--- Page 4 ---
<meta>This page is the primary title page of the "Regenten Buch" (Book of Rulers). It follows the handwritten provenance page from 1699, establishing the formal identity of the printed work published in 1579. This title page acts as a table of contents for the entire volume, which contains not only Lauterbeck's work but also translations of other legal and political treatises.</meta>

# **Book of Rulers**

# **Of the Highly Learned and Widely Renowned**

## Lord Georg Lauterbeck, Princely Brandenburg Councilor, etc.

-> In which many and various useful instructions, excellent counsels, and plans for praiseworthy and successful governance, the establishment, improvement, and maintenance of good <term>public order<note>original German: "Policey." In the 16th century, this referred to the overall administration, morality, and social welfare of a state, rather than just modern law enforcement.</note></term> in times of peace and war, as well as the promotion of the <term>common good<note>original German: "Gemeinen nutzes." A central concept in Renaissance politics emphasizing the welfare of the entire community over private interests.</note></term> among the subjects, and whatever else may be conducive to a stable government, are collected from the most prominent ancient and new histories, as well as from the writings and books of other excellent and highly learned men, and most diligently prepared for print. <-

<image-desc>A small ornate floral heart-shaped typographical ornament.</image-desc>

-> **Almost necessary and useful for all potentates, kings, princes, counts, lords, rulers, and authorities to read, so that they may know how to conduct themselves in all occurring dealings and matters.** <-

-> **Likewise, his treatise and booklet on courtly life.** <-

-> **Furthermore, the work of Lord Claude de Seyssel <note>original: "Claudij de Sissellijs"</note>, sometime Bishop of Marseille, being two books on the office of kings and the government of the common good.** <-

-> Also, two treatises by Guido de Suzara <note>original: "Guidonis de Susaria"</note> and Paolo Grillandi of Castiglione <note>original: "Pauli Grillandi Castilionici"</note> regarding criminal matters and <term>interrogations<note>original German: "Fragen." In a 16th-century legal context, this specifically refers to judicial examination, often involving torture (the "question").</note></term>. <-

-> Likewise, the treatise of Lord Ulrich Zasius <note>original: "Vlrichi Zasij"</note> on feudal law. <-

-> **The aforementioned author <note>Referring to Georg Lauterbeck</note> has most faithfully and diligently translated the first of these from the French language, and the others from the Latin language, for the benefit of the common fatherland of the German Nation.** <-

-> All now revised once again from the start, expanded and improved, the likes of which has never been seen in print before. <-

-> **Printed in the Imperial Free City of Frankfurt am Main, etc.** <-

-> 1579. <note>original Latin: "M. D. LXXIX."</note> <-

# THE LIVING IMAGE OF THE
# MOST LEARNED AND ILLUSTRIOUS MAN,
# MR. GEORG LAUTERBECK, OF PIOUS
# MEMORY.

<image-desc>A woodcut portrait of Georg Lauterbeck set within an ornate oval frame. The frame is decorated with scrolls, architectural flourishes, floral swags at the bottom, and two putti (cherubs) at the top holding a central emblem. The subject is an elderly man with a long, dense beard, wearing a scholar's gown with a prominent collar. His hands are clasped together in a pious gesture. A laurel-like branch or feather is tucked into the left side of the frame.</image-desc>

Behold the countenance of Lauterbeck in a living image:
Behold the face and gentle features of the learned old man:
He who wrote here, with great skill and much labor,
A book desired by kings and princes—
Handing down the deeds and examples of men of old,
While also adding new instructions to them:
From which our leaders may take guidance and methods,
By which they may improve and establish their own affairs.
There is a city in the land of the Bavarians, small and ancient,
Schongau; <note>original: "Singinga." This is the Latinized name for Schongau in Upper Bavaria.</note> that city brought forth this man for us.
There he was born of praiseworthy parents,
And there he first drank in the seeds of sacred learning.
He was steeped in honorable character and studies there,
In the manner that is proper for boys to be raised.
Then venerable Leipzig <note>original: "Lipsia."</note> received the youth as a student,
And for a long time, like a mother, cherished him in her friendly bosom.

<summary>This page features a portrait and a Latin poem honoring Georg Lauterbeck, identifying his Bavarian origins and his education at the University of Leipzig. The text frames his "Book of Regents" as an essential fusion of ancient wisdom and modern advice for rulers.</summary>

<meta>This page serves as a laudatory poem, or commendatory verse, common in Renaissance and Early Modern scholarly books. It introduces the author of the work, framing his professional career as a legal advisor to princes as the foundation for the expertise found in this volume.</meta>

Having been advanced by various skills and honors,
-> he was at last commanded to serve among leading men: <-
So that, as a protector of the Law <term>Iuris patronus: a legal advocate or scholar</term>, in the courts,
-> he might guide and advance public affairs with his counsel. <-
He performed that service for many years with great praise,
-> a service full of hard toil <note>original: "sudoris," literally "sweat"</note> and envy. <-
But however many and great his labors were,
-> they could not draw him away from his studies. <-
He devoted himself to reading books night and day,
-> so thirsty was he for vast knowledge: <-
And sometimes he even composed some writing himself,
-> bringing forth the riches of a fertile mind. <-
But among all the other books he published,
-> this very book stands out and is most prominent, <-
Which he wrote concerning the affairs of kingdoms, and which
-> we now provide, helpfully expanded, dear reader. <-
You, whoever enjoys his labor, give thanks to the author,
-> and hold his name in high esteem. <-

-> Master Henricus Brem, <-
-> of Chur. <note>original: "Curiensis," referring to the city of Chur in the Grisons, Switzerland.</note> <-

# To the Illustrious, High-born
# Prince and Lord, Lord George Frederick,
# Margrave of Brandenburg, in Prussia, of Stettin, Pomerania, of the
# Kashubians and Wends, also in Silesia, Duke of Jägerndorf, etc.,
# Burgrave of Nuremberg, and Prince of
# Rügen, etc., our Gracious Prince
# and Lord.

<image-desc>A large, ornate woodcut initial letter 'D' decorated with detailed floral and foliate scrolls within a square frame.</image-desc>Illustrious, High-born Prince, to Your Princely Grace <note>original: "Euwren Fürstlichen Gnaden," a formal address abbreviated later as E.F.G.</note> we offer our humble, yet faithful, submissive, dutiful, and obedient services, with ready diligence beforehand, etc. Gracious Prince and Lord. We, the undersigned, have no doubt that it is well known and manifest—especially in the Holy Empire of the German Nation, our much-beloved Fatherland—how our dear father, Georg Lauterbeck (of blessed and good memory), who was Your Princely Grace's former Court Councilor and servant in the mountains at Culmbach <note>Referring to the Margraviate of Brandenburg-Kulmbach</note>, several years ago (namely, at the time when he was Chancellor of Mansfeld and still in his vigorous years) wrote a book called the *Regentenbuch* <term>Regentenbuch: literally "Book of Rulers," a genre of "Mirror for Princes" literature intended to advise leaders on governance and morality</term> and had it published in print. And with it (as we do not doubt, though we mention it without boasting), he served many Christian, kind-hearted rulers who love peace and the common welfare, to their benefit, good, and gracious pleasure. The first edition <term>Edition: the original publication run</term> of this work, although a goodly large number of copies were printed, was nevertheless soon and quickly exhausted, and consequently came into great demand. Because of this, our aforementioned dear father—prompted and diligently urged by several excellent, loyal-hearted people—was moved and caused to revise and improve the said *Regentenbuch* anew. And because precisely then and at that same time, he was graciously summoned by Your Princely Grace to be a Councilor and servant (for which reason...

->### Preface.<-

...and then several others followed) to prepare and publish in print such a work with a new Preface <note>original: "Præfation"</note> to Your Princely Grace in the year—of the lesser count <note>An archaic way of dating; "sixty-seven" refers to 1567</note>—after the incarnation of our **Lord** and Savior Jesus Christ, sixty-seven, etc.

But since, Gracious Prince and Lord, the second edition <note>original: "Edition"</note> as well as the first was well-received by everyone, sold at a good price, and moved well, yet regarding the aforementioned second edition and printing, as is evident, something improper was transacted. Namely, that the bookseller obtained a privilege <term>Privilegium: a legal protection or "copyright" granted by an authority, preventing others from reprinting a work for a set time</term> based on an unfair report, without the prior knowledge of our dear late father, the author <note>original: "Authoris"</note>, and incorporated it into that edition of the book.

For such reasons, our frequently mentioned father—once again in his old age and shortly before his passing—carefully revised <note>original: "recognoscirt"</note>, reviewed, and usefully expanded the aforementioned *Regentenbuch* with special diligence. He was also fully determined, after His Roman Imperial Majesty, Emperor Maximilian—of highest, most laudable, and Christian memory—had most graciously granted him a new privilege for this book for ten years, to have it published and printed once again and anew after the expiration of those years, and to humbly dedicate <note>original: "dediciren"</note> it to Your Princely Grace for a second time. 

However, our much-mentioned dear late father did not live to see the end of those ten years. Yet, he often and many times gave us, as his heirs, his fatherly command that should he pass away before the expiration of those ten years (as has indeed happened according to the will of Almighty God), we should then hand over the work—which he had prepared and adorned <note>original: "adornirt"</note> for a third edition—to be printed without delay, as much as possible, and that we should humbly and obediently dedicate it to Your Princely Grace above all others, etc. Since then, Gracious Prince and Lord, [it was] our dear fa-

<meta>This page concludes the dedication of Georg Lauterbeck’s "Regentenbuch." ### Preface.

<sig>* iiij</sig>

...his last will and fatherly command, we recognized our duty to be obedient; the aforementioned ten years have passed, and all copies <note>original: "Exemplaria"</note> of both editions <note>original: "Edition"</note> of the often-mentioned book have been distributed and sold everywhere. Therefore, several booksellers made many requests to us, the heirs, to allow the book to be printed for them once again, to grant permission, and to hand it over. We gladly granted and allowed this to happen, as we also had long wished to see such a work undertaken and performed according to our dear father’s command and desire, etc. 

Since now, by God’s grace, this is completed and accomplished in the manner our father left us in his command, we hereby (as mentioned, by virtue of the fatherly command) submissively and humbly dedicate <note>original: "dediciren"</note> this book, now newly prepared and printed, to Your Princely Grace <note>E. F. G.: *Euer Fürstlichen Gnaden*, a formal address for the ruler George Frederick, Margrave of Brandenburg-Ansbach</note>. With this we attach a humble request that Your Princely Grace would be our Gracious Prince and Lord, and let this useful work of our late blessed father (as we hope) and this dedication, repeated by us, find your gracious favor; and further, to keep us—as the surviving heirs of the deceased author <note>original: "Autoris"</note>—at all times under your gracious protection and patronage. In return, we shall at all times be found as Your Princely Grace’s faithful, obedient, and thankful servants. Done and dated at Culmbach, Thursday, the nineteenth day of this month of March, after the birth of Christ our only Redeemer and Savior, in the year one thousand, five hundred, and seventy-nine.

Your Princely Grace’s

# IN COMMENDATION OF THE POLITICAL BOOKS OF THE MOST ILLUSTRIOUS MAN, ETC., LORD GEORG LAUTERBECK.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'P' featuring floral patterns and scrolling foliage.</image-desc>

->*First glory is deservedly owed to the sacred books,*<- <note>original: "Prima sacris meritò debetur gloria libris"</note>
->*Which the right hand, full of divine power, gave from above.*<-
->*These reveal to us the memorable mysteries of God,*<-
->*Which the Son himself brought from the Father’s bosom.*<-
->*From there come comforts to the struggling mind,*<-
->*Which trembles and shudders at the sad burden of death.*<-
->*From there the firm hope of future life blooms again,*<-
->*And faith flourishes, overcoming all hardships.*<-
->*Afterward, praise is due to those writings*<-
->*Which indeed assist the public benefits of life—*<-
->*Those which the noble power implanted in our mind brought forth,*<-
->*And that little flame remaining from the first light.*<-
->*Or the wisdom of things born from long experience,*<-
->*Learned <term>Minerva<note>The Roman goddess of wisdom, here symbolizing statesmanship and intellectual skill.</note></term> aided by your discoveries.*<-
->*Such are the bonds which urge a peaceful peace,*<-
->*And which establish the measures of law and justice.*<-
->*Or those which shape the public governance of Kings,*<-
->*And rule morals with just skill.*<-
->*Or those which recount the examples of men of old,*<-
->*Who cultivated virtue by their deeds.*<-
->*Such writings, collected with great labor,*<-
->*Were offered by men serious in the nobility of their spirit.*<-
->*Whose famous names our time also holds,*<-
->*And returns thanks with a mindful mouth, as is fitting.*<-
->*To these men, he joins himself as a companion—who, friend reader,*<-
->*Gives you this book with great diligence.*<-
->*Virtue itself has extolled the man, and his outstanding learning,*<-
->*And the knowledge acquired over a long period of time.*<-
->*He was present at the <term>scepters<note>In this context, the "scepters" refer to the royal courts and the administration of sovereign power.</note></term> of leaders and in the conduct of affairs;*<-
->*As a prudent man, he saw many things that must be seen.*<-

# Preface to the Christian Reader.

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'E' featuring scrolling foliage and floral motifs.</image-desc>
It is held by scholars, beloved reader, that every person or station in this world has need of a certain rule by which to guide and direct their life and being, so that they do not act or behave in their course and calling in a way that is disadvantageous to them, or by which they might be led away from the proper path. However, if one considers and rightly reflects upon all stations of life, it will be found that such a rule and order is most necessary for those appointed to the governance of the <term>common good</term> <note>original: *gemeinen Nutzes*, referring to the commonwealth or public welfare</note> and who must preside over land and people. This is because they face particularly many temptations and causes that might lead them astray and move them to act against their command and calling.

Although many great and brave men have written various books concerning the governance of the <term>common good</term> and <term>civil administration</term> <note>original: *Policey*, which in this era referred to the general internal order, regulation, and "policed" state of a community, rather than just modern law enforcement</note>, in which they gave rulers much good teaching and instruction (and would to God it were as easy to lead a government in deed as it is to write and speak of it!)—namely **Aristotle**, **Plato**, **Xenophon**, **Isocrates**, and others among the Greeks; **Cicero**, **Plutarch**, along with several more among the Romans; **Contarini** and **Sabellico** among the Venetians; **Claude de Seyssel** among the French—it is nevertheless considered that nothing on earth can be presented or proposed to those who must eventually govern the <term>common good</term> that is more useful than the science of <term>history</term> <note>original: *Historien*</note>. This is because history not only provides measure and instruction on how to fit oneself for government and how to behave therein, but also frequently reminds rulers of human frailty, so that they learn to act more gently and not to exalt themselves too highly in their power. By such arrogance, they might overstep their calling, thereby angering God or otherwise becoming lazy and negligent in their office, as one sees happening from time to time in all governments.

And such deficiency comes from nowhere else but our warped and evil nature, which even the heathens recognized. For **Socrates**, who in his time was regarded and held to be the most noble and pious of men, used to say that human nature is of such a kind and quality that if a person had the room and could undertake, do, and act as they pleased without hindrance—even if they were the most pious of all—they would ultimately fall into arrogance and <term>tyranny</term>. One has a clear example of this in the Emperor **Nero**, who governed so laudably and well for the first five years that few emperors before him had done the like; but afterward he became such a ghastly, evil tyrant that

<summary>This preface argues that rulers require the study of history to temper their power and guard against the natural human tendency toward tyranny. It cites classical philosophers and the example of Emperor Nero to illustrate how even the best-intentioned leaders can succumb to arrogance without moral guidance.</summary>

# Preface to the Reader.

...for whom no tyranny or debauchery was too great; for he killed not only his wife, but also his mother, and likewise his tutor **Seneca**, an excellent, learned, and pious man, along with many other honorable people. It would take too long to write of all that here; therefore, we shall let him pass for now.

And since necessity also requires—whenever one must speak of great matters—that a person possess certain "commonplaces" <note>original: *Locos communes*; these were thematic headings or categories used by Renaissance scholars to organize knowledge and rhetorical arguments</note> from which he can prepare himself for what must be undertaken in any business and what advice to give. This is exactly how **Demosthenes** (as one reads of him) conducted himself. He so loved the historian **Thucydides**, and read him with such diligence, that he transcribed his works eight times with his own hand. Therefore, I have also undertaken and endeavored to pull together several examples from Greek and Latin, ancient and modern histories—first and foremost for myself, and subsequently for others who may not know better, or who, due to other business, do not have the time to run through all the histories and books. Such histories serve particularly well to help one better conduct oneself in all kinds of affairs and dealings, and to see how similar cases were handled. Let me provide an example of this.

**Xenophon** writes of a captain from <term>Byzantium</term> <note>original: *Bisantz*, the ancient Greek city that later became Constantinople and now Istanbul</note> who surrendered the city to the enemies laying siege to it because of a Great Famine. When he was later strictly accused in **Sparta** for surrendering such a strong city to the enemy instead of letting them take it by storm, he answered and defended himself thus: He could not bear to see the innocent women and children within die of hunger. Nor did he believe that the <term>laws of war</term> <note>original: *Kriegsrecht*</note> should extend so far that these persons—whom enemies usually spare because of their innocence—must be starved to death before a city is surrendered. Had he waited, those innocent people would have been killed by their own captain and protector, yet the city would not have been saved; for if everyone inside had died of hunger, the enemy could have captured it easily and without any effort afterward. This defense was accepted, and the captain was acquitted. One can guide oneself by this example in similar cases. Not to mention that lords and rulers often find in such books things that their advisors do not tell them, nor dare to remind them of—namely, what they should do or leave undone, etc.

For thus one reads of King **Antiochus**, that when he once wandered too far while hunting, he had to stay the night alone in the small hut of poor people who did not recognize him. When they began to speak of King **Antiochus** at the table, they said that he was indeed pious, but that he entrusted several offices to wicked men, whose evil dealings he ignored, and that through his constant hunting, he neglected necessary affairs, which caused him to be spoken of poorly. # Preface to the Reader.

...was, until the morning when they brought him the crown and the red purple robe, Antiochus began to speak against the crown and the purple robe: "Come now, since I have put these on, only yesterday did I first hear the truth about myself." That is: "Well then, now that I am surrounded and dressed in these, yesterday was the first time I heard the truth told about me." <note>This anecdote refers to Antiochus the Great, who realized that his royal status often prevented people from being honest with him.</note> For all those who wish to be at court strive for this: that they say nothing to princes unless it is pleasant to the ears <note>original Latin: *Nisi blandum auribus*</note>, which is to say, only what they like to hear, as **Erasmus** <note>Desiderius Erasmus (1466–1536), a famous humanist scholar who wrote extensively on the education of princes</note> writes.

I have therefore gathered these examples and histories into separate books and chapters, much like "Commonplaces" <note>original: *Locos Communes*; a Renaissance method of organizing knowledge by thematic headings like "Justice" or "Greed" for easy reference</note>, so that they might be more easily remembered and found. In these, as if in a small mirror, one can see and be reminded of what is right, what is wrong, what should be followed, and what should ultimately be avoided, etc.

Accordingly, **Suetonius** <note>A Roman historian known for his biographies of the first twelve emperors</note> also writes that the Emperor **Augustus**, in his reading and studies, paid the most attention to such historical examples and frequently made use of them when he wished to issue written orders. This was not only in matters of war and toward his servants and officials, but also toward the Senate in Rome and others. Indeed, he often copied them out word for word and sent them in place of a formal command to those he wished to instruct. For as a wise prince, he well knew and saw that such historical examples achieved more for the cause than if he had used many words and long letters.

In addition to this, I have occasionally included several sharp and subtle sayings—Latin maxims—which the Greeks call <term>Acroamata</term> <note>Literally "things heard"; in this context, it refers to intellectual entertainment or pithy sayings shared during meals or leisure time</note> and the like. Great lords are accustomed to using these and apply themselves to them, as one reads of the great and noble prince **Charlemagne** (*Carolo Magno*): when he sat at the table in the evening, he would either have something read aloud to him (after the custom of monks) or make use of such short *acroamata* and sharp sayings.

Although such sayings are usually very short, they provide much understanding and various reminders. Because of their brevity, they can also be easily grasped and retained. Therefore, I do not know what could be presented to young rulers and lords that would be more useful—after Holy Scripture—since they cannot always attend to so many books in which histories are scattered and contained here and there, due to their other business. Countless such short, magnificent, and useful sayings are found throughout Greek books, as can be seen in **Erasmus**, who recounts them in great numbers in his <term>Apophtegmata</term> <note>A famous collection by Erasmus of concise, clever sayings by historical figures intended to teach moral lessons</note>. These are things that all lords and rulers ought rightly to read.

But those among the rulers who are so minded that they pay no heed to their calling, nor ask after such wholesome and necessary things—likewise those who will not suffer or have any certain rule by which they might conduct themselves in government and their office, but instead pay more and greater attention to their luxury, hunting, and other plea[sures]...

Or, they otherwise govern "into the wind," entrusting and commending such great and weighty matters to luck and their advisors alone; such men one may let go their own way.

But since these individuals are greatly mistaken, they should consider how, in time—which does not fail to arrive—they will answer for it before God. For to these matters belong not only understanding, skill, and wisdom, but also the fear of God, grace, and blessing, as well as great care, effort, and labor, historical examples, and more besides. This is clearly seen, known, and experienced by those who deal with these things daily. For they are certainly not appointed and called by God as rulers as if they were invited or summoned to a wedding or a parish fair <note>A "Kirchmeß" (Kermesse) was a local church festival or fair, often associated with heavy drinking and revelry rather than serious duty.</note>. ## Chapters of the Third Book.

Of War / what a harmful thing it is / and that no one should lightly advise for War. Chapter 1.

That our Lord God has often indicated and announced such terrible wars through preceding signs <note>These "signs" often referred to astrological events, comets, or unusual natural phenomena interpreted as divine warnings.</note>. 2.

That great lords in war have sometimes endeavored to fight and overcome their enemies more through bravery <note>original: *Manheit*</note> than through trickery. 4.

That one is also duty-bound to keep faith <note>To keep one's word or honor a promise.</note> with enemies. 5.

Concerning the Law of War / and what discipline and order the ancient commanders maintained among their soldiers when they took to the field / and what they had to swear. 6.

How the ancient soldiers were sometimes punished for their transgressions. 7.

How often small groups have defeated and struck down large and powerful armies in war. 8.

Concerning Fortifications / and that one should not place too much trust in them. 9.

That one should not lightly enter into alliances. 10.

That one should faithfully keep alliances / oaths / and vows / And that God is vehemently opposed to unfaithfulness and the breaking of promises / and therefore does not leave it unpunished. 11.

That one should not covet another’s government / land / or people. 12.

That a Prince or Lord / in great and important matters / and especially in affairs of war / should not hear one counsel alone / but as many as he can have. 13.

That some hold it to be better / that great Princes and Lords / when they have business with one another / should not meet in person / but rather settle the matter through their advisors. 14.

That a supreme commander <term>Feldherrn</term> <note>The highest military rank, equivalent to a General or Commander-in-Chief.</note> must consider and deliberate with the highest diligence / once he has accomplished his business with his soldiers / how he may best discharge them / And if this does not happen / what danger may arise for him from it. 15.

Concerning military regulation / order and laws / directed toward our current time / and composed as briefly as possible. 16.

That soldiers / when it comes time for battle / should diligently commend themselves to God / and call upon Him for victory and good fortune. 17.

That one should not lightly make any changes to the statutes / laws / and ordinances in a land / or in a city. 2.

That the governors should make provision so that the poor do not suffer want. 9.

# The First Part of the Book of Rulers /
### Drawn together with diligence from many excellent old and new histories / For all rulers and authorities for the establishment / improvement / and preservation of honorable and good <term>governance<note>original: "Policey". ## On the distinction of governments /

## The First Chapter.

<image-desc>An ornamental drop cap 'E' at the beginning of the text, depicting a seated man in classical or academic robes holding a staff, set against a background of intricate floral and architectural engravings.</image-desc>
It is first to be known / that until now in the world many kinds of governments have existed / and have been maintained / according to how / and how one was able to adapt to them at any given time / and in any given place. The first government / has been called <term>ARISTOCRACY<note>original: "ARISTOCRATIA", from the Greek meaning "rule by the best."</note></term>, where several wise / and some of the best people / had the duty to rule / excluding the <term>rabble<note>original: "Pöfel". A derogatory term for the common masses or uneducated populace.</note></term> / as such people / who are fit for government / are always found in the smallest numbers / if they are to lead others rightly with virtue and wisdom / And this way of ruling / takes place in those locations / and is used / where the best / in a city / or the most prominent / in a land / hold the government in their hands.

The second is called <term>DEMOCRACY<note>original: "DEMOCRATIA", meaning "rule by the people."</note></term>, in which all estates / have a voice in commanding and consenting / as was the case in former times in Rome / where the commonality / alongside the Council / and those of the <term>knighthood<note>original: "Ritterschafft". Likely referring to the Roman equestrian order or the social class of knights.</note></term> / ruled together. It is not to be understood / however / as some have thought / that this is DEMOCRACY / when and if the mad and insane rabble / rules alone / but rather when / alongside the most prominent estates / the commonality has the right to give consent / and it is esteemed / that in such places / and in such governments / there is true freedom and <term>liberty<note>original: "Libertet".</note></term>. But where the common rabble has the right to rule alone / there can be not only no freedom / but also no government. However, where it proceeds through all estates at once / where the law / and justice give as much to one as to the other / and no one has an advantage / then things cannot easily go wrong. Such a government the <term>Lacedaemonians<note>The ancient Spartans.</note></term> once had / which was composed and established by all estates / For although they had a King / as a monarch / they nevertheless had the Council alongside him / as the few among the many / and finally the <term>Ephors<note>original: "Ephoros". Ancient Spartan magistrates who shared power with the kings and represented the interests of the people.</note></term> on behalf of the common man / and the Ephors even had the power to command the King.

# The First Part
<meta>catchword: then/</meta>

The third government / is called **Monarchy**, where one entrusts / and hands over the government to a single person / or an entire kingdom / land or city / just as for several years now / the Empire of the German Nation / has been entrusted and commanded to a Roman Emperor / to whom the other members of the same Empire / such as Electors / Princes / Counts / Prelates / Cities and Communities / must be subject / and obedient.

With which Monarchy the fourth estate / that is / the Tyrants / would like to compare themselves / and mix themselves in / like mouse droppings among pepper <note>A common early modern proverb meaning something foul or worthless mixed in with something of quality.</note>. But these are the differences between them / that the Monarchs / however high they may be / use the laws and justice / and use force against no one contrary to justice / just as the Roman Emperors / have subjected themselves to the Law / <term>The Law "Digna Vox" in the Code on Laws<note>original: "L. Digna Vox. C. de Legibus". This refers to a famous decree in the Code of Justinian (C. 1.14.4) stating that it is a statement "worthy of the majesty of the ruler" to profess himself bound by the laws.</note></term>, and in other places of the Law more / as shall be heard hereafter. The Tyrants however proceed and act simply with force / without law / respecting neither trust nor faith / Therefore also such Tyrannical power / and unlawful government / has always and everywhere been rejected / and held for injustice. Such rulers and tyrants have been / **Dionysius** / the King of Syracuse / the Emperor **Nero** / and others more / of whom the histories report / and of whom enough examples shall be heard hereafter.

Concerning these three aforementioned different governments / a fine and pleasant dispute is introduced by **Herodotus** the Greek historian / between three powerful men / and most prominent princes in the Kingdom of Persia / And such a dispute arose from this cause / After King **Cambyses** had taken his own life / and the Magi <note>A group of priests in ancient Persia who briefly seized power.</note> had spread a rumor among the people / that his brother **Smerdis Cyrus** was still alive / although he had been murdered long before / but such an uncertain rumor / could not last or endure for long / so that the Magi were not only shamed by it / but also miserably perished at the last. Accordingly it happened following this / that the highest imperial councilors / who were indeed honorable brave people / who could speak wisely and reasonably of matters / among whom also none stood under suspicion / or were held to be / seeking the kingdom / to bring it to himself by cunning or force / but rather that they gladly wanted to advise and help promote that / which might be most excellent and useful for the Empire.

Firstly **Otanes** <note>original: "Othanes"</note> was of the opinion / that one should elect no monarch or king / and thus not grant the government / and the power to one alone / because Cambyses had behaved so badly / but held instead / it were best / that one should let the government rest / and remain with the entire common assembly of all Estates / of the Empire. For in such a case / they would not need to fear / that their wives and daughters / might be dishonored / shamed / or someone violated / or killed in unproven matters / But such violent handling must cease / because one could not achieve it before the other / nor would it be permitted to one over the other / desired therefore / that they would give place to this his opinion. But in the case / that they would have other concerns /

**Megabyzus** <term>Megabizus<note>One of the seven Persian noblemen who conspired to overthrow the Magi usurpers in 522 BCE.</note></term> opposed this opinion, and with many brave and adorned words, preferred **OLIGARCHY** <term>OLIGARCHIA<note>A Greek term meaning "rule by a few." In this historical context, it refers to government by a select group of the "best" or most capable citizens.</note></term>, that is, the government of the few and the best, of which was spoken above. In contrast, he struck down the opinion of **Otanes** <term>Othanis<note>Otanes was the noble who argued for "isonomia" or a form of democracy where the people rule.</note></term> and would in no way give it his approval, indicating that it required little proof, for the work itself showed what kind of good and stable government could exist among the many and the common, mad **mob** <term>Pöfel<note>A derogatory term for the common populace or "rabble."</note></term>; for it is customary for things to go haywire in places where the commoners have to rule; nevertheless, he placed his opinion at the consideration of the others.

After this, **Darius** <term>Darius<note>Darius the Great, who eventually became the King of the Persian Empire.</note></term> began to speak, and after he first refuted the previous two opinions, he next diligently advised for **Monarchy** <term>Monarchi<note>Rule by a single individual.</note></term> and preferred the same over the other two governments, alleging that neither the mob nor a few of them could rule as well, and that matters would proceed more easily if the authority, command, and government were entrusted and commanded to one alone. The opinion of Megabyzus could also not stand for this reason: that among those who were in an equal government, a grudge and secret ill-will could easily arise, since each would gladly be the foremost, from which ultimately nothing more certain than murder, war, discord, and other mischief would result. It was also not to be hoped that a lasting peace could be established in the Empire unless one had first weeded out the others, and the one who was finally to remain King had obtained and taken over the Empire. And **Darius** not only remained fixed in his opinion by such speech but was also shortly thereafter accepted, declared, and proclaimed a powerful King of the **Persians** <term>Persen</term>.

However, it happened with **Darius** <term>Dario</term> in this way: namely, that the aforementioned princes agreed that they would come together again early the following day at a notable place, and whichever horse should neigh first, its rider should be King. Now when **Darius** came home, he reported this to his **Steward** <note>The original refers to a "Hoffmeister" (court official). In Herodotus' original account, this is Darius's clever groom, Oebares.</note> and asked him if he knew any advice for it, to which he answered: Yes. Thereupon, he led **Darius's** stallion and a mare to the place that same evening and let them together, so that when the stallion came back the next morning, he would neigh for the mare. When the princes came together again in the morning, **Darius's** horse neighed first, and a clap of thunder occurred in the clear sky; because of this, the other princes fell from their horses and worshiped **Darius** <term>Darium</term> as a King.

It is, however, likewise important to know that regarding these different governments, there are many and varied **opinions** <term>Opinion</term> even among the learned and highly intelligent as to which among these governments might be the best. For although they generally all conclude and hold the government of the common mob to be unfit and rejected, as well as the Ty—

> The fickle crowd is split into opposing factions. <note>original Latin: "Scinditur incertum studia in contraria vulgus." Also from Virgil.</note>

And just as it is impossible for everyone in a house to rule at once—rather, the father of the house alone, or whoever he commands to govern, must rule, provide for, and restrain the household—it is likewise impossible for everyone in a land, kingdom, or city to hold the government at the same time. Nevertheless, those same learned and highly experienced people held the other two forms of government in high regard. Among them were several brave and great men who, for all sorts of reasons and stately considerations, thought more of the government where the best people are appointed than where the rule is commanded to one alone. **Aristotle** <term>Aristoteles<note>The Greek philosopher whose "Politics" remains a foundational text for Western political thought.</note></term> is one of these, who says in his **Politics** <term>Politicis<note>Aristotle's work "Politics," which categorizes different types of constitutions and governments.</note></term> that two people can see better and more than one alone. Likewise, the German proverb says that twelve men are placed in a council for this reason: what one cannot see or understand, another may. Furthermore, **Plautus** <term>Plautus<note>Titus Maccius Plautus, a Roman playwright.</note></term> writes:

No one can be wise enough alone. <note>original Latin: "Quòd nemo solus satis sapiat."</note>

By this, he meant to suggest that no one person could be wise and cautious enough in a matter by themselves. Therefore **Agamemnon** <term>Agamemnon<note>The leader of the Greeks in the Trojan War.</note></term> also wishes, as **Homer** <term>Homerus<note>The legendary author of the Iliad and the Odyssey.</note></term> writes, that he might have ten advisors who, in their wisdom, might be equal to **Nestor** <term>Nestori<note>Nestor was an elderly king and advisor known for his great wisdom and eloquence.</note></term>.

But regardless of these arguments and the reasons cited, it is finally concluded by the others that **Monarchy** <term>Monarchi<note>The rule of a single sovereign.</note></term> should be preferred over the other governments. Likewise, it is more useful and profitable for land and people to be ruled by one alone than to have many rulers. For just as the **bees** <note>original: "Bynen"</note> have no more than one king, ruler, and leader, and just as the Heavens have no more than one sun, so also should there be only one regent, one Emperor, one King, one Prince, and one Lord in a land. This is what Homer points out when he says:

> It is not good for many to rule; let there be one king. One ruler, to whom great Jupiter has given the golden scepter and commanded to provide laws to protect his subjects. <note>original Latin/Greek: "Nec multos regnare bonum, Rex unicus esto. Vnicus imperium, cui Iupiter aurea magnus Sceptra dedit, Iustitq́; suis dare iura tuendis." A famous passage from Homer's Iliad.</note>

->That is:<-

> It is not good where many rule,
> One alone should lead the government.

Likewise, **Domitian** <term>Domitianus<note>Roman Emperor (reigned 81–96 AD), known for his authoritarian rule.</note></term> in **Suetonius** <term>Suetonius<note>Gaius Suetonius Tranquillus, a Roman historian who wrote "The Twelve Caesars."</note></term>:

So one also reads how, when **Alexander the Great** <term>Alexander Magnus<note>King of Macedon and creator of one of the largest empires in history.</note></term> had put **Darius** <term>Darius III<note>The last King of the Achaemenid Empire of Persia.</note></term> to flight, and captured his mother, wife, daughters, and sons—and treated them so princely that for the sake of such virtue Darius offered to make peace with him, proposing to share his kingdom with him and give him his daughter with a great dowry. That is: Just as the heavens, if two suns were in them, could not have their beauty and order, so also the world, if two want to rule at the same time, cannot be governed without war and rebellion.

Accordingly, things also rarely go well where there are many regents; there, the subjects are not served for the best, as one reads that **Caria** <term>Caria<note>A region in western Anatolia (modern Turkey).</note></term> was lost through a multitude of captains. As the pagans say: *So many people, so many minds; every man has his own head.* Therefore, wise people also advise that no one should easily move to and settle permanently in a land or city over which many have to rule. For it is impossible that one can do right by them all and please them all at once, while one commands "black" and the other wants "white." Accordingly, it remains once again the case that it is more convenient and beneficial to have one regent rather than many. But as for what was said about "the few and the best," as mentioned above, I would (if it were proper for me to judge) have that understood and interpreted only in regard to cities. Since, however, I recognize myself as too small in this matter, I will leave every man to his own opinion herein.

# The First Part
<meta>catchword: would have.</meta>

...measure. <note>original Latin: "fura" (completing "mensura" from the previous page). "Ea conditione natura constituit singula, vt in occasum atque interitum vergant."</note> Nature has established each thing under this condition: that they should verge toward decline and destruction. That is: human things fall away and flow like water; much less can they remain in a fixed state, for all things are so ordered by nature that they must incline toward their downfall and must perish. Accordingly, I will briefly recount here how the great **Monarchies** and **Empires** <term>Keyserthumb<note>The German term for Empire, specifically relating to the authority of a Caesar or Emperor.</note></term> in the world began, and how they later changed in wondrous ways and passed away again. For just as all other things—and especially all human beings—first have a small beginning, and as they have grown, increased, and reached their highest point, they then decrease again, fall, and perish. Therefore, man is called a **microcosm** <term>eine kleine Welt<note>Literally "a little world"; the Renaissance idea that the human body reflects the structure and laws of the entire universe.</note></term>. And just as it does not help a man to be strong, beautiful, clever, and wise, so it does not help even if a Kingdom, Empire, or land is established and strengthened with power, as well as with statutes, laws, and courts, and with a great multitude of men. Rather, when it has reached its highest point, it must decrease again, just like a human being, and finally go to the ground—as one reads in history, from one kingdom to another and from one monarchy to another.

First, the Empire was with the **Assyrians**, although this same monarchy—as **Xenophon** <term>Xenophon<note>An ancient Greek philosopher and historian, known for his writings on the history of his own times and the sayings of Socrates.</note></term> writes—first began with the **Chaldeans**. However, it did not remain with them for long, and their rule did not last long; instead, the Assyrians, who bordered them, conquered the realm. It increased greatly under the Assyrians and their kings, such as **Ninus**, the Queen **Semiramis**, and others. But when **Sardanapalus** <term>Sardanapalus<note>The legendary last king of Assyria, often depicted in literature as a symbol of decadence and effeminacy.</note></term> came to the throne, he concerned himself more with women than with the kingdom and the whole monarchy. As one reads of him, he allowed himself to be found among the womenfolk in women's clothes, picking up the spindle for the women, and even spinning himself, while his fingers were covered and shone with golden rings and precious stones. And **Justinus** <term>Justinus<note>Marcus Junianus Justinus, a Roman historian who edited the works of Pompeius Trogus.</note></term> writes that he had a more whorish face than any loose woman. Consequently, the **Medes** and **Babylonians** defected from him, and the empires were separated from one another. Thus, this same monarchy—which at that time had lasted over twelve hundred years (or 1,300 years, as Justinus calculates it)—passed away and came to the **Persians**. But how that happened would be too long to tell, so I will omit it; it is enough to know here that the second monarchy was with the Persians, starting with **Cyrus** and lasting until **Darius** the last, who was overcome by **Alexander the Great**. Nevertheless, the Medes also held the empire for a time according to the historians, namely 350 years.

The third **Monarch** was **Alexander the Great** from Greece in Macedonia, who brought all of Asia under his rule with such great luck and victory that no attack of his ever failed or went wrong. This was despite the fact that he faced great resistance from kings, princes, and powerful cities. He was a great, active, and virtuous prince, who nonetheless also stumbled at times and had his flaws—as there is no human being who does not have a fault or a physical infirmity.

# How and in what manner the government among the Romans changed.

## The Third Chapter.

<margin>Rome.</margin>
From the histories of the city of **Rome's** beginnings, when it first received an established government, it cannot be known or found that they had a true **MONARCHY** <term>Monarchiam: A system of government where supreme power is held by a single person.</term>. For although the kings held the upper hand, their power was so structured and tempered that, alongside the king, the elders and the best of the city (who numbered one hundred at that time) also had a share in governing and commanding. And if one wished to elect mayors <note>German: *Bürgermeister*; in this Roman context, the author refers to the Consuls or similar high magistrates.</note> or otherwise appoint other offices, or if a war was at hand, it was necessary to summon the other estates as well as the common man and hear their thoughts; for without their consent, a final decision could not have been reached.

And it is true. The Romans at that time did not yet have a written law, and the government rested with the kings—yet within these bounds, as mentioned, with the consent of the elders and the commonality. Thus, the same government cannot be considered or held to be a tyranny.

However, after the kings—and especially the **Tarquins** <note>The Tarquin dynasty was the final line of kings in Rome, known for their arrogance.</note>—presumed much in Rome, such as with **Lucretia** <note>The rape of the noblewoman Lucretia by the king’s son triggered the revolution that overthrew the monarchy.</note> and the like, as the histories say, they were finally driven out, and mayors were appointed in their place. Afterward, for a time, matters of government between the knighthood, the council, and the commonality proceeded in a strange and marvelous way. For the government was sometimes held solely by the council and the most noble families, against which the common man rebelled and forced his way in, as he also wished to be informed and have a hand in affairs. Finally, they brought it to the point that not only several guild-masters <note>German: *Zunfftmeister*; here referring to the Tribunes of the Plebs, who protected the rights of the common people.</note>—who were called **Tribunes**—but also one of the mayors had to be elected from the commonality. This caused much unrest, as both parties were powerful and had many followers, and neither wished to yield to the other.

<margin>To the people who, through flattery, greeted Julius himself as King, Caesar said, "I am Caesar, not King." <note>original Latin: "Populo per adulationem Regẽ ipsum Iuliũ salutãti, Cesar inquit, sum, non Rex."</note></margin>
And this discord lasted until, unexpectedly, **Emperor Julius** [Caesar] arrived and began to take a hand in the game, especially regarding the nobility; he took the best people to himself, along with the government, and appointed the other offices. Because such an undertaking was a great thing and almost appeared as if he wanted to bring the royal state back into the city, and because Julius knew how violently that name was opposed and loathed by the Romans, he did not allow himself to be called a King, but rather a Commander or **Emperor** <note>German: *Keyser*; derived from the name *Caesar*.</note>. Nor was he satisfied with that, but took the best offices [for himself]...

However, such an unjust and headstrong government could not endure. Therefore, when Emperor Julius was stabbed in the Senate House <note>German: *Rahthauß*; the author uses the contemporary term for a town hall to describe the Roman Senate House.</note> in Rome by **Brutus** and **Cassius** along with their accomplices, and likewise when **Antony** and **Lepidus** were subdued (to pass over things briefly), the government—which had now become an Empire—fell to **Octavian Augustus**, whom Julius had adopted. This corruption took hold and increased more and more under subsequent emperors until finally the Roman civil order <term>Policey: Derived from the Greek *politeia*, referring to the organized administration, law, and moral order of a state.</term> and honorable customs—especially under the Popes—completely decayed and were extinguished. This is plain to see today and requires no proof; therefore, I shall refrain from writing further on the matter.

# Of the Mayors of
# Rome, and what their office was.

## The Fourth Chapter.

<image-desc>An ornamental woodcut initial letter 'N' decorated with foliage and floral patterns.</image-desc>

Since I have set forth in the previous chapter the reasons why the kings, who had ruled in Rome for two hundred and forty-four years, were driven out and the mayors began to rule in their place, necessity requires me to show—as briefly as possible—what the office of a mayor was at that time, seeing as it was such a great office that they stood in the place of kings.

In this regard, it is to be known that the mayors held a very heavy and most prominent office, and there were always two of them at once. For both of them had to govern and provide for the common good <term>Nuß: From the German *Nutzen*, meaning the public benefit or common welfare.</term> both abroad in the provinces and at home in the city, whether in times of peace or war. They were also bound to protect and defend the common good from harm at the risk of their own lives, and whenever a war was at hand, they had to lead it, provide for the troops, and serve as the supreme commanders. The years were also numbered by their time in office. The first two mayors were **Junius Brutus** and **Lucius Collatinus**. However, so that their jurisdiction might have a limit, if it happened that a criminal matter <note>German: *peinlich*; historically referring to legal matters involving physical punishment or the death penalty.</note> arose involving a citizen, one could appeal the mayor’s decision. He could also pass no judgment in criminal cases, nor [take] a citizen’s life—

# What a Dictator Was Among the Romans, and Concerning Their Office.

## The Fifth Chapter.

<image-desc>Decorative initial 'D' featuring elaborate scrollwork and floral motifs within a square border.</image-desc>Those who have written about the office of the <term>Dictator</term> <note>In the Roman Republic, a Dictator was a magistrate with extraordinary powers, appointed during emergencies.</note>, or Supreme Commander, have reported and indicated among other things that they were called <term>Masters of the People</term> <note>Latin: *Magistros populi*</note>. It was a great and excellent office, which was not only equal to a prince but almost to a king, as anyone can easily conclude for themselves when considering how great the power of the Romans was at that time, when they occasionally—and as often as necessity required—elected Dictators. If, however, anyone wished to imagine that Rome was a lowly city <note>German: *schlechte Statt*; in this context, "schlecht" means simple or insignificant rather than "bad."</note>, as one might find even among the most powerful, it would be a small matter. But it was quite another thing; however that may be, upon the Dictator in Rome often rested the welfare of the common good and the entire empire. He was not elected until the greatest emergency was at hand. At that time, the entire empire—justice and law, liberty, honor, life and property, and whatever the Romans had under their power—was entrusted to him. He could make and establish war, peace, alliances, and the like, without being questioned by the Council or the community. For as soon as a Dictator was elected, the power and governance of the other offices had to cease, and all were subject to him alone, whether they were <term>mayors</term> (consuls), judges, or master builders, only the <term>Tribunes</term> <note>German: *Tribunos*; officials elected to protect the interests of the common people (plebeians).</note> or guild masters excepted. He could not only have citizens physically punished without the consent of the community, but also remove those who were in office (among whom the mayors were included) and appoint others in their place. Therefore, he constantly had 24 city-servants <note>German: *Statteknecht*; referring to the lictors who carried the symbols of authority.</note> or attendants <term>with rods and axes</term> <note>Latin: *cum fascibus & securibus*; the fasces were bundles of wooden rods, sometimes surrounding an axe, symbolizing the power to punish and execute.</note>, whereas another, such as the mayor, was only permitted to have twelve. Also, whenever a Dictator came to a place where a mayor was present, the mayor...

Furthermore, whatever alliances, treaties, or transactions were established during the Dictator's rule without his foreknowledge and consent were considered invalid; he had the authority either to confirm them or to obstruct and abolish them.

Yet, despite such high might and power, he still lacked one thing. Specifically, as long as his term of office lasted, he was not permitted to sit upon a horse without the permission of the community. This was provided for among the Romans by a special statute <note>German: *Statut*</note>; it was also believed that this was done for a specific reason and significant consideration: namely, so that the power of the Dictatorship might have a limit <note>German: *ein maß haben*</note>, and the Dictators or Supreme Commanders would not think they could act, do, or allow everything according to their own whim. Accordingly, the custom was that if a necessity arose where the Dictator had to ride, he first had to bring the request before the community. Instead, he carried out his business on foot—however far it might be—only letting a horse run alongside him to carry his clothes and bundles. Finally, one should also know that the Dictatorship lasted no longer than half a year, or six months. This remained the case unless, out of favor or for particularly important reasons, he was granted permission to stay in office a few weeks longer—until **Julius Caesar** undertook to keep that same office permanently.

## The Sixth Chapter.

<image-desc>A large ornamental woodcut drop cap 'Z' featuring a blackletter letterform decorated with elaborate floral and scrollwork patterns within a rectangular border.</image-desc>In Rome, until the year three hundred and ninety, they had no <term>Praetors</term> <note>Latin: *Pretores*; the high-ranking Roman magistrates primarily responsible for the administration of justice.</note> or judges to manage legal disputes and pronounce judgment. At that time, the same office was handled by the Mayor <note>German: *Bürgermeister*; the author uses this contemporary title to refer to the Roman Consuls.</note> or whoever else held supreme power in Rome at the time. However, because business increased daily to such an extent that the Mayors could not attend to these matters—due to the distraction of their other duties, and especially because of impending wars—the people's legal rights were often delayed and obstructed. Therefore, the Romans were compelled by necessity to appoint someone for the administration of such legal disputes: namely, a <term>Schulthes</term> <note>A traditional German term for a local magistrate or administrative judge, used here to translate the role of the Roman City Judge.</note> or city judge.

# Of the Book of Regents.

But as they began at that same time to speak and deliberate upon this matter, a disagreement soon arose concerning the **City Judge** <note>German: *Stattrichter*; here referring to the Roman office of the **Praetor**</note>. For the **Council** <note>German: *Raht*; referring to the Roman Senate</note> desired that he should be elected and accepted from among their own number. However, the **Commoners** <note>German: *Gemein*; the Plebeians</note> opposed this and would not grant it, but instead wanted him to be elected from among the Commoners. And although the common man would not be quieted at that time unless the Judge were chosen from their ranks, the Council finally managed to prevail upon the Commoners so much that he was to be, and could be, chosen from among the Councilmen. And the first Judge was **Spurius Furius**, a son of **Marcus Furius** <note>Marcus Furius Camillus, a famous Roman general and statesman</note>. It was also a very great and magnificent office (as it still is) and he had his own chair <note>The *sella curulis*, a ceremonial chair used by high-ranking Roman magistrates</note>, just like a Dictator or a **Mayor** <note>German: *Bürgermeister*; used here to translate the Roman office of **Consul**</note>.

However, it did not last long that the Judge could only be taken from the Council; rather, it happened shortly thereafter that not only the **Praetor** <term>Praetor: A high-ranking Roman magistrate primarily responsible for the administration of justice</term> or Judge, but also one of the Mayors, had to be elected from the Commoners. And **Publius Philo** was the first Judge from the Commoners. But because the estate of the Judge began at the very time when the Romans started to become powerful, they consequently gained much to do, so much so that one Judge was soon too few. Thus, at first two, and subsequently three, were elected at the same time. Also, the Praetors at that time did not only have the courts to care for, but were appointed like the Mayors to govern the **Provinces**, and also to go to war. In this, they had particularly great fortune above other Regents, as is found in the records of their dealings, and therefore they accomplished much good for the common wealth. When later **Sardinia**, as well as **Spain** and **Sicily**, came into Roman hands, six Judges were elected at once. This increase continued annually until, under the **Emperor Augustus**, it reached sixteen, and under **Claudius**, eighteen.

Now, as far as their office is concerned, it was great and extensive, as can be understood in part from the following law, which was called the **Praetorian Law** <note>Latin: *legem prætoriam*</note>, which says:

> Let there be a **Praetor** to be the arbiter of law, who may judge private matters or order them to be judged. Let him be the guardian of the Civil Law. Let all obey this power. As many as the Senate shall decree and the People shall order, let there be that many. <note>original Latin: *Iuris disceptator, qui priuata iudicet, iudicariue iubeat, Prætor esto: Iuris Ciuilis custos esto: huic potestati parento: quotcunque Senatus decreuerit, Populusq; iusserit, tot sunto, &c.*</note>

That is,
A Praetor shall have the authority to judge cases or command such to be done; he shall be a guardian of the civil rights, and the citizens shall render him obedience. There shall be as many of them at any time as the Council in Rome shall ordain. And a Praetor did not only have to do with legal proceedings—as judges are appointed now—but they also had the power to give all kinds of laws to the people, which is still called **Praetorian Law** <note>Latin: *Ius prætorium*</note> to this day. Therefore, they were able to abolish old laws. And if someone was wronged because of their age, they were **restored** <note>Latin: *restituirt*; referring to *restitutio in integrum*, a legal remedy to cancel the effects of a contract or action</note> and reinstated to their previous standing by the Judge. He set the servants free <note>referring to the manumission of slaves</note>, and whatever else belonged to his office at that time. He also oversaw not only the common citizens, but also those who were in office, such as the building masters and treasurers <note>German: *Bauw vnd Rentmeister*; referring to the **Aediles** and **Quaestors**</note>, and others who...

# The First Part

...people did not have the power to demand, or to seize and punish. The Emperor **Octavius Augustus** also granted this freedom to the city judges <note>German: *Stattrichtern*; referring to the Roman Praetors</note>, that they might pass judgment on the appeals of the common man within the city. But for those who appealed from the countryside, only the **Mayors** <note>German: *Bürgermeister*; used throughout to refer to the Roman **Consuls**</note> were permitted to administer justice.

Beyond this, it also belonged to the Judge's office to announce feast days to the people, to arrange public games, to oversee the waterworks <note>referring to the maintenance of aqueducts and public fountains</note>, and to inquire into how every magistrate conducted himself in his office. He was responsible for appointing and choosing **Two Men** and **Ten Men** <note>likely referring to the *Duumviri* and *Decemviri*, specialized Roman administrative boards</note> for whatever pertained to public discipline and morality. I will remain silent here regarding the lesser things that the Judge was responsible for overseeing and executing: such as granting the **possession** <term>possession: the legal right to occupy or use property, often distinct from ultimate ownership</term> of goods, allowing the heirs of the deceased to receive their inheritance, appointing lower judges, confirming guardians, and presiding over all manner of contracts—such as buying, selling, lending, renting, settling disputes, and so on. Likewise, he was to protect the pious and punish the wicked. For who does not know that a judge, even to this day, has the duty to judge and administer such matters?

It is also important to know that when the Mayors of Rome had to depart for war or to the provinces, it fell to the Judges in the meantime to summon the **Council** <note>the Senate</note> and to hold the **Comitia** <note>original: *Comitia*; the public assemblies of the Roman people</note> or gatherings. They were to deliberate on whatever the necessity of the common good required at that time. They held nearly as much power as the Mayors themselves, for they had their own **Legates** <note>high-ranking military or administrative assistants</note> whom they could employ in case of necessity, especially in war, and the soldiers—who were the **Quaestors** <note>financial and administrative officials who also served in military capacities</note>—were commanded by them. However, within the city, they were not permitted to use more than six attendants <note>the *Lictors*</note>, who walked before them carrying **rods** <note>the *fasces*, bundles of rods symbolizing the power to punish</note>, so that a distinction might be made between them and the Mayor, who employed twelve such attendants.

But when they failed in their duty and behaved improperly (for they were not all virtuous), they were dealt with severely, as can be seen in the case of **P. Lentulus**. He was also a judge, but he nonetheless joined himself to the rebellious **Catiline**. Because of this, he was led into the terrifying **Tullianum** prison, which is a desolate, dark, stinking, and horrible hole, two levels <note>German: *schuhe* (feet/shoes); used here as a measure of depth</note> beneath the earth. He was lowered into this hole and strangled with a rope by the executioners, as **Sallust** writes.

The name of **Praetor** was also known among other nations, such as the Macedonians and Egyptians. Likewise, it was known among us **Germans** as well as the Romans, and remains so to this day. For what would the law be in a city or a land if there were no people at hand to execute it, which the judges must do? One also reads that in **Syracuse**, the judges were held in great esteem and possessed much power; however, **Dionysius**, who held that same office, took it as an occasion and an entry point to become a tyrant.

Of the Book of Rulers.

# Of the Censors in Rome,
## and what their office was.
### The Seventh Chapter.

The **Censors** in Rome at first had a quite humble beginning, but in a few short years, they rose to great heights. They were originally elected and appointed so that they might keep diligent watch over the **morals** and customs of the Roman people. This they carried out with great earnestness, severely punishing those they found to be in violation of public decency <note>German: *brüchtig*; referring to those whose reputations were damaged by scandalous behavior</note>. Additionally, they kept watch over those who were ordered by the court to swear an oath, observing whether they swore a true or a false oath.

Likewise, they ensured that no one led a life of excessive expense or consumption in the city; that no **adulterer**, **usurer**, or other unfit person should be tolerated or endured in the **Council** <note>referring to the Roman Senate</note>, nor in other honorable guilds and societies. Instead, they were to remove such people and appoint honorable and capable individuals in their place. They also watched those who did not tend their fields well, those who behaved rudely and shamelessly toward honorable people, women, and maidens, or those who wastefully and shamefully squandered their goods with immoral folk.

It is particularly noted that they had to keep a diligent eye on the young citizens, so that they did not remain **unmarried** and without lawful wives, but were compelled to wed. In short, they were ultimately concerned with all classes, all districts, and all lineages—noble and common, rich and poor. They were to observe what kind of life, nature, business, spending, trade, and conduct every individual practiced, and in what manner he governed his house, wife, children, servants, and property. For they held a strong and explicit command regarding this, which in Latin reads word-for-word as follows:

> The Censors shall take account of the people's children and families; they shall protect the city’s funds, the temples, the roads, the treasury, and the tax revenues. They shall distribute the parts of the people into Tribes and divide the wealth among the ranks of the city; they shall record the lineage of the cavalry and infantry, forbid men from remaining unmarried, rule the morals of the people, and leave no disgrace within the Senate. They shall be two in number and hold their office for five years <term>five years: known in Latin as a *lustrum*, the period between censuses</term>, while other offices are held for only one year; and this power shall always remain.
<note>original Latin: "Censores populi soboles familiasq; censento, pecuniasq; vrbis, templa, vias, ærarium, vectigalia, tuento: populiq; partes in Tribus distribuunto, & pecunias in ciuitatis ordines partiunto, equitum peditumq; prolem distribuunto, cœlibes esse prohibento, mores populi regunto, probrum in senatu ne relinquunto, bini sunto, magistratum quinquennium habento, reliqui magistratus annui sunto, eaq; potestas semper esto."</note>

That is, the Censors should not only keep the families of the Roman people in good discipline, but also guard the city's treasury, the temples, the public roads, the customs, and the **tolls** <term>tolls: fees paid for the safe passage of goods or people</term>. They were to divide the whole population of the city into its four parts <note>referring to the four urban *Tribus* or administrative districts</note>. They were not to permit the citizens to remain unmarried; they were to rule the people's morals and tolerate no public vice or shame in the Council. There shall not be more than **two** of them; their government shall last **five years**, while that of others lasts only one...

...last for a year, and the Censors shall retain such authority at all times.

By virtue of this law and command, the Censors also had charge over the Council Chamber <note>The Roman Senate house</note>, the temples, and public roads. They were responsible for dividing the people into quarters <note>Administrative districts or wards of the city</note>, and for ordaining and collecting customs and tolls. From this, it is sufficiently clear what a magnificent, great, and powerful office it was.

It is also to be known that such censorship was not only established and ordained in Rome and in Italian lands <note>German: *Welschen Landen*; historically used by German speakers to refer to Italy or Romance-speaking territories</note>, but also in several other noble places. For one reads that in Sicily, in particular, the Censors were held in high regard. Likewise, in Carthage in Africa, they had overseers and masters of morals and of the whole life and conduct of the citizens. One of these, at a certain time, punished Hamilcar, a great and powerful captain, because he spoke and associated with Hasdrubal (who was of ill repute). In Argos, the Censors were made to pay diligent attention to idle and lazy people; these people had to give an account of what their trade was and how they supported themselves. This was also the custom and practice in Athens; indeed, every citizen there had to give an account of his income and livelihood to the judges (whom they called <term>Areopagites</term> <note>Members of the Areopagus, the high court of Athens</note>), of which I will say more hereafter.

I must also mention here, among other things, that the Censors in Rome became so powerful over time and rose so high that it became necessary to restrain them and, in part, to humble them. This was because they overreached and attempted too much; in the excessive power they had attained, they began to think they could act as they pleased—appointing, dismissing, taxing, punishing, mastering, governing, and pushing people around as they wished, and that no one should have a say in the matter. This is what usually happens when someone receives too much power: they dare to undertake anything.

Because everyone was terrified of them and no one dared to speak against such power, the <term>Tribunes</term> <note>officials elected to protect the interests and rights of the common people</note> earnestly undertook to oppose them. Thus, P. Clodius <note>Publius Clodius Pulcher</note>, during his term of office, issued a <term>Plebiscite</term> <note>original: *Plebiscitum*; a law or decree enacted by the common people</note> and decree stating that henceforth the Censors should have no power to dismiss or punish anyone unless that person had first been legally accused and convicted. Metellus was also banned because he had punished someone unfairly while he was Censor. More could be written here concerning the Censors, but I will leave it at this brief account,

->so that I do not annoy the reader with<-

# Concerning the Tribunes, whom they called *Tribuni*, and their Office.

## The Eighth Chapter.

After it came to pass at one time in Rome that a great discord arose between the Council <note>The Roman Senate</note> and the Common People, to such an extent that the Commons marched out of the city against the Council, it was found that they could not be calmed in any other way unless the Council agreed that they might elect several Tribunes <note>German: *Zunfftmeister*, literally "guild-masters," an early modern term the author uses to explain the Roman *Tribuni plebis* to his readers</note> from among the Commons. This was not with the intent that they should pass judgment or help to hear and decide the citizens' cases in the Council, like other magistrates and councilors, but rather that they should provide assistance to the common man against the Council and the Mayors <note>The Consuls</note> if they sought to oppress the common man too heavily or impose too much upon him. Likewise, they were to keep a diligent watch over the freedom of the Commons. Accordingly, they were neither permitted to wear purple clothing nor to have any attendants with them; however, they were not forbidden from keeping a lackey or a messenger.

On the other hand, they possessed this liberty: even at a time when a Dictator was elected and all other offices ceased and had to stand still with their governance—so that they were not permitted to use their jurisdiction, as was mentioned above in the chapter on the Dictator—the Tribunes remained in place, one way or another, and exercised their office. However, they did not have the power to summon anyone or to hear and decide the cases of the parties involved; rather, they alone held the authority to take people into custody, regardless of whether they were Mayors, Judges, or Censors. This is indeed what Marcus Drusus did, who imprisoned Philippus the Mayor <note>Lucius Marcius Philippus, the Consul</note> when he tried to prevent him from speaking, and dealt so roughly and violently with the good man that his mouth and nose bled from it. Also, if the Tribunes saw that someone from the Commons was about to be violated by force or insulted, they were permitted to protect him; and what is more, the Tribunes could impose a monetary fine upon both the Mayors and the Dictator himself. Furthermore, if the Tribunes among themselves wished to act, undertake, or conclude something, and one among them had a different opinion and would not consent to it, the others had to stop, and they could not reach a conclusion on the matter.

Beyond this, no Tribune was allowed, as Macrobius writes, to be out of the city for an entire day, so that the Commons might not be abandoned or remain without help on their account. However, Franciscus Floridus Sabinus does not wish to accept this command from Macrobius as good or true. For he writes of it thus: *For who would agree with Macrobius, that the Tribunes of the people were not able...* <note>original Latin: "Quis enim concedat Macrobio, Tribunos plebis, non potuisse"</note>
