...last for one year, and the Censors shall retain such power at all times. By virtue of this law and command, the Censors also oversaw the Senate chamber, the temples and public roads, the division of the people into quarters, and the regulation and collection of customs and tolls; from which it is sufficiently clear what a magnificent, great, and mighty office it was.

And it is to be known that such censorship was not only established and ordained in Rome and in the Italian lands, but also in several other noble places. For one reads that the Censors were held in high regard especially in Sicily. Similarly, in Carthage in Africa, they also had overseers and masters of morals and of the entire life and conduct of the citizens. Among these, one there once punished Hamilcar <note>original: *Amilcarem*</note>, a great and powerful captain, for the reason that he had spoken and held company with Hasdrubal <note>original: *Haſtrubale*</note> (who was of ill repute). In Argos, they had the Censors keep a diligent watch over loose and lazy people, who also had to give an account to them of what their trade was and by what means they supported themselves. This was also the custom and practice in Athens; indeed, every citizen there had to give an account and explanation of his income and livelihood to the judges (whom they called *Areopagites* <note>Members of the Areopagus, the high court of Athens</note>), about which I will say more hereafter.

Nevertheless, I must mention here among other things that the Censors in Rome became so powerful over time and rose so high that it became necessary to restrain them and, in part, to humble them, because they were reaching too far around themselves and attempted too much. For in such immoderate power into which they had come, they allowed themselves to think they might act as they pleased—to appoint, remove, tax, punish, master, rule, and drive people about as they themselves wished—and that no one should have a say in the matter; as it usually happens when someone acquires too much power, that they dare to attempt everything.

However, because everyone was terrified of them and no one dared to speak against them in such power, the Tribunes <term>Tribuni: officials elected to protect the interests of the common people</term> earnestly undertook to oppose them, so that P. Clodius, during his term as guild-master <note>The author uses the German term *Zunfftmeiſterampt* to explain the Roman Tribunate to a contemporary audience</note>, issued a plebiscite <note>original: *Plebiſcitum*; a law enacted by the common people</note> and decree that henceforth the Censors should have no power to remove anyone or take them into punishment, unless that person had first been legally accused and convicted. Metellus was also sent into exile <note>original: *in die acht gethan*; placed under the imperial ban or exiled</note> for this reason, because he had punished someone unjustly while he was Censor. There would be much more to set down here concerning the Censors—

After a time, it happened in Rome that a great discord arose between the Senate <note>original: *Raht*</note> and the Commons <note>original: *Gemeine*, referring to the Plebeians</note>, so much so that the Commons withdrew from the city in opposition to the Senate. They could not be pacified in any other way until the Senate agreed that they might elect several Tribunes from among the Commons. This was not intended for them to dispense justice or to help hear and decide the affairs of the citizens in the Senate, as other magistrates and councilors did, but rather so that they should provide assistance to the common man against the Senate and the Consuls <note>original: *Bürgermeister*</note> if they sought to oppress the common man too heavily or impose too much upon him. Likewise, they were to keep a diligent watch over the freedom of the Commons. Accordingly, they were permitted neither to wear purple garments nor to have any official attendants with them, although they were not forbidden from keeping a footman or a runner.

On the other hand, they possessed this liberty: even when a Dictator was elected and all other offices ceased and had to halt their governance—such that they were not permitted to use their jurisdiction, as was mentioned above in the chapter on the Dictator—the Tribunes continued on just as before and exercised their office. However, they did not have the power to summons anyone or to hear and decide upon the cases of parties; rather, they alone held the power of seizure, to take people into custody, regardless of whether they were Consuls, Judges, or Censors. This is what Marcus Drusus did, who imprisoned the Consul Philippus when he tried to interrupt him in his speech, and dealt so roughly and vehemently with the good man that his mouth and nose bled because of it. Furthermore, if the Tribunes saw that someone from the Commons was about to be violated or disgraced, they could protect him. What is more, the Tribunes could impose a monetary fine upon both Consuls and even the Dictator himself. Also, if the Tribunes wished to negotiate, undertake, or conclude something among themselves, and one of them had a different opinion and would not consent to it, the others had to stop, and they could not come to a conclusion on the matter <note>This refers to the power of *intercessio*, or the veto, where a single Tribune could block the actions of his colleagues or other magistrates.</note>.

# Of the Bishops of Rome,
## and what their office was 
## in the time of paganism.

### The Ninth Chapter.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'E' featuring scrolling foliage and floral motifs.</image-desc>
In former times, soon after the beginning of the city of Rome, the bishops arose there and were called *Pontifices*, that is, "bridge-masters" <note>original: *Brückenherrn*</note>, namely *a Ponte*, which is "from the bridge." For as often as the bridge called the *Sublicium* <note>The oldest bridge in Rome, made of wooden piles</note> was in disrepair, these same gentlemen had to rebuild and maintain it. Otherwise, it was a great and magnificent office, not to be regarded lightly, to which not lowly men, but the most prominent and powerful people and the highest regents—such as kings, emperors, mayors <note>original: *Bürgermeister*, used here to denote Roman Consuls</note>, censors, and the like—were elected and employed. Thus, Numa Pompilius, the second king of Rome; Titus Vespasian, the emperor; and many other great people were bishops. Julius Caesar also sought and desired this episcopal office, as did Q. Catulus <note>The text reads "Q. Carulus," likely a misspelling of Quintus Lutatius Catulus, a prominent Roman statesman</note> alongside him, who was a powerful man and held in great esteem by the Romans. But when Julius Caesar was about to leave his house to petition for this office, and his mother accompanied him to the door, he said:
> "Today, O mother, you will have either a son who is Supreme Pontiff <note>original Latin: *Pontificem maximum*</note> or an exile."
That is: "O mother, today you shall have either a high bishop or an exiled man for a son." A stout and brave heart, which he proved afterward. And it was almost such an office as the current bishops in the Papacy <note>original: *Papiſterey*</note> have held, and in part still have; for they were commanded to manage and provide for the ceremonies: such as which gods were to be served and sacrificed to on which altar and with what kind of offerings at each time; when one should observe holidays; how one should behave at funerals; and what special honor must be shown to each particular god—and so much of this foolishness that I cannot recount it all.
      Among other things, however, this was also their office (for which reason I have primarily set down this chapter): that the greatest and highest bishop had to keep and maintain the year-books, which were called *Annales* <note>Latin for yearly records</note>, in which he had to write...

...to be recorded—whatever happened and occurred from one time to another throughout the entire year, whether it was good or bad, provided it was worthy of being remembered, known, and written down. Subsequently, he had to have all these histories placed upon a tablet, which was called the **Album** <note>In ancient Rome, the *Annales Maximi* were recorded on a whitened board or *Album*</note>, so that they might be copied by the mayors <note>original: *Bürgermeistern*; referring here to the Consuls</note>, judges, wardens, or guild masters, and diligently preserved and taken into safekeeping not in one, but in many reliable places. In addition, a Bishop must not only be personally innocent of all matters of blood <note>Cases involving the death penalty or violence</note>, but he was also not permitted to be a party to such things, nor to have any knowledge of them. And just as he had to be pure and unstained by all vices and misdeeds in his own person, so too must his wife be chaste and virtuous, and lead an innocent life.

Finally, at that time, both the knowledge and the interpretation of the Law, as well as its explanation, resided with the Bishops. It remained so for several hundred years thereafter, as they were the best and holiest of people, because the Law was esteemed and held to be a precious and holy thing—as indeed it is in truth. Therefore, no one was permitted to know, interpret, or profess the Law except the Bishops, until later when the Law came to the **Jurists** and now, in our own times, in some places, to the magistrate courts <term>Schöffenstüle: local courts presided over by lay judges or "Schöffen"</term>.

And it would not be a bad thing if this noble gift of God—the holy Law—once again had such guardians, overseers, directors, advocates, and holy people, so that it would not be so shamefully falsified, torn apart, and abused by every person, as happens now in some places. In these times, people care little for how the Law is administered, which is a particular harm and ruin to the common good, the land, and the people. For this reason, **Seneca** said not without cause:

> Where there is no shame, nor care for the law, no sanctity, piety, or faith, the kingdom is unstable. <note>original Latin: *Vbi non est pudor, Nec cura iuris sanctitas, pietas, fides, instabile regnum est.*</note>

As one can see, things are almost reaching that point in some places because people defer to the nobility, the rich, and the powerful against the Law, and look on as they sometimes dare to oppress the poor. They use the Law no differently or further than it is beneficial to them; likewise, the advocates for their part do not hesitate to defend evil causes with the noble laws, so that it looks as if everything is about to collapse.

<margin>Right lies in arms; fear oppresses the laws, says Seneca. <note>original: *Ius est in armis, opprimit leges timor*</note> And Cicero: All things are wretched in wars. <note>original: *Omnia sunt misera in bellis*</note></margin>

## The Tenth Chapter.

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap initial 'D' with floral or vine patterns inside a square frame.</image-desc>Since these names, such as the Two Men, Three Men, Ten Men, Hundred Men, etc., are mentioned many times here and there in the histories, especially in **Livy** <note>Titus Livius, a Roman historian famous for his monumental history of Rome</note>, necessity requires that a brief mention be made of them. It should be known that the **Two Men** <note>Latin: *Duoviri*</note> were sometimes appointed to manage the sacrifices to the idols, in order to soften and still their anger. Likewise, the **Sibylline Books** <note>A collection of oracular utterances used by the Roman state in times of crisis</note> were entrusted to them. These were first chosen and ordained by **Tarquinius**; one of them, **M. Attilius**, was punished as a <term>Parricida</term> <note>literally a "parricide" or parent-killer</note>—that is, one who strangles his parents—because he revealed the secrets of the Sibyl.

Subsequently, after some time, the **Ten Men** <note>Latin: *Decemviri*</note> were appointed in their place by the guild masters <note>original: *Zunfftmeistern*; likely referring to the Tribunes of the Plebs</note> Sertius and Licinius: namely, five from the Council <note>the Senate</note> and five from the Commoners. This number remained for several years until the time of **Cornelius Sulla**, when fifteen were then chosen to provide for the sacrifices and likewise to pay heed to the ceremonies and the books. For as **Dionysius** writes:

> The Romans guard nothing so strictly, neither anything holy nor anything sacred, as the Sibylline oracles sent from heaven. <note>original Latin: *Romani nihil ita custodiunt neque sanctum, neq; sacrum, quemadmodum Sybillina diuinitus missa oracula.*</note>

These books were bought by Tarquinius for 300 Philippic Guilders <note>the author uses a contemporary 16th-century currency to describe the ancient cost</note> and were later burned in the Capitol during the time of Sulla.

There were also other **Two Men** chosen, partly from the Council, partly from the judges, and also partly from the commoners, who among other things had to organize and repair the armada and naval equipment when the Romans wanted to go to war by water. They were required to provide them with soldiers, money, artillery, provisions, and all necessary supplies.

The **Three Men** <note>Latin: *Triumviri*</note> had the duty to judge and pass sentence in criminal matters <note>original: *peinlichen sachen*; cases involving physical punishment or death</note>. These first began when **Curius Dentatus** triumphed over the **Samnites**. Likewise, there were also <term>Triumviri</term> who, in times of war, had to travel around the cities to assemble, enroll, and deploy the soldiers, and to hold musters among them. This happened at the time when the Romans were defeated and slain by **Hannibal**, so that they lacked soldiers; then these same *Triumviri*, or Three Men, gathered not only the free people but also the bondservants and

The office of the **Four Men** <note>Latin: *Quattuorviri*</note> was to establish **colonies** <term>Colonias</term> <note>Establishing a colony meant settling Roman citizens in new or conquered territories to ensure loyalty, manage population, and provide land for veterans.</note>—that is, to settle cities with Roman citizens. If some new or unforeseen danger arose which brought peril, they had to take precautions so that the common good suffered no harm. 

The **Five Men** <note>Latin: *Quinqueviri*</note> were responsible for distributing the fields, and likewise for repairing the city walls and towers. To those who were burdened by debts and could not pay, they were permitted to provide an advance from the common treasury; this occurred at the time when the citizens of the city of Rome were burdened with great debts. It is written that this was a significant advancement and arrangement—as is easy to judge—to maintain the community in good peace and unity with the Council.

In short, whenever something difficult was at hand from which a disadvantage might arise for the city and the Roman people, and for which one required pious, faithful, diligent, and cautious people, they chose either two, three, four, five, or six, according to what the weight of the matter required. These men attended to such difficult and laborious tasks, diligently considered them, and finally performed and settled them. When that same matter reached its conclusion, they thereafter waited upon their own affairs again and were satisfied.

The **Seven Men** <note>Latin: *Septemviri*</note> dealt with spiritual <note>religious or ecclesiastical</note> matters. The **Ten Men** <note>Latin: *Decemviri*</note> were of various kinds, as has been partly heard above; for one finds among others that they organized, leased, and managed the customs and tolls. These were thereafter expanded and improved by the **Ten Men** <term>Decemuiris</term> and set into a proper order, out of which the **Law of the Twelve Tables** <term>zwölff Tafeln</term> <note>The Twelve Tables (c. 450 BCE) was the foundational legal code of ancient Rome, making the laws public for the first time.</note> was formed. 

This same law is the foundation and origin of all statutes and the entire Imperial Law. Because of this, **Cicero** says: *Though everyone may rage, I will say what I feel: the one little book of the Twelve Tables seems to me to surpass the libraries of all the philosophers (by Hercules!) in its weight of authority and its abundance of utility, if one happens to see the sources and heads of the laws.* <note>original Latin: "Fremant licet omnes, dicam quod sentio, Bibliothecas (me herclè) Philosophorum omnium vnus mihi vdetur 12. tabellarum libellus, si quis fortè legum fontes & capita videre, & authoritatis pondere, & vtilitatis vbertate superare." From Cicero's *De Oratore*.</note> That is: though they all might wish to be angry, the Law of the Twelve Tables—if one wishes to see the ground and origin of the Law—is a brief summary of all philosophy, so many excellent and useful things are contained therein. ...had to manage legal disputes, just as in certain places today, in the absence of the Judge, the **Jurors** <note>German: *Scheffen* (Schöffen); lay judges or assessors who assist in legal proceedings.</note> are accustomed to doing and carrying out. In addition to these, there were also **Twenty Men** who had to settle and adjudicate all kinds of legal matters, as if at a seat of judgment.

Finally, they also had the **Centumviri** <note>Latin: "Centumviros", meaning "The Hundred Men".</note>—that is, one hundred men—who held the highest and supreme **Capital Court** <term>Halßgericht</term> <note>Literally a "neck court," referring to jurisdiction over crimes punishable by death or physical punishment.</note>, from which no one could appeal. Later, Domitian also had the judgments and decrees of the 100 men abolished and rescinded as unnecessary.

## Of the Treasurers, who were called
->Quaestors, when they first arose in Rome,<-
->and what their office was.<-

### The Eleventh Chapter.

<image-desc>A large decorative woodcut initial 'E' containing a seated female figure holding a sword and a pair of scales (Lady Justice), surrounded by floral ornamentation.</image-desc>Pomponius, Fenestella, Cornelius Tacitus, and others write that the **Quaestors** <note>Latin: *Quaestores*</note> or **Treasurers** arose in Rome shortly under King Romulus and thus have a very ancient origin, although some believe they were first established by Tullus Hostilius, which is also uncertain. It is found, however, that when the kings were driven out of Rome and Valerius Publicola and Brutus were **Mayors** <note>German: *Bürgermeister*; the author uses this contemporary term to describe the Roman Consuls.</note> and began to build a common treasury, the Council appointed two from their midst as Treasurers—namely Publius Veturius and M. Minutius—to preside over that same treasury and common purse. As soon as this was put into practice and the commonalty perceived that it was beneficial to the city and an honorable office, it happened (as mentioned above regarding the judges) that the common man interfered, demanding that some from the commonalty must also be chosen as Quaestors. From this it followed that, to remedy these matters, four Treasurers were appointed. Two held the common money of the Council in their administration, receiving and paying it out. The other two had to wait upon the Mayors when they went to the field <note>i.e., went to war.</note> to pay the soldiery, acting as paymasters, and these two were elected by the Council or the commonalty.

In ancient Rome, the Quaestors were the junior-most officials who supervised the treasury and financial accounts.</note>, such a commotion arose between the Council and the Common people that no one from the Council was elected among the four, namely, Fabius Ambustus. This number remained the same until the Picenes <note>An ancient people of the Adriatic coast of Italy who were defeated by Rome in 268 BC.</note> were forced by necessity to join the Romans. At that time, their number became six, as necessity required, because the income from rents, customs, and tolls increased daily with the Roman power. Consequently, more people had to be appointed to take over the administration of that income; for this reason, the number of Treasurers eventually grew to twenty and more. 

Regarding what the Treasurers had to do beyond this office, various things are written: namely, that one of them had to be in every Roman field camp to take charge of the **war spoils** <note>German: *Brandschatzung*; money or goods seized during war.</note> and other money and property captured in war. Likewise, they collected customs and other dues here and there in the provinces on behalf of the Romans. For this, they had to keep special account books of their income and expenditure, which were then deposited and kept in the Treasury <note>German: *Renterey* or *Schatzkammer*.</note> from one year to the next.

In particular, however, they were commanded to keep an eye on foreign people who came to Rome and were sent away, whether in person or as messengers, and to take care with all diligence that they did not suffer any lack of lodging, quarters, food, drink, and all necessities. This practice was held among the Romans for a long time, until there were so many envoys from all places, kingdoms, principalities, cities, and lands of the whole world that they could not all be maintained and hosted. Therefore, it had to be discontinued; however, those envoys and embassies had a certain place where they were lodged and assigned. There they had to report to the **Quaestors**, have their names recorded, and await further instructions. And when they wished to depart again, they honored the Quaestors with costly gifts; and if one of them died, he had to be buried at the expense of the public treasury.

It is also important to know that the Romans had an inner and secret treasury in the Temple of Saturn, in which they gathered an excellent supply of pure gold, so that they might use it in impending necessity; otherwise, they were not allowed to touch such a treasure. Everyone had to give the **twentieth penny** <note>Latin: *vicesima*; a 5% tax usually levied on the value of manumitted slaves.</note> toward this supply, for which reason the tax was called the *Vicesimarum*. Such an unspeakable treasure of gold was brought together there that Julius Caesar, at the beginning of the Civil War against Pompey, seized that same treasure. He took from that inner and secret treasury up to twenty-six thousand gold bricks—or gold cakes cast in the form of bricks—along with a notable sum of minted gold coins, which the Quaestors also had under their hands. And Pliny says, <note>original: "Nec fuit alijs temporibus Respublica locupletior."</note> that the city of Rome was never richer in its reserves at any other time. And such an office remained with the Quaestors for a very long time, until it was later given to the...

## The Twelfth Chapter.

<image-desc>Large decorative woodcut drop cap initial 'E' depicting a figure or mythological scene.</image-desc>
THERE were otherwise many more offices among the Romans, such as **Architects**, **Councilors**, and **Governors**—whom some now call a **Vice-Steward** <term>Vitzdom</term> <note>Derived from the Latin *vicedominus*, an administrative official representing a lord or bishop.</note>—and the like, which I will omit for the sake of brevity. These aforementioned ones, however, I have set down so that one may see how many different offices are necessary in a kingdom, land, or city, and that from them all kinds of teaching and instruction, useful for the establishment and preservation of good and honorable **Public Order** <term>Policey</term> <note>Derived from the Greek *politeia*; in this context, it refers to the broad administration, moral governance, and civil order of a state, rather than modern law enforcement.</note>, may be taken.

First, so that one may see the differences in offices which are used now or are no longer used. Second, that it has always and at all times been the custom that the **Regents** and **Mayors** have had to swear an oath; the only difference is that they now swear at the beginning of their rule, whereas in those times they had to do so when their government reached its conclusion <note>The author highlights that Roman officials were held accountable *after* their term, providing a final report on their conduct.</note>. Third, that in criminal cases one should not hasten to judge the citizens, especially when it concerns life and limb. For this reason, the Romans did not wish to trust or grant such power to the Mayor alone, but it had to happen with the prior knowledge of many—concerning which I will write and set down something further at the end of this book.

Fourth, it is also to be noted that nothing is so good or so well-established that it might not, with time, fall into misuse, as one clearly sees with the **Censors**. They held such a magnificent and precious office, from which so much good followed for the public order and the whole city that one cannot write enough about it; yet such an office became changeable over time, so that the Censors began to abuse it and reach further around themselves than they were commanded, for which reason they had to be humbled again.

One had to do the same with the **Dictators**, so that they would not assume too much power for themselves. And would to God that the **Authorities** <term>Oberkeit</term> would one day open their eyes, and that the rulers, especially in cities and lands, would again establish such a **Censorship** of good morals, since people are now so coarse and wild that it would have been too much even among the heathens; it will...

and should have kept them for themselves. Now, if the Romans had also been so negligent and had not had their **Annals** <note>Year-by-year historical records.</note> recorded with such diligence and earnestness, from where would **Titus Livy** and others have been able to describe and take their histories? For he could not, after all, have been there himself to see and hear everything, nor could he have lived so long; therefore, he had to inform himself from the histories and yearbooks. Furthermore, **Livy** lived during the time of the Emperor **Octavius** <note>Augustus Caesar.</note>, a full seven hundred and eighty-some years after the founding of the city of Rome.

Beyond this, it is also to be seen that no office among the Romans was so minor that one could not notice and learn something special from it; with such foresight and great diligence were all things in that same city ordered and provided for. Therefore, it is not to be wondered at that they increased so remarkably. For although the **Treasurer’s Office** <term>Quaestorship</term> <note>original: *Rentmeisterampt*; the author is referring to the Roman Quaestors, who managed the treasury and often handled the logistics for foreign embassies.</note> was not one of the most prominent offices, it nevertheless had several magnificent and fine duties which other cities ought rightly to follow and take to heart. Namely, when the embassies of foreign people or lords come into a city wherein they have something to petition or achieve, they should be honorably received, provided with lodging and all necessities in the best way, subsequently heard kindly at a convenient time, and finally also honorably dismissed. This is exactly what you see the Romans did, considering that among the ancients throughout the whole world, **Legates** <note>Diplomatic ambassadors.</note> were a sacred thing whom one must not dare to violate nor harm. Whoever laid hands upon them, however, violated and transgressed the **Law of Nations** <term>Ius Gentium</term> <note>original: *Ius Gentium*; the customary law held to be common to all mankind, which provided "diplomatic immunity" to messengers even during war.</note>. Yet some have acted so forgetfully that they did not even spare the legates, and held them not only in contempt but also sometimes struck them down and miserably murdered them—disregarding that such a gruesome and godless undertaking turned to their own significant disadvantage and harm, as can be understood from the following examples from history.

Firstly, **Titus Livy** writes that the **Aequi**—who bordered the **Volsci** and had many battles with the Romans—at one time desired and obtained a peace from the Romans. After they did not keep it, however, but attacked the Romans again in the following year and took to the field under **Gracchus**, their commander, doing much damage, the Romans dispatched two legates to them in their camp to complain that the peace had not been kept. But when they came into the camp and wished to deliver their message, the commander pointed them to an oak tree that stood not far away, stating that if they had anything to announce on behalf of the Council at Rome, they might complain and report it to the oak. Thereupon one legate went there and spoke these following words toward the oak:

> "And let this sacred oak," he said, "and whatever gods there may be, hear that the treaty has been broken by us; and let them be present now for our complaints, and soon for our arms, when we shall avenge the violated laws of both gods and men." <note>original Latin: "Et hæc, inquit, sacrata quercus, & quicquid Deorum est, audiant fœdus à nobis ruptum : nostrisq; & nunc querelis adsint : & mox armis : cùm Deorum, hominumq; simul violata iura exequemur."</note>

> "And you, sacred oak, and whatever other gods there are, may they be our witnesses that the alliance has not been kept with us, and that we intend to avenge this with deeds."

And the legates thereafter returned home.

That is to say: What should I say of **Lucius Mummius**? He who destroyed the most beautiful and magnificent city of **Corinth**, which was ahead of all others and wealthy in all things, and subjected many brave cities in **Achaia** and **Boeotia** to the Roman Empire. Furthermore, to come to the **Greeks**, King **Darius** of **Persia** sent several legates to the **Spartans** (or **Lacedaemonians**) for **water and earth** <note>This was a traditional Persian demand for submission, symbolizing the surrender of the land and its resources.</note>. This is to say, he demanded that they should surrender to him. They did not wish to do this, however, but instead threw the legates into a well and drowned them. And although King Darius did not have the time to avenge himself on the Spartans for such shame and injury, the histories say that they had an **idol** <note>A god or hero-spirit.</note> named **Talthybius**, who, because of this evil deed, inflicted so much plague and misfortune upon them that they had to hold a council on how they might escape such hardship and reconcile with the idol again. 

After they learned from their own consciences that they had sinned against the innocent blood of the legates, and that they must be reconciled and stilled with human blood in return, they had it proclaimed that if someone were available who would give themselves over to death for the common city, they should report to the council. Soon two of them came, namely **Sperthies** <note>German: *Spertus*.</note> and **Bulis**, and not only volunteered but also traveled to King Darius. There, they offered to pay with their lives for the legates. However, Darius did nothing to them, but wondered at such **manhood** <note>Referring to their courage and nobility.</note> and admitted that he was not the equal of the Lacedaemonians. He also asked these two men to remain with him, since they had shown such loyalty to their fatherland. But they answered him:

Because of this, the poor man met his final ruin, for they perhaps found in him that which would otherwise have remained hidden.

Likewise, when **Philip** the King of **Macedon** <note>This refers to Philip V of Macedon, who allied with Carthage against Rome.</note> learned that **Hannibal** had been victorious over the **Romans** in three consecutive battles and had beaten them severely, he dispatched a formal embassy to establish friendship and an alliance with him. However, since they were not being watched closely and no deception was suspected, they escaped along the way before reaching Rome and made it to Hannibal. Once they had completed their business and errand there and wished to sail back to Macedonia, Roman ships intercepted them again and demanded an explanation. Xenophanes once more began his deceitful tale, saying he had been sent to make an alliance with the Romans but had been prevented by enemies and thus had to return home empty-handed. However, because Hannibal's legates—**Mago** and others—were also with him, the matter became suspicious. # On the Origin of Fiefs among
## the Germans.
### The Fourteenth Chapter.

<image-desc>A large decorative woodcut initial 'D' depicting a landscape scene with figures and foliage.</image-desc>Since the previous chapter briefly mentioned the origins of certain estates in the German lands, it seems appropriate to me to set down something here regarding the origin of **Fiefs** <term>Fiefs <note>original: "Lehen"; land or rights granted by a lord to a vassal in exchange for loyalty and service.</note></term>, as these are in constant use and practice, especially among the nobility. Now, when I look at the legal scholars who have written on this, I find that, in my opinion, they have not established the proper foundation nor sufficiently weighed the matter. However, so that one may know how things stand, it is held by brave and highly learned men—such as **Zasius** <note>Ulrich Zasius (1461–1535), a famous German jurist and humanist.</note>, **Haloander** <note>Gregor Haloander (1501–1531), a German jurist who restored Roman legal texts.</note>, and others—that fiefs had their origin in the customs and habits of the ancient **Romans**.

For some write, such as **Dionysius of Halicarnassus** <note>A Greek historian and teacher of rhetoric who lived in Rome during the reign of Augustus.</note>, and likewise **Gellius**, that the first king, **Romulus**, allowed and permitted the inhabitants that each might choose a **Patron** and **Protector** <note>original: "Schutzherrn"</note> according to his circumstances, to represent and defend him if he were to be oppressed by the rich and powerful. These people were then called **Clients** <note>original: "Clientes"</note> by the patrons, and it was a great honor at that time if a patron had many clients. Thus **Valerius** writes of **Appius Clausus**, that he moved from the Sabines to Rome with five thousand clients. It is believed that fiefs later originated from such a custom; for after the Romans had been victorious here and there, not only in **France** but also in **German lands**, and had thereby brought many kingdoms, principalities, lands, and people under their control, the Roman soldiery for the most part settled and inhabited those lands. Those areas they could not inhabit, they granted to the lords whom they had conquered (changing their titles as mentioned in the previous chapter) or to neighboring people, who in turn pledged themselves to them; and such granted and loaned

Doctor Ulrich Zasius <note>A famous humanist jurist (1461–1535) known for reforming legal studies in Germany.</note>, an excellent jurist, has written specially about this, which [I] have translated into German and published in print, so that those who do not understand Latin feudal law may learn of it there. But this is the summary of it: that a lord is obligated to do and provide for his vassal that which the vassal has sworn to him; and if he did not do so, he would have forgotten his loyalty to him and [therefore] may be sued by him. If it were such a case where the vassal had been in breach of duty, such that he would have lost the **useful ownership** <term>useful ownership <note>original: "utile dominium"; the right to use and profit from property, though the ultimate title stays with the lord.</note></term>, and the lord had trespassed against the vassal in such a case, then the lord would have forfeited and lost his **direct ownership** <term>direct ownership <note>original: "directum dominium"; the ultimate legal title to a property.</note></term> against the man, as stated in the chapter "On the form of fidelity," at the end. And in the chapter "Otherwise the Lord is deprived of the property of the fief," in the *Books of Fiefs* <note>original: "vibus feudorum" / "Libri Feudorum"; the standard collection of feudal law in the Middle Ages.</note>. And the *Gloss* says in the same place: "And it is no wonder if the lord loses the property ownership, since the lord himself is bound to reciprocate to the vassal in those things for which the vassal is bound to him." That is: It is no wonder if the lord must lose the ownership of the fief in those cases, since he is obligated to keep for the vassal exactly what he promised him, etc.

# The First Part

[The land] which the LORD your God will give you, and you take possession of it, and dwell therein, and shall say: "I will set a king over me, as all the nations around me have," then you shall set him as king over you whom the LORD your God shall choose. But you shall choose one from among your brothers as king; for you cannot set any stranger, who is not your brother, over you. Only, he shall not have many horses, nor lead the people back into Egypt for the sake of the multitude of horses. He shall also not take many wives, so that his heart is not turned away, and he shall also not collect much silver and gold. And when he shall now sit upon the throne of his kingdom, he shall take this second Law <note>original: "ander Gesetz"; this refers to the book of Deuteronomy, which literally means "Second Law."</note> from the priests of the Levites, and have it written in a book. That shall be with him, and he shall read therein all his life, so that he learns to fear the LORD his God, that he keeps all the words of this Law and these customs, so that he acts accordingly. He shall not exalt his heart above his brothers, and shall not deviate from the commandment, neither to the right nor to the left, so that he may prolong his days in his kingdom, he and his children in Israel.

So God also says to Joshua, in the first chapter of that same book: "Only be comforted and joyful, that you keep and do all things according to the Law which Moses my servant commanded you. Do not deviate from it, neither to the right nor to the left, so that you may act wisely wherever you go. And let the book of this Law not depart from your mouth, but meditate upon it day and night, so that you keep and do all things according to that which stands written therein; then you will prosper in your ways and will act wisely."

These are excellent, beautiful words and commandments which God prescribes for a king. Namely, that he should not maintain a great display of horses, nor burden himself with many wives, which can hardly be maintained without the **taxation** <term>taxation <note>original: "Schatzung"; refers to the levying of taxes or tributes upon subjects.</note></term> of the subjects. Likewise, that he should live in the fear of God and occupy himself with His word, reading it continually and following it. Lastly, also, that he should not exalt himself too high above his **subjects** <term>subjects <note>original: "Vnterthanen"; those living under the rule and protection of a sovereign.</note></term>, and not deviate from the right, neither to the left nor to the right. Thus, if a king or prince were to guide himself by this short rule, it would not be possible for him to do or act unjustly. A temporal promise is also attached to it in Joshua: namely, that those same kings shall succeed—that is, it shall go happily and well for them, and they shall live long in their royal reign. 

But God Himself saw that the kings would not leave it at that, but would take more power and right for themselves than is proper for them, as the Scripture makes mention of in the first book of Samuel, in the 8th chapter, when the Jews desired and wanted to have a king. But kings in that same position should not understand the Scripture to mean that they had the right, cause, and power to take the children and goods of their subjects by force. Otherwise, God would not have punished Ahab together with his wife, the evil Jezebel, so severely because of the vineyard that they took from Naboth. However, because the world will not have it otherwise, it happens that people sometimes receive rulers who treat them in such a way as the Scripture reports in the aforementioned chapter of the first book of Samuel—much like the stork with the frogs. <note>This refers to the Aesop's fable where frogs asked for a king and were eventually given a stork that ate them; it is a common historical metaphor for a people who, unsatisfied with their lot, receive a predatory ruler as punishment.</note>

As far as the anointing and coronation of kings is concerned, this is also an ancient and magnificent custom, which also carries many beautiful interpretations. And although every kingdom has its own particular style and ceremonies for the coronation and anointing of kings, I will nevertheless recount a brief form here which was observed when the current, powerful, and praiseworthy King of Denmark, Christian, was crowned. From this, the interpretation of the ceremonies usually employed in this matter can be easily understood. I do not believe that one will find such a magnificent and beautiful example of a coronation and the interpretation of its ceremonies in any other histories. For this reason, I have wished to set it down here at length, just as the aforementioned King sent it in writing to the well-born, my gracious Lord, Count Albrecht of Mansfeld, of blessed memory, and His Grace honored me with it. The history of the coronation proceeds briefly as follows:

In the year one thousand, five hundred, and thirty-seven, on the Sunday after St. Lawrence <note>original: "Sontags nach Laurenti"; this refers to August 12, 1537.</note>, Christian, a Duke of Holstein, was elected King of Denmark after a long-lasting war. First, before the day of the coronation, the church was decorated most beautifully with fine tapestry; likewise, organs and all kinds of stringed instruments were prepared. Not far from the high altar, two tents with high poles were set up, completely covered, in which the King and Queen could change their garments.

When the elected King came to the church, the <term>Regalia</term> <note>the emblems or insignia of royalty</note> were carried before him through the streets and into the church. The same was done for the elected Queen by the Lords of the Realm to whom it was proper. The King’s regalia were the sword, crown, scepter, and orb <note>original: "Apffel"; literally "apple," referring to the globus cruciger, a symbol of planetary authority.</note>. The Queen’s regalia were the crown and scepter. The King went into his tent, and the Queen into hers as well. But those who carried the regalia stood before them for a short time. The altar was decorated, and a chair placed before it. For the <term>Ordinator</term> <note>the presiding official or bishop conducting the ceremony</note>, a chair was also prepared below before the altar, where the King and Queen could kneel, with a low bench upon which they could lean. The Ordinator was dressed in an alb and a cope, standing not far from the altar with the other priests, who wore white surplices and commended this matter to God in their private prayers.

Also, the Elder of the Realm then went to the altar with the <term>Regal</term> <note>original: "Regal"; used here to mean a specific item of the regalia</note> he was carrying. And as he approached, he knelt down upon the earth, stood up again immediately, and offered the regalia upon the altar, returning then to his place. After him, the one with the second item did the same. Then the one with the third, and also the one with the fourth item of the regalia.

## stament.

After the King had taken such an oath, the Council of the Realm <note>original: "Reichs Rähte" — the high-ranking nobles and clergy who advised the monarch.</note> brought the Queen to the Officiant <note>original: "Ordinator" — the clergyman, likely a bishop, presiding over the ceremony.</note>. Her hair was loosened and spread over her shoulders; however, she was not dressed as a Queen, but only as a Princess. The Officiant stood up; the Queen knelt down; soon after, the Officiant sat back down in his chair. Then one of the Councilors began to speak in Danish, and the other in German, saying: "We ask once again, worthy Lord and Father, that you—as a servant of Christ—would, in the name of God, confirm and establish this our chosen Queen (for whom we thank God) with the regalia <note>The physical symbols of royalty, such as the crown and scepter.</note> and such worthy power as befits a Queen." 

To this, the Officiant answered: "Noble, valiant, and honorable Lords, I do this with all my heart. It is godly and just, as you see your Lord crowned, that such honor be given also to His Grace’s lawful consort, and that she be confirmed here before God. For this is God’s ordinance: man and wife are one body, so also should their honor and name be inseparable. Although their offices should not and cannot all be the same, we hope in God that this shall also prosper to God’s honor and the common peace."

The Officiant then addressed the Queen in the following manner: "High-born Princess, Gracious Lady, one reads in the Holy Scriptures of several noble women and their great, godly deeds, which must be praised. One reads of Deborah in the Book of Judges, in the fourth chapter, that she ruled the people of Israel for forty years in good peace; she delivered them from their enemies and restored among the people the beloved Word of God, which the priests and the godless had rejected, for she was a prophetess.

Thus we also hope that Your Grace will apply special diligence and counsel so that good preachers and schools are once again provided for the Word of God in these lands, and also in Norway, where many people have not come to church for several years—may God have mercy; we truly should not be so indifferent. 

Likewise, one reads in the first book of Samuel, in the 25th chapter, of the godly and wise woman Abigail (who afterwards became Queen), that she turned King David away from his anger when he wished to slay the defiant squire and drunkard Nabal. 

Likewise, of the great Queen Esther, how she prayed to God: 'LORD, you know that I do not value my crown more than filth <note>original: "Vnflat" — something repulsive or worthless; Esther is portrayed as wearing her crown out of duty to her people rather than vanity.</note>, but for the honor of the King and the Kingdom I wear it.' And she delivered her people from death, which would have befallen them all through the court-devil Haman, who received a gallows as his reward. 

Therefore, everyone in the land expects much good from Your Grace, following the example of these holy Queens. Yet they desire that Your Grace would also publicly promise this to us here before God."

### It follows how the King swore the oath.

I, Christian, by the grace of God, elected King of Denmark and Norway, confess joyfully from my heart that—alongside the holy Gospel of our Lord Jesus Christ, which is our salvation and through which I have received all this power and honor—in order that I may not be ungrateful to the heavenly Father, my dear <term>Liege Lord</term> <note>original: "Lehenherrn." In this context, the King acknowledges God as his own feudal superior, from whom he holds his kingdom.</note>, I promise before this, my land, and to all, and I vow to God: that I will uphold this teaching of Christ with everything that belongs to it (namely with faithful preachers, good schools, and their decent and honorable sustenance). I will also help pray that God, out of grace, may let His wholesome Word and Gospel always remain with us and not take it away in His displeasure. Furthermore, I promise that I will uphold the law, and strive for justice for the lowest as well as for the highest, for peace, for good governance, and for the common good. I will maintain the <term>Council of the Realm</term> <note>original: "ReichsRähte." The high council of nobles and clergy who advised the monarch and governed the state.</note> along with my other faithful subjects in their proper honor, so far as God gives me grace, according to my ability, knowledge, and understanding, and according to the advice of my faithful counselors. God give grace that I neglect nothing. But if I, as a human being, should neglect something, may the merciful God forgive me for the sake of Christ His dear Son, our Lord. However, I will not, God willing, act or allow action to be taken knowingly or willfully against this my promise. So help me truly, our dear Lord Jesus Christ, with His Gospel, etc.

And when he came to the anointing, the officiant stood up and anointed the King—who was kneeling—with his thumb, between the hand and the elbow, and between both shoulders, with the sign of the cross. Likewise, he also anointed the Queen in the prescribed manner, and explained the anointing with the following words:

That kings are anointed is a very ancient custom. It was common not only among the Jews—as Saul, David, Solomon, and other kings were anointed by God's command—but also among the Gentiles. For we also read in the Holy Scriptures, in the First Book of Kings <note>original: "dritten Buch der Könige" — in older German Bibles, 1 and 2 Kings were often titled as the 3rd and 4th Books of Kings</note>, in the 19th chapter, that Hazael was anointed by God's command by the prophet Elijah to be King in Syria, etc. Therefore, when one says *Messiah* <note>original Hebrew: "Messia"</note>, which in Greek is *Christ* <note>original: "Christus"</note>, in Latin *Anointed* <note>original: "Vnctus"</note>, and in German *Gesalbet*, one means nothing else by the word than a King. Thus, when we Christians speak of the King of all Kings, Jesus Christ, it is the same as saying Jesus the King. Yet it is to be understood that this Christ is the King appointed for us by God and promised through the prophets, who has power in heaven and on earth.

We certainly confess here that such anointing is not commanded of us, as if no King or Queen could be such without the anointing. On the other hand, we also know quite well that such anointing is not forbidden. Therefore, we do not make a necessity or a matter of holiness out of it—as the priests <note>original: "Pfaffen" — a derogatory term used by Reformers for the Catholic clergy</note> have done without God's command in their consecrations with their foul oil—but because it is customary and has a divine and noble meaning, which matters greatly to all these lands, we anoint our King and Queen in the name of God with balsam or precious waters. I say this against the factious spirits <term>Rottengeister: a term used by Lutherans to describe radical reformers or Anabaptists whom they viewed as socially or theologically disorderly</term> who consider such freedom a sin, so that we may give account of what right and fitness we have before God to do such a thing.

But the meaning of such anointing concerns all authorities, of both high and low status, just as everything else that will be dealt with here regarding the regalia <note>The physical symbols of sovereignty, such as the crown, scepter, and orb.</note>. This is so that every authority should have painted before their eyes and depicted <note>original: "abconterfeyen"</note> a royal image with all the regalia—just as our King is honored here—and receive their command before the face of God and His dear angels (of which there is no doubt). From this, they would always be reminded of what they are before God and what their office is. But when I speak of oil, you must not think of our stinking fasting-oil <note>Common vegetable oil used during Lenten fasts, which the author contrasts with high-quality ritual oils.</note>; in those lands <note>The biblical Middle East.</note>, there is fragrant and precious oil; besides that, precious water is sometimes called "anointing" in the Scriptures, as we read in the Gospel.

The precious anointing of which we speak cannot mean severity, for it strengthens the limbs, soothes, smells sweet, and makes a joyful countenance, as was the custom in Syria, though it is unusual among us. Of this Christ says in the sixth chapter of Matthew <note>the source says "seventh chapter," but the quote is from Matthew 6:17</note>: "When you fast, anoint your head and wash your face, so that you do not appear sad, but cheerful." And if one may bring a comparison here from the eternal kingdom of Christ: it is written in the twenty-first Psalm <note>likely Psalm 45:7 in modern numbering</note> that God anointed him—that is, made him King—with the oil of joy, which is the Holy Spirit, not

...not that he alone should be joyful because of it, but also all Christians, and the entire Kingdom of Christ.

### What the anointing of the arm signifies.

Thus, the anointing of the arm signifies here the chosen King and Queens—and truly also all authorities, however humble they may be—that everyone among the subjects hopes and expects of them that they shall be the subjects' fathers and mothers; not tyrants, not defiant and raging, but mild, gracious, comforting, and helpful. Just as they are titled "Most Gracious and Gracious Lords and Ladies," they should joyfully, in good peace and governance <term>Regiment: the system of rule or government</term>, care for their people as if for their own children. The subjects may rejoice in this, thank God, and seek refuge with them in their times of need. The arm represents the government, but specifically a government of grace and joy, in which the Kings and Queens desire to be fathers and mothers. This is the true, mild "Oil of Joy."

### What the anointing on the shoulders signifies.

Isaiah <note>Referencing Isaiah 9:6</note> prophesies that the dominion of Christ shall be "upon his shoulders"; surely no king or LORD will ever match Him in that. For who can carry a dominion—that is, land and people—upon his shoulders? But He carries the lost sheep—that is, the whole of Christendom—on His shoulders, as it is written in the Gospel. Nevertheless, a King and Queen, and indeed every authority, must "carry" the people in their worldly government, each according to his measure. In times of famine and other common hardships, they must seek counsel for the people and always have *patience* <note>original Latin: "patientiam"</note>—that is, endurance—when things do not always go smoothly, provided that no outrage or wantonness is at hand. God has commanded the princes to rule and to improve the lands. Whatever can be improved through grace requires no severity. It is also not good to be quickly defiant and to draw the sword when our enemies speak ill of us, or are otherwise wicked, or for the sake of some old, forgotten title; for God has brought about many such changes in kingdoms and principalities. Those lords who have not practiced such *patience* or endurance have often lost land and people because of it. It is said: "he who has a broad back and strong shoulders can carry well." And of lords, it is wisely said: *He who knows not how to look the other way, knows not how to rule* <note>original Latin: "Qui nescit dissimulare, nescit regnare"</note>. He who cannot endure or "look through his fingers" <note>A German idiom meaning to turn a blind eye or be indulgent toward minor faults</note> cannot govern. And indeed, Your Grace <note>original: "E. G." (Eure Gnaden)</note> has faced resistance in these lands with war; that must from now on never be remembered against those who have submitted themselves in obedience to Your Grace. Furthermore, such a "government of grace" demands much effort, labor, care, and danger—all of which a regent must take upon his neck, so that the peasants...

...and the common man/ you may drink your mugs of beer with joy. Such a governance of grace <term>Gnadenregiment: a style of ruling defined by mercy and divine favor rather than mere force</term>, patience, and care, is the anointing of the arm and the shoulders, which Your Graces shall never forget. Christ, the spiritual and eternal King, reigns among us with pure grace; the sign of which—that is, the Cross—is brushed upon Your Graces’ arm and shoulders with the balsam. Thus does a father also; he does not like to use the rod, but is happy to be joyful with his children and provides for them. Thus God also depicts for us a portrait of grace of the King in Daniel <note>Referencing the vision in Daniel 4:10–12</note>, where a king is compared to a beautiful tree that nourishes all animals and lets them rest under its shadow; for God gives and maintains—through the authorities—rest and peace, protection and shield, nourishment and goods, and the whole of temporal life. In this God has a great pleasure. The subjects shall enjoy the benefit of their lords; but greed or avarice, and tyranny, have cost many lords their inheritance and fiefs. Conversely, Solomon says: "Benevolence and truth preserve a king, and through grace his throne is made firm" <note>Proverbs 20:28</note>. We do not speak so much of the governance of grace of the King and Queens, or the authorities, in vain; for all these lands wait for it and desire such, as the crown also signifies, as we shall hear. And this is called the Day of Coronation, and not the Day of Swording <note>original: "Schwerttung" — the ceremonial bestowing of the sword</note>, even though the sword is also given here, to signify that everyone is to hope for a blessed, peaceful, and gracious government from their King and Queen. Amen.

# The First Part
<meta>catchword: us</meta>

One of the priests stood before the altar, turned toward the people, and read the Epistle for the season in German. Afterward, the cantors sang a short piece to accompany it. Then, the King was led forward by two Councilors of the Realm. The Ordinator <note>The presiding official or bishop; in this instance, the reformer Johannes Bugenhagen.</note> stood up, took the sword from the altar, and while the King knelt, the Ordinator placed the naked <note>An unsheathed sword, symbolizing readiness and the raw power of justice.</note> sword into his right hand. And while one of the other preachers held the scabbard, the Ordinator spoke to the King as follows: "High-born Prince and Lord, may Your Grace take the sword, which I give to you by command in the name of God; you should not doubt that you and all legitimate authorities receive the sword from God's hand. As Paul says, as was read previously: 'There is no power but of God.' The power that exists everywhere is ordained by God, so that whoever resists the power resists the ordinance of God. Those who resist shall receive judgment upon themselves. Therefore, just as Gideon cried out with his army against the enemies, 'The sword of the LORD and of Gideon!' <note>A reference to Judges 7:20</note>, Your Grace may certainly also cry out against enemies in battle: 'Here is God's sword and the King of Denmark's!' May God protect us from war and discord. And even if the words do not match exactly—for Gideon had a special command from God to act in a wondrous and singular way—the intent and courage should still be there: that the sword is God's sword. By the sword is understood not only <term>high justice</term> <note>original: "Halßgerichte", referring to jurisdiction over capital crimes involving life and limb.</note> but also the proper measure to punish in all variety of ways. Therefore, whoever is punished, whether severely or lightly, according to their merit for their misdeeds, should certainly consider that God Himself punishes them with His judgment. For judgment belongs to God; let the authorities see to it that they wield it rightly."

At this point, the King gave the sword to the Marshal, who took the scabbard from the preacher, placed the sword inside it, and kept it with him. The Ordinator, however, continued to say the following words: "It is truly a fine ceremony <note>original: "Ceremonia"</note> that one first soothes and anoints the King's arm before placing the sword in his fist. Firstly, one also anoints the shoulders before directing him to his armor, so that the power does not turn into a tyrant, and so that the anointed arm might pull back when the fist with the sword—that is, with severity—wishes to go too far. Thus, an authority, like King David, can sing of a good governance <note>original: "Regiment"</note> in thanks to God, saying: 'Of mercy and justice will I sing, and praise you, Lord.' <note>Psalm 101:1</note>"

Here, however, a Christian Prince should know—though he should have the courage and heart to know that God is with him when he uses the sword, spear, and lance rightly as King David did—that he should not rely on such power. Instead, he should humbly pray to God to grant success and to help toward a good governance. Thus he can also say with David: "God, You are my King, You who promised help to Jacob; through You we will push down our enemies; in Your name we will trample those who rise against us. For I do not trust in my bow, and my sword cannot help me; but You help us from our enemies and put to shame those who..."

Here the King swung the received sword toward the people, to the side, so that it gleamed—yet quite decently—in four directions, and put it back into the scabbard.

And the Ordinator said: "You all see that our chosen King has shown the back side of the sword all around, meaning that he wishes to mercifully protect all lands and subjects. He has also grasped it so that he can turn it for a strike, meaning he will also punish the wicked and disobedient. All these lands should rejoice in this, for no one has anything to fear except those who act with wicked violence. For Paul says again: 'Rulers are not a terror to good works, but to the evil' <note>Romans 13:3</note>. If you do not want to fear the power, do good, and you shall have praise from the same; for she is God’s minister <note>original: "Gottes Dienerin"</note> to you for good. But if you do evil, be afraid, for she does not bear the sword in vain; she is God’s minister, a revenger to execute punishment upon him who does evil. Oh, that I could persuade all supreme heads <note>The rulers or monarchs.</note> so that they would clearly mark what it means that Paul so often calls the authorities God’s minister!"

Here the King knelt again upon the earth to receive the crown. The Ordinator took the crown, sat down, and addressed the Councilors of the Realm <note>The *ReichsRähte*, the high-ranking nobility who advised the King.</note> in the following manner: "Noble, Valiant, and Honorable Councilors of the Realm, you have requested of me to crown the King in the name of God. But now that it has come to the crowning, I admonish you all to reach out and touch the crown and help crown our King. And he who cannot reach the crown because he stands far off, let him nevertheless extend his arm toward the crown. For such honor belongs to you, and it is of great importance to you, as you shall hear hereafter."

After this, the Ordinator stood up and, alongside the Councilors of the Realm, placed the crown upon the King. Saying: "Most Gracious King, receive from us the crown of the realm, in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. May the merciful God give you grace. As the crown signifies that Your Majesty should hold to all subjects as previously mentioned, and in turn, the citizenry and all subjects should hold to Your Majesty with love and obedience—so do Head and Crown fit well together before God and the world, through Jesus Christ, His dear Son, our Lord. Everyone say: Amen."

Afterward, the Ordinator said to the Councilors of the Realm: "Step back on both sides, so that people can see and hear." Immediately, the Ordinator...

For women are overcome by friendship and can achieve much through pleading, admonishing, weeping, and other means of interceding, and at times they might take the sword out of their lord's hand. If it is a matter for which one may intercede, let that happen, and it may well belong to the Rule of Grace; even if something has been transgressed, let Your Grace show such mercy, not only to noble and great lords but also to poor people, for there is much frailty among the poor. But if it is not such a matter, and the sharp law must proceed against mischief and insolence, then Your Grace should think: "The sword is not commanded to me, but to my dear Lord King; I let happen what is right; God give me grace for that which is commanded to me."

# The First Part

In this manner: what else should the King’s and Queen’s crown be, but the people together with the rulers? If this is true, then see, you Imperial Councillors, how rightly you have the honor today of having crowned your King and Queen before God, and His holy angels, and this world itself; I will make this even clearer. Paul says to those whom he brought to God through the Gospel, as to the Philippians in the 4th chapter: "My beloved and longed-for brothers, my joy and my crown, stand firm thus in the Lord." <note>Philippians 4:1</note> And to the Thessalonians in the 2nd: "Who is our hope, or joy, or crown of rejoicing? Is it not even you before the Lord Jesus Christ at His coming? For you are indeed our glory and joy." <note>1 Thessalonians 2:19-20</note> It was said before that for the true Evangelical <term>Evangelical: here referring to the Protestant tradition centered on the "Gospel" (Evangelium) rather than Catholic tradition</term> bishops and priests, the scepter or bishop’s staff is the beloved Gospel, with which the eternal King Christ rules in His church or Christendom.

Now hear that they also have a glorious bishop’s crown, which shall shine on the Last Day at Christ’s coming; though it may have no prestige before the mad world, their crown is the people whom they bring to the kingdom of Christ through the Gospel. The Pope’s bishops despise such a staff and crown and occupy themselves with foolish antics and blasphemy; of that we will say no more now. Now, if Saint Paul’s crown is his people whom he brought to Christ, what else is the King’s and Queen’s crown in worldly government but their subjects? Solomon says: *In the multitude of people is the king's honor.* <note>original: "In multitudine populi dignitas Regis." Proverbs 14:28</note> If a King has many people, that is the King’s honor; thus the head that you have crowned is the King and the Queen, but the crown is the land and the people. When the crown fits the head well, things go well—that is, when the authorities and their lands hold together well, then there is peace among the people, and they help each other toward their livelihoods, just as the crown closes and holds itself together in all its parts; then it is also purely God’s way, just as the crown is golden, with obedience, proper discipline, and all prosperity. Flies and dust may land upon the crown; that does not harm the crown, for it is easily mended. Likewise, a kingdom cannot be without frailties; these must be mended, and at times one should not proceed with severity. If a piece breaks off but can be patched or soldered back on, well and good. But if it falls from the crown into the filth, it is lost or trampled underfoot and never returns to its former honor in the King’s crown. Thus, if some become disobedient and willful, and it can be mended, well and good; if not, the whole crown must not be broken because of it. For God upholds the authorities, but those rebels lose their necks or fall into other dangers for which their children’s children must pay, and they must moreover have a guilty conscience, knowing they have well deserved it. Solomon thus admonishes: "My dear child, fear God and the King, and have nothing to do with the rebellious, for their destruction comes before they can even look around." <note>Proverbs 24:21-22</note>

One more thing, my dear lords, I had almost forgotten, and it is the best part of the crown, but no goldsmith thinks of it and the world does not regard it: that is, the crown is open at the top, toward Heaven, so that over King, Queen, lands, and noblemen, God alone from Heaven shall rule. Therefore, keep GOD before your eyes, hear and learn His Word, and He will also bless you with peace and prosperity in this earthly kingdom. # Of the Book for Rulers.

schools, so that God in Christ may be praised through them, also among our descendants, and that they may thus rule and lead the nations with constant peace and good **government**, to the honor of Almighty God, Amen.

Secondly, because human hearts sometimes interpret these matters differently, and the <term>Anabaptists: a radical Reformation group that often rejected civil oaths and state authority</term> and other erroneous spirits indiscriminately make a sin of them—and it is no wonder, for they also despise authority and power, though it is from God—therefore the elected King and Queen should know, through instruction in the truth, that such honorable splendor and royal ceremonies are not in themselves, or of themselves, sin or against God. This is for the sake of these kingdoms or peoples, who all wish and desire to see that their King and Queen are confirmed and conformed in the Church, with the presentation of the <term>regalia: the physical symbols of royalty, such as the crown, scepter, and orb</term>, as if from God, through a minister of God, with divine power and command; for such power is undoubtedly from God and is God's ordinance. 

Additionally, they should know that these royal ceremonies are not merely a proper display of splendor but also have a divine meaning from God's Word, for a good and blessed reign, as was heard publicly during the coronation. Yet they should pray to God through Christ that they may remain in the fear and trust of God, and that their hearts do not rely on such power and honor; nonetheless, they should be joyful and accept with thanksgiving such peace and honor as great and high gifts of God. 

Most of all, however, they should pray to God after this time of coronation that the lords and princes, and all the people, may also be joyful before God with thanksgiving during this time, so that nothing happens that is an abomination to God and for which we would later have to repent, but rather that we may say afterward: "Praise be to God that everything proceeded honorably and joyfully." Thus did holy **Job** (Chapter 1) offer sacrifice and pray for his sons and daughters when they invited one another to feast, so that nothing wrongful might occur or be counted as sin against them.

Thirdly, one should not only provide for the poor during the coronation while the splendor lasts—so that the poor **Lazarus** does not hunger before the door of the rich glutton <note>A reference to the biblical parable of the rich man and the beggar Lazarus</note>—but also have a holy and godly mind and purpose in the heart to help poor people, to protect them, and to establish old and new hospitals. May other lords and subjects of high and low estate take a good example from such a Christian deed, so that they also learn to do such good works.

But above all, every elected King and Queen should take care and prevent that there never comes upon them that great offense and sin with which entire kingdoms and principalities are burdened (as much as lies within them): that they allow the preachers of the **Gospel** and the school servants to leave their office because of poverty, whereby the people thereafter become "Turks" <note>In the 16th century, "becoming a Turk" was a common metaphor for losing one's Christian faith or falling into "barbarism" and unbelief</note>, and God pours out upon us blindness, hardening of hearts, and His wrath, to the ruin of body and soul. May God's fathomless mercy graciously prevent this, Amen. Instead, they should much rather, with good ordinances and honorable provisions (since a worker is worthy of his hire) provide good teachers and the holy Gospel to maintain our salvation, not only for themselves and for

not only for those living now, but also for posterity. Such a divine and Christian deed is truly to be wished and desired for Christian princes and lords, for these are joyful and happy deeds. I will remain silent on whether they should be considered burdensome, as human madness suggests, for these matters are provided for in good, quiet peace, to the honor of God and for the good of one’s neighbor.

Christ will also acknowledge on the Last Day that such acts are the true <term>Sacrificia: sacrifices</term> and offerings made to Him through humanity. And He comforts us with His promise in the Gospel that He will return it a hundredfold, even in this life—namely, through mercy, justice, wisdom, foresight, peace, obedience, good government, good counsel, friendship, sufficient goods, etc. Just as He gave to Solomon when he prayed, and he had enough and more than enough, as long as he feared God and stayed with His Word. However, those who do not wish to perform such minor expenditures in peace with joy and a good conscience should know that they or their heirs will have nothing to enjoy or improve from it; rather, the devil will snatch it away through his own and put it elsewhere. And they must, through God's judgment, afterward spend everything they have—and more than they have—on war and other displeasure and damage with fear and trembling and all kinds of danger. Then God says in their conscience: "Take this for that," etc. <note>original: "Habe diß für das," a proverbial way of saying "this is your reward for that behavior."</note>

It is truly a great grace of God when princes and lords fear God and allow themselves to be persuaded to such good deeds; for God Himself provides for and protects the principality and government of those dear ones, as Solomon often promises in these proverbs.

At this point, it would be appropriate to set down at length the election, coronation, anointing, oath, and papal confirmation of a King of the Romans. But because the <term>Golden Bull: the foundational 1356 law governing how the Holy Roman Emperor was chosen</term> is available, and mention is also made of it in the Canon Law, primarily in the chapter *Venerabilem* regarding elections <note>original: "C. Venerabilem, de electione," a reference to a specific papal decree in the Corpus Iuris Canonici</note>, I will not write about it at length, nor would it be proper for me to do so. I will only briefly run through the process: how a King of the Romans is first elected and proclaimed at Frankfurt by the Prince-Electors; subsequently, how he must swear an oath to the Prince-Electors; and how it proceeds with the coronation and the <term>regalia: the physical symbols of royalty, such as the crown, scepter, and orb</term>. ## The Oath follows, which the Imperial Majesty must swear to the Prince-Electors.

I PROFESS and promise before God and His Angels, henceforth and from this time forward, to preserve the law, justice, and peace of God's holy Church; to be of service to the people subject to me, and to perform justice, and to preserve the rights of the Kingdom, saving a worthy respect for divine mercy. <note>original Latin: "PROFITEOR & promitto coram Deo... legem & iustitiam, pacemq; sanctæ Dei Ecclesiæ seruare." Those things also which have been granted and bestowed by Emperors and Kings to the Churches or to men of the cloth, I shall preserve for them inviolably and cause to be preserved. To the Abbots and orders of <term>vassals: those who held land or titles in exchange for loyalty</term> of the kingdom, I wish to bear and exhibit honor. Our Lord Jesus Christ granting me aid, strength, and glory.

# The First Part

Following this, the Emperor traveled to Rome with the intention of speaking with the Pope regarding Church matters. He kept his army close at hand, in case the Pope should attempt anything. He then held a friendly conversation and discussion with the Pope, recounting what had been reliably reported to him, both in writing and in person, by prominent individuals; he exhorted him kindly, with a request to desist from such actions, etc.

But when the Emperor noticed that such friendly reminders would bear no fruit with the Pope, but rather that he intended to persist in his pride and arrogance, he also became indignant and told the Pope to his face that if he would not conduct himself differently in the matter, he would consider ways so that the Church should not be left abandoned. He then arranged that a Council <note>original: "Concilium." A formal assembly of Church leaders to decide on doctrine or discipline.</note> be organized on a designated day and primarily ordered the bishops whom he knew to be pious and righteous to attend.

However, when the day of the Council arrived, the Pope made himself scarce and, undoubtedly due to his evil life and conscience, did not wish to await the proceedings; instead, he withdrew to Campania, into the Hernici Mountains. Although he was publicly summoned and called before the Council three times, he nevertheless remained disobediently absent and showed contempt for the Council.

Because of this, the Emperor was moved to let the Council be informed of the grievances he had against the Pope—what he himself had experienced and what he had understood from others regarding the Pope's evil, un-Christian life and conduct. He then brought the matter to the point where, by the approval and decree of a General Council, Leo VIII was elected and proclaimed Pope in place of Octavian <note>Pope John XII, born Octavianus, was deposed by Emperor Otto I in 963 AD on charges of various crimes.</note>.

After the Emperor had, through this means, put a stop to the Pope's devilish and un-Christian conduct, he resolved to remedy the other grievances of the Church, particularly since the Popes, through their greed, had wrongfully seized much and, furthermore, falsely claimed that Emperor Constantine had given the Western Empire <note>original: "Occidentisch Reich." Referring to the Western Roman Empire or the territories of the Holy Roman Empire.</note>, or the Imperial dignity, to Pope Sylvester as a gift. Emperor Otto would not concede this, but rather wanted such a Donation <note>original: "Donation Constantini."
