Humanist scholars of the 15th century proved it was a fake.</note> to be annulled and abolished again, since it was in itself false, null, and void. Therefore, such possession should be restored and returned to the Empire, from which it had been unfairly withdrawn, as it was in no way fitting for him to allow the Popes to withdraw the Western Empire from secular authority in such a fictional manner.

Thereupon, he held a stately negotiation with the new Pope, who then admitted that the Popes had little right to this. Therefore, with the unanimous consent of the Cardinals, he placed the power over such Donation of Constantine into the Emperor's authority. He also gave him a letter and seal [affirming] that the Western Empire belongs and shall remain with the Emperor and his descendants, and not with the Pope.

Fourthly, when a Roman Emperor is elected, he may receive consecration from the Pope, or from another bishop if the Pope should refuse to perform it. Since this consecration is a newly invented ritual <note>original: "newer dichtet werck." A forged Roman imperial decree by which the 4th-century emperor Constantine the Great supposedly transferred authority over Rome and the Western Roman Empire to the Pope. Likewise, when the Council of Basel was held, Nicholas of Cusa—a Cardinal of the title St. Peter in Chains <note>original: "tit. S. Petri ad vincula." Referring to his titular church in Rome.</note>—sent his written opinion in Book 3, Chapter 2, stating among other things: "One thing I cannot pass over in silence, as almost everyone believes that Emperor Constantine gave the Western Empire to Pope Sylvester and his successors forever. Although I have researched this matter with the greatest diligence—even setting aside the question of whether Constantine actually had the power to make such a gift (a question which has not been resolved and will likely remain so)—I find it highly questionable."

"It is most astonishing to me that if this were truly the case, as is claimed, one finds absolutely nothing about it in the noted writings and histories. I, for my part, have read through all the records of the Emperors and Popes ever written with special care. I have also read the writings of Saint Jerome—who recorded everything with great diligence—Saint Augustine, Ambrose, and other excellent learned men, as well as the proceedings and histories of the holy Councils as far as they occurred after the Council of Nicaea <note>The first ecumenical council of the Christian Church in 325 AD.</note>; yet I can find nothing that compares or aligns with what is contained in this supposed Donation. Pope Damasus, at the urging of Saint Jerome, compiled the histories of his predecessors; however, even in those, nothing is found regarding Pope Sylvester that supports the common talk of this Donation. It is true that one reads in the histories how Emperor Constantine was baptized by Sylvester, and that the Emperor magnificently adorned several churches in Rome and endowed them with great income—which is recorded here and there in the Papal books. To write at length about these things, since it has been done more than enough before now, I consider unnecessary; nor is it my intent or desire to burden myself with it. Nevertheless, it is true that the Pope, following the saying of Peter, **“Lord, here are two swords,”** <note>original: "HERR, da sind zwey Schwert." For this reason, one of his bishops once interpreted the saying of Christ—where He says, **“When I am lifted up, I will draw all things to myself”** <note>John 12:32.</note>—to mean that the Pope shall take both spiritual and worldly power for himself.

It is also to be known here that various peoples have held many different and strange customs and considerations regarding the election of kings. In **Meroe** <note>An ancient city-state on the east bank of the Nile in modern-day Sudan.</note>, no one was admitted to this reign or rank unless he surpassed all others in strength. The same custom also existed among the **Sydri**. Whoever wished to become king among the **Gordians** <note>original: "Gordijs." In **Cathea** in India, kings are chosen according to their beauty. Thus, the more beautiful and well-formed one is in body and stature, the more easily he is accepted as king in that place. And it is written that among all the soldiers that **Xerxes** <note>The Persian King Xerxes I (the Great), who invaded Greece in 480 BCE.</note> led into Greece—which, according to the histories, is said to have been as many as ten times one hundred thousand <note>One million soldiers.</note>—there was not one who surpassed him in stature, size, and beauty. This is indeed a wondrous thing to hear.

### The First Chapter.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial letter 'A' with intricate floral and scrollwork flourishes.</image-desc>
In order that I do not forget God in this matter, nor set Him aside, but rather hold Him as the Founder, Lord, Patron, Protector, Sustainer, and supreme Overlord <term>Lehenherrn — a feudal lord who grants land or authority to others</term> of all authority and governance—just as even the poets and heathens held such a view, as Homer writes:
> ->There is one King to whom Jupiter gave the Scepter and the venerable laws.<-
<note>original Latin: "Rex vnus cui Sceptra dedit, venerandaq; iura Iupiter."</note>

So I will here recount a clear and noteworthy history from the Holy Scriptures, which teaches and shows us that kings, princes, potentates, and great lords do not come to power by mere chance or "by a sudden plunge" <note>original: "plumps halben." An idiomatic expression meaning something happening abruptly or without cause, like falling into water.</note> (as the saying goes), nor do they remain in power or are sustained by their own strength and might; rather, it comes from God, who distributes kingdoms according to His pleasure. For thus writes the prophet Daniel in the 4th chapter, that King Nebuchadnezzar had such a dream, in which it seemed to him there stood a tree in the middle of the land, which was very tall, large, and thick, and reached with such height unto heaven, and spread itself out to the ends of the entire land. Its branches were beautiful and bore much fruit, from which everyone had enough to eat; all the animals on earth found shade under it, and the birds under heaven sat upon its branches, and all flesh was nourished by it.

But as he looked upon it, it seemed to him that a Watcher <note>original: "Wächter." In the Book of Daniel, this refers to a celestial being or angel sent as a divine messenger.</note> called down from heaven and said: "Chop down the tree, and lop off its branches, strip off its leaves, and scatter its fruit, so that the animals lying under it run away, and the birds fly from its twigs. Yet let the stump with its roots remain in the earth, but let it be bound in iron chains and bands, and walk in the grass of the field; it shall lie under the dew of heaven and become wet, and shall graze with the animals on the herbs of the earth. And let the human heart be taken from him, and a beast-like heart be given to him, until seven times have passed over him. This is decided in the council of the Watchers and deliberated in the conversation of the holy ones, so that the living may recognize that the Highest [has] power..."

"I, King Nebuchadnezzar, have seen such a dream," he said. "But you, Belteshazzar," <note>original: "Belsazer." In the Book of Daniel, the prophet is given the Babylonian name Belteshazzar, not to be confused with the later King Belshazzar.</note> he said to Daniel, "tell what it means; for all the wise men in my kingdom cannot show me what it means."

Then Daniel, who is otherwise called Belteshazzar, was astonished for nearly an hour, and his thoughts troubled him. But the King spoke: "Do not let the dream and its interpretation trouble you." Belteshazzar began and said: "Ah, my lord King, may this dream apply to your enemies, and its interpretation to your adversaries. The tree that you saw, which was so great and thick, reaching with its height unto heaven and spreading over the whole land, whose branches were beautiful and whose fruit was plenty, from which everyone had to eat, under which the beasts of the field dwelt, and upon whose branches the birds of the air sat—that is you, O King, who are so great and mighty; for your power is great and reaches unto heaven, and your authority extends to the ends of the world."

"But that the King saw a holy watcher <note>original: "heiligen Wächter." This refers to an angelic being or 'messenger' from the divine realm.</note> come down from heaven and say, 'Hew down the tree and destroy it, yet leave a stump with its roots in the earth; let it be bound in chains of iron and bronze in the field, in the grass, and lie under the dew of heaven and become wet, and graze with the beasts of the field until seven times <note>historically interpreted as seven years</note> have passed over him'—this is the interpretation, my lord King. And such a decree of the Most High concerns my lord the King: you shall be driven away from people and must stay with the beasts of the field, and you shall be made to eat grass like oxen, and you shall lie under the dew of heaven and become wet, until seven times have passed over you, so that you may recognize that the Most High has power over the kingdoms of men and gives them to whom He will."

"But as it was said that the stump with the roots of the tree should nonetheless be left, it means that the kingdom shall remain yours once you have recognized the power in heaven. Therefore, my lord King, let my counsel please you: break free from your sins through righteousness, and be rid of your misdeeds through kindness to the poor, so that He may have patience with your sins."

All this befell King Nebuchadnezzar. For after twelve months, as the King was walking upon his royal palace in Babylon, he began and spoke: "Is this not the great Babylon that I have built as a royal house through my great power, to the honor of my glory?" Before the King had finished speaking these words, a voice fell from heaven: "To you, King Nebuchadnezzar, it is said: your kingdom shall be taken from you, and you shall be driven from people, and shall stay with the beasts that go upon the field; you shall be made to eat grass like oxen until seven times have passed over you, so that you may recognize that the Most High has power over the kingdoms of men and gives them to whom He will." Since God Himself portrays it so and is so well pleased by it, praising and adorning it so highly, a Lord and Regent should indeed carry out and fulfill his office with joy and love, faithfully attending to his calling. He should not consider whether it costs trouble and labor; likewise, we should not focus on how evil the tyrants are, but rather on what a magnificent and precious office they hold from God, established for the good and salvation of us all.

Alongside this, it is also to be considered how poor and wretched we are on account of our evil and distorted nature, such that we cast God’s stern judgment to the wind. Even though we are often and frequently reminded and warned through the prophets and servants of the Divine Word, it is all in vain. Thus, this King also goes his way, forgetting not only the dream and its interpretation, but also becoming boastful, exalting himself in his power and wealth as if he had obtained it all by himself. Yet he rightly should have thanked God for such great and noble gifts; it would be no wonder if this King had thought of such a dream every moment for his entire life and lived in constant concern as to when what Daniel had told him would come to pass. Consequently, he should have converted and done penance, just as the King of Nineveh did—as Jonah writes in the 3rd chapter—who rose from his royal throne, laid aside his purple robe, wrapped himself in sackcloth, and sat in the ashes, etc. But it was in vain; he despised it and wished to experience the cruel judgment, just as happens now, when we are warned so many times with signs, sermons, and writings, but nonetheless do not wish to do penance, but rather despise everything until one day God's terrible wrath comes upon us unexpectedly, and we must then experience the warning through the event itself.

Finally, special attention must be given to the little word that stands at the end in the Prophet (**Those who are proud, He is able to humble**). For the great lords are to learn from this that they also have a Lord and Judge who can discipline them; and when they forget their calling and begin to be proud and haughty and to oppress their subjects, He can reach into the dice bag <note>original: "in die Würffel greiffen." An idiom suggesting that God can intervene in the "luck" or fate of a ruler as easily as one reaches for dice.</note>. And though they think they sit most securely, He can humble them in wondrous ways and cast them down. It is truly terrible and pitiable when such a great King or Lord must fall so deep and sit down so harshly—just as Fortune <note>original: "Glück." Often personified as Lady Luck or Fortuna in early modern texts.</note> is accustomed to exalting some so high so that they must thereafter fall all the harder. *For as that man says, fortune exalts many to the heights so that they may fall with a heavier ruin.* <note>original Latin: "Multos enim, vt ille ait, fortuna extollit in altum, vt lapsu grauiore ruant." This is a famous line from the Roman poet Claudian.</note> That is: Fortune exalts many so high so that they must thereafter fall all the more heavily. And such a Lord must then not only bear God's wrath upon him—which is already far too heavy—but also be a laughingstock to the world, suffering poverty and misery, so that it might have been more tolerable for him if he had been a poor shepherd or a peasant than that he should suffer such a swift judgment and be disciplined in such a manner. Therefore, it is said that one should fear God and not boast too much, lest one come who can humble you, as happened to Nebuchadnezzar above, and as he himself afterwards confessed: that no injustice was done to him, but that he had deserved it with his pride.

# The Second Part

However, so that I do not entirely leave out the histories and examples, as I promised, I believe it is plain as day how God has made true in thousands of cases—and still carries out daily in His work—this sentence: **"He is able to humble those who walk in pride."** <note>This is a reference to Daniel 4:37, the central theme of the preceding commentary on Nebuchadnezzar.</note> For a brief indication, I will mention only a few histories here one after another. Did God not thoroughly humble the pride of Emperor Valerian? This man persecuted the poor Christians who, for a time, had been increasing everywhere in godly fear and piety. He began to tyrannize the Christians and pursue them with cruel fury, sparing not even small children. He was misled by his own doctor—whom Eusebius <note>Eusebius of Caesarea was a 4th-century historian often called the "Father of Church History."</note> calls the **worst teacher and prince of the Egyptian sorcerers** <note>original Latin: "pessimum Magistrum, & Principem Ægyptiorum Magorum"</note>. Valerian believed that through such atrocities he would make the Roman Empire more stable and long-lasting.

But while this magnificent enemy of Christ was still wet and damp with the innocent blood of the poor Christians whom he had martyred and killed in various ways, God sent another tyrant upon his neck, who was just as wicked as he: namely, Shapur <note>original: "Saporem"; Shapur I was the second Shahanshah of the Sasanian Empire.</note>, the King of the Persians. He invaded Mesopotamia with the strength of an army and took the entire land. He also made war upon and won the provinces of Syria, Lycia, and Cappadocia, cruelly destroying everything where he went with fire and weapons of war. Emperor Valerian set out to help these lands and, in the first attack, drove back and defeated the Persians. He reached Mesopotamia, where King Shapur himself came to meet him. When both sides attacked each other earnestly and bravely, the Romans were ultimately put to flight by the sheer number of the barbarian soldiers. Sabellicus <note>Marcantonio Sabellico (1436–1506) was a Renaissance historian.</note> writes that he believes God punished the Emperor's tyranny, which he had used against the Christians, in this way. Therefore, Valerian was captured alive after the battle and such a heavy defeat. The historian Trebellius <note>Trebellius Pollio, one of the purported authors of the "Historia Augusta," a collection of Roman imperial biographies.</note> suggests that one of his captains, whom he trusted, had thus misled and betrayed him. After such a victory, Shapur returned to Persia, leading the captive Emperor with him to the eternal mockery of the Roman name. He not only kept him in iron chains but also had his eyes gouged out. So that he would not rot away in such a wretched prison, he additionally had to serve as Shapur's footstool; whenever the King wished to sit upon his horse, he stepped upon the Emperor's back. And when he was perhaps no longer fit for this due to old age—for he lived for 70 years—Shapur had the skin pulled over his ears from his head down to his feet and thus, as Agathias <note>Agathias was a 6th-century Greek poet and historian.</note> writes, had him pitifully flayed. I do not know what Crinitus <note>Pietro Crinito (1475–1507), a scholar and disciple of Poliziano.</note> was thinking when he attributed this history as having happened to Emperor Aurelian.

We have similar examples from the Turkish Emperor Bayezid <note>original: "Basaite" or "Baiazite"; referring to Bayezid I, who was famously captured by Tamerlane.</note>. What a great enemy and persecutor of Christians he was is as plain as day, so that many words need not be made of it. Among other things, he besieged Constantinople for eight years and had to withdraw only because of other wars. But when he had finished those, he besieged it again for two years and would have conquered and won it if God

## for Wisdom.

### The Second Chapter.

Since I have stated above that all **government** <note>original: "Regiment"; here meaning the authority or system of rule.</note> comes from God, and He gives it to whom He wills, it will also be necessary to remind the regents and great lords that at the start of their reign—and also daily—they should diligently pray to God and call upon Him from the heart to give them understanding and wisdom to rule their subjects rightly and in a Christian manner. As **St. James** teaches in his epistle: *If any of you* (he says) *lacks wisdom, let him ask of God, who gives to all men simply and reproaches no one; and it shall be given him. But let him ask in faith, and doubt not. For he who doubts is like the waves of the sea, driven and tossed by the wind. Neither let such a man think that he shall receive anything of the LORD; a doubter is unstable in all his ways.* <note>A paraphrase of James 1:5–8.</note>

Although we all together—each in his own calling, deed, and undertaking—need wisdom and understanding for the **governance of our household** <note>original: "Regierung seiner Haußhaltung"; refers to the early modern concept of the 'Oikos' or household as a micro-state.</note>, wife, and children, and therefore should rightly call upon and pray to God daily and every hour to give us understanding and wisdom so that we act rightly in all our deeds and being, presiding over our domestic servants, wife, and children in the fear of God, etc. Yet, it is primarily the regents, princes, kings, emperors, and other great lords who need it; and the more land and people one has to rule, the more diligently and frequently he should call upon <note>catchword: "anruffen" (to call upon)</note> God for wisdom and understanding.

### The Third Chapter.

THE excellent and wise man **Plato** writes that those kingdoms, lands, and cities are in the best condition and are to be considered blessed which are governed by wise people, or whose regents, princes, and lords strive after art and wisdom. This sentiment the Emperor **Marcus Antoninus the Philosopher**—as **Capitolinus** <note>One of the supposed authors of the "Augustan History."</note> writes—constantly had in his mouth. Likewise, **Prudentius** <note>A Roman Christian poet.</note> artfully set it into three verses, where he says:

> Truly, as a most learned man once beautifully said:
> the state would be fortunate enough if
> either kings were wise, or if the wise were kings.

In addition to this, many kings in **Samaria** were also cruelly murdered for this reason.

...such are the thoughts of the heart, which no one can know but God himself.

But I testify before the face of God, and will testify at the **Last Judgment** <note>The final and eternal judgment by God of every nation.</note> when God demands an account from me and all people of how we spent our lives here on earth in thoughts, words, and deeds: that in this I seek nothing other than the honor of His Almightiness, and how I might be accepted as a child and heir of eternal life. May **His Imperial Majesty** <term>Key. May.</term> <note>Abbreviation for *Kaiserliche Majestät*, referring to Emperor Charles V.</note> not doubt this, and graciously bear with my entangled and imprisoned conscience, as well as the fact that I regard God's unbearable wrath and displeasure so highly.

As far as external matters are concerned, I have always been eager to show His Imperial Majesty most submissive obedience with all loyalty—God knows this—and I will continue to do so from now on. What I have promised, pledged, and sworn to His Imperial Majesty, I will keep in a princely, sincere, and unbreakable manner.

May the Merciful God soften His Majesty's heart toward me, so that I might obtain mercy regarding my long imprisonment and be released by his fatherly grace. I hope that I might not be the first prince and blood relative <note>John Frederick was a cousin to the Emperor through their royal lineages.</note> of His Imperial Majesty to spend his life in His Majesty's prison. To him, I hereby commend myself in all submissiveness and humility.

->John Frederick the Elder, etc.<-
->signed with his own hand.<-

Secondly, rulers <term>Regenten</term> must also know how to conduct themselves wisely in their office regarding external and worldly matters. Although this subject is extensive and much is required so that rulers are sufficiently learned and instructed to fulfill their office and calling, I will nevertheless write about it as briefly and simply as possible. The rest will be provided by the examples and histories set down in this book. Firstly, it would be highly desirable that every prince, ruler, or king be raised and instructed in all kinds of good arts <note>In the 16th century, "arts" or *Künste* referred to the liberal arts—the branches of knowledge like rhetoric, history, and philosophy necessary for a leader.</note>. They should remember the magnificent maxim of King Alexander the Great, which he used to say: *He would rather excel in learning than in riches.* <note>Original Latin: "Malle se disciplinis antecellere, quàm opulentijs."</note> That is: He would rather be rich in the arts than in great possessions.

# Of the Book of Rulers #

Likewise, there is the beautiful praise of the Roman Senate when they shouted in the *Curia* <note>The Senate House in ancient Rome.</note> in honor of Emperor Tacitus <note>Marcus Claudius Tacitus, Roman Emperor (r. 275–276 AD), known for his respect for the Senate.</note>: **"Who commands better than a man of letters?"** <note>original: *Quis melius, quàm literatus imperat?*</note> Who should more rightfully be a ruler than an educated man? This is so that the subjects might take an example from it, also keeping their children to good arts and virtues. But primarily, it is so that he might lead others more wisely in his government, and likewise lead a fine, moderate, virtuous, peaceful, and godly life for himself. For the subjects are usually accustomed to modeling themselves after their lords and authorities, as the saying goes: **"As the leader, so the people."** <note>original: *Qualis Princeps, talis Populus.*</note> As the shepherd is, so are the sheep. **"The citizens tend to be such as the leaders in the Republic are,"** according to the opinion of Plato, which Cicero also mentions. For men usually (as the author Herodian <note>A Roman civil servant and historian of the 3rd century AD.</note> testifies) strive to emulate the life of the Prince. As the regents and princes are in the commonwealth, so also are the subjects; for people usually model their own conduct after the customs of the princes. As the poet Claudian <note>Claudius Claudianus (c. 370–404 AD), a court poet for the Emperor Honorius.</note> also writes about this in the following verses:

> Do not let what is permitted to you come to mind, but what is fitting to have done; let a regard for what is honorable master your mind. <note>original Latin: *Nec tibi quid liceat, sed quid fecisse decebit, Occurrat, mentemq; domet respectus honesti.*</note>

**That is:**

> A Lord should not always seek
> To carry out what his mind and will desire.
> Rather, he should look in every way
> To ensure he does what is honorable,
> And upholds that which is right.

### AND A LITTLE FURTHER.

> Let him behave as a citizen and a father; you must consult for all, not for yourself. Let not your own interests move you, but the public vows. If you command anything to be held or observed in common, be the first to undergo those orders: then the people become more observant of justice, and do not refuse to bear it when they see the author himself obeying his own law. The world is shaped according to the example of the King; human senses are not as powerful at swaying minds through edicts as is the life of the ruler. The fickle commoners always change along with the Prince. <note>original Latin text by Claudian.</note> **That is:**

> O Imperial Majesty,
> I will give you this counsel:
> That you should wish to be as a father,
> By no means advising yourself alone.
> Rather, wish to help everyone,
> And do not let your own wealth
> Enter your heart. And if you
> Have commanded anything, let that same thing
> Also be commanded to yourself;
> You should be the first to do it.

For if a prince arranges his government and conduct honorably, rightly, and Christianly, it cannot fail; it must result in good for many people. Conversely, when a prince or regent errs and deviates from the right path, this must occur to the noticeable disadvantage and ruin of many people. As Nazianzenus <note>Gregory of Nazianzus (c. 329–390 AD), an influential theologian known as "The Theologian" in the Eastern Orthodox tradition.</note> says: **"For just as through a Prince, when he acts well, the life and safety of very many are provided for: so also, the error of a Prince leads to the destruction of many."** <note>original: *Sicut enim per Principem, cùm benefacit, plurimorum vitæ & saluti consulitur: ita, & error Principis, ad multorum perniciem pertinet.*</note> For just as many people are served by a prince when he acts rightly and well, so also are many harmed through him when he errs. And the foremost and greatest form of rule in a prince is when he can rule and moderate himself, so that he does not indulge his whims too much, as the aforementioned poet <note>Claudian, a Latin poet under Emperor Honorius, whose work was a staple of Renaissance political education.</note> says:

> Though you may rule far and wide through the farthest Indies,

> Even if you, all the way to India,
> Rule, and Arabia.
> And all the world worships you,
> And yet your anger, fear, and greed for gold
> Hold you captive.
> Then you are still a servant therein;
> For you shall only then become truly free,
> And will also be truly powerful,
> When you can be master over yourself.

Therefore, a Prince or authority should not take up the government while inexperienced or unwise, but should be so skilled that he himself may see and recognize what is right and what is wrong. And when great, weighty matters arise, he should know how to adapt and conduct himself therein, so that he does not need to rely solely upon his counselors in such things and all other matters, and be forced to use them. For where such Lords and Regents are who let themselves be ruled by other people, there such people usually bargain for their own benefit, seeking and considering not the Lord’s or the common good, but their own profit. From this, much trouble results for the poor subjects, and things go badly and miserably for them. And when such evil and self-seeking counselors gain the upper hand, the people are worse off than where the Lord himself is self-seeking and the counselors are pious and God-fearing. And to this belongs the saying of Plato, of which mention was made at the beginning of this chapter: that those kingdoms are best governed in which the regents strive for wisdom, or where the wise have the administration of the government.

[...his] own, but much more look to the profit and piety <note>The German "frommen" here refers to the general welfare or "the good" of the people.</note> of the land. A prince should also gladly follow his people in fair and equitable matters, and according to their counsel and deliberation, establish his government. He should ordain law and justice with the highest diligence, so that no one therein is delayed, and undertake nothing according to his own personal opinion. Rather, he should do everything according to the order of the **written laws**, which he shall hold, protect, and defend as nothing less than a **Divine Order**.

This is how the praiseworthy princes and emperors acted, namely **Antoninus Pius** <note>Antoninus Pius (reigned 138–161 AD) was a Roman Emperor known for his peaceful and judicial focus; he was one of the "Five Good Emperors."</note>, who handled nothing—neither in matters of war nor in civil affairs—concerning which he had not first consulted with his best and wisest people. He also held these advisors not as servants, but as his best friends. For he used to say: *It is more fitting that I obey so many good friends and follow their counsel, than that so many should follow me alone, as a single man, and my own head and whim.* He was, therefore, of a far different mind than some lords found today, who are so impulsive and unrestrained that they dare to say, when something good is advised to them by their people: "I have a head that hears what it wants, but it also does what it wants; therefore, I buy it a new hat every year," etc.

But one should in no way give place or belief to such hypocrites, but rather follow the example of the aforementioned Emperor Antoninus Pius.

Hatred, evil gossip, secret malice and persecution, strife, quarreling, danger
to body and life, abandonment of wife and children, property and goods, etc. And if two
paths stood open to everyone at the beginning—so that he should either
go into the government <term>Regiment</term> <note>The word 'Regiment' refers to the act of governing or public administration.</note>, or to a place where nothing was more certain
than that he would immediately perish with body and property and go under—
then every person would rather hasten to their ruin a thousand times over than allow
themselves to be used for governing. Unless he were completely mad and insane, so that he
might at once escape the danger and anxiety in which he must continually stand
and expect within the government.

This is indeed a serious and excellent saying, which the great
and highly sensible man <note>Demosthenes (384–322 BC), a famous Greek orator known for his speeches against Philip of Macedon.</note> learned not from hearsay (as they say) but
from great and long experience; since, as shall be heard hereafter,
all kinds of danger and difficult conditions met him in government.
For he was not a poor orator, such as one might sometimes find among the lawyers
today, but one who was employed in great matters, as mentioned, and also in
military affairs, upon whom King Philip of Macedonia especially had an eye.

And Demosthenes, with the aforementioned saying, clearly wanted to indicate and
remind that those who wish to commit themselves to the government of the common good <term>gemeinen Nutzes</term> <note>The 'common good' or public welfare was the primary duty of a Renaissance ruler.</note>
must expect nothing other than pure danger, worry, trouble, and labor.
Which Antisthenes <note>A Greek philosopher and a pupil of Socrates, often considered the founder of Cynic philosophy.</note> also indicated when he was asked
how one should undertake the common good. He said: *One should approach the state*
*as one approaches a fire: not too close, lest you be burned, nor too far, lest you*
*freeze.* <note>original Latin: "Ad Rempubl. est accedendum vt ad ignem, neque nimis propè ne vraris, neque longius ne frigeas."</note> That is: Just like a fire, where you do not place yourself too
closely to it, so that you do not burn yourself. Nor too far from it, so that you do not
freeze. Likewise, when Chrysippus <note>An influential Stoic philosopher who was prolific in his writing on logic and ethics.</note> was asked why he did not govern
the common good, he said: "Because if one governs badly, it displeases the
gods; but if he governs well, it does not please the citizens."

However, since one nevertheless finds people who strive for it and
seek with the greatest diligence to enter the government, it is
easy to consider and conclude what kind of understanding they must
have and how they can be beneficial and helpful to the common good.
Indeed, it also commonly happens that when they see how things go
in the government and begin to feel the burden, they would then gladly be
away from it, if they could honorably escape it. But it happens to them just like those
who do not know the way and nature of the sea and therefore are at first
joyful when they board a ship, intending to travel far across the sea.
But when they have set sail and a little storm wind comes, they begin
to be afraid, quake and tremble, fearing they might drown.
Indeed, even if it remains calm, they still become sick and unwell from the water
because they are unaccustomed to it; they begin to feel dread, as if they
would vomit, and they retch day and night, such that neither food nor
drink tastes good to them. Thus, they do nothing else but constantly think and
wish for how they might be delivered and freed from the voyage.

...helped him to land. He even agreed that if he were ever to return to the sea, the fisherman should simply let him drown. In such a way it also goes with those who enter into government <term>Regiment</term> <note>The word 'Regiment' here refers to the act of governing, public administration, or the holding of high office.</note>. For at first it pleases them well that they achieve great honors, and that people call them wise and gracious lords. But when they see the burden of the government beginning to weigh them down, and the toil and labor gain the upper hand, they not only lose their desire to eat and drink, but at times become so anxious that they do not know what to do or how to rid themselves of that burden again. And if they could only regain their previous status, they would gladly be idle and free from the government, etc.

However, those among the rulers usually bear the greatest burden, and must also endure the greatest danger, who have least deserved it and have most faithfully intended the common good <term>gemeinen Nutz</term> <note>The 'common good' was a central concept in Renaissance political thought, emphasizing the ruler's duty to the public over personal gain.</note>, having put their bodies and goods in danger for its sake. And if one were to recount here all the examples from all histories—ancient and new, from Greek and Latin historians—which testify that things have gone worst for the most pious people in government, one could not fit them all into a large book, let alone into this short chapter. As we daily experience, see, and hear, this is how things go in the world. Therefore, I will only recount here a few examples which are well known in history and cited in many places. First, concerning Themistocles.

This Themistocles <note>Themistocles (c. 524–459 BC) was an Athenian politician and general whose naval strategies saved Greece from Persian invasion.</note> was an excellent, wise, and sensible regent in the city of Athens, which is well evidenced by this alone, among his other magnificent deeds of which Plutarch <note>original: "Plutarchus"</note> and others write at length. Namely, when King Xerxes moved into Greece with ten times a hundred thousand men <note>A traditional figure for the massive Persian army, though modern historians estimate it was smaller.</note>, not only to make war upon it, but also to bring it entirely under his power or even to exterminate it. The Greeks, according to ancient custom, asked their god Apollo <note>original: "Apollinem"</note> at Delphi <note>original: "Delphos"</note> for advice on how they should protect themselves and hold off the enemy. Thereupon the god answered them that they would find victory in "wooden walls." Themistocles interpreted this to mean that they should arm themselves with ships and prepare for battle at sea, which was then done. The Greek cities defended themselves mightily against Xerxes on the sea, cut down many of his people, and also sank many of his ships. Thus the King fled; and after the weather had torn apart the bridge he had built across the Hellespontine Sea <note>The Hellespont, now known as the Dardanelles, is the narrow strait connecting the Aegean Sea to the Sea of Marmara.</note> in many places, he had to cross back in haste upon a small boat, in which he nearly drowned, leaving his army behind.

Themistocles brought all of this about mostly through his own schemes; for he pretended to side with the King and warned him that he should watch his position and get out of Greece, for the Greeks intended to destroy his bridges again. He suggested that if they were to trap and enclose him there with his army, they would then attack him in earnest and with their full power. This warning made the King so fearful that he immediately took flight and left the Greeks unburdened further.

It happened with Miltiades that when those of Athens helped to invade and burn Sardis, King Darius of Persia sent a great host of soldiers—one hundred thousand on foot and ten thousand horse—into Greece to punish and invade those of Athens. This same army came to within two miles of Athens. Although some advised that one should not go before the eyes of the enemy, but rather protect the city as best as possible and defend oneself from within, Miltiades pointed out that the common man could not endure a siege. He held, therefore, that if one went quickly to the enemy and attacked them before they recovered from their difficult journey, they might be defeated. The Athenians finally followed this counsel and made Miltiades the supreme captain. And since they could have no help from the other cities in such haste, excluding those of Plataea, they marched against the enemy with eighteen thousand men and defeated them.

Of the Book of Regents.

# That the Regents / Kings / Great-
# Potentates and Princes / must bear the greatest danger /
# care / toil / and labor.

### The Fifth Chapter.

<image-desc>Ornamental drop cap 'E' featuring intricate vine-like scrollwork and a small bird perched within the decoration.</image-desc>

Many people believe and maintain—especially the common, inexperienced masses—that it is a very precious thing to be a regent, king, prince, lord, or great potentate, because they seem to lack nothing that belongs to a "blessed life" (at least as the public defines it). They possess lands, cities, subjects, honor, money, property, food, drink, exquisite clothing, jewelry, and everything else the mind can imagine. Because of this, they must endure much envy and hatred from the people, and sometimes even from their own subjects. The majority of the crowd thinks there is no more fortunate thing on earth than when someone can become such a great and powerful lord. Every man wishes for himself that he might attain such high status, wealth, honor, lands, and people. Indeed, why do I speak only of wishing? Look around and read all of history, and you will find that for this sake, men have left nothing undone that was humanly possible to do or devise—including treachery, murder, betrayal, and poison. Such paths often end in misery. It has commonly happened that once a man has seized another’s property, empire, kingdom, lands, people, honor, and power, he must soon lose them again in the same fashion. Therefore, the situation of these high-ranking heads is quite different than some might think. If one examines it by the light of day, it is more a matter of pride, toil, and labor, mingled with great peril, rather than true happiness. This was recognized by King <term>Antigonus</term> <note>Likely Antigonus II Gonatas (c. 319–239 BCE), a Macedonian king known for his philosophical approach to rule.</note>. When he saw his son acting tyrannically toward those he commanded and treating them with contempt, he said: "Do you not know, O son, that our kingship is almost nothing other than a splendid and glorious servitude?" <note>original: "An ignores, ô fili, regnum nostrum non ferè aliud esse, quàm splendidam & gloriosam seruitutem?"</note> That is to say: Do you not know, my son, that our government is hardly anything else but a magnificent, visible slavery?

This is also evident from the fine history of King <term>Dionysius</term> <note>Dionysius I (c. 432–367 BCE), the tyrant of Syracuse, central to the "Sword of Damocles" legend.</note> of Syracuse. Once, while he was speaking with one of his flatterers named Damocles, Damocles highly praised and lauded King Dionysius as a mighty, rich, powerful, and fortunate king and lord. He spoke as if he believed no one had ever been more blessed or lived in greater glory than he. The King then said: "Do you then wish, O Damocles, since this life delights you, to lead it yourself and experience my fortune?" <note>original: "Visne ô igitur Damocle, quoniam haec te vita delectat, ipse eandem degere, & fortunā experiri meā?"</note> That is: Damocles, do you wish to experience what a magnificent life and luck I have? And when Damocles desired this, the King...

Part Two

<margin><note>original: "Euripides Solet enim inuidia ad res illustres prosilire. Malisq; gaudet, & bonis tristatur."</note> Euripides says: For envy is accustomed to leap upon illustrious things. It rejoices in evils and grieves at good things.</margin>
...iness, to these the shadows must follow. So it is also for those in high positions of dignity; envy follows after them. And if the envious can offer them a draft <note>original: "etwas zu trincken können"; a metaphor for providing an opportunity or "bitter cup" that leads to a leader's downfall</note> whereby they might fall into decline or be diminished, they leave nothing undone, but apply all possible diligence to that end. However, this persecution is also frequently caused by the fact that selfish people cannot tolerate it when affairs proceed rightly for the <term>common good</term> <note>original: "gemeinen nutz"; the public welfare or "commonwealth"</note>, because their own schemes and corrupt practices are thereby hindered. When someone comes along who speaks up a little and "looks into their cards" <note>An idiom meaning to see through someone's secret plans or deceptions.</note>, preventing them from their designs so that they cannot seek and drive their own profit, they devise so many lies and tricks that they eventually push him out of the way, so that they may remain unhindered by him.

Since this has always and everywhere been the way of the world—to such an extent that even the most pious <term>regents</term> <note>The author uses "Regenten" to encompass all levels of high authority, from local lords to kings.</note> could not be exempt from criticism—as one sees with Samuel, whom the Jews grew weary of. They wished to have a king instead, despite the fact that they could find no fault in him. Accordingly, matters will likely remain so. And regents should by no means let such ingratitude trouble them so deeply that they fall into despair, or cast aside their office and calling and want to run away from it, as some have entered monasteries for that reason. For even if some have fared so that they were driven out or had to suffer otherwise because of it, many others alongside them have nonetheless been preserved in government. And it is evident that God stands by the authorities and the regents and preserves them, however horribly Satan rebels against them and would gladly suppress and exterminate them through rebellion and tyranny—just as he is most highly opposed to all divine orders.

Furthermore, it is no small comfort that those who are persecuted, driven out, killed, or otherwise mistreated in such a manner die with greater honor than if they had remained at home in their government and in their highest honors. As Livy writes of Camillus <note>Marcus Furius Camillus (c. 446–365 BC), a Roman soldier and statesman who was honored as the "Second Founder of Rome" despite being sent into exile.</note>, that he lived more honorably in his misery than when he was a citizen in Rome. In the same way, it is said of Scipio <note>Scipio Africanus, the general who defeated Hannibal, who later retired to his estate in Liternum in a self-imposed exile due to political attacks.</note> that when he moved from Rome to Liternum, several robbers came to him. They had a great desire not only to greet such an excellent man but also to touch his right hand, with which he had performed so many knightly deeds and overcome so many enemies. Therefore, in my simple opinion, I think no one would be so foolish and insane as to not prefer being such an exiled citizen and regent (like those mentioned above) rather than being a great Emperor who is also an evil and raging tyrant, such as Nero,

->Domitian, Caligula, Julian,<-
->and the like.<-

<header>Of the Book of Regents.</header>

# That Regents / Kings / Great
## Potentates and Princes / must bear the greatest danger /
## concern, trouble, and labor.
### The Fifth Chapter.

Many people hold and believe—especially the inexperienced **common folk** <note>original: "gemeine unerfahrne Pöfel"; the author uses this to describe those without direct experience in the complexities of government</note> through and through—that it is a very precious thing to be a **regent**, **king**, **prince**, **lord**, and **great potentate**, because they lack nothing that belongs to a prosperous life and being (as they perceive it), such as lands, cities, people, honor, money and goods, food, drink, costly clothing, jewelry, and everything one can imagine. Because of this, they must endure much envy and hatred from the people, and sometimes from their own subjects. Most people think there is no more <term>blessed</term> <note>original: "glückseliger"; a term implying both material success and divine favor</note> thing on earth than for one to become such a great and mighty lord. Everyone wishes for themselves that they might come into such a great station, wealth, and honor, land and people. Indeed, why do I speak of wishing? Look around you and read all history, and you will find that for this sake, nothing has been left undone that was humanly possible to do or devise—such as **treason**, **murder**, **faithlessness**, **poison**, etc. It would be far too long to recount it all here. And it has commonly happened that when one brought another's goods, empire, kingdom, land and people, honor and wealth to himself, he had to lose those same things in like manner shortly thereafter. Therefore, the situation regarding such great heads is quite different than some might think. And if one looks at it in the light, it is more a matter of pride, trouble, and labor, mixed with great danger, than a true prosperity. This was recognized by **King Antigonus** <note>Likely Antigonus II Gonatas, a Macedonian king known for his philosophical outlook on kingship.</note> when he saw his son reigning tyrannically over those he was to command and holding them in contempt; he said:

> <note>original: "An ignores, ô fili, regnum nostrum non ferè aliud esse, quàm splendidam & gloriosam seruitutem"</note> Do you not know, O son, that our rule is almost nothing other than a splendid and glorious servitude?
That is: Do you not know, O son, that our government is almost nothing else than a magnificent, apparent bondage?

This also appears in the beautiful history of **King Dionysius of Syracuse**. For when he was speaking at one time with one of his flatterers named **Damocles**, and Damocles highly lauded and praised King Dionysius as a mighty, rich, powerful, and prosperous king and lord—so much so that he held that no one had ever been more blessed or in greater glory than he—the king said:

> <note>original: "Visne ô igitur Damocle, quoniam haec te vita delectat, ipse eandem degustare, & fortunā experiri meā?"</note> Do you wish then, O Damocles, since this life delights you, to taste it yourself and experience my fortune?
That is: Damocles, do you wish to experience what a magnificent life and fortune I have? When Damocles desired this, the

<header>The Second Part</header>

The King immediately had a table prepared, very precious with golden pieces and sideboards, in the most magnificent way; and as **Cicero** <note>Marcus Tullius Cicero (106–43 BC), a Roman statesman and philosopher who famously recounted this story in his "Tusculan Disputations."</note> writes: He ordered the man to be placed on a golden couch, spread with a most beautiful woven coverlet, painted with magnificent works, and he adorned many sideboards with chased silver and gold; then he ordered selected boys of exceptional beauty to stand at the table and to serve him diligently at his glance. Ointments were present, and garlands; perfumes were burned, and the tables were piled high with the most exquisite delicacies. <note>original Latin: "Iussit collocari hominem in aureo..."</note> **That is:** He had a golden table prepared for him with beautiful tapestries, and filled the sideboard before the table with golden drinking vessels. At the table, upon which was exquisite food, chosen boys had to stand and serve him according to his pleasure. All kinds of fragrant herbs were also lit. And **Damocles** thought he was now a truly <term>blessed</term> <note>original: "glückseliger"; referring to a state of perfect worldly happiness and good fortune</note> man; he ate, drank, and was merry, and conducted himself in the most magnificent way. 

But as he happened to look up, he became aware that a bare, sharp sword was hovering and hanging over his head by a silk thread (some write it was a **horsehair** <note>original: "Seta equina"</note>), at which he was so terrified and frightened that he begged the King to let him go, indicating that he had had enough of this royal splendor and bliss. The King, however, said that from this he—and everyone—might well understand what kind of joy a <term>regent</term> <note>original: "Regent"; a general term for a ruler or sovereign</note> has, who must spend his life and being in constant fear and daily terror. Since, however, this story is described by **Eusebius** <note>Eusebius of Caesarea (c. 260–339 AD), a historian and bishop often cited for his moral and historical anecdotes.</note> with special circumstances, I have wanted to place his words here, in case someone would rather read them in English than German. And they go as follows:

For when someone was extolling the life of <term>Tyrants</term> <note>original: "Tyrannorum"; in the classical sense, this refers to an absolute ruler or autocrat, often one who seized power, rather than necessarily a "cruel" ruler</note> in the presence of **Dionysius**, praising it as if it were blessed, Dionysius is said to have called the man to a dinner prepared with royal splendor. He suspended a sharp sword by a very thin thread over the head of the man as he sat. After the guest suddenly looked at it, he did not dare to rise from there for fear of the tyrant, nor was he able to drink or eat. Struck by danger, with his neck and eyes fixed on the hanging sword, he awaited death. When **Dionysius** saw this, he said: "Do you not understand how blessed our life is? For such it is, unless we wish to flatter ourselves. For although we have an abundance of all things, because of the frequency of dangers and the impending dread, we can enjoy nothing. We are like those who are often deceived by unsightly prostitutes who, being greatly adorned with clothing and gold and hiding their facial ugliness with paint, attract young men like fish with a hook, capturing them with these snares. We are oppressed by this unhappiness, we who seem happy to many. And just as many are forced by tortures to reveal the secrets of their minds, so sometimes, overcome by the trouble of this life, we let out the truest voices about our misery. For we tyrants are certainly like those animals that are fattened, to whom an abundance of eating and drinking is offered for nothing other than their own destruction." <note>original Latin quote: "Nam cùm quidam vitam Tyrannorum..."</note>

**Horace** <note>Quintus Horatius Flaccus (65–8 BC), a leading Roman lyric poet.</note> also remembers this story when he writes:

> For him, over whose impious neck
> A drawn sword hangs, the Sicilian feasts
> Will not produce a sweet flavor,
> Nor will the songs of birds or the lyre
> Bring back sleep. <note>original Latin: "Districtus ensis cui super impia..." from Horace’s Odes, 3.1.</note>

# Of the Ruler's Book #

That is: When a bare sword hangs over one's neck, even if one had the finest food, one cannot enjoy the taste. Nor can harps or the song of birds bring back sleep.

Therefore the Emperor **Saturninus** <note>Gaius Julius Saturninus, a Roman usurper in the 3rd century AD; his story is found in the "Historia Augusta."</note>, as **Vopiscus** <note>Flavius Vopiscus, traditionally one of the six scriptores (writers) of the "Historia Augusta," a collection of Roman imperial biographies.</note> writes, spoke well of this when he said:

> You do not know, friends, what an evil thing it is to rule. Swords and spears hang over our necks, spears threaten from every side, darts from every side; the guards themselves are feared, the companions themselves are dreaded. Food provides no pleasure, travel brings no authority, wars are not conducted by judgment, nor arms by choice. Add to this that every age in power is criticized. Is someone old? He seems unfit. If not, there is madness. For in wanting me to be Emperor, you drag me toward the necessity of death. But I have the consolation of death: I shall not be able to perish alone. <note>original Latin: "Nescitis amici, quid mali sit imperare. Gladij & tela nostris ceruicibus impendent, imminent hastæ vndiq;, vndiq; spicula, ipsi custodes timentur, ipsi comites formidantur, non cibus pro voluptate, non iter pro authoritate, non bella pro iudicio, non arma pro studio, Adde quòd omnis ætas in imperio reprehenditur. Senex est quispiam, inhabilis videtur, sin minus, inest furor, nam quòd Imperatorem me cupitis, in necessitatem mortis me trahitis. Sed habeo solatium mortis, solus perire non potero."</note>

**That is:** O dear friends, you do not know what a burdensome thing it is to rule; there we are safe from no one, but must daily worry about our own guards and those who travel with us. Spears and swords lie daily upon our necks. We cannot eat or travel with pleasure, much less conduct war according to our liking. If one is old, he is held to be incompetent; if one is young, he is regarded as insane. Therefore, in making me Emperor, you do nothing other than demand my death. Yet I comfort myself with this: that I cannot die alone.

**Stobaeus** <note>Joannes Stobaeus (5th century AD), a compiler of an extensive anthology of Greek literature.</note> writes similarly of the aforementioned King **Antigonus** <note>Likely Antigonus II Gonatas (c. 319–239 BC), a Macedonian king known for his philosophy.</note>: When an old woman highly praised his good fortune, he answered her: *If you knew, O mother, with how many evils this rag was filled (showing his <term>diadem</term> <note>original: "Diademate"; here referring to the royal headband or crown of a Hellenistic ruler</note>), you would not even pick it up if it were lying on a dunghill.* <note>original Latin: "Si nosses, ô mater, quantis malis hic panniculus esset plenus (ostenso Diademate) ne in sterquilinio quidem iacentem tolleres."</note> **That is:** O mother, if you knew what great evil and burden lay in this little cloth (meaning the crown), you would not lift it up from the manure. Which the Poet has captured in magnificent verse:

> It is noble, I confess, and weighed down with glowing stones,
> But it comes accompanied by innumerable cares.
> If everyone could weigh it properly, there would be no one,
> No one, who would wish to lift you from the ground.
> <note>original Latin: "Nobilis est fateor, rutilisq; onerata lapillis, / Innumeris curis sed comitata venis. / Non benè si possent omneis expendere, nemo. / Nemo foret, qui te tollere vellet humo."</note>

King **Seleucus** <note>Seleucus I Nicator (c. 358–281 BC), founder of the Seleucid Empire.</note> also considered and took this to heart when he said: many would be found—if only they knew what great trouble and labor it was to read and write letters—who would not pick up the crown even if it lay before their feet. *If many knew how laborious and troublesome it is to only write and read so many letters, they would not even lift up a diadem cast before their feet.* <note>original Latin: "Si nouissent multi, quàm sit operosum & molestum, tot duntaxat literas scribere, legereq;, Diadema etiam abiectum ante pedes, ne subleuarent quidem."</note> And the Poet writes correctly when he says:

> The shining diadem sustains innumerable labors,
> And under the greatest empire, the greatest care lies.
> <note>original Latin: "Sustinet innumeros fulgens Diadema labors, / Maximo & imperio, maxima cura subest."</note>

And these are indeed kingly speeches and wise words. However, these kings would also be considered wise if they had not only despised such kingly finery with words but had also cast it away from themselves in deed. Therefore **Petrarch** <note>Francesco Petrarca (1304–1374), an Italian scholar and poet in Renaissance Italy.</note> says: There are many lords over land, people, and worldly goods. But there are few who cast the same away or renounce them:

<header>The Second Part</header>

Therefore, the Emperor Augustus is praised because he was twice willing to resign the Imperial office, and would have done so if only someone wiser and better than he had been available to take up the government. <note>original Latin: "Illum enim diem lætißimum cogitabat, quo magnitudinem suam exueret."</note> **That is:** He considered that the most joyful day on which he could again lay aside the high status into which he had come.

One also reads that when Antiochus the Great <note>Antiochus III, ruler of the Seleucid Empire (222–187 BC).</note> was driven beyond Mount Taurus by Lucius Scipio <note>Lucius Cornelius Scipio Asiaticus, a Roman general and statesman.</note>, losing Asia and all surrounding lands, he diligently thanked the Romans for relieving him of such great governance, trouble, and labor, and was thus content and satisfied to manage with a smaller power. For he had well discovered and learned what the Emperor rightly said: <note>original Latin: "Nihil est difficilius, quàm benè imperare."</note> **That is:** There is nothing harder than to rule rightly and well. And Catullus <note>Gaius Valerius Catullus, a Roman poet.</note> says artfully: <note>original Latin: "O quid solutis est beatius curis."</note> Oh, what is better than to live without care.

Now, just as a person knows where the shoe pinches—as the saying goes—only if he is the one wearing it, so too no one knows what a laborious thing it is to be a regent except the one who carries the burden upon his neck.

Regarding this, Seneca <note>Lucius Annaeus Seneca, the Roman Stoic philosopher and advisor to Nero.</note> writes a beautiful maxim where he says: <note>original Latin: "Omnium istorum, quos incedere altos vides, bracteata felicitas est. Inspice & disces, sub ista tenui membrana dignitatis, quantum mali iaceat."</note>

All these who travel along so high have merely a painted splendor; if you were to look at them rightly, you would find it so, and see what evil lies hidden beneath such a thin veneer of dignity.

### The other Seneca, the Tragedian, says the same:

> Scepters never held calm peace,
> Nor a day certain of itself.
> One care tires after another,
> And a new storm vexes the soul.
> The sea on the Libyan sands
> Does not rage so, rolling wave after wave,
> As Fortune spins the headlong
> Downfall of Kings: they desire to be feared,
> And fear being feared: for them the kind night
> Offers no safe retreats:
> Nor does sleep, the conqueror of cares,
> Release their hearts. <note>original Latin: "Nunquam placidam Sceptra quietem, Certúmue sui tenuere diem. Alia ex alijs cura fatigat, Vexatq́; animos noua tempestas. Non sic Libycis Syrtibus æquor Furit alternos voluere fluctus. Vt præcipites Regum casus Fortuna rotat: metui cupiunt, Metuiq́; timent: non nox illis Alma recessus præbet tutos: Non curarum somnus domitor Pectora soluit."</note> **That is:**
> 
> However high the King's estate may be,
> It cannot have stability.
> For one care here, another there,
> Drives like one storm after another.
> Though the sea is indeed stormy,
> And brings many to a grisly end,
> Yet such a fall is even greater,
> And entirely perilous everywhere.

# From the Book of Regents.

->All this is the work of Fortune,<-
->Which always rules through its trickery.<-
->Though great lords wish to be<-
->Feared, and think themselves quite grand.<-
->When people tremble before them,<-
->I do not always consider it a good thing.<-
->For they must, in equal measure,<-
->Fear others just as much or even more.<-
->Consider this: by day and by night,<-
->They cannot sleep in safety.<-

This was confirmed and experienced by King **Alfonso** of Aragon <note>Alfonso V (1396–1458), known as "the Magnanimous."</note> when he was eating dinner one night. An untimely old chatterbox <note>original: "Schwezer"</note> would not stop talking and stayed awake late. The King said openly: <note>original Latin: "Alinorum conditionem longè meliorem, quàm Regum. Nam illis quidem comedentibus dominos parcere, Regibus neminem."</note> **That is:** Donkeys have it better than kings; for when donkeys feed, their drivers leave them in peace, but no one leaves a king in peace.

King **Philip** of Macedon <note>Philip II (382–336 BC), father of Alexander the Great.</note> testified to this as well. When he wished to set up his camp in a pleasant and beautiful spot, it was pointed out to him that there was no pasture or fodder for the horses and animals in that place. He said: <note>original Latin: "O Hercules, cuiusnam modi vita est nostra, si ad Asellorum commoditatem, & occasionem, viuere cogimur."</note> **That is:** O Hercules, what kind of life do we lead, if we must arrange our lives according to the convenience of donkeys?

Therefore, **Poggio** <note>Poggio Bracciolini (1380–1459), an Italian humanist and scholar.</note> writes that Pope **Adrian** <note>Likely Pope Adrian IV (c. 1100–1159), the only Englishman to be Pope, who famously complained about the burdens of the office.</note> said that <note>original Latin: "Neminem videri sibi Romano Pontifice miserabiliorem..."</note> **That is:** He considers that there is no more miserable thing on earth than a Pope. He asserted that the chair upon which the Pope sits is full of thorns; the cloak with which he is dressed is full of the sharpest spikes and is so heavy to carry that it crushes even the strongest men; and the triple crown <note>The Papal Tiara.</note> might burn one’s head with its heat.

Regarding this **Adrian**, **Petrarch** <note>Francesco Petrarca (1304–1374), the famous Italian poet and scholar.</note> also writes that **Policrates** <note>This likely refers to the *Policraticus*, a book on government by John of Salisbury, which records these quotes from Adrian IV.</note> often heard from him that he could wish no greater plague or punishment upon any of his enemies than that he should become Pope. For in truth, it is a heavy burden that appears blessed but is full of hatred. If one wishes to conduct oneself well in the Papacy, he finds enough work to do; but if he does not wish to do right, he soon goes to ruin. **Pinitianus** <note>Johannes Pinitianus, a 16th-century humanist poet.</note> testifies to this when he says:

> *He runs toward death of his own accord, who for the Papacy*
> *Competes, where deceit and cruel poisons rule.*
<note>original Latin: "Sponte sua in mortem currit, qui Pontificatum / Ambit, ubi fraus & sæua venena regunt."</note>

**That is:** Whoever desires the Papacy gives himself over to death, because nothing is to be found there but poison and deceit.

Therefore, for both good and evil Popes, it is a terrifying status,

# The Second Part

If a man who was Pope for only a short time could recognize this, what then would those complain and say who have grown old in the Papacy?

And Emperor **Domitian** <note>Titus Flavius Domitianus (51–96 AD), a Roman Emperor often portrayed as a cruel autocrat.</note> spoke rightly and well when he said: *The condition of Princes is most wretched.* Similarly, **Vulcatius** <note>Vulcatius Gallicanus, one of the traditionally attributed authors of the *Augusta History*.</note> writes that the Emperor **Hadrian** <note>Publius Aelius Hadrianus (76–138 AD), known for his extensive travels and the wall in Britain.</note> also said: *The condition of Emperors is a miserable one.* **That is:** It is a poor thing to be a great Lord. For one need only consider the danger to their bodies and lives, which they must expect from wicked people in the fields, in the forests, in houses, in wars, and in peace—all of which the common man does not have to fear at all. Or that he might be given poison, or dispatched with a "little Italian soup" <note>original: "Welschen Süplein." In this period, "Welsch" (meaning Italian or foreign) was often used in German to imply sophisticated or treacherous methods of assassination, such as poisoning.</note>. Therefore, such lords and potentates must have their <term>Credenzer</term> <note>From the Italian "credenza," this refers to the ceremony of "credence" where a servant (the cup-bearer or sewer) tastes food and drink in front of the lord to prove it is safe.</note>. This was also observed by the poet **Juvenal** when he wrote:

->No poisons are drunk<-
->From earthenware; then fear them, when you take up<-
->Gemmed cups, and the wine glows in deadly gold.<-
<note>original Latin: "Nulla aconita bibuntur / Fictilibus, tunc illa time, cùm pocula sumes / Gemmata, & leto Setinum ardebit in auro."</note>
->And Seneca says:<-
->Poison is drunk from gold; I speak from experience.<-
<note>original Latin: "Venenum in auro bibitur, expertus loquor."</note>
->And another, on the anxious life of the powerful:<-
->Immense power always brings various cares,<-
->And forbids the limbs to be restored by peaceful sleep.<-
->The Prince does not go forth unless surrounded by soldiers and arms;<-
->Unlucky man, he always fears some enemy.<-
->Whenever he must eat, someone must taste it first;<-
->They drink the wine before he himself drinks.<-
->Such things declare that a king is hardly safe;<-
->What a heavy burden a great tyranny sustains!<-
->Indeed, the bodyguard indicates enemies to be feared,<-
->And the one who tastes the poison warns of things to be avoided.<-
->Therefore, what place is free from fear here? You see those very things<-
->Which drive away fear are themselves full of fear.<-

**That is:** The greater a Lord is, the more danger he must expect, such that he can neither sleep, eat, drink, nor travel in safety. For when he eats or drinks, he must have it tasted and worry about poison. Because he has so many guards <note>original: "Trabanten," referring to the halberdiers or bodyguards who attended a sovereign.</note> around him, it is understood that he is not safe from violence either, but must ultimately even worry about those who are supposed to take away his fear.

To conclude this chapter, however, I will introduce another beautiful and entertaining text (similar to the matter related here) from the Greek writer **Lucian** <note>Lucian of Samosata (c. 125–180 AD), a satirist. The text referenced is his dialogue "The Dream" or "The Cock."</note>. There, the **Cock** <note>original: "Gallus." To this, the Cock answers, as **Erasmus** <note>Desiderius Erasmus (1466–1536), the famous humanist who translated Lucian’s Greek into Latin.</note> translated it into Latin, as follows:

Do not bring it back to my memory, O Micyllus, for I was then beyond measure unhappy. For as far as external matters were concerned, as you said, I seemed clearly fortunate; but within, I was distracted by innumerable cares. Truly, I [was] unpr...

I ruled a region by no means small, Micyllus <note>Micyllus is a character from the Greek satirist Lucian’s dialogue *The Cock*. In the story, a rooster—who was once a king in a previous life—explains to the poor cobbler Micyllus why being a king is actually miserable.</note>, remarkable for the abundance of all good things, the density of its inhabitants, and the beauty of its cities. Furthermore, it was blessed with navigable rivers and a harbor-filled sea. To these were added a huge army, a most distinguished and excellent cavalry, a large personal guard, warships, a greater sum of money than could be counted, a vast supply of silver vessels, and all the other joys of a principality—a clamor and apparatus of state built up and accumulated beyond what one can believe. 

Thus, when I went forth, most people would worship me, thinking they saw some god among them; others, pushing one another, would run together just to catch a glimpse of me. Some, having climbed onto the roofs, thought it a great thing if they could fully contemplate my carriage, my robe, my Diadem, as well as those walking before me and those following behind. 

I, meanwhile, conscious of how many things were torturing me, judged those people worthy of forgiveness on account of their ignorance; but I pitied myself, for I seemed very much like those great **Colossi** <note>Massive statues, like the Colossus of Rhodes.</note> manufactured by **Phidias**, **Myron**, or **Praxiteles** <note>Three of the most famous sculptors of ancient Greece, known for creating lifelike and monumental statues.</note>. For each of those statues, as far as their outward appearance goes, is Neptune himself or Jupiter, wonderfully decorated with gold and ivory; in his right hand he holds a thunderbolt, a flash of lightning, or a trident. But if you were to stoop down and look at what is inside, you would see bars, pegs, and nails protruding within, as well as beams, wedges, pitch smeared about, and other such deformities inhabiting the interior. I will not even mention the swarms of flies and weasels that sometimes live inside them. 

The life of kings surely seems to be something of this sort. Why should I tell you of the fears, the **biting cares** <note>original: "curas mordaces"</note>, the suspicions, and the hatred with which those who live with the King pursue him? Or the plots, and because of them, the rare sleep—and even that being very light—and the nightmares full of tumult, the perplexed thoughts, and the always wicked hopes? Or the lack of leisure, the distracting occupations, the decrees, treaties, and consultations? By these things it happens that not even for a moment is one allowed to enjoy anything sweet; rather, it is necessary to look out anxiously for all matters and sustain a thousand pieces of business.

# The Second Part

And the Emperor **Domitian** spoke rightly and well: *The condition of Princes is most wretched.* <note>original Latin: "Conditionem Principum, miserrimam esse."</note> Similarly, **Vulcatius** <note>Vulcatius Gallicanus, a Roman historian and one of the supposed authors of the *Augustan History*.</note> writes that the Emperor **Hadrian** also said: *A wretched condition is that of Emperors.* <note>original Latin: "Misera conditio Imperatorum."</note> That is to say: it is a poor thing to be a great Lord. That is: the greater a Lord is, the more danger he must expect, so that he can neither sleep, eat, drink, nor travel in safety. For if he eats or drinks, he must have it tasted and worry about poison. Because he has so many guards around him, it is to be understood that he is not safe from violence; rather, he must ultimately also worry about those who are supposed to take away his fear.

When I first undertook to write this book, my mind was set upon only placing the bare examples and the histories under each of their titles, and letting it rest there. ...[is preached], schools are established, good laws and public order <term>order: the original German "Policey" refers to the general regulation and civil administration of a community, rather than just modern law enforcement</term> are maintained, the noble arts along with all good customs and virtues are cultivated, and discipline and honor flourish. For this reason, Aristophanes says: <note>original Latin: "O veneranda pax, largitrix omnium rerum, quo te nomine appellabo, & vnde verbum satis magnificum accipiam?"</note> "O venerable peace, giver of all things, by what name shall I praise you, and where shall I find a word grand enough for you?" And another: Peace gives people the best things on Earth, namely, wealth, etc. This is what the Greek poet Homer intended to show when he writes how Achilles had two cities painted or engraved upon his shield; in one, people are in good spirits and everything proceeds quietly and peacefully; in the other, however, there is nothing but war, fire, and murder, etc. This can be understood from the following verses (which are found in the *Iliad*, Book 18 <note>The OCR says "Iliados M."; while 'M' is the Roman numeral for 1000, the description of the Shield of Achilles is famously located in Book 18 (Sigma) of the Iliad</note>, and read as follows in Latin):

# The Ruler’s Book

->And sets fire to the houses/<-
->So that they must go forth naked from them.<-
->Which one should now take note of/<-
->And constantly strive for peace.<-

From these verses, one can sufficiently perceive and understand how fine, lovely, joyful, wholesome, and useful a thing the noble Peace is. For there everything proceeds well and happily, and nothing else is heard but joy and delight, of which Cicero also says: <note>original Latin: *Dulce est nomen pacis, Res vero ipsa, quum iucunda, tum salutaris.*</note> "The name of peace is sweet, but the reality itself is as pleasant as it is beneficial." Accordingly, it is also a very comforting and high virtue in a prince when he is patient and does not allow himself to be easily moved to war, but seeks all humanly possible ways and means, sparing no expense, toil, or labor, so that he may have peace, thereby preventing much untimely damage and misfortune. For this reason, the poets also devised the fiction that when Jupiter wished to thunder, hail, and strike with lightning, he first had to summon all the other gods and obtain their consent. However, when he wished to let a quiet, gentle rain fall, by which the earth was refreshed, he did not require such consent—this was to demonstrate that a prince or lord should not abandon peace or undertake war without great cause and careful deliberation.

Thus we read of Agesilaus, the King of the Spartans <note>original: *Lacedemonier*</note>, that when he wished to wage war against the King of Persia, he first asked the gods—namely Jupiter and Apollo, Father and Son—for counsel; likewise the Ephors <term>Ephors: a group of five high-ranking Spartan magistrates who held the power to oversee and even check the authority of the kings</term>, who were five councilors or judges whom even the kings had to obey. And when the war was advised by all parties, only then did he take up armor. Now, whoever will not follow such an example, but instead has a lust for war, putting his own life and soul, as well as his subjects, land, and people, into ultimate danger, let him look upon war [with caution]; for many can be found who were inclined toward both war and peace. Thus Thrasybulus overcame great treachery in Athens with patience; likewise Scipio in Rome. Thrasybulus also made a law in Athens that those who had been victorious in war and civil strife should forget what had happened therein and how they had been treated by the conquered. They were also forbidden from reclaiming their property from those who were defeated, but rather, for the sake of peace and the common good, they were to forget it—which was a laudable and princely consideration for the promotion of peace. Similarly, Scipio, out of a noble spirit, despised certain loud-mouthed and rebellious rascals and preferred to withdraw from the city of Rome to his estates, saying: <note>original Latin: *Ingrata Patria, ne ossa quidem mea habebis.*</note> "O you ungrateful fatherland, you are not worthy to have my bones," rather than giving cause for war, bitterness, and unrest. And although he, as a powerful lord, could have defended himself with force and avenged himself on such loud-mouths, as can be seen in Gellius <note>Aulus Gellius, a 2nd-century Roman author of the *Attic Nights*</note>, book 4, chapter 18.
