# The Second Part

As he [the prince] possessed such an undaunted and princely spirit, he nevertheless set it aside for the sake of the common peace and overcame his impulses with patience. Such a prince was also **Duke Frederick, the Elector of Saxony**, of highly praiseworthy memory, who loved peace so much that he would not even build any fortifications, so that he might not have cause to take up or engage in war.

One reads similarly of the **Emperor Marcian**, that he would not allow himself to be moved to war unless he was driven to it by the utmost necessity. And this was his proverb: <note>original Latin: *Donec in pace liceret viuere, non decere Principem sumere arma.*</note> "As long as one may live in peace, it does not befit a Prince to take up arms." And every prince should remember the sentence of **Sallust**, where he says: <note>original Latin: *Omne bellum facilè sumitur, cæterum egerrimè definitur. Non est in eiusdem potestate initium & finis.*</note> "Every war is easily started, but most difficult to end. The beginning and the end of a war are not within the power of the same person."

Therefore, **Suetonius** writes of **Titus Vespasian**, the Roman Emperor, that he had himself consecrated and chosen as the High Priest for this reason: so that he might not have to stain his hands with blood. This Prince possessed such a peaceful heart. For those who were chosen and accepted into such a priestly office at that time had to swear that they would entirely abstain from bloodshed for the duration of their lives, even if they were harmed or provoked to it, as I also partially mentioned above. This the aforementioned Emperor faithfully kept after he became High Priest. For one reads of him that when he learned that two of the most prominent councilors in Rome had secretly conspired against him, he did not kill them—even though he would have been justified in doing so because they sought his life and had fallen under the penalty of **High Treason** <term>original Latin: *Læsæ Maiestatis*. This refers to "injured majesty," a crime against the dignity of the sovereign or the state</term>, and he could have proceeded against them with the sword as against rebels and insurgents to serve as a deterrent to others. Instead, he summoned them to him at the marketplace and let them sit down beside him. Then he gave each a two-edged sword into their hands with the command that they should feel how sharp it was, thereby giving them to understand what they had deserved and how dangerous it was to conspire against the authorities and turn rebellious. Beyond this, he took no further action against them.

Likewise, **Seneca** and others write of the **Emperor Augustus**, that when he was forty years old and living in France <note>The author uses "Franckreich" (France), though in a Roman context this refers to the province of Gaul</note> at the time, it was reported to him how the noble youth **Lucius Cinna**, a nephew of Pompey, was seeking his life; and he was told how, when, and where he intended to attack him—namely, he wanted to strike him dead in the church. <note>The German text uses "Kirchen" (churches), though in Augustus’s time this would have been a pagan temple.</note> The judgment was reached that he should be driven into exile, although the Emperor allowed various opinions to be heard. Finally, **Livia**, his spouse, came and said: "O Emperor, will you not also take advice from a woman? Do as the physicians do: when the usual medicines will not help, they try the opposite ones. You have accomplished nothing with your severity thus far; so try goodness instead and forgive L. Cinna. For his plot and intention are already revealed; it can—

And the Emperor began and recounted to him many and great benefits; among others, that he had preserved him and granted him his life, even though he had found him among his enemies. # The Second Part

Since he <note>Cineas, a student of the orator Demosthenes</note> was an exceptionally eloquent man, he attempted to persuade the King to desist from war and make peace with the Romans. Therefore, he said to him: "Lord King, since the Romans are the best warriors, if we have conquered them, what do we intend to do next?" Pyrrhus answered: "Then we shall take all of Italy." "When we have Italy, what shall we do then?" "We shall next move against Sicily." "What after Sicily? Shall we then keep the peace?" "By no means," said Pyrrhus, "rather, this shall only be a beginning to greater things. For we still have Libya and Carthage before us." To this, Cineas said: "If you conquer these lands, you can thereafter easily overcome Macedonia and all of Greece. But when you have accomplished all this and brought it to an end, what will you do then?" Then Pyrrhus said: "Then we shall have good days, be merry, banquet daily, keep the peace, and delight one another with friendly conversation." Then Cineas answered: "O King, why then will you not grant peace and have good days *now*? For these your schemes will cost much blood, and yet you cannot know whether it will turn out according to your plans, and whether you will attain that which you strive for or not." As it happened, things turned out much differently for Pyrrhus than he intended. For when he had fought two battles with the Romans and defeated them, it was with such great loss that he said:

> If we defeat the Romans in just one more such battle, it will be the end of us, and I shall return to Epirus without any soldiers. <note>original Latin: "Si vno adhuc Romanos vicerimus bello, actum fuerit de nobis, & sine vllo Milite Epeirum reuertar."</note>

If we hold such a battle with the Romans once more, it will be the undoing of our people, and we shall return home without any army—just as he indeed did not return home, but was struck dead in Argos, Greece, by a woman with a stone.

Here one might say: should one then wage no war at all, and never use earnest force when necessity requires it? To this, sensible and wise people give this answer: If a pious Prince or Lord is so highly provoked and pushed to war that all human ways and means have failed him, and he thus cannot reach peace through other paths—but must fear nothing other than riot, invasion, rebellion, and the like, and cannot quiet these in any other way than through a regular war—then he must make a virtue of necessity (as they say). Alciatus <note>Andrea Alciato (1492–1550), a famous Italian jurist and author of the "Book of Emblems."</note>, an excellent jurist, also holds this view when he says:

> Let weapons lie far away, yet it is lawful to take up war,
> If otherwise the art of peace cannot be enjoyed. <note>original Latin: "Arma procul iaceant, tamen est fas sumere bellum, / Sin aliter pacis, non licet arte frui."</note>

->That is:<-

> Weapons should be cast far away,
> After peace we must strive every day.
> But if it simply cannot be,
> Then strike with joy and bravery.
> See that you gain the upper hand,
> For trembling fists lose hold of the land.

Likewise: *War must be waged so that peace may be sought.* <note>original Latin: "Bellum gerendum est, vt pax quaeratur."</note> However, a commander should especially pay diligent attention to the following points.

# Of the Book of Regents.

Firstly, he should strive with all diligence and before all things to consider how he may conduct the impending war in such a way that his entire Fatherland, along with all his subjects—the nobility, citizens, and peasants—as well as his loyal neighbors where possible, suffer the least damage. Only those who have given cause for such a war should be harmed. Thus, he should prevent, as much as he is able, his subjects, land, and people from being led into misery, distress, anxiety, poverty, and ruin.

For his subjects—whether they be noble or common, citizens or peasants—should be as dear to a Christian Regent as his own body. Just as he would not willingly lose the smallest limb from his body, he should also not willingly lose even the least of his subjects or throw them away to slaughter <note>The original German "in die schanck schlagen" is an idiom for sacrificing or risking something carelessly, often in a military context.</note>.

<margin>Princely speech and example of the Roman Lucius.</margin>
Secondly, it should be his highest desire that in such a war, he seeks the benefit, salvation, and welfare of his own people more than his own profit. He must direct all care, effort, and diligence toward ensuring that his wars do not fill the land with poor people, widows, orphans, and beggars. Instead, he should, as much as possible, prevent unnecessary bloodshed, strangling, and murder. He should remember the example of the Roman (and yet pagan) regent, **Lucius**, when he said: He would rather rescue one of his citizens and soldiers from the hands of the enemy than inherit and possess all the goods of the enemy.

<margin>Antoninus Pius</margin>
Similarly, Emperor **Antoninus Pius** <note>Roman Emperor from 138 to 161 AD, known for a peaceful reign.</note> greatly loved the splendid saying of **Scipio** and had it constantly in his mouth, saying: *Se malle vnum ciuem seruare, quam mille hostes occidere.* <note>original Latin: "He would rather save one citizen than kill a thousand enemies."</note> That is: He would rather preserve one citizen than strangle a thousand enemies. This Emperor (says **Vopiscus** <note>Flavius Vopiscus, one of the purported authors of the Augustan History.</note>) esteemed peace far higher than war. He also held that it should be the foremost office and concern of a commander how he might attain victory at any time without great bloodshed.

<margin>Caecilius Metellus</margin>
**Caecilius Metellus** followed this same opinion. When someone pointed out to him that if he would risk ten men and throw them to slaughter, he could thereby capture a fortified place, Metellus asked him: "Would you like to be one of the ten and give yourself over to the danger and the slaughter?" God help us, one finds few such commanders and captains today! There are some to be found now and then who do not have such a great conscience, even when they have placed a great heap of soldiers in peril, and they do not care much how they might escape such peril again.

<margin>Agesilaus.</margin>
Thirdly, the commander should also reflect that he, in his own person, should not rage too cruelly, nor should he permit his soldiers to do so, following the example of **Agesilaus**, King of the **Lacedaemonians** <note>The Spartans.</note>. He often exhorted his soldiers in the ranks that they should not torment or torture prisoners and wrongdoers, but should treat them as human beings. Regarding young children in war, he ordered that they must be gathered together in one place so that they would not perish when the camp moved. He had the same care for the elderly prisoners, so that they would not be harmed since they could not keep up with the young. This gentleness earned him, among friends and enemies alike, a wonderfully

# The Second Part

...made a good name and goodwill; now those claim to be the bravest warriors who spare neither old nor young, neither women nor virgins, of which more shall be said in another place.

A warlord should also not think that he has done well if, after conquering a city, he slaughters everyone within and razes it to the ground. For it is much easier to destroy and break things with fire than to build them anew. As Agesipolis <note>A King of Sparta who reigned in the early 4th century BCE.</note> said when someone boasted that King Philip of Macedon had destroyed the fine and magnificent city of Olynthus in a short time, he answered: "By the gods, as powerful as he is, he will not build such a city even in a much longer space of time." <note>original: *Atqui per Deos, talem Ciuitatem, longè maiore temporis spacio, non extructurus est.*</note>

And to return to those who do not like to see their soldiers placed in danger: we read of Lycurgus, the King of the Lacedaemonians <note>The Spartans.</note>, that he would not allow any castle, tower, or other fortress to be stormed, so that a magnificent or brave warrior might not be wounded or pelted to death by a woman or a boy. He said: "Lest better men be killed by a woman or a child, or by any other person who is no different than a child or woman." <note>original: *Ne inquit, à fœmina pueróue, aut alio quopiam homine, puero aut fœminæ non dissimili, viri præstantiores occidantur.*</note> As indeed happened to King Pyrrhus, struck by a woman <note>Pyrrhus of Epirus was famously killed in a street fight in Argos when an old woman threw a roof tile at him.</note>, as mentioned above.

Likewise, when King Archidamus saw a new instrument brought from Sicily called a catapult <term>Catapulta: an early siege engine used to hurl bolts or stones</term>, with which people could easily be shot and killed, he cried out with a loud voice: "O Hercules, the bravery of man has perished." <note>original: *O Hercules, viri periit virtus.*</note> That is: Now it is over with the manhood and strength of man. For against such weaponry <term>Geschük: a term used here for mechanical artillery or early cannons</term>, a strong-hearted man cannot prove his courage. What would Archidamus say if he lived in our current time and saw the cruel artillery and terrifying war-armaments, compared to which those instruments are mere child's play and worth nothing? Today, a worthless scoundrel often shoots several brave men at once, though he would not otherwise dare to speak to any of them with a free heart, let alone fight them.

Finally, war also requires money—and not a little, but a great and significant sum—no matter how precisely the war is planned. For so much goes to the cavalry captains <term>Rittmeister: the military rank for a captain of a troop of horsemen</term> and other appointments. So much goes to the artillery, guns, and war-gear. So much goes to the infantry. So much to provisions. Often one must also have money to silence those who might otherwise join the enemy. And who can count all the costs? The proverb will surely remain true: *War desires no counsel.* <note>The German "Krieg wil kein raht haben" suggests that once war starts, it becomes unpredictable and cannot be managed by simple advice or plans.</note> And as the aforementioned Archidamus answered when he was asked how much money and property was required for a war: "War," he said, "does not seek defined limits." <note>original: *Bellum, inquit, non quærit definita.*</note> That is, one cannot prescribe a measure or set a goal for war. He wanted to indicate that those who have started a war must be prepared for all the necessities of war in every way. For war, as mentioned, wants nothing fixed, and many unforeseen things happen within it.

Therefore, if someone wishes to go to war, let him only see to it that he has money. For they are...

# Of the Regent's Book.

...money is the sinews of war and the force that brings things to fruition. <note>original: *nerui bellorum, & rerum agendarum effectrices pecuniæ*</note>. For money is required for war—and indeed, money and enough of it—if you wish to accomplish anything. Otherwise, let the warring be, for the ruler will otherwise achieve nothing, and no one will serve him. The imprisoned King of Denmark, Christian, <note>Christian II (1481–1559), the last monarch of the Kalmar Union, who was deposed and spent much of his later life in captivity.</note> once undertook to reconquer and take back his kingdom; however, because he lacked money, he could accomplish nothing. And though I have heard from afar that he even pawned his royal crown for this purpose and has not redeemed it to this day, it still was not enough to reach his goal, and thus the war went backwards.

It would be a different matter if someone took the thought that he wanted to pay his war-force out of another’s purse and lead them into a land that was not his own, etc., as such captains are sometimes accustomed to say. But what kind of foundation and reputation this has, any sensible person will easily consider for themselves: that one picks a quarrel out of nowhere <note>The German "eine vrsach von einem Zaun bricht" literally means "breaking a reason off a fence," an idiom for picking a fight for no reason.</note> and then lets a crowd of wicked, godless rascals—whom he no longer needs—run through the land, plundering towns and villages to recover their pay. Although it may have happened this way at times, it is neither princely, honorable, nor Christian; it is contrary not only to the ancient customs of the heathens but also to natural and common written laws. It is more to be called a **robbery** <note>original: *Latrocinium*</note> than a war when it proceeds in this manner.

A Christian prince, when forced into war, should consider all of this and the like, especially what the poet writes concerning peace and war <note>original: *de pace & bello*</note> with these words:

> As nothing can be more accursed than war,
> So nothing can be more excellent than Peace.
> Peace nourishes genius, and stirs up the noble arts:
> Peace gives all good things to man with a generous hand.
> But the madness of war plunders whatever nourishing peace provides,
> Setting it on fire and filling all things with slaughter.
> Mixing the highest with the lowest, iron-hearted Mars <note>The Roman god of war.</note> calls forth
> the Furies <note>original: *Eumenides*; the vengeful deities of the underworld.</note> from the depths, and brings every evil upon the earth.
> War is the rod of an angry God: Peace is the noble gift
> Of that same God when appeased, and his chief favor.

In short, just as nothing is more harmful than war, so nothing is more comforting than peace.

And indeed, if someone has been in a war once, or has conducted a war, I have no doubt that his desire for warring will vanish, and he will look about for noble peace. For the proverb says: **War is sweet to those who have not experienced it.** <note>original: *dulce bellum inexpertis*</note>. That one also soon grows weary of war, the poet Homer sought to teach with these verses, where he says in the *Iliad*, Book 9:

> In a short space of time, men are sated
> With the love of bitter war.

and write [these reminders] in their chambers, so that they might be reminded of their office, and consider why God has placed them in power over land and people. Thus, they should occasionally take heed themselves of how the poor people are treated, inquiring after them and speaking to the captains. And when a poor man has a just cause, perhaps against a wealthy man, the ruler should not allow him to be oppressed or look the other way, but should stand by him, protecting and defending him—for that is what it means to "open one's mouth" <note>This refers to the biblical proverb (Proverbs 31:8): "Open your mouth for the speechless, in the cause of all who are appointed to die."</note>. However, such things can rarely happen in places where people are drunk <note>The original German "voll" literally means "full," a common idiom for being intoxicated.</note> day and night. Many a poor "nose" <note>A colloquial term for a person or individual.</note> must be crushed under such conditions. Such behavior was not only forbidden to the Jewish kings, but even the heathens concerned themselves with it; for if a prince in Athens was drunk, he had thereby forfeited his life. Likewise, the ancient Romans so hated those who were prone to drunkenness that the Censors <term>Censors: high-ranking Roman officials responsible for public morality and the census</term> thereafter deemed none of them worthy to be employed in the government or the public good. For this reason, they were often removed from their offices and regarded as disreputable people. The Egyptians, however, so that their king might have no cause to burden himself with drink and lead a disordered life, gave him a daily allowance of wine with which he had to be satisfied.

Although there is now a different opinion and circumstance, such that it is not considered fitting to give lords and rulers a set measure of what and how much they should drink—nor is this why I have written this—nonetheless, drinking has so taken the upper hand everywhere, both among subjects and rulers, especially in the German Nation, that it can hardly be changed or abolished. One can scarcely find a citizen or a craftsman who would tolerate his servant prescribing a measure for what he should eat or drink. Yet it remains necessary that rulers occasionally remind themselves of this and see that not only Holy Scripture but also the heathens held such a life of gluttony and drunkenness in no regard. It does not matter if some laugh at this and make a mockery of it when one speaks of these and similar vices—especially those who are at the lords' courts. For among them, heavy drinking is considered the greatest art, and they even wish to be praised for it, even when they do it in the coarsest manner and one drinks the other down so that he must die from it. As it is written of the Great Alexander of Macedonia, how he once offered a golden crown to whoever could drink the most. A man named Promachus earned and won the crown by guzzling, but he lived no longer than three days afterward, and so, with a full belly, he traveled into Nobis’s Jug <note>original: "Nobis Krug." A German folk expression referring to a tavern in the afterlife or hell; to "go to Nobis's Jug" means to die, often specifically from overindulgence.</note>.

Therefore, if one can reach an agreement and peace, he should seize it. For an agreement or peace—even if it is not entirely advantageous in all things—may easily be better than a war in which everything is destroyed and brought to the ground at once, as shall be spoken of further hereafter in the section concerning war. For this reason, Livy <note>Titus Livius, a Roman historian</note> also says: A certain peace is better than a hoped-for and uncertain victory. <note>original: "Quòd melior sit certa pax, quàm sperata victoria."</note>

# That Rulers,
## Princes, and Great Lords Should Especially Remain Moderate,
### and should guard against drunkenness.

### The Seventh Chapter.

Although all Christians are strictly commanded in the Holy Gospel of Luke to guard against drunkenness, where Christ says: "Take heed to yourselves, lest your hearts be weighed down with excess eating and drunkenness, and the cares of this life," etc. Likewise, Saint Paul says in more than one place that the drunkards shall not inherit the kingdom of heaven; yet, rulers are especially bound to guard themselves against drunkenness. Indeed, the wise man Solomon desires that they should use no strong drink at all, such as wine, mead, and anything that makes one drunk. For thus he says in Proverbs, in the 30th chapter <note>In modern Bibles, this passage is found in Proverbs 31:4-9.</note>: You shall by no means give kings wine to drink, for where drunkenness reigns, nothing can remain hidden; and kings might forget the law, and pervert the cause of the poor man's child. Give strong drink to the sorrowful, and wine to those who have a troubled and heavy spirit, so that they may forget their poverty and suffering. Open your mouth for the mute, and promote the cause of all those who pass by; open your mouth, and discern what is right, and stand by the needy and poor.

Which saying is so worthy that all great lords, rulers, and potentates should know it by heart, or have it written with golden letters in their chambers

and write [these duties] in their chambers, so that they might be reminded of their office and remember why God placed them in government over land and people. Thus, they should occasionally take heed themselves of how the poor people are treated, inquiring about them and speaking firmly to the captains <note>In this context, 'captains' (Häuptleute) refers to local officials or military governors</note>. When a poor man has a righteous cause against a rich man, the ruler should not let him be oppressed or look the other way <note>literally: "look through the fingers"</note>, but rather stand by him, protect him, and defend him—for that is what it means to "open one's mouth" <note>A reference to Proverbs 31:8: "Open your mouth for the speechless, in the cause of all who are appointed to die."</note>.

However, such things can rarely happen in places where people are "full" <note>drunk</note> day and night; many a poor man must be oppressed under such conditions. Such behavior was not only forbidden to the Jewish kings, but even the pagans concerned themselves with it. For if a prince in Athens was drunk, he forfeited his life because of it. Likewise, the ancient Romans so hated those who were prone to drunkenness that the Censors <note>Roman officials responsible for maintaining public morality</note> thereafter deemed no such person worthy of being employed in the government or for the common good. Indeed, they were frequently removed from their offices for this reason and were regarded as disreputable people. As for the Egyptians, so that their king would have no reason to burden himself with drink and lead an Edwardian or disorderly life, they gave him a set amount of wine daily, with which he had to be satisfied.

Although the current opinion and circumstances are now different, such that it is not easily done or considered fitting to give Lords and rulers a specific measure of what and how much they should drink, this is not the reason I have written this. Rather, because drinking has gained such a massive upper hand in all places—among both subjects and rulers, and especially in the German nation—it will be difficult to change or abolish it. One can hardly find a citizen or a craftsman who would tolerate his servant prescribing a measure of what he should eat or drink. Nevertheless, it is necessary that rulers occasionally remind themselves of this and see that not only Holy Scripture, but also the pagans, held nothing of such a "full" life and drunkenness.

It does not matter if some people laugh at this or make a mockery of it when one speaks of these and similar vices—especially those who are at the courts of Lords. For among them, [drinking] is the greatest art, and they even want to be praised for it, even when they do it in the crudest manner, and one drinks against another until he must die from it. This is written of Alexander the Great <note>original: "Alexandro, zu Macedonia"</note> of Macedonia: he once offered a golden crown as a prize to the one who could drink the most. A man named Promachus earned and won the crown by guzzling, but he lived no longer than three days afterward, and thus with a full belly he traveled to the Nobis Inn <note>The "Nobis Inn" (Nobiskrug) is a traditional German folk metaphor for hell or the grave; a place of no return for the godless.</note>.

It is no wonder that Alexander was a cause of this death and the intoxication of Promachus, for it is written of him that he himself was a great and powerful drinker. # The Second Part

[Ki]ngs <note>Completing the word from the previous page</note> / but also princes have the custom / that those / who serve them drink / must first taste the cup <term>Credenzen</term> <note>From the Italian 'credenza', this refers to the practice of a servant tasting a drink to prove it was not poisoned before handing it to a superior</note> / so that no poison might be mixed in. And because **Xenophon** / in this speech of **Cyrus** / says / "and you are not ashamed to do that which is forbidden to us children" / I will tell the history / that **Plutarch** writes of the **Spartans** or **Lacedaemonians** / who were provided with good laws by their King **Lycurgus**.

Therefore they had the custom / when they wished to discourage their youth from drunkenness / as from the most shameful of acts / they would take the coarsest and most boorish servants / who were called **Helots** <note>The Helots were a subjugated population in Sparta, often treated harshly to serve as a negative example to Spartan citizens</note> / and make them drunk and full as sows. When they were thus burdened with wine and excessive drink / and displayed strange and wondrous behaviors / as drunken, foul people are prone to do / the **Lacedaemonians** commanded / that these men / so drunk and full / must be led before their young sons and citizens / in their gatherings. This was done so that they might see and perceive / the great clumsiness and shameful gestures / of such drunken people / and be horrified by it as if by a misshapen / ugly / and stinking work / and guard themselves against it for their entire lives. For it appears quite strange / when such a drunken, senseless person comes among people / who are sober / and it is impossible / for one who possesses reason / not to be horrified and feel a localized dread toward it.

For this reason, **Plato** not unjustly forbade wine to rulers / such as mayors and the like / as long as they were in their office. Likewise, he—along with **Aristotle**, **Eusebius**, and the excellent physician **Galen**—praises the law of the **Carthaginians**. For as long as they were in times of war / and conducted military campaigns / no one was permitted or allowed to drink wine / but all were required / throughout the entire war / to drink water.

*You, with those jaws, with those flanks, with that gladiatorial strength of your whole body, had drained so much wine at Hippia’s wedding that you were forced to vomit the next day in the sight of the Roman people. Oh, what a thing, not only foul to see, but even to hear! If this had happened to you during dinner, amidst those massive cups of yours, who would not consider it disgraceful? But in an assembly of the people, while conducting public business, as the Master of the Horse <term>Magister Equitum</term>—for whom it would be shameful even to belch—you, by vomiting, filled your own lap and the entire tribunal where you sat with wine-smelling morsels of food.* <note>original Latin: "Tu istis faucibus, istis lateribus... gremium suum & totum tribunal impleuit."</note>

That is to say: With your gluttony and your whole body, you swilled so much wine at **Hippia’s** wedding that you had to give it back the following day before the entire Roman people. Now, whether this is a shameful thing not only to see but also to hear—even if such a thing had happened to you in the evening during a nightcap, it would still be regarded as nothing other than shameful frivolity. But you, before the entire Roman people, in an official public proceeding, a **Master of the Horse** <note>A high-ranking Roman official, second only to the Dictator</note>—to whom it would not even be appropriate to let out a belch—you filled not only your lap but the entire chair upon which you sat with the pieces you vomited up, which reeked of wine.

The **Locrians** <note>An ancient Greek tribe in southern Italy</note> had a law from **Zaleucus**, as **Aelianus** <note>Claudius Aelianus, a Roman author and teacher of rhetoric</note> writes: whoever among them was sick and drank unmixed wine without the command and order of a doctor—even if that person recovered and became healthy again—was nevertheless punished with death because he had drunk wine without an order.

If the heathens thus punished and hated such a vice as drunkenness, what would then be rightly becoming of us, who wish to be Christians? And although everyone should guard themselves against this to the highest degree, and drunkenness is becoming to no one, regardless of their station, it nonetheless appears most scandalous in great lords and rulers. What sometimes follows for them from this is something all potentates should mirror in the example of the **Emperor Zeno** <note>The Eastern Roman Emperor from 474–491 CE</note>, of whom the histories report that he was accustomed to swilling so much wine that he often lost all reason and senses; and when he had drunk so, there was no difference between him and a dead corpse. Once, when he had swilled much wine and lay there as if he were about to die, his own wife, the **Empress Ariadne**—who was an enemy to him on account of such swilling—ordered him to be carried into the imperial tomb as if he were a dead man, and had a great stone placed upon him. When he had slept off the wine and came to himself again, he howled and cried out loudly, but in vain; for no one dared to help him or open the grave by order of **Ariadne**. And this Emperor, who had been an adversary to everyone and had practiced much tyranny for seventeen years, died a miserable and yet well-deserved death, paying for his drunkenness and carousing with his life.

# That it is a Princely work, and fitting for great Kings and Princes, to establish Libraries.

## The Eighth Chapter.

It is hardly possible to believe how difficult it was for the ancients to produce books, unless one considers, firstly, that all books had to be written by hand, which took a great deal of time and leisure. And if one had to pay another to copy such books, it cost a great deal of money. Secondly, those same books were commonly written entirely upon parchment, which also had to be produced at great expense. Although, for lack of parchment, some also wrote upon birch bark, from which books were then called *Codices*, as if they were *Cortices* <note>The author is noting a Latin etymological theory: *codex* (book/trunk) is related to *cortex* (bark/outer layer).</note>. From this, it is not a little surprising that the ancients devoted such diligence to study and were able to attain such great art and wisdom, as well as bringing together such a great multitude of books. But regardless of this, it is found in the histories that great kings and princes spared no expense to bring the best books from all over the world to themselves, from which their descendants might recover all kinds of knowledge.

So did **Ptolemy Philadelphus** <note>Ptolemy II (308–246 BCE), king of Ptolemaic Egypt, famous for the Library of Alexandria</note>, the Egyptian King, who established a beautiful and magnificent library, which has been described as: *A most beautiful monument of royal wealth, which was an extraordinary work of royal elegance and care.* <note>original: "Pulcherrimum regiæ opulentiæ monimentum, quod elegantiæ Regum curæq; egregium opus fuit."</note> A beautiful and magnificent work, which well becomes a king and creates an eternal memory. In this he was aided by **Demetrius Phalereus** <note>An Athenian orator and statesman who helped found the Library of Alexandria</note>, an

# The Second Part

[...What a] treasure must have been among those very best of books? What would they have cost to write and witness? How many excellent authors must have perished there, never to come to light again?

But here, the reader might find it unbelievable that I have written of four hundred thousand books burning at Alexandria, and might think me "taking a shot" (as they say). This is especially true for those who have read Seneca on this matter, who mentions only forty thousand. However, I have not done this without reason, but have looked widely enough through historical accounts.

Therefore, the reader will cease to wonder when he reads what Eusebius writes in *The Preparation for the Gospel* <note>original: *de præparatione Euangelica*</note>, Book 8, Chapter 1. There he records the words of Aristeas, which in English <note>original: "Teutschen" (German). The author is quoting a German translation of a Greek source; I have rendered the quote into English for the modern reader.</note> read as follows: When the administrator or head of the Royal Library in Egypt received a significant sum of money and used it to buy and transcribe books from far and wide, wherever he could get them, the King asked him in my presence (says Aristeas): How many books had he already collected? To which he answered: There were more than two hundred thousand, and he hoped they would shortly become no fewer than five hundred thousand—not only from all of Greece, but also from the Jews, who had many good and useful books. From this, it can be easily understood that many more books must have been available in that place than Seneca indicates. It is true, it is a large number and almost unbelievable, and even for a wealthy king, it is not easy to produce. This is especially true when one considers how books were produced at that time; one had to buy a single book for a hundred <term>Guilders</term> <note>A gold coin used throughout Europe; in the early modern period, 100 Guilders was a massive sum, equivalent to the annual salary of a master craftsman.</note> or more. This is easy to believe, since only 70 years ago, Cicero’s *Familiar Letters* <note>original: *Familiares Ciceronis Epistolæ*</note> were bought in Milan for ten <term>Ducats</term> <note>A high-purity gold coin. The author is highlighting how the price of books plummeted after the invention of the printing press.</note>, as Philelphus writes to Petrus Perleo; yet today one can buy them beautifully printed for barely five <term>Groschen</term> <note>A common silver coin of much lower value than a Ducat.</note>.

Therefore, Gellius writes in Book 6, Chapter 17—and Sabellicus, Hedio, and others agree with him—that such a mass of books was brought together by the Ptolemies in Egypt that their number reached seven hundred thousand. He says and asserts that they all burned and perished at once during the war in Alexandria, as mentioned above. However, he says: **"Not intentionally, nor by a planned act, but set on fire by chance by auxiliary soldiers,"** <note>original: *Non sponte, neq; opera consulta, sed à militibus fortè auxiliariis incensa*</note> meaning that it was not done on purpose, but happened by accident because of the soldiers. I had to point this out so that no one would think that four hundred thousand was put in place of forty thousand by mistake or ignorance.

Nor should anyone wonder at this great number of books. For the potentates, kings, and emperors of old had more passion for books and the fine arts than is seen in the present time. As Opsopoeus also testifies when he writes: **"This was once a notable pursuit of Kings and Princes, to ensure with the greatest diligence that the monuments and books of ancient writers were preserved."** <note>original: *Fuit hoc quondam Regum & Principum memorabile studium, summa diligentia curare, vt veterum scriptorum monumenta ac libri conseruarentur.*</note> That is: In former times it

-># Of the Book of Rulers.<-
<page-num>61</page-num>

...it was a special diligence among the great kings and princes to make this provision, that good and useful books might be diligently kept. Therefore, Capitolinus <note>Julius Capitolinus, one of the authors of the *Augustan History*.</note> writes that **Serenus Sammonicus**, in his will, bequeathed and left sixty-two thousand books to the Emperor **Gordian the Younger** <note>original: *Gordiano Juniori*</note>, which was counted as one of the greatest honors for this Gordian.

Likewise, Leonicus writes in *On Various Histories* <note>original: *De varia Historia*</note> that **Epaphroditus of Chaeronea** <note>original: *Epaphroditus Cheroneus*</note>, who lived under the Emperor **Nero** and was one of his scribes, possessed thirty thousand of the very best books.

Also, Calvisius <note>original: *Caluisius*</note>, Caesar’s friend, added to the increasing shame and vice of **Mark Antony** <note>original: *Antonio*</note> that Antony gave Queen **Cleopatra** a whole library of parchment, in which there were two hundred thousand books.

In the same way, **Lucius Lucullus** <note>original: *L. Lucullus*</note> diligently had many beautiful books written and brought together. The use and enjoyment of these brought him more praise and honor than the fact that he was otherwise a great lord. For he allowed all learned people free access and entry to these books of his, so that they might use them. Therefore, the Greeks, when they were at leisure, retreated there as if to **the most pleasant lodging-house of the Muses** <note>original: *velut amœnissimum quoddam Musarum diuersorium*</note>—that is, like a delightful inn of all the good arts—and spent the day there in great pleasure and joy, speaking and disputing. Whenever Lucullus learned that the most learned people were gathered and disputing, he would join them there.

**Charlemagne** <note>original: *Carolus Magnus*</note> also had a great desire for the free arts, which are called in Latin the **liberal arts** <note>original: *Artes liberales*</note>. He honored them most highly, held their doctors in magnificent regard, and bestowed great honors upon them. Regarding his books—as he had a beautiful library <note>original: *Bibliothecam*</note> and a great quantity of them—he ordered that those who desired them after his death should buy them at a fair price, and he decreed that the proceeds from these sales should be given to the poor.

Likewise, history records that under the Emperor **Zeno** <note>original: *Zenone*</note>, there was a powerful and heavy fire in **Constantinople**, during which the greater part of the city burned, and among other things, one hundred and twenty thousand books were destroyed. Among these were also the books of **Homer**, which were written there in golden letters on a dragon's skin one hundred and twenty feet <note>original: *Schuch* (feet)</note> long.

And this single work of art is indeed to be mourned, for Homer was so highly loved by the potentates of old. As **Pliny** reports, when **Alexander the Great** <note>original: *Alexander Magnus*</note>—among the spoils of the defeated King **Darius** of Persia <note>original: *Darij*</note>—obtained the chest of all his jewels, in which there was gold, pearls, and a great many precious stones, and Alexander’s surrounding counselors suggested various uses for it, he said: "By the god **Hercules**! One should preserve the books of Homer above all things, so that such a magnificent work of human reason may be kept in a precious vessel." Oh, what a beautiful and brave speech, befitting such a king.

# The Second Part
<meta>catchword: this</meta>

**Matthias Corvinus, King of Hungary**, kept a distinguished library in **Buda** <note>Now part of Budapest. Matthias Corvinus (r. 1458–1490) was one of the most significant patrons of the Renaissance in Central Europe.</note>. He sought out the most select Greek and Latin authors from Asia, Greece, and Italy, and everywhere else, making it not only the most ornate but also the most abundant in every genre of books. That is: Matthias, King of Hungary, established and gathered at Buda a magnificent and beautiful library of the best authors in the Greek and Latin languages from all of Asia, Greece, and Italy, arranged in the most splendid manner.

Regarding this, I will here relate several examples of how dearly and highly the ancients valued certain special books. For one reads that **Largius Licinius** wanted to give **Pliny the Elder** <note>original: *Plinio Maiori*. Pliny was a Roman author and naturalist.</note> for his *Commentaries*—which were not as numerous then as they are now—**four hundred thousand sesterces** <note>original: *quadringentos mille nummûm, siue quadringenta sestertia*</note>. That amounts to over ten thousand guilders <note>A significant sum of gold coins in the author's time</note>, and yet he could not obtain them. Likewise, Pliny reports that **Isocrates**, the excellent Greek orator, sold a single oration for **twenty talents** <note>original: *viginti talentis*</note>; that makes twelve thousand crowns.

Therefore, **Budé** <note>Guillaume Budé (1467–1540), a famous French Renaissance humanist and scholar.</note> writes not without reason: *“What king now would wish to buy a most crowded library for ten thousand gold pieces? For how much did a single private citizen dare to bid for certain impromptu writings from Pliny? And yet Pliny did not wish to sell them for so much.”*

Which king now spends ten thousand guilders at once on a fully equipped library, which a citizen once offered to Pliny for a single book, and yet could not get from him?

And even if, because of these current evil times, all of this is despised and turned into a joke, I must still point out one history which is just as much to be wondered at as the others. For we read in the Greek author **Athenaeus** that King **Alexander the Great** <note>original: *Alexander Magnus*</note> spent **eight hundred talents** <note>original: *octingenta talenta*</note>—which makes four hundred and eighty thousand French crowns—on the books *On the History of Animals* <note>original: *de Historia Animalium*</note>, concerning the nature of all animals. Through this, hunters and all sorts of people were commissioned to obtain and maintain the animals. Concerning this, Pliny relates more of the reasons when he writes thus:

> *Aristotle records various things; he is a man whom I believe should be followed in large part in these matters. King Alexander the Great, inflamed with a desire to know the natures of animals, delegated this commentary to Aristotle, a man supreme in all learning. He ordered several thousand men throughout the regions of all Asia and Greece to obey him—all those who lived by hunting, fowling, and fishing, and those who had charge of game preserves, herds, beehives, fish ponds, and aviaries—so that nothing anywhere in the world would be unknown to him. By questioning these men, he composed those fifty famous volumes on animals.*

That is: When Alexander the Great desired to know the nature of all animals and commanded the description of them to **Aristotle**—as an excellent man in all the arts—he assigned to him in Asia and Greece several thousand men and commanded them to obey him, so that he might inquire of them everything belonging to hunting, bird-catching, and fishing. These men also prepared ponds, game parks, aviaries, and other houses for nature, so that he would lack nothing...

# Of the Book of Regents

...of this inquiry was necessary, lest something be missing; for which reason he <note>Aristotle</note> also wrote fifty precious books on the nature and character of animals.

It is also counted as a special praise for the Lacedemonians <note>The Spartans</note>, when they devastated the Boeotians and Thebans with fire and flame, that they spared the house of the poet **Pindar** and refrained from damaging it. This same act is also attributed to King **Alexander the Great** by Arrian <note>Flavius Arrianus, a Greek historian of the Roman period</note> and Pliny.

However, since one now has such convenience for producing books as has never existed since the beginning of the world: firstly, that paper can be produced as a necessity; and secondly, and most importantly, that we have the benefit of the **printing press** <term>Druck: movable type printing</term>—which was invented roughly a hundred years ago in **Germany** for the advancement of such matters—with which one can accomplish more in a single week than many could previously have written by hand in an entire year. Therefore, in our times, the best **authors** <note>original: *Authores*</note>, as many as remain available, have come to light again, and a great number of books can be obtained for little money.

Thus, one may well find a citizen or some other scholar in a city who has more good books than a king or prince could have possessed or produced in former times; as I have seen in the house of an honorable citizen in **Naumburg on the Saale**, named **Balten Beier**. Consequently, princes and lords should also strive with the highest diligence so that they do not let such convenience pass by in vain. For many a book is printed now that will hardly be available again in a hundred years if one does not keep them with diligence. Considering that a prince today may well gamble away so much in one evening that he could have established a magnificent library <term>Liberey: an early modern term for a library</term> with it. 

But nevertheless, the princely counselors usually have these thoughts: once they have brought their lord's affairs to the point where he has a precious game park for hunting, and they have arranged his chamber estates and income to the highest degree, and have equipped the armory <term>Zeughauß: a building used for storing weapons and armor</term> with all necessities, with cannons and other artillery <term>Artalerey</term>—regardless of the fact that it was done to the detriment of the poor subjects—they feel they have accomplished everything well. And meanwhile, they do not think even once of **religion** or the **fine arts**, with which we are richly graced by **GOD** in these final and dangerous times, so that we might not only preserve them in our times but also pass them on to our descendants.

And such things would most befit bishops, abbotts, cathedral canons, and the like, since they have enough wealth and income for it; it would also not be ill-suited to their office and calling. But I do not know how it happens that they prefer to concern themselves with other profane matters and worldly dealings and governance, and thus desire to be worldly against their name and calling; also that they prefer to apply their income—with which they were richly endowed and gifted by emperors, kings, and princes—to other ways than for the establishment of schools or public libraries. For tell me, which bishop concerns himself in these times with such things? Are they not almost all, with few exceptions, more directed toward their pomp...

# That a Prince or Regent
## should be subject to the Law.

### The Ninth Chapter.

<image-desc>Large decorative woodcut initial 'E' featuring an architectural frame and a seated figure holding a book or scroll.</image-desc>
There is a great dispute among many people, both learned and unlearned, as to whether a King, Prince, or Regent is also obliged to conduct himself according to the Law, and to be obedient and subject to it. And when one looks at the old written laws, it is found that they say and intend that an Emperor or Prince should be unbound by the Law, as Ulpian <note>Domitius Ulpianus, a prominent Roman jurist of the 2nd century AD</note> says: **The Prince himself is released from the laws** <note>original Latin: *Princeps autem ipse legibus solutus est*</note>.

I understand this text to mean that the subjects have no right to prescribe laws to a Prince or Regent, but rather the Prince prescribes them to the subjects. However, whatever the Prince agrees upon, vows, or promises to his subjects, he is nevertheless obliged to keep. If it were to have any other meaning—namely, that a Prince wished to be bound by no laws at all—then it would be more likened to tyranny than to the Law.

Accordingly, it is written <note>Referring to the *Decretum Gratiani*, a collection of Canon Law</note>: **It is just.** <note>original Latin: *9. dist. c. Iustum est*</note> It is just for the Prince to obey his own laws, for then he may consider his own rights worth guarding when he himself pays reverence to them. Princes are held by their own laws, nor can they condemn in themselves the rights which they establish for their subjects. For the authority of their voice is just if they do not allow themselves what they forbid to the people.

That is: It is indeed a fair thing that a Prince follows the laws he has given and conducts himself accordingly. For he should only truly expect that the laws be guarded and kept by everyone if the Prince himself guards and keeps them with diligence. For Princes cannot make the laws—which they have prescribed and commanded others to keep—ineffectual for themselves. Rather, it is much more fitting, as it is inherently fair and right, to take heed that when they forbid something to their subjects, they also consider it forbidden to themselves.

The praiseworthy Emperors **Theodosius** and **Valentinian** <note>The text says "Valerianus," but historically refers to the 5th-century emperors associated with the *Digna Vox* decree</note> also considered and weighed this, and deemed it fair and just that an Emperor should submit himself to the Law. As one reads in the law: **A Worthy Voice.** <note>original Latin: *l. Digna vox. C. de legibus, & constitutionibus Principum*</note> There it stands: It is a voice worthy of the majesty of one reigning to profess that he, as Prince, is bound by the laws; so much does our authority depend upon the authority of the Law, and in truth, it is greater than the empire to submit the principality to the laws...

Of the Book of Regents.

<meta>catchword: power</meta>

...and by the oracle of the present edict, we judge what we do not allow to ourselves. <note>Original Latin: *tum, & oraculo præsentis edicti, quod nobis licere non patimur, iudicamus.* This is the conclusion of the *Digna vox* decree from the *Codex Justinianus*, a foundational legal text which states that it is a statement worthy of a ruler's majesty to profess themselves bound by the laws.</note>

The meaning of this law is roughly this in English: that an Emperor should not be ashamed even if he is bound by the Law or subject to the same, because all his authority and power flow from the Law, etc. And although some wish to interpret this law or legal maxim to mean that Emperors, Kings, Princes, and Regents are not obliged to be subject to the Law in any other way or further than they choose to do so voluntarily and of their own accord, rather than out of duty—yet no one, if they consider the matter rightly, can give this law any other interpretation more in accordance with the Law, honor, and equity for many excellent reasons, other than that we must all confess and say: if a Prince or Lord wishes to govern a realm or principality rightly, or if matters in that kingdom or land are to proceed correctly, then the authorities as well as the subjects must be bound and subject to the Law. This means they are just as obliged as others to do and act according to what is right, honorable, and equitable <term>Billigkeit: a legal concept referring to fairness and justice beyond the strict letter of the law</term>, and they should seek no advantage beyond their due taxes, rents, and what properly belongs to them. It is also not advisable that they be granted so much leeway that they might act according to their whim and against the Law. For if the idea were to prevail that everyone could rule as they pleased, a "fine" sort of government <note>The author is being sarcastic here: "ein fein Regiment" implies a chaotic or poor one.</note> would soon arise in the world; since human nature is so entirely evil and perverse that very few are found in the world who do what is right and equitable of their own accord and without compulsion, even if they are among the most pious.

Accordingly, Socrates (who was praised and held by the whole world to be not only clever and wise but also pious and just) said that human nature is so fashioned that even if a man were the most pious, and if fortune favored him and he gained such power and might over people that he could do with them as he pleased, he would nevertheless become proud and arrogant because of it. For it is not in every man's nature and character to be able to moderate himself in a state of good fortune and high power so that he does not exalt himself. As the Poet <note>Referring to the Roman poet Ovid</note> says:

->Minds usually run riot in prosperity,<- <note>original Latin: *Luxuriant animi rebus plerunq; secundis*</note>
->And it is not easy to bear favorable circumstances with an even mind.<- <note>original Latin: *Nec facilè est æqua commoda mente pati.*</note>

That is, as the common proverb says: **It takes strong legs to bear good days.** <note>A German idiom meaning it requires a strong character to remain humble and disciplined when experiencing wealth or success.</note>

Therefore, praiseworthy Regents, Kings, Princes, and Lords, who are accustomed to leading an upright government <term>Regiment: the act or system of ruling</term>, usually conduct themselves in such a way that they leave their subjects to their old customs, protect and maintain them in equality and justice, and adhere to the Law themselves. Likewise, in their councils, they employ such people who speak of matters in no other way than what is according to honor, the Law, and equity. For it is easy for anyone to consider and conclude for themselves that if power were given to an individual person to act outside the Law and solely according to their own whim...

# The Second Part

...granting power and might, so that it could not well fail that many things must happen contrary to Law and Equity <term>Equity: from the German 'Billigkeit,' referring to fairness and justice that follows the spirit rather than just the letter of the law</term> and be tolerated by such regents.

From which it follows that these cities and lands are best governed where one person as well as the other must be satisfied with equality and Justice, and no one can have any preference or advantage. Accordingly, Demaratus, the King of Sparta, when he was asked why he had allowed himself to be deposed and driven out since he was King, gave as an answer: It happened because in that place the Law was more and greater than the royal power. By this, he wished to indicate and give to understand that a King should be subject to the Law just as much as his subject. Therefore, Archidamus, when he was asked what kind of regents the Lacedemonians <note>Lacedemonians: another name for the Spartans of ancient Greece</note> had, he answered: "The Law, and the Authorities who behave according to the Law," thereby indicating that the supreme power should not reside with the regents, but should be placed and lie with the Law, and that no regent should be permitted to begin or undertake anything contrary to the Law.

In such a manner, Chilo the Lacedemonian also exhorted his citizens that they should, above all things, be obedient to the Law, which is said to regents and princes just as much as to subjects. For although they may imagine, and would sometimes like to direct matters so that they might be "freer"—as the saying goes—and not subject to the Law, yet that is wrong. For where could a better and more stable government be established than where the Law binds one as well as the other? The Lord as well as the subject. And it is not possible, where one governs in such a manner, using the Law alone, and no one has to fear violence or any tyranny and inequality, that things can go poorly there. Therefore, the historians write of the Emperor Trajan that when he was once before the Roman Magistrate, he drew his sword and gave it unsheathed to his Marshal, saying:
> Receive this sword; if I am good, use it for me; if not, use it against me.
> <note>Original Latin: *Accipe hunc gladium, & si bonus fuero, pro me, sin minus, contra me vtere.*</note>
> That is: Take the sword; if I act rightly, use it for me; if I do wrong, use it against me.

Someone once asked Pausanias why the old laws and statutes in Sparta were not allowed to be changed. To him, this answer was given: That the laws were more than the citizens, and the citizens had no power over the laws, but the laws over the citizens.

# Of the Book of Regents.

...servant of the Law, and has no right to assume or employ anything further against the Law.

One reads of King Agesilaus <note>Agesilaus II (c. 444–360 BC) was a prominent king of Sparta known for his military leadership in Asia Minor.</note> that when he had conquered a large part of Asia and intended to march directly against the King of the Persians to attack him—for although the latter led no open war, he nonetheless hired other people with money to attack the Spartans and besiege the city—Agesilaus was therefore called home to save the city. As soon as he saw the letters from the Council, he halted the war and departed, saying that no one is a true captain who is not obedient to the Law and the Council. Likewise, at another time when he was called out of Asia, he gave this written answer to the Ephors: <note>The Ephors were five senior Spartan magistrates who oversaw the kings.</note> "Although we have conquered the greater part of Asia, driven the enemies therefrom, and fought and won several battles in Ionia; nevertheless, because you have set a day for me and called me away by command of the Council, I will follow this letter, or perhaps even arrive before it. For I rule not for my own sake alone, but for the sake of the Common Good, and for those who have united and bound themselves to it."

But as soon as a regent or prince sets the Law aside and lets it go, then either pure tyranny or else a shameful, devilish, and un-Christian life and being must follow, as one may sufficiently see from the following history. The histories say that Antonius Caracalla, <note>Marcus Aurelius Antoninus, known as Caracalla (reigned 198–217 AD), a Roman Emperor famous for his cruelty.</note> the Roman Emperor, once happened by chance to come upon his stepmother <note>The text refers to Julia Domna. While she was his mother, historical rumors often styled her as his stepmother to emphasize the scandal of their supposed relationship.</note>—a very beautiful woman—when she was uncovered, and he said to her: "If it were possible, I would gladly have you as my wife." To this she answered him: "If it pleases you, then it is also fitting for you. Do you not know that you are the Roman Emperor, who may give the Law to everyone, but needs to take the Law from no one, and are subject to no one?" Because he was thus permitted to do and allow as he pleased, the Law could not hinder him if he only had desire and love for her. By this speech, the Emperor was moved to a shameful and unseemly deed, which was against Law, Nature, and Reason, in that he took his stepmother as his wife.

The histories also report that someone asked Acamenes <note>Likely referring to Alcamenes, an early King of Sparta.</note> why he had refused the gifts and presents that the Messenians had offered him.

> Because if I had accepted them, he said, I could not have remained at peace with the Laws. <note>original: "Quoniam si recepissem, inquit, cum Legibus pacem habere non poteram."</note>

Therefore (he says), if I had taken them, I could have had no peace with the laws. This is a spirit truly worthy of an empire, which held the authority of the Law in higher esteem than great and personal profit. And where are those (says Erasmus) <note>Desiderius Erasmus (1466–1536), the famous Renaissance humanist who wrote extensively on the education of a Christian prince.</note> who cry out:

> What has pleased the Prince has the force of Law, and the Prince indeed gives laws, but is not bound by laws? <note>original: "Quod Principi placuit, Legis vigorem habet, & Principem dare quidem leges, at non tenere legibus?" This is a reference to the Roman legal maxim *Lex Regia*.</note>

That is: What pleases the prince has the strength and power of Law, and the prince indeed gives laws but is not subject to them.

Has not this King bravely struck down and answered the speech of the flatterer, who wanted all things to be fitting for a King? For the King is not the ruler <note>original: *Richtscheid* — a carpenter’s straight-edge or leveling tool, used here as a metaphor for the standard of truth.</note> of honor and fairness; rather, he is a servant of that which is honorable and fair. Oh, would to God, says *Erasmus*, that the ears of our Christian Princes did not hear such flattering speech, or if they heard it, that they would despise and reject it with the same earnestness as *Antigonus*. What else do they do, those who whisper in the ears of Princes and say—as mentioned above—*What has pleased the Prince has the force of law*? <note>original: *Quod Principi placuit, legis vigorem habet* — a famous maxim of Roman law used to justify the absolute power of the Emperor.</note> Those who deny that the Prince is bound by the laws? That is: there are some who give the Prince two kinds of power: namely, an ordinary power and a general one. The ordinary power extends no further than the laws, treaties, and judgments. But the other extends to everything in general. But are these not shameful and harmful hypocrites, and desperate scoundrels, who undertake to blind Princes and Lords with such clumsy and unfair talk?

Likewise, it is written of the tyrant, Emperor *Caligula*, when his grandmother *Antonia*—who was of great standing—admonished him and argued that he acted wrongly in many things, he answered her: *Remember that everything is permitted to me over everyone.* <note>original: *Memento mihi omnia in omnes licere.*</note> Such *monsters* <note>original: *Portenta* — literally "omens" or "prodigies," used here to describe the freakish nature of tyrants.</note> and sea-wonders the world produced as Emperors at 그 time. > *He who is allowed more than is right, desires more than is allowed.* <note>original: *Cui plus licet, quàm par est, plus vult, quàm licet.*</note>

So also *Arrianus* writes that he who respects this sentence of a "wise man" is far astray:

> "It is not necessary for a King to act with a choice of what is just; rather, whatever is done or decreed by him, whatever its nature, must be held as just, etc." <note>original: *Non oportere Regem cum delectu iusta agere...*</note>

Here it might well be said that such regents have followed the defiant word from the tragedies, where it is said:

> "Yes, to be holy and to fear God—the common people may consider such things good; but Princes do as they lust and as they will."

Therefore *Livy* writes a fine sentence: *Kings at home draw all things and times to themselves and do not follow them; nevertheless, only what is just and honorable is permitted to a Prince who truly rules.* <note>original: *Reges domi rerū temporumq; trahunt cuncta, non sequuntur, Attamen quæ iusta sunt & honesta, ea licent Principi, verè principianti.*</note> That is: although Kings in their houses draw everything after themselves and need follow no one, it nevertheless becomes a Prince well that he reaches no further in his dealings than law and honor extend.

...but I will let it rest at that. Every sensible person will be able to judge for themselves and understand what the truth is in this case—namely, that a Prince should look more toward what is honorable, right, and fair, rather than what he has the power to do. Whoever wishes to be overly clever, to flatter great lords, and to court their favor when they occasionally overstep their bounds and forget the Law, may do so. However, it befits an honest man to confess and speak the truth and the Law, rather than to flatter anyone and thereby strengthen their vice. For it happens far too often already that people overreach, even if one does not point the way, open the doors and windows for them, or excuse them when they grab for too much.

To this also belongs the proverb used by vassals <term>Lehenmañ: a feudal tenant who holds land from a lord in exchange for service and loyalty</term> against their lords, which says: **Faithful Lord, faithful servant.** For the Lord is duty-bound to show the same faithfulness to the vassal as the vassal must show to the Lord. For these are the words in the chapter on the form of faithfulness: *The Lord must also return the favor to his faithful subject in all these things; if he does not do so, he shall rightly be judged unfaithful.* <note>original: "Dominus quoq; in his omnibus vicem fideli suo reddere debet, quod si non fecerit, merito censebitur malefidus." From the *Libri Feudorum*, a collection of feudal law.</note> This means: In all these cases, the Lord is bound to the vassal in the same measure as the man is to the Lord. And if he behaves otherwise toward him, he may not unfairly be scolded for unfaithfulness.

Therefore, let a pious, faithful, and honorable Jurist take heart from an excellent man named **Papinianus**, whom history calls the *Refuge of the Law and the Treasury of Legal Learning.* <note>original: "Iuris asylum, & doctrinæ legalis thesaurum." Aemilius Papinianus was a celebrated Roman jurist of the 2nd century AD.</note> This honest legal expert <term>Iurisconsultus: a professional legal consultant and scholar</term> was asked by the Emperor **Antoninus Caracalla**—of whom we just spoke—to excuse the shameful murder he had committed against his brother Geta, and to justify it before the Council in Rome. But Papinianus would not do it. Instead, he said to Bassianus <note>Bassianus was another name for Emperor Caracalla.</note>: *It is much easier to commit a murder than to excuse it.* <note>original: "Multò facilius est parricidium fieri, quam exculari."</note> Because of this, the aforementioned Emperor had him beheaded and strangled before his very eyes. And he did so with these words: *You should have carried out my command with the sword.* <note>original: "Gladio te exequi oportuit meum iussum." Caracalla's retort implies that a soldier obeys with the sword, and the lawyer's duty was to provide the "verbal weapon" of an excuse.</note> Therefore, this man is worthy of eternal praise and is an ornament to all faithful Jurists, for he chose to be killed rather than to approve of and defend injustice.

In our times, however, almost everyone follows **Favorinus**. The Emperor **Hadrian** once entered into a dispute with him and rebuked him for a word that could actually have been defended as right and good. When Favorinus's associates and good friends criticized him for yielding to Hadrian's unfairness regarding this word—since it had been used by excellent authors—he answered with a laugh, saying: *You advise me poorly, my friends, for you cannot bear it that a man who commands thirty legions should be considered more learned than I.* <note>original: "Non rectè, sed malè mihi suadetis familiares, qui non illum me doctiorem haberi ab omnibus, æquo animo feratis, qui triginta Legionibus imperet." This anecdote is recorded in the *Augustan History*.</note> That is to say: You do not advise me well, dear friends, because you cannot stand it if he, who has over thirty legions to rule and command, is seen as more learned than I.

# That one should judge according to the written Law, and not according to personal Reason; and concerning Jurists.

## The Tenth Chapter.

<image-desc>An ornate woodcut initial 'N' depicting floral vines and scrollwork in a square frame.</image-desc>

NOW, since in these times of ours many people are heard and found—of both high and low standing—who hold the opinion that because the Law is so extensive, and because **Jurists** <note>The term "Jurist" refers to those professionally trained in the law. In the 16th century, they were often criticized for over-complicating cases and causing expensive delays.</note> at times not only handle it with great delay, but also grossly abuse it for their own advantage—to the extent that there is almost no case so bad or "leaky" <note>The original German *löcherig* literally means "holey," referring to a case full of legal flaws or gaps.</note> that the Jurists do not dare to defend and pursue it through legal means—it is often said of them that it would be better if one did away with the Jurists and the written Law altogether. Instead, it is argued that matters should be judged by **Honorable People** according to **Reason**, since Law itself ultimately flows from Reason. Those who hold such thoughts are not simple folk; rather, one finds among them great Princes, Lords of the nobility, and other worldly-wise and sensible people. And if I am to speak and confess the truth, I have also occasionally been of that same opinion. However, if one wishes to rightly weigh and consider the matter, it is found that this opinion is false and incorrect. It is much better and more convenient to have a constant and written Law than to have one person hold this, and another person hold that, to be right and fair, as may be understood from the following reasons.

For firstly, I would like to see it if six or seven of you—more or fewer—sat down together, and someone came and brought a bad and tangled case which required much debate (as not all matters are clear and bright), how those who were seated would accord space to **Equity** <term>Billigkeit: a legal concept where a judge rules based on fairness and conscience rather than the strict, literal letter of the law</term> and pronounce judgment according to Reason in such a way that they hit the mark and did not miss the right path. I fear that if it concerned me, it would go for me as it did for that character in **Terence** <note>Terence (Publius Terentius Afer) was a Roman playwright whose comedies were staple texts in Renaissance education. The author is referencing a scene from the play *Phormio*.</note>, who said after his friends had given him long advice: *I know much less than before where I stand; for one says this, the other that, and the third considers it further for deliberation.*

It is indeed true and not without merit that there are many sharp-witted heads and fine, wise, clever people in the world who, with their understanding and speech, far surpass many a Jurist. Nevertheless, it would not be good, nor advisable, that the direction of the Law should be left entirely to them. For as much as **Passions** <note>Original: *Affect*. In this context, it refers to human emotions, biases, or personal interests that cloud objective judgment.</note> and various paths exist by which a man can be led astray from the right track, man is also so inclined that the more leeway he is given, the worse he becomes. Additionally, even if they thought they had hit upon the best solution and settled it, every person would still not be satisfied or content with it,

<summary>The author argues against the popular Renaissance-era idea of abolishing codified law and lawyers in favor of "natural reason." He contends that without written laws, judgments would become inconsistent and biased by human emotion.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the argument that judging based on written laws is superior to relying on the subjective "reason" of an individual. The previous page ended by stating that it is much better to follow established law than to let a ruler decide cases based on his own whims.</meta>

<header>Of the Book of Rulers.</header>
<page-num>66</page-num>

...or even to be satisfied with it. For I have seen many people—and they are found elsewhere as well—who are of such a nature that they would rather do anything than yield even slightly to their opponent once they have fallen into strife and quarreling with them, unless they are compelled to do so by the utmost force of the law. From this, one can easily conclude that such people would not be satisfied by a mere instruction <note>An "instruction" here refers to a judge's informal guidance or a ruling based on personal opinion rather than statute.</note>, but rather the judge would fall into danger if he could not justify his pronounced judgment with the foundation of the law.

On the other hand, you will also find those who sometimes entrust their affairs to their friendships, or at other times to honorable and upright men, so that they do not have to quarrel or fight in court. Some are also so minded that they would rather let everything go, or patiently suffer what happens to them or what is taken from them, before they would involve themselves in a legal dispute with someone. But since there are not many such people, and this happens quite rarely—whereas the majority, as one sees, tends to make use of the law—it must finally be concluded that it is necessary to maintain a certain rule and measure, so that people may be judged regarding their failings and the disputes between them may be settled.

Since it is not feasible to judge and pronounce sentence simply according to reason—as was mentioned and explained above—one can have no other or more certain rule than to adhere to the **written laws** as they are currently in use, to follow them, and not to let oneself be pushed or led away from them. For it is certain that even the wisest of men, if they were to speak and judge according to reason, would not do it more certainly or better.

And although some might say that the Emperor himself preferred <term>Equity</term> <note>In a legal sense, "Equity" (Billigkeit) refers to the principle of fairness that balances or softens the application of strict, literal law to prevent injustice in specific cases.</note> to strict law—as is indeed true in the law *Placuit* in the Code *concerning Judgments* <note>original: *l. Placuit. C. de Iudicijs*</note>—this is not to be understood in any other sense than that of **written equity** <note>original: *& sic de æquitate scripta*</note>, and not according to every man's personal whim. In my opinion, it would be the same thing to set aside and abolish written law as if one wanted to burn and eradicate the books of medicine written by **Galen**, **Hippocrates**, and other excellent physicians, and then every person would attempt to help and advise another regarding their health according to their own whim—not according to medicine—as sometimes happens when everyone tries to meddle in this noble art: priests, Jews, wanderers, old women, barbers, and the like.

Likewise, it would be the same as when in former times **Lycurgus** <note>The legendary lawgiver of Sparta.</note> commanded the **Lacedaemonians** <note>Another name for the Spartans.</note> to root out the vineyards because people were enticed to drunkenness by them. As **Pliny** also says: "We owe it to wine that we drink even when we are not thirsty" <note>original: *Vino debemus, quòd non sitientes bibimus.*</note>. For all kinds of vices arise from drunkenness, yet this is not the fault of the wine, but of those who shamefully abuse the noble gifts of God. And so it is true that it is better to hold to a written law than to judge according to reason—
