# The Second Part 3

Emperor **Alexander Severus** loved **Ulpian**, the excellent jurist who was then Chief Chancellor <note>Ulpian (c. 170–223 AD) was a famous Roman jurist and Praetorian Prefect under Alexander Severus.</note> and held in such high regard at the Imperial court that the Emperor honored and loved him as a father. Because of this, Ulpian faced significant danger and envy. As is common at the courts of great lords, those who stand in favor and have more influence than others are often hated and persecuted by others. Anyone who refuses to say only what people want to hear, or who does not simply agree with everyone’s opinion and let things be, must expect such risks.

When Ulpian attempted to talk sense into the great masses, the commanders, and the officials—intervening so that they would not overreach or become too arrogant in the luxury and pride that grew during times of peace, but instead remain satisfied with equity and justice—they became so embittered against him that they rioted several times in open audience in the Imperial hall and in the presence of the Emperor. They would have eventually stabbed him to death if he had not been protected by the Emperor, who covered him with his own cloak and offered his own body as a shield.

By this example, the Emperor intended to show great princes and lords that they should not only protect their faithful advisors as their own limbs but also defend the **teachings of the law**—by which justice and right are maintained—even at the risk of their own bodies and lives. This is what princes and lords have done until now and continue to do, regardless of the fact that it annoys some.

It is true that some jurists occasionally abuse the law, as mentioned before. However, if the authorities would remember their office and do what is right, they would break the power of such jurists and not tolerate or suffer them in the **consistories** <term>consistory: a high administrative or ecclesiastical council or court</term> or at the courts of lords.

That legal matters are sometimes delayed for so long is not always the fault of the jurists, but mostly of the parties involved, and partly of the judges. For when people have become entrenched in a legal battle, they cannot drag the matter out long enough or devise enough defensive maneuvers; they spare no expense or effort simply to bring damage and costs upon their opponent. In such cases, the judges are such "fine people" that they just sit there and watch how one person leads the other around by the nose so grandly and willfully. They allow one **interlocutory decree** <term>interlocutory decree: a provisional or temporary court order made before the final decision is reached</term> to be obtained after another, as these are for sale for money. 

As **Speculator** <note>Speculator was the nickname for Guillaume Durand (c. 1230–1296), a famous legal scholar who wrote the 'Speculum Iudiciale'.</note> writes, a case once hung before the Roman court that began before he was born; by the time it reached him, he was twenty-four years old. Yet, even then, the **legal contest had not yet been formally established** <note>original: "der Krieg noch nit befestiget"—referring to the 'litis contestatio', the formal stage where the issues of a trial are fixed.</note>. This is despite the fact that judges have the power and authority to compel the parties to bring forward their defenses all at once and then proceed to the main issue.

It is also provided for in the law that civil matters should be completed within three years, and criminal matters within two years after the legal contest is established (up to the point of appeal); and the appeal itself should be finished within a year’s time, unless there is a specific cause for delay. And the Emperor **Justinian** says in the same...

# On the Kindness of a Regent,
## or Prince.

### The Eleventh Chapter.

<image-desc>Ornate decorative drop cap 'E' with floral and scrolling leaf patterns.</image-desc>
Some regents or lords may believe they cannot rule better than by using the greatest severity against their subjects in their governance, bringing things to such a point that the subjects must live in fear of them, and then, out of such fear, do everything that is imposed and commanded of them. Others, however, are kind and mild, ruling with leniency <note>Original: "glimpff," meaning fairness, mildness, or proper moderation.</note> more than with severity. Regarding these two types of government, it shall be set down one after the other what kind of outcome each usually tends to achieve. And first, it is to be known that it is far more becoming and useful for a regent to deal with his subjects kindly and gently than to accomplish everything with blustering and pounding, which is evident from the fact that some have received their surnames because of such goodness and gentleness, being called "The Kind." Such as **Antoninus Pius** <note>Roman Emperor (reigned 138–161 AD) known for a peaceful and benevolent reign; "Pius" refers to his dutiful and gentle nature.</note>, who was so kind that he not only [protected] from Emperor **Hadrian** several powerful councilors, whom he [Hadrian] out of... <note>The text ends mid-sentence; the catchword "Tyran-" suggests the next page discusses Hadrian's "tyrannical" impulses which Antoninus Pius mediated.</note>

...from the hands of tyranny, which sought to strangle and kill him. He even looked after Hadrian himself in such a way—when Hadrian later wished to bring about his own death—that he was unable to accomplish it <note>This likely refers to Antoninus Pius, who famously prevented the ailing Emperor Hadrian from committing suicide and saved those Hadrian had ordered to be executed.</note>.

Similarly, some have been called "Fathers of the Fatherland" <note>Latin: *Pater Patriae*</note>. By this name, rulers were reminded that they should deal with their citizens and subjects not as a master with his slaves, but as a father with his children. As one reads of the Emperor Augustus: when he was greeted, named, and proclaimed "Father of the Fatherland" by Valerius Messala on behalf of the Roman people, he rejoiced so greatly in this name and title that he wept for joy. He said that nothing dearer could have happened to him on Earth, and he prayed to God that he might keep such a name with honor until the end of his life.

Subsequently, some were called "the very best," such as Trajan <note>Known as *Optimus Princeps*, or "The Best Prince."</note>. It is recorded to his high praise that his friends once criticized him for having too little regard for his imperial majesty, because he made himself too approachable to everyone. He answered: "I will be such an Emperor to my subjects as I myself would wish to have if I were a subject." <note>Original: "Talem præstabo Imperatorem priuatis, qualem ipse priuatus."</note> This is truly a beautiful and magnificent name. And although some believe they have achieved much when they act in such a way as to be called "Great"—as Alexander, Pompey, Charlemagne, Otto the Great, and others have done—such a title is still not equal to "the Best." Indeed, anyone who loves honor and virtue should much rather be and be called "the best" than "the greatest." For whoever wishes to be great and raise himself above other people cannot achieve or accomplish this without the oppression of many people; therefore, he must be hated and envied by many. This also happened to Alexander, of whom Hannibal gave testimony when Scipio Africanus asked him whom he considered the greatest captain. Hannibal replied: "Alexander," because he had often slain and defeated great and powerful hosts with few people, and in a few years had conquered almost the entire world.

Homer also writes that kings were called "Shepherds of the People" <note>Original: *Pastores Populi*</note>, and undoubtedly not without reason. For just as a shepherd applies all possible diligence to ensure that his sheep and the entire flock take no harm nor suffer want, but are provided with fodder, pasture, and other necessities, and thus remain beautiful and lovely, growing and increasing; so also should a regent or prince strive with the highest diligence to ensure that his subjects are everywhere provided with laws, officials, and, in expensive times, with grain. Just as it is glorious for a shepherd when he has a beautiful and joyful herd of cattle that is healthy, well-grazed, and has survived the winter well, so it is an honor for a prince when he has a beautiful and rich land in which the subjects are in good circumstances. # Of the Ruler's Book #

Duke **Georg of Saxony**, of highly praiseworthy memory, was once challenged with the suggestion that he should not permit such luxury to the people of **Leipzig**, but rather should take away their gold chains and similar finery. He answered: He wished that he had many such cities in which the people could produce such adornment. For princes should be nothing other than guardians <term>Vormünden: legal protectors of those unable to care for themselves</term> who direct everything to the benefit and welfare of their wards <term>Mündlin: the subjects, viewed here as legal wards</term> and do them no harm, since they have been commanded by God to look after them for the best.

But those lords who look upon one person and not the other, promote one and suppress another, are favorable or gracious to one and ungracious to the other, and thus act according to favor rather than equality and fairness—they stir up nothing but disunity and discord in their cities and lands. From this, great and significant damage follows, and at times the ruin of land and people. For as soon as the despised and suppressed party gains opportunity and cause, they seek how they may take revenge and recover their losses. To prevent such things, it is necessary for a regent or prince to remember—if he wishes to fulfill his calling—that the relationship between the ruler and his subjects is no different than that between the **head and its limbs**. Now, if a regent did not provide for the common good and the subjects, but instead let them fall into ruin and suffer need, he would be doing nothing other than neglecting his own body, being negligent toward himself, and becoming a murderer; whereas if he spares his poor subjects, he spares himself.

The Emperor **Aurelianus** used to say that the people were never happier than when they were full, just as the proverb goes among us Germans: *A happy head stands upon a full belly.* <note>Original German: "Auff einem satten Bauch stehet ein frölich Häupt."</note> By this, he wished to indicate that it is fitting for regents and superiors to ensure that their relatives and subjects suffer no lack of grain in times of shortage <term>Thewrung: price inflation or scarcity of goods</term>, as mentioned above, since they are duty-bound to do so by their office. For this reason, the **Romans** are primarily praised for having applied great diligence, effort, and labor during times of famine so that their citizens might have supplies and be sustained. As **Livy** <note>Titus Livius, the Roman historian.</note> writes, **Minutius** was the first provant-master <term>Prouiant Meister: an official in charge of food logistics</term> in Rome. Likewise, it was grandly decreed by the Emperor **Julius** and others that one should not artificially create shortages or practice grain usury <term>Getreide Wucher: the practice of hoarding grain to sell it at an exploitative price</term>. Whoever would not uphold this, but instead violated it, should be banished from the land—especially if he used a false bushel or measure, as **Ulpian** says <note>Original Latin reference: "in l. annonam. para. final. ff. de extraord. criminibus," referring to Roman legal codes regarding the food supply and extraordinary crimes.</note>.

However, this legal ordinance has so far declined and been extinguished that a large portion of people now practice grain usury. They not only apply themselves to it but also nourish and sustain themselves by it. In just a few years, it has gone so far that even those who ought to forbid it—such as treasurers <term>Kastener</term>, bailiffs <term>Vögte</term>, and administrative officials <term>Amptleute</term>, sometimes noble and non-noble alike—are not ashamed of it. Because of this, such expensive years have occurred continuously for some time, even though no crop failure in the grain could be perceived; thus, the poor people can only with great effort earn enough so that they might pay for their bread

# THE SECOND PART #

...[the subjects] may and must go bare and naked during their hard labor. And if one were now to drive out all these grain speculators <term>Korn Jüden: a derogatory historical term for those who hoarded grain to drive up prices, often using antisemitic tropes to scapegoat speculators</term> and usurers from the land, then many places in German lands would for the most part stand desolate; even those who—by virtue of their office—rightly should have punished, prevented, and forestalled this vice would themselves have to flee.

Therefore, necessity requires that one pay diligent attention to such matters, and not burden many poor people for the sake of one or two who might be favored, nor allow oneself to be moved and led by their flowery words to permit such usury. Instead, one should strictly forbid it and not let the matter rest there. It is also necessary to command and decree that in cities and communities, granaries and storehouses <term>Schüttheuser: buildings designed for the bulk storage and "shucking" or pouring of grain</term> be built, and a supply of grain be procured, so that in times of dearth <term>Tewrung: a period of famine or inflated food prices</term>, it may be provided again to the poor—and especially to the citizens—at a fair price. This is no small help to the citizens and inhabitants, as I have seen in **Leipzig**, **Nuremberg**, and other places. Thus, the Emperor **Trajan** is praised for providing the city of **Rome** with provisions for seven years. Likewise, the Roman **Septimius** is praised for leaving behind a seven-year supply of grain in such quantity that seventy thousand bushels could be distributed weekly.

**Mamertinus**, in his panegyric <term>Panegyrico: a formal public speech delivered in high praise of a person</term> to the Emperor **Julian**, also gave him this praise: that he provided for the city of **Rome**—which at that time was most heavily burdened with hunger and dearth—in such a way that not only did the famine cease, but the city also received a great supply and abundance. In doing so, he spared no expense but had grain brought in from all parts of the world. Such provision once brought great praise to **Pompey the Great**; for when he entered **Rome** in victory and triumph from the East and the West, it so happened that when he had gathered a great sum of grain from **Libya**, **Sicily**, and **Sardinia** in many ships, and a powerful storm arose at sea so that the sailors did not want to sail but rather cast their anchors, **Pompey** stepped forward, cut the anchors away again, and said: "To sail is necessary; to live is not necessary" <note>original Latin: "Navigare necesse est, viuere non necesse est"</note>.

And since I have just spoken of ships, it occurs to me that **Plato** compared a ruler to a mariner, and called him a shipman for this reason: Just as the shipman must constantly look about and take care so that the ship and those within it do not perhaps drown and take harm, and thus must carry more worry and care than the others sitting in the ship—some of whom eat and drink while they travel, and some of whom sleep without worry. As that soldier said, who also slept as he stepped from the ship: "If you had drowned me, I would have stabbed you."

Thus it is also fitting for a regent and sovereign to [be more active] than others...

# BOOK OF THE REGENT #

<note>The following section contains reconstructions where the original German page was damaged on the left edge.</note>

...[It is necessary to always] be watchful and diligent, and to look here and there, so [that] his cities, land, and subjects, which are entrusted to him by God, [may] live in [good] peace, be joyful and in good spirits, and not suffer any harm. [A]nd just as the mariner directs himself according to the course of the heavens, the wind, and the clouds, drawing in or spreading the sails accordingly, so also should [a] ruler always consider and look above himself at what kind of office God has [la]id upon him. And where perhaps a storm—such as a feud, war, or unrest—[th]rough which land and people might be damaged, begins to weave and rise, [he should kno]w how he might prevent the same and rescue his poor subjects from such [misfor]tune and sorrowful evil. For what a wretched [thi]ng war is, has been sufficiently told above in Chapter 6, and hereafter in Chapter 1 of the Third Book, and shown at length.

From this it appears clearly enough that a ruler or prince cannot have many idle or restful days, nor much time for banqueting, hunting, tournaments, and other joyful games, if he wishes to faithfully preside over and fulfill his office <term>Ampt: a divinely ordained duty or position of authority</term> and calling. This is because so much care, unrest, effort, and labor belong to it; which indeed pious, faithful rulers well feel and become aware of. But otherwise, no one can easily see or believe this, because people look only at the outward pomp—how the princes and rulers hold only costly banquets, wear golden chains, precious stones, and marten-fur gowns <term>Mardere Schauben: expensive, fur-lined overcoats worn by the upper classes as a status symbol</term> (as **Duke Charles of Burgundy** <note>Known as Charles the Bold (1433–1477), famous for his immense wealth and the extravagant court of Burgundy</note> had a garment which was estimated at the least to be worth two hundred thousand ducats), and also ride with many horses, and possess many kingdoms, principalities, lands, and people. But they cannot see the care, unrest, effort, fear, and labor that they have daily, and how they must be the servants of every man, in that all unpleasant and erroneous matters come before them, etc. And sometimes such cares, effort, and labor, which are hidden under the golden pieces and marten gowns, oppress them in such a way that one would rather wear a coarse smock <term>Kittel: a simple, cheap tunic worn by peasants</term> and be unburdened of such cares, effort, and labor.

However, since it is not possible to carry such a burden, effort, and labor forever and have no refreshment, they are not to be terrified <note>In this context, "not to be blamed or discouraged"</note> if they sometimes seek refreshment with hunting, tournaments, and other festivities and knightly games. And the **Egyptians** did nearly wrong in that they punished their **King Amasis** <note>Amasis II, a Pharaoh of the 26th Dynasty mentioned by the historian Herodotus</note>, who sat in judgment in the market from morning until high noon and heard the cases himself with great diligence, because he drank and was joyful and in good spirits after noon. For this reason he also answered them: "Those who have bows are not accustomed to keep them strung except when they wish to shoot; when they have nothing to shoot, they let the bows slacken. But if one wished to carry a bow constantly strung, it would not be able to last long, but would easily become weak or break altogether."

But so that I may return to the mildness and gentleness of princes and lords, one reads of the great and powerful **King Agesilaus** <note>Agesilaus II, a famous King of Sparta known for his simple lifestyle and wisdom</note>, when he was asked how and by what means one might obtain praise and honor among the people, he answered: "When he applies himself to speak the best, and [does the] same..."

## The Second Part ##

...are able and must, despite their bitter labor, go bare and naked. And if one were now to drive all these grain speculators <note>original: "Korn Jüdẽ," a pejorative historical term for those who hoarded grain to drive up prices</note> and usurers out of the country, many places in German lands would mostly stand desolate, and those who, by virtue of their office, should have rightly punished, resisted, and prevented this vice, would in part have to flee with them.

Therefore, necessity demands that diligent attention be paid to such favors, lest for the sake of one or two people who are perhaps favored, many poor people are burdened, or lest one be moved and led by their flowery words to permit such usury. Instead, one must strictly forbid it and not let it rest there. It is also necessary to command and ordain that in cities and communities, grain houses and storehouses <term>Schütheuser: public granaries designed for bulk storage of threshed grain</term> be built, and a supply of grain be procured. This is so that the grain may be made available again to the poor, and especially to the citizens, at a reasonable price in times of dearth <term>Tewrung: a period of inflation or famine where the cost of living becomes unbearable</term>. This is no small help to the citizens and inhabitants, as I have seen in Leipzig, Nuremberg, and other places. Thus, the Emperor Trajan is praised for providing the city of Rome with provisions for seven years. Likewise, the Roman Septimius is praised for leaving behind a supply of grain for seven years at his death, in such an amount that seventy thousand bushels <note>original: "Scheffel," a historical unit of dry volume</note> could be distributed weekly.

Mamertinus, in his panegyric <note>a formal public speech of high praise</note> to the Emperor Julian, also gave him this praise among others: that he provided for the city of Rome—which at that time was most heavily burdened with hunger and famine—with grain in such a way that not only did the famine cease, but the city also received a great supply and abundance. In this, he spared no expense but had grain brought in from all parts of the world. Such provision once brought great praise to Pompey the Great; for when he entered Rome with victory and triumph from the East and the West, it so happened that as he had gathered a great sum of grain from Libya, Sicily, and Sardinia in many ships, a mighty storm arose on the sea. The sailors did not want to sail but rather cast anchor; however, Pompey stepped forward, cut the anchors away again, and spoke: "It is necessary to sail, but it is not necessary to live." <note>original: *Nauigare necesse est, viuere non necesse est.*</note>

And since I have just spoken of ships, it occurs to me that Plato compared a regent to a mariner, and called him a mariner for this reason: just as the mariner must constantly look about and take care so that the ship and those within it do not perhaps drown and suffer harm—and thus must bear and have more care than the others sitting in the ship, some of whom play and drink while they travel, and some of whom sleep without care—like that soldier said, who had also been sleeping when he stepped off the ship: "If you had drowned me, I would have stabbed you."

Thus it is also fitting for a regent and sovereign, more than others...

<meta>The text begins with the suffix of a word from the previous page, likely "others" (andere).</meta> ...to watch over others and to be diligent, also to look here and there so that his cities, lands, and subjects—which are entrusted to him by God—may live in good peace, be joyful and of good cheer, and not suffer any harm. And just as the pilot <term>Schiffmann: a sailor or captain of a vessel</term> guides himself by the course of the heavens, the wind, and the clouds, and draws in or spreads the sails accordingly; so also should a regent constantly reflect and look above him to the office laid upon him by God. And where a storm—such as a feud, war, or unrest—might begin to spin and arise, through which land and people might be damaged, he must consider how he may prevent it and rescue his poor subjects from such misfortune and sad evil. For what a miserable thing war is has been sufficiently told above in Chapter 6, and hereafter in Chapter 1 of the third book, and shown at length.

From which it sufficiently appears that a regent or prince cannot have many idle or restful days, nor much time left for banquets, hunting, tournaments, and other joyful games, if he wishes to faithfully lead and fulfill his office and calling. <header>The Second Part</header>

...demonstrates and fulfills the same through deeds. There is nothing that better suits a ruler on earth than to gladly allow his people and subjects to come before him, to grant them a kindly hearing, to give them a gracious dismissal, and not to behave so cruelly in words, gestures, and countenance that the people are terrified of him and lose their ability to speak. In this regard, the great man Pompey the Great <note>Pompeius Magnus (106–48 BCE), a leading Roman general and statesman.</note> is excellently praised by Cicero. Likewise, the Emperor Trajan is praised by the younger Pliny <note>Pliny the Younger (61–112 CE), a lawyer and author whose "Panegyricus" praised Trajan's humility.</note> for gladly hearing the people and dismissing them kindly. For this reason, the Emperor Augustus used to say—when someone reached out to hand him a letter while trembling—that one should not present a letter and petition <term>Supplication: a formal written request or petition to a person in power</term> to lords in such a manner as one offers food to elephants and lions: namely, with worry and trembling.

Therefore, it is also provided for by law that the governors <term>Landpfleger: administrative officials or provincial governors</term> and other officials should hear the people kindly and gladly let them come before them; of this, I must here tell an example of a great prince. It is said of the current Archbishop of Salzburg, a Duke of Bavaria <note>Likely referring to Ernst of Bavaria (1500–1560) or a contemporary successor who held the Archbishopric.</note>, that he commanded his advisors and servants that if even the lowliest of his subjects desired to come before him, they should not keep it secret from him but let the person approach. He also occasionally disguises himself in peasant’s clothing and hears how the judges and officials deal with the poor people; and wherever a judge or official behaves improperly, he is immediately removed from his office.

It also happened once, when he saw that the butchers <term>Fleischhawer: an archaic term for a butcher</term> did not want to let the poor people have meat for their money, that he went to the meat stalls in peasant’s clothing and asked—saying he had a pregnant wife—if they would let him have a pound of veal. And when they dismissed him rudely, he had them all put into the tower and punished in other ways those who had behaved improperly in their office, and he secured justice for everyone, as is fitting. Because of this, an old woman once said to King Philip of Macedon <note>Philip II of Macedon (382–336 BCE), father of Alexander the Great.</note> when she asked for a hearing and the king answered her that he was not at leisure: “Then you should also not rule nor be king (said she) if you will not hear the people.” The king wondered at this speech and was startled by it; thereafter, he diligently heard not only that woman but all others. However, things have reached such a point among us Germans that if someone said such a word to a village headman <term>Schultheissen: a local official or magistrate in a village</term> in a village, he would have to lie in the deepest tower or give ten thalers as a penalty.

Therefore, neither fortune nor salvation is any longer at hand, because the officials have so completely forgotten their calling and only pay attention to their own profit. Just as King Philip is praised, so it is not unjust to scold Demetrius <note>Demetrius I Poliorcetes (337–283 BCE), a King of Macedon known for his extravagance and perceived arrogance.</note> in contrast. For it is written of him that the Athenian envoys followed him for two whole years regarding an important and necessary matter, and yet could not be heard by him, but instead had to return home unheard.

And when the Lacedemonians <note>Spartans</note> sent no more than one envoy to him, he became angry and asked why those from Sparta sent no more than one...

# Of the Book of Rulers

...dispatched envoys to him? The envoy answered: "They thought it was enough if they sent one to one." <note>original: "unum ad unum"</note> Following this, the same Demetrius <note>Demetrius I Poliorcetes (337–283 BCE), a King of Macedon known for his initial brilliance but eventual arrogance.</note> had it proclaimed that all those who had business with him should come and present their needs in writing, and he would graciously hear them. Now, when a great many people had come and handed him their grievances in writing, he received the letters in a friendly and gracious manner. But when he came to the River Axium <note>The Axium (modern Vardar) is a major river in Macedonia.</note>, he stepped onto the bridge and let all the letters, which he had gathered together in his cloak, fall into the water all at once. By this act, he caused a great and noticeable defection among the Macedonians.

In contrast, others were of a far different mind, such as Trajan, as was mentioned above. Likewise, all rulers and princes should diligently take to heart the speech of Titus Vespasianus, who used to say that a prince should never let anyone leave his presence feeling sad. Indeed, the Emperor Alexander <note>Likely referring to Alexander Severus (reigned 222–235 CE), noted for his moderate and approachable rule.</note> frequently called his servants to him and asked why they asked nothing of him: "How does it happen that you desire nothing from me? Do you wish to make me your debtor? I would rather you ask something of me than that you complain about me in secret." Therefore, Solomon says in his Proverbs, "The kindness of the prince is like a lovely evening rain." <note>A reference to Proverbs 16:15: "In the light of a king's face there is life, and his favor is like the clouds of the spring rain."</note> Now, the fewer such rulers are found in our times—who deal with their poor people in this way, hearing them personally and dismissing them kindly—the more such virtue is to be admired and praised in those who possess it, just as Your Grace is particularly praised in this regard.

Julius Pollux <note>A Greek grammarian and sophist from the 2nd century CE.</note>, as Erasmus writes, clearly illustrated for the Emperor Commodus (whom he had instructed in his youth as a tutor) the names and titles of a pious king or ruler in the Greek language. And although these names, by virtue of their specific character, are of such a nature that they cannot easily be transformed into Latin, much less translated into German by me now, I will nonetheless recount some of them here—as many as I have been able to obtain—so that one may see what thoughts the heathens once had. For Julius Pollux was a heathen, and he also wrote to a heathen emperor.

And would to God that such beautiful and magnificent titles could truthfully be attributed to all rulers, all of whom wish to be called Christians—some even writing of themselves as "Most Christian"—for then perhaps one would see a different and better government in the world. The names and titles of pious and righteous rulers in Pollux are as follows: Father, Gentle, Mild, Pleasant, Cautious, Consistent, Affable, Magnanimous, Not Greedy, Not Vengeful, Master of Himself, Despiser of Lust, Rational, Understanding, Wise in Counsel, Just, Sober, Diligent, Steadfast, Sincere, Concerned with Great Things, Dignified, Industrious, Upright, Caring for Subjects, Savior inclined toward charity, Gracious, Kind, Gladly hearing the poor, Protector of the obedient, Skilled but not eager for war, Peaceful, Peace-loving, Peacemaker, Skilled in improving the morals of the people, and in giving good laws.

...proves and fulfills the same with deeds. Nothing, however, suits a regent on earth better than that he should gladly allow his people and subjects to come before him, hear them kindly, give them a gracious dismissal, and not present himself so cruelly in words, gestures, and countenance that the people are terrified before him and lose their speech. # The Second Part

...proves and completes the same through action. Nothing, however, better becomes a ruler <term>Regent: a sovereign or person who exercises ruling power</term> on earth than to let his people and subjects come before him willingly, to give them a kind hearing, to grant them a gracious departure, and not to present himself with such harsh words, gestures, and facial expressions that people are terrified of him and lose their power of speech. In this regard, the great man **Pompey the Great** <note>Gnaeus Pompeius Magnus (106–48 BCE), a celebrated Roman general and statesman</note> is excellently praised by **Cicero**. Likewise, the Emperor **Trajan** is praised by the younger **Pliny** for willingly hearing the people and dismissing them with kindness. For this reason, the Emperor **Augustus** used to say, when someone tremblingly handed him a letter, that one should not hand over a letter and petition <term>Supplication: a formal written request or humble petition</term> to a lord in such a manner as one offers food to elephants and lions—namely, with fear and trembling.

Accordingly, it is also provided for by law that the governors <term>Landpfleger: regional administrators or high-ranking local officials</term> and other officials should hear the people kindly and let them come before them willingly. Concerning this, I must tell an example of a great prince. It is said of the current **Archbishop of Salzburg**, a **Duke of Bavaria**, that he commanded his councilors and servants that if even the lowliest of his subjects desired to come before him, they should not keep this secret from him, but let the person come before him. He also occasionally disguised himself in peasant's clothing and listened to how the judges and officials dealt with the poor people; and where a judge or official behaved improperly, he was immediately removed from office.

It also happened once, when he saw that the butchers <term>Fleischhawer: an archaic term for butchers</term> did not want to let the poor people have meat for their money, that he went to the stalls in peasant's clothing and begged, saying he had a pregnant wife and asked if they would let him have a pound of veal. And when they dismissed him poorly, he had them all thrown into the tower <note>original: "Thürn" (tower), referring here to a prison or dungeon</note> and punished in other ways those who behaved improperly in their office, ensuring justice for everyone, as is fitting. Because of this, an old woman once said to **King Philip of Macedon** <note>Philip II (382–336 BCE), father of Alexander the Great</note> when she begged for a hearing and the King answered that he was not at leisure: "Then you should also not rule or be king," she said, "if you will not hear the people." The King was astonished by this speech and was shaken; thereafter, he diligently heard not only that woman but all others as well. Although among us Germans it has come to such a pass that if one were to say such a word to a village mayor <term>Schultheissen: a local administrative official or village head</term> in a village, he would have to lie in the deepest tower or pay ten thalers as a fine.

Therefore, there is no longer any fortune or salvation at hand, because the officials have so completely forgotten their calling and pay attention only to their own profit. Just as King Philip is praised, it is likewise not unjust to scold **Demetrius** <note>Demetrius I Poliorcetes (337–283 BCE), King of Macedonia, often depicted in literature as a contrast to more accessible rulers</note> in contrast. For it is written of him that the Athenian legates <term>Legaten: ambassadors or official representatives</term> followed him for two whole years in an important and necessary matter, and yet could not be heard by him, but had to return home unheard.

And when the **Lacedaemonians** <note>The people of Sparta</note> sent no more than one legate to him, he became angry and asked why those from **Sparta** had sent no more than one

Subsequently, this same **Demetrius** <note>Demetrius I Poliorcetes (337–283 BCE), a King of Macedon known for his erratic and often arrogant behavior</note> had it proclaimed that all those who had business with him should come and present their needs in writing, for he wished to hear them graciously. Now, as many came and gave him their grievances in writing, he accepted the letters in a friendly and gracious manner; but when he came to the River **Axium** <note>The Axius or Vardar River in Macedonia</note>, he stepped onto the bridge and let the letters, which he had gathered in his robe, all fall into the water at once. By doing this, he caused a great and noticeable desertion among the Macedonians.

In contrast, others were of a far different mind, such as **Trajan** <note>Roman Emperor (r. 98–117 CE) celebrated as a "just prince"</note>, as was mentioned above. Likewise, all rulers and princes should diligently take to heart the speech of **Titus Vespasianus** <note>Roman Emperor (r. 79–81 CE) famous for his generosity</note>, who used to say that a prince should never let anyone leave him feeling sad. Indeed, the Emperor **Alexander** <note>likely Alexander Severus (r. 222–235 CE), known for his mild rule and concern for justice</note> often called his servants to him and asked why they requested nothing from him: "How does it happen that you desire nothing from me? Do you wish to make me your debtor? I would rather you ask something of me than that you secretly complain about me." Therefore, **Solomon** says in his Proverbs, "The favor of the prince is like a lovely evening rain" <note>A reference to Proverbs 16:15, comparing royal favor to life-giving rain</note>. Now, the fewer such rulers are found in our times who deal with their poor people as mentioned—hearing them personally and dismissing them kindly—the more such virtue is to be wondered at and praised in those who do, just as Your Grace is particularly praised for this.

**Julius Pollux** <note>A Greek grammarian and sophist from the 2nd century CE</note>, as **Erasmus** writes, depicted the names and titles of a pious king or ruler quite distinctly in the Greek language for the Emperor **Commodus**, whom he had instructed as a tutor in his youth. For Julius Pollux was a heathen and wrote for a heathen emperor.

And would to God that such beautiful and magnificent titles could truthfully be attributed to all rulers who all wish to be Christians—some even writing of themselves as "the most Christian"—for then perhaps one would see a different and better government <term>Regiment: the system or manner of rule</term> in the world. But the names and titles of pious and righteous rulers in Pollux's work are as follows: Father, Meek, Mild, Pleasing, Prudent, Equitable, Affable, Magnanimous, Not greedy, Not vengeful, Master of himself, Despiser of pleasure, Rational, Understanding, Mighty in counsel, Just, Sober, Diligent, Steadfast, Undeceiving, Concerned with great things, Respected, Hardworking, Sincere, Caring for subjects, Savior inclined to do good, Gracious, Kind, Hearing the poor gladly, Protector of the obedient, Skilled but not eager for war, Peaceful, Peace-loving, Peacemaker, Skilled at improving the morals of the people, and at giving good laws,

## On Tyranny, and how the 
## same is usually punished.

### The Twelfth Chapter.

<image-desc>A large decorative drop cap 'W' showing a figure seated on a throne or chair within an ornate architectural frame, surrounded by floral motifs.</image-desc>

What a horrible and inhuman thing tyranny is, I touched upon briefly at the beginning, and there would indeed be no need to write further about it, since almost everyone can grasp it—to say nothing of seeing and noticing it—both from history and daily experience. There is a great difference between a righteous authority <note>original: "rechtschaffenen Oberkeit"</note> and a tyrant. Nevertheless, as a warning, I wish to set down several histories and examples of how tyrants have been punished in every age, so that such cruel people may learn from them what a horrible and hateful thing it is before God and the world when tyrants practice violence and injustice against their subjects, and that God cannot endure it. For this reason, they should desist from such behavior and should rule and live in the fear of God and according to His will and command.

But before I come to the examples and histories, I must remind the reader that among the Ancients, the name "Tyrant" was not hateful, nor did it mean anything other than a "King." This appears in the writings of **Xenophon** <note>a Greek historian and philosopher (c. 430–354 BCE)</note>, where the poet **Simonides** <note>Simonides of Ceos (c. 556–468 BCE), a famous Greek lyric poet</note> frequently calls King **Hiero** <note>Hiero I, the ruler of Syracuse from 478 to 467 BCE</note> a "Tyrant" in a dialogue. He undoubtedly would not have done this if a distinction had existed at that time between a king and a tyrant. Otherwise, it would have been no more polite than if I were to speak friendly with a highwayman <note>original: "Strassenräuber"</note> and insist on calling him a "highwayman" throughout. It would be like that gentleman who once heard someone called a **Plafteucker** <note>original: "Plafteucker," an archaic German term of abuse or insult, often used for a sycophant, a "plate-licker," or a person of ill repute</note> and did not know it was a disreputable name. Therefore, when he met the man, he spoke to him quite friendly and invited him to be his guest, but kept calling him a "Plafteucker," etc. 

However, when tyrants began to abuse their power, that same name subsequently became hateful to subjects throughout the whole world. Thus, even to this day, those are scolded and called "tyrants" who do not behave toward their subjects according to law and equity <note>original: "Recht vnd Billigkeit"</note>, but solely according to their own cruel whims, violating and oppressing them. Yet, because such behavior is unjust, and since no one dares to oppose the tyrants, God—who cannot endure it—usually overthrows these cruel monsters <term>Wüterich: an archaic term for a bloodthirsty tyrant or a person acting with insane rage</term> in a terrifying manner, so that others may take offense at their example and diligently guard themselves against such tyrannical and violent deeds.

<summary>This page defines tyranny and explains how the term evolved from a neutral word for "king" into a title of reproach due to the abuse of power. It warns that while subjects may be unable to resist a tyrant, God inevitably punishes such rulers as a warning to others.</summary>

Herodotus writes of King Cambyses that he was such a tyrant that he strangled his own biological brother and thereafter took his sister as a wife, contrary to natural and established law <note>original: "wider natürlich vnd ordentlich beschrieben Recht"</note>. As it happened at one time, while Cambyses was in Egypt, that he allowed a young lion and a dog to bite one another before the table, and the lion—as was easily seen—was superior, the dog's brother joined in and helped him, and the lion was strangled by the two of them. The King was joyful at this, but the Queen, his sister, became distressed and began to weep. When the King wanted to know why she wept, she gave him this answer: she was reminded by this occurrence of the dogs and the lion of her deceased brother, who had no one who could have helped him. From this answer, Cambyses became so violently enraged that he had the Queen led away from him and immediately strangled.

Following this, the same Cambyses asked one of his best advisors named Prexaspes what the Persians thought of him, to which he answered: the Persians had a good opinion of him everywhere, except in one matter they were displeased: that he applied himself too much to wine and overloaded himself with drink, thereby doing damage to his reason. When the King heard this, he grew furious and angry, and then said to him: "You shall soon experience whether I am still in my right mind when I have drunk." He had a banquet prepared, drank his fill of wine, then took Prexaspes' son, stood him on the threshold, and spoke: "Now take heed whether I can hit your son in the heart with an arrow; if I miss, then you and the Persians have won; but if I hit his heart, then you have accused me of the impropriety of drinking unjustly." He then took his bow and shot an arrow into the boy. When they had then cut him open, and the King saw that he had hit the boy’s heart, he became joyful and said to Prexaspes: "Now you yourself will undoubtedly have to confess and say that it is not I, but you and the Persians who are senseless." If the good man Prexaspes had flattered the King, then he would have been a beloved man and far removed from this, as **Croesus** <note>referred to as "Crefus" in the text; the famously wealthy King of Lydia who served as an advisor to the Persian court</note> did, whom the King also asked what he thought of him, and whether he was not to be held in higher esteem than his father **Cyrus**? And **Croesus** replied to this: "No, for the reason that he has not yet left behind such a son as Cyrus left in Cambyses." But because he told him the truth and kindly reminded him of what flaw he had, and that he should moderate his excessive drinking, he had to lose his son for it—as indeed has often happened to many others. Cambyses practiced much more of such tyranny afterward, until he finally strangled himself <note>While the text says he strangled himself, historical accounts often state Cambyses II died from an accidental self-inflicted wound from his own sword.</note>.

One reads of the King of the Goths named **Dietrich** <note>Theodoric the Great (c. 454–526 AD), King of the Ostrogoths</note> that he had both mayors of Rome—namely **Symmachus** and his son-in-law **Boethius** <note>Boethius was a celebrated philosopher and statesman, author of "The Consolation of Philosophy"</note>, two great and brave men—miserably put to death on account of very slight suspicion. The Emperor Valens, who was an Arian <note>Arianism was a theological movement that argued Jesus Christ was a created being, subordinate to God the Father; it was considered heretical by the orthodox church.</note>, wished to force Basil the Bishop of Senis <note>likely referring to Basil of Caesarea; "Senis" may be a corruption of a Latin geographic name</note> by power to join the side of Arius. He used this threat: that if he did not do so, he would drive him from the land and punish him horribly. To this, Basil briefly replied that he should present such threats to children; Valens could well take his life, but he would not let him take the Truth of the Divine Word.

And so there was for several days a violent dispute between the Emperor and Basil, which was finally interrupted by a visible miracle from God. Namely in this manner: when the Emperor was so violently embittered and maddened that he himself ran into the church with his household and guards with the intent of taking the Bishop out by force. But as he came before the seat, such a violent dizziness came upon the Emperor that his sight and hearing failed him; he would have fallen down upon the pavement had one of the Bishop's deacons not caught and held him. From this, Valens became terrified, trembled, and quaked, so that his servants had to lead him out of the church—he who had come with the intention (as mentioned) of leading the Bishop out. After this fall, the Emperor's wrath was somewhat softened. However, as he departed, he nevertheless had a mandate posted by the governor <term>Landpfleger</term> <note>A regional administrator or prefect acting on behalf of the Emperor.</note> against Basil, stating that he should vacate the area.

But the congregation at Senis would not abandon Basil. Therefore, the tyrant let him remain there, more out of fear than out of good will. Not long thereafter, the Emperor set out with a large army against the Goths, and when he saw that the battle was lost, he took flight and came into a shepherd's small house, which the soldiers pursuing him set on fire. Inside it, he had to burn and perish shamefully. This was the end of the great and angry tyrant, who would have gladly removed and driven all pious and righteous preachers from the Church—as he had indeed vigorously begun and had driven many away—so that he might spread the Arian poison even further. Yet he had to let some of them remain and be brought to shame thereby, as an example to others and as a comfort to pious preachers, that they should not be too greatly terrified by such tyrants.

The Emperor Carus had two sons, Carinus and Numerian. Now, after Phalaris had tortured and killed many pious and honest people, the people were moved against him, so that they burned him along with his wife and children in that same bull.

Aelian <note>Claudius Aelianus (c. 175 – c. 235 AD), a Roman author whose *Varia Historia* is the source for many such anecdotes.</note> writes of a tyrant named Tryzus <note>likely a reference to a story from Aelian regarding a tyrant of Thasos.</note> that he was so furious and insane that he even forbade his subjects from speaking to one another, whether in secret or in public, so that they might not think of ways by which his tyranny might be stopped. This was an intolerable and impossible thing, as people cannot conduct their business and affairs through any other way than speech. Nevertheless, he brought them so far that they obeyed this command and had to abstain from all speech with one another—one can well imagine with what hardship. But because the poor and troubled people still had to deal with one another, and since they were not allowed to hold any speech or conversation, they began to wink at each other and to make their gestures and thoughts known to one another through signs and expressions; depending on the matter, they appeared angry or happy, etc. The devilish tyrant would not tolerate this either; therefore, he strictly forbade such winking with the eyes and other limbs through a special law, wishing to turn the people into sticks and stones. This moved one of the subjects to pity; he therefore stepped into the market and began to weep violently. Almost all the others ran to him and lamented their miserable plague and servitude with weeping. # The Second Part

...[the people] beat the tyrants to death and delivered themselves from such intolerable tyranny.

In Thessalia <note>Thessaly, a region in northern Greece.</note> there was a cruel tyrant named Alexander Pheraeus <note>Alexander of Pherae (ruled 369–358 BC), a ruler notorious for his extreme cruelty.</note> who plagued the people so severely that he had many men sewn into the skins of bears, lions, and wolves. However, when he attempted to shamefully abuse one of his wife's brothers, the wife conspired with her brothers and strangled him in his bed at night, so that they might be delivered from his cruel tyranny.

In Vicenza <note>The text uses "Vincenz."</note> in Italy <note>The original uses "Welschlanden," an archaic German term for Italy or Romance-speaking lands.</note> there was once a tyrant called Carrarius <note>Likely referring to a member of the Carraresi family (da Carrara), who vied for control of northern Italian cities.</note> who first murdered the Lord of Scala <note>The Della Scala or Scaliger family, rulers of Verona and Vicenza.</note> along with his son, so that he might obtain power and mastery over that same city. Once he had attained this, he sent for a citizen and demanded that he send him his daughter, who was very beautiful. However, both the father and the daughter refused. Therefore, the tyrant was moved to anger and had the daughter taken from the father’s house by force. After two days, he sent her back to the father in a basket, chopped into pieces. When the father saw this, he was (as is easily imagined) deeply distressed. He reported it to the Council and his kinsmen, begging them for help and counsel. After much deliberation, they brought the matter before the Venetians, sending along the basket with the hacked-up maiden. For this reason, the Venetians quickly armed themselves, drove out the tyrant, and took the city into their protection, under which it remains to this very day.

Such cruel tyranny and wanton violation also gave the Swiss cause to make themselves free by their own hands. This was caused, according to the Swiss Chronicle, because they had a governor named Gessler <note>Original: "Grießler." Hermann Gessler was the legendary Habsburg bailiff whose cruelty sparked the Swiss uprising.</note>, an evil tyrant. On one occasion, he came to Uri <note>Original: "Vri."</note> and had a pole placed under a linden tree where everyone had to pass by. Upon it he placed a hat and had it publicly proclaimed that whoever passed by should do reverence to the hat and bow, as if he himself were sitting there in person. Whoever mockingly ignored the command, however, he would punish without any mercy. He also kept a guard there constantly, who had to watch the people to see who kept the command or not.

Now it happened by chance that a man named William Tell, a pious and honest man, passed the pole several times and did no reverence to the hat. This the guard reported and indicated to the Lord. The governor had Tell summoned before him and asked him why he had not kept his command and had thus not bowed to the hat. Tell answered: "Gracious Lord, it happened by oversight; I did not think that Your Grace <note>Original: "E. G." for "Eure Gnaden."</note> would take it so much to heart. I have no understanding of such matters, for if I were cleverer, I would be named something else; therefore, I beg for forgiveness." Now the governor knew that Tell was a good marksman; therefore, he had all his children secretly brought and asked Tell if they were his, and which among them he loved most. To this he answered that they were all his, and they were all equally dear to him.

# Of the Book of Rulers

Then the Lord <note>Referring to Hermann Gessler, the legendary Hapsburg bailiff (tyrant) of Altdorf.</note> spoke further: "Since you are such a good marksman, as I have heard of you, you shall now prove it to me and shoot an apple from the head of one of your children. If you hit the apple, I shall hold you to be a good marksman." Tell was greatly terrified and begged the Lord to spare him from this, for it was unnatural for a father to do such a thing. Whatever else the Lord might impose upon him, he would suffer it patiently. But he could obtain nothing from the tyrant; rather, he was forced by him and his servants to shoot the apple from the child’s head. This he did, and he succeeded so well that he did not injure or harm the child in the slightest.

Now, when the Lord saw this, it pleased him well. However, since Tell had two arrows—one with which he had shot the apple, and the other tucked behind in his doublet <term>Goller: an archaic term for a wide collar or a garment covering the neck and shoulders, here used to hold the spare arrow</term>—the Lord wanted to know what he intended to do with the other one. Tell said at first that it was the custom of marksmen. But the Lord would not be satisfied with such an answer; instead, he pressed him to say why he had tucked the arrow into his doublet, with the assurance that it should not result in any disfavor toward him, promising him also that his life should be spared and made secure. Upon this promise and vow, Tell said that he had tucked the arrow there so that if he had missed the apple and injured the child, he would not have missed the Lord and his men. When the Lord heard this, he said: "Well then, I have promised you security of life; however, because I perceive that you were of a mind to shoot me, it will likewise be necessary for me to think of ways that I may remain safe from you." Therefore, he had him bound and placed in a ship along with his shooting gear, with the intention of leading him to Schwyz <note>The original text uses "Schweiß," an archaic spelling of the Swiss canton Schwyz.</note> and holding him there as a prisoner.

As they sailed from the land, however, such a cruel and tempestuous wind arose that they believed nothing else but that they must all drown. Therefore, one of the men addressed the Lord, crying out and begging that he would let Tell be untied, because he was a strong man and could help with the rowing. The Lord allowed it, because the need was at hand; thereupon he was untied, stepped to the rudder, and steered vigorously along. Yet he watched constantly for his advantage and his shooting gear. In the meantime, they came to a great flat rock, which is still called "Tell’s Plate" <note>Tellsplatte: a famous site on the shores of Lake Lucerne.</note> today.

When it seemed to him that it was time to escape, he called out to the servants to row freshly, for it was necessary; but once they were past that spot, there would be no danger. But while they were pulling so hard, he grabbed his shooting gear, leaped over the side onto the flat rock, and pushed the ship away from him, letting them drift. He, however, ran the nearest way toward Schwyz, and when he came to a "hollow way" <note>Hohle Gasse: a famous sunken lane near Küssnacht where the assassination of Gessler traditionally occurred.</note> through which Gessler <note>Original: "Grießler."</note> had to ride past, he hid himself in a thick bush and waited there until he came by. And when he heard them speaking of him, he spanned his crossbow and shot the Lord through with an arrow so that he died.

Afterward, he ran back again toward Uri <note>Original: "Vri."</note>, where he found his companions; for several of them had already conspired together that they [would no longer suffer] such arrogance and injustice...

# The Second Part

...tyrants beaten to death / and freed themselves from such intolerable tyranny.

In Thessaly there was a cruel tyrant / named Alexander of Pherae <note>original: Alexander Pheræus; a 4th-century BC ruler of Thessaly notorious for his bloodthirsty nature.</note> / who tormented the people so severely / that he had many people sewn into bear, lion, and wolf skins <note>Ancient accounts suggest he then set hunting dogs upon them for sport.</note>. When he attempted to shamefully abuse one of his wife's brothers / the wife joined together with her brothers / and strangled him in his bed at night / so that they might be delivered from his cruel tyranny.

In Vicenza in Italy <note>original: "Vincenz in Welschlanden." Welschland was an archaic German term for Italy or other Romance-speaking lands.</note> / there was once a tyrant / named Carrarius <note>Referring to the Carraresi family of Padua, specifically Francesco I da Carrara (1325–1393).</note> / who first murdered the Lord of Scala <note>The Scaliger family, who ruled Verona and Vicenza.</note> / together with his son / so that he might obtain the power and upper hand over the city. Now, when he had attained this / he sent for a citizen / and demanded / that he should send him his daughter / who was very beautiful. However, both the father / and likewise the daughter refused. Therefore the tyrant was moved with anger / and had the daughter taken from the house by force from the father / after two days he sent her back to the father in a basket / chopped into pieces. When the father saw this / he was (as can easily be imagined) heavily troubled by it / he reported it to the Council and his kinsmen / and sought their help and counsel. They, after much deliberation / let the matter reach the Venetians / and sent the basket with the hacked-up maiden along with it. For that reason, the Venetians armed themselves in haste / drove out the tyrant / and took the city / under their protection / under which it remains / to this day.

Such cruel tyranny / and wanton violation / also gave the Swiss cause / to free themselves by their own hands. This was caused / according to the Swiss Chronicle / by the fact that they had a governor / named Gessler <note>original: Grießler.</note> / an evil tyrant / who came at one time to Uri / and had a pole placed under a linden tree / where everyone had to pass by / upon which he set a hat / and had it publicly proclaimed / that whoever passed by there / should do reverence to the hat / and bow / as if he himself were sitting there in person. However, whoever should contemptuously overlook the command / he would punish without any mercy. He also kept a watchman constantly there / who had to watch the people / to see who kept the command or not.

Now it happened by chance / that one named William Tell / a pious and honest man / several times walked past the pole / and did no reverence to the hat. This was then reported and shown to the Lord by the watchman. The governor had Tell summoned before him / and asked him / why he had not kept his command / and thus had not bowed to the hat. Tell answered / "Gracious Lord / it happened by chance / I did not mean / that Your Grace should take it so deeply to heart / I have no understanding of such things / for if I were wiser / I would have a different name <note>Tell suggests here that if he were truly clever, he wouldn't be called 'Tell'—an old term related to "Talp" or "simpleton." He is playing the part of a humble, uneducated man to avoid the tyrant's wrath.</note> / therefore I beg for forgiveness." Now the governor knew / that Tell was a good marksman / therefore he had all his children secretly fetched / and asked Tell / if they were his / and which among them he loved most. To this he answered / they were all his / and they were all equally dear to him.

Then the Lord <note>Referring to the Habsburg bailiff Hermann Gessler, often spelled Grießler in early German texts.</note> spoke further: "Since you are a good marksman, as I have heard of you, you shall now prove this to me and shoot an apple from the head of one of your children. Whatever else the Lord might impose upon him, he would suffer it patiently. But he could obtain nothing from the tyrant; instead, he was forced by him and his servants to shoot the apple from the child’s head. This he did, and he was successful, so that he did not injure or harm the child in the slightest.

Now when the Lord saw this, it pleased him well. However, because Tell had two arrows—one with which he had shot the apple, and the other tucked in the back of his <term>doublet</term> <note>original: "Goller"; an archaic term for a short jacket or a wide collar worn over the shoulders.</note>—the Lord wanted to know what he intended to do with the other. Tell said at first that it was the custom of marksmen. Upon this pledge and promise, Tell said that he had tucked the arrow there for this reason: if he had missed the apple and injured the child, he would not have missed the Lord or his men either. When the Lord heard this, he said: "Well then, I have promised you security of your life; but because I perceive that you were of a mind to shoot me, it will likewise be necessary for me to think of ways that I may remain safe from you." He therefore had him bound and placed in a boat, along with his shooting gear, with the intention of taking him to <term>Schwyz</term> <note>original: "Schweitz"; here referring specifically to the town or canton of Schwyz, though it later became the name for the entire Swiss Confederation.</note> and holding him there as a prisoner.

Therefore, one of the men addressed the Lord, crying out and begging that he would have Tell unbound, because he was a strong man and could help with the rowing. The Lord permitted this because the danger was at hand. Thereupon Tell was unbound, stepped to the oar, and rowed stoutly along; yet he watched constantly for his advantage and for his shooting gear. But while they were pulling so hard, he grabbed his shooting gear, leapt out over the side onto the ledge, and pushed the boat away from him, letting them drift. ### Of the Regent’s Book.

...then died, and his lineage ruled after him until the sixth Mithridates. This man dared to wage war against the Romans. And although he had at first been a friend of the Romans—to the extent that he sent aid to Crassus against Aristonicus <note>Aristonicus of Pergamum led a revolt against Rome in 133–129 BC.</note>—after he began to fight with Nicomedes, the King in Bithynia, he turned away from the Romans. He also attacked them with force in Phrygia, first defeating and capturing Aquillius, and soon after the governor <note>original: "Bürgermeister"; likely referring to the Roman proconsul or praetor Quintus Oppius.</note> Oppius. Through that part of Asia, he issued a general proclamation to all commanders and regents: that on a certain appointed day—namely the thirtieth—each man, as far as his authority reached, should, upon pain of the highest punishment, have all Roman citizens and Italians <note>original: "Welschen"; used here to denote the Italian allies and residents who were not ethnic Romans.</note> stabbed and killed, whether they be man or woman, young or old, noble or common, and that no one should be spared. From this it followed that on that same stated day, throughout all Asia, up to one hundred and fifty thousand Romans and Italians were miserably murdered without any guilt—though Valerius reports only eighty thousand—as Appian of Alexandria clearly reports in his *Mithridatic Book* <note>Appian's "Mithridatic Wars" is a primary source for the "Asiatic Vespers" massacre in 88 BC.</note>.

Though this is viewed as a great number, it is yet to be believed that it is consistent with the truth and likely, since the Romans and Italians were at that time in such power and had such great trade in Asia. It was a most pitiful affair that in so many cities, towns, and everywhere throughout all Asia, so many Romans, Italians, and everything belonging to them had to be slaughtered on a single day without cause; that the hearts of the hosts changed so quickly and unexpectedly against their guests, and they either had to lay hands of death upon them themselves or look upon it with a sorrowful and terrified heart, as many of them were undoubtedly related and bound by friendship. But just as Haman—who would have gladly given the Jews such a "gift" <note>original: "Packet"; a figurative expression for a death warrant or a disaster.</note> according to the report of Holy Scripture—met a shameful end, so it ultimately went for Mithridates. For he was so distressed and pressured by his own son, Pharnaces, that he had to kill himself with poison. And when the poison would not work on him, he begged a Gallic <note>original: "Französischen"; here referring to a soldier from Gaul, likely the Chieftain Bituitus.</note> warrior and offered his neck, who then struck off his head after his son would not hear his begging and pleading. "Since Pharnaces my son," he said, "bids me to die, I pray you, O you gods of my fatherland, that he also in time may hear this voice from his own children which he has heard from me, his father." Which was undoubtedly God’s punishment and providence on account of his tyrannical heart.

And it is always a pity when such a person turns out so badly, for he was not only possessed of a magnificent, brave, and strong body, but also of great understanding and reason. And what is most to be wondered at: he was so eloquent and experienced in twenty-two languages that he could give speech and answer in each one as necessity required, without any interpreter. But it usually happens that when such people begin to go astray and forget themselves, then no shame...

...no treachery, no tyranny, and finally no wickedness is too much, as can be sufficiently seen in Nero <note>Nero (r. 54–68 AD), the last Roman emperor of the Julio-Claudian dynasty, was famously depicted by early Christian and Roman historians as a cruel and decadent tyrant.</note>.

Julius Pollux <note>A 2nd-century Greek grammarian and rhetorician whose work *Onomasticon* categorized Greek vocabulary, including terms for rulers and tyrants.</note> also painted the tyrants with their own colors, just as he did above for the pious regents. However, the colors of the tyrants look much different, and the words sound quite different; namely this: A tyrant is cruel, raging, a seizer of others' goods, a money-eater <note>original: "Geltfresser"; a person consumed by greed.</note>, arrogant, proud, harsh in speech, angry, terrifying, a slave to lust, immoderate, thoughtless, inhuman, unjust, godless, insane, fickle, easily deceived, unkind, one who refuses to be reminded of his duty, an instigator of war, burdensome, annoying, and entirely intolerable, etc.

Lastly, it is held by many that a tyrant is such a cursed, harmful, and hateful thing that they are worse than the Devil himself. For Eusebius <note>Eusebius of Caesarea (c. 260–339 AD), a historian of the early Christian church.</note> says that the pagan gods—whom he considers to be devils—are like lanterns or lights: when they burn, they give light to everyone and harm no one. But when they go out, they emit a horrific stench. Likewise, these same gods or devils, when they are "living," they are merciful to the people; but when they die, they poison the land and the people with their stench, causing hail and storms. But tyrants are much worse, for even during their lives they do nothing but harm, plaguing and torturing the people worse than the Devil himself; and after they have died, they leave an evil and hideous stench behind them—that is, a bad name and reputation, which is not forgotten as long as the world stands, as one sees in Nero, Domitian <note>Domitian (r. 81–96 AD), a Roman emperor often grouped with Nero for his authoritarian rule and conflict with the Senate.</note>, and many others. For tell me, have they not left a hideous stench behind them in the world?

# Of the Justice of Regents.
## The Thirteenth Chapter.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial N featuring foliage and scrollwork patterns.</image-desc>

Now that we have spoken of the goodness and tyranny of regents, it will also be necessary to provide several examples of their justice. For Cicero <note>Marcus Tullius Cicero (106–43 BC), the Roman statesman and philosopher.</note> says that Justice is the queen of all virtues; and where it is absent, then kingdoms, lands, and cities must be nothing other than great and harmful dens of robbers <term>Raubhäuser</term> <note>This is a reference to St. Augustine’s famous line in *The City of God*: "Justice removed, then, what are kingdoms but great bands of robbers?"</note>, as Augustine writes; and according to the opinion of Plato, the regime must soon collapse. Therefore King Agesilaus <note>Agesilaus II, a famous King of Sparta known for his leadership and modesty.</note>, when he was once asked which virtue was the most noble between fortitude and justice, answered: "We would have no need for fortitude if we were all just," and if each did for the other what he was duty-bound to do. By this, he meant to indicate that one should use no force and undertake nothing against the Law, which was spoken in a truly right and princely manner.

# Of the Book of Regents. #

Likewise, when Agis, the King of the **Spartans** <note>original: "Lacedemonier"; the people of Lacedaemon, more commonly known as Sparta.</note>, was asked by his parents at one time to assist and stand by them in a matter that was not particularly costly, he refused and asked them to excuse him from it. But as they persisted and would not cease, he finally gave them his decision: "While I was at home with you, I knew nothing of **Justice**. But once you handed me over to the Fatherland and allowed me to be instructed in the **Ancestral Laws** together with Justice, I will follow such laws as much as is possible for me. And since I know that your will and intention is that I should do that which is best—and nothing can be better than that which is **right**, both for the **Rulers** and the **Subjects**—I shall remain with that which you truly want, which is right in itself. However, regarding what you now request: since it is contrary to what is Right, I can neither advise nor help you in it."

This laudable King held so firmly to Justice that he would not approve or assist his own parents in anything against it, but instead politely declined them.

After **Phraates**, the King of the **Parthians**, sent word through his ambassadors to **Pompey the Great** <note>Pompey (106–48 BC), a leading Roman general and statesman during the late Roman Republic.</note> requesting that he should let the **River Euphrates** be the border that divided him and the Romans, Pompey answered: "One should rather let **Justice** decide that same boundary." By this, he meant to indicate that the King had no right to dictate to the Romans how far they should extend their borders; for in this, neither mountains nor water would hinder them, but they would only turn back when they no longer had the right or justification to step further.

When someone once praised the people of **Elis** <note>An ancient district in Greece, famous for hosting the Olympic Games.</note> for having applied themselves to **Justice** above all others during the **Olympic Tournament** and for using no unfair advantage, **Agesilaus** <note>Agesilaus II (c. 444–360 BC), a powerful King of Sparta.</note> answered: "Is it such a wonder if someone acted rightly once in five years?" By this, he wished to give it to be understood that no one was to be praised for the sake of Justice unless they held it before their eyes in all their deeds and being.

**Marsias**, the brother of King **Antigonus** <note>Likely referring to Antigonus I Monophthalmus, a successor of Alexander the Great.</note>, had a legal case to carry out against someone. He asked the King, however, that he would not take it to public court, but rather hear the case at home in a private hearing. Whereupon the King answered him: "If we are to act legally, then such a thing can happen nowhere better than before the **Court** and in public, where everyone may hear and judge it." Thus, he would not allow himself to be moved or led away from Justice in the slightest, regardless of the fact that it was his brother. Therefore, he said further to him: "If you know that you have a bad case, why do you quarrel? But if you have a good case, why do you flee or shy away from the **light of the court**, and why do you wish to have matters that belong before a court decided at home in the dark? Which could not happen without suspicion, even if you had the very best case."

When **Satibarzanes**, the chamberlain of **Artaxerxes** <note>Likely Artaxerxes II of Persia (r. 404–358 BC).</note>, once asked for something unjust from the King, and the King noticed that he would gladly [receive] several thou-
