## The Second Part ##

...had [many] guilders from him and since it was a matter of money, he had his treasurer fetch thirty thousand ducats, gave them to Satibarzanes, and said: "Now, take this sum of money; for if I had granted your request, I would have become more unjust because of it, but through this gift of money, I become neither poorer nor more unjust."

**Phocion** <note>An Athenian statesman and general (c. 402–318 BC) known for his extreme frugality and honesty.</note> would not stand by his son-in-law **Carillus** in an evil matter, as **Plutarch** writes, but said: he had chosen him as a son-in-law because he was a pious and just man. And when he had spoken these words, he let him stand alone before the court and walked away.

**Themistocles**, when at one time the poet **Simonides** requested that he deliver an unjust verdict in his case, gave him this answer: "Just as you would not be a good poet if you wanted to sing outside the rules of music—which would also not sound well—so too would I not be a good prince if I were to undertake to pass judgment against what is right."

When **Antisthenes of Athens** <note>A Greek philosopher and a pupil of Socrates.</note> was asked through what things the good government of cities perished and decayed, he answered: "When no distinction is made between the godly and the rogues, but rather when the unjust are worth just as much as the just." By this, he meant to show that kingdoms and governments do not remain stable where no upright governance <term>governance: the original term 'Policey' refers to the total civil order, administration, and moral regulation of a state</term> is maintained, where **Virtue** is robbed of its honor and deserved praise, and where villainy and shame remain unpunished through unjust negligence. For such a thing strives against the rule of **Justice**, which gives and preserves for each what is his own, according to the reward they have earned. Just as for adulterers, ravishers of maidens, murderers, and highway robbers—regardless of whether they are great men or small, noble or ignoble—their rightful punishment belongs to them: the sword, the gallows, the wheel, and the like. Conversely, a prince and regent shall protect the just and the godly, preserve the upright and honorable from injustice, and show them all honor, friendliness, and grace.

For from this fountain of **Justice** wells up and flows innocence, friendship, harmony, godliness, love toward God, and all honorable, pious men. As **Macrobius** <note>A Roman provincial who lived during the early fifth century, known for his writings on philosophy and grammar.</note> describes when he says: *From justice come innocence, friendship, concord, piety, religion, and humanity. By these virtues, a good man is made first the ruler of himself, and then of the Republic.* <note>original: "De iustitia veniunt innocentia, amicitia, concordia, pietas, religio, humanitas. His virtutibus vir bonus primum sui, deinde Reipublicae Rector efficitur."</note>

Therefore **Plato** also says, regarding the institution of the Republic: *The love of justice must be infused into the soul, without which not only the State, but not even a small gathering of men, nor even a small house, will stand.* <note>original: "de Republicae inſtitutione. Infundendum animis iuſtitiae amorem, ſine qua non ſolùm Reſpublica, ſed ne exiguus hominum coetus, nec domus quidem parua conſtabit."</note> That is: One should diligently instill in people, especially great lords, the love of justice, without which not only the common good, but not even a tiny cottage or a single house can be governed or persist. And it is not without reason written by the ancients that nothing appears more magnificent in a prince or king than **Justice**. *For kings, as Homer says, it is proper to exercise and guard not city-destroying engines and brass-clad ships, but justice received from Jove.* <note>original: "Reges enim, vt inquit Homerus, non expugnatrices vrbium machinas æratasq; naues, ſed iuſtiam à Ioue ſumptam exercere, cuſtodireq; decet."</note> That is: Kings should pay more heed to **Justice**, which is commanded to them by God, than to military armaments with which one can conquer a fortress.

# Of the Book of Rulers #

Thus the ancients, such as **Chrysippus** <note>A Greek Stoic philosopher (c. 279–206 BC) who was influential in shaping the logic and ethics of the Stoic school.</note>, in former times painted the image of **Justice** as a neat and beautiful maiden, but with an unfriendly, serious, and formidable face, and with bright and sharp eyes. She was depicted as neither defiant nor humble or downcast, but of a venerable and brave appearance, unmixed with any sadness. By this, they intended to teach that a lord or regent should act with purity and integrity toward his pious subjects. Yet, he must also have sharp eyes and not be merciful toward great misdeeds; rather, he should be resolute and penetrate through all things without fear, watching over matters with such earnestness that right and equity are protected, carried out, and provided. This ensures that all those who act uprightly and lead an honest, quiet life may enjoy the fruits of such piety. Those, however, who lead sinful, wicked, and punishable lives—whether they be of high or low station, noble or common—he shall punish without indulgence, regarding neither the pleas of friend nor foe. Therefore, **Erasmus** <note>Desiderius Erasmus of Rotterdam (1466–1536), a leading humanist of the Northern Renaissance.</note> aptly writes: "Nothing is more dangerous than leaving crimes unpunished, as it always invites worse behavior." <note>original Latin: "Nihil esse periculosius criminum impunitate, cùm ea semper ad deteriora inuitet."</note> And the elder **Cato** <note>Cato the Elder (234–149 BC), a Roman statesman known for his traditional morality and strictness.</note> spoke a fine maxim that was common for him to say: "He would rather receive no gratitude for a favor bestowed than fail to impose punishment for a crime committed." <note>original Latin: "Se malle pro collato beneficio nullam reportare gratiam, quàm pro maleficio perpetrato, non dare pœnam."</note>

As when once **Harpalus** <note>An aristocrat of Macedon and childhood friend of Alexander the Great.</note> pleaded with **King Philip** <note>Philip II of Macedon (382–336 BC).</note> that he should excuse his cousin or natural friend **Craterus** from the monetary fine he had incurred for his offenses and misconduct. Furthermore, he asked that the King graciously decree that Craterus should not have to stand trial before anyone else, but be declared free and innocent by His Royal Majesty, held as pious, and remain beyond the reproach of the people. The King answered: "It is better that he himself should have a bad reputation than that we should because of him." <note>original Latin: "Præstat vt ipse malè audiat, quàm vt nos propter illum."</note> He meant by this that it was far better for Craterus to suffer shame according to his deserved punishment than for His Majesty to be found unjust for his sake. **Plautus** <note>Titus Maccius Plautus (c. 254–184 BC), a Roman playwright.</note> also agrees with this when he says:

> For it is not fitting for unjust things to be obtained from the just, 
> but to ask for just things from the unjust is foolishness; 
> for indeed those who are unjust are ignorant of the law and do not uphold it.
> <note>original Latin: "Nam iniusta ab iustis impetrari non decet, Iusta autem ab iustis petere, insipientia est. Quippe illi iniqui ius ignorant, neq; tenent."</note>

->That is:<-

It is not proper to ask for something unjust from a just person; but to ask for fair things from an unjust person is folly, because the unjust do not know nor understand what is right.

**Plutarch** also writes that the Egyptian kings, according to ancient custom, compelled all judges in their lands to swear an oath that they would not deliver or pronounce any unjust verdict, nor otherwise act unjustly, even if they were permitted to do so freely or were even commanded by the kings themselves. Therefore, the following text by **Petrarch** <note>Francesco Petrarca (1304–1374), an Italian scholar and poet in Renaissance Italy.</note> is well worth considering, where he writes:

# The Second Part #

> There is one Judge, one incorruptible tribunal; before it, you mortals shall stand. What need is there for the skin of a false judge to be impressed upon the judicial seat, and for a barbaric reminder of justice? <note>original Latin: "Vnus est Iudex... & barbarica admonitione iustitiæ opus est?" This refers to the legend of the Persian King Cambyses, who flayed a corrupt judge named Sisamnes and used his skin to upholster the judge's chair as a warning to his successors.</note> Each person who judges sits in that very seat; where, if judgment is rendered unjustly, neither money, nor favor, nor false witnesses, nor unworthy prayers, nor empty threats, nor eloquent advocates will be of any use. <note>original Latin: "Ea in sella quisq; sedet... nec diserti proderunt Patroni."</note>

O you people, there is a Judge and a judgment seat before which we must appear. What need is there for the skin of the false judge nailed to the judgment seat, or for the barbaric reminder of justice? Every judge sits upon that very chair. If he now judges unjustly, then neither money nor favor, false witnesses, pleas or threats, nor even the lawyers—who protect people before the court—will be able to help him.

Therefore the aforementioned **Antisthenes** <note>A Greek philosopher and student of Socrates (c. 445–365 BC) who emphasized virtue as the only path to happiness.</note> rightly spoke when he pointed out the only way by which an eternal name and fame might be attained. "He used to say that those who desired to be immortal ought to live piously and justly." <note>original: "Eos qui cuperent immortales eſſe, oportere dicebat, piè viuere, atq; iustè."</note>

In Pedalia <note>Likely a reference to a legendary location in India found in classical travelogues or accounts by authors like Ctesias or Pliny.</note> in the land of India, it is not the priest who slaughters the sacrifice, but rather the one among them esteemed as the wisest. He is permitted to ask nothing else of the gods but justice alone.

**Plato** says: He is truly to be honored who does no one wrong. But he who does not tolerate wrong being done is to be honored more than twice over. For the former is compared to only one man, but the latter to many people, because he makes equity known to other leaders. But he who punishes injustice alongside the authorities, as much as he can, shall be praised as a great and perfect man in the city.

**Philemon** <note>A Greek poet and dramatist of the New Comedy (c. 362–262 BC), known for his moralizing maxims.</note> says: A just man is not he who does no wrong, but he who will commit no inequity, even though he might be able to. Nor is it he who refrains from taking small things, but he who does not allow himself to seize great things, even if he could have them and obtain them without danger. Nor is it he who does all this in order to gain fame thereby; rather, he who is endowed with a pure, free spirit is just, especially if he does not wish to be seen as such for that reason alone.

These are now all heathen examples and sayings, written by those who knew nothing of God. What, then, should Christians do, seeing that they are exhorted to justice so often and in many places in the Divine Scriptures? As in **Exodus 23**: "You shall not follow the multitude to do evil, nor answer in a court of law to turn aside after the multitude to pervert justice; you shall not favor the poor man in his cause," etc. And **Isaiah 5**: "Woe to those who justify the wicked for a bribe, and turn away the righteousness of the righteous from them." **Wisdom 1**: "Love righteousness, you rulers of the earth. For it is perpetual and immortal." <note>original: "Illa enim perpetua est, & immortalis."</note> That is, it endures forever and is immortal. Likewise, **Proverbs**: "To do wrong is an abomination to kings, for the throne is established through righteousness." And other sayings more. Although, alas, it is little considered, and one experiences daily how poorly things go in the courts in some places, of which I will, God willing, write further hereafter.

# From what causes rulers,
## and especially great potentates, kings, princes,
### and lords, should show themselves merciful toward their subjects and servants, and regarding taxation.

### The Fourteenth Chapter.

<margin>
See Cassiodorus, book 9, the letter to Magnitudo and the following. <note>original Latin: "Vide Cassiodorum lib. 9. Epistola magnitudinis et sequenti." Flavius Cassiodorus (c. 485–585 AD) was a Roman statesman and author whose "Variae" contained model letters and instructions for administrators.</note>
</margin>
Many lords hold these thoughts, and indeed sometimes speak them aloud: that if they do not tax their subjects, they could not rule them. For [they claim] the subjects exist for that purpose, and the lords have the legal right and power to deal with them in such a manner—especially the nobility with their peasants. They even say: "One must tax them once every three years, just as one trims the branches and hair from willow trees every three years." And just as willows do not grow if they are not pruned at the right time and become overgrown, so too the peasants do no good if one does not know how to tax them soundly. To support this, they cite Holy Scripture, which says: "Give to Caesar what is Caesar’s." <note>Matthew 22:21. The author suggests that while this scripture commands obedience, it is often misused by rulers to justify greed.</note> Although it is true that no one should be permitted to be rebellious in such cases, but must give while the means are available, the lords should nevertheless remember that they are human, and they should not burden the poor subjects so heavily. For they were not ordained by God for the sole purpose of taking. This is the very thing the Scythians <note>An ancient nomadic people from the Eurasian steppes, often portrayed in classical literature as plain-spoken critics of imperial excess.</note> threw in the face of Alexander the Great when he had himself publicly proclaimed a god, yet simultaneously seized one principality and land after another, only to give them away again as he pleased. Their ambassadors said to him: "If you wish to be a god, you should give to people and not take; but if you are a human, remember what you are, for it is foolish to strive for other things and forget yourself."

Accordingly, lords should think more on how their subjects might grow and increase, which can happen in no better or more fitting way than if they spare them from <term>taxation</term> <note>original: "Schatzung," a general term for assessed taxes or tributes.</note> and <term>levies</term> <note>original: "Vngelt," specifically referring to indirect taxes or excises on goods like beer or wine.</note> as much as possible. This is how several pagan kings acted, and for this reason they are highly praised. For under King Cyrus and his son Cambyses, no taxation was imposed; instead, everyone gifted and honored the king with whatever they wished. But when Darius came to the throne, he established taxes and tribute in all lands. Therefore, the Persians called Cyrus a "Father" for the sake of his goodness and piety; Cambyses a "Master" because he was strict and serious; but Darius a "Huckster" or "Merchant," because they perceived that for him, everything was about the money.

Thus one reads of Charles VII, the King of France, that the people had to give him twelve hundred thousand francs in taxation annually.

# The Second Part

His son Ludovicus <note>Likely referring to King Louis XI of France (reigned 1461–1483), who was notorious for significantly increasing royal taxes.</note> however, was not satisfied with that, but instead increased the assessment so high that the people had to give him four million crowns annually, not including what was required for his buildings. Now, in some places, things have reached such a point that there is neither measure nor end to it. Yet, one occasionally finds pious lords and regents who do not wish to burden their subjects with taxes.

One such prince was Duke George of Saxony, <note>George the Bearded (1471–1539), a Duke of Saxony known for his administrative reforms and his opposition to the Reformation.</note> of highly praised memory, as I have often heard his own subjects praise him for this. Thus, I have heard that a Prince of Saxony once levied a tax, but when it seemed to him that it was too much and his conscience was troubled by it, he commanded that the money be returned to the people—contrary to the common proverb: "What once enters the Devil's maw," etc. <note>The full proverb "Was dem Teufel einmal in den Rachen kommt, das gibt er nicht wieder heraus" means "What the Devil gets in his throat, he never gives back."</note> When he also learned that one of the officials had acted dishonestly and kept the tax money, refusing to give it back to the poor people, the Prince became violently angry and severely punished the greedy wretch.

Furthermore, Philippus Comineus <note>Philippe de Commines (1447–1511), a writer and diplomat whose *Memoirs* are a primary source for 15th-century European politics.</note> writes that Mehmed, the Turkish Emperor, <note>Mehmed II (1432–1481), known as "The Conqueror."</note> in his testament and last will, felt nothing more heavily on his heart or lamented more than the fact that he had once burdened his subjects with a tax beyond their proper tribute. This man was a Turk; yet today, some Christians dare to levy a new tax almost every month, by which the land and people are immeasurably weakened and ruined. And because God's blessing is not upon it, such money also vanishes so shamefully that it is of little use to the lords. A large part of it goes to the financiers, <term>Finantzer</term> <note>In this period, "Finanz" often carried a negative connotation of usury, trickery, or unscrupulous money-dealing.</note> and the rest is spent on banquets, gambling, or otherwise uselessly wasted. But how will it be when the Turk wakes up again and we must defend ourselves against him? Then it will be seen—when we are supposed to give, but nothing is at hand. It is even less tolerable when someone invents a false excuse <note>The phrase "eine Ursache vom Zaun brechen" literally means "to break a cause off the fence," meaning to fabricate a pretext or start a quarrel out of nowhere.</note> to take what belongs to another, or permits others to do so, as sometimes happens; for God has forbidden such things in the Ten Commandments, where He says: "Thou shalt not covet thy neighbor’s house, nor anything that is his." If we are not even to covet it, we can much less take it from them by force. That God has a great displeasure in such violent undertakings is easily considered from the history of King Ahab, who, by the counsel of the damned Jezebel, took the vineyard of the pious Naboth, for which he had to expect a terrible punishment. <note>1 Kings 21. King Ahab coveted a vineyard, and Queen Jezebel had the owner, Naboth, falsely accused and executed so Ahab could seize the land.</note> People ought to take such examples diligently to heart; if they did, many would lose the desire to take what belongs to another. Though some of them are worse than Ahab was, for he at least wanted to pay Naboth for his vineyard or compensate him in some other way. Since God punished Ahab so severely, what do you think will happen to those who act even worse, and not only take people's property by force, but sometimes even burn down their house and home, and will not even give a poor man a kind word?

It is much more princely and honorable for a lord to be merciful, and...

# The Ruler’s Book

...and gives gladly. Those same princes are also highly praised in all histories who not only did not burden their subjects with <term>taxation<note>The original German uses "Schatzung," referring to special levies or assessments beyond regular feudal dues.</note></term>, but also gave many great and rich gifts from their own rents and income. Among these, the most powerful King Cyrus <note>Cyrus the Great (c. 600–530 BC), founder of the Achaemenid Empire, often cited in the Renaissance as the ideal "Mirror for Princes."</note> is considered the most prominent. For, as Xenophon <note>A Greek historian whose work, the *Cyropaedia* (The Education of Cyrus), was a popular manual on leadership.</note> writes of him, among other princely virtues, he was especially diligent in seeking how he might make his friends and subjects rich. He did not strive to bring great wealth and vast riches to himself, but rather said that a prince or king should be of no other mind than that of a **shepherd**. For just as a shepherd is bound to look after his flock so that it takes no harm, and is well-tended and protected, so too should it befit a prince to watch over his subjects, ensuring they grow, increase, and are well-governed; for this reason, he gave away much money.

But when Croesus <note>The King of Lydia, legendary for his wealth, who became an advisor to Cyrus after being defeated by him.</note> (whom he used as a counselor) saw how generous he was, he reminded him and said that if he continued in this way, he would fall into poverty and impotence, even though in such good fortune he could instead gather great treasures and become rich and powerful. To this, Cyrus replied to Croesus, saying: "How much money do you think, Croesus, I could have gathered if I had been stingy <note>original: "kranck"; in this context, it implies being miserly or "tight" with money rather than physically ill.</note> and had not given so much away?" And when Croesus named an incalculably large sum, Cyrus said further: "So that you may see how rich I am and what treasures I possess, go at once and arrange with Hystaspes <note>A high-ranking Persian official and father of Darius the Great.</note> to travel among my friends and inform them that I am in need of money, and have them record specifically what each is able and willing to send to me."

Hystaspes carried out his royal command, traveled about, spoke to the people, and recorded what each promised to give; this then amounted to a far greater sum than Croesus had previously named. Thereupon, Cyrus turned to him, saying: "Do you see that I am rich and have many treasures? For in making my good and faithful friends rich, I do nothing other than gather treasures for myself, which are kept and held together for me much more faithfully than if I had locked them away at home." The same great King Cyrus also said that he sought money primarily for this reason: so that he might come to the aid of his friends in their time of need.

We also read in Ammianus Marcellinus <note>A 4th-century Roman soldier and historian.</note> of the Emperor Julian <note>Julian the Apostate (reigned 361–363 AD).</note> that he highly extolled and praised the answer of Alexander the Great. When Alexander was asked where he kept his treasures, he answered: "**With my good friends.**" King Dionysius <note>Dionysius I of Syracuse, or perhaps his son Dionysius II.</note> agreed with this; when he came into his son’s chamber and saw a large <term>sideboard<note>The original "Credenz" refers to a display of silver and gold plate used for serving and showing off wealth.</note></term> of silver and golden cups and drinking vessels, he said: "Eh, you do not have a kingly spirit, nor are you fit for the government, since you have made no friends with such **dead treasure**." He meant that without the goodwill of the subjects, one could neither obtain nor maintain a kingdom. However, a lord earns particularly good will when they are freely generous. In this manner, the fine Emperor Theodosius <note>Theodosius the Great (reigned 379–395 AD).</note> was also praised, of whom the excel—

# The Second Part

...the poet Claudian <note>Claudius Claudianus (c. 370–404 AD), a late Roman Latin poet who wrote panegyrics for the imperial court.</note>, where he writes of him: **"Bestower of great wealth, bestower of honors."** <note>original Latin: *Magnarum largitor opum, largitor honorum.*</note> This is to say that Theodosius <note>Theodosius the Great (r. 379–395 AD), the last emperor to rule over both the Eastern and Western halves of the Roman Empire.</note> gifted many people not only with great property, but also with great honors. Some great lords give only honors, such as when they ennoble someone or dub them a knight; this man went further and gave them money and property to go with it. For if someone is made a noble or a knight but does not have the income to match, he might as well be without the nobility. But when he receives property alongside it, he can better maintain his noble and knightly standing.

To this also belongs what the Emperor Trajan <note>Roman Emperor (r. 98–117 AD), famous for his vast public building programs and social welfare policies.</note> said: that the <term>Fiscus<note>The *fiscus* was the personal treasury of the Roman emperors, distinct from the public treasury of the state.</note></term>, or the Imperial Chamber, is to be compared to the **spleen** in a human body. For in the same way that when the spleen grows in a person, the other limbs must waste away; so too, when the Prince’s treasury grows and increases, the subjects must become impoverished and decline.

Plutarch <note>A Greek-Roman historian and philosopher (c. 46–120 AD) whose "Parallel Lives" was a standard text for Renaissance education.</note> writes that among the Corinthians a decree was issued and strictly upheld that all their ambassadors, wherever they were sent, should accept no gifts or presents. Therefore, when the tyrant Dionysius <note>Dionysius I of Syracuse (c. 432–367 BC), often used in literature as the archetype of a cruel but occasionally witty tyrant.</note> wished to give gifts and honors to the Corinthian ambassadors, they could not accept them because of their law. At this, he became greatly incensed and said: *“You do a shameful thing, for you take away and abolish the one good thing a tyrant has, while you teach that it is dangerous to receive a benefit even from tyrants.”* <note>original Latin: *Rem absurdum facitis, qui, quod vnum bonum habet Tyrannus, hoc tollitis, dum docetis etiam beneficium à Tyrannis accipere, periculosum esse.*</note>

Nonetheless, such mildness in this tyrant is praised to this day; and a Prince or great lord should, in this matter, follow our Lord God, who is mild and charitable toward everyone and yet requires nothing in return, nor desires any repayment. Regarding this, Seneca <note>Lucius Annaeus Seneca (c. 4 BC – 65 AD), a Stoic philosopher and advisor to Emperor Nero.</note> says a beautiful proverb: *“The duty of generosity is to give to everyone who asks, and in this to imitate the Gods. If you imitate the Gods, give even to the ungrateful. For the sun rises even upon the wicked, and the seas lie open even to pirates.”* <note>original Latin: *Officium liberalitatis est omni petenti dare, Deos imitari: Si Deos imitaris, da etiam ingratis. Nam & sceleratis Sol oritur, & Pyratis maria patent.*</note>

Artaxerxes Longimanus <note>Artaxerxes I (r. 465–424 BC), King of Persia, whose nickname "Longimanus" means "Long-handed," allegedly because his right hand was longer than his left.</note>, the son of King Xerxes, used to say commonly that it was more princely and magnificent to give something than to take it. He believed it was more fitting for a King and Prince to increase the property and holdings of his subjects than to diminish them.

Ptolemy <note>Ptolemy I Soter (c. 367–282 BC), a companion of Alexander the Great who became the ruler of Egypt.</note>, a son of Lagos, often ate and drank with good friends and even stayed overnight to sleep at their homes. However, when he invited these same good friends back as his guests, he made use of their own household goods, borrowing drinking vessels, tapestries, tables, and other items from them. For he kept no more than what necessity required, saying: **"It is far more kingly to make others rich than to be rich oneself."**

# Of the Book of Rulers

Lampridius <note>Aelius Lampridius, one of the purported authors of the *Historia Augusta*, a collection of biographies of Roman Emperors.</note> writes of the Emperor Severus <note>Alexander Severus (r. 222–235 AD), known for his efforts to improve the administration of the Roman Empire.</note> that he kept a register in which were recorded those to whom he had shown favor. And when he learned of an honorable and God-fearing man, he would call for him and say to him:

> **"What is it? Why do you ask for nothing? Do you want me to be your debtor? Ask, so that you do not complain about me as a private citizen."** <note>original Latin: *Quid est, cur nihil petis? An me vis tibi fieri debitorem? Pete, ne priuatus de me queraris.*</note>

Why do you not desire or request something from me? Do you want me to remain in your debt? Desire and ask for something, so that you have no cause to complain about me.

However, there is currently much complaining in many courts that those who have served faithfully enjoy very little benefit from their loyal service, while those who have the least trouble and labor are rewarded the best. But Emperor Sigismund <note>Sigismund of Luxembourg (r. 1433–1437 AD), Holy Roman Emperor, known for his role in the Council of Constance.</note> dismissed this—showing that it was not the fault of the lords—with a polite story, which I will also briefly recount here.

Emperor Sigismund had a faithful servant for a long time to whom he had rewarded or given little, even though the Emperor was praised for having a mild and imperial spirit. Once, as the Emperor rode through a body of water, a horse relieved itself. The servant, who was riding close by his master, said to his companion in a joke: "This horse has its master’s ways." The Emperor heard this and asked why he said it. The servant answered: "The horse holds its water in the water where it is already wet. Likewise, the Emperor gives to those who are already rich and do not deserve it." The Emperor noticed his meaning—that he had politely insulted him for not giving him, as an old servant, anything special—and said: "It has never been a lack of my will, for the gifts of lords are not for those who deserve them, but for those to whom they are destined by fate." He promised to prove this to him as soon as he reached a place of rest. Now, when the Emperor was staying at a certain place, he ordered two boxes of the same shape and size; he put gold in one and lead in the other, both of the same weight. He called the servant before him and told him to choose, for in one box there was gold and in the other lead. The servant became anxious; he lifted the boxes one after the other, not knowing which to grab. At last, he chose the lead box. Then the Emperor spoke: "Here you see that it was not a lack of my will, but a lack of your fortune <note>In the original German *Glück*, meaning luck, fate, or divine providence.</note> that has prevented you from being richly rewarded until now." And it appears from this that the Emperor saw and noted that all prosperity is God's gift and present.

Furthermore, one reads of Titus <note>Roman Emperor (r. 79–81 AD), often remembered for his generosity and his role in the destruction of Jerusalem before becoming emperor.</note>, the son of Vespasian, that he made many promises to everyone but could keep few of them. When his friends reproached him for this, he answered: ***"It is not fitting for anyone to depart sad from a conversation with Caesar."*** <note>original Latin: *Non oportet quenquã à Cæsaris colloquio tristem discedere.*</note> This is in itself a laudable imperial saying, provided the work and the deed follow it. But that he made great promises and held none is an unprincely levity and worthy of no praise. Therefore Seneca <note>Lucius Annaeus Seneca (c. 4 BC–65 AD), a Stoic philosopher and advisor to Nero who wrote extensively on the ethics of giving and receiving benefits.</note> teaches that one should consider what he wishes to give away and what to refuse, and also take to heart: to whom, how, and when. For these are his words: **"One must consider what, to whom, in what manner, when, where, and why something is to be given."** <note>original Latin: *Considerandum, quid, cui, quali- quando, vbi, & quare dandum.*</note>

Therefore, a lord should give in such a way that no lack for himself...

# The Second Part

...arises, and it follows thereafter that he must tax his subjects and collect again from the poor. As I once saw a Bishop who made many people rich through his gifting, and thereby deeply indebted himself, so that he had to levy great taxes upon his subjects; even three bishoprics could not provide enough for him. Therefore, Cicero very skillfully says: **Many squander their family estates by giving thoughtlessly.** <note>original Latin: *Multi patrimonia effundunt, inconsultè largiendo.* From Cicero’s *De Officiis*, warning that prodigality leads to the exhaustion of resources.</note> Likewise Seneca:

**Plunder follows after excessive giving; for when they begin to lack through giving, they are forced to lay hands on the property of others.** <note>original Latin: *Largitionem ſequuntur rapinæ, cùm enim dandô egere cœperint, alienis bonis manus inferre coguntur.* Seneca argues that when a ruler runs out of his own money to give away, he is tempted to seize the assets of his subjects.</note> He who gives away too much looks for where he might get it back, even if he must take it from another.

I also do not know what it is that now, in our times, Princes and Lords show the greatest generosity by giving away Church lands, being so liberal with things belonging to others. <note>original Latin: *de alienis*</note> Of this, Luther also said: **The time is most pestilential when the Church is neglected; nothing is given to it, but it is plundered. Once, Kings and Princes confirmed church properties, but now they plunder.** <note>original Latin: *Tempus eſt peſtilentiſſimum, ubi Eccleſia negligitur, nihil illi datur, ſed ſpoliatur. Olim Reges & Principes confirmabant, nunc verò ſpoliant.* Martin Luther was highly critical of secular rulers who used the Reformation as an excuse to seize church wealth for personal gain rather than supporting schools or the poor.</note> That is to say: It is truly a harmful time when little regard is paid to the Church. In former times, Kings and Princes increased and confirmed church properties, but now they are taken away again—properties which were nonetheless given and established by the ancients for the honor of God and the preservation of religion. Or otherwise, they manage them such that the Church enjoys very little of them. And where previously a crowd of idle monks resided (who are now driven out), in their place someone is often appointed who does little better than the monks. As a learned man once traveled past a monastery and composed this epigram <term>epigram: a short, pithy, and often satirical poem</term> on the spot:

->Once monks held these seats and kingdoms,<-
->Whose life was their belly, and foul food their goal.<-
->Who, like drones, devoured the food of the bees—<-
->The wealth that the flock of Christ produces with constant labor.<-
->But now that the drones are cast out, the Centaur,<-
->Disturbing the hives, plunders the riches of Christ.<-
->Thus fortune drags many things toward the worse: yet still,<-
->Christ Himself preserves and feeds His own flock.<-
<note>original Latin: *Has Monachi quondam sedes & regna tenebant...* The poem uses a nature metaphor: the monks were "drones" who ate the honey of the "bees" (the working Christian community). Now, "Centaurs" (greedy secular administrators) have replaced them and are even more destructive.</note>

->In ancient times, right here,<-

> Thus everything becomes far worse

However, this depends on each person's own accountability; nor is it cited by me in any other way than that I wished to mention it here in good faith alongside other things; otherwise, for my part, it will be neither whiter nor blacker. <note>A German idiom meaning that the author’s reputation or the truth of the matter remains unchanged regardless of how the reader reacts to the advice.</note> If also in a land the schools and churches are so well provided for <note>The original "vergessen" is likely a transcription or printer's error for "versehen" (provided for/endowed), as the context implies they suffer no want.</note> that they suffer no lack, together with the poor, then one may fairly bear with other expenses with patience.

I must also include here in this chapter the history of the aforementioned Emperor Sigismund. <note>Sigismund of Luxembourg (1368–1437), Holy Roman Emperor and King of Hungary and Bohemia.</note> Concerning his generosity, Cuspinianus <note>Johannes Cuspinian (1473–1529), a humanist scholar, historian, and diplomat in the service of the Habsburgs.</note> writes, among other things, that forty thousand Hungarian guilders were sent to him from Hungary. When these had been placed in the treasury and the Emperor wished to go to sleep, he deliberated and pondered how he might best invest such money. But as he wrestled with this in his sleep and fantasized until he woke from it, he roused his chamberlain with the command that he should urgently summon his counselors, captains, and the leaders of his knighthood to him. When they were summoned at midnight and were terrified—fearing that some misfortune had befallen the Emperor—they came in haste, desiring to hear the reason for such a sudden summons. Then the Emperor commanded the aforementioned money to be brought before him and divided it among them with these words: "Take away these shameful executioners and enemies" (he meant the gold coins) "who have broken my sleep; now I wish to sleep safely and peacefully."

One reads similarly of King Alphonso, <note>Alfonso V of Aragon (1396–1458), known as "the Magnanimous," a famous patron of the arts and literature.</note> when ten thousand guilders were brought to him by his treasurer, and a sycophant who happened to be present said: "This sum of money alone would be enough to make a man rich and blessed." The King answered: **"Take it, however much it is, and be blessed."** <note>original Latin: *Accipe quantacunque ea est, & beatus esto.*</note> From this and what follows, it appears how some court-parasites <note>original: "Hoffschrantzen." A derogatory term for sycophantic courtiers who consume the ruler's wealth.</note> are so coarse and shameless that they not only ask the lords for gifts, but take from them beyond all measure. Therefore, Panormitanus <note>Antonio Beccadelli (1394–1471), called Panormita, an Italian jurist and poet who wrote a famous biography of King Alfonso.</note> writes of the same King Alphonso that a nobleman named Johannes Calaguritanus asked for and received so much from him that the King could hardly tear himself away from him, and finally said: **"I would be lying if I did not fear, among so many and various things he asked for, that my knight would even demand my wife herself from me."** <note>original Latin: *Mentior, ni inter tam multa, & varia quæ petebat timuerim, ne uxorem etiam ipsam a me deposceret Eques meus.*</note>

Such and similar examples should sometimes be presented to lords, especially while they are young, so that they may be moved to a degree of generosity and take care not to burden the people and their poor subjects with excessive taxes and levies. However, now in some places—just at the time when all good and fine arts, the noble languages, and foremost the Holy Gospel have come to light and resounded in all places—

...had a Count with him at court who was rich and powerful. When, however, the Count once rode with the Duke on a hunt and stopped before a wood by a beautiful meadow, and there noticed a poor young maiden—a peasant’s daughter—cutting grass in the meadow, it happened that the Count, as a young man, allowed himself to be overcome by fleshly lust. Therefore, he rode silently to the maiden and thus forced her there in the meadow to satisfy his will.

But when the maiden came home, she showed this to her father with weeping eyes. And although the father heard this with great pain and was so dismayed by it that he did not know what to do—since he did not know the perpetrator, only that the maiden told him it had been someone from the Duke’s court—he nonetheless took heart and went with his daughter to the aforementioned Duke and complained of this to him with a troubled spirit. When the Duke had graciously heard him, he asked the maiden, among other things, whether she knew the person who had forced her. To this she answered: "If he had his clothing and horse again, just as he did at that time, then I would certainly know him." Therefore, the Duke had it announced by trumpet <note>original: "vmbblasen" - literally "blown around," referring to a public herald's announcement</note> that everyone should be prepared again, each in his usual clothing, to go out on the hunt the following morning.

When the morning had come that they were to be ready, and everyone was present and waiting for the Duke, the Duke took the maiden to a window with him and let the entire court household, noble and commoner alike—among whom was also the Count—pass by. He commanded the maiden to keep a close watch for the perpetrator, but to point out the correct one and not make a mistake. As the Count then passed before the Duke, the maiden began to speak to the Duke and said: "That was the one who forced me." At this, the Duke was not a little horrified. He had the court household return inside, hid the maiden in a chamber, and immediately had the Count summoned. He informed him that it had come to his attention how he, on the previous day's hunt, had forcibly violated a poor man's child. But the Count would not confess to this and denied it with indignation. 

Therefore, the Duke had the maiden brought forward. As soon as the Count looked at the maiden, however, he was terrified, fell at the Duke’s feet, confessed the deed, and asked for grace and forgiveness. But he could obtain no other decision or answer from the Duke than that he should prepare himself to be lawfully wedded to the peasant's daughter whom he had violated within a few days. Thereupon, she was honorably provided for by the Duke with clothing and all necessities. When the wedding day had passed, the Duke asked the young woman how the Count had behaved toward her. She answered: "Gracious Lord, he did to me just as he did in the meadow." <note>This response highlights the ongoing nature of the Count's behavior or perhaps the girl's trauma, as the Duke's attempt at "justice" through forced marriage does not necessarily change the Count's character.</note>

As everyone now thought the Duke had done more than enough to him by forcing a Count to take a poor peasant's daughter in marriage, thereby making her a Countess, nothing else was thought—

<header>The Second Part</header>

[The Count] thought that [the Duke] would let the matter rest and be settled with such a penalty. However, the Duke unexpectedly ordered a day of court to be held. He had the Count criminally indicted <note>original: "peinlich anklagen" – a legal term for a capital charge involving physical or "painful" punishment</note> for the aforementioned deed, and after the verdict was delivered, he had him executed by the sword. Furthermore, he ordered that the lordship and estates which the Count had owned be settled as a life estate <term>Leibgedinge: a legal provision, often a widow's dower, ensuring the use of property for the duration of one's life</term> upon the peasant's daughter, who was now a rich Countess. 

Because this proceeding seemed to some to be too hasty, the Duke was addressed by them and asked why he had behaved in such a manner toward the Count and imposed a twofold punishment upon him, contrary to the common proverb: *No one should be beaten with two rods* <note>A reference to the legal principle of double jeopardy—that one should not be punished twice for the same crime.</note>. To this he answered: With the first punishment, justice was done only to the woman, so that she might receive some compensation for her honor; however, to him, as the Judge, the crime had not been sufficiently satisfied in other ways unless the Count received his well-deserved [capital] punishment.

If such swiftness were practiced today with an ordinary citizen or a nobleman—which, in my opinion, would not be contrary to the Law, as one can indeed legally impose a twofold punishment on someone in many cases—God help us, how people would wonder at it! How they would cry out that it was handled too hastily! Especially if it were a case where someone had, perhaps, shamed the child of a poor peasant. For today, this has become so common in some places that it is no longer considered a disgrace, nor is it punished. Instead, when something of this sort happens to a poor man and he complains of it, he is snapped at in such a way that he thanks God if he can only keep silent in safety, or he allows himself to be turned away and satisfied with a small amount of money. Some are even punished because they complained, being told they should have rightly spared the young lord <term>Junckern: young noblemen or squires</term>; that it had happened before, and that one must teach such a person how to complain so that others might take offense at it, etc.

Although it has, alas, come to this with the authorities—that they let such things go unpunished as a matter of course, or at least do not use the earnestness they rightly should—it is nevertheless wrong. Everyone will find it difficult to answer to God for this on that [Judgment] Day. For if the authorities do not punish, nothing else follows but that vice becomes so common that no one is any longer ashamed or terrified by it. How many thousands, indeed how many hundreds of thousands of people throughout all of Brabant, the Netherlands, Zeeland, Holland, Flanders, and as far as this mighty Prince had command, must have taken this example to heart and thought to themselves: "If the Duke has used such severity with the Count for the sake of a poor peasant girl—who has thereby become rich and attained such a status as she otherwise could never have reached, so that she became a magnificent Countess—how would he deal with me if I should undertake to deceive a poor girl or force her by violence, etc.?" And especially, he must have instilled a fear among the young nobles, who otherwise are accustomed to making a joke or a laughingstock out of it when such a case occurs among them. But because the authorities, as mentioned, withdraw their hand and will not punish further, the government also proceeds much less...

Of the Book of Rulers.

...captain in Asia named Sysamnes, who, for the sake of money <note>That is, he accepted a bribe.</note>, delivered an unjust verdict in a major legal case. When this came before the King, he had this unjust judge flayed—ordered the skin to be pulled over his ears. And after he had that same skin stretched over the judge's chair, he appointed that captain's son as the new judge, with this warning: if he did not conduct himself in his office properly and uprightly, the same punishment that befell his father would happen to him. It should also be noted here that this Sysamnes was not a lowly village or peasant judge or magistrate, but a powerful lord who had an entire land to rule; therefore, this deed is to be considered all the more significant.

Likewise, one reads of Emperor Frederick Barbarossa <note>Frederick I (1122–1190), Holy Roman Emperor, known for his red beard and firm rule.</note> that he imposed a severe punishment on the Count Palatine of the Rhine because, in the Emperor's absence, the Count had unlawfully seized several towns from the Bishop of Worms. Specifically, the Count was forced to carry a dog on his shoulders through the entire city of Worms, holding it by its front legs; for at that time, this was the required punishment for princes and the nobility <note>This was a humiliating public penance known as "Hundetragen" (dog-carrying), used to shame high-ranking nobles who broke the Landfrieden (imperial peace).</note>.

With these preceding histories, one might well compare the example of Mettius Fufetius <note>original: "Metij Suffetij"</note>, who was a dictator in Alba and was called upon by the Romans for help against the Fidenates. Now, when the battle lines were drawn, he moved to one side, wanting to see where the victory in the battle would fall. When fortune and victory went to the Romans, Tullus the Roman King <note>Tullus Hostilius, the legendary third king of Rome.</note> summoned him, confronted him with his piece of treachery, and subsequently had him torn apart by two horse-drawn wagons. This was a truly severe and previously unheard-of punishment. Regarding this, Sextus Caecilius says (as Gellius writes): <note>original: "Nouum atq; asperum supplicij genus, quis negat? sed quid elegantissimus Poeta dicat, vide." A quote from Aulus Gellius’s *Attic Nights* referencing the poet Virgil.</note> "A new and harsh type of punishment, who can deny it? But look at what the most elegant poet says:"

> ->But you, O Alban, should have stood by your word.<-
> <note>original: "At tu dictis Albane maneres." From Virgil's *Aeneid*.</note>

That is to say: It is indeed a new and quite severe and violent punishment, as no one can deny. But see what the fine poet says: "You, man of Alba, should have kept your faith." It is as if he wanted to say: In such cases, one must make an example of a person so that many others may take heed of it.

# That rulers at times should hear and not hear, see and not see.
## The Sixteenth Chapter.

There is a common proverb among us Germans: He who wishes to be a ruler must sometimes see and not see, hear and not hear. By this they mean to indicate that whoever wishes to be in government must "dissimulate" <term>dissimulieren: the art of strategically ignoring certain minor offenses or pretending not to notice things to maintain social or political order</term> many things and let them pass in silence, or act as if he often [sees] a matter...

<meta>catchword: [sees] a matter...</meta>

<meta>This page transitions from the previous discussion of harsh, exemplary punishments (like flaying and public humiliation) to the tactical necessity of "dissimulation"—the art of a ruler knowing when to overlook minor offenses to maintain peace and avoid unnecessary hatred.</meta>

### The Second Part

who did not know this. For if one wished to defend all matters with total severity, he would have much to do and would never be able to sheath the sword. This would cause rulers much trouble and would achieve nothing other than awakening envy and hatred against them. Even the heathens recognized this, partly through reason and partly through experience: namely, that such forced and tyrannical governance, in which one wishes to use the extreme of severity, cannot be lasting or stable. This was seen with the "Thirty Men" in Sicily <note>Likely a reference to the Thirty Tyrants of Athens or similar despotic councils in Greek history known for their short, bloody rule.</note>. The proverb that Marcus Cicero uses in *On Duties* <note>original: "in Officijs"</note> also states this clearly: *They hate whom they fear, and whom each man hates, he does not wish to see live.* <note>original: "Oderunt, quem metuunt, quem quisque odit, non expetit viuere."</note> That is, one hates the person they fear, and whomever one hates, they would rather know him to be dead than alive.

Emperor Frederick, the father of Maximilian <note>Emperor Frederick III (1415–1493).</note>, used to say: *He who knows not how to dissimulate, knows not how to rule.* <note>original: "Qui nescit dissimulare, nescit imperare." Dissimulation here means the tactical art of feigning ignorance or "turning a blind eye" to maintain political stability.</note> Hutten <note>Ulrich von Hutten (1488–1523), a famous humanist scholar.</note> attributes this to Emperor Sigismund, saying: *He said that he who does not know how to feign, does not know how to govern.* <note>original: "Qui nesciat simulare, eum nescire regere, inquit."</note> That is: He who cannot occasionally allow things to pass his ears and eyes and "look through his fingers" <note>An idiom meaning to deliberately overlook a minor offense.</note> does not make a good ruler. This is captured in the following couplet:

->*Those who wish to reign are often wont to sleep through many things,*<-
->*And to overlook much with wise counsel.*<-
<note>original: "Qui regnare volunt, multis dormire, sagaci / Multaq; consilio dissimulare solent."</note>

From this, one must conclude that if a Prince or Lord wishes to rule rightly and well, he must choose not to know many things—especially what is not openly against the common peace, but rather concerns the Lord's person or his administration. Otherwise, if he were to strike immediately with severity, he would draw nothing upon himself from the people but one enmity after another.

However, where a matter is against the common peace and serves to cause an uprising, there a Lord should know, see, and hear, and follow through with punishment. For with good words and hard punishments, one keeps the common rabble in check and in good obedience. Therefore, let a Lord or Ruler be kind toward everyone; but if he encounters one who has deserved it and will have it no other way, let him hold him fast and show such punishment against him that others must take note. For it is better (as the saying goes) to leave a godly man unrewarded than to leave a wicked rogue unpunished.

And so that I do not forget the examples, one reads that in the time of Alexander the Great, there was a pirate or sea-robber named Diomedes.

When he was captured and led before King Alexander, he prepared himself to die. Therefore, he wished to earn his death honorably and speak enough for his life. When Alexander now asked him how he was so bold that he dared to take what belonged to people on the sea like a robber, he gave him this answer: "Because I, O King, have only a single ship on the sea, I am brought before you and must be called a sea-robber. But you, who do the very same thing with power..."

# The Ruler’s Book

...you commit violence, and not only on the sea but also on the land, robbing all people, taking entire kingdoms and principalities, yet one must worship you and call you a King and Emperor. In our actions, there is no difference, except that you are a greater robber than I, because you do everything with force and have the favor and help of the people. No necessity drives you to this, but only insatiable greed, a thirst for honor, and pure wantonness. As for me, poverty and the reduction of my livelihood force me to this. If I had your luck, I would not wish for this robbing, but would be satisfied with the ten-thousandth part of your fortune. As far as the law is concerned and that which is forbidden to me, you are indeed much worse than I, because you rob a thousand before I rob one. Only you carry out your robbing with force and tyranny and trample the laws with your feet; yet it must be considered right. I, however, who sought my sustenance out of necessity and great poverty, must be a robber and die for it. At this unheard-of answer and great boldness, Alexander <note>Alexander the Great (356–323 BCE).</note> wondered; he not only released him unpunished but ordered him to be counted among his servants.

In the same way, several mercenaries were reported to Pyrrhus at Tarentum <note>Pyrrhus of Epirus (318–272 BCE). Tarentum was a Greek colony in Italy where he fought the Romans.</note> for having spoken much evil of him while drinking. But when one of them said during the interrogation: "It is true, Gracious King, and if we had had more wine, we might perhaps have strangled Your Majesty altogether." Pyrrhus did nothing to them because of it, but let them go free and clear.

The philosopher Diogenes <note>Diogenes of Sinope (c. 412–323 BCE), the Cynic philosopher famous for his extreme poverty and blunt honesty toward the powerful.</note>, when Philip, the father of Alexander, overran the Greeks with the power of his army, went into Philip's military camp. When the King saw him, he cried out at him: "A spy! A spy!" Thereupon Diogenes answered: "It is true, you have guessed it, for I have come to find out if you are as insane as people say of you. For you could well have good peace and comfort in your kingdom, yet you set yourself against the Greeks, not without great and noticeable danger to your kingdom, as well as to your body and life." Philip heard this speech without any particular annoyance and let Diogenes go from him.

Likewise one reads of the much-mentioned King Alexander, that he came to the wise people in India who are called Gymnosophists <note>The "naked philosophers," early Indian ascetics whom Alexander encountered during his eastern campaigns.</note>. He told them to ask and desire of him whatever they wanted. Thereupon they asked: "Give us that we may never die, which we wish for and desire above all things." Alexander said to them: "Since I myself am mortal, how can I make you immortal?" *If you know yourself to be mortal,* they said, *why then, not content with your father’s seat, do you trouble everyone and try to subject the whole world?* <note>original Latin: "Si ergo, inquiunt, mortalem te esse cognoscis, cur non contentus Patrijis sedibus, omnibus infestus, totum orbem subjicere conaris?"</note> Since you then confess yourself to be mortal, why are you not satisfied with your father’s empire and royal seat, but instead make yourself hostile and hated to all people, wanting to bring the whole world under you and make it subject to you?

While often remembered as a tyrant, this anecdote highlights his philosophical stance on dissent.</note>; yet when those who had spoken such things about him were brought forward and reported, he did nothing more about it nor gave any other answer than saying: *In a free state, even tongues must be free.* <note>original Latin: "In libera ciuitate, oportet etiam linguas esse liberas."</note> That is: In a free...

## The Second Part

In such a place, one should also have the power to speak freely. In this present time, if perhaps a poor man speaks a word too many, and does so out of thoughtlessness and not out of a wicked heart, and does not think that any danger shall arise for him from it—since it was not done to insult anyone—some places will immediately seize his body and goods. This occurs regardless of what the Imperial Law decrees in the case of <term>l. Unica. C. Si quis Imperatori maledixerit</term> <note>original: "The single law in the Code [of Justinian] regarding whether anyone has spoken ill of the Emperor." This Roman law suggested that such talk should often be ignored rather than punished.</note>. Some men are even driven from house and home without a hearing. Such haste was not even used by the heathens, as a fine example shall hereafter be set down concerning <term>Ruffus</term> <note>Likely a reference to a Roman citizen named Rufus who was accused of slandering the Emperor.</note>, who had spoken ill of the Emperor <term>Augustus</term>.

Yet, I do not wish to have defended those who wantonly presume to insult the authorities and other high-ranking people, whom we should rightly hold in all honor according to the teaching of Saint <term>Peter</term>, who says: "Honor the King," etc. If something happens to such an unrestrained mouth because of it, he is not to be pitied, much less defended, since one should not scold or insult anyone, whether they be of high or low station. For indeed, sensible, wise, modest, and prudent people well know how to distinguish between those who speak of people perhaps without evil intention or thought, and those who intentionally insult people. There is also a common proverb: "One speaks what he wants, but he does not therefore get what he wants." One must tolerate speech (unless one wants to make all people mute), but one should punish evil deeds. However, he who wants to contest every word, as mentioned, and stop everyone’s mouth, would give himself much to do and yet accomplish nothing more than that people would talk about him all the more. Therefore, <term>Hillebrand</term> says to <term>Dietrich von Bern</term> <note>Characters from the "Nibelungenlied" or associated Germanic heroic legends; Hillebrand is the wise old mentor to the hero Dietrich.</note>, as he rebukes him:

-> If you wish to be a wise man, <-
-> Then let speech pass by your ears. <-

In Rome, they have a special place in front of a Cardinal’s house where there stands a statue called <term>Pasquillum</term> <note>Known as Pasquino, the most famous of the "talking statues" of Rome where people posted anonymous satirical verses (pasquinades) criticizing the Pope or the government.</note>, enclosed by a grate. Every year, all kinds of writings are thrown and posted there, in which even the Pope himself is sometimes heavily attacked. But no one takes these writings to heart, nor is any inquiry or investigation made into where such writings, <term>Carmina</term> <note>original Latin: "verses" or "poems."</note>, or poems come from. Of this, enough for now.

# On Slanderers and Evil
## Backbiters: that Regents and great Lords should not tolerate them, nor give them any credence.

### The Seventeenth Chapter.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial D featuring floral patterns and a bird-like figure within a square border.</image-desc>Because there is no worse or more harmful vice on earth than to cut away a man's honor and to malign or secretly denounce him before the authorities—whereby many an honest man, through no fault of his own and even before he is aware of it, is deprived of life, honor, and property—and because I know in part from experience that this vice is especially common at court, so that lords and authorities usually have this failing: that they not only listen to such people gladly, but also hold them in great honor and dignity and exalt them above other pious people. And the more pious and simple <note>In this context, "simple" means guileless or well-meaning, rather than unintelligent.</note> a lord is, the more easily and light-mindedly he can be deceived by such <term>ear-blowers</term> <note>original: "Ohrenbläsern"; a vivid term for sycophants or informants who whisper poisonous lies into a ruler's ear.</note>. Thus, it is not the fault of the lords, but of those same loose people who know how to worm their way in and persuade people with sweet words so that they believe them. And though one might wonder how such a thing could happen or be possible, he will soon cease to wonder if he considers within himself how entirely human nature is perverted and corrupted through the fall of our first parents <note>A reference to the biblical Fall of Adam and Eve in Eden.</note>, and that no one can be so pious and righteous that he does not love himself. But because love is such a foolish and nonsensical thing—for no one is more easily deceived than those who are bound by such love—it follows naturally that when hypocrites and ear-blowers come and praise us, but conversely scold and diminish others, we may easily be moved to give them credence.

However, since this is so harmful, and we should warn people as much as possible because of the damage that results from it, I will therefore set down several examples here. From these, one may learn what kind of hardship often follows and encounters pious, honest people through such slanderers, informants, and ear-blowers, so that the rich and powerful, and especially the <term>Regents</term> and authorities, may know how to guard themselves against them, and so that they do not grant them place or room so quickly, but rather investigate the matter better, lest they burden someone without guilt and thereby put their own consciences in danger.

One writes among other things of <term>Apelles</term> <note>Apelles of Kos (c. 330 BCE), the most renowned painter of ancient Greece.</note>, the exquisite painter, that he was at one time denounced and accused before <term>Ptolemy</term> <note>Ptolemy I Soter, the Macedonian general who became King of Egypt.</note> the King of Egypt, as if he had made and concluded a conspiracy against him at <term>Tyre</term> <note>A major ancient port city in modern-day Lebanon.</note> with several others, especially one named Theodorus, although he...

Now, when the King (who was not of particularly great understanding and believed far too much in <term>ear-blowers</term> <note>original: "Ohrenblasern"; sycophants or informants who whisper poisonous lies into a ruler's ear.</note>) learned of this, he was fiercely enraged. Instead, he simply had these thoughts: that since he had done much good for Apelles, and Apelles had shown himself so ungrateful in return, he wanted to punish him all the more severely, and he intended by no means to release him.

And Apelles would undoubtedly have been executed, though innocent, passing from life to death, had not one of those who had actually made the alliance against the King been captured. Apelles was most strongly exonerated by this man, who testified that Apelles had nothing to do with the matter. When the King heard this, he came to his senses again and not only set Apelles free and released him, but also gave him many thousand gold pieces as a gift. He also delivered Antiphilus, his detractor and accuser, into Apelles' hands to be his servant.

To prove the first charge, not much effort was needed, for they could easily find a loose and flighty woman who would say that she had been forced by Athanasius. Now, as *Athanasius* was pious and holy, so too was he wonderfully shrewd in his plans and a very wise man. Therefore, he commanded that *Arsenius* should keep himself hidden and let no one see him. The woman had been taught and instructed by them to say that she had given lodging to *Athanasius*, and that he had forced her to satisfy his lust during the night. Upon this, *Athanasius* was summoned to defend himself. *Athanasius* ordered the priest *Timothy* to speak for him and give answer, for he knew for certain that the woman had never known or seen him in her life, much less been given lodging by him. Accordingly, *Timothy* said to the woman, "How do you dare, woman, to be so shameless as to say that I have committed violence against you and forced you?" To this, the woman answered out of her frivolity, "Yes, exactly you have done it; in this place and at this time, I gave you lodging and was dishonored by you."

Although many in the Council were astonished, and even the accusers themselves were partly ashamed that the woman’s false and fabricated accusation was discovered and brought to light so easily in such a manner, *Athanasius* was nevertheless not counted as acquitted, nor was the woman called to punishment, for the accusers were also the judges. Therefore, they proceeded with great earnestness to the second point of accusation, and the *Arians* said that *Athanasius* would surely not be able to deny that this was the arm of *Arsenius*; therefore, he must also show why he had severed it and what he had to do with it. In this accusation, *Athanasius* again used his prudence and asked the *Arians* if they truly knew *Arsenius*. To this, they gave answer that they knew him well. Then *Athanasius* requested that he might be permitted and allowed to call for one whom he required for this business, which was then granted to him. So he had *Arsenius* called for and brought him before the Council healthy and fresh, saying: "Since you gentlemen all see that *Arsenius* still lives and also has both his arms, I expect that I shall be released from this accusation and that the accusers be held to show whose arm they have cut off and where they obtained it."

But one might ask: what excuse could the adversaries offer, since they had been so publicly defeated and put to shame on both counts of the accusation? <note>Referring to the failed attempt to frame Athanasius for both murder (using the hand of Arsenius) and assault.</note> To this it is answered: they cried out and said that *Athanasius* was such a sorcerer, black magician, and deceiver of the land that no one could resist him, and therefore he should by no means be left alive; and that the matter with *Arsenius* was likewise nothing but pure sorcery. Thereupon, the lords of the <term>Council</term> <note>The Council of Tyre (335 AD), dominated by theological rivals of Athanasius.</note> were summoned together again, and *Athanasius*, that holy man, was condemned and sentenced just as if he had been legally and properly defeated. They were not satisfied with this, but sent letters out against him into all lands, and horrible rumors spread about the good man; he was hunted in all places, and a high price was set upon his head, so that if he could not be taken alive, he should be killed and strangled. Therefore, he lay hidden for six whole years in a dry cistern; for thus *Eusebius* <note>Eusebius of Caesarea, a contemporary historian, though some accounts of this event come from later histories.</note> writes of this: <term>He is said to have remained hidden for six continuous years in the pit of a cistern that held no water, so that he never saw the sun.</term> <note>original Latin: "Sex continuis annis ita latuisse fertur, in lacu Cisternæ, non habentis aquam, vt Solem nunquam videret."</note> That is: he lay hidden in a cistern that had no water for six whole years, so that during that time he never saw any sunshine. All of this the *Arians* <note>Followers of Arius, who held different views on the nature of Christ than Athanasius.</note> had falsely orchestrated against him. Therefore, God also rescued him in a wondrous way and afterwards brought his innocence to light, though the full account of this must be omitted for the sake of brevity. It follows further.

The Emperor *Justinian* had two excellent military commanders, *Narses* and *Belisarius*, and *Belisarius* in particular was fortunate and victorious in matters of war, according to the histories; for he defeated the Persians, conquered all of Africa, and protected Syria from enemies, not to mention the Goths. Yet he was so slandered and falsely accused by his enviers to the Emperor that the Emperor had his eyes put out, and he was afterwards forced to beg for alms from the people. <note>This account of Belisarius being blinded and becoming a beggar is a popular medieval legend, though modern historians believe he was actually pardoned and restored to favor before his death.</note> It is indeed a pity that the dear hero should be so shamefully rewarded for his chivalrous and manly deeds. Therefore, a little house or hut was built for him by the side of the road, and when people passed by, he called out to them and said, "Give a penny to *Belisarius*, whom his great and manly deeds honorably exalted, but whom the envious and false slanderers have brought low again and deprived of his sight." And therefore *Sidonius* writes <term>concerning the miserable condition of mortals</term> <note>original Latin: "de misera mortalium conditione"</note>, and not unjustly:

->O wretched necessity of being born,<-
->Miserable in living, hard in dying.<-
<note>original Latin: "O necessitas abiecta nascendi, Viuendi misera, dura moriendi."</note>

That is: O Lord God, what a miserable thing is human life!

# Of the Book of Rulers

life, where the beginning is slight, the middle miserable, and the end or death is quite burdensome.

In the same manner, it would no doubt have gone for Narses <note>Narses (c. 478–573 AD) was a high-ranking Byzantine general under Justinian I who completed the conquest of Italy.</note> had he returned to Constantinople. When Lady Sophia, the Emperor's wife, summoned him, he would not appear, but remained in Italy and said: If he came, he would give the Empress such a distaff <note>original: "Rocken." A tool used in spinning wool; Narses was implying the Empress should stick to "women's work" rather than meddling in military affairs.</note> that she would have enough to spin from it for her whole life. For he had also been denounced in such a way and falsely accused. From this, one can clearly see what great harm such slanderers do at court and elsewhere, and how easily a lord or ruler can err and commit an injustice if he gives too much credit to such people and follows them without thoroughly investigating the causes. Therefore, Antisthenes says (which is also attributed to Diogenes) that he would rather fall among ravens than among slanderers, for ravens attack only the dead, but slanderers do not even spare the living. Even Nero, as cruel and tyrannical as he otherwise was, did not like to hear them. Therefore, Saint Jerome teaches: Do not have itching ears to hear the slanders of others. <note>original Latin: "Noli habere aures prurientes, ad audiendum alienas calumnias."</note> That is: You should not have greedy ears to hear when another person is being disparaged.

One also reads of Domitian that when he noticed there was no poison on earth more harmful than the backbiter and slanderer, he had them all driven out and banished from the city of Rome, and furthermore said: A prince who does not punish informers incites them. <note>original Latin: "Princeps, qui delatores non castigat, irritat."</note> A prince who does not punish the backbiters provokes and entices them. Alfonso <note>Likely referring to Alfonso V of Aragon, known as "the Magnanimous."</note> used to say that flatterers were not unlike wolves. For just as wolves are accustomed to devour donkeys by tickling and scratching them, so flatterers strive for the destruction of princes through blandishments and lies. <note>original Latin: "Alphonsus, adulatores Lupis haud absimiles dicebat esse. Nam quemadmodum Lupi titillando ac scalpidando asinos vorare soliti essent, Sic adulatores ad perniciem Principum blanditiis ac mendacijs contenderent."</note> That is: Alfonso scolded and held the hypocrites to be nothing other than wolves. For when wolves come upon a donkey, they scratch it before they begin to eat it; so also do the flatterers, giving the princes and lords good, flattering words in order to destroy them. And would to God that all lords and rulers followed Domitian in this, and likewise the praiseworthy Emperor Alexander Severus. Although he was a heathen, born in Syria, and furthermore quite young in age, he was so vehemently hostile toward backbiters, ear-whisperers, slanderers, false judges, and other harmful, wicked people that—though he was otherwise kind and gentle—he could have no patience at all with them.

In the same way, the Emperor Sigismund once said that he hated sycophants, flatterers, and slanderers like harmful poison and the pestilence. His counselor, Brunorius of Verona, spoke: "There is no race of men that you love and promote more; for what would they be or what power would they have with you—Marcus Bauus, Laurentius Palatinus, Ursacius Michael, and Caspar Schlick <note>Caspar Schlick (c. 1396–1449) was a prominent diplomat and chancellor under Sigismund.</note>—if they had not earned and obtained such grace with you through hypocrisy, flattery, and slandering?" The Emperor answered him: "Brunorius, it is so arranged that when we say flatterers should be avoided..."
