## The Second Part

...then we most especially give them our ears. Nor would you have been with me so long, unless you had accustomed yourself to flattering me. <note>original Latin: "tum maximè illis aures damus. Nec tu mecum tamdiu fuisses, nisi mihi blandiri assuevisses."</note> That is: it is so ordained that even when we say flatterers should be avoided, they are still heard by us. And if you, Brunori, had not flattered me, you would not have stayed with me for so long.

Macrinus <note>Marcus Opellius Macrinus (c. 165–218 AD) was a Roman Emperor; the text here uses him as an example of a ruler's policy toward informants.</note> had this custom: that he made traitors infamous <term>anrüchtig</term><note>Meaning to be held in low public regard or stripped of honor.</note> if they proved a deed against someone; but if they could not prove it, he had them punished with the sword, as they were worthy of no better reward. For it often happens that such a villain, who has scarcely been at court for three days and—due to his lack of skill and understanding—cannot dare to trust that he might gain prestige in the same way as those he intends to slander. Therefore, he schemes and strives day and night how he might falsely accuse and report them, and can easily invent some petty and base pretext <term>farbe</term><note>Literally "color," used here to mean a false appearance or a manufactured excuse.</note>. Then the Lord is at hand and believes it so quickly, from which it follows that a Lord often treats his most faithful servants and best friends with suspicion, even casting them off entirely. Some become so senseless that, based on such mere words and empty accusations, they dare to seize the life and property of one who has served them faithfully and well for many years, without any defense or hearing—even though they have much to consider in this matter. 

Firstly, their conscience: that they can never answer for such actions before God. Secondly, their good reputation and fame; for it cannot fail that one’s good name will be greatly weakened and darkened by such forgetfulness when a Lord begins to behave in such a manner toward his servants or subjects. Thirdly, they should know the nature and character of the slanderer: namely, that they deal in nothing but lies and false, fabricated charges, and use no truth. They know nothing and can do nothing but be hateful toward everyone, reporting falsely and speaking the worst behind people's backs. They envy the rich their goods, the learned their art, the clever and wise their skill, and even the pious their piety. In short, they wish no one any good, only every evil.

These are the dragons and snakes who crawl through every corner of the court and are more harmful and destructive to people than any poison or any pestilence. For they often cause many a man to shamefully lose the faithful service he has rendered to a Lord for many years. And some Lords like to keep such slanderers near them for this reason: so that through such a path, they need not give their servants what they have promised, signed for, or vowed, and which those good people have earned over a long time. As one often sees, they manufacture a reason out of thin air <note>original idiom: "ein ursache vom Zaun brechen," literally "to break a reason off the fence."</note> so that they may nullify a man's faithful service.

To this is added the cursed proverb which all princes and lords have daily in their mouths and use, and which is said to come from Emperor Sigismund <note>Sigismund of Luxembourg (1368–1437), Holy Roman Emperor.</note> (as was further cited above), which reads: "The goods of lords do not belong to those who earn them, but to those to whom they grant them or for whom they are destined." Now, what kind of heart must a man have for such a Lord, who uses and speaks this proverb before his servants...

Against such slanderers, **Apelles** (mentioned above) took his revenge with a certain painting. Namely, he painted a man sitting on a throne with large ears, reaching out his hand to **Calumny** <note>The personification of false accusation or slander.</note> or False Speech, inviting her to come to him. For it is not possible, when a Lord has allowed himself to be misled by slanderers in such a way and afterwards learns the truth, that he should not feel shame and horror at it, wishing he had not done it but had been more cautious, heard the other side, and properly investigated the matter, as the Greek poet teaches: **Do not judge before you have heard the case of both parties.** <note>original: "Ne ante iudicaueris, quàm vtriusq; partis causam audiueris."</note> That is: you should not judge or give a verdict before you have heard both sides.

**Ammianus** <note>Ammianus Marcellinus (c. 330–400 AD), a Roman historian who recorded the deeds of the emperors.</note> writes that in the time of the Emperor **Julian**, there was a man named **Cephidius** <note>Likely referring to the orator Delphidius, who famously accused Numerius before the Emperor Julian.</note> who made it his business to accuse people in criminal matters. After he had, at one time, vehemently accused **Numerius** of being a thief before the Emperor, **Numerius** defended himself in such a way that the accuser could bring nothing against him. **Cephidius** then began to shout loudly at the Emperor, saying: "Most powerful Emperor, who will ever be found guilty if he is allowed to deny the charge and answer the accusation with 'no'?" To this, **Julian** answered: "Who then could remain innocent if one were allowed to accuse anyone without proof?" # The Second Part

"...it is then that we most give them our ears. Nor would you have been with me so long, had you not grown accustomed to flattering me." <note>original: "tum maximè illis aures damus. ...ly to condemn. Now, just as Julian is praised for such wise speech, so is Constantius not unfairly criticized for giving too much place and room to slanderers and <term>ear-whisperers</term> <note>original: "Ohrenbläsern"; people who secretly whisper gossip or accusations into a ruler's ear to manipulate them.</note>—something that the Emperor Augustus and other high leaders did not do. For one reads of the aforementioned Emperor Augustus that when someone once accused a man named Helianus before him, claiming he had spoken ill of the Emperor, Augustus said nothing to Helianus (who was present in person). Instead, he looked sternly at the accuser and said: "If you can prove this against Helianus, he shall find that I too am not speechless, and can say more about Helianus than he can of me," and with that, he let the matter drop. Later, when <term>Tiberius</term> <note>Tiberius (42 BC – 37 AD) succeeded Augustus as the second Roman Emperor; while Augustus is depicted here as lenient, later history often views Tiberius as more paranoid.</note> complained about Helianus in the same manner, Augustus gave him this answer: he should not take it to heart on his account if someone spoke ill of him; it was enough that no one could do him any actual harm. There was one among the flatterers and slanderers of <term>Alexander the Great</term> <note>original: "Alexandri Magni"</note>, acting as a leader or captain, named Medius. He commanded and ordered the other slanderers to simply strike out boldly and vigorously with accusations and betrayals. For even if the wound of the slanderer heals, he said, the scar remains. Therefore, Anarilas said: "Flatterers are the worms of the rich" <note>original Latin: "Adulatores esse diuitum vermes"</note>. That is: flatterers are the worms or lice of the wealthy. Now, if great lords and rulers would show themselves toward backbiters, slanderers, and ear-whisperers in the same way as those mentioned above have partly done, there would not be so many of these shameful people found; and in our times, so many good and honest people would not be brought into disadvantage and undeserved hardship by them.

But let no one come to me here with the <term>Papian Law</term> <note>original: "Lege Papia"; referring to the Lex Papia Poppaea, a Roman law that encouraged the reporting of various legal infractions through financial rewards.</note> and say that a certain and good reward was ordained for such people by that law—namely, half of the penalty of those they had accused. For that same <term>law</term> <note>original: "Lex"</note> speaks of informants whom a lord must occasionally use when he has rebels in his land, or if people are secretly conspiring against him, or if someone wishes to harm him, etc. These people take their payment for it, and one knows well enough what to think of such people. However, that same law did not remain in full effect for long, for Emperor Nero reduced their share to only a fourth part, from which they were then called <term>Quadruplators</term> <note>original: "Quadruplatores"; Roman professional informants who received a fourth (quadrans) of the convicted person's property.</note>, just as they are called "four-and-twenty-ers" or "eight-and-twenty-ers" among us. And although Tiberius, Vitellius, and several others held to it so fiercely that they believed everything and gave credit to every person, it lasted until betrayal gained the upper hand to such an extent that one traitor turned in another, and no one dared trust another anymore, whereby many innocent people were deprived of life, honor, and property. Yet the succeeding Emperors, such as Vespasian and his son Titus, changed it all back and not only abolished the <term>Papian Law</term> <note>original: "Legem Papiam"</note> again but also had those accusers publicly beaten with rods, so that they might develop a dread of betraying people. ...that there is a great difference between the secret informants whom a Lord must sometimes employ and pay for their services, and those who to this day remain unsolicited, falsely slandering people yet wishing to appear as if they have done no such thing. Much less do they wish to be regarded or held as such <term>Quadruplatores</term> <note>original: "Quadruplatores"; in ancient Rome, these were public informers or professional accusers who received a fourth part of the criminal's goods as a reward.</note>; they even have the audacity to defy anyone who would dare accuse them of such behavior.

For this reason, the laws have also decreed that slanderers and false accusers, if they are convicted of the same, shall be punished with the same penalty that the accused would have had to suffer. Just as the <term>Lex Remia</term> <note>A Roman law concerning "Calumniators" or false accusers.</note>, *on Slanderers*, states: *The accuser shall suffer that which the accused would have suffered, had he been convicted.* <note>original Latin: "Calumniator id patiatur, quod reus, si fuerit conuictus."</note> This means: The informant shall suffer what the accused would have had to suffer if he had been overcome. <term>Isocrates</term> <note>An ancient Greek rhetorician (436–338 BC) known for his influential speeches on ethics and politics.</note> agrees with this, saying: *Inflict an equal punishment both on those who slander with lies and on those who actually commit a crime.* <note>original Latin translation of the Greek: "Pari poena afficito, & qui mendacio calumniantur, & qui facinus admittunt."</note> Therefore, it is a particularly great gift and grace of God when a Prince or Lord does not easily believe such <term>Delators</term> <note>original: "Delatorn"; professional denouncers or informants.</note>, slanderers, and <term>Calumniators</term>. In ancient times, the old Emperors used to send such people across the sea into misery and to the island of <term>Gyaros</term> <note>A small, barren island in the Cyclades used by the Roman Empire as a place of exile for political prisoners.</note>, which was only twelve thousand paces in circumference. This is described by the <term>Epigrammographus Poeta</term> <note>The "Epigrammatic Poet," likely referring here to the Roman poet Martial or a similar contemporary, describing the clearing out of informants from Rome.</note> with these verses:

->*A mob heavy for peace, and an enemy to tranquil rest,*<-

->*And the informer now possesses the exile he once caused others to suffer.*<-

# The Third Part of the Ruler’s Book.

## On War: What a harmful thing it is, and that no one should lightly advise for war.

### The First Chapter.

<image-desc>A large ornamental woodcut initial 'W' featuring scrolled foliage and floral motifs within a square frame.</image-desc>

Although the senses and thoughts of man—according to the testimony of Holy Scripture <note>A reference to Genesis 8:21, "the imagination of man's heart is evil from his youth."</note>—are inclined toward evil from youth due to our corrupt and wicked nature, which is why so much evil occurs daily in the world among people and is instigated by them, it would nonetheless be impossible to believe that people could fall into such blindness and folly that they would set aside the Noble Peace (of which we spoke above) and commit themselves to war and discord for a trivial or frivolous cause, if we did not find this to be the case in all histories and books, and likewise, unfortunately, experience it all too much through current events.

Yet nothing more harmful can or may be conceived on Earth than war, from which so much evil and distress arises in the world at once, as soon as it is even slightly stirred. For then religion and the Word of God are hindered, the servants of the church are driven away, the schools are devastated, the common chest <term>common chest</term> <note>original: "gemeine Kasten"; a communal fund established in Reformation-era German towns to support the poor, education, and the church.</note> is exhausted and emptied, the rich are made poor, the poor are utterly destroyed, and everyone is left without rights or help. All good laws and order, through which human society should be maintained, are overturned and entirely abolished. In their place, only cruel tyranny, robbery, murder, theft, seizure, harassment, cursing, and swearing govern; people are plundered, everything is made a prize of war, and women and maidens are dishonored. Even the heathens of old were ashamed of such things and therefore refrained from them—as one reads of Alexander <note>Alexander the Great, known for his respectful treatment of the captured family of the Persian King Darius.</note> and Scipio <note>Scipio Africanus, a Roman general celebrated for his "continence" in returning a captured maiden to her fiancé.</note>—and even the Turks themselves could hardly make it worse. Likewise, everything is burned and ravaged, and nothing remains but the bare foundations of the homesteads; poor widows and orphans are made, so that one must see nothing but pure weeping, howling, misery, and wretchedness. What has been collected and saved by many people over many long years is all taken, ruined, consumed, and devoured in a few days. For a lion does not kill another, nor a dragon another—despite them being the most cruel beasts on Earth. Thus there is a common proverb: *It must be a cold winter before one wolf eats another.* How then do humans—who are governed and instructed by reason and so many Christian and other good laws, and also hear daily in every sermon how they should behave toward their neighbor in all their deeds and being—allow Satan to lead them into such forgetfulness? Since Satan is a founder of war and such discord, I will here cite the beautiful text of the excellent, learned man Erasmus <note>Desiderius Erasmus of Rotterdam (1466–1536), a famous Christian humanist who wrote extensively against the madness of war.</note>, with which he briefly describes the misery, harm, disadvantage, and ruin that follow from war, which Satan awakens, where he says:

Desolated matrons grow barren at home; laws are silent, humanity is mocked, equity has no place. Religion is a mockery; there is no distinction at all between the sacred and the profane. Moreover, he is impious whoever summons war. Too much, alas, too much was the evil by which miserable mortality is constantly vexed, worn down, and swallowed up, whether it wishes it or not, etc.

That all of this is true will be clearly and sufficiently understood from the following histories.

The great and mighty King Xerxes <note>Xerxes I (r. 486–465 BC), the Persian King famous for his massive invasion of Greece.</note>, of whom mention was made above, according to the Greek histories, after the death of his father Darius <note>Darius the Great, who had previously lost the Battle of Marathon against the Greeks.</note>, when he was chosen as king, intended to overrun the Greeks—and especially those of Athens and their allies—with force and to attack them with war. The causes of this war were (as usually happens) quite minor; the most prominent was that the King of Thessaly <note>original: "Thessalonia". Thessaly was a region in northern Greece that collaborated with the Persians.</note>, along with others, sent their embassy to him and urged him to invade the Greeks, promising and pledging great help for such an invasion.

Subsequently, several soothsayers were brought before him, who said he should fear no danger in this war, but that it would turn out happily for him everywhere—regardless of whether they knew otherwise. His father Darius, though also intending to undertake such a war, would not have refrained from it had he not died so soon. Therefore, Xerxes summoned the most prominent estates of the Persian Empire <term>Reichsstände</term><note>The political representatives or noble counselors of the realm.</note> and revealed his intention to them. For it is fitting for a prince, when he wishes to begin something that puts land and people in danger, that he should first weigh, deliberate, and consider it well, and also take counsel from the estates of the land, and not act in such a case without their prior knowledge. Although Xerxes’ intention was not to obey the estates—since he had already decided within himself what he would do and what he would stand upon—he wished only to announce his opinion and intention to them and to hear their thoughts on the matter. Once the estates of the realm had come together, the King (so that the matter might have even more and greater prestige) spoke in his own person and presented the following opinion to them:

> You men, you Persians: Since our ancestors have always been diligent in expanding the borders of their kingdoms and lands since ancient times—just as Cyrus <note>Cyrus the Great, the founder of the Persian Empire.</note> first brought the empire from the Medes to the Persians and defeated Astyages <note>The last king of the Median Empire, overthrown by his grandson Cyrus.</note>. Similarly, the other kings have worked toward this goal continually, and God himself has excellently promoted this work and given grace and luck to it, more than one might have dared to expect. As we would know how to tell at length: what great and manly deeds Cyrus, Cambyses <note>Cambyses II, son of Cyrus, who conquered Egypt.</note>, and our father Darius performed, and what kingdoms, cities, and lands they conquered and brought under their power. Since, however, this is still fresh in all your memories, we consider it unnecessary to point it out now, but for the sake of brevity will omit it this time. Since we have now come to these royal dignities after the death of our father, we would by no means wish to behave differently than our ancestors, as is fitting for us. Rather, we are no less inclined than they were to increase your power—the power of the Persians—and to protect and maintain it in every way.

### The Third Part

Now we have considered a way by which, in our estimation, we may not only finally avenge the disgrace that has in many ways befallen our father and the Empire, but also intend to attain notable benefit and profit, as well as glory and honor, with divine help. For we cannot withhold from you that we are fully intent on preparing for war as quickly as possible, and to lead the assembled army across the **Hellespont** <note>The narrow strait now known as the Dardanelles, which separates Europe from Asia.</note> into Greece, to avenge once more the disgrace that those of **Athens** have brought upon both our father and the Empire in many ways. Accordingly, we are intent on speedily carrying out that which our father could not accomplish, for which we have, as heard, sufficient cause, since those of Athens first attacked our father and us with disgrace and injuries. For how they conducted themselves when we came to **Sardis** with **Aristagoras of Miletus** <note>Aristagoras was a leader of the Ionian Greeks who rebelled against Persia; the Athenians assisted him in burning the city of Sardis.</note> would take long to relate; what they dared to undertake subsequently at the time when **Darius** and **Artaphernes** traveled through their territory, you yourselves well remember. Because of this and other things, we are moved to attack them most earnestly and powerfully, and with divine help to bring them under our power. How greatly your power—that of the Persians—will then be strengthened, you may easily conclude and perceive for yourselves. Since we already hold other surrounding kingdoms and lands for the most part in our hands, we have no doubt that we will also easily conquer the rest of Greece and bring it under our power; for we are informed that none of the other lands will then be able to resist or escape our might.

Therefore, we expect that you will, at our requirement, join us most strongly for such an impending war, and as members of the Empire and faithful subjects, be helpful in this; which we shall then note and accept with gracious pleasure from you. We have also herewith offered to reward with grace and all good things those who show themselves obedient and willing. Although we have no doubt that you will take this our opinion to heart no less than we do ourselves and be pleased with it, we nevertheless desire that you also voice your opinion and good judgment on the matter, and advise us therein, as we wish to place this matter before you for your counsel and consideration. And herewith the King concluded his speech.

### The Third Part

[God] strikes down and attacks, but leaves the small shrubs and low huts in peace. In the same way, large and powerful masses are often defeated by a small number of people when God does not wish to grant them victory; through this, many have fallen into great danger and ultimate ruin and harm. <note>This is a classic Greek philosophical trope: the gods are jealous of human greatness and strike down the "tallest trees" or most arrogant men.</note>

There are some who would hold that it is better to proceed with a matter in haste rather than delaying for a long time. But they are mistaken, for they do not know what significant harm haste brings, according to the common proverb: *Haste brings no good.* <note>Equivalent to the English proverb "Haste makes waste."</note> Conversely, they also do not recognize what benefit and advantage come from endurance and proceeding with a matter slowly. Because such benefit and advantage are not immediately apparent or visible, it is ultimately found that they do not fail to appear; and one must generally conclude that it is better to act slowly than to rush into a matter and thereby put land and people into distress and danger.

I have wished to say this regarding this matter and to advise Your Majesty with the most faithful and best intentions. I would have expected that you, **Mardonius**, would have spoken differently and not so foolishly regarding this business, nor have so greatly despised and slandered the **Greeks** with your speech before the Lord King, simply so that you might more easily move him to war. It is quite clear from your speech that you must have a particular lust and desire for this war, and for that reason, you have belittled the **Greeks**, who are not present and cannot defend themselves. Therefore, a two-fold injustice is done to them: on one hand, by those who revile them, and on the other, by those who believe it before they have heard the **Greeks'** answer.

But since you hurry so vehemently toward this war—well then—let the King remain at home among the **Persians**, and let us set both our children as a <term>pledge</term> <note>A legal or physical guarantee; here, Artabanus suggests a "blood wager" where their children would be executed if their respective predictions fail.</note> to the realm. Furthermore, take as many soldiers as you need for this quarrel and march forth against those of **Athens**. If the matter then ends successfully, as you now claim, then let me and my children be killed. But if it goes otherwise, as I fear, then your children shall be killed, and you likewise, if you indeed return home. But if you hesitate to accept this proposal and yet persist in insisting that the **Greeks**, and especially those of **Athens**, should be attacked with war, then I hope to live to see the day that the **Persians** will say: **Mardonius** perished in **Greece** and was shamefully consumed and devoured by the birds and dogs.

This was a wise and sensible counsel which the King should rightfully have followed, for in the end, it happened exactly as **Artabanus** had indicated. But when he had finished speaking, the King became so vehemently angered and embittered by such talk that he could no longer restrain himself, but broke out with these unseemly words and said to **Artabanus**: "If you were not our father's brother, **Artabanus**, you would now receive your right and deserved reward for your foolish and nonsensical counsel. Although you shall enjoy the benefit of that relation for this time, we shall nevertheless arrange the matter so that this disgrace shall be laid upon you..."

However, they had to let the matter go and allow it to rest for the time being.

When evening fell, the King—having been troubled all day by Artabanus's opinion and having weighed it back and forth—finally concluded within himself that it was neither feasible nor advisable to begin a war against the **Athenians** at this time. ...and with that, he fell asleep. But the **Devil**, noticing this and fearing that the game he had set in motion might be undone, appeared to the King in the guise of a handsome, tall man while he slept, and spoke to him thus:

When day broke, the King did not allow himself to be troubled by what had appeared to him in his sleep during the night and the threats made by the man; he did not mention it with a single word. However, we do not doubt that you will forgive us for pressing so vehemently for war yesterday, for due to our lack of age, we have not yet attained the understanding necessary to know how to consider all things as required. Therefore, when **Artabanus** advised against this war, we were somewhat moved by hot-headed youth and received the counsel of such an old, experienced, and wise man otherwise than was fitting. Therefore, you may henceforth remain unconcerned regarding this matter.

The Persians were exceedingly gladdened by this speech of the King. Especially since he himself had rejected the opinion of **Mardonius** <note>original: "Mardonij"</note> and abolished the war with clear words.

<meta>This page continues the dialogue between King Xerxes and his advisor Artabanus. Following the previous page, Artabanus agreed to test the King's recurring vision by dressing in the royal regalia and sleeping in the King's bed to see if the spirit would appear to him as well.</meta>

### The Third Part ###

Your Majesty <note>The original text uses the abbreviation "E. M." for *Eure Majestät*.</note> had hardly returned to the right path, and since wicked people could achieve nothing in this matter, I had truly hoped that it would have remained settled.

However, I have heard that another hindrance intends to arise—namely, that Your Majesty is being urged by a divine vision in a dream to attack the **Greeks** with war. But I cannot conclude, My Lord King, that this vision comes from **God**. Rather, I believe that because Your Majesty has been troubled by these matters for several days and has deliberated upon them, they have appeared to Your Majesty again in sleep. It is common for that which occupies a person's mind during the day to return to them in dreams at night. No one can fully express how often people have been deceived by dreams here and there. But regardless of all this, if this action is truly **God’s** ordaining, then I neither can nor will hinder it; instead, according to Your Majesty’s desire and command, I shall behave obediently and assist with all my power, being both helpful and supportive.

After these words, **Artabanus** sat upon the royal throne and subsequently lay down in the King’s chamber. As soon as he had fallen asleep, the same figure mentioned above appeared to him as well, addressing him with the following words: "Are you the one who prevents King **Xerxes** from making war against those of **Athens**? Who appointed you as his guardian, or commanded you to do such a thing? Or do you think you can settle this matter with your own cleverness? Since you now dare to advise against that which must and shall happen through the providence of the **Gods**, it shall not go well for you, but shall ultimately fail. Moreover, if **Xerxes** allows himself to be delayed any longer by you and procrastinates in the matter, I have already informed him of what shall befall him." And the figure looked upon him so earnestly and terribly that he felt as if it intended to gouge out his eyes with a fiery iron. Because of this, he was so violently terrified in his sleep that he began to scream, which caused him to wake up. Immediately afterward, he went to the King, recounting what he had seen in his sleep. He further indicated that, as one who had experienced many kinds of wars, he had occasionally advised the King out of good and faithful intentions, so that he might not undertake too much in his youth. For he had seen how it had gone for **Cyrus** <note>Cyrus the Great, founder of the Achaemenid Empire, who died campaigning against the Massagetae.</note> against the **Massagetae**, for **Cambyses** against the **Moors** <note>Original: "Mohren." In this historical context, this refers to the ancient Ethiopians during Cambyses II's failed military expedition.</note>, and for his father **Darius** against the **Scythians**, and in what danger all of these had been with their armies. Therefore, he had held the opinion that nothing better or more fortunate could happen to such a mighty and powerful King than to devote himself to rest and peace, establishing good laws and order within his kingdoms and lands, as far as it could be done without disadvantage or significant harm to his country and people.

But since it now appeared that it might be so ordained by the **Gods** that those of **Athens** had earned a punishment, and should be punished and humbled by **Xerxes** for the sake of their pride, he could and would not hinder it further, but rather with his counsel and consideration...

Thinking [to himself] that he would gladly yield to the King and desist from his opposition, **Artabanus** therefore saw it as good that the King should announce to the **Persians** and command them to make themselves ready for war as quickly and strongly as possible. This the King then did, and Artabanus himself afterwards exhorted the others to war, despite having previously most vehemently advised against it. # The Third Part #

<note>Artabanus is speaking to the King</note> Your Majesty <note>original: "E. M." for "Eure Majestät"</note> has barely returned to the right path, and since wicked people could achieve nothing in this matter, I had truly hoped that it would have remained so.

But I have heard that another hindrance intends to arise; namely, that Your Majesty is being urged by a divine vision in a dream to attack the Greeks with war. However, Lord King, I cannot consider that this vision comes from God. Instead, I hold that because Your Majesty has been troubled by these things for several days and has deliberated upon them, it has therefore appeared again to Your Majesty in sleep. This is what usually tends to happen: that which one deals with during the day returns to a person in their dreams at night. How often people have otherwise been deceived here and there by dreams, no one can sufficiently express. But be that as it may, if this action is to be God's providence, then I neither can nor will hinder it; instead, according to Your Majesty’s desire and command, I shall conduct myself obediently and help, serve, and be as productive as is in all my power.

After these words, **Artabanus** sat himself upon the royal throne and subsequently lay down in the King’s chamber. As soon as he fell asleep there, the image mentioned above also appeared to him and addressed him with the following words: "Are you the one who prevents King **Xerxes** from going to war against those of **Athens**? Who has appointed you as his guardian, or commanded you to do such a thing? Or do you think to carry this matter through with your own cleverness? Since you now dare to advise against that which shall and must happen by the providence of the **Gods**, it shall not go well for you, but will ultimately fail. Moreover, if **Xerxes** allows himself to be delayed longer by you and procrastinates with the matter, I have already announced to him what shall happen to him because of it." And the image looked at him so earnestly and cruelly that he thought nothing else but that it intended to gouge out his eyes with a fiery iron. For this reason, he was so violently terrified in his sleep that he began to scream, which caused him to wake up.

Following this, he went immediately to the King with the account of what he had seen in his sleep. He further indicated that as one who had experienced many and various things regarding wars, he had occasionally spoken against the King's plans. This had been done with good and faithful intentions so that the King, in his youth, would not undertake too much. For he had seen how it went for **Cyrus** against the **Massagetae**, for **Cambyses** against the **Moors** <note>In this historical context, "Moors" refers to the Ethiopians or North Africans</note>, and for his father **Darius** against the **Scythians**, and in what danger all of these had been with their armies. Therefore, he had held the opinion that nothing better or more fortunate could happen to such a mighty and powerful King than to devote himself to rest and peace, making good laws and order in his kingdoms and lands, so far as it could ever happen without disadvantage or significant harm to his land and people.

Since it now appeared, however, that it was perhaps thus provided by the Gods—that those of **Athens** had earned a punishment and should be punished and humbled by **Xerxes** for the sake of their pride—he also could not or would not hinder such a thing, but rather with his counsel and consideration...

<note>original: "met/ und saget/" — the sentence continues from the previous page where Xerxes is responding to Pythias.</note> with [him], and said: He could not even spare himself, his own children, or his friends, but had brought them all along; and Pythias should remember that as a servant and subject, he was duty-bound to follow the King with his wife and children. And though the King would not have spared him were it not for the tribute <note>original: "verehrung," referring to the massive financial gifts Pythias had previously given Xerxes</note> he had provided, he would let Pythias enjoy the benefit of that gift and grant life to him and four of his sons. This was a cruel reward for such a great favor as **Pythias** had shown the King. But fortune is such that it blinds great lords when they come into such power and means, so that they do not know what they are doing. Instead, they become tyrannical and practice great arrogance, just as **Xerxes** committed other such acts. Some write that he became so senseless that he ordered the sea to be whipped <note>referring to the scourging of the Hellespont after a storm destroyed his bridge</note>; and if anyone wished to speak much of death or the uncertain outcome of the war—as his cousin **Artabanus**, being a wise and experienced man, sometimes did—the King could not tolerate it.

Yet such great lords can also sometimes appear pious. For this same **Xerxes**, when he saw the great multitude of people he was leading into **Greece** gathered together, began to weep, realizing that of such a great crowd, not one would still be alive in a hundred years. Likewise, **Alexander** [the Great] acted lamentably when, in a drunken fit, he stabbed **Clytus**, his faithful friend who had saved his life, without just cause.

And indeed, the majority of that same army perished in **Greece** and was unable to achieve anything there; instead, [Xerxes] had to flee shamefully in a small boat <term>nachen|a small, simple rowing boat or skiff</term>, as was shown above in the example of **Themistocles**.

**Mardonius**, the captain and war councilor, remained in **Greece** with three hundred thousand men. Because he had been the first to advise for the war and had largely encouraged it—and had not least caused the King to march into **Greece**, as mentioned before—he feared that if he returned home, the King might punish him. He therefore attacked the **Athenians** with great force, plundering and burning the city. Subsequently, he fought several battles with the other cities until he and all his people were finally defeated and beaten.

This was the end of the great and perilous war, from which great princes and lords should take note and learn not to enter into war lightly, and not to rely upon their great power, but rather to live in the fear of God. For God cannot tolerate such pride and inhuman rage, but punishes the same and brings them to shame along with their great power. This also happened to **Croesus** and others, in addition to what was heard at the beginning of this chapter regarding what an unchristian, harmful, and inhuman thing war is.

Of the Book of Regents.

Finally, those who are at the courts of great kings, princes, and lords have this to learn: they should take great care that they do not give the lords cause for war with their advice, or advise them toward it when the lords believe they have found or obtained some cause that has a semblance of justification under which they might start a war. This is especially true where one might avoid it and use other means and ways, so that it does not ultimately end badly for them, according to the common proverb: <note>original: "Malum consilium consultori pessimum."</note> **Bad counsel is worst for the counselor who gave it.** Ovid also testifies to this when he says:

> <note>original: "Neque Lex iustior vlla est, Quam necis artifices arte perire sua."</note>
> No law is more just on earth than that a person should perish by the very path they prepared for another.

As one sees in this **Mardonius**: after he advised for war, he also perished and was slain in the war. <note>Mardonius was the Persian general left in command by Xerxes; he died at the Battle of Plataea in 479 BCE.</note> So, too, have some experienced such advisors falling into despair and stabbing themselves, or otherwise perishing shamefully. Whoever will not believe this or pay it any mind, but instead takes pleasure in warring, may try it and see what he gains from it. When he has then tried it and satisfied his desire—so much so that he has "warred away" <note>meaning to lose everything through the costs and consequences of conflict</note> all his goods, along with his wife, child, best friends, and his land and people—he will then surely grant peace and desire it. This is as the **Athenians** did, who always wanted to war and never have peace, until they had first taken a heavy blow. <note>original: "tapffere Schnappe," an idiom for a stinging setback or defeat.</note> Therefore **Demades** <note>an Athenian orator and contemporary of Demosthenes</note> said, when they once undertook an untimely war and would not keep the peace: The people of Athens would not become peaceful until they wore black bands around their hats. <note>A reference to the mourning attire worn after suffering massive casualties in battle.</note>

<header>The Third Part</header>

A Christian must rightly be terrified by this, for nothing is more certain to be feared than this: while such signs appear daily, ever more frequent and more terrible, we nevertheless do not turn from our ways nor improve ourselves. Therefore, a much greater punishment remains behind and will certainly follow, just as has always happened according to the accounts of history.

As it was before the destruction of Jerusalem in the year 72 AD, among other signs, a burning sword was seen hovering in the air over the Temple for an entire year. So too it is written that when Tarquinius <note>Tarquin the Proud, the last legendary King of Rome.</note>, the King of Rome, was chased and driven from his kingdom because of the tyranny against **Lucretia** and others, a dog spoke with a human voice and a snake barked like a dog; soon after, the King's ruin and misery followed. One also finds that when the rich and powerful King **Croesus** of Lydia was to be defeated and captured in war, shortly before, a small child of only half a year spoke clearly <note>original: "bescheidenlich" — here meaning with the reason or clarity of an adult.</note>. This undoubtedly signified the gruesome damage and defeat, as well as the transformation of the entire kingdom. Likewise, at the time when the **Galli Senones** <note>The Senone Gauls who famously sacked Rome in the 4th century BC.</note> marched against Rome to wage war on the city, a clear, bright voice was heard on the street called the "New Road," which announced and proclaimed the coming of the Gauls. Because of this, the Romans later built a church at that same place and called it the **Temple of the Warning Voice**. <note>original: "Allocutionis Templum"</note>

And what more should I say? Indeed, several signs occurred when **Xerxes** undertook his mighty campaign into Greece, which was mentioned at length in the preceding chapter. History says that a comet appeared, and likewise there was an eclipse of the sun. And what is even more, a horse among the cavalry gave birth to a hare; by this it was signaled that if they would not desist from the war, their horses would be forced to flee <note>The hare is a traditional symbol of flight and cowardice.</note>.

And so that I may leave behind the ancient histories and examples, I will recount here a sign which happened somewhat more recently—namely, around the time recorded as 1452. When the Turkish Emperor **Mehmed** <note>Mehmed II, known as "The Conqueror."</note> intended not only to wage war against the noble imperial city of **Byzantium** or **Constantinople**, but to bring it entirely under his power, there was seen in a city called **Como** <note>original: "Comum"</note>—belonging to the crown of France—a great, gruesome, and terrifying pack of mad dogs in the air shortly before sunset. They made a gruesome cry that terrified the people. These were followed by many other animals and a great multitude of soldiers, both on horse and foot; and such visions lasted until the falling of the night. This certainly signified nothing other than the cruel Turks, as experience and the event itself soon proved. For Byzantium was conquered by storm by the Turkish Emperor in the year 1453, on the 29th day of the month of May. What cruel tyranny he practiced there! How he had a crucifix pelted with filth <note>original: "Kot"</note> and had written above it: *This is the God of the Christians.* How he stuck the Emperor's head upon a long spear and carried it around the city. # The Third Part

should similar things happen to us, we might bear them more easily. For according to the proverb, it shall be called nothing other than: **today it is me, tomorrow it is you.** 

*Polybius* <note>Polybius (c. 200–118 BC) was a Greek historian whose work "The Histories" covered the rise of the Roman Republic.</note> writes that he stood by *Scipio* when he saw the excellent city of *Carthage* burn to the ground. *Scipio* wept, and when *Polybius* asked him why he wept—seeing as he had achieved such a magnificent victory in such a great and difficult war against the Carthaginians—he answered with a heavy sigh. He said that he felt a heartfelt compassion for this excellent city, which had stood for seven hundred years and had risen to such great prestige and renown, that he should now see its downfall. He added that it was impossible for him to think or speak without great pity of the downfall of ancient empires, or of that which might, in time, also befall the city of *Rome*, since we are all subject to fortune. ->The time will yet come here,<-

->And also *Priam* <note>The legendary King of Troy during the Trojan War.</note> likewise,<-

Therefore, we should rightly be terrified of the Turkish and other wars, improve our lives, and each pay better attention to his own rank and calling. We should also, with constant sighing and weeping, pray to God from our hearts that He would not allow His holy Church to be so miserably devastated by these Turkish, un-Christian, and inhuman people. Indeed, such devastation has already taken hold of the greater part of the world, especially as far as the **Mahometan tyranny** has spread.

And such an undertaking by the Turks should move our hearts and minds all the more because it was prophesied long ago by the Prophet *Ezekiel*, where he mentions *Gog* and *Magog*. For he writes that they shall come from the side of the North <note>original: "Mitternacht," literally 'midnight,' which historically denoted the North in German geography.</note> and lead an uncountably large army and many people, and shall wage war against the saints of God.

Likewise, *Josephus* <note>Titus Flavius Josephus (37–c. 100 AD), a Romano-Jewish historian.</note> maintains that *Magog* is the father and ancestor of the **Scythians**, whom people now call **Tartars**. Furthermore, one can clearly see in the *Apocalypse of John* <note>The Book of Revelation in the New Testament.</note> that *Gog* and *Magog* shall be the last and mightiest kingdom on Earth, which shall have a great and uncountable multitude of people and wage war against the saints of God—that is, against the Christians—whom *Christ* shall visit and exterminate at His coming.

Similarly, we should not cast to the wind certain recent prophecies of *Joannis Hiltenius* <note>Johannes Hilten (c. 1425–1502) was a Franciscan monk in Eisenach known for his apocalyptic predictions, some of which were later cited by Lutheran reformers.</note>. He was held in no small regard in his time, despite being a monk in the Franciscan monastery at Eisenach. Among other things that have since come to pass, he also indicated this: that around the year one thousand six hundred, the Turks would rule in *Germany* and *Italy*.

# Of the Book of Regents

Since things in Christendom are currently in such a poor state—where Christian leaders themselves are frequently at great odds with one another, and where sin and vice increase daily, while the false teachings and idolatry of the shameful Pope and his followers are defended—it could easily happen, by God's punishment and providence, that we face a similar fate. Indeed, nothing has advanced the rise and prosperity of the **Turks** <note>The Ottoman Empire, led at this time by Sultan Mehmed II, "the Conqueror."</note>, or allowed them to set foot so far into our lands, as much as our internal discord and other shameful vices.

Because I have been preoccupied with these matters this very day, I could not refrain from investigating how the noble city of **Athens**—which was overthrown by those same tyrants who destroyed **Byzantium** <note>Constantinople, which fell to the Ottomans in 1453.</note>—came to its end. In this account, those who read it should primarily consider the Divine judgment and punishment. The downfall of the city of Athens occurred briefly as follows:

A Florentine merchant named **Nerius** <note>Nerio I Acciaioli (d. 1394), an Italian noble who established control over the Duchy of Athens.</note> came to Athens and achieved so much there that he became the supreme regent of the city. When he died, he left behind his wife and a small child. Through gifts and bribes, the wife obtained enough favor from **Mahomet** <note>Sultan Mehmed II.</note> that he allowed her to remain in the government of Athens after her husband's death. It did not last long, however, before this woman became acquainted with a Venetian merchant. They fell in love, and the woman promised him that if he left his wife in Venice, she would take him as her husband and make him the Prince of Athens.

The Venetian soon grew greedy for rule. He traveled home and killed his wife with poison, **in the Italian fashion** <note>original: "nach Welscher art." In 16th-century German, "Welsch" referred to Italians or Southern Europeans, who were stereotypically associated in literature with the use of poison.</note>. He then returned to Athens, wooed the widow, and took over the government. However, when he began to practice great tyranny against the nobility and other great and honorable people—which the citizens of Athens could not endure—they filed a complaint against him before **Mahomet**. When the Sultan summoned him, the Venetian attempted to quiet him with money, but **Mahomet** had him strangled.

Thus, the Venetian first received his well-deserved punishment for killing his wife with poison. Subsequently, as the young heir had a relative <note>original: "Freund," which in this period often meant a kinsman or blood relative.</note>, **Mahomet** handed the government over to him until the boy should reach his majority. This man seized the woman—who, under the pretense of marriage, had handed the government to the Venetian—by the neck and had her led to **Magaris** <note>Megara, a coastal town between Athens and Corinth.</note> and put to death there. Thus, the woman was also punished through Divine providence.

Now, when the young heir had lost his mother and saw that his relative was also attempting to deprive him of the princedom, he complained to **Mahomet** that the man had strangled his mother. Because of this, when **Mahomet** saw that there was to be no end to the strangling, he was moved to command his governor in **Thessalia** <note>Thessaly, a region in northern Greece.</note> to seize the city of Athens. Thus, **Mahomet** brought the aforementioned city into his power. And after the citizens later showed themselves to be rebellious and disobedient, he did not only

### Part Three

...not only the castle but also a large part of the city was razed and torn down; now nothing remains of it except for several small huts where fishermen live, and a gathering of common folk.

This is the end of that excellent city, which once possessed many glorious and beautiful examples of all kinds of virtues, and served as a dwelling and inn for the finest arts on earth. It also performed many honorable and great deeds—both wise and knightly—against the **Persians**. And, not to remain silent on this point, while it held the upper hand in **Greece**, its government was far more kind and moderate, and did not exalt itself as high as the **Thebans** and the **Lacedaemonians** <note>The Spartans, known for their strict and militaristic society.</note>. From the time of **Solon** <note>The famous Athenian lawmaker (c. 638–558 BC) who laid the foundations for democracy.</note> until **Mahomet** <note>Sultan Mehmed II, "the Conqueror," who took Athens in 1456.</note> destroyed and overthrew it, two thousand years passed.

I have found it necessary to recount this, dear lords, so that we might look about us a little and diligently consider the reasons why cities, lands, and peoples are overthrown. For this reason, we should conduct ourselves with moderation in our government and all our dealings, keeping God before our eyes and calling upon Him for grace, protection, and help.

It would be greatly desired that the **Germans** <note>Original: "Teutschen".</note> read and investigate the histories of the **Turks** with great diligence, and that they were more united and earnest in the protection of their fatherland. For if they truly knew the Turks—the kind of government they lead, the tyranny they employ, and finally their manner of waging war—their noble minds would be so moved by the gravity of these matters that they would apply greater diligence and care to protect their aforementioned praiseworthy fatherland, the true religion of the **Christian Church**, the courts and the law, the distinction of the social estates, the fine arts, discipline, and decency, and a righteous and honorable **civil order** <note>Original: "Policey," which in this era referred to the general administration, peace, and moral regulation of a community.</note>, and to defend these with their own blood against Turkish barbarity, under which all such things are abolished.

What I have just recounted was recently translated from the Greek language into Latin from the works of **Chalcondilo** <note>Laonikos Chalkokondyles (c. 1423–1490), a Greek historian who witnessed the fall of the Byzantine Empire and wrote about the rise of the Ottomans.</note>, who was once a citizen of Athens. This man saw and was present for much of the misfortune that befell the city, which is why he wrote about it. In his description of nations, he says of the Germans, among other things: "I know of no people who have such honorable customs as the Germans; and if they were united, they would be invincible."

See, dear lords, how much even a short time ago foreigners esteemed your ancestors. Therefore, we must pray to God that the customs and practices of these times might be compared favorably with those of old.

But help me, God! Where has my great grief and sorrow led me, now that I have begun to speak of the Turkish histories? My intention was only to mention the noble city of **Byzantium** <note>Constantinople, modern-day Istanbul.</note> at this time. And it should be known that there is a place in **Thrace** located by the **Hellespontine Sea** <note>The Dardanelles, the narrow strait in northwestern Turkey connecting the Aegean Sea to the Sea of Marmara.</note>, which is extremely convenient and well-situated for an Imperial seat, because

# Of the Book of Rulers.

Asia and Europe nearly meet at that place; thus, it is also easy to reach Africa from there by water. It is found in the ancient histories that those of **Carthage** built **Byzantium** <note>The author likely refers to the Phoenicians or early colonists; historically, Byzantium was a Megarian colony, but the author cites a Phoenician linguistic origin.</note>, and it was well-armed and provided with ships, and many kinds of goods were fetched from afar. Some also believe that this city received its name from the **Phoenicians** and was called *Bethzonia* in their language, meaning a "guesthouse" or "tavern." This is because in ancient times, as **Phylarchus** <note>A Greek historian of the 3rd century BC.</note> writes, they were people who lay in taverns day and night and consumed their wealth there.

Subsequently, the **Megarians** from **Greece** settled this same city with their citizens and made a colony out of it—just as the **Romans** also did many times. For that reason, they also brought the Greek language and their rights and laws with them to **Byzantium**. After the war that **Xerxes** <note>The Persian King (r. 486–465 BC) who invaded Greece.</note> waged in **Greece**, they sometimes held with the **Lacedaemonians** <note>The Spartans.</note> and sometimes with those of **Athens**, making alliances with them. But when **Philip**, the King of **Macedonia** <note>Philip II, father of Alexander the Great.</note>, came before it and besieged it long and fiercely, they finally had to surrender themselves into his power.

In the times of the **Romans**, when **Pescennius** and **Severus** <note>Septimius Severus (r. 193–211 AD) and his rival Pescennius Niger.</note> quarreled over the Empire, and Pescennius first occupied the city of **Byzantium**, **Severus** besieged the city for three and a half years. After many people within had perished in various ways, they could no longer hold out due to hunger but had to surrender to **Severus**, who then almost entirely destroyed the city and had the walls torn down. **Herodianus** <note>A Roman historian of the 3rd century AD.</note> writes that the walls were made so skillfully and strongly that it was a wonder they could be broken down at all.

From **Severus** until **Constantine**, one hundred years passed, during which time the city remained unbuilt and the walls lay thus torn apart. But **Constantine** was finally moved by the convenience of the site not only to rebuild the city but also to adorn it with magnificent, beautiful, and mighty buildings and great honors; he especially desired that it should be esteemed and held equal to the city of **Rome** in every way.

Furthermore, there was also a cathedral church there which had many fine, learned people, among whom were many righteous bishops. It can be demonstrated with truth that, after the school at **Alexandria**, there were nowhere so many noble arts until the final conquest as there were in **Byzantium**.

However, when this city fell under the power of the **Turk** <note>The Ottoman conquest of Constantinople in 1453.</note> and the learned people no longer had a place there—such as **Argyropoulos**, **Lascaris**, **Theodore Gaza**, **George of Trebizond**, **Chrysoloras**, and others <note>These were famous Greek scholars who fled to Italy, sparking the Renaissance.</note>—they had to go to **Italy** <note>Original: "Welschland".</note> and brought the Greek language along with philosophy there with them. At that time, after **Italy** first tasted the sweetness of the Greek language, it was able to learn the Latin language all the better and more righteously. Specifically, the Greek language provided the entrance to understanding philosophy correctly and thoroughly.

### The Third Part

From these same sources in **Italy**, several small streams of the **Greek language** flowed into **Germany**. For as soon as **Johannes Regiomontanus** <note>Johannes Müller von Königsberg (1436–1476), a pioneering German mathematician and astronomer.</note> had mastered the Greek language, he undertook to explain **Ptolemy**. **Rodolphus Agricola** <note>Considered the "Father of Northern European Humanism."</note> had a good acquaintance in **Ferrara** with **Theodorus Gaza** <note>A Greek scholar who fled the fall of Constantinople and became a leading figure in the revival of Greek learning in Italy.</note>, an excellent, learned, and very well-mannered man.

Finally, it may be written with truth that this city—named after **Constantine I**, from whom it also took its name and was called **Constantinople**—was the most beautiful city in the world, and an excellent church and harbor for all noble, great, and righteous arts.

I have had to recount this so that all nations and peoples who still profess the Christian faith might grieve and lament all the more that they have lost such an ornament of all **Christendom**. Now follows the account of the siege by the **Turkish tyrant**.

We read that the siege began in **April**, and that in the city there were no more than six thousand **Greeks**, in addition to the citizenry and **Venetians**, and three thousand **Genoese**. Against them, however, **Mehmed** <note>Mehmed II, the Ottoman Sultan.</note> brought up to four hundred thousand men to the city; such a great multitude of people was gathered, for the most part, from the neighboring nations that still bear the Christian name, such as from **Greece**, **Illyricum**, **Wallachia**, **Thrace**, **Bulgaria**, etc. Yet few **Turks** were among them, save for those who had come from **Asia**, **Bithynia**, **Galatia**, **Lydia**, and **Cilicia**.

Thus the Turkish tyrant wages war against us Christians by forcing the lands closest to us to be used in wars against us.

Those in the garrison defended themselves knightly; their commander was **Justinianus of Genoa** <note>Giovanni Giustiniani Longo, a professional soldier who led the defense of the city walls.</note>, who had much fellowship with the excellent and highly famous knight called in the histories **Joannes Grandis Almanus** <note>original: "Joannes Grandis Almanus." This refers to Johannes Grant, an engineer (often called German or Scottish) who famously counter-mined the Turkish tunnels.</note>; for that reason, they bravely drove the Turks back in their assault.

Although many Turkish soldiers were shot down before the city with both bows and firearms, the few soldiers could not withstand such a great multitude—attacking the city in three places—for long; primarily because both sides dug mines against each other, although the Turkish mines could achieve nothing.

The Turkish tyrant gathered up to two hundred and fifty ships from many surrounding places on the sea so that he could besiege the port of **Byzantium** with them, and so that one might cross from one shore to the other on the ships, just as if on a bridge.

Against such Turkish ships were set seven ships of the **Genoese**, three from the **Cretans**, and several that had come from **Chios**, and the port was closed with an **iron chain** <note>The Great Chain that blocked the entrance to the Golden Horn.</note> so that the Turk could not force his way in with his ships. It happened, however, that those in the garrison moved out with their ships against the Turks and fought knightly with them, undertaking to set fire to the Turkish armada; thus, the Turks could accomplish nothing with their ships for several days.

# Of the Book of Rulers.

Finally, the **Turks** found a way to enter the **harbor** <note>This refers to the Sultan’s tactical feat of transporting ships overland into the Golden Horn to bypass the defensive chain.</note> by force. As soon as this was accomplished, they began to bombard the city for the assault from both water and land. Because the walls were breached in many places, the **Tyrant** <note>A common contemporary label for Sultan Mehmed II.</note> hoped to capture them soon; furthermore, the city was easily attacked from the port. For this reason, on the **29th day of May**, he began to storm and fall upon the city from all sides with a great cry.

The **Tyrant** stood not far away on a hill and watched as the assault began, exhorting his men to attack manfully. Wherever he saw his men driven back or struck down, he screamed horribly and encouraged those who were terrified.

Those within the city defended themselves so gallantly and manfully that a large part of the **Turkish army**—seeing and feeling that so many of their own had been struck, shot, and slain—began to retreat and abandon the assault.

This gave the heroes in the city no small hope and great heart to hold the city. Conversely, the great damage and danger made the **Turkish Tyrant** so anxious and distressed that he raised a gruesome cry and wailing. He threatened to punish those who retreated and fled; he also commanded those who usually served as his bodyguards <note>Likely referring to the Janissaries.</note> to kill and strangle all those who would withdraw or retreat from the assault.

On the other hand, the **Greek Emperor** gained great hope that the **Turk** would achieve nothing. He therefore exhorted his people—since they could see that **God** was visibly helping them and was with them—to show themselves gallant and undaunted. However, when **Justinianus of Genoa** <note>Giovanni Giustiniani Longo, a Genoese professional soldier who was the primary commander of the land walls.</note>, mentioned above, was wounded, fortune soon turned back again. For although **Emperor Palaiologos** <note>Constantine XI Palaiologos, the last Byzantine Emperor.</note> diligently reminded him not to leave his tower, as the wound he received was not fatal, he could not be restrained from fleeing. He was weakened more in spirit than in body; he also appointed no one to take his place who could have addressed, comforted, and led those assigned to the defense.

Now that this same position had been abandoned by the captain **Justinianus**, and his soldiers had followed him, the location was found by the **Turks** to be entirely unmanned and unguarded. They fell into the city there in great crowds. **Justinianus** fled to the nearest part of **Chalcedon** <note>The author likely means the district across the Golden Horn.</note>, which is now called **Galata**. However, as he later intended to sail to **Chios**, he died—either from his wound or perhaps from a broken heart <note>The original German "bekümmerniß deß Gemüts" implies a death from extreme grief or distress.</note>.

After the **Turks** had gained the upper hand in this manner, **Emperor Palaiologos** knew of no other counsel to find than how he might escape by flight. Therefore, he set out with many others. He perished, however, in the flight, or was trampled in the gate; for in the gate, up to eight hundred people were found who had been crushed, wounded, or left dead.

### Part Three

Several small books in the Greek language also flowed from Italy into Germany. For as soon as **Johannes Regiomontanus** <note>original: "Joannes Regiomontanus"; a famous German mathematician and astronomer who studied Greek to better understand ancient scientific texts.</note> had mastered the Greek language, he undertook the task of explaining **Ptolemy**. Likewise, **Rodolphus Agricola**—while in Ferrara—maintained a close acquaintance with **Theodorus Gaza**, an excellent, learned, and thoroughly disciplined man.

Lastly, it may be written with truth that this city—from **Constantine** the First, from whom it took its name and was called **Constantinople**—was the most beautiful city in the world, and a magnificent church and harbor for all noble, great, and righteous arts.

I have found it necessary to recount this so that all nations and peoples who still profess the Christian faith may all the more grieve and lament that they have lost such an ornament of all Christendom. Now follows the account of the siege by the Turkish Tyrant.

We read that the siege began in April, and that there were no more than six thousand Greeks within the city, in addition to the citizenry and the **Venetians**, and three thousand **Genoese**. In opposition, however, **Mehmed** <note>original: "Mahomet"; referring to Sultan Mehmed II.</note> brought up to four hundred thousand men to the city. This vast multitude of people was gathered for the most part from the neighboring nations who still bear the Christian name, such as from Greece, **Illyria**, **Wallachia**, **Thrace**, **Bulgaria**, etc. Yet few Turks were among them, save for those who had come from **Asia**, **Bithynia**, **Galatia**, **Lydia**, and **Cilicia**.

Thus the Turkish Tyrant wages war against us Christians by forcing the lands nearest to us to be used in wars against us.

Those in the garrison defended themselves knightly. Their commander was **Giustiniani of Genoa** <note>Giovanni Giustiniani Longo, a Genoese captain and specialist in defending walled cities.</note>, who had much fellowship with that excellent and highly renowned knight called in history **Johannes Grandis the German** <note>original: "Joannes Grandis Almanus"; likely John Grant, a master engineer whose origins are debated but who was instrumental in counter-mining operations.</note>. Together, they valiantly drove the Turks back in their initial onset.

Although many Turkish soldiers were shot down before the city by both arrows and firearms, the few defenders could not long withstand such a great multitude attacking the city in three places—principally because both sides were digging <term>mines</term> <note>original: "Gräber"; referring to the practice of sapping or digging tunnels under walls to collapse them.</note> against each other, though the Turkish mines were unable to achieve anything.

The Turkish Tyrant gathered up to two hundred and fifty ships from many surrounding places on the sea, so that he might besiege the port of **Byzantium** with them, and so that one might cross from one shore to the other upon the ships just as if on a bridge.

To oppose these Turkish ships, they had set seven ships of the **Genoese**, three of the **Cretans**, and several that had come from **Chios**. The port was closed with an iron chain so that the Turk could not force his way in with his ships. It happened, however, that the garrison moved out with their ships against the Turkish ones and fought knightly against them, venturing to set the Turkish armada on fire, so that for several days the Turks could achieve nothing with their ships.

### Of the Book of Rulers

Finally, the Turks found a way to enter the harbor by force; as soon as this had happened, they began to bombard the city for an assault by both water and land. Because the walls were breached in many places, the Tyrant <note>The author uses "the Tyrant" to refer to Sultan Mehmed II, a common epithet in 16th-century European histories.</note> hoped to soon conquer them. The city was also easily attacked from the port side; therefore, on the 29th day of **May**, he began to storm and fall upon the city from all sides with a great cry.

And the Tyrant stood not far away upon a hill, watching how the assault proceeded, exhorting his men to attack manfully. Wherever he saw his men driven back or stabbed, he cried out terribly and comforted those who were frightened.

Those within the city defended themselves so chivalrously and manfully that a great part of the Turkish army—seeing and feeling that so many of their own had been stabbed, shot, and slain—began to give way and abandon the assault.

This gave the heroes in the city no small hope and a great heart to hold the city. Conversely, the great damage and danger made the Turkish Tyrant so anxious and pained that he set up a terrible screaming and wailing. He ordered that those who gave way and took flight be threatened with punishment; he also commanded those who usually guarded his person to kill and strangle all those who should step back or retreat from the assault.

On the other hand, the **Greek Emperor** <note>Constantine XI Palaiologos, the last Byzantine Emperor.</note> gained great hope that the Turk would be able to accomplish nothing; he therefore exhorted his men—since they saw that God was visibly helping and was with them—that they should show themselves chivalrous and undaunted. But when **Justinianus of Genoa** <note>Giovanni Giustiniani Longo, a Genoese captain and specialist in fortifications who led the defense of the land walls.</note>, mentioned above, was wounded, fortune soon turned back again. For although the Emperor **Palaiologos** diligently reminded him not to retreat from his tower, since the wound he had received was not fatal, he could not be kept from fleeing, as he was weakened more in his spirit than in his body. He also appointed no one to take his place, or to speak to, comfort, and lead those assigned to him.

Now, as that same place was abandoned by Captain **Justinianus**, and his soldiers followed him, that location was found entirely unmanned and unguarded against the Turks; they fell into the city there in great crowds. **Justinianus** fled to the nearest point in **Chalcedon** <note>The text likely conflates Chalcedon with the district across the Golden Horn.</note>, which is now called **Galata**; but as he later intended to sail to **Chios**, he died either from his wounds or perhaps out of distress of the spirit.

After the conquest by the Turks had prevailed in such a manner, Emperor **Palaiologos** knew of no other counsel to find than how he might escape by flight; therefore, he set out with many of his people. He perished, however, in the flight, or was trampled in the gate; for in the gate, up to eight hundred people were found who had been crushed, wounded, and remained dead.

### The Third Part

The Turks, however, having now gained the victory and the upper hand, ran through the city, striking and strangling not only those they encountered, but also those who had hidden themselves in the houses, sparing neither young nor old, women nor virgins. There, many honorable women and maidens were forcibly, pitiably, and miserably violated; and not only the houses, but also the houses of God <note>The author refers to the numerous Byzantine churches and monasteries, most notably the Hagia Sophia.</note> were plundered, just as Mahomet <note>Sultan Mehmed II, often called "the Conqueror."</note> had promised them: that if they conquered the city, they should keep all the loot for themselves. And what is entirely unchristian to hear is that the Turks desecrated the images and paintings of our highest Lord and Savior Jesus Christ in the most grievous way. Thus, during these three entire days in this most ancient, beautiful, and wealthy city, so much shame, indecency, and tyranny occurred as only an unchristian, inhuman people, through their insatiable greed and tyranny, could dare to devise and undertake—so much so that it cannot be sufficiently grasped or expressed here with words.

After three days, Mahomet himself moved into the city and the castle and quieted the raging Turks. Whatever noble and good people he could still find—for whom he had a most diligent search conducted—who had not fled or been strangled, he had them all hacked to pieces.

And the histories say how, during banquets <note>original: *Pancketen*</note>, the Turkish scoundrels <note>original: *vnfläter*</note> [defiled] many honorable and noble pious women and matrons, some of whom were born of royal lineage; after they had been violated to the utmost, they were hacked to pieces as if in a theatrical spectacle. Thus, I do not know or cannot find whether a more terrifying, cruel, or unchristian example has ever occurred in the conquest of a city than what happened then. Therefore, these events should justly remind and move us all to fear God, so that we might not have to expect his similar punishment, and that we might lead our lives more moderately and, as much as possible, guard ourselves against sin. Finally, we should also diligently pray to our Lord God that, for the sake of His dear Son, He might graciously preserve His Church among us; and since we have in many ways well deserved a greater punishment, which will hardly be avoided, that He might mitigate the same out of His divine grace and mercy.

Since this noble, beautiful, and magnificent city—which might well have been called a crown of all cities in the whole world—has not only been conquered by force and shamefully plundered, but has also had to suffer and experience such murder, shame, and indecency from the most cruel, impudent, and murderous villains, it is easy and well to consider what punishment other cities and lands have to expect. Certainly, the terrifying examples in the Holy Scripture are not painted before our eyes in vain, and we should not think we are so secure that they do not concern us: as when God destroyed the entire human race, save for eight people, through the Great Flood <note>original: *Sündflut*</note>; that He burned Sodom and Gomorrah with fire from heaven; that Samaria was destroyed; and likewise the magnificent, beautiful, and powerful cities of Jerusalem, Athens, and Constantinople, along with countless other cities, which all...

# That nothing can be more **honorable** and **praiseworthy** for a prince than to show himself **merciful** toward the defeated enemy after a victory, and to consider that such **misfortune** could also happen to him.

### The Third Chapter.

Just as it usually happens that those who are defeated in the course of war <term>Kriegsläufften: a term referring to the fluctuating events, campaigns, and outcomes of warfare</term> become discouraged and humble themselves, hoping thereby to obtain mercy; so it happens, conversely, that those to whom God has granted victory and triumph become proud and arrogant. They do not know how to take sufficient revenge upon the enemies over whom they have gained power through their victory. Some even become so senseless that their subjects, as well as poor servants, and—what is even more—poor women and maidens, along with innocent children (whom even the heathens spared), must sometimes pay the price.

So that these [victors] might reflect a little when they are blessed by God with a victory, it will be necessary for them, above all things, not to exalt themselves too highly, as does occasionally happen. I could well set down examples of this here, even concerning common people who are not of the nobility, but will omit them for the sake of brevity. It is, however, no small wonder that people change their disposition so quickly and become so blind that they cannot look back far enough to remember that they, too, are human, and that such misfortune can happen to them—as happened to Croesus, who was a great and powerful king in Lydia <note>Croesus (reigned c. 560–546 BCE) was the King of Lydia famous for his immense wealth; he was eventually defeated and captured by Cyrus the Great of Persia.</note>. Therefore, I wish to portray several histories for these proud victors, in which they may see themselves mirrored and learn from them what is fitting for them to do in such a case: not to be too severe, but rather, seeing as they have surpassed many others through fortune...

One also reads a not-too-dissimilar history regarding the King of the Spartans, **Pausanias** <note>Pausanias (died c. 477 BC) was a Spartan regent and general who won a great victory over the Persians at Plataea but later fell into disgrace.</note>, as he was making a great boast and clamor regarding his fortunate dealings and deeds.
