Simonides answered him with a laughing mouth: **Remember that you are a man; let it not escape you.** <note>original Latin: "Esse te hominem, ne exciderit tibi."</note> That is: I admonish you that you should think on this, and by no means forget, that you are a mortal human being. At the time, Pausanias despised this magnificent philosophical admonition and held it for nothing; he only became more puffed up and proud, being well-pleased with himself. He had intended that the poet should have praised him—that he was being hosted by such a king, invited as a guest, and honored with a royal meal; he felt the poet should have said something glorious and wise about this or the like.

But not long afterward, when the Spartans were in great fear and very troubled, Pausanias, the Spartan war-leader, took 500 marks of gold from King Xerxes <note>The Persian King of Kings during the Greco-Persian Wars.</note> with the promise to betray the city of Sparta to him. He wrote to him regarding this, among other things, that whatever messenger he might send to him, the King should kill him, **so that the matter might not be betrayed by the talkativeness of men.** <note>original Latin: "ne res loquacitate hominum proderetur."</note> That is: In order that the plot might not be revealed.

However, when his father **Agesilaus** <note>While the text says his father Agesilaus, historical accounts often focus on the Spartan authorities (the Ephors) and his mother discovering the plot.</note> learned of this treachery through the interception of the messenger and the opening of the letters, he helped to pursue and hunt his son (who was caught in the act) until he fled into the Temple of **Pallas** or **Minerva** <note>The Temple of Athena of the Bronze House (Athena Chalkioikos) in Sparta.</note>. There, all the doors were quickly bolted and walled up from the outside with bricks. Furthermore, his own mother—who was then an old, frail woman—carried the first stone. Both father and mother helped to keep watch over the son until he died of hunger therein. But before it came to that, **as he struggled with death due to hunger** <note>original Latin: "quòd cum fame luctaretur."</note>, he often thought of the aforementioned admonition of Simonides. And as these thoughts distressed and struck his burning spirit, he spoke this sentence three times: **O guest from Ceos, your speech was indeed a great thing, but because of my madness, I myself thought it was nothing.** <note>original Latin: "O Cæe hospes, magnum igitur quiddam oratio erat tua, sed prę amētia, esse nihil ipse opinabar."</note> "O Simonides, my dear guest, you indeed gave me a fine speech, but I was so senseless at the time that I held it for foolishness." # The Third Part #

<meta>catchword: Likewise</meta>

Rome; finding gathered there also several people of knightly rank and many young citizens, he undertook nothing against them. Rather, he had them guarded with earnestness and diligence so that no shame might be brought upon them by the soldiery. He even had them escorted into their own custody and allowed them to depart from him without any ransom or tribute <note>original: "Ranzon oder Schatzung." This refers to the practice of demanding payments for the release of high-status prisoners of war.</note>, just as the Romans had sent their wives there on account of the war. But war is such an uncertain thing, as is the inconstant, shifting victory, that one cannot sufficiently protect or provide for oneself. Thus, when someone thinks he has protected himself or his people well enough—as I myself have experienced—he shall find himself right in the middle of it. Therefore, **Homer** not unjustly calls **Mars**, the god of war, *cunning and changeable, who accommodates himself to all places, clinging now to this one, now to that one. That is, victory falling alternately, now to those, and in turn, now prevailing with these, now with those* <note>original Latin: "Versutum, mutabilem, qui se omnibus locis accommodat, nunc huic, nunc illi adhærens. Id est, victoriam alternatim, nunc illis obtingentem, & vicissim, nunc apud hos, nunc apud illos pollentem."</note>. That is: one who is now with this person, now with another, and thus knows how to **hang his cloak according to the wind** <note>A German idiom meaning to be an opportunist or to adapt to changing circumstances to survive.</note>.

Following this, so that I do not forget the Germans, the historians indicate that a great discord and fierce war arose between **Emperor Conrad** the Swabian <note>Conrad III (1093–1152), the first King of Germany of the Hohenstaufen dynasty.</note> and **Welf** <note>original: "Guleffen". This refers to Welf VI, a member of the powerful House of Welf, rivals to Conrad’s family.</note>, the Duke of Bavaria. And because the Duke did not dare to attack the Emperor in the field nor fight him, he took the knighthood and his best soldiery with him and placed himself in the city of **Weinsberg** <note>original: "Winsberg".</note>, fortifying it. After he was besieged therein by the Emperor, he held fast and endured several assaults; however, they eventually began to lack provisions and other necessities, so that Welf could no longer hold out, but had to surrender himself and his people to the Emperor's mercy or lack thereof. The Emperor also commanded that the Duke, along with the knighthood who had been with him in the war and garrison, should be taken prisoner immediately.

But it happened, before the gates were opened and the <term>capitulation</term> <note>The formal agreement for surrender.</note> was concluded, that the women—namely the Duchess and the noblewomen and the wives of the prominent knights—approached the Emperor with a plea. Specifically, that they all, collectively and individually, might depart in safety with whatever they could carry with them. This the Emperor, as a kind German prince, granted and promised them. And while everyone thought they would carry out their jewelry, such as silver, gold, and pearls, each woman took her husband upon her back and carried the children in her lap, and thus marched out of the city toward the camp, with the Duchess and her lord leading the way.

However, after some said that this was a deception, which did not accord with the treaty and agreement, and therefore would have liked to see the Emperor not allow it—as it usually happens in such cases that people speak and act only for the worst, and men are no longer men but sheer devils—nevertheless, the pious Emperor not only kept his promise and allowed it to happen, gifting the women their husbands, but he also praised and graciously received them for such a clever plan and for their loyalty.

# Of the Book of Rulers #

In the same manner, it also occurred with this current ruling Emperor, **Charles, the fifth of that name** <note>Emperor Charles V (1500–1558), who ruled the Holy Roman Empire and the Spanish Empire.</note>, when **King Francis of France** <note>Francis I (1494–1547), the lifelong rival of Charles V.</note> lay before **Pavia in Lombardy** <note>The Battle of Pavia (1525) was a decisive victory for the Imperial forces over France.</note> with a great army of horse and foot. Having been defeated and captured by the Emperor's soldiers—especially the Germans—and taken to Spain, the Emperor not only graciously released him from imprisonment but also gave him his sister, **Queen Eleanor**, as a lawful wife in marriage.

And so, through such a deed, this Emperor earned great praise and honor for his goodness throughout the whole world, and was more highly lauded than if he had burned and overturned all of France. For although a prince should show himself earnest and firm against his enemies, it is yet becoming for him to show grace toward those who surrender to him, or who have been forcibly constrained and overcome, and to use <term>victory</term> <note>original Latin: *Victoriam*</note> with moderation; of which the Poet also said:

> If victory itself does not have fixed laws,
> As often as it was good, it is prone to be harmful.
<note>original: "Ipsa nisi certas habeat victoria leges, / Quàm bona sæpe fuit, tam solet esse nocens."</note>

Which **Virgil** also intended to show with a beautiful verse, where he speaks:

> To spare the humble and to battle down the proud.
<note>original: "Parcere subiectis, & debellare superbos." A famous line from Virgil's *Aeneid* describing the Roman ideal of governance.</note>

->That is:<-

> Whoever turns and begs for grace,
> Should rightly be shown mercy.
> But whoever wishes to act with pride,
> Should be rewarded accordingly.

For no one can be called a true victor who cannot so much restrain and overcome his own anger that he can set aside and refrain from part of the vengeance against his enemies. Rather, if we wish to be Christians, to whom God says: *Leave vengeance to me*, or, *Vengeance is mine; I will repay, says the LORD.* <note>A reference to the biblical principle found in Romans 12:19 and Deuteronomy 32:35.</note>

Among the ancients, **Philip** and his son **Alexander, Kings of Macedon**, are praised for this virtue. Particularly when Philip overcame the **Athenians** in a war or battle and captured many noble and brave citizens therein. After the victory, he made merry and prepared a great banquet, which the captured citizens watched. As the King then became overloaded with drink and behaved strangely—uttering many arrogant words and acting shamefully—**Demades** <note>An Athenian orator captured at the Battle of Chaeronea (338 BC).</note>, despite being one of the captured citizens, could not endure it. However, it is clear from your gestures and speech that you would rather follow **Thersites** <note>A character in Homer’s *Iliad* known for being vulgar and insolent to his superiors.</note>, which is not becoming of such a great King."

This man was a pagan and a powerful king; today we all wish to be called Christians. But if a prisoner were to speak in such a way to a colonel or captain of the present time—even if he were no king, prince, or great lord—especially if he had been drinking, God help us! What oaths, martyrdom, and "thousand wounds" <note>A common soldier's oath of the period.</note> would be shouted! How he would throw the man into irons and keep him imprisoned! In this way, all human kindness, discipline, and honor have ceased among the Germans. Thus, when one is among a troop of soldiers, he hears such terrifying words and sees such gruesome things that he imagines nothing else than that he is among pure devils. For even if a military leader <term>War-prince</term> <note>original: *Kriegßfürst*</note> would often like to use his **victory** <note>original Latin: *Victoria*</note> for the best, he cannot achieve it or maintain it because of such wicked men. As **Cicero** testifies with a beautiful maxim:

> All things, he says, are wretched in wars. Yet nothing is more wretched than victory itself, which, even if it comes to the better side, nevertheless renders them more fierce; and so indeed, even if they are not such by nature, they are compelled by necessity. For a victor must do many things at the will of those through whom he conquered, even against his own will.
<note>original Latin: "Omnia, inquit, sunt misera in bellis. Nihil tamen miserius, quàm ipsa victoria, quæ, etiam si ad meliores venit, tamen eos ipsos ferociores reddit, & ita quidem, & si natura tales non sunt, necessitate tamen cogantur. Multa enim victori eorum arbitrio, per quos vicit, etiam inuito, facienda."</note>

->That is:<-

Although nothing good is found in war, but everything proceeds in a piteous and miserable way, yet this is the most wicked and lamentable thing of all: that even if victory falls to the best of men, they cannot use it well, but become insolent and proud because of it. And though they may not be of such a nature, they must sometimes show themselves so out of necessity, because a prince who has conquered must often do something to please those through whom he attained such victory and triumph. Therefore, although one may still find pious and God-fearing warriors, they are very few at this time and are not the ones meant here. Because they have so completely forgotten all moderation, there is almost no fortune or welfare left among them; rather, it appears as though it is all over for Germany and the praise and glory she once had, though it is not necessary to write of that at length here. Now we shall also set down an example regarding **Alexander**.

When this same **Alexander** captured **King Porus** <note>A king of the Pauravas in ancient India, defeated by Alexander the Great at the Battle of the Hydaspes in 326 BC.</note> in a battle, he not only set him free again and let him remain with his kingdom, land, and people, but gave him even more land and people besides, so that he became more powerful and richer than he had ever been before. As one reads of others whom the aforementioned Alexander received into grace after a victory and endowed richly, so that one rightly doubts whether he is more to be praised for his triumphant conquest or for the kindness he showed toward the vanquished.

I also recognize myself as duty-bound to do this for my deceased friend and his surviving daughters, since he showed me loyalty and friendship until his grave and gave me shelter."

This speech pleased the entire banquet and was received with great joy and wonder by everyone who heard it. The King was also so moved by it that he ordered the two young women to be fetched and delivered to him; he gave them an honorable and royal <term>morning gift</term> <note>original: *Morgengabe*; traditionally a gift from a husband to a wife, but here used as a royal endowment or dowry.</note>, regardless of the fact that their father Apollophanes, along with his entire lineage, was in the highest disgrace because he had helped to murder Alexander, the King's brother. He asked for and desired a sum of money so large that one friend could hardly hope to obtain it from another. The Emperor not only graciously gave him the money, but also paid for the freedom of the servant who, out of loyalty, had so diligently warned his master of harm and given him such good counsel.

# THE THIRD PART #

Historians testify of those who, though they received many such letters and whole chests full of them, nonetheless read none of them but burned them instead, so that no further unrest might arise from them. In such a manner did the Elector, of highly praised memory, Duke Maurice of Saxony <note>Maurice (1521–1553) was a powerful Elector of Saxony known for his strategic shifts during the Schmalkaldic War.</note>, conduct himself in the past war. For although his Electoral Grace received all kinds of letters, some of which were written by prominent persons, he did not make them pay for it, but let them remain in their rank and dignity and took no action against them.

Otherwise, one may well find a "Centaur" <note>likely used here as a derogatory term for a brutish or greedy minor official</note>, a magistrate <term>Amptmann: a local administrative official who exercised judicial and executive power over a district</term>, or one who otherwise has a small command, who dares to break open an honest man’s letters and run through house and yard, rummaging through everything for the sake of a slight suspicion to see if he might find some little letter from which he could draw cause to defame him before the high authorities, and thereby gain grace and favor at court. But these people should rightly look upon the example of Emperor Frederick <note>Frederick III (1415–1493), Holy Roman Emperor.</note>, to whom a bundle of letters was brought that Master Caspar Schlick, at that time the Imperial Chancellor, had written to several Hungarians. For this reason, the Emperor was urged by his advisors to break them open, for they doubted not that he would find all sorts of treachery and secret plots therein. But the Emperor answered: "I consider Caspar Schlick to be an honest man and one who is fond of me; if I am now deceived, I would rather the error come to light on its own than that it be investigated through my own diligence." <note>original Latin: "Casparum ego & probum virū, & mei amantem existimo, si fallor, malo per sese error pateat, quàm mea diligentia inuestigetur."</note>

Here also belongs, and it cannot be omitted to mention, that some are so utterly forgetful when they have dealings with another—having chased him away, suppressed him, or otherwise gained power over him—that they cannot sufficiently avenge themselves upon his servants and subjects. Instead, they catch, entrap, put in stocks, torture, plague, tax, chase away, and sometimes even banish them entirely. Yet the poor, innocent servants and subjects can do little about the situation. These poor people are so utterly drowned in revenge that they do not consider that such a thing might also meet and happen to them and their own servants. And if it were to happen, it would not please them, but they would cry out over it and decry it as an act of violence. I would know well how to show examples of this, but I will omit it for the sake of brevity and other reasons.

By this, however, I do not mean to imply that pious and faithful advisors, servants, and subjects—who sometimes learn of something intended to be to the disadvantage of their lords and superiors—should remain silent. Indeed, our Lord God sometimes ordains it so that they learn of it and should report it to their lords and warn them; they are also bound by their oaths to do so. For what else is their oath when they pay homage to the lord and say they wish to be "loyal and holden" to him, than that they should report his harm and work for his benefit? And those who fail to do so are to be scolded and regarded as nothing other than perjurers. And would to God that such faithful

<page-num>109</page-num>
## Of the Book of Rulers. ##

Advisors, servants, and subjects, as many as have the ear of their lords, would be held in much higher regard if they reminded them of things out of heartfelt, good, and faithful intent, and warned them of harm and misfortune, rather than acting as loose traitors and false accusers.

It usually happens, however, that such people are despised, and their warnings are held to be either suspicious or otherwise worthless. From this, it follows that many a man falls not only into danger, misery, and distress, but eventually perishes entirely. When this has finally occurred, only then does one think of the pious and faithful people—how well they meant it, and how they would have gladly prevented such damage and misery; but the wait was too long, and the damage has been done, which can never be restored.

Just as it is a form of flightiness to listen to all "ear-blowers" <note>German: *Ohrenbläsern*; a colorful term for sycophants or informants who whisper rumors into a ruler's ear to gain favor.</note> and accusers without distinction and to believe them, bringing whatever they will, whether it be true or not; so too would it be a great lack of foresight if a Prince or Ruler would listen to no one at all, and refused to be warned even in great danger. Those who would block such people—who intended to warn the lord of his harm—do not mean well or faithfully. If anything disadvantageous follows from such a hindrance, one should take the matter up with them and punish them for it. Therefore, a lord must maintain a middle path in this, and listen to those whom he has found and known to be truthful and loyal. He should also protect them, and if they are accused by others out of unfairness or envy, he should give those accusers no place or belief. Instead, he should investigate the matter most diligently. And if he finds that the betrayer has dealt in lies and cannot prove that which he has alleged, he should punish him in such a way that others take offense at it <note>In this context, "take offense" means to be deterred or shocked into better behavior by the severity of the punishment.</note>.

In the same way, he should not leave those unpunished whom he has discovered with truth to have acted unfaithfully, or who at least intended to undertake something untimely against the lord, or to seek after his life, honor, and property—no matter how great a personage he may be.

By this path, he can bring it about that not only will no one easily accuse another before the lord without grounds, but also that no one will dare to undertake anything dangerous or unfaithful against the lord, since both parties must expect punishment. For it cannot fail that such earnest punishment must create a sense of dread in others. As Plato also says: *Punishment of the guilty is necessary, not because of the past crime—since that cannot be corrected—but so that he does not sin again, and so that others do not sin by his example.* <note>Original Latin: "Castigare noxium oportet non ob præteritum delictum quuum id corrigi nequeat, sed ne iterum peccet, tum ne ipsius exemplo cæteri quique peccent." This is a classic legal principle often attributed to Plato or Seneca regarding the deterrent nature of justice.</note> That is: one should and must punish criminals, not for that which has already happened and passed—since that can never be brought back—but so that he sins no further,

->and that others take an example from him not to sin,<-
->but rather have a dread, and must<-
->be terrified of the punishment.<-

<header>The Third Part</header>

# That Great Lords in
## War Should Strive More to Contend with and Overcome
### Their Enemies Through Valor than Through Cunning.

## The Fourth Chapter.

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial 'E' featuring ornate foliage and floral scrolls.</image-desc>

Some have held the opinion that it is and counts for just as much however one overcomes his enemy, whether it be with valor, strength, or with cunning; for this they employ the verse from Virgil, where he says:

> Deceit or valor, who would ask when dealing with an enemy? <note>original Latin: "Dolus an virtus, quis in hoste requirat."</note>
> Force and guile,
> At the same while,
> Are both deemed right,
> Against the enemy in fight.

If one wishes to consider the matter rightly, however, one finds that this opinion does not hold, and that this verse is not to be followed. Rather, he who wishes to act honorably should look his enemy straight in the eye and overcome more through valor <note>German: *Mannheit*; specifically referring to the traditional masculine virtue of courage in battle.</note> and strength than with cunning. For what Aeneas says in Virgil occurred in the utmost and final necessity, when the city was full of fire and enemies, and he could no longer hold off the Greeks nor save his fatherland further, though he would have gladly done so. Though, in truth, he should have rather lost his life than abandoned his fatherland.

Furthermore, Aeneas also displayed a feat of deception toward Queen Dido, who expected much loyalty and goodness from him, and who took him and his people into her city of Carthage and treated them magnificently after their shipwreck. For although he had promised her marriage, he became faithless to her, left her sitting there, and departed when he saw his advantage. He claimed that the gods willed it so, and that he must go to Italy, etc. I shall not even mention that he also left his own wife behind, as Virgil writes at length. Therefore, in this case, one should not refer so much or so highly to Aeneas.

Instead, we should rightly set before our eyes the examples of the ancient Romans, so that we may learn what a noble and brave thing it is to make use of one’s valor, and not only to deal in cunning. Although in this present time of war, things have reached such a state that—on account of the cruel <term>artillery</term> <note>German: *Geschütz*; refers here to cannons and early firearms which the author views as dishonorable.</note>—one can very rarely use his strength and valor. Instead, it often happens that a worthless and despondent knave <note>German: *loser vñ verzagter Bube*; literally a "loose and faint-hearted boy," implying someone of low social standing and little courage.</note>, who otherwise would not dare to open his mouth or address one cheerfully, shoots to death such a brave and manly hero who could have easily held his own and defended himself against three or more others through his strength and valor.

Now, if one wishes to use cunning alongside the artillery, it cannot be possible otherwise: valor must be extinguished in response, just as it is now extinguished almost everywhere. For where does one hear that in thirty years and

<summary>This chapter argues that true honor in warfare comes from open valor rather than deceit, critiquing Aeneas as a model and lamenting how modern artillery has destroyed the noble art of combat.</summary>

<header>Of the Book for Rulers.</header>

...and longer, an honest battle took place—as one often reads of the ancients—even when great military preparations were underway. Therefore, the Romans are to be praised above others in this regard (as mentioned above). We read that when King Pyrrhus warred against them, a deserter from his camp came into the hands of the Romans and offered to Fabricius (who was the commander) that, if he were promised a reward, he would secretly kill the King with poison.

Although Pyrrhus was a powerful warrior who caused the Romans great distress and had already cut down many of their people, they would by no means consent to such a dishonorable act. They did not wish to overcome the King through this means, even though it would have been easy to do. Instead, Fabricius sent the treacherous defector back to the King and had him warned. The entire Senate in Rome approved of this and praised his conduct.

This beautiful story is described by many, though not with one and the same opinion <note>The author acknowledges that different historical sources provide slightly varying accounts of this exchange.</note>, which I shall pass over for the sake of brevity. Whoever wishes may read Gellius, Book 3, Chapter 8; Plutarch, in *Pyrrhus*; both of whom provide a particular example of what was written to King Pyrrhus. Also Valerius, Book 6, Chapter 5; Cicero, *On Ends* Book 5 and *On Duties* Book 3; Eutropius, Book 2; Seneca, *Letter* 121; Frontinus, *Stratagems* Book 4, Chapter 4.

Because of this, Pyrrhus released all the Roman prisoners he held at any given time without any ransom <term>Ranzon: A payment demanded for the release of a prisoner of war</term> (as it is called today) and taxed none of them. As Ennius writes of him:

> I do not demand gold for myself, nor shall you pay me a price;
> Let us not haggle over war like merchants, but wage it as warriors.
> Let us decide the lives of both with steel, not with gold.
> Whether Lady Fortune wishes you or me to rule, or whatever she brings,
> Let us test through valor. And hear this word as well:
> Those whose valor the fortune of war has spared,
> It is certain that I shall spare their freedom.
> Take them as a gift; I give them with the blessing of the great gods.
> <note>original Latin: "Nec mî aurum posco, nec mî precium dederitis / Nec cauponantes bellum, sed belligerantes / Ferro, non auro vitam cernamus utriq; / Vosne velit, an me regnare hera, quidve ferat fors / Virtute experiamur. Et hoc simul accipe dictum / Quorum virtuti belli fortuna pepercit / Horundem me libertati parcere certum est / Dono ducite, doq; volentibus, cum magnis dijs."</note>

->That is:<-

> I want no money or goods on earth,
> Only to fight with the sword.
> It is my desire, whoever in the field,
> Retains the victory through fortune alone.
> He has obtained a good prize;
> Since now these poor people
> Have kept their lives through fortune,
> So I will also set them free.
> Therefore take them away forever,
> From them I desire no profit.

In our times, soldiers are of a very different mind; indeed, most of them pursue war for the purpose of obtaining money...

<meta>This page continues the discussion of military honor and the rejection of treachery, specifically transitioning from the example of King Pyrrhus and Fabricius to another famous Roman example involving Camillus and the schoolmaster of Falerii.</meta>

->### The Third Part<-

...whether it be with ransoms <note>original: "Rankonen," referring to the practice of buying back prisoners of war</note>, or however it may be; and those captured are not only each assessed a price according to their wealth, but are often stripped of their weapons, clothing, and everything they own.

Likewise, Livy <note>Titus Livius, a Roman historian known for his monumental history of Rome</note> writes that it came to pass when the excellent Roman Camillus—who was attacking and besieging the Faliscans <note>The Faliscans were an ancient people of Italy who lived in the city of Falerii</note> after they had rebelled against the Romans—that a schoolmaster, to whom the most prominent citizens in the city had entrusted and commanded the instruction of their children, led these same boys out for a walk through the gate, as he had often done in times of peace. Through trickery, he led them so far that they came first to the guard, then into the camp, and finally before the commander Camillus. The traitor was not satisfied merely with handing the boys over to the enemy, but also pointed out to the commander that these were the children of the most prominent and wealthiest people in the entire city. Therefore, he claimed there was no doubt that if Camillus kept them as his prisoners, the city would not hold out against him for long, but would soon surrender. 

But when Camillus looked upon the unfaithful man and heard his proposal, he gave him this answer: "You traitor, you have come with your shameful booty neither to such soldiers nor to such a commander who would be like you or who would find pleasure in such dishonorable acts. For although we have no special alliance with the Faliscans, we still wish to conduct ourselves as honorable people, blamelessly and as is proper, according to what nature teaches both sides about how one should behave in times of peace and war; and we shall carry out this war against them not only with manhood, but also with justice. We know, however, that our weapons achieve nothing against those who are not of an age to practice war or defend themselves—since it is customary to spare such people even when they are captured. Instead, we wish to use our weapons against those who, without cause, fell upon the Roman camps at Veii <note>A reference to the long conflict between Rome and the Etruscan city of Veii</note> and attacked us. Although that was unjust, your undertaking is far worse and more shameful, and in this matter, you are far surpassed by the Faliscans. But it does not befit me to overcome with such untimely plots, but rather with Roman dealings—namely with justice, manhood, and weapons." 

When he had spoken thus, he had the schoolmaster's clothes stripped off, his hands tied behind his back, and gave each boy a rod in his hand, with the command that they should whip him back out of the camp all the way into the city; which was then done.

But after those in the city observed such treachery from their own man, and likewise such honor and justice from the Romans—even though they were enemies—they were completely changed by this action. Although they had previously been bitterly angry at the Romans and had fully decided that they would rather all die than surrender into Roman hands, they then sent their embassy to Camillus and, after a discussion, offered to surrender to the Romans. He then considered it good that they also send to the Senate in Rome to make this known.

This act of Roman integrity so impressed the besieged Faliscans that they voluntarily surrendered to Rome.</summary>

...should let them go, for he had no doubt that the Council would willingly accept them. When the envoys of the **Faliscans** <note>The Faliscans were an ancient Italian people whose capital was Falerii.</note> arrived in **Rome**, they spoke roughly to this effect:

"We have indeed been overcome by you and your commander, O Fathers, which we now confess before you. However, we live in the hope that such a victory over us shall serve only for our best. Accordingly, we have been commissioned and sent here on behalf of our common city to surrender ourselves and the entire city into your power. For we find and perceive that we can live and walk more conveniently and better under your rule than under our own laws. Such praise is, above all, most honorable and glorious for a victor. And in this war, two beautiful examples have appeared and occurred, which may be useful and beneficial to anyone who takes them to heart. First, that you would not allow yourselves to be moved toward any injustice or cunning, even though you had cause for it; instead, you considered trust, faith, and honor more highly than the victory itself. Second, that we were so moved and prompted by your upright spirit and justice that we have surrendered ourselves and our common city to you and your power, willingly and without compulsion. As we now actually submit ourselves to you, it is with the intent that we wish to be subject and obedient to you. Therefore, you will know how to command your men to march into the city and take possession of it (as it shall stand open to them), and not only demand hostages and armaments from us according to the custom of war, but also impose what further we must do, in the confidence that we shall not regret this action." This was then carried out, and the **Romans** took the city. And **Camillus**, through this honorable deed, gained more and greater thanks and favor—not only from his friends, such as the Council and citizens of **Rome**, but also from his enemies because of such justice—than if he had conquered the city by a powerful storm and razed it to the ground.

**Alexander the Great** <note>Alexander III of Macedon (356–323 BCE), the famous Greek conqueror.</note> also possessed such an upright and great spirit. For when **Parmenio** <note>One of Alexander’s most trusted generals.</note> and others advised him that he should attack **Darius** <note>Darius III, the King of Persia.</note> by night—as Darius had prepared against him a second time and was otherwise far too strong for him—and finish him off all at once, which the other advisors and the entire army also liked, **Alexander** would neither do nor allow such a thing. Instead, he preferred to leave the matter to fortune or to forgo the victory entirely, indicating that he did not care so much for it if it meant people might say or write of him that he had overcome someone with cunning (which is not befitting of honorable kings, but rather of other people). As **Galterus** <note>Walter of Châtillon (12th century), a writer and poet who wrote the 'Alexandreis', an epic poem about Alexander the Great.</note>, the Flemish poet, magnificently described the King's answer in beautiful verses, saying:

> The king looked upon him (for he could no longer bear to argue with Parmenio, or to offend him with swollen words)
> <note>original Latin: "Hunc rex intuitus (nec enim iam Parmenionem / Sustinet arguere, & tumidis offendere dictis)"</note>

gen <note>This is a continuing word from the previous page, likely "those."</note> / so that those who do not understand Latin may know the content and not be displeased that it remains un-translated <note>The author is likely referring to legal or scholarly terms left in the original Latin in the source text, though they are explained here for the reader.</note>.

Plutarch, Cicero, and Valerius also write how Themistocles, after the battle with the Persians, announced to a public assembly of the Athenians that he had found a plan which would be beneficial to the common good and highly advantageous. However, it was of such a nature that it had to be kept secret and entrusted to very few. Thereupon, the community decided and decreed that he should show this plan and secret deliberation to Aristides alone; if it pleased him, it would displease no one else, but rather be accepted.

Now, when Themistocles reported to Aristides what he had in mind—that if all the Greek ships were set on fire and burned while they were anchored at the port (which would be easy to do), then the Athenians would rule over all of Greece and be its masters—Aristides then reported back to the community that Themistocles' revealed plan was very useful, but on the other hand, it was utterly dishonorable and not right. As soon as the community heard this answer, Themistocles was forbidden from thinking of his plan any further. In this, the common people performed a wise act, refusing to mix profit with shameful dishonor. One also senses from this how much the reputation and virtue of an honest man matters, given that the entire community entrusted the welfare of the common good to Aristides alone.

All of this, however, is to be understood as referring to traitors, dishonorable people, and similar cunning practices. But when it comes to battle and a commander uses an advantage, which are typically called <term>stratagems</term> <note>original: "Stratagemata"; clever military tactics or ruses used to outwit an opponent.</note>, he is not to be blamed for it. For example, if one sets an ambush, takes a mountain or hill, etc. And the Canon Law <note>original: "Geistliche Recht"; ecclesiastical or church law.</note> is to be understood in that way, which says in 23. q. 1. c. *Dominus noster*: *When you have undertaken a just war, it matters not whether you fight by ambush or openly.* <note>original: "Cum iustum susceperis bellum, nihil refert, an ex insidijs pugnes, an apertè."</note> Yet it remains a requirement that one must have a just cause; if the cause is evil, and one wants to use improper ways on top of that to achieve victory, it is not to be praised.

The king, having just struck down the advice given with sharp satire,
Said: "This is the habit of a bandit, this the cleverness of thieves,
Which is suggested to me; whose only hope of prayer, and

Plutarch, Cicero, and Valerius also write how Themistocles <note>A famous Athenian politician and general (c. 524–459 BCE) known for his cunning and his role in the naval victory at Salamis.</note>, after the battle held with the Persians, announced to a public assembly of the Athenians that he had found a plan that would be useful and highly advantageous for the common good. However, the circumstances were such that it had to be kept secret and entrusted to very few. Thereupon, the community decided and decreed that he should reveal his counsel and secret deliberations to Aristides alone; if it pleased him, it would displease no one else, but rather be accepted.

Now, when Themistocles informed Aristides of his idea—that if all the Greek ships were set on fire and burned while they were anchored at the port, which would be easy to do, then the people of Athens would rule over all of Greece and be its masters—Aristides then announced to the community: Themistocles' proposed plan was very useful, but on the other hand, it was profoundly dishonorable and not right. As soon as the community heard this answer, Themistocles was forbidden from ever thinking of this plan again. In this instance, the common people performed a wise deed by refusing to accept a profit that was mixed with base dishonor. One also senses from this how much the reputation and virtue of an honest man matters, as the entire community entrusted and submitted the welfare of the common good to Aristides <note>Aristides "the Just" (c. 530–468 BCE), an Athenian statesman renowned for his integrity.</note> alone.

All of this, however, is to be understood as referring to treachery, dishonorable acts, and similar cunning practices. But when it comes to a battle and a captain makes use of some advantage, which are usually called <term>stratagems</term> <note>From the Greek 'strategema', referring to a military maneuver or ruse used to outwit an enemy.</note>, he is not to be blamed for it. Such as, for example, when one sets an ambush, occupies a mountain or hill, etc. And that is how the Canon Law <note>The body of laws and regulations governing the Church, referred to here as 'Geistliche Recht'.</note> is to be understood, which says in 23. q. 1. c. *Our Lord*: "When you have undertaken a just war, it matters not whether you fight by ambush or openly." <note>original: "Cùm iustum susceperis bellum, nihil refert, an ex insidijs pugnes, an apertè."</note> Yet it is also stated alongside this that one must have a just cause; if the cause is evil, and one still wishes to use improper means to achieve victory, that is not to be praised.

# That one is also bound to keep faith with enemies.

## The Fifth Chapter.

Just as in all other dealings it is right and fair that a person holds to what he has once vowed and promised, it is also proper that what one enemy promises to another must be kept. From this comes the practice of pledges <note>original: "Bestrickung," referring to formal bonds of honor or parole often used by the nobility when captured.</note> among those of the nobility and others, although the abuse

<header>Of the Book of Rulers.</header>

...so that those who do not understand Latin may know the content, and not be displeased that the verses remain untranslated <note>The author is referring to the German translation of the Latin poem on the previous page.</note>.

Plutarch, Cicero, and Valerius also write of how Themistocles <note>An Athenian politician and general (c. 524–459 BCE) known for his cleverness and for building the Athenian navy.</note>, after the conflict with the Persians, announced in the public assembly of Athens that he had found a plan which would be serviceable and highly beneficial to the common good. However, the nature of the plan was such that it had to be kept secret and shared with very few. Therefore, the people resolved and decreed that he should reveal his counsel and secret considerations to Aristides <note>Aristides "the Just" (c. 530–468 BCE), an Athenian statesman renowned for his integrity and a frequent rival of Themistocles.</note> alone; if it pleased him, it would displease no one and be accepted.

Now, when Themistocles reported to Aristides what he had devised: that if all the ships of the Greeks were set on fire and burned while they were anchored at the port—which would be easy to do—then Athens would rule over all of Greece and be its masters. Upon hearing this, Aristides reported to the assembly that the counsel revealed by Themistocles would be very useful, but on the other hand, it would be utterly dishonorable and not right. As soon as the people heard this answer, they forbade Themistocles from ever thinking of this plan again. In this instance, the common man performed a wise deed by refusing to have utility mixed with base dishonor. One also senses from this how much the reputation and virtue of an honest man can achieve, in that the entire community trusted and deferred the welfare of the common good to Aristides alone.

All of this, however, is to be understood as applying to traitors, dishonorable acts, and similar cunning practices. But when it comes to battle, and a captain uses an advantage—which are typically called <term>Stratagemata</term> <note>Stratagems: clever maneuvers or tricks used to outwit an enemy in war.</note>—he is not to be blamed for it. This includes things such as setting an ambush, seizing a mountain or hill, etc. And the Canon Law <note>original: "Geistliche Recht", referring to the body of laws and regulations made by Church leadership.</note> is to be understood in this way, which says (23. q. 1. c. Dominus noster): "When you have undertaken a just war, it does not matter whether you fight by ambush or openly." <note>original Latin: "Cùm iustum susceperis bellum, nihil refert, an ex insidijs pugnes, an apertè."</note> Nevertheless, it is also stated that one must have a righteous cause; for if the cause is evil, and one then wishes to use improper means alongside it to achieve victory, that is not to be praised.

...very often happens, and one is taken into a snare by another for a trivial reason, as tends to happen in other matters as well. Yet, nothing is more fitting than for a man to keep what he has promised, to both friends and enemies alike. As one reads of the honorable man Marcus Regulus <note>Marcus Atilius Regulus was a Roman general and consul during the First Punic War (c. 250 BCE).</note>, who was captured in the Carthaginian War, which lasted 22 years. This Regulus was sent from Carthage to Rome to negotiate an exchange, so that they might release the captured enemies; if he achieved this, he was to be set free. If, however, he could not achieve this, he was to return again to Carthage. When he arrived in Rome, he himself advised that this exchange of prisoners should not be made, considering that he was an old man whose life was henceforth of little account. He also brought it to pass that the Senate finally followed his counsel, and he returned to Carthage, where he was then horribly and in various ways tortured. And it is indicated, among other things, that they cut off his eyelids and tormented him with forced wakefulness. Therefore, his loyalty is praised first, in that he esteemed the common good higher than his own welfare, body, and life. Secondly, his faith is praised, in that he returned even though he knew they would torture him horribly.

With this—letting the other examples pass—the Spiritual Law <note>Also known as Canon Law, the internal religious law governing the Catholic Church.</note> also agrees, which says: <note>original: "Fides enim quando promittitur, etiam hosti seruanda est, contra quem bellum geritur, quantò magis amico, pro quo pugnatur."</note> *For when faith is promised, it must be kept even with an enemy against whom war is waged; how much more so with a friend for whom one fights.* That is: If we are bound to our enemy, against whom we struggle, to keep that which we have promised him, much more should we keep such things with our friend, for whom we fight.

Likewise, Baldus <note>Baldus de Ubaldis (1327–1400) was one of the most influential legal scholars of the Middle Ages.</note> says in the first book of the Code concerning the constitution of money: <note>original: "Alexandrum Magnum ab Aristotele, qui fuit ipsius Præceptor, prudenter admonitum esse, vt pacta seruaret, Alioqui malum finem sequuturũ."</note> *That Alexander the Great was wisely reminded by Aristotle, who was his instructor and tutor, that he should diligently keep what he once promises; otherwise, it would come to a bad end for him.* However, according to the opinion of some, this only applies so long as faith is also kept with us by them, according to the rule: <note>original: "Frustrà sibi fidem."</note> *In vain [does one expect] faith [to be kept with oneself if one does not keep it with others].* For it is surely unjust that one would want me to keep faith regarding that which I had promised him, yet would fail me regarding that which he had promised me. Secondly, no deceit must be used through which we think to be rid of that which was promised by us. As happened when Hannibal was petitioned by a Roman who asked for permission to leave the camp; the Roman promised and swore that he would return, and so he departed. Soon he returned, as if he had forgotten something in the tent, thinking that he had thereby fulfilled his vow and oath <note>By physically "returning" to the camp for his forgotten item, the soldier technically fulfilled the words of his oath while violating its intent.</note>. But this was a deceit that does not befit an honorable man. Therefore, I will tell the following history of such deceit.

Through this, he fell into such disfavor with the Emperor, as can easily be imagined, that no one could quiet or settle the matter. Albert, however, fled from the vengeance...

### Of the Book of Rulers.

...anger and punishment of the Emperor, [Albert retreated] into the strong Castle of Babenberg <note>Now known as Bamberg. This refers to the Babenberg Feud (c. 906 AD) between the Frankish Babenberg family and the Conradines.</note>, wherein he remained for seven years, so that nothing could be taken from him. Finally, the Emperor laid siege to the castle. But as he could achieve nothing by force, he sought to overcome him with cunning and deceit. For this reason, he asked Hatto, the Bishop of Mainz, for advice on how to proceed. Hatto, who was at that time a particularly cunning man, gave him this answer: "Be content; I will relieve you of this worry and the war. I will bring the Count to you; see to it that he does not escape you again." Thereupon, Hatto went into the castle to the Count as a mediator and friend, spoke much with him there, and finally advised that he should travel with him to the Emperor himself; he would either reconcile them or bring him back to his castle with his life unharmed.

And so that he would have no doubt about this, he swore a solemn oath to Albert. The Count believed all of this, especially because this was a holy bishop and a spiritual man. He then asked the Bishop to share a meal with him, which the Bishop cunningly declined. They therefore rode out through the city without delay; some write they rode past the castle. The Bishop led Albert by his right hand and said: "How often is something offered to a person, and they do not want it. I am thinking of the long journey, and that we must ride without eating, yet we could have easily changed and prevented this." When Albert heard this, and suspected no danger or cunning from the holy Bishop, he asked him with all respect to ride back and share a meal with him. Thus, the Bishop led Albert back into his stronghold, with the intent that he would thereby be released from his sworn oath and promise, because he had returned him to his place unharmed. After the meal was finished, Albert set out again with the Bishop and was delivered to Emperor Louis <note>Louis the Child (reigned 899–911), the last Carolingian ruler of East Francia.</note>. Thereupon, a court was immediately held, and the Count was sentenced to death by the princes and lords who were present. But when he called upon the Bishop's oath, safe conduct, and promise, the Bishop answered: He had kept it, and had brought him before the castle and led him back inside without harm; he was not obligated to keep anything further. Thus it went for the brave Count; by the Bishop's treacherous unfaithfulness, his head was taken from him. The Emperor gave the Bishop the castle and all the villages and income of Count Albert as a reward, and he was buried in this very castle, called Tharisia <note>Referring to the former castle and later monastery of Theres in Franconia.</note>. God himself punished this unfaithfulness of the Bishop, such that thunder struck him dead.

# The Third Part

...was led to the fiery Mount Etna in Sicily with this cry:
> "Thus shall you be punished and fall." <note>This refers to a popular medieval legend that Bishop Hatto was cast into the volcano for his sins, or in other versions, devoured by mice in the "Mouse Tower" at Bingen.</note>

And Otto of Freising <note>A famous 12th-century German chronicler and bishop.</note> writes that regarding this priest, others may judge as they wish, and they may defend this deed as if it were done for the good of the Empire. However, I say for my own part that it does not befit any Christian, much less a bishop, to deprive any person of life and limb for the sake of any benefit, and to circumvent them in such a treacherous manner. And therefore Cicero <note>The Roman statesman and philosopher, likely referencing his work *De Officiis* (On Duties).</note> says that while we can be injured and attacked in two ways—either by force or by cunning—and although both are wrong, wicked cunning is considered the worst. He argues that the injustice of those who deceive someone is most harmful when they still wish to appear as if they have acted rightly in all ways; this is neither honorable nor just.

For what a person has once promised and pledged, they are bound to keep. It is not valid to put forward a "colored pretense" <note>A false or misleading legal justification.</note> or to interpret a promise with cunning, as has just been told, and as Cleomenes <note>Cleomenes I, a King of Sparta.</note> did in ancient times. Cleomenes took one of his trusted friends, named Archonides, and desired that he should help him establish a matter under the obligation of an oath. The oath stated that since the matter concerned him, he would henceforth direct and handle all affairs "according to his [Archonides'] head." 

But when it happened that they carried out the matter to his liking, Cleomenes not only failed to keep his faith and the trust he had promised his friend, but he actually strangled him. Nevertheless, he claimed to have kept his promise, oath, and duty; he took the strangled man’s head, placed it in a barrel of honey, and whenever he was about to conduct business, he went to the barrel and looked at the head, believing that he had thereby fulfilled his oath to consult his friend's head. 

Among the foolish, one might put forward such an excuse to give the transaction a fair appearance. Among the wise, however, such a thing is "sealed with snow" <note>An idiom suggesting a defense that is transparently flimsy and will quickly "melt" under scrutiny.</note>. For even if a person achieves their ends before the world through either force or cunning and manages to mislead people—which happens but rarely—they will not deceive God. He will surely judge and knows how to punish such unfaithfulness, as was just demonstrated and proven in the case of Hatto the Bishop.

# On Military Law, and the discipline and order the ancient captains maintained among their soldiery when they took to the field, and what they were required to swear.

### The Sixth Chapter.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut drop cap initial 'I' with floral and foliate patterns.</image-desc> I was indeed of the mind to write more and at greater length regarding matters of war, as there is so much mention of it here and there in the histories. I find, however, for several reasons, that this is unnecessary. Firstly, I am entirely inexperienced in such things and have seen little of them. Secondly, war today is a completely different matter than it was in ancient times, especially on account of artillery <note>The author refers to the "Geschütz," noting how the invention of gunpowder and cannons fundamentally changed the nature of combat compared to the classical era.</note>, as everyone can see with their own eyes. Thirdly, several others long before me have already written stately and sufficient accounts of this business, such as Vegetius, Julius Frontinus, Aelianus, and Modestus <note>These were the primary classical authorities on military strategy and discipline studied during the Renaissance.</note>, who have very skillfully brought the art and practice of knighthood to light, and have partly translated it into German. Furthermore, people are already more than enough prepared and inclined toward war in these times; would to God that we were as willing for peace as we are for shameful war, for then the world might perhaps be in a better state, as would better befit and suit us as Christians if we would only heed our calling. For these reasons, I have refrained from writing at length about it, and will only set down several chapters concerning the ancient customs of soldiers, what they had to swear, as well as the discipline and punishment of ancient soldiers, along with several other chapters.

But before I come to the examples and histories in which military order and knightly discipline are handled, I wish to briefly set down here how the ancients described Military Law in Latin: **"Military law is the solemnity of waging war and the bond of making treaties. It is the marching out against the enemy or the joining of battle when the signal is given. Likewise, when the signal is given, it is the retreat; the discipline and restraint of military misconduct, if the situation requires it; the method of pay, the grades of rank, the honors of rewards—such as when a crown or a collar is given. Likewise, it is the decision of booty and its just division according to the quality and labors of the persons, and finally, the prince's portion."** <note>original: "Ius militare est belli inferendi solennitas foedera faciendiq; nexus. Signo dato egressio in hostem vel pugnæ commissio. Item signo dato, receptio flagitij militaris disciplina & coertio, si locus desiderat, Stipendiorũ modus dignitatũ gradus, præmiorũ honores veluti cum corona vel Torques donatur. Item prædæ decisio & pro personarū qualitatibus & laborib. iusta diuisio, ac deniq; principis portio."</note>

That is to say: Military or Knightly Law is nothing other than a public and grand manner of harming and making war upon another, of reconciling that same war again, of making alliances, of arranging the order of battle, of attacking the enemy, of summoning the soldiery back from the battle by the trumpeter, of punishing the crimes of the soldiers where necessary, of ordaining each man’s pay according to his skill, of appointing and distributing offices, and of ordaining brave gifts for those who acted knightly and stood before others against the enemy—just as in former times one would give a...

[granted] a torque <note>original: "Kranck," likely referring to a *torques* or neck-ring given as a military decoration, paired here with a bracelet.</note> or bracelet. Finally, [he describes] the division of the spoils, so that equality is maintained as is due to each, and so that the colonel or general may receive his proper share. Beside this, I will also, as briefly as possible, relate what kind of persons the ancients used as soldiers and what age they had to be.

It is to be known that the ancient Romans accepted no one under seventeen nor over forty-six years of age. This was because those under or over this age were considered unable to endure or grow accustomed to the heavy and difficult labors of war. However, it did not matter to them if such soldiers were raised in the city or in a village under the open sky; for they held that the latter could better endure both heat and cold, as well as the labor with which soldiers are burdened, more so than those raised in the city and in the shade.

Furthermore, in the recruitment of new soldiers, the captains paid diligent attention to their physical build and the skill of their gestures; for they usually accepted those who had a straight neck, a broad chest, strong limbs, and a free, steadfast spirit—as experienced captains could quickly see such things—so that they might enlist people in whom the common <term>benefit</term> <note>original: "Nuß," an archaic spelling of "Nutz," meaning utility or public good.</note> could find comfort in the face of impending war. But those who were too fat or had an ugly body, likewise the lame, the sluggish, the lazy, and the sick, were mustered out and considered unfit. Thus, <term>Cato Censorinus</term> <note>Cato the Elder (234–149 BC), a Roman statesman famous for his strict adherence to traditional customs and military discipline.</note> dismissed one who had a heavy and fat body.

Once a man was enrolled and accepted as a soldier, however, he could not be discharged against his will unless he conducted himself so improperly and against his sworn oath that he made himself unfit to be a soldier. Certain articles were also immediately presented to them, which they had to confirm with an oath. Among these, the most prominent was that each was duty-bound to be faithful to the others, and that no one would desert the field from another.

When the new <term>recruits</term> <note>original: "Tyrones," the Latin term for soldiers in training.</note> and soldiers were accepted, they were given a drillmaster <note>original: "Zuchtmeister," a master of discipline or trainer.</note> who had to teach them military customs for the first year, so that they knew how to conduct themselves better in all matters, to use weapons properly and usefully, and not to neglect them. Emperor <term>Julius</term> [Caesar] applied such diligence to the soldiers so that they might be rightly led and instructed, that he even employed the most prominent people and councilors in Rome who were experienced in war for this purpose. Among these, the first was <term>P. Rutilius</term> <note>Publius Rutilius Rufus, a Roman consul who, in 105 BC, introduced professional gladiatorial training methods into the Roman army to improve combat skills.</note>, who taught the young warriors how they should look out for themselves in battle and before the enemy so they would not be wounded, and how they should attack others and fight with them. Only after they had learned such things over the first year were they then considered true soldiers. Thus, every...

every captain must keep watch over his soldiers, ensuring that they diligently practice the **art of knighthood**.

The Persians had several old and experienced warriors, none of whom were over fifty years of age; by these, the young and inexperienced were instructed—first in moderation and proper conduct, and subsequently in all serious knightly matters. For this purpose, they established an <term>order of battle</term> <note>original: "Schlachtordnung," referring to the specific tactical formation of troops.</note>, and both the young companions and the men from age forty up to fifty were required to serve in the war. Likewise, the military law of the Romans did not include those who were over fifty years of age; among some, the custom was that no one was enrolled as a new soldier who was over forty years old.

The Scythians, however, had a law stating that no one over sixty years of age could be accepted as a soldier.

Among the Egyptians, the <term>Calasirians</term> <note>A hereditary caste of warriors in ancient Egypt mentioned by Herodotus.</note>, who were their best soldiers, were permitted to be prepared and instructed for war by no other master than their own parents. However, Phocion in Athens, in order to restrain his people because he saw they were all too eager for war, issued a decree and commanded that even the old, frail men over eighty years of age must enroll and serve in the war.

Thus Camillus, when he undertook a great war against the Latins and Volscians, mustered the elderly who were still capable as soldiers. Alexander did the same against Darius.

The Romans enrolled no one as soldiers except Romans or Latins; those who were foreigners were mustered with light armor. But Cyrus was of the opinion—saying that just as one fetches the best horses from far away, so it is with soldiers—that those who come from afar and are unknown are the best. For such people are terrifying to hear about, let alone to see or to fight against. Thus, those of Alexandria for a long time used no others but foreign soldiers.

One also finds that among the ancients, it was provided that soldiers should usually wear red clothing, so that if they were wounded in battle, they would not easily see the blood on themselves and be terrified, but might instead remain all the more stouthearted and bold. Thus Artaxerxes clothed his soldiers in red when he wished to war against Cyrus. Cyrus, however, clothed his in white. The Thracians used black clothing in war. The Moors also used white. The Samnites usually used multicolored or divided clothing. It was also the custom of the Moors to paint themselves for war, half with <term>minium</term> <note>original: "Menig," a bright red-orange lead pigment.</note> and half with clay-color.

Furthermore, the war-princes and great captains often—especially in battle—dressed themselves in such clothing and armor that they could be recognized above others. Such as Alexander the Great, Julius Caesar, and Lucius Lucullus. Although some among the Greeks, namely Agesilaus, Agis, and Gylippus, used humble clothing,

...so that they might not be recognized among others and common soldiers, despite the fact that they were great, excellent kings, princes, and captains, and their soldiers along with their cavalry equipment—especially those of Agesilaus <note>Agesilaus II (c. 444–360 BCE), a famous King of Sparta known for his military leadership.</note>—were most finely and beautifully adorned. A law was also given by C. Gracchus <note>Gaius Gracchus (154–121 BCE), a Roman statesman who enacted the "Lex Militaris," which provided soldiers with clothing at the state's expense.</note> that every Roman soldier must be given a garment, and that the cost of such should not be deducted from his pay.

And to return to the <term>Tyrones</term> <note>Latin: *tiro*, meaning a recruit or a novice soldier.</note> and their training: it should be known that when they marched out from Rome to war, the soldiers were first all recorded on tablets so that it could be seen who returned and who remained behind or was slain in the war. When they arrived at the place where they pitched camp, secured their wagon-fort, and built their fortifications, they did not drink, gamble, or bicker with one another, as the modern profligates do—who are partly unworthy of being called soldiers. Instead, both winter and summer, before and after noon, as soon as the trumpet was blown or an alarm sounded, each had to hurry to his <term>Feinlein</term> <note>An archaic term for a "Fähnlein," a company of soldiers gathered under a single flag or standard.</note>, where they were then commanded to do all manner of tasks. For they were required to dig trenches, throw up ramparts, march in formation, or stand for a time in battle order, conduct false alarms, and do everything else that is proper and customary in wartime, or whatever each was commanded by his captain. Iphicrates <note>An Athenian general who revolutionized Greek warfare with better training and equipment.</note> was a particular master of this; he kept his soldiers in constant exercise so that they knew how to handle themselves in all matters: throwing, running, jumping, shooting, wrestling, etc. The Romans also had their young soldiers learn to swim, and whatever else could be devised for combat and military training.

But primarily they had a large <term>post</term> <note>original: "Pfal," referring to the Roman *palus*, a wooden stake used for target practice with swords and shields.</note> upon which they had to test themselves daily. This same post was about three cubits high and shaped like a man; against it the young warriors fought and practiced to use their knightly weapons properly. The Cretans and Cydonians <note>Ancient inhabitants of Crete, renowned in the ancient world as elite archers.</note> had to practice constantly with the hand-bow. Cyrus <note>Cyrus the Great, founder of the Achaemenid Persian Empire.</note>, however, exercised his soldiers with constant labor, such that they were not permitted to eat their food until they had first exerted themselves with work until they sweated, just as he himself used to do. The Persian kings used to give gifts and prizes to their warriors when they practiced fighting, running, and other knightly games. In the same way, Alexander the Great did also, making captains of those who conducted themselves virtuously and well in knightly games above others. Emperor Aurelian let no day pass without spending some time in shooting and other knightly games. Bassianus <note>The Emperor Caracalla, who often lived and marched like a common soldier to win the favor of his troops.</note>, beyond other knightly exercises, also walked on foot in his full armor. And what is even more, one reads of the Emperor Severus that in wintertime, in cold frost and snow, he went with a bare head over great mountains and through entire forests, and with such patience could endure such great hunger and labor that it is almost unbelievable.

# The Book of Rulers. 116

...carried heavy armor, both for horse and foot; breastplates and helmets were covered with bear skins, some with horse manes or horse tails, so that they might appear all the more terrifying and cruel to the enemy. Some used leopard and lion skins in war. Pyrrhus and Philip <note>Pyrrhus of Epirus and Philip II of Macedon.</note> wore goat horns on their helmets. The Hammonians <note>Followers of the oracle of Jupiter-Ammon.</note> used a bull's head. Alexander the Great wore beautiful white feathers around his helmet. The Thracians wore ox horns. And others bore similar signs, as one still sometimes sees today, where a man bears something special on his helmet, such as ostrich feathers or elk hides <note>original: "Elendshäut". In Early Modern German, "Elend" often referred to the elk.</note>.

And it was especially an ancient custom among the Romans that the soldiers had to act cautiously in all matters, exactly as if the enemy were right at their throats, particularly when they went out for foraging <note>original: "auff die Fütterung gezogen", referring to the gathering of fodder for horses and supplies for the camp.</note>. They also had to be ready day and night, and as soon as anything occurred, each had to report to his company <term>Fähnlein</term> <note>A small military unit or company gathered under a single banner.</note>; whoever was tardy was either branded a scoundrel or otherwise severely punished. However, some among them also used a milder punishment, such as Scipio Aemilianus; although he otherwise strictly maintained military discipline, if he caught someone who had broken ranks, if he was a citizen, he had him beaten with grapevines; if he was a foreigner, with clubs. When they went out for foraging, the infantrymen were not allowed to mix with the cavalry, nor were the soldiers allowed to sell the grain given to them; even if they obtained cattle as booty, they were not permitted to trade it for wine. Also, no lowly infantryman was allowed to keep a baggage train or a horse; no captain could become a guide <note>original: "Führer", here likely a specific lower rank or scout.</note>, nor could a guide become a common soldier.

Moreover, the soldiers always had to be belted in their clothing and armed with their weapons. Those who went unbelted were considered lazy and incompetent warriors. For this reason, the Macedonians had a law that whoever had not killed an enemy had to gird himself with a halter <note>original: "Holfftern", usually a rope or headstall for an animal, used here as a mark of shame.</note> and not with a military belt. Likewise, the Carthaginians considered those who were unbelted to be the most dissolute and worst of people. When they were on the march, every soldier had to carry his armor, shield, sword, flask, bellows <note>original: "Blasbalg".</note>, and sometimes provisions for half a month on his back, using a pack-frame or "horse" <note>original: "Troß oder Pferd". In this context, it likely refers to a wooden T-frame or "mule" used by Roman soldiers (muli Mariani) to carry their gear.</note>. It was also strictly forbidden for anyone to leave the formation to fight or brawl with another without orders, even if he had been challenged. Anyone who was not enrolled <note>original: "geschrieben", meaning registered on the official muster rolls.</note> and sworn into the war was not permitted to mix with the other soldiers or attack the enemy.

Likewise, whoever was not enrolled and slew an enemy was punished in his body just as if he had strangled a friend or companion. In the same way, it was punishable if, when the army was recalled from battle by the trumpet, someone was tardy and did not immediately cease attacking the enemy. For this reason, Cyrus praised a soldier who had his sword drawn and...

# The Third Part

As for the oath of the soldiers <term>Kriegsleute</term> <note>Literally "war-people," a general term for soldiers or mercenaries.</note>, one reads that initially ten cavalrymen and a hundred infantrymen voluntarily swore to one another; however, once Paulus Aemilius and Terentius Varro <note>Lucius Aemilius Paullus and Gaius Terentius Varro, Roman consuls during the Second Punic War.</note> became Mayors <note>original: "Bürgermeister"; here referring to the Roman Consuls.</note>, the voluntary oath of the soldiers ceased, and the soldiers were first required to swear to one another. First, the High Commander or War-Lord had to swear, then the legates or commissioners, lieutenants, cavalry captains, captains, sergeants, quartermasters, and squad leaders <term>Rotmeister</term> <note>The leader of a "Rotte," a small file or squad of soldiers.</note>, and finally the common soldiers. And these were the articles which they had to swear: That they would be obedient to the captain; that they would not leave the tents or camp without permission for any reason whatsoever that might be imagined; and that they would not step out of formation, unless it were to retrieve an arrow, to strike an enemy, or to protect a citizen in mortal danger. Also, when they lay in the field, no one was to go further than ten thousand paces from the camp, nor take more than one silver groschen as loot; and whatever booty he obtained beyond a spear, bellows, keg, fodder, or wood, he was to bring to the captain or Mayor. Sometimes, when a necessity or a hard battle was at hand, they swore together that none of them would return to his tent unless the enemies were first overcome and put to flight. Now, when the entire army had to swear to the commander, they usually followed this custom: only the Centurions or captains and squad leaders swore such articles with a loud voice on behalf of the others; the rest of the host stood by and silently consented, keeping those same articles with such loyalty as if they had all sworn and repeated the articles word for word.

Among the Lacedaemonians <note>Spartans.</note>, the custom was that the soldiers swore to their commander that whoever was his enemy should also be their enemy, and that they would suffer together in good and bad, and remain together in life and death. And because the Megarians <note>Inhabitants of Megara, a city-state in Greece.</note> had done many injuries and grievances to those of Athens, acting against the laws of nations, the Athenians became such enemies to them that whenever they went to war, they had to swear among other articles that they would not return home from the war until they had plundered the fields and villages of the Megarians, done them damage to the best of their ability, and "plucked a feather" <note>original: "eine Feder gezogen"; likely a symbolic reference to a successful raid or a minor act of military aggression.</note>.

This was roughly the military custom, practice, and the articles which the soldiers had to swear and keep, from which it can be seen that everything proceeded honorably and modestly, and in great obedience. Likewise, because men strove for honor and manhood, and the soldiers were in constant knightly exercise <term>Ritterlicher vbung</term>, such beastly drinking, dicing, gambling, and such unchristian cursing and swearing, or the shaming of women and virgins, did not exist, nor was it heard of. Then, the soldiers did not dare to so shamefully mutilate and brawl with one another over wine or otherwise. Furthermore, they were also forbidden from bringing women with them into war, even if...

# How the ancient soldiers
### were punished for their crimes.

## The Seventh Chapter.

As far as the punishments of the ancient soldiers are concerned, it is to be known that in olden times there were two types of punishment among the soldiers. For some escaped with a minor punishment, while others were punished strictly and harshly, according to the nature of the crime. Thus, those who staged a mutiny in the camp, deserted their watch, or otherwise became fugitives from the field were punished with gravity and with their lives. For in these matters, one had to use such severity so that others might have a horror of it and guard themselves against mutiny and other offenses, and not abandon the watch upon which so much depended, etc. But if the mutiny was so great that a large crowd became rebellious, the most prominent instigators and ringleaders were either impaled or had their heads chopped off with an ax. The others had to draw lots with one another, and every tenth man had to be surrendered to be beheaded <term>Decimation</term> <note>A form of military discipline used by Roman armies to punish mutiny or cowardice; one-tenth of a group was selected by lot to be executed.</note>.

**Germans** <note>original: "Teutschen"</note> lost his shield, it was forbidden for him 
to be present when a public assembly was held or when sacrifices were offered to the gods.
