# Of the Book of Regents.

Those, however, who have deserted or committed treason were punished in their bodies without any mercy. **Fabius Maximus** <note>Quintus Fabius Maximus Verrucosus (c. 280–203 BC), the Roman general famous for his delaying tactics against Hannibal.</note> had the right hands cut off of those who, contrary to their oaths and duties, defected to the enemy. **Publius Scipio** <note>Likely Scipio Africanus the Elder.</note>, however, had those same oath-breaking and deserting scoundrels hanged on a gallows if they were Romans; but if they were Latins <note>The Latin allies of Rome, who held a different legal status than full Roman citizens.</note>, he had their heads cut off with an axe according to old Roman custom. **Africanus** <note>Likely Scipio Africanus the Younger.</note> had those same men thrown to wild beasts. **Paulus Aemilius** <note>Lucius Aemilius Paullus Macedonicus (c. 229–160 BC).</note> gave them to the elephants. The **Germans** hanged them from trees and had those who were unfit for war drowned; but those who surrendered to the enemy out of negligence or fear had their rank changed. Thus, if a man had previously been a horseman <term>Reuter</term> <note>A cavalryman or knight.</note>, he was forced to become a foot soldier, and was also required to keep his quarters outside the rampart and the **wagon-fortress** <term>Wagenburg</term> <note>A fortification made of wagons, common in both Roman and medieval German warfare.</note>. Just as **Domitius Corbulo** <note>A prominent Roman general under Nero.</note>, when he was sent by Nero into Armenia, drove two wings and three companies out of the wagon-fortress for this reason.

Likewise, one reads of **Vitollo** <note>Vytautas the Great (c. 1350–1430), Grand Duke of Lithuania.</note>, who ruled in **Lithuania** about a hundred years ago, that whenever he went to the field with his army, he always carried a drawn bow; and whichever soldier stepped out of order or otherwise behaved improperly, he would shoot an arrow into him. Similarly, **Sylvius** <note>Likely Enea Silvio Piccolomini, later Pope Pius II, who wrote histories of the region.</note> writes of him that all his subjects so feared his cruel tyranny that when he said to one, two, or more: "Go at once and hang yourselves," not one refused this command. And in this regard, some were heard who, while running, exhorted their companions, saying:

> Let us go as quickly as possible, lest we stir up the master's wrath. <note>original: "Eamus quam properanter, Ne bilem Domino commoueamus."</note>

**Tamerlane** <note>Timur (1336–1405), the Turco-Mongol conqueror.</note>, the King of the **Scythians**, kept his army under such strict discipline that when a soldier was accused before him of having stolen a pot of milk from a poor woman, he not only had him beheaded but also cut open, and had the milk poured out of his body again.

**Pescennius Niger** <note>A Roman usurper (r. 193–194 AD).</note>, while he held **Gaul**, had a captain pelted to death with stones when he learned that he had cheated his servant out of every tenth penny of his wages.

It was once reported and made known to the **Emperor Macrinus** <note>Roman Emperor (r. 217–218 AD) known for his legal severity.</note> by his proviant-master how several soldiers in an inn had forced a maid to satisfy their desires. Therefore, he had them summoned immediately to investigate the matter. Since they could not steadfastly deny it, he immediately had two large oxen cut open and placed the soldiers inside them, sewing them up again. However, their heads remained outside so that he could speak with them and scold them bravely until they died.

This **Macrinus** also had a captain—who had permitted and looked on while the watch was abandoned—bound to a wagon and dragged alive the entire way.

# How small groups have often defeated and struck down large and powerful armies in war.

## The Eighth Chapter.

It will not be inappropriate here, while writing of military affairs, to report among other things from history and to recount several notable examples from which it may be seen that sometimes large and powerful masses were defeated by a small number of troops. I will, however, mention nothing here of **Xerxes** <note>Xerxes I, the Persian King who invaded Greece in 480 BC.</note>, because mention was partly made earlier in the first chapter of this third book regarding the army he led into Greece and how it was defeated, lest I make the reader weary.

Only this I cannot leave unmentioned: how Xerxes crossed the Hellespont <note>The narrow strait between Europe and Asia, now known as the Dardanelles.</note> with his army and intended to seize a pass, which was already occupied by the Greeks, even though they were very few in number compared to the great host of Xerxes. For there were no more than three hundred **Lacedaemonians** <note>Spartans.</note>, four hundred **Thebans**, and about three thousand men from other parts of Greece; and yet, before it came to the final battle, first the **Phocians**, then the others, except for the Lacedaemonians, Thebans, and **Thespians**, withdrew. Nevertheless, that small group struck down up to twenty thousand of Xerxes' men, and they themselves all perished there, save for two.

And one reads of no such battle in all the histories, except that the noble **Swiss**—at the time when the **Council of Basel** <note>Held between 1431 and 1449.</note> was held, and the Pope sent the **Dauphin of France** <note>The future King Louis XI.</note> into Germany with a large army of poor young nobles whom they called the "Jacks" <term>Jäken</term> <note>A nickname for the Armagnac mercenaries who invaded the region in 1444.</note>, who then committed great tyranny in Alsace—showed themselves courageous. For as they came before the city of Basel, three thousand Swiss set upon them and slew up to twenty thousand of the French; and the Swiss, though they held the field, for the most part perished as well. <note>This refers to the Battle of St. Jakob an der Birs in 1444.</note>

Initially, one reads of **Cyrus**, the King of the Assyrians <note>Historically the King of Persia, though early modern authors often conflated ancient Eastern empires.</note>, when he ventured to make war upon the **Scythians**: although he hit them hard at first, he was later paid back by **Queen Tomyris** in such a manner that she defeated him and his entire army decisively, striking them so that not even a messenger remained who could have reported this gruesome loss to his people. Secondly, when the **Locrians** and the **Crotoniates** <note>Inhabitants of Greek colonies in Southern Italy.</note> had come into intense enmity with one another, they took to the field against each other. The Locrians struck down up to one hundred and twenty thousand of their enemies, even though they had no more than fifteen thousand men on their own side.

Thirdly, it is found in the histories that when the King of Macedonia, **Alexander the Great**, fought several battles with King **Darius**, Alexander once struck down one hundred thousand foot soldiers and ten thousand horsemen belonging to Darius; at that time, Alexander lost no more than thirty-two foot soldiers and one hundred and fifty horses from his own side. On another occasion, Darius lost twenty thousand foot soldiers and two thousand horses by the River **Granicus**, while Alexander did not miss thirty-two persons from his army.

As far as the **Romans** are concerned, although they fought more fortunately than others and had many victories, it is nonetheless no small cause for wonder that **Fabius Aemilianus**, who was barely thirty thousand strong, struck down more than two hundred thousand Gauls <note>original: "Frantzosen." In this classical context, it refers to the Gallic tribes, specifically the Allobroges and Arverni at the Battle of the Isère River.</note> at one time, which battle took place by the River **Rhône**.

Similarly, they struck down more than fifty thousand men belonging to King **Antiochus**, and in contrast lost no more than twenty-four cavalrymen and three hundred foot soldiers. I will remain silent on how **Gaius Marius**, with a small force of soldiers, gallantly defeated a great heap of **Cimbri** and **Teutons** who had invaded Italy <note>original: "Welschland," a term historically used by Germans to refer to Italy or Latin-speaking lands.</note>.

When **Pompey the Great** attacked with his military might the proud king and evil tyrant **Mithridates**, who was the worst enemy of the Romans, forty thousand men were struck down; in contrast, Pompey lost no more than twenty men.

And what is even more, and almost unbelievable, one reads of the excellent Roman **Lucullus** that he marched against King **Tigranes**. And although he was barely a twentieth as strong as the enemy, he nevertheless slew over one hundred thousand of those enemies with his small force. And the histories say that everything went so fortunately on the Romans' side that not more than one hundred of them were wounded, and no more than five were killed. This is indeed something to wonder at in the highest degree: that such a great mass, such a vast multitude of people, should be defeated while one's own side takes so little damage. Therefore, **Alexander of Naples** <note>Alessandro d'Alessandro (1461–1523), a legal scholar and author of *Geniales Dies*.</note> says, no doubt out of amazement: *Such an extraordinary victory was gained at such a small cost.* <note>original Latin: "Tam paruo impendio tam insolens victoria stetit."</note> This means: with such minor damage was such a magnificent victory achieved. One would have enough work simply to destroy and strangle such an army, even if none of the enemies defended themselves but simply allowed themselves to be put to death.

Yet the Romans also occasionally made mistakes <note>original: "die schanck versehen," an idiom meaning to make a blunder or suffer a mishap.</note> and had to experience the adverse fortune of war just like others. Although the defeats they suffered at **Cannae** and **Lake Trasimene** <note>Two disastrous Roman defeats against Hannibal of Carthage during the Second Punic War.</note> are not so much to be wondered at,

# The Third Part

It is no wonder, since their opponent Hannibal attacked them with such a well-equipped and fresh army, and not only proved himself a soldier but also drove them to learn to be cautious and to take better care of their affairs. Yet, this is a great and notable loss: that **Lucius Baebius**, with all the army he led into **Spain**, was so completely destroyed when he strayed from the right path and was ambushed by the **Ligurians** in a forest, that the people of **Marseilles** <note>original: "Massilien"</note> had to report the news to the Romans.

In the same manner, the Romans were met by the **Cimbri** and **Teutones** before **Marius** overcame them; for they slaughtered up to eighty thousand Romans and their allies under **Gaius Manlius** and **Quintus Caepio**. And according to the histories, from such a magnificent host, both horse and foot, not more than ten men escaped.

To this also belongs the shameful defeat that the Romans encountered under **Claudius**. <note>The author likely refers to the Battle of the Caudine Forks (321 BC). While the primary consuls involved were Postumius and Veturius, the author may be citing a source attributing leadership differently or referring to a related engagement.</note> It is true that they were not slaughtered there, but only captured; yet through such imprisonment, into which they fell through lack of foresight, they came into the hands of the **Samnites** and were so surrounded and besieged that they could have all been strangled and killed—as would have soon happened, for the counsels of **Herennius** were partly directed toward that end. And because they were made to run through the yoke <note>original: "Galgen," literally "gallows," but here referring to the *sub iugum*, a humiliating ritual where defeated soldiers passed under a spear-gate.</note> stripped, half-naked, and without any weapons, and were thus shamefully sent back to Rome, this disgrace so affected their spirits that they would all have preferred to perish a thousand times in a free field battle, had it been possible. As **Titus Livius** <note>The Roman historian Livy.</note> has magnificently described these histories in Book 9 of *From the Founding of the City* <note>original: "ab urbe" [condita].</note>. And many more such examples could be brought forth and cited here, but it is proper for me, as in other matters, to observe moderation and not overwhelm the reader.

These examples, however, remind **Princes and Lords** that they should not rely too much on their own power, nor despise their enemies, even if they are few, but should keep their affairs in good care; and also remember that war depends more on fortune and to whom God wishes to grant victory, than on great might. For this reason, **Livy** also says: *Often even a despised enemy has produced a bloody struggle, and famous peoples and kings have been defeated and overcome with very little effort.* <note>original Latin: "Sæpe etiam contemptus hostis cruentum certamen edidit, & inclyti populi, regesq; perleui momento, victi sunt."</note> This means: A despised enemy has often caused a bloody war, and great kings and nations have been slain and conquered with slight effort; and **Homer** says of the uncertain outcome of war:

> For victory is doubtful for men, and does not remain in a fixed turn; it is now flattering to one, now grim to the same man. <note>original Latin: "Namq; viris dubia est victoria nec vice recta Constat, & est nunc blanda vni nunc tristis eidem."</note>

->And shortly thereafter:<-

> That the coming victory should bring earned praise lies in the hands [of the gods] and in the equal will of the divine. <note>original Latin: "Qui meritam ventura ferat victoria laudem In manibus positum est & in æquo numine diuum."</note>

# On Fortresses: That One Should Not
## Trust Too Much in Them

### The Ninth Chapter

No one should assume that I would venture to advise a Prince or Lord against having or building any fortresses in his cities or lands, for that is not my intention. Rather, my point is that those who possess fortresses should not rely upon them too heavily. For no fortress is so large, well-protected, or well-equipped that it cannot be surrendered or conquered through treachery or a long-lasting siege. For this reason, King Philip of Macedon <note>Philip II (382–336 BC), father of Alexander the Great.</note> says, as Cicero writes: "All fortresses can be captured, provided a donkey laden with gold can climb into them." <note>original: "Omnia castella expugnari posse, in quæ modo asellus onustus auro possit ascendere."</note> This means there was no castle so firm that he could not conquer it, if only he could get a donkey carrying gold inside. Therefore, the aforementioned Cicero rightly says elsewhere: "Nothing is so sacred that it cannot be violated, and nothing so fortified that it cannot be conquered with money." <note>original: "Nihil esse tam sanctum, quod non violari, nihil tam munitum, quod non expugnari pecunia possit."</note>

<margin>Oracle of Apollo</margin> Even the *Oracle of the Pythian Apollo* <note>The famous oracle at Delphi.</note> reports on this: "If you fight with silver arrows, you will overcome all things." <note>original: "Argenti pugnatelis atq; omnia vinces." This refers to using bribes (silver) as a weapon.</note> And tell me: was not Jerusalem a fortified city? Where is it now? Tell me further: was not Babylon a fortified city? What did it help? Was it not conquered regardless? So that the reader might see how things stood with that city, I will omit its description for the sake of brevity, as it cannot be fully described in few words.

<margin>Description of Babylon</margin> But whoever wishes to, let him read Strabo, book 16 of his *Geography*. And in book 15, he says that Alexander the Great favored this city above all others. Thus Pliny and Solinus call it "The capital of the Chaldean peoples," <note>original: "Chaldaicarum gentium caput."</note> which was prized above others in the entire world, and because of which Mesopotamia and Assyria were called Babylonia. Therefore Mela says: "Babylon, a city of wondrous size." <note>original: "Babylon urbs miræ magnitudinis."</note> Aristotle agrees with this when he says that when Babylon was conquered and taken, the citizens in certain parts of the city did not know or learn of it for three days. See more on this in Justin, book 1; Valerius, book 9, chapter 3; Orosius, book 1, chapter 4, and book 2, chapter 9; Herodotus, book 1; and Gellius, book 8, chapters 11 and 12. I will therefore briefly recount the story of how it was won. When Cyrus died in Scythia, many lands fell away from him, among which was the city of Babylon; however, it was reconquered by Darius, the son of Cambyses, in the following manner.

### The Third Part

...his son, named Zopyrus; this same man cut off his own ears and nose and informed King Darius <note>Darius the Great (r. 522–486 BC), King of the Persian Achaemenid Empire.</note> of what he intended and planned to do. He then came, all bloody, before the city of Babylon and acted as if he were enraged, claiming that the King had mutilated him so disgracefully because he had advised that they should abandon the siege of the city. He therefore sought protection within Babylon, declaring that for this reason, he had become the King's enemy. The Babylonians believed Zopyrus, and as a besieged people, they welcomed him gladly so that they might have a leader. Zopyrus even struck down several "lost hope" <note>A term for expendable or vanguard troops (German: *verlorne hauffen*).</note> units of Darius's army, so that the Babylonians would trust him all the more; however, it was all a staged deception. For once Zopyrus had been made captain by the Babylonians and held power over the city, he let Darius in, after the King had lain before it for a full year and six months—and perhaps would have had to lie there even longer, or retreat in shame, had Zopyrus not done this. Since the Babylonians were well-armed for war with provisions and all necessities, and the fortress, as mentioned, did not fail them. And Herodotus <note>The Greek historian known as the "Father of History."</note> writes that they even hanged the majority of their women—except for those they absolutely needed for washing and baking—so that they would not have to maintain and feed many useless people during the time of the siege.

Of this Zopyrus, King Darius often said he would rather have one upright Zopyrus than capture or conquer a hundred Babylons. Babylon, as briefly mentioned, was an exceptionally rich city, yet the King valued a loyal friend higher than a hundred Babylons. "O," says Erasmus, <note>Desiderius Erasmus (1466–1536), the famous Dutch humanist and scholar.</note> "how lacking in such spirit are certain princes, who often value a jester, a horse, or a dog higher than a pious, loyal, and learned friend." And to say nothing of other examples, we have seen in recent years how many fortresses in German lands were won, conquered, surrendered, and yielded one after another.

For this reason, the Germans also say: "He who has a beautiful wife and a strong house must guard them with great diligence and pay close attention." By this, they mean to indicate that fortresses can easily be lost through treachery and negligence, as experience demonstrates. Therefore, it is said of Archbishop Ernst of Magdeburg <note>Ernst of Saxony (1464–1513), Archbishop of Magdeburg.</note>—who was a born Prince of Saxony—that he said there was no better fortress or wall than for one to have many of his neighbors as friends.

> *For to protect the wealth of a Prince, nothing is more suitable than the goodwill of his subjects. These are the firmest defenses, these the impregnable citadels. And (as Cyrus says in Xenophon) <note>Xenophon (c. 430–354 BC), a Greek historian and student of Socrates; Cyrus refers to Cyrus the Great.</note> It is not a golden scepter that preserves a kingdom. But many friends are the truest and most secure scepter for Kings. Dionysius the Tyrant <note>Dionysius I of Syracuse (c. 432–367 BC), known for his harsh rule.</note> used to say that "adamantine bonds" <note>A poetic term for unbreakable chains.</note> are fear, violence, the fleet, and ten thousand armed men. But who does not see that goodwill, justice, beneficence, and clemency both are, and ought to be called, the truer adamantine bonds?* <note>original: "Ad opes enim Principis tuendas, nihil aptius beneuolentia subditorum. Hæc sunt munimenta firmissima, hæ arces inexpugnabiles. Et (vt ait Cyrus apud Xenophontem) Non est aureum sceptrum, quod regnum seruet. Sed amici multi sceptrum sunt Regibus verissimum, maximeq; securum. Dicere solebat Dionysius Tyrannus, Vincula adamantina esse metum, violentiam, classem, & decem millia armatorum. Sed quis non videt magis vincula adamantina, & esse & dici debere beneuolentia, iustitiam, beneficentiam, atq; clementiam?"</note>

To protect a Prince’s property, nothing is better than obedient, loyal subjects; they are the true fortresses. And (as Cyrus says in Xenophon)

(Xeno)phon) <note>original: "phonte" — the end of the name Xenophon, the Greek historian and philosopher.</note> A golden scepter does not protect a kingdom; rather, friends are the true and safest scepter. Dionysius the Tyrant <note>Dionysius I of Syracuse (c. 432–367 BC), a ruler famous for his military innovations and his profound paranoia regarding assassination.</note> once said that fear is a good piece of ship-equipment <note>original: "Schiffrüstung" — likely used here metaphorically to mean a necessary provision or defense for the state.</note>, and that ten thousand mercenaries <note>original: "Landsknecht" — the specialized infantry of the late 15th and 16th centuries.</note> were a strong bond. But who does not see that kindness and justice are much more enduring and firm?

The wise King Alfonso <note>Alfonso V of Aragon (1396–1458), known as "the Magnanimous," who was celebrated as a model of the Renaissance prince.</note> also confirmed this. When he was once walking alone without any servants, he was rebuked and exhorted by certain flatterers: *that, after the manner of other Princes, he too should walk surrounded by a band of armed men.* <note>original: "Vt more aliorum Principum, & ipse armatorum manu stipatus graderetur."</note>

That is to say: that like others, when he went out, he should make arrangements to have a crowd of guards <note>original: "Trabanten" — refers to the life-guards or halberdiers of a prince.</note> around him, and not move about so alone. He answered them in a truly royal and wise manner: *that they should by no means believe him to be alone, but that he traveled accompanied by innocence; nor was there any reason to fear anything while relying on the goodwill of the citizens.* <note>original: "Se quidem minimè solum vt istum crederent, sed innocentia associatum vadere, neque esse quòd beneuolentia ciuium fretus, quippiam extimescat."</note> And in another place he says: *Those whom you have subdued by terror through severity and cruelty, it is necessary that you always fear; but those whom your own piety and mercy have won over to you, you shall find forever faithful.* <note>original: "Quos sæuitia, & crudelitate territos subegeris, vt metuas semper necesse est, quos autem tua tibi pietas misericordiaq; conciliauerit, perpetuò fidos inuenias."</note> This means: He was not alone, as they thought, but had innocence with him; and since he expected nothing but good from his subjects, he need not be anxious before them. And elsewhere he says, what is forced by violence and tyranny must be dreaded; but what one obtains through kindness, there one finds loyalty, and need not worry about it.

Furthermore, such fortresses often give Princes a reason for war, which they might otherwise avoid; and thereafter, those who live around the fortress are in very great danger and must suffer much when a castle or city is besieged. For there everything is devastated, plundered, burned, and killed; meadows, fields, gardens, and vineyards are laid waste. Indeed, even the fish in the ponds cannot remain in peace, so that some people are afraid to settle near a fortress. As has been seen in these past years at the old city of Magdeburg <note>Referring to the Siege of Magdeburg (1550–1551) during the Schmalkaldic War, which left the surrounding area devastated.</note>, how everything all around was ruined, burned, and torn apart. And although it is known to everyone that it is a strong city, it was to be feared that it would have been leveled to the ground, had the noble House of Saxony <note>Refers to Maurice, Elector of Saxony, who negotiated the city's surrender on relatively lenient terms.</note> not acted and moved the Emperor's heart to kindness.

And this is more honorable and glorious for His Imperial Majesty and the House of Saxony than if they had let the city go to ruins, razed it to the ground, plundered it, and let everyone inside be stabbed to death. This is because so many innocent people would have had to suffer with the rest, such as women, children, and the old and weak. For it is said that in Magdeburg there were up to forty-two thousand people who did not serve in the war, all of whom would have had to suffer—regardless of their innocence—even if those of Magdeburg had actually committed some offense.

Thus Bartolus <note>Bartolus de Saxoferrato (1313–1357), one of the most famous jurists of the Middle Ages.</note> also writes that Emperor Henry <note>Likely Holy Roman Emperor Henry VII, who besieged Brescia (Brixien) in 1311.</note> condemned the city of Brescia *to the plow* <note>original: "ad aratrum condemniert" — a symbolic punishment where a city is razed and a plow is run over its site to signify total destruction.</note>, but out of mercy he undoubtedly retracted that sentence for such reasons. Therefore, those people should

...to watch out, those who have fortifications, that they do not place too much trust in them; for it was perhaps better when there were not many fortifications, while there was peace. > When towns stood surrounded by ruined walls,

> Now you lack courage, now of your own accord you reach out
> Your helpless hands to all weak enemies.

> So do your walls surrounded by ditches help you.

> Because once among the Germans,
> There was no danger before rampart and ditch.
> And the walls were quite slight,
> No fortifications were seen at all.
> In cities and in the countryside,
> As they are now known.
> Then the German nation was
> Already widely renowned for manliness. <note>original: "Mannheit" — in this context, it implies both physical courage and the moral virtue of a warrior.</note>
> So that they were safe from foreigners,
> And traveled into other lands.
> Since now, however, everywhere,
> In walls, ditches, and ramparts,
> There is no lack, we are discouraged,
> As soon as we are hunted out of the fortification.
> And we let foreigners move in;
> God knows if we are still Germans.

# That one should not easily
## enter into alliances.
### The Tenth Chapter.

Although it is an ancient custom <note>original: "alt herkommen" — a traditional practice or established precedent.</note> that people have made alliances and unions with one another, of which the Scripture also makes mention, as will be heard; yet there is no small danger in it if these same alliances are not kept faithfully and with earnestness, and one person leaves the other in the lurch.

### Of the Book of Rulers.

On the other hand, however, it is a notable comfort to those in the aforementioned distress when they have faithful allies. We wish to examine the examples from history regarding both of these, one after the other, in this chapter.

But before I come to the histories, I must here show the reader that it is neither un-Christian nor evil to make alliances <note>The German word *Bündniß* refers to both political treaties and religious covenants, blurring the line between diplomacy and faith.</note>, provided that one uses them rightly. > Behold, the time is coming, says the LORD, when I will make a new covenant with the house of Israel and with the house of Judah; not like the covenant that I made with their fathers on the day when I took them by the hand and led them out of the land of Egypt, which covenant they did not keep, and I had to compel them, says the LORD. But this shall be the covenant that I will make with the house of Israel after that time, says the LORD: I will put my law in their hearts and write it in their minds; and they shall be my people, and I will be their God. And no longer shall each one teach his neighbor and say, "Know the LORD," for they shall all know me, from the least to the greatest, says the LORD. For I will forgive their iniquity and remember their sin no more.

Secondly, God has also made alliances with specific individuals. For it is thus written in the 17th chapter of Genesis, how God made a covenant with Abraham, where the Scripture says:

> When Abram was ninety-nine years old, the LORD appeared to him and said to him: I am the Almighty God; walk before me and be blameless. You shall circumcise the foreskin of your flesh, etc. Thus shall my covenant be in your flesh as an eternal covenant.

### The Third Part

...come into his father’s house. And Jonathan and David made a covenant with one another, etc.

And just as it is useful and good, and carries no danger, when we make a covenant with God—because God is faithful and righteous, and holds firmly and truly to that which he has once promised and vowed, as the Scripture clearly shows—it is, conversely, entirely perilous to enter into alliances with people. This is especially true if one does not find faithful allies, or if they are faithful, they allow themselves to be separated through some means and set apart from one another. As Philippe de Commines <note>original: "Philippus Comineus" — Philippe de Commines (1447–1511) was a diplomat and chronicler for the French court, famous for his analytical memoirs on the politics of his day.</note>, who was mentioned before, writes with these beautiful and excellent words: *For whenever those who are joined by a treaty create a separation and allow themselves to be scattered, it can no longer be doubted that they will all gradually suffer some disaster; and this pertains as much to Princes as to cities. And since there are many proofs of this matter, there is no need for a longer discourse.* <note>original Latin: "Quoties enim illi, qui foedere coniuncti sunt, secessio-nem faciunt, & se dissipari patiuntur, dubitari amplius non debet, quin paulatim omnes cladem aliquā accipiant, idque pertinet tàm ad Principes, quàm ad ciuitates. Et quoni-am eius rei plurima extant documenta, longiori sermone nihil est opus."</note> That is to say: As soon as those who have been together in an understanding allow themselves to be sundered and separated again, they have nothing more certain to expect than that they must suffer harm and fall into misery and distress, whether they be Princes or cities. And since enough examples are before our eyes, there is no need to make a long chatter about it. And he also provides an example of two cities situated on the Mosa <note>The Meuse River, which flows through parts of modern-day France, Belgium, and the Netherlands.</note>, which also had an understanding and union with each other. But as soon as they were separated, and one of them came to terms with Duke Philip of Burgundy, they went to ruin.

How it went for the Saguntines <note>The inhabitants of Saguntum, an ancient city in Spain whose siege by Hannibal sparked the Second Punic War.</note> with their allies, the Romans, and what a miserable harm they had to suffer from Hannibal because of it, is described at length by Livy <note>Titus Livius, the Roman historian.</note>. And although the Romans, as honest and brave people, used no falseness or unfaithfulness toward them, but rather the time was otherwise too short for them to be able to help, they nevertheless fell into danger and extreme distress on their account. However, the delay was primarily caused by the fact that the Saguntines were far distant from the Romans, being in Hispania <note>Spain</note>.

Secondly, the Saguntines first sent their message and envoys to Rome, seeking and praying for help against Hannibal. But when the Romans heard these same legates and deliberated on the matter, they resolved to send an embassy back to Spain, which was to inquire specifically how things stood with the Saguntines, as well as the entire war, and likewise regarding Hannibal, as a new enemy and military captain. This was with the instruction that these same legates should not only have the command to address Hannibal and report to him on behalf of the Council that he should leave their allies unburdened and in peace, but also, should necessity require it, to sail on to Africa and complain about Hannibal to the Carthaginians. In the meantime, however, and while these things were being handled—and even before these same resolutions were put into effect—one message after another from the Saguntines reached the Senate in Rome, by which they were not a little dismayed, in

# That one must faithfully keep Alliances, Oaths, and
## Vows; and that God is vehemently opposed to Unfaithfulness and Failure to keep them, and therefore will not leave them unpunished.

### The Eleventh Chapter.

Just as one sees that people sometimes fall into such a state and develop such wide consciences <note>A "wide conscience" (German: *weite Gewissen*) is a historical idiom for a lax or flexible moral compass, describing someone who easily justifies breaking their word.</note> that they pay little heed to their oaths and vows, so too does history show that such things occurred in ancient times. However, these same histories also show that God takes special displeasure in such unfaithfulness and the failure to keep one’s word, and for that reason, He will not leave them unpunished. I will relate a powerful example of this which occurred among the **Greeks**. It is an example that all those who do not shrink from acting against law and equity, or against their oaths and duties, should take to heart and be terrified by; it occurred in the following manner:

After the **Lacedemonians** <note>The Lacedemonians are better known today as the Spartans, the famously disciplined and warlike citizens of the city-state of Sparta.</note> had risen to such heights in **Greece**, and had come into such prosperity that they were far superior in power and might to the other cities, and no one dared to oppose or rebel against them, it happened unexpectedly that they were finally subdued, conquered, and humbled by the **Thebans**, whom they had very heavily oppressed and burdened while under their servitude. It is considered and held that this change and unexpected downfall was caused by the following:

The **Lacedemonians** had pledged and bound themselves to the other **Greek** cities with an oath, that they would [grant] to none of the other cities...

He argued that because the **Peloponnesians** were the true Greeks and the **Arcadians** alone were native-born to the **Peloponnese**—while all others were merely newcomers—they were in no way comparable to the **Arcadians**. It was also well known how bravely and powerfully the **Arcadians** were accustomed to conduct themselves in war. Therefore, he argued it would be in no way feasible or advisable for them to look to other cities or peoples for leadership, particularly regarding how the **Lacedemonians** might be suppressed or the **Thebans** elevated. Much less should they be helpful or serviceable to either side; instead, it would befit them to look to their own advantage.

He further argued that although the **Lacedemonians**, as well as the **Thebans**, might have been seen as somewhat powerful, they were never in such a position of power that the **Lacedemonians** would have dared to march into the **Athenian** region, or the **Thebans** into the **Peloponnese**, without the help of the **Arcadians**. And because the **Arcadians** had not considered this, but instead had helped and strengthened the **Lacedemonians** with their power, they had accomplished nothing other than letting the **Lacedemonians** grow "over their heads," so that they must now be warred against by them. This would certainly also happen to them from the **Thebans** in time, should they increase and progress in such power.

When the **Arcadians** heard this, it pleased them, and they immediately took heart; they also showed **Lycomedes** such honor as had never before been shown to anyone. They followed his advice, completely abandoned the **Thebans**, and considered for themselves how they might obtain the upper hand in **Greece**. When the **Thebans** noticed this, they want[ed]...

### The Third Part

...they did not trust them any further, from which it followed that they could not wage the war as grandly as had been done until then.

The same thing occurred when several cities in the **Peloponnese** <note>The southern peninsula of Greece.</note> grew into discord with the **Arcadians**, because they wished to elevate and assert themselves in such a manner—principally the **Eleans** and **Messenians**, who until now had held a defense and alliance with them.

**Lycomedes** <note>An Arcadian statesman who sought to increase Arcadian independence from both Sparta and Thebes.</note> also persuaded the **Arcadians** that they should make an alliance with the **Athenians**. But as he was sent there on a legation and had concluded that same alliance with those of **Athens**, and wished to travel home again, he was strangled on the way by exiled citizens. However, the established alliance remained, which nonetheless awakened a great displeasure in the **Athenians**. Namely, the **Corinthians**, who previously had been in union with the **Lacedemonians** <note>Spartans</note> and **Athenians**, conceived a suspicion because of this and therefore joined the **Thebans**. In like manner, **Epaminondas** <note>The famous Theban general and statesman.</note> applied himself to preventing the **Achaeans** <note>original: "Acheer"</note>—who at that time were held in great prestige—from assisting [the enemies of] the **Thebans**. He therefore set out and took those same cities and brought them under the power of the **Thebans**, which would have been very beneficial to them if they had kept those cities.

But it happened that the captains and governors whom those of **Thebes** had sent into those same cities drew the **common rabble** <note>original: "Gemeinen Pöfel"</note> to themselves against the nobility and the powerful. They thus incited mutiny between them, because of which those same cities were caused to defect from the **Thebans** again and to betake themselves to the **Lacedemonians**. In the meantime, it also happened that the **Eleans** were at odds with the **Arcadians** because they would not give back their cities; thus they also defected from the **Thebans** to the **Lacedemonians**, from which a strange and wondrous disruption and change followed between the cities. For those of **Thebes** and **Athens** stood with the **Arcadians** against the **Eleans**, regardless of whether they were enemies with one another; likewise, the **Lacedemonians** stood by the **Eleans**, though they were otherwise in union with those of **Athens**.

The war was also fiercely undertaken by all parties: first for **Cromnum**, then at **Olympia**. For the **Arcadians** retook **Cromnum**, which the **Eleans** had forced from them shortly before. Subsequently, they marched toward **Olympia** at the very time when the **five-year games** <note>The ancient Olympic Games.</note>—with racing, tilting, running, fencing, and other such **knightly games** <note>original: "Ritterspielen"; the author uses 16th-century terminology to describe ancient Greek athletic contests.</note>—were to be prepared and held; they drove the **Eleans** away and occupied the **Temple of Jove** <note>original: "Tempel Jouis"; the Temple of Zeus.</note>. The knightly games then had to be held and distributed according to their pleasure.

Now when the time came that the games were to begin, the **Eleans**, together with their allies, armed themselves as strongly as they ever could, intending to drive the **Arcadians** out again and to reconquer the temple, which they had occupied against right and with vain force; and this they indeed did. For when the games were at their height, they marched forth, and the **Arcadians** came against them by a water called **Cladaum** <note>The Cladaus River.</note>, where they then...

He therefore proceeded to seize the envoys in the middle of a banquet where they were gathered and threw them into prison; he especially would have liked to have the **Mantineans**, but they had already ridden away. 

And after they learned what the captain at **Tegea** had undertaken against the envoys, they wrote of it to the other cities with an exhortation that they should arm themselves; they also had it sternly signaled to the captain that he should not judge or allow any of the prisoners to be killed, as they first wanted to know what the cause was and why they were detained. And if they were found to be at fault, they would not leave them unpunished, etc. They also indicated to him that all **Arcadia** was in arms and would not allow their people to be shamed and violated in such a manner.

When the captain heard this, and being uneasy in his mind, he released the prisoners. Therefore, he had to keep a sharp eye on the fortification and take the envoys into custody until he could inquire into the matter and see how things stood, whether there was anything to it or not. ...occurred; however, they had not yet dissolved the alliance with the **Thebans** thereby, but only sent word to those of **Thebes**, and through their **envoys** <note>original: "Oratores"; refers to diplomatic representatives or ambassadors</note> lodged a complaint against the captain, indicating that he should rightly be punished, since he had presumed to do that which was not his place to do.

Now, **Epaminondas** <note>A celebrated Theban general and statesman known for transforming Thebes into a leading Greek power</note> was at that time at the head of the government in **Thebes**, and after he had heard the **Arcadian** envoys, he immediately gave an inept and unfriendly answer: namely, that the **Tegean** captain had not sinned or trespassed so greatly by taking the envoys prisoner as he had by releasing them again. "For since we" (he said) "are engaged in war on your behalf, it has certainly not happened by chance—and it looks not unlike treachery—that you make alliances behind our backs and leave us stuck in the war. Therefore, you may go your way; we shall not be far from you, and alongside our allies, we will know how to seek you out at home and teach you how you ought to make treaties and peace without our consent."

When this speech was recounted in the common council and assembly of the **Arcadians**, the **Mantinaeans** and other cities of the **Arcadians** defected from **Thebes** and sent their envoys to the **Lacedaemonians** <note>The Spartans</note>, making peace and an alliance with them, with the condition and agreement that when the war was conducted in **Arcadia**, it should be done so by the **Arcadians**; but if it were conducted in the territory of the **Lacedaemonians**, the **Lacedaemonians** might also be the army leaders. They also immediately incited the **Eleans** and **Achaeans** against **Thebes**, with the report that it was well-noted that the **Thebans** sought nothing other than that the cities in the **Peloponnese** should war against and weaken one another, so that they might thereafter the more easily overpower them and bring them under their control.

While this was being negotiated in the **Peloponnese**, **Epaminondas** was elected by the **Thebans** as the war-captain; he then equipped himself magnificently, was tireless, and drilled the troops he had mustered at home. He also received help from **Thessaly**, **Euboea**, and **Boeotia**, with whom he marched in great haste into **Nemea**. However, he lay still there for some time for the reason that he intended to encounter and strike those of **Athen**, who were coming to the aid of the **Lacedaemonians**, before they could join the main force. But when the **Athenians** decided to reach the **Lacedaemonians** by sea, and **Epaminondas** learned of this, he broke camp in **Nemea** and moved with all his troops toward **Tegea**, and encamped with them within the city. This was useful to him, as he not only lay more securely than in the field, but also because the enemy could learn less of what designs he was making, how he had prepared for war, and how strong he was, etc. Thus **Epaminondas** waited in **Tegea** until he might see his advantage, sending out his intelligence-gatherers everywhere to the enemies' camps, which then lay not far from him; therefore, he also hoped that it should soon come to a battle.

In the meantime, **Agesilaus** <note>The aging but experienced King of Sparta</note> was called upon and requested by the **Lacedaemonians** to allow himself to be used as a captain over their troops that lay at **Mantinea** against those of **Thebes**; he allowed himself to be persuaded to this, and took

They showed themselves joyful and quite willing, and each prepared what was necessary for him: one polished his helmet, another his sword, the third his spearhead, another the bridle and other gear for the horses, all of which **Epaminondas** himself inspected with diligence.

When everyone was ready, **Epaminondas** commanded the soldiers to eat, and then marched out of the city into the field with them—not directly toward the enemies, but leaving them on the right hand, and took another path across a plain until he reached a mountain. There he commanded his soldiers to stand still and lay down their weapons. To the enemies, this had the appearance as if **Epaminondas** intended to strike camp there, not that he intended to fight soon. But in the meantime, he most diligently and skillfully prepared his **battle order** <note>original: "Schlachtordnung"</note>. The other groups were arranged more for appearance than for necessity, among which he assigned one against the **Athenians** (who had pitched their camp separately) so that they might not be attacked from behind. Of the Regent's Book.

# That one should not covet another’s 
### government, land, and people.

## The Twelfth Chapter.

SINCE it is a common custom in all the world, but especially among rulers, that one always has an eye on another and would gladly force from him what is his, or at times even displace him entirely—as *Julius Caesar* <note>Gaius Julius Caesar (100–44 BC), the Roman general whose rise to power effectively ended the Roman Republic</note> did—*Marcus Cicero* <note>The Roman statesman and philosopher known for his writings on duty and governance</note> admonishes with the greatest diligence that rulers should take care not to let such thoughts deceive them or lead them into error. Even though *Lucan* <note>A Roman poet who wrote about the civil war between Caesar and Pompey</note> says:

> There is no faith between partners in a kingdom, and all power 
> is impatient of a companion. <note>original: "Nulla fides regni socijs omnisq; potestas Impatiens confortis erat."</note>

Likewise, the poet *Ennius* <note>An early Roman writer often called the "father of Roman poetry"</note> said: "That no partnership is sacred." <note>original: "Quòd nulla societas sit sancta."</note> This is to be understood especially regarding rulers and great potentates, for ambition usually runs alongside them, which ensures that no one can, with good will, endure or tolerate another beside himself. Here someone might say: "You promised at the beginning that you would bring historical accounts to market; I see well that you are running short at the last, and now you come dragging in the poets?" To this I give this answer: Although the poets are also not to be rejected and contain many good teachings—as appears from *Homer* and many others—I could still cite enough histories regarding this matter.

So that I do not use many vain words, however, and to bring forth a history, *Livy* <note>Titus Livius, the Roman historian who wrote a monumental history of Rome</note> writes: After the two brothers *Romulus* and *Remus* had come to their years, and were so informed that they were not the children of a lowly shepherd, as they first believed, but were born of noble and royal stock, they also wished to establish a particular government and kingdom, and began to build a great city. They could not, however, agree with one another for long regarding the government.

And after they came to discord over this, *Remus* was slain by his brother. And although *Romulus* put forward other reasons—such as that he had supposedly jumped over the city wall, etc., and had therefore forfeited his life—it is nevertheless commonly held that it was done so that he might keep the government for himself alone. Therefore *Lucan* also speaks further:

> Lest examples be drawn from too far afield, 
> the walls first grew wet with a brother’s blood. <note>original: "Ne longius exempla trahuntur Fraterno primùm maduerunt sanguine muri."</note>

This was also the reason that the war arose between *Pompey* <note>Pompey the Great, Caesar's former ally and later rival</note> and *Emperor Julius*; for *Caesar* would not suffer that anyone should rule over him

## covet another’s government, land, and people.

### The Twelfth Chapter.

SINCE it is a common practice in all the world, but especially among rulers, that one always has an eye on another and would gladly force them out of what is theirs, or sometimes even suppress them entirely—as Julius Caesar did—Marcus Cicero admonishes with the greatest diligence that rulers should take great care. They must not let such thoughts deceive them or lead them into transgression. For as Lucan says:

->No trust exists between partners in power, and all sovereignty<-
->is impatient of a sharer.<-
<note>original Latin: "Nulla fides regni socijs omnisq; potestas / Impatiens consortis erat." from Lucan's Pharsalia, an epic poem about the Roman Civil War.</note>

The poet Ennius also said: "No fellowship is holy." <note>original Latin: "Quòd nulla societas sit sancta."</note> This means: one finds no partnership that is entirely pure or sacred, which is to be understood especially regarding rulers and great potentates. For in such circles, ambition <term>Ehrgeitz</term> <note>literally "honor-greed"; an excessive or toxic desire for status and power</note> usually creeps in, which ensures that no one can kindly tolerate or endure another beside him. Here someone might say: "You promised at the beginning that you would bring histories to market <note>an idiom meaning to provide historical evidence or examples</note>; I see well that you will lack them in the end, and now you come dragging in the poets?" To this I give this answer: although the poets are not to be rejected and contain much good teaching within them—as is evident from Homer and many others—I could nevertheless also cite enough histories for this purpose.

To the end that I do not waste many words and may bring forth a history, Livy writes: After the two brothers Romulus and Remus came of age and were informed that they were not the children of a simple shepherd (as they first thought) but were born of noble and royal stock, they wanted to establish their own government and kingdom and began to build a great city. However, they could not agree with one another for long regarding the government.

And after they came to discord over this, Remus was slain by his brother. Although Romulus pretended other reasons—such as that Remus had jumped over the city wall and had therefore forfeited his life—it is nevertheless commonly held that it was done so that he might keep the government for himself alone. Therefore Lucan says further:

->Lest examples be sought further afield,<-
->the walls first grew wet with a brother’s blood.<-
<note>original Latin: "Ne longius exempla trahuntur / Fraterno primùm maduerunt sanguine muri." This refers to the fratricide that founded Rome.</note>

This was also the reason that the war arose between Pompey and Emperor Julius; for Caesar would not suffer that anyone should rule over him—

<header>The Third Part</header>

...should rule, so Pompey could tolerate no one who was his equal, which amounted to the same thing. And Emperor Julius Caesar had such a desire to rule, as Suetonius <note>Gaius Suetonius Tranquillus, a Roman historian famous for his biographies of the first twelve Roman rulers.</note> writes, that he often let it be heard that it would be harder for him if he had held the first and highest position in government and were now to receive the second, than if he had the second and were to become the very last. And as he traveled to Spain and passed by a small little spot <note>original: "Flecklein," meaning a tiny, insignificant village.</note>, someone began and asked whether people also crowded for power in such a little spot as they did in Rome? Then Julius Caesar answered: He would rather be the first there than the second in Rome.

It has now come to the point that almost all great lords are more inclined toward war than peace. For this reason, they also deliberate about it more and more often. The lords' advisors are also well-trained in this; when they come onto the track with such deliberations, they arrange their votes <note>original: "Suffragia," meaning formal expressions of opinion or support in a council.</note> accordingly, giving their approval, and devising all sorts of tricks and schemes through which the matter might proceed. In one place, they advise that an alliance should be made, and yet the same should not be held longer than it is necessary or convenient; thereafter one may easily find a reason to untangle oneself from it again. In the second place, that people should be bribed with money. In the third, to make the most prominent advisors of the opposing side defect and draw them to oneself. In the fourth, that one should commission horsemen and foot-soldiers.

<margin>Utopia.</margin>
It is also put to deliberation whether one might not make promises to some through marriage, so that all things are prepared, everything provided for, and nothing left behind. Such advisors then believe they have come to court with great favor for the lord and advised him for the best, yet they achieve nothing else by it but putting the lord, along with his land and people, in danger of life and limb. And even if it turns out for the best that one man displaces another, he has no other gain from it than that he must have more worry, anxiety, toil, and labor, and additionally a worse conscience than he had before. For this reason, those on the island of Utopia, as Thomas More <note>Sir Thomas More (1478–1535), the English statesman and author of "Utopia," which describes an ideal society.</note> writes, are praised, who—when another kingdom had fallen to their king by inheritance long ago, and they not only had to win it for him but also maintain it—perceived that they had less money, peace, and quiet alongside their king than before. They gave the king the choice to select one of the two realms and let the other go. For when the king was in one place, rebellion and discord arose in the other; in the other place, enemies invaded, plundering villages and towns. From this followed that one had to keep soldiers perpetually, for which an immense amount of money is required. And where it goes thus, people become accustomed to robbery, harassment, murder, and theft, which they could not tolerate. Nor did they wish to be ruled by a "half-king," as they explained it, and said: No village community would gladly accept a shepherd who had a herd of cattle to guard or protect in another village. Therefore, the good king also had to let the other kingdom go and be satisfied with the previous one.

# That a Prince or Lord, in
## great and important matters, and especially in
### wartime affairs, should not listen to one advisor alone, but
### rather hear as many as he can have.

---

->The Thirteenth Chapter.<-

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'P' featuring elaborate foliate and scrollwork designs.</image-desc>
Philippe de Commines <note>original: "Philippus Comineus"; a celebrated diplomat and chronicler whose memoirs provide a detailed account of the lives of the Dukes of Burgundy and King Louis XI of France.</note>, an excellent man and a French historian, has written that when the people of Liège <note>original: "Leodienser"; inhabitants of the city-state of Liège who were frequently in revolt against Burgundian rule.</note>—who at that time were allied with the French—invaded the lands of Duke Philip of Burgundy and caused great damage, which occurred around the year 1466. Because Duke Philip was an old man and no longer capable of waging war, he commanded his son, Duke Charles <note>Charles the Bold, the last Valois Duke of Burgundy.</note>, to march against them and punish them. Accordingly, Duke Charles prepared himself and besieged the city with a powerful army. Now, when the people of Liège learned of this, they soon became faint-hearted and despondent, unable to endure the siege. They therefore sent word to Duke Charles, pleading for a truce, and sent him several hostages <term>original: "Gysel"; individuals held as security to ensure that the terms of a treaty or agreement are honored.</term> or sureties, with the understanding that if they did not keep the agreed-upon truce, he might deal with the hostages as he pleased. But despite this, they rebelled again shortly thereafter, broke the peace agreement, and intended to defend themselves against the Duke. Because of this, the Duke was moved to great anger against the city and held a council regarding how he should deal with the hostages. The advisors were divided in their opinions. One, named Contcus (who was a fine, well-mannered, clever, and sensible man, and otherwise quite kind), was the first the Duke questioned; he wanted all the hostages to be hanged immediately. But the other, named Imbercortus <note>Jean de Brimeu, Lord of Himbercourt, a loyal and influential advisor to the Burgundian dukes.</note>, advised that the Duke should, above all things, be careful and take heed that he did not anger God with such a cruel undertaking. Instead, he should conduct himself in this matter in such a way that people might recognize and feel that he was more inclined toward goodness than toward cruelty and tyranny, and was not bloodthirsty. Therefore, his opinion was that the Duke should set the hostages free, because these good people had never hoped or intended anything other than that their Lords and superiors would keep faith, just as they had promised and for which they had been given as security.

For if they had perceived or known that their Lords would turn back and would not keep faith, they would undoubtedly not have allowed themselves to be used as hostages; they had therefore fallen into such a burden and distress because of the guilt and treachery of others. However, when they were sent away, they should be strictly forbidden from forgetting such mercy and kindness, and should remind the citizens of peace and unity. And even if they achieved nothing with the others, they would nevertheless, for their own part, remain as grateful

This opinion pleased the other counselors, as well as the Duke himself; he then released the hostages <term>original: "Gysel"; individuals held as security for a treaty</term>, regardless of the fact that their lords had not kept the offered truce. ### The Fourteenth Chapter.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'W' decorated with scrolling vines and floral motifs.</image-desc>
Although one might think to oneself that it would be more convenient and better when great potentates, princes, and lords—when discord, war, and strife arise, or they otherwise have great, important, and notable business with one another—that they should personally meet and reconcile or agree with one another. This is because it often happens that means and ways arise for which the counselors have no command to accept, and they must therefore write back or return home themselves with nothing accomplished to seek further commands from their lords, from which damage, effort, expense, and a prolongation of time grows. Yet some hold, and especially Philippe de Commines, whom I mentioned above in the previous chapter, that it is better if they send their counselors together. For as far as the expense is concerned, the legates <term>original: "Legaten"; diplomatic messengers or ambassadors</term> must travel back and forth for a long time, consuming, gambling, banqueting, and giving away as much as if the lords had met together themselves. As for the prolongation of time...

...go, one must also have patience, even if things cannot proceed so quickly and hastily; and it is sometimes better to go slowly and not hurry so much. For hurrying, as they say, brings no good.

However, one must also consider what the necessity and circumstances of the case require. Accordingly, it is considered that great potentates <term>original: "Potentaten"; high-ranking rulers or monarchs</term>, princes, and lords act unwisely—especially when they are of equal power, such as certain kings and mighty lords, etc.—when they meet in person. This is acceptable only if they are still at an age where they cannot handle great and weighty matters, but instead come together solely for joy, hunting, and other pleasures. But once they have reached their full age and it happens that they must speak and negotiate with one another personally regarding important matters, disputes <term>original: "irrung"; errors or legal disputes</term>, and grievances, it very rarely fails that a secret grudge, envy, and ill-will grows between them—even if they are satisfied with the matter itself before they depart—and they later find in practice that it would have been more convenient and better if the matter had been handled and settled through counselors and legates <term>original: "Räthe vnd Legaten"; diplomatic representatives and ambassadors</term>.

Lest anyone should think that this opinion (which at first seemed somewhat strange and unusual even to me) was something I simply dreamed up, I will here cite, prove, and provide several true examples from credible histories—written by those who saw and heard these things better—so that one must recognize that I have not invented this.

First, as Philippe de Commines <note>original: "Philippus Comineus"; a famous 15th-century diplomat and historian whose memoirs are a primary source for European court history.</note> writes, it happened that King Louis of France <note>Louis XI, known as "the Cunning" or "the Universal Spider."</note>, not long after he came to the kingdom, reached an agreement with Henry, the King of Castile <note>Henry IV of Castile.</note>, that they would meet at a place called Schnellenbrunnen <note>original: "Schnellenbrunnen"; likely referring to the historical meeting on the Bidassoa River near Saint-Jean-de-Luz (Fontaine-les-Gués).</note>. The Queen of Aragon was also summoned there, with whom King Henry was in dispute over certain matters; this place was right by a body of water that divides Spain and France. Now, as they came together from all sides and had spoken with one another barely twice, the servants in the meantime became dissatisfied with one another, and each disparaged and criticized the other's lord. King Henry was of an ugly appearance and was not well dressed, for which reason he was mocked by the French. Louis wore short clothing that was not very costly, which the Spaniards criticized and interpreted as a sickness in the King <note>The Spaniards, accustomed to grand ceremonial dress, viewed Louis XI’s plain, practical attire as a lack of royal dignity or a sign of a troubled mind.</note>. They then departed from one another in this manner. And although they had previously and always been constant good friends, a secret grudge then arose between them because of the quarrel mentioned above. And after Louis was chosen as an arbitrator between the Spaniards and the Aragonese, it annoyed the Aragonese that he had sided with the Spaniards in his judgment. Consequently, a fierce war broke out between them afterward, which lasted for sixteen years.

### The Third Part

The Duke displayed such splendor and incurred such excessive costs; for he wore a robe that was estimated at the time to have cost at least two hundred thousand Guilders, as Rodolphus Agricola <note>Rodolphus Agricola (1444–1485) was a preeminent Dutch humanist scholar and diplomat.</note> writes. But when they began to deliberate together, many great and important matters arose that were of significant concern to the Empire and Christendom, particularly regarding the Turkish War <note>A reference to the ongoing conflicts between the Holy Roman Empire and the Ottoman Empire.</note>. At that time, a marriage was also discussed and negotiated, which was only finalized between their children after both of their deaths; thus, nothing was actually accomplished in any matter at that time. Instead, after they had stayed in Trier for several days, hosting one another as guests at great expense to both parties, the Emperor departed from the Duke without a formal blessing <note>original: "ungesegnet"; implies an abrupt departure without the customary diplomatic farewells or mutual agreement</note>, which led to no small ill-will between them. It is said that both parties forgot their proper measure: the Emperor in that he envied the Duke’s prosperity and hated him for it (though the Emperor may have been unfairly judged in this regard), and the Duke in that he looked down upon the Emperor—as the greater and higher authority—and was too ostentatious.

Furthermore, it is recorded that the courtiers of both sides spoke ill of and mocked one another. The Germans criticized and scolded the Duke's splendor, saying he was proud and full of haughty words. The Burgundians, however, despised the Emperor because he arrived in Trier to meet the Duke so plainly and with such a small retinue, and did not adorn himself as expensively as the Duke. Ultimately, it went so far that they fell into open hostility with one another, and Duke Charles besieged the city of Neuss <note>The Siege of Neuss (1474–75) was a key event in the Burgundian Wars.</note>. Because of this, the Emperor was forced to rouse nearly the entire Empire against him. Whoever wishes to read more about the conversation between these two princes and desires a full account should read the letter of Rodolphus Agricola, who translated this matter from the French language into Latin, and it is quite pleasant to read. However, the citizens, after taking counsel, decided it would not be honorable for them to admit such a powerful prince—especially since they did not know for certain whether he was a friend or a foe—and thus allow him to enter while so heavily armed. Consequently, they informed him that they would receive him only with a small number of horses and servants, so that they might still hold power over him should the Prince attempt any act of force. The Prince replied that he would rather obtain what he sought through courtesy than demand it by force, even though he "held the keys to the gate in his hands" <note>This is a metaphor for his massive army; he is implying that he could take the city by force if he chose.</note> (referring to his military forces). His army had established its camp in the Prince-Bishopric of Trier, scattered here and there among the villages, stretching three miles wide and two miles long. 

When the Emperor arrived in Trier with his son <note>The future Emperor Maximilian I.</note> and the son of the Turk <note>Likely referring to a noble Ottoman hostage or a member of an embassy; at this time, the "Turkish threat" was a major concern for the Empire.</note>—and the city of Trier lies on the Moselle, roughly sixty miles above where the Rhine and the Moselle flow into one another. It is also a very renowned city, not only for great and magnificent deeds, but also because of its great age. For it is said that it was built during the time of the Trojans <note>A popular medieval legend claimed Trier was founded by Trebeta, son of the Assyrian king Ninus, centuries before Rome.</note>; it was formerly French until the Germans expanded their borders, at which point the city of Trier was also drawn into the Roman Empire. 

And when the Duke was informed that the Emperor had arrived there, he set out the next day to travel toward Trier. Once this became known in Trier, the Emperor set out with all his splendor, as did the Archbishop, and whatever other knighthood was in the city, riding out nearly a mile to meet the Duke. When the two parties came together and saw each other, the Duke first jumped from his steed as a mark of honor and uncovered his head. Subsequently, the Emperor also dismounted and embraced the Duke—who had fallen on his knees before him—and raised him up again. After they had greeted one another, and those who were entitled to do so had received and given greetings, they mounted their horses again. The Emperor and the Duke rode side by side, and following them rode the Emperor's son and the son of the Turk. After them followed everyone else according to their nobility or rank. Each party had a great number of trumpeters who marched before them and blew their horns. The Emperor did the Duke the honor of allowing the Duke’s own trumpeters to go first and play alone. 

As many lands as Duke Charles possessed, he had just as many heralds who marched before him <margin>The office of the heralds.</margin> in their customary clothing, such as is used in France, Germany, and the entire West <note>original: "Occident"</note>, though they are not particularly well known in Italy <note>original: "Welschland"</note>. Their office is to know the arrival, excellence, honor, and coats of arms of the princes, counts, and those of noble descent, and to know (or rightly be expected to know) what excellent, commendable, good, or even evil and unseemly things have been done by each of them and their ancestors. These heralds are also held to be secure and almost sacred, so that even in the course of war, though they travel as swiftly as they wish, no one ever...

### The Third Part

...no one offends. These **heralds** have the power to announce the misdeeds of the princes, although their power is no longer as great today as it once was. In former times, they would step before the tables of kings and princes and place bread behind their backs <note>This was a ritual of public shaming; placing the bread behind a person's back symbolized that they were being "turned away" from honorable society.</note> (which was then a particular mark of belittlement) and cut the tablecloth in two once it was laid out. They would also assign other similar marks of dishonor because of a prince’s crimes. But, like all other things, this custom has fallen away, as vice has gained such a high hand that the heralds have no longer been able to use their office as they did before. Only the bare name and the memory of the old, honorable lineage of the heralds remain, rather than their actual authority. 

Each of these heralds displayed the name and coat of arms of his land before the princes, as has been said. However, Duke Charles <note>Charles the Bold, Duke of Burgundy.</note> left the sword to the Emperor, as to the supreme head, as was only right and proper. Here one might have seen how everything proceeded in a most bountiful and magnificent manner, befitting His Majesty. The entire city echoed with trumpets, trombones, and other instruments. There were so many brave torches, candles, and other fireworks present that the night was made equal to the day. Everything shone with gold and precious clothing; there was a clamor of people and horses that was beyond words, yet everything proceeded so peacefully that everyone was able to behold it safely and without danger. 

His **Imperial Majesty** <note>Emperor Frederick III.</note> wore a garment of cloth-of-gold which reached down to his feet, with a lapel in the Turkish style; the sleeves and the hem were most preciously embroidered with pearls. And although His Majesty was of a venerable age, he was nonetheless perceived as young and strong. The Duke was about forty years old and in the very prime of his life, both in terms of his moderation and his glorious deeds. He wore a full **cuirass** <term>cuirass: a piece of armor consisting of a breastplate and backplate fastened together</term>, which was covered by a mantle so adorned with pearls, carbuncles <note>A term used in the Middle Ages and Renaissance for any red gemstone, usually a deep red garnet.</note>, and diamonds that it was estimated to be worth at least two hundred thousand **ducats** <term>ducat: a gold coin used as a trade currency throughout Europe</term>. 

And Agricola <note>Likely referring to the humanist scholar Rudolf Agricola.</note>, or whoever wrote this epistle, says that in truth many peasants must be made into beggars before one can pay for such a mantle. As Agricola—being an excellent and learned man—concluded this with a fine and beautiful proverb, which reads as follows: "It costs the poverty of so many that one person may be clothed." <note>original: "Tam multorum paupertate constat, vt vnus veſtitur."</note> And whoever dares to squander such immoderate money on a single person must have no sense of moderation, but surely takes all things out of an insatiable greed. 

The Emperor's son <note>The future Emperor Maximilian I.</note> was in his eighteenth year, with a handsome face and such high intelligence that he might already have been deemed worthy of his father’s fortune in receiving the Empire and leading it. He followed his father, dressed in red velvet sprinkled with silver. 

The **son of the Turk** <note>This likely refers to a high-ranking captive or envoy from the Ottoman Empire. The text claims he was captured during the wars with the Emperor of Trebizond, a Byzantine successor state that fell to the Ottomans in 1461.</note>, as they say, was captured in the war that the Emperor of Trebizond waged against the Turks; he was subsequently sent to the Pope in Rome and is said to have been given to the Emperor as a gift. He was dressed in the Turkish fashion, in a garment of cloth-of-gold; his hair was tied up, and his face was cruel and terrifying, from which one might recognize the Turkish tyrants at first glance <note>This reflects the typical 15th-century European perspective and fear regarding the Ottoman "Turks" during the period of their expansion into Europe.</note>. In this entry, there were also other princes and great lords...

# Of the Book of Regents

...each of whom, had they been alone, could have held a magnificent **grand entry** <note>original: "Einzug" — a formal, ceremonial entry into a city by a ruler, serving as a display of power.</note>. But in the presence of such great leaders, they were regarded only as outriders. From the Bishopric of Trier came the most prominent men, up to six hundred strong, dressed entirely in red; they rode out to meet the Duke primarily to honor him, as they were in awe of his power, and showed themselves to be at his service. As they traveled, it could be seen from the way the Emperor and the Duke looked at and behaved toward one another that they spoke very kindly together. But when they reached the center of the city at the market square, each wished to escort the other to his lodgings, and there were great pleas from both sides, so that the Emperor wished to escort the Duke, and the Duke the Emperor. Since neither side would be persuaded otherwise, they blessed one another and each departed to his own quarters. His **Imperial Majesty** stayed at the market square in a large and magnificent house. But the Duke stayed outside the city, in the Monastery of **Saint Maximin**, of the **Benedictine Order** <note>Saint Maximin's Abbey was one of the oldest and most powerful Benedictine monasteries in western Europe.</note>.

On the following day, after the midday meal was eaten, the Duke came to the Emperor's lodgings, where the Emperor had already been waiting for him for a long time. His Imperial Majesty stood in a hall decorated most magnificently with tapestries of **cloth of gold** <note>original: "Güldenstücken" — a luxurious fabric woven with real gold thread.</note> and precious silks; he was leaning against a sideboard while lost in thought. However, when he was informed that the Duke was arriving, he went to meet him halfway into the courtyard and greeted him most warmly, then led him by his right hand into the hall. There they spoke alone, alongside one of the most prominent secretaries, for a long time and at great length, though one cannot know what they discussed and negotiated.

When this conversation ended, drinks and fruit were served. And when they wished to depart from one another, the Emperor again wanted to escort the Duke; however, the Duke would by no means permit this. But when the Duke was halfway down the stairs and saw that the Emperor intended to follow him, he quickly turned back, led the Emperor into the middle of the hall, and then departed.

On the very next day, the Duke visited the Emperor again and persuaded His Imperial Majesty to travel with him to **Saint Maximin**, where he was quartered (as mentioned above). The Emperor wore a red velvet cloth of gold; the Duke was dressed in no other way than in princely attire, aside from his banner <note>original: "Pannets" — likely referring to the Duke's personal heraldic display or pennon.</note>. The Emperor’s son <note>Maximilian I, who would eventually succeed his father and marry the Duke's daughter, Mary of Burgundy.</note> was dressed in green damask. Among the others who belonged to both parties and followed them, there was such splendor and clothing—such as velvet, cloth of gold and silver, as well as so many gold chains and other things—present and worn at that time, that one would not have thought or believed that so much finery existed in all these lands at that time if one had not seen it. Thus, those who said that the **Germans** have sold and exchanged their ancestral glory and honor for foreign splendor did not speak entirely wrongly. They could not believe that their ancestors—who clothed themselves in the skins they stripped from captured wild animals—could have so often defeated and beaten the **Romans**...
