### The Third Part

...and have so gloriously expanded their borders, for they now conduct themselves in no other way than like a painted peacock, preening and admiring their own reflection.

When the **Emperor** <note>Emperor Frederick III (r. 1452–1493).</note> withdrew into a private chamber with the **Archbishop of Mainz**, to whom he entrusted all his secret matters, and the **Duke** <note>Charles the Bold, Duke of Burgundy.</note> with his **Chancellor**, the Archbishop began to speak on behalf of his **Imperial Majesty**. He spoke of matters concerning all of **Christendom** <note>At this time, "Christendom" referred to the collective Christian states of Europe, then facing perceived threats from the Ottoman Empire.</note> and the heavy burden it currently faced. He earnestly exhorted the Duke to come to the aid of his Imperial Majesty, adding many words to encourage him to consider his great lineage and the praise he had already won in his blooming youth through his magnificent deeds. For, he said, this was a truly princely work, befitting such a **potentate** <term>potentate: a monarch or ruler with great power</term>, to help advise the Imperial Majesty on how and in what manner the heavy obligations of Christendom might be relieved. Since this was the most noble of undertakings, it would also be the safest and most unshakeable path above all others.

After the Archbishop had spoken at length on this matter, the Duke replied that he would prefer to relocate to a more spacious place, so that his necessary response might be heard and understood by many. At this, they were shown into a large and magnificent chamber, adorned and hung everywhere with **tapestries** <note>These famous tapestries depicted the life of Alexander the Great and were a prized possession of the Burgundian court, used to project an image of world-conquering power.</note> depicting the great deeds and dealings of the mighty King **Alexander the Great**, who conquered the entire Orient. It is said by those who knew the Duke’s inclinations best that he took particular delight and held a great admiration for the history of Alexander. In the middle of the chamber was a chair of the most magnificent sort, raised up several steps and covered everywhere with **cloth of gold**. On the right side sat the three Bishops of **Mainz**, **Trier**, and **Metz**; the Emperor’s son <note>The young Archduke Maximilian, who would eventually marry Charles the Bold's daughter, Mary of Burgundy.</note>; the **Margrave of Baden**; Duke **Ludwig** and **Albrecht of Bavaria**; and the two Counts of **Wachenberg** and **Württemberg**. On the other side sat the **Duke of Burgundy** and the two Bishops of **Liège** and **Utrecht**, along with the rest of the **knighthood** from the nobility. 

Closest to the Duke stood his Chancellor, wearing a velvet robe in the French fashion. He was very eloquent, though even more courageous than he was well-spoken. This man began to speak in the **Latin language** <note>original: "Lateinischer sprach" — Latin was the international language of diplomacy, law, and high-status formal addresses.</note>. First, he repeated the oration of the Bishop of Mainz; then, he recounted the favors that **Duke Philip** <note>Philip the Good (r. 1419–1467), father of Charles the Bold.</note> had shown to the **King of France** <note>Louis XI. The Chancellor is reminding the audience of when Philip gave refuge to Louis while he was still the Dauphin, rebelling against his father, Charles VII.</note> when the King was unsafe from his own father, and how the Duke had taken him in. He described how the King was later restored to his kingdom with the Duke's help and advancement, what wars had arisen between them because of it, how these were later settled and brought to treaty, and whatever else was necessary to relate regarding this business. Whatever needed to be said concerning the **Duke of Aquitaine** <note>Charles of France, Duke of Berry and Aquitaine, the younger brother and rival of Louis XI, whose death in 1472 had significant diplomatic consequences for Burgundy.</note>, he highlighted with great diligence.

Finally, he gave an answer to the Emperor’s request, stating that it was a source of the highest sorrow and regret to his gracious Prince and **Lord** that matters in Christendom were not going better. He also knew very well...

# Of the Book of Regents.

...that in a few short years the same <note>Referring to Christendom.</note> has suffered great and insurmountable damage. Although it might not be fitting for him—since there are so many high and mighty kings and princes present—to undertake anything himself or to urge and move others toward such a great work, he nevertheless wished that, in the event his dukedoms, lands, and people could be peaceful and secure, he would so prove and demonstrate himself that there would be no lack in him. Rather, everyone should say that he lacked neither courage, fortune, wealth, nor the outward devotion to the Christian religion. Now, when he had finished speaking, the Duke escorted his **Imperial Majesty** back to his lodgings.

The **Duke of Aquitaine** <note>Charles of Valois, Duke of Berry and later Duke of Guienne (Aquitaine), the younger brother of King Louis XI of France.</note>, who was mentioned previously, was the brother of the **King of France**. The King was violently opposed to him, so much so that he would have gladly disinherited him, believing that he was a cause of the **Burgundian War** <note>Part of the "League of the Public Weal," a 1465 revolt by French nobles against King Louis XI.</note>, in which the King was defeated by the Duke, and even besieged in **Paris**, and therefore forced to come to an agreement with him. A few years later, the King’s brother died of the cruel **pestilence** <note>The plague.</note>, as they say, although he had been severely ill and no one knew what ailed him; his nails fell off his hands and the hair from his head, and because of this, many believed that **poison** had been administered to him. As the common people are always inclined to speak the worst of great lords rather than to do them any good, they also wanted to attribute this to the one for whom his death was most beneficial, and who had been most opposed to him while he lived. A few days later, Duke Charles invited the Emperor to be his guest again, where the banquet was prepared in the most magnificent and costly manner, so that it almost compared to his own **wedding** <note>Duke Charles's marriage to Margaret of York in 1468 was legendary for its extravagance.</note>, of which there had been a great cry and rumor throughout all of France and Germany.

Up to this point (says **Agricola**) <note>Rudolph Agricola (1444–1485), a preeminent Dutch humanist whose writings often recorded these diplomatic histories.</note> I have set down the epistle; what follows I have from those who were present at the transaction at that time. It was primarily concerned with how one might marry the Duke’s daughter <note>Mary of Burgundy, the most eligible heiress in Europe.</note> to the **young King Maximilian** <note>The future Emperor Maximilian I.</note>, since the Duke had no son. However, nothing was finally concluded at that time. The Emperor would have made Duke Charles a **Governor** <term>Governor: In this context, the title of "Imperial Vicar" (Reichsvikar), which would have granted Charles legal authority over Imperial lands</term> in the Empire if he had first declared himself regarding the marriage. But the Duke wanted to play it safe; before he consented to the marriage, he wanted to be assured of the office of Governor. It was intended at that time that the Duke should undertake with all his power to bring back everything that had ever been taken from the **Holy Empire**. This would truly have been no small task, enough to keep one who was equally bold and virtuous quite busy.

It was also mentioned alongside this that Duke Charles sought all kinds of things from his Imperial Majesty, and although none of them were refused him, he nevertheless received no final answer regarding them. Throughout the entire time, all kinds of **knightly games** of racing and jousting were held, and both sides made brave use of their wealth and splendor. And although the Emperor [was accompanied by] excellent princes, both spiritual and temporal, and counts...

### The Third Part

and the **Knighthood**, were superior to the Duke, yet the Duke conducted himself with much greater magnificence, so that it was said by some that a secret envy existed between them, and both parties forgot their proper measure <note>Meaning they exceeded the bounds of decorum or their social stations due to pride.</note>. It was suggested that the **Emperor** begrudged the Duke his prosperity, and the **Duke** held the **Emperor** in contempt; however, this cannot be written as a certain truth, for an injustice may well have been done to the good Prince <note>Likely referring to the Duke, suggesting these rumors might be unfair gossip.</note>.

Thirdly, the histories recount that at one time **Edward**, the **King of England**, came to the aforementioned **Duke Charles** (as he was the husband of the King's sister <note>Charles the Bold married Margaret of York, sister of Edward IV, in 1468.</note>). They had been together no longer than two days when a dispute soon arose between the households of the two lords. And after the Duke—to whom both sides brought their complaints—favored one side more than the other, the resentment and hostility between them grew much greater. And although the Duke grandly came to the aid of **King Edward** with money, soldiers, and several ships to help him regain his kingdom (from which he had been driven out), they were never truly friends again from the time they were together, but instead always spoke ill of and held a poor opinion of one another.

Likewise, when the **Count Palatine of the Rhine** once came to **Duke Charles**, the Duke hosted him honorably and well in **Brussels** for many days. But the **Burgundians** were biting toward the **Germans**, calling them "slovenly" and "crude." They were particularly displeased that the **Germans**, as they accused them, were accustomed to throwing their boots into the sleeping chambers—and some even onto the beds—which were most magnificently adorned with beautiful tapestries, silk covers, and curtains. For this reason, they did not regard the Germans as honorably as before. Conversely, the **Germans** did not care for the excessive luxury of the **Netherlanders**; thus, they clashed over these matters and parted from one another in ill-will.

Furthermore, it happened at one time that **Sigismund**, **Archduke of Austria**, came to the frequently mentioned **Duke Charles** and mortgaged the **Lordship of Pfirt** <note>The County of Ferrette in Alsace.</note>, which borders High Burgundy, for one hundred thousand guilders, because he could not defend it against the **Swiss**. Later, **Sigismund** reached an agreement with the **Swiss**, but the Duke, as they say, lost his money along with the lordship.

Item: The two kings, **Louis of France** <note>Louis XI.</note> and **Edward of England**, met near the **Amiens** <note>original: "Ambianis"</note> and conferred with each other on many matters. And although they did not act against each other openly or with force, they showed little friendship to one another after that conversation, and very little of what they promised each other at that time was ever kept.

There have indeed been many other great potentates and lords who occasionally came together—some related by marriage or even by blood, who held friendly conversations and were on the best of terms—but who nevertheless later damaged one another with wars and otherwise to such an extent that even their descendants will not be able to extinguish the bitterness. to recount what is written, I will let it rest with these examples. And the great lords and potentates will certainly perceive from this that it is not good or advisable to engage too much in personal conversation and to come together with their equals. Rather, they should let their legates <term>Legates: official diplomatic representatives or ambassadors acting on behalf of a ruler.</term> and faithful embassies carry out such matters, if they otherwise wish that friendly goodwill should be and remain between them. For it is hardly possible, when they come together, that their servants and attendants should not occasionally reproach one another and speak of matters and dealings that occurred in times past, which vexes the other party and which they cannot and will not tolerate; from this, then, more often than not, strife and discord arise among the servants, especially when they have been drinking.

So it also happens at times that one lord is more renowned than the other for beauty, stature, skill, eloquence, wisdom, and wealth. When that person is then praised, it vexes the other, as I will also say hereafter concerning clothing. When people come together in this way, such talk breaks out—first secretly, then openly—for almost nothing is so secret that it will not be brought to light in time, which the poet testifies, saying: *Everything that is under the earth, time brings into the open.* <note>original: "Quicquid sub terra est, in opertum profert ætas." A quote often attributed to Horace or similar classical sources regarding the revealing power of time.</note> This is according to the proverb: "Nothing is so finely spun that it does not come to the sun." <note>A traditional German idiom meaning that no matter how carefully a secret is hidden, it will eventually be revealed.</note> And Christ himself says in **Matthew**: *Nothing is covered that shall not be revealed, and nothing hidden that shall not be known.* <note>original: "Nihil opertum, quod non reuelabitur, & occultum quod non scietur." # The Third Part

take good care; and when they have burdened themselves with soldiers and have accomplished their objectives with them, how they may be rid of the same with the best propriety. And briefly, the history follows as such.

As soon as the peace between the Romans and those of Carthage regarding the Kingdom of Sicily was concluded, Amilcar <note>Hamilcar Barca, the Carthaginian general and father of Hannibal.</note>, as the supreme general of Carthage, moved into Lilybaeum <note>original: "Liliben"; an ancient city on the western coast of Sicily.</note> with his entire army and handed it over to a captain named Gesto <note>likely Gisco, a Carthaginian commander.</note>, who was stationed at Lilybaeum and commanded to bring them to Carthage in Africa, while [Amilcar] resigned from his office.

Gesto, as a wise captain, feared that if such a multitude of soldiers were to arrive in Africa all at once, a troublesome mutiny might result, especially since they had not been paid for a long time and were owed much in large wages, which the Council of Carthage could not pay because they were entirely exhausted by the war. Therefore, he made this provision: that the troops should not be sent to Africa all at once, but one after another, and he also made the arrival times different, so that the first could have been settled before the others arrived.

Those of Carthage were partly sluggish and negligent, and partly lacked money. They not only failed to settle with the soldiers who arrived first but also told them to wait in the city for the others until they all came together, at which time they would negotiate regarding payment. But after much misconduct occurred daily from the soldiers, and the Carthaginians could no longer endure it, they summoned the captains and asked them to lead the soldiers—as many as had come into the city—to the city of Sicca, and to wait there until the others also arrived in Africa. To make the waiting easier, they ordered that a little money be given to each man.

The captains were willing. But when they began to lead the troops away, every soldier wanted to leave what he had brought with him in Carthage, thinking they would soon return for their wages. But the Carthaginians feared that some of them, because of their wives and children, would not want to move away, or would soon return to the city, and therefore this proposal would be of little help to them. They did not want the soldiers to leave anything behind, but finally forced them with power to vacate the city with wives, children, and all their possessions.

But as the soldiers were led to Sicca and had nothing to do (which is most detrimental in a camp and the beginning of all mutiny, uprising, and disadvantage), they began to grow willful and commit all manner of misconduct. They all cried "Money! Money!" and wanted more and larger wages than they had previously desired. But nothing came of it. When they were all gathered at Sicca, the Carthaginians sent their magistrate <term>Schultheiß: a local administrative official or magistrate; here referring to Hanno the Great acting as a representative of the Carthaginian government.</term> named Anno <note>Hanno the Great, a wealthy Carthaginian aristocrat and political rival of the Barcids.</note> to them, who not only brought no money with him but also complained at length to the soldiers...

### Of the Book for Rulers.

...how entirely the city was exhausted by the long-lasting military forces, and therefore they diligently sought from them that they would allow some reduction in their pay. When the soldiers heard this, however, they were immediately most vehemently stirred up and became mutinous, so that a terrible alarm arose in the city. To this, it helped not a little that the soldiers had flocked together from many different tongues and lands. Although such a thing is not bad in itself—in that the soldiers are less able to talk with one another and organize a mutiny, and might thus obey their captains better—it has, on the other hand, this defect: when a riot arises in such a camp and the commander or captain wishes to address them, he cannot be understood by everyone, and therefore they cannot be calmed. This is exactly what happened at that time. For there were Spaniards, Gauls <note>original: "Frantzosen"; historically referring to the Celtic mercenaries</note>, Greeks, Africans, Ligurians, and a great number of those who had deserted from all lands. For this reason, one could not address them all at once, nor could any other counsel be found; and just as the magistrate <note>original: "Schultheis"; here referring to the Carthaginian leader Hanno the Great</note> could not speak to each nation individually, it could not be achieved through interpretation either. And although there was no other way at that time than for the captains to handle this, each addressing his own—which Hanno <note>original: "Ammo"; likely a variant spelling or OCR error for Hanno</note> most diligently attempted—even this would not hold, for some could not even understand their own captains; partly they spoke differently than they had been commanded, which happened partly out of misunderstanding and partly out of malice. Therefore, there was no remedy, but only sheer riot, cursing, and scolding at hand.

Among other things, the soldiers complained not a little about this: that none of the commanders (under whom they had served in Sicily) had been sent to them. Thus, they wanted nothing to do with the magistrate, but broke camp and, in such ill-will, marched back toward Carthage with weapons in hand. They pitched a camp at Tunis, fifteen Italian miles <note>original: "Welsche Meilen"; an "Italian mile" was a common unit of measurement in early modern German texts, roughly 1.5 kilometers</note> from the city. The entire host numbered about twenty thousand. Then those of Carthage saw for the first time what they had done and how far they had erred. But they could think of no remedy for the matter, for it was truly a great folly that they had allowed so many mercenary soldiers to gather in one heap after the end of the war, and that they had not kept their wives, children, and other property with them in Carthage; for they might have kept these as hostages in case of necessity. However, so that the crowd might be calmed, they applied all possible diligence, had provisions and all necessities brought to the camp, and allowed them to be paid at their own pleasure, sending one delegation after another to them.

But the soldiers devised one new demand after another, becoming bolder and more wanton from day to day. They noticed that those of Carthage were terrified of them, because they were experienced in the Sicilian war, whereas the Carthaginians were provided with no military force of their own. For this reason, they not only demanded their back pay as before, but also wanted to be paid for the loss of horses and for grain over many years <note>The soldiers demanded compensation for horses killed in battle and for rations at inflated prices</note>, which was previously unheard of.

# The Third Part

The most wicked villains and rebels in the camp were considered the best and held the most influence. Those from Carthage offered to do everything that was required of them, and matters easily reached the point where the entire dispute and discord was to be placed in the hands of one of the commanders who had been with them in Sicily.

Even though Hamilcar <note>original: "Amilcar"; referring to Hamilcar Barca, the famous Carthaginian general and father of Hannibal</note> was the most prominent among them, as heard before, they could not entirely tolerate him because he had not come to them personally during these negotiations and had also resigned from his command. For this reason, they all unanimously voted for Gisco <note>original: "Gestonem"</note>, as he had also been a captain in Sicily and had behaved kindly toward them, especially during the return of the military forces to Africa.

Gisco soon set out and arrived at Tunis <note>original: "Thunes"</note> by water with money. First, he summoned the captains to meet, and afterward, each nation individually. Once they appeared, he not only punished them for the things they had committed thus far but also diligently reminded them of what was proper for them to do at this time. He exhorted them to remain loyal to the Carthaginians, whom they had served for so long, and to keep their interests in view. Finally, he arranged for everyone to receive their pay and be satisfied with it, offering to distribute the wages through the various nations.

Now, there were two desperate villains among the crowd. One was from Campania, who had escaped from the Romans during the Sicilian War; he was a man of very strong physique who dared to attempt anything in military matters, named Spendius. This man feared that if the matter were settled with the Carthaginians, he would be handed back to his master and receive his due punishment according to Roman law <note>As a fugitive slave or deserter, Spendius faced execution if returned to Roman jurisdiction</note>. For this reason, he strove with all his might—through both words and deeds—to ensure the treaty was hindered and the rebellion made even greater.

The other was Matho, an African. Although he was a free man and had fought for the Carthaginians in Sicily, he had stirred up much rebellion and unrest, from which he expected nothing more certain than his own deserved punishment. Therefore, he called together the entire host of Africans and exhorted them to look well to their own affairs. He told them not to doubt that as soon as the other nations were paid and had returned home, the Carthaginians would vent their anger upon the Libyans <note>original: "Lybiern"; referring to the local African recruits who were Carthaginian subjects</note>. These words moved the entire crowd, especially because mention had been made only of the wages <term>Besoldung</term> <note>the basic salary</note> and not also of the compensation for lost horses and the arrears of grain. They therefore ran together to deliberate on how to proceed.

When this had happened, the captains—namely Spendius and Matho—stepped forward and vehemently scolded Gisco and the other Carthaginians. They received a great hearing. If anyone else dared to speak, he was not heard, whether he agreed with Spendius or not; instead, he was immediately stoned to death. Thus, many captains and others perished in this way, and in this tumult, nothing else was heard but "Strike him dead! Strike him dead!" <note>original: "wirff todt, wirff todt"; literally "throw [him] dead," referring to the act of stoning</note>. The shouting was even louder because they were all quite drunk from their evening meal.

# Of the Book of Rulers

...had arisen in a drunken stupor. Therefore, if anyone cried out "strike him dead," there would be such a hurling of stones that it was impossible for anyone to escape.

Since no one else wished to put themselves in such danger or offer any further advice, the entire crowd unanimously chose both Spendius and Matho as their commanders. Although Gisco <note>original: "Gesto"; referring to the Carthaginian general Gisco, who had been sent to negotiate the mercenaries' back-pay</note> saw that he could accomplish nothing in such noise and riot, he nevertheless considered the welfare of his Fatherland more than his own safety. Therefore, when he noticed that the insurrection was gaining more and more ground—placing the people of Carthage in great peril—he exerted all possible diligence, even at the risk of his own life. He summoned the two captains of the rebellion and then each nation individually, earnestly exhorting, pleading, and begging them to desist from such an untimely undertaking; he also did not fail to make many promises. But when they still insisted on receiving the outstanding grain, Gisco offered to provide it if they would deliver Matho into his hands. This word was so poorly received by the common men, and they became so embittered by it, that they plundered the money he had brought for the payment of the back wages, captured Gisco and his associates, and cast them into irons.

Now, so that the war might be set in motion all the sooner, the two commanders, Spendius and Matho—having nothing good in mind—praised the common men. They took not only what belonged to the Carthaginians but also whatever else they had with them, and held them all captive. They also made such a cruel alliance among themselves, the likes of which had never been heard of before that time, and thereafter undertook the war against Carthage. These were the causes and the beginning of the war known as the African War <note>Known to modern historians as the Mercenary War (c. 241–237 BC), which nearly destroyed Carthage after the First Punic War</note>.

To further their plan, Matho and Spendius sent their legates and messengers to all places throughout Africa, calling the people to freedom and requesting that they come to their aid against the tyranny and the unbearable and cruel rule of Carthage. Since everyone was well-disposed toward this, and sent them not only provisions but also men for every necessity, the two commanders divided their forces: one marched with his part of the army toward Utica, while the other took his path toward Hippo <note>original: "Hippon"; likely Hippo Regius or Hippo Diarrhytus</note>, intending to overrun those two cities because they had refused to join their conspiracy.

The Carthaginians, who until then had sustained themselves through agriculture while taking money from land taxes and conducting their wars with hired soldiers, were so dismayed when their land and people were stripped away and turned against them—leaving them nothing to hope for from that quarter—that they did not know what to do. This burden was all the greater for them because they had not expected it in the least at this time; for they had become so weary in the Sicilian War <note>The First Punic War (264–241 BC) against Rome</note> that they had been forced to enter into a treaty with the Romans in the hope of recovering a little in the meantime. This, however, was not to be.

## The Third Part

...but were instead suddenly overtaken by this war, just as by a sudden fire. Previously, they had fought with the Romans for the possession of the kingdom of Sicily; now they must fight for their own city, for wife and child, and for life and limb, against their own people. Furthermore, no supplies, no ships, nor anything belonging to such things were at hand, for they had been worn down by the previous naval war; likewise, no help was to be expected from either friends or allies. From this, they first recognized what a great difference there was between an external and an internal war. 

And the Carthaginians themselves were a great cause of this evil. For although they may have had a rightful cause in the previous war, they had dealt quite arrogantly with the peoples in Africa and had been all too greedy. They had doubled every tribute and taken away half of all the crops. No one could be excused from punishment by them, even if they had sinned out of ignorance. And the regents who were most esteemed among them were those who had collected the most money, and not those who had governed best—as was the case with Hanno <note>original: "Anno"; referring to Hanno the Great, a wealthy and influential Carthaginian leader</note>, who was mentioned before and was also such a regent. From this it followed that there was no need for much exhortation or persistence; rather, the peoples in Africa could have been made rebellious or defiant with a single messenger.

Because those of Carthage had previously made slaves of many people who could not pay the customs tax, the women—in order to avert such <term>servitude <note>original: "Seruitut"; the state of being enslaved or subjected to a master</note></term> from happening to their husbands and children—did not hide their jewelry. Instead, to pay the wages, they willingly gathered their feminine ornaments (which is almost hard to believe) and sent them into the camp. From this, Matho and Spendius received so much wealth that they not only paid the soldiers their outstanding wages but also kept a good necessary amount of money left over to carry out the intended war. Therefore, those who wish to give right counsel and act with foresight must look not only at present things but also at things to come.

Although those of Carthage were surrounded on all sides by so many burdens, they did not entirely despair. Instead, they sought soldiers as quickly as could be done and made Hanno <note>original: "Annocnem"</note> a chief commander. They also armed the young citizens in the city; likewise, they mustered whatever cavalry they had in the city. Subsequently, they gathered what ships remained and ordered new ones to be built.

Spendius and Matho, who were now 70,000 strong, divided themselves (as mentioned above) and besieged the two cities of Utica and Hippo <note>original: "Hypfan"; likely Hippo Diarrhytus, modern-day Bizerte</note>. Yet they had not entirely decamped from Tunis <note>original: "Thunes"</note>, by which all of Africa was cut off from those of Carthage. For Carthage lies upon a mountain that stretches into the sea, much like an island, and has no more land touching Africa than three Italian miles <note>original: "Welsche Meilen"; approximately 4.5 kilometers</note>. On the side where Carthage lies in the sea, the city of Utica is not far. On the other side, toward the lake, lies the city of Tunis. Since the enemies now, in part, themselves

<meta>This page continues the account of the Mercenary War. On the previous page, the author described the inner turmoil of Carthage and the arrogance of its leaders, particularly Hanno, which led to a widespread rebellion among the African subject populations.</meta>

...[one part of the enemy army] was positioned before Tunis, and the other before Utica, so that those from Carthage could not reach the rest of Africa. The enemies moved toward the city day and night, and sometimes during the day, right up to the city walls, instigating skirmishes and alarms in such a way that those within the city did not know how to stop their trembling.

Meanwhile, Hanno <note>original: "Anno"; referring to Hanno the Great, a wealthy Carthaginian political leader and general</note> prepared himself and diligently organized everything for war; for he was a man who knew how to handle such matters and was full of great plans. However, because he did not know how to strike at the right time, he soon moved against the enemy and displayed the great inexperience of a commander. For when he was sent to aid the people of Utica, whom the enemy was besieging most harshly, he did indeed attack them bravely. Because the <term>elephants <note>War elephants were a staple of Carthaginian warfare, used here to break enemy formations</note></term> terrified the rebels, they were soon scattered and took flight. But after such a victory, Hanno behaved so clumsily that the besieged people he had come to help fell into the utmost distress. 

For when the Carthaginians brought all kinds of ammunition and war equipment—which was used in those days for the conquest of a city—with them to Utica and set up his camp before the city, and the enemy fled in terror of the elephants to the nearest mountain, Hanno did not think the enemy would regroup so quickly. Having previously only fought against the Numidians <note>A North African people known for their light cavalry; the author implies their tactics were less disciplined than the current veteran rebels</note> (who, once scattered, hardly come back together even by the third day), he instead entered the city and indulged himself in comfort.

The enemies, however, had been accustomed in Sicily under Hamilcar <note>original: "Amilcare"; Hamilcar Barca, the famous general and father of Hannibal</note> to retreat multiple times a day and then quickly turn back. Therefore, as soon as they learned that Hanno had moved into the city and had left his soldiers lying in the camp in a state of false security because they had won, they ambushed the Carthaginians in the camp. They slew many of them and forced the others to flee shamefully into the city. From this victory, the enemy captured all the war equipment, <term>siege engines <note>original: "Sturmzeug"; machines like catapults or rams used to attack fortifications</note></term>, and other supplies. And Hanno did not only harm the Carthaginians this time through his lack of foresight, but also later when the enemy lay before Geron <note>likely referring to a geographical feature or town near the Macar River</note>. Even though he had twice drawn up the battle lines and could have broken and defeated them with the elephants, he neglected it all through his carelessness.

When the Carthaginians saw that Hanno had handled military matters so unseasonably, they unanimously chose Hamilcar again as a commander. They immediately provided him with seventy elephants, as well as whatever professional soldiers they had, all the deserters, and whatever men they could raise in the city on horse and foot—totaling nearly ten thousand men. He set out in great haste and, through his knightly virtue and manhood, broke the courage of the enemy all at once. He relieved the city of Utica and proved himself entirely as he had done before, and as the Carthaginians had expected and hoped of him. His intelligence was first recognized by this: The mountains upon which Carthage is built have a very sharp ridge and several wooded hills where the land joins with Africa. Because of the difficult terrain, much of which had been modified by hand <note>referring to man-made defensive earthworks or narrow passes</note>, it was impossible to cross.

### The Third Part

<meta>catchword: Matho</meta>

Matho <note>A leader of the mercenary rebels against Carthage.</note> had occupied all of these and diligently garrisoned them. At that same location, there was also a river which usually flowed very swiftly and had quite high banks, so that there was no way to cross it except in one place where there was a bridge. Beyond the bridge lay a city named Sephyra <note>Likely referring to a fortification near the Bagradas River.</note>, which Matho also held, by which the way into Africa was closed off not only to the Carthaginian army but also to private individuals. Now, when Amilcar <note>Hamilcar Barca, the father of Hannibal and the new Carthaginian commander.</note> saw this, he thought back and forth about how he might enter Africa and spared no effort. Eventually, he realized that the aforementioned river, on account of the wind, would stand still, with almost nothing flowing from it into the sea. Having noticed this, he realized he could cross by the sea with little difficulty, but he revealed this to no one; instead, he simply ordered that whatever was necessary for the march be prepared.

When he saw that his opportune time had come, he crossed at the aforementioned place in the water during the night with his entire army, so that no one noticed. But when it became day, and the enemy—as well as those in the city—saw this and were greatly terrified by it, Amilcar first moved against those who were besieging Sephyra. Spendius <note>Another primary leader of the rebellion, a former Roman slave.</note>, however, soon set out with his army, wishing to come to the aid of his companions. Ten thousand men lay at Sephyra, and 5,000 at Utica. Their plan was that if they attacked the Carthaginians at the same time—one part from the front and the other from behind—they would surely be defeated. Therefore, they moved toward Amilcar with their full force by the nearest route.

Amilcar was not deterred; he marched onward in his battle formation, with the **elephants** at the front, followed by the <term>mounted troops <note>German: *Reisigen Zeug*; refers to the heavy cavalry or armored riders.</note></term> and the <term>vanguard <note>German: *verlornen hauffen*; literally "the forlorn hope," referring to the frontline troops who initiated the skirmish.</note></term>, and finally the <term>Double-pay men <note>German: *Doppelsöldner*; veteran soldiers who received twice the standard pay because they fought in the most dangerous positions and provided their own superior armor.</note></term>. When he saw that the enemy was attacking his men so fiercely, he wheeled the battle formation so that those in the front appeared as if they intended to flee. However, those in the rear were ordered in such a way that they came to the front of the points. From this, the Libyans, who were moving against the Carthaginians from both sides, believed nothing else but that they were taking flight; they abandoned their battle formation and ran toward them. But when they saw that the mounted troops, along with the entire host, pressed upon them with force, they were terrifyingly scattered and finally put to flight. Quite a few were slain by the **Double-pay men**; others were trampled by the **elephants** and killed by the mounted troops. Thus, six thousand of the enemy remained on the battlefield, and two thousand were captured; the others fled, one part toward the city of Sephyra and the other part to the camp that was before Utica.

Now that Amilcar had accomplished these things so successfully, he followed the enemies who had fled toward Sephyra and soon took and conquered the city. The army that was within it fled toward Tunis. He, however, moved about the land there, taking one city after another. Some surrendered, and others he had to win by storm. Because of this, the people of Carthage—who a short time ago did not know what to do and were entirely despondent—regained their power.

# Of the Regent’s Book.
Aa ij
<meta>catchword: concluded-</meta>

Matho was stationed at this time before Hippo <note>original: "Hisson"; likely referring to Hippo Acra or Hippo Regius</note> and advised Spendius and Autharitus <note>original: "Autharico"</note>, a Gaulish <note>original: "Frantzösischen"</note> captain, to follow the enemies. However, they were to avoid the plains because of the elephants and instead stay in the mountains, and for various reasons that might arise, they were to stay not far from the enemy.

Furthermore, Matho sent messengers to the Libyans and Numidians, pleading and begging them intensely to come to the aid of his people and not to hinder or neglect the freedom for which Africa now stood. Therefore, Spendius, with six thousand elite soldiers chosen from the entire host stationed at Tunis, set up his camp in the mountains not far from Carthage. He also had with him two thousand Gauls who had been under Autharitus in the Sicilian War <note>The First Punic War (264–241 BCE)</note> when the Romans besieged Eryx <note>original: "Eryncen"</note>, and who had deserted to join them.

Now, while Hamilcar <note>original: "Amilcar"</note> lay in a plain with all his army, surrounded on all sides by mountains, a mighty multitude of soldiers from Numidia and Africa marched to join Spendius. Thus, the Carthaginians were besieged by three groups: the Africans were in front, the Numidians behind, and Spendius was on the flank. Because of this, Hamilcar remained in doubt for a long time as to what should be done.

At that time, there was among the Numidians a magnificent and prominent nobleman named Naravas <note>original: "Narua"</note>, who had always been well-disposed toward those of Carthage and especially thought highly of Hamilcar because of his virtue. This man felt that he now had an opportune time to make friendship with Hamilcar; therefore, he set out with about one hundred horses and went to Hamilcar’s camp.

When he arrived quite close to the camp, he signaled with his hand and requested a parley. Hamilcar wondered at the boldness of the man and sent a rider to him, to whom Naravas indicated that he had come for the purpose of speaking with the commander. But as Hamilcar doubted and would not yet give him any credit, Naravas dismounted, gave his horse and his spear to his servants, and walked alone and fearlessly to the commander. Everyone in the camp marveled at this—that a Numidian should be so bold. When he was called into conversation with Hamilcar, he explained how he had always been well-disposed toward the best interests of Carthage and had desired nothing more than to have long ago entered into friendship with Hamilcar. Therefore, as he was now present, he offered to risk his life and his fortune for Hamilcar and those of Carthage, faithfully and without any deceit.

When the commander heard this, he was so greatly rejoiced that he swore an oath to him that he would give him his daughter in marriage <note>This daughter is often identified by later traditions as the inspiration for the character Salammbô, though her historical name is unrecorded.</note>. He was also particularly pleased that Naravas had come to him so boldly, addressed him, and spoken so honorably and simply without any deceit; he only reminded him to remain faithful to Carthage. Upon this, Naravas returned to his people and, on the following day, moved into Hamilcar's camp with all those he had under him. Once this happened, Hamilcar had at his disposal...

# The Third Part

Matho had occupied all of these locations and garrisoned them with great diligence. There was also a body of water in that same place which usually flowed very swiftly and had steep banks, so that it could only be crossed at one place where there is a bridge. Beyond the bridge lay a city named Sephyra <note>historical: This likely refers to a fortified position near the Bagradas river, which controlled access to the interior of Africa</note>, which Matho also held. Because of this, the road into Africa was closed off not only to the Carthaginian army but also to private individuals. When Hamilcar <note>original: "Amilcar"</note> saw this, he pondered how he might reach Africa and spared no effort. Finally, he realized that the aforementioned river becomes obstructed because of the wind <note>Hamilcar observed that certain winds blew sand into the river mouth, creating a temporary natural ford</note>, and almost nothing of it flows into the sea. Having noticed that he could pass through by the sea with little effort, he revealed this to no one, but instead only had the necessary supplies for the army's march prepared.

When he saw his opportunity, he crossed at the mentioned place in the water by night with his entire army, so that no one became aware of it. However, when day broke and the enemies—as well as those in the city—saw this and were greatly terrified, Hamilcar first moved against those who were besieging Sephyra. Spendius quickly set out with his army to come to the aid of his companions. There were ten thousand men stationed at Sephyra and five thousand at Utica. Their plan was that if they attacked the Carthaginians simultaneously—one group from the front and the other from the rear—the Carthaginians would be defeated. Therefore, they moved with their full force directly against Hamilcar.

Hamilcar did not let himself be deterred but advanced in his battle order. He had the elephants in the front, followed by the cavalry <term>Reisigen Zeug: The mounted troops or heavy cavalry of the period</term> and the vanguard <term>verlornen hauffen: literally the "lost group," these were front-line troops tasked with breaking the enemy line, often at high risk</term>, and finally the elite infantry <term>Doppelsöldner: veteran soldiers who received "double pay" for their experience and superior equipment</term>. When he saw that the enemies were rushing them so violently, he wheeled the battle order so that the front ranks appeared as though they intended to flee. The rear ranks, however, were arranged in such a way that they moved to the front of the formation. Because of this, the Libyans, who were advancing from both sides against the Carthaginians, believed nothing other than that they were taking flight; they abandoned their battle order and ran toward them. But when they saw that the cavalry along with the entire host pressed upon them with great force, they were terrifyingly scattered and finally put to flight. A great many were slain by the elite infantry, others were trampled by the elephants, and others were killed by the cavalry. Thus, six thousand of the enemy remained on the battlefield and two thousand were captured. The others fled, partly toward the city of Sephyra and partly into the camp that was before Utica.

Once Hamilcar had accomplished these things so successfully, he followed the enemies who had fled toward Sephyra and immediately took and conquered the city. The army that was inside fled toward Tunis <note>original: "Thunes"</note>. He, however, marched throughout the surrounding countryside, capturing one city after another. Some surrendered, while others he had to take by storm. Because of this, the Carthaginians—who only a short time ago did not know what to do and were completely despairing—regained their strength.

# Of the Book of Regents

Matho was at this time besieging Hippo <note>original: "Hiffon"; likely referring to Hippo Diarrhytus or Hippo Regius</note> and advised Spendius and Autaritus <note>original: "Autharico"</note>, a Gallic captain <note>original: "Französischen Hauptmann"; the German text uses the contemporary term for "French" to describe the ancient Gauls</note>, to follow the enemies. Furthermore, Matho sent messengers to the Libyans and Numidians, pleading and begging them urgently to come to his aid and not to hinder or neglect the freedom that now stood before Africa. Therefore, Spendius, with six thousand elite soldiers chosen from the entire host stationed at Tunis <note>original: "Thunes"</note>, set up his camp in the mountains not far from Carthage. He also had with him two thousand Gauls <note>original: "Franzosen"</note> who had been under Autaritus during the Sicilian War when the Romans besieged Eryx <note>original: "Eryncen"</note>, and who had deserted to join them.

Because of this, Hamilcar remained for a long time in doubt as to what he should do.

Now, at that time, there was among the Numidians an excellent and distinguished nobleman named Naravas <note>original: "Narua"</note>, who had always been well-disposed toward those of Carthage and especially held Hamilcar in high regard for his virtue. He felt that he now had a favorable opportunity to make a friendship with Hamilcar; therefore, he set out with approximately one hundred horses and went to Hamilcar's camp.

Everyone in the camp marveled at this, that a Numidian should be so bold. When he was called into a conversation with Hamilcar, he explained how he had always been well-disposed toward the Carthaginians and had wanted nothing more than to have established a friendship with Hamilcar long ago. ### The Third Part

<meta>catchword: Matho</meta>

Matho had taken all of these places and occupied them with diligence. There was also in that same place a river which used to flow very swiftly and had quite high banks, so that there was no way to cross it except at one place where there is a bridge. Overlooking the bridge lay a city named Sephyra <note>historical: Likely referring to the fortified position or town at the bridge of the Bagradas (modern Medjerda) River</note>, which Matho also held; from there, the way into Africa was closed off not only to the Carthaginian army but also to private individuals. Now when Hamilcar <note>original: "Amilcar"</note> saw this, he turned over in his mind how he might reach Africa and spared no effort. Finally, he realized that the aforementioned river, on account of the wind, stands still <note>The text describes a phenomenon where specific winds could push the sea into the river mouth, creating a temporary fordable shallow</note> and almost nothing of it flows into the sea. Therefore, noticing that he might pass through at the sea with little trouble, he revealed this to no one, but only ordered that which was necessary for the march of the army to be prepared.

When he saw that his time had come, he crossed over at the aforementioned place in the water during the night with all his army, so that no one was aware of it. But when it became day, and the enemy—including those who were in the city—saw this and were greatly terrified by it, Hamilcar first marched against those who were besieging Sephyra. Spendius, however, soon set out with his army, wishing to come to the aid of his companions. Ten thousand men lay at Sephyra, and five thousand at Utica <note>original: "Vtica"</note>. And this was the plan: that they would attack the Carthaginians at once—one part from the front, the other from the rear—so that they would already be defeated. Therefore, they moved toward Hamilcar with their entire force by the nearest way.

Hamilcar allowed nothing to lead him astray and marched forth in his battle order <term>Schlachtordnung: A formal tactical arrangement of troops on a battlefield</term>. He had the elephants in front, then the cavalry <term>Reisigen Zeug: A contemporary German term for mounted troops or cavalry</term> and the "forlorn hope" <term>verlornen hauffen: The vanguard or skirmishers who took the initial, most dangerous brunt of the fighting</term>, and finally the "double-pay" soldiers <term>Doppelsöldner: Elite heavy infantry who received twice the standard pay for their skill and placement in the front ranks</term>. When he saw that the enemies were charging his men so fiercely, he wheeled the battle order around so that those in the front appeared as if they wished to flee; those in the rear, however, were ordered in such a way that they came to the front of the point. From this, the Libyans—who were marching against the Carthaginians from both sides—believed nothing else than that they were taking flight. They abandoned their battle order and ran toward them. But when they saw that the cavalry along with the entire host pressed upon them with force, they were terribly scattered and finally put to flight. Quite many were slain by the "double-pay" soldiers; others were trodden down by the elephants and struck down by the cavalry. Thus, six thousand of the enemy remained on the field of slaughter <note>original: "Wallstat"</note>, and two thousand were captured. The others fled, part toward the city of Sephyra and part into the camp that was before Utica.

Now that Hamilcar had accomplished these things so successfully, he followed the enemy who had fled toward Sephyra and took and conquered the city immediately. The army that was within it took flight toward Tunis <note>original: "Thunes"</note>. He, however, marched about in the land there, taking one city after another. Some surrendered, and others he had to win by storm. Because of this, the people of Carthage—who a short time before did not know what to do and were entirely despondent—recovered their power once again.

And it happens with these tyrants, if one wishes to consider it rightly, just as with human bodies, which sometimes become so severely corrupted and decayed <note>original: "anbrüchig"</note> that they can no longer be helped. For just as ulcers <note>original: "Geschwäre"; sores or abscesses</note> break out when one wants to heal them, yet if one leaves them be and does nothing to them, they naturally spread further and do not stop until they have corrupted the entire body. So too are the minds of men, which sometimes become so entirely inflamed and corrupted that no animal on earth can become so evil and poisonous; in such a way that if one occasionally shows kindness toward them and wishes to grant them some leniency, it has no place or standing with them, but everything is interpreted and received by them in the worst way, and they become even worse than before one showed them goodness. But if one opposes them and wishes to restrain them, nothing on earth can be thought of so cruel, so tyrannical, and so evil that they would not dare to do and use against it, even considering the same to be glorious, until they go so far that they forget themselves and cast off all human nature. The beginning and the greatest part of these things come from bad habits and bad upbringing, after which one addition follows another. But primarily in war, the greed <note>original: "Geitz"</note> and tyranny of the commanders and captains do great damage, all of which was found at once in this crowd, and especially among the captains.

In the meantime, **Amilcar** <note>Hamilcar Barca</note> summoned **Annonem** <note>Hanno the Great</note>, the other captain from Carthage, with his army to him, in the hope that with both forces they could more easily withstand the enemy and carry out the war. And Amilcar threw all enemies he had and thereafter obtained to the wild beasts, and found so much that no other means could be found to end this war than that the enemies must be completely rooted out and exterminated.

Though things then began to look as if they were going reasonably well for those of Carthage, luck soon turned. For when the two supreme commanders came together, they became violently at odds with one another, in such a way that they cared much more for how one might suppress the other...

From which untimely state of affairs, the two captains of the enemies, namely **Matho** and **Spendius**, became so proud and arrogant that they dared to undertake a siege of the city of **Carthage** itself.

**Amilcar** <note>Hamilcar Barca</note> at that time had **Hannibal** alongside him as a fellow supreme commander, for they had dismissed **Hanno** <note>original: "Annoni"</note> from the same office because the soldiers had chosen to keep Amilcar, as mentioned above. And because they were personally present, this carried great weight, not only in that matter but also in other things they accomplished.

Now, while the Carthaginians were thus besieged on all sides by the enemies, they intended to call upon their confederates and cities for help. At that time, **Hiero of Syracuse** <note>original: "Hieran von Syracuse"</note> gave them great and notable help, providing whatever the Carthaginians desired. For he believed that if things went well for the Carthaginians, it would not be disadvantageous to him; he feared that if the Carthaginians were suppressed, the Romans might thereafter wish to deal with him and others as they pleased, since no one would be able to offer them any resistance.

In the same manner, the **Romans** were also bound to the Carthaginians by treaty; therefore, they omitted nothing that could be furtherance and help to them, regardless of the fact that a short time before a grudge had arisen between them for the following reasons. As soon as the city was besieged, the Carthaginians had captured and put in irons up to five hundred men who, for the sake of their own profit, had carried provisions and all necessities into the camp of the enemies—which the Romans never

little annoyed. However, when they dispatched their envoys to the people of Carthage a few days later regarding this matter, the Carthaginians released the prisoners quite willingly and without any payment. This pleased the Romans so well that, in return, they released all the prisoners they had held from the **Sicilian War** <note>The First Punic War (264–241 BC), fought primarily over Sicily.</note> without any ransom. They also provided all proper assistance and permitted Carthaginian merchants to replenish their stores of grain and other necessities among them. However, no one was allowed to transport provisions into the camps of their enemies. At that time, the soldiers who were in **Sardinia** refused to give an answer to the legates who demanded that they should surrender and hand over the island to the Romans.

Thus, the people of **Utica** <note>original: "Vticenser"</note> surrendered themselves and all they owned to the Carthaginians shortly thereafter, and bound themselves anew to remain as allies and not to act against them. From this, the people of Carthage took heart and endured the siege much more easily, as they hoped for relief.

But **Matho** and **Spendius** <note>The primary leaders of the mercenary revolt; Spendius was a former Roman slave and Matho was a Libyan.</note> were no less besieged than they themselves were besieging the Carthaginians; for through the diligent observation of **Hamilcar** <note>original: "Amilcaris"; Hamilcar Barca, the Carthaginian general and father of Hannibal.</note>, they were driven into such distress and hunger that they were forced to retreat from Carthage in shame. They took the best soldiers and marched with fifty thousand men directly toward Hamilcar. However, because of the elephants and the cavalry under **Naravas** <note>original: "Narua"; a Numidian chieftain who defected to Hamilcar's side.</note>, they would not venture onto the plains, but always kept to the high ground. And although they were strong enough against the Carthaginians, because they did not entirely understand the customs of war, they were frequently overcome by the Carthaginians. From this, it can be easily and well understood what a great difference there is between a sensible and wise warlord or commander and a heap of inexperienced people. For while they lay against each other and skirmished daily, Hamilcar took the greatest care to ensure he did nothing rashly or to his own disadvantage. He subsequently broke the spirit of Spendius, for at times he pretended he wished to flee, but as he turned back, he did great damage to the enemy. Sometimes he fell upon them unexpectedly, so that they were completely terrified and discouraged. All those whom he captured alive, he had torn apart by wild beasts. Finally, Hamilcar pitched his camp next to the enemy’s camp, yet in a location that was most inconvenient for the enemy but most favorable for the Carthaginians. From this, the enemy was so distressed that, out of fear of the elephants and the **cavalry** <note>original: "Reisigen Zeuges"</note>, they could neither fight nor—since they were surrounded by trenches and ramparts—conveniently flee. And there was such a hunger in their camp that, in the end, one had to eat the other. It is easy to believe that God ordained such punishment upon these cruel people for the sake of the wretched tyrants, so that they had to perish in such a way.

Since they now saw that the Carthaginians were superior to them, and feared how they would be treated if they were to be defeated, they

They also dared not ask for any treaty, for their own conscience taught them that no mercy would be obtained from those of Carthage on account of the tyranny they had committed. For this reason, they refrained from it and daily placed their hope only in those who still lay at **Tunis** <note>original: "Thunes"</note>, waiting to see if they would come to their aid.

Now, when they had cruelly eaten and consumed all the captive and dead bodies—with which they had sustained themselves for a good while—they stood in such famine and fear of punishment that they were in doubt as to what they should do. Finally, they decided to approach the enemy for a treaty; therefore, they dispatched a herald to seek from **Hamilcar** <note>original: "Amilcare"; Hamilcar Barca, the Carthaginian general.</note> whether they might send their embassy to him. When they had obtained this, the legates came to the commander, with whom he made an agreement in this manner: namely, that from the entire host of the enemy, ten should be delivered into the Carthaginian camp at their pleasure; in that case, they would let the others go without ransom, though without weapons and wearing only a single tunic. When this was concluded and agreed upon, Hamilcar took those who were then present. Thus **Spendius** and **Autaritus** <note>original: "Authoricus"; a leader of the Gallic mercenaries.</note>, together with others of the most prominent of the entire host, fell into the hands of Hamilcar.

But when the **Libyans** heard that their commanders and leaders had surrendered to the enemy, they alleged that the people of Carthage had not kept the peace, because the treaty had been executed without their prior knowledge; they therefore sought safety and wished to remain in their camp. Hamilcar, however, set upon them with the elephants and scattered the entire host, so that they could achieve nothing, and over forty thousand were struck dead. This occurred at a place called **The Saw** <note>original: "die Sege"; referring to the mountain pass known in Greek as 'Prion' because of its jagged shape.</note>, because it was shaped exactly like that instrument.

After these things, the people of Carthage, who had been quite despondent, took heart again a little. Hamilcar, **Naravas** <note>original: "Narua"; a Numidian prince who allied with Carthage.</note>, and **Hannibal** <note>A Carthaginian general under Hamilcar, not to be confused with Hamilcar's famous son.</note> traveled hurriedly throughout Africa, and the Carthaginians again gained a large following. When they had recovered many cities, they moved with their army before Tunis and there besieged **Matho**, along with those he had with him. Hannibal pitched his camp on the side of the city that lies toward the Carthaginian works. Hamilcar, however, camped on the other side, opposite him. There they brought out Spendius and the others whom they had put in irons and hanged them before the noses of the enemy.

Meanwhile, Matho saw that Hannibal had pitched his camp somewhat carelessly and that he could easily be overcome; he rushed out of the city and attacked the Carthaginians, striking many of them dead while the others took flight. Consequently, Matho plundered the camp. Hannibal was captured alive, and after they had cruelly tortured him, he was immediately hanged on the gallows in Spendius’s place, and thirty of the most noble citizens were cruelly hewn to pieces. Thus, fortune saw to it that both sides received their rightful punishment. Hamilcar learned of this outcome somewhat late, and even when it was made known to him, he could not come to Hannibal's aid because of the difficulty of the terrain; therefore, he retreated from Tunis and pitched his camp by the water called **Macar** <note>original: "Machera"; the Bagradas River.</note>.

### The Third Part

When those of Carthage heard of such unforeseen damage <note>referring to the capture and execution of the mercenary leaders described on the previous page</note> suffered by their own, they were violently terrified and became quite despondent. Yet they took heart again, and therefore ordered the drums to be beaten and mustered some new soldiery. They sent a stately embassy to **Hamilcar** <note>original: "Amilcare"</note>, namely thirty councilors, and with them the former captain **Hanno** <note>original: "Ammonem"; Hanno the Great, a political rival of Hamilcar Barca.</note>. They gave these delegated councilors the command that they should, through suitable means, settle and reconcile the discord between the two captains. When the ambassadors arrived at the camp and summoned the two captains before them, they gave them so many reminders that they completely settled their error and discord. The captains accepted and arranged all things on behalf of the city, following the command of the Carthaginians in all respects and thereafter acting with common counsel. And since only **Matho** <note>the last major leader of the rebel mercenaries</note> remained to be fought, after much effort, danger, and labor experienced and endured at **Lepta** and elsewhere, they agreed with him to a free pitched battle. They also summoned not only their fellows and confederates but also the soldiery they had stationed in the cities, all with the intent that they would and must try their last hope this time and put an end to the war once and for all.

When both parties were prepared and ready for battle with all necessary supplies, they attacked each other bravely and manfully at the same time. And although it stood hard for both sides, the Carthaginians ultimately held the field and won the battle. In this battle, the greatest part of the enemy was struck dead. Those who remained fled into the city situated nearest by, but soon afterward surrendered to the Carthaginians, because they saw that all was lost.

And only two cities, namely the **Uticans** and **Hipponensians** <note>the cities of Utica and Hippo Diarrhytus</note>, persisted in their stubbornness and disobedience, because they could well judge for themselves that they had so trespassed against Carthage that they could not be accepted into grace. From this, one may well and easily conclude what a great thing **moderation** <term>original: "Mittelmässigkeit"; here referring to the classical virtue of the "golden mean" or avoiding extremes</term> is, and that one should see and be considered in every way so that one does not do too much out of wantonness and without compulsion.

But finally, when these same cities had no hope of help, comfort, or relief, and were heavily besieged by the two commanders, they surrendered their power to the Carthaginians **unconditionally** <note>original: "auff gnaden vnd vngnaden," literally "on mercy and un-mercy."</note>. From this, these terrible and bloody wars gained such a fortunate outcome on the side of the Carthaginians that they not only brought all of **Africa** <note>referring to the Libyan territories surrounding Carthage</note> back into their power, but also all those who had offered resistance to them in this war received their proper punishment. For Matho and the others who were captured were led through the city of Carthage in a magnificent triumph by the young citizenry of Carthage, and subsequently received their deserts <note>a euphemism for their execution</note>.

And this war lasted nearly three years and four months. **Polybius** <note>the Greek historian who is the primary source for these events</note> also writes that he never heard of a more hideous, shameful, cruel, and unheard-of war. And it is especially, to put it briefly—

Of the Book of the Ruler.

To conclude briefly: here one may see how easily fortune can turn in war, what depends upon an upright commander or captain, and that he who assembles a host of soldiers should see to it how he might dismiss them with propriety and honor. It will hardly end without damage, whether he wins or loses; whoever will not believe it may try it at his own peril.

# On Military Rule, Order, 
->and Laws, Adjusted for Our Present Time,<-
->and Compiled in Brief.<-

### The Sixteenth Chapter.

<image-desc>Ornamental initial 'D' depicting a small figure or putto surrounded by decorative leaf-like scrolls within a square frame.</image-desc>Since I promised above in the sixth chapter to include a brief form of military preparation, I will briefly report on it according to the common custom of the **German Nation**, as it has come down to us from our ancestors (for from the disorder of warfare in the present time, unfortunately, no teaching or example is to be taken). This is intended, however, in a general and non-binding way, as various differences are found according to the regions and other circumstances. Therefore, I do not wish to prescribe such military law to anyone as something that must be strictly followed in this manner (although some hold it would be good if it were), but rather as I have heard it generally from military experts and as it has been briefly summarized in several published treatises on military ordinances.

First, it is fitting that every sovereign <note>original: "Kriegßherr"; literally "War-Lord," referring to the prince or ruler who possesses the right to wage war.</note> who wishes to undertake a war should take care with all diligence and earnestness—among himself, his friends, and wise, faithful advisors (as well as legal scholars)—that he need fear no sin before God, no reproach before the world, and no dishonor among posterity. He must ensure he has an honorable, fair, urgent, and lawful reason for his warring. For to wish to wage war without necessity, law, or propriety—solely out of greed, hatred, envy, or a thirst for glory through mere violence—was considered scandalous and unpraiseworthy even among the heathens. It has never done well in the long run and has always yielded a bitter reward in the end, as can be seen from countless examples in the ancient **histories** <note>original: "Historijs"</note>.

Secondly, if a sovereign is of such a Christian and honorable mind and yet must and shall go to war, it is also his duty to ensure that, just as he himself is not inclined toward injustice, he likewise allows his soldiery as little room as possible to act against law and honor.

Such provision, however, can happen no better than through the serious maintenance of good **governance** <term>Regiment: the systematic rule, discipline, and administrative structure of a military force</term> (which is of the highest service to obedience and general welfare).

# The Third Part
## On Status and Governance.

Every great and powerful war or campaign usually has, and must have, three types of governance <term>Regiment: here referring to the distinct branches of military administration and command</term>. And where one of these is missing, nothing grand or noteworthy can be accomplished.

Namely: the lords, princes, and knighthood, together with all the mounted troops <note>original: "Reisigen Kriegsvolck"; refers to armored cavalrymen</note>, have their own command.

The supreme master of ordnance <term>Feldzeugmeister: the high official in charge of artillery, weaponry, and technical supplies</term>, along with all the artillery, has his own command.

The colonel of all the foot soldiers <note>original: "Fußknecht"; the infantry, typically mercenary pikemen or Landsknechte</note> has his own command.

These three aforementioned commands have one supreme field captain <note>original: "obersten Feldhauptman"; the commander-in-chief</note>, who is the superior over the entire field camp, provided that the true Principal or Sovereign <note>original: "Kriegsherr"; the ruler who commissioned the war</note> is not present in person. Where, however, the Sovereign is himself in the field, then the Supreme Captain acts as the Sovereign's lieutenant.

Furthermore, all mounted troops usually have their commander, who is called the Field Marshal. He holds a magnificent office and also has his own provost <note>original: "Profosen"; a military official responsible for discipline and justice</note>, who is called the provost of the knighthood. He also has under him the captains of all the mounted troops; they always seek and receive orders and instructions from the Marshal on what to do and what to leave undone, for he is by heritage one of the foremost military leaders.

The second command is that of the supreme master of ordnance, who has under his power the entire artillery, together with all the guns and munitions; he also has his own provost.

The third is the command of the foot soldiers; they also have a colonel of all foot soldiers, who has under him all other subordinate captains, and he also has his provost and his own command.

Now, over these three commands, yet another is appointed by the Sovereign as a supreme field captain over all three other military offices or commands; he also has a provost, namely the supreme field provost, which is the same as a field judge. This same man has in his charge the punishment of capital crimes <note>original: "Malefitz"</note> and the setting of prices for provisions <note>original: "Prouiant zu schätzen"</note>. He also has his "staff-men" <term>Steckenknecht: assistants to the provost who carried out arrests and maintained order</term> who help him manage his office. He has his magistrate <note>original: "Schultheißen"</note> and court, and also his executioner <note>original: "Nachrichter"</note>. Whatever he is commanded to punish by the supreme field captain and other military councilors, that he must do, appearing before the judge and military court as a legally appointed official and commanded by the law.

Thus, there must be three commands in every powerful campaign, and none may work fruitfully without the others; rather, one must extend a hand to the other. The reason: the foot soldiers cannot run down the riders; likewise, the riders cannot do much against foot soldiers in high mountains, narrow woods, or in bogs and trenches. Furthermore, one cannot easily knock down walls, towers, bulwarks <note>original: "Bolwerck"</note>, and bastions with horses' heads and long pikes; one must have powerful guns and artillery, which can do it. Artillery is also useful in field battles, but if it has no mounted troops and no foot soldiers with it to protect it, watch over it, and hold it with force, then the artillery is of no use. Therefore, they are all three best when they are together.

<meta>catchword: Because</meta>

Since all three [divisions] belong together, they shall also govern, advise, and make war plans with one another. They shall all pull together equally <note>original: "an die Stangen greiffen"; literally "to grab the poles," a metaphor for working together on a shared task</note>. In this way, the three commands <term>Regiment: here referring to the distinct branches of military administration</term> become one and have a single supreme leader, who is appointed over the three commands by the Sovereign <note>original: "Kriegsherr"; the prince or ruler who commissioned the war</note> (if he is not in the field himself); this makes, in sum, a single command.

### How the War Council should be established.

First, those belonging to the Supreme Commander as war councilors are: the Field Marshal, then the Master of Ordnance <term>Feldzeugmeister: the high official in charge of artillery and weaponry</term>, and thirdly, the Colonel of all the foot soldiers.

Thereafter, the Supreme Field Captain may, together with the three war councilors just mentioned, summon from the sub-captains of the cavalry <note>original: "Reisigen"</note> those who are the most famous and respected or the most experienced in war—in certain cases—to serve as war councilors, whether many or few, according to the opportunity and nature of the situation. The same should also be done with the sub-captains of the foot soldiers, yet in equal measure or number, so that the cavalry do not think the plans are made lightly, nor the foot soldiers think the councils are made only to please the foot soldiers. Conversely, it ensures that the captains do not act only for the pleasure of the cavalry or seek some advantage for one side over the other; therefore, ill-will should always be prevented.

Although the three military divisions do not equal one another in number of persons, more is spent on the horses, so that in cost, the cavalry compares well to the infantry. Although the artillery has the smallest group of men, much is spent on the wagons, horses, and the multitude of "Double-Pay" soldiers <term>Doppelsöldner: experienced veteran soldiers who received twice the standard wage for their skills or equipment</term> and others, as well as powder, balls, and other ammunition; thus, the cost in the end is almost equal for all three.

## Hereafter follow the commissions, laws, rights, and benefits of all high offices.

Since the commission, law, right, freedom, and benefit of every high office in times of war is primarily to be understood from the appointments <term>Bestallungen: formal contracts of employment or commission</term> for which they were accepted and the oaths they were burdened with, I will indicate those same appointments and oaths (which amount to the same thing) here, and provide further reporting on them.

It is to be known that this form is not always kept exactly the same throughout, but is changed, increased, diminished, or improved from time to time in one point or another, according to the nature of the land and the pleasure of the Sovereign.
