# Articles upon which the Supreme
## Captain shall be commissioned.

Namely, that he shall be faithful and loyal in such commission to the Illustrious [Highness], etc. <note>original: "Durchleuchtigen / &c."</note>; he must faithfully warn of harm to His Imperial Majesty or Princely Grace, avert it, and promote their welfare. He shall have the troops, assigned to him on account of [N.] <note>The letter "N." is used throughout as a placeholder for specific names or numbers to be filled in later</note>, faithfully under his command, and according to his best foresight, use and act boldly against the enemies of [N.]. And if His Imperial Majesty and his war councils consult with him on how he should move, encamp, and act against the enemies, the Captain of [N.] shall consider these proposals and other matters himself, and according to his understanding, advise the best for those or other purposes. If it seems good to him, he shall conduct inspections and reconnaissance. Furthermore, with such movements and encampments, he shall do for [N.] or [N.] and others what seems to him most effective, honorable, and useful, according to the circumstances and the orders of [N.]. In all this, he shall maintain diligent oversight so that he does not lead his commissioned troops to their ruin through contempt or negligence to the detriment of [N.].

The Supreme Captain shall also not take on any special servant or anyone else on his behalf or in his name <note>This clause was likely intended to prevent the common practice of "ghost soldiers," where officers would claim pay for non-existent servants or soldiers</note>.

Furthermore, the Supreme Captain shall be diligent with all industry so that [N.] is not defrauded in the muster <term>Musterung: the formal inspection and counting of soldiers to ensure the rolls matched the actual men present for pay</term> or other matters, and that good order <term>Regiment: here referring to military discipline and the administrative governing of the troops</term> and obedience are maintained among the troops.

And otherwise do all that a pious <note>original: "frommer"; in this era, the word implied being honorable, skilled, and loyal to one's duties, rather than strictly religious</note> captain is obliged and duty-bound to do for his Lordship and Authority.

And if a dispute should arise between the said Captain and the aforementioned [N.] regarding his service and commission, which cannot be settled amicably, such dispute shall be decided by [N.] and [N.] jointly or by the majority, honestly and without any refusal.

And the aforementioned Supreme Captain [N.] shall be commissioned for [N.] months, with thirty days counted as one month. For each month, he shall be given [N.] Rhenish Guilders <term>Rheinischer Gülden: a standard gold coin used for high-level accounting across the Holy Roman Empire</term> for his captaincy. His pay, like that of the other troops, shall begin shortly on [N.] day and be counted into [N.] month.

In addition, he shall be given [N.] Rhenish Guilders per month for his supply wagon <note>original: "Kammerwagen"; a heavy wagon used to carry the captain's personal effects, documents, and administrative tools</note>. He shall take twelve bodyguards <term>Trabanten: personal guards, typically armed with halberds, who served as a status symbol and for protection</term> from among the other simple paid soldiers, each of whom shall be given an additional pay every month for this reason.

To his clerk, three pays; to his interpreter, two pays; to his musicians <note>original: "Spiel"; specifically the drummers and pipers who signaled commands and maintained morale</note>, four pays; to his chaplain, two pays.

Also, if it is necessary to appoint a lieutenant for him, he shall take him from among the sub-captains of the soldiers; for this reason, his pay shall be doubled. However, if the Supreme Captain does not take his lieutenant from other commissioned sub-captains, he shall not be given more than any other such captain. And all these aforementioned articles shall the Captain [N.], or someone on his behalf, be [ordered]...

# Commissioning of the Sub-Captains
### over a company of soldiers.

It is deemed appropriate that each sub-captain <note>original: "Vnterhäuptmann"</note> should lead no more than one company <note>original: "Fähnlein," a military unit of the 16th century, literally meaning "small flag" or ensign</note> of soldiers, and that each company should consist of four hundred soldiers, counted by person.

Also, although it has not been the custom until now, it is considered useful and good that whichever captain has been accepted on behalf of [N.] <note>The letter "N." is used throughout as a placeholder for specific names, dates, or numbers to be filled in later</note> to lead a company of soldiers, a formal commission should be established with him according to the following measures and articles.

Namely, that you shall deliver to each a copy of the Articles of War <note>original: "Artickelbrieff," the code of conduct and legal regulations soldiers were required to swear an oath to follow</note> which the soldiers must swear to, along with what the lordship and the common soldiers are to appoint in terms of offices. Also, it must be specified that their service shall begin on [N.] day and last for [N.] months; and in what manner those who depart with the Supreme Captain's passports <note>formal leave of absence or discharge papers</note> shall have [N.] days counted for their departure, so that they may know how to prepare for the raising of their soldiers.

Secondly, it shall be indicated in the commission of the sub-captains whether they lend money to any of their soldiers for the purpose of raising them <note>hiring and equipping them</note>; in such a case, [N.] shall be owed nothing further for this than what such soldiers would later earn in wages.

Thirdly, if soldiers should depart between musters <note>the formal inspections where troops were counted for pay</note> and the sub-captains take on others in place of those departed soldiers, they shall immediately bring and present them to the Supreme Captain and the Muster-Master, and they shall not enroll them without their permission.

No sub-captain shall have the authority to grant passports to his soldiers or others; this right shall belong solely to the Supreme Captain.

Fourthly, in conducting the muster of the soldiers, they shall not report more soldiers or pay-units to the Muster-Master, nor demand payment for more than were knowingly permitted and inspected in their commission. They shall not seek any advantage or use deceit in this or other matters whereby His Imperial Majesty <note>original: "Key. May." (Kaiserliche Majestät)</note> might be defrauded or burdened. Furthermore, they shall not provide advice, help, or promotion for such fraud in any way.

Fifthly, he shall not hire any clerk or use one for the enrollment of his soldiers or for the muster unless that clerk has first promised and sworn an oath to the Supreme Captain, as a special oath will be ordered for this purpose; a copy of this oath shall be given to each such sub-captain.

Sixth: Whether during the time of such commission <term>Bestallung: a formal appointment or military contract</term> disputes should arise among themselves or with other captains, which cannot be settled amicably with the knowledge of both parties, they shall abide by the final decision of the Supreme Captain and the War Councilors whom he chooses to consult.

Seventh: That he shall faithfully serve [N.] months for which he is commissioned, and shall be following and obedient to the Supreme Captain.

Eighth: That he shall, as far as is possible for him, be diligent with his soldiers so that they faithfully serve [N.] according to the wording of their commission and Articles of War <note>original: "Artickelsbrieffen"</note>, and that they follow the same Supreme Captain. That every such Sub-Captain shall vow and swear to all the aforementioned articles to the person who succeeds [N.], and shall accordingly give and receive letters of commission and formal pledges <term>reversal: a "Revers" was a legal document where an officer formally accepted his duties and the terms of his service</term>.

Each such Sub-Captain shall be given forty Guilders, and in addition, a simple wage for a boy <note>this refers to a servant or page who assisted the officer</note>. He shall also take two bodyguards <note>original: "Trabanten," specialized guards who protected the officer</note> from the paid soldiers; for each of these, he shall be given an additional half-wage, and to all of this, two simple wages for a chaplain. This is done so that one may have more honorable and capable Sub-Captains—which is of no small importance—for such a captain must undergo many expenses because of his captain’s rank. Therefore, if one wishes to have honorable Sub-Captains, it will be necessary to make their pay better; one arrives much closer to the goal this way than by giving them less and letting them seek other advantages to the detriment of [N.].

The soldiers of each Sub-Captain shall be mustered in the presence of the Supreme Captain, shall swear to their Articles, and shall immediately thereafter be given half a month's pay so that they may march out straight away.

# On Mustering Masters.

Likewise, at least two Mustering Masters <term>Musterherrn: officials responsible for inspecting troops to ensure they are present and fit for duty</term> shall be appointed and salaried. It is considered appropriate that one of these should be given as much per month as was previously specified for a Sub-Captain over a company of soldiers, for his own person, his pages, and his bodyguards <note>original: "Knaben vnd Trabanten"</note>.

### Mustering Master’s Oath.

I, [N.], vow and swear to God that for the [N.] months for which I have been appointed by the Imperial Majesty or [N.] for the mustering of the soldiery, I will faithfully serve [N.], warn of harm, and promote their interests. I will also be ready and obedient to the Supreme Captain and will, in every muster of the soldiery, prevent and turn away as much as is possible for me any situation whereby the lordship might be cheated or burdened with improper wages <note>this refers to the common fraud of "ghost soldiers" or "dead pays," where officers claimed wages for soldiers who did not exist</note>. And whatever instructions are given to me in writing regarding such mustering on behalf of the War Lord, those I shall and will follow. Should any dispute arise regarding my aforementioned service that cannot be settled amicably, I will finally abide by the unrefused decision of the Supreme Captain and the War Councilors whom he chooses to consult. So help me God.

Now, this article shall also be placed in the Mustering Masters' standing orders given to them by the War Lord, so that they may follow it as is proper. And as many well-qualified soldiers as the Mustering Masters find in such a muster, they shall provide the Paymaster <term>Pfennigmeister: the official in charge of the military chest or treasury</term> and his Counter-Scribe <term>Gegenschreiber: a clerk who kept a second set of books to prevent embezzlement</term> with the number of their qualified soldiers and their due wages, recorded by their own hand and, in addition, secured with their personal seal. According to these records, the Paymaster shall then give money to the Captain of each company of soldiers, and shall receive from each such Captain a written, sealed receipt <note>original: "Quitanten"</note> for the money he, the Captain, has received from him for his own pay and the due payment of his soldiers.

### Oath of the Paymaster or Customs Clerk, which he shall swear to the War Lord.

I vow and swear bodily by God that I shall and will be faithful and true to N., my gracious Prince and Lord, warn of harm, promote honor and benefit, and faithfully record, calculate with earnestness and diligence all Artillery personnel—how they are appointed, according to the letter of appointment <term>Bestallbrieff: a formal contract or commission defining duties and pay</term> and the register which the Master of Ordnance has signed with his own hand and accounted to me—and pay them, knowingly neither less nor more than what each person's appointment dictates and states. Furthermore, I shall do and refrain from all else that a pious, honest, and upright man is duty-bound to do for his Lord as his superior authority, faithfully and without any deceit; so help me God.

### Appointment of the High Master of Ordnance.

The Master of Ordnance <term>Zeugmeister: the high-ranking officer in charge of all artillery, ammunition, and siege equipment</term> shall be given one hundred guilders a month for his own person.

Likewise, for six equipped horses, ten guilders a month for each; and for his baggage horse, five guilders.

In addition, he shall be provided with a chamber wagon and a kitchen wagon, with the eight horses and persons belonging thereto.

Likewise, he shall be maintained with six bodyguards <note>original: "Trabanten"</note>, with two pay-units <note>original: "Sölde" — a "Sold" was a single share of standard infantry pay</note> for each; one Chaplain, at two pay-units; one Interpreter, at two pay-units.

Likewise, for his page whom he uses for the equipment transport <note>original: "Führrüstung"</note>, one single pay-unit.

For his musicians <note>original: "Spiel" — likely a small ensemble of drummers and fife players used for signaling and ceremony</note>, four pay-units. For his Artillery Scribe, four pay-units.

Likewise, for his Artillery Surgeon, a wagon shall be maintained with four horses, upon which he may carry his medicines and other necessary tools; in addition, he and his servant shall be given 30 Guilders every month. For this, he shall heal all Artillery personnel who are wounded or injured by either enemies or friends. Whatever medical services he otherwise performs in the field camp outside of the Artillery, he may charge for according to the nature of the case and the means of the person. However, he shall be at the disposal of the Artillery before all others, by his oath, healing the poor as well as the rich without further demand, unless something is given to him out of free will.

Likewise, if both the Master of Ordnance, the Clerk, the Paymaster, and also the Surgeon wish to keep a fully equipped horse <note>A "gerüst Pferd" is a battle-ready horse equipped with necessary armor and tack.</note> for themselves that passes inspection at the muster, the Master of Ordnance shall give each of them 10 Guilders every month for its upkeep.

## The Privileges and Perquisites of the High Master of Ordnance, which belong to him.

When castles or towns are won that are fortified, whether they be many or few, and whether they surrendered or were taken by storm, all the munitions belong to the Master of Ordnance <term>Feldzeugmeister: the high-ranking officer in charge of all artillery and siege operations</term>—such as cannons, powder, shot, and everything pertaining thereto. Likewise, all weaponry, armor, spears, and all handguns, and what belongs to handheld weaponry, are his. However, if the War Lord <term>Kriegsherr: the sovereign prince or commander-in-chief</term> should have need of such items or wishes to take them for his own use, the Master of Ordnance shall allow him to redeem them at one-third less than their actual value. And the War Lord shall be satisfied with the fiscal assets, the conquered territories or lordships, or the city’s usual guilders, rents, interests, and other belongings.

## Instructions for the Armory Keeper.

The Armory Keeper <term>Zeugwart: the officer responsible for the storage, maintenance, and transport of the artillery and supplies</term> shall have all the equipment and the entire store of munitions under his command, as he is the one who leads it into the field. It shall be entrusted to him with an inventory, so that the Master of Ordnance can show the War Lord what equipment and other items have been used at a city or castle, or what remains in stock, or what the entire field artillery has consumed in shot, powder, and other expenses, so as to govern further actions accordingly.

Likewise, he shall diligently record how many shot, how much powder, and thus all munitions throughout. Also, every night, he must record what was used that day; and whatever he thinks is running low, he shall tell the Master of Ordnance in secret and reveal it to no one else. Then the Master of Ordnance can report in the War Council that such a shortage should be replenished, or the War Council will know how to conduct themselves otherwise.

And if the Armory Keeper is asked by others whether there is a lack of this or that, he shall always present himself with good cheer and say that he still has enough and that there is no shortage yet, so that less faint-heartedness <note>original: "weiche", literally "softness" or weakness of spirit</note> may spread among the soldiery.

The Armory Keeper shall also, during the march, place the powder wagons every night, or order them to be placed in their designated spot, as indicated by the Quartermasters and Master of Ordnance. After that, the other artillery wagons shall be arranged around them like a wagon-fort <term>Wagenburg: a defensive circle or barricade made of wagons to protect the camp</term>, so that other artillery servants may assist him in ensuring that no one can reach the powder with fire—neither friend nor foe—during an alarm or otherwise.

Every morning, once the drivers have hitched their teams, he shall again indicate to the head driver how he should proceed, so that he keeps the wagons in order. It requires careful management <note>original: "Es wil sein maß haben"</note> to see how each wagon should go, so that one could...

### The Third Part

...tell every ordnance servant: "You will find that wagon there, and the other one there." Many a driver does not know himself what he is carrying, and it would not be good for it to be known at all times. <note>Keeping the specific contents of wagons secret helped prevent theft and ensured that enemy spies or even disgruntled soldiers didn't know where the most valuable supplies—like gunpowder—were located.</note>

The monthly salary for the **Armory Keeper** <term>Zeugwart: the officer in charge of maintaining and distributing military equipment</term> himself is **sixteen Guilders**. For the **Armory Keeper’s Clerk**, **eight Guilders**. For the **Armory Keeper’s Boy**, **four Guilders**.

If the Armory Keeper wishes to keep a battle-ready horse <note>original: "gerüst Pferd"</note> in addition to his own—one that meets the requirements of the cavalry muster—the Master of Ordnance shall provide him with **ten Guilders** a month for its upkeep.

Furthermore, when horseshoes, horseshoe nails, and similar items are needed within the **Artillery** <term>Artalarey: the department responsible for heavy guns and their logistical support</term>, the Armory Keeper shall sell them to those who need them for money, at the price set by the Lieutenants. He must provide an accounting of this and make payment at the proper time. Likewise, he shall provide pikes for money to those who need them, whether they be mounted riders or foot soldiers.

Similarly, he shall provide armor and guns, as well as match-cords, gunpowder, and priming powder to the hand-gunners for money.

Furthermore, should it happen that an assault or a battle is undertaken, or expected, it is customary for a drum to be beaten throughout the camp <note>Beating a drum was the standard way to announce orders or gather troops for distribution of supplies.</note> for all hand-gunners to come to the Artillery to collect powder and lead. At that time, the Captains shall muster their gunners and count how many they have under them or within their company. Each Captain shall then, upon his oath and under his seal <term>Petschier: a personal signet used to authenticate official documents</term>, send the number of gunners to the Master of Ordnance via two Sergeants or his guards. Then, the Master of Ordnance shall have his Clerk copy that note into a register or book and command the Armory Keeper as to how much powder and lead should be given to that Captain for each gunner. Additionally, the Master of Ordnance shall hand over the sealed note from the Captain to the Armory Keeper, so that the Armory Keeper may settle his accounts.

Thus, it is customary to give each gunner one **quarter-pound of powder** and **half a pound of lead**; for if one gives too much, much is lost and wasted in unnecessary shooting. If they then require match-cord or priming powder, it shall also be given in the same manner for day and night, and shall be diligently recorded by the Comptroller.

Furthermore, it is the common custom, when an assault or battle is expected, to have a drum beaten to announce that whoever needs armor should report to his Captain. Armor will then be provided for a reasonable price. And whoever cannot pay for it immediately shall have **one Guilder** deducted at every muster until the armor is paid for. <note>This was a form of military credit, allowing soldiers to be properly equipped for battle even if they lacked the upfront cash to buy expensive plate armor.</note>

Afterward, the Master of Ordnance shall command the Armory Keeper to give the armor to the Captains themselves. That same Captain shall give the Armory Keeper a written acknowledgment under his seal and signature, stating how much armor he has taken. This same handwriting or Captain’s note shall be copied and entered by the Clerk into the Master of Ordnance’s register, as mentioned before.

Thereafter, the Captain shall [distribute] the armor to his soldiers for the money...

And immediately, the **Armory Keeper** <note>original: "Zeugwart"</note> provides a transcript of each **Captain’s** <note>original: "Hauptmañs"</note> acknowledgment regarding how much **armor** <note>original: "Harnisch"</note> he has taken. The Customs Clerk or **Paymaster** <note>original: "Pfennigmeister"</note> who pays the **foot soldiers** <note>original: "Fußknecht"</note> gives the money to the Captains at every muster for the foot soldiers based on those same slips.

Thus, the money for the armor remains in the power of the **War-Lord** <note>original: "Kriegsherrn", referring to the sovereign or prince</note>, and the Master of Ordnance provides his accounting for the armor based on the Captains' acknowledgments.

The same procedure is followed with the long pikes among the soldiers; likewise for the cavalry’s armor, even when they desire knee-guards, small helmets, or forehead-plates <note>chanfrons</note> for the horses. Their Captains must be responsible for this, either through the wages or by making payment with cash. The same also occurs when the soldiers take **hand-guns** <note>original: "Handrohr", early matchlock firearms</note> from the **Artillery** <note>original: "Artalerey"</note>; they are paid for in the same manner as described above.

It often happens that it is publicly proclaimed and announced by drum-beat <note>original: "umbgeschlagen"</note> that any soldier who carries a hand-gun will be given one "thick penny" <note>a higher-value coin</note> more per month, or perhaps half a Guilder more than one who carries a long pike—usually when a battle is expected. However, the Armory Keeper should take the pike from the **mercenary** <note>original: "Landsknecht"</note> if he requests a gun, deducting it from the money as he distributes the pikes among the men.

It happens at times that the trumpeters, by order of the high Captains, sound their horns throughout the camp and make a proclamation through the **herald** <note>original: "Ehrenholt"</note>—especially when a battle is expected—asking which men, noble or common, independent riders <note>original: "Einspennig"</note>, young lords, or soldiers, lack their cuirasses and armor. These will be provided with helmets, knee-guards, and also forehead-plates for the horses from the artillery’s stock to supplement the usual armor they have. This is done so they might remain more protected in the crush of battle, among friends and before enemies. Anyone who accepts this shall have two more Guilders per month for his horse than he had before. The Captains shall also record those who wish to accept this and the armor they have taken.

Furthermore, when the wagons of powder, shot, and other ammunition are lightened, one may dismiss the drivers who wish to leave and let them travel back; those who are best equipped and most reliable should be kept. Unless, of course, a castle or city is captured; it then often happens that guns, powder, shot, and other ammunition are seized, and more horses, wagons, and people are needed than before.

It is also common practice that many of the shot balls are found again, whether they belonged to the enemy or to friends. The Lieutenant should buy them back from those who bring them. Specifically: for a **Large Mortar** <term>Metzen: a heavy, large-caliber mortar</term>, **Basilisk** <term>Basilisken: a heavy cannon named after the mythical serpent</term>, **Nightingale** <term>Nachtigal: a type of long, medium-heavy cannon</term>, **Songstress** <term>Singerin: another melodic name for a specific type of cannon</term>, and **Heavy Cannons** <term>Carthonen: the heaviest class of siege guns</term>—these are the **wall-breakers** <note>original: "Mawrenbrecher"</note>—four Kreuzer shall be given. For **Dragon** <term>Tracken: a medium-weight cannon</term> and **Culverin** <term>Schlangen: literally "snakes," long-barreled cannons</term> balls, two Kreuzer. # Of the Regent’s Book.

...pay money as the **Master of Ordnance** <note>original: "Zeugmeister," the high-ranking officer in charge of all artillery and weaponry</note> has appraised it for him, and record it in his payment register; thus, at the time of every **muster** <note>the formal inspection of troops</note>, he deducts the **Guilders** <note>gold coins</note> until the debt is paid.

In this way, the money for the armor remains in the power of the **Warlord** <note>the sovereign or high commander</note>, and the Master of Ordnance provides his accounting for the armor based on the Captains' acknowledgments.

The same process is customarily followed with the **long pikes** <note>original: "langen Spießen"</note> among the soldiers. The same is done for **cavalry armor** <note>original: "Reuterey Harnisch"</note>; also, if they desire **knee-guards** <note>original: "Kniebuckeln"</note>, **helmets** <note>original: "Helmlin"</note>, or **chanfrons** <note>armor for a horse's head; original: "Stirn auff die Geul"</note>, their Captains must be responsible for it, making payment from their wages or in cash. The same also occurs when the soldiers accept **handguns** <note>original: "Handrohr," early portable firearms</note> from the **Artillery** <note>original: "Artalerey"</note>, being paid for in the same manner as described above.

It often happens that it is publicly proclaimed and announced by drum-beat which soldier carries a handgun; such a man is to be given one **"thick penny"** <note>a higher-value coin</note> more per month, or perhaps half a Guilder more, than one who carries a long pike, usually when a battle is expected. However, the Armory Keeper shall take the pike from the **mercenary** <note>original: "Landsknecht"</note> if he desires a gun, deducting the cost just as when he gives the pikes out among the soldiers.

It happens at times that the **trumpeters**, by order of the high Captains, sound their horns in the camp and have it announced by the **heralds** <note>original: "Ehrenholt," an official messenger or master of ceremonies</note>—especially when a battle is expected—that those who are present, whether **noble or commoner**, **independent horsemen** <note>original: "Einspennig"</note>, **squires** <note>original: "Junckern"</note>, or soldiers, who do not have their **cuirass** <note>torso armor</note> and armor, may be issued helmets, knee-guards, and horse-chanfrons from the Artillery to supplement the armor they already have. This is done so that they may remain more courageous in the press of battle, among friends and before the enemy. Whoever chooses to accept this shall have two Guilders more per month for his horse than he has had previously. The Captains shall also keep a record of those who wish to accept these terms and the armor they have taken.

Furthermore, when the wagons of **powder, shot, and other ammunition** are emptied, one may dismiss the **drivers** who so desire and let them travel home, keeping those who are best equipped and most encouraged. This is unless it happens that a castle or city is won; it often follows that one captures **cannons** <note>original: "Büchssen"</note>, powder, shot, and other ammunition, and thus requires more horses, wagons, and people than before.

It is also common practice that many of the **fired cannonballs** are found again, whether they belonged to the enemy or to friends. The **Lieutenant** should redeem them from those who bring them. Specifically: for a **Mets**, **Basilisk**, **Nightingale**, **Singer**, and **Cannons of Battery** <note>The author lists colorful nicknames for different sizes and types of heavy siege engines. original: "Metzen / Basilissken / Nachtigal / Singerin / vnd Carthounen"</note>—these are **wall-breakers**—four **Kreuzer** <note>small silver coins</note> shall be given. For **Dragon** and **Snake** <note>original: "Tracken vnd Schlangen," types of culverins</note> balls, two Kreuzer. For a **Falconet** <note>a small, light cannon</note> ball, one Kreuzer. This is useful because the balls...

<note>original: "geln", completing the word "Kugeln" from the previous page</note> ...cannonballs are brought back; if there were no reward for it, they would seldom be returned. And when the **Lieutenant** has the cannonballs, the **Armory Keeper** <note>original: "Zeugwart," the officer in charge of the physical inventory of the armory</note> shall receive them from him into the **Artillery** <note>original: "Artalerey"</note> and give the Artillery Lieutenant a receipt for them, under his signature or **seal** <note>original: "Petschier"</note>, stating how many balls he has received. After that, the **Artillery Clerk** <note>original: "Zeug Zollschreiber"</note> or **Paymaster** <note>original: "Pfennigmeister"</note> takes that same receipt and pays the Lieutenant for the balls accordingly. In this way, the **Warlord** <note>the sovereign or commanding prince</note> is once again protected from loss, unless two or three villains are conspiring together.

Afterward, the Armory Keeper takes them and passes these same balls through the **gauges** <note>original: "lehr," a tool used to measure the diameter or caliber of ammunition</note> of the guns he has; whatever he finds to be of the correct size, he adds to his existing stock of balls to be fired again. Whatever is not of the correct size, he sets aside and keeps until he eventually acquires the specific guns that match them.

## The Trench Master’s Commission.

The **Trench Master** <note>original: "Schantzmeister," the officer responsible for fortifications, earthworks, and engineering</note> is to consult with the **Master of Ordnance**, his Lieutenant, and others appointed by the **War Council** to inspect the site and layout of the castles and cities where they intend to encamp. He shall help determine how to best proceed with the equipment, by day or night; whether the ground can support the large pieces—such as the **Heavy Mortars** <note>original: "Metzen," likely referring to Scharfmetzen, a type of heavy siege gun</note>, **Basilisks** <note>original: "Basiliskon," exceptionally long and heavy bronze cannons</note>, and other heavy guns—or not; and whether ditches, bogs, or other watercourses might hinder progress, or if the enemy’s defenses might be driven back or not.

The Trench Master shall also always proceed ahead with several **Tool Masters** <note>original: "Geschirrmeister"</note>, **Trench Laborers** <note>original: "Schantzbauren," laborers or sappers who dug trenches and built fortifications</note>, carpenters, and others, equipped with axes to fell wood and to build bridges, footpaths, and roads. He shall travel ahead with the **scouting parties** <note>original: "Rennenden hauffen"</note> and their guides who are familiar with the countryside and know the paths and ways. They must inspect whether the artillery can pass through or not, and improve the bridges, paths, and roads so that the entire train of equipment may follow more easily. To this end, the Tool Masters know well how to advise and make plans, especially regarding the **narrow passes** <note>original: "Rencken"</note> in the mountains; otherwise, the long **trails** <note>original: "Züge," the rear part of a gun carriage</note> of the cannons cannot manage as well as common wagons that do not have such long trails; for this reason, one must often seek out strange and unusual paths.

The Trench Master’s salary is that of a **Captain’s** pay: forty **Guilders** <note>gold coins</note> a month. For one servant, one unit of pay; for two **guards** <note>original: "Trabanten," personal bodyguards or halberdiers</note>, four units of pay. If he wishes to keep one or two armored horses in addition to his own, that is up to him, provided that they—as stated before—pass inspection with the **cavalry** at the muster and are fit for use in every way like other artillery servants. For these horses, twenty Guilders a month is allotted. This makes a total sum for the Trench Master of eighty Guilders per month.

Furthermore, the Trench Master and the **Captain of the Trench Laborers** shall be responsible for and oversee the making of **gabions** <note>original: "Schantzkörbe," large wicker baskets filled with earth used to provide cover for gunners</note>. To this, the Master of Ordnance shall also assign several artillery servants and **gunners** <note>original: "Büchssenmeister"</note> to ensure that the baskets are made neither too large nor too small, nor too high or low.

## Regarding the Trench Diggers and 
## their Captains.

For the **Artillery** <note>original: "Artalerey"</note>, no fewer than four hundred **trench diggers** <note>original: "Schantzbawren," laborers, often recruited from the peasantry, used for heavy manual labor and engineering</note> should be paid and maintained; one often has great need of them, and they are a very useful people. Before one should do without them or suffer their lack, one should rather have four hundred fewer **soldiers** <note>original: "Knechte"</note> in the troop. They perform much necessary labor that benefits and advances the entire **camp** <note>original: "Läger"</note>. When a field camp is stationary and cannot obtain from the local land such things as bridges, fords, footbridges, and roads, these are made by the trench diggers. What expense does the **Warlord** <note>the sovereign or prince</note> incur for the entire camp? What happens when one must dig trenches in a single night, and it cannot otherwise be done in three? What disadvantage and disruption does that bring to the camp and perhaps the entire war? What might the enemies build against us in that same night, such that one must shoot for five or six days longer than otherwise—indeed, at times, one might even have to retreat in shame, which would not happen if the trenching and shooting were done expeditiously? Therefore, no Warlord should regret the expenses required for the trench diggers; one hour of their work pays back what is spent on them in two months.

Furthermore, the **Captain of the Peasants** <note>original: "Bawern Hauptmann," the officer commanding the trench diggers</note> shall have an armored horse; he is used like any other **ordnance officer** <note>original: "Zeugdiener"</note> and shall be registered as such.

Furthermore, he shall also see to it that the peasants have their **quarters and lodgings** <note>original: "Quartier vnd Losament"</note> right next to the artillery, so that when they are needed, they are close at hand.

The Captain shall also [promise] by his oath that he will neither recruit any peasant nor allow any to leave without the knowledge and will of the **Chief Master of Ordnance**.

By the same oath, he shall also report and not conceal when a trench digger is injured or otherwise dies, or if one or more run away, so that others may be recruited in their place or removed from the **register**. Regarding those who have run away, he is to write to their respective **Lords** <note>their local feudal authorities</note> to deal with them as perjured, faithless people, according to what is proper.

Furthermore, twelve peasants shall always form a **squad** <note>original: "Rott"</note>; they shall choose a **Squad Leader** <note>original: "Rottmeister"</note> from among themselves, and then report that same Squad Leader to the Captain and the **Artillery Clerk**. He will then [work] with his squad separately...

### The Commission of the Trench Master.

The **Trench Master** <note>original: "Schantzmeister," the officer responsible for siege works and engineering</note>—along with the **Master of Ordnance** and his Lieutenant, as well as others appointed by the **War Council**—shall inspect the sites and locations of the **castles and cities** (where one intends to lay siege) and help determine how best to approach with the equipment by day or night. He must judge whether the ground can support the **large pieces** <note>heavy cannons</note>, such as the **Metzen** <note>original: "Metzen," a type of heavy, large-caliber siege gun</note>, **Basilisks** <note>original: "Basilissken," exceptionally long, heavy bronze cannons</note>, and other heavy guns, or not; whether ditches, marshes, waterfalls, or other obstacles might hinder them; and likewise where the enemy's defenses might threaten them or not.

The Trench Master shall also at all times travel with several **equipment masters** <note>original: "Geschirrmeister"</note>, **trench diggers** <note>original: "Schantzbauren"</note>, **carpenters**, and others, to fell wood with axes and to build bridges, footpaths, and roads. He shall move ahead with the **scouting parties** <note>original: "Rennenden hauffen," fast-moving reconnaissance units</note>, using his scouts who are **knowledgeable of the land** <note>original: "Landkünstig"</note> and know the paths and tracks. They must inspect whether the artillery can pass through or not, and improve the bridges, paths, and roads so that the entire **ordnance train** <note>original: "Zeug"</note> can follow more easily. In this, the equipment masters know well how to advise and make plans, especially regarding the **sharp turns** <note>original: "Rencken"</note> in the mountains; otherwise, the **long carriages** <note>original: "langen Züge," the extended frames used to transport heavy cannons</note> of the guns cannot pass as common wagons do, which do not have such long frames; for this reason, one must often seek out strange and unusual paths.

The **salary** <note>original: "Besoldung"</note> of the Trench Master is the pay of a **Captain** <note>original: "Hauptmans Sold"</note>: forty **guilders** <note>original: "Gülden"</note> a month, one pay for a servant boy, and two **guards** <note>original: "Trabanten"</note>. He should have these for himself, provided that—as previously stated—they pass muster with the cavalry and allow themselves to be employed in all ways like other artillery servants. For their salary, twenty guilders a month is allotted. This makes a total sum belonging to the Trench Master’s office of eighty guilders a month.

Furthermore, the Trench Master and the **Captain of the Trench Diggers** shall see to it and ensure that **gabions** <note>original: "Schantzkörbe," large wicker baskets filled with earth used for fortifications</note> are made. To this end, the Master of Ordnance shall also appoint several artillery servants and **gunners** <note>original: "Büchssenmeister"</note> to see that the baskets are made neither too large, nor too small, nor too high, nor too low.

### Concerning the Trench Diggers and
### their Captains.

Likewise, no peasant shall move outside the camp without the Captain’s permission, whether the distance is far or near.

The Ensign, squad leader <note>original: "Rottmeister"</note>, and drummer are all paid the same wage in this unit: that is, four guilders. The total is one thousand six hundred guilders.

He may sell this for his own profit to whomever he wishes. Whether it be hurdles <note>portable frames of woven twigs used for protection</note> or bridges upon which one shoots, it is all his.

### The Master Gunners' Perquisites
->and advantages.<-

The Master Gunners <note>original: "Büchssenmeister"</note> are entitled to certain perquisites <note>original: "Proueit," referring to traditional military benefits or privileges</note>: if a city or castle is forced to surrender or is taken by storm, the cannonballs and powder remaining in the cannons belong to them. Furthermore, any opened or partially used powder kegs must be bought back from them by the Lord at a fair value. To them also belong the largest "storm bells" <note>original: "Sturmglocken," the large bells used to sound alarms during an attack</note> of that castle or city, which are then redeemed from them for a fee. Additionally, the officials of the artillery and the Master Gunners should be given a "gratuity" <note>original: "verehrung," a formal gift or bonus</note> of at least one month's pay. It has sometimes occurred that everyone in the artillery was given a month's pay if the artillery's power alone forced a surrender without the need for a physical storming of the walls.

---

### The Equipment Master's Command
->and Office.<-

The Equipment Masters <note>original: "Geschirrmeister," the officers in charge of transport, harnesses, and wagons</note> usually select carters <note>original: "Fuhrleuten," the drivers of supply wagons</note> who have spent many days on the road and are well known to other drivers; they know best which carters are courageous and have good horses or gear. They are usually sent out by the Master of Ordnance to recruit and hire the wagons, horses, and carters.

The Equipment Masters shall ask the Master of Ordnance every evening at his lodgings <note>original: "Losament," from the French "logement"</note> for instructions, so that they can tell the carters at what time they should hitch the horses, when to wait for the move-out, and in which direction they should point the wagon poles to begin the journey. The Master of Ordnance shall also let them know the destination, but no further than that single day's journey; the Equipment Master must keep this secret under his oath.

# The Third Part

But it is necessary that the **Equipment Master** <term>Geschirrmeister|The officer responsible for the transport wagons, draft animals, and the movement of the army's heavy gear</term> has a certain knowledge of these things; he must always help the **Trench Master** <term>Schantzmeister|An officer in charge of field fortifications, road building, and earthworks</term> prepare the ways and inspect them during the advance, offering advice and speaking on how to construct the bridges and roads. Therefore, much depends on an Equipment Master; they usually understand better than other people what the long wagon trains are capable of during **pivoting maneuvers or turns** <note>original: "Rencktöre oder Kheren"</note>.

They also know better than others what the bridges may or may not carry; furthermore, when they see the ground, they can recognize better than others whether the **cannons** <note>original: "Büchssen"</note> will sink into it or not.

Likewise, when one comes to the mountains, one must take care to see if the **hollow ways** <note>sunken lanes or narrow passes</note> are wide enough for the axles of the large cannons, as they are sometimes made wider than those of ordinary wagons. If it is in the hollow ways, among rocks and stones, then one must dismantle the largest barrels <note>referring here to the cannon barrels</note>; for this, the **fast-carts** <note>original: "Schneller," a lighter type of transport wagon</note>, blacksmiths, carpenters, and wheelwrights are needed to place them onto other, smaller wagons that fit the wheel-tracks, and have them led through piece by piece; afterward, they should be unloaded again and reassembled.

If the hollow ways are made of sand or earth, one may have them cleared by the trench laborers. However, the commanders should always provide the Trench Master and others appointed to the vanguard with people who know the land and are knowledgeable—those who have knowledge of the paths, **fords** <note>original: "Führt"</note>, and roads—for if the advance is false and incorrect, the entire campaign will go astray. For this reason, much depends on **scouts** <note>original: "Kundschafftern"</note>. Yet, the commanders should not reveal the scouts' objective further than a single day's journey, and the scout should keep this secret and reveal it to no one until those he is to lead are gathered together, so that mutiny may be prevented.

This brings two fruits <note>meaning two benefits</note>: first, that the enemies do not know where the campaign will turn next, and are thus less warned of potential harm.

Secondly: That the enemies may be less able to hinder the army camp in its intentions—such as guarding the passes, tearing down bridges, barricading the mountains and hollow ways, **felling trees to block paths** <note>original: "Hölzer zuuerhauwen"</note>, perhaps opening dams and ponds to fill the narrow valleys with water, whereby the cannons and powder might be soaked before one can make it through the fords.

Therefore, it is not good for the enemies to have knowledge of where the "head" of the camp intends to turn; although they cannot always thwart the camp's intentions, it still causes great hindrance until one breaks through, builds, or repairs a bridge, resulting in long delays and significant costs for the camp, and bringing particular benefit and courage to the enemy. Therefore, one should carry the powder in good, sealed barrels that are well-wedged, so that no water may enter when one must drive through swollen waters.

The Master Gunners should also, when crossing, tilt the loaded guns as high as possible at the breech, so that no water can reach the powder bag through the muzzle; additionally, they should seal the **touch-holes** <note>the small hole where the spark ignites the powder</note> with wax. If this is done, it does not matter how deep the muzzle or the forepart of the barrel hangs in the water.

<header>Of the Book of Regents.</header>

Once the roads have been scouted and prepared as far as the **assembly site** <note>original: "Malstat," the designated location for the night's camp</note> where the camp will be established for that night, the **Equipment Master** <term>Geschirrmeister|The officer in charge of transport wagons and draft animals</term> shall ride back toward the heavy artillery. He is to ride ahead of them to show them the ways he has helped prepare, whether by day or by night, so that they may remain on the correct, prepared tracks.

However, if there is more than one Equipment Master—as often occurs—the others, one or two of them, shall remain with the heavy artillery. Should a **cannon** <note>original: "Büchß"</note> sink into the ground or become stuck, or should a hill be so steep that he cannot bring his gun over it, the Equipment Master shall demand horses from other wagons to be hitched in front until the gun can travel over the land again.

Likewise, it is customary to have one Equipment Master for every two hundred wagon-horses.

It is a very good thing for fifty or a hundred spare horses, with their harnesses, to travel alongside the **ordnance** <term>Zeug|The collective term for artillery, weaponry, and military machinery</term>; this brings great benefit to the **commander** <note>original: "Kriegßherrn," literally "War-Lord"</note> and the entire camp. It would be good at times to have these, and to have that many fewer **cavalry horses** <term>Reissiger Pferde|Horses intended for mounted combatants rather than draft work</term>, should one wish to avoid the extra cost. No one knows how much this aids the march except those who have been present for many of them. For this reason: no wagon may or should be left behind, and the order of the **march** <note>original: "Feldzug"</note> must be maintained. Whatever is assigned to the **vanguard** <note>original: "vorzug"</note> must remain in the vanguard; likewise, the **rearguard** <note>original: "nachzug"</note> must leave nothing behind that belongs to the front. Thus, one must keep things moving with the main body as ordered. Otherwise, the entire camp might have to stand still because of a single wagon or cannon.

The Equipment Masters shall also ride or walk ahead of the **carters** <note>original: "Fuhrleuten," the wagon drivers</note>, by day or night, when the artillery is to be led into the **entrenchments** <term>Schanze|Field fortifications or earthworks</term>, to show them the way and to help and advise them so that the guns are correctly guided, positioned, and mounted.

Likewise, when powder, shot, wheels, vessels, or other necessities must be brought into the entrenchment, the Equipment Master shall command the carters responsible for them to do their work, and he shall see to it that this is done efficiently, both in loading and transporting.

The **Master of Ordnance** <term>Zeugmeister|The high-ranking officer in charge of all artillery and technical equipment</term> shall also decree that every month a **muster** <note>an official inspection and roll-call</note> be held by the Lieutenants, **Trench Masters** <term>Schanzmeister|Officers in charge of fortifications and road-building</term>, Equipment Masters, **Ordnance Clerks** <note>original: "Zeugschreiber"</note>, and other ordnance servants. At this time, all wagon-horses shall be inspected, and any that are unfit shall be culled.

And the Master of Ordnance shall perform a "blind" muster, without warning, while the train is on the move. He should have the Ordnance Clerk with him with the muster-roll, along with the Equipment Masters; in this way, he will discover during the driving and hitching of the teams who has his required number of horses and who does not.

# The command, office,
### and labor of the Hoisting Crew.

The Master of Ordnance shall also have eight **Hoisting Assistants** <term>Schneller|Specialized laborers used for heavy lifting and maintaining the artillery</term> who lift the large pieces of artillery from one wagon to another. They shall help grease the guns as often as is necessary and help load and unload the gear and munitions.

## The Office of the Artillery Provost.

The **Artillery Provost** <term>Profos|A military official responsible for discipline, market regulation, and legal matters within the camp</term> has this command: he must ensure, alongside other provosts and **provision masters** <note>original: "Prouiantmeistern"</note>, that the artillery is supplied with provisions. He must procure meat, wine, bread, beer, and other necessities for the artillery, appraise their value, and permit their distribution.

Should any driver sell any provisions before the Provost has appraised the price, the Provost may seize the provisions entirely, in accordance with custom and martial law.

Furthermore, if a seller offers provisions at a higher price or marks them up more than they were appraised, the Provost has the authority to seize all the goods as well as the money earned above the appraised value. This rule is established so that the poor, hungry **soldier** <term>Kriegsknecht|Literally "war-servant," referring to the common infantryman or mercenary</term>—who has no wagon to carry his own food—is not charged beyond what is fair.

The Provost shall also appraise the provisions so that the seller receives a fair and honest profit. This allows him and other sellers to benefit from the camp and makes them more willing to return with more supplies, so that the camp does not have to be abandoned due to hunger.

Furthermore: everyone is permitted to sell provisions for *less* than the appraised price, but never for more. The discount happens naturally; whoever wishes to sell quickly will offer a lower price.

Furthermore: If anyone within the artillery causes damage or violates the prohibitions set forth in the general **Articles of War** <note>original: "Artickelsbrieff," the formal code of conduct for the army</note>, and especially in cases of **criminal acts** <term>Malefitz handel|Serious crimes or capital offenses</term>, the Provost—with the help of the Master of Ordnance’s **guards** <term>Trabanten|Personal guards or life-guards assigned to a high-ranking official</term>—shall seize the offender. He shall chain them to a wagon or put them in irons until further orders from the Master of Ordnance, or whatever other punishment the Master of Ordnance commands for the disobedient in such cases.

Otherwise, he shall also attend to the Master of Ordnance like a guard. Such a Provost is not provided with a **bailiff's assistant** <term>Steckenknecht|A low-ranking assistant to the provost who often performed arrests or corporal punishment</term>. His monthly **pay** <note>original: "Soldt"</note> is—depending on the circumstances—three times the standard rate, and one rate for his servant boy.

Furthermore: If a person within the artillery should die who has no rightful master, and whose name is not found in the war registers—meaning he was not a paid soldier in this camp—the Provost shall inherit whatever is found on him. This applies unless the deceased's father, mother, sister, brother, or wife is present and comes forward...

# The Freedom of the Artillery.

The **Freedom** <note>This refers to the right of sanctuary or asylum within the artillery's bounds</note> and ancient custom in the military practice of the **Artillery** <note>original: "Artalerey"</note> is as follows: should it happen in the field camp, among the soldiery—whether they be of horse or foot, of high or low standing—that one person kills another or wounds them unto death, and this occurs out of a **heated temper** <note>original: "hitzigem Gemüte"</note>, over a game, over debts of money, due to insulting words, or because one provoked the other to fight (provided that such a thing did not happen by a treacherous plot, in a murderous way, or with cold premeditation); if that person should flee into the artillery and seek and desire the Freedom of the Artillery, then he shall be taken into custody neither by the **Provosts** <term>Profosen|Military officials responsible for discipline and arrests</term> nor by others from the artillery. Instead, he shall be allowed to remain with the artillery. 

This is unless the injured party was the perpetrator's own **Captain** <note>original: "Hauptsman"</note> or superior, in which case he would have no freedom within the artillery; likewise, no murderer or traitor [is protected]. The freedom applies only to what happens out of provocation and a heated temper. Whichever lord or Provost acts against this out of defiance commits no less a crime than one who acts against **Imperial Freedom**.

And as a further strengthening of the power of such Freedom, it is established that should an infringement occur by force from the authorities, all **Artillery Personnel** <note>original: "Artalerey Personen"</note> are released from their duty by such an act, and have the full right to march out of the field, to friends or enemies, without any injury to their honor.

However, should a subordinate, of high or low name, act with a defiant hand against such Freedom, he has (without mercy) forfeited his head, and all regiments shall remain in order as before.

The deed may, however, be properly adjudicated before the ordained **Field Judges** <term>Feldrichtern|Military legal officials</term> to determine if it was done presumptuously, suspiciously, by conspiracy, with premeditation, with old threats, in violation of a peace-order, murderously, or from behind, or for other such causes. The judge may then declare with a clear voice what is right; by their judgment, the perpetrator’s Freedom may well be revoked. Then the Colonel, with the knowledge of the **Field Marshal** <term>Feldmarschalck|One of the highest-ranking military commanders</term> and first the Master of Ordnance, acting as an authority, shall have the Provost take the perpetrator and let further proceedings happen as the law allows.

Furthermore, if someone possesses the Freedom with all fairness, and it cannot be revoked, and the camp breaks up, then the perpetrator must stay by a **cannon** <note>original: "Büchssen"</note> within twenty-four paces, or even sit upon it, until the next camp is reached; thus he remains once more with the artillery. This is how far the Freedom extends for the perpetrator; but should he go further away, he must face his own **peril** <note>original: "ebentheüer"</note>.

## Of the Duties of the Common Soldier.

Since the **Articles of War** <term>Artickelsbrieff|The formal code of conduct and legal contract read to soldiers upon recruitment</term> provided to the common soldiers is presented to them, and they are taken into service and sworn an oath upon it—as the standard by which they must conduct themselves in all they do or refrain from doing—it contains and comprises [all their duties]. Therefore, dear reader, for the sake of brevity, I will include the form of the Articles of War here instead of a separate report.

# Articles of War for the Infantry.

These following articles you, **N. and N.** <note>The letter "N" was used in historical legal documents as a placeholder for names, much like "Name Here" or "John Doe"</note>, shall swear to your Colonel and appointed Captain.

Namely, that you shall warn of any harm to our **Gracious Lord** <note>original: "G. H." (Gnädigen Herrn)</note> and promote his benefit, and be willing to be submissive and obedient to **N.** as the **Colonel** <term>obersten Hauptmann|Literally "Highest Head-man," the commanding officer of the regiment</term>, or whoever is appointed in his place. You must also be obedient to the **Ensign** <term>Fähnrich|The junior officer who carried the company's flag (the 'Fähnlein')</term> and the **Sergeants** <term>Webeln|Non-commissioned officers responsible for discipline and organizing the ranks</term> who are set over you from the common men according to the terms of his commission, in all their reasonable business and commands, as befits pious soldiers.

Whatever the Colonel, the other Captains, the Ensign, Sergeant, musicians, and soldiers should command or order you to do, you shall be submissive and obedient to them.

You shall also not demand or require more from **N.**, by whom you are employed, than four **Rhenish Guilders** <note>original: "vier Gülden Reinischer wehrung"</note> per month for a single soldier's pay, with each [guilder] to be paid at the [established] rate, and you shall be obliged to serve thirty days for one month. Likewise, the Ensigns and other officers shall also be satisfied with their promised pay, all according to the sound and content of the **commission** <term>Bestallung|The official document of appointment and contract</term> and **letter of obligation** <term>Reuersbrieff|A formal written promise or bond</term> given by the Captain who accepted each of them.

Furthermore, at the **muster** <term>Musterung|The formal inspection and enrollment of troops where names and equipment were checked</term>, everyone shall give and have recorded their proper first and last names, as well as the town in which or near which they were born. Also, in the muster, no one shall pass under another's name, nor use other advantages, nor help, advise, or promote anyone else in doing so, so that **N.**, by whom you are employed, is not cheated or burdened with unfair and inadmissible wages, in whatever way that might or could happen. Whoever is convicted of this shall not only be considered faithless but also **perjured** <note>original: "meineidig"</note> and shall be held as a rogue; furthermore, he shall be physically punished by the **executioner** <note>original: "Hencker"</note>.

Furthermore, whoever receives money for which he is still obliged to serve, and yet departs without the known permission of the Colonel...

Furthermore, if one or more should shoot or throw his weapon at another, or stab or strike someone while they are down, whether before or after the peace [is declared], he shall be punished in his body.

No one shall start a **mutiny** <term>Meuterey|A collective rebellion against military authority</term>, riot, uprising, or alarm; whoever is unruly or contemptuous in such matters shall be punished without any mercy, according to the judgment of the **captains** <note>original: "Heuptleute"</note>.

Where one or more become aware that someone is practicing treason or other evil deeds against the **War Lord** <note>original: "N."</note> or their appointed supreme captains, he shall report this to the **Provost Marshal** <term>Profosen|The military officer responsible for police duties, discipline, and executions within the camp</term>, who then has the duty to act according to the command of the supreme captain.

### The Third Part

->Catchword: Order<-

No one shall move out of the camp, whether for booty or elsewhere, without his **Captain's** <term>Hauptmann|The commander of a company, responsible for the discipline and pay of his men.</term> knowledge and will, under penalty of corporal punishment.

No one shall hold speech with the enemy without the **Colonel’s** <term>Oberste|The highest officer of the regiment; the term is the root of the modern word 'Colonel.'</term> knowledge, in any way whatsoever.

Item: Where **mounted men-at-arms** <term>Reisige|Heavy cavalrymen, typically armored and serving on horseback.</term> or **foot soldiers** <term>Fußknecht|Infantrymen, often mercenaries such as Landsknechts.</term> lie together in a camp, the foot soldiers shall yield to reasonable necessity so that the mounted men may stable their horses, and they shall tolerate one another.

Item: Each man shall also be satisfied with the place where he is lodged by his **squad leader** <term>Rottmeister|A sub-officer in charge of a 'Rotte' or squad, usually consisting of 10 to 15 men.</term> and **quartermaster**, and shall behave peacefully and kindly.

Item: No one shall fire off [weapons] in dangerous places, especially at night, whether in the camp, towns, or castles, whereby damage might arise or an alarm might be caused, under avoidance of corporal punishment.

Item: No one shall damage any mill, nor shake or tear anything upon it, without the command of the Colonel, under penalty of corporal punishment.

No one shall in any way demand **extortion money** <term>Brandschatzen|The practice of demanding 'fire-tax' from a town to prevent it from being burned down.</term> nor burn [property], nor set fire to any camp, without the Colonel’s command, under penalty of corporal punishment.

Item: Should there be one or more who take flight in the field, or otherwise during battles or skirmishes, then the nearest person who can reach him shall stab him or strike him dead; in this, nothing is forfeited, but rather he shall be given great thanks. But if such a person escapes, he shall be reported to the Lords and Captains so that he may be recognized as a **scoundrel** <term>Schelme|A formal legal status of infamy; a 'scoundrel' lost all legal protections and honor.</term>.

Item: When **provisions** <note>original: "Prouiant"</note> come into the camp or army, no one shall fall upon them or seize them before they are first valued; and where you march into N. or other lands of friends, each man shall pay fairly and damage no one. Also, no one shall sell or take provisions outside the camp, under penalty of corporal punishment.

If the **Provost** <term>Profoß|The military official in charge of the police, arrests, and the execution of sentences within the army.</term> or his men wish to take into custody one or more who are disobedient and have committed a misdeed, no one shall hinder them, nor advise against it, nor interfere, under penalty of corporal punishment.

And if one or more should prevent the Provost or his men from taking a prisoner, and the wrongdoer thereby escapes, then the same person or persons who helped in this shall be punished in the wrongdoer’s stead and be taken by the Provost.

**Toasting** <note>original: "Das Zutrincken" refers to the social pressure of competitive drinking or forced toasts.</note> shall be forbidden in such a way that if someone commits a misdeed while in a drunken state, he shall be punished just as if he were sober; also, no one shall compel another to such drinking.

Item: When a march occurs, no one shall pull out of the order without proper cause. But where one is so disobedient and contemptuous, the Captains or **Sergeants** <term>Webel|Also known as a 'Waibel,' an officer responsible for maintaining the physical formation and order of the troops.</term>, with the help and hand of the common soldiers, shall drive the disobedient back into the order by common force, take their prize, rob them, and take from them what they have.

Where battles, storms, or conquests occur, however they may be, no one shall concern himself with goods or looting, nor [break] out of the order...

No one shall take anything by force against another's will at the playground or during gaming. Furthermore, no German shall play against a member of another nation, so that less ill-will may arise, under penalty of heavy punishment. <note>Gambling was a frequent source of violent disputes in mercenary camps; restricting games to one's own nationality was a common de-escalation tactic.</note>

Every man shall also leave the **executioner** <term>Nachrichter|The official responsible for carrying out corporal and capital punishment. In military life, he was a necessary but socially shunned figure.</term> to his own freedom. <note>This likely means soldiers were forbidden from harassing or interfering with the executioner while he performed his duties.</note>

Item: When an alarm is raised, whether in the field or in the camp, every man shall go to the place where his **banner** <term>Fähnlin|Literally 'little flag,' referring to a company-sized unit of infantry.</term> is assigned, and shall run nowhere else without the permission of the **Captain**.

If one or more should depart from the field camp without a **passport** <term>Paßporten|A written leave of absence or safe-passage document.</term>—which only the **Colonel** <term>Oberste Hauptmann|The supreme commander of the regiment.</term> has granted—everything they own shall be taken from them. Furthermore, they shall be punished by the Colonel in the field; or, if they have escaped, a warrant shall be written after them, and they shall be further pursued for their punishment.

Item: When a company is assigned to the watch, the Captain, **Ensign**, **Sergeant**, nobles, and commoners <term>Edel vnd Vnedel|Literally 'noble and ignoble,' emphasizing that guard duty was a universal requirement regardless of social class.</term> of each company shall march to the watch and keep watch as is proper. Whosoever does not come to the watch, or leaves the watch before the appointed time, shall be punished without any mercy by his comrades with the consent of his Captain, by a **heavy fine** <note>original: "dicken Pfennig"</note> or according to the circumstances of the time and the discretion of the Captain.

No one shall appoint another watchman to stand in his place without the permission of his Captain.

Finally, if one or more do not keep or should break the prescribed Articles, he or they shall be corporally punished according to the judgment of the Colonel. And should anything have been forgotten or not named in the aforementioned Articles which soldiers are bound to uphold, all such offenders shall also be punished according to the decision of the Colonel.

And if one or more has not rightly noted or has forgotten these Articles, he may find this **Letter of Articles** <term>Artikelsbrieff|The formal code of military law and conduct read to soldiers upon enlistment.</term> with N. or the Colonel, and with the **Provost** <term>Schultheissen|A military judge or legal official responsible for maintaining order and administering oaths.</term>; from one of whom he should and may seek further instruction.

---

->Note.<-

This Letter of Articles shall, by order and in the presence of the Colonel, be read clearly by his clerk to the soldiers in the **Ring**. <note>The 'Ring' was the traditional assembly where soldiers stood in a circle to hear laws or voice grievances, a key element of the Landsknecht military democracy.</note> Afterward, the Provost shall administer the proper oath of duty to them.

Item: The common soldiers have the right to elect the common **Sergeants** <term>Webel|Non-commissioned officers responsible for drills and internal discipline.</term> and **Quartermasters** <term>Forirer|Officers responsible for scouting and arranging lodgings for the troops.</term>; however, all other offices shall be appointed by the Colonel on behalf of N.

# The Third Part

...then occurred upon prior public renunciation and warning of honor, etc.

If someone is captured in a public and honest war, and gives his hand <note>original: "gibt seine Hand von sich"; a gesture of surrender and a pledge of one's word</note>, he shall keep his faith as an **upright man**, steady and firm, as befits a prisoner.

If he should fail to do so, and attempted to flee from an **honorable imprisonment** where he was otherwise being treated rightly, thus forgetting his word of honor, the victor may then deal with him through strict confinement or even through a **question of honor** <note>Interrogation or legal proceedings regarding his status and conduct</note> without violating the victor's own reputation.

Conversely, if the prisoner conducted himself rightly, and the victor nonetheless wished to exercise his own caprice upon him through strict imprisonment or interrogation, or other such treatment, then the prisoner is—according to the **laws of war**—released from his duty and oath. Should he then escape the victor's imprisonment, he may with good honor rejoin the war and the **conflict** <term>Bhede|A formal state of private war or feud, often used interchangeably here with the general state of hostilities.</term> in the same manner as before.

If one enemy wishes to ransom another in captivity, no one shall, according to the laws and customs of war, set the ransom higher than one-third of the prisoner's assets. For example: if he were worth three thousand **Guilders** <term>Gülden|A standard gold or silver coin used across Europe, particularly in the Holy Roman Empire.</term>, he should not be ransomed for more than one thousand Guilders; however, whatever was found on his person is also lost to him.

When a field battle is fought, or a castle or town is stormed, the custom or law of war is (unless otherwise ordered in the **Articles of War** <term>Artickelsbrieff|The formal contract and code of discipline read to soldiers upon their enlistment.</term>) that the month's pay begins and ends on that very day; furthermore, a month's **wages** <note>Sold</note> shall be given throughout the entire year, and all captured movable property (except as follows below) belongs to the common **booty**.

To the **Sovereign** <term>Kriegsherr|The lord or prince who has commissioned the army.</term> belongs all provisions found in the garrison, as well as all weaponry, with the exception of the artillery.

To the **Master of Ordnance** <term>Zeugmeister|The high-ranking officer responsible for the army's artillery, ammunition, and engineering equipment.</term> belong specific cannons, powder, and shot, etc. However, the Sovereign must buy these back from him as they can agree, though for no more than two-thirds of their fair value.

Whatever privileges and profits other offices may have has been indicated above.

If a **banner** <term>Fähnlein|The company flag, which represented the honor and soul of a unit; capturing one was a supreme achievement.</term> is won, the **Colonel** <note>Oberste Hauptmañ</note> shall buy it from the one who first brought it into his hands for one month's pay—calculated at the double or triple rate that the soldier receives under his captain. Otherwise, the Colonel shall not take the banner from the soldier.

Furthermore, the same man who won the banner has the full right to walk and stand alongside the other **Ensigns** <note>Fenrich</note> when they march in formation, holding his captured banner in his hand, open and flying. However, he must carry it by the iron tip in his fist, with the pole turned toward the sky, as a sign of a defeated and captured banner. This brings the soldier special honor, for he is recognized by it as having conducted himself honorably against the enemy.

If the enemies must retreat without success from a fortification which they have bombarded (even if only three or four shots were fired into it from heavy pieces), then, as is currently common in the **Articles of War**...

Otherwise, there are many other customs of war; however, in these times and circumstances, they are poorly observed. ### General Rules of Conflict.

No counsel or plan is better than those kept hidden from the enemy before you execute them.

In the event of a lack or depletion of food, or in cases of ambush and surprise, the enemy is always more easily overcome than with the sword; for in battle, fortune holds more sway than valor <term>Mannheit|Bravery or physical strength; in this context, the inherent quality of the soldier versus the luck of the field.</term>.

Good planning, cunning, and prudence are always better in conflicts than mere bravery.

Bravery is better than a great multitude.

Nature gives birth to few bold or stout-hearted men; but through good instruction and leadership, skill <note>original: "Geschicklichkeit"; refers here to the technical proficiency and discipline gained through training.</note> makes many men courageous.

An army <term>Kriegsvolck|Literally "war-people," the collective body of soldiers or troops.</term> grows through labor, but through idleness, it diminishes.

If a spy <term>Kundschaffer|A scout or intelligence-gatherer.</term> of the enemy is suspected to be in the camp <term>Läger|Military encampment.</term>, then on a given day everyone, to a man, should be ordered into their own tents; thus, the spy will be found immediately.

Should you realize that the enemy has become aware of your plan, it is necessary that you change your intentions.

Discuss what *ought* to be done with many; but discuss what you *intend* to do with few, and those the most faithful, or even with yourself alone.

It is a great skill to overcome the enemy more through hunger than with the sword.

In what manner and with what weapons you intend to fight should be kept from the enemy, so that they cannot devise a counter-strategy.

## Of Military Governance.

If you must ever enter into war,

Everything that you must have for it,
So that you do not come to mockery and harm.

## On Good Governance among the Soldiers.

I will leave the aforementioned things be
And go back among your soldiers <term>Kriegßuolck|The collective body of soldiers or the army at large.</term>.
Among them are many a mother's child
Who are not of one mind and spirit.

I have not yet heard it said much
That one has struck an enemy with an internal enemy <note>Meaning: You cannot defeat an external foe if your own army is composed of men who are enemies to one another.</note>.

## On Field Battles.

Should you wish to enter a field battle’s fray,
Observe the terrain and site without delay.
Scout your enemy’s power well in advance,
Neither sparing effort nor leaving their strength to chance.
Contempt has many an army brought low,
So be always mindful of the coming blow.
Take heed if a place can be found in your mind,
Where the enemy cannot attack from behind.
Do not surrender an advantage with ease,
Nor boast of future luck as you please.
The wheel of fortune <note>The *Rota Fortunae* is a common historical metaphor for the unpredictability of fate; the author warns that a commander's luck can turn instantly.</note> is fickle and round,
Turning itself within the hour to the ground.
Arrange your field artillery <term>Feldgeschütz|Mobile cannons or guns used on the battlefield rather than for static sieges.</term> before you begin,
With people who know how to manage the din.
To the enemy, they are worse than a bane,
Especially when their aim is steady and plain.
There is no more terrifying thing on the earth;
Against them, no weapon, armor, or horse has much worth.
If your mounted troops <term>Reisigen Zeuges|A collective term for cavalry or men-at-arms who fought on horseback.</term> are few in number,
Assign a portion to the skirmish <term>Scharmützel|Brief, preliminary fights between small groups of soldiers before the main battle begins.</term>.
Let the others then break forth with force,
Running and striking before the foot soldiers' <term>Fußzeug|The infantry or foot soldiers who formed the bulk of the army.</term> course.
They can withstand the thrust and the blow,
If they have good armor and horses to show.
Among them are many of noble birth,
Who prize their honor above all plunder on earth.
Though others may also be trusted, it’s true,
The nobility offers more to build upon for you.
They consider the honor of parents and kin,
While the common soldier <term>Knecht|Refers to the infantry or mercenaries (like the Landsknechte) who were often seen as less motivated by family honor.</term> thinks little of such within.
Establish your formation in plenty of time,
Better to wait than to rush into the climb.
Trust not so much in your own might and pride,
But keep your eyes on the advantage as your guide.
For the front rank, let those men be sought,
Who have more boldly in previous wars fought.
For as the frontmost hold their ground and stay,
So will those in the rear follow the way.

It argues that the front ranks must consist of experienced, honorable men to ensure the stability of the entire formation.</summary>
