# The Third Part

If the front ranks stand **knightly**,
Then those in the rear will also fight **manfully**.
The strike and sport <note>The original "schertz" (jest/sport) refers here to the "play" of weapons or the initial skirmishing, which sets the morale for the rest of the army.</note> of the first clash
Are the hope and heart of both sides.
It is also quite useful in **battle**
That one forms units called wings <term>Flügel|Tactical formations positioned on the sides of a main army to protect the center or outflank the enemy.</term>.
One may well divide the force into two groups,
Letting them both run to do the enemy harm.
In the field, it is a truly fortunate hour
When one unit <term>Hauffen|A general term for a body of organized troops, similar to a battalion or a tactical "heap" of men.</term> comes to the aid of another at the right time.
Arrange your affairs with the advice of your **captains**,
So that the enemy does not harm you or them.
When it comes to the actual **battle**,
Exhort your people; take heed of yourself.
Even if your dignities should lie low,
You can restore them afterward.
You are not finished by a single battle;
You may endure more than one.
But if you were to perish or die,
Many lands and people would be ruined.
No honor comes from excessive exuberance;
It is often regarded instead as mad **recklessness**.
Much depends on great and many princes;
They should not easily be **rash**,
Risking their bodies in danger,
For from that comes great hardship and sorrow.
If your enemy gives way or flees,
Follow them in good **order**.
Do not let your people break formation;
Let only certain units run after them.
In case the enemy should turn back,
So that you might defend yourself without harm.
If it should then happen
That your enemy is stronger in the field,
And you might suffer a disadvantage in the **battle**,
Do not be ashamed to prevent disaster.
Withdraw to a certain position,
Let anyone say what they will. <note>The author emphasizes that a strategic retreat is more honorable than a foolish defeat, warning the Prince not to be swayed by those who value pride over survival.</note>
Do not risk it lightly through pride or anger;
Be mindful: what is not achieved today may happen tomorrow.
And if you cannot retreat,
Think of how else you might defend yourself.
Dig in, build defenses, use old and young,
Until rescue or relief <term>Entschätzung|The military act of lifting a siege or providing reinforcement to a trapped or surrounded force.</term> comes to you.

Of the Book of Regents.
Dd iiij
<meta>catchword: Have</meta>

Thereto, the wagon-fortress <term>Wagenburg|A tactical fortification formed by circling wagons, famously used by the Hussites, providing mobile defense for infantry and supplies.</term> serves well as a defense,
Just as it was kept in use in times of old.
He who can gain an advantage through reason
Is to be considered a seasoned war-captain <term>Kriegshäuptman|A chief military leader or commander.</term>.
There are many types of advantages on the field;
Conduct and hold yourself according to what you encounter.
One cannot plan everything ahead of time;
One must also act according to how events unfold.
Lengthy deliberation is not always good;
Sometimes one arrives far too late.
It is not only the battle itself that matters;
One must often consider many other factors.
In former times, a King's heart and power depended
Upon the knightly deeds and battles in the field.
In those days, not so many lands were devastated,
Nor were the poor people so ruined and destroyed.
Then, one knew a knight's heart and hand;
Men did not fight from behind walls or barriers.
Since then, a different way has been devised,
And many strong castles <term>Schloß|In this context, a fortified castle or manor house.</term> and cities have been built.
So that it is difficult to draw men out from them;
Behind those walls, both the brave and the cowardly feel secure.
Often, behind a great wall, stands
A wicked and despondent lurker <note>The original "Lawr" (modern: Lauerer) implies someone lying in wait, a scout or a low-status soldier who hides rather than fighting openly.</note>.
One who would not dare speak a harsh word to his face
Now steals the life of a knightly man.
Only with great labor, expense, and loss
Can one manage to drive the scoundrel out.

### On Siege and Storming.

Besiege castles and cities in their proper season;
Winter provides no progress for such things.
Take note of the area surrounding the city;
Observe what defenses, towers, and moats <note>The text uses "Graben" which could mean a ditch, trench, or moat.</note> it possesses.
Examine the situation of the waters—
Whether they are bottomless, narrow, or broad.
Whatever you wish to storm "from the stirrup" <term>Stegreiff|To do something "from the stirrup" means to do it immediately or spontaneously without extensive preparation; a surprise attack.</term>,
Do so in haste, secretly, and quietly.
For this, there is no better help or counsel
Than having understanding and intelligence <note>Original: "kundschafft." In a military context, this refers to reconnaissance or gathered information.</note>.
Attack at the right time when they are unwarned;
Once prepared, do not delay long or stay far off.

# The Third Part

Pay close attention and be diligent,
To first tear down the defenses.
<margin>3</margin>
With your artillery, fireworks, and lead <note>The "lead" refers to leaden bullets or cannonballs used in early modern siege warfare.</note>,
Force them so that they cannot endure it.
Upon the wall, use your hand-guns <term>Hakengeschütz|Literally "hook-gun," an early heavy firearm or arquebus with a metal hook under the barrel to hook onto a wall or rest, helping to absorb the recoil.</term>,
Drive them from their positions; it will bring you benefit.
Pay good heed to all your equipment yourself,
Lest the ladders be made too short.
If they are, much will be neglected,
Costing both people and goods—let whoever will, take note.
Now, if God gives you the grace of victory,
So that you prevail in the assault,
And you become master of the castle or city,
Spare those who are not actually bearing arms.
Do not let them be slaughtered,
Be they woman, child, or men <note>The author distinguishes between "wehrhafft" (those capable of defense/combatants) and civilian men who should be spared.</note>.
Do not shed innocent blood,
For it rarely brings any good.
If you take what is his by force,
Another then becomes your subject.
For where mercy shines alongside power,
That praise and honor usually endure long.
In all things give the honor to God,
From whom luck and victory come.
I would still have much to write of war,
But will let it be for this time.

## Examples to follow the Ancients.

One thing, however, I advise you faithfully;
If you follow me, you will not regret it.
With diligence, read of the deeds of the Ancients,
Their manly actions, honor, and standing.
Whereby they, for themselves and their lineages,
Have established an eternal name.
Adorning their glory and their kin,
So that they shall no longer be forgotten.
Follow after them—that is my teaching—
Thus will your praise, luck, victory, and honor grow.

Of the Book of Rulers.

# That Soldiers, When Battle
## Is Imminent, Should Diligently
### Commend Themselves to God
### and Call Upon Him for Victory and Fortune.

# The Seventeenth Chapter.

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial 'I' depicting classical figures and foliage.</image-desc>

I have written more in this third book about military matters than I would have liked, or than I had intended; however, since I have already entered into the subject—and although war is such a thing in which (as has been heard) not much good is to be found or hoped for, and it is a business into which one is sometimes forced out of necessity, since, according to the common proverb, "No one can have peace any longer than his neighbor wants"—nevertheless, soldiers should not be so devilish, wild, and crude that they fail to commend themselves to Almighty God with the highest earnestness through diligent prayer when battle is imminent. For in such a moment, no one can be assured of their life, and often one is taken away by the cruelty of the artillery <note>The original German "Geschützes" refers to the heavy cannons and firearms that were revolutionizing warfare in the 16th century.</note> before he is even aware of it. This was done with great earnestness by our ancestors, who would first prostrate themselves <note>original: "einen Fußfall gethan," a physical act of kneeling or lying face down in prayer.</note>, even though they did not have such light <note>The author, likely writing from a Protestant perspective, suggests that while his ancestors were devout, they lacked the "true light" of the Reformation's teachings.</note> that they knew how to call upon God rightly and in faith; instead, one commended himself to the Mother of God, another to the Knight Saint George, and thus one to this saint and another to that one. Furthermore, no Prince or Supreme Commander should rely on his own power and great might, but should fear God and call upon Him for grace and victory. For it must truly come from God, as David says at the end of the 60th Psalm:

> Who will lead me into a strong city? Who will lead me into Edom? Will You not do it, O God, You who have cast us off and do not go out with our armies? Give us help in our distress, for the help of man is useless. With God we will do great deeds; He will tread down our enemies.

In addition to this, we have many beautiful examples here and there in the Holy Scriptures, some of which I must recount here because they are so finely and briefly expressed—as much confidence is worth little when it comes to the clash of battle—so that soldiers may see themselves reflected in them.

Firstly, the Scripture says in 2 Chronicles 16 <note>original: "2. Paral. 16." This refers to Paralipomenon, the Latin name for the Books of Chronicles.</note> that the Prophet Hanani stepped before the King and spoke to him:

> Because you have relied on the King of Syria and have not relied on the Lord your God, the power of the King of Syria has escaped your hand. Were not the Moors <note>original: "Moren." In 16th-century German Bibles, this typically referred to the Cushites or Ethiopians.</note> and Libyans a great multitude, with many chariots and horsemen? Yet the Lord gave them into your hand when you relied on Him. For the eyes of the Lord look upon all lands, that He may strengthen those who are with Him with their whole heart. You have acted foolishly; therefore, from now on you shall have war.

Secondly, there follows a prayer of Asa, King of Judah, from 2 Chronicles 14, as follows:

## Exhortation of Judas Maccabeus to the People
### 2 Maccabees 3 <note>While the text cites 2 Maccabees 3, this narrative of the battle against Seron is found in 1 Maccabees 3.</note>

Then Judas marched against him with a small company; but when they saw the enemies, they said: "We are few, and moreover we are weary from fasting; how should we be able to fight such a large and strong company?" # The Fourth Part of the Ruler’s Book.

## On the Governance of Cities.

### Preface.

Until now, I have related the examples and histories which pertain to great princes and lords. And although I did not originally undertake this work for that purpose, nor was it my intent or opinion to broaden my thoughts so far—for I know what a great thing it is, and how difficult it is, to advise such great leaders, especially when they are young. As it is said, *It is difficult to give counsel to a king.* <note>original Latin: "Difficile est Regi dare consilium."</note> But because it has turned out this way, it goes for me like that potter of whom *Horace* <note>The Roman poet Horace in *Ars Poetica*.</note> writes, who wanted to make a wine jug, but when the wheel spun out, a water pitcher came of it instead. <note>A metaphor for a project that changes its form or scope as it is being created.</note> Therefore, I have let it run its course and have had to follow this order as it presented itself, until I have finally come to the **governance of cities**. In this, I only intend to set down and indicate what seems most necessary to me, as I have done until now; for who can think of and record everything that is needed here? Moreover, it is the way of the world that every house has its own particular governance, and much more so does every city. Therefore, it would be a folly to establish such a city law or <term>Regiment: In this context, the word refers to the system of administration, governance, or "rule" of a municipality rather than a military unit.</term> to which all cities must conform. And just as it would not be proper for me, as a private person, to do so, I also confess that I am not sufficiently qualified for it. But for the remembrance of the most important points, I thought in my simplicity that it would not be bad to pay good attention in cities to the following examples, as I have found them in histories. ## The First Chapter.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial letter 'N' depicting a merman or triton blowing a conch shell amidst scrollwork foliage.</image-desc>
It was not in vain, nor without specific reason or consideration, that the ancients—who were nonetheless pagans—held rights and laws, or statutes, to be sacred. For truly, it is in itself a very precious and holy thing, these laws and statutes in a city or a land, as it is through them that human society, lands, and cities must be governed, protected, and preserved. This, Demosthenes <note>An influential Greek statesman and orator of ancient Athens.</note> expresses and confirms with a beautiful maxim when he says: The law is the soul of the city; for just as the body collapses when the soul departs, so too is a Republic finished when its laws are removed. <note>original Latin: "Lex vrbis anima est, Nam quemadmodum corpus decedente anima concidit, ita sublatis legibus actum est de Republica."</note> The law is the soul of the city; for as the body falls away when the soul leaves it, so too does a city fall apart when it has no law, or loses its laws. Therefore, a lord cannot do better for his subjects, cities, and lands than to give them good laws and order, which are in accordance with reason, honor, and equity, and to ensure they are faithfully upheld. For it is impossible that they should not improve thereby, and that everything there should proceed rightly and well. And there is a great difference between those who have evil and worthless statutes and those who have honorable and good ones, as can be seen from the following examples.

Herodotus <note>Known as the "Father of History," a Greek historian from the 5th century BCE.</note> writes that the city of Sparta of the Lacedaemonians <note>Another name for the Spartans.</note> was initially quite disordered and poorly provided with laws; because of this, the citizens therein led a very wild and strange life, and had no trade or dealings with anyone outside. From this, it followed that they could grow neither in manpower nor in wealth. For where such a wild and disjointed <term>Regiment: The system of governance or administration.</term> exists in a city, things cannot go well, nor can any welfare or prosperity be at hand; instead, the citizens must perish, one running here and the other there. Especially when they do not go out, trade, and work, but lie at home behind the stove, or go walking in the market, or lie in the beer houses; for this reason, no one easily turns toward such a place.

But after Lycurgus <note>The legendary lawgiver of Sparta who established the military-oriented reformation of Spartan society.</note> came to the Lacedaemonians, and as a wise, clever, and experienced man saw such disorder, he abolished it with gentleness, furnished the city with good laws and order, and established a proper <term>Policey: In this historical context, "Policey" (from the Greek *politeia*) refers to the entire civil order, administration, and public welfare of a community, rather than just modern law enforcement.</term>, according to which the citizens had to conduct and hold themselves. Consequently, they immediately thereafter increased in wealth and

# The Fourth Part

It should be known, however, that the Lacedaemonians <note>The citizens of Sparta.</note> had no written laws or statutes; instead, they followed whatever Lycurgus <note>The legendary lawgiver of Sparta, who established the city's famous communal and military systems.</note> had once commanded and imposed upon them. He strictly required that these be observed, from which it can be concluded that the laws were not long, nor were there many of them. Rather, they were created in such a way that they could be easily understood and remembered. Indeed, laws should be brief and not invite much dispute. Such laws are the Ten Commandments <note>original: "zehen Gebot"</note>, which were given to us by God Himself; likewise, the Laws of the Twelve Tables <note>The foundation of ancient Roman law, originally inscribed on twelve bronze tablets.</note>. Nowadays, one finds every book filled with laws, along with various interpretations and explanations. Furthermore, every land and every city has many and varied statutes, which are sometimes more harmful than useful or advantageous to a city. Nor is any earnestness applied to ensure they are strictly followed, even though everything depends on this, as shall be heard hereafter.

And although some rulers sometimes act as if they wish to hold firmly to their laws, statutes, and ordinances, it lacks endurance and stability. As soon as the law would affect them or their own associates, they find a different "gloss" <note>A term for a legal interpretation or explanatory note, often used here to imply a "loophole" or creative excuse.</note> and claim the meaning is not the same as if it had affected someone else. They act just like that judge who, when one of his neighbors came to him and said, "Lord Judge, my cow has gored yours to death," the judge replied, "If that is so, you are obligated to pay me for the cow." But when the neighbor reversed it, saying, "Lord Judge, your cow has gored mine to death," the judge replied, "Oh, that is a different case," etc.

And since I mentioned the Ten Commandments <note>original: "Decalogo"</note> above, for further explanation of these matters, it should be briefly known: First, that all rulers, when they wish to make other laws alongside the Decalogue, should strive to frame them in such a way that they do not contradict or oppose Divine Law. Second, that rulers should be nothing other than a living voice of that same Divine Law. For although the "light of nature" shines in the hearts of men and teaches them to some extent what they should do—and that they are bound to keep God’s commands—the magistrate <note>term: Magistrate: Civil authorities or government officials responsible for upholding the law.</note> must nevertheless remind the people of this and wake them up through his command and voice.

Third, because men are not governed by laws alone, but some are so unruly that they despise the teaching of the law and show themselves disobedient and resistant. Therefore, God has commanded and charged the authorities to punish such transgressors of the laws and statutes. And it is certainly true that God Himself punishes such criminals as murderers, adulterers, tyrants, and the like; yet He usually employs the authorities for this, through whom He allows such punishments to be executed. Thus, God punished the shameful and unchaste life and other vices of Antony <note>Mark Antony, the Roman general and ally of Cleopatra.</note>, but He did so through Emperor Augustus. And what...

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the necessity of law and the role of the ruler as its enforcer. What would magistrates and authorities be, what would courts and justice be without punishment, other than a poor reward? For this reason, many praise the saying of Aeschines <note>An ancient Athenian orator and rival of Demosthenes.</note>, which Demosthenes included in his own speech, where he says:

> A city that has no sinews <note>The "sinews" refer to the strength or enforcement power of a state.</note> against the wicked has no value. <note>original: "Nihil valerere ciuitatem, quæ neruos non habet aduersus facinorosos."</note>

So too says Pomponius <note>A Roman jurist of the 2nd century AD.</note>, in the second law of the *Digest* regarding the origin of law, that laws are of little value in a city unless there are those who put them into execution. <note>original: "parùm valeant in ciuitate esse iura, nisi sint qui ea mandent executioni."</note> That is: Where there is no **punishment**, all laws are in vain. Accordingly, all kinds of lawsuits have been devised according to the nature of the crime; from this, it should be noted that lawsuits—both **criminal** <term>peinlich: referring to corporal or capital punishment</term> and **civil**—are not the least part of the law. It is for their sake that authorities were ordained and given to the human race. They are called not only *Guardians of the Laws* <note>original: "Custodes Legum"</note>—that is, protectors of right and the statutes, so that they preserve and keep the teaching of the law in books—but also so that they use **earnest punishment** against transgressors. Through this, the hearts of men are stirred and moved toward virtue, and deterred from shameful vices.

Therefore, Plato wishes that those who are placed in charge of preserving the laws should be most incorruptible. <note>original: "Ideo Plato vult, Eos qui seruandis legibus præfecti sunt, incorruptissimos esse."</note> That is: Such people who are to preside over justice and the laws must be without any failing and beyond reproach, according to the opinion of Plato. Therefore, a pious prince should punish no one more harshly or earnestly than those who do not righteously uphold the laws and justice.

A prince, however, should be the first and foremost protector of the law, and above all things, he must guard himself against misusing good laws, lest it be said of him: *The highest law is the greatest injustice.* <note>original: "Summum ius, summa iniuria." This proverb warns that the strict application of the letter of the law without regard for equity or common sense can result in deep unfairness.</note> Rather, every prince, ruler, and lawmaker should take to heart and remember the manly deed performed by **Charondas of Thurii** <note>original: "Charondas Tyrius"; a celebrated lawgiver of Sicily and southern Italy.</note>, who reconciled his citizens when they were rebellious and divided even unto bloodshed. To prevent such great danger and ensure it would not happen again, he issued a law or command for the good of the common wealth, which everyone, without exception, had to keep. Namely: whoever entered the public assembly and councils girded with a weapon or a sword should be immediately stabbed and struck dead. It happened, however, not long afterward, that he had been out in the fields and called the citizens together for urgent matters. He went to them, keeping his sword at his side just as he had come from the field.

But the man standing closest to him said, "You have issued a law that no one should come here with a sword, and yet you do not keep this law yourself?" Charondas answered, "Since I have broken my own law, I will also confirm it with my own blood." With that, he drew his sword, fell upon it, and stabbed himself to death. He did this despite the fact that he could have offered the excuse that he had been in the field and had done it without intent, evil meaning, or contempt. Yet he was so upright that he would suffer no gossip that he had made a law and failed to keep it himself. For he undoubtedly understood that just as the authority rules over and has command over the people, so...

**The Fourth Part**

...laws also stand over the authorities. It was aptly said by **Cicero**: *The magistrate is a speaking law, while the law is a silent magistrate.* <note>original: "Magistratum legem esse loquentem, Legem autem mutum Magistratum."</note> That is to say: The authority is a law that speaks, but the laws are a silent authority.

Fourthly, rulers should also know that although they are bound to hold the **Ten Commandments** <note>Also referred to as the Decalogue.</note> as the highest, most prominent, and best law—as it certainly is in itself—and in truth no one, no matter how wise or clever they may be, will ever be able to create anything better, for God Himself wrote them with His own fingers, detailing how one should conduct oneself toward both God and fellow human beings; yet they nevertheless shall and may create other laws, provided that these are not contrary to the **Decalogue** or the Ten Commandments (as mentioned above) but rather explain and interpret them. To provide an example: When God says, "Thou shalt not steal," He implies that not all things are held in common, but rather that the ownership of goods should be distinct; and if someone should attempt to alienate another from their property, they would thereafter have committed a theft.

However, since the **Decalogue** only mentions property in a general sense, and yet there are many ways and legal means by which people come into such property and acquire it, it was necessary for the magistrate and the legislators to write specifically and in detail about these things, and by what means one can make something one's own property. For this reason, **contracts** were invented, such as buying, selling, exchanging, and the like. It is also expressed therein which contracts are valid and which are invalid. For if I give someone a pledge with the agreement that if I do not redeem such pledge by a certain time, it shall be forfeited—such a contract is invalid and rejected by the law. <note>original: "C. de Pactis pignorum & lege commissoria." This refers to the Justinian Code regarding pacts of pledges and the 'lex commissoria,' a clause that automatically voids a contract under certain conditions.</note>

From this it now appears that the magistrate and rulers are bound to provide the cities and lands with good and capable laws, and that these same laws must not be contrary to the Divine commandments. The subjects should also observe them with diligence, as **Empedocles of Akragas** <note>A Greek Neopythagorean philosopher from Sicily.</note> rightly said: *Citizens must fight for their laws no less than for their city walls.* <note>original: "Ciues non minus oportere pugnare pro legibus, quam pro mœnibus."</note> This is because without laws, no city can be maintained in its prosperity, whereas it can indeed survive without walls and fortifications. Yet **Erasmus** <note>Desiderius Erasmus, the famous Renaissance humanist.</note> provides a fine teaching regarding the establishing of laws when he says:

> In establishing laws, one must first and foremost take care that they do not smell of the treasury’s profit <note>The "fiscus" refers to the state treasury.</note>, nor should they be directed toward the private advantage of the elites, but everything should be referred to the public utility. Otherwise, it will not even be a law, unless it be just, unless it be equitable, and unless it consults the public good. <note>original: "In condendis Legibus illud inprimis cauendum, ne quid oleat fisci lucrum, nec ad priuatam procerum commoditatem, sed ad publicam vtilitatem referantur omnia. Alioqui ne lex quidem erit, ni iusta sit, ni æqua, ni publicis commodis consulens."</note>

That is: When one wishes to make and establish laws, one must primarily prevent them from being directed toward private gain or "smelling of the treasury," but rather everything must be set for the common good. For it cannot be a law unless it is consistent with right or equity and established for the benefit of the common good. It is also to be considered here that several laws which are...

People should not regard this as something that happened by chance, but rather that it is God’s will, provided we strive for good laws and order so that people are kept in check and do not disturb human society.

And many examples could be told here of those cities which, through good laws and order, grew into great power and prosperity. However, since this would almost require an entire separate book—indeed, I fear it could not all be contained within one book—I will therefore only briefly point out a few with my finger, as it were, in which the reader may see a reflection and which rulers may follow, so that they might likewise provide their own cities with good, Christian, and sensible laws, and strictly uphold them.

Among many, the ancients primarily praised the <term>Lacedaemonians</term> <note>The Spartans.</note> and the Athenians among the Greeks, and the <term>Romans</term> among the Italians. It cannot happen otherwise where there is no compulsion and the wicked are not punished. Therefore **Plato** also said:
> Whatever pious people existed in Athens had to be exceptionally pious of their own accord, since no one was accustomed to being held to virtue by force, but rather everyone lived as they pleased.

There was also a time when a man from **Sparta** returned home, and someone asked him how he liked those from Athens. To this he gave this answer: That they pleased him thoroughly and were all to be praised. At this, the other man marveled and asked the reason for his answer, to which he further said: This was the reason—that in Athens, nothing was considered a shame, nor would anything be held against a person.

Undoubtedly, the <term>big shots</term> <note>original: "grossen Hansen," a period idiom for powerful or arrogant men of high status.</note> and the powerful did and acted as they pleased, just as even today they shy away from no command or law and force their way through all statutes. Concerning this, **Anacharsis the Scythian** spoke very wisely:
> Laws are like spiderwebs, in which the weaker creatures get caught, but the stronger ones break through. <note>original: "Leges aranearum telis esse similes, in quibus infirmiora animalia hærerent, valentiora perrumperent."</note> Thus laws constrain the humble and the thin, but are violated by the powerful with impunity.

That is: The laws are like spiderwebs; for just as the spiderwebs hold the small flies but the large hornets tear through them, so too do the laws seize the poor and the lowly, but spare the great. **Stobaeus** attributes this to **Zaleucus**, the lawgiver of the <term>Locrians</term>, and says:
> Laws are like spiderwebs. For if a fly or a gnat falls in, it is held fast; but if a wasp or a bee falls in, they tear the web and fly away. So it is also with the laws. <note>original: "Leges aranearum telis similes esse. Nam si musca aut culex inciderit, retinetur: si vero vespa aut apes, disrupta tela auolant. Ita se res habet etiam in Legibus."</note>

that such a thing must henceforth have been wrong. From which it followed—because the Locrians <note>The Locrians were an ancient Greek tribe; their lawgiver, Zaleucus, is credited with creating one of the first written Greek law codes, famous for its rigidity.</note> held so stiffly and firmly to their laws—that no one thereafter dared to undertake or propose a new statute or bring it to the floor unless he had a noose around his neck. # The Fourth Part

It has been said / that things go better in a city / which does not have overly magnificent laws / but where they are strictly upheld / than in a place / where many new, good laws are made daily / which no one bothers to enforce with any seriousness. With this, Plato also agrees / when he says: <note>original: "Hunc esse optimum & præstantissimum ciuem, qui summam gloriam in ciuitate ducat esse, non triumphos, non vllas victorias, sed vincere alios diligentia parendi legibus."</note> *That man is the best and most excellent citizen / who considers the greatest glory in the city to be / not triumphs / nor any victories / but to surpass others in the diligence of obeying the laws.* That is: We regard him as the most excellent and best citizen / who is so minded / that he holds the welfare of the city and the preservation of the law higher / and seeks to obey the laws more diligently than others / rather than seeking any triumph.

Here one might ask / whether one must be so bound to the statutes and laws / that in a case of necessity one might not deviate from them / and, according to the opportunity of the time and current circumstances / might not be permitted to make new laws? To this it is answered / that this opinion does not apply to the <term>Rights</term><note>Referring to the body of established jurisprudence.</note> of all laws / that have ever been given / excluding what God Himself and Nature have ordained. All other laws should and may be ordained / abolished / increased / diminished / and changed according to the opportunity of the time and circumstances / especially / when one finds cause to do so. Thus writes Gellius <note>Aulus Gellius (c. 125 – 180 AD), a Roman author known for his "Attic Nights," a collection of notes on grammar, philosophy, and history.</note> in Book 20, Chapter 1: <note>original: "Non enim profectò ignoras, legum opportunitates & medelas, pro temporum moribus, & pro rerum publicarū generibus, ac pro utilitatum præsentium rationibus, proq́; vitiorum, quibus medendum est feruoribus, mutari atque flecti, neque vno statu consistere, quin vt facies cœli & maris, ita rerum atque fortunæ tempestatibus varientur, &c."</note> *For surely you are not unaware / that the timeliness and remedies of laws / according to the customs of the times / and the types of commonwealths / and the reasons of present utility / and the heat of the vices which must be healed / are changed and adapted / and do not remain in one state / but just as the face of the sky and the sea / so are they varied by the storms of circumstances and fortune, etc.* That is: For you will surely know / that the laws are invented no differently than medicine / according to the opportunity and welfare of the common good / and solely to encounter the prevailing vices / and must therefore be judged and changed accordingly / and like the weather in the sky / they must have their changes.

Thus the Law of the <term>Twelve Tables</term><note>The ancient legislation that stood at the foundation of Roman law.</note> / concerning injuries / was changed. Therein it was provided / that if one person injured and insulted another / he had to give him twenty-five <term>shillings</term><note>The German text uses "Schilling" to translate the Roman "as", a small unit of currency.</note> as compensation / just as the <term>Saxon Law</term><note>The 'Sachsenspiegel' or Saxon Law, one of the most important law books of the German Middle Ages.</note> still ordains to this day / that one should give thirty shillings to a person for their shame and injury.

But when it happened in Rome at one time / that a man named Lucius Neratius / a wicked fellow / who took pleasure only in being vexatious to people / and inflicting shame / had a servant carry a purse of money behind him. Whenever he encountered someone / he struck them in the face / and then commanded the servant / to give them twenty-five shillings. Therefore Favorinus says in Gellius, in the aforementioned book: <note>original: "Quis erit tàm inops, quem ab iniuria facienda viginti quinq; asses deterreant? Itaque cùm eam legem Q. quoque Labeo vester in libris, quos ad 12. Tabulas conscripsit, non probaret, inquit, L. Neratius fuit egregiè homo improbus, atq; immani vecordia. Is pro delectamento habebat, os hominis liberi, manus suæ palma verberare. Eum seruus sequebatur crumenam plenam assium portitans: & quemcunq; depalmauerat, numerari statim secundum 12. tabulas, 5. & 20. asses iubebat."</note> *Who will be so poor / that twenty-five pennies would deter him from doing injury? Therefore, since your Quintus Labeo also did not approve of that law in the books he wrote on the Twelve Tables, he said: Lucius Neratius was an extraordinarily wicked man, and of immense madness. He took it as a delight to strike the face of a free man with the palm of his hand. A servant followed him carrying a purse full of coins; and whomever he had slapped, he ordered twenty-five pennies to be counted out immediately according to the Twelve Tables.*

<header>Of the Book of Regents.</header>

*Propterea, Prætores, postea hanc abſoleſcere, & relinqui conſuerunt, iniurijs æſtimantur recuperatores ſe daturos edixerunt.* <note>original: "For this reason, the Praetors later allowed this [law] to fall into disuse and be abandoned, and they proclaimed that they would appoint judges to assess the damages for injuries." Quoted from Aulus Gellius.</note> That is: Dear Lords, who is of such small means that he would not dare to give someone a slap in the face for the sake of twenty-five shillings? Therefore, Labeo <note>Marcus Antistius Labeo (d. 10/11 AD), a highly influential Roman jurist.</note> in his book written on the Law of the Twelve Tables <note>The foundational 5th-century BC legislation of Roman law.</note> could not praise the fact that Lucius Neratius, a wicked rogue, out of sheer wantonness, struck people in the city here and there on the mouth. He had a servant follow him with a bag of money, and whenever he had given someone a blow to the jaw, he had him handed twenty-five shillings, with which the victim had to be satisfied. Because of this, the Praetors abolished such a law. Since the situation is just the same with the **Saxon Laws** <note>Referring to the *Sachsenspiegel* or related regional German legal codes.</note> in this case, where it is customary to award thirty shillings for one's shame and **injuries**, which is quite burdensome to honorable people—as I have often seen, heard, and experienced. Therefore, it is no small wonder that this is not also abolished and that people are not permitted to **estimate** <note>To legally assess the financial value of damages based on the victim's status and the severity of the act.</note> their insult according to the capacity and permission of the **Imperial Rights** <note>The Roman Law (Corpus Iuris Civilis) as applied in the Holy Roman Empire, which allowed for flexible damages.</note>, since a person can have nothing better or dearer on earth than their honor and good reputation, which is weakened and cut off by such **slanderers**. It also happens that one person murders another because of such insults and injuries, which would otherwise be avoided if they were punished in earnest.

This is even more surprising: that such slanderers are still aided, and the Saxon law is softened so that one does not become **infamous** <note>original: *infamiam*; a legal status of disgrace that stripped a person of certain civil rights.</note> when the thirty shillings are to be awarded by judgment and law. For if he is to avoid infamy, he is advised to place the thirty shillings in court before the sentence is passed, or to appear through a <term>procurator</term><note>A legal representative or agent acting on behalf of a party in court.</note> and not in person. That, I believe, is simply giving people cause to insult and injure others—opening the doors and windows to it. These are the fruits of self-interest, in which the whole world is now drowned, so that from the highest to the lowest, almost no one considers the welfare of the **common good**, but only what each person’s own necessity requires. Therefore, things are going so poorly everywhere that both Lords and subjects are nearly ruined by it.

->Enough of that.<-

# That idleness should neither be
# tolerated nor suffered in a city,
# and that diligent attention should be paid to foreign people.

## The Third Chapter.

Regarding how harmful a thing idleness <term>Müssiggang: laziness or the state of being unemployed and without purpose</term> is for all people, both of the male and female sex, the heathens (to say nothing of Holy Scripture) have written much. Primarily, however, they almost all agree that it is a cause of much shame, vice, and sin—such as adultery, theft, gluttony, and the like. As Ovid <note>Publius Ovidius Naso (43 BC – 17 AD), a Roman poet.</note> testifies when he says:

> If you do away with leisure, Cupid's bow will perish,
> and his neglected torches will lie without light. <note>original: "Otia si tollas periere cupidinis arcus Contemptæq; iacent, & sine luce faces."</note>

->And Lucan <note>Marcus Annaeus Lucanus (39–65 AD), a Roman poet.</note> says:<-

> Leisure always breeds a wandering mind. <note>original: "Variam semper dant otia mentem."</note>

Accordingly, every person should arrange their life and being for themselves in such a way that they do not spend their time—and especially their young years, which pass away like flowing water and never return—in idleness, but rather take up an honest trade or business <term>Handtierung: a manual craft, trade, or occupation</term>. In particular, a city or community should keep watch so that they suffer no idlers among them, and also keep an especially diligent eye on foreign and unknown people, so that they may be questioned and called to account at any time as to what their trade, business, and means of support may be. As Sabellicus <note>Marcantonio Sabellico (c. 1436–1506), a Venetian historian known for his universal history.</note> writes of the Florentines—whose city lies in Etruria <note>An ancient region of Central Italy, modern-day Tuscany.</note>—that they have had this laudable custom since ancient times: when they found and caught such a person who went about idly in their city and could give no good account of his trade, being, and conduct, they would sentence him from life to death, or banish him forever from the city as an unfit and harmful person. Such a law was also given by Draco <note>An Athenian lawgiver (7th century BC) known for the "Draconian" severity of his legal code.</note> to those in Athens: that those convicted of idleness must be punished by the head—that is, from life to death. For as wise people, they noticed and understood that such idlers can achieve nothing good nor have anything good in mind, but must usually support themselves with stealing, robbing, or other dishonest dealings.

In these lands <note>Likely referring to the German territories during the Holy Roman Empire.</note> I have indeed seen in several places that an unknown person has been allowed to loiter and go about for a year and a day, and no one knew, nor even asked, what his trade and business was. And if

<header>Of the Book for Rulers.</header>

If they are sometimes questioned, they may easily give a deceptive answer <note>original: "einen blinden bescheid" — literally a 'blind answer', meaning a vague or misleading response</note>, and people let it rest at that, making no further inquiry, but letting everyone spend their time and lie about until they cause some trouble <note>original: "einen stanck anrichten" — literally 'stir up a stench', meaning to cause a scandal or public nuisance</note>, or at least have brought in as much to the host as they have consumed with him, and people only become wise through their own loss.

Of such idle, worthless, and useless people, the learned Count Pico della Mirandola <note>Giovanni Pico della Mirandola (1463–1494) was a famous Italian Renaissance nobleman and philosopher.</note> writes and inveighs quite vehemently and truly satirically: 

> "For what," he says, "can be more unjust or more wicked in life than to pass time itself—certainly the most precious thing—most shamefully in sleep and sluggishness? For those who live lazy, cowardly, and yawning do not, by Hercules, live any more than stupid cattle and mere beasts. Nor do they live, but merely draw breath as cattle are wont to do; which is why some have established the sharpest penalties against those lazy and idle ones, and have rightly called them infamous. For Solon himself, in his Laws, most severely condemned this inertia and shameful cowardice. He who has followed idleness, he says, shall be liable to accusers." <note>original: "Nam quid, inquit, esse in vita iniquius aut scelestius potest, quàm tempus ipsum, rem scilicet preciosissimã, somno, inertiaq; turpissimè transigere... Qui desidiam inquit, sectatus est, is accusantibus esto obnoxius."</note>

That is to say: What can be more harmful and worse in the whole of human life than to shamefully spend time—the very best and most precious treasure—with sleep and laziness? For those who live in laziness and idleness in this manner are no different than irrational and wild beasts; indeed, they do not live, but merely draw breath as such animals do. From this it follows that some have devised great and excellent punishments against such lazy people and branded them as scoundrels, just as Solon <note>Solon (c. 630 – c. 560 BC) was an Athenian statesman and lawmaker known for his efforts to legislate against political, economic, and moral decline.</note> did in his laws when he said: He who wishes to devote himself to idle days must also suffer being accused for it.

Therefore, the Lacedemonians <note>The ancient Spartans.</note> rightly held it quite high and honorable to employ time well. They gave everyone something to do and did not tolerate any citizen spending time in idleness or in joking and entertaining games, so that through these dealings virtue would not be set aside and taxes and duties <note>original: "Steuer vnd Geschoß" — types of civic or military contributions</note> would not be needlessly lost or paid. And Aelian <note>Claudius Aelianus (c. 175 – c. 235 AD), a Roman author who wrote in Greek about natural history and anecdotes.</note> sets down this testimony among others: When it was reported to the Ephors <note>The Ephors were high-ranking Spartan magistrates who oversaw the conduct of citizens and kings.</note>—who were the Spartan authorities and had to watch and take note of all irregularities—that those who occupied Deceleia <note>A village and military outpost in ancient Attica.</note> were accustomed to being idle and going for walks after midday, the Ephors sent word to them, ordering them and proclaiming this mandate:

> "Do not walk about to indulge your whims, but rather to exercise the body. For Lacedemonians ought to obtain and maintain good health not by strolling, but by useful bodily exercises." <note>original: "Ne deambuletis, vt genio indulgeatis potius, quàm vt corpus exerceatis. Nam oportere Lacedemonios non deambulationibus, sed exercitijs bonam valetudinem parare, & tueri."</note>

That is to say: You should not go walking for the sake of pleasure, but only move your bodies as physical necessity requires. For the Lacedemonians do not obtain and preserve their health through strolling, but through useful exercise of the body.

From this it appears how greatly the ancients hated idleness and strolling. What would they say now if they were to see our city-fops <term>Stattsjunckern: young noblemen or fashionable men-about-town who focused on status and leisure</term>, night-revelers, wine and beer spoilers, gamblers, drunkards, and whoremongers, who do nothing else day and night but gluttonize, guzzle, wander the streets, gamble, and sleep? Dionysius the King <note>Likely Dionysius I or II, tyrants of Syracuse known for their complex relationship with philosophy.</note> was once asked if he were idle? "Where then are those who spend the better part of the day on dice and trifles?" says Erasmus. <note>original Latin: "Vbi sunt igitur qui bonam diei partem, alea nugisque transigunt? inquit Erasmus." Xenophon writes that Socrates said: "Business is no disgrace, but idleness is a disgrace." <note>original Latin: "Negotium non est opprobrium, otium autem opprobrium est."</note> As one reads elsewhere, he used the verse of Hesiod <note>An ancient Greek poet.</note> like a proverb:

The wise philosopher Plato, whenever he finished a disputation, would admonish his disciples and listeners: "See to it, boys, that you turn your idleness toward an honorable and honest business." By this, he wished to show them that idleness teaches youth nothing but evil. As Sallust <note>A Roman historian known for his moralizing accounts of Roman politics.</note> says: "Plans for treachery are taken during idleness, when the opportunity of the place permits." <note>original Latin: "Proditionum consilia per otium ex loci opportunitate capiuntur."</note>

Someone asked the Prince Cleomenes <note>Cleomenes III, a reformist King of Sparta.</note> why the Spartans had not entirely rooted out and exterminated the Argives, since they had defeated them so often? He said: "We do not wish for them to be entirely rooted out, for we must have someone against whom our youth can practice and exert themselves." "The excellent leader had clearly seen," says Erasmus, "that youth would be corrupted if allowed idleness, which is the master of luxury and all evils." <note>original Latin: "Perspexerat egregius dux, inquit Erasmus, corrumpi iuuentutem si permittatur otio, luxus ac malorum omnium magistro."</note> That is: For the brave man saw well that youth would be completely and utterly ruined by idleness, since it is a promoter of all things bad. Appius Claudius <note>A Roman statesman, possibly Appius Claudius Caecus.</note> used to say similar things often: "It is better for the Roman people to have something to do than to be idle." In the same manner, it is also the duty of rulers in cities and elsewhere—as has been partially taught and cited in this current chapter—to pay attention to their citizens and their <term>livelihoods</term> <note>original German: "Nahrung," referring here to a person's trade or means of supporting themselves.</note>, so that they do not squander, gamble away, drink away, or destroy their property in vain and useless ways. ->We are but numbers, born to consume the fruits of the earth.<-
<note>original Latin: "Nos numerus sumus, & fruges consumere nati." A quote from the Roman poet Horace, Epistles 1.2.27, describing those who live without purpose.</note>
->That is:<-
->We are the very worst of swine,<-
->Who only consume everything here.<-

And as another writes regarding the idle monks:

->If you ask what they do: they snore, they drink, and they defecate;<-
->In these three things, every duty of the belly is performed.<-
<note>original Latin: "Si quæras quid agant, stertunt, potantq́;, cacantq́;, / Ventris in his munus vertitur omne, tribus."</note>

Therefore, it is more difficult for these same <term>wine-skins</term> <note>original German: "Weinschläuchen," a derogatory term for drunkards or gluttons who consume without producing.</note> to squander and run through that which they have inherited from their parents and friends than it was for their kin to earn it. However, whether a government—which perceives and finds such sin, shame, and ruin among the sons of its citizens and does not prevent it—will be excused before God, I will leave for them to discover. For God did not say in vain: "In the sweat of your face you shall eat bread." And as Paul says: "He who does not work, shall not eat." <note>referencing Genesis 3:19 and 2 Thessalonians 3:10.</note>

Dionysius the King <note>likely Dionysius I or II, rulers of Syracuse known for their complex relationship with philosophy.</note> was once asked if he were idle. He answered: "God forbid that this should ever happen to me." <note>original Latin: "Absit ut hoc mihi unquam accidat."</note> By this, he meant to convey that it is dishonorable and shameful for a king to be found idle and not to occupy himself solely with the affairs of the <term>commonwealth</term> <note>original German: "gemeinen nußes," referring to the public good or the state.</note>. "Where then are those who spend the better part of the day in gambling and trifles?" says Erasmus. Therefore, Erasmus <note>Desiderius Erasmus (1466–1536), a leading humanist scholar of the Northern Renaissance.</note> asks: Where are those now who spend the great part of their time with games and useless fables?

Xenophon writes that Socrates said: "Work is not a disgrace, but idleness is a disgrace." <note>original Latin: "Negotium non est opprobrium, otium autem opprobrium est."</note> As one reads elsewhere, he used a verse from Hesiod like a proverb:

->Work is no shame, but idleness is shame.<-
<note>original Latin: "Non probrum est operari, at est cessatio probrum." Derived from Hesiod's "Works and Days."</note>

The wise philosopher Plato, when leaving a debate, would admonish his disciples and listeners: "See to it, boys, that you turn your idleness toward an honorable and upright business." By this, he intended to show them that idleness teaches youth all manner of evil. As Sallust <note>Gaius Sallustius Crispus (86–35 BC), a Roman historian.</note> says: "Plans for treason are seized through idleness when the opportunity of a place arises." <note>original Latin: "Proditionum consilia per otium ex loci opportunitate capiuntur."</note>

Someone asked Prince Cleomenes <note>Cleomenes I, a King of Sparta.</note> why the Spartans had not utterly rooted out and destroyed the Argives, since they had defeated them so often. He spoke: "We do not wish for them to be entirely rooted out, for we must have someone against whom our youth may practice and exert themselves." "The eminent leader saw," says Erasmus, "that youth would be entirely ruined by idleness, since it is the master of luxury and all evils." <note>original Latin: "Perspexerat egregius dux... corrumpi iuventutem si permittatur otio, luxus ac malorum omnium magistro."</note> In the same way, Appius Claudius <note>Appius Claudius Caecus, a Roman statesman.</note> often used to say: "It is better for the Roman people to have work to do than to be idle." Not that he...

# That it is the Duty of Rulers to Pay Close
## Attention to their Citizens and Subjects, so that they do not Uselessly Squander their Goods or Engage in Improper Trades.

### The Fourth Chapter.

In the same way, it is proper for rulers in cities and elsewhere—as has been partly taught and cited in the current chapter—to pay attention to their citizens and their livelihoods, so that they do not uselessly and fruitlessly squander, **gamble away**, drink away, or destroy their goods. For it is of great importance to a lord and ruler, as well as to a city, to have wealthy subjects. Likewise, no one should be permitted to engage in **improper trades** and businesses through which they harm the livelihoods of other citizens and subjects, such as <term>forestalling</term> <note>original German: "Vorkauff," the unethical practice of buying up goods before they reach the market to create a monopoly and inflate prices.</note>, <term>usury</term> <note>original German: "Wucher," the practice of lending money at unreasonably high interest rates.</note>, and the like. As was once done in **Argos**, where they paid particular attention to lazy and negligent people and idlers; these people had their own overseer, much like a <term>Censor</term> <note>a Roman official responsible for monitoring public morality and maintaining the census.</note>, to whom they had to give an account and explanation of how they supported themselves. This was also the custom in **Athens**; indeed, every citizen there had to give an account of his income and maintenance to the magistrates, whom they called the <term>Areopagites</term> <note>members of the Areopagus, the high court of Athens which held significant moral and judicial authority.</note>. King **Amasis** of Egypt did the same; he provided a special law that the <term>Praetor</term> <note>here referring to a high-ranking judicial official.</note> must receive an account from everyone regarding their life and maintenance, and whoever was found to be supporting themselves through usury or other dishonest trades was punished as a criminal.

One also reads that the **people of Marseille** expelled their soothsayers and priests—who traded their sacred things for the sake of profit or money—from the city, *lest they pursue idleness and luxury under the pretext of religion.* <note>original Latin: "Ne religionis prætextu otium sectarentur, & luxum."</note> Among the **Nabataeans**, it was a custom that those loose, lazy rogues who diminished and consumed their paternal inheritance were heavily punished; but those who managed their households well and [increased] the same...

For as **St. Paul** says:
> If someone does not know how to manage his own household, how will he care for God’s church?
<note>A translation of the author's German paraphrase of 1 Timothy 3:5.</note>
Therefore, I also hold that such people can be of little benefit to the **common good**, for they have not progressed far enough, or do not have enough understanding, to know how they should usefully provide for their own families.

In particular, it would be quite necessary—since in many places parents are so very negligent in raising their children to learn something so they may honorably support themselves—to address this issue. Instead, after the children have attended school for a year or two, the parents let them walk about at home and become **young squires** <note>original German: "Jungherrn," a title for young nobles, here used pejoratively to describe idle young men who think they are too good for manual labor.</note> until they take wives. And even if the parents leave them money or property, it cannot last in the long run because they know not how to earn anything; they must ultimately become beggars, leave their wife and children behind, and run away. The **authorities** <note>original German: "Oberkeit," referring to the local government or ruling magistrates.</note> should also look into this.

<margin>Regarding Jews.</margin>
Here it would also be necessary to remind the authorities regarding the **damned Jews**, that they should not tolerate or suffer them in their cities, principalities, and lordships; or at least, they should not hold them in such high regard or allow them too much room and indulgence. However, since I see that people are so completely drowned in **greed** and self-interest that nothing helps anymore, and the admonitions of that dear man, **Doctor Martin Luther** of holy memory (which he undertook with the greatest earnestness in writing against the Jews, almost concluding his life's work with them), have achieved nothing with these rulers, I will not presume to write further of this here or waste effort on their account. Whatever **Christian authorities** exist who highly value and esteem God’s word and the honor of His dear Son, **Jesus Christ**—to whom the Jews are bitterly hostile and whom they most extremely and hideously dishonor and blaspheme—they will well know how to conduct themselves. But for those to whom the Jews are so important that for their sake they dare to set aside God’s word and the honor of His dear Son, as well as the welfare of their subjects, for the sake of a little profit or other reasons: they may do so at their own peril and set the Jews in the place of honor until the **Last Day**, and prize and worship them as nothing but **holy relics**. I expect that no one will trouble themselves much on their account.

Yet I have occasionally heard that several rather sensible people held the opinion and had these thoughts: that for those who think so highly of the Jews, it must be a poor matter regarding their **religion**, and they must not hold Christ (whom the Jews cannot leave un-insulted) as their Savior, but must be secretly resentful of Him. Just as those who occasionally harbor a Lord’s enemies, honoring and promoting them, are also considered to be secretly against that Lord, proving by such a deed that they undoubtedly do not...

Since the power and stability of every city depends heavily upon those by whom it is to be governed and maintained, one should strive with all diligence to ensure that the **Council** <term>Raht: the governing body of a city, similar to a city council or senate</term> is at all times provided with capable, wise, pious, honest, and prudent people. A man stepped forward who was full of shameful, evil habits and a truly wicked person; yet he spoke so excellently and well about how matters should be handled everywhere that his opinion could not be improved upon. Thus it stood that the entire Council along with the **Community** <term>Gemein: the general body of citizens</term> wished to conclude upon his opinion and fully follow it. From this, it easily follows that over time, few capable, learned, and sensible people are drawn into the government in such places, and it becomes a strange sort of administration. Indeed, some are so mad and reckless that they even elect people to the councils with whom everyone in all governments and cities across the whole world must deal, negotiate, and struggle for the sake of their own profit. This refers primarily to butchers, bakers, usurers <term>Wucherer: moneylenders who charge excessive interest</term>, and the like. These people are allowed to rise so high and go so far that they gain the upper hand, governing and acting according to their own will and pleasure, while others must yield to them. 

Then one sees a strange and wondrous government, enough to make one’s hair stand on end, in which the poor common man must endure much distress and anxiety, being pressed hard and severely. Therefore, such regents remind me exactly of the common proverb: it is like "setting the goat to be the gardener." <note>A German idiom meaning to entrust something to the person most likely to misuse or destroy it.</note> This is also sufficiently indicated by the rhymes which I read in the town hall at Gotha in Thuringia, which run approximately like this:

->Where the Mayor pours the wine,<-
->The butchers in the council shine,<-
->And the baker weighs the bread,<-
->The people suffer great dread.<-

->Where the butcher, baker, innkeeper, and usurer rule,<-
->What safety remains for the wretched citizens in that city?<-
->Their Republic is bound to flourish just as well<-
->As a sheepfold cared for by a hungry wolf.<-

This is partly because people are intimidated by them due to their power and the fact that they are "in the game," and partly because people are related to them by marriage or friendship. Thus, both sides look to ensure they do not anger them. In the meantime, the righteous man suffers. <note>original: "Interim patitur iustus."</note> Meanwhile, the poor man must "lose his hair" <note>An idiom meaning to suffer loss or be fleeced.</note> and surrender his sweat and blood. # The Fourth Part

...[where more] is no longer tolerated, and where they strive to be rid of such capable people from the Council, rather than considering how they might be brought in collectively.

Beyond this, there is also a wicked and harmful abuse among some others: they promote only the sons of citizens <note>In many early modern cities, "citizenship" was a specific legal status passed from father to son; the author is criticizing this hereditary gatekeeping.</note> and choose them as regents. On the other hand, they despise those who are newcomers, regardless of the fact that these outsiders are sometimes more capable and skillful. One should instead look only to whether a person is fit and skilled for the task or not.

Thus, the people of Athens frequently chose not only foreigners and newcomers as regents for the common good, but also appointed them as commanders and captains in times of war, preferring them over the locals when they found them to be capable, honest, pious, and upright. One such captain was *Apollodorus of Cyzicus*, whom the Athenians often requested as their supreme military leader when they were burdened by war. Likewise, *Heraclides of Clazomenae*—both were honorable and brave men. For this, the Athenians were praised not a little. For as *Aelian* <note>Claudius Aelianus, a Roman author and teacher of rhetoric who wrote in Greek around 200 AD.</note> says: *And for these things the city is to be extolled with praise, which did not betray the truth to please its citizens, but even frequently entrusted the highest affairs to those who were joined to them by no kinship, yet were most worthy of honor because of their virtue.* <note>original: "Atq; ob hæc laudibus extollenda ciuitas est, quę non ciuibus veritatem gratificando prodiderit, sed etiam ijs non rarò summam rerum impertiuerit, qui nulla ipsis cognatione coniuncti essent, propter virtutem tamen honore dignißimis."</note> And for this reason, the city of Athens is rightly praised, for it did not only entrust its welfare to its citizens in times of need, but in such impending danger also took counsel from foreigners—those to whom they were not bound by blood—so long as they were honest men.

Finally, one must look carefully and diligently during such an election to ensure that people are not chosen for the councils based on wealth or great power, for such choices do not always turn out for the best. It often happens that the common good <term>gemeine Nutz: the well-being of the whole community over individual profit</term> is placed in great danger and led into significant harm because of such people. This is especially true when they are otherwise unfit and unskilled, as one commonly sees that those who have the most property are often the least fit for government, or at least do not concern themselves much with the common good, but instead strive more for goods and money.

Of this, *Plato* gives a splendid example when he says in the old book:

> Just as those who wish to cross the sea are in great danger if they have an inexperienced sailor or pilot <term>Patron: the master or owner of a ship</term> who cannot steer the ship—even if he has much money and is rich and powerful—so too must the citizens in a city endure and expect much danger if they receive such an unskilled, unfit regent who knows and can do nothing but strive for money and think of how he might create his own profit and become rich. One also sees clearly that such fellows hold the other citizens in very poor and contemptuous regard and oppress them heavily, especially if they are not fond of someone. Thus, it is not good to live under such regents or to be a citizen under them. On the contrary, one might well find those who are more skilled, more learned, and therefore more fit for government; but because the former has more money and goods...

# Of the Book of Regents.

[such a man] will be preferred over the other. And it usually happens that those who earnestly concern themselves with skill, honor, and the common good cannot apply themselves so diligently to money and property, nor strive for how they might become rich. Instead, they are satisfied with daily and modest sustenance, yet they turn and direct all their thoughts and affairs toward how they might best and most faithfully serve the common good. Such a regent was *L. Nummius* <note>Likely Lucius Mummius, a Roman general and statesman known for his integrity; despite his high status, he died so poor that the state had to provide a dowry for his daughter.</note>, who was so poor, as mentioned above, that the Council of Rome had to provide his daughter with a marriage dowry.

And since it is also the custom in certain cities, such as *Venice*, *Strasbourg*, and the like, to involve the nobility and those of the knighthood in the government, it will be necessary to take great care that the nobility does not gain too much of an upper hand, nor that they be granted too much power, so that one cannot manage them afterward. As *Claudius Sesellius* <note>Claude de Seyssel (c. 1450–1520), a French jurist and diplomat; the author refers to his work *The Monarchy of France*, which also discussed the Venetian Republic.</note>, an excellent man, writes in *The Republic of Gaul* <note>Original: *de Republica Galliæ*.</note>, in *Venice* only those from the knighthood and the established lineages are brought into those offices which can support greater dignity, honor, and income. Because of this, the other citizens—who are not only equal to them in understanding and wealth but are often superior—feel a noticeable resentment. It has come to the point where the citizens there who are not of the nobility have almost no hope of attaining any office in the government. And *Sesellius* writes that although it is true that the *Venetians* have such a well-ordered government—the likes of which for stability, justice, and good order cannot be better arranged or found—it is nonetheless to be feared that because they have granted the nobility so much, a great disadvantage could one day arise for them from it.

Accordingly, the people of *Strasbourg* are praised as wise people for having so moderated the power of the nobility in their government that they [the nobility] cannot achieve any dominance or lordship among them. For none of them—as I have been informed by many—are admitted to the office of *Ammeister* <term>The highest political office in Strasbourg during this period, serving as the head of the city's guilds and council.</term>, which is the most prominent office in *Strasbourg*. Rather, the *Ammeister* must be a "peasant" through all four of his grandparents—that is, he must come from and be born of a common citizen and not of a noble lineage.

And just as the *Venetians* have powerfully elevated and promoted the nobility in their city, so too in other cities subject to the *Venetian* jurisdiction and territory, the nobility is held in very low regard and is not brought into the councils. Some believe that this is done because

# Part Four

## That Above All Else, Regents in the Cities and Elsewhere Are Obliged to Ordain That Consistories and Spiritual Courts be Established for Many Reasons, Especially to Maintain a Christian Way of Life and Discipline Among the People.

### Chapter Six.

<image-desc>A large decorative woodcut initial 'D' featuring scrolling foliage and a human figure.</image-desc>Since the Holy Apostles—and especially Saint Paul throughout his writings—most faithfully and diligently exhort that among those who have recognized the truth of the Gospel, all things should proceed honorably and in a Christian manner, according to the will and command of God and His dear Son, our **LORD** Jesus Christ.

He also learned that those in Corinth conducted themselves otherwise, and tolerated one among them who had taken his father’s wife—and thus his own stepmother—as his wife. Saint Paul was so moved by this that he intended to place that man under the <term>Ban</term> <note>Excommunication or exclusion from the church community.</note>, wishing to show through such an example the proper way to establish and use the Ban.

Accordingly—and because everywhere among us only the smaller portion of people conducts itself according to the Gospel, and because one must therefore constantly restrain, exhort, and remind them, and where exhortation and reminding will not help, punishment must follow—it will be necessary to establish <term>Consistories</term> <note>Administrative and judicial bodies in the Protestant church that oversaw moral conduct and marriage law.</note> and <term>Spiritual Courts</term> in cities and lands. When such failings occur, these bodies shall decide them according to the regulations that have been agreed upon.

To such a Consistory, however, belong fine, Christian, learned, and God-fearing people who are of good reputation and irreproachable. They must also be undaunted in confronting people regarding their vices, proceeding against them according to the measure and teaching of our Savior Christ in <note>original: "Matthei am 18. Cap."</note> Matthew, chapter 18. These members should include <term>Superintendents</term> <note>High-ranking clergy who oversaw the conduct of other ministers and the spiritual life of a district.</note>, pastors, and preachers, as well as wise jurists where they can be found. For it is impossible to say what great and excellent benefit such a Christian work brings, and what a difference there is between those places where Christian discipline is maintained and those where everything is allowed to go as it goes, and everyone lives as they please—where there is no greater sin than if one wishes to rebuke vice and punish people for it.

Furthermore, such discipline and Spiritual Courts cannot be well-established or maintained in a stable manner unless the secular court lends its hand. For the <term>Secular Authority</term> <note>Original: "Oberkeit"; the governing lords or city councils.</note> is obligated and duty-bound to do this by virtue of the office they hold. Indeed, what is even more, the secular authority—insofar as it wishes to be Christian and considers itself as such—is just as much...

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the necessity of church discipline. The previous page introduced the concept of the Consistory as a tool to maintain Christian conduct, citing Saint Paul’s use of excommunication (the Ban) in Corinth as a biblical precedent.</meta>

[A ruler] identifies as a Christian, just like other Christians, and is therefore subject to such a <term>Consistory</term> <note>A church court or administrative council established in Protestant territories to oversee moral and ecclesiastical discipline.</note> and spiritual court, and thus to <term>church discipline</term> <note>original: "Kirchenstraffen"</note>. Those, however, who do not wish to be Christians may be let go, as they are outside the community of God, as can be found in Saint Paul, 1 Corinthians chapter 5. "For what," he says, "does it concern me to judge those who are outside?" etc. In this manner, Saint Ambrose, Bishop of Milan, placed the Emperor Theodosius under the <term>Ban</term> <note>Excommunication; exclusion from the sacraments and the community.</note> because he had shed innocent blood in an unheard-of massacre at Thessalonica; and the pious Emperor accepted such punishment with humility, performed public penance for it, and was afterward <term>absolved</term> <note>original: "absoluiert"; formally forgiven and restored to the church community.</note>.

From this, it is clear and easy to understand what distinction exists between worldly courts and punishments and church courts and punishments, and that the Church must, by necessity, have its own special discipline. For the **LORD** Christ himself ordained such punishment in Matthew 18. The <term>pastors</term> <note>original: "Seelsorger vnd Pfarrherrn"; literally "soul-carers and parish lords."</note> and ministers should abide by this and not make matters more severe or harsher, so that it does not appear as if they have more desire for tyranny than for bringing their little sheep to improvement in all gentleness. On the other hand, what reasons and thoughts those people have who will not tolerate Consistories or the Ban at all, and yet still wish to be considered Christians—that I cannot understand, nor will I argue it; rather, I will let them answer for it themselves.

Furthermore, these spiritual courts primarily handle the legal processes and the resulting judgments that must be used against those who live in public, external sins and refuse to desist from them. Alongside this, should a dispute regarding doctrine arise, it may be settled through appropriate means and without excessive long-windedness.

Thirdly, <term>matrimonial matters</term> <note>original: "Ehesachen"</note> are also usually decided before the Consistories, which provide a great deal of work. For this reason, the bishops formerly created many <term>Canons</term> <note>original: "Canones"; church laws.</note>, some of which, however, require change. For in these matters, one person leaves another without cause; or the married couple cannot otherwise get along and one seeks the life of the other; or there is always a failing on one part such that they must be divorced. Likewise, one has no less trouble and work because of <term>secret vows</term> <note>Clandestine betrothals made by young people without the knowledge or consent of their parents, a major legal issue in the 16th century.</note>, which occur daily without the knowledge of the parents.

To write at length about all of this would be too much and would take too long, requiring a special book of its own. But since Doctor Luther, of holy memory, Philippus Melanchthon, and many others have already written much on this, and since several Consistories have already been established with their processes and spiritual court orders, it would be superfluous for me to undertake such a task—as I also recognize myself as too small and humble for it. Therefore, I will let it rest with this brief and simple reminder: namely, that I consider it a necessary piece of governance—if one wishes to maintain an honorable and Christian way of life—that one must resist vice through this path of the Consistory and the Ban, and that such a path is Christian and right, as I...

# That it is the duty of rulers,
-> among other things, to pay diligent attention <-

### The Seventh Chapter.

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial 'E' featuring a bird and floral scrollwork.</image-desc>

The great and excellent man Aristotle describes and admonishes in his *Politics*, among other things, that those who have the authority to command for the common good, or to establish laws, statutes, and ordinances, should primarily direct their care and thoughts toward ensuring they neglect nothing in the area concerning the upbringing and instruction of the youth. For where this is neglected, it cannot fail but that a great harm must result for a city or community. And if one desires to have a well-ordered city or common good, one must first begin with the youth, building them up with good arts and Christian morals. And Aristotle says finally that not only is such a thing highly necessary, but also that rulers are obligated to maintain and promote it.

Therefore, Apollonius wrote a fine, short epistle to the Roman Prefects, which reads as follows: <note>original: "Porticuum, ædificiorum, mœnium, & ambulationum quibuſdam vestrum cura est, Liberorum verò & iuuentutis atque mulierum in ciuitatibus, neque vos curam geritis, neque leges, Quod si fieret, quàm honesta erat res Magistratus?"</note> "Some of you take care for porticos, buildings, walls, and walkways, but regarding the children, the youth, and the women in the cities, neither do you provide care, nor do the laws. If this were to happen, how much more honorable would the office of the Magistrate be?" That is to say: Your buildings, city walls, and walkways are decently provided for by some of you; if you also cared for your wives and the youth in the cities so that they were properly supported—which currently neither you nor your statutes provide for—how much better would it go for the rulers of the city of Rome?

In this way, Emperor Trajan is praised for having commanded and decreed that five thousand honorable boys be raised and provided for annually from the public treasury. Likewise, Charlemagne is praised for establishing three magnificent universities: one in Paris in France, the other in Bono- <note>The text continues on the next page: "nia" (Bologna).</note>
