Similarly, the same Emperor established many powerful monasteries in German lands, which at that time were nothing other than schools, in which the youth were raised rightly and Christianly in good morals and the <term>liberal arts</term> <note>The "freyen Künsten" or *artes liberales* were the traditional curriculum of grammar, logic, rhetoric, arithmetic, geometry, music, and astronomy.</note>. Here it would also be necessary to remember that primarily great lords should apply their utmost diligence so that their children might be instructed in the best way. For they should especially consider that their children are born for the benefit of the fatherland, and therefore the common good should be considered more by them than what should benefit them alone and for themselves. Many are found who erect a memorial for themselves with burials or other great monuments, but no lord can leave a better and more laudable memorial behind him than if he leaves behind a pious son who is like his father in virtue and honorability. He cannot be considered dead who leaves such a living image of himself behind. And so that he lacks nothing, he should appoint from his best people—those who are honorable, upright, understanding, wise, pious, and faithful—several to be with and around the young lord, for whom he must have a respect on their account. These men should speak, do, and act nothing frivolous, shameless, or dishonorable, but be of an honorable and modest life. They should not keep the "young blood" too strictly, so that he does not begin to hate virtue before he has recognized it; and in turn, they should not leave the rein too long for him, so that he might go to ruin and turn out otherwise than he should.

# That rulers should make provision so that the poor do not suffer want.

## The Ninth Chapter.

<margin>Deuteronomy, Chapter 15</margin>
<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut drop cap 'E' featuring a bird-like creature entwined with scrollwork and foliage.</image-desc>It is fitting and proper for a Christian authority <note>The German "Oberkeit" refers to the governing body or magistracy of a city or state.</note> in every way to see to it and make provision so that the poor and needy do not suffer want. Beware lest there be a wicked thought <note>original: "Belials tück." <margin>Matthew, Chapter 25</margin>
See with how many words, and how diligently and earnestly God commands and desires that we should look after the poor and lend them a helping hand. This is particularly true if we wish to be Christians. For Christ commands this upon the penalty of losing salvation, as He says in Matthew, Chapter 25: "Inasmuch as you did not do it to one of the least of these, you did not do it to Me. For all the rich, however great they may wish to be, are all too poor before God. Therefore, we rightly buy our Lord God through this virtue alone, since through this virtue alone we follow Him. No wise, strong, or moderate man should boast of himself before God, especially of following Him, since such things cannot even be a shadow compared to Divine virtues. And therefore, a human being can follow God in nothing better than through a generous hand toward the poor. Oh, what a blessed merchant he is who, with a small amount of money, can buy himself away from his enemies—that is, from vices—and buys not only humanity, but also God. And then no one can be counted as poor who is rich in God and humanity. A poor man can do nothing better than to lift himself up in such a manner. Likewise, a great lord can do nothing better than to humble himself in such a manner toward the poor.

<note>The following paragraph is the original Latin source of the passage translated above.</note>

God, God Himself is for sale. But with what coin is God most especially bought? With that which He Himself buys others: that is, through a certain liberal charity toward the poor. For God, out of immense love, grants all things to all people for free, and gives only to the poor. For all, though they may seem very wealthy, are far too destitute before God. Rightly do we buy God by this virtue alone, because by this alone do we most truly imitate Him. Let no wise, strong, or temperate man boast that he emulates God. These virtues are but shadows of Divine virtues, the reason of an image. Only the man who is generous toward the poor exactly imitates Him. For the liberality of men and of God is the same in giving. Oh, too happy a merchant! Who for a small price redeems himself from his enemies—that is, from vices—and at the same time gains both men and God. He will never be poor who is rich in men and God. He who, in the midst of great wealth, often considers what it is to be poor, never ends up at the bottom; he who, being placed at the top, mercifully looks down upon the lowest things. A lowly person never achieves anything better than when he humbly ascends on high. A great man does nothing greater than when he magnificently descends to the depths, etc.

Part Four

Therefore, those places and locations where common chests <note>original: "Gotteskasten" — a central fund established during the Reformation to collect and distribute resources for the poor and the church.</note> have been established should rightly be praised. Into these chests, money is placed to support the poor, and alongside them, magnificent hospitals <note>In the 16th century, a "Hospital" functioned more as an almshouse or shelter for the elderly and destitute than a modern medical facility.</note> have been built and provided with all necessities for the maintenance of the needy. All Christians should take this as an example and a model, and establish such beautiful Christian orders among themselves. The authorities <note>original: "Oberkeit" — the magistrates or governing body.</note> should especially ensure that this happens and, in places where it is already established, see to it that it remains in practice and is not torn down or abolished by godless, lazy, or greedy people.

## The Tenth Chapter.

<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial N featuring dense floral and vine patterns.</image-desc>

Since it is clear as day and before everyone's eyes—requiring no further proof—that excess and vanity in clothing have gained the upper hand to such an extent that it is believed such heights have not been reached since the beginning of the world as they are now. This can be clearly felt by the fact that people are becoming so poor and destitute through this that they can hardly nourish or support themselves anymore; rather, everything dissolves and becomes too little. It is most astonishing that people have fallen into this, becoming so mad and blind that even though they notice such costs for excessive clothing are harmful and detrimental to their livelihood, they still do not desist, but would rather be ruined and destroyed by it.

Furthermore, they refuse to be moved by the honorable and laudable examples of various principalities and cities, and especially of the Estates of the Empire of the German Nation <note>Refers to the Holy Roman Empire.</note>, in which ordinances and reforms <note>These were "sumptuary laws" intended to curb luxury and maintain clear social distinctions between classes.</note> have been undertaken and established. In these, a measure is given to the subjects regarding how each should behave concerning clothing, and what is permitted or forbidden according to their social standing—all of which is now despised and set aside.

And although it was the case not only among the ancients but also within living memory that one could recognize one person from another by their clothing—not only who was a member of the clergy or the laity, learned or unlearned, but also what degree each of the learned held—this has now, despite the reforms established at the universities and everywhere else, so fallen and ex-

There are the rulers in the cities, and those who should act, who are such fine folk that they always watch and let things go as they will, fearing they might encounter something burdensome if they should undertake to moderate such **pride and splendor**. Just as this is not new in our times; even the mighty Emperor Tiberius despaired and lost heart regarding the abolishment of such excessive splendor, useless abundance, and haughty adornment, as appears from the valiant writing he sent to the Senate at Rome, in which his words, among others, read thus:

> What should I attack first, or undertake to reform? Should I take on the great splendor of the water-houses <note>original: "Wasserhäuser" — likely referring to private baths or elaborate fountains.</note> and carriages, for which almost entire countries are built up? Or the excessive household staff and servants who follow the lineages and the nobility? Or the great useless silver and gold vessels used for banqueting? Or the painted panels and bronze vessels, which are also an abundance of wonders? Or the unchaste and extravagant clothing used by both men and women without distinction? Or should I start with the women's jewelry, for the sake of which (so they may get enough rare and expensive gemstones) our money and goods must be taken to foreign lands and even among our enemies? For all these things are so excessive and beyond all measure that I cannot well see or think where one should or might begin first. I know well, however, that there is much talk and complaining everywhere when people gather in the taverns and on the bleaching greens <note>original: "Plehen" — open fields where linen was spread to whiten in the sun; a common place for public gathering and gossip.</note>, and everyone desires that an inspection be made and a limit be set. And how one wants to target the best and greatest citizens and bring them to ruinous harm, and how there was no one in the whole city who was guilty or punishable regarding such abundance and splendor.

## Of the Regent’s Book.

...and the **Pope** has brought a great, notable amount of money out of German lands with the fictional and shameful **Indulgences** <note>original: "Ablaß" — certificates sold by the Church to reduce punishment for sins, a major grievance of the Reformation</note>; likewise, much taxation is daily imposed by the Princes against the **Turks** <note>Referring to the Ottoman-Habsburg wars, where "Turk taxes" were common levies for defense</note> and otherwise. However, if one compares those costs against this present splendor, and rightly weighs the damage and disadvantage that continuously follows from it—since it has now become the custom for everyone, and there is no measure or end to it—then a much greater taxation will be found. Everyone will have to say that the business with the Indulgences was mere child's play by comparison. Now, if someone were ordered by the **Authorities** <note>original: "Obrigkeit"</note> to maintain such notable splendor, he would complain that they intended to ruin him and his livelihood.

In the same way, foolish people behave regarding **feasting** <note>original: "Wirtschafften" — here meaning extravagant hosting, banquets, and public displays of hospitality</note>. If the Authorities were to issue a mandate that one *must* hold such excessive feasts, God help us, what a complaint would arise! How they would cry out that they were being burdened, etc. But because it is forbidden for their own good, everyone wants to arrange great feasts or banquets, regardless of whether he does himself harm and must lose not only house and home, but sometimes even the wedding clothes over it.

Thereafter, Princes, Lords, and Regents in the cities and elsewhere should abolish such abundance and maintain it with earnestness. They should not leave so much room to the **rabble** <note>original: "Pöfel"</note> that, once the authorities have made a Reformation and Ordinance, the people may transgress them without punishment. For if one grants them so much in one piece that they may treat the statutes with contempt, then such laws are finished, and they will not stop until the **civil order** <term>Policey: from the Greek 'politeia', referring to the overall regulation, morality, and good governance of a community</term> goes completely to the ground—which the Regents are duty-bound to prevent if a government in a city or a land is to be preserved. They should also hold the citizens to the standard that they must be satisfied with the clothing that their parents and ancestors used. Thus **Cato** presided with great earnestness over the **Oppian Law** <note>original: "Lege Oppia" — a Roman sumptuary law restricted women's luxury during the Punic Wars</note>, as **Livy** writes, in which a measure was given to women as to what expense they should put into jewelry and clothing.

So one reads of **Emperor Augustus**, that when he noticed the Romans had a desire for foreign clothing, and that this would result in notable damage and disadvantage, he admonished them with an excellent and long speech to break away from it and be satisfied with Roman clothing. He cited the verse from **Virgil** which says:

->“Romans, the masters of the world, and the race that wears the toga.”<-
<note>original Latin: "Romanos rerum dominos gentemq; togatam."</note>

We should rightly follow this example of great and wise people, and not be so inquisitive—especially with foreign clothes—as we have done until now with Italian, Spanish, and French clothing. As to what benefit and piety these have brought us, we have, in my opinion, partially found out.

**Xenophon** also writes that **Lycurgus** commanded the Spartans <note>original: "Lacedemoniern"</note> among other things that they should train their children so that when they walked in the streets, they should keep their hands under their clothes and not gape here and there, but walk straight ahead. Xenophon highly praises this.

...and he considered it to be an arrangement, so that people throughout their whole lives and beings might become all the more chaste and modest, if they are accustomed and held to it in their youth.

**Diogenes** <note>A Greek philosopher known for his extreme simplicity and for challenging social norms</note>, when he came to **Olympia**, saw several young men from **Rhodes** dressed excessively and magnificently, and delicately adorned. He spoke with mockery: "*These are truly signs of vanity.*" <note>original: "Superbiæ prorsum indicia sunt hæc."</note> That is: Such is an indication of vanity. However, when shortly after some **Lacedaemonians** <note>Spartans, famous for their austere and disciplined lifestyle</note> arrived in torn and soiled clothes, he said: "*This is a far different kind of vanity.*" <note>original: "Hæc longè alia est superbia."</note> That is: Here is a much different sort of pride. Therefore, it would be honorable to keep to the middle path in this matter, as **Cicero** <note>The famous Roman orator and statesman</note> teaches: "*In dress, as in most all things, moderation is best.*" <note>original: "In vestitu, sicut in plerisque, omnibus mediocritas optima est."</note> That is: One should maintain moderation in clothing, as in all other things. For if someone dresses too conspicuously and expensively against their proper station—slashing, fluttering, cut-up, and multicolored—and mirrors and gazes at themselves like a **peacock**, they easily fall into shameful gossip, of which **Lucian** <note>A Syrian-Greek satirist</note> also writes: "*Spring is at hand; where does the peacock come from?*" <note>original: "Iam ver adest, & unde nam pauo?"</note> That is: Spring is here; from whence comes the peacock?

When **Julia**, the daughter of the Emperor **Augustus**, had once dressed too boldly and boyishly, and she noticed that her father the Emperor was moved to anger by it, she changed such clothes the next day and approached the Emperor anew. Then he said to her—having held his anger from the previous day—"Oh, how much better this clothing adorns the Emperor's daughter." But Julia met him with a polite and cunning answer, saying: "Yesterday I dressed to please my husband, but today to please my Lord Father."

**Demonax** <note>A Cynic philosopher who lived in Athens</note>, when he saw one who wore a scarlet coat and showed himself magnificent and proud within it, whispered into his ear: "*Hey you, a sheep wore this before you, and it was a sheep.*" <note>original: "Heus tu, Hoc ante te gestabat ouis, & ouis erat."</note> That is: Listen here; before you, a sheep wore this, and it remained a sheep. He showed him by this that he was nonetheless a coarse and haughty fool, even if he wore scarlet.

**Dionysius**, the tyrant of **Sicily**, sent beautiful and precious clothes and jewelry as a gift to the daughters of **Archidamus** (some call him **Lysander**). Archidamus did not want to accept them and said: "These clothes and jewels do not adorn my daughters; rather, they make them more misshapen and dishonor them." This wise father understood well that one could adorn young women with no better clothing than modest and simple attire, and that through silk, gold, and gemstones, they would become more misshapen and ugly rather than pretty and adorned. For excess and splendor of clothing indicates no moderate mind, and causes those who see it to be moved more toward dishonorable advances than toward an honorable reputation. "*It is proper, however, that a maiden be a maiden in her entirety and in every way,*" <note>original: "Decet autem vt virgo tota & vndique virgo sit"</note> says **Erasmus** <note>Desiderius Erasmus, the great Renaissance humanist</note>, "*nor should she in any part give a sign of a corrupted mind. Therefore **Sophocles** said: 'This is not an ornament, O unhappy one; rather, it will be seen as a disgrace and the madness of your mind.' For an ornament is, as **Crates** says, that which adorns; however, that which makes a woman more honorable adorns her; yet it is not gold, nor emerald, nor scarlet color that provides this, but whatever provides an example of gravity, moderation, and modesty.*" <note>The author provides a lengthy Latin quote synthesizing views from Erasmus, Sophocles (the playwright), and Crates (the philosopher) on true beauty</note> That is: A young-

# Of the Regent's Book

A maiden should be a maiden in all places, and give no indication of a deranged mind. The true adornment is that which graces a person; but that which graces and makes a woman more honorable is no gold, no emerald, nor any scarlet, but much more an honorable, moderate, virtuous, and modest spirit.

Likewise, **Fabius** <note>Quintilian, the famous Roman rhetorician and teacher</note> says:
> "Dress that is appropriate and magnificent adds authority to men, as attested by a Greek verse; but womanly and luxurious dress does not adorn the body, but rather exposes the state of the mind." <note>original: "Cultus concessus atq; magnificus addit hominibus, vt Graeco versu testatum est, autoritatem: at muliebris & luxuriosus, non corpus exornat, sed detegit mentem."</note>

Oh, if only some German cities today had a **Pythagoras** <note>The famous Greek philosopher and mathematician</note>, who could talk the haughty pride and useless clothing out of people's hearts. For it is written how Pythagoras taught the women in **Croton** <note>A Greek city in southern Italy</note> about chastity and obedience toward their husbands, and instilled in them moderation, as if it were a mother of virtue. Through his diligent teaching and disputation, he brought it to the point that the honorable matrons and wives cast away their gilded clothes, rings, jewelry, and other ornaments of their status, as if they were tools of unchastity. They carried them into the **Temple of Juno** <note>The Roman queen of the gods, often associated with marriage and womanhood</note> and offered them all there. And there stands a beautiful sentence in history, namely:
> "The true ornaments of matrons are their modesty, not their clothes." <note>original: "Vera ornamenta matronarum pudicitiam, non vestes esse."</note>

That is: The true and genuine ornament and jewelry of honorable women are not clothes, but discipline, shame, and honorability.

**Aristotle** <note>The influential Greek philosopher</note> established an authority called the <term>Gynaeconomon</term> <note>From the Greek 'gynaika' (woman) and 'nomos' (law); essentially an 'Overseer of Women'</note>, whose office was to take care that womanly jewelry did not become excessive, or unsuitable for one’s age or station. And such authority remained among the Greeks, so that they had special <term>Inspectores</term> <note>Latin for 'Overseers' or 'Inspectors'</note> who were called <term>Gynaeconomos</term>. These people had the power and command to pay attention to the clothing of women; and where they noticed excess in one or more, they put a stop to it and set a limit. And in summary, they applied serious oversight so that no woman dared to dress above her means, but rather according to each one’s income and wealth. Those who violated such a command were subject to heavy fines. Indeed, what is even more, in **Athens** they had a law that any woman who walked immodestly in the streets had to pay a fine of a thousand **Drachmas** <note>An ancient Greek silver coin; this was a very high fine</note>. And **Pollux** <note>Julius Pollux, a Greek grammarian and lexicographer</note> writes that twenty such overseers were appointed and present.

Such excess also crept in among the **Venetians** and took the upper hand significantly. And although that city—through its great commerce, as well as the kingdoms, islands, cities, lands, and people they acquired—grew in wealth and prosperity to such an extent that many a citizen in Venice possesses a princely treasure; nevertheless, because they rose so high with jewelry and clothing (especially that of the women) and with the dowries of their children, they felt a reduction in their livelihood, trade, and business. Some of them even became beggars or <note>The original term 'Eisern' likely refers here to 'iron-clad' debtors or those whose assets were frozen/seized</note> impoverished, and thus went to ruin. Therefore, they were also moved, not very many years ago, to counter such unbearable, excessive, and entirely unnecessary costs, and to set a limit,

### Part Four

They also strictly and earnestly uphold these rules: namely, that from now on no woman or maiden, when she leaves her home, may put on any velvet or silken garment, unless it be on her wedding day, or otherwise at weddings and festivals where it is customary. This is despite the fact that so much feminine adornment and jewelry is found among them—even those from a humble background—that even a queen or a princess would not need to be ashamed of it. Furthermore, they have also made a statute that no one may wear a golden necklace or bracelet with precious stones, a belt studded with gold, and golden rings all at the same time; instead, one may choose and wear one of these, and must leave the others aside.

Thirdly, which was of no small importance, they have decreed that no citizen, no matter how rich he may be, may give his daughter more than six thousand **ducats** <note>A high-value gold coin used throughout Europe for trade</note> as a marriage dowry. And if he wishes to have guests, he may serve only one, or at most two, **capons** <note>A castrated rooster, considered a luxury meat</note> and beef, which must be strictly observed. For what destroys not only citizens in the cities and peasants in the countryside, but also the nobility, and even great princes and lords, other than such excessive ostentation and haughty clothing, dowries, grand households, and deadly banquets? Therefore, if one wished to do well by a city or a land, it could be done through no better or more convenient way than by setting a measure for these things. The Romans also had their **laws concerning food and clothing** <note>original: "Leges cibarias & vestiarias"</note>, through which the abundance of food and clothing was prevented and abolished.

Indeed, we do not need to seek examples from so far away; one finds even in our own times, praise be to God, still princes and rulers who have applied and still apply no small care and earnestness to this order. Primarily the honorable House of **Saxony** <note>One of the most powerful states in the Holy Roman Empire</note>, as well as the aforementioned cities, along with several others. In some places, where such pride can be taxed, and the preachers occasionally speak of it and punish such pride in dress, the women become resentful. When they wish to go to a feast or a wedding, as it is called, they might even send for the priest and mockingly ask what clothes, rings, and chains they should wear.

And it is truly a matter of no small wonder that people, who otherwise think and strive so much for goods and money day and night, are so hostile and hateful toward it that they are willing to spend so much money on a single garment, whereas in former times five or six people could have been decently clothed. As it happened, a man in **Leipzig** <note>A major German trade city</note> had seven **ells** <note>A unit of measurement, roughly 22–45 inches depending on the region</note> of London cloth cut for a single pair of breeches and was banished from the city for it. Another used ninety-nine ells of **sarcenet** <note>A fine, thin silk fabric used for linings</note> for the lining under his trousers and **doublet** <note>A man's snug-fitting jacket</note>. If that is not an unheard-of excess, then I do not know what excess means. And it is even more wonderful to behold how not only the nobility but also other wealthy people are so hostile to merchants and shopkeepers, yet turn over heaps of money to them for their wares, such as velvet and silk, though these are but mere rags and soon torn. Many people, however, hold it to be...

...must be a form of blindness, because it has come to the point where no order is maintained, but everything is in disarray. People are no longer ashamed to acquire money, whether by right or wrong, becoming or unbecoming, only for it to be squandered again, according to the proverb: *Ill-gotten, ill-spent.*

It is also a shameful and completely devilish abuse that people disguise themselves with such shameful clothing to the extent that they no longer resemble humans, but the devil himself—especially among the cavalrymen and mercenary soldiers <note>original: "Landsknecht"</note>. Indeed, <term>Musculus</term> <note>Andreas Musculus (1514–1581), a prominent Lutheran theologian and social critic</note> writes that a man commissioned a painting of the Last Judgment and ordered the painter to make the devils ugly enough. But when he painted them wearing <term>puffy breeches</term> <note>original: "Pluderhosen"; voluminous, multi-layered trousers with decorative slashes that were a controversial fashion trend in the 16th century</note>, someone came to him and gave him a sharp blow to the mouth for painting the poor devils so shamefully, since they were not accustomed to using such clothing. That God must also find this displeasing can be seen from the fact that a child was recently born whose skin hung from its legs in such a way that it looked exactly as if it were wearing puffy breeches.

Here, however, one might ask: should people then not adorn themselves with clothing at all? To this it must be answered that such things should be ordered according to each person's social standing, with which they should be content. And if people are so intent on applying much finery to themselves, I would, in my simple opinion, hold and advise them to focus more on silver and gold than on precious stones, pearls, velvet, and silk. They should strive for that, just as one sees was the custom among our ancestors, who wore silver hairbands, clasps, and little buttons on their clothing. The reason for this is that silver and gold, and whatever is made from them, can be used in times of impending need. For this reason, the Netherlanders, who maintain this custom, acquire more silver than those who own silver mines. And although they can make velvet and silk themselves, they do not make much use of them, because they know what money, silver, and gold are useful and good for, and that those other things are wares that easily perish and lead to strife.

# That diligent provision should be made
->so that strangers may at all times be provided with lodging in cities / And concerning the law of hospitality.<-

## The Eleventh Chapter.

In many places in the Holy Scripture, the virtue of welcoming people gladly—which in Latin is called <term>Hospitalitas</term> <note>hospitality</note>—is not only praised but also commanded, stating that we should gladly lodge one another. Primarily, Abraham, Lot, Laban, Rachel, the <term>Widow of Zarephath</term> <note>a biblical figure from the Books of Kings who provided for the prophet Elijah</note>, the <term>Shunammite</term> <note>a woman who provided a room for the prophet Elisha</note>, Job, and others are praised for this, as the Bible demonstrates. Likewise, the ancient heathens, both among the Romans and Greeks, were praised for lodging people gladly, so much so that they established a special law for it, which they called the <term>Ius hospitalitatis</term> <note>the right or law of hospitality</note>. Whoever violated, injured, or broke this law was considered a perjurer and an evil person. They even set Jupiter himself as the judge over this matter, as <term>Virgil</term> <note>Publius Vergilius Maro, the Roman epic poet</note> says:

> Jupiter, [be favorable] to guests (for they say you give the laws). <note>original: "Iupiter hospitibus (nam te dare iura loquuntur.)"</note>
> And <term>Homer</term> <note>the legendary Greek author of the Iliad and the Odyssey</note>:
> The gods care for strangers.
> For from Jupiter comes the suppliant, the poor man, and the guest.
> Whatever is given to these is like a great gift;
> Though it be small, it is nevertheless fitting to offer it. <note>original Latin translation of Homer: "Peregrinos numina curant. / A Ioue nam supplex, pauper procedit & hospes. / His quodcunq; datur, est magni muneris instar? / Sit licet exiguum, tamen est præbere decorum."</note>

Thus, almost no bond was held so great and holy as the law of hospitality; <gloss>for it was a divine crime to violate guests</gloss> <note>original: "Hospites enim nefas fuit violari"</note>. Therefore, the ancients first set <term>salt</term> before their guests, which they took and tasted together, to show that they wished to be of one mind and constant friendship, suffering both bad and good together. And indeed, it is no small friendship when one has to travel across the land and to foreign places, to know what kind of host he has, so that he need not worry about him, nor be forced to move into a common inn where everyone turns in and stays.

But that there is a great difference between such private lodgings and common inns, <term>Cicero</term> <note>Marcus Tullius Cicero, the Roman orator and philosopher</note> writes a fine story in the first book of *On Divination* concerning two <term>Arcadians</term> <note>residents of Arcadia, a region in ancient Greece</note>. He writes that there were two good companions in Arcadia who traveled together to <term>Megara</term> <note>a historic city in Greece</note>. When they arrived there, one moved into a private lodging with his friend, and the other moved into a public inn. Now, when both had gone to rest after their evening meal, it seemed to the first one in his sleep that his companion from the public inn came to him and pleaded with him to come to his aid, for the innkeeper was seeking his life. When he awoke from such a dream and sat up, intending to go to his companion, he reconsidered and thought it was just a dream; therefore, he went back to rest in vain. Not long after, the companion appeared to him again and pleaded, since he [was] at his...

Likewise, a **History** <note>original: "Historia"</note> is written by **Gastius** <note>Johannes Gast, a 16th-century Protestant pastor in Basel known for publishing "Convivialium Sermonum," a collection of moralizing anecdotes</note> about a guard <term>Trabant</term> <note>a mercenary or bodyguard, often part of a ruler's retinue</note> who wished to travel home from the wars. Since he had to stay and lodge with a thievish and robber-like host, he gave him a bundle—in which was a good purse full of gold coins <note>original: "Gülden"</note>—to keep for him, with the request to guard it so that he might receive it back. Now, when the guard wanted to be up and away in the morning, he demanded his bundle back, which he had entrusted to the host’s hands. The host brought it; however, he had thievishly taken the gold out of the purse and put stones in its place so that the previous weight remained. The guard was suspicious of the host's manner and behavior, and his heart sensed nothing good. Therefore, he untied and opened the bundle in the presence of the host. When he found stones instead of gold, he **remonstrated** <note>original: "expostuliert"</note> with the host regarding his lost gold. The host said he had received no money, nor had he given him any to keep; he said he was a rogue <note>original: "Bub"</note> who was accustomed to taking where he had laid nothing down.

They quarreled with such and similar words for a good half-hour until it finally came to blows. The guard cried out with a loud voice for rescue and help, for the host would have soon strangled him for the money; for the host was cunning and had been "at the net" <note>an idiom meaning he was an experienced predator or criminal</note> many times before. Therefore, the host accused and blamed the guard himself for theft, indicating that he had lost money that same night and found his chest broken open. The guard said in turn what had happened to him, and showed his purse, which he had handed to the host full of gold to keep but had received back from him with stones. In **short** <note>original: "summa"</note>, everyone believed the host; his words were held as true and certain. The guard not only lost his money but was also imprisoned and kept for a long time in a stinking dungeon <note>original: "Kärcker"</note>. To whom finally the Devil came, saying: "Dear mercenary <term>Landsknecht</term> <note>a professional, often flamboyant German mercenary soldier of the Renaissance period</note>, if you would follow me and surrender yourself into my power, I would know how to advise you so that you should get your lost money back." When the guard heard this, he was horrified; he doubted who it was speaking to him thus, wondering how he had come so quietly into the stinking and locked dungeon. He asked by whom he was sent, how he had come into the dungeon, and who he was. To this, the Devil gave him a clear answer. When he heard that it was the Devil, he signed himself with the cross, was greatly terrified, and said: "I have nothing to do with you, who can only bring ruin and lead to eternal damnation..."

The guard <term>Trabant</term> <note>original: "Trabant"; a term for a mercenary or bodyguard, often part of a ruler's retinue</note> took heart when he heard that he was to hang (though he knew that the Devil is a liar); nonetheless, he asked to hear his advice, and if it were not harmful to his soul, he would follow it. Satan said: The roguery, sin, and vice of the innkeeper shall be made truly manifest; he shall also receive the rightful punishment and reward for his practiced shame, for tomorrow he shall dine <note>original: "Collah halten," likely referring to a "collation," a light meal or meeting</note> with me and Cerberus <note>original: "Cerbero"; the multi-headed hound of the classical underworld</note> in Hell.

The guard, however, stood there alone without his Advocate. And as they were all violently terrified and looked in vain here and there for the innkeeper, they acquitted the guard and went with him into the innkeeper's house; there they found the money, just as Satan had reported to the court, and returned it to him based on the full report.

That is: It is said that this was a frivolous, false, and perjured person and a deceiver of the land, and therefore well deserved the punishment.

Although such special lodgings, mentioned above, are not so common at this time, and few people know what such a law of hospitality <term>Herbergrecht</term> <note>The traditional rights and duties governing the relationship between hosts and guests</note> is—likewise the common inns are so well provided with people, especially in the cities, that one need not fear such danger—yet things are better arranged in one place than another. One place is also praised more than another by those who travel the lands, just as those of Athens were once praised for their willingness to provide lodging and for taking good care of foreign people; for which they were primarily encouraged by Cimon <note>A famous Athenian statesman known for his generosity</note>. For this reason, they in turn met with kindness when they were once besieged in war; having driven their wives and children out of the city for fear of the enemy, they were taken in by the Troezenians <note>People of Troezen, an ancient Greek city</note> and maintained from the public treasury. By decree of the Council, their children were also permitted to gather fruit in all places, and no one was allowed to forbid them.

# The Fourth Part

...who was named Pacunius, invited as a guest and provided lodging for Hannibal. However, because the son of Pacunius was very much on the side of the Romans, he undertook to stab Hannibal to death during the evening meal. He would have accomplished it, too, if his father had not prevented it. For although they had to expect great danger and burden from the military forces, the father did not want to allow the sacred right of hospitality <term>Herbegrecht</term> <note>The ancient custom of "Gastfreundschaft," where a host was divinely obligated to protect their guest.</note> to be stained by such a murder. Furthermore, there is such a lovely and friendly thing concerning a host and a guest—where they hold themselves rightly toward one another—that even the wild animals recognize such friendliness. Thus, the swallows seek out their nests and lodgings again. 

So writes Apion <note>Apion was a 1st-century grammarian and scholar known for his stories of wonders; the story of Androclus is his most famous account.</note>, a very learned man, that a certain thing happened in Rome at a time when they wished to hold a public game. Many cruel beasts were brought into the enclosures, among which were several lions. It was the custom to throw those who had forfeited their lives due to their crimes before these beasts. Among them was a servant named Androdus <note>Better known in classical literature as Androclus.</note>, who had run away from his master and had been captured again. 

When one of the lions saw him, it first looked at him intently. Then, it approached him as if it should know him; it proceeded to lick his hands and legs with its tongue and wagged its tail in a friendly manner. At this, the entire Roman people were greatly astonished, and the Emperor had Androdus summoned before him to ask: From whence had this friendship between the lion and him arisen? 

To this, he gave this report: After he had been so badly beaten and treated by his master, he had been forced to run away. He had even considered that, although he could have no provisions in the wilderness, he would rather have shortened his own life there. However, after there had been a very great heat one day, he crept into a large and deep cave to seek shade. It was not long thereafter that the lion also arrived; and when the beast became aware of him, it came to him quite gently and showed him one foot, which was injured by a splinter or thorn. The lion wailed as if it desired that he should help it. Therefore, he inspected the foot, and after he found a large splinter in it, he pulled it out and cleansed the wound of the pus and blood. Because of this, the lion let its foot lie in his lap and rested before him after the days of pain. 

Once the lion became healthy again, he lived with the lion in a cave for three whole years and used the same food; for whatever wild game the lion caught, he brought the best of it to the man. The man had to dry this in the sun, since he had no fire.

However, he finally became weary of the wild and animal-like life and therefore, while the lion was out on the hunt, he went away and was captured by soldiers. And when he was brought back to Rome from Africa to his master, the master immediately sentenced him and commanded that he be thrown to the wild beasts. Since the lion then recognized him, it showed itself to be thankful toward him in such a manner. Upon this report, both the servant and the lion were given their freedom and set loose, and the lion followed the servant wherever he went.

## Another *History* follows.

Titus Livy <note>original: "Titus Liuius"</note> writes of a beautiful and magnificent example concerning the Etruscans <note>original: "Hetruscis"</note>, who came before the city of Rome with their King Porsenna to restore the exiled Tarquinius <note>Tarquin the Proud, the last king of Rome.</note> to his throne. When Porsenna could achieve nothing with his own men, he sent his son with a portion of the army against the Aricians <note>original: "Ariciner"</note>. Although the Aricians had not expected such an attack, they strengthened themselves and attacked the enemy so earnestly—with the help of the Cumaeans <note>original: "Cumaner"</note>—that the Etruscans, along with their prince, were defeated. Those who escaped in flight, having nowhere else to go and no lodging or shelter nearby, traveled instead to Rome, naked and wounded. There, they were willingly let in by the Romans and received in a friendly manner. They were not only provided with housing and quarters here and there, but the Romans also had those who were wounded bandaged and healed. Some of them later returned home and proclaimed such Roman kindness throughout all of Etruria. The others, however, were mostly moved by this to remain in Rome and to leave their own fatherland, friends, and neighbors; they were given a place to live in Rome which was called the Tuscan Street <note>original: "Thuscum Vicum"; a famous street in ancient Rome.</note>. Thus, the Romans sheltered their own enemies—who had besieged them with military force shortly before—in their time of need and distress, showing them all goodness and support.

It also happened at one time that a very great pestilence raged violently in Rome, which had perhaps arisen from the storms of the previous winter or other causes. Then the *Duumviri* <note>A board of two men in Roman government responsible for specific public or religious duties.</note>, or "Two-Men," knew no other counsel than to build a public guesthouse in the city. There, they prepared three magnificent tables and invited the gods Apollo, Mercury, Hercules, Neptune, Juno, and Diana to be guests, in order to reconcile with them <note>This refers to the "Lectisternium," a religious ritual where images of gods were placed on couches and offered food.</note>. The other citizens followed this example and placed all kinds of food and drink in their houses, which were left open. They invited both acquaintances and strangers, friends and enemies, sheltered them, and showed them every kindness. They even released the prisoners. From this, one can understand that they believed one could show the gods no better pleasure than by sheltering people, feeding them, giving them drink, and showing them other acts of kindness.

And after Badius had been burdened with sickness, he was again with him...

had him healed / from which they then formed a special friendship with each other / and became well-acquainted. Crispinus also showed him great kindness in his house. But the Campanian began defiantly / and said: "If you are an honorable soldier / then do battle with me on horseback / so that one may see who prevails." Crispinus replied with mildness / that if they both had a desire for it / each side could easily find his equal / but he was not inclined to strike him / even if he encountered him in battle / he would still yield to him / so that he might not violate the law of hospitality <note>original: "Herbergrecht"; the ancient moral code governing the relationship between host and guest.</note> / and act against it.

When the Campanian heard this / he became even bolder / scolded Crispinus as a despondent man / because he did not dare to fight him / and wanted to disguise his womanly spirit by saying he had stayed at his house / although it now had a different meaning / because he was no longer a guest / but an enemy / from which it was easy to conclude / that Crispinus must be afraid of him / and dared not stand his ground / since it was easily seen / that because the common alliance between the Romans and Campanians had ended / that between the two of them must also be dissolved / which then weighed on Crispinus' mind / especially because Badius was not satisfied with that / but also publicly / so that the soldiers on both sides heard it / renounced the hospitality / and offered combat. But as Crispinus still wanted to consider it / his companions cried out to him / that he should save his honor / and not let himself be so defied and bullied by the Campanian / therefore he went to the consuls <note>original: "Bürgermeistern"; literally "mayors," but used here for the Roman Consuls or high-ranking military commanders.</note> / informed them of this / and also requested leave / that he might do battle with the enemy outside of the battle / which was then granted to him. Now when he had armed himself / he bravely met Badius / so that he knocked him over in a heap with his horse / and also ran through his left shoulder over the shield / and Crispinus would have stabbed him to death as he lay there / had he not quickly gotten up again / and fled / and left the horse with its armor lying there / which Crispinus then kept / as a sign of victory / for which he was not only praised by his own / but also endowed with gifts.

Such praise, however, is not recorded of King Prusias <note>Prusias I of Bithynia, who reigned c. 228–182 BC.</note>, to whom Hannibal <note>The famous Carthaginian general and enemy of Rome.</note> fled and was taken in by him as a beloved guest. But when Quintus Flaminius <note>Titus Quinctius Flamininus, the Roman general and diplomat.</note> came from Rome and diligently sought to have Hannibal handed over to him, the unfaithful host and King would have surrendered him against his pledged word, had Hannibal not provided for himself with poison. For these were his last words: "We shall release the Roman people from their long-lasting worry, since they will not wait nor tarry for the death of me, an old man."

Yet Flaminius will carry away no notable victory from a defenseless and betrayed man. How greatly the Roman people have changed their customs and virtue will be shown for all time by this day. Their fathers and ancestors let Pyrrhus <note>King Pyrrhus of Epirus, a formidable opponent of early Rome.</note>, the King who was their enemy in arms and who kept his army in Italy, be warned that he should guard and protect himself against poison <note>Referring to the Roman general Fabricius, who famously informed Pyrrhus of a plot to poison him, valuing honor over an easy victory.</note>. The current Romans have sent their embassy and had King Prusias requested to sacrifice and kill his welcomed guest with shame and vice upon the slaughter-bench <note>original: "Fleischbanck"; a butcher’s stall, implying Hannibal was treated like livestock for the slaughter.</note>. And hereupon Hannibal cursed and maledicted King Prusias and his entire kingdom; he also called upon and took as witnesses the gods of hospitality <note>original: "Götter der Gastung"; likely a reference to Jupiter Hospitalis, the protector of guests.</note> that the faith and safe-conduct promised to him had been so shamefully broken; he then drank the poison and died.

# How the willing and friendly housing of guests is 
also a great virtue, and that one should support and sustain the wretched and banished people, especially those who have neither money nor provisions; this appears from this old epigram which was once inscribed at the <term>Xenodochium</term> <note>From the Greek 'xenodocheion', meaning a house for guests, pilgrims, or the poor; a hospice.</note> in Constantinople, which reads thus in English <note>original: "Lateinisch" (Latin)</note>:

> You who previously wandered, poorly known in the whole city,
> Whether you come as a stranger by land or by sea.
> Now set down your cares, let anxious fear be banished, and now
> Stay your foot, behold, a house is prepared for you.
> Yet if by chance you wish to know who first built 
> This roof, it was the Prelate Pharies.

->That is:<-

> You who are a stranger here,
> Having come by water or land.
> And have had to worry for lodging,
> Be still, I will relieve you of this care.
> For the lodging is prepared for you,
> Whenever you may come here.

# The Fourth Part

->Bishop Pharies, I tell you here,<-
->Was the first to found me here.<-

Likewise, the following distich <note>A poem or verse consisting of two lines.</note> indicates in the same place to some extent how the ancients used to lodge people and what distinctions they made in their customs, since all strangers are in need of such kindness at the same time:

->You shall be a welcome citizen and guest; for who you are<-
->And from where you were born, the laws of hospitality forbid us to ask.<-
<note>original: "Ciuis & hospes eris gratus, nam qualis & vnde, Natus es, hospitij quærere iura vetant."</note>

Also, <term>Cicero</term> <note>Marcus Tullius Cicero, the famous Roman orator and statesman.</note> writes a beautiful praise regarding <term>Hospitality</term>. There he speaks thus: "Hospitality was also rightly praised by <term>Theophrastus</term> <note>A Greek philosopher and successor to Aristotle.</note>. For it is (as it seems to me) very becoming for the homes of illustrious men to be open to illustrious guests. This is also an honor to the Republic, that foreign men in our city do not lack this kind of generosity. It is also extremely useful for those who wish to have great influence honorably, to prevail in wealth and favor among foreign peoples through their guests."

->That is:<-

Kind lodging is rightly and fairly praised by <term>Theophrastus</term>. For it seems to me to be quite elegant and a particular sign of prosperity—also very beneficial to the common good and very useful for gaining the favor of foreign peoples—that the houses of highly venerable men are open to honorable guests, and that in our city foreign people do not suffer from a lack of such kindness. This <term>Cicero</term> also praises <term>Philodomus</term> <note>Likely referring to a Roman citizen noted for his hospitality, or perhaps a corruption of a name in Cicero's orations regarding Piso.</note> for his hospitality, where he says that among the Romans he was always considered <term>most hospitable</term> <note>original: "hospitalissimus"</note>.

So says <term>Pontanus</term> <note>Giovanni Pontano (1429–1503), an Italian humanist and poet.</note>: "It is, moreover, the highest praise not only for individual private citizens, but even for the cities themselves, that private homes stand open to those coming from abroad."

->That is:<-

It is not only praiseworthy and honorable for special and individual citizens, but for entire cities, when the house and yard of the citizens and inhabitants stand open as a lodging for foreign people.

Similarly writes <term>Sabellicus</term> <note>Marcantonio Sabellico (1436–1506), a Venetian historian.</note>: This man performs and gives much who, as far as it lies within him, protects the guests from shame and injustice. But much more so he who, as a host, rightly places the guest's needs before his own affairs and would much rather let his own house be damaged than the guest. But he who gives himself over to death for the sake of the guest is to be praised above all others. This was done by <term>Herbonius</term> <note>Usually identified as Saint Cerbonius, the 6th-century Bishop of Populonia.</note>, the Bishop of <term>Populonia</term> <note>An ancient city in Tuscany, Italy.</note>. For when he fiercely and steadfastly protected and shielded his guests—who were sought for punishment by <term>Totila</term> <note>The King of the Ostrogoths who fought against the Byzantine Empire in Italy.</note>—he was, by order of the barbarian King <term>Totila</term>, thrown to the bears so that they might tear him apart. But they did not harm him. Therefore, the King was ashamed to rage further against him whom even the most cruel beasts had spared.

# Of the Book of Regents

...suffer [want, I will] set down afterwards; and after I have returned to common lodgings, I shall then also conclude this chapter.

Among the **Indians**, no stranger was permitted to lodge or remain in one place for more than three days, lest their own people—through long habit—might adopt foreign customs and fall into foreign ways and practices.

Among the **Lucanians** <note>An ancient people of Southern Italy.</note>, there was a regulation that anyone who turned away foreign people who arrived at their home after sunset and refused them lodging—even if they were unknown—must undergo the punishment established for it, being seen as an unkind person and guilty of the *crime of inhospitality* <note>original: "Criminis inhospitalitatis"</note>.

Likewise, one reads of their neighbors, the **Calabrians**, that they showed themselves entirely friendly toward foreign people by providing them with lodging.

Among the **ancient Germans**, the *law of hospitality* <note>original: "Ius hospitij"</note> was held quite honorably and earnestly. They were so inclined toward it that they considered it a cardinal sin if someone were to reject those who had perhaps sat with them at the table or sacrificed with them, or if they were to lock the door against them when they approached.

When there was a great drought and a lack of water for nine years in **Egypt** during the time of King *Busiris*, a man named *Thrasius* came to the king and said he should sacrifice the strangers and guests who arrived there to the gods, for through this they would have enough water and abundance. But *Busiris* began with this same advisor and sacrificed him first. And as he continued in this manner and sacrificed other foreign people in the same way, *Hercules* finally came upon him and dealt him the exact same punishment as he had done to others.

It is also written that when the *Megarians* and *Corinthians* once waged war with one another, they treated the prisoners on both sides so well, just as if they were not enemies, but rather bound to one another by the *law of hospitality* <note>original: "Iure hospitij"</note>. For it was otherwise customary that almost everyone had a regular host in the places where he had business or trade. This same *law of hospitality* was held in high and dear regard among the ancients as a special bond, so much so that they even named *Jupiter* with the surname *Xenium* <note>A title meaning "the Hospitable," referring to Jupiter/Zeus as the protector of travelers and guests.</note> and honored him as a patron of such friendship.

*Heraclides* also writes of the *Aphytenfers* <note>The inhabitants of Aphytis, an ancient city in Greece.</note> that they led such a godly and blameless life that they never touched anyone's door, even if it stood open. He relates how a stranger once bought a jug of wine while traveling through, but as he was ready to depart and the ship was about to sail away, he left part of the wine behind and neither gave it to anyone nor entrusted it to anyone's care. It was kept for him for a long time, until the next fair <note>original: "Messe" – likely a seasonal trade fair.</note> when he returned, and it was brought back to him undamaged and unconsumed.

*Lucullus* <note>A Roman general famous for his immense wealth and lavish banquets.</note> was particularly renowned for his hospitality (as his virtue was also partly mentioned above), which he demonstrated toward other people, but especially toward the *Greeks*, so that one regarded his house as

### The Fourth Part

...held a refuge and a certain stage for the learned people of Greece. For our ancestors (says Pontanus) wished to maintain the <term>Right of Hospitality</term> <note>original: "Ius hospitii"; a legal and social code in antiquity that protected the relationship between host and guest.</note> in its dignity and inviolate.

**Philippus Maria**, a Duke of **Milan**, conducted himself not only with great mildness and hospitality toward foreign people, but also sent princely gifts and offerings to brave and honorable people whom he knew of in the surrounding cities and places of **Italy** <note>original: "Welschlandes"; a historical German term used to refer to Latin-speaking or Romance-language lands, particularly Italy.</note>.

**Cimon of Athens** made and ordained a private and special house as a common hostel, which stood open to citizens and foreigners alike. He also allowed everyone to gather the fruits of his cultivated fields. No time passed that he did not hold a banquet. Therefore, he was called "divine" and "the most friendly toward guests" by the poet **Cratinus**.

And **Critias** the Tyrant, when he wished for the wealth of the **Scopadae** and the victory of **Agesilaus**, added to his wish the free generosity of **Cimon**.

The old custom and diligent practice of the city of **Athens** regarding hospitality and entertainment also had to yield to the magnificent generosity of **Cimon**, and could not be compared to it.

**Lychas**, a citizen of **Sparta**, is also summoned and highly praised for no other reason than that during the **festal games** <note>original: "Thurmer spielen"; likely referring to the Gymnopaediae, an annual festival in Sparta where Lychas was famous for hosting strangers.</note>, he was accustomed to kindly inviting and lodging strangers as his guests.

But before the conclusion of this chapter, I shall return to the common hostels and inns where foreigners and travelers must seek their night's lodging and shelter. Accordingly, it will be necessary to remind here that it is the duty and obligation of the Lords and Regents in the countryside to keep a diligent eye so that people—whether they be on horse or on foot—are not only gladly sheltered (since no one can carry their lodging with them), but that the people are provided for, each according to his station, and cared for in exchange for their money; also, that the guests should not be **overcharged** <note>original: "vbernemmen"; to take advantage of or exploit someone, usually through unfair pricing.</note>.

In this regard, I wish to tell an example of a city in **Thuringia** called **Arnstadt**. Namely, when in the past year of [15]39, several Electors and Princes, Counts, and envoys of many cities came together there and remained together for several weeks, the Council there sent messengers to all the inns. They had the guests and envoys kindly addressed and asked whether they were being well-served for their money, and whether they were being unfairly overcharged by the innkeepers. This was done with the assurance that if such a thing had happened to them, it would be abolished and the innkeepers would be given a fair punishment. This is a fine and magnificent example that I did not wish to leave unmentioned, out of honor for pious and honorable people, and for two reasons.

First, so that one does not blame the **Thuringians** by saying they do not like to provide lodging—which I experienced quite differently at that time. Not only can one obtain lodging and other necessities for money in the land of Thuringia, but one can also get by more easily than in many other places regarding the cost of provisions, due to the fertility of the land. Secondly, because I also well in large and mighty...

# The Ruler’s Book #

In many places, such diligence was not observed; instead, people were more inclined to overcharge their guests to the highest degree. And although complaints were made, the situation remained unchanged, and no special oversight was exercised.

From this, it follows that one finds certain innkeepers who already know and have calculated what the guest will consume before he has even rightly come through the gate. Whether he eats and drinks much or little, he must give what and as much as the innkeeper demands, and without receiving a single kind word in return. Some are even so wicked that guests occasionally vanish while staying with them, so that no one knows where they have gone—such men are truly like **Lycaon**. For as the poets write, **Lycaon** was an innkeeper in **Arcadia** who slaughtered, cooked, and ate his guests. However, when this came to the attention of **Jupiter**, who did not want to believe it, he disguised himself in the form of another guest so that **Lycaon** would not recognize him. Had he been successful, **Lycaon** would have slaughtered and eaten him too, by a hair’s breadth. Therefore, **Jupiter** cursed him so that he had to become a wolf. **Pausanias** <note>A Greek traveler and geographer of the 2nd century AD.</note> considers this a true story and history, which is said to have occurred and happened in his time.

> For at that time, he says, on account of justice and piety, men were the guests and table-companions of the gods; and those who were good men, the gods held in high honor, but they were angered by injustices. <note>original Latin: "Eo enim tempore, inquit, propter iustitiam homines & pietatem Deorum hospites erant & conuictores, & qui viri erant boni, iis euidenter dij honorem habebant, at iniurijs irascebantur."</note>

Be that as it may, the poets intended to use this story to depict such innkeepers and how they treat their guests. It also shows that lords and superiors are duty-bound to keep a diligent eye on and investigate such innkeepers, so that they do not go unpunished, as **Jupiter** did to this **Lycaon**. In truth, this is no small matter that belongs to <term>Policey</term> <note>In the 16th century, "Policey" (Policy) referred to the overall civil administration, social order, and the promotion of the common good, rather than just modern law enforcement.</note>, and one cannot watch over it diligently enough. It is indeed necessary, for otherwise, a city can suffer much ill repute because of it. It should be especially considered that a guest entrusts his body and property to the innkeeper. If one allows this to continue and does not set a standard or ordinance for the innkeepers on how they should charge their guests—as has been done and undertaken several times by the **House of Saxony**—there will be no measure or end to the flaying and overcharging. Moreover, they do not care for the guests accordingly but for the most part "feed them with words."

I will tell an example of this here, concerning an innkeeper who had guests at a certain time. Since he considered himself a good **Lutheran**, he first spoke much with the guests about the **Gospel** <note>original: "Euangelio"; refers to the Lutheran/Evangelical teachings of the Reformation.</note>, saying how it was such a grace-filled and wholesome doctrine. Yet, alongside this, he gave the guests little good to eat or drink.

When it came time for the bill, however, and the guests wanted to be on their way again, the innkeeper did not forget the chalk <note>Innkeepers often used chalk to tally a guest's debt on a board.</note> and charged dearly enough. Therefore, one of the guests was moved to address the host politely, saying: "Sir Host, you would not have made a good **Evangelical** preacher." When the host wanted to know the reason (since he imagined he knew as much about the Scriptures as any other man), the guest said further: "True **Evangelical** preachers are accustomed to [feed] their listeners..."

# How the Ancients kept themselves so moderate in eating, drinking, and clothing, and what is to be learned from it.

## The Twelfth Chapter.

<image-desc>A large historiated decorative drop cap "E" depicting a small child or cherub-like figure nestled within intricate curling foliage and floral motifs.</image-desc>

Many excellent indications are found here and there in the histories and other writings that the ancient world kept itself quite moderate in eating, drinking, and clothing. For instance, wine was once entirely forbidden to women; if they were found to have partaken of it, it was considered no different than if they had been caught in adultery. From this also came the custom among the ancient Romans that brothers-in-law and blood relatives would offer a kiss to the women, in order to discover whether they had been in the habit of using wine, as was also mentioned above. In the same manner, the Massilians, the Milesians <note>Massilia (modern Marseille) and Miletus were ancient Greek city-states known in antiquity for their strict social laws.</note>, and other foreign peoples had this custom: that women had to abstain from wine and drink water. Indeed, the men themselves had to abstain from wine, especially before their thirtieth year. As for the servants, they were not permitted to drink wine their entire lives, except when they sacrificed to the idols. Because of this, it was easy to grow enough wine for everyone.

But now, everything is a mess; everyone drinks wine without any distinction—not only men and women, servants and maids, but even the children in the cradle. They learn not only to drink wine but also how to get quite drunk before they reach two, three, or four years of age. Therefore, it is no wonder if one cannot grow enough wine, despite the fact that agriculture is significantly weakened because vineyards are planted in places where precious grain used to grow. And since the authorities in this case exercise no oversight or insight into whether their lands suffer more from a lack of grain or wine—but instead only look to ensure there is plenty for gluttony and carousing, allowing everyone to waste and squander as much in their house as they desire, and permitting vineyards to be laid where a cornfield would better stand—it follows that a famine easily arises in those same lands whenever there is a slight failure of the grain...

### Of the Book of the Regent.

...falls at the same time; then there is no supply among the people, and they must recover themselves with great effort and expense from others.

<margin>As in the year 1529.</margin>
Indeed, I have clearly seen that one could not obtain food even for money; that the people had to bake bread from peas, acorns, sawdust, and the like, and were forced to boil grass with milk. The people could not digest such things; instead, it stuck in their throats, and they died from it. However, if the people would strive after agriculture with such diligence, and were held to it by the authorities, so that everyone—according to their ability—was required to produce a supply of grain to be used in the face of such need, then a <term>dearth<note>A period of high prices and food scarcity, often preceding a famine.</note></term> could not be so easily feared.

I have seen this in several well-ordered cities: every citizen was required to have a year’s worth of provisions in reserve. This is not only to be done for the sake of war—for more is required for that than just a supply of grain, as I see it—but so that when a price-hike arises, the citizens do not have to suffer want, but instead have such a supply at hand. However, there are also other reasons why agriculture is terribly weakened, especially because of <term>forestalling<note>original: "Vorkauff"; the practice of buying up goods before they reach the market to manipulate prices.</note></term> and <term>usury<note>original: "Wucher"; lending money at high interest or exploitative trade practices.</note></term>, which have become so common among the people that a great part of humanity now dilgently applies themselves to these practices. Because of this, they despise and abandon agriculture, since trade brings in more profit and requires less effort and labor. But this should rightly not be suffered by the authorities; rather, it should be abolished, and the people should be diligently kept to agriculture, and also be protected and defended in it.

But to return again to wine and to drunkenness: it is easily gathered from what was mentioned above regarding women, men, and servants, that the ancients took no pleasure in such excessive drinking. For that reason, it was not permitted for everyone to drink as much as they wanted. This is understood from the history of Romulus; for when he was once invited as a guest and he abstained from wine because he had business to attend to the following day, someone began to say: "If everyone drank as little wine as you, wine would become much cheaper." To this Romulus replied: "Indeed, if everyone drank as much wine as I do, it would become expensive; for I drink as much as I want." <note>Romulus’s wit implies that his "will" is governed by extreme moderation; if others followed his example of drinking only what they truly needed, the demand (and thus the price) might actually rise if their "will" was less disciplined, or perhaps he suggests he drinks exactly as much as he desires, which happens to be very little.</note>

Afterwards in Rome, the Censors were also such fierce enemies of drunken people that they considered none of them worthy to be used for an honorable office or to lead the common good. The Cretans, Lacedaemonians <note>Spartans</note>, and those of Athens did the same; they forbade wine so strictly that they would not even allow their soldiers to drink wine. This was first forbidden by Plato, who also would not allow the regents to drink wine as long as they were in office. And if a prince in Athens had been found drunk, he would have been punished with death. Pittacus <note>One of the Seven Sages of Greece.</note> gave a law that anyone who committed an offense while in a state of drunkenness...

## The Fourth Part

Zeleucus <note>Zaleucus, a 7th-century BCE Greek lawgiver known for his strict legal code.</note> was such an enemy of wine that he would not even allow it for the sick. Similarly, Lycurgus <note>The legendary lawgiver of Sparta.</note> ordered the grapevines to be uprooted so that the people might not get drunk and carouse. These two opinions, however, are not right, but in my judgment are too extreme. For wine is a noble creature of God, created for the good of man; therefore, one may use it in moderation, and especially the sick. Just as Paul permitted Timothy to drink wine occasionally for the sake of his weak stomach <note>A reference to 1 Timothy 5:23.</note>. Thus, it is not the fault of the wine, as Pliny <note>Pliny the Elder, Roman author and naturalist.</note> maintains, that people become drunk, where he says: *We owe it to wine that we drink when we are not thirsty.* <note>original: "Vino debemus quod non sitientes bibimus."</note> For one reads that certain peoples, such as the Scythians, Babylonians, and those in Thrace, who have no wine, make a drink from the smoke of certain herbs that they throw into the fire, and some also from date pits and other fruits, and thus become drunk. And let this be enough concerning drinking.

As far as eating is concerned, the Romans were also exceedingly moderate in this, so that for several hundred years they used and ate no bread in the city of Rome, but rather vegetables or porridge. There were also no bakers in the city for up to six hundred years. And the porridge was cooked from water, barley, or bean flour. Some also, before grain became common, sustained themselves in the forests solely on acorns; I will say nothing of others, some of whom were satisfied with milk, some with fish, and some even with locusts. This is written as a certainty regarding Epicurus <note>The Greek philosopher often wrongly associated with luxury; here the author defends his actual lifestyle of simple living.</note> (who is nonetheless held to be a great glutton by many learned and unlearned people), that he satisfied himself not only with meager food and drink, such as water-porridge, barley bread, fruit, and the like, but also held that he could have more pleasure from a piece of bread than if many costly dishes were brought before him at once. Just as it is also true that a piece of bread tastes better to one who is hungry than when another has fish and partridges which he must consume without pleasure or hunger.

And so that the people might indeed learn to keep themselves moderate in eating and drinking, among the ancients, the young people had to take their food in the presence of their schoolmasters—or in their absence, in the presence of their closest friends—and were not allowed to eat in a corner at their pleasure or as much as they wanted. This was done under the open sky, especially in the summer time, but in the winter by the fire, so that the elders might see how the youth learned to remain moderate in eating and drinking. And there were not many costly dishes available there; rather, a piece of dried meat or bacon, or a salted fish, was the best fare with which one was satisfied. And the young fellows learned to sing fine <term>master-songs<note>original: "Meisterlied"; a formal type of German lyric poetry and song practiced by the guilds of Meistersingers.</note></term> and songs of praise about great and worthy heroes, and in the evening, they escorted the elders home out of honor.

The great leaders also distinguished themselves as an example to others...

One also finds those who claim that the penny was minted for the purpose of usury; otherwise, it would be nothing else but a "money cow" that gives no milk—contrary to the opinion of <term>Aristotle</term> <note>Aristotle famously argued in his *Politics* that money is "sterile" and cannot naturally reproduce; therefore, charging interest (making money "breed") was unnatural.</note>. Regarding all of these views, I will set them down one after another as briefly as possible, so that one may see how the matter of usury stands today, though I leave the better opinion of others on this matter unpunished.

For the first point—that usury is a sin and is earnestly forbidden by God in the Old and New Testaments—we have clear sayings. For instance, in **Leviticus 25**, where God says: "If your brother becomes poor and falls into decay beside you, then you shall take him in as a stranger, that he may live with you; and you shall not take usury from him, nor too much, but shall fear your God, so that your brother may live beside you. For you shall not give him your money for usury, nor your food for <term>excess</term> <note>original: "vbersatz," referring to the practice of charging a higher price for goods when sold on credit.</note>. For I am the LORD your God, who led you out of the land of Egypt." Likewise, the **15th Psalm** says: "Lord, who shall dwell in your tabernacle, and who shall remain on your holy hill? He who does not give his money to usury and does not take bribes," etc. Also, in **Ezekiel, the 18th chapter**, God says among other things: "He who gives back the debtor’s pledge, who takes nothing from anyone by force, who shares his bread with the hungry, who does not practice usury," etc. "He is a righteous man; he shall have life," says the LORD.

And Christ himself says in **Luke, the 6th chapter**: "Do good and lend, hoping for nothing in return; then your reward will be great, and you will be children of the Most High." From these sayings, it appears sufficiently clear that we are obligated, under the highest punishment and the displeasure of the Holy Divine Majesty, to avoid usury if we wish to be Christians and children of the Most High; and that for God, it must be a gruesome sin for whoever practices usury, since He warns us so faithfully and forbids usury with such earnestness. Therefore, the opinion of the young <note>Likely referring to the "younger" school of legal or theological thought.</note> may not be wrong when they say that those who do not consider usury a sin are to be regarded as heretics; and their opinion is grounded in **Clementine 1, extra de usuris** <note>A reference to the *Clementines*, a collection of papal decrees in Canon Law, specifically the decree "Ex gravi," which declared that anyone who obstinately maintained that usury was not a sin should be punished as a heretic.</note>.

This also refutes and sets aside the opinion of those who say that Christians may practice usury and put out money for interest and usury; among whom **Bucer** <note>Martin Bucer (1491–1551), a prominent Protestant Reformer from Strasbourg who held more flexible views on lending at interest than many of his contemporaries.</note> is one, who maintains that usury is not always a sin, but rather, if our neighbor is capable of paying, it is for us...
