# The Fourth Part

...conceded/something to gain in order to take back that which we have lent to him. However, if he is not in a position to pay, then we should not press him to give anything, whether it be the principal sum or the interest. And the sayings of the Old Testament are to be understood more in the sense that we should not overcharge or burden our neighbor, rather than that we should never (where it can be done without his disadvantage) take some usury-profit from him. Primarily, this applies when no deceit or malice is involved, but rather when we deal and trade with our neighbor as we would wish to be treated by him.

<term>Bucer</term> <note>Martin Bucer (1491–1551), a prominent German reformer who took a more moderate or pragmatic stance on social and economic issues compared to some of his contemporaries.</note> also desires that one might name the Imperial Laws, which were established and ordered by <term>Justinian</term> <note>Justinian I, the Byzantine Emperor (r. 527–565) known for codifying Roman law.</note>, namely <term>Centesimas usuras</term> <note>original: "Centesimas usuras," a Latin legal term for interest at the rate of one percent per month, or twelve percent per year.</note>. That is, one guilder every month for every hundred guilders; thus the interest equals the principal in one hundred months—that is, in eight years and four months. This amounts to twelve per hundred annually, primarily for those who trade in merchandise across the sea. For other usurers, it is eight, and for those of the nobility, three. This may not have been ill-intended by Justinian, provided one left it at that and did not shamefully abuse and exceed everything. Yet one sees that those who are permitted the least usury are the very ones who practice it most and "cut far beyond the line." <note>original: "weit vber die Schnur hauwen," a German idiom meaning to overstep boundaries or behave excessively.</note>

However, so that one may see how usury was situated within the Imperial Laws, it was framed in this way: the ancient <term>Laws</term> <note>original: "Leges," referring to Roman civil laws.</note> permitted usury, and merchants in particular were allowed to practice usury as they pleased. Thereafter, Justinian set a measure for usury; yet in both instances, this provision was made: that one was not allowed to take usury upon usury—that is, that no one should have to pay interest on the interest itself, or give interest upon interest. <note>This refers to the prohibition of compound interest.</note>

Now the question is: may one also take usury by virtue of the cited Imperial Laws, according to the opinion of Bucer, and especially according to the laws of Justinian? Answer: No, and for the following reasons.

Firstly, the Emperor himself changed such laws through another decree, as one reads in the <term>authentic decree on Ecclesiastical titles</term> <note>original: "authentica de Ecclesiasticis titulis," a section of the *Corpus Juris Civilis*.</note>. In this decree, the Emperor submits himself to the four main Councils—namely the <term>Nicene</term>, <term>Constantinopolitan</term>, <term>Ephesian</term>, and <term>Chalcedonian</term>—commanding and desiring that one must abide by them and judge accordingly. Now, the Council of Nicaea clearly stipulates, among other things, that usury shall be abolished and forbidden <note>original: "c. quoniam. 27. distinct. gloss. in authentica, ad haec. C. de usuris in verbo cadat." These are citations to the *Decretum Gratiani* (Canon Law) and the Justinian Code.</note>. Likewise, usury is otherwise strictly forbidden in Ecclesiastical Law, such that if someone took even a single penny above the principal sum, it would be recognized and held as usury. Secondly, it cannot be tolerated that a subject should overturn the laws of his sovereign and ordain the opposite. Just as a servant cannot change or abolish the laws of his master, so too, because the Holy Scripture in the Old Testament has forbidden and abolished usury—and especially as Christ speaks: "You shall lend, and hope for nothing (He says) from it" <note>A reference to Luke 6:35.</note>—one cannot permit or approve usury according to Imperial Laws. Nor can one introduce any statute or custom...

# The Book of Rulers. 197

But all this should not be understood as applying to anything other than **loaned money**, and no other <term>contract</term> <note>original: "Contract." Here referring to a specific legal agreement or transaction type.</note>. For whatever one takes from loaned money is usury, even if it were only a single <term>penny</term> <note>original: "Pfennig." Used here as a generic term for the smallest unit of currency.</note>. However, in other contracts, if one gives or takes something, such a thing cannot be cited as usury. For instance, if I have lent someone a horse or rented out a house and take some rent for it, that cannot be considered usury. Nevertheless, other contracts should also, as much as possible, be regulated and maintained according to the **Law of Love**, so that no malice or deceit creeps in, and so that we do not deal with our neighbor in any way other than how we would wish to be treated by him.

But since some set all this aside and say that one should and must practice usury, claiming the penny was minted for that purpose, etc., as mentioned above: such a thing is not to be understood regarding loaned money. Rather, it may be understood regarding other legitimate trades and businesses that one must use in the world. But to say that the penny was minted for the sake of usury is a false and unjust statement, and is against the opinion of <term>Aristotle</term> <note>The Greek philosopher Aristotle argued that money was "barren" and should only be a medium of exchange, not a way to create more money through interest.</note>, who says that the penny was first devised and invented so that people might more conveniently and easily conduct trade with one another. For since in the beginning and among the ancients there was no coinage, they traded only with goods—as appears in <term>Homer</term> <note>The author refers to the Homeric epics, where values are often measured in cattle (barter) rather than coins.</note>—and it often happened that one could not always agree on the goods without disadvantage, or sometimes one person did not have what the other desired. Therefore, out of necessity, they were forced to think of ways that people could trade conveniently with one another. For this purpose, then, coinage and the penny were devised—not so that one should practice usury with them, nor should the authorities tolerate or suffer such a thing.

Although this is the truth, which even the gates of hell could not contradict unless one wished to entirely deny God’s Word, usury has nevertheless gained such a strong upper hand that it is regarded as a mere joke when someone writes, speaks, or wishes to say something against it. Where is the book that <term>Doctor Luther</term> <note>Martin Luther (1483–1546). Rather, he said they should let them die like wild animals, not offer them the sacraments, nor let them enter the Christian community.

Has not all this been silenced? Where does one see anyone in all these lands—where we nevertheless wish to be **Evangelical** <note>In the 16th century, "Evangelical" was the common term for those following the Reformation (Protestants).</note>—being driven away from the **Sacrament of the Altar** <note>Holy Communion.</note> and **Holy Baptism** on account of usury? A dishonorable burial ground for criminals or outcasts, outside of consecrated church soil.</note>, even if he had been the worst usurer all his life and even the children on the streets could tell stories about it? Indeed, they are...

# Of the Book of Rulers

...authorities <note>The OCR fragment "stium" likely refers to "Magistratium" (magistrates) or a similar governing body.</note> approve such <term>contracts</term> <note>original: "Contract." Legal agreements for loans or property.</note> that are legally binding, then a Christian may use them safely and well, no differently or less than any other ordinance established in the <term>civil administration</term> <note>original: "Policey." Not "police" in the modern sense, but the general regulation and good order of the community.</note>.

And one might clearly grasp the distinction—as if feeling a wall—that it is one thing if I lend someone a thousand <term>guilders</term> <note>original: "Gülden." A common gold coin of the Holy Roman Empire.</note>, perhaps for one, two, or three years, and take ten, twelve, or less or more from every hundred. Indeed, from one <term>Leipzig Fair</term> <note>original: "Leiptzischen Marck." One of the major trade fairs in Germany where debts were settled.</note> to the next, perhaps five percent is charged; then comes the fourth fair, the <term>Peter and Paul Fair</term> <note>original: "Petri Pauli Marck." Held around June 29th.</note>, which brings the total to twenty guilders per hundred for the year, or two hundred guilders on a thousand-guilder loan for one year. However, it is different if I sell someone a thousand guilders with a proper and permanent <term>right of repurchase</term> <note>original: "widerkauff." A legal loophole where a loan was framed as a sale of income from property, which the "seller" could eventually buy back.</note>, in such a way that I do not have to demand the sum back according to the law of repurchase. This is what the Imperial statutes address, so that no one might accuse me of undertaking to condemn them. For I know that His Imperial Majesty himself is displeased by such unseemly usury. Thus, Cato compared all usurers to murderers.

For when he was asked, *What would be the best method for managing a household's affairs?* <note>original Latin: "Quæ esset optima ratio parandæ rei familiaris."</note> he answered: *Concerning agriculture* <note>original Latin: "de Agricultura."</note>. But the one who asked meant *concerning usury* <note>original Latin: "de Vsuris."</note>, to which Cato replied: *What is it to kill a man?* <note>original Latin: "Quid est hominem occidere?"</note> That is to say: when asked what the best way was to make a living, he answered it was farming. But when the questioner understood him to mean usury, Cato responded further: "What is it to kill a man?" And so it truly is: when someone falls into the hands of usurers, he is not only ruined, but because he is so distressed, he must also eat himself to death with worry. Therefore, in the most recent <term>Imperial Diet</term> <note>original: "Reichstag." The deliberative assembly of the Holy Roman Empire.</note>, when the <term>Common Penny</term> <note>original: "gemeine Pfennig." A tax intended to fund the war against the Ottoman Empire.</note> against the Turks was approved, it was decreed that anything someone takes over five guilders per hundred should be taxed specifically and higher than other money, according to and by virtue of the <term>Imperial Recess</term> <note>original: "Reichs abscheid." The official summary of the Diet's decisions.</note>, especially the one established at **Speyer**.

Finally, it should be known that usury among the **Romans** also had its limits, and not everyone was allowed to take as much money on usury as they wanted or as much as they could spend. A Senator in **Rome** was not permitted to take more than two thousand shillings on interest, as **Sulpitius** the <term>tribune</term> <note>original: "Zunfftmeister." Literally "guild master," but here referring to the Roman office of Tribune of the Plebs.</note> made a law regarding this, though he did not keep the law himself. For after his death, it was found that he was in debt for up to three hundred thousand guilders. Later, **Caesar** also set a limit on usury. And specifically, provision was made that one should not lend money on usury to children during the lifetime of their parents. This was later provided for in the Imperial laws and is called the *Macedonian Decree of the Senate* <note>original: "Senatus consultum Macedonianum." A Roman law preventing lenders from collecting debts from sons who were still under their father's legal authority, meant to prevent sons from murdering their fathers to pay off debts.</note>, a law which originally flowed from **Solon**. Among the **Indians** and **Germans**, usury was once entirely unknown. Some nations were such enemies of usury that they punished it most severely, such that usurers were considered much worse and more harmful than a thief. Therefore, they punished a thief with a double fine, but a usurer with a fourfold fine. And if one is to tell the truth, stealing...

But it is no small wonder that people are so utterly reckless, mad, and blind that they pledge for another with such frivolity, even though they are not certain whether he wishes to pay or not. For he did not have <note>original: "nicht einen stecken gehabt." An idiom meaning he possessed absolutely nothing of his own.</note> a single stick of his own in all of Germany. It should have been a great wonder how people could be so willing and seal [contracts] so recklessly without once thinking how they might be released from their suretyship; for the proverb is never far off which says: <note>original: "Bürgen sol man würgen." For I knew a stately man thirty years ago who, in Bohemia, lost his livelihood through suretyship to such an extent that he had to abandon all his property and goods, despite having been a rich lord. And when he died, his widowed wife had to marry the mayor in a small town, and his daughter a butcher. Now, when one hears such examples, he should rightly reflect and not be so frivolous as to put himself, his wife, and his child into such danger...

# On Coinage, and what is its
## origin, and how it is to be used.

### The Fourteenth Chapter.

<image-desc>Decorative initial O with floral scrollwork and architectural elements.</image-desc>

In the previous chapter above, I pointed out from <note>Homer, the legendary Greek poet, author of the Iliad and the Odyssey.</note> Homer that for a long time there was no coinage at all—neither of gold, silver, copper, brass, ore, iron, tin, or any other metal. Instead, the dealings among merchants and other people were directed such that one gave one commodity for another, as the Emperor <note>Justinian I (reigned 527–565 AD), the Roman Emperor known for codifying Roman law.</note> Justinian also testifies. We have an example of this today among the "wild" <note>The author refers to the Sami people of northern Scandinavia, historically called Lapps or Pilapen.</note> Lapps or Pilapen, as has been written about them; these people have neither wine nor grain in their land, nor do they till the fields. Instead, they nourish themselves through hunting, birds, and fishing, which they then trade for grain, salt, cloth, and other necessities. Such a custom was also once common among the Armenians, Scythians, Tatars, and the like. Afterward, some began to cast pieces of ore, but not to stamp them as coins, such as the Essenes and the Indians. The Portuguese also used a large piece of ore or silver in place of coinage; indeed, they still have such large pieces of gold, though with a stamp, where one is worth up to fifteen or more <term>Thalers</term> <note>The Thaler was a large silver coin used throughout Europe for centuries; the word is the origin of the modern "dollar."</note>.

Lycurgus forbade the <note>The Spartans.</note> Lacedaemonians from having or using silver or gold coinage; instead, they had to accept payment in iron in place of such coins. One reads of the Carmanians and Bambicatians that they diligently gathered all kinds of metal together and afterward buried it as deep as possible in the earth, so that they might not be led from virtue into greed and other vices. Similarly, among the <note>The author uses the historical term "Moors" to refer generally to North African peoples.</note> Moors in ancient times, gold was held in such contempt that they made nothing else from it but chains and fetters, which were forged onto criminals so that they could not run away. And in short, it was the custom throughout the whole world to exchange one good for another—such as iron or leather, and today skins of oxen—to trade for wine or other things, as the verses of Homer state in the 7th book of the *Iliad* at the end. The Roman Emperor Justinian later repeated this from Homer in the <note>original: "titulo de empt. & venditio. lib. 3. Inst." # That Rulers Shall Provide Correct Measures, ells, and Weights, and Shall Tolerate No Fraud Therein.

## The Fifteenth Chapter.

<image-desc>A large decorative drop cap 'D' featuring floral and scrollwork patterns.</image-desc> Although in all lands, cities, and communities, there is a great burden and hardship in that people are so accustomed to falsifying all wares—to the extent that almost no ware is so insignificant that it comes to market honestly, but must instead be mixed and diluted—yet Satan has especially possessed the shopkeepers, merchants, hucksters <note>Small-scale retailers or peddlers, often viewed with suspicion in early modern trade.</note>, citizens, and peasants in such a manner that they are not satisfied with such falsification of goods. Rather, they additionally use false ells <note>An "ell" (German: *Elle*) was a historical unit of length, often the distance from the elbow to the fingertip, which varied by region.</note>, measures, and weights, so that the poor man is twice harmed and cheated. To this, the authorities, especially in the cities, remain silent and look on, or at least do not apply the seriousness they are indeed obligated to show. Namely, that one should sentence such a fraud to a double fine, or banish them from the land, or, according to **Saxon Law** <note>Refers to the *Sachsenspiegel* or similar influential legal codes in the German-speaking world that dictated harsh penalties for market fraud.</note>, have them flogged at the pillar. And even if they were allowed to pay a fine instead, they should nonetheless be stripped of their honor and declared **infamous** <note>original: *infames*. In a legal sense, this meant the loss of standing and certain civil rights.</note>. But the rulers manage this poorly, or strive only for their own profit, not thinking even once a year that it is their office to pay attention to such things. Help us, God! How will they answer for this on that Day <note>The Day of Judgment.</note>, that they let the poor be cheated in such a way? What reason will they give for watching and allowing all trade to be so filled with falsehood and fraud, and letting such things go unpunished?

I have heard that in **Amberg** in the **Palatinate** there was an executioner who, after he had collected some money, resigned his service to the Council and became a shopkeeper. However, when he found that he could not compete with the others unless he used fraud—both with the goods and the weights—and saw that the other shopkeepers were such scoundrels, he gave up the trade, went back to the Council, and asked for his old job back. When the Council wanted to know the reason, he informed them that he did not know how to practice such fraud, and that without it, he could not thrive among the others. Now, such things are strictly and clearly forbidden in Holy Scripture, as where God speaks in **Leviticus 19**: *You shall do no injustice in judgment, in measures of length, weight, or quantity. Honest scales, honest weights <note>original: *Pfund* (pounds).</note>, an honest **ephah** <note>A dry measure, roughly 22 liters.</note>, and an honest **hin** <note>A liquid measure, roughly 4 to 6 liters.</note> shall you have. For I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, that you should keep all my statutes and laws.* Following this in **Deuteronomy 25**, God says: *You shall not have in your bag two kinds of weights, large and small, and in your house there shall not be two kinds of measures, large and small. You shall have a full and just weight, a full and just measure, so that your life may be long in the land which the LORD your God is giving you.*

In response, it would be highly necessary to apply the law of the Thebans <note>The inhabitants of the ancient Greek city-state of Thebes.</note>, of which Aristotle writes: that they accepted no such fellows into the council or other honorable offices unless they had ceased their trade <note>original: "Mercatur," referring to large-scale commerce.</note> and shopkeeping for ten years and had completely abstained from it.

Now, what kind of government results in those places where things are allowed to proceed in this way requires no proof; rather, it is seen before one's eyes. It is also not possible for it to persist in the long run; instead, when the people are completely ruined and it is found that the damage was largely caused by this, the authorities will then be forced by necessity to take action, or they will have to give a difficult account of it before God.

# What Kind of Persons are Necessary
## for the Common Good in a City.

### The Sixteenth Chapter.

Among the ancient Romans, nothing was more highly esteemed than when someone was called a good field-worker or farmer, for the ancients primarily applied themselves to and honored agriculture. Thus, one reads of Lucius Quinctius Cincinnatus <note>A Roman statesman (c. 519–430 BC) who became a legendary symbol of civic virtue for resigning his near-absolute power as Dictator to return to his farm.</note> that he was called from the plow to be Dictator. In this dictatorship, he bore himself so valiantly against the enemies that he struck and overcame them, thereby achieving a magnificent victory and triumph along with great praise—so much so that he could easily have remained a powerful citizen in Rome. However, after his triumph, he left the city again and returned to his farming. Therefore, it is held that those who sustain themselves through agriculture should rightly be counted among the most distinguished part of a city.

# The Fourth Part

In his *Politics*, regarding the **estates** <note>term: "estates" (German: Stände) — the social classes or professional groups that make up a society, each with specific duties.</note> into which a whole city should be divided, or from which a city or community should be constituted, it is important to know that he first established the **farmers**, for the reason that they must grow the grain for us, through which we sustain our life. Though today no one is more despised or held in lower esteem than the poor peasants. Second, Aristotle places the **craftsmen**, without whom a city cannot exist, such as bakers, shoemakers, tailors, carpenters, stonemasons, and the like. Third, he places **merchants**, shopkeepers, and hawkers. Fourth, the **day laborers**. Fifth, those who make use of **warfare**; but not those who let themselves be hired by anyone for money, but rather those who defend their own and common city, fatherland, freedom, and the insults and injuries <note>original: "schmähe vnd Iniurien"</note> inflicted upon them, and who protect and maintain peace. And finally, those who preside over the common good and the entire city, ruling the same and the general citizenry, which is the most noble estate, without which a city can in no way exist or endure; such as judges, mayors, and councilors, etc. Now while it is true that a city cannot do without such people and, as mentioned, cannot endure without them—as anyone can well judge for themselves—there are nevertheless several other estates of which Aristotle makes no mention in the aforementioned book, but which one can even less dispense with. These are the **superintendents**, school and church servants, pastors, and preachers, who instruct the people in the Christian faith and the Word of God, administer the sacraments to them, and maintain them in Christian discipline. Following these are the **physicians**, who know how to advise people when they are burdened with weakness <note>meaning illness or physical infirmity</note>.

Beyond this, a city also needs **legal scholars**, who are called lawyers <note>original: "Juristen"</note>, and who can inform the people of the law. Therefore Cicero says: *That the house of the legal expert should be the oracle of the city.* <note>original Latin: "Quòd domus Iuriconsulti sit oraculum ciuitatis"</note> Likewise good master builders and carpenters; for how much a city depends on such persons is clear as day and before one's eyes. But despite this, one sees daily here and there how lazy and sluggish people are in cities when it comes to seeking out such people, unless the utmost necessity is at hand. And although one is not inclined to lack for lawyers, or likewise for physicians, they are nevertheless in part more skilled at filling their purses than at helping the poor. Thus, the school and church servants are also held in very low esteem, and there is always a quest for how they might be maintained as cheaply as possible.

And I have seen in a city that people held a **painter** and a **mirror-maker** in higher regard, and commissioned and brought them in at greater expense, than a good preacher or schoolmaster, even though the latter is a thousand times more important. It is, however, easy to gather from this that we care more for the body, temporal goods, and pleasure than for our soul and conscience, and that our children might be raised in a godly and Christian manner; otherwise, we would exert ourselves more diligently for such people and hold them in greater honor. Now, where a city has ordained such estates, it can easily be preserved. But one must be just as well...

# Of Concord, that the
## same is most highly necessary
## in a city or a land.

### The Seventeenth Chapter.

<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial 'D' featuring a figure in a natural landscape, surrounded by leafy scrollwork.</image-desc>THE excellent man Sallust <note>Gaius Sallustius Crispus, a Roman historian famous for his accounts of political struggles.</note> writes that through concord small things increase and grow, and conversely, great things fall apart and diminish through discord. In the same way, discord grew between the Council <note>term: "Council" (German: Raht) — referring here to the Roman Senate.</note> and the Commons <note>term: "Commons" (German: Gemeine) — the Plebeians, or ordinary citizens of Rome.</note> in Rome, because the Commons felt they were being too harshly oppressed and burdened by the Council and the rich. But a man named Menenius Agrippa <note>A Roman consul famous for the following fable, which he used to end the First Secession of the Plebs in 494 BC.</note> came and quieted them with a very short speech and made them peaceful. "At one time," he said, "the limbs of the human body became at odds with one another and revolted against the stomach. For they complained and lamented that it alone consumed more than all of them could acquire with great effort, despite the fact that it could not and would not do any work for itself. They therefore resolved that they would give the stomach nothing further, nor do any more work." But while they were withholding food from the stomach, the other limbs also became faint and weak; and if they had not given food to the stomach again, they would have perished altogether. "It is exactly the same way," he said, "with the Council and you, the Commons." From this, the Commons realized they had done wrong, and therefore they reconciled with the Council and moved back home.

Now, when it happens that such dangers and discord arise, one should be mindful of these examples. In such cases, nothing is better than for both parties to yield somewhat to the other; for where that does not happen, and each person wants to push through with their own stubborn opinion, no peace can be achieved, nor can it end without damage. This is as Pliny <note>Gaius Plinius Secundus (Pliny the Elder), a Roman author and natural philosopher.</note> demonstrates with a fine parable, saying that once two little roe deer met on a high, narrow bridge, under which a deep water flowed. The bridge was so narrow and small that neither could yield to the other, nor could one pass by the other.

Although these were poor, irrational animals who could not possess much understanding or wisdom, Nature nevertheless showed them the way, whereby they both crossed past each other unharmed. Specifically, one lay down and let the other walk over him, which was but a small effort and only a matter of a step or two. If neither had been willing to yield to the other, but instead had butted heads, it could easily have happened that they both fell into the water and drowned.

Where then do people, who are gifted by God with reason and understanding—and especially Christians and <term>Evangelical people</term> <note>term: "Evangelical" (German: Euangelischen) — in this 16th-century context, this refers specifically to the Protestant reformers and their followers.</note>—get the idea that they fall into such forgetfulness that they would rather put themselves, as well as their land and people, into ruin and danger, than to yield anything to their neighbor? But in spiritual matters, and those concerning God's Word, there is no yielding, nor should there be, no matter what it costs. For this reason, the prophets, apostles, and all martyrs had to suffer and staked their bodies and lives on it; which they undoubtedly would not have done if they could have yielded with God and a good conscience, as is sometimes suggested by some.

So that I may now return to the histories, Plutarch writes of one named Scilurus <note>A legendary king of the Scythians mentioned in Plutarch’s "Sayings of Kings and Commanders."</note> that he had eighty sons; and when he was about to die, he is said to have tied a bundle of long spears together and commanded each one individually to break that bundle in two. But as none of them was strong enough to finish it, he had the bundle untied again and gave each of them one of the spears in his hand and let them break them in two, which they then could easily do. And he thereby showed and gave them to understand that if they would remain united, no one could easily harm them; rather, they would remain in peace and become great and powerful. But if they were to stir up discord among themselves and separate from one another, they would already be weakened and ruined.

...has its captains who keep the soldiers in check, so that they do no more and reach no further than they are commanded, or else they must expect punishment. For the ancients especially maintained such <term>discipline</term> <note>original: "Disciplin"</note> and military law, and likewise there were several captains in our own times who showed themselves to be very strict toward their soldiers. These verses show sufficiently what a dangerous and terrifying thing <term>rebellion</term> <note>German: "Auffruhr" — referring to civil unrest, riots, or sedition against established authority.</note> must be, in which people become so mad and insane. Indeed, if they were not completely foolish, but were in their right minds, they would not dare such shameful and dangerous undertakings against the authorities, whereby they must expect danger not only to the body, but also to the soul, if they persist and perish in such a game. For such rebellion and insurrection is most strictly forbidden in the Holy Scriptures. For the Scripture says in Proverbs 24: "Fear the King, and do not mingle with the rebellious." <note>Proverbs 24:21.</note> But if anyone goes beyond this and wishes to set his cause right through rebellion, or otherwise come forward with it to make a name for himself, his skill will fail him greatly and he will be wrecked by it. For all of history is full of such examples, both in the Holy Scriptures and in the books of the Heathens; therefore, I wish to recount some of them, from which one may perceive and learn what an excellent displeasure God has for such rebellious people.

I must, however, remind the reader here that this is a plague and pestilence that misleads and afflicts not only the common man and lowly people, but also great lords and clever, wise people—as was seen in the first example above, where captains and councilors rebelled against Moses and Aaron <note>Referring to the rebellion of Korah, Dathan, and Abiram described in the Book of Numbers, chapter 16.</note>. It happened thus in Rome as well; for although Sallust writes that Catiline’s initial following was nothing other than a crowd and a drain-pipe full of wicked and godless knaves who had squandered, consumed, and wickedly wasted their own property, and therefore wished to recover their losses through rebellion against others, yet among them were found several brave and prominent people, both from the nobility and the council. Such as Lentulus, Cethegus, Lucius Cassius, Antonius, Fulvius, Statilius, Capito, and others more; it is no small wonder that such brave people let themselves be so blinded, seduced, and incited to enter into such shameful rebellion and mix with such idle and seditious knaves.

When one wishes to look at the causes and the source of this shameful undertaking, it will be found that it usually flows from this: that these same rebels are enemies of authority, they hate them, and they covet the seat of government. For their minds are so directed that they despise their authorities, being not only disobedient to them, but also wishing to place themselves in their stead, and would rather rule and govern themselves than render proper obedience to other rulers. And since they have shamefully squandered and wasted their own wealth, they hope that if they gained the upper hand, they could then attack the rich at their pleasure and seize their goods by force—which is, however, against both Divine and Natural Law. For God says: "You shall not covet the goods of others." Likewise, Natural Law says: "What you do not want done to you, you should not do to another." Imperial Law also forbids such things, stating that one should not become seditious. <note>original: "C. de seditiosis" — referring to the Code of Justinian, Book 9, Title 30, "On Seditious Persons."</note> Also, in the law *Denunciamus*. <note>original: "l. denunciamus. C. de his, qui ad Ecclef. confugerunt" — referring to a specific law in the Code of Justinian regarding those who seek sanctuary in a church.</note>

From this, one can see how God watches over those in authority and punishes rebels, so that they not only come to shame but must also perish in such terrible punishment. For in their desire to stab and oppress the authorities, they must be stabbed themselves; indeed, they are also frequently executed upon the wheel and, in some cases, quartered, whereby they are then truly made into "quarter-masters" for the first time. <note>This is a dark pun in the original German: the officials called *Viertelmeister* (district or "quarter" masters) were punished by being *geuierteilt* (quartered).</note>

<margin>God punishes the rebels.</margin>
This severity should have rightly made those of Lübeck fearful, so that they would behave as obedient citizens toward their authorities. They, however, devised a reason by which they might rightfully depose the Council and thus force their way in. Namely, they alleged that the Council managed the household poorly and did not represent the common good, which was evident from the fact that they were heavily in debt here and there—debts which the citizens would ultimately have to pay and therefore be burdened with taxes. They claimed they could no longer endure this and thus cried out that the Council should be deposed. When such a clamor gained the upper hand and the Council could not withstand such rebels, they departed from the city and moved to Hamburg to stay there.

<margin>Lübeck.</margin>
In the meantime, the district masters in Lübeck used their "cleverness," for they asked the Bishop there for advice—what he thought of this business and how it pleased him (which they rightfully should have done before they began such a game). For despite the fact that the Bishop was ill-pleased with their undertaking and most vehemently advised against it and expressed his displeasure, they nonetheless persisted in their rebellious intention: the old gentlemen of the Council had to be deposed, and others elected in their place, among whom the rebels were the most prominent, serving as Mayors.

<margin>Rostock and Wismar.</margin>
And since the Scripture says that we are all inclined toward evil from our youth, such that one can easily give people cause and instruction to undertake something untimely and to follow the bad examples of others: as soon as the rumor reached Rostock and Wismar that the commons—and especially the guild masters—had dealt with the Council in Lübeck in such a way, they also changed and deposed their Mayors and Councilmen. In their place, they appointed sixty from among the commoners, who were supposed to do a better job.

But just as the rebellion and change first began in Lübeck, so too did it first end there, and the old Council was reinstated. This reinstatement was brought about by the fact that it happened just as the Council of Constance <note>A major ecumenical council of the Catholic Church (1414–1418) that addressed church reform and heresy.</note> was being held regarding the trial of Jan Hus <note>original: "Johann Hussen"; a Czech reformer whose execution for heresy at the Council of Constance sparked the Hussite Wars.</note>. For it often happens that many long for government, but when they have obtained it and do not know how to handle it, finding themselves inadequate for the task, they then wish to be relieved of it again. So it went here as well. Consequently, the Emperor sent his legates to Lübeck and had the banished Mayors and councilors reinstated. It also helped this cause significantly that King Eric of Denmark <note>Eric of Pomerania, ruler of the Kalmar Union, who was often at odds with the Hanseatic League.</note> was heavily troubling the people of Lübeck, and they did not know how to resist him.

Now, the lords of the old Council had good cause to address them in a much harsher way, considering that they had not only been insolently removed from their honors and offices, but had also been forced to flee the city and had been unsafe in body and life. However, they acted as wise and sensible men, forgetting and setting those grievances aside so that no further discord would follow, but rather that the quarrel might come to an end. Therefore, the chief Mayor, **Jordan Bleßkoppf** <note>Jordan Pleskow (or Bleßkoppf) was a significant historical figure and Mayor of Lübeck during the early 15th century.</note>, gave them this answer with very friendly words and said: "Dear friends, just as we pray to our dear Lord God that He might have mercy on us and forgive us our sins, so we wish to forgive you from the bottom of our hearts for the transgression you committed against us. We will not make you pay for such ill-timed actions; rather, you shall find us kinder, friendlier, and more well-disposed than we were before."

This speech by the Mayor so moved all those standing around and listening that they could hardly keep from weeping. And such a speech was a certain sign that this Mayor was a very wise, clever, sensible, and kind man who had experienced much, and thus learned from his own experience how to yield to fortune and adapt himself to the times. For this reason, he wished to think of this matter no longer, for which he is justly to be praised; and these verses from Virgil, which follow below, may justly be said of him:

Of the Book of Regents.

# That one should suppress those things 
# which lead to rebellion, rather than 
# bring them to light.

## The Nineteenth Chapter.

During the time when Agesilaus was the King of the <term>Lacedaemonians</term> <note>Another name for the Spartans.</note>, a man named Lysander rose up against him, gathered a following, and arranged that when Agesilaus returned home from Egypt, they would rebel against him and accuse him falsely. He even had an oration <note>A formal speech.</note> prepared which he intended to learn by heart and deliver against Agesilaus before all the people.

However, after Agesilaus learned of this, and Lysander died in the meantime, he demanded the letters and obtained the oration. He intended to have them read publicly so that people might see what a rebellious man Lysander had been. Therefore, he asked advice from Cratidas, who was the most prominent among the <term>Ephors</term> <note>The Ephors were high-ranking magistrates in ancient Sparta who oversaw the kings.</note>, as to how he should conduct himself in this matter. The same man, having read through the oration, advised him that he should by no means bring it to light. Firstly, because it was written somewhat vehemently, and the common man might take all sorts of reasons from it to start an innovation <note>In this context, "innovation" refers to political upheaval or revolution.</note>, as the common folk are more inclined toward novelty than toward what is good. Secondly, since Lysander was now dead, it would not be fitting for the King to engage in a dispute against him. Agesilaus—despite being a powerful King—obeyed him in this, looking more to the common good (so that the public would not be made restless by this business) than to the injuries that had been inflicted upon him by Lysander.

One also finds similar examples among the Romans. For it is written of Julius Caesar that when he had defeated Pompey and Scipio, he did not read their letters—of which he had captured entire chests full—but rather had them all burned. This was a truly princely act, of which Pliny writes thus: <note>original: "Illa fuit vera & incomparabilis inuicti animi sublimitas, captis apud Pharsaliam Pompeij Magni scrinijs Epistolarum, ite-rumq; apud Capsum Scipionis, concremasse ea optima fide, atq; non legisse."</note> "That was the true and incomparable loftiness of an unconquered mind: having captured the letter-chests of Pompey the Great at Pharsalia, and again those of Scipio at Thapsus <note>The Latin text says "Capsus," likely a reference to the Battle of Thapsus in 46 BC.</note>, he burned them in good faith and did not read them." Which means: I consider this a truly princely high-mindedness of an unconquered spirit, that Julius Caesar obtained Pompey’s letters at Pharsalia but did not read them, burning them unread instead. Pompey did the same thing: when he had defeated Sertorius and received his letters from Perpenna, he would not accept them, but instead had Perpenna beheaded and the letters burned. For he feared that the war might spread further because of them. As it cannot fail to happen: when one receives such letters, one must become embittered by them and be provoked to further war. It is also the case that a rebellion often rises from minor things. For just as...

Furthermore, a fire does not always begin in the Town Hall, in the church, or other public places, but sometimes in a poor, humble hut or in a small stable, yet it destroys an entire city. Likewise, a rebellion often arises among lowly persons and spreads in such a way—unless one prevents it with clemency <note>The original German uses *glimpff*, meaning leniency or a mild approach to de-escalate tension.</note> and timely counsel—that the whole city is forced to deal with the consequences.

Therefore Agesilaus <note>A famous king of Sparta known for his leadership and legal mind.</note> also says: "I truly judge those to be most worthy of praise who always meet rising evils head-on and destroy and extinguish them before they have gained any strength." <note>original Latin: *Ego vero illos potisſimum laude dignos iudico, qui naſcentibus malis ſemper occurrunt, & ea priuſquam virium aliqua ſit acceſſio facta, delent & extinguunt.*</note> That is: I primarily consider those worthy of praise who are willing to timely prevent arising evils and prefer to extinguish and suppress them before they spread further, rather than allowing them to come to light.

## That a citizen is obligated to protect his fatherland in times of imminent need, and not to abandon it.

### The Twentieth Chapter.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'E' featuring scrolling foliage and a serpentine creature entwined with the letterform.</image-desc>

It is written by the Greeks that Philip, the King of Macedonia, was once engaged in war with those of Athens. When both parties came to battle at Chaeronea <note>The Battle of Chaeronea in 338 BCE, where Philip II of Macedon defeated a coalition of Greek city-states, effectively ending Greek independence.</note>, the Athenians were overcome and defeated by the King. Consequently, the Council of that city was intensely terrified by such a downfall and loss; for it is easy to imagine that the side which is defeated must become despondent, while the side that has conquered becomes arrogant in its victory. Yet, after taking counsel, they decided to defend themselves from within the city and hold off the enemy. The Council issued a public decree <term>Decret</term> <note>An official order or law issued by a legal authority.</note> stating that no citizen should depart the city, but instead, everyone should remain at home and wait to see what fortune would grant and what the Council would do with them. 

However, it happened that a man of Athens named Leocrates fled from the city, taking his goods and property with him, and stayed for a time in Rhodes and the rest of the time in Megara. Because of this, when he later returned, he was severely accused <note>The German *peinlich angeklagt* implies a criminal prosecution involving capital punishment or severe physical penalty.</note> by Lycurgus <note>Lycurgus (c. 390–324 BCE) was a famous Athenian statesman and orator, not to be confused with the Spartan lawgiver of the same name.</note> as a traitor to his fatherland.

And because it is delightful to read how bravely and earnestly Lycurgus framed his complaint against Leocrates—how diligently he recounts the matter, proves the same with witnesses of his misdeed, and admonishes the judges that they should not let such a crime go unpunished, etc.—it is truly a wonder. And because this same oration <note>A formal speech.</note> of Lycurgus is well worthy of being specially translated into German and printed, so that one might learn from it...

...and so that one might learn how each person should conduct themselves toward their fatherland, and what each owes to the same, I have translated this oration into German and set it here as an example, and it reads as follows.

## Oration of Lycurgus against Leocrates, who
## abandoned his fatherland.

In order that I may make a proper and fitting beginning to this criminal indictment <term>Peinliche Notklage: A formal legal accusation in a case involving capital punishment</term>, so that it may be fruitful and profitable for the common good <term>Gemeiner nutz: The public welfare or the shared interests of the community</term>, and that God may be given his due honor, I first pray to Almighty God—since I rightfully and justly accuse this Leocrates before you for having treacherously surrendered and abandoned the religion, churches, sacrifices, and whatever else was established by our ancestors and received by us—that He would, through His divine mercy, grant me help and assistance today on this day. I pray He directs this accusation of mine so that it may be healing to the common good, and that your hearts and minds might be so moved that they finally consider their parents, wives, children, fatherland, and religion. And after you have taken this traitor into your hands, I pray He would strengthen you, so that you do not let the shameful and offensive deeds of this Leocrates—or any other in the future who might commit the same offense—go unpunished. But if I accuse Leocrates without cause, such that he did not betray his fatherland and did not abandon the city of Athens, then I pray to God that He might graciously release him from this capital trial <term>Halßgericht: Literally a "neck-court," referring to a high court with the power to sentence a defendant to death</term>.

I could wish for nothing more than what is necessary for the common state: that we must have people to accuse wicked rascals and harmful citizens for their crimes, yet that they likewise do not burden anyone with unjust accusations. For if one were to undertake to accuse an innocent person in such a manner, and did not bring the charge out of love for justice and for the rescue and salvation of the fatherland, he does nothing other than put himself in danger and heavy hatred, and through such severity, brings others into distress.

You should know, however, that three things are highly necessary for the preservation and protection of the common good: namely, the Law or Statute, the judicial Verdicts and Sentences, and lastly, the Accusations <note>Lycurgus argues that laws are useless without trials, and trials are impossible without citizens willing to step forward as accusers.</note>, through which those who have committed an offense may be brought before the court and thereby be brought to justice. The Law and the statutes or ordinances show the citizens what they should do and what they should avoid. The accuser brings the matter before the court and charges those who have acted against the law and have thereby fallen under the punishment of the Council. The judge, however, must punish those whom the law and the voice of the accuser prove to be guilty and who have forfeited their lives according to the law; then, according to the importance—

<header>### The Fourth Part</header>

...[the gravi]ty of the crime, pass a judgment, and finally allow the execution of that sentence to actually take place. Therefore, it must also necessarily follow, and conclude of its own logic, that accusers are necessary for the common good <term>Gemeiner nutz: The shared welfare and interest of the community</term>; we cannot do without them, for without their voice, the laws and the courts would be entirely mute and in vain.

Now, as far as my own person is concerned: because I knew that Leocrates treacherously abandoned his fatherland and thereby incurred the highest punishment and penalty, I felt it was my duty to bring this complaint forward. I was not driven by envy or a desire for quarreling, but I considered it utterly shameful that such an evildoer should remain unpunished. It is a disgrace that he should use the marketplace alongside other honest citizens and participate in the common sacrifices of the entire city, bringing noticeable insult and shame upon us all. I must also declare to myself that it does not befit an honest and just man to drag someone innocent before the court out of specifically harbored envy.

However, when someone accuses another for the sake of the common good, he cannot and should not be reasonably held under suspicion of malice.

And although all public lawsuits serve the preservation and protection of the city, this particular case—which I intend to bring forward and argue legally today—is of primary importance. For if someone were to complain that a person had introduced a new law that did not align with our other laws or statutes, nothing more would need to be done than to change or abolish it. But this matter of ours does not merely affect some small part of the city, nor does it bring only a slight or minor harm; rather, it concerns the entire common good of this city. It shall serve as an example <term>Exempel: A legal or moral precedent meant to instruct future generations</term> which should be rightly considered and taken to heart by all our descendants. For the shameful deed of Leocrates is to be esteemed so grave and great that no existing indictment for a penalty can be found, nor is one expressed in the law, by which he could be sufficiently punished. For what penalty can he have forfeited who abandoned his fatherland and, so far as it lay within his power, surrendered the religion, the temples, and the graves of our ancestors, along with the entire city, to the enemies?

It is true that one cannot punish a person more severely than by taking them from life to death; yet such a punishment is far too small compared to the forfeiture and shameful deed of Leocrates. I can find no other conclusion than that no specific legal complaint was established or ordained in the law for such a shameful vice<sup>a</sup> because, until our own time, no such evil example had ever been heard of. Nor could our ancestors have suspected that in future times such a thing would occur. Therefore, no sufficiently sharp penalty or punishment can be found for this crime, and in this matter, you will have to be not only judges in the usual and proper manner, but also new lawmakers. For as for the punishments for crimes that occur daily...

For my own part, I will complain and argue nothing in this matter other than what is right. I will not invent, speak, or pretend anything that is not useful to the case, regardless of the fact that I know many accusers who make a habit of bringing all sorts of improper things into their complaints. ### The Fourth Part

...the accuser might have cause to invent false and fictional charges in court; for no judge can speak and pass a lawful judgment unless he has been rightly and thoroughly informed of the matter by the accuser or the orator.

In addition, you will certainly consider this: that the trial to be held over this *Leocrates* cannot proceed and remain hidden as with other private and individual persons. For if the situation were such that you were to judge and pass sentence upon a man who was unknown to the other Greeks, it would not matter so much how the trial was conducted, or whether he was handled rightly or wrongly. However, since all of Greece will pay heed to this your judgment and see what kind of verdict you pass in these highly important matters, it requires much further consideration. This is especially true in view of the flight he committed, and because he reported as a certainty <note>The speaker uses irony here; Leocrates told the people of Rhodes that Athens had already been destroyed, spreading panic and disgrace.</note> to the people of *Rhodes*, along with all the merchants who gather there from the greater part of the world for their trade, that the city of *Athens* had been conquered by the enemy—whereby he became known almost everywhere.

Since everyone now knows and can easily conclude for themselves that such an example does not usually originate among the people of *Athens*, it will be necessary to look into this with all the more diligence and earnestness. For just as you wish to be praised above all other people—not only for your reverence toward God and your kindness toward parents, but also for being foremost in the protection of the fatherland—so too would you rightly be judged to have forfeited such a calling and the good name of these aforementioned virtues if you let this man escape unpunished. Therefore, and because it has come to this, that the court is convened today for his sake, I ask that you hear this my accusation at length. I ask also that you take no offense that the great harm which befell our fatherland must be recounted anew by me, but rather that you be angry at those who caused it, whose damage is revealed in the following manner.

After the rumor spread here that the people of *Athens* lay defeated in the Battle of *Chaeronea* <note>The Battle of Chaeronea (338 BC) was a catastrophic defeat for the Greek city-states against Philip II of Macedon, effectively ending Athenian independence.</note>, and the people here gathered together, it was resolved and provided for in the common council that women and children should be brought from the fields and villages into the city; the commanders and captains should occupy and secure the city, and the remaining citizens should obey the captains. *Leocrates* knowingly despised this command and had his servants bring his belongings to the ship, in which he intended to make his escape toward nightfall. This is indeed what happened; for this reason, he went to the ship through a small side-gate with his mistress and shamefully abandoned the fatherland. In this, he showed no regard for the gates or the city walls, which, so far as it depended on him, were left without any guards or protection—whereas he should have rightly been terrified before the sight of the temple of *Jupiter* <note>original: "Jouis"</note> and *Athena* <note>original: "Palladis"</note>, whom he will now call upon. However, **Leocrates** did not turn back from his ways but committed even more gross and terrible evils. For when he settled in **Megara** and lived there, having brought his property there and seeing the opportunity of the place, he bought a great deal of grain from **Queen Cleopatra of Epirus** <note>Cleopatra of Macedon, sister of Alexander the Great, who served as regent of Epirus.</note> and traded it again among the other **Greeks** for the sake of profit. Will you now let such a reckless man—who abandoned his fatherland in the distress of war, sold grain elsewhere, and moved his household goods away to other places—go unpunished? But you must see from this whether I did not have a fair reason to investigate this matter, so that I would not have to complain against him before you based on a poor assumption, but rather, after bringing the truth to light, you would have to judge and speak upon it. ### should be publicly read here.

Since he did not obey this announcement and did not follow it, he has thereby made himself guilty and declared himself a traitor to the fatherland. For it must certainly follow that whoever refuses such an investigation <note>original: "inquisition"</note> and flees from it reveals himself to be guilty of that vice. You also know that when a matter stands in doubt, so that the true ground cannot be discovered, it is customary to have such an investigation of the servants who have knowledge of it. One gives more credit to them than to what the accuser brings forward, especially in highly important matters where the common good <note>original: "gemeinen Nutzk"</note> is significantly at stake.

I would have liked to undertake and handle the matter so completely justly that I would have gladly confirmed it through the testimony of his own household. But because he has a bad conscience, he could not be persuaded to present them so that one could have searched for the truth through them. It would have been quite possible that the servants, in judicial interrogation, would have denied things concerning their masters rather than confessing and testifying to something fabricated against him.

### The Fourth Part

...will be [found guilty] and thereby fall into danger. Regarding this, I provide this report so that you, gentlemen, all know that those who wish to falsely accuse someone and make them hated by others usually employ such arguments and subject matter that have a grand appearance and can easily move others to anger and hatred. Conversely, those who bring right and truthful complaints against someone desire to overcome the accused more with deeds and truth than with empty and invented words. Accordingly, I leave it to your own consideration: who would have been impossible to deceive with words? Is it not true that these are the slaves <note>original: "Knechte." In Athenian law, the testimony of slaves—often obtained through "basanos" or judicial torture—was considered more reliable than the word of free men.</note>? For by the command of nature, they would have had to speak the truth in the interrogation, by which one could have clearly judged. However, Leocrates, despite the fact that they were his own, would not allow them to be brought forward. But who can be softened to mercy with words and weeping? Is it not the judges? This traitor now seeks refuge with them, but for no other reason than his fear that the accused and the witnesses might be summoned from the same house at once.

But what can this invented excuse profit him? The law is simple and straightforward; the discovery of the truth is easy; the evidence and proof lie on a short path. If he confesses that the accusation is truthful and just, then let justice be done to him according to the order of the law. But if he denies it, why does he not allow the menservants and maidservants to be brought forward, so that the truth could be learned from them? For when one comes under suspicion of treason, it is not fitting that he should wish to flee the most certain evidence of his innocence. Since he now refuses this, and thereby confesses himself a traitor through his actions, it is easy to conclude that a judgment may justly be spoken against him based on such a confession. No forgiveness is to be granted to him, since he himself removed his own defense. Through this refusal, he intends to mock and nullify your court regarding the crime which he has admitted through his deeds.

With this, I shall consider that regarding the announcement I desired—that the witnesses might be presented—as well as the shameful vice which the accused, as you see, admits to, sufficient evidence has been given. Now it will be necessary for you to take to heart at what time and in what danger Leocrates shamefully abandoned his fatherland.

->Here the Council’s Decree shall be read,<-
->that the citizens shall remain at home.<-

Here you have heard the Council’s Decree, in which it was ordered that the Councilmen should betake themselves down to the **Piraeus** <note>The primary port of Athens, vital for the city's defense and food supply.</note> with their armor, to take command there, to protect and hold the **Piraeus** against the enemy, and also to ordain that which would be most necessary for the people. Now, as this status of the Councilmen, who otherwise in the war...

exempted from being drawn into service, yet in his armor, out of the prevailing necessity of the common good, he should have deliberated; and while the city was in great terror and fear, Leocrates fled from it. Despite such sustained damage and great distress, the common state nevertheless remained of a steadfast mind, and the people placed all their hope in the eldest councilors. Honorable women were seen everywhere in the streets and at the gates, utterly mournful and terrified; some asked after their husbands, some after their fathers, and some after their brothers, as is customary in such cases, and they were deeply troubled for their sake. But alongside them went the old men, who were no longer fit for war due to their infirmity and therefore had to remain at home; they walked about the city in their armor to oversee everything. And although many terrifying things occurred daily, and the city was stunned by the damage taken—making for a very mournful spectacle in **Athens**—one nevertheless saw the people, who had always held most fiercely to their **freedom**, decide because of the great danger to bestow freedom upon those who were bondservants, and to grant citizenship to the foreign guests. Furthermore, those who had become infamous because of their misconduct were restored to their former status and made right. From this, such a reversal of fortune could be seen: that this city, which previously protected and maintained other cities in their freedom, was now forced to attempt its final salvation to preserve its own liberty. And although it had frequently delivered and liberated others from foreign nations in the past, it now had to struggle and fight with the **Macedonians** for its own salvation, freedom, and welfare. Ultimately, the people—who in former times, when they rescued the **Lacedaemonians** <note>original: "Lacedemonier," referring to the Spartans.</note> and others, were called a helper or savior—were driven by fortune to the point that they now stood in need of help from other and lesser cities.

Now, if someone were so forgetful as to shamefully leave his fatherland stuck in such terror and in such great danger, and had not armed himself or reported to the captains to stand up for and protect the city alongside them: Which judge, who otherwise loved his fatherland, would declare him free or innocent? Which orator or speaker would venture to defend him or speak for him? Since he thereby...

### The Fourth Part

...did nothing else than defend the one who neither mourned the common harm that befell the city, nor did anything for the protection of the common state, nor took it upon himself as would have been proper. For at that time, not only did people of every sex and age rush to the city's defense and apply themselves with earnestness, but even the earth itself gave its trees, the dead gave their graves, and the temples gave their shields <note>In the panicked aftermath of the defeat at Chaeronea, Athens took extreme measures to fortify itself, including using timber from sacred groves and stones from funerary monuments.</note>. Beyond this, some were appointed to repair the **city walls**, others the ditches and ramparts—indeed, no one in the entire city was idle, except this Leocrates alone, who took no part in such labor. Therefore, you are duty-bound to consider this and do justice to him, especially since he was not even present. When the bodies of those most precious men were brought back—those who perished in the battle of **Chaeronea** while fighting for their **fatherland**—and their remains were buried (men who, for his sake, might as well have remained unburied), he even shunned their graves when he first looked upon his fatherland again in the eighth year after that defeat.

And since I have once begun to mention these things, I ask that you do not find it a burden to hear me further, and do not think that such a narrative is in vain. For in praising the pious, the accusation in which the traitors are rebuked becomes all the more clearly understood. Moreover, it is right and just that the praise of the pious not be left behind, as it is a reward for those who surpass others in virtue; therefore, we are duty-bound to grant this praise to these brave heroes who so faithfully laid down their lives for the fatherland. They were the first to encounter the enemy at the **Boeotian border**, with the intent that they might strive and fight for the freedom of all **Greece**. They did not place their safety and comfort in the **city walls** <note>original: "Rinckmawer," referring to the circuit of defensive walls.</note>, nor did they allow the countryside to be devastated and plundered. Instead, because they held that their **valor** <note>original: "Mannheit," translating the Greek *arete*, meaning manly excellence or courage.</note> was a stronger wall than those built of stone, they ventured to protect and defend the land in which they were born and raised—as is only right. For just as we should feel a greater favor toward our true parents who gave us birth than toward those by whom we were chosen and adopted as children, so too should we love and esteem the land in which we were born and raised more than any other to which fortune has led us or where we have otherwise happened to arrive. This was the conviction held by our citizens; while they stood in equal danger alongside other **allies** and honorable, pious people, they met a different fate and fortune. Yet they did not receive their prize while living, but in death—not as the vanquished, but as those who remained in their place, on the ground and in the footsteps where they had been stationed in the battle-line, where they were struck down and perished. And if you will allow me to say something more wondrous and rare, which is nevertheless the truth...

Furthermore, the entire People made a common Decree that those who fled the city to avoid the common danger should be regarded as traitors, condemned, and punished with their lives.

Since the judgments and Decrees everywhere agree and harmonize—namely, the Senate in the **Areopagus** <term>Areopagus</term> <note>The ancient high court of Athens, known for its prestige and strictness in matters of homicide and religious sacrilege.</note>, the judges who condemned **Autolycus** <note>Autolycus was an Athenian official who was executed for sending his wife and children to safety after the defeat at Chaeronea, even though he stayed in the city himself.</note>, and likewise the Decree of the whole People which established such a law—it can be neither right nor fair for anyone to wish to speak or pass a judgment that would contradict them. This lie can first be refuted with this argument: that merchants, when they wish to go to sea, do so freely and openly; they take their best friends with them to give them a send-off and wish them a prosperous journey. They do not slink out secretly through a small side gate, nor do they take a mistress and maids with them, but rather depart alone with a servant. Furthermore, how else could it be proper to judge a citizen of **Athens** who lived for five full years in **Megara**, sent for his household gods <note>In antiquity, "household gods" (the Penates or Lararia) represented the spiritual heart of a home; moving them signified a permanent change of residence and an abandonment of one's ancestral city.</note> to be brought to him, and dared to sell the house and yard he had here? You must recognize him as a traitor to the fatherland and guilty of the gravest of vices. It would be entirely shameful if you were to release one man for such a crime, while others have been recognized as deserving of punishment and condemned for the same offense.

Perhaps he will also try to cover his conduct with this pretext, saying that no one who is absent can be condemned or held as a traitor unless they were commanded to guard a specific part of the city, such as the armory, the gates, or some other charge in the city. But I consider that those who are appointed to a specific place in the city betray only a part of the common good; however, because he surrendered the entire Common Good, he is unjust not only toward the living, but also toward the dead, and likewise against the temples of the gods, which were thereby abandoned and could not have their proper service and honor. # Of the Book of Regents

Even though the city is surrendered by those currently present, and even though it has entered into servitude, it is nonetheless still inhabited.

But if it is abandoned—as this **Leocrates** has abandoned it—then it becomes a devastation and a wasteland. Even if cities suffer some grievous blow, they can recover themselves and return to their previous state. But if they are completely razed and destroyed, no hope remains that they might be rebuilt and restored. Just as a human being, as long as he lives, can disentangle himself from his troubles, but when he is dead, he can have no hope remaining; so it is with cities. When they are devastated and razed, it is their death; but if the people remain within them and are not completely destroyed, they can recover themselves. Our own city may serve as an example of this, which at times had to suffer much from tyrants and was hard-pressed; subsequently, it was conquered by the **Lacedaemonians** <note>Also known as the Spartans, the long-time rivals of Athens.</note>, who then tore down the city walls and appointed thirty men to be our Regents <note>The "Thirty Tyrants," a pro-Spartan oligarchy installed in Athens after its defeat in the Peloponnesian War in 404 BCE.</note>. Although we suffered not a little from those same tyrants, we were nonetheless finally delivered from both dangers, and have also regained our freedom, government, and authority. However, cities that have been razed and devastated have never afterwards been rebuilt nor inhabited, as can be seen with **Troy** (for I would rather use this ancient example, since Troy was the greatest city of its time and held dominion over nearly all of Asia). When that city was once destroyed and razed by the **Greeks**, it has never since been rebuilt or inhabited. In contrast, **Messene** was destroyed to its foundations; however, after five hundred years had passed, it was rebuilt through the help of **Epaminondas** <note>A Theban general and statesman who broke Spartan power and helped the Messenians reclaim their land.</note> after the **Leuctran** <note>The Battle of Leuctra (371 BCE), where Thebes defeated Sparta.</note> defeat, when the citizens, because of the love they bore for their fatherland, found their way back together again. Therefore, **Virgil** <note>The Roman poet Publius Virgilius Maro.</note> also says:

->And a field where Troy once was.<-
<note>original: "Et campus ubi Troia fuit." A famous line from the Aeneid used to illustrate total desolation.</note>

But someone might say here that so much does not depend on a single person, nor could such damage to the fatherland—as has been suggested—result from his flight. To that, however, it must be answered that this excuse (which is impudent enough) is in itself rightly worthy of corporal punishment. For if he confesses that he abandoned the fatherland, nothing more is needed than to leave it to the court to recognize what a great transgression and evil deed it is. If he does not confess, it is foolishness to say that nothing depends on one person; I cannot agree with such a view. Rather, I say the opposite: that much depends on every individual specifically. For if every person keeps his place in the city, then the city stands rightly and cannot easily be harmed. But if one place within it remains neglected or abandoned, then the entire city must indeed fall into danger because of it.

# The Fourth Part
<meta>catchword: they their</meta>

all thieves and temple-robbers <note>German: *Kirchenräuber*; in the Athenian context, this refers to those who stole from sacred temples, a capital offense.</note>—whether they have stolen much or little—should be punished with death; likewise all murderers, whether they have slain a servant or a free man. For the law does not look solely upon the specific damage they committed, but considers what would happen if such acts were to prevail: it would be harmful and detrimental to the entire city. It is only right that we stick to this understanding, and it is not fitting to interpret or explain such a statute and ordinance in any other way. If a man were to come across the book of your laws and statutes and erase no more than one of them, and then try to excuse himself by saying he only removed a single law and therefore it was of little consequence, would you let that be? Would you not much rather punish him with death?

I, for my part, can judge or rule no other way than that such a person should be rightly punished, if we intend to maintain and defend the remaining laws. Since this is the case, this **Leocrates** must also be punished if you wish to bring your citizens to improvement. And you should not let yourselves be moved by the argument that he is but a single man; rather, take the weight of the matter to heart. For that there were not more than one, and that it remained with him alone, you must rightly thank God. It follows then that he should be punished all the more harshly, because he alone abandoned the other citizens and withdrew to a private place.

But I cannot at all be satisfied with those who defend him with the opinion that a departure should not be called treason, and that our ancestors also left the city and sailed to **Salamis** <note>The Battle of Salamis (480 BCE), where the Greeks defeated the Persian fleet.</note> when **Xerxes** <note>The King of Persia who invaded Greece.</note> led his naval forces into Greece to engage in battle. What foolishness it is to try to compare such an honorable deed of our ancestors—which is so highly to be praised—with this shameful flight; it is easy to see.

For this great virtue and manliness of our ancestors is praised with eternal honor throughout the whole world. I hold that no one is so wicked, or even so sluggish and lazy, that he would not wish he had been present at that same honorable deed and had kept company with the others in such danger. Thus, they did not "leave" the fatherland; rather, they chose and sought out a favorable place where they might meet the enemy.

And when **Eteonicus**, **Lacedemonius**, **Adymantus**, and **Corinth**, along with the fleet of the **Aeginetans** <note>Commanders and contingents from various Greek city-states (Sparta, Corinth, Aegina) who were hesitant to fight the Persians at Salamis.</note>, were considering fleeing from the enemy because they had been abandoned by other Greeks, they were preserved by our ancestors. Our ancestors brought them into the narrow sea at **Salamis**, where they then had to fight. Thus, our ancestors at that time overcame both friend and foe: the friends with kindness, and the foes in battle.

Whether this flight—where one can reach **Rhodes** by water in four days—can be compared with this magnificent and glorious deed, I leave for you yourselves to judge. Indeed, our ancestors would have tolerated such a traitor nowhere, but would have stoned him to death. For...
