# Of the Book of Rulers

...they loved their fatherland to such an extent that they nearly stoned King Alexander of Macedonia <note>This refers to Alexander I of Macedon, who served as an envoy for the Persian King Xerxes during the Persian Wars.</note> to death when he, on behalf of **Xerxes**, demanded that we should surrender ourselves to him.

Since they then judged even such a great king worthy of punishment for the sake of a single word, they would have much less allowed a man to go unpunished who betrayed the city through his actual deeds. Because they acted so chivalrously, they maintained their rule throughout all of Greece for seventy years; they plundered and waged war in **Phoenicia** and **Cilicia**; likewise, through great manliness, they successfully defeated and overcame the Persian naval fleet at **Eurymedon** <note>The Battle of the Eurymedon (c. 466 BC), where the Athenians won a double victory on both sea and land.</note> and the army they had on land, all in a single day. They took one hundred galleys from the enemy, in which they captured the spoils of all **Asia**; and they did not merely think of how they might erect a *tropheum* <note>original: "Tropheum"; a victory monument or trophy.</note> or sign of victory at **Salamis**, but rather preserved the freedom of all Greece. They also refused to make peace with the Persians in any other way than that no large ship should come past the **Cyanean Rocks** <note>Rocks at the entrance of the Bosphorus, marking a boundary for Persian naval movement.</note>, and that the Greeks should keep their laws in Europe and Asia and be allowed to live according to them. Now, if they had abandoned their fatherland at that time, as **Leocrates** has now done, these manly deeds would not have happened, and you would not be sitting in this place today. Just as it is fair and right that you honor, laud, and praise pious people and brave heroes, it must also follow by necessity that you are duty-bound to hate and finally punish the wicked—and specifically this **Leocrates**, who neither feared nor respected you, from which you may well perceive and measure the city's intent.

The voice of the city, however, is nothing other than the laws and statutes of those who established and ordained the common good. If you now obey them, you will do rightly and well; you will also be regarded and held as being truly worthy of such a government. For all citizens, when they reach their manly years, must swear an oath with these words: **"I swear that I will not disgrace or dishonor the holy weapons, nor will I abandon the battle-line; I will defend the fatherland and help to improve it as much as is within my power."**

If **Leocrates** took this oath, then he has publicly become a perjurer and a rogue, and has not only acted unjustly toward you but has also broken faith with God. But if he did not swear this oath, then he has deceived the city and has long gone about seeking how he might cause the city harm; therefore, it is also just and pertains to the honor of God that he be punished for it.

->Here the <term>oath</term><note>original: "Jurament"</note> shall be<-
->read aloud.<-

Since this oath is honorable and godly, and **Leocrates** has transgressed it in all its points, it follows that he has thereby publicly become a perjurer. For how could one hold the holy weapons more [firmly]...

# The Fourth Part
<meta>Sig: *</meta>
<meta>Catchword: unjust</meta>

...more savage <note>original: "tiger"; likely used here as an adjective meaning ferocious or cruel, akin to a beast.</note> and shameful dishonor than if he refuses to use those same weapons against the enemies? How can he be scolded as anything other than one who has abandoned his ensign or the battle formation? How much can a man be said to fight for the sanctuary when he intends to take no part in the common danger anywhere? How could he have more severely and shamefully betrayed his fatherland than by leaving the city, which—as much as it depended on him—has fallen into the hands of the enemies? Since he has now become notorious and guilty of so many vices, should he not justly be put to death? Or should only those be punished who have transgressed only a part of the oath <note>original: "Jurament"; refers to the Ephebic Oath taken by young Athenian men to defend the city and its laws.</note>? If that were the case, those who have committed many great vices would have less danger to expect than those who have offended in a minor and small matter.

But you should justly consider that upon the oath, as upon a bond, the entire common state of the city wavers and hangs. For since there are three members of the city—the Council <note>The Boule, or the governing council of Athens.</note>, the Judges, and the Citizens—each in particular, as the oath has bound all three of them together; and this for the sake of this reason: that many people escape the punishments which are customarily imposed upon them physically, but no one can flee the Divine Judgment and the divine punishments. And even if they do not come upon him immediately, they yet affect his lineage and descendants, so that they must fall into heavy pain and punishment. Therefore it also came to pass that the Greeks, before the battle that occurred at **Plataea** <note>A decisive 479 BC battle where a Greek alliance defeated the Persian invasion force.</note>, all bound themselves together with an oath; although they did not first devise it at that time, but took an example from our city, which you should justly consider, as it is still at hand and recorded in small letters; and therefore, you should feel wonder at the virtue of the citizens, your ancestors.

->Here the second oath shall also be read,<-
->as follows hereafter.<-

I swear that I will not value my life higher than freedom, nor will I abandon my captains, whether they be alive or dead; following this, I will bury my comrades who have fallen in battle; and when I have triumphed, I will not eradicate any city of the Greeks which took part in this battle. On the contrary, I will help to exterminate those who have sided with the **Persians**. I will also not rebuild the temples which the enemies have burned down, but will let the broken walls be a temple <note>Here used in the sense of a memorial or a sacred reminder.</note> of the malice which the Persians have practiced and undertaken in these our lands. Now, because the Greeks everywhere faithfully kept such an oath, they also felt the Divine help alongside it. And although they were all manly, brave heroes, yet the citizens in your city had the preference before others.

And since they were so manly and bold that they dared to stake and risk their lives for the fatherland, it would surely be shameful and in the highest degree...

# Of the Book of Regents.

...unjust <note>This continues the thought from the previous page: that it would be unjust for the judges to show leniency.</note> that you should not be allowed to punish those whose evil and shameful deeds result in the shame and dishonor of such a praiseworthy city. Nor should you allow the praise and glorious fame, which your ancestors earned through their **heroic deeds**, to be darkened by such shameful vices; for it is your duty, above all other Greeks, to preserve the honor of your city with diligence.

I will, however, recount a few examples here, which should remind you of what is proper for you to do regarding this accused man, as well as how you should conduct yourselves in many other great and important matters. For our city surpasses others in this regard: it can provide many more beautiful and bold examples. And just as it leads others in age, so too is it superior to others in **virtue and manhood**.

First, it happened at the time when **King Codrus** <note>Codrus was the legendary last King of Athens (c. 1089–1068 BC). According to myth, his self-sacrifice saved the city from invasion.</note> reigned here, that the peoples who lived in the **Peloponnese** <note>The southern peninsula of Greece.</note> moved out of their fatherland due to infertility and famine to attack our city with war. They had decided that once they had driven out our ancestors, they would divide the fields among themselves. But when they asked **Apollo at Delphi** <note>The Oracle of Delphi was the most important shrine in Greece, where the god Apollo was said to give prophecies through a priestess.</note> for advice on whether they would conquer the city of Athens, the answer given to them was that they would conquer the city, provided they did not kill King Codrus. When they heard this answer, they began the siege. However, this answer from Apollo was secretly reported to the Athenians by someone from Delphi who had heard it. Such was the favor our people held even among foreigners, that they cared for us and were concerned for our welfare.

What, then, did our ancestors do at that time when the city was besieged? They truly did not take to flight and abandon the fatherland as **Leocrates** has done. Nor did they surrender the city along with the sanctuary to the enemies. Rather, as they were too weak for the enemies in open battle, they stayed within the ring-wall and endured the siege. At that time, there was such great virtue in the kings that they preferred to lay down their lives for the welfare of the city rather than leave their dwellings while alive and grant them to the enemies. Therefore, it is said that Codrus commanded the citizens to take note of his death; subsequently, so that he might deceive the enemies, he put on a **beggar's cloak** and went out of the city in secret to gather wood. When some of the enemies lying before the city wanted to capture him—so that they might inquire of him how things were going in the city and what plans they had within—he killed one of them with a **sickle**. Because of this, the other enemy was moved to strike back and stabbed the King (whom he took for a beggar) with a sword. When this had happened, the Athenians sent a trumpeter into the camp to the enemies to request that they return King Codrus so that they might bury him, and they informed the enemies of the King's plan...

### The Fourth Part

...recount. Now, since the enemies realized that God did not wish for them to conquer the city, they returned the body of the deceased King to the citizens of Athens and departed. But for Cleomantis of Delphi, who revealed Apollo's answer to them, the city, out of gratitude, decreed that he and his descendants should be granted their maintenance in the **Town Hall** <note>original: "Rathhaus"; referring to the *Prytaneion*, a public building in Athens where distinguished citizens and foreign envoys were fed at the state's expense.</note> here.

You see, then, how this and similar examples compare to Leocrates. The kings at that time knowingly and willingly allowed themselves to be slain by the enemies, purchasing and preserving the salvation of the common city with their lives—so much so that they even had to deceive the enemies to make it happen. For this reason, the names of their lineages have descended from them, and they have been granted such honors as are usually paid to the immortals. Thus, the dead are not unjustly honored in that place where they endured such danger during their lives.

In contrast, Leocrates is not worthy of being buried in his ancestral soil even after his death; because he abandoned it, he should justly be rejected and driven from it. For the earth should not cover **virtuous and manly heroes** and shameful traitors at the same time.

He might perhaps try to argue further, claiming that if he knew himself to be guilty of such gross misconduct, he would not have come before the criminal court. But with such pretenses and excuses, thieves and sacrilegious robbers often attempt to delay and protect themselves. Such an excuse can carry little weight; rather, it is a testament to his impudence. One is not excused by this answer; instead, it is necessary for Leocrates to prove that he did not flee, that he did not abandon the city, and that he did not dwell in **Megara** <note>original: "Megaris"; a neighboring city-state where Leocrates fled after the Battle of Chaeronea.</note>. That would be an answer with "hands and feet" <note>A German idiom (Hand und Fuß) meaning an argument that is solid, well-grounded, and makes sense.</note>—one that Leocrates could stand upon.

But that he has come back here, I believe, has happened through a special providence of God, so that he might receive his due punishment. Since he escaped such an honorable and glorious danger, he must now, in contrast, die a shameful death, captured by those whom he betrayed by his flight. For even if he were to fall into trouble elsewhere, it would not appear as if he were being punished for this specific crime and shameful deed. Thus God does not punish such evildoers before He has first struck their consciences with fear and terror, so that they know not where to stay. Therefore, it seems to me that the ancient poets left behind these following verses as a prophecy:

> ->When a man has sinned greatly,<-
> ->And God wishes to punish him for it,<-
> ->He makes him entirely mad and blind,<-
> ->So that he no longer recognizes his own deeds.<-
> ->And he goes on sinning ever more,<-
> ->Until his final hour arrives.<-

->That he shall receive his punishment,<-
->For then he will be well and truly repaid.<-
->Nor can he escape the penalty,<-
->Since God has so ordained it.<-

Who among the elders does not remember, and who among the young has not heard, that Callistratus <note>Callistratus of Aphidnae (c. 410–355 BCE) was an Athenian politician and orator who was eventually condemned to death and fled into exile.</note> was criminally accused? While he wandered about in misery, he asked the **Oracle** how he would fare, and the answer given to him was that if he returned to Athens, he would receive his due. Not long after, he did return, and although he fled into the **Temple of the Twelve Gods** for sanctuary, he was nonetheless taken out by force and punished. Indeed, no injustice was done to him in this, for he received his rightful portion—which was nothing other than receiving his deserved reward for his transgressions. For this reason, the divine voice directed him there, so that he might be punished by us.

It is not likely that God performs the same signs for the righteous and the godly as He does for those burdened with harmful vices. However, I will nonetheless maintain that God looks upon all our deeds and affairs and provides for them, especially concerning the honor and kindness shown toward parents. Since we received the beginning of our lives from them, as well as great benefits, we should not only refrain from mistreating them but also refuse no danger on their behalf, if we wish to escape the vice of ungodliness.

A fine example of this is set (even though it is a story that is difficult to believe, yet it is not bad to present it to the youth). It is said that in **Sicily**, in a certain place, there is a high mountain <note>Referring to Mount Etna, the most active volcano in Europe.</note> which at times is said to spew and hurl fiery brands, ashes, stones, and other things for many miles around. At one time, these were carried into the city of **Catania**, among other surrounding towns and villages, so that the people had to flee from there and make a miserable escape, lest they be suffocated, burned, and perish within.

Among them was a young fellow who had a father who, due to his age and weakness, could hardly walk, let alone flee from the fire. Now, when the fire had reached nearly as far as the entire city, it is said that the young man took his father upon his shoulders; but when he could not make progress and the father was too heavy for him, so that he ended up in the middle of the fire, God showed that those who show kindness toward their parents are dear to Him and that He cares for them. It is said, therefore, that the flames burned many who were far ahead of him and had left their parents behind; but around this man, the fire divided on both sides and let them both pass through unharmed. Accordingly, that same place is said to be called and named the **Field of the Pious** <note>original: "Campus piorum"</note> or the **Field of Kindness** even to this day.

Among others, **Panormitanus** <note>Nicolaus de Tudeschis (1386–1445), an influential Italian canon lawyer known as "Panormitanus" because he was the Archbishop of Palermo.</note> mentions this mountain in the **Chapter on Judgments** <note>original: "c. de iudicijs"</note>. Likewise

[This city] surpasses others / and is not

    namely, from the Attic land <note>original: "Attischem Land"; refers to Attica, the region of Greece where Athens is located. Lycurgus emphasizes the Athenian belief that they were "autochthonous," or born from the soil of their own land, unlike other cities founded by migrants.</note>.

There, no one agrees with the other,

there, one wants this and the other that,

# The Fourth Part

It is a great thing / provided that by it /
the fatherland is rightly served.
As we are all duty-bound /
to ensure that the city alone /
might remain / and it is much better,
as it seems to me at this time:
That one person should die willingly now /
than that the whole city should perish.
If God had granted me a son /
and if that same son were required
for war / so that he might help strike down
and drive the enemies out of the land,
then I could not and would not refuse it /
even though it often happens otherwise
with other women / when they see
that their sons wish to go
and enlist themselves for war /
then they begin to wail.
Yet truly, that is not to be praised /
even though it frequently occurs among them.
Rather, they should much prefer to see /
how they might rightly consider
that their sons be held in fine manhood <term>Mannheit: refers to the Greek concept of 'andreia' or manly courage/virtue</term> /
and in honor.
So that they might thereby attain /
immortality and eternal praise.
Just as my daughter shall receive /
when she performs such a pious service <note>original: "frommen"; here meaning a beneficial or godly act for the community.</note>.
By her death alone, she shall save /
the other two little sisters <note>In the myth of Erechtheus, one daughter was sacrificed to save Athens from an invading army, and her sisters chose to die with her.</note>.
Therefore, I give her up quite willingly /
and ask not whether I am her mother.
And though she was indeed born of me /
I have no more claim to her
than that I planted <note>original: "gepflanzt"; used metaphorically for rearing or raising a child.</note> her.
But were the city to be entirely destroyed /
then I would have to watch the downfall /
of my entire lineage and everyone else.
And with that, the scepter and the whole government
would come to a total end.
Therefore, much more is at stake for me /
concerning the common city and its honor,
that they may be preserved /
than for any other thing on Earth.

### The Fourth Part

There is no more wretched thing at this time /
To be found anywhere upon this Earth /
Than to flee from war in shameful retreat /
And to wander to and fro in misery.
With father, mother, wife, and child /
Finding very few places of shelter.
Those who might welcome such people /
Or provide them with food and drink /
Are few; instead, everyone looks on with resentment /
And their situation may quickly go to ruin.
Especially if one begs too much /
One is very soon commanded to be silent /
And told to move along /
To find shelter in some other place.
At this, a man’s heart grows weak /
When his affairs stand in such a wretched state /
That no one wishes to take his side /
And everyone feels ashamed of him.
Therefore, let us be undaunted /
And strike out with honest joy.
Let us offer up our lives /
For the <term>fatherland</term><note>German: *Vaterland*. In this context, it refers to the Greek *polis* or city-state, specifically Sparta.</note>, for we /
Truly all owe it this duty.
Therefore, we must bravely stake our lives.
Under penalty of death, take heed as well /
That no man gives cause to another /
To turn coward through his flight /
And thus show his back to the enemy.
Instead, you must remain with your bodies /
And your weapons by the <term>standard</term><note>German: *Fähnlein*. Literally "little flag," referring to the military unit’s banner or the company itself.</note>.
Attack the enemy with earnestness /
And do not hold your lives too dear.
Instead, consider your honor /
As you learn from this teaching.
Take heed of the <term>elders</term><note>Tyrtaeus’s poetry often emphasized that young men must not let the older soldiers—whose knees are no longer nimble—die on the front lines while the youth flee.</note> as well /
So that not a single one of them /
Is left behind; for it would be a great shame /
If they were to faithfully for the fatherland /
Stake their very lives /
While the entire troop of young men /
Were to flee and leave them /
To fight the enemy all alone /
Leaving them abandoned in their time of need /
To be struck down and killed.

How laudable and glorious it is to recount and hear the memory of such knightly deeds, you must consider for yourselves; and just as these deeds adorn and make such actions respectable, so are they primarily to be spoken of in praise of this city. Conversely, however, the flight of Leocrates most highly obscures, shames, and diminishes the honor and glory which the city has acquired and maintained over so many long years. Now, if you punish him severely as he has deserved, you will give the other Greeks to understand that you take no pleasure in such misconduct. But if you should acquit him and let him go unpunished, you will completely cover up the honor and glory of your ancestors, and this example will be harmful and offensive to the entire citizenry. For those who do not hold your ancestors in high regard will follow the example of this Leocrates; they will attempt to turn affairs so that manhood, honor, and virtue may well be acceptable elsewhere, but among you, only shamelessness and treachery have a place.

## Of the Book of Rulers

to have; For just as they were tireless in all honest, honorable, and manly deeds, they also conducted themselves with severity and earnestness at all times regarding the punishment of crimes and misconduct. For look only at the severity and earnestness with which they punished those who were traitors and enemies of the common state. Namely, when Phrynichus was murdered <note>German: *erwürget*; while this often means strangled, in this historical context it refers generally to the assassination of the oligarchic leader Phrynichus in 411 BCE.</note> at the well in the willow thicket by Apollodorus and Thrasybulus during the night, and the friends of Phrynichus had those two seized and captured, they were declared free and released by the whole people. This was after it was investigated and found that Phrynichus had been engaged in treachery, and therefore was justly killed, but the two men had been unjustly imprisoned. It did not stop there; Critias also considered it right that Phrynichus, though already dead, should be accused of the crime of high treason <note>Original Latin: *laesae Maiestatis*; a legal term referring to an offense against the dignity or security of the state.</note>. If he were convicted and sentenced, he was to be dug up again, and his bones carried out and cast away from the entire Athenian land. Thus, he was to be robbed of the honors of burial in the land and city which he had betrayed.

Furthermore, a public decree was also made that if the dead Phrynichus were thus condemned, those who had dared to defend him should be held guilty of the same punishment. Our ancestors used such earnestness at that time because they considered it not only improper, but indeed the greatest injustice, to provide support and help to such traitors. Rather, they firmly believed that those who undertook to defend traitors should themselves be judged and punished as nothing other than traitors. Because they were so opposed to such wicked people and confronted evildoers in such a manner, they never allowed them to rise up, but immediately suppressed and rooted them out.

Thus, they also preserved the freedom of the fatherland in great and magnificent wars, for they did not have to fear any internal treachery from their own citizens at home, and they manfully struck down and overcame the enemies.

->be read here.<-

Now that you have heard the decree, you should remind yourselves of your office and consider what is your duty to do in this matter. Those ancestors dug up the bones of the traitor and cast them outside the Athenian borders; they not only had his advocates and defenders, such as Aristarchus and Alexicles, put to death, but also deemed them unworthy of being buried in the Attic territory <note>German: *Attischen Pflege*; referring to the land under the jurisdiction of Athens.</note>. And you here have the traitor before the court in the flesh, alive and present, and yet you would let him go free and unpunished? By my life, you must never allow it to be said of you that you ignored the examples of your fathers, which guide you toward a far different path; for such a thing would undoubtedly result in a significant loss of your own standing.

If no more than this single decree existed concerning these matters, one might argue that it was born of anger or envy, or that you acted with too much haste rather than deliberating the matter as necessity requires. However, since a similar punishment has been ordained until now not only in this court but in all others as well, it clearly appears that the judges, out of a love for justice, were so inflamed against this hideous and harmful vice <note>The "vice" referred to here is high treason and the abandonment of the city during wartime.</note> that they established this very penalty.

When they held a criminal trial over Hipparchus, and he did not wait for the day of judgment nor defend himself, he was to be punished in his person. Since his person was gone and had escaped the penalty, they removed his statue from the castle <note>German: *Schloß*; referring here to the Acropolis, the fortified heart of Athens.</note>, desecrated it, and had it melted down into a bronze pillar. Upon this pillar, they ordered the names of traitors and the condemned to be inscribed, placing the name of Hipparchus at the very top, followed by the other traitors. Now, let the first decree be read, in which it was determined that the statue of Hipparchus should be torn down from the castle. Subsequently, let the writing on the pillar be read.

This Hipparchus was a friend of Pisistratus <note>Pisistratus was a famous tyrant of Athens; his "friends" or relatives were often viewed with suspicion by the later democracy.</note>; and when he drove away his children, he himself sought after the tyranny and the seat of government.

Do you not see that the same punishment was always imposed upon this vice? When they could not capture the traitor’s body, they attacked his memory, doing away with it and punishing his likeness—not because the image itself could suffer or feel anger, but so that descendants might keep such an example in mind and see how our ancestors were minded toward traitors.

I also ask that the second decree be read, concerning the citizens who fled to the enemies at Decelea <note>A strategic outpost in Attica that was occupied by the Spartans (Lacedaemonians) during the Peloponnesian War, serving as a base to harass Athens.</note> while our city was besieged by the Lacedaemonians, so that the judges may recognize and perceive that a unanimous sentence <term>Sentence: original *Sententz*, a formal judicial decision or judgment</term> has always been rendered and passed in these cases.

Although at first they had to proceed very slowly and deal with matters wisely, they finally brought it to the point that the entire citizenry swore to the decree. Namely: whoever should undertake to become a tyrant, or to betray the city, or lastly to change the established government, could be strangled <note>In this context, *erwürget* (strangled/slain) implies being killed with impunity or summarily executed.</note> by anyone who noticed it or heard of it without penalty. And it was considered at that time that it would be better to slay the one who gave cause for suspicion, rather than waiting so long until he had put his designs into action; for if one watched too long and thereby lost their freedom, the matter could no longer be helped. ### The Fourth Part

...that one should seize citizens as soon as any one of them makes himself known <note>In this context, it means showing the first signs of traitorous intent.</note>, so that they might learn to be so cautious that no one could truthfully harbor any suspicion or mistrust against them.

These things have been written upon the pillar that stands in the **Town Hall**, so that when the **Councilmen** <note>original: "Rahtsherrn"</note> gather for the Council, they might be reminded of them. To this end, the citizens have ordained by a solemn oath that if any man be found who deals in treacherous dealings and counsel, he may be immediately strangled by any private person. In other crimes and misdeeds, the punishment of forfeiture must follow; but in **treason** <term>High Treason: crimes against the state or its sovereignty</term>, and when one would dare to bring the city into servitude through **tyrannical practices**, there must be no rest or delay. Instead, the highest necessity requires that such a thing be prevented as soon as is possible. Should one wait so long that such treason or tyranny is actually put into effect, then the wait would have been far too long, and the city, once it was overwhelmed, could not withstand the danger, nor defend itself, nor bring those who caused it to their proper punishment.

Such foresight of your ancestors, and these examples, you should weigh and take to heart today, on this day and in this court. You must also conduct yourselves accordingly and, by your lives, do not forget your lineage when delivering the verdict, nor let it slip from your minds. Rather, you should encourage and exhort one another so that a lawful judgment might be found by you, as you have heard and read enough examples from the decrees to understand them as a **guiding rule** <note>original: "Richtschnur," literally a plumb line or builder's string used to ensure a wall is straight</note>. Indeed, you have also sworn an oath to the **Decree of Demophantus** <note>Demophantus was an Athenian statesman who, in 410 BCE, passed a law authorizing the killing of anyone who attempted to overthrow the democracy.</note>, that you would punish with death all those who dare to surrender or betray the fatherland, whether in words or in deeds. And you must in no way think that you can be partakers of your paternal inheritance if you do not participate in the oath which your ancestors swore with such earnestness, as the welfare of the common city must be maintained through it.

Lest it appear that our city alone held such a strict court over traitors, I can clearly demonstrate that the **Lacedaemonians** <note>The Spartans</note> conducted themselves in the same manner. Although I wish to pray here that you do not set yourselves against me or be vexed that I mention the Lacedaemonians so often and so much in this, my necessary and unavoidable case and grievance, upon which so much of the common city's welfare depends. For it is surely fitting that we take a pattern and example from such a city which has righteous and good laws, and is subject and obedient to the same, since everyone can more easily inform himself from such an example as to what he should recognize and judge in this case, by virtue of his oath.

As can be seen from the example of **Pausanias** <note>A famous Spartan regent and general who led the Greeks to victory at the Battle of Plataea but was later accused of conspiring with the Persian King.</note>, who defeated the **Macedonian** <note>The German text says "Macedonij," though historical context usually refers to the Medes or Persians in this specific story of Pausanias.</note> army and shortly thereafter dared to establish a **monarchy** in Greece and treacherously subject the Greeks to the Persians...

...to make the city subject to himself, the **Ephors** <note>The Ephors were five senior magistrates in ancient Sparta who oversaw the kings and maintained the laws.</note> as soon as they learned of this, sought after him so that they might seize him. But because they could not capture him—as he had fled into the **Temple of Pallas** <note>Referring to the Temple of Athena Chalkioikos in Sparta; traditionally, temples provided sanctuary (asylum) where no one could be forcibly removed.</note>—they had the gates of the temple barred on all sides and stationed guards there so that he could not escape. Therefore, he was kept and watched in the temple for so long that he died of hunger therein, so that others might have an abhorrence for such an example and might take heed from it.

Furthermore, the temples of the gods should not help or offer sanctuary to such traitors, for the reason that traitors first violate the religion and the gods of the **Fatherland** <term>Fatherland (Vaterland): Here referring to the Greek "patris," the ancestral city-state which the traitor has abandoned.</term>. Therefore, they should not hope for any protection or comfort from those same gods.

Here I must tell another magnificent and brave example. The Spartans enacted a law that all those who refused to fight for the Fatherland should be killed. By this, they wished to demonstrate that even if such fellows flee death in the heat of battle, it shall not help them; rather, because they sought to escape death through flight, they shall be condemned to death. And so that you may see that I speak the truth and that the matter is fundamentally as I say, I will have that same statute read publicly here.

### Statute.

From this, dear Lords, you can clearly see how honorable and also wholesome this law and statute was devised, not only for the **Lacedemonians** <note>Another name for the Spartans.</note> but also for other people. For fear compels men, since in war they must endure and expect all kinds of danger. For who would want to abandon the Fatherland if he sees that by doing so he has forfeited his head? Who would want to escape from war or battle for the sake of saving his life if, through such flight, he attains exactly what might have happened to him in war, and thus has nothing else to expect but death? Instead, every citizen must consider that since he must expect nothing but death on either side, he would rather die honorably before the enemy than be punished with life-taking shame before a court because of the flight he took.

But he who has abandoned the city is punished much more justly than if he had fled from the military camp. For the soldiers who lie in the field fight for the city so that they may maintain a safe place in which they can reside and protect themselves from the enemies. But he who flees from the city thinks only of how he alone might be safe in his own body, and fights neither for his house nor for the common city. Instead, he throws away the ancestral and essential rights of all men—rights which are so fundamental that they are observed even in other animals that have no understanding, showing that even they carry a remarkable natural affection for such rights.

For although birds, on account of their speed, are most likely to...

# The Fourth Part

...are prepared for flight, yet they allow themselves to be struck dead upon the nest rather than abandon it. As we may read concerning this in the works of a poet:

> ->When the bird has made its nest,<-
> ->And brought its eggs therein,<-
> ->It does not fly away out of fear,<-
> ->And leave another to sit<-
> ->Upon its eggs within the nest,<-
> ->But rather stays to be strangled there.<-

But because Leocrates, regardless of this <note>The speaker is contrasting the natural instinct of a simple bird with the shameful behavior of Leocrates.</note>, abandoned his **Fatherland** <term>Fatherland (Vaterland): In this context, referring to Athens, which Leocrates fled after the city’s defeat at the Battle of Chaeronea in 338 BC.</term> out of fear, it is only right that he be granted refuge in no city. Instead, wherever he goes, he should be driven out and hunted away more than any murderer. For those who wander in misery because of a murder may occasionally find a place where they receive lodging—since the one who fled has no friends in that place who might prevent it. But when someone has treacherously abandoned his own fatherland, what city would dare to take him in and provide him shelter? For if he did not wish to come to the aid of his own fatherland, how could he be expected to put himself in danger for another or a foreign city? And just as every man is accustomed to having in his fatherland his fellow citizens, inhabitants, guests, and especially trusted friends and kinsmen—who enjoy the common goods of that fatherland alongside him—so too is nothing else proper for them but that, as soon as a common danger arises, they should immediately come running and help to turn it aside so long as their bodies have strength.

Since, therefore, other and foreign cities—which he did not even offend—have cast him out and would not tolerate him, you should tolerate him much less. Rather, because he has injured you to the highest degree, you should punish him most severely. Indeed, if any punishment could be devised that were harsher and more cruel than death, that same punishment would rightly be inflicted upon this Leocrates. For others, when they have treachery in their minds and are caught at it, are punished before they can complete the deed; but this man is brought to judgment a long time after he committed his treason.

I would also like to see—since the **advocates** <note>In Athenian law, "advocates" (synegoroi) were often friends or influential citizens who spoke on behalf of a defendant.</note> dare to protect Leocrates—with what excuse they intend to escape the punishment they have thereby earned. Perhaps they are his good friends. But I cannot consider them innocent for that reason, nor do I believe this insolent deed should be forgiven them on that account. Rather, I say freely that they are worthy of being punished with their lives. For before Leocrates became a traitor, one did not know what these fellows were planning <note>original: "was sie am Schilde füren." Literally "what they carry on their shield," an idiom for one's hidden intentions or true character.</note>. But now they reveal themselves openly: that they maintain friendship with wicked people—because they themselves are no different and share the same morals—and would gladly defend them. It will be necessary for them to answer for themselves before they bring this defendant out of danger.

And if there could be any understanding or thought among the dead, I am certain that his father would be most vehemently opposed to him and would pass a judgment upon him that would be too heavy to bear. This is because he abandoned his own column in the Temple of Jupiter <note>This refers to a memorial or statue dedicated to his father's military service, likely in the Temple of Zeus Soter.</note> and left it to the enemies to overturn in their predatory way. Thus, to his own shame and disgrace, he surrendered such a magnificent witness to his father’s **manhood** and **virtue** to be destroyed by the enemy. For it would surely cause his father great pain to be named and called the father of a traitor. For this reason, I have been addressed and questioned by many as to why I did not also accuse Leocrates of being a traitor to his own paternal memory in the Temple of Jupiter. To these I answered that I well know this vice is worthy of no small punishment, but I will nevertheless not forget Jupiter the Preserver <note>original: "Iouis Seruatoris." This is the Latin form of Zeus Soter (Zeus the Savior/Preserver), to whom the Athenians looked for protection.</note> in my accusation.

But to return to the advocates and protectors of Leocrates, I am most of all amazed that these people—who are bound to the defendant neither by blood relation nor by friendship, but have simply been bought with money—dare to take up Leocrates's cause and wish to defend him. For there is no doubt that such men ought not rightly be spared from being punished with death themselves. For whoever dares to undertake the defense of such capital crimes gives sufficient understanding that he might also be willing to keep company with those who commit such vices. Such citizens are not to be strengthened in this pursuit against you. Instead, they must be instructed and brought to a point where they are more intent on how they might defend you, the courts and the law, and freedom and the **Fatherland**. And it matters not that some of these advocates claim they are not there to overwhelm and overcome us with their speech, but only wish to obtain through their prayers that the defendant might be granted mercy (perhaps because they themselves have earned merit for the **common good** <term>Common good (Gemeiner nutz): The general welfare of the state or public interest.</term>). I am not at all satisfied with this. For if they have done something good for the common good—so that they and their lineage might gain honor and fame thereby—or have spent money for its sake, they should rightly be satisfied with the honor shown to them for it. They should not desire that which might result in shame for the common good. For those who have kept horses for the benefit of the common good, or have organized magnificent games, or those who have built new ships, repaired the **city walls**, or otherwise shown themselves generous and liberal toward the common city, are honored in return with a crown. While it is not unjust to highly praise such liberality in citizens—notwithstanding that today, pomp and extravagance in other useless things have risen very high—no good deeds should be considered so great that, for the sake of gratitude, a traitor should be gifted his life in return. No one should be so insane that, if he wishes to stand with honor and fame in his fatherland and surpass other citizens...

### The Fourth Part

...would strike him down, and that he would never hold with or favor those who intend to destroy the place where he is to be honored.

And although it is otherwise not customary to bring a wife and children before the law in criminal matters, it would nonetheless be unjust if this were not done in cases concerning **treason**. The defendant's wife and children, as those who have the most at stake, should also be present to see and hear how the traitor is accused, so that their compassion and distress might give the judges cause to pass a sentence that is all the more vehement and earnest.

However, since it is not usual to allow such a household to come before the court, and it is your duty by virtue of your office to consider and protect their welfare in such trials, I therefore also ask you to recognize and pronounce that this traitor be sentenced from life to death. Thus, when you return home, you will have this example to show and report to your own wives and children. For you must consider that it would be entirely unjust if Leocrates were to have the same rights as other citizens who protected and defended the **Fatherland**. He was the first to abandon the city; he did not fight at the front, and finally, he did not defend the city walls. But regardless of this, he has now returned and presumes to use the communal sacrifices, the marketplace <note>The marketplace (Agora) was the heart of Athenian civic and religious life; a traitor was considered "polluted" and was religiously forbidden from entering such sacred public spaces.</note>, the common law, and the entire form of the common good just like any other citizen. It was for the sake of preserving these very things that at **Chaeronea** <note>The Battle of Chaeronea (338 BCE), where Philip II of Macedon defeated the Greek city-states, including Athens. This defeat led to the end of Greek city-state independence.</note> some thousand men had to sacrifice their lives. The city had them buried collectively, yet this hard, stubborn, and iron-hearted man did not revere their graves, even though they stood before him as he entered the city. He even dares to desire that he might be permitted to walk openly among those who are in great mourning and distress—and who even until this hour bewail the deaths—of their sons, husbands, brothers, and fathers who perished in the war at Chaeronea.

But since he asks to be heard according to the laws of this city—as the laws state that one side must be heard as well as the other—I ask you to question him as to which laws he calls upon for protection: are they the ones which he previously betrayed and shamefully abandoned? You, however, should in no way grant him permission to dwell within these city walls, nor to enjoy the laws and honors of other honest citizens, since he did not protect them alongside the other citizens. If he calls upon the gods, then ask him which gods he seeks refuge with. Are they the ones whose temples, altars, and images he betrayed? But if he turns to the citizens and begs for mercy, asking that you should have pity on him, then in that case no mercy, nor even the safety of the common city, should preserve him or come to his aid.

Instead, he may go off to **Rhodes** <note>Leocrates famously fled to the island of Rhodes after the defeat at Chaeronea, taking his wealth with him.</note> and call upon them for help, since he saw fit to believe that he would have more protection there and be better secured than here in his own Fatherland. And I would gladly [hear] from him...

# Of the Book of Rulers.

I would ask of him to know what age or gender of people he intends to call upon for help here, that they might have mercy upon him. Should it be the elderly? But as far as it was within his power, he has stripped the elderly of all their comfort and help in which they might have rejoiced; for they could not have been supported by the young, nor, had they died, could they have been buried in a free land. Is it the young? Certainly not; for if those very men—who still have it fresh in their memory how their comrades were slain in the war—wished to set him free and release him from this judgment, they would be doing nothing other than condemning those same slain men with their verdict. This they will surely not do, nor will they set this traitor free and clear, as if he were innocent.

Or do you wish, by such an example, to embolden other **wicked rogues** and thereby give cause for everyone to attack the **common good** and be harmful to it as they please, both in word and deed? For if Leocrates were to be seen in this city—he who previously stayed in **Megara** <note>A neighboring city-state to Athens where Leocrates fled to escape the war.</note> for five or six whole years as a resident—nothing would more certainly follow than that not only all the exiled and orphaned, but even our worst enemies (who passed such a judgment that all **Attic cities** should be turned into cattle pastures) would return once more.

Since this speech has now drawn on for a long time, I ask you to bear with me, for I wish to step down soon, once I have read only the **Decree** concerning the oath of the judges. This is useful to me for this matter, and it should be justly considered and weighed before the passing of the verdict.

### Decree.

Now that you have heard what your sworn oath entails, and I as a prosecutor have brought this evildoer here before you, I ask—since it stands in your power—that you take him into proper punishment. For it is indeed right and just that he be punished for God's sake, and for the sake of your own welfare, on account of his crimes. For a person is guilty of a vice which he has committed even before the verdict is handed down; but when the trial has been held, if one does not use proper earnestness therein, the guilt remains upon the judges, in such a way that they must find it difficult to answer for it.

In addition, you should also know that although you cast your **stones** <note>In ancient Athenian courts, jurors voted by placing bronze discs or stones into two different urns (the "buckets" mentioned here) to signify guilt or innocence.</note> secretly into the bucket in passing your judgment, our **LORD God** will nevertheless look upon your sentencing and will judge it Himself. Furthermore, this case is of such a nature that in this single verdict you must declare yourselves against many vices and shameful deeds, which are exceedingly great. Firstly, against **treason**, because Leocrates surrendered the abandoned Fatherland to the enemies; against the crime of <term>High Treason</term> <note>original: "crimen læsę Maiestatis"; Latin for "the crime of injured majesty," referring to an offense against the state or its sovereignty.</note>, or that he acted against the authorities, in that he would not await the danger for the sake of protecting the **Common Government** of this city.

# The Fourth Part

...against his godlessness; for he, as far as he was able, was a cause for the **Church and Religion** <note>original: "Kirche vnd Religion". In this context, the translator uses "Church" to refer to the sacred institutions and temples of Athens.</note> to have been completely destroyed. He acted against the honor of his parents, because he destroyed the graves and commemorations of the dead. Finally, he also acted against the military order by fleeing from the battle line and abandoning the camp, having escaped in secret so that the **captains** <term>Hauptleute: military commanders or officers</term> might not assign him to a specific post.

In former times, when a person was legally accused and the **judges and jurors** <term>Schöpffen: lay judges or assessors in a court</term> were to pass a verdict upon it, the judgment was not composed in writing or pronounced orally. Instead, they used a **bucket** <note>original: "Eymer". Referring to the voting urns used in ancient Athenian courts.</note> which was covered. Into this, each judge and juror would cast a **stone**, either white or black. If more white stones were found in the bucket than black ones, the accused was acquitted; but if there were more black ones, he had to be punished.

Who would now wish to acquit such a defendant, who has been publicly convicted of his misdeeds? Who would want to leave unpunished so many shameful vices, which he committed not only intentionally and knowingly, but also in a deceitful manner? Who would be so foolish and reckless as to put his own life in danger for the sake of this traitor—by counting him as acquitted—and thereby give hope to other traitors that they too would remain unpunished? Who would have compassion for him when he considers how unmercifully the enemies would have treated our poor wives and children, as well as the poor, helpless people, had the city been conquered? They would have plundered, strangled, and burned everything. Who, finally, would show any kindness to a traitor, knowing that God is angered by it and that punishment must be expected for it?

Now, so that I might fulfill my bounden duty to the **homeland** <note>original: "Vaterland". Lycurgus refers to the city-state of Athens.</note>, and likewise come to the aid of the laws and religion, I hope that I have brought this, my painful indictment, in a right and proper manner with all the necessary circumstances. I have also not allowed myself to be troubled by what else **Leocrates** might have forfeited or committed in his life, which might have caused me to go too far in my speech; rather, I have said only what necessity required. You, my Lords, will consider that if you find this Leocrates innocent, you thereby condemn your homeland, citizens, wives, and children. For since two buckets are set out—one by which the city is betrayed, the other by which it is preserved—and the stones are cast into them either for the destruction or the salvation of the homeland: if you acquit Leocrates, you will remind the people of nothing other than how they too may betray the fatherland, the religion, and the **naval fleet**. But if you punish him according to his merit, it is certain that many will take this as a reminder to protect and preserve the homeland and this government. If you truly look upon the earth, the trees, the harbors, the ships, the city walls, the temples, and the religion, it will be found that they all cry out and plead together that they might be protected and preserved through your righteous judgment. Therefore, and because this is so, I pray that you would show yourselves by this example in such a way

and

> I swear that I will do or commit nothing unseemly in war. And whichever **ensign** <term>Fähnrich: a standard-bearer or the military unit gathered under a specific flag</term> I am assigned to in battle, I will be found with him at all times and will not shrink from him. I will fight faithfully for the temples and religion, both alone and with the multitude. I will not make the fatherland worse, but rather better than I received it. Whatever is justly imposed upon me, I will show myself obedient at all times, as well as to that which the whole people shall henceforth harmoniously decree. But if anyone should venture to change the laws or make them contradictory, I will not side with him, nor will I—as far as it lies within my power—allow it, but will instead defend them, whether I am alone or among the crowd. Furthermore, I will hold the religion of my fathers in honor; and upon these words, I desire to call the gods as witnesses.

Previously, according to the opinion of some, the example of **Timagoras** <note>Timagoras was an Athenian envoy sent to the Persian King Artaxerxes II; he was later executed for accepting bribes and failing to coordinate with his fellow envoys.</note> also belongs here. He was accused in Athens when he went on an embassy with **Pelopidas** <note>A prominent Theban general and statesman.</note> to the King in Persia. There, he accepted gifts and did not stay in the same quarters as his fellow envoy. For this reason, when he returned home, he was accused as mentioned, convicted, and finally punished with death, as **Xenophon** and **Plutarch** write in the *Life of Pelopidas* <note>original: "vita Pelopidæ"</note>.

It is also read that when a powerful and wealthy citizen once secretly slipped out of the city of **Venice** and abandoned his fatherland, the Council ordered that his house be torn down to its foundations and a monument of dishonor be set in that same place for eternal memory.

But to return again to **Leocrates** <note>Leocrates was an Athenian merchant who fled Athens after the defeat at the Battle of Chaeronea in 338 BCE, fearing the city would be besieged.</note>: if the matter is weighed, it is true that by leaving the city against the Council's decree, he acted against his proper duty. Nevertheless, he did not act so grievously against his fatherland as to surrender it or fight against it. Rather, he merely departed without permission and in silence, taking with him what he could carry at the time. And though he started a rumor in **Rhodes** that the city of Athens had been conquered—which he perhaps heard from others—he held no special office in Athens. He was not a member of the Council or a commander, but followed his trade; therefore, to such a city, not much could have depended on such a minor person. But regardless and notwithstanding this, the people of Athens took it so much to heart, and **Lycurgus** <note>The orator and statesman who prosecuted Leocrates for treason.</note> accused him so vehemently, that he even said there was no law in existence that sufficiently expressed his guilt, nor could any penalty be devised that could properly match his crime...

For if Lycurgus <note>The text refers to Lycurgus of Athens (c. 390–324 BC), the orator who famously prosecuted Leocrates for deserting the city after the Battle of Chaeronea.</note> accused this man so fiercely, what would he have done if he had fought against the fatherland, which he was bound to defend? As we have certainly experienced and seen in our own times—though to write about that here would be a bit too long.

But I must say this nonetheless: that some have allowed themselves to be used extensively against their fatherland, the praiseworthy German Nation, which is little to their credit to record or say of them; yet it stands on every man's own responsibility.

And just as Leocrates and others acted unfaithfully toward their fatherland, for which they received their due punishment, one also reads that many others, by contrast, held to it faithfully and even gave their lives for it. For did not M. Curtius <note>Marcus Curtius, a legendary Roman hero who sacrificed himself by leaping into a mysterious chasm in the Roman Forum to appease the gods and save the city.</note> plunge himself into the pit, which could be filled with no earth, so that the city of Rome would no longer need to stand in worry? Did not Mucius Scaevola <note>Gaius Mucius Scaevola, a Roman youth who attempted to assassinate the Etruscan king Porsenna and famously burnt his own right hand to show his resolve.</note> despise his life and risk everything by going into the enemy camp with great boldness and audacity, and undertaking to stab King Porsenna so that his fatherland might be delivered from the heavy siege? Did not Agesilaus <note>Agesilaus II, King of Sparta, known for his military leadership and devotion to the Spartan state.</note> turn all his honor and fame, which he had gained in wars, solely to the benefit of the fatherland? To say nothing of Cicero, Cato, Sertorius, Pompey, and others—for who can recount all those precious and honorable people in brief, since a separate book could well be written about them.

# That the subjects are bound to show proper obedience to the authorities, and how far this extends.

## The Twenty-first Chapter.

I have taught and shown throughout the whole book until now how and in what manner the sovereigns and rulers should behave toward their subjects, and what they are duty-bound to do for them. However, because it will not suffice for a prince or ruler to be diligent in his office and to establish good laws and order if the subjects do not also faithfully keep those same laws and be obedient to the authorities. Therefore, it is appropriate here to provide an account and notice to the subjects on how they should behave toward the authorities, and what they are duty-bound to do for them: namely, to diligently observe their statutes, laws, commands, and prohibitions. This was also seen and considered by Cambyses, King of the Persians, as is written of him, that he made two rules for the cities and lands: The

# Of the Ruler’s Book

...one: That the rulers know how to rightly govern the common man and to command with laws. The other: that the subjects do not make themselves resistant to the lord’s command, but rather know how to render obedience to the same.

And these two rules took their origin from the **Law of the Twelve Tables** <note>The foundation of Roman law, drafted mid-5th century BC, which defined the rights and duties of citizens.</note>, which says: Let the commands be just, and let the citizens obey them modestly and without refusal. <note>original: "Iusta imperia sunto, ijsq; ciues modestè, ac sine recusatione parento."</note> That is: The government shall be just, and the citizens shall also be submissive to it and obey without hesitation. For just as it is not enough for a schoolmaster to be diligent with his pupils, making good laws and order for them and leading a righteous way to instruct and govern the boys—unless the pupils also learn to pay diligent attention and be obedient.

So it also goes between the **authority** <term>Oberkeit: a term used for the governing powers or magistracy</term> and the **subjects**. And just as a righteous ruler is a rare thing, so too is a pious, faithful, and obedient subject a much "rarer bird." When they are meant to master, judge, and sentence the lords and authorities, and give no one anything, they are well-suited for it. But when they are meant to do what is proper for them, and what the authority requires of them, then "no one is home" <note>An idiom meaning they avoid their responsibilities or are nowhere to be found when work is required.</note>; otherwise, there is no end to their criticisms. At one moment the authority is too pious; at another, it is too "quick" <note>meaning harsh or impulsive</note>; so that it can never do right or hit the mark, regardless of how it governs. And the poor people do not recognize or know what a heavy and unbearable burden governance is—as they would certainly experience if they were to take it into their own hands and try it; then they would see that it is not as easy to be a ruler as they perhaps think and talk about on the **beer benches** and over wine.

But should one let the subjects have their way when they are so disobedient and "want the stools to climb onto the benches" <note>A proverb used by Count Albrecht to describe an upset in the natural order, where the low seek to command the high.</note>, as my Gracious Lord **Count Albrecht von Mansfeld** <note>Albrecht VII, Count of Mansfeld (1480–1560), a prominent supporter of the Reformation and friend of Martin Luther.</note> used to say? The answer is no. For just as a father should not permit his children to live as they please and show themselves disobedient, or presume to interfere in the household management, but should rather take them into proper punishment—so too does a lord or authority have the power to punish such disobedience in his subjects by virtue of his office. However, one sees in sensible parents how they kindly admonish their children to be pious and obedient, and do not use the **sharp rod** before good words and admonition have failed entirely. Authority should follow this example: first, kindly remind the subjects of their duty. But if such reminders do not help or take hold, then they may also use severity, so that the subjects know they have a master. Yet all things must be done with measure, and not too harshly, as pious and Christian, sensible rulers will well know how to do.

But so that the subjects also see that they are bound to obey the authority, they should know that things must proceed in a city no differently than with a human body: that every limb holds to its own kind, its command, and its office. So that the eyes see, the ears hear, the mouth speaks, the hands work, and

### The Fourth Part

the feet walk; and no limb dares to perform the work of another, for it is indeed impossible for them to do so. Especially, all must follow the head. And it would become a very strange and wondrous thing if the hands and feet were to encroach upon the eyes and ears, interfering in their office, and thus wishing to hear and see for themselves. Just as one also sees among the **subjects** <term>Unterthanen: the common people living under the rule of a prince or magistrate</term>, that they always wish to be cleverer and to see and hear more sharply than the rulers themselves, who are commanded to look after the others. Although these poor people let themselves think they have wondrously sharp eyes which can see through an oak board—claiming there is a deficiency in the government—it only fails, in their opinion, because the matter is not entrusted to them and the power to oversee is not commanded to them. Especially when they stand in the market or sit over their wine and there contemplate the needs of the Empire, the land, or the city; then you hear great "wisdom," and how they know how to find a fault in every ruler. And these same limbs have so completely forgotten that they are hands and feet and not eyes, yet they let themselves think no differently than that they are the true eyes, standing ready in the middle of the head and seated in their rightful office.

Although it would also not be bad, but rather to be wished for, that things in the **government** <term>Regiment: the system of rule or administration</term> went so well and were done in such a way everywhere that the hands and feet were not given cause to speak against or watch the eyes; that the eyes also did not sleep too much or look upon other things, but rather, according to their nature and property, kept diligent watch and oversight so that the **common good** <note>original: "Gemeine nutz" — the welfare of the entire community or state.</note> would take no harm. For if it reaches the point that the feet and hands must open the eyes of the head and show them what is lacking, and the eyes thus refuse to see until they are reminded of their office by the other limbs, then things do not stand for the best in the common good. But since I have given sufficient indication of this elsewhere and confirmed the same with examples, it is unnecessary to write further of it here. And it is to be found not only from this parable, but also from the Holy Divine Scripture, that subjects should be obedient and following of their authority. Just as St. Paul primarily writes: Let every man be subject to the authority that has power over him, for there is no authority except from God. <note>A reference to Romans 13:1, a foundational text for the "Divine Right of Kings" and civil obedience during the Reformation.</note>

Now, whoever resists the authority resists the ordinance of God, etc. And this teaching serves this purpose: so that we do not fall into such madness as to think we have no need of authority, as the **Anabaptists** <note>Widertäuffer: a radical Reformation movement that often rejected state authority and practiced adult baptism, seen as a threat to social order by both Catholics and Lutherans.</note> have done and taught. Where would the fault be if we could all live strictly according to the **Gospel** <note>original: "Euangelio"</note> and were pious Christians, such that everyone did to the other what he wished to have done to himself? Then we would need no authority, because authority is ordained not for the sake of the pious (as indeed upright Christians ought to be pious) to punish them, but for the sake of the wicked. As Paul further says: The powerful are not to be feared for good works, but for the evil.

But since there are few of you, as one sees, who obey the Gospel and arrange their lives accordingly, but rather the greatest part remain wicked, and...

# Of the Book of Rulers.

...often shamefully abuse the Gospel, whereby the **godly** <note>Referring to those who live according to Christian virtues</note> are offended. Thus, we must of necessity have **authority** <term>Oberkeit: the governing body, magistrate, or prince</term> to restrain such wickedness and wantonness, so that the godly may be protected and common peace and obedience maintained.

At this point, however, a question arises: to what extent should one be obedient to the authority, and are the subjects also bound to show obedience to the authority in all things? To this, it must be answered: that one is bound and obligated to show obedience to the authority in all external, honorable matters, so far as body and goods extend. But if it should happen that the authority attempted to force its subjects to deny the known truth, or to accept the Pope's or other false and idolatrous teachings and worship, or even commanded one to steal, rob, murder, or commit adultery, then the external obedience of the subjects toward the authority ceases. In such a case, the rule is: *One must obey God more than men*, as Peter says in the Acts of the Apostles in the fifth chapter.

The highly learned man ***Jacobus Omphalius*** <note>A 16th-century legal scholar known for advising princes on their duties</note> also clearly demonstrates this in his work *On the Office and Power of a Prince* <note>original Latin: "de officio & potestate Principis"</note>. For in such cases, even a servant is not bound to obey his master, according to the order of the written Imperial Law, in the law titled "A Slave" under "Actions and Obligations" <note>original: "l. seruus. ff. de actionibus & obligationibus," a reference to the Roman Digest</note>. And ***Zasius*** <note>Ulrich Zasius, a famous German jurist of the era</note> says regarding the same law, *Because the master must command honorable things* <note>original Latin: "Quia Dominus debet honesta iubere"</note>.

That is: A master should command that which is honorable. Now, if even one’s own servants are not bound [to obey dishonorable commands], how much less then are the subjects obligated.

So that I do not forget history, ***Ambrose*** <note>Saint Ambrose, the 4th-century Bishop of Milan</note> cites a rare story of ***Julian*** <note>Julian the Apostate, the last non-Christian Roman Emperor</note> and says: Although Julian was a denier and an apostate Christian, he nevertheless used Christian soldiers. These soldiers conducted themselves under him in such a way that when he commanded them to march out for the protection of the common good, they marched and showed him obedience. But when he commanded them to march against fellow Christians, they would not do so, but looked instead to the supreme Emperor in Heaven and showed obedience to Him; as is written in the legal collection under the section titled "Julianus," question 11, case 3.

If people would also open their eyes a little, and recognize and look upon themselves, they would easily have to conclude and confess: That they are far from being equal to God, and that there is a great difference between the **creature** and the **Creator**. Likewise, that they themselves cannot tolerate it if their subordinate judges, commanders, and rulers were to command something that was contrary to them. Therefore, they also should not command that which is contrary to God, the highest Majesty in Heaven and on Earth, nor change or cancel His command. For no matter how high the worldly authority may wish to be, it must nevertheless remain within the **Second Table** <note>The second part of the Ten Commandments, which governs human-to-human relationships. The "First Table" governs the relationship between humans and God</note> and cannot enter into the First Table.

For this reason, ***St. Augustine*** also says: It is indeed true that whoever resists power or authority resists God’s ordinance. But what if the authority wished to impose something that was not fitting for you to do, and which you could not do with a good conscience? Here (he says), let the worldly authority stand and

### The Fourth Part

...and pay attention to the order of the **secular government** <term>Weltliches Regiment: the civil administration and social order of the world</term>, how things usually proceed within it. Namely, when the **under-bailiff** <term>Vnteruogt: a local subordinate official or deputy</term> commands something, one should and must keep it. But if the **Mayor** commands something else, you naturally let the under-bailiff's command stand and follow the Mayor, as he is the greater authority. And the subordinate should not be angry that the superior is preferred over him.

But if the Mayor then commands something, and the **Emperor** commands otherwise; or if the Emperor commands something, and **God** orders another, here you must judge that God is a higher power. Therefore, O Emperor, may you be willing to forgo and hold us excused that we cannot follow your command. For although you may threaten us with the **dungeon**, God threatens even more harshly—namely, with **hell and eternal damnation**. Thus says Augustine <note>original Latin: "Hæc Augustinus 11.q.3.c. Qui resistit"</note> in the eleventh Question, third Case, on *He who resists*. Beyond this, we also have beautiful examples in **Mattathias**, **Eleazar**, and the dear **Maccabean martyrs** and their mother <note>Jewish figures from the 2nd century BCE who resisted the forced Hellenization of King Antiochus IV</note>. In addition, we have other fine verses which teach us this. Such as Matthew in the 10th chapter: *Whoever loves his father and mother more than me is not worthy of me.* Also: *Fear not him who kills the body, but rather him who can cast both body and soul into hell and destroy them eternally.*

However, this is not to be understood to mean that we should, in such a case, rise up against the **authority** <term>Oberkeit: the established government</term> and seize the sword against them, as the **insurrectionist peasants** <note>A reference to the German Peasants' War (1524–1525), which the author views as a sinful rebellion</note> did. Rather, we should withdraw from the tyrants, according to the teaching of Christ, where he says: *When they persecute you in one place or in one city, flee to another.* But if a person cannot flee, he should rather suffer whatever happens to him for the sake of the truth, rather than act against God’s Word and command. This is what the **Apostles** did, of whom it is written in the **Acts**: *They departed from the presence of the Council rejoicing that they were counted worthy to suffer shame for His name's sake.* And the dear holy martyrs **Saint Maurice** and his companions <note>The Theban Legion, a Roman legion that supposedly converted to Christianity and was decimated for refusing to sacrifice to pagan gods</note>; when the Emperor commanded them to fight against the Christians, they would not do it, threw their weapons away, and said: "If he wished to fight against Christians, he need not seek others; they were right there, as Christian people, ready to suffer whatever he willed."

From all this, it can also be concluded that the poor people under the godless **Bishops**, **Abbots**, and godless, damned **Monks**—who were held like property against God's command and against all equity, solely for the sake of the clergy's bellies and pride, and were kept away from the Word of God—are not bound to show them obedience. Rather, they may freely confess God's Word, receive the right use of the **holy Sacraments**, and not let the unchristian tyranny and power of the priests and monks hinder them. Instead, they should say: *We must obey God more than men.* Yet, they should not fight for anything with their hands, but as the holy Apostles and martyrs did, suffer whatever God's will is. Let the godless tyrants be as wicked as they wish, they will still not achieve what they desire, but must ultimately perish and leave God and His Word alone—as we have indeed heard and seen with our own eyes for these past **forty years**.

<header>The Book of Regents.</header>

# The Fifth Part of the Book of Regents.

## Concerning Judges and Their Office.

### Concerning the Office of a Judge, and what kind of man a Judge should be.

### The First Chapter.

<image-desc>Large decorative initial 'E' featuring a classical figure, possibly a deity or personification, amidst scrolls and foliage.</image-desc>
A judge is so named for this reason: because he is meant to speak the law <note>German: *das Recht außsprechen*</note> and to decide and judge that which is held in dispute between two or more parties. A judge should be nothing other than a leader and protector of justice, and such a man who is pious, brave, holy, and upright <term>auffrichtig: honest and straightforward</term>. He must be one who allows himself to be led away from the right neither by gifts nor bribes, nor by hypocrisy and false lies, or whatever else of that nature may occur. Instead, he must uphold justice and equity <term>Billigkeit: the principle of fairness that tempers the strict letter of the law</term> in such a way that no one dare attempt to seek anything unfair from him or desire it of him. For this reason, the laws have also called a judge a "pious man."

And the heathens <note>Referring to the classical authors of ancient Greece and Rome</note> write—as was also cited above in the Second Book, thirteenth chapter—that the ancients once had the image of Justice sketched and painted in this form: Namely, that she first had a beautiful, straight, virginal, and unblemished body; a serious countenance; and sharp eyes—yet not cruel nor tyrannical. Rather, she showed herself earnest, powerful, upright, and entirely invincible only toward the wicked and those deserving of punishment, appearing terrifying through the power and majesty of truth and justice.

Now, how far judges in many places today are from this description and portrait can be easily found by anyone who looks around the world a little, or otherwise has business to do with people. Thus, one sometimes finds those who are so coarse and ignorant, and also so tyrannical, that they would scarcely be worthy to judge a stable full of oxen or pigs (as Petrus Ferriensis <note>Petrus Ferrariensis, a prominent 14th-century Italian jurist known for his work on legal practice</note> says). I shall remain silent about the fact that in many places everything proceeds with "poison and gifts" <note>A rhyming German idiom, *Gifft vnnd Gabe*, referring to bribes and corruption</note>. Sometimes people are also overtaken in such a manner that no one considers whether the punishment is consistent with the law and the offense—even though the law clearly provides that the punishment should not be greater than the transgression. Instead, they simply take the fine <term>Busse: a legal penalty or financial restitution</term> from a person according to whether they happen to need money at the time, or according to how they...
