# The Fifth Part
<meta>catchword: not</meta>

...to be swayed or unswayed, gracious or ungracious toward anyone. This is something the high authorities <term>Oberkeit: the governing body or lords</term> who appoint and establish such judges should in no way tolerate or suffer. Instead, they should punish them earnestly, or at the very least forbid such conduct, while remembering that it is a great and heavy sin before God when judges deal with people in such a manner and the high authorities permit and indulge it. For the Scripture says:

> See to it what you do, for you hold judgment not for man, but for the LORD, and He is with you in judgment. And as you judge, so it shall come back upon your own neck. Therefore, let the fear of the LORD be upon you, and take heed and do it; for with the LORD our God there is no injustice, nor respect of persons, nor taking of bribes.

And in the first chapter of Deuteronomy, Moses speaks:

> I commanded your judges at that time, saying: Hear your brothers and judge righteously between every man and his brother, and the stranger. You shall not recognize any person in judgment, but shall hear the small as well as the great, and be afraid of no man, for the judgment is God’s.

In this matter, even the heathens <note>Referring to the pre-Christian Greeks and Romans</note>—so that they might do no one an injustice—attempted everything humanly possible. This was especially true of those in Athens, who weighed all things in this case with such diligence that those who spoke before the court were not permitted to use any preamble or introduction, nor to stir any emotion <term>Affect: an emotional appeal meant to manipulate the judge's feelings</term>. Instead, they were required to speak and recount or complain using only the bare words necessary to the case, and nothing more. Therefore, Chilo <note>Chilo of Sparta, one of the Seven Sages of Greece</note> says: "The best Republic is that which listens most to laws, and least to rhetoricians <note>original Latin: *Optimam esse Remp. quæ maximè leges, minimè autem Rhetores audiat.*</note>." That is to say: in those cities things go best where the laws are most respected and heard, but the orators are least regarded. This same court in Athens was also held only at night, so that they might judge by hearing alone and might not see who was friend or foe, rich or poor.

The Thebans <note>People of the ancient Greek city of Thebes</note> were of a similar mind and applied themselves to holding and carrying out an upright judgment. And so that the judges might better and more easily remember this at all times, they had the image of the judge painted without hands, and the image of the prince painted without eyes, and had them placed in the location where judgment was usually held. By this, they intended to show that judges should not reach out too much and take gifts <note>meaning bribes</note> or otherwise exploit the people; likewise, the great princes and lords should not look upon the person <note>i.e., show favoritism based on status</note> and سپس command the judges to speak a righteous verdict. For judges do not always speak according to their own heads, but either seek the law in a place where it is for sale, or must take their lead from the high authorities.

Now, as to how much the common good <note>German: *Gemeinen nutz*</note> depends upon an upright judge, and what a harmful thing a wicked judge is—a great long oration could be written here about that. For no one can deny that human society cannot be established, rightly exist, or be maintained so long as so many contracts and dealings must occur and be upheld daily—such as buying, selling, lending, and renting; likewise, marriage contracts, wills, inheritances, succession, and the like—which cannot [continue]...

# Of the Ruler’s Book

...will not always remain correct and steady, but for the most part must be judged as erroneous before the court. This is to say nothing of the injuries, strife, and quarreling that arise daily among the people.

If God gives a pious and God-fearing man to a city or a land, who upholds what is right in such cases and contracts, and otherwise lets equity <term>Billigkeit: the principle of fairness and justice that balances the strict letter of the law with common sense and mercy</term> be done to everyone—punishing evil and promoting good—then it cannot be said nor expressed what a noble gift this is. For this, one should thank God daily, as one is duty-bound to do for all other authorities <term>Oberkeit: the governing body, lords, or magistrates</term>, and pray that He would graciously preserve and sustain such regents who faithfully oversee the common good. 

But it happens with this gift as it does with all other gifts and blessings of God with which we are occasionally graced. For when God has provided such a man, he can do nothing right for anyone. If he is gentle and handles everything with kindness, he is considered useless, is despised, and has no following—although negligence is also a cause for many people to sin. Therefore, the authorities who must administer jurisdiction <term>Jurisdiction: the legal power to hear and decide cases</term> should always be active and not lazy, <note>original Latin: "Ne videlicet indulgentia & nimia leuitate peccent"</note> lest they sin through indulgence and excessive leniency. 

If, however, a judge is earnest—as a judge must be—people also cry out against him, saying he is too strict and hard, and for that reason they will not tolerate him. Regarding this, Gellius <note>Aulus Gellius (c. 125 – after 180 AD), a Roman author whose work was popular in the Renaissance for its moral and historical anecdotes</note> writes a charming and practical text where he says: 

It is necessary that he who is a priest of justice be grave, holy, severe, incorruptible, and not to be flattered; against the wicked and harmful, he must be merciless and inexorable, upright, lofty, and powerful, terrifying through the force and majesty of equity and truth. <note>original Latin: "Oportere eum qui iustitiæ antistes est, esse grauem, sanctum, seuerum, incorruptum, inadulabilem, contraq; improbos, nocentesq; immisericordem, atq; inexorabilem, erectumq; & arduum ac potentam, vi & maiestate æquitatis, veritatisq; terrificum."</note>

That is to say: To him who is to stand for justice, it is fitting in every way that he be brave, earnest, holy, and entirely unswerving and immovable against the guilty and the wicked—unmerciful, inexorable, powerful, and upright—and one who maintains oversight through the help of truth and equity. 

Therefore, it usually happens to such people, whom no one can please, as it did to the frogs: when they had a log for a king, they trampled it underfoot and did not know how to hold it in enough contempt. Therefore, Jupiter gave them a stork, of whom they must now be so afraid—no matter how much they otherwise cry—that they dare not open their mouths, for he strikes them upon their heads and greedily devours them. Regarding this, Waldis <note>Burkhard Waldis (c. 1490–1556), a famous German fabulist whose rhymed versions of Aesop's fables were used to teach moral lessons</note> says:

->The present state we always rue,<-
->And gape always for something new.<-
->A pious ruler is always despised,<-
->Even when he does all for the best.<-
->His goodness never receives their praise;<-
->It is right that frogs also have storks.<-

And although people experience daily that this is how things go in the world, they are yet so careless that they do not consider it. There is also no regent so pious and righteous that they do not know how to find fault with him, and...

### The Fifth Part

...grow weary of the same rulers and always desire another, hoping to obtain a pious one; yet they usually fail in this, according to the proverb which says, *Every successor is worse than his predecessor.* <note>original: "Omnis successor deterior."</note> This was precisely what the woman thought who prayed for the life of the tyrant **Dionysius** <note>Dionysius I of Syracuse (c. 432–367 BC), a famous Greek tyrant known for his cruelty.</note>. He had taken a cow from her grandfather, then two from her father, and finally three from her. So that a fourth and even worse ruler would not follow him, she prayed for the life of Dionysius—although the historian **Maximus** <note>Valerius Maximus, a Roman author who compiled historical anecdotes.</note> tells this story differently.

As far as the office of the judge is concerned, they can learn it nowhere better than from Holy Scripture, as mentioned above. Thus says the fifty-eighth Psalm:
> Are you then mute, that you will not speak what is right, and judge what is fair, you children of men?

And in the eighty-second Psalm it is written:
> How long will you judge unjustly and favor the person of the godless? Provide justice for the poor and the orphan, and help the miserable and the needy to their rights; rescue the lowly and the poor, and deliver them from the power of the godless.

From this we must note that God especially commands and desires that judges and regents pay heed to widows and orphans, the poor and the oppressed, and protect them from the power of the rich and the godless, upholding them in their right. For God knows the hearts and minds of men—how they are disposed, how easily they let themselves be bent, and how many causes there are by which they are moved to abandon the right. This is especially true when some "Rich and Powerful Hans" <note>A German colloquialism for a person of high status or influence, similar to "Big Shot."</note> comes along who has great prestige, and a poor man stands against him. How unequally they are regarded! It is so lopsided that everything the rich man does must be considered right so as not to anger him, while everything the poor man does is considered wrong. Added to this are self-interest, friendship, enmity, poison, bribes, and other shameful and devilish vices of certain judges, about whom **Palladas** <note>A Greek poet of the 4th century known for his cynical epigrams.</note> among the Greeks wrote a beautiful epigram. I will set it all down here in English, and it reads as follows:

->No upright judge was ever also a lenient one,<-
->For these two qualities conflict with one another by their own nature.<-
->The upright man offends the oath-breaker; the lenient man offends through foolishness,<-
->When these two things, joined together, provide the cause for evil.<-
<note>original: "Nemo probus Iudex idem fuit atq; benignus, Namq; sua pugnant hæc duo lege simul. Fœdifrago peccat probus, furiusq; benignus, Materiam quum dant hæc duo iuncta, mali."</note>

Therefore, God forbids such sins and warns that one should guard against them. But where things proceed so unequally, and such warnings will not help, then punishment will not be long in coming, so that the land and the people go to ruin because of it. For the aforementioned Psalm says further:
> But they will not be told; they pay no heed, but go always into the darkness. Therefore all the foundations of the land must fall. I have said: You are gods and children of the Most High; but you shall die like men, and perish like a tyrant.

Therefore, it is the duty and responsibility of the high authorities to look upward, as **Eusebius** <note>Likely referring to Eusebius of Caesarea, an early Christian historian and counselor to Constantine the Great.</note> teaches them when he says:
> If you carry the sword, think of no enmity or discord, even if you had such with someone before.

For you are not...

...therefore you were appointed as a regent, not to avenge yourself, but so that you should safely protect the subjects of your territory from foreign enmity and violence. And **Epictetus** <note>A Greek Stoic philosopher (c. 50–135 AD) who taught that virtue is the only good.</note> says: *If you wish to make a right judgment, desire to know neither party, but the case itself.* <note>original: "Si rectum vis facere iudicium, neutram cupias partem cognoscere, sed ipsam causam."</note> If you wish to pass a righteous judgment, do not think about how you [favor] the party, but how you rightly recognize the cause. Therefore, I wish to tell the following story of a righteous royal judge, which goes as follows:

When the King in **Hungary**, named **Andreas** <note>Andrew II of Hungary (reigned 1205–1235), who led the Fifth Crusade.</note>, wished to travel to **Syria** with many princes and lords against the unbelievers, he first—before he undertook this far journey—appointed a dear and noble lord named **Bancbanus**, a very faithful and wise man, as governor over the entire kingdom. He was to manage and rule the royal court and all his power, and additionally to have the Queen, along with her children, under his protection and shield.

He was given this exhortation: that he should govern the kingdom with all justice and, in the King’s absence, allow no one to suffer shame, violence, or injustice; furthermore, he was to keep peace with the neighbors and should promote and plant that same peace, rest, and honor within the kingdom, omitting nothing, just as if the King himself were present. This governor and administrator of the kingdom accepted such a laudable command with a knightly spirit and hoped to carry out all matters faithfully and honorably. 

Fortune, however, was hateful toward this pious man and broke his honorable intentions. Namely, the Queen, named **Gertrud** <note>Gertrude of Merania (c. 1185–1213), whose historical assassination is the basis for this story.</note>, received her brother from **German lands** into Hungary. He had traveled to her to comfort her regarding her departed lord <note>The "departed lord" refers to the King's absence on the Crusade.</note> and for other reasons, and he remained with her for several weeks, for she loved him as his sister, as is fitting. 

Now, the aforementioned governor's wife had to be with and near the Queen day and night; she was of a particularly beautiful and famous form, which she greatly enhanced with her discipline, modesty, and honorable conduct. Therefore, the Queen bore a special love and favor toward her. The Queen's brother, however, was ignited with a burning and hot love for her, from which he became so inflamed within a few days that he fell into sickness on her account. 

When the Queen became aware of her brother's burning yet unseemly love, she had a reckless compassion for him—as such things commonly reside in women—so that she indulged him too much. Thus, she led and called the governor's wife to speak with her brother, and often invited her to her table. Sometimes she would slip away from them so that they might talk with one another, giving them room under an honorable appearance to show their friendship toward each other.

But after the Queen found that this noble woman held so honorably and virtuously to her lord that the brother could not bring her to a fall with good words, she secretly provided her brother with a special chamber. There, the pious woman was deprived of her honor and virtue by force. The good woman did not keep this painful misfortune secret any longer than until she came to her husband.

But when her lord received her and wished to embrace and hold her according to his custom, she said to him: "O, what an unhappy, wretched woman you now wish to embrace; alas, I am no longer your lawful spouse, but a stinking whore. Where you think to hold your wife to your heart, you will be miserably deceived, for instead of your wife, you have a shameful, impure whore, because your bed and my body are desecrated. For she <note>The Queen.</note> whom you trusted with your dear wife as her lady, has handed her over to her brother, acting as a **procuress** <note>original: "Kupplerin" — a person who facilitates illicit sexual encounters; a panderer.</note>, to be violated. This has happened to my body, even though my heart, will, and mind are innocent. Therefore, although I am stained more by another than by myself, you should nevertheless execute and strangle me, so that I do not have to become a murderer of my own poor body and soul, and your praise and honor be thereby weakened and defiled. For this reason, I beg that you would stab me unawares, and thereby avenge the goddess of chastity," etc.

Although the noble man was greatly moved by these words and acted like a raging lion, he nevertheless suppressed his inner pain and comforted his weeping and wailing wife, who expected death. And as she offered him her body to be killed, he first embraced her, held her, and comforted her, asking her for the sake of their marital loyalty and love—since this misfortune happened not by her will or guilt, but because she was weakened and shamed through the wantonness and violence of others—that she should hide and conceal their common shame and disgrace, for which he would avenge himself at an appropriate time with a grim example.

When he had thus persuaded and pacified the woman, he could not long tame his hidden fury and anger; thus, after a few days, he went with several of his companions to the Queen in her chamber. There, after he had pointed out her wickedness to her, he pierced her through with his sword. Drawing the bloody sword out of her, he displayed it and said that he had killed her rightfully and justly, since she, acting as a procuress, had forced his dearest wife and helped her brother so that she was shamed by him and her honor was violated and robbed. When a great uproar arose, he said publicly that he desired no pardon for this deed, for he would be up by morning to ride with several lords of the land to the King, and there submit himself to his court, judgment, and power; with this, he stilled the uprising.

Thereupon, he arrived without delay with several lords before the King (whom he found at **Constantinople** <note>Andrew II was in Constantinople in 1218 during his return from the Fifth Crusade.</note>), before whom he stepped fearlessly and spoke thus: "Most Gracious Lord King, here is the governor of your kingdom, whom some might perhaps regard as a shameful murderer and slayer. However, I have relied upon your royal justice and righteous judgment, and have committed such a deed that I do not think to excuse myself by flight; rather, by presenting my own body, I have sought the justice of the most equal and holy seat of judgment. I come to you as my lord and righteous judge, so that, if I have acted wrongly according to the law, I may take my punishment immediately. Furthermore, I desire no other judge but you alone—"

...to you, whom I have offended; you who shall be not only my rightful accuser and avenger, but also my own judge. I declare and lament, therefore, that your spouse the Queen—to whom I entrusted my highest treasure, my dearest wife, as a lady-in-waiting—handed her over to her wanton brother to be shamed. And as I could not restrain my righteous anger (for I would rather die than leave such an insult unavenged), for that reason I have stabbed the Queen to death with this sword. And this, O most just judge, is that very sword, stained with the Queen's blood. If I have sinned by saving myself from such unbearable disgrace and shame, then you may put me to death immediately with this same sword. But if you can recognize that I acted rightly and fairly, then please declare me acquitted through your judgment as a righteous judge. For such upright justice of yours will be an eternal memory among all peoples, for it is upon this alone that I have relied, presenting myself in person before your Majesty, etc.

The King listened to such a speech with such a steadfast and brave spirit that he changed neither his expression nor his color, and said: "Bancbanus <note>original: "Banebane" — referring to Bánk bán, a historical Hungarian palatine.</note>, your trust in me and my just judgment may sufficiently advise you to place your hope in me. If it is as you have reported to me, then return to my kingdom and faithfully carry out your office as my **governor** <term>Statthalter: a high-ranking official acting as the King's deputy or regent.</term>; when I return to Hungary from this journey <note>A reference to the Fifth Crusade (1217–1218) led by King Andrew II.</note>, I will pronounce the verdict after sufficient inquiry." He thus allowed him to return to Hungary and traveled to Asia with his army.

When he had completed this campaign and many of his lords and subjects in Hungary came to meet and receive him, King Andrew was deeply troubled by the Queen's death when he entered his royal chambers; he remained firm, however, in his resolve. He therefore summoned his governor, Bancbanus, to trial the following day. And when he understood the reported guilt and misconduct of his spouse and was truly informed, he recognized—as an eternal example of feminine honor and purity—that [Bancbanus] had acted rightly and fairly, and thereby declared him acquitted and free.

->In this King and just judge, all potentates, judges, and<-
->commanders should rightly see themselves reflected, and<-
->in similar cases, they should also judge and rule accordingly.<-

# The Fifth Part

## Of Pious and Just Judges.

### The Second Chapter.

Although it is almost a rare thing to find a pious judge—and for that reason it is not so easy to compile a <note>original: "Catalogum"</note> catalog of pious judges from the histories—one nevertheless finds that at all times there have been pious and upright people who faithfully presided over their office. They did not allow themselves to be led astray or deceived by greed or other passions <note>original: "Affect"</note>. These men were undoubtedly sustained by God and given by Him so that others might see themselves reflected in them and take them as an example. Therefore, to honor such an office, I cannot avoid including a chapter on this subject for the benefit of all pious judges, and as a warning to the wicked, godless, and tyrannical judges, so that they might improve themselves. This is so they do not receive such a reward as was mentioned in the previous chapter; indeed, it is a warning and reminder that they should not invite God's wrath upon themselves and thereafter be eternally damned.

But so that I do not make a long preface, look, dear Christian reader, at <term>Samuel: a biblical prophet and the last of the Hebrew Judges, known for his integrity</term> and the testimony that Holy Scripture gives of him. Then look around here and there in the world to see if the judges behave according to his example, and if they may boast with a good conscience of that which this holy man boasted. For thus says the Scripture, in the first book of Samuel in the twelfth chapter:
> Behold, I have listened to your voice in all that you have said to me, and I have made a king over you. And now behold, there goes your king before you. I, however, have become old and gray, and my sons are among you; and I have walked before you from my youth until this day. Behold, here I am; have I taken anyone’s ox or donkey? Have I done violence or injustice to anyone? Have I oppressed anyone? Have I taken a gift <note>original: "Geschenck" — implying a bribe.</note> from anyone’s hand and kept it secret? If so, I will restore it to you. They said: You have done us no violence, nor oppressed us, nor taken a gift from anyone’s hand. He said: The LORD be witness against you, and His anointed this day, that you have found nothing in my hand.

What the poets say of pious judges—not only of <term>Minos</term> and <term>Rhadamanthus</term>, who are now said to be the court-holders in Hell <note>In Greek mythology, Minos and Rhadamanthus were kings famous for their justice, later becoming judges of the dead in the underworld.</note>, but also of <term>Ripheus</term>, <term>Emathion</term>, and <term>Erichtheus</term>, of whom <term>Virgil</term> and <term>Naso</term> <note>Naso refers to the Roman poet Ovid (Publius Ovidius Naso).</note> make mention—I will leave unmentioned here, as my intention is to stick to the historical records. Now, to come to the pagan histories, <term>Plutarch</term> writes that <term>Cato</term> among the Romans, and <term>Phocion</term> among those of Athens, defended justice and equity with such diligence that they even to...

...often stood against their best friends when they perceived and saw that they held evil and unjust causes.

<term>Mycerinus: an Egyptian Pharaoh of the Fourth Dynasty, known for his piety and fairness</term> surpassed all other Egyptian kings with his justice; and if anyone complained to him that something had been stolen from them, he would make restitution to them from his own money. Thus <term>Aelianus: Claudius Aelianus, a Roman author and teacher of rhetoric who wrote in Greek</term> writes that among the Egyptians, the judges were almost one and the same as their priests. And their judge had to be the most just and pure among them all, also wearing a figure or jewel around his neck in which a beautiful blue sapphire was set, which was called "The Truth." But the aforementioned author says:

> <note>original Latin: "Ego verò iudicem non tam in lapide sculptam aut expressam veritatem circumferre, quam in animo menteq; insitā & in infixam habere velim."</note> But I would wish that a judge would not carry the truth carved or expressed in stone about him, as much as having it implanted and fixed in his soul and mind.

That is: I would wish that a judge might not carry the truth cut into a noble stone, but rather have it printed in his heart and mind, carrying it with him constantly. Thus was <term>Glaucus: a Spartan known for his reputation for honesty, though later tested by a temptation to keep a trust</term> so renowned among the Lacedemonians <note>The Spartans</note> for his justice that many foreigners came to Sparta for no other reason than to see this man.

It also happened that when <term>Titus Manlius: a Roman consul famous for his strictness</term> was to be the judge between the Macedonian plaintiffs on one side and his son, the defendant, on the other, and he perceived that the son was in the wrong and had been convicted, he spoke such a judgment between them: "Since it has been sufficiently demonstrated and proven that my son Syllanus has unjustly taken money in his office and taxed the people against equity, I will no longer hold him for my son, but he shall have herewith made himself unworthy of it." And therefore, he earnestly commanded that the son be removed from his presence immediately, and also brought it about that he should be judged from life to death.

And what is even more, one reads of <term>Zeleucus: Zaleucus, the legendary Greek lawgiver of the Locrians</term> that he made a law in <term>Locris: a region in ancient Greece</term> that anyone who committed adultery should have both eyes gouged out. But when it happened that his own son was the first to be caught in adultery, he had one of the son's eyes and one of his own eyes gouged out, so that the law might be more firmly and magnificently upheld.

Furthermore, one reads of <term>Lucius Brutus: Lucius Junius Brutus, the founder of the Roman Republic</term> that when he learned his sons wanted to help restore <term>Tarquinius: Tarquin the Proud, the last king of Rome</term> (who had been driven out of Rome because of his tyranny), he first had them beaten with rods according to Roman custom and then beheaded. Regarding this, <term>Virgilius: the Roman poet Virgil</term> also writes:

> <note>original Latin: "Natosq; pater, noua bella mouentes, Ad poenam pulchra pro libertate vocabit."</note> And the father shall call his sons, who were stirring up new wars, to punishment for the sake of beautiful liberty.

<margin>An example of Roman fortitude.</margin>
And what shall one say of men? For even women, as the histories report, have sometimes applied themselves so fervently to justice. For one reads of a woman in Sparta named Thalantia: when she heard that her son ruled badly and unjustly among the <term>Chians: the inhabitants of the island of Chios</term>, she wrote to him that he should reflect and behave better in his government, or not show himself in Sparta; for if he were caught there, he should certainly know that he would be punished with his life.

# The Fifth Part

The poet <term>Philoxenus: a Greek poet who lived at the court of the tyrant Dionysius I of Syracuse</term> also possessed such a sincere and steadfast spirit that he would rather have himself thrown into the stone quarries as a prisoner than to praise the wretched poems of Dionysius. For he said: <note>original: "Longè satius esse in Lapidicinis vitam agere, quàm eius Poemata audire."</note> "It is far better to spend one’s life in the stone quarries than to listen to his poems." Such an honorable and sincere spirit was also held by the esteemed and eloquent man <term>Xenophon: a Greek philosopher, soldier, and historian</term>; for when he alone possessed the histories of <term>Thucydides: the author of the History of the Peloponnesian War</term>, he did not wish to suppress them or publish them as his own, but freely confessed that they had been written by Thucydides. This is despite the fact that Xenophon otherwise possessed many magnificent gifts and virtues; he was not only a historian but also performed many noble deeds with his own hand under King Cyrus and elsewhere in war.

However, it is to be noted here that it is not enough for a judge to be pious; he must also be just. For if, out of a sense of piety, he wished to let the guilty go free or "look through his fingers" <note>an idiom meaning to intentionally overlook a wrongdoing</note> at them, he would be just as much in the wrong as if he wished to punish or suppress the innocent out of envy. Therefore <term>Cato: likely referring to Cato the Elder, known for his strict morality</term> says that a judge should neither pray for the righteous nor allow himself to be moved by pleas for the unrighteous. For if a man is righteous, he needs no intercession; rather, the judge—if he truly wishes to be a pious and just man—should let him be, and protect and uphold him. But if the man is unrighteous, the judge should not allow himself to be moved by pleas, even though one cannot prevent people from pleading. If the judge allows himself to be swayed by pleas, he has already deviated from what is right, has not fulfilled his office, and is to be punished.

Furthermore, it should be noted that piety is a very subtle thing, which can easily be lost in a person, so that he does not know where to find it. As one reads of <term>Glaucus: a citizen of Sparta mentioned in Herodotus's Histories</term>, a citizen of Sparta, who for the sake of his justice and piety was renowned not only in the city but also elsewhere in the countryside. But listen now to what <term>Herodotus: the Greek historian</term> writes of him in his sixth book—how the "rogue" <note>referring here to the temptation of greed or a personified spirit of trickery</note> wrestled with him, and what happened to him and his descendants because of it. He writes as follows:

Among many other virtues worthy of praise, Glaucus was highly lauded and renowned among the Lacedaemonians <note>The Spartans</note> for his justice, not only in Sparta but also in other surrounding cities and lands. Because of this, it happened that a man from <term>Miletus: an ancient Greek city on the western coast of Anatolia</term> came to him to make his acquaintance and addressed him with the following intent: "Although I am a Milesian, my dear Glaucus, I take comfort in your justice; therefore, I come to you to make use of it. For since your name and good reputation have resounded throughout all Greece, and especially in <term>Ionia: the central coastal region of ancient Anatolia</term>, so that your equal is not to be found, I have weighed this in my mind. I considered that because Ionia must constantly be subject to danger, from which they can keep nothing safe, while the <term>Peloponnese: the peninsula forming the southern part of Greece, where Sparta is located</term> is quiet and secure, I have turned half of my income into money. I am intent on laying this down in your faithful hands for safekeeping. Therefore, I ask that you would take this money and give me in return a confession and a written statement..."

...give [the coins], with the instruction that whoever brings these to you, you should return and deliver that money to him; which was done accordingly.

However, after much time had passed, the children of the <term>Milesian: a citizen of Miletus, a powerful Greek city in Ionia (modern-day Turkey)</term> came to Glaucus and demanded the deposited money, according to the acknowledgment of the debt. Glaucus, however, gave them the answer that he had no memory of these things, nor did they concern him; therefore, he would admit to nothing. Yet, he said he would consider the matter, and they should return after four months. If it were then found that he had received something, he would return it; if not, he intended to take legal action against them for such an improper demand, according to the custom of the land. The Milesians had to be satisfied with this answer for the time being and depart. 

But Glaucus, who wished to keep the money for himself, traveled to <term>Delphos: Delphi, the site of the most important oracle in the Greek world</term> and asked <term>Apollinem: Apollo, the god of prophecy</term> for advice: whether he might clear himself with an oath so that he would not have to return the money to the Milesians. To this, Apollo answered: It might well benefit him for a short time if he cleared himself with the oath, but afterwards, it would be found that his house and his children would have to pay the price for it. When Glaucus heard this, he begged Apollo for forgiveness and confessed that he had done wrong; thereafter, he summoned the Milesians and gave them their money back. 

But Apollo said it was just as bad to tempt our Lord God and to act against Him in intent as in deed. Therefore, it went the same for Glaucus: because he had desired to keep the deposited money and had been willing to swear [falsely] for it, his entire lineage at <term>Sparta: a prominent city-state in ancient Greece known for its military discipline</term> perished—regardless of the fact that he did not actually swear the oath—and no one of them remained. 

How do you think it will go for those who falsely swear away someone else's property in actual deed, or take and extort it by force? Must their descendants not also pay for it and realize the cost? Because I have made mention of this in another place, I will not cite it further here.

# That a Judge is Obligated
## to Hear One Party as Well as
## the Other.

### The Third Chapter.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial letter 'U' featuring leaf and vine motifs within a rectangular frame.</image-desc>

Among other irregularities that occur in courts and among the authorities, this is not the least: that judges sometimes hear one side and not the other. Rather, as soon as they have heard one side—namely the complaining party—especially if he is rich or powerful, they rush headlong into judgment before they have heard the other side or have thoroughly investigated the matter. They then condemn or punish the poor man. Yet every judge is obligated to hear one side as well as the other, and to hold an equal scale... <note>The "equal scale" refers to the scales of Lady Justice, symbolizing weighing evidence without bias.</note>

...to let [it] happen / Also to condemn no one unheard / which God himself likewise upheld / with the first man Adam / For although He already knew / that Adam had transgressed the commandment and sinned / He nevertheless wished to hear him / and not condemn him in his absence / But called out and said: Adam, where art thou? <note>Genesis 3:9. > He who decides anything without hearing the other side, 
> even if he has determined what is fair, is not himself a just judge.

Likewise, one reads of Alexander the Great, the King of Macedonia / when he first began to sit in judgment / and someone brought his complaint before him / that he heard the plaintiff with only one ear / and held the other shut. After he was asked / why he did such a thing / he answered / He must also keep one ear for the defendant / to hear and receive his answer and defense. <note>This famous anecdote illustrates the "audi alteram partem" (hear the other side) principle.</note>

At this point, I must also relate what is written about **Demosthenes**, the Greek orator (who has been mentioned several times before). Specifically, it is said that he once stood in a capital court <note>German: *peinliche Gericht*. Historically, these were "penal" or "painful" courts dealing with serious crimes, often involving corporal punishment or death.</note>, where one is especially duty-bound to pay diligent attention to every word so that no one is wronged. He intended to stand by and represent someone, but the judges paid little heed to his speech; instead, they chatted amongst themselves, one about this, another about that. When he noticed this, he asked them to listen to him for a moment, saying he had a fine and amusing story that had recently occurred, which he wished to tell them. As they all immediately pricked up their ears to hear what this new story might be, he began and said:

There was a young fellow who rented a donkey from another man to carry some goods from **Athens** to **Megara**. Now, when it was midday and the heat became overwhelming, the owner of the donkey, as well as the young fellow who had rented it, both wished to lie down in the shade. Since they could find no other shade, the renter sat down beneath the donkey. But the owner would not permit this, 
<margin>Concerning the shadow of a donkey. <note>original: "De asini umbra."</note></margin>
saying he had rented him the donkey, but not its shadow. The other replied that he had rented the donkey for the duration of the time to use as he saw fit. Thus, a great quarrel arose between them, to the point that they even came to blows and finally appeared before a judge. Once **Demosthenes** had spoken these words, he walked away from the court. But because the judges were eager to hear how this quarrel ended—how the two had reached an agreement before the court, and especially who had won the right to the donkey's shadow—they called **Demosthenes** back, requesting that he finish the story he had started.

Then **Demosthenes** said to them: "You men, you judges! You are perfectly willing to listen diligently to a story about the shadow of a donkey, but this poor man’s case, which concerns his very life and limb, you found too burdensome to hear with such diligence. Instead, you behaved in such a way that I was forced to fall silent and step away." One also reads of **King Ptolemy**, how he was once playing a board game when someone came and sat with him, reading a list of names of those condemned to death. As the man pointed out their crimes and offenses and asked the King to decide by what manner of death each should be executed, **Berenice**, the King's wife, snatched the papers out of the reader's hand and said: "No one should judge or decide such grave matters where a person's life is at stake with such a careless spirit and lack of attention; rather, one should do so with great deliberation, setting aside all games. For it is not the same thing to play with dice as it is to play with the human body." When the King heard these words, he took them to heart and stopped playing. Furthermore, for the rest of his life, he never again heard or judged a capital case while playing games.

### The Fifth Part

# Of Wicked and False Judges, and Their Punishment.

## The Fourth Chapter.

Although it is legally provided that judges, when they are chosen for their office, shall swear to represent their office faithfully and to take neither bribe nor gift <note>original: "Gifft noch Gabe." While "Gift" means poison in modern German, in this historical legal context it often serves as an alliterative pairing with "Gabe" (gift) to denote any form of corruption or "poisoning" of justice.</note>, etc., which they nevertheless swear daily, the examples of history clearly show that legal proceedings in many places forget their sworn oath. They allow themselves to be moved by gifts so that they rule against the law and occasionally pass false judgments, for which they are also dreadfully punished. Therefore, Emperor **Pescennius** provided his councilors and judges a grand salary, so that they should not feel burdened to take anything from anyone; for he said, *A judge should neither give nor receive.* <note>original: "Iudicem nec dare debere, nec accipere."</note>

Just as the law has also provided an express punishment for this, *The Code concerning the punishment of a judge who has judged poorly, etc.* <note>original: "C. de poena Iudicis, qui malè iudicauit, &c." This refers to a specific section of the Justinian Code, the foundation of Roman law in Europe.</note> Though such punishment is considered somewhat mild compared to the old examples of history; for the Emperor ordained in money or civil matters that the judge, if it is proven that he has taken something, shall be punished three times as much as the gifts were, and shall also be removed from his office. However, if it is a penal case <term>penal case: a "painful" or criminal matter (peinliche sache) involving physical punishment or death</term>, he has forfeited all his goods and shall be banished from the land. But in times past, great lords imposed even harsher punishments on such false judges. For as **Cambyses**, King of **Persia**, punished such a judge, named **Sisamnes**, which was told at length above <note>The author likely refers to the famous account where Sisamnes was flayed alive for his corruption, and his skin was used to cover the chair where his son was then forced to sit as the new judge.</note>. It is also written that when King **Darius** learned that **Sandaces**, a governor, had spoken a false judgment for the sake of money, he became so violently embittered against him that he had him hung on the public gallows, as a horror to others.

What displeasure the Romans also felt for such unlawful judgments may also be understood in part from the following history. Specifically, **Titus Livius** writes that at one time the **Ardeans** and **Aricinians** came to discord over their borders, and since they could not agree in any other way, they came to **Rome** and related the business to them. They requested the Romans from both sides to be arbitrators <term>arbitrators: neutral third parties chosen to settle a dispute</term> and entrusted their matters heavily to them, as they had suffered many kinds of damage and displeasure from both sides and were weary of the quarrel. Now, as they came to a hearing, and each side brought forward its necessity, led witnesses and other evidence, and the Romans were called to step into four parts to deliberate on the verdict, one from the common people, a very old man named **P. Scaptius**, stepped forward and requested from the mayors that he [of the...]

# The Fifth Part

...belonged to the Ardeans. And although they might have intended for the matter to be settled and decided by other judges, it was neither proper nor tolerable to be both a party and a judge at the same time. Therefore, the Mayors and the Council were as deeply concerned about this as the Aricians or the Ardeans themselves.

Laws have indeed been ordained concerning how false judges—and those who allow themselves to be bribed and corrupted with money—should be punished. However, these laws have partly faded away, so that no one pays attention to them. Just as it is otherwise permitted for both judges and officials to tax, punish, and plague poor people as they please, they have brought things to such a point in many places that they no longer wish to allow any limit to be set for them.

Therefore, I will introduce one or two more examples of false judges and courts, and then leave it at that. It happened in the year 1537 that a mercenary <term>Landsknecht: a professional, often brightly dressed, German mercenary infantryman of the 15th and 16th centuries</term> came to a notable village, which Johannes Gastius <note>Johannes Gastius (c. 1490–1552) was a Protestant reformer in Basel who collected stories of moral and divine justice.</note> does not name for sensitive reasons. There, the peasant judges condemned the mercenary to death for a minor matter. Some say that because he had a large sum of money, that was the primary cause of his death. But when the sentence of death was passed, the mercenary spoke to the judge and the jurors with an undaunted heart: "You are unjust and false judges, for you condemn me innocently and sentence me to death. You do this either to please your superiors and lords, or because I have some money, and not because of any crime of mine. Therefore, take my money and not my life, and let me go."

"I will finally promise you to do no harm, as I could not even if I wanted to. I will also never again come to this place or into your territory. Therefore, do not spill such innocent blood; fear the righteous Judge to whom nothing is hidden, and who will repay everyone according to their merits and works, whether they be good or evil." But as he could obtain or achieve nothing with this, he spoke further: "Very well, since all of you together in this court have deaf ears to my plea, I summon and call you before the righteous judgment of God, in the Valley of Jehoshaphat <note>A biblical reference to the site where God will judge the nations; here used as a summons to meet the victim at the Final Judgment.</note>. There, you unjust and money-hungry judges will find how falsely and unjustly you have condemned and killed me on this day." What followed after this? Before a year had passed, four of the men from this court perished miserably. The first was struck by lightning. The second, while at a merry feast, was stabbed with a sword. The third was hanged for theft. The fourth suffered great agony and the heat of a violent fever, in which, as he was about to die, he said: "Satan, why do you delay? Why do you not take my soul from my body? I have served you until now; therefore, I am yours. I do not want to be led into the Valley of Jehoshaphat to the mercenary." <note>original Latin: "Sathan cur cessas? quando animam e corpore tollis? tibi hactenus seruiui, tuus igitur sum. Nolo in vallem Iosaphat duci ad militem."</note>

### A terrifying history, by which all judges and judicial officials should be warned, that they judge rightly and according to the truth, and condemn or judge no person for the sake of any personal gain.

->*Another, but more cruel, example.* <note>original: "Aliud, sed crudelius Exemplum."</note><-

There was a father who had a biological son, born of his own body, whose death the son desired from his heart, so that he might possess and squander the goods and property which the father had brought together with effort and labor throughout his life. Because the father lived too long for him, the son falsely defamed him, claiming he had committed an act with livestock <note>This refers to the capital crime of bestiality, which in the 16th century was often punishable by death.</note>. Upon this, the father was imprisoned. And when he was subjected to <term>torture: specifically 'Marter,' the legal use of physical pain to extract a confession</term> and severe torment, he confessed to this shameful vice. However, as soon as he was released from the cruel torture, he denied this deed; but when he was stretched again, he confessed it once more. For he had such a delicate body that he could not endure the agony and pain. He said he would much rather die than be tortured again.

But when he was questioned and accused before the open court, he denied this shameful deed, indicating that the previous confession had been caused by the great torture. He stated that not only had he never done it in all his days, but he had never even thought of doing it. However, seven witnesses were presented there who had heard the deed from his own mouth while he was in prison under torture. Now that he was overcome by witnesses, he was sentenced to the fire. But as he was led to the <term>place of execution: 'Malstatt' in the original German</term>, he cried out to all the people, denying and disclaiming this deed and vice—stating that he had not done it, nor had it ever entered his heart or mind in his entire life, but rather that his son had devised such a thing against him out of malicious hatred so that he might inherit his property.

But the poor father was burned; he suffered the shameful death with a steadfast spirit, and commended and offered his spirit to the LORD. It happened, however, that all these judges and witnesses perished and died miserably within one month afterward, and the treacherous son strangled and hanged himself with a rope. Thus God is accustomed to avenge innocence and bring it to light.

> I swear that in all matters I will speak and pass judgment according to the Law and the common statutes of the people of Athens, likewise according to the opinion of the Council of the Five Hundred. Furthermore, I will not allow anyone to come to any office who has previously held another office and has not yet given an account of it—be he from the Nine Men, or those who handle the common sacrifices, or finally from those who are chosen by beans <note>Athenian officials were often selected by lot using colored beans</note> alongside the nine princes whom they call <term>Pretores: chief magistrates or archons</term> <note>original: "Pretores"</note>, or from the legates and assistants (for these were all among the foremost of the city). I will take no gift nor present, nor pervert justice for the sake of greed; nor shall such be permitted to any other with my knowledge.

# Whether a judge should judge and pass sentence according to conscience, or according to the records and evidence.

## The Sixth Chapter.

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'E' with a serpent or dragon coiled within and around the letterform.</image-desc> There is an old dispute between the <term>Glossators</term> <note>Scholars from the 11th-13th centuries who wrote explanatory notes, or "glosses," on Roman law</note>, such as <term>Martinus</term> and <term>Johannes</term> <note>Referring to the famous medieval jurists Martinus Gosia and Johannes Bassianus</note>, which in my opinion is not unworthy of reflection. For this reason, it has since been extensively disputed and handled by legal scholars: namely, whether a <term>judge</term> in cases pending before him should judge and pass sentence solely according to his conscience, or according to the records and the submissions of the parties, as far as they provide proof.

This question is understood by the <term>Doctors</term> <note>Doctors of Law</note> to mean that it must be a significant case in which the judge clearly and distinctly believes the truth of the matter to be different from what the party has submitted and proven. To give an example: suppose a matter between two people is brought before the judge and they are in dispute. The plaintiff brings forward some evidence to support his claim, upon which a judgment must be passed. However, the judge knows for certain that the situation is fundamentally different and the evidence is false; or conversely, that someone has a good and just case but lacks the necessary evidence.

In such a case, <term>Martinus</term> the <term>Glossator</term> argues that the judge should speak and judge according to his conscience. <term>Johannes</term>, however, argues that he should follow the evidence and speak accordingly. Between these two, <term>Accursius</term> <note>The jurist famous for compiling the "Great Gloss," the standard commentary on Roman Law</note> interposes himself, making a distinction and saying: A judge should have two kinds of conscience—one as a judge, through which he understands and hears what is being handled before him, and the other for himself personally. And thus they commonly understand the law *Illicitas regarding the office of the governor* <note>original: "l. Illicitas de off. præsid." Referring to a specific passage in the Digest of Justinian</note>. "The truth of things," says <term>Ulpian</term> <note>One of the most influential Roman jurists</note>, "is not corrupted by errors in the proceedings, and therefore the presiding judge should follow what is appropriate for him to follow based on the credibility of what is proven. Because truly concerning the office of the delegate..." <note>original: "Veritas rerum (inquit Vlpia.) erroribus gestorum non vitiatur, & ideo præses id sequatur quod conuenit eum ex fide eorum quæ probantur, sequi. quia verò de offi. dele. Vbi gloss. & Alb."</note>.

And they commonly posit such a case: Someone has slain another in the street; the judge happens to look out the window and sees the killing, and knows the perpetrator well who committed such a murder. The kin of the slain man accuse the perpetrator; but since he denies the deed, they cannot overcome him with evidence, because

<summary>This page explores a fundamental legal debate: whether a judge's personal knowledge of the truth should override the formal evidence presented in court. <meta>This page continues the legal discussion regarding whether a judge should base his ruling on personal knowledge (conscience) or on the formal evidence presented in court. It argues in favor of the judge's personal knowledge of the truth.</meta>

<page-num>135</page-num>
<header>The Fifth Part</header>

...no one was present who saw it, except the judge alone, as previously mentioned. Now the judge wishes to compel the defendant through the <term>painful question</term> <note>original: "peinliche frage"; this refers to judicial torture used to extract confessions during the early modern period</note> so that he might confess the truth, and he seeks a legal ruling to permit this. However, the legal scholars do not wish to allow the defendant to be interrogated under torture based solely on the judge’s own conscience, since no other suspicion or evidence is at hand.

Even though this common opinion carries great weight and is universally regarded as law—and the legal scholars have written quite a bit about it—it is nonetheless fundamentally false. Even if they debate it at length, it is no different than asking whether a judge, in passing sentence, should follow the truth or a lie. Since the judge knows for certain—to return to our previous case—that the perpetrator committed the murder, and that everything brought against this fact is nothing but lies, why should he not follow the truth more than the lies? For he ought to be a pious and righteous man who should only support the truth and condemn the lie. <note>original citation: "l. Cæteræ. paragr. male. ff. Fami. her." Refers to the Digest of Roman Law concerning the division of inheritance.</note> Wicked people are accustomed to dealing in lies and to speaking and acting differently than what they know to be true; therefore, they should not be unfairly spared from punishment. <note>original citation: "c. 1. de crimine falsi..." Citations referring to the laws against forgery and falsehood.</note>

Furthermore, it is not only against nature but also against all law and <term>equity</term> <note>original: "billigkeit"; the principle of fairness that balances strict, literal legal rules</note> that an authority or judge should possess a twofold conscience. For the conscience is such a thing that cannot be divided, but must remain singular and unified. Whatever is done against the conscience is also done against the truth and builds a path toward the fires of hell, as <term>Innocentius</term> <note>Pope Innocent III (c. 1160–1216), a major influence on Canon Law</note> says. <note>original: "c. literas. de restitut. spoliato." A citation from the Decretals regarding the restoration of seized property.</note>

From this, it sufficiently appears that the opinion of <term>Martinus</term> <note>Martinus Gosia, a 12th-century jurist who famously argued that a judge should prioritize equity and his conscience over strict legal technicalities</note> is right and true: namely, that a judge, who is but a single human being, can have no more than one conscience which he must follow through the law. For this is indeed the primary office of the judge: to seek out the truth in the courts and to judge and decide the matter according to equity. This cannot happen unless he acts with a good conscience, as mentioned above. Nevertheless, we shall cite further reasons to demonstrate that the aforementioned opinion of the legal scholars is erroneous and false.

Firstly, it is certain and legally established that the presentation of evidence is made to the judge. For if one were required to prove the matter to the opposing party, it could never be done to his satisfaction. <note>original citation: "L. Quinquaginta in fine. ff. de probationibus." A reference to the Roman Digest on the rules of proof.</note> How can a judge recognize what is right other than through what he knows for certain, having seen and heard it himself? Such personal knowledge is indeed weightier than any other evidence that might be brought against it. <note>original: citations from the Digest and Canon law regarding court proceedings and appeals.</note> However, when the judge stands in doubt and does not know which party is in the right or the wrong, then he must and may rely upon what each party presents and how much can be proven, and pass judgment accordingly.

<summary>This page argues that a judge should prioritize his personal knowledge of the truth (his conscience) over contradictory evidence presented in court. It rejects the idea that a judge can have separate "private" and "public" consciences, citing both legal tradition and the threat of divine punishment.</summary>

->Secondly.<-

Firstly, if one wished to speak and judge according to the strictness of the law, one might well say that a <term>corporation</term> <note>original: "Vniuersitet"; here referring to a "universitas" or legal corporate body</note>, city, or community cannot sin or forfeit anything criminally. # The Fifth Part

...raged and had seven thousand people stabbed in a theater in that same city. For this, he was heavily rebuked by **St. Ambrose** <note>Bishop Ambrose of Milan famously excommunicated Emperor Theodosius I for the Massacre of Thessalonica in 390 AD, forcing him to do penance.</note>, who would not allow him to re-enter the church until he issued a law stating that if he ordered anyone to be punished, they should wait thirty days before carrying it out <note>This thirty-day delay was intended to allow for the cooling of tempers and the possibility of mercy.</note>.

That one may and should sometimes change a punishment for certain reasons is provided for in the law and has occurred before. <note>Original Latin citations: l. Quid ergo. Par. pœna grauior. ff. de his qui notan. infa. l. hos accusare, Par. omnibus. ff. de accuf.</note>

But if someone should ask why an entire city should not be put to death for a single misdeed as one would a single man, **Bartolus** <note>Bartolus de Saxoferrato (1313–1357), a highly influential legal commentator on Roman law.</note> answers and says that such severity cannot be used against a city or community for the reason that it would result in the highest injustice, as mentioned above—namely, that many innocent people would suffer. Indeed, he says this also applies to monetary fines; if the Emperor or Prince fines a city or a whole community for a crime, those who are innocent and gave no cause for the crime are not legally bound to contribute by law. <note>Original citation: arg. l. Circa princ. ff. de magistratib. Conueniend.</note> And he says that he saw this applied in a judgment by Emperor Henry <note>Likely Emperor Henry VII (c. 1275–1313).</note>.

Upon this, **Bartolus** asks: if an entire city or **community** <note>original: "Commun"</note> went out to slay someone, would the entire city or community be guilty and suffer for it? He answers: No, unless they had done it intentionally and with specific deliberation. For in that case, they would all be guilty. <note>Original Latin: "l. semper aduersus Par. si in sepulchro. ff. quod ui aut clam." The jurist Ulpian says: "For a deed done by several as an undivided whole binds each individual for the total."</note> Indeed, **Bartolus** says that even if a community went into such a conflict with raised banners—as when the alarm bell has been struck—and killed someone, an entire **corporation** <note>original: "Vniuersitet"; here referring to the legal body of the city.</note> or community could not be punished for it throughout, unless it happened through a deceitful deliberation or if the act was later publicly or silently ratified and approved. Otherwise, such an act is to be considered more of a riot, according to the title *Regarding the Seditious*. <note>original: "C. de seditiosis."</note> And just as the misdeeds of subjects do not bind or make a city or corporation guilty, so too do the crimes of their **officials**, servants, and magistrates not bind them, as it is not to be presumed that they were told or ordered to do evil. <note>Original Latin: l. si procurator. Par. Celsus ait. ff. de Condic. indeb.</note>

As far as the **ban** <note>original: "acht"; referring to the Imperial Ban (Reichsacht), a form of outlawry where a city lost its rights and protection.</note> is concerned, into which cities or communities are sometimes placed, the Emperors speak of this in various ways in their **Constitutions** <note>Formal imperial decrees.</note>. <meta>catchword: That</meta>

...that the ban <note>The "Imperial Ban" (*Reichsacht*) was a form of outlawry in the Holy Roman Empire where a person lost all legal rights.</note> may be understood as a monetary fine and not only as corporal punishment. And shortly thereafter, he speaks of a harsher punishment of the ban, saying: "If anyone is found who, after a year's time, should despise our Imperial Constitution, then those goods shall be forfeited throughout the whole Empire, such that they may be seized and taken by anyone; yet with the reservation of other pains and punishments expressed against such despisers in the common Council."

According to this understanding, those who break the public peace <note>original: *Landtfriedbrecher*; those who violated the *Landfrieden*, or the "territorial peace" laws designed to end private feuds.</note> might perhaps be punished if they are individual persons. But a community or a city cannot be punished in such a manner because of natural equity <note>Natural equity refers to the principle of fairness and justice inherent in human nature, often contrasted with the strict letter of the law.</note>.

Accordingly, Emperor Frederick I <note>Frederick Barbarossa (r. 1155–1190).</note> established the <term>Constitution on maintaining peace among subjects <note>original: *Constit. de pace tenen. inter subditos*</note></term>. If anyone should dare to break the said public peace out of their own malice, if it is a city, it shall pay as punishment to our Imperial Chamber one hundred <unclear>S</unclear> Marks of fine gold; this punishment is somewhat milder and more measured according to equity than the one mentioned above.

But the most severe punishment of the ban was adopted at Worms under Emperor Maximilian <note>Maximilian I (r. 1508–1519). The 1495 Diet of Worms established the "Perpetual Public Peace."</note>, under the title "The Penalty of Peace-Breakers," with these words: "And if anyone, of whatever dignity or status they might be, should act or dare to act against one or more of the points set forth in the previous article, they shall, by the very act, according to the law, together with other penalties, fall into our and the Holy Empire's ban; which we also hereby recognize and declare as being under our and the Holy Empire's ban: So that their bodies and goods are permitted to all <note>This meant the person was "fair game"; anyone could harm them or take their property without legal consequence.</note>, and no one shall or may commit a crime or trade with them. Also, all contracts, obligations, or alliances belonging to them, upon which they might have a claim or demand, shall be null and void against those who were punished; also the fiefs, as many as the violator used, shall be forfeited to the liege lord; and they shall not be obliged to grant those fiefs or parts thereof to him or other lords, or to allow his portion of the profits to follow, as long as the peace-breaker lives." Whether this constitution of the ban is measured according to equity and can be maintained according to Imperial Law, I will let others judge. However, this constitution was nevertheless confirmed anew by Emperor Charles V in the year 1521 under the title "The Penalty of All Peace-Breakers," with the addition that for one who is violently attacked and seized, self-defense shall not be forbidden but rather permitted.

# That it is entirely dangerous to
# sentence someone from life to death
# based on a confession from painful questioning.

## The Eighth Chapter.

<image-desc>A large decorative woodcut initial 'E' at the start of the main text, set against a background of intricate floral and leaf-like scrollwork designs within a square border.</image-desc>

**E**it is a common, but entirely dangerous and wicked abuse, almost throughout all the German lands, that when a poor person is brought to prison on some slight suspicion, the judges and authorities immediately begin to plague and attack the same poor prisoner with <term>painful questioning <note>original: *peinliche Frage*; a legal euphemism for judicial torture used to extract confessions.</note></term>. They often do so repeatedly before they have sought legal counsel to determine whether the suspicions and <term>indications <note>original: *indicia*; the legal signs or evidence of guilt required to justify the use of torture under Imperial law.</note></term> of such painful questioning are sufficient or not. Yet the law clearly and expressly provides that no one should be attacked painfully unless there is an <term>open notoriety <note>original: *offene Notoritet*; a crime so public and obvious that it requires no further proof.</note></term> present, or the indications have first been recognized through a lawful judgment, establishing that one may be questioned and addressed painfully. Some judges are so crude and reckless that they do not think it necessary to seek legal instruction regarding such matters.

And the judges are not satisfied with questioning them about that for which they were accused and detained; rather, they even dare to address, prosecute, and have people questioned regarding foreign matters <note>Refers to crimes or events unrelated to the original charge.</note> of which they have perhaps never heard in their entire lives. And even if they deny it once or twice, the same executioners and <term>jailers <note>original: *Stockmeister*; the official in charge of the prisoners and the instruments of restraint.</note></term> do not let up, but continue to question, and as they say, "once more into the fresh wounds," stretching and tormenting the poor people so long and so much until they finally confess everything they are asked, with many circumstances, such that no one could think otherwise than that it happened just as they confess—regardless of the fact that they were never guilty of such dealings in their entire lives. From this, it follows that many people are killed and executed entirely innocently, as the following excellent and true histories—some of which occurred recently and within human memory—clearly and sufficiently demonstrate.

First, it happened in Metz in Lorraine—as Dr. Martin Luther writes (though some say of a city in Saxony, and that it occurred in the year 1500)—that there was a wealthy merchant who had traveled across the sea for his business. During the time he was away, the executioner of that same city stole very secretly into the merchant’s house one evening when the door happened to be left open. He hid himself in the cellar for the night and remained there until the following day at noon, when the household was about to eat. Then, the maid first went into the cellar to fetch wine, whom the executioner immediately strangled. But when the maid delayed and did not return, the mistress sent her daughter after her, who was also strangled by him, and thus in the

While she was staying with her friends, it happened that a woman drowned in the Rhine and came floating by, dressed in exactly the same clothes as the wife who had left her husband used to wear. Since the murderers did not know how to lure the maid and the mistress out of their chamber, and they noticed a goat, they pinched or squeezed it so that it began to cry out loudly. When the woman heard this crying, she sent the maid down to see what the goat lacked. ### The Fifth Part

And although some judges have such crude and wide consciences that they can forget their deeds for a time, the hour of reckoning will not fail to arrive—so much so that the world can become too narrow for them, and one might wish he had never held such an office. Indeed, some have been driven so far in their consciences by such cases that they left their office and entered monasteries. As one reads of **John of Capistrano** <note>Johannes Capistrano (1386–1456) was a famous Franciscan friar and preacher who, before his religious life, served as a secular judge and governor in Perugia.</note>, who was a judge for **King Ladislaus**; once, in his official capacity, he had a Count and the Count’s son—who were notorious for treason—questioned. He found the treason to be with the father and not with the son, and he reported this to the King. The King commanded, under a pretense, that the son be sentenced alongside the father; this was done by Capistrano to investigate whether the son was truly guilty or not. And when they were both brought to the place of death, as the father was beheaded, the son also fell down out of fear of death and died. Because of this, Capistrano—who at that time was still a secular man—was so deeply distressed that he left the world (as it was then perceived) and entered the **Order of Saint Francis**.

Furthermore, it also happens sometimes that an entire land, a city, or a community must pay for such a reckless proceeding, as one could clearly show from history, though it would take too long. These histories are cited solely so that those who hold court should learn to proceed with deliberation, and not allow people to be so easily subjected to <term>Judicial Torture</term> <note>original: *peinlicher frage*; literally "painful questioning," the legal use of torture to extract confessions in capital cases.</note>. As the **Lacedemonians** <note>The Spartans; known in the Renaissance as models of stern but deliberate law-givers.</note>, being wise and diligent people, used to do. # That one should not lightly lay hands upon the servants of the court,
## however lowly they may be.

### The Ninth Chapter.

<image-desc>A large decorative historiated initial 'E' depicting a figure or scene, likely biblical or classical.</image-desc>Justinus Gobler <note>Justinus Gobler (1504–1567) was a German jurist and historian, famous for translating legal codes and writing regional chronicles.</note> writes in the Chronicle of Lübeck that around the year counted as one thousand, three hundred and thirty-three, it happened in Lübeck that a criminal was to be executed with the sword. However, when the executioner missed the first stroke, the mob <note>original German: *Pöfel*; the common people or a disorderly crowd</note> was immediately upon him and struck to death not only that same executioner <note>original German: *Scharff oder Nachrichter*</note> but also four others with him. When this is recounted in a social gathering or to the common man, it is regarded as a trivial and laughable thing when one hears that a hangman or five of his kind were struck dead. But if one considers God's commandment and will, it is truly a great sin to kill a human being—however lowly he may be—and especially the servants of justice, while they are innocent. At that time, the people of Lübeck cared nothing for this; for regardless of the fact that the one who was to be executed had well deserved his punishment, they looked more upon the executioners than upon the criminal. On that same day, Burgomaster Marx Meyer <note>A prominent military leader and politician from Hamburg/Lübeck in the early 16th century; his mention here alongside a 1333 event suggests the author is blending historical anecdotes or referring to Meyer's later involvement in Lübeck's turbulent history.</note> had come riding from Hamburg with a stately, well-armed mounted retinue, as he was holding a wedding that day. The Captain and his servants were present, who should have protected the innocent blood; but at that moment, they set that duty aside and focused instead on their own pomp.

Nevertheless, God—who leaves no innocent blood unavenged—afterward showed His displeasure such that the people of Lübeck later recognized and felt that they had no luck either with the obedience of the citizens or with their legal affairs, as the words of the history record. For Justinus Gobler writes thus:

> Truly, a grave sin was committed against God and justice through the murder of the court officers <note>original Latin: *Lictorum*; referring here to the executioners</note>, for it is established that from that day forward, the legal order and obedience in the city of Lübeck were miraculously subverted and fell away. Therefore, this example is a terrifying one, warning everyone toward modesty and obedience toward magistrates and their ministers—namely, that they are not to be offended or harmed. For such a manifest outrage and sedition against the judgment, which belongs to God, He does not leave unpunished, as happened to the city of Lübeck after this riot and insolence. May God grant that such sins are recognized. That is:

# An account of how and in what manner great transgressions and capital cases were punished in many places by the ancients.

## The Tenth Chapter.

Since I do not intend to present a formal judicial process <note>original German: *Gerichtlichen Proceß*; the technical steps of a legal trial</note> here—because these are common and well-known, and better described elsewhere than I could manage—I will write no more of judges and courts than merely how wrongdoers were punished by the ancients. For I intend to remain only with histories and certain fine maxims <term>Sententzen: derived from the Latin 'sententia,' these are authoritative moral sayings or legal principles</term> and the like, as I have done until now. Whoever desires and wishes to have a formal judicial process will know how to find it through other means. 

But to come to the punishments of the ancients, I find that the wise man **Plato** (who also wrote much and variously concerning the polity <term>Policey: in this era, the term referred to the overall civil order, administration, and governance of a community, rather than just modern 'police'</term>) held that there are two ways one may punish. 

The one is friendly: as when one addresses another kindly with words, reminding, correcting, and exhorting him to improve and desist from his evil intent, or otherwise punishes him with a small sum of money, which is done for the benefit of those punished in such a manner. 

The other way is serious: namely, that one punishes a person physically, as a horror to others, so that they may take warning from it. This is as is done here in this land to adulterers, church and highway robbers, murderers, and thieves. For all humans are of the opinion by nature that when they perceive they can escape unpunished, then no vice, no shame, no evil deed, and finally no treachery is too great or too much for them. Therefore, law and justice were of necessity moved to devise and ordain appropriate and public punishments for such evildoers. Thus, some were punished in their property, some banished, some had their ears cut off, eyes gouged out, and fists struck off; some also were sentenced to death and lose their lives, and are still so sentenced. For those who have sinned against God and their own parents, and committed some crime, or robbed the temples,
