Such distinctions were signified by the *fasces* or bundles of rods, as well as the axes, which the Romans used; some were to be simply disciplined with rods, while others were to have their necks struck off. For it was the custom of the Romans that those who had committed grave offenses were punished with death or cast down from a rock, while others were beaten with rods or condemned to the stone quarries. Likewise, in Thessaly there was a rock called the "Raven-stone" <note>German: *Rabenstein*; a common term for a place of execution where scavenging birds would gather</note>, over which wrongdoers were thrown. The Persians had a prison which they called "Death," for the reason that no one was placed therein unless he had forfeited his life. At Syracuse, they had a very deep pit hewn into a rock into which they threw wrongdoers. By the Messenians, the prison was called "The Treasury," and it was so difficult and cruel that neither daylight nor air could enter. In Rome, the prison was called "The Abyss" <note>original: *die Helle*; likely referring to the *Tullianum* or the *Barathrum*</note>. Those of Athens called their prison a "House"—even though it was also difficult and severe—so that the people might be less terrified by it. This example was later followed in Rome by Appius Claudius, who called the prison a "Common Inn." In the same way, the dungeons among us Germans have also acquired special names. Thus, the prison in Dresden is called "The Emperor." In Regensburg, "The Wolf." In Leipzig, "The Dog-house." In Eisleben, "The Snurr" <note>Likely referring to a "spinning house" or a local nickname</note>. In Naumburg, "The Donkey Stable." In Magdeburg, "The New Cellar." In the New Town there, "The Coal Chamber," etc.

Now as far as punishments and penalties are concerned, these were many and varied among the ancients, depending on the nature of the crime. And although **Metius Suffetius** received a heavy and hard punishment for his unfaithfulness and treachery—as was mentioned above:
> *It does no harm (as Plato says) to say twice what is well said.*
<note>original Latin: *Non enim nocet (vt Plato ait) bis dicere, quod bene dicitur.*</note>
That is: as Plato says, a good little song may well be sung twice—namely, that he was torn apart by two chariots; yet such punishment was not used against others thereafter. Although even among us to this day, it is still the custom to cut traitors into four parts and hang them in four locations.

But regarding fines <term>Geldtstraffe: financial penalties paid as punishment</term>, the ancient Romans also had a measure for them. Specifically, no one could be fined in money higher than the value of thirty oxen and two sheep. An ox was valued at 100 Groschen, and a sheep at 10 Groschen, which made about 100 Ducats. Furthermore, the sheep always had to be named first in the imposition of the fine, and not the oxen, so that they wished to show that they were more inclined toward the lesser rather than the great and hard punishment. Such a manner of punishing was also common in ancient times among the Germans; namely, if someone committed manslaughter, he had to pay for it with a certain number of cattle. Just as the Saxons now pay for the same with a "blood-money" <term>wehrgelt: from 'Wergild,' the value placed on a human life paid as compensation to the family of a victim</term>, which is 24 old *Schock* <note>A 'Schock' was a unit of sixty</note>, amounting to 22 florins and 18 Groschen according to the Territorial Law, Book 1, Article 65, in the gloss.

# The Fifth Part

<warning>Text at the right margin is partially obscured due to tight binding and cropping.</warning>

Those of Athens also used to punish people with fines, and they placed that money in the temple treasury of Jupiter. Once money had been placed there, no one could ever reclaim it. This practice flowed from Plato, who had ordained a monetary fine for every kind of misconduct, thus punishing people by their purses. Minor offenses among the Germans were paid for with a head of cattle or with a horse. Some among the Romans were banished from the city in such a way that no one was permitted to give them shelter or have any fellowship with them—much like when someone today is placed under the Imperial ban <note>German: *Reichs acht*; a medieval legal status where an individual was declared an outlaw, stripped of all rights and property.</note>. For some, fire and water were forbidden <note>Latin: *interdictio aqua et ignis*; a Roman form of exile.</note>. The greatest punishment was that people were thrown to wild animals. Such punishment was usually applied to servants who were unfaithful to their masters or had run away, or to those who were enemies of the city or otherwise harmful people. Likewise, it was commonly inflicted on those who had defected from the Roman alliance or had deserted from war, and were thus considered unworthy of any mercy. It was also the custom that some were assigned to the gold mines and others to the stone quarries, where they performed their labor in chains; some had to spend their entire lives there, and others for a set number of years. But those who were stained with such evil deeds that such punishment was deemed too light in comparison were also thrown before wild animals to be torn apart, or were otherwise tortured to death.

Marcus Malleolus was the first parricide <note>One who kills a parent or close relative.</note> in Rome who strangled his own mother, and after him came Lucius Hostilius, who was stuffed into a leather sack and thrown into the water. This punishment remained thereafter until this time, except that the law ordained that an ape, or in the absence of that, a cat, a rooster, and a snake should be stuffed in with him. Thus, in such agony among wild animals, he was made to die as a murderer of his own parents or blood-relatives. <note>original: "ff. ad l. Pompeiam de parricid." refers to the Digest of Roman Law, specifically the Lex Pompeia concerning parricide.</note> Among the Egyptians, such parricides who strangled their parents or children were so hated that they were pricked in every limb with sharp styluses over their whole body, and subsequently burned with thorns. However, if a father there strangled his son, he had to sit by the corpse for three whole days and look at it continuously. The Egyptians held that one could not punish or torment such a father more severely than by forcing him to look upon his own deed and crime against his own flesh and blood for so long, thereby torturing him in his heart and conscience.

The Lusitanians or Portuguese led such evildoers to the border and stoned them to death. But Julius Caesar, beyond the punishments expressed in the law, also had the goods of those who strangled their parents or children confiscated and seized. Solon and Romulus—as Cicero and others write—gave no law regarding parricide, because they did not believe it was possible that such evil people could be found in the world who would dare to kill their parents or children.

<page-num>241</page-num>
# Of the Book of Regents.

The Greeks punished temple robbers <note>German: *Kirchenräuber*; literally "church robbers," but in a Greek context refers to those who plundered sacred temples.</note> severely, such that they were either drowned, burned, or thrown to their deaths from a cliff. In Macedonia, parricides <note>those who kill their parents or close relatives</note> and those who acted against the King were also stoned to death. However, anyone who presumed to act against the common good had a rope placed around their neck and was led through all the streets while being beaten with rods until they died; only then was the body finally thrown down from a cliff.

Although the penalty and punishment varied from one place to another, and the court proceedings in one city were different from another, we read of the court in Athens called the Areopagus. The judges and assessors of this court, called Areopagites, held their proceedings with great solemnity and strictness, not by day, but by night. Furthermore, no one was permitted to speak in a way that might move the judges to mercy, so that no one would place more hope in such mercy than in the merits of the case itself. After this court had almost entirely fallen into decay and vanished due to the many wars and misfortunes that befell the Athenians for many years, it was later restored and returned to its ancient form and custom by Cimon <note>Original: *Chinonem*; likely referring to the Athenian statesman Kimon.</note>. In the same manner, the Lacedaemonians <note>the Spartans</note> held their court at night, with the judges locked in a room so that they could only hear and not see anyone. The Bithynians, however, held their court facing and under the sun, to demonstrate that the law should proceed clearly and purely for everyone, like the bright sun. This is as the Emperor Justinian says: In criminal matters, the proof must be clearer than the bright sun at midday. <note>Original Latin reference: *l. dicta sciant cuncti. C. de probationibus*; referring to the Justinian Code, Book 4, Title 19, Law 25, which begins "Let all know..."</note> In Rome, no judgment could be passed upon a person before ten o'clock if they were absent. Likewise, no one could be put to death at night, as such punishments were meant to be known to everyone so that they might have a horror of the crime. In Macedonia, in ancient times, wrongdoers were stoned to death. Among the people of Memphis, murderers were not tolerated in the city, nor were people allowed to have any fellowship with them; instead, they had to wander in exile in great misery and contempt until they were again absolved and received back by their priests, whom they called Gymnosophists <note>literally "naked philosophers"; a term usually applied by Greeks to Indian ascetics, but here associated by the author with Egyptian priests.</note>. In Meroë <note>an ancient kingdom in what is now Sudan</note>, if the King committed a grave offense, no special punishment was inflicted upon him, except that no one was allowed to have any further fellowship with him. Thus, he had to spend his life in sadness and grief, abandoned by all.

Furthermore, it was the custom among the Egyptians that when they wished to judge a wrongdoer, they placed a rope around his neck and a bit in his mouth, like a horse, and led him about in this manner. He...

### The Fifth Part

...the King also sent food from his own table the evening before. This practice later took root among certain Emperors in Rome; if they intended to have someone put to death (as some of them were such tyrants), they sent him a magnificent and exquisite meal the evening before—a meal that one would surely have preferred to do without.

The Moors <note>Historically referring to North African or Muslim peoples</note> in ancient times had their criminals bound with golden chains. As soon as the King sent that person a sign of death, he was required to inflict death upon himself and strangle himself. It is said of the Turkish Emperor <note>The Ottoman Sultan</note> today that he commands such obedience from his own people: if he indicates to someone that they must strangle themselves, it is done without any refusal.

In some places, major crimes such as homicide and the like were paid for with a small fine. For instance, if someone killed a Boeotian <note>People from Boeotia, a region in ancient Greece often stereotyped as rustic</note> peasant or someone from Thessaly, he only had to give the deceased's kinsmen a bushel of lentils or a similar pottage. Conversely, some nations used severe physical punishment for minor offenses. Thus, if someone in Thessaly killed a stork, he had to die for it; the same was true in Egypt for killing a hawk. Likewise, if someone in Phrygia <note>An ancient kingdom in central Anatolia</note> stole a plowshare or a rake. Also, if someone in India evaded the escort or the toll <note>original: *Zoll*; customs taxes or transit fees</note>, he forfeited his life. The Persians also punished minor offenses with such gravity, particularly the breaking down of tall trees: they would tie people to them and then have them torn asunder.

And although many other penalties for various criminals could be recounted, it is partly a foolish matter, and therefore I do not wish to burden the reader with it. However, it is important to know that adultery was punished in various ways by the ancients. Although among the Indians, Massagetae <note>Ancient nomadic people of Central Asia</note>, and Moors, the adulterer and adulteress faced no punishment but were free, the Nomads held their wives in common. And among the Lacedaemonians <note>Spartans</note>, adultery was so rare that they did not even make a law concerning it. Yet the wise man Plato, as well as Solon, held and decreed that adulterers should be punished with the sword. The Thracians and Parthians punished no vice as heavily as adultery—despite the fact that they considered it no crime if one caused a maiden to fall <note>refers to the seduction of an unmarried woman</note>, for that was free to everyone. In Tenedos <note>An island in the Aegean Sea</note>, both man and woman were punished with the sword for adultery. The Jews struck their adulterers to death with stones. In Pisidia <note>A region in ancient Asia Minor</note>, adulterers were placed upon a donkey and paraded around, which was a great disgrace. But whoever defiled a maiden there had his male member removed <note>emasculation or castration</note>. This was also used at times in Rome; for when Bibienus caught Carbo in adultery, he treated him in the same manner. Zaleucus of Locri <note>A celebrated Greek lawgiver known for his "eye for an eye" style of justice</note> put out both eyes of adulterers.

# A Reminder Follows / regarding
## the reasons why people / and especially rulers / princes, and lords / should read histories with diligence.

<image-desc>A large decorative drop-cap 'W' featuring intricate vine and floral patterns.</image-desc>We see daily before our eyes / and experience / that the world proceeds no differently than on the wild sea. For just as the sea is never still / but ebbs and flows many times a day / likewise when the billows <note>original: *Bülgen*; large waves</note> rise from the turbulence of the wind / one ship is raised up even to heaven / while another is cast down into the depths / as if plunged and thrown into hell / and yet eventually some return to safety / while others drown and perish. This is also how things tend to go in the world / among the people / and especially among the great leaders / that now one rises / another falls / and the one who has fallen soon brings himself forward again. Thus, no one is so fortunate / or so great and powerful / that he does not stand in danger / that some misfortune might seize him and cast him down from his seat <note>meaning his throne or position of authority</note>. Some of these / when they overreach in their power / and show themselves to be harsh and cruel toward the people at all times / become so hated / that they are finally abandoned / and must ruin and perish in their misfortune / especially if they have been godless as well. Others, however / when they recognized their misfortune / and prayed to God for forgiveness and grace / have come forward again / into their former standing / as can be seen in the case of Manasseh <note>A King of Judah who, according to the Bible, was taken captive to Babylon but was restored to his throne after repenting.</note>.

Furthermore, we also see / and experience daily / the change / downfall / destruction / and ultimate ruin of many kingdoms, principalities, lands, and cities. However, because the causes and origins of such great, remarkable, and harmful changes / misfortunes, and destruction are of many kinds / and not known to everyone / they must therefore be explored and considered with the highest diligence. Yet these can be recognized and seen nowhere better or more clearly / than in the old and past stories <note>original: *Historien*</note> / which occurred at every period of time. Therefore, necessity requires / that we diligently inquire into such things from histories / since we can see and learn the same therein as if in a mirror. Indeed, such stories from the beginning of the world / have been composed into histories with great diligence by brave / experienced, and highly learned people / and have been preserved until this time / without doubt not without the special providence <note>original: *schickung*; the unfolding of God’s will</note> of Almighty God.

For since humans, out of their perverse nature, are so blind and un-

<note>original: "besonnen/" from the previous page</note> mindful, and finally become so completely forgetful that they can neither see nor recognize the causes from which such changes, as mentioned above, spring and flow. Rather, for the most part—like unreasoning cattle—they think no further, nor look around, beyond that which occurs daily and lies before their eyes. But when it leaves their sight, it is also soon forgotten. In such great instability of human affairs, they do not consider that some misfortune might occur and befall them, or that their skill might fail them, until they suddenly fall to the ground. Through such blindness, they are finally driven to the point where they hold the highest and worst vices to be the best virtues, choosing evil and setting aside good; which is more to be pitied than wondered at.

Accordingly, out of special grace, the Almighty has awakened several excellent people who undertook this labor and have described with great diligence such things as have occurred from of old. In this, they have earned no small merit for posterity and all the world; indeed, they could have undertaken and accomplished nothing more useful on earth. For they have captured in writing the past things—which otherwise would have been forgotten a thousand times over (however great and noteworthy they may have been)—with such diligence that we and other descendants might also have knowledge of them. Thus, through such examples of things past, we might better direct and adapt ourselves to present and occurring affairs. Likewise, so that the things which are necessary for us to know in all of human life might not escape us; for we are all by nature so disposed that we are first to neglect that which is most necessary for us to know.

From this, it can be sufficiently understood and inferred that histories <note>The author uses "Historien" to mean both the study of the past and the written accounts themselves.</note> were written first and foremost because it is impossible for us, given the vastness of the world and so many kingdoms and lands, to see everything with our eyes and experience it in deed. Similarly, our life here on earth lasts only a short time; yet, through such diligence and the investigation of histories, we might have a true account and knowledge of absent, past, and distant things. By this, we attain such an excellent benefit and advantage that when we read such stories and histories, we feel not as newborn people, but as though we have come down from ancient times and many centuries past. From this, we are instructed in such a way that even if we are young, we may not only know and learn such old stories and histories but also be able to instruct others.

Furthermore, the greater part of mankind is so minded that they are more easily informed and instructed by examples of past history <note>original: "Exempel ergangener Geschicht"; the use of historical "examples" was a primary method of moral teaching in the 16th century.</note> than by verbal commands and laws. Such examples also have much more power to move people than simple words—no matter how serious they may be or if they come from the philosophers. Thus, those commands are in no way to be compared with history; rather

# Reminder

<meta>catchword: than</meta>

...on account of their utility, are far preferred over commandments. This is because they explain a matter to a person much more richly and powerfully, and place it right before one's eyes when it happens that a difficult situation arises—what should be done or avoided, how one should guard against <term>vices</term><note>The original German "Untugend" refers to a lack of virtue or bad habits.</note>, and how one should strive for <term>virtue</term>. For histories encompass all virtues in general, and paint before our eyes their causes, hindrances, growth, and final outcomes. Although this is primarily done so that when such foreign stories and histories are told, the reader may perceive and notice what is evil or good within them—how to praise the good and follow it, and likewise how to punish the evil and guard oneself against it.

As **Cornelius Tacitus** <note>A famous Roman historian (c. 56–120 AD) known for his moral commentary on the Roman Empire.</note> also says of this, when he speaks thus: "I consider this the greatest and best fruit of history: that the virtues and brave deeds are praised, and conversely, that which was handled evilly and shamefully is also placed and modeled before the eyes, so that descendants may have all the more reason to guard themselves against such shame and such evil."

Since virtue is of such a nature that it not only highly adorns a person and suits everyone finely and well, but also frequently guards and preserves them from great danger and disadvantage. For this reason, however, shameful vices so disguise and mislead people that they fall into extreme ruin because of them. Who would not most diligently cling to virtue and follow it? And conversely, who would not flee from evil and offensive vices, avoiding them like the worst poison? Who would not most earnestly punish and scold the womanish, shameless, and completely perverted customs of **Sardanapalus**, **Heliogabalus** <note>Sardanapalus (Assyria) and Heliogabalus (Rome) were historical figures frequently used as examples of extreme decadence and moral failure.</note>, and other such foul persons? Who would not feel a sense of loathing at the shameful deed of **Paris** <note>Referring to the abduction of Helen, which sparked the Trojan War.</note>, or likewise at the unseemly marriage of **Masinissa** and **Sophonisba** <note>A tragic story of political marriage and suicide during the Punic Wars.</note>? Who, finally, would not be horrified by the cruel tyranny of **Phalaris**, **Nero**, **Dionysius**, and others? This is to say nothing of the faithlessness, falsehood, treachery, murder, as well as the uprisings and other gruesome vices that people have used and practiced against one another—both the authorities against their subjects, and conversely the subjects against their authorities; likewise, children against parents, one friend against another, one lord against another, and servants often against their masters. To elaborate on this with examples would become too long, and it has already been partly discussed earlier in this book.

But now, when someone sees such vices in another and condemns them, and feels a displeasure and notices what kind of end those who pursued such vices and evil deeds met, then he can provide for himself so much better and more easily, and guard himself against such vices and misdeeds, which often cost a person their body, soul, honor, and property.

For when we consider such vices in another and subsequently search our own hearts and minds, we sometimes find that we have committed similar shames and misdeeds, or at the very least, have had the will and inclination to do so. For it is unjust to [judge] that in others... <note>The text ends mid-sentence; the next page likely continues with "at which we ourselves fail."</note>

# Reminder

...to hate [vices] which we ourselves commit, as **Aristotle** <note>The famous Greek philosopher (384–322 BC) whose works on ethics and politics were foundational to Renaissance thought.</note> says: 

> *For we do not feel indignation when others do the very things we do ourselves.* <note>original Latin: "Non enim indignamur cum alij ea faciunt, quæ nolipsi."</note>

That is: we should rightly not be angry when others do the things that we ourselves have done (since we are all more inclined toward evil than toward good). Thus, we should remember such foreign examples and turn away from our own wicked intentions and evil purposes, so that we might not also meet such a shameful, evil, and terrible end. For just as a person’s **virtue** and **honor** cannot remain hidden for long but must break forth, so too can **vices** and shameful sins (even if they can be hidden for a time) not remain covered forever. They must be revealed and finally receive their punishment; indeed, they will not be able to escape it.

From this, it appears clearly enough—if one views histories correctly and considers them with diligence—that they instruct us quite clearly and brightly on what to follow and what to flee. They point, as if with a finger, to what one should or should not do, as well as the great praise and honor one attains through honest deeds and actions. Likewise, they show how some fall so horribly and terribly, and in their fall, drag many others down with them, thus perishing and going to ruin miserably together. Similarly, they show how some rise so strangely, increase in power and wealth, and come to a high station—which God primarily and occasionally allows to happen so that He can punish them all the more terribly and cast them to the ground. As that fine sentence of **Aristotle** indicates, where he says:

> *To many, God grants great prosperity not out of benevolence, but so that their calamities may become more notable.* <note>original Latin: "Multis non ex beneuolentia Deus ingentes præstat prosperitates, verum ut nobiliores suæ fiant calamitates."</note>

That is: God sometimes gives someone great fortune, not out of grace, but so that He may thereby make their misery all the greater.

Likewise, history shows what a bad name and reputation a person acquires from shameful misdeeds. Furthermore, histories show how many have deceived others under a false appearance, and deliberately preferred evil over good, and what is worst of all, persisted in it and perished.

Therefore, one must confess and say that everyone—and especially the **great regents** <note>Rulers, princes, or high-ranking officials.</note>—should consider histories with the highest diligence and practice them, so that they may direct and arrange their reign and their entire lives thereby. For first, they will see in the evil and godless **tyrants** and kings, who spent their lives in <term>unchastity</term><note>The original German "Vnzucht" refers to immoral behavior, often sexual, but generally implying a lack of discipline.</note>, tyranny, and the lust for worldly things, that they met a miserable, wretched end. They will see what great change, disruption, and final ruin of kingdoms and lands followed. For who would not be moved by the local rages and murders that **Marius** and **Sulla** <note>Gaius Marius and Lucius Cornelius Sulla were Roman generals and rivals whose bloody civil wars led to the destabilization of the Roman Republic.</note> caused in Rome? And since the godless can have no peace, it often happens that one dares to wage war against, ruin, and kill another for the sake of envy, hate, or other minor causes, as is seen with **Caesar** and **Pompey** <note>Julius Caesar and Pompey the Great, whose power struggle led to the Roman Civil War (49–45 BC).</note>.

Furthermore, one sees in these histories what a cruel, evil, and harmful thing **anger** is in men, and how we are all of the opinion...

## Reminder

...if anger seizes us, so that we would gladly overturn and destroy everything if we could manage to do so; that out of anger and for the sake of small matters, we often commit gruesome murders and rages. Therefore, **Heraclitus** <note>A pre-Socratic Greek philosopher known for his teachings on change and conflict.</note>, as **Aristotle** writes, rightly said: *It is hard to fight against anger, for I have bought this with my life.* <note>original Latin: "Durum est pugnare aduersus iram, Vita enim id emi."</note> This means: it is difficult to struggle against anger, for I have paid for this lesson with my very existence. 

For what great reason did **Saul** <note>The first King of Israel, whose jealousy of David led to several acts of madness.</note> have to set fire to the city of **Nob** and stab everyone inside, other than that the priest **Ahimelech** had sheltered and fed **David**? What great reason did the Emperor **Theodosius** <note>Theodosius I (r. 379–395 AD), who ordered a massacre of 7,000 citizens in Thessalonica after a riot.</note> have to allow several thousand people to be gruesomely murdered in **Thessalonica**, simply because some of his servants were slain in a riot for which they themselves had given cause? 

Therefore, and because anger is such a harmful thing, rulers and great lords should look out most diligently <note>original: "fleissigsten"</note> against such a raging evil. Histories faithfully warn of this: that one should not use such cruelty in government, nor otherwise, but should instead hold to **justice**, **virtue**, and **decency**.

For just as those who allow themselves to be moved by anger or otherwise become **tyrants** may very easily fall into noticeable harm and ruin, so too can those who strive for justice, virtue, and goodness more easily escape burdens when they encounter them. Indeed, nothing truly unfortunate can easily happen to such people; and even if it does, they have this advantage—since they have the favor of everyone—that in the face of impending need, they can more easily rescue themselves, their wives, children, friends, subjects, lands, and people, and receive help.

Now, when one sees how many brave heroes received eternal praise and a great name for the sake of their beautiful virtues and magnificent deeds—as are found here and there in history, such as **Hercules** and the like—why does he not allow himself to be moved to follow them, so that he might also attain such a name and honor? Who would be ashamed to endure poverty when he reads with what constancy **Phocion** <note>An Athenian statesman and general (c. 402–318 BC) known for his extreme honesty and refusal of gifts.</note> in Athens despised the huge sum of money that King **Alexander of Macedon** <note>Alexander the Great.</note> sent to him? He pointed out that it was not fitting for an honest man living in a free city to take money from foreign princes and allow that money to move him toward something dishonest.

Similarly, consider with what a great and steadfast spirit **Marcus Curtius** <note>Though the text names Marcus Curtius, this anecdote of refusing gifts usually refers to Manius Curius Dentatus, a Roman hero famous for his incorruptibility.</note> turned down the gifts of the **Samnites** and would not take them. Yes, and what is more, when one reads how **Paulus Emylius** <note>Lucius Aemilius Paullus Macedonicus (c. 229–160 BC), a Roman general who refused to enrich himself from the spoils of the Macedonian War.</note> would not even look at the gold sent to him by the King of Macedon. Just as such moderation and steadfastness raised the **Roman Empire** to the highest level, so too did **greed**, **pride**, and great **extravagance** ruin it to the ground, as **Sallust** <note>Gaius Sallustius Crispus, a Roman historian who wrote about the moral decline of the Roman Republic.</note> writes of it. How can one better or more conveniently restrain and defend against his desires, or cast out of his mind the worry over lost things, than if he reads in the histories how many powerful people among great wealth... # Reminder

...and govern people justly, healthily, and well; they should not consider their own profit, but much more the common good. History also reveals how rulers upheld justice even with great danger to their own bodies and lives, how they took great earnestness in avenging insults directed at their friends, and how they took up arms for war not out of any triviality, but only in extreme necessity. Thus they also—so that such cruel and inhuman things resulting from war (as discussed above) might be avoided—patiently overcame all kinds of insults and injustice for the preservation of peace and unity.

One also reads what care these same rulers took for the sake of the youth, out of which one must establish the governance of the common good, as well as churches and schools. Namely, that the youth should be properly instructed, taught, practiced, raised, and kept in check. Likewise, that they physically provided for and supplied their kingdoms, lands, and cities not only with good, honest laws, customs, and policies, but also with the right religion and its ministers. For we have fine, clear, and magnificent examples from Holy Scripture in **Josiah** <note>A king of Judah celebrated for his religious reforms and rediscovery of the Law.</note> and **Hezekiah** <note>A righteous king of Judah who removed idols and restored the temple.</note> that the authorities are duty-bound to abolish false worship and to plant and maintain the true religion. <margin>Thrift</margin> <note>original Latin: "Frugalitas."</note>
And although moderation in clothing, eating, drinking, and all other things has in current times—especially among us Germans—completely ceased and been extinguished, one finds from history that this same moderation was a fine arranger and sustainer of the human race in ancient times. Back then, people were so moderate in all things and let themselves be satisfied with so little—both in eating, drinking, clothing, and other human necessities—that now the very least among us cannot be sated and satisfied with that which a powerful lord might once have made do with.

Since this same virtue is now abandoned, despised, and set aside by everyone—especially by us Germans—and every person, however lowly, strives only for how they might waste much, consume much, and spend on clothing, in which we are so completely drowned that we no longer see or consider the great damage and ruin resulting from such luxury and immoderate waste, nor can we recognize the great benefit of moderation. As **Cicero** <note>The Roman statesman and philosopher Marcus Tullius Cicero.</note> says: *Men do not understand how great a revenue thrift is.* <note>original Latin: "Non intelligunt homines, quàm magnum sit vectigal parsimonia."</note> Instead, we regard such luxury as a magnificent virtue, and conversely, moderation as a shame and a vice. Thus, if someone nowadays attempts to arrange their life moderately, whether in clothing or otherwise, people do not know how to speak shamefully enough about him; they are held in almost worse and more contemptuous regard than murderers and usurers were held by the ancients. One can also, in all places, better tolerate a drunkard, adulterer, or usurer than such a man who strives for moderation. Such abundance...

Although many things also happen so that we may be disciplined and punished, to the end that we might repent and not be condemned with the world, as **Paul** says to the **Corinthians**. <note>A reference to 1 Corinthians 11:32: "But when we are judged, we are chastened of the Lord, that we should not be condemned with the world."</note>

They are exactly like a mariner who sails upon the sea and yet pays no attention to the ship or how it is steered; nor does he ask whether it occasionally strikes an obstacle, but instead waits upon his own business, eating, drinking, playing, and being lighthearted. Now, such a ship stands in great danger and cannot remain whole for long; also the people who sail within it must drown and perish along with their mariner. In the same way, subjects under such a government cannot live without danger, but must expect the imminent distress of harm and ruin.

For from where else should so much harm, misery, war, murder, and misfortune have arisen for the human race at all times, than that kings, princes, regents, and great lords in the world have sometimes been so reckless and paid no heed to the examples of history, but instead wished to carry out everything without thought and according to their own heads. Now, the more the harm that follows from such thoughtlessness and negligence increases, the more great lords should accustom themselves to reading history, so that they might learn from it to act prudently and wisely, and to guard themselves against harm. And if, among so many thousands of histories, a single example should come—if one considers it rightly and follows it—which could preserve a lord's life, honor, property, friendship, land, and people, which he would otherwise have to lose if he despised it.

<margin>What History is.</margin>
If such great lords, as well as the regents in cities, could err without the harm, disadvantage, and ruin of other people, then such error might still be suffered and forgotten. But because that cannot be nor happen—but rather, when these great people err and fall, that same fall and error usually falls upon the poor subjects, whereby land and people fall to the ground and must perish with them—they should indeed learn and read history with great diligence, especially in their youth, which instructs one in all these things. For History, as **Cicero** <note>Marcus Tullius Cicero (106–43 BCE), a Roman statesman and orator. The quote is from his work *De Oratore*.</note> says, is a witness of time, a light of truth, a life of memory, and a messenger of the ancient world and its stories. And histories and examples serve not only when the sky begins to grow dark, or when hail and storms break in, to show how one should conduct oneself; but also when the sky is bright and beautiful, so that one does not fall asleep and become over-confident, and through such security and lack of foresight perhaps awaken a storm—as can easily happen. Likewise, so that one knows when to hurry, like **Camillus**, <note>Marcus Furius Camillus (c. 446–365 BCE), a Roman general honored as the "Second Founder of Rome" for his swift and decisive actions.</note> or when to delay and restrain oneself, like **Fabius Maximus**. <note>Quintus Fabius Maximus Verrucosus (c. 280–203 BCE), known as "Cunctator" (the Delayer) for his strategy of exhausting Hannibal through attrition rather than direct battle.</note> It is also not enough that one knows such examples merely superficially; rather, it will be necessary for him to know how to use them rightly.

I have written this book not to master anyone, or to give any measure <note>original: "einige Maß zu geben" — meaning to dictate terms or set limits to one’s behavior</note> to anyone who knows better, especially great lords; much less to criticize <note>original: "tarieren"</note> and attack anyone with it, which I wish to have testified here before the whole world. Primarily because I know how difficult it is to give advice to others, especially to high-ranking people, and because Fortune will have its course and wishes to master all things. It often happens that even bad advice achieves a good outcome, and good plans turn out poorly. 
> As Cicero himself experienced and testified when he said: The best-conceived plans often turn out worst. <note>original Latin: "Quod & Cicero ipse expertus testatur, cùm inquit: Optimè cogitata sæpe pessimè euenire."</note> 
That is: Things that are best thought out often gain a bad and troublesome end. Thus, no one can be far-sighted enough in future things. Rather, I have written, compiled, and put this into print for the benefit of the simple, the young lords and regents, and the common man—but primarily for myself. It is like one who places a "hand" <note>A reference to a wooden signpost shaped like a hand, common at early modern crossroads</note> along the path so that travelers may guide themselves by it. Most powerful and most gracious King and Lord, it is written that in former times no one dared to come before the King of Parthia <note>An ancient empire located in what is now Iran and Iraq; they were famous for their courtly protocols</note> with empty hands. In the most humble hope that it shall not be displeasing to Your Royal Majesty, I have resolved to report this to Your Royal Majesty and to most humbly send a copy of the same book.

# A Beautiful and Wise Speech /

I wish to look around in foreign books and do as those who, perhaps for honors or weddings, borrow money or clothes when they are in need of them, but under pressure can find nothing more suitable in their haste than the beautiful and magnificent speech and reminder of Musonius the Philosopher. <note>Musonius Rufus (c. 20–101 AD) was a famous Stoic philosopher known as the "Roman Socrates."</note> He lived during the time of the Emperor Nero and was even persecuted and killed <note>original: "erwürget vnd getödtet"; though Musonius was actually exiled by Nero and survived him, 16th-century accounts often emphasized the martyrdom of philosophers under Nero's tyranny.</note> for the sake of his truth and free speech. He gave this speech to a King of Syria who had visited and addressed him, and I have now translated it here into German <note>now English</note>.

Even though it is true that today things are viewed quite differently than in the time of Musonius, and not everything depends on philosophy as it perhaps did then—since Almighty God, out of mild grace and mercy, has revealed and given us His holy eternal Word through Christ His only Son in these latter times—from which great potentates, kings, princes, and authorities can be more and better informed and instructed as to what their office is, and what they should do or leave undone (of which I have made further mention in my *Politia* <term>Politia: Referring to Lauterbeck's own work, "Regentenbuch" or "Politia Historica," a handbook on governance and statecraft.</term>), it can still be sufficiently understood from this short speech of Musonius that even the heathens <note>Pagans; here referring to the pre-Christian Greeks and Romans.</note> saw through reason and the light of nature that it befits a regent to be pious, just, and irreproachable in his own person. They saw that he should protect and maintain his people and subjects with equity and justice, and violate no one, but rather show himself as a father toward them.

They also saw, alongside this, that the office of government requires great diligence, and that regents should concern themselves with those arts by which one is made fit to properly oversee the state <term>Regiment: The 16th-century term for the administration, rule, or governance of a territory.</term>—to know what is right or wrong, evil or good, fair or unfair, and what is to be done or avoided. It was primarily the philosophers of old who taught and wrote about these things. Therefore, one had to seek out such art among them and learn from them, just as Alexander the Great did from Aristotle.

And Musonius was not the least among them, as is clearly shown by the fact that such a powerful king was not ashamed to address him and listen to his report regarding the government. This undoubtedly would not have happened if such a great reputation had not echoed here and there throughout Greece and everywhere else concerning him. Musonius also proved his arts and wisdom in many other ways and left behind magnificent sayings from which his wisdom could be perceived. One such saying is found in Gellius, book 16, chapter 1, <note>Aulus Gellius (c. 125–180 AD), author of "Attic Nights," a collection of notes on grammar, philosophy, and history.</note> which reads as follows:

> <note>original Latin: "Si cum labore honeſti quippiam egeris, labor abit, honeſtum manet. Si cum voluptate turpe quippiam feceris, quod ſuaue eſt, abit, quod turpe eſt, manet."</note>
> If you perform an honorable deed with toil and labor, the labor passes away and ceases, but the honorable deed remains forever. But if you perform a shameful deed with pleasure, such pleasure is soon gone and passes away, but the shameful deed remains.

With this, he intended to incite people toward honorable deeds and away from evil and shame-

For to such a great leader, [eloquence] is not only elegant, laudable, useful, and excellent, but also highly necessary—not only in deliberations but also when it occasionally happens that he must speak before many people (as can easily occur), so that he is not then completely mute.

# A Beautiful and Wise Discourse/

It is well for those who have looked through foreign books and done as those do who—perhaps for honors or weddings—borrow money or clothes when they are in need of them but can find nothing more suitable in a hurry among many things than the beautiful and magnificent speech and reminder of *Musonius* the Philosopher. He lived under the Emperor *Nero* and was also strangled and killed for the sake of his truth and free speech <note>Musonius Rufus was a famous Stoic teacher. While he was famously exiled by Nero, Lauterbeck reflects a common historical tradition that grouped him with other Stoic martyrs like Seneca who were killed by the tyrant.</note>. He gave this discourse to a King of Syria when he was visited and addressed by him, which I have brought here into German.

Although it is certainly the case, and true, that things are understood much differently now than in the time of *Musonius*, and not everything depends on philosophy as it may have then—since Almighty God, out of mild grace and mercy, has revealed and given us His holy eternal Word in these last times through Christ His only Son—from which great potentates, kings, princes, and authorities can be more and better informed and instructed as to what their office is and what they should do and leave undone (of which I have made further mention in my *Politia* <term>Politia: Likely referring to Lauterbeck's famous work, the 'Regentenbuch' or 'Book of Rulers', which provided moral and practical guidance for governing.</term>), yet it is sufficiently clear from this short speech of *Musonius* that even the heathens, through reason and the light of nature, saw that it befits a regent to be pious, just, and irreproachable in his own person. They saw that he should protect and maintain his people and subjects in equality and justice, and violate no one, but rather show himself as a father toward them.

They also saw, alongside this, that great diligence is required for such an office of government, and that regents should concern themselves with those arts by which one is made fit to preside over a government <term>Regiment: Here meaning the act or system of ruling/governing.</term> properly—to know what is right or wrong, evil or good, fair or unfair, to be done or to be left undone. Of these things, the philosophers primarily taught and wrote in former times. Therefore, one had to seek such art from them and learn from them, just as *Alexander the Great* did from *Aristotle*.

And *Musonius* was not the least among them, which appears clearly enough from the fact that such a powerful king was not ashamed to address him and to listen to his report regarding government. This would no doubt not have happened if such a great reputation had not resounded here and there in Greece and everywhere else concerning him. *Musonius* also proved his arts and wisdom in more ways and left behind his magnificent sayings, through which his wisdom could be felt. Such as the saying in *Gellius, book 16, chapter 1* <note>Referring to the 'Attic Nights' by Aulus Gellius, a 2nd-century collection of notes on grammar, philosophy, and history.</note>, which reads: <term>If you do something honorable with toil, the toil departs, the honor remains. If you do something shameful with pleasure, the pleasure departs, the shame remains.</term> <note>original: "Si cum labore honesti quippiam egeris, labor abit, honestum manet. Si cum voluptate turpe quippiam feceris, quod suaue est, abit, quod turpe est, manet."</note> That is: When someone completes and carries out an honorable deed with effort and labor, the effort and labor pass away and cease, but the honorable deed remains forever and ever. But if someone completes a shameful deed with pleasure, such pleasure is and goes away quickly, but the shameful deed remains. With this, he wished to incite people toward honorable deeds and away from evil and shameful ones—

# A Beautiful and Wise Discourse /

...but rather that they should apply themselves, out of philosophy and the foundation of the law, to learn what is right or wrong, good or evil. And if something is put forward for deliberation, or otherwise comes to light, that is not in accordance with the law and equity, and yet someone wants to press for it based on their rights or otherwise—that the King should not sit there like a mute character in a comedy <note>A "mute person" refers to a silent actor or an extra who has no lines in a play.</note>, but rather should know how to refute such inequity with the consistency and foundation of the law and the truth, and how to counter those who desire such unjust things. It is indeed true that such great lords think they have people and lawyers who understand such things, and therefore they do not need to concern themselves with them. But yet there is a very great difference between those lords who understand a thing themselves and are able to say more than just "Amen" or "I approve" <note>original: *placet*, a Latin term used by rulers or officials to signify formal consent to a proposal.</note>, and those who are personally ignorant of all things and must rely solely on their advisors and lawyers, and leave all matters to them, as commonly happens. It is also not meant that such great lords and potentates should not have other learned, wise, and highly intelligent people with and beside them, and make use of them for speaking, advising, and other necessities. Rather, it has only this meaning: if it should happen out of necessity that a regent or King himself must speak, that he would then be prepared and not so entirely unpracticed and unskilled in speaking, as mentioned above. For fortune and the time of the entire human life very often change, and for such great heads, many difficult, important, and strange matters and dealings occur, for which not only art and wisdom but also skill and practice in speaking are necessary. Such regents were Philip of Macedon, as Aelian <note>Claudius Aelianus, a Roman author of the 3rd century who wrote in Greek about history and natural wonders.</note> writes of him, Julius Caesar, and Marcus Cicero—just as Your Royal Majesty is also highly renowned in this regard. So it happened with King Dionysius <note>Dionysius II, the tyrant of Syracuse, who was exiled and reportedly became a schoolteacher in Corinth.</note>, when he was driven from his kingdom because of his tyranny, that he had to establish a school in Corinth and teach boys, which he undoubtedly could not have done if he had not been educated and practiced in the good arts from his youth.

Likewise, one reads of Nero that he lamented nothing so bitterly when he was to die than that so many great and excellent arts, which he had however misused more than used, should sink and perish with him. Therefore, this reminder is also not to be despised, for it could happen that one might not only regret such a lack but that it might also result in harm—as one can see, since regents and princes cast such things to the wind and do not apply themselves to speaking, nor see what great disadvantage and damage follows from this in kingdoms, principalities, and lands, about which, however, no more can be written here at length. Musonius the Philosopher.

# A beautiful, glorious, and wise
## discourse of Musonius the Philosopher, which he
## gave to a King of Syria, when
## he visited him.

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial 'V' featuring intricate foliage patterns and small figures. Below the centered title and above the initial is a small ornamental printers mark representing a cluster of fruit or a stylized flower.</image-desc>

Among the many other excellent arts with which the highly learned philosopher Musonius <note>Gaius Musonius Rufus (c. 20–101 AD) was a Roman Stoic philosopher known as the "Roman Socrates."</note> was gifted, and which he left behind in his books, he especially applied himself to wisdom. In this, he far surpassed others, and his reputation rang out through all the world. Therefore, at one time, the King of Syria <note>Historically, Musonius was exiled to the island of Gyaros, but this text likely refers to an encounter during his travels in the East.</note> came to him so that he might hear him. When they had greeted and received one another, this excellent man—who was the most learned and clever of his time—began to speak to the King in the following manner:

Although, most gracious King, many are of the opinion that it is not necessary for a king and regent to concern themselves with philosophy and the art of wisdom—and they put forward several reasons for this, especially that they have people <note>Referring to professional advisors or lawyers.</note> whom they can employ in case of necessity—Your Majesty should not allow yourself to be persuaded of this. In no way should you give it room or belief. Rather, you should certainly believe and hold it to be true that for no person on earth is it more or greater a necessity to strive after philosophy and the art of wisdom than for Your Majesty. This is for the reason that Your Majesty has such a beautiful, large, and glorious kingdom, as well as so many lands and people, to rule. For the most important office of a king is to know how he may protect his people and subjects, and with what he can do them the most and best good.

But whoever wishes to protect, manage, and well oversee the people and do them good, it is necessary for him to know what is useful and beneficial to man, as well as what is harmful and disadvantageous. He must know how he should defend the godly <note>In this context, the "godly" or "pious" refers to the virtuous and law-abiding citizens.</note> and punish the wicked, so that each person receives what is due to him and what he is worthy of, or has earned by his works—so that the wicked perish and the godly are preserved. But what is right, good, or evil, and how one can show goodness to someone, no one knows better how to distinguish than the philosopher, as he concerns himself daily with such thoughts and deals with them. He alone also knows what makes one, in a worldly sense, fortunate or unfortunate. From this, it clearly appears that philosophy is of the highest necessity for kings, princes, and great potentates <note>A potentate is a person who possesses great power, such as a monarch or ruler.</note> to know, and it is especially fitting for them to concern themselves with it and to arrange their government accordingly.

# A beautiful wise discourse

Furthermore, it befits a king—when he intends to give to one person here and another there—that he maintain the right measure in this, so that one does not receive more than he deserves while something is withheld or taken from another. By doing so, he would violate equity <note>The original term is "Billigkeit," referring to fairness or the spirit of the law rather than just the literal word of the law.</note> and take what he should have let remain. Instead, giving and taking should be conducted according to each person's merit and worth. But how can anyone maintain such a measure if he has never known or learned what justice is? For no one can be just if he has no knowledge of justice.

Therefore, it follows once again that a king should strive after philosophy and concern himself with it, so that he may learn from it what justice is. For without philosophy, no one will know what is fair or unfair. Now, he who does not know what is fair also does not know what is right. For this reason, people often quarrel among themselves, each claiming to know best what is most fair; yet this would not happen if they truly knew what was fair or unfair. People quarrel as little over what is black or white, what is warm or cold, or what is hard or soft, because they all agree on these things and everyone is certain of them. No one is so foolish as to call that which is white, black, or that which is hard, soft. Therefore, there is no dispute among people regarding these things. Without a doubt, the same would happen regarding justice and equity if people were certain of them, as mentioned above; they cannot be in harmony because they neither know nor understand these matters.

Since this discourse, in my opinion, also concerns Your Majesty, it will be necessary for Your Majesty to strive to rightly learn and know what justice and equity are. And as much as Your Majesty surpasses your other subjects and private persons, so much more is it required of Your Majesty to avoid being ignorant of that which is most necessary for you to know: namely, justice.

Furthermore, it also befits a king to be decent and moderate, and to maintain moderation in his government <note>original: "Regiment," referring here to the act of ruling or the king's administration.</note>, so that his subjects may yield him all the more obedience. Neither side should undertake anything untimely, nor should the king conduct himself with too much magnificence and excess. For such excess and magnificence befit neither the lord nor the subjects, and nothing more harmful can happen to either party. I would, however, like to hear and see how someone could rightly use wisdom if he has never learned how to govern himself and control his own desires. If he himself lives in all magnificence and luxury, how could he reasonably make others decent and moderate, or raise them to be so? Now, there is indeed no other art that can bring a person to moderation <term>Moderation: known as "Mässigkeit" or temperance, one of the four cardinal virtues</term> than philosophy. For philosophy teaches us to overcome magnificence and luxury, to curb greed, to love moderation, to hold discipline and shame in honor, to mind our speech, and to faithfully protect and defend the people. Whoever has learned these things knows how to conduct himself bravely and magnificently, and—when necessity requires—also moderately. Such virtues especially adorn a king and regent in such a way that he is compared to the gods and is held in the highest honor for the sake of such virtue.

### Musonius the Philosopher

In addition to this, a king must also be courageous; however, such courage—and the fact that we do not fear death, nor other dangers, troubles, or labor—comes from nowhere else than from the art of philosophy. Philosophy teaches us that in death, and in the other tribulations that are assigned to and befall humans in their lives, there can be nothing inherently evil. Those who are not informed of this will never attain true fortitude <note>The original term is "starckmůtigkeit," referring to a strength of spirit or magnanimity that allows one to remain unshaken by adversity.</note>, but will frequently be burdened and overtaken by fear and anxiety.

Therefore, if a king wishes to become strong of mind—since this virtue is no less necessary to him than the others—he can obtain it from nowhere better than from philosophy. For this reason, it is also fitting for him to learn it with diligence. But among all the things that are necessary for a king to know, nothing is more glorious, better, or more princely than for a king to make himself skilled in eloquence <note>The original term is "wolredenheit," literally "well-speaking," which encompasses the classical art of rhetoric and persuasive speech.</note>, and to be superior to all others in it. If he is defeated by someone else in this regard, he should consider it no less a loss than if he had been struck down and overcome by that person or his enemies with their fists. For when kings show themselves to be weak and unskilled in speech, they cannot fail to be frequently misled, deceived, and talked into allowing things that are false and unjust. Conversely, they may set aside that which is upright and good. This is a certain sign of ignorance, indicating that there cannot be much wisdom, understanding, or foresight within them. Therefore, I believe nothing more suitable or useful could be granted to a king on earth to serve his eloquence than philosophy, if he wishes to remain undefeated. For whoever is properly informed and instructed in it can easily distinguish good from evil and falsehood from truth; he can also refute and strike down evil with little effort, while protecting and defending the good alongside the truth.

Consequently, when it happens that the rhetoricians or orators are to debate with the philosophers—God help them—how quiet they become! It even happens sometimes that they must fall completely silent or speak contradictory things. Now, if the orators—who apply all their diligence to being superior to others in speech—must give way to the philosophers, what should other people expect to gain from them? Truly, it is easy to believe that they would be able to accomplish far less against them. Therefore, if someone comes to such royal dignity and does not wish to be overcome by others in speech, let him strive after philosophy. Thus, he will easily be able to overcome others, and he need not worry about being defeated by others in speech; rather, he will remain truly intrepid and victorious in all things.

And let this be enough concerning speech. Furthermore, it should be known that an upright king behaves in all ways such that he acts unjustly neither in words nor in deeds, but in all his actions, life, and being, remains entirely un-

# A Beautiful and Wise Discourse

->...[steadfast] and perfect he shows himself. For the ancients held a King to be a living Law or Statute <note>This refers to the classical concept of *Nomos Empsychos* (the "living law"), where the ruler's character is the ultimate source of justice.</note>, who strives solely for unity and justice, punishes rebellion and all misconduct, and shows himself toward his subjects entirely fatherly and gracious, just as Jupiter <note>original: "Jupiter." The king of the gods in Roman mythology, often used by Stoic philosophers like Musonius as the archetype of the ideal, benevolent ruler.</note> does. But how can one show himself in such a manner, and be so capable, unless he is far distinguished from other people, and instructed in all kinds of good arts and morals, and has also obtained such virtues through great diligence and effort, which this kingly office requires?

If now there are any arts available by which human nature can be adorned, and which lead and draw one toward honor and virtue, the King should also be instructed in them, and one should see which of these is most fitting and makes people most capable of governing—so that the King, who wishes to rule rightly and well, does not merely present a semblance of being pious and just, but also proves this through his deeds. However, is there any other art available which could be compared with this task and with Philosophy? Indeed, no other can or may be demonstrated. For some arts are directed solely toward the body, and even if some concern the soul, one cannot attain so much through them that they could make one more moral or temperate. But Philosophy drives and brings a person to the point where he can avoid wickedness and love and acquire good virtues. Therefore, nothing can be found in the world that a godly, righteous King should value more greatly or highly, nor what could be more useful to him, than Philosophy.

For this reason, I cannot consider anyone to be a righteous, godly King unless he is at once a philosopher. Conversely, I hold no one for a philosopher who might not also rightly be a king. Now, as far as the first part is concerned, we wish to examine it and ask: Can a man who is not godly be a godly, righteous King? It is generally held that this is in no way possible. Furthermore, no one can be a truly godly man unless he is a philosopher, for Philosophy is nothing other than an art in which one strives for honor and piety. Therefore, one must also confess and say that a King must also immediately be a philosopher.

That a philosopher is also a king can easily be demonstrated. For since it is a kingly office to rule principalities, kingdoms, cities, and lands righteously and well, where in the world would one find a better and more suitable regent over kingdoms, cities, and lands than a philosopher? For such people—if they are indeed true philosophers—should not only be prudent, temperate, and of a steadfast mind, as well as protectors of justice and equity, but also undaunted in all matters and shrinking from no labor. Likewise, they should be ones whom others must respect and fear, yet who are nonetheless friendly, kind, and modest toward everyone. Can a more suitable or better regent be imagined than a philosopher? Truly, no.<-

### Of the Philosopher Musonius

Although such a king or philosopher may not have many lands and people to rule, and likewise may have few people who are obedient and subject to him—indeed, he might even be commonly despised by the world—not much depends on that. Instead, it is enough that he presides over his friends, his wife and children, or lastly over himself, ruling them and commanding them. For such a person is just as rightly called a physician when he helps only a few and makes them healthy, as one who has helped many, provided he alone possesses the art of healing and medicine. And he who learns to sing even a little is called a musician just as well as if he had taught and instructed many, provided he himself can sing. Likewise, a man is just as much a rider if he has two or three horses as one who has ten or more, provided he alone can ride. In the same way, one can with good reason call someone a king or a regent who rules over little, just as much as one who rules over much, if only he is experienced and knows how one ought to rightly govern people. This is what Socrates knew well, and for that reason, he called philosophy a civic and kingly art.

The king took such great pleasure in this discourse of Musonius that he not only thanked him in a friendly manner immediately afterward, but also informed him that he should ask of him whatever he wished, with a gracious promise that he would grant and give it to him. To this, Musonius replied: "Since Your Majesty <note>original: "E. May." abbreviation for 'Eure Majestät' (Your Majesty).</note> is pleased by these words, I diligently pray that Your Majesty might follow and hold to them. If that happens, I desire nothing further, but find in it a good sufficiency. I know also that it will turn out to Your Majesty's benefit and toward all that is good." And with that, they departed from one another. 

It is brought into question which of the two should be considered more powerful: the king, who promised and offered to give so much, or Musonius, who did not wish to have it, but was satisfied that the king accepted his words with thanks and desired to abide by what Musonius had shared with him from the art of the philosophers. For such people were the philosophers of old; they cared for neither money nor property, but sought only wisdom and good character. Thus, Crates <note>Crates of Thebes (c. 365–285 BC), a Cynic philosopher who famously gave away his large fortune to live a life of poverty in accordance with his principles.</note> even threw his money into the sea. 

One also reads that Alexander the Great once came to Diogenes and, among other things, offered and promised to give him much money. To this, Diogenes neither thanked him nor gave any answer, except to ask him to move out of the light <note>This refers to the famous meeting where Diogenes the Cynic, living in a tub, told the world-conqueror Alexander to stop blocking his sunlight.</note> and not to take from him what he could not give him. At this, Alexander wondered so greatly that he even said: "If he were not Alexander, he would wish to be Diogenes." That is to say: if he were not a regent or king, he would concern himself with nothing so much as with philosophy. Through his high understanding, he well noted and saw that these two things were almost alike, and that a king must be a philosopher—just as he was, without doubt, instructed and taught by his tutor <note>original: "Preceptore." From the Latin 'praeceptor,' meaning teacher or instructor.</note>, Aristotle.

### A Beautiful and Wise Discourse/

...unwavering <note>The original OCR reads "uerrückt" (displaced/crazy), but contextually it is likely "unverrückt" (steadfast/unmoved).</note> and perfect; for the ancients held a king to be a **living right or law**, who strove only for unity and justice, punished rebellion and all misconduct, and behaved toward his subjects in a completely fatherly and gracious manner, just like **Jupiter** <note>The king of the gods in Roman mythology, often cited as the model for the ideal ruler.</note>. Furthermore, the king who wishes to govern rightly and well must not only put on an appearance of being virtuous and just but must also prove this through his deeds. There is, however, no other art to be found which could be compared with this matter and with **philosophy** <note>Musonius Rufus was a Stoic philosopher; here philosophy is presented as a practical training for leadership.</note>, nor can any other be demonstrated. And it is considered that such a thing is by no means possible. For such people—provided they are true philosophers—should not only be prudent, moderate, and of a steadfast mind, as well as protectors of justice and equity, but also fearless in all things and shun no labor. Likewise, they are people whom others must stand in awe of and fear, yet who are simultaneously friendly, kind, and reserved toward everyone. # Musonius the Philosopher.

<meta>catchword: Of</meta>

Although such a king or philosopher may not have much land or many people to rule, and likewise few people may be obedient and subject to him—being instead commonly despised by the world—not much depends on that. Rather, it is enough that he presides over his friends, his wife and children, or ultimately himself, governing them and commanding them. For such a man is just as worthy to be called a physician if he helps only a few and makes them healthy, as one who has helped many, provided he alone possesses the skill to heal and to practice medicine. And he who learns to sing a little is called a musician just as much as if he had learned and instructed many others, provided he himself can sing. Likewise, he is just as much a horseman who has two or three horses as he who has ten or more, if only he knows how to ride. In the same way, one can with good reason call him a king or regent who governs little, just as much as him who governs much, if only he is experienced and knows how people should be rightly governed. Socrates <note>A foundational Greek philosopher from Athens, known for the Socratic method and his influence on Western logic and ethics.</note> knew this well, and for that reason, he called **philosophy** a civic and royal art.

The King took such great pleasure in this speech of Musonius that he not only thanked him kindly at once but also informed him that he should ask of him whatever he wished, with a gracious promise that he would grant and give it to him. To this Musonius replied: "Since this speech has pleased Your Majesty, I diligently ask that Your Majesty would direct and hold himself according to it. If this is done, I desire nothing further, but am well satisfied. I also know that it will thrive to Your Majesty’s benefit and all goodness." Thereupon they departed from one another. And it is called into question which should be considered more powerful: the King, who promised and offered to give so much, or Musonius, who did not want to have it, but was satisfied that the King had accepted it with gratitude and desired to live according to what he had shared with him from the art of philosophy? We also read that **Alexander the Great** <note>The King of Macedon who created one of the largest empires in history; he was a student of Aristotle.</note> once came to **Diogenes** <note>Diogenes of Sinope, a Cynic philosopher known for his lifestyle of extreme simplicity, famously said to have lived in a large ceramic jar.</note> and, among other things, offered and promised to give him much money. # Of the Government of the Common Good
## and what pertains to it / composed in Latin from Plato by the highly learned Master Johannes Sleidanus <note>original: "Johanne Sleydano"; Sleidanus (1506–1556) was a famous historian and diplomat known for his history of the Reformation.</note> / and subsequently brought into German <note>original: "Teutsch"</note> by Georg Lauterbeck / quite pleasant and useful to know.

# To the Prudent, Honorable, and
## Right Wise Lords, the Mayor and Council of the City of Lüneburg, my very favorable Lords, I, Georg Lauterbeck, offer my most willing service beforehand.

<image-desc>A large ornamental woodcut initial 'V' decorated with intricate foliate patterns and containing a pomegranate-like fruit at its center.</image-desc>

Prudent, Honorable, and Right Wise, Very Favorable Lords: It is considered and held by everyone who has received instruction in **philosophy** that the books which the precious and highly understanding man **Plato** <note>A foundational Greek philosopher whose work "The Republic" and "Laws" form the basis of Western political theory.</note> wrote concerning the **Laws** and the <term>Common Good</term> <note>original: "Gemeiner Nutz"; refers to the "commonwealth" or the collective well-being of a community, a central concept in Renaissance political thought.</note> are not a little useful and serviceable for the government of the same. However, since Plato, out of his high intellect, wrote all his books in such a way that they cannot be understood or grasped by everyone (as I, for my part, also confess), it so happened a few years ago that an excellent and highly learned man, Master **Johannes Sleidanus** of Strasbourg, composed those same books of Plato on government and the common good into a short summary in Latin for the benefit of all. When I saw this summary, it pleased me so much that I did not wish to neglect bringing it into **German**, as I have indeed done (although somewhat hastily and amidst other business). I did this first and primarily so that I might better and more diligently impress those same writings upon myself and learn to understand them; and subsequently, for the benefit of the regents in cities and for the <term>common good</term>, since there is indeed much therein...

...contained within, which is found to be useful for the building and promotion of the **common good** <note>original: "Gemeinen nutzes"; refers to the collective well-being of the state.</note>. For this reason, legislators and jurists have held **Plato** in such high regard that his opinions are still felt here and there in legal texts even today. Indeed, his very words are included and read in some places, although occasionally something is mixed in that is little or not at all suited to our present times.

Just as Plato also wrote some things not with the intention that they must be literally so, but rather intended to imply something else beneath the surface—though it would take too long to explain that here as thoroughly as necessary. However, I must clarify this with an example or two. Plato writes that those who have done much good for the **common good** are rightly served when they receive nothing but ingratitude in return, and often lose their lives and property because of it; for through their good deeds they achieved nothing other than strengthening the arrogance of the common rabble. Likewise, where he writes that one should have all things in common, he intends to indicate that the hearts and minds of the rich and powerful are so oriented that they would gladly possess everything and leave nothing to anyone else as their own.

Thirdly, it was not the least of the reasons that, at that time, I was an unworthy <term>Syndicus</term> <note>A legal official or counsel representing a city or corporation.</note> in a city, and for that reason, I wished to read and write everything that might be useful for the establishment of a good, honorable, and Christian <term>Policey</term> <note>original: "Policey"; in the 16th century, this term referred to the general civil order, administration, and moral regulation of a community.</note>. Since Plato wrote on this with particular diligence, I felt compelled to examine him.

Finally, I was moved to translate this book into German <note>original: "verteutschen"</note> and release it in print so that everyone might see how great and significant a difference there is between the teachings of **Holy Scripture** and **philosophy**. For although this man possessed such high understanding that no one could ever advance further through the **light of nature** <note>original: "liecht der Natur"; a philosophical term referring to human reason without the aid of divine revelation.</note>, it is nevertheless pure darkness compared to the Light—
