-># Preface.<-

...of the holy Divine Word. For this reason, one must give high and great thanks to the Almighty, who has gifted us in these our latter times with such a light out of grace and mild mercy. We should not allow ourselves to be led away from it by any path; much less should we give room to those who venture to compare and mix together these two noble and glorious gifts—namely, **Holy Divine Scripture** and **Philosophy**. Instead, each should be allowed to remain in its own place and at its own value. For although Philosophy is not only pleasant but also useful, and teaches rationally about the governance of the **common good** <note>original: "Gemeinen nutzes"; the collective welfare or the state.</note> as well as about honorability and good morals, it can nevertheless achieve nothing further than what concerns outward conduct.

But if a person should face some adversity or temptation, they would find no such comfort in philosophy as they would in the **Holy Divine Scripture**. Thus, the philosophers have never been able to reach the true knowledge of God through their own reason. Therefore, John says rightly: No one has ever seen God, except the only-begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father; He has revealed Him. <note>Referring to the Gospel of John 1:18.</note>

These are the reasons, favorable Lords, that moved me to write about these things at the present time and to bring this book into our **German language** <note>original: "Teutsche Sprach"</note>, so that one may know how to distinguish these arts. Since it has always been the custom from of old that such and similar books be dedicated to Princes, Lords, and Cities, I wished to **dedicate** <term>Dediciren</term> <note>To formally present a work to a patron.</note> this little book to Your Wisdoms—as much as is fitting and proper for me—and to honor you with it. For I have been informed and told by many brave and highly learned people (some of whom were also related to Your Wisdoms) that you are so well-disposed regarding the governance of the common good, and also for the sake of religion (praise God), that one [could find] such cities almost...

...would find few such examples in the whole German land. Therefore, God’s blessing also allows itself to be seen so richly and generously among them. And would to God that other cities—which for their part pay more attention to their pomp and pride, likewise to immorality and **usury** <note>The practice of lending money at unreasonably high interest rates, frequently condemned by 16th-century reformers.</note>, than to good, honorable customs and Christian, good **governance** <term>Policey: In the 16th century, this term did not mean "police" in the modern sense, but rather the overall administration, public order, and moral regulation of a community.</term>—would take **Your Worships** <note>original: "E. W." (Eure Weisheiten); a formal title for city council members or magistrates, literally "Your Wisdoms."</note> as a mirror for themselves and follow your example; then things would without doubt proceed in a more Christian, better, and more beneficial way.

For, given that such wars and rebellions have persisted here and there in the **German Nation** <note>original: "Teutscher Nation"; referring to the German-speaking lands of the Holy Roman Empire.</note> for some time, I can, in my simplicity, consider them as nothing else than a punishment and a rod sent for the sake of our sins. This is because not only has all honorable, good governance almost entirely ceased, but on the other hand, sin and shame, immorality, usury, and faithlessness have taken the upper hand to such an extent that one can almost no longer restrain or resist these things. Furthermore, some have even reached the point where they allow themselves to be moved to make changes in religion, regardless of the fact that the public and recognized truth is as clear as day. This is indeed terrible to hear, and it is to be feared that if we do not recognize such error and fault and do penance, we must expect even harsher punishment for it; however, there is no time to write further of this now.

I most humbly ask Your Worships that you would accept this modest tribute with favorable pleasure; I shall be found willing to earn this from Your Worships again with the highest diligence. And herewith I commend myself to Your Worships. Dated **Mansfeld** <note>A significant mining town and the childhood home of Martin Luther.</note>, on the sixteenth of the month of **April** <note>original: "Aprilis"</note>, in the lesser count of the **year fifty-four** <note>original: "vier vnd fünffzigsten Jar"; shorthand for 1554.</note>.

# A Dialogue or Conversation
## concerning the Platonic teaching / whether / and how far the same may be useful for the government of the Common Good.

->Burgomaster. &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; Secretary.<-

**Burgomaster.** Recently, Mr. Secretary, you brought up a strange and wonderful dispute when we were together at the light meal; and although I was somewhat tipsy at the time, so that I could not remember everything, I have nevertheless thought about it several times since then, especially because you engaged so deeply with the Judge. And I recall no differently than that it was about Plato. Therefore, I have now sent for you, so that we might speak and deal with this matter alone, soberly, and in private. But I will not hide from you—as much as I could perceive then during the drinking—that it seems to me to be a very strange and foreign teaching as far as government is concerned, which would not sit well here in our city.

**Secretary.** It is so, Mr. Burgomaster, and I remember well that I spoke recently of the Platonic teaching. As I have for some time now, for the sake of the common city's benefit, applied myself to reading and writing everything that I think is considered necessary for the establishment of honorable, Christian, and good **governance** <term>Policey: In the 16th century, this term referred to the overall civil administration, public order, and moral regulation of a community, rather than modern law enforcement.</term>, as you have occasionally heard from me, and as I acknowledge I am duty-bound to do by virtue of my office. For this reason, I came upon Plato among others, who is rightly held as the most prominent of all those who have left behind writings on these matters.

But I would like to hear from you for what reasons such teaching seems so strange, foreign, and useless to you. For in my simplicity, I would not know what could be more useful or beneficial for the common good than what Plato has written on this, especially if it were slightly modified according to the circumstances of these lands, times, and current affairs.

**Burgomaster.** Firstly, it is a completely new teaching to me, of which I have heard nothing, or at least very little, except for the saying attributed to Plato which states that those cities shall be blessed in which **philosophers** <term>Philosophi: Here meaning learned scholars or lovers of wisdom, particularly those trained in classical Greek thought.</term> govern, or where the rulers occupy themselves with philosophy. Secondly, that Plato wants to have all things held in common <note>A reference to Plato's *Republic*, where he suggests communal property among the guardian class.</note>. And whatever else he may have written about **Ideas** <note>original: "Jdeis"; referring to Plato's Theory of Forms.</note> and **Atoms** <note>original: "Atomis"; though the concept of atoms is more associated with Epicurus or Democritus, the Burgomaster may be conflating various ancient philosophical concepts.</note>. I would like to see, however, where a city could be found today where philosophers govern, much less where one has all things in common. Unless you intend to come to me with the **Anabaptists** <term>Widertäuffer: A radical Reformation group that often advocated for communal living and the rejection of private property, most famously during the Münster Rebellion of 1534-35.</term>, who are accustomed to leading such a regime. 

**Secretary.** It may be that this teaching, if it were to come to light among us Germans, would seem to many rulers...

<header>Concerning the Common Good.</header>

...it might seem that [this teaching] was new and strange, because people have concerned themselves little with it until now. But that it should be as useless as you say, you will find otherwise once you hear my report on the matter. And as far as the saying is concerned which Your Worship mentioned, it would not be a bad thing if such people were employed in cities who had been raised from youth in those arts that serve the government of the common good; for Plato means such people <note>Plato argues in *The Republic* for "philosopher kings" or specially educated guardians to lead the state.</note>, and then undoubtedly a better **government** would be maintained. For currently, unlearned and inexperienced people are used for this, who look only toward their own profit—such as merchants, shopkeepers, usurers, butchers, bakers, and the like. **Burgomaster.** In large cities, it may well be that one can find learned people, but in common cities <note>By "common cities," he refers to smaller, ordinary towns without university resources.</note>, such as ours here, one must take and choose "whatever the ladle serves up" <note>original: "was die Kelle gibt" — a German idiom meaning one must make do with the available options.</note>. However, in several places, Jurists are nevertheless retained, such as Doctors and Licentiates. Also, Town Clerks and Secretaries, who are meant to remind and inform us of that which we do not know and which necessity requires at any given time. **Secretary.** Would to God that you followed them sometimes; perhaps things would stand better in the government. But whether it is sufficient, and also advisable, to rely on a single person in all matters—upon which the welfare, prosperity, and ruin of a city may depend—that I will consider further later.

Now I must answer Your Worship on the second point: namely, that you unfairly compare the teaching of Plato with the sect and teaching of the **Anabaptists** <term>Widertäuffer: A radical Reformation group that often advocated for the communal ownership of property, which the ruling classes viewed as a threat to social order.</term>. For the situation is fundamentally different. For although Plato, among other things, mentions something regarding the community of goods, he also points out the basis and reason why it would be good to employ such community—specifically, that much strife and quarreling would be avoided, which otherwise occurs daily over property. Yet, he confesses that one will hardly find a city in which such a government and community of goods can take place; for which reason he also prescribes other fine teachings and laws which may be used in other cities and governments. And it is a very different thing with the Anabaptists, as they not only have nothing of their own, but they also wish to have (as is said of them) no law, government, cities, nor authority, nor will they tolerate any. In contrast, Plato teaches with the highest diligence about laws and authority, to honor them and to be obedient to them. **Burgomaster.** If that is the meaning of it, then I would not only be satisfied with Plato, but would gladly consult with my council-colleagues and you whether it might be permissible for us to direct ourselves accordingly here, as much as is possible and useful.

Therefore, please inform me, as briefly as possible, what teaching Plato proposes for rulers to use; afterward, we will consult further on it. **Secretary.** Although the writings of Plato on these things are somewhat extensive, high, and difficult—so that one cannot dispute, speak, or show much of them in a short time—I will nevertheless gladly do Your Worship the favor, and as much as I [can] from his...

# Concerning Government

...retained in those writings / from which they will then also know how to judge his other teachings / as far as my meager understanding extends / I shall give my report. Firstly, Plato maintains / that it is not possible for a ruler / without divine help and grace to uprightly fulfill the duties of his office / and he provides this as his reason / that since a man can hardly govern himself happily and uprightly / he would be able to do so and establish such much less in a whole community / in which there are so many strange and evil people <note>original: "seltzamer böser Leut" — in this context, "seltzam" suggests people who are peculiar, unpredictable, or difficult to manage.</note> / and where daily so many wants and defects arise among them / without divine help and grace. 

**Burgomaster.** This beginning pleases me well / and it agrees with Holy Scripture. For Christ says: "Without me you can do nothing" <note>John 15:5.</note>. Likewise Solomon also held this view / and therefore called upon God for grace and wisdom. It is also written there / that God took pleasure in such a request / and therefore provided and gifted him not only with wisdom / but also with honor, wealth, and power <note>A reference to 1 Kings 3, where Solomon asks God for an "understanding heart" to judge the people.</note>.

**Secretary.** Further, he teaches / that one should not draw ungodly people or those who despise the Divine Majesty / into the government <note>original: "Regiment" — referring to the administration or the ruling body.</note> / nor should one tolerate or suffer them within it. Likewise / he says / just as justice is the foundation of all government / and the salvation of the city / so also is injustice the destruction and downfall of all cities and lands. Following this, he desires / that the burgomasters and rulers in cities should be nothing else / than protectors / overseers / and watchmen <note>Plato’s *Republic* describes the ruling class as "Guardians" or "Watchmen" (*phylakes*) of the state.</note> over the laws. And just as a watchman should be diligent / alert / sober / courageous / and besides that gentle / one who addresses people kindly / and gives a good account of himself. Thus also a ruler should be formed / and instructed from youth in the art of philosophy. For such people should rightly be drawn into the government.

**Burgomaster.** But if one cannot have such people / I deem it does not matter so much / if only a city is established and provided with good laws / For we cannot all be Doctors, Jurists, and Philosophers. 

**Secretary.** Laws without an upright / sensible, and wise ruler / are dead and in vain / however good they may be. Therefore, much depends / on how the rulers are prepared / and where a city is provided with sensible rulers / even if it does not have many written statutes and laws / yet those same rulers are a living law <note>original: "lebendig Gesetz" — the concept of the *lex animata*, or the idea that a wise ruler’s judgment is a vital, flexible application of justice compared to the static "dead" letter of written law.</note>. However, so that one may continually have people in a city / who are raised in the good arts and philosophy / and afterward drawn to the government for the common good / Plato desires / that one should give diligent attention to the youth / and keep those / who are useful and skilled for such study / to it with the highest diligence / or send them to the places / where such arts are taught / otherwise there will soon be a lack of them. For just as a farmer hopes in vain / that he will harvest fruits / when he has not sown the field / so a city will also hope in vain for good and wise rulers / if it has not made provision / that they be instructed for it from youth. He desires, moreover / that the rulers or those / to whom it is commanded / should give diligent attention to such boys and young fellows / as to how they [behave] in their conduct and life / and also in all their speech, play, and gestures/

# Of the Common Good

...behave, conduct, and prepare themselves, so that one may perceive what comfort one may hopefully expect from them.

**Burgomaster.** But why does Plato insist on such diligence? 

**Secretary.** Because he believes that otherwise all effort and expense is in vain, and the City is not helped, if the regents are not raised, instructed, and taught in such a manner. He sees it as being just like a sick person who cannot keep a regimen <term>Regiment: here referring to a "medical regimen" or a disciplined way of life</term>; even if the physician tries many treatments on him, it is all in vain. 

**Burgomaster.** Should such young fellows then not play and enjoy pastimes? 

**Secretary.** That is not Plato’s meaning; rather, he means that such games should be honorable. For games are of such a nature that where one becomes accustomed to them, they transform into habits and studies <note>original: "sitten vnd studia"</note>. Therefore, he also forbids the youth from playing any games other than those they learned from their parents, and forbids them from constantly undertaking and devising one new game after another. 

**Burgomaster.** Why is that? 

**Secretary.** So that they do not become accustomed—when they are eventually employed in serious matters and enter the government <term>Regiment: here referring to the administration of the state</term>—to dealing with the laws and statutes in the same way they dealt with their games: changing them at their pleasure and choosing new ones. For in a City, no thing can be more harmful than if one continually makes one innovation after another regarding the statutes and laws. And just as it is not necessary for a healthy person to take many and varied medicines if he simply knows how to keep himself temperate in eating and drinking, so too is it unnecessary for a well-ordered City to issue new laws daily; indeed, the City is not helped by doing so.

Following this, Plato desires that the citizens be held to strive much more for the "goods of the soul," and to apply themselves to obtaining these first and foremost, rather than the "goods of fortune" and the "goods of the body." 

**Burgomaster.** What does Plato mean by such a distinction of goods? 

**Secretary.** The "Goods of the Soul" he calls Justice, Honesty, Virtue, Prudence, Wisdom, Fortitude, Temperance, Piety, and whatever other such virtues there may be. These a person should learn first and strive after. Once he has acquired and learned these, he may then strive for the "Goods of the Body," such as health, strength, beauty, and wealth. Plato also maintains that no one should be accepted or chosen as a regent unless his life and conduct are better than his office requires, and unless he has neither desired nor begged for that same office.

Furthermore, he describes a judge, and insists that he should be a pious man of an honorable mind—namely, understanding and wise—who has also known many people, both good and evil. 

**Burgomaster.** Nowadays, judges usually strive to ensure they collect many fines <note>original: "Busse" — refers to monetary penalties or atonement payments</note> from the people. 

**Secretary.** That is the fault of the authorities <term>Oberkeit: the governing body or high-ranking officials</term> who appoint such people to the judicial bench. However, because I have written extensively on this elsewhere, we shall turn away from the judge with this brief mention and return to Plato, to see how he wishes for us to use money. 

**Burgomaster.** And how is that? 

**Secretary.** Not that we should use it for usury, dicing, or gaming, nor waste it uselessly or abuse it in other unseemly ways. Rather, we should use it for those...

...satisfy them and set their minds at ease, to whom we have promised something, or otherwise owe payment.

**Burgomaster.** This opinion may well have held weight among the ancients, but now the situation is quite different, because the greatest portion of trade is conducted with money. And although the theologians have taught and written vehemently against it—among them also **Dr. Luther**, of holy memory—they have nevertheless been unable to accomplish anything <note>The Burgomaster is likely referring to the practice of usury or charging interest, which Martin Luther and many reformers condemned, though it became an economic necessity in the burgeoning mercantile world of the 16th century.</note>.

Yet because so much precious and earnest teaching is found therein, which is useful for the common good—so much so that there should be no regent who has not learned and grasped something from Plato concerning government—so that there be no lack in this regard, I will not begrudge the effort, but will apply my diligence so that Your Worship might receive such a booklet as soon as possible, as it is not very long and is very pleasant and useful.

**Burgomaster.** But what if my council servants do not wish to hear or accept it?

**Secretary.** That matters little; it is also not intended that one must follow it so strictly in every point, for that would not be well tolerated among us. Rather, Your Worship, as the man of understanding and the head, should make an effort to read this excerpt from time to time and hold your statutes and laws against it. From this, Your Worship will easily see what may be tolerated and what is beneficial to the common city or not.

**Burgomaster.** I will do so with diligence; I also hope it will not be without fruit if the matter is taken up in such a way. But what do you think of the law <term>Juristerey: the profession and practice of law</term>?

For that reason, one must inquire of the law when a dispute arises. But when one hears of the origin of the laws, they have come forth from philosophy. # On Governance

...satisfy them and put them at ease, those to whom we have promised something or whom we otherwise owe payment.

**Burgomaster.** This opinion might well have held weight among the ancients, but nowadays things are quite different, since the greatest trade is conducted with money. And although the theologians have argued and written fiercely against it—and among them also Dr. Luther, of blessed memory—they have nonetheless been unable to accomplish anything.

**Secretary.** We shall let that pass for now. And for some time, those same usurers <note>Money-lenders who charge interest; usury was a major theological and legal debate in the 16th century</note> have been so punished in their spirits—since they despised God’s Word and all honorable and good governance <term>Policey: This term refers to the overall administration, moral order, and public welfare of a city, not just the modern police force</term>—that many of them do not know where their principal or interest have gone. W." (Eure Weisheit), a formal title for a city magistrate meaning "Your Wisdom"</note> to that work.

From this, Your Worship will easily see what is applicable and what is beneficial to the commonwealth or not.

# On the Governance of the Common Good / and what pertains to it / quite pleasant and useful to know.

<image-desc>Large decorative initial 'A' featuring a human figure entwined in elaborate floral and vine-like scrollwork.</image-desc>Initially, it is to be known that Socrates—although he was the most prominent, best, and wisest among all philosophers—left nothing behind in writing. This is cited as a reason: that he held the view that writing would be more harmful than beneficial to the memory. For as soon as a matter is composed in writing and put onto paper, one no longer pays as diligent attention to it as when it remains unrecorded. But be that as it may, so that these teachings of Socrates regarding the common good <term>Gemeiner Nutz: A central concept in Renaissance political thought referring to the collective welfare of the community over individual interest</term> would not be forgotten again, but might remain with posterity, the excellent and highly learned man Plato compiled them into several books. However, because they are not only somewhat lengthy but also difficult to understand correctly—so much so that there have been many learned and brave people who could not grasp their deep meaning—the contents are briefly summarized as follows.

In the first book, Socrates begins a very friendly conversation with several people concerning old age; and among other things, as they are speaking together, a question arises among them: what kind of thing might it be that is called "Just," or "Justice"? To this, the others reply that Justice is such a virtue that "gives to each his own" <note>This is the classical definition of justice: *suum cuique*</note>. But Socrates examines this and says: it is not always fair and right to give someone what is theirs and to let them have it. He provides an example of a senseless or insane person: if such a person had deposited something in the "faithful hands" <note>A legal term for a trust or safekeeping</note> of another, one would not be obligated, nor would it even be good, for that item to be returned to him while he is in that state. Therefore, this definition or description of Justice could not stand or be sufficient.

The third opinion was that of Thrasymachus, who believed that justice was nothing other than what was useful to the powerful and to those who held an office of authority. Socrates, however, completely rejected this and proved with many fine arguments that an honest and pious man in government should seek not his own advantage, but the <term>common good (Gemeiner Nutz): the collective welfare of the community</term> of those over whom he presides. And although Thrasymachus was moved by this, he dared to suggest—in order to strengthen his opinion—that injustice was stronger and more powerful than justice. He argued that a person could have more benefit and profit if he employed injustice than if he were to live according to justice. Socrates would not let this stand either, but provided the report that injustice cannot endure; instead, out of necessity, it must ultimately fail and perish shamefully.

When Thrasymachus was silenced and could bring nothing further against Socrates, the brothers Glaucon and Adeimantus began an extensive dispute regarding injustice. they suggested that everyone must confess that humans are by nature inclined toward injustice; for this reason, they would never cease to pursue it if only they had the opportunity. By such means, some had achieved great and royal honors, which could never have happened to them had they chosen to follow justice. This is seen in the case of Gyges <note>original: "Gige"</note>, who was a poor shepherd and yet became a great king, which happened as follows:

As Gyges was then keeping watch over the livestock alongside others, they were forced to flee, each wherever he could. Gyges saw that there was a great chasm in a mountain; he fled into it and saw many strange and wonderful things therein. Among other things, a large cast-bronze horse stood there, which had a door or window in its side. When Gyges looked inside, he found a very large man lying within, who wore neither clothing nor ornament, except for a golden ring with a noble stone on his finger. Gyges took the ring, and when the storm became quiet again, he went back out of the cave or chasm, and a few days later returned to his companions. He tested this so often until he was certain of the matter. Furthermore, **Socrates** demonstrates beautifully and wittily that some are born to rule, some to be assistants and subjects, others for farming or for handicrafts. He distinguishes these from one another, just as craftsmen are accustomed to distinguish metals such as **gold, silver, copper, iron, tin, lead**, etc. He proves that often from a golden father, an iron fruit is born, and from an iron father, a golden one. Therefore, one should pay diligent attention to the nature of children and what they are most capable and fit for by nature; to that, one should hold them with the highest diligence. For indeed, in the breeding and instruction of boys, one can easily notice what each is primarily inclined toward.

The <term>guardians</term>, overseers, and officials of the **common good** <note>commonwealth</note> should possess nothing of their own but should be maintained from the <term>public purse</term>. For it commonly happens that when they are supposed to consider and provide for the common good, they instead seek their own profit, improve their own estates, and forget or leave behind the welfare of the commonwealth.

In the following book, he answers **Adeimantus** <note>original: "Adinanto"</note>, who challenged this opinion, and proves alongside this that a moderate fortune or wealth is the best and safest. He shows that abundance has its faults and crimes just as much as poverty and indigence. For from poverty arise all kinds of evil deeds, such as theft and the like; but from abundance come <term>luxury</term> <note>original: "ubirkeit" / "Üppigkeit"</note>, laziness, rebellion, and a desire for all kinds of innovation. And he says that if one wished to exercise special diligence in providing for cities, one would not permit the citizens to take on evil, mad, and unseemly habits, such as becoming accustomed to gambling, drinking, whoring, and indecency, nor to practicing thievery, robbery, swearing, cursing, and likewise rebellion and disobedience against the authorities, etc.

And so that a city may always have brave, strong, and courageous men and women, **Socrates** suggests that from the whole number of the citizens' children, the strongest and best young men and the most beautiful young women should be selected and married to one another, so that they may bear children together. The lottery must be used so that no party has cause for complaint, but instead lets themselves be satisfied and appeased by what they have received through the lot.

Men may apply themselves to fathering children from the age of twenty until fifty-five. And women from the age of twenty until forty. **Socrates** desires that married couples primarily keep **modesty and discipline** <note>original: "scham vnd zucht"</note> before their eyes during the breeding of children and in their station. When children are born and raised in this manner, they shall be reared and nourished at the expense and provision of the **common good**. For this purpose, a special, convenient, and well-situated place in the city shall be built and designated. Yet, with this distinction: those who are born of the best parents should not be mixed among the lowly. 

In common, however, no father shall know which child is his own, whether they be sons or daughters; likewise, the mothers shall not recognize their sons. Instead, the children altogether shall call the male and female citizens **"Father"** and **"Mother."** In turn, the male and female citizens shall call all children **"Sons"** and **"Daughters,"** according to what the age of each person requires. **Socrates** believes that through this, a great and notable friendship, unity, love, and kinship shall arise among all the citizens, such that everyone will think that whatever happens to another has happened to his own children or to himself. Likewise, whatever he does for another, he does for his own child, and therefore one will risk his life and property for the other. He considers that a city cannot be better established and ordered than through this way of unity and kinship, where everyone treats the affairs of others as his own.

Furthermore, **Socrates** desires that the citizens use friendly and kind words among one another, addressing each other with gentle speech. The rulers shall not call themselves **Princes** or **Lords**, but rather **Guardians and Helpers**; the subjects shall call them **Providers and Sustainers**. For he desires, as mentioned above, that the rulers have nothing of their own, but be maintained from the **common purse** and from the common income. This is for the reason that they should not become greedy, and not only hinder the other citizens in their livelihood, but also distress and suck the life out of the **commonwealth**.

He also desires that the men should lead their wives and their sons with them into war, so that they may behold their manhood and virtue, and from youth onward accustom themselves and make themselves skillful in war. To this end, he gives several fine rules which the soldiers should keep: namely, that no one should flee from his **company**, but rather defend himself manfully in battle, and as long as he has life, not surrender to the enemy. And how one should honor and praise those who have conducted themselves well in war, and those who have perished therein.

He distinguishes, however, between wars, and says that one should conduct war differently against foreigners than against the **Greeks** and neighbors. The foreigners should be attacked most harshly because they are enemies by nature. But with the Greeks, one should act gently. For since the Greeks are all of one nation, and therefore related to one another by friendship, alliance, and other ways, even if they occasionally become dissatisfied with one another—as can easily happen—such a thing is not to be counted as a war, but rather as a mere **tumult and uprising**; and therefore the war should be arranged in such a way as if one wished soon to be reconciled with one another again. One should also, in such a war against the Greeks, entirely abstain from fire and the devastation of fields, the plundering of the common people, and similar inhuman undertakings. <note>Socrates argues that Greeks should treat other Greeks as if they will eventually be reconciled, sparing the land and non-combatants, unlike their "total war" approach to non-Greek "barbarians."</note>

After such things, Socrates was interrupted by his friends, who said that one would hardly be able to find or establish such a <term>Common Good</term> <note>original: "Gemeinen Nutz," referring to the *Res Publica* or the ideal Commonwealth</note> as he had spoken of and desired to have. To this he answered and said: although it might not be possible to establish such a **Common Good**, nevertheless, it would not fail that those cities would be magnificently arranged which most closely resembled such a fine form and opinion. One could not expect any good government in any city unless it were ruled by **Philosophis**—that is, by the lovers of wisdom. He says and describes also, alongside this, what a **Philosopher** is: namely, a lover of truth, of good arts, and of wisdom, so that through these he might come to the knowledge of those things which remain eternally and can be changed neither by birth nor by displacement.

In the **sixth book**, **Plato** describes the nature and character of the Philosopher quite extensively: namely, that he should despise the pleasures of the body and seek and strive only after that which enlightens the mind; and that he should be moderate in all things, not greedy, but a diligent researcher of the truth and of all virtue. Whosoever is thus constituted, to him one may and should rightly entrust the government of the **Common Good**.

Against this, however, **Adimantus** objects to **Socrates**, saying that those who once devote themselves to philosophy usually persist in it and are rarely fit for the government of the **Common Good** and worldly affairs.

To which **Socrates** answers and confesses that it is true that **philosophers** seldom come to the seat of government. It is, however, not their fault, but rather the fault of those who do not call upon and make use of them. **Philosophers** are also the kind of people who do not strive after great honors or do anything for the sake of fame; for this reason, they do not put themselves forward, but remain in seclusion <note>original: "im Winckel," literally 'in a corner'</note> and with their books, whereby they are more often despised by other ignorant people than they are brought forward. As for the fact that some turn out badly despite being instructed in the art of **philosophy**, **Socrates** says the fault lies in their being poorly raised; as commonly happens, youth are corrupted and spoiled by their parents before they ever reach school.

It is also not quite possible for one to become truly upright among such evil and deranged customs of the world, unless he be specially preserved through God's help and grace.

Although wealth and what the world considers good are great hindrances to **philosophy**—since she desires people who are otherwise free in all things, concerning themselves only with the art of wisdom and not allowing themselves to be turned away by the talk of men. Finally, **Socrates** concludes, as before, that no government can be fortunate unless **philosophers** rule, or the rulers concern themselves with **philosophy**.

In the seventh book, **Socrates** creates a fine allegory <note>original: "Gleichniß"</note> of those who sit in a deep pit or cave under the earth, into which they receive so little light that they can only see a little. Yet the inhabitants of that cave know no better than that there is no better or more pleasant place and life on earth than their own. When they come out from there into the light, into the bright sun, they can only look upon it with great difficulty. But when they gradually grow accustomed to the sun, only then do they first bewail their misery and see what a wretched life they led under the earth and in such a dark place. Afterward, he explains this same allegory and says that it is the same with a person who is still coarse and unlearned; because he knows nothing at all of the light of wisdom and the good arts, but when he is afterward instructed in such arts, he then first begins to contemplate in his mind those things which are not subject to change. He also recounts, alongside this, which arts are necessary for those who intend to reach such perfection, and he lists **arithmetic** <note>original: "Rechenkunst"</note>, **geometry** <note>original: "Erdmessung"</note>, **astronomy**, and finally **dialectic** <note>original: "Dialecticam"</note>—that is, the art of how one should rightly dispute and judge properly of every matter. This art is praised and exalted by **Socrates** above all other arts; he also desires that it be presented to young men last, when they have reached their years of maturity, and that they should then be taught it.

He commands, however, with the highest diligence, that the youth should by no means be harshly forced to learn, but rather that they should be taught and instructed as if through play. ...to argue or to quarrel with the people. Accordingly, he also teaches how to maintain a distinction among those whom one teaches. He argues that one should only share the art of **dialectics** <term>Dialectica: the art of logical investigation and the pursuit of truth through reasoned argument</term> with pious, honorable, and well-mannered men who love the truth, rather than those who pervert everything with their **sophistry** <term>Sophisterey: the use of clever but false arguments, especially with the intention of deceiving</term>. Furthermore, just as young men are instructed in such arts, **Socrates** wishes that young women should also be practiced and instructed in them, especially those who are suitable and capable.

In the eighth book, he begins to recount the various forms and distinctions of government within the **commonwealth** <term>Gemeinen nutz: the public welfare or the state</term>. Although he concludes that this government is best when the most prominent men in a city or land hold the rule, he nevertheless confesses that it may very easily be disturbed and corrupted. This happens when those few rulers begin to "blow into one horn" <note>idiom: to act in collusion or conspire together</note> and oppress the others. From this, nothing can follow but hardship, toil, and labor. When they overreach to the point that the **common people** <term>Pöfel: the masses or the general populace</term> can no longer endure it, the people will overthrow them or seize the government themselves. Thus, a change occurs, creating a government that also cannot last very long. Consequently, nothing follows more certainly than **tyranny**, murder, and misfortune.

After he had spoken these things, **Glaucus** says that such a government (as had been described before) would not easily be troubled or displaced from its standing. To this, **Socrates** answers that while that may be true, all things are subject to transience; therefore, no government can be established so firmly that it might not eventually be displaced and perish. However, governments are nowhere more harshly challenged, displaced, and disturbed than through disobedience and rebellion. This is mostly caused when the customs and wealth of the citizens are unequal and set against one another. Furthermore, children often develop different characters and dispositions than their parents, especially if the parents do not pay attention to the proper time in which they should conceive children.

Therefore, it also happens that sometimes from a "golden" father, a "copper" or "iron" fruit is born <note>This refers to Plato's "Myth of the Metals," where citizens are born with souls of different value—gold, silver, iron, or copper—determining their role in society</note>. Because of this, the quality of the cities does not improve but instead steadily worsens and declines.

Next, he speaks further on the distinctions of government, especially when the rule falls to the nobility or the powerful. In such cases, these rulers strive only to become wealthy as quickly as possible. The result is that the offices of the commonwealth are distributed only among those who have the most money, regardless of whether they are otherwise suitable or capable for the role. This does not help the government at all. For just as it is on the sea—if those who wish to sail across the ocean are given an inexperienced sailor simply because he is rich and has much money—they remain in great danger of life and limb. Likewise, the subjects and citizens in cities must live in danger if their rulers, though they have much wealth, are unskilled in governance. For to govern requires more art, wisdom, honor, and virtue...

If it also happens that these same rich misers <term>Filß: a stingy, greedy person</term> gain the upper hand, they do nothing but strive after property and how they might satisfy their insatiable greed. Through this, the other citizens and the **public welfare** <term>Gemeine nutz: the common good or the state's resources</term> are sucked dry and completely ruined. It follows further that among the poor and common masses, many are found who devote themselves to all kinds of evil tricks, such as theft, highway robbery, church-robbing, and the like. Now, when these people notice that the **government** <term>Regiment: the ruling order or administration</term> operates in this way, they also begin to feel resentment toward it. Since they exceed the others in number (as there are always the most "bad boys" everywhere), they either slaughter the rulers or drive them away and set themselves up as rulers in their place. Thus, the government comes to the **common man**, where things proceed strangely and miraculously, because many vices are left unpunished which should rightly be punished, and everyone is free to do or not do as he pleases, as it sometimes happened in **Athens** <note>Plato uses Athens as the primary example of a democracy that decayed into chaos due to excessive liberty</note>.

From such a government there usually follows at last a harmful and cruel **tyranny**. This is caused by the following: namely, when the common rabble <term>Pöfel: the masses or general populace</term> gets the upper hand, they can no longer be restrained or fended off. Therefore, out of necessity, they are forced to elevate one from among them, to whom they entrust and hand over the power and might to rule the others and to restrain them if they attempt something unjust. But when he comes to power, he soon adopts a wolfish nature <note>original: "Wolfffart"; a reference to the Platonic myth in Book VIII where the "protector of the people" tastes blood and turns into a wolf</note>. In order to clear out of the way those whom he fears might hinder his plans, he devises all sorts of accusations against them. He also immediately demands help and assistance from the people for the sake of "security," such as **mercenaries** <term>Söldener: hired soldiers</term> and **guards** <term>Trabanten: armed attendants or bodyguards</term>. These are given to him because no evil is suspected of him. For a time, he gives good words and acts entirely kind and gentle so that he may build a following; he shows much kindness to some. But primarily, when a war arises, he strives to direct matters so that such a war may be entrusted to him. Then, when that happens, he does not rest; and all those who are of an honorable mind, or otherwise will not obey his rule, he sends into the fray <note>original: "schlägt er in die schank"; an idiom meaning he exposes them to mortal danger or sacrifices them</note> and places them in locations where they must suffer damage from the enemy and perish, so that he no longer has to fear any honest man. And such a tyrannical ruler acts nothing like a physician; for a physician only cuts away from the body that which is evil, but the tyrant cuts away only the good, for otherwise he can come to no power or dominion. He and his followers also strive to take the weapons out of the hands of the citizens, so that when he begins to deal and behave with them as he pleases, they cannot reach for any defense. Then the poor people see what they have done—what a harmful beast they have raised, which they cannot get rid of again without harm, even if they dearly wished to.

# Of the Commonwealth #

Xr iiij

...governance in a city, but that the minds and hearts of honorable and pious men are also offended and corrupted thereby.

And so that he may be believed all the more firmly, he proves this with several <term>Locis: rhetorical "places" or points of argument</term> from Homer—who never governed a Commonwealth with good laws, nor served cities in other useful ways as Lycurgus <note>The legendary lawgiver of Sparta</note> did; nor did he help lead any war with his advice, or prescribe good, honest, and useful commandments for posterity to live by, as did Thales of Miletus <note>One of the Seven Sages of Greece</note> and others. Finally, Homer led no special discipline or way of life, nor instructed others therein, as did Pythagoras <note>The philosopher who founded a famous school based on a specific communal lifestyle</note>. For these reasons, he concludes that poets are not to be held in such high esteem, for they never reach the true, inner, and perfect knowledge of the Truth, but only occasionally grasp a shadow of virtue, which they then follow.

However, he speaks these things with very friendly and mild words, with a kind request to forgive him for speaking his mind so bluntly and being unable to hide it.

And although there is an old and constant grudge between poets and philosophers—so that they hate one another and cannot agree—he will not let himself be troubled by this or use any <term>Affect: emotional bias or passion</term> here; moreover, since childhood, he has honored and loved Homer as a precious and good author.

Socrates also confesses that poetry is useful for the refreshment of the <term>Gemüt: the mind, soul, or inner disposition</term> and for an honest and fitting pleasure, for which purpose it may be used. But he will by no means concede that one should govern the Commonwealth with it, or use it for important, serious, and brave matters.

At the end, he disputes concerning the immortality of the soul, indicating that after this life, either an eternal reward or an eternal punishment is ordained for it, according to how each person acted well or poorly here. He tells a fable of one named Erus Pamphilus <note>Known in Plato's Republic as "Er, son of Armenius, a Pamphylian."</note>, who died, and when he became alive again, told the people many strange things about how it goes with souls in the next life, what they must suffer, and what state they finally lead after this life; with this, he concludes the last book of the Commonwealth.

This Pamphilus was, according to the account of some, slain in war and lay dead on the battlefield for twelve days; and when he was taken up and placed on the funeral pyre three days later, he only then became alive and told of wondrous things from that life which he had seen while he was dead.

# Of Governance #

In all laws and systems of government, one should primarily be mindful to arrange things so that they serve God’s honor, justice, prudence, fortitude, and temperance <note>These are the four cardinal virtues—prudence, justice, fortitude, and temperance—combined with religious duty</note>. Concerning other goods which are of lesser value—such as health, beauty, strength, and wealth—one should let them follow after. According to this principle, Socrates generally begins to reach the main point, taking up the laws of both the Cretans and the Lacedaemonians <note>The Spartans</note> to examine them. However, he first lets the young fellows depart and keeps only the old men with him. For it was strictly forbidden for the young fellows to inquire about the laws or to dispute them; but it was permitted for the elders, when they were alone together, to discuss and deliberate upon them.

Therefore, they let the young fellows go, and the Athenian <note>The "Athenian Stranger," the lead character in Plato's Laws who often speaks for the author</note> begins to speak vehemently against the laws of the Cretans, rejecting them as unfit—especially regarding excessive drinking and other pleasures in which the Cretans indulge. And to give their actions a semblance of legitimacy, they take Jupiter <note>original: "Juppiter" (Zeus)</note> himself as an example, claiming he took Ganymede to be his cupbearer, and they further accuse him of I know not what indecencies <note>A reference to the myth of Zeus and Ganymede, often used in antiquity to justify pederasty</note>, which is not at all becoming of them to do.

Upon this, the Lacedaemonian says that the customs and practices in his city please him best; for there, no one is permitted to indulge in drunkenness or other pleasures or incitements to evil, and drunkenness is punished most severely among them. The Athenian allows this to be good, saying also that it is fine and right to maintain such discipline and honor so that people remain sober and do not grow accustomed to heavy drinking. But he nevertheless insists that in such conversations—where one man brings forward this point and another that, and each gives his best thought—one should not judge so quickly, nor either scold or praise a thing immediately. Rather, one should first see and consider on what grounds and for what reasons such things are established and maintained. And although he also scolds drunkenness as that which makes men unskillful and unfit for all things, and violently awakens and ignites the <term>Affecten: the passions, emotions, or irrational impulses</term> within a man, takes away the memory, and withdraws from the understanding its actual power—yet, if someone wishes to know the character of his citizens, he cannot achieve this with easier effort or greater convenience than when they are drinking and have become intoxicated with wine <note>Plato suggests that wine acts as a "touchstone" for character, revealing a person's true nature without lasting harm</note>. And he adds thereafter a very useful and fine maxim: namely, that those who wish to be esteemed as excellent above others in any matter should be instructed and practiced in it from youth. This is so they become so accustomed to it that they can speak and act upon it as if in play. He says this because he wishes to show that people usually turn out according to how they are raised, whether good or evil, depending on the instruction, which then remains with the person throughout their entire life.

Concerning wine, he says that it is of such a nature and kind that it first makes a person cheerful; then, the more he drinks, the bolder he becomes, and the more he thinks of himself, until he...

In the second book, he <note>Plato</note> returns to the subject of music. After indicating that it is primarily useful for calming the <term>Affects</term> <note>original: "Affect"; refers to the passions or emotional states of the human soul</note> of men, he admonishes young fellows to abstain entirely from wine before their eighteenth year. This is so that they do not "pour oil onto the fire" (as the saying goes) or stir one fire with another. However, when they begin to occupy themselves with labor after that time, they may then use wine in moderate measure until their thirtieth year. Yet they should guard themselves with the highest diligence so that they do not, for the sake of their bodies, become drunken. After the fortieth year, however, one may drink a little more easily to honor the gods, especially <term>Bacchus</term> <note>original: "Bacho"; the Roman name for Dionysus, the god of wine and theater</note>, who allowed wine to grow for the benefit of mankind as a medicine. With this medicine, we can occasionally soothe the vexing burdens of old age and immediately wake up and become lively again. Wine also serves to help us occasionally forget heavy thoughts and great worries, and it ensures that our heart and mind are refreshed and warmed by it—as if by a fire—and made joyful. Thus, the mind can be better guided and bent, just as we see that iron is made soft by fire and then bent however one desires.

When young men and fellows sit together and drink, a fine, elderly, and modest man should always be assigned to them. He should, like an overseer and watchman, diligently pay attention to the gestures and morals of the young fellows. If he notices anything shameless, untimely, or disgraceful from one or more of them, he should not leave it unpunished. However, he must see how and for whom it is best suited to take such punishment in hand. In summary: he desires that one should use wine in such a way that we do not forget shame and discipline, but rather remain mindful of them continually while drinking, just as we are at other times. We should seek nothing else when we occasionally use wine than that our powers and strength be increased and our spirits refreshed.

Now, if people come together and drink in such a manner, there would be no danger in it. But if they wish to run together indiscriminately and engage in unchaste behavior through drinking and other vices at their pleasure—refusing to have or tolerate anyone with them who might watch their morals and gestures as just mentioned—then they should in no way be permitted to do so. In that case, it would be better to do as those from <term>Carthage</term> <note>A powerful ancient city-state in North Africa</note> did, who forbade wine-drinking entirely; for the Carthaginians were not permitted to drink any wine when they were in the field for war.

It would also not be unfitting for rulers to abstain from wine while they are performing their official duties; likewise for men when they wish to conceive children. In conclusion, he <note>Plato</note> argues that the noble gifts of wine should not be so poorly despised and left unused, even though some condemn wine altogether. This is similar to how the <term>Lacedaemonian</term> <note>A Spartan</note> criticized the custom of the <term>Cretans</term> regarding <term>toasting</term> <note>original: "Zutrinckens"; the social practice of drinking to someone's health or challenging others to drink</note>, even though they themselves could not entirely avoid the same practice in their own city.

Socrates
</margin>
Following this discourse, Socrates turns to the growth and decline of cities. After long consideration, he asks what the cause is that some cities have a humble beginning yet nonetheless become rich, mighty, and powerful—while others, once they have become powerful and have stood for a time in their growth and prosperity, fall apart again and decline. From that point forward, he speaks of the time in which almost the entire circuit of the world was drowned and destroyed by the Great Flood <note>original: "Sindflut"; referring to the cataclysmic Deluge, which in the Greek context of Plato's "Laws" refers to the flood of Deucalion</note> and the human race was reduced to only a few persons. He says that at that time, among those same few people, there was a great favor, friendship, and love, on account of the vast and monstrous wasteland they saw before their eyes, which they could neither contest nor make use of because of their small number. Therefore, they also had no cause to stir up any riot, war, or ill-will because one had too much or too little. For in whatever place or assembly of men it happens that no poverty or wealth flows forth or is present, there can neither be envy, hatred, injustice, riot, or ill-will present.

<margin>
The first
Polity
</margin>
At that time, the people were also provided with no written laws or arts, nor did they know them. And just as they had no quarrel or strife among them, so were they also entirely simple, just, and moderate; no one inflicted any annoyance on another. They also lived for a good long time in this way, each one alone and separately, and had no one to command but his wife, children, and servants. How their ancestors behaved was their right and law, and they had to guide and conduct themselves accordingly. But after they multiplied again, and each had trained and instructed his servants and children in the paternal old traditions and customs, it happened that some of them occasionally joined together and built huts, and fortified them with fences and other things so that they might live more safely from wild animals. And because they could not agree among themselves for long unless they had judgment and law by which everyone must abide, they agreed in such a way that each should bring forth from his house—as if from his fatherland—the laws and customs of his ancestors. They wanted to bring these all together and weigh them according to necessity, to see which would then be the best and most in accordance with reason, honor, and equity. Everyone should then follow and abide by these. Finally, it came to pass that from such assemblies, cities, market towns, and villages were formed, and that subsequently many cities and villages elevated and elected a single man as a king or prince, by whom they wished to be governed. They also joined and bound themselves together and perhaps chose one city which should rule the other surrounding inhabitants, protect them from unjust violence, and maintain them in their freedom and old traditions. Such an alliance the cities in the Peloponnese <note>The southern peninsula of Greece</note> had, namely the Lacedaemonians <note>The Spartans</note>, Argives, and Messenians.

### Of the Common Good. ###

<meta>catchword: -ment (completing "Regiment" or "goverment" from the previous page)</meta>

[It is right for] children, clever and wise people to command the improvident and fools, and to rule over them. Besides this, he also mentions the rulers who are chosen by lot. But he holds this to be the best among other forms of government: when the most prominent, best, and wisest take over the government. From the beginning, however, he recounts two types of government from which the others (just as from a well) have taken their origin and flowed: namely, **Monarchy**, where one alone has the upper hand, and **Democracy**, where all rule together. And **Monarchy** was primarily in vogue among the Persians, while **Democracy** was prevalent among the Athenians. And herewith he takes cause to speak of the kings of **Persia**, namely of **Cyrus**, **Cambyses**, **Darius**, and **Xerxes**. And although he admits that **Cyrus** was a fine, pious, and magnanimous prince, he acted quite poorly in this regard: that he paid so little heed to his sons and let them be raised quite softly among the women. From this, they were so corrupted and led astray by shameful sycophants <note>original: "Ohrenbläser"; literally 'ear-blowers', referring to flatterers who whisper into a ruler's ear</note> that after the father's death, one shamefully murdered and killed the other. **Cambyses** was also so poorly raised from childhood that he almost entirely ruined and overturned the empire.

After **Cambyses**, **Darius** came to the government. This king also showed and conducted himself moderately enough in his rule; however, he also failed in that he raised his son **Xerxes** so shamefully that he was little fit for government. Therefore, it reached just such an end with him as it did with **Cambyses**. From that same time on, and after those mentioned above, there was no powerful king in **Persia**, and they are to be called kings more in name than in deed. This did not happen by mere chance <note>original: "plumbs halben"; suggests an accident or a sudden, mindless occurrence</note>, and should thus not be attributed to luck, but rather to the evil and shameful government that the tyrants conducted. He also says that the children and descendants of those same tyrants can rarely be brought to a good character, neither in youth nor in old age, because they are hung with so many vices that they are thereby hindered from a good and righteous government and cannot preside over it righteously. He says this for the reason that he might prove that the Persian government went to ruin because the kings were too strict with the people. Conversely, the government of the Athenians was weakened because they gave the common man too much freedom and let them live and act as they pleased; for he desires that one should maintain moderation in both governments. He also wishes to apply the proverb mentioned by **Hesiod**, which in Latin reads *Dimidium plus toto* <note>original: "Dimidium plus toto"; Latin for "The half is more than the whole."</note>. The half part is better than the whole. With this, he wants to indicate that it is better to have a little with love and peace than much with strife and bickering. Likewise, that a moderate government is better than one established in the sharpest or mildest manner.

Thus he rebukes the **Messenians** and **Argives**, because they used too much freedom in their government and did not follow in the footsteps of the **Lacedaemonians** <note>The Spartans</note>, whom he praises and extols to the highest degree, because they [gave] to the nobility in the govern[ment]—

From this argument, they take further cause here to speak with one another. Secondly, whether another city is located near it. Thirdly, whether the location has fertile soil. Fourthly, whether there is much timber in that place from which one can build ships.

To this he replies that the location is somewhat distant from the sea, does not have overly fertile soil, and possesses no wood at all from which one could build ships. Thereupon Socrates <note>In Plato’s *Laws*, the primary speaker is the "Athenian Stranger," but this commentator identifies him as Socrates, Plato's usual protagonist.</note> says it is good; the matter is well-ordered, and the place is so situated that one can build a city there to every advantage—one suited to all honor and virtue. It cannot easily be defiled by those vices which cities near the sea usually possess, where all sorts of people from many kingdoms and lands arrive and bring such vices with them, whereby people are corrupted and become effeminate <note>original: "Weibisch"; in this context, it refers to a loss of traditional masculine martial discipline due to the luxury and comforts of trade.</note> and unfit for all matters. That there is also no wood available from which to build ships has this meaning: that citizens are usually bolder and more courageous in war when they have no hope of escaping on ships. And he proves this with the city of Athens, how it once performed many manly and knightly deeds, but now, since they began to build ships, they have become quite different and no longer dare to venture as they once did.

He also relates how Ulysses <note>Odysseus</note> rebuked Agamemnon for venturing to build an *armata* <note>original: "Armata"; a fleet or naval armament.</note> or naval equipment at the very time when they were most heavily besieging and battling the city of Troy. Following this, he asks the Cretan (since he stated above that he is to build and establish a new city) what kind of people he wants to take for it—whether they shall be purely Cretans or partly other Greeks. For it matters not a little whether a people flows from one nation with the same customs, or from many together. It also matters not a little whether they moved together of their own good will to build another city because they could not sustain themselves in their own place due to the narrowness of the land, or whether they were driven out by rebellion or war, or otherwise [gathered] from all sorts of people.

[...and have] run together, because one part can be better governed with laws and held in check than the other.

Next, he comes to the age of Saturn <note>original: "Saturni"; referring to the mythical Golden Age of Cronus, a time of peace and plenty before the current age of man.</note> and shows what kind of government he led. In particular, he notes that when Saturn perceived that if the government is entrusted and commanded to an individual—such as a king or a monarch—he usually dares to take too much power and does not remain within the right measure of rule. Accordingly, he gave humans angels—whom he calls *daemons* <note>original: "Dæmones"; in Platonic philosophy, these are intermediary spirits between gods and humans, acting as guardians rather than "demons" in the modern sense.</note>—as regents in his cities, who knew how to govern them with moderation and foresight. For he did not want to set one human as a regent over another, but rather something higher and better, just as we see that one ox cannot govern another, nor one goat the other, but they must have another regent, namely, a human.

He speaks this way (for he admits that the story of Saturn is a fable) because he wants it to be understood that those who govern other people—such as cities and lands—should be endowed with greater virtue, piety, honorability, art, and wisdom than others, and not be coarse oxen or donkeys. He also intends that the laws in cities and lands should be established and ordered not for the benefit or pleasure of one part, but for the welfare and best of the entire common good <note>original: "Gemeinen nutz"; the central principle that laws must serve the whole community rather than special interests.</note>. And those who act otherwise do not behave like pious, honest, and just citizens, but like rebels and villains. Therefore, the authorities should not tolerate such things, but see to it that the laws are established equitably, as they are also meant to be the servants and guardians of the laws.

After he has said this (as a kind of preface) regarding the office of a lawgiver, he continues and shows how the legislator <term>Legislator: a lawgiver; the person responsible for drafting the fundamental statutes of a society.</term> should position and conduct himself when he wishes to provide a city or land with new laws. Namely, that he should first exhort the people with the greatest diligence toward honorability and virtue, and also impress upon them the punishment of the wicked and the virtue and honorability of the pious, even in this temporal life. Likewise, how one should honor the gods, what honor one should show to parents and good friends, and that this should by no means be neglected. Finally, he teaches quite finely and pleasantly how subjects and the common man can be persuaded with good and gentle words rather than forced with words, so that they submit to the statutes and laws and be obedient to them, which he then proves with such an example:

The council or the mayor <note>original: "Bürgermeister"</note> commands that all young men shall marry and take wives after their thirty-fifth year; and those who do not obey this command but hold it in contempt and remain unmarried after such a time shall fall under the council's punishment and, in addition, be dishonorable and of ill repute.

# On Government #

Plato is of the same opinion / with a clear indication / that great wealth and power can seldom be reconciled with piety and justice / and whichever city wishes to be secure from rebellion and discord / should be neither poor nor rich / but in a moderate state among all trades / sustenance, and commerce / which are nevertheless of many kinds. And Plato especially praises **agriculture** and **livestock breeding** / as an honest and divine sustenance. In addition, he teaches / that one should first and foremost pay attention / to the goods of the **soul** / and strive after them. Secondly / to the health and welfare of the body. And thirdly / to money and property.

He who wishes to build a city / shall strive above all things / that it be placed in a convenient location / where it does not lack wood and water / which things are indispensable for daily necessity / And it is of no small importance / for a city to succeed / that it be established and built in a good location.

In the sixth book, Plato demonstrates / that although a city may be established with good laws / it cannot endure in the long run / without good governors / who have been raised and instructed for government from their youth. Thereupon he teaches / what kind of guardians of the law should be chosen / how they should record the names of the citizens / and indicate to each his tax and tribute. <note>The original terms are "Geſchoß vnd Zinſe," referring to specific types of early modern property taxes and interest-based dues.</note> Likewise / how one should choose captains / cavalry commanders / sergeants / ensigns / and other commanders for war.

But the election of the **mayors** and **councils** in cities / shall be so arranged / that it does not proceed as between masters and servants / and a governor should treat the citizens / as a master treats his own servants. That the wicked should also not be elected to government / to rule over the good. For such a government cannot endure for long. And although nothing is more laudable and better among citizens / than that equality be maintained among them everywhere / yet this can have no other permanence / than that one should nevertheless pay attention / to the virtue / morals / life, and character of each individual / And that one should then, according to those same virtues, choose them for and admit them to honorable offices. In some matters / concerning the government / one should use the **lot** <note>The "lot" refers to sortition, the practice of choosing officials by random drawing to prevent corruption or political factionalism.</note> to avoid offense and ill-will.

For the maintenance of the public buildings / such as churches / town halls / streets / paths / watercourses / and the like / Plato desires / that one appoint dedicated and special **master builders** / who shall have such buildings in their charge and care / likewise for the protection of the public money / chamberlains or treasurers. Thirdly / he also establishes people to be appointed / who pay attention to the boundary stones / so that they are not moved / who patrol the borders / and maintain the land-defenses as necessary / both with trenches / ditches / and ramparts / so that the enemy may not surprise the city unawares / Also that the wells and water-flows should be most diligently adorned with structures / such as pipe-casings and cisterns. <note>The text mentions "Rörkaſten vnd beumen," referring to the wooden pipes and basins used in early water management.</note>

The other reason is / that one usually employs / some forms and ways in the government / which cannot well tolerate or suffer / having excellent and skilled citizens / especially where the rulers are tyrants / whom he then does not want in his city / and therefore holds / that such military exercise could well be established and maintained therein.

Subsequently, Plato gives several laws regarding farmers / and first / that one should not move the boundaries and landmarks at the corners of fields / as often happens. Regarding craftsmen / he does not wish / that a craftsman should practice two kinds of trades / but should remain with one alone / and attend to the same with diligence. Of food / that one brings into or out of the city <note>original: "S" (Stadt)</note> / he does not wish / that one should take a toll. One should also bring nothing from other lands into the city / except what one cannot do without for necessity's sake. In the same manner, he forbids / letting that be taken out of the city / which one cannot spare in the city or in the country / and needs for oneself. And no goods shall be sold / unless they have first been inspected by the appointed *Censores* <term>Censores: officials responsible for public morals and the regulation of trade</term> / whether they are good and upright / and not falsified / so that no one may be deceived.

In the following book / when he wishes to treat of the courts and punishments / of crime and misconduct / he makes such an introduction / where he considers it unnecessary and superfluous / that in a city / which is best arranged and provided with good / honest / and equitable laws / one should speak and treat much of courts and punishments / of crime / because it is not to be expected / that it could reach such a point / that people would become so evil / wicked and godless <note>original: "geſſen" (likely vergeſſen) — literally 'forgotten,' used here to mean those who have abandoned moral or divine law</note> / that they would dare to act and undertake something against such laws.

But because times always become worse and more evil / and people do not / as in olden times / shrink from punishment and laws / and vice is too much for them / so one must of necessity also treat of this / and not leave this part of the *Policey* <term>Policey: an early modern term referring not just to the police, but to the entire civil administration and the maintenance of public order</term> behind. # Of the Common Good

<meta>The catchword "gessen" from the previous page likely completed a word such as "vorgessen" (forgotten) or "angemessen" (appropriate), though the OCR begins mid-sentence.</meta>

...cannot by any means be dispensed with. For where one does not have laws, statutes, courts, or justice, there a truly cruel, monstrous, and inhuman life must follow. This is based on the principle that no human is by nature of such piety, honor, and virtue that he could sufficiently recognize what belongs to the welfare of the **common good**. And even if he does recognize it, he nonetheless occasionally takes the **wrong path** <note>original: "holtzweg" — literally a logging path that leads nowhere; an idiom for being on the wrong track</note> and considers nothing too much for himself if he feels there is no law present to stop him and that he can escape without punishment. However, where cities are provided with good laws, and the citizens all together seek that which is serviceable to the welfare of the **common good**, there they flourish and increase. Conversely, where **self-interest** <note>original: "eigen Nutz"</note> reigns, and people strive more for their own ends than for the common good, then the cities must decline, decay, and finally perish.

¶ Concerning those who **take their own lives**, he has spoken above; yet he makes a distinction among them and believes it is worse if one kills oneself out of a despondent spirit than if one does so due to the accident of an illness or because of shame.

¶ Whoever violates or shames a maiden or a woman may be put to death by her friends—such as her father, brother, son, or husband. He also speaks likewise of other shames and insults, which are inflicted upon neighbors, the authorities, **graves**, and lastly even the gods.

¶ And he says that the insults against the gods are of three kinds. For some say that there are **no gods**. Others indeed confess that there are gods, but that they do not concern themselves with humans or provide for them. The third group concedes both—that gods exist and care for humans—but they believe the gods allow themselves to be very easily reconciled by all kinds of sacrifices from those who sin against them. However, because this view and <term>opinion</term> <note>The author uses the Latin-derived "opinion" to signify a formal but false belief</note> are entirely false—or where they are held in a city or community and gain the upper hand, they do much damage—he provides instruction on what one should hold instead.

¶ Initially, he rejects the opinion of those who say that the **body** was made before the **soul**. He says that this motion, which moves both itself and other things, is the noblest and best motion of all; for the soul moves itself first, and thereafter moves the body as well. From this, it can easily be concluded that the soul existed before the body. Indeed, the body must be subject to the soul, just as a servant is to his master. **God**, however, is the best and noblest soul, who stirs and makes alive all things that dwell in heaven, on earth, and in the depths of the sea; therefore, all things are filled with the divine.

¶ But as for what some say and pretend—that God does not care for human affairs—this happens primarily for the reason that the worst villains, and those who apply themselves to all injustice, have the greatest **good fortune** in this life. If the gods cared for men, they would by no means let this happen. Plato rejects this opinion and false delusion, saying that the gods are not of such a sort or nature that they would forget this or that...
