# Of Governance

...forgotten or neglected out of fear, but rather that they govern, order, and provide for all things at once.

For it is not to be believed that the **gods**—who far surpass all humans in their power and wisdom—would be more negligent and careless than mortal men. One must admit that no **doctor** is so forgetful and negligent of his medicine, no **builder** of his art, and no **father of a household** <note>original: "Haußuater" — a term referring to the head of a domestic estate, responsible for its economic and moral welfare</note> of his management, that he would willfully neglect or leave out anything necessary to his craft, trade, or household.

Therefore, people should not imagine that when they sin, the gods will forget it and let them escape unpunished; rather, when the time comes, they will receive their due penalty. And though it may appear that the **ungodly** enjoy better fortune here on earth than the **pious**, this is not to be considered true happiness. The greater the prosperity they have here on earth, the more harshly they will be tormented and tortured in the next life.

Furthermore, those who believe that the gods can be appeased with **sacrifices** do nothing differently than **dogs** who allow **wolves** to give them a piece of meat so that they remain silent, while the wolves meanwhile tear apart and devour even more sheep. Or, they suggest the gods are like a **sailor** who allows himself to be swayed by a good drink of wine to let the ship go adrift and be tossed and overturned by the winds. Since even a man (who possesses at least a little reason and conscience) cannot be persuaded to set justice aside for the sake of **bribes and schemes** <note>original: "finanzen vnd gesch" — "Finanzen" in this period often referred to deceitful financial dealings or usury</note> and look through his fingers at a **villain**, it would be shameful to say or hear that the gods are worse than men. It would be an insult to claim the gods could be moved by sacrifices to permit injustice and let evil go unpunished.

Plato took up this debate so that people might be reminded not to speak or think of God so shamefully, but rather to look to Him for all good things, to fear, love, and trust Him. He also desires that those who wish to give laws should admonish the citizens to turn away from their evil lives and be converted. If someone is found who speaks mockingly and evilly of God, he should be brought before a court and punished. Since it is to be expected that many various sins arise from such a misunderstanding of the **Divine Majesty**, he considers it right that the **authorities** <note>original: "Oberkeit" — the ruling magistrates or governing body</note> should punish them—some more harshly and some more leniently, according to the circumstances and the nature of the person. For although there are some who do not hold much regard for God, they nonetheless love honor and **virtue** and are highly opposed to vice and wickedness. Such people should be dealt with gently and punished only with imprisonment, while being exhorted toward improvement with friendly words. But the others, who not only hold wrong views of God, but...

->### Of the Common Good<-

...those who also lead a wicked, godless life, and for whom no malice is too great, shall be punished more severely. Furthermore, a specific law should be made for their sake: that no one may choose or invent their own **gods** contrary to the common laws and commands, nor build any private chapels or churches in their own house. He <note>Plato</note> also remarks how difficult it is to turn people away from a false opinion of God once they have first received it.

In the eleventh book, he deals first with **treasures**, and he dictates that one should not take found treasures that belong to others, based on the principle that the rule says: *What you did not lay down, you shall not take up.* <note>original: "Was du nicht hingelegt hast / soltu nicht wegnemmen" — a classic legal maxim regarding lost property</note> If someone has left something behind in a certain place, it should not be taken, but should remain and be left in that place. Those **servants** who have been set free by their masters <note>This refers to manumission, the legal act of freeing a slave</note> shall hold those same masters in great honor and dignity because of the kindness of being freed. Therefore, they must present themselves at least three or four times every month to offer their service to their masters, so that they are not found ungrateful. They shall also marry only with their master's advice and knowledge. Finally, they should not be wealthier than their **patron**; any excess wealth they acquire should be turned over to him.

Next, he turns to **contracts** and trade, such as buying and selling. He dictates that after receiving the purchase price—if it was more than thirty **shillings** <note>original: "Schilling" — a unit of currency used here to translate the Greek drachma or similar denomination</note>—the seller must remain in that place in the city for ten days. This is so the buyer knows where to find him if the sold goods prove not to be upright or merchantable, so that he may address the matter or, in case of necessity, bring a complaint. In such a case, the seller would have to take back the defective goods—especially if the goods, such as **horses**, **servants**, and the like, were sold to someone who does not know how to judge or value whether they were bad or good. If the seller concealed a defect which he rightfully should have disclosed, and which the buyer ought to have known, then because such deceit is harmful, he <note>Plato</note> wants it heavily punished. Specifically, the seller must return double the purchase price to the buyer.

However, if a **doctor** or a **fencer** <note>original: "Fechter" — likely referring to a trainer of gladiators or athletes who would have professional knowledge of physical health</note> buys a servant who has a defect, he may keep him and blame himself for not being more cautious, since he should have rightfully recognized such a flaw or defect. Therefore, he cannot be heard with such a complaint as mentioned before. Furthermore, regarding this contract of buying and selling, he forbids anyone from selling false goods or selling upright goods too dearly. He also does not want people to boast about the goods or swear oaths over them, as **merchants** and **tradesmen** are accustomed to doing. Whoever sells false goods despite this shall forfeit the goods and suffer as many lashes as the number of shillings he received for the goods. To oversee this, he wants specific **Market Masters** and **Treasurers** <term>Schatzherrn</term> <note>officials appointed to oversee trade and public finances</note> to be appointed.

After this, he comes to the **innkeepers** or hosts who keep public inns. And because they are generally all greedy, skinning people and overcharging them, he holds them in lower and more dishonorable esteem—not because they are hosts and innkeepers, but because...

# Of Governance

...is a nearly necessary thing that one cannot do without; however, it is for the sake of **self-interest** <note>original: "E-", likely *Eigennutz* or self-interest</note> that such people are occupied with it.

For it is the nature of most men that even if they are not inherently evil and have been well-raised, they are rarely satisfied or satiated with a modest and fair profit. Instead, they strive for the highest amount of money they can get, especially when they are oppressed by poverty or otherwise seized by a lust for gold.

Since one cannot do without such people as **innkeepers** and those who provide **lodging**, it is the duty of the Council <note>The governing body of the city</note> to take precautions so that their numbers do not become excessive. They should allow no more to arise than are strictly necessary, and these should serve only travelers and strangers, not native-born citizens. Furthermore, they must ensure that these innkeepers are not notorious or disreputable for wicked vices and greed. And so that people are not overcharged, the authorities should prescribe an **ordinance** stating what they may charge for fodder, meals, and drink, according to whether things are currently expensive or cheap. This should be done in such a way that the innkeepers do not suffer a loss, but instead may have a reasonable profit and maintain their livelihoods.

Regarding **craftsmen**, Plato gives such a law: they must finish their work by the promised time, they must not ruin the materials, and they must not charge more than the work is worth.

As for those who have been **soldiers** and have served the <term>common good</term> <note>The public welfare or the state's interest</note> well and been useful to it, he wishes them to be held in honor. They should not be allowed to suffer want, so that they have no cause for just complaint.

Regarding **wills** and testaments, Plato does not wish a person to have total freedom to bequeath and distribute their goods as they please, especially if the will is made on a deathbed and in the final hour. This is because people usually become stubborn and strange when illness takes hold of them; sometimes they are not even in their right minds. Consequently, they often dictate wills that go against legal order and the customs of the land, distributing their property here and there while forgetting those whom they should rightly provide for and consider. Therefore, he does not wish such testaments to be valid or upheld. He also rebukes and rejects the opinion of ancient legislators who permitted those in their final moments on their deathbeds to bequeath their goods. Instead, he provides another law for how inheritance should be handled, both with and without a testament, in the following manner:

That a father may, according to his pleasure, make one of his sons the heir to his goods, and ordain for the others their fair share, or give his other children to others <note>This likely refers to adoption or marriage arrangements to ensure other households have heirs</note>. If he has only daughters, he shall choose husbands for them and make them his heirs. If he leaves no children behind, he may choose others and appoint them as heirs. If a father should die without a testament and leave daughters behind, the nearest <term>male relative</term> <note>original: "Schwertmagen" — a legal term for relatives related through the male line or "sword-side"</note> may marry one and take over the inheritance. But if he should die without a testament and leave no children, the nearest male-line relatives shall be admitted as heirs.

->### Of the Common Good<-

Regarding **guardians**, he first and foremost establishes the most prominent ones as those appointed in a testament; after these, the closest **paternal relatives** <term>Schwertmagen: literally "sword-kin," meaning relatives on the father's side of the family</term>, and finally those whom the Council or an authority is accustomed to appoint. He commands all of them with the utmost seriousness to faithfully oversee the welfare of their **wards** <note>original: *Mündlein*, a diminutive form of *Mund* (mouth), used here to refer to minor children under legal protection</note>, indicating that they can perform no service more pleasing and acceptable to God than to properly provide for their ward. Furthermore, God is displeased with those who act unfaithfully toward minors; for they should consider such foster children no differently than their own children.

Whoever has a son who will not allow himself to be raised well should summon his closest friends and accuse the son before them; also, if he will not improve, he may **disinherit** him and cast him out from the estate with their advice and knowledge.

Conversely, a son may also complain against his father before the court if the father intends to waste too much and uselessly gamble away or consume his assets; however, the complaint must be moderate and not filed hastily. If it is found before the authorities that the father has indulged too much, they should **restrain his hand** <note>original: *in die Würffel greiffen*, literally "reach into his dice," meaning to restrict his gambling and financial freedom</note> and forbid him from managing the estate.

Plato also permitted **divorce** between those who cannot suitably remain together, provided they have not conceived children with one another, so that they may marry again, each according to their own preference.

He most strictly forbade any master from having any dishonorable dealings with his maid, or a mistress with her servant, under penalty of banishment.

He commands children to hold their parents in honor and to show them proper obedience, indicating that God demands and desires this from them. If parents also complain in their prayers about such disobedient children, there is no doubt that God would hear such prayers and punish the children—as he proves with examples, namely with **Oedipus**, **Amyntor**, and **Theseus** <note>Classical figures whose children—Polynices/Eteocles, Phoenix, and Hippolytus—suffered due to parental curses</note>, who also complained about their children, and the children were severely punished by God.

All **sorcerers**, and those who poison the pastures, or otherwise do harm to livestock or people with poison or in other ways, shall be put to death.

No one shall insult, revile, or slander another; instead, whoever has a claim against another should do so before the court, for which he has given a specific law. He also mentions the **poets** here, who sometimes shamefully attack people in their writings, which he also will not tolerate—especially what constitutes serious slander; however, what is written in a joking manner and is not defamatory, he allows to pass.

He will tolerate no **beggars** or vagrants <note>original: *Schützen*, literally "shooters," likely referring to wandering mercenaries or idle vagabonds</note>; rather, they shall all be driven away.

If someone has an animal that causes damage to another, the owner of the animal shall pay for it and settle the debt.

# Of Governance

If he knows nothing of the matter, then he shall no further be coerced. But if one is found who has three times borne false witness, he shall have **forfeited his head** <note>meaning he shall face the death penalty</note>.

Lastly, he comes to the **Procurators** <term>Procuratores: legal representatives or attorneys</term> and **tongue-thrashers** <term>Zungendrescher: a derogatory term for lawyers who use aggressive rhetoric to manipulate or confuse the court</term> who serve people before the court and, for the sake of greed, embitter people against one another and spin one war out of another so that they may obtain more gold. With these, he is ill-pleased; he scolds them not only as thieves, but he also desires—if they do such things for the sake of fame and wish to be seen as superior to others—that they should be **forbidden from practicing their trade** for a time until their pride passes. If they do it for the sake of money, however, he makes a distinction: he desires that a stranger, who is not a citizen, be eternally banished, but a citizen should be punished with death.

In the final book, he treats various matters, all of which are worth knowing and necessary. First, however, regarding the **Legates** <term>Legaten: ambassadors or official envoys sent on diplomatic missions</term>, that they should carry out their commissioned business with faithful diligence. Those found to act otherwise shall be punished according to the greatness of their forfeiture.

All manner of **theft**, whether it be great or small, he wishes to have treated with equal penalty, thereby indicating that he punishes the **will** and the **habit of stealing** as much as the deed itself. However, regarding servants and strangers who are caught in theft or otherwise apprehended, he leaves them to the judge to be punished. But citizens shall be punished with death, so that they might have a dread of such vice and not stain the government of such an established city.

He admonishes the people that they should not accustom themselves to living alone, but rather to keep company with other humans, because such solitary people live for no one but themselves and are useful to no one.

Following this, he admonishes parents that they should accustom their children from youth onward to be satisfied with meager food, to endure heat and cold with long patience, and that they should by no means spoil the head and feet with any covering, but keep them as nature created them. For if these outermost limbs are left in their natural state, there is no telling how much the entire body is strengthened thereby.

Regarding **matters of war**, Plato gives the following laws: First, when a soldier is commanded to do something by his captain and refuses or abandons the task, he shall be brought before the regiment and made a **rogue** <note>original: *Schelmen*, a term of deep public dishonor</note> in such a fashion that henceforth he shall no longer be used as a soldier, nor be permitted to bring complaints against others for their offenses. Whoever, however, conducts himself honorably and manly in war, he shall be honored above others and gifted with a **laurel wreath**, which the captains shall afterwards hang in the churches and write his name therein for eternal remembrance. Whoever **deserts the banner** <note>original: *panerflüchtig*, refers to fleeing from one's military unit or flag</note> or throws his armor away shall be earnestly punished. Yet he commands that the **Provosts** <term>Profosen: military officials responsible for discipline and punishment</term> or **Magistrates** <term>Schultheiß: local administrative and judicial officials</term> shall make diligent inquiry into what cause each man had for throwing away his armor, whether it happened without danger or under compulsion, so that no one might suffer an injustice. And he leads...

# Of the Common Good

For example: *Patroclus*, who, after he was slain, was plundered by *Hector* and stripped of his armor. If another had then come and accused *Patroclus* of having thrown his armor away <note>implying cowardice in battle</note>, *Patroclus* would have been done an injustice by that person.

Furthermore, *Plato* considers it necessary that the officials and regents of the **Common Good** <term>Gemeiner Nutz: the public welfare or the state interest</term> shall give an account annually, or at the conclusion of their offices. If anyone is found to have committed a transgression, or otherwise cannot settle his accounts as an honorable man, *Plato* describes how he should be punished, who should be appointed to hear such accounts, and how the punishment should be determined.

Since one should rightly always choose the best and most pious people as regents, he says that it is quite difficult—should one of them fall under suspicion—to find a better and more pious man to judge him, one who knows how to punish the others in such a case and examine their accounts as necessary; for these must be very pious and beyond suspicion. And he immediately thinks of *Rhadamanthus* <note>In Greek mythology, a son of Zeus famed for his integrity, who became a judge of the dead</note>, noting that he was a righteous judge and upright man who did not allow himself to be moved to injustice by gifts <note>bribes</note>, but dealt with people firmly and freely and did not delay. He also maintained the custom of requiring an **oath** from everyone who had business before him. However, *Plato* adds that at that time there were God-fearing, honorable, and pious people who were terrified of **perjury** <term>Meineyd: the act of swearing a false oath</term> and held it in dread, because they respected God and believed that He not only watches over and governs mankind, but also wishes to severely punish the godless, evil, and perjured. This way of doing things no longer suits the courts today, for the spirits and hearts of men have changed greatly toward God; they no longer fear Him, but are diligent in doing wrong, swearing falsely, and committing all manner of evil against their neighbor. For this reason, one must also change the courts, the regulations, and other laws, and arrange them accordingly, and likewise withdraw the use of oaths. For if every person were allowed to clear themselves with an oath, the city would be filled with perjured people. Accordingly, *Plato* did not wish for judges to allow people, when they litigate before the court, to swear oaths to justify themselves or their kin, nor to weep or use other womanly gestures whereby the judges might be moved to mercy; instead, they should simply state how the matter stands. However, those who are strangers having business before the court may be allowed to swear an oath, for it is not to be presumed that anyone can be scandalized by those who do not remain or hold residency in any particular place or city.

After this, he speaks of **travel** <term>Wanderschafft: the practice of traveling abroad or wandering</term> and says that it is not possible for people not to travel to and fro, and that it would be a form of arrogance <note>original: "obermut"</note> if one did not wish to host foreign people or grant citizens and inhabitants the right to visit foreign places. Therefore, he admonishes with great diligence that cities should carefully guard against the reputation that they do not like to harbor strangers. It also matters a great deal,

Whoever has received stolen goods and concealed the theft shall be

Whoever has also harbored an exile, or someone who was **under the ban** <term>in der Acht: a legal state of being an outlaw, where one is stripped of rights and protection</term>,
Plato wished to have punished with death. For this reason: that
every citizen, according to his duties, is bound to regard as an enemy whomever
the Council or the common city has regarded and condemned as an enemy.

Plato wished that no citizen, without the knowledge of the community, should either
make peace or incite war, or else be severely punished for it.

Should some of the citizens have ventured to do such a thing, the
agitators and primary instigators of the same should be punished for it
by the superiors or regents.

Whoever has served the common good and been helpful shall take no
gift or present for it. And Plato desires that one should not take gifts even
in good matters, let alone for evil or to deceive; for once
one has accustomed himself to taking gifts, he can only with great
difficulty restrain himself from it again.

# Of the Common Good

Regarding **legal disputes** <term>haddersachen: contentious quarrels or lawsuits</term>, he considers it good that one should first choose arbitrators or **mediators** <term>Teidingsleut: negotiators appointed to settle disputes amicably</term>, and let them judge such erroneous matters in a friendly spirit. Where such a friendly resolution fails, the matter should be brought before the **district officials** <term>Viertelmeister: local administrators or 'quarter-masters'</term>. If the defendant is found liable before them, he shall pay a penalty equal to one-fifth of the value of the main claim. However, if he then appeals further to the court and is found liable for the third time, he shall pay the entire sum and an additional half of that amount as a fine. This penalty is established so that no one may willfully undertake to prolong war or strife, or to appeal from one judge to another out of sheer stubbornness.

Following this, he returns to the public courts and their administrators. Although he has mentioned this before, he cites the proverb that "one may well sing a good little song twice" <note>This suggests that important moral or legal advice is worth repeating for emphasis.</note>. He diligently exhorts that the pious should be kept under good protection and care, while the wicked should be punished. Yet, among the latter, a distinction must be kept: those in whom there is still hope for improvement, and who have sinned more out of oversight than out of malice, should be granted mercy and restored. But where there is no hope, he wishes to have no compassion for them; rather, like **scabby sheep** <note>original: "reudigen Schaaff" – a common metaphor for individuals whose corruption threatens to "infect" the rest of society</note>, they should be removed as quickly as possible so they may do no more harm.

Plato also does not wish for anyone to set themselves against the court or to revile and scold the judges. Should anyone venture to do so, they should be punished with their life, as they are those who will suffer neither judgment nor justice, but would gladly see the same suppressed so that they might live according to their own pleasure.

After this, he comes to the matter of **burials** and desires that one should not incur great expense for them. In particular, he wants the graves to be placed in no fruitful location where something might otherwise grow and be useful to mankind; rather, where the ground is stony and barren, the graves should be made there. For since the earth was created to bear fruit and be of use, he also does not wish for excessive, large tombstones to be placed upon graves. Following this, he comes to the debate and distinction between the **body and the soul**, and is entirely of the opinion that the soul is immortal, and when it has departed from the body, it returns to God, where it must give an account of its deeds and dealings. He therefore exhorts, in summary, all people—young and old, woman and man—to live honorably and well. And if someone’s father, mother, child, or friend dies, the
->Magistrate should not allow nor permit unseemly<-
->howling and screaming, especially<-
->in the streets.<-

# Conclusion to the
->Reader.<-

As I (favorable reader) have held and compared this short excerpt—concerning the laws and government of the **common good**—against the whole of **Plato** (as much as he has written on this matter), I have found that Plato’s writings extend somewhat much further. However, they rhyme little with our current deeds and nature. Therefore, I have let the matter rest there. Indeed, I confess that I have not translated everything contained in this excerpt word-for-word. This is something that **Horace** <note>The author refers to the Roman poet Horace, who in his *Ars Poetica* famously advised against being a "faithful interpreter" who translates word-for-word, suggesting instead that the sense and spirit of the text are more important.</note> neither praises nor desires; instead, I have remained with the meaning and that which the German language was able and willing to provide and endure. I consider it enough that the rulers alone have a taste of Plato and see a little how the ancients concerned themselves with government. And if they find anything good therein, they should not be ashamed to take the same into their **administration** <term>Regiment: the act or system of ruling and governance</term> for assistance, and to improve their **order** <term>Ordnung: the legal and social regulations of a territory</term> thereby. For just as the **bees** collect the best juice from all flowers into a heap and make the precious and lovely honey from it, so too should the **legislators** and rulers gather the best from all books, so that they may establish such an order and government which is not only Christian, but also useful and beneficial to the **subjects**.

->MARTIALIS.<-

->A book that is to live must have spirit.<- <note>original: "Victurus genium debet habere liber." — a quote from the Roman poet Martial (Epigrams, Book 6, No. 60), meaning that for a book to endure through the ages, it must possess a certain spark of genius or vital spirit.</note>

## Contents of the Platonic Doctrine.

Various questions concerning a new city and how it should be built, with all its circumstances.
What kind of people belong in a city.
The reign of Saturn. <note>A reference to the "Golden Age" or the mythical rule of Cronus, which Plato uses to discuss the ideal relationship between divine wisdom and human governance.</note>
The lower nature desires to be ruled by the higher nature.
Regents should not be oxen and asses. <note>A metaphorical warning that rulers must possess intellect and wisdom rather than mere brute strength or stubbornness.</note>
Laws should serve the common good.
Uniformity of the laws.
What the office of a lawgiver consists of.
Subjects are to be persuaded toward obedience more with kind words than with coercion.
When men should marry.
Praise for the state of marriage.
When laws are given, they must also be upheld, and the transgressors must be punished.
Praise for the mind <term>Gemüt; the inner spirit, disposition, or soul of a person</term> in man.
Becoming virtuous is the highest honor of the mind.
Praise for moderation <term>Mässigkeit; temperance or self-control</term>.
Honor of the body.
The elderly should provide the young with an example to follow.
How one should behave toward strangers.
Two noble virtues of the authorities: to hate the wicked and to be gracious to the good.
Authorities should avoid ambition <term>Ehrgeitigkeit; here meaning vainglory or the selfish pursuit of status</term>.
Maintaining moderation in both good fortune and distress.
Citizens and farmers who belong to a new city or district.
How all the goods of men should be held in common. <note>Refers to Plato's controversial idea in *The Republic* that the ruling class should not have private property.</note>
One citizen should know the other.
The benefit of such acquaintance.
Citizens should maintain their property in good repair and improvement.
Making or appointing heirs.
The begetting of children.
What kind of citizens should be accepted or not accepted.
Citizens should not practice usury <note>The lending of money at high interest rates</note>.
Where wealth and power are found in cities, there is generally little piety and justice.
A city should guard itself against insurrection.
Praise for agriculture.
Goods of the mind should come first, then the health of the body, and thirdly money and property.
Suitable locations for building cities.
Good laws cannot exist without good regents.
Guardians of the laws.
Commanders for wars.
What kind of people are to be chosen as regents of the cities.

## To the Reader.

Friendly and dear reader, I myself am of the opinion that in this Platonic doctrine <note>original: "Platonischen Lehre"</note> there are many things which perhaps do not fit so well with Christian government, administration, and civil order <term>Civil order; original: "Policey." In the early modern period, this term referred to the broad regulation of community life, morality, and public welfare, rather than just modern law enforcement.</term>. Furthermore, this little book was not published with the intent that every government must or should be modeled exactly after it. Rather, it is intended only so that the rulers of our times might find reason within this Platonic doctrine to establish good governance <note>original: "Regiment"</note>. This has often been discussed at Imperial Diets <term>Imperial Diets; original: "Reichstagen." These were the formal deliberative assemblies of the Holy Roman Empire where princes and representatives met to discuss imperial law.</term>, yet it has never truly been put into practice. And should anyone perhaps desire to know upon what points a proper and useful civil order rests, I have wished to recount them below, just as they were presented at the Imperial Diets.

->❦<-

<vocab>Platonic doctrine, Christian government, Administration, Civil order, Imperial Diets</vocab>

<summary>In this preface, the author clarifies that while Plato's ideas might not perfectly align with Christian states, they serve as a vital inspiration for improving governance and public order. He notes that although these reforms are often discussed at Imperial Diets, they are rarely implemented.</summary>

->Issued in the year 1549 at the Imperial Diet of Augsburg.<-
<note>original: "CAPITA REFORMATIONIS IN REBVS POLITICIS, Anno M. D. XLIX. in comitijs Augustanis ædita." This refers to the legal decrees enacted by the Holy Roman Emperor and the Estates to regulate public morality and commerce.</note>

On Blasphemy.
On swearing by and cursing God.
On the blaspheming of the Mother of Christ and God's Saints.
On the swearing by and cursing of God by the Nobility and their Mounted Retainers <term>Mounted Retainers; original: "Reisigen Knechten." These were armed men, often of lower noble birth, who served as a lord's military escort and cavalry.</term>.
On Blasphemy in the land and in war, as well as oaths and cursing.
What is exempt <note>original: "gefreyet." Refers to legal privileges, protections, or tax-exempt statuses granted during military campaigns.</note> in times of war.
On masterless soldiers <note>original: "Herrnlosen Knechten." Armed men without a formal employer or lord, often viewed as a source of social unrest and crime.</note> who venture to gather together and burden the poor.
On toasting <note>original: "zutrincken." The social practice of competitive or excessive drinking, which authorities frequently tried to curb.</note>.
On disorder and extravagant clothing <term>Extravagant clothing; original: "köstlicher Kleidung." This section deals with sumptuary laws, which dictated what fabrics and styles each social class was permitted to wear.</term>.
Of Citizens, Peasants, and other Subjects.
Of the Nobility.
Of Doctors <note>original: "Doctoren." Refers to those holding the highest academic degrees, usually in Law, Medicine, or Theology.</note>.
Of Counts and Lords.
On horse equipment.
On certain articles in which the authorities are commanded to establish order.
On Weddings.
On Baptisms.
On Burials.
On the Ell-measure <term>Ell-measure; original: "Ellenmaß." A traditional unit of length, roughly the length of a man’s arm, used primarily for measuring fabric.</term>.
On Measures.
On Weight.
On the excessive charges of Innkeepers.
On Workers.
On Day-laborers.
On Messengers.
On the wages, labor, and pay of all artisans.

On Carters.

On the sale of woolen cloths.
On drunkenness.
On bankrupt merchants.
On the sale of ginger.
On Mounted Retainers and domestic servants.
On frivolous cohabitation <note>original: "leichtfertiger beywohnung." Refers to unmarried couples living together or illicit sexual relations.</note>.
On Beggars and Idlers.

On Gypsies. <note>original: "Zigeunern." Historically, this term referred to the Roma and Sinti people, who were often subject to restrictive and exclusionary laws in the early modern period.</note>
On slanderous nicknames. <term>Slanderous nicknames; original: "Schalcksnamen." This refers to the use of insulting names that could damage a person's legal standing or social honor, which were punishable offenses.</term>
On musicians and messengers. <note>original: "Pfeiffern" (literally pipers or fife players).</note>
On vagabonds, singers, and rhymers. <term>Vagabonds; original: "Landfahrern." Literally "land-travelers," a term for itinerant people, performers, or peddlers who lacked a permanent legal residence.</term> <term>Rhymers; original: "Reimsprechern." Performers who recited verse in public, often associated with traveling entertainers.</term>
On the guardians of minors. <note>original: "Tutorn der vnmündigen." Legal guardians appointed to manage the inheritance and welfare of children who had not yet reached the age of majority.</note>
On judges, advocates, and patrons. <note>original: "Aduocaten/vnd Patronen." This section regulates the conduct of lawyers and those providing legal representation.</note>
On pharmacists. <note>original: "Apoteckern." Apothecaries responsible for the preparation and sale of medicinal remedies.</note>
On libelous writings, images, and fabrications. <note>original: "Schmäheschrifften/gemälde/vnd gemächte." This covers various forms of defamation and forgery, including written satires and insulting drawings.</note>
On goldsmiths.
On trades in general.

**D**istinguished, High-born Prince, gracious Lord: In worldly matters, it is perhaps the greatest and most important thing to consider how those whom Almighty God has appointed and ordained into authority to lead, govern, protect, and maintain other people, should rule in a godly, wise, and sensible manner and be instructed therein. For this reason, from the beginning and at all times, several highly understanding people have concerned themselves with this matter and, for the benefit of the common utility and welfare <note>original: "gemeinen nuß vnd wolfart." This refers to the "common good," a central principle of early modern governance suggesting the state exists to serve the collective benefit of its people.</note>, have committed their thoughts on such things to paper.

Although it is true that in this regard the Greeks—such as Plato, Aristotle, and Xenophon, along with several others—and likewise Marcus Tullius [Cicero] and Plutarch among the Romans, have written with such great reason and wisdom on these things (as everyone must admit) that there is not much left to improve; nevertheless, it seems to me that those who have since left behind something in writing regarding these matters should also not be rejected. This is primarily for the reason that in former times and among the ancients, there was a somewhat different understanding, both among the Romans and the Greeks, than government subsequently acquired. For governance is so constituted that sometimes, quite quickly and unexpectedly, and even in a wondrous way, changes are undertaken within it. And although we (praise God) have a well-ordered and established government <term>Government; original: "Regiment." This refers to the system of rule and the institutional order of the state.</term> among us Germans, it still constantly appears as if it might one day undergo <note>The catchword "winnen/" indicates the next page continues the word "gewinnen" (to undergo/attain).</note> a change.

# Preface.
Au

As for the military preparation and bravery of the Germans in war, it is more than evident—so much so that nothing can be detracted from it by me, as a single, humble, and private person; nor is that my intention. And the French know well, when they wish to wage war or are forced into it, how much they rely on German assistance.

And would to God that the noble Germans truly recognized and understood their own power; perhaps things would stand differently in Germany, and it would not have reached the point where, through misunderstanding, they have fallen into burdening and destroying one another <note>The translator is likely lamenting the internal strife and civil conflicts, such as the religious wars, that fractured the Holy Roman Empire during the 16th century.</note>.

Therefore, I have no doubt that whoever reads this book by Claude de Seyssel, even if he is not French, will nonetheless find within it matters—especially regarding Lords and Rulers—that will be highly useful to him. Furthermore, the author has such an engaging style <term>engaging style: original "lustigen stylum," referring to a rhetorically pleasing or readable prose</term> that once someone begins to read it, they do not wish to put it down. Although I confess that, due to my age and other difficulties I have faced, I have not been able to do full justice to this author in my translation <term>translation: original "Version"</term>, I have nonetheless done as much as was possible and omitted nothing.

If the opinion were to hold that the writings and books of foreign nations should not be read, then one would have to leave unread the books of almost all the most excellent men, both of the Greeks, the Romans, and other nations.

# Preface of Johannes Sleidanus
## to King Edward in England.

<image-desc>Decorative initial 'E' set within a square woodcut border featuring ornate floral and foliate scrolls.</image-desc>

The most excellent men, Plato and Aristotle, among other branches of philosophy, especially devoted themselves to that part which concerns human society and the governance of the <term>common good: "Gemeinen nutzes," a central 16th-century concept referring to the collective welfare of the state rather than private interests.</term> They handled this with diligence and according to every necessity. For they considered it not enough simply to write about how one might reach a correct understanding of philosophy, or how to attain honorable morals above others, or finally how to receive delight or comfort in one's own mind. Instead, they also strived and took care to be useful and to serve the public and the world at large. Whatever certainty and understanding they had gained through their constant diligence, long practice, and experience, they wished to bring out of the darkness and into the light. They could find no better way to act, nor any way to produce greater fruit with such diligence.

Doubtless they were moved to this because they felt and saw in governments and among the <term>authorities: "Oberkeit," referring to the ruling class or magistrates.</term> how unfairly, prematurely, and unjustly rule was conducted in many places. They saw that the greater part of men tended to pursue ambition and their own private profit, and to pull all things toward their own welfare and utility. So that they might succeed better in this, they took to their aid favor, grace, envy, hatred, and other evil <term>passions: "Affect," in the classical sense of unruly emotions that overcome reason.</term> rather than reason, honor, and equity.

And it often happens that people are talked out of their freedom by those using a colored and learned kindness, and that the kingdom and the authorities are overtaken by evil tricks. In such times, God and religion—as they then stood—were spoken of and held in poor regard, and the good arts, along with honorable morals, were despised and not held in their proper dignity and respect.

For these reasons, those same highly intelligent men were moved to record their thoughts. They took what they had gained—not only through their diligent study of the liberal arts and philosophy but also through experience and long practice, and from what they had heard and weighed in councils and other friendly conversations with many wise, virtuous, honorable, and pious people. From this, they selected what they deemed the most prominent and best ideas and set them down in writing. They did this so that those who come after might have a guide to follow, and might see the form of government for the common good that they had envisioned and described. And although they could not change the state and nature of the world as it was in their own time, they nevertheless wished to leave such opinions and writings behind for posterity.

# Preface of Johannes Sleidanus.

Just as their writings and books—because they contain and are filled with so much good, excellent, and useful teaching and instruction—remain at hand to this day and are read with great profit, fruit, and wonder, they shall also, as long as the <term>good arts: "die guten Künste," referring to the liberal arts and humanities</term> maintain their dignity and standing, remain in high regard, not only in libraries but also among the people whenever they are remembered.

<margin><note>original Latin: "Tyranni quomodo cognoscantur"</note> How tyrants are recognized</margin>
For since nothing can be dearer, more convenient, or more desired by human nature and an honorable civic life than to live under a tolerable and equal government and authority, and since we are all most highly opposed to <term>servitude: "Seruitut," from the Latin *servitus*, meaning slavery or forced subjection</term> and hate and flee from it, so too must the regents be mindful to arrange their government in such a way that they are not placed under suspicion of tyranny or excessive power by the <term>Estates: "Ständen," the social and political ranks of the Holy Roman Empire</term> and the subjects of the Realm. Instead, they should show themselves to be more inclined toward justice, equity, moderation, and ultimately the protection of the whole people. Furthermore, these writings clearly show by what signs a tyrant may be recognized: those who overtake a free people and force them under a yoke, or otherwise do not conduct themselves according to their royal office and fail to fulfill its duties. These and similar evil regents are rejected, scolded, and condemned by the aforementioned men; they consider them not as human beings, but as monstrous, cruel, wild beasts, because they present themselves as fathers and shepherds while nonetheless sucking the life out of, devouring, and completely exhausting lands and cities. They consider them all the worse because they carry out their intentions under a good appearance and inflict such damage upon the common good.

<margin>Claude de Seyssel</margin>
I have perhaps recounted this at somewhat greater length than I intended, but I will now get to the heart of the matter. Following these two excellent men I mentioned above—namely, Plato and Aristotle—several others have concerned themselves with these things and written about the governance of the common good. Among these, <term>Claude de Seyssel: "Claudius Seysselius" (c. 1450–1520), a French jurist and diplomat whose work "The Monarchy of France" became a standard text on constitutional thought.</term> is not the least, nor has he applied the least amount of diligence. This man was initially a jurist and held a great reputation. Subsequently, due to his excellent standing, he was elected Bishop of Marseille and was employed for several years by Louis XII, King of France, as an ambassador to <term>Pope Leo: Pope Leo X (reigned 1513–1521)</term>. He was an excellently learned man, as his books—of which he left many behind that are still at hand—sufficiently testify and prove. <margin><note>original Latin: "Thucydides Xenophon Hist. # Preface of Johannes Sleidanus.

When it happened that he became weary and tired of life at court, he retired to a life of rest at his church—to which he had been appointed as shepherd—so that he might attend to his office and remain with his studies. But when King Louis passed away, he dedicated and addressed this book, *The Monarchy of the Crown of France* (as he titled it and wrote it in the French language), to King **Francis the First**, who came to the throne after **Louis**. For although he had removed himself from the court and withdrawn from its affairs, he still wished—out of the love and favor he bore for his fatherland and the common good—to remain a counselor and a useful servant to his Lord and King even in his absence. He was primarily moved to do this because the <term>customs of court life: "Brauch deß Hoflebens," referring to the complex social and political maneuvers inherent in Renaissance royal courts</term> were not unknown to him; rather, he knew well how things tend to go at court, and how easily kings and great lords can be misled and led astray from the right path by so many "ear-whistlers" and flatterers, especially while they are young.

For this reason, he brought together with great diligence everything that belongs to a good government. In this work, he followed not only those who wrote of these things in ancient times, but also those who lived in his own day and made their well-meaning views known. He did this so effectively and skillfully that he was able to draw everything toward his own central argument, gathering and presenting it as necessity and opportunity required.

<margin><note>original Latin: "L. digna vox. C. de legib. & constit." referring to a famous decree in the Code of Justinian stating that it is a "voice worthy of the majesty of the ruler" to profess himself bound by the laws.</note> A worthy voice. Code: On laws and constitutions.</margin>
Although this book has the appearance of being written specifically and primarily for the King of France, it nevertheless pertains and applies to all kings alike, since all of them (with few exceptions) are **monarchs** in their own kingdoms. And although they may wish to be subject to no superior lord, or recognize any higher authority, nothing is more glorious, better, or more laudable for them than to submit themselves to the same laws with which they govern their people and subjects, and to allow themselves to be bound by them.

These are the matters upon which he bases his discourse and opinion: namely, the office and the <term>duties: "Officia," the moral and legal obligations of a person in a position of power</term> or commissions that belong to a king or prince in his government and which he is obliged to carry out. By following these, he may have fame, praise, honor, and renown before God and the world. However, should he set these aside, believing he needs to answer to no one and is not bound to obey any law or commandment, he has already lost all favor and his royal name and reputation among all pious, honorable, and sensible people.

This author, **Claude de Seyssel**, encompasses the office and commission that a king must carry out in three parts: namely, **Religion, Jurisdiction**, and **Policey**, with which he also divides and completes the entire book. Regarding the second and third parts, he treats them quite wisely, extensively, and sensibly, so that anyone can learn from them and judge correctly and be satisfied. # Preface of Johannes Sleidanus.

...lived. For he wrote this book approximately fifty-some years ago, when little or nothing was known of the light of truth, but the entire world lay hidden and concealed in darkness, much like the dark cave of which Plato writes <note>Sleidanus refers to Plato’s Allegory of the Cave, an image of people who only see shadows of reality until they are brought into the light.</note>. Therefore, when he writes that kings should pay diligent attention to religion, protecting and defending it, and that they should root out heresy and not allow it to arise, holding spiritual prelates in honor and dignity, and above all, conducting themselves according to the Apostolic Church—this is indeed right and true if it is understood correctly. He means it in a way that many today still understand and wish to maintain: that it is the intention of our Lord God to have established and ordained a specific person in the Church who should be held high above others, shining and brought forward, according to whom all of Christendom should be guided. But we must understand it differently and more generally regarding religion and the Church where God’s Word is preached, and thus as applying to all persons who belong to the holy Christian Church.

Therefore, it is right and proper that kings should promote, honor, and defend religion, for God primarily demands such work from them. However, they must also ensure that it is the right, true religion, and not a false, colored, or self-devised religion. Instead, it must be one that has the testimony of the writings of the Apostles and Prophets and agrees with them. Similarly, it is right and true that kings should allow no heresy <term>heresy: "Ketzerey," meaning beliefs that contradict established religious doctrine. Sleidanus argues that Scripture, not tradition, must define what is truly heretical.</term> or false teaching to arise in their kingdoms. But one must look at how the word "heresy" is used. When one wishes to scold someone as a heretic or make them out to be one, they should not judge according to the opinion of the common man or those whose judgment is suspicious. Instead, one must let the Scripture be the judge, along with the books that testify of Christ and were dictated and written through the inspiration of the Holy Spirit, from which the true light and life are to be received.

No less is it true that kings, as mentioned, should show spiritual persons their due reverence. But these persons must also do and accomplish what is their office—teaching and living a good Christian life—for which they were ordained. For otherwise—just as it is the duty of a king to have pious, Christian, God-fearing overseers in his churches and to hold them in all honor—his office also requires him to look diligently to ensure that the people and the subjects do not take harm through negligent, lazy, or puffed-up <note>original: "auffgeblasene," meaning arrogant or prideful</note> and unrighteous shepherds.

Here you say that one should give the highest honor to the Church—or as they say now, the Papal Chair <term>Papal Chair: "Bäpstlichen Stuel," referring to the office and authority of the Pope in Rome.</term>—and follow its lead. I hear that. But no regime can be so powerful as to bring people to do this, unless those who occupy such a chair are like those who led the papacy before **Pope Sylvester the First** <note>Sylvester I (Pope 314–335 AD). Protestant reformers often pointed to his era as the start of the Church's decline into worldly power and corruption.</note> in their righteous doctrine, holy life, humility, and fear of God. For just as each of those early leaders was the most learned and innocent, they also had the least of the honors which the Popes now wish to have.

He also scolds the kings for appointing unworthy and incompetent men over the poor people, and for allowing ambition, favor, grace, "finances" <note>original: "Finantzen"; in this era, the term often referred to political scheming, intrigue, or corrupt fiscal manipulation rather than simple accounting</note>, and the like to carry more weight in these matters than the desire to attain worldly honors and offices.

For although Your Majesty has inherited a magnificent, beautiful, and powerful kingdom from your lord father, Your Majesty is to be considered primarily blessed because, even in your childhood years, you have begun to acquire for yourself the true riches—which are so named and truly are—as a possession, estate, and kingdom: namely, the knowledge of the liberal arts <term>liberal arts: the traditional curriculum of grammar, rhetoric, and logic essential for a free citizen and ruler</term> and of honorable virtue and morals.

To this end, it may also be justly counted as a great gift and stroke of luck that Your Majesty was assigned such a tutor and guardian <note>This likely refers to the scholars Richard Cox or Sir John Cheke, who oversaw Edward VI's famously rigorous education</note> by your father—one who, for the sake of his virtue, has also attained great fame and praise among many foreigners. Since this is so, it is only fitting for Your Majesty to turn and apply the noble gifts of God—which you have received in understanding, in art, and by nature—to the honor of His divine name and to the welfare and best interests of the entire realm.

I will say no more at this time, nor will I exhort you further, lest it appear as if I wished to prescribe the goals and limits for Your Majesty's teachers and doctors, who instruct you so excellently. I only ask this: that Your Majesty might occasionally read these two books by Commines <note>Philippe de Commines (c. 1447–1511), a diplomat and historian whose memoirs provided a pragmatic, often cynical view of statecraft</note> and Seyssel <note>Claude de Seyssel (c. 1450–1520), whose 'The Monarchy of France' argued for a balanced government restrained by religion, justice, and custom</note>—one being political and the other historical—while you are otherwise fully dedicated to your studies. And when you are grown and take up the government, make these two books your own, for Your Majesty will not regret it. I do not know of any other French books ever written that might be compared to these, as Your Majesty will discover for yourself once you have reached full and proper understanding, and you will judge and rule no differently. Commended to God. Given at Strasbourg,

->in the month of June, 1548.<-

# Claude de Seyssel on the 
## Common Weal in France and on the 
## Office of Kings.
### The First Book.

<image-desc>A large ornamental drop-cap 'Z' intricately decorated with floral and vine patterns within a square frame.</image-desc>

In writing of the government of the **common weal** <note>original: "Gemeinen nutzes"; this refers to the 'res publica' or the public good of the state</note> in the praiseworthy Crown of France and the office of kings, we wish to set aside the tedious disputes of the philosophers which they are accustomed to introduce concerning such government—for they are of little practical use—and instead grasp the matter directly. We shall speak here of three kinds of government: namely, of **Monarchy**, when the rule is entrusted to one alone; **Aristocracy**, when several persons—and those the foremost and best among the people—hold the government; and **Democracy**, when the rule remains with the common man. Among these three governments, Monarchy is considered the best, provided the Prince or King is pious, sensible, and wise, and loves the common weal and intends for it to be handled with loyalty. However, because it is quite difficult to maintain the proper measure under such great power, it is considered that the other government—that of the best and foremost—might be more tolerable and sustainable, and also stand upon a better foundation. Namely, when those who surpass others in virtue, understanding, and wisdom are made regents from throughout an entire realm. For even if one among them should wish to take the **wrong path** <note>original: "Holtzweg"; a forest path that leads to a dead end, used here as a metaphor for a moral or political error</note>, the others can **interfere with his game** <note>original: "in die Würffel greiffen"; literally "to reach into the dice," meaning to intervene or check someone’s actions</note> so that he must remain on the right track. As for what concerns the third government, which rests upon the common rabble, it has always been held as suspicious and rebellious, and is usually dangerous and hostile to the best people.

It also happens at times that an **Aristocracy** is changed into an **Oligarchy**. Namely, when a few among the "best" in a city take over the government and, as if they had conspired together, draw the greatest honors and incomes to themselves and distribute them among each other. Thus, they strive more for how they might improve their own profit and income than how they might rightly and well preside over the common weal, though they ought to consider and provide for it above all else. Therefore, it is concluded that none of the three governments is permanent or perfect, for with time all things change and become worse. And such change happens most quickly when a kingdom is accustomed to increase and begins to flourish; for then such disruptions often occur, and one follows the other before one even truly realizes it.

And so that I may set down an example, one sees this in the Roman gov—

# Of the Government of the Crown of France

government and the **Common Weal** <note>original: "Gemeinem nutz"; refers to the *res publica* or the public good</note>, which was once the most preeminent in the whole world, and how it has changed. For first, the Kings ruled the same; thereafter the **Consuls** <note>original: "Bürgermeister"; literally 'mayors', used here to denote the Roman Consuls</note>; following them the **Decemviri** <note>original: "Zehenman"; the 'Ten Men' who briefly ruled Rome to codify laws</note>; sometimes also the **Tribunes** <note>original: "Zunfftmeister"; literally 'guild-masters', used here for the Tribunes of the Plebs</note>; and lastly the Emperors. But among them all, the government of the **Consuls** and the **Senate** <note>original: "Rahts"; the Roman Senate</note> was the most magnificent and longest-lasting. For the City and the Common Weal increased most excellently under their rule, for the reason that their government was **tempered** <note>original: "temperirt"; balanced or moderated</note>, composed, and measured.

The Consuls had great power and prestige in many things and were mighty, especially among foreign nations. Following this, it concerned the Senate at Rome, who were truly select, excellent, and in short, the most prominent men in the City of Rome; they were indeed as mighty and held as much prestige as if they were truly magnificent Princes (concerning which I shall write no further) and thus held great power because they governed the State and the Common Weal. Everything of importance also had to be brought before the Senate and resolved there. Likewise, the community of the Roman People also had their prestige and dignity in great matters, which could not be concluded without their consent. They also had certain offices to elect and distribute. Furthermore, when it happened that one had to deliberate and counsel on matters of war or peace and the like, for which reason the **Tribunes** <note>original: "Zunfft oder Viertelhster"; literally 'guild or ward-masters'</note> were elected annually; without their knowledge and consent, the Senate’s decree and command could not be confirmed nor be effective. And finally, it came so far that under the power of the Senate and the whole people of Rome, the most important matters of almost the entire world had to come to be judged and decided.

However, if one nonetheless considers these things—as they stood at that time—rightly and with diligence, one will find that this same government of the Romans was also not perfect in all things. For, to say nothing of the other defects, I will recount only one: namely, that they did not act with wisdom, whereby their great power and might were heavily weakened, and finally the government was rolled onto a **single person** <note>refers to the rise of the Roman Emperors following the collapse of the Republic</note>, who yet could not maintain or defend such a regime, but finally can barely defend and maintain the name. For in the beginning, when the Kings were driven out of Rome, the Senate (along with the Nobility) took upon itself all too much and too great a power, and the common citizenry was esteemed as almost nothing. Therefore, the commoners were heavily moved by such contempt, in such a way that they fell away from the Senate entirely, and could not be satisfied in any other way than by promising them that they would also be mindful of them. From this it followed that more was thereafter conceded and granted to the common man than was proper or good for the City; and from this there flowed, as if from a **spring-well** <note>original: "Brunquell"</note>, all kinds of error and discord between the Senate and the Commoners, which lasted for so long that they finally could hardly be stilled, as

# The First Book.

...had to deal and work with their neighbors and foreigners, which did not happen under the reign of the Kings. For humans are by nature so disposed that they would rather obey and be subject to one alone than to many. For they think that where many are in the government, the others are just as much as those very rulers. If one then yields to them a little, and they feel that they have power with a single word, they want to have more and more. From this, ultimately, great disruption and discord follows, as also happened in Rome, where the common people <note>original: "Pöfel"; refers to the masses or plebeians</note> wanted to venture too much, primarily at the instigation of the Tribunes <note>original: "Zunfftmeister"; literally 'guild masters', but used here to denote the Tribunes of the Plebs</note>, who frequently hindered the very best plans and intentions. This happened partly because of the distribution of public offices and because of the votes when great matters were to be deliberated and decided. For in such cases, usually those gained the most votes who had the most to give and had the greatest following. On the other hand, the best and most capable people, who could have best looked after the **Common Weal** <note>original: "Gemeinen nuß"; the public good or *res publica*</note>, had to stay behind, and in their place, self-interested, godless, and wicked rascals were brought forward.

Now, when such fellows came into the government, all their affairs and thoughts were primarily directed toward how they might recover that which they had given away and distributed here and there to attain their office. Following this, how they might proceed with such gifts and presents to maintain favor and goodwill. Therefore, the allies of the Romans, and those who held friendship with them, had to bear the brunt and "lend their hair to it" <note>A German idiom meaning to pay the price or suffer the loss for another's gain</note>. This was then permitted to the commanders and the soldiery also—partly so that the rulers might have their favor, and partly out of fear, because the rulers themselves were guilty and used such tactics.

From this it followed that the honor, integrity, and wisdom of the government of the old **Common Weal**—which the most excellent, best, and wisest people had established with great effort, diligence, and labor, and which had remained thus unmoved and preserved for several hundred years among their descendants—was through this path entirely corrupted and brought to shame, so that almost nothing good remained in the Roman government. Instead, the vice of which we spoke above took the upper hand like a Great Flood, and ultimately gave cause for the **Civil Wars**. For those who could not come forward and to honor through their integrity, virtue, and piety, clung to the common man, courted him, and said what he gladly heard, with the pretense that things were going poorly in the government, and the **Common Weal** was little considered, and the like. Through this, the common populace (who were already hostile and opposed to the Senate) were vehemently embittered, and thereafter obeyed and supported such agitators <note>original: "Auffwicklern"</note>, so that they oppressed or drove out the pious, righteous rulers and got the government into their own fists.

The **Gracchi** <note>Tiberius and Gaius Gracchus, Roman brothers who attempted land reform</note> also used this path when they devised the law regarding the distribution of the fields <note>The *Lex Agraria*, laws meant to redistribute public land to the poor</note> among the Roman people, which stirred up great riots, and thereafter spread further between **Marius** and **Sulla** <note>Gaius Marius and Lucius Cornelius Sulla, whose rivalry led to the first major Roman civil wars</note>, through

# Of the Government of the Crown of France

...by which the **Common Weal** <note>original: "Gemeine nuß"; the public good or *res publica*</note> was heavily plagued, torn, and weakened. 
For military discipline was no longer maintained, and the 
authority that the state once held over the military commanders and captains was entirely lost. 
And it came to such a point that whoever was superior to others in power and military forces 
practiced the greatest wantonness and followed his own whims. This was 
handled not only in war, but also within the city of Rome among the citizens. 
They did not respect the Council <note>The Roman Senate</note>, but instead, whomever they 
conceived a grudge against, they persecuted most vehemently according to their pleasure, 
inflicted every possible plague upon him, and killed countless many in this way.

Thus acted Lucius Sulla and Marius. Likewise Julius Caesar; and when 
these were killed, it was Mark Antony, Lepidus, and Octavius, the **Triumvirs** <note>A group of three men holding power; specifically the Second Triumvirate of Rome</note>. 
And Octavius did not rest until he had cleared his companions out of the way 
and brought the government and the lordship of the whole Empire and the 
Imperial office under his own power. At the beginning of his reign, he also 
managed things in such a way that the **Common Weal** suffered harm. And 
thereafter, almost all Emperors followed this example, except that some 
made it even worse.

And all this damage occurred because the common man <note>The ordinary citizens or plebeians</note> 
held the government. Many wise, pious, and learned people 
had feared and seen these things coming and had warned of them 
in their books. But when it was put into action, no one could 
stand against them or resist them.

Therefore, this form of government (even if it is a mixed one) cannot 
be productive or perfect, because the common rabble <note>original: "Pöfel"</note> has a hand in it. 
And it is much better that the government be held by a few, and the best (which 
is called **Aristocracy** <note>original: "Aristocratia"; government by the best-qualified citizens</note>), as the Venetians have established their government. 
There, a certain number of the citizens are used and chosen for the government; 
there is one Mayor, whom they call a **Doge** <note>original: "Hertzogen"; literally 'Duke', but referring to the Venetian head of state</note>, which 
is a piece of **Monarchy**. But from the government of the common people and the rabble, 
nothing is suffered or found there. For the common man 
in Venice has absolutely nothing to do with the government, but must do 
what the Council commands in all matters, or expect a harsh punishment. 
Because of this, the city has grown into such power and prosperity that she 
has often defended and maintained her own against great potentates and princes, 
and still defends and maintains it today.

Yet it is not as if there is nothing at all lacking in the Venetian 
government. This lack is of such a nature that they 
occasionally fall into great anxiety and distress. If they do not 
provide for themselves, it could happen to them further. For just as a human 
body is composed of the four elements and has opposing humors <note>original: "feuchtigkeit"; refers to the four bodily fluids (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile) believed to control health and temperament</note>, 
which are partly warm, partly cold, or rather partly evil 
and partly good fluids—as long as they remain balanced in the human 
body, he remains healthy and fresh. When, however, one takes 
the upper hand over the other, be it heat or cold, the body cannot 
remain healthy but must fall into sickness because of this inequality.

# The First Book

Eee iij

And since there are many members in one body, even if one wishes to come to the aid of one limb, another is harmed in its place; thus, it is difficult and requires great effort to restore the whole body to its former health. This same principle applies to human society—namely, in a city, which is joined and held together like a body <note>original: *Corpus*</note> with laws, just as if with elements and bonds. It first increases gradually and grows, and when it has climbed to its highest point, it remains in that state for a time. But when, thereafter, regents come who are not like one another, and one wishes to go this way while the other goes that way—and none of them are good or upright—then their power must vanish once more. And the more powerful such fellows are, the sooner and more horribly the government and the entire city fall apart and go to the ground.

It is customary to divide the human age into five stages: namely, childhood, youth, manhood, maturity <note>original: *recht alter*</note>, and childish or the final age. In this same way, some learned people have divided the Roman Empire. And if one wishes to consider the matter rightly, it is found that it happens in much the same way with almost every city, principality, or kingdom.

And to return again to the city of Venice: it is certain that they have such defects in their government that, if these are not abolished or improved, great harm will result for them over time. Among these, the foremost is that the highest, greatest, and best offices—even those that bring some profit—fall only to the nobility <note>original: *Adel*</note> and are administered by them. This greatly vexes the other citizens <note>original: *Bürger*; referring here to the *Cittadini*, a class of non-noble but privileged residents</note>, because they must look on while they are often far superior to the nobility in understanding and wealth. This is all the more so because the nobility increases daily in number and power. However, those of the nobility who live in their other cities and territories are considered as nothing; they are neither used nor drawn into the government or into offices. This has the appearance of being done so that they might not start an uprising in the countryside. As for the other citizens in the city of Venice who are not of the nobility, they dare not have any hope of attaining great offices and dignities, because the nobility prevails to such an extent that there are hardly enough positions to provide for all of them.

The second defect is also not small: namely, that when they wage a war on land, they do not appoint one of their own as a commander, but rather appoint foreigners. For they fear that if they chose a Venetian, he might—should he be successful—reach for the upper hand and turn the state into a kingdom <note>i.e., seize absolute power as a monarch</note>. Furthermore, the Venetians are otherwise by nature more suited to merchant trade than to war; for this reason, very few stately and experienced soldiers are found among them. But in this matter of which we have just spoken, the defect is that foreigners—whom they hire for money for war—do not long regard the common good with such loyalty as the citizens do, for whom it truly matters if the war goes badly. And they are accustomed to assign to the commander certain legates, whom they call in their language *Prouisores* <note>Provisors or *Provveditori*; civilian officials who supervised military leaders to ensure loyalty to the state</note>, or...

...to appoint administrators or overseers <note>The original German uses "walter oder Vorsteher," referring to the Venetian *Provveditori*, civilian officials who supervised military commanders</note>, upon whom the entire provision of the war rests. Without their knowledge and consent, the Colonel <note>original: "Oberste"</note> can or may accomplish nothing of significance or importance. However, this does not help matters, as these legates are usually inexperienced in war and can easily err out of ignorance, which brings great harm to the entire city. Beyond this, the members of the nobility of that place are not at peace among themselves, but have all sorts of quarrels and discord. For those who have been in the government from the beginning and have their origins there <note>Referring to the "Case Vecchie" or "Old Houses" of the Venetian nobility</note> consider themselves much better and higher than those who were elected and accepted later <note>The "Case Nuove" or "New Houses"</note>, even as they also exceed them in number. These two parties tear at each other so much over <term>fools' caps</term> <note>A metaphor for vanity, prestige, or empty titles of office</note> and over which part is better than the other, or who is closest to the government, that great ill-will often arises among them. This happens because they strive more for their own profit, pomp, and glory than for how the <term>common good</term> <note>original: "Gemeine nutz," referring to the welfare of the state or commonwealth</note> may be best provided for; for they, just like other men, have their faults and defects and allow themselves to be moved and ridden by self-interest.

And although no particular disadvantage has arisen for the Venetians yet or up to this point—which has undoubtedly been prevented by the particular wisdom and foresight of some—it is nonetheless to be feared that one day, when the <term>evil moisture</term> <note>A medical metaphor based on the four humors; here it refers to political corruption or social imbalance reaching a tipping point</note> (as mentioned above) takes the upper hand, it might break out and become so violent that the evil can no longer be restrained. This should not be understood as if I intended to criticize or reform the Venetian commonwealth and government, for one will hardly find a better or more powerful commonwealth and government in all of Christendom that could equal it. Rather, I wish to show that it is not well possible that in such a government and commonwealth—especially where a city is large and powerful—there could not be more defects than in a **Monarchy**. For where one alone has the upper hand, he can much more easily remedy a defect and change it than where there are many of equal dignity and power. For we see that people are by nature and kind so minded that they hold a single person, whom the others have set over them as a ruler, in higher regard and fear him more than an entire crowd where one rules today and another tomorrow. Reason also dictates this, that in all other things we look to and pay attention to one thing, just as to the head and a spring from which other things flow; and that nothing is more harmful or dangerous than where many have the government at the same time.
