### The First Book. 292

It can also be easily demonstrated that *monarchies*—even when they are changed by the passing of princes or by some other human accident—are nevertheless more steadfast, quiet, and peaceful than those other forms of government mentioned above. This is seen among the *Assyrians*, *Egyptians*, and *Parthians*. Indeed, to use examples closer to us and more familiar, it is seen among the *Spanish*, in *England*, and in *France*. No other kingdom can be compared to these in terms of longevity, much less be preferred over them.

Hereditary kingdoms, where one member of the lineage always follows the other and succeeds according to the right of inheritance, are also much more blessed and flourishing than those where a ruler is called upon and elevated through election. This is clearly shown by the Roman Empire <note>The author refers here to the Holy Roman Empire, where the Emperor was chosen by Prince-electors rather than by simple inheritance</note>. This usually happens because elections rarely proceed correctly; instead, many reach such high office through political maneuvering and corrupt schemes. This has occurred many times when a Roman Emperor has passed away and a new one had to be elected.

And would to God that it did not also happen this way with the Popes and other spiritual prelates, among whom only virtue and skill should be considered.

For these and several other reasons, which I shall omit for the sake of brevity, it is in my opinion sufficiently demonstrated that a *Monarchy*—where one alone has the power to rule and command—is far better than the others and is to be preferred above them. And if any kingdom is well-ordered and to be praised for its government—not only for its stability and longevity but because it has always been better suited for growth and advancement than others—it is the glorious Crown of France. It will likely remain so for a long time, provided that certain defects, which we will discuss later, are changed and abolished, which can be done easily and well.

Primarily, there is one particularly magnificent and precious thing about the Crown of France: only male heirs succeed to the kingdom and belong to the realm. This is provided for and ordered by a special law called the Salic Law <note>original: "legem Salicam"; an ancient law code of the Salian Franks that, in this context, was used to exclude women from inheriting the throne</note>. Truly, this was not established in vain or without great deliberation. For in any place where women may follow or inherit a kingdom, it is impossible that it will not eventually fall to a foreign <term>potentate</term> <note>A monarch or ruler with great power</note>. This cannot happen without significant harm and danger, for such a lord, being raised by habit and nature in different customs and another language, will naturally believe his own ways are best. Therefore, he remains attached to them. Furthermore, the advisors and servants he brings with him into the kingdom must then be preferred over the locals. The best and most profitable offices, in terms of both dignity and income, are granted to them. Meanwhile, the local people—even if they are more capable and skilled—are overlooked. From this, great resentment, envy, and hatred can easily arise, not only among the nobility but also among the common man.

Then, the entire people—of both high and low standing—accept, honor, love, and fear him as their natural authority, ordained and granted by God. It matters little if he is of a more distant line or degree to the deceased King, as has recently occurred and as we have seen when King **Charles VIII** <note>Charles VIII (1470–1498) died without a male heir, leading to the crown passing to his cousin, Louis XII.</note> and **Louis XII** <note>Louis XII (1462–1515) succeeded his cousin, demonstrating the stability of the French line even when a direct son was not available.</note> passed away. It was also provided for and confirmed through a special law <note>The author is likely referring to the Salic Law, which dictated that the French throne could only be inherited by male descendants.</note> such that in future times no dispute is to be feared on this account, and no doubt can arise regarding the **succession**.

However, so that I may demonstrate and clearly bring to light that the **Kingdom of France** is set up and ordained to be governed more wisely than others, I will briefly explain the current state of its government and the **commonweal** <term>common good</term> based on the previous old statutes and laws which they have used. First, one must acknowledge it as a great and useful thing that the royal power and all the other **Estates** <note>The "Estates" refers to the social orders of the realm: the clergy, the nobility, and the common people.</note> throughout the whole kingdom are so reconciled and equally bound to one another that a great discord cannot easily arise therein. It is indeed true that in human life nothing is eternal or permanent, and by God’s providence, it may well happen that this kingdom—as mighty, powerful, magnificent, and vast as it is—might fall into decline. This has happened from the beginning to one **monarchy** after another, and to one kingdom after another, as we mentioned above: that the healthier a man is and of a good **constitution** <term>complexion</term>, and the more moderately he lives in eating and drinking, the longer he remains in good health. So it is with kingdoms and principalities as well: the better they are established and provided with good laws, the more resilient and stable they are, and the less harm can come to their government.

But in those **monarchies** and kingdoms where succession takes place, as in this Kingdom of France, it is nevertheless not good, but rather harmful and very dangerous, when many new lords follow one another and many pass away. For it can often happen that a powerful, wise, and sensible King is followed by one who is equal to him neither in understanding, virtue, nor manhood, but is instead entirely unfit for rule, or perhaps even still a **child**. From both of these flaws, much discord and damage can follow—not only because of the King’s person, but also because of the malice and roguery of those assigned to him as advisors and guardians. This usually happens when God wishes to punish a kingdom, land, or city according to what they have deserved. # The First Book.

...the kingdom stands in its highest bloom and has risen to its most powerful state, and thus floats in fortune and honor, one expects and fears the least. This flows from the fact that men do not consider the inconstancy of fortune, but live on in their prosperity, just as one sits joyfully with good wine until he is full and drunk. They do not thank God for the grace of such prosperity even once, nor do they consider that both fortune and downfall stand in His hand.

&emsp;&emsp;If, however, such a storm were to occur in the Crown of France—which Almighty God forbid—there are nonetheless (praise God) ways and means by which the King can be kept in check, should he step too far in his government or conduct himself improperly, or if he cannot come to rule due to age, through his overseers, guardians, and councilors. For although the King has an appropriate status, his honor, and dignity, he is not permitted or allowed to rule and act in all matters according to his own pleasure. Rather, he must leave it and let it remain with that which is measured by right and equity, just as one has most diligently provided for this with quite magnificent laws and decrees, and has intended for the same, which also cannot be overturned or changed without great effort, trouble, and labor, regardless of the fact that one sometimes attempts to do so with force.

<margin>**Julius Caesar** writes in *Book 6 of the Gallic Wars* <note>original: "libro 6. belli Gallici"</note> that the **Druids** among the French or **Gauls** <note>original: "Gallis"</note> in ancient times, and before they came to the Christian faith, held the supreme power. They usually traveled once a year to a place located in the middle of **France**, where people would go and bring their grievances before them, and what they decided had to be strictly followed.</margin>
&emsp;&emsp;There are primarily three pieces, like three chains or halters, with which the power of the Kings of France is bound, linked, and moderated: namely, **Religion**, **Jurisdiction**, and **Policey** <term>this refers to 'Polity' or civil administration and public order</term>. As far as **Religion** is concerned, it is found that the French have always and at all times applied themselves to religion to the highest degree and held it in great esteem, even at the time when they had not yet come to the true knowledge of God and the Christian faith, and had their **Druids**, who were their bishops and priests, and were in great standing among them, as **Julius Caesar** reports. After the Gauls <note>original: "Galli"</note> recognized the Christian religion, they were the first and foremost among the far-flung peoples who accepted it. They also hold to that which they have once recognized with all seriousness and diligence to this day, and allow no heresies to take root among them, as **Jerome** <note>Saint Jerome (c. 347–420 AD), a prominent early Christian scholar.</note> wrote of them. They also hold to this so stiffly and firmly, and are so far superior to others, that Spain, England, and Germany have more than once reformed and improved their churches according to the French rule. In addition, our kings have always and at all times had the calling that they, especially before others, applied themselves to preserve the churches from error, and had a diligent watch so that no heresy might arise among them. Therefore, all other nations turned toward **Paris** and, as if from a pure spring, learned the knowledge of religion. For this reason, the Kings of France also attained and received the name ***Christianissimus***, that is, the **most Christian** <note>original: "der aller Christlichste"</note>. Whichever King now wishes to be well-accepted and well-regarded by the people, he must apply himself to faithfully and earnestly uphold religion,

## Of the Government of the Crown of France

And when a harm arises in the kingdom, they immediately blame it on the ungodly king—as has happened more than once—although it is sometimes more the fault of other people than of the kings.

&emsp;&emsp;If, however, the king conducts himself and his nature in accordance with religion, then he does not act against the Law; he does not behave proudly, nor does he let himself be tempted by greed. But if he does not do so, then every bishop or clergyman who is of a good and blameless life, and who has a reputation among the community, has the right and power to rebuke the king and to remind him of his office. Such a man need not shy away from or fear anyone; for the king must be concerned that if he lays a hand on such a person, he might fall into disfavor with the people. This freedom, to my knowledge, exists in no other kingdom—or is at least not so great—to deal with a king in such a manner. Furthermore, kings are instructed from childhood and held to be God-fearing, and to keep the clergy in honor and dignity. Now, if the common man believes that the king has a merciful God and therefore prospers and fares well, they will be much more favorable toward him than otherwise, and he will have all the more followers in times of need.

# The First Book.

...to inspect and consider letters and mandates; and if they find anything suspicious or unseemly within them, to reject the same. As for criminal matters <note>original: "peinlichẽ Sachen" — referring to capital crimes or cases involving physical punishment</note> regarding a misdeed someone has committed, even if the King has forgiven such a crime, the Parlements <note>In France, a *Parlement* was not a legislative body like in England, but a high court of justice</note> uphold the law so earnestly that almost no one dares to rely on the King's intercession to undertake something great or to sin. Even if the judges occasionally allow themselves to be swayed by the King’s petition and mercy, and must remit the punishment of the offender, it often happens later—when the King’s grace and favor have diminished or been lost—that they take that same offender into greater punishment than if the King had never petitioned for him at all.

&emsp;&emsp;Furthermore, such judges of the Parlement remains in office once they have entered it, and none shall be removed from such an office (unless it be for the sake of a great crime). If he is to be blamed for something he is said to have done, or is to be accused thereof, it must happen before the Council in which he previously sat. However, if one is removed by the King’s command without a legal judgment, and another is appointed in his place, the successor should not rejoice too greatly in this. For it is customary to watch his conduct so closely <note>original: "auff die schanze zu sehen" — an idiom meaning to keep a sharp eye on someone's actions</note> that he can hardly escape without punishment when his accounts are settled. And because they remain in their office continually, and can easily see for themselves that nothing can harm them as much as their own misconduct, they must be all the more diligent in legal proceedings so that no one suffers injustice.

&emsp;&emsp;For this reason, the authority and power of the Law in all of France is held in such great and high esteem that it may perhaps occasionally be attempted to be changed or bent, but it can in no way be overthrown. Although it also has its flaws and failings which require change and improvement—as there is nothing in the world that cannot become changeable over time.

&emsp;&emsp;The third band, or the third fence, is the Administration <note>original: "Policey" — this refers to the broader civil order, statutes, and public governance</note>; these are the laws and decrees which the Kings of France have made, established, and confirmed one after another, and which cannot easily be changed or abolished. And if the Kings were to attempt this, they would make the people resentful and disobedient, especially regarding the laws of the Royal Domain <note>original: "Patrimonij"</note>, which the Kings may not change, provide for, nor alienate <note>To "alienate" in a legal sense means to sell or transfer ownership of land or assets</note> unless the highest and most extreme necessity is at hand. Even then, such matters are weighed with such great diligence by the Royal Councilors and granted with such conditions that no one easily undertakes to buy them.

&emsp;&emsp;Though the Kings have the power to use the kingdom's income as they please, all expenses are nevertheless brought before the Treasury and the Master of Accounts. They have the power to weigh and reduce those expenses if they find that they have been too excessive, or useless and in vain. This is directed toward the highest equity and is not acted against the common good, but rather happens for the common...

# On the Government of the Crown of France

...for the best of the common good. For if such public income, rents, tolls, and public interest <note>original: "Zinse" — here referring to various forms of tax or tribute</note> assigned to the Kings were to be entirely spent, and no public reserve were set aside and kept for when a war or other necessity requiring money should arise, the people would be forced to make a levy from their own pockets and give money to their great detriment. However, because it is maintained (as mentioned) that they cannot act according to their own pleasure, the Kings are thereby held in check <note>original: "im Zaum gehalten" — literally "held in the bridle"</note> so that they do not become too indulgent or give away too much.

Beyond these, there are many other laws of the Crown of France which I shall omit for the sake of brevity, letting it rest with these principal ones through which the royal power is significantly moderated. This redounds primarily to their great praise; for if they had unconditional power to act as they pleased, they would be much less perfect. Just as God is Almighty, yet nonetheless not imperfect—for He cannot sin, but His perfection is rendered all the more glorious and wonderful thereby—so too do Kings become all the more praiseworthy when they submit themselves to their own laws and conduct themselves accordingly. They are, and become, closer to perfection through this than if they had the power to deal with all the realm's income as they saw fit, or to command and provide everything. In this case, as stated, this government is closest and most similar to an Aristocracy <note>The author uses "Aristocracy" in the classical sense: a government balanced by the "best" men or institutions, rather than an absolute autocracy</note> and endures the longest.

Furthermore, there are three principal Estates <note>original: "Stende" — the formal social orders of the realm</note> in France: first, the Nobility; second, the People and the Cities; and third, the common populace <note>original: "Pöfel" — referring to the lower classes or common masses</note>. Each of these three Estates has its own circumstances, laws, and statutes which they must use and uphold. These are so reasonably moderated and balanced against one another that no one part can overpower or suppress the other, nor can they join together against the King to create a mutiny. I will speak of the [other] Estates hereafter. Concerning the Estate of the Nobility, it is the case that the nobility is provided with great income and also with great freedoms. For this reason, they also hold the Kings very strictly and firmly, and are ready to stake body and life for him and the common Fatherland. Therefore, they pay no tribute <note>meaning they are exempt from certain taxes</note> and may carry their armor everywhere. They also have enough income and advantage that they can maintain themselves honorably and have no cause to pursue usurious or other dishonorable dealings—which, according to the custom of this land and our Kingdom, is not permitted to them. But when they must go with the King and wait upon his service, they are maintained in such a way that they need suffer no want. For there are so many offices and services in the Kingdom of France for which only those of the nobility are employed, that one might serve in an office for a quarter or half a year and look after it, and for the rest of the year he may be at home attending to his own affairs. All these of the nobility have their annual salary from the King, and there is not one among them who does not have hope for a higher office. As for the princes and great lords in France, they also have much influence among the nobility...

# The First Book.

...especially for those who otherwise do not have all too much; for such gentlemen may likewise expect various favors and benefits from the King in return.

Beyond this, it is a fact that the Kings in France continually maintain and support a large and powerful mounted force <note>original: "Reisigen Zeug" — referring to the heavy cavalry or Gendarmerie of the French royal army</note>, for which they employ the nobility. Within this mounted force are many offices distributed among the nobility, though this occurs more in times of war than in peace. The most prominent members of the nobility—after each has distinguished himself, conducted himself well, and striven for honor and virtue—are appointed as Colonels, Lieutenants, Marshals, Cavalry Captains, and so on. Others are employed as legates <note>original: "Legaten" — diplomatic or military envoys</note>; some become Ensigns, some Cuirassiers <note>original: "Kürisser" — armored cavalrymen</note> (of whom there is a great number), and some are Archers. Those who are unable to wear armor due to their age must serve the others. When no war is at hand, they may remain at home, and they can save a good portion of their pay if they are willing to live a somewhat modest life.

Furthermore, it is hard to believe how many offices there are throughout all of France which are distributed solely among the nobility. Some of these extend over an entire province or territory, some over cities, some over market towns, others over various borders, citadels, villages, castles, and the like. This is to say nothing of the highest offices, which are granted only to princes, such as those we call in our language the Constable, the Marshals <note>original: "Marescalli"</note>, the Admirals, and many more. In their special generosity, the Kings also tend to distribute annual gifts among many of the nobility who are in their service; these individuals are called pensioners <note>original: "Pensionarios"</note>, soldiers, or mercenaries, regardless of whether they are currently being utilized in active service.

From all this, it appears clearly enough that the nobility in France enjoys a great advantage and is held in honorable and high regard. In my opinion, this is not without justification, as they must protect the fatherland from enemies and are preferred over others for their virtue and manhood—traits for which not only they, but also their ancestors, are praised.

The second estate <note>The author here groups merchants and the "nobility of the robe" (lawyers/officials) into this second category</note> also possesses no small advantage. To this estate belong the traders and merchants, who can generate such great profits that they may trade and conduct business throughout almost all of France. The nobility in France does not apply itself to the business of trade, yet they nevertheless tend to spend great sums on clothing and finery. To this second estate are also usually assigned the positions in the cavalry and other offices that deal with money, such as those concerning escorts, customs, and the like. Likewise, they hold the offices of Judge and Bailiff <note>original: "Schultheißamt"</note> and all that pertains to legal proceedings, which are truly not only honorable but also profitable offices. Indeed, in France <note>original: "Gallia"</note> there are more judges, bailiffs, advocates, proctors <note>original: "Procuratores" — legal representatives</note>, court clerks, and the like than in any other place in all of Christendom.

Thus, this part of the second estate has the advantage that, even if they leave off their merchant trade, they may instead make use of such profitable offices. However, because this estate carries so much profit, they are hated not a little by the nobility for it. Those who are not part of it...

In the <term>Third Estate</term> <note>The "Third Estate" (German: *Dritte Stande*) refers to the commoners—everyone who was not a member of the clergy or the nobility.</note> are the common people and those of low birth, who

so that the <term>Knightly Estate</term> <note>The nobility or "Ritterstand."</note> may be maintained in its dignity,

military exercises and cannot otherwise easily sustain itself. Secondly,
so that the people have reason to strive for virtue, honor, integrity,
and manliness, so that they might thereby reach the first and best estate.

For through such hope, those who are in the lowest rank
can reach the second, and if they persist therein for a time, they may
finally reach the first estate. From this, it follows that so much less
envy, hatred, and resentment arise among the estates when they see and
realize that for those who strive for honor and virtue, a way is made to
move from one grade to another and thus obtain goods and honor.
If this means were not available—if the middle and lowest estates had
no hope of rising—then these two estates would find cause to
harbor hatred and rebel against the first estate, especially among
those who are proud and ambitious people who are pained by contempt.
Such people could easily incite those of their own estate against
the powerful. From this, all sorts of danger and trouble could arise,
which, however, cannot take place here, because one has such means by
which even one of low estate can come to high honors and dignity.

# The First Book.

...and maintained. For one who was a common citizen could first reach the <term>knighthood</term> <note>German: *Ritterstand*; the rank of the lower nobility, often achieved through service or royal favor.</note>, and subsequently be taken into the Council.

Thus, with us, the <term>clerical estate</term> <note>German: *Geistliche stand*; the clergy was considered the First Estate and offered the most significant path for social advancement through education.</note> is open and common to everyone—to whoever has the desire to study. From this it follows that often those who are of a quite lowly origin, through their skill and virtue, reach the highest honors and dignities. Thus, Cardinals and Bishops, and wealthy prelates are sometimes made from them. This gives young fellows a reason to apply themselves all the more diligently to their studies and the liberal arts.

I have also, for my own part, always considered it necessary for the <term>common good</term> <note>German: *Gemeinen nutz*; the welfare of the state or public interest.</note> that <term>church benefices</term> <note>German: *Pfründen*; an ecclesiastical office, such as a parish or bishopric, that provided a guaranteed income (a "living") to the holder.</note> should be granted to those for whom there is hope that they might serve the Church with their skill and good life. If this does not happen, most church properties remain with the princes and bishops, who then distribute them among their servants and stable-hands as payment. If someone has applied all diligence to his studies, but does not have a good friend at Court, it does him no good. From this it follows that the "unlearned asses" <note>The author uses a sharp metaphor here—*vngelchrten Esel*—to criticize those who hold high church offices without the necessary education or moral character.</note> hold most, and even the best, benefices. Therefore, it is necessary to keep watch, not only in our Crown of France, but also at the Roman Court, that a middle ground might be reached. I will say no more of this for now.

But what has been said here regarding the order of the estates is to be understood so that one may see how appropriately, finely, and pleasantly all three estates are joined together, and how one gives his hand to the other. And if one of them commits a fault, it is easily remedied. For if the nobility ventures to attack, injure, or burden the others, they are checked by those who pronounce the law and hold <term>jurisdiction</term> <note>German: *Jurisdiction*; referring to the legal authority and the court system, particularly the Parlements of France.</note>, since their power and reputation are so great that everyone else, however great they may be, must obey their decrees and commands. In the same manner, if the common people, or even the <term>rabble</term> <note>German: *Pöfel*; a dismissive term for the lower classes or an unruly mob.</note>, venture anything, as sometimes happens, the <term>knighthood</term> <note>German: *Ritterschafft*; the armed military class of the nobility.</note>, as those who have their armor and know the use of war, can easily restrain and defend against them, so that they remain in their station and undertake nothing wanton, but live peacefully with one another. Because they have no cause for rebellion and can achieve nothing but putting themselves in danger, they love, honor, and uphold the King from all estates, as a founder and beginner of such great benefit and magnificent order. If it also happens that he desires something from them, they are obedient and willing to perform it and to come to his aid in common need.

But if some specific persons occasionally "overstep the line" and become disobedient, a remedy and means can soon be found for the matter so that it is stilled, like a fire that is about to start burning, so that it goes no further.

And let this be enough said of that which I mentioned above: namely, that I have more clearly indicated and brought to light how and in what manner the praiseworthy Crown of France is quite magnificently [established] with good laws and ordinances...

# Of the Government of the Crown of France /

...royally provided for. Now I wish to come to the second part, which is no less difficult than it is useful; for therein is reported and shown what great failings and defects exist in our <term>common good</term> <note>German: *Gemeinen nutz*; this term refers to the "res publica" or the collective welfare of the state and its people.</note> in France, and how these might be changed and improved. Although I must confess that this is a great matter, which does not depend on the understanding of one single man alone, but rather requires many sensible and wise people, yet the love I bear for the fatherland and the common good compels me to bring to light here—as far as my ability extends—what I have learned through my modest understanding, actions, effort, and labor until now.

However, I do not wish to prescribe any law or command to anyone, but simply and plainly to bring to light that which seems good and right to me in this case, and subsequently let others, who understand it better, judge and pass verdict upon it. And since [the responsibility] for this common good rests primarily with the King, it must be the first, highest, and best requirement that he be a pious, wise, and sensible man. For if he has the subjects of the realm obedient and willing in all things, he can easily ensure that the good, wholesome, and useful laws remain in force and effect, and, conversely, that the harmful and useless ones be abolished. Secondly, if he arranges his conduct and character rightly and honorably, he gives cause through such an honorable and good life to all estates and the entire structure of the Crown of France to also lead such an upright, honorable, and modest life and to follow him. Thus, the other officials and governors will also be less likely to overstep their mandates; instead, each one individually and in particular will strive to do what befits his office and not commit any offense for which he might be punished, but rather follow the King's example.

Now, if these four virtues were present in a king—namely, understanding, experience, prudence or wisdom, and love for the common good—then one should desire nothing further from him and should rightly be perfectly satisfied with that. But because (as I fear) few will be found who are endowed with such virtues and graced by God, and even if some were found, nevertheless—since the kingdom is obtained through inheritance and not through such virtue, and since these things depend solely on the King's actions and practice—we must here take hold of those matters with which a pious and righteous regent should concern himself and expand upon them further. This is just as Aristotle, the <term>tutor of Alexander the Great</term> <note>original Latin: *Alexandri Magni Preceptor*</note>, and other great, experienced, and learned people have done, and prescribed to such great lords how they should conduct themselves in their entire life and being.

In what manner a <term>common good</term> should be righteously governed, how a regent should be formed, and what virtues he should possess—of these things both the Greeks and Latins write so abundantly and magnificently, as do some in our French language, that it would be far too long to recount it all here, and it would be foolish to try to add anything to what they have written. For in my opinion, nothing new or better can be devised or brought to light that is useful for the government of the common good.

# The First Book.

...could also bring nothing to light that the ancients had not already considered. Rather, some have treated these matters in the manner of a dialogue—such as **Aristotle**, **Xenocrates**, and **Thomas Aquinas**. Others in a historical manner, such as **Xenophon** in the book called *The Education of Cyrus* <note>original: "Paediam Cyri," referring to the *Cyropaedia*.</note>, in which he describes him as a king and recounts his life, customs, and deeds; not that he actually lived, acted, and conducted himself in that exact way, but rather so that those who wish to be righteous rulers should adopt such customs and live as he prescribed for them. Others have attempted and brought such things to light with *Panegyric Orations* <note>original: "Orationibus Panegyricis"; these are formal public speeches delivered in high praise of a person.</note>, or powerful, beautiful, and long speeches of praise, as **Cicero** praises **Pompey** and the younger **Pliny** praises the Emperor **Trajan**. Likewise, similar things have also been written in our French language. Beyond this, there are still others who describe the lives and conduct of princes, <margin>Erasmus also praises King Philip of Spain.</margin> not that they actually lived, acted, and conducted themselves so, but as an example to others, whereby they give the pious cause and incitement to do good, and deter the others from their evil nature and life; just as **Valerius Maximus** used this argument masterfully and well, and has with great diligence collected and magnificently described not only the Roman but also the Greek examples of pious and honorable people, as well as evil and shameful ones.

Now, if the princes and great lords were to read such books themselves, or hear them read by others, and take to heart the magnificent, beautiful commands, examples, and reminders—of which such books are full—and diligently impress them upon their minds, then they would not need much more or greater instruction. However, because they cannot retain all such things due to their quantity and length—partly because of the weakness of human understanding and memory, but primarily because of the great business and affairs with which they (if they otherwise have wit and understanding) are occupied daily, and thus have so very little remaining or idle time; or, if they are still young, they spend more time in pleasure, gaming, and "good days" <note>An idiom for a life of ease or leisure.</note>—for these and other prominent reasons, I am moved to grasp as briefly as possible that which seems to me necessary for the government of the <term>common good</term> <note>German: *Gemeinen nutzes*; the collective welfare of the state.</note> in France. From this, it will follow that the lords who are occupied with serious business will not be held back or hindered from their work, nor can I be tedious with this short instruction to those who do not care much for such magnificent, useful, and necessary things, such that they would grow weary of it.

In which endeavor I hope to succeed all the better and more easily, because our current King in France is of such magnificent understanding that he will most gladly receive that which is best and most useful; to which end Almighty God will grant him luck, blessing, and all prosperity. And since God holds the hearts of kings in His hand, we wish to call upon Him from our hearts and pray that He would grant him His Holy Spirit, to arrange his reign in such a way that it may redound to the honor of His Divine Name and to the welfare and best interests of the realm.

## Concerning the Government of the Crown of France

...belong to these dealings and are necessary to discuss before we come to those matters which lie hidden beneath common knowledge. Just as physicians are accustomed to do when they encounter a patient in whom they sense something that might bring a great sickness, they tend to focus solely on that and take care to prevent it with good counsel and remove the cause, rather than thinking only of how they might quickly make the patient healthy again. Therefore, it will be primarily necessary for the King that he, by all means, does not act in haste or undertake anything thoughtlessly, whatever it may be. Instead, he should take his people into counsel, just as the best and most prominent people and rulers have always done and practiced. For even our Lord God assigned the wisest and best people from the whole nation to the prophet Moses, whose counsel he was to use in his governance <note>This refers to the biblical account in Exodus 18 or Numbers 11, where Moses is advised to delegate authority to seventy elders.</note>. For it is not well possible that one person alone—or even a few, let them be as skilled, clever, and wise as they will—can bear and perform the burden of such a great government as this Kingdom. Rather, they would be so blinded and overwhelmed if they burdened themselves so heavily with affairs that they would not know what they were doing or which task they should take up first, since they can have neither the understanding nor the time enough to reflect upon matters everywhere and as necessity requires. And one can easily commit a great sin if he rushes into a matter and does not consider it sufficiently.

In addition, the King must also consider that he should look out for himself and not bring those things that should be kept secret and private among many people, nor let them come before a general council. For it often happens that one must include certain people in a council because of their dignity and rank, and whatever pleases the larger part is accepted and held as right. This, however, often carries great danger, because it is always the minority who, through understanding and experience, can recognize and judge what is best and what is right.

And even if nothing is at hand that must be put to deliberation, such a magnificent gathering is nonetheless laudable in itself, and highly glorious for the King and the entire Kingdom. It also rarely fails that in such a Council and advisory body something does not arise to be spoken of that might, in time, bring some benefit to the Kingdom.

But no one should force himself into this Council who is not appointed or enrolled for it—unless something is entrusted to someone who does not belong to such a Council to be considered or carried out because he possesses more and better information and knowledge of it. But such a thing should not be done often or commonly, but should happen only for important reasons, so that not everyone takes cause to force themselves into such a Council.

And so that all things proceed in their proper order, necessity requires that either the King himself sit in the Council, or that he constitute and appoint one from the most prominent or from the entire assembly of councilors as <term>President</term>. This person should be of such a character that the other councilors honor, love, and hold him worthy of such an office more for his virtue and understanding than for the sake of honor and the presidency. But in truth, it would be most useful if the King’s Majesty himself sat in the Council, especially when great and highly important matters are at hand for deliberation. For it is not enough that one reports the <term>Decree</term><note>A formal decision or law reached by the council.</note> and what has been decided to the King, if he is not himself present during the deliberation and hears the reasons why the Decree was so made and decided—principally when it is somewhat obscure and cannot be easily understood by the King.

# Of the Government of the Crown of France

[The King] learns from the counsel, understanding, reason, wisdom, and eloquence of each; he hears each one speak separately on matters, discerning who excels the others in handling affairs and who is most useful for business. Also, the advisors are thereby made alert and diligent in their deliberations, as they must consider all things rightly and well and allow no falsehood to slip in <insert>secretly</insert>, since they see the Judge <note>The King is here described as the "Judge" of the counsel he receives.</note> before their eyes, who can bear witness to the advice they have given.

From such advisors, the King should choose three, or at most four, whose virtue and skill he holds in the highest regard. With these he may converse privately about the affairs that have arisen and are to be put to deliberation before he enters the <term>Council</term><note>The "Concilium" refers to the broader royal advisory board.</note>. For it can happen that in such matters something occurs which is not appropriate for everyone to know, but must be kept in secret; or perhaps someone within the Council is personally involved, making it unwise to bring the matter before the full assembly. Therefore, the King can deliberate much more securely with these few, and based on their assessment, he can subsequently recognize and weigh the opinions of the other advisors more <unclear>easily</unclear> and see how they are formed. Even if something has been decided in the Great Council, he may still discuss it with these few; for it is not always the best course simply because the majority has decided upon it and deemed it good.

When the King notices that the advisors are not in agreement, or are divided in their deliberation, or if he dislikes what the whole body has deemed best, he should not let his feelings be known in their presence. Instead, he should save his thoughts until he has the opportunity to further move and consider the matter in an inner circle. And even if he finds that his own opinion has better grounding than that of the Council, he should not become <unclear>hostile</unclear> or attack them rudely. Rather, in the next <margin>☛</margin> Council, he should most graciously and gently indicate what caused him to be unable to accept their advice and why, for this or that reason, he had to conclude upon the other path. This, however, must and should only happen rarely, and only for great and highly important reasons—that the King should deviate from the Council and reject their opinion. For disadvantage might follow from it; if the advisors noticed that their counsel no longer carried weight with the King, they might harbor <unclear>discontent</unclear> toward him and would no longer reflect on matters with such earnestness and diligence. Therefore, the King must act cautiously so that he does not do too much in this regard; he must not value the few advisors mentioned above too highly, nor the others too little. Above all, he must not prefer one advisor so far above the others that he alone has the King’s ear, forcing all others to conform to him in their speech and actions. For that person would prepare nothing other than a <term>servitude</term><note>original: "Seruitut"; referring here to the King's potential political enslavement or total dependency on a single favorite minister.</note> for him. By pulling everything toward his own profit, such a person inflicts great damage on the common good. For it is very difficult for one who floats above others and has everything according to his pleasure to maintain <unclear>modesty</unclear> everywhere and not occasionally "overstep the line" <note>The German idiom "über die Schnur hauen" literally means to chop over the chalk-line, meaning to behave excessively or overstep boundaries.</note>.

And just as it is a frivolity to believe everyone without distinction in such cases, so too would it be a great imprudence if a Prince or King refused to trust or hear anyone who wished to report something to him and warn him of his danger. Therefore, he should maintain a middle ground: even if he has given someone great power, he should not grant him so much that the person would dare to do anything without shame or fear. One should not let such things pass, but rather keep them in fear, so that if they commit a crime or act unjustly, they are certain that it will not be overlooked or end well for them.

Now, that the King should have one among all his <term>Advisors</term><note>The "Rähte" are the members of the royal council.</note> who is more private than the others, and with whom he speaks and deliberates on his private affairs and the management of his household—that I will not oppose. Indeed, if a Lord lacks such a man, he is missing no small piece of his welfare and happiness. But in great, serious, and important matters, it is not intended that a Lord should crawl into a corner with one man alone and deliberate with him. For it is impossible for one man alone to know, understand, provide for, consider, and execute the affairs of an entire Kingdom. And the more cautious and sensible a person is, the more reluctantly he should want to load and take such a great and important burden upon himself—unless <term>ambition</term><note>Original: "Ehrgeitz," meaning a craving for honor or status.</note> and <term>pride</term><note>Original: "Hoffart," referring to haughty arrogance.</note> have so blinded him and made him so senseless. As one sometimes sees, people allow themselves to be so "ridden" and blinded by the Devil that they take everything upon themselves.

Therefore, the King should by no means keep such great matters of high importance hidden, but rather reveal them to those whom he trusts the most. For sometimes there is as much danger in silence as when someone reveals something at an inopportune time and brings it to light. <meta>This page continues the discussion on the King’s relationship with his advisors, specifically focusing on the dangers of false accusations and the necessity of discretion in matters of state.</meta>

# Concerning the Governance of the Crown of France

...entrust something great in secret / so that he should reveal and show it to no other person. For if such informers are rascals and rogues / they may thereby easily find opportunity / to lay a trap for some good man / and out of envy invent and present something / from which one can draw a great suspicion / so that the King must then torment and worry himself / because he promised not to mention it / which he must later regret / and be ashamed of.

Therefore / it will be necessary for him to know such people well beforehand / that they are faithful and discreet / before he entrusts them with so much / so that he may speak and act with them no less freely and safely / than with himself. For many great, brave, and important affairs have failed / and come to nothing / because they were not kept secret. So it also happens at times and quite often / that even when there are people / who have thoughtfully considered something useful and good / they do not dare to bring it to light out of fear of the envious / who <term>calumniate</term><note original="calumniren">To calumniate is to make false and malicious statements about someone to damage their reputation; to slander.</note> everything / and interpret it for the worst / because they must fear that it might come to harm.

In particular, it will be highly necessary that the <term>counsels and deliberations</term><note original="Rahtschläge vnd Deliberation">This refers to the formal processes of debate and decision-making within the King's inner circle.</note> / mentioned above / be kept in the strictest secrecy. And although the counselors / by virtue of their sworn oath / are bound and obligated to keep the counsels secret / it can nevertheless do no harm for the King / when great and important matters occur which should be kept quiet / to remind them of their sworn oath and duty / that by virtue of the same / they should keep the matter secret within themselves. If he also learns that something has leaked out / he may well have an inquiry made as to who revealed it / and if he finds that person / he should punish him in such a way that others take offense at it / and have a dread [of doing the same]. For it can easily happen that a matter placed in counsel / if something leaks out / the whole matter falls apart / and comes to nothing / as when one deliberates on a war, etc. For this reason, the King should certainly hear every person's opinion and thought / but not conclude in a general council; rather, whichever counsel is best / he should follow / and arrange the business accordingly. Although it seems safest to me / that he should open his mind to one or two [trusted advisors] / regarding what he intends to do / especially when he informs them that he does not sufficiently understand the matter / that has been deliberated and is at hand. And it is better for the King in this case / to keep himself a little humble / than to hold himself too high / and thereby despise the counselors out of arrogance.

In my opinion, I consider this to be especially necessary concerning the business / of what the <term>Council</term><note original="Concilium">The author uses the term "Concilium" here to refer to the formal body of political advisors.</note> does. For if a Council or assembly is established in such a way / then it is not easily possible that such a danger or so great a misfortune can occur / which cannot be easily countered / since nothing can arise for deliberation of which there has not previously been noble speech and consideration. It follows from this / that one can prevent things with less lengthiness, harm, and disadvantage to the <term>common folk</term><note original="meinen Volcks">The general population or subjects of the kingdom, whose lives are impacted by the state's decisions.</note> / than if one acts without any deliberation.

# The First Book.

...or premeditated / when the need and the business are at hand / to speak to the matters / and to deliberate upon them.

And although, in my opinion, enough might have been said regarding these things / since usually many / the more learned and wise they are / the more doubts and considerations they have / and the more they weigh in their deliberations / and have various sudden ideas / for which reason I am prompted / to set down and show something further here / which will be useful and necessary for the preservation and increase of the whole Kingdom / some of which belong to <term>domestic governance</term><note original="Haußregiment">This refers to the internal management of the royal household and the immediate affairs of the court.</note> / and some to <term>civil administration</term><note original="Policey">From the Greek 'politeia', this refers to the general regulation, public order, and governance of the state for the common good.</note> and external government. Therefore, it shall and must be confirmed and established from those same origins / and also increased and preserved henceforth.

Because these things require a further explanation / and our people have for a time and until now taken little interest or concern in them / I must describe and explain it a little better. That we have previously made mention of the **three bands** / with which the Kings (so that they may not act according to their own pleasure) are held in check / did not happen without reason / for such things carry nothing other than the highest <term>equity</term><note original="Billigkeit">The principle of justice and fairness that balances the strict application of the law with mercy and common sense.</note> within them. And the King could do no more pleasant favor for Almighty God / and no more useful and wholesome thing for the whole people / or what would be more honorable and glorious for him / than that he strictly uphold this Law / and live according to it; for through this / and for the sake of such Royal and magnificent virtue / he can make himself so deserving / that he may justly be called a **Father and protector** or guardian of the people. If he, however, should do the opposite / and wishes to act in all things according to his own pleasure / he will soon lose the praise and favor of the people / and will be hated by everyone / and held for a tyrant.

And since we should entrust the beginning and end of all our affairs to God / and look to Him alone / Kings or Princes should primarily provide for religion with diligence. This is especially true for the Royal dignity in France / because he is endowed by God with such a powerful / magnificent and fruitful / most beautiful Kingdom / whose ancestors / with their magnificent / most powerful / Christian and laudable deeds / earned the name of the **Most Christian** <note>The title 'Rex Christianissimus' (Most Christian King) was a hereditary title of the Kings of France.</note> / and it would therefore be a great and eternal shame for them / if the current Kings did not wish to walk in the footsteps of their ancestors / and did not pursue their virtue. Therefore the King should be diligent / and see to it / that religion and the holy Christian faith remain undefiled in the Kingdom / and that long-condemned <term>heresies</term><note original="Ketzereyen">Beliefs or doctrines that contradict the established teachings of the Church.</note> are not tolerated among the people / so that the name of our Savior Christ is not shamed or dishonored / which many have a very fine and frivolous habit of doing. But such frivolity should be earnestly punished by the King / so that others may carry a dread of it / if he wishes to have a gracious God; for unfortunately more wickedness and vice sticks in our customs / than we believe.

# On the Governance of the Crown of France

...[they] do not consider such vice to be a disgrace any longer. Primarily, however, they should hold the <term>Apostolic Church</term><note>In this 16th-century context, this refers to the Roman Catholic Church, emphasizing its claimed descent from the Apostles.</note> in honor and high esteem; and all the more so, because their ancestors received such great fortune and welfare from it. In addition, the King should be diligently commanded to ensure that the churches everywhere in France remain undisturbed in their liberties and <term>justices</term><note original="Gerechtigkeiten">This refers to the legal rights, privileges, and jurisdictions held by the Church.</note>, and that they may be protected and prayed for. On the other hand, the clergy should also do that which their office [requires]; and where they are negligent in this, he should have them earnestly punished by those to whom it belongs and who have the power to do so. For it is not enough that one [knows] what is right, honest, and Christian; rather, one must see to it that [it is] put into practice, and lived and done accordingly, which is proper for those who lead others, but most especially for the [King], whose deeds and dealings cannot be hidden. And since the [people] usually are accustomed to judge themselves according to their Lord, King, or Prince in his life, as the saying goes: <note>original: "wie der Herr ist/ so ist auch das Volck"</note> "As the master is, so are the people." Therefore, the King should strive to shine before his subjects with a beautiful example of an honorable, good, and Christian life, and hold the clergy—especially the most prominent who are in office and government—in their [honor] and dignity, yet in such a way that the King's majesty and dignity are maintained.

There is much mistreatment in this, not only here but also in [other places], in that the clergy are held so poorly and unjustly; to which they perhaps give cause by their unchaste, disorderly life. Which, although it is [as clear as day], one should nonetheless not [disregard] the entire clerical estate, but rather keep and maintain it in its proper honors and dignity. Just as with the King—regardless of the fact that he does not always behave properly for his station, but often <note original="vber die schnur tritt">Literally "steps over the cord," an idiom meaning to overstep one's bounds or behave immoderately.</note> oversteps the bounds—nothing is taken away from his royal [dignity]. It is certainly true that shame and vice rule enough among the people, and there is no <term>estate</term><note original="stand">The "Estates" were the social classes of the time: the Clergy, the Nobility, and the Commoners.</note> that does not need reforming and [improvement], especially among the clergy. But one may blame the Kings for this, who sometimes—indeed, most often—allow such evil, incompetent people to become <term>prelates</term><note>High-ranking church officials, such as bishops or abbots.</note> and enter the clerical estate, and place them there themselves. This carries with it a greater harm than can be believed; for the people's salvation and bliss are put in danger by it, and the common man, seeing such a reckless life, takes offense at it, follows such an evil life, and also becomes such a wicked rogue. Therefore, the Princes and great Lords may well believe that they will provoke our Lord God to the highest degree through this, and must give an account of it on that day <note>A reference to the Day of Judgment.</note>. They should reasonably consider that while they otherwise pay such diligent attention and inquiry to other servants and household staff—on whom not so much depends—such as cooks, hunters, falconers, barbers, and the like, and appoint them with such foresight, as well as stable masters, guards, archers, and military captains; they should have done much more in the appointment of clerical offices. How they (because they are negligent in this) will stand before the judgment seat [of God], when they shall give an account of it, there they will [see].

# The First Book.

...[to] find that they set the Church and religion—which our Lord Christ redeemed with his [own] blood—so far aside, and (as mentioned) pay greater and more diligent attention to other minor things. They provide for the poor churches with such people who, with their evil unchristian customs, nature, and conduct, lead the common people away from the right path toward Hell; and even if they are not punishable in their lives, they are yet so coarse and unlearned that they cannot fulfill their <term>office</term><note original="Ampt">This refers to the specific ecclesiastical duties and spiritual responsibilities assigned to a clergyman.</note> in teaching.

But since we nevertheless (as we have the name) wish to be Christians, we should also prove it with deeds. If we also give belief to the holy Gospel and God's Word, we may certainly hold it to be true that in a Christian <term>commonwealth</term><note original="gemeinen nutz">Literally 'common utility,' this refers to the well-being of the whole society or the state.</note> no greater plague can exist than where the churches are burdened with loose, wicked people, or coarse, unlearned asses. For from such a source, as from a spring-well, all other vices flow out. Meanwhile, the spiritual heads—Bishops and Prelates—usually provide for the lower offices and parishes to care for the poor people with those of their own kind: that is, unlearned and incompetent evil rogues. Thus, such spiritual goods, which in former times were brought together with good-hearted and Christian intent and were ordained for right and honorable use, are now to be so shamefully and wickedly applied, consumed, and wasted. And what is most highly to be lamented: religion thereby falls into mockery and contempt.

Although I have also entered into the <term>spiritual estate</term><note original="Geistlichen stand">The clergy or the social class of those in religious orders.</note> myself, I must nevertheless confess and say that this is the truth regarding how things now proceed in the spiritual estate. This is not to say that they should be removed or driven out for that reason, but rather that each one should do what is suitable and proper for him by virtue of his office, so that the great scandal might finally cease. They should consider not only the harm to the common people entrusted to their care, but also the harm to the entire Church; for among many of us clergy, one will hardly find even a few who could rightly change and improve these defects, or who could be in a general <term>Council</term><note>A formal meeting of church leaders (like the Council of Trent) to decide on matters of doctrine and administration.</note> with honor and dignity, to speak, propose, and deliberate upon what is necessary for the common good as the need requires. And if only a small number were at hand who were capable of this business, there is no doubt that things would soon be brought into a better state. For the Truth—when it is brought to light in an upright and skillful manner—always remains in its position and cannot be overturned; moreover, the Almighty always comes to the aid of His own with His counsel, as has always been experienced, and has happened more than once in our time.

It is certainly true that these words benefit me little, but rather are more against me, if I were to consider and look toward self-interest. But the truth is so strong that even those who deny it with their deeds and their customs—even if they do not do so publicly with words—must yet confess it in their conscience and silently. Since I know, then, how heavily the spiritual estate sins in this and acts wrongly, in that they do not fulfill their office and represent it rightly, I must confess the same...

I do this also willingly, and I consider that the primary and great sin in this matter is that the bishops do not themselves reside with their people, to whom they have been assigned. The King would also have many on his side who would agree with his opinion and will in this and would be helpful to him. ### The First Book.

...out of ambition or for the sake of attaining wealth, pushing themselves into such places, yet accomplishing so little there that would benefit the common good; indeed, countless many are scandalized by their profligate and evil lives. And so much we wished to have said concerning the **first bond** <note original="erstẽ band">Refers to the first of the essential pillars or obligations of the French monarchy.</note> of the praiseworthy Kings of France—namely, concerning **Religion**, which pertains to our holy Christian faith.

**The Second** is that they apply themselves to the highest degree so that **justice** is done to everyone, and that they earnestly uphold justice within their kingdom, protecting and maintaining it. For through justice alone are all kingdoms, principalities, and lands maintained and made stable. And where there is no law, nothing else can exist there but pure robbery, injustice, and harassment, murder, and every misfortune. And because—praise be to God—the noble Crown of France is especially provided with magnificent laws above others (as was partly mentioned above), the King shall earnestly uphold them, since after religion there is no more necessary, useful, nor magnificent thing. Kings and Princes should also know that they are primarily ordained by God to order their kingdoms and principalities in such a way that justice may be done to everyone, whether they be poor or rich. And nothing is so highly contrary to the Royal **Office** <term>Office</term><note original="Ampt">The divinely ordained duty and function of a ruler.</note>, and against its nature, as if he were to fail to organize <term>jurisdiction</term><note original="Jurisdiction">The legal authority and system of courts.</note> or wished to weaken it. Just as those who are appointed to provide for the churches and the judgment seats cannot rightfully demand their wages unless they faithfully and uprightly preside over their office and administer it. Indeed, in such a case, one can even hold them to the requirement that they must return what was given to them. In the same manner, one could also speak of Kings if they refuse to inquire after the law, for God earnestly demands such from them. Thus, after the provision of religion, nothing on earth gives a King or Prince such a magnificent reputation and favor as the **administration of justice**. And people can be moved further by this than by war and great severity to do what they are duty-bound to do. For by nature we are all so minded that we cannot well tolerate force, and can be moved much further with good words and equity—as histories sufficiently show—than with violence.

Although much and at great length could be written and dealt with concerning jurisdiction and the law, and what deficiencies occur therein daily, I will nevertheless recount and explain only three things which befit a King in this regard. **The First** is that the King appoints pious and learned people to the judgment seats. And since he does not have so much understanding that he can judge them himself—whether they be capable and sufficient in skill and learning in every respect—he shall command other understanding people to look out for learned and sensible people and to declare upon their oaths that they know nothing else but that such persons are fit for such an office, as the ordinances and statutes of the Realm require and allow. But he, the King, shall earnestly address and remind the judges, counselors, and <term>assessors</term><note original="Beysitzer">Associate judges or legal experts who sit on a judicial panel.</note> that they should faithfully preside over the law and their office...

For since there is no lack of laws in the Crown of France, but rather a lack of faithful people who preside over them and love the **common good** <note>original: "Gemeinen nuz"</note>, it follows that when these **judicial officials** <term>judicial officials</term><note original="Gerichtshelter">Refers to magistrates, judges, or court assistants who administer the law.</note> either pay attention to their own profit—to increase and improve it—or judge according to favor, they thereby inflict unspeakable and horrific damage upon the common good. And because the office of the judicial officials lasts indefinitely once they are accepted, and they are not removed without particularly great and important causes (as mentioned above), so that they may act rightly and preside well over their office and satisfy it, necessity will require that the King occasionally have them summoned and speak to them personally, with reminders and earnest presentation that all sorts of complaints and grievances are brought to him from the people concerning them. It should, therefore, be his earnest command for them to behave differently and better, so that the people have no reason to complain, with mention of punishment where he finds them at fault. But those whom he knows to be diligent and faithful in their office, he shall honor and promote, and also be more gracious to their children for the sake of such faithfulness, to give others cause for **integrity** <note>original: "redligkeit"</note>.

Especially he shall diligently prevent gifts and bribes from having a place or intervening in the courts, which usually happens when those who have no understanding of such matters petition on behalf of others, relying on the fact that they have free access to the King. But the King should give no place to such intercessors, nor allow himself to be moved by anything. And if such an office should be vacated, he should consult in secret with his own advisors, and if he finds from their report that the one who has applied for it—or rather, who has been indicated by the law—is fit for such an office, the King should let him have it for free, and not for the sake of any intercession. Furthermore, he should prevent with the utmost diligence, when two parties come to court in a dispute, that he by no means grants any favor to one side against the other through writings or oral intercession at the court. For the King’s name carries such great weight even with judges; though they have sworn to uphold the law, they may nevertheless be moved to waver when they hear the King's name, especially if the matter is of great importance. This can happen all the more easily in our courts because there is a custom of judging more according to **equity** <term>Equity</term><note>original: "Billigkeit"; a legal principle where judges apply fairness and common sense rather than strictly following the letter of the law.</note> than according to the written laws, in which much disadvantage and harm can occur. Although what has been said should primarily be understood regarding civil matters, **capital cases** <term>Capital cases</term><note>original: "Peinliche Sachen"; legal matters involving physical punishment or death.</note> should no less be included regarding intercession. Therefore, he should also earnestly reject those who intercede for such wrongdoers—such as willful murderers, adulterers, rebels, and the like—so that others may fear to approach him, and wicked rogues may guard themselves against such shameful deeds and crimes. It is much better for a lord to show himself earnest and unyielding in this regard; for if he is lenient and easily moved, he does nothing other than give cause for many great and evil deeds.

Although much more could be said regarding this part, it would be too long here; therefore, we must let it rest and proceed further. Yet one more thing remains, which is highly necessary to remember: namely, that the King, with the common counsel of sensible, honorable, and pious people who wish for the **common good** <note>original: "Gemeinen nuß"</note>, should consider and deliberate how long-winded legal disputes and quarrels might be shortened, and how they might be resolved appropriately and according to equity. For it is almost too common in our land for matters to be so prolonged and drawn out that many fall into the deepest poverty through this alone. Likewise, not a few, because of the great expense and because they do not trust themselves to withstand the power of their adversaries, must sometimes let even the best cases lie and fall, and abandon them.

Therefore, if the King—who should be a protector of the Law—knowingly entrusts such a knightly **office** <note>original: "Ampt"</note> and such a great thing to evil, greedy, unskilled, and unfit people, or allows them to attain it, he is, by all fairness, guilty and obligated to compensate for whatever damage and disorder results from it. Just as **merchants** are accustomed to compensating for whatever their **factors** <term>Factors</term><note>original: "Factor"; business agents or managers who acted on behalf of a merchant or company.</note> and agents negotiate. 

And since the office of judge lasts indefinitely once they are accepted (and they are not removed without particularly great and important causes, as mentioned above), in order that they act rightly and oversee their office well and fulfill its requirements, necessity demands that the King occasionally have them summoned and speak to them personally. He should remind them and earnestly hold before them that all sorts of complaints and grievances are brought to him by the people regarding them. It is therefore his earnest command that they behave differently and better, so that the people have no cause to complain, mentioning the punishment he will impose where he finds them in breach. However, those whom he knows to be diligent and faithful in their office, he should honor and promote, and be all the more gracious to their children for the sake of such faithfulness, to give others cause for integrity.

Above all, he should diligently prevent **gifts and bribes** from having a place or creeping into the courts. This tends to happen when those who have no understanding of such matters intercede for others, relying on the fact that they have free access to the King. But the King should give no place to such **intercessors** <note>original: "Vorbittern"; those who use their influence or proximity to the King to request favors for others.</note>, nor allow himself to be moved by anything. # Of the Governance of the Crown of France

I

...the customs, order, and habits of the entire Crown of France are contained. It is under these that this kingdom has flourished and expanded to such a degree. The King shall strive to follow these same statutes and decrees himself without hesitation and to uphold them. Furthermore, he should earnestly command that they be kept throughout his cities and lands, especially because at the beginning of his royal reign, he must promise with an **oath** <note>This refers to the Coronation Oath, where the King swears to uphold the laws and privileges of the realm.</note> that he intends to do so. Now, if he acts against this, he will not escape the punishment of God, who does not leave such things unpunished; he will also be plagued by a restless and evil conscience. In addition to this, he will cause great resentment among his people, so that they will hold him in less regard, and thus he weakens himself.

The first and most important thing, however, is that the King diligently prevents himself from alienating or selling any more of his **patrimony** <term>patrimonii</term> <note>original: "Patrimonij". This refers to the "Crown Estate"—the lands and revenues traditionally belonging to the monarchy which were legally considered inalienable (could not be sold) to ensure the King remained financially independent.</note> (that is, the property of the Kingdom) than is permitted to him by custom and the statutes of the Realm. For otherwise, he would give cause for much disorder. If he waives or grants something to one person, others will soon appear who believe the King should likewise favor them because of their merit and great status. And if he then refuses them, he has already soured his relationship with them; immediately, a secret resentment and opposition arises among the servants, which otherwise would not have happened if he had treated one the same as the other and granted nothing to any, but instead gave a refusal to everyone at once.

For where one estate is not at peace with the others and does not mean well toward them with loyalty, no stable government can be hoped for. Therefore, the King should pay special and diligent attention to the **Nobility**, which is the first and foremost estate. He should not only let them remain peacefully in their old and existing privileges and rights, but also conduct himself toward them in other matters so that they understand he has great trust in them and wishes them to increase in all welfare and prosperity. For through this estate—and through their virtue, integrity, diligence, and labor—the Kingdom first and primarily took its beginning, was subsequently greatly increased, and finally confirmed and maintained unto this day. These are the ones who, when the common Fatherland was in distress and hardship, rescued and preserved it from enemies; for these men, no danger is too great or too heavy so that the King may remain in honor and dignity. They also love and honor the King more highly and more than the other estates, just as they have more opportunity and cause for this than other estates, as they are of more honorable descent and are raised and kept in virtue, honor, and integrity from their youth. Therefore, it is also fitting that they precede others with manliness and virtue, and look after...

...that they do not speak, do, or act in any way that does not well become their noble heritage.

Therefore, the high offices and captaincies <term>Hauptmanschafften</term> <note>These were military commands and administrative positions traditionally held by the aristocracy.</note>, be they spiritual or secular, should more rightfully be distributed to them, those of the nobility, than to those from other estates, and they should be provided for with such roles. This is rightfully done and is not contrary to our laws, provided that they are capable of performing them. But if they are not fit for such offices, they should not be used for them, nor should they be allowed to attain such offices, so that the disorder previously mentioned <note>Referring to the potential for administrative chaos or corruption if incompetent men hold power.</note> may be prevented. For if the King were to look only at lineage and heritage, and not at understanding, skill, and knowledge, and were to distribute offices poorly based on favor, then the greater part of the nobility would rely upon their birth and strive for neither skill nor honorable deeds. But when they see that the King holds those in highest regard who strive for good skills, honor, and virtue—regardless of the lineage or tribe from which they come—then they must of necessity also apply themselves to the same, if they wish to stand out before other nobles and be elevated to noble honors, dignities, and status. And this applies not only to those offices common to both estates <note>Likely referring to positions that could be held by either the nobility or the "Third Estate" (commoners), such as certain judicial or financial roles.</note>, but also to those which the nobility alone can claim and which are specifically designated for them. A distinction is also to be made among the nobility, as some come from a greater lineage than others, and one surpasses another in valor <note>original: "Mannheit"</note>, virtue, skill, and integrity.

Beside this, the King should also see to it that he does not concede or give in to the nobility so much that they oppress the other estates or forget their own condition and fail to show him his due honor. For from this, great disruption usually follows, as has happened several times in France. Therefore, the King should preserve the upper hand and supreme power with diligence and not let it be taken from him. Instead, he must ensure he retains such authority among all estates that they recognize and hold him as their rightful superior and lord. He should indeed show himself kind and gracious toward his people, yet in such a way that he does not lose his honor and royal dignity thereby. Regarding his duty to govern and judge, as well as his oversight of the officials to whom he has commanded such tasks to be carried out, he should maintain strictness and earnestness. This was reasonably and wisely provided for by our ancestors, and supreme necessity also requires that it be maintained with earnestness so that it remains so, for this is one of the highest and greatest ornaments and protections in the Crown of France.

But the King should not allow his officials <note>original: "den seinen" — referring here to the King's direct agents or royal administrators.</note> to impede or hinder the great lords and the nobility in their courts and jurisdictions <note>original: "Gerechtigkeiten" — the legal rights and feudal privileges that allowed nobles to hold their own local courts.</note>, unless for great and important reasons which have been deliberated upon with all necessity. For if the King, without sufficient inquiry, wanted to grant standing and belief to every complaint, the result would be that no matter would be so minor that a person would not dare to complain against the lords and nobility before the King, to the disadvantage and harm of the nobility themselves.

Secondly, so that everything in the courts proceeds in a uniform manner, the King must see to it that criminal and capital matters <term>Malefitz vnd Peinlichen Sachen</term> <note>From the Latin *maleficium* (wrongdoing) and the German *Pein* (pain/punishment); these were serious crimes involving physical or capital punishment.</note> do not go unpunished, but are punished most earnestly, and that no one is easily pardoned—especially among the soldiery.
