However, to completely waive a person's punishment is in no way to be tolerated, nor is it advisable; for punishment must be carried out so that others may have a dread of it and be kept in fear. And in times of war, the punishment should be all the more severe, as I shall say hereafter when I come to the military regulation <term>Kriegßregiment</term>.

Regarding the distribution and provision of offices, a King should pay close attention to the character, nature, and understanding of those known to him, such as those of princely status or other powerful men. And if one comes before him who is of a proud and rebellious spirit, he should not allow that person to attain any office, so that he cannot abuse his evil disposition against the King himself, or the Realm, or the common good <term>Gemeinen nutz</term>. For such people, when they have power, can easily reach that point and take cause for such evil intentions over a minor matter and be moved toward them. But those whom he recognizes as being by nature and character pious and virtuous, the King should prefer above others, honor them, and provide them with great offices, so that they have cause to serve the common good well. In this way, the people will be all the more willing to be obedient and submissive to them.

But the King is likewise advised to be cautious and not grant anyone too much power—certainly not more than he deems proper for his Majesty, or more than would be good and useful for the same. Rather, he should conduct himself in such a way that they and their subjects honor him and keep him before their eyes as their rightful head, from whom they have received their high status and office. When great matters arise, they should have recourse to him alone and look toward him. For if he does not use the means of distributing offices to reserve this authority for himself, he cannot maintain his standing among the people. Then those who are in great offices and in the provinces—likewise their governors, legates, and officials—will venture into untimely and headstrong dealings, and in time undertake such counsels as will be of little benefit to the King and the common good, just as is known to have happened in the Roman Empire.

But all this is not only for the sake of this present time...

It will also be necessary to watch diligently that the middle estate <term>mitlern Stande</term> <note>The "middle estate" refers to the rising class of townspeople, lawyers, and officials who stood between the peasantry and the high nobility.</note>, mentioned above, is not granted so much power that they might surpass the nobility and diminish their estates and income. For there are primarily three things which greatly weaken and diminish the holdings of the nobility. The first of these is that they have many legal disputes <term>Hadersachen</term> in the courts, and one lawsuit follows another, which are drawn out for an immoderately long time and incur a mighty great cost. From this, we see and experience that court-holders and judges come to own and possess the estates of the nobility, through which the nobles fall into such incapacity that they can no longer maintain their status or fulfill their duties. Thus, they are forced to do and undertake much that does not befit or suit them. This grievance could well be prevented if only the King and those he employs as advisors would pay attention to it with earnestness and diligence.

It is much the same with the questors <term>Questorn</term> <note>From the Latin *quaestor*, these were high-ranking financial officials or treasurers.</note> or stewards <term>Rentmeistern</term>. For although they must have no small power and authority so that they may collect the money belonging to the King’s chamber, there should nevertheless be a limit for them. They should not be permitted to use such means by which they become rich and powerful while, in contrast, many others who come from better lineages fall into poverty.

In the same way, one should also keep the merchants <term>Mercatanten</term> <note>Derived from the Italian *mercatante*, referring to large-scale traders or wholesalers.</note> or tradesmen (who were named last among the three) in check and give them their limits so that they do not rise too high. One sees that the nobility live sumptuously and ostentatiously, spending much on clothing, through which two things they suffer a great decline in their livelihood. Great damage to the common good results from this, in that an unspeakably large amount of money is led out of the kingdom annually by the merchants. By this, the common good is weakened no differently than if one draws the blood from the veins of the human body. Therefore, in this case, nothing would be better, nor could the King perform a more useful work, than to abolish all such superfluous and vain expenses. For God is greatly angered by this. And even if the King increases their salaries—as must happen if they are to carry out their services and the offices to which they are appointed—it is nonetheless in vain. For the more one gives them, the more and greater expenses they incur, and the more the subjects of the realm, who must provide this, are burdened. Those of the nobility who do not hold office then wish to maintain such superfluous expenses as well, especially those who have their military commissions and are in the King’s Guard. Therefore, those who wish to strive for honor and virtue find that their income—when they pursue such splendor and...

And when they have spent everything, they must resort to robbery and harassment. Although this is forbidden among us with harsh penalties and is also seriously punished, it is in vain as long as the root of this evil is not uprooted. It is just as when a limb of the human body becomes diseased through bad "fluxes" and moisture <note>The author uses the "humoral" theory of medicine, where illness was caused by an imbalance of bodily fluids.</note>; even if one can sometimes soothe the pain, all medicine is in vain and for nothing unless the causes of the illness and bad moisture are removed through purging <term>Purgation</term> <note>original: "Purgation"; a medical treatment to clear the body of waste or "bad humors."</note> and other medicines.

Accordingly, nothing would be more useful for cutting off this inappropriate and excessive splendor of clothing than for the King to make a beginning with himself and his courtiers. As has been well experienced elsewhere, his greatest fame and honor do not rest in the splendor of clothing; rather, such excess diminishes his authority <term>Authoritet</term> and reputation more among the people. And while he cannot be sufficiently and magnificently adorned with clothing for his person and the office he holds, one can certainly find someone of the lowest rank who can outdo him in this regard, so that the King must yield to him in finery.

->Therefore, it would be best and most laudable to maintain moderation in clothing, rather than being overly concerned with it. For it is certain and true, as they say: "Too much is unhealthy."<-

This should not be understood as meaning that those who are with and around the King should be dressed too poorly, from which dishonor might result for the King. Rather, only the great excess of splendor should be cut away; and a measure should be prescribed for everyone according to their status <term>Stande</term>, condition <term>Condition</term>, and office <term>Ampt</term>, which they must observe. For it is indeed unseemly that everyone, regardless of their status, should be allowed to dress as they please. If the King were to take a serious look into this, it would greatly benefit the common good <term>Gemeinen nutz</term>. For just as a leech sucks the blood out of the human body, so also is the common good exhausted, so that no money remains with anyone and it vanishes before one realizes where it has gone.

Next is another matter that primarily concerns the merchants. Neighboring kingdoms, principalities, and lands have the custom—and strictly forbid it—that no money be carried out of their lands. This custom, however, is not observed by us in France. And even if something is commanded regarding this, it is bypassed and not kept even by those who rightly should observe it. This happens frequently, as they say, for the purpose of serving and complying with the neighbors so that they remain friends and are not angered. For what reasons could they put forward, if they received as much from us as

### The First Book.
<meta>catchword: let</meta>

...let them come to us. Furthermore, it is indeed the case that France is so fertile in all growing grain and fruits—which is such an abundance—that one can well do without other lands in what they might bring to us. Thus, it cannot easily be lacking; because of this, many among them are all the more negligent in the cultivation of crops. He, however, would be worthy of great praise among all descendants who could provide all estates of this kingdom throughout with good ordinances and laws. If this were to happen, there would be no doubt that France would surpass all other kingdoms, which I would easily demonstrate in case of necessity if it were needed, but it does not belong here.

Now as for what concerns the Third Estate <term>Third Estate</term> <note>original: "Dritter Standt"; in the social hierarchy of the time, this referred to the commoners, including peasants, artisans, and merchants, who were distinct from the clergy (First Estate) and the nobility (Second Estate).</note>, as the common people, regardless of the fact that it is easy to understand from what I said above what is proper for them to do; yet I do not mind—since it is nevertheless significantly important—to repeat the same here and briefly recount it. Initially and first, the King should be mindful that he does not overburden the common man with taxation and tribute <term>Tribute</term> <note>original: "Schatzung vnd Tribut"; various forms of taxes or assessments paid by subjects to their ruler.</note>. Rather, he should show himself so that they may perceive that he would gladly grant them their advancement and welfare, and cares for them. For in this, a special pleasure is done for our Lord God; the King maintains thereby a good and quiet conscience, and it serves him for luck and all welfare. For he can lay no great taxation upon the common man without their great and noticeable harm, since through this, that which their entire welfare depends on is withdrawn from the poor people, and which they can in no way do without, since they, their children, and servants are to have their sustenance from it. Which is then very unjust; nor do I doubt that our Lord God will be moved to heavy anger by such unrighteous undertakings and the sighing of the poor as often as it happens. Nor should the lords think that such taxation benefits them, or that they will become richer from it.

Kings should weigh and consider this, and also know that a government will not gain much goodwill through this way from the common man if they have no measure for their greed and taxation. From this also, rebellion and other mischief can easily arise, especially if some misfortune occurs at the same time. And where the people do not want to die of hunger, they must leave house and home and betake themselves to other places, which then results in disadvantage and shame for the King. And where such people then go and settle, they will cry out against such tyranny and unrighteous taxation and give the King a bad name. The others, when they are ruined, will leave farming aside and take the beggar's staff in hand.

Therefore, the King should cut off and moderate all excessive splendor and costs, so that the assets taxed from the poor people do not turn to harm. For the assessment of money, as much as is customary, should have a measure, since an immoderate amount of money is collected and brought in, but yet is spent for the best neither for the King nor for the common utility <term>Common Utility</term> <note>original: "Gemeine Nutz"; the general welfare or public good.</note>. Instead, the treasurers, because they rely on their power and authority...

# On the Government of the Kingdom of France

...let [the money pass] / and often handle the same money poorly / using it for their own benefit and to increase their own livelihood.

It is indeed true that one cannot do without treasurers <term>Treasurers</term> <note>original: "Rentmeister"; officials responsible for collecting and managing the revenues of a lord or the crown.</note>, nor can affairs proceed without daily expenses. However, many defects creep into this business, such that great and very diligent oversight is necessary. This is especially true because greed and pride—which usually accompany such positions—do not fade, but rather gain the upper hand more and more.

How these things should be moderated and improved, however, will rest solely in the King's hands.

The second point is that the King should not permit the poor common man to be oppressed by the powerful, nor allow anyone to suffer injustice. Instead, justice should be done for one as much as for the other, and both poor and rich alike should enjoy it. But above all, care should be taken that no violence or harm is inflicted upon the poor by those who follow the profession of war <note>original: "welche sich deß Krieges gebrauchen"; referring to soldiers or military personnel.</note>. Although this is sufficiently provided for in our statutes and strictly forbidden, it does not seem to help, but is all in vain. From this, a two-fold mischief follows: First, that the poor people are so plundered by the soldiery <term>Soldiery</term> <note>original: "Kriegsvolck"</note> that they cannot give the King what they owe him. Second, that they become bitter enemies of the soldiers and wish from their hearts that they might simply be killed.

The last point is that the poor common man should be left with his old traditional justice and freedom, and nothing of it should be diminished. Rather, allow them to practice and carry out the trades, arts, and crafts that befit their estate and are permitted to them. Likewise, one should not prevent them from practicing the trades through which they can rise from the lower to the middle estate: namely, commerce <term>Commerce</term> <note>original: "Kauffmannschafft"</note>, learning the liberal arts, and participating in military exercises. And whatever else they can do, practice, and trade with honor and renown, the King should allow. He should graciously promote them, protecting and upholding them so that others, perceiving and noticing this, may likewise find reason to strive for honor, virtue <note>original: "Tugend"</note>, and integrity <note>original: "Redlichkeit"</note>. For if someone from the lower rank comes forward in such a manner through his virtue and integrity, and others see this, they can take a great example from it to distinguish themselves in the same way and strive for honor and virtue. And the fewer and rarer learned people are, the more the King should apply himself to give his subjects cause and incentive toward virtue, honor, and integrity—whether through the promotion of good arts, through military exercise, with commerce, seafaring <term>Seafaring</term> <note>original: "Schiffahrt"</note>, or however he can—so that they may be praised and lauded above others.

And since the welfare, salvation, and prosperity of this kingdom rest upon the arts of war and peace, I will hereafter write and treat of them in the Second Book, as far as my understanding and ability extend.

# The Second Book of Claude Seys-
## sel, on the Common Welfare of the Crown of France,
## and the Office of Kings.

<image-desc>A large ornamental woodcut drop cap 'D' featuring intricate scrolling foliage and floral patterns within a square frame.</image-desc>

THE entire power, strength, and welfare of the Crown of France consists primarily of four parts. First, that all Estates <term>Estates</term> <note>The social classes of the realm: the Clergy, the Nobility, and the Third Estate (commoners).</note> are unified and show the King his due reverence, honor, and obedience. Second, that they are powerful in wealth and resources and continue to increase in them. Thirdly, that the French are well-practiced and experienced in matters of war. And fourthly, that the cities and castles located on the frontier <note>original: "Frontir"</note> are most strongly fortified. These four parts must be deliberated with the highest diligence and, after deliberation, continually put into practice. For it is a futile thing—which could otherwise bring great benefit—to wage war abroad (as the saying goes <note>Likely a reference to the Roman statesman Cicero: "Leadership abroad is of little worth unless there is wise counsel at home."</note>) unless the same has been previously planned at home.

Regarding the first two points, it is not necessary to say much, as we have already made sufficient mention of them above in the previous book. That I should say and remind much of the latter point is also unnecessary, as it is clearer than day that the highest necessity requires it more than I can write about. For everyone knows and understands how highly necessary it is that the King and the Realm have proper fortifications, which are best guarded, on the borders and frontiers. For such a fortress, being provided with provisions <note>original: "Prouiant"</note>, artillery <note>original: "Geschütz"</note>, and all necessities, and being so designed and garrisoned with soldiers that it can endure a siege until it is relieved <note>original: "entseze"; meaning to have the siege broken by outside reinforcements.</note>, can often bring great salvation, comfort, and benefit to the entire Realm. This has been sufficiently experienced not only in times past but especially now in our own times. Therefore, the King should consider this with special diligence and spare no expense, also allocating money and creating a fund for it—particularly in the region where the fortress is located, so that the country folk in times of war may have a refuge for their belongings and property and find comfort therein.

This, however, can most conveniently be done in times of peace. For it is less burdensome to the people; likewise, the fortress can be made more stable and better since one does not need to hurry so much, and the people are not as panicked as when one proceeds to such a work in haste, without any order, and must provide what is necessary in a rush.

Although the commanders <term>Commanders</term> <note>original: "Befelchhaber"; officers or governors in charge of specific districts or military installations.</note> are often very negligent in this, which results in noticeable harm and disadvantage to the King and the entire Realm. Therefore, they should hereby be reminded—if they otherwise wish well for the King and the common welfare—that they should by no means be dilatory in this matter.

<header>Of the Government of the Crown of France!</header>

However, since not everyone understands these matters, but rather only those who know how to handle them properly, and since a great deal of money can easily be wasted and spent in vain on building—as some men pay more attention to their own profit than to the common good—it would therefore be advisable for the King to moderate himself and travel from one province to another. He should primarily inspect the frontiers <note>original: "Frontir"</note> or borders and deliberate upon which locations are most suitable and necessary for building fortifications. Alongside this, he could also inquire as to how the subjects are governed and how the offices and officials <term>Amptleute</term> <note>Local administrators and magistrates who held authority in the King's name.</note> are managing their houses, where he would then discover many improper things. No matter which place he visits in the entire kingdom, he should show and conduct himself everywhere in such a way that the subjects recognize that he gladly oversees their welfare. Also, he should graciously hear those who have a grievance to bring before him, and whatever he finds to be unjust, he should seek to turn and amend. For through this, he can gain much more favor and goodwill among the people and achieve much more than through written mandates. Besides this, the officials and commanders, as well as the war-captains, are kept in fear, obedience, and restraint, so that they attend to their offices all the more diligently and do not overstep <note>original: "vber die schnur hauwen," an idiom meaning to "overstep the line" or behave immoderately.</note> their bounds, which they often do when one does not keep a close eye on them <note>original: "nicht auff die Eisen sihet," literally "does not look at the irons," referring to checking the quality of tools or horseshoes.</note> or occasionally catch them in the act.

Now we wish to take up the third part, namely what concerns military matters and affairs, of which it is not so easy to speak or treat. At the beginning, we mentioned above that military affairs belong primarily to the Nobility <term>Adel</term>, and that the common man should not be permitted to concern himself much with them. However, this point requires further reflection and explanation. For firstly, it cannot be denied that if the common people become accustomed to war, they can easily be moved to disobedience and may defy the King and the Nobility, rising up against them and even completely suppressing the Nobility, as happened just a short time before living memory. Conversely, it is also dangerous enough if the subjects are entirely inexperienced and unpracticed in war. For if we are attacked by foreigners, we cannot have an upright infantry <term>Fußuolck</term>, which one cannot do without when the English, Germans, or the Swiss wage war against us, for these nations usually fight for the most part on foot. Now, when our people perceive that such enemies are moving through the land with a great army—be they few or many—and even though our side may be strong and have their mounted troops <term>Reisigen Zeug</term> <note>The heavy cavalry or "Gendarmes," which was the traditional backbone of the French noble military.</note> with them, the people nonetheless huddle together and become faint-hearted, despondent, and terrified. Because the mounted troops notice this, they also begin to lose heart, considering that without the infantry they cannot long withstand the attack of the enemy. From this it follows that the enemies, to whom this is no secret, are all the more eager to wage war against the French <note>original: "Francken"</note>. This would not happen if the people—who are so very numerous—were permitted to practice themselves in matters of war.

<header>The Second Book.</header>

It is certainly true that the King, by virtue of his power and wealth, can easily and well hire foreign and overseas mercenaries <note>original: "Kriegsvolck"</note> when a war arises, and when it has reached its conclusion, he can let them go again. However, this cannot happen without noticeable damage; rather, it is more dangerous than if he had used the French for this purpose. For firstly, they carry a remarkably large sum of money out of the kingdom. Furthermore, it is not possible to trust them (especially when they are common folk, as the infantry usually are) as much as if they were French. Thus, they cannot be kept under constraint like our own people, nor do they yield such obedience; and when it comes to payment, one cannot satisfy them, or if they have committed a crime, one cannot take revenge upon them with punishment. Rather, it may well happen that the crimes are of such a nature that the entire kingdom is thereby put into harm and danger—such as when they are the cause of a battle being lost, or a city or castle being surrendered. Beyond this, there is also this to be feared from foreign mercenaries: that they might seize some place in the kingdom if they become too strong and gain the upper hand, so that they cannot be driven out again—as has indeed happened and taken place not only in France but also in other lands.

So it may also well happen, when foreign mercenaries have been hired, that they—either out of wantonness or because they are hindered by various causes—delay and remain absent, and in the meantime, the enemies inflict great damage upon the realm and the common good. In addition, it is even less advisable to accustom those who are by nature and disposition inclined to war to oneself with money and great promises, so that they explore all our circumstances—how we conduct our wars, what deficiencies we have therein, how discouraged the common people are, which parts of the country are fortified and which are open. Finally, they also learn how rich and powerful in goods we are, through all of which they then have all the more cause and will to wage war against us—which has happened to many kingdoms and lands, and recently to this kingdom as well.

For these reasons, it seems to me quite dangerous to allow the people and subjects in France to remain forever so inexperienced in military exercise <note>original: "Kriegsübung"</note> and to rely solely on foreign mercenaries. For one can demonstrate and prove from many histories that those who have overburdened themselves with foreign mercenaries have thereby come into remarkably great harm and danger—as happened to those of Carthage, as Polybius <note>A Greek historian (c. 200–118 BC) famous for his work *The Histories*, which detailed how the Roman Republic became dominant; he often wrote about the dangers of mercenary armies.</note> writes. Since danger is now present on both sides—with both foreign and domestic soldiers—it seems to me best advised that one should take up the path that has often been spoken of and deliberated upon: namely, that in all provinces of the entire kingdom, one should select a few from among all the people who are not infirm and have the appearance of having a desire for war, and who may be suitable and trained for it. One should appoint captains <term>Häuptleute</term> <note>Military leaders or heads of companies.</note> for these men from the same region, who know them and can therefore answer for them. But

# Of the Government of the Crown of France

These same captains should be honorable and upright people—not greedy, nor showing favoritism or partiality, especially in matters concerning the King and the common good. Furthermore, they should instruct their soldiers, according to ancient custom, in discipline and moderation. The Constable and the Marshals, as superiors, shall have command over them, as shall the captains of the cities and provinces. All of these shall apply themselves in times of peace to training young <term>recruits <note>original Latin: "Tyrones"</note></term> and soldiers. For this purpose, they shall appoint and take counsel from certain foreign, veteran, and experienced soldiers on how to conduct themselves, what weapons they should use, how to form battle lines and prepare for combat, and whatever else pertains to such military exercises. And when they hold a <term>muster <note>A formal inspection and counting of troops to ensure they are present and properly equipped.</note></term>, it shall be conducted with earnestness and diligent oversight, so that no fraud may creep in. Above all, this military support should be organized and maintained at the lowest possible cost to the common people, so that they may manage and sustain themselves. In the meantime, however, while our soldiers are being trained and learning how they should conduct and hold themselves in the field, and before one can rely on them entirely in an emergency, one must nevertheless hire a regiment of foreign <term>mercenaries <note>original: "Landsknecht," referring to professional, often German, infantrymen.</note></term> or foot soldiers to be used alongside our own. This is also for the event that, even if our soldiers are well-trained, we might be better equipped with infantry and our own men might have reinforcement. Furthermore, we would then have nothing to fear from the nation from which the soldiers are hired; rather, we could rely on them as friends, so that they do not act against us. However, before such a hiring is made, one must diligently consider and see to it that soldiers are recruited from a nation that acts honorably, uprightly, and faithfully, and in whom we can place our trust. Secondly, these should not be as strong as our own forces. For then they will not dare to attempt anything untoward, because they lack the power and cannot overwhelm our men. And if they should do something wrong, they can easily be forced to desist. When they see that not only our <term>cavalry <note>original: "Reisiger Zeug," referring to the heavy mounted men-at-arms.</note></term>—which is then most excellently equipped and trained, as well as strong and mighty in number—but also our infantry is capable and well-armed for war, they will not only refrain from daring any violence against our men, but must also bow before ours so that they are not overpowered by them. They will remain peaceful and united before our men; indeed, they will even have to take care and apply themselves so that they do not anger our men or provoke them.

From this it will then follow that so much money is not taken out of France, and the people are not so highly burdened with levies and <term>tributes <note>original: "Schatzung," referring to special taxes or assessments for military funding.</note></term>. Consequently, no uprising or tumult is to be feared. For the soldiers, who are appointed and mustered here and there in the French provinces, will

# The Second Book

...few of them and not gathered together, but lying scattered here and there, they cannot incite others to disobedience and rebellion or form alliances among themselves. Furthermore, they have no reason to stir up unrest, as their pay and maintenance are provided, and they otherwise enjoy privileges above others. Indeed, it is rather to be expected that for the sake of this kindness, they will help to prevent and forestall such trouble, and be at hand whenever they are needed.

However, I do not wish this to be understood as if it were my opinion that those who dwell on the borders of the Kingdom should not be more and better armed and practiced for war than those who sit in the middle of the Kingdom and dwell farthest from the borders. For that is not the intention. Rather, the <term>captains and governors <note>original: "Häuptleute vn Landpfleger"</note></term> who live on the borders should keep them to it and, on holidays or other convenient times, occasionally have them shoot for prizes with crossbows, bows, or <term>matchlocks <note>original: "Züntroren," an early type of firearm ignited by a match cord.</note></term>. Alongside this, they should exhort and earnestly command that everyone should prepare themselves with equipment for war, such as guns, armor, swords, and long pikes, and occasionally hold <term>musters <note>A formal inspection and counting of troops to ensure they are present and properly equipped.</note></term> among their people and let them practice. Yet, not with everyone indiscriminately, but primarily with those who are physically fit for it and have a natural inclination for war.

For it is indeed necessary that those who dwell on the border or <term>frontier <note>original: "Frontir"</note></term> have equipment so that they may defend their own when they are to be attacked and harmed by their neighbors. For without this, much bickering and quarreling arises across the border. If one were only then to order and summon soldiers from afar in such an emergency, that part of the country would have to suffer in the meantime before one could come to their aid and relieve them. It is also in the character and nature of things that those who live on the borders do more for their Lord's sake and hold more firmly to him than others, even allowing themselves to be beaten for it. Therefore, it is only fair that they should be exempted from the <term>taxes and tribute <note>original: "Schatzung vnd Tribut"</note></term> that others must give, for such reasons and because of the constant danger and damage they must always expect—just as happens among us. For they maintain the soldiers who are usually stationed on the border, keep watch, and must also work on the construction of the fortifications themselves.

Of the <term>armada <note>original: "Armata," referring here to a naval fleet.</note></term> and naval equipment I will speak hereafter: how it is to be established and why it is important. And because much depends on keeping the soldiers, both horse and foot, in check, obedient, and under constant <term>discipline <note>original: "Disciplin"</note></term> in times of peace as well as in war, both inside and outside the country, I will also say a little about that. For more depends on this than one can believe, and from it flows—just like from a spring—whatever good and useful things one may hope for from war. # Concerning the Government of the Crown of France

...kingdom and the <term>common good <note>original: "Gemeinen nutz," referring to the collective welfare of the state and its people.</note></term> significant damage arises when discipline is not maintained during war, but rather allowed to fail. Once we have explained how this occurs, we shall then entrust the instructions to other kings and those whom the King has appointed and ordained for this purpose.

Initially, the importance of such <term>discipline and military order <note>original: "Disciplin vnd Kriegzucht"</note></term> is known to all who have read the ancient stories and histories, especially those of the Romans. For they, in particular, maintained it with all diligence and earnestness, and achieved more through it than through their sheer power. Because of this, they ultimately achieved such great success, as <note>Valerius Maximus (c. 20 BC – AD 30) was a Roman author famous for a collection of historical anecdotes used to teach moral and military lessons.</note> Valerius Maximus and many others testify. They also name several generals and captains who overcame their enemies solely through this: by restoring the ancient military customs, despite the fact that those same enemies could not previously be broken by other means because discipline had not been maintained among the soldiery but had been allowed to decay.

This and similar examples should give cause to kings, generals, and captains to follow suit. Such military discipline consists of two parts which must and should remain together and cannot be divided or separated. The first is that a <term>general or commander-in-chief <note>original: "Oberste oder Feldtherr"</note></term> who leads the war and to whom the government of the troops is entrusted, must be a virtuous man and a brave hero. Secondly, the soldiers must yield obedience to him in all <term>reasonable matters <note>original: "billichen Sachen," implying orders that are just, fair, and within the laws of war.</note></term>.

For if a commander is <term>upright <note>original: "rechtschaffen," meaning both morally sound and professionally competent.</note></term>, and the other captains and officers, along with the common soldiers, are compliant and obedient to him, there is no doubt that everything must proceed correctly, well, and fortunately. But if there is a lack on either side—no matter which one—it is not well possible for things to turn out right or for anything righteous and praiseworthy to be accomplished. And if a commander is not experienced in all aspects of warfare and does not know how to conduct himself in all cases, or fails to actually carry out the punishment decreed by military law, he will be despised by his own men as well as by the enemy. And even if he ventures to achieve something with his troops, they will be unwilling, fearful, and resentful toward it—men who would otherwise be willing and bold if they had a competent commander who understood the situation. They would then consider no task or danger too heavy. For it is unspeakable what damage and disadvantage it brings when a commander is negligent, lazy, unskilled, and timid. For he considers nothing, deliberates on nothing, seeks no advantage, and settles nothing; rather, he is often deceived and fails so greatly that the entire common good is placed in danger.

And it is not enough that skillful and experienced people are assigned to him to help advise him. Rather, he himself should be cautious, wise, experienced, and understanding, so that he may comprehend what is being proposed in counsel. And when various opinions arise, he should know which is the—

We, however, find the opposite view to be more pleasing. For one with manliness and virtue, if he is faithfully assisted with good counsel, can achieve more than one who relies alone on experience and knowledge where there is no manliness.

This is evident in *Alexander*, *Hannibal*, and *Scipio*; likewise in *Pompey*, who became a <term>Commander <note>original: "Oberster," meaning a high-ranking military leader or Colonel-General.</note></term> before he had ever been a common soldier. They could not have possessed this through experience because of their youth, which otherwise would have been far too little and insufficient to accomplish such things. Because they possessed an innate manliness and <term>courage <note>original: "Herßenhafftigkeit," literally "heartedness" or bravery.</note></term>, they accomplished many and greater things than many others who were equally well and most highly experienced in war, but were not so bold and manly.

If only two men were presented to you: one who is most highly experienced in matters of war, but lacks the earnest manliness and courage necessary for a Commander; the other, though he might not have great experience, yet were a courageous, bold hero and undaunted in all things—I would truly prefer the latter over the former. This is partly for the reasons just mentioned, and partly because he who is manly can also gain experience over time. However, the former will only slowly acquire steadfastness and strength of spirit if he does not already possess it. Since it can hardly fail that one who has spent many years in war should be courageous and brave, and since, on the other hand, many are found who are courageous enough and ready to do everything, but entirely inexperienced in war—without a doubt, for this reason, *Marcus Cicero* would have given second rank to the science of warfare among the virtues necessary for a Commander, and awarded the prize [to courage].

If, however, a Commander is chosen from a high rank and noble lineage, such a thing gives him an excellent and magnificent reputation, as well as favor and love. Therefore, if someone of such high standing is available who is capable of serving as an <term>Imperatorem <note>Latin: "General" or "Commander-in-chief."</note></term> or Commander, he should be appointed or summoned before one of lower standing. # The Second Book.

...courageous and eager to put things into action. Such a high-ranking person, in my understanding and judgment, is rightly to be preferred above all others. He should also be assigned wise, honorable, and good people who can fulfill and carry out whatever he might perhaps lack.

Whether these things are primarily the responsibility of the King’s <term>Legates <note>original: "Legaten," referring to high-ranking representatives or lieutenants acting with the King's authority.</note></term>, since the administration of war is commanded to them in this case—nevertheless, even when the King himself is in the camp in the field, though he may have great experience in these matters, he should see to it that he undertakes no highly important or significant matter on his own, unless he has first deliberated and most diligently considered it.

The second thing with which a <term>Commander <note>original: "Oberster," a term for a high-ranking officer or general.</note></term> should be equipped, and which is necessary for him, is that he be eloquent and well-read and experienced in both ancient and modern <term>Histories <note>In this context, "Histories" refers to the study of past events as a guide for moral and strategic conduct.</note></term>. For when a difficult time or a great, important matter occurs that carries danger with it, requiring that one must address the soldiery, a fine and brave speech from a Commander does much for the cause. It can refresh the troops and make them <term>courageous <note>original: "hertzenhafftig," literally "stout-hearted."</note></term> even in the greatest need and danger. Otherwise, if they only look at one another while the need and danger are at hand, they must surely become despondent and faint-hearted. This can be seen and understood in more than one place in the *Commentaries* of *Caius Caesar*. For what such eloquence can achieve, when it is composed and provided with fine maxims and reasons, is sufficiently understood from the oration he gave at that time when he set out for <note>original: "Besantz," the city of Besançon.</note> and marched with the force of his army and all his soldiery against *Ariovistus*, the King of the Germans.

Many such examples and the like are found in *Xenophon*, in the book where he describes King *Cyrus's* military campaign into Persia—which book I have translated into our French language from the Greek. The same is found in *Sallust*, *Titus Livius*, *Quintus Curtius*, and almost all other historians. Therefore, this is my opinion, and I conclude thus: if the ancient custom of how one spoke to and addressed the soldiery in former times were brought back into practice, so that our Commanders also applied themselves to it, then great and notable benefit would arise therefrom for the Realm and the common good. And let this be enough said concerning the office of a Commander, or the King's Legate (that is, the one who holds the upper hand, commission, and command in the camp on the King's behalf).

Now we wish to briefly show what, on the other hand, it is fitting for the King to do. Initially, it is necessary—and indeed right in itself—that when he appoints a Commander or Field Marshal, all power over the entire soldiery be conferred upon him: to command, to forbid, to do, and to leave undone. Thus, there should be no one in the entire army camp who does not look to him and must be obedient to him. And should anyone make himself resistant, the Commander must have the right and power to punish him earnestly for it. ...while this is connected to the first part, I wish to speak of it specifically—not at great length, but only as much as is necessary for our present times, based on what I have seen myself and understood from other great and widely experienced people.

Principally, however, it is held that the entire discipline of soldiers is contained in three commands, among which the first and foremost is that the soldiers render due obedience to their Commander; concerning this, enough has been said previously. The saying of <note>Publius Cornelius Scipio Africanus (236–183 BC), the Roman general famous for defeating Hannibal.</note> *Scipio Africanus* is highly praised in this regard, when he said that a thousand obedient soldiers are better than ten thousand disobedient ones.

Obedience, however, depends for the most part—and primarily—upon the Commander himself. For if he conducts himself according to his office and fulfills its requirements, and if he is granted as much authority by the King as belongs to his office, then there is no doubt that his troops will indeed obey him. This is because no <term>nation <note>original: "Nation," here referring to a specific ethnic or regional group of soldiers.</note></term> or people is so wild and untamed that they cannot be brought to obedience through laws and punishment, and made to do what they are duty-bound to do.

A Commander must use severity for the reason that otherwise no order can exist; instead, everything becomes confused, and everyone does as they please. Everyone knows what harm such disorder brings to a camp and what evils result from it. Therefore, those Commanders and Captains who—for the sake of keeping favor and goodwill among the common men—easily forgive soldiers even when they have committed a gross offense, and at times <term>dissimulate <note>original: "dissimuliren," meaning to intentionally ignore or overlook a transgression for tactical or political reasons.</note></term>, are more to be scolded than praised. This is all the more true if the soldiers have acted against the Commander himself or against their <term>Articles of War <note>original: "Artickelsbrieff," the legal code and contract of service that every soldier swore to uphold.</note></term>. If such transgressions are allowed to go unpunished, it is impossible for anything other than great disobedience and wantonness to follow among the other soldiers, causing discipline to collapse. For the nature of soldiers is such that it is more fitting for a Commander to be serious with them than to be kind and gentle.

*Julius Caesar* was otherwise, and in other matters, almost entirely a kind man, but toward his soldiers, he was serious. Yet his soldiers did not hate him for it; indeed, they loved him intensely. For it commonly happens that Commanders and Captains who, for the sake of favor, allow the soldiery everything, are ultimately despised by them. Those who keep them in check and are firm with them, so that they must do what they are duty-bound to do, are held most dear by them—provided only that they do not employ any tyrannical behavior. 

When they live according to their Articles of War and are punished for their transgressions, the Commander must take diligent care that this happens as often as an individual—or even several who hold no office—commits an offense worthy of punishment. However, if the entire regiment or a part of it has transgressed, he must <gloss>feign ignorance</gloss> and show patience, so that something worse and a greater outcry does not follow. But when things have become quiet, he should see that it may be <term>avenged <note>original: "gerochen," in this context meaning to see that justice is eventually carried out or the discipline restored.</note></term>. Even if it cannot be conveniently done, he should nevertheless show and express himself in such a way that everyone may perceive and see that he bears a great displeasure because they acted so forgetfully toward him and set aside their duty. He should also—

...warn them earnestly that they should not dare to engage in such ill-treatment any further, for it shall not go unpunished for them.

Alongside this, the <term>Colonel <note>original: "Oberste," the high-ranking officer in command of a regiment or the entire force.</note></term> should also diligently ensure that he does not himself give the soldiers cause for mutiny, which could easily happen if he were to withhold or diminish anything of their rights. He must therefore not let greed deceive him or be too grasping; instead, he should show himself to be generous toward those who are worthy. He must not reduce their pay or use any deceit regarding it; rather, he should work and apply himself to see that they receive it at the right and proper time, and not intentionally delay the payment. If, however, the money is not at hand, he should demonstrate that this is most regrettable to him, and furthermore, spare no possible diligence to ensure they are paid, showing himself to be kind and helpful in the meantime. Should it also happen that there is a lack of provisions, he should comfort them as best he can, and think of ways and means by which supplies may follow. He should also indicate that he is in the same need alongside them and is willing to risk life and property with them, and that their misfortune is as grievous to him as his own. Yet, he must do this in such a way that he does not forget his status and office, nor let his bravery falter or become faint-hearted. As for the <term>Captains <note>original: "Haupt vnd Befelchsleute," referring to the various levels of commissioned officers.</note></term> and commanders, as well as distinguished veteran soldiers, he should maintain a friendly relationship with them. From all the regiments—specifically those containing the best and bravest soldiers who distinguish themselves above others and bear themselves most gallantly—he should choose [certain men] and show them friendliness and goodwill. He should also let it be known how much he values them, though this must be done with discretion so that the others do not take offense or begrudge them for it (which could well result in a mutiny). Rather, it should be done so that the others might also wish to bear themselves bravely and manfully, following their example and yielding nothing to them. A Colonel can achieve this if he elevates those who have conducted themselves well and shows them favor with good deeds, just as one reads that Emperor Julius [Caesar] behaved toward the <note>The original text says "Legation," but this is a likely error for "Legion," referring to Caesar's famous Tenth Legion.</note> Tenth Legion. If a Colonel conducts himself toward his soldiers in such a manner, no mutiny can easily arise among them. Even if some unrest should occur, it can be settled again with little effort.

The second part of <term>Military Discipline <note>original: "Kriegsdisciplin," the code of conduct and moral regulations for an army.</note></term> is that the soldiers conduct themselves honestly, moderately, and soberly, so that they do not act against God and the common good, and thereby anger God. Therefore, they should not be permitted—and the Colonel should forbid them in the <term>Articles of War <note>original: "Artickelsbrieff," the legal document read to soldiers outlining their duties and the penalties for misconduct.</note></term>—to curse or swear by God’s name. Furthermore, they shall not rob churches, hermitages, or hospitals; likewise, they shall leave poor widows and orphans unburdened. The Colonel shall strictly forbid all such things under high penalty and ensure the rules are kept. In particular, they must not dare to violate, force, or abduct women and maidens, under penalty of death. ...the way the people behave, especially among us in France, where the **soldiers** live so magnificently and expensively in the **camp** with eating and drinking, **just as if** they were at home in their own houses. And there are many among them who wear no **armor** unless the need is at hand, such as when one fears a sudden attack from the enemy, or when one is meant to fight. Even in such cases, they wish to spare themselves and do not want the effort, but **rather** have the **baggage train** or **servants** <note>original: "Droß," referring to the massive crowd of non-combatants, servants, and supply wagons that followed early modern armies.</note> who wait upon them carry their weapons and armor behind them. This is no small harm or **misuse**, for firstly, the soldiers lose their **manhood** <note>original: "Mannheit," meaning their courage and martial vigor.</note> through this, and become so soft and **effeminate** that they can no longer achieve anything honorable or brave. This is exactly what happened to <term>Hannibal <note>original: "Hannibali." A reference to the Carthaginian general whose army supposedly grew soft and undisciplined while wintering in the luxury of Campania (specifically the city of Capua) during the Second Punic War.</note></term> and his army when they lay in **Campania**.

Secondly, such **gluttons** require a great deal of **provisions**, because they are not satisfied with simple food, such as wine and bread, but insist on having the best in the camp. And if there is a lack of anything, they immediately want to start a **mutiny** and **uprising**. Also, when they must live differently than they are accustomed to due to the times, they fall into **illness**, which would not happen to them if they kept themselves moderate. 

Furthermore, a great **disorder** in the camp must follow from this, because one must maintain such a large **baggage train** and so many horses and wagons. And when one is meant to fight the enemy, one must have a great number of soldiers to protect them, who must wait upon them. From this it often follows that the cavalry, because they worry for the wagons—lest they be plundered by the enemy—leave the **battle formation** and come to the aid of those who were assigned to the wagons and the baggage train.

Lastly, when the soldiers have squandered their **pay** on gluttony and drunkenness and have nothing left, they begin to rob the **country folk** <note>original: "Landuolck," the local peasantry.</note> and plague those whom they are supposed to protect and defend, even more than the enemy themselves. From this it follows that they become hated by the country people, and if a war arises, one must be just as terrified of them as of the enemy. This often causes the poor people to leave house and home standing and move away with wife and child.

Such a burdensome evil must be countered, and the **Authorities** <note>original: "Obrigkeit."</note> must look into it and arrange it so that the country people are satisfied with us and are not terrified of us when they come into our power. And there is no doubt that if our government is rightly ordered and established, people will be better satisfied with it than with any other.

Now that we have indicated our thoughts on how the government, both at home and abroad—that is, in times of peace and war—should be well and properly established: It follows now how the King should behave toward his **neighbors** round about, both in war and in times of peace. This is a more difficult matter to speak of, to advise upon, and to handle than the others. For how all things should be ordered and arranged at home in the Kingdom is known to many excellent people. But how the surrounding nations and **friends** are to be appropriately maintained requires great foresight, wisdom, and [experience].

One must watch what their actions and intentions are, and indeed prevent with diligence that they have no power or cause to do harm; this must be done according to the opportunity of the time and place, and also regarding the person of whom we are wary. For we have more to fear and look out for from one who wishes to press us and is powerful enough to do us injury—believing he has a case against us or otherwise carrying an old grudge—than from one who does not have so much power or cause to act hostiley against us. For such a person must refrain from it for one of those two reasons. Likewise, if one is cunning and craftly and strives for honor and property, we have more to look out for from him than from one in whom we have no deceit to fear, or who is not of such power that he could inflict violence and harm upon us. Accordingly, we should live most peacefully in times of peace with those of whom we are most wary, in such a way that they have no complaint or cause...

...took hold, as can be seen in the case of **Gnaeus Pompey** <note>original: "Cneo Pompeio." Gnaeus Pompey Magnus (106–48 BC), a Roman general who was famously granted extraordinary powers to clear the Mediterranean of pirates in 67 BC.</note>, who within sixty days cleared the entire sea of pirates. By doing so, he ensured that all cities—even those allied and bound by treaty to the Romans—could sail freely and safely from such sea-robbers. Previously, these same pirates had shown themselves almost at the very gates of the city of **Rome**, and no one could sail safely or take to the sea unless it happened by the pirates' grace and will. This truly could not have been achieved on land without great and significant expense and a vast multitude of soldiers. From this, one can easily conclude what great benefit can be created through such an **Armata** <note>original: "Armata." Used here to mean a standing navy or organized fleet of warships.</note> or naval armament.

For although the **Pyratæ** <note>original: "Pyratæ." Latin for pirates.</note> and sea-robbers were low-born people and wicked rascals of little means, they nevertheless relied on their mastery of seafaring. Because of this, they dared to undertake anything and brought not only Rome's allies but the city of **Rome** itself into such anxiety and distress that they could not have been easily restrained had **Pompey’s** courage and successful resistance not intervened. While I am well aware of the great and significant costs required for this, and that it can hardly be established without some burden to the subjects and the whole people—since a special tax would have to be ordained and applied—necessity nevertheless demands it, especially should a great and serious war break out. And our present times and difficult dealings should rightly teach us enough, through the significant damage to our own and the common good, how much depends on the fact that we were not prepared with an upright and stately navy to resist dangerous wars.

It is indeed true that when no war is at hand, one should not incur greater costs than the people can well bear. But just as the **cavalry** <note>original: "Reisige Zeug." Referring to the standing mounted troops of the realm.</note> is maintained continually and is not only an ornament to the whole Reich but also a help and comfort—indeed, even a terror to enemies—so it would also be with the **navy**. If we were continually and stately prepared with it, according to our power and means, there would be no doubt that we would remain at peace in **France** and in a short time attain great power and authority. For it would bring a magnificent contribution to the King's income, and much great benefit would come to the whole realm regarding **trade** <note>original: "Kauffmanschafft." Referring to merchant commerce and the shipping industry.</note>, which many would pursue once not only the danger but even the fear of danger was driven away.

How often does it happen that a rumor arrives as if an invasion were occurring by those coming by water? Then we run together in great terror and trembling, and when we finally must offer resistance, it must be done at double the great cost. This damage could easily be prevented if we were prepared and provided with a naval armament. For they would either have to leave us entirely in peace, or if they did venture something, they would accomplish nothing or very little; and before they could do us any harm...

# Of the Government of the Crown of France

In particular, the French should apply themselves earnestly so that they never withdraw from what they have once decided; for by their nature they are particularly hot-headed <note>The author refers to the common early modern stereotype of the "furia francese," or French fury, suggesting they are brave in the initial charge but lack stamina.</note> at the start of military matters, but such heat soon fades and eventually grows cold. Therefore, one must do whatever is possible, and whatever can be accomplished with money, gifts, and promises should be employed as an aid, leaving nothing undone until we obtain what we have sought and desired.

Although those who understand these things know best what is to be done in such cases, I must nevertheless offer my perspective here, as I have seen many times in my day how things became quite difficult, resulting in significant harm to the common good and the entire Kingdom. Therefore, I must state here how we should preserve and maintain the territories we have conquered through war. And though one can learn and take little from experience, common usage, or history regarding what is necessary and what should be done here, I cannot refrain from offering my opinion and what I see in this case, according to my custom, insofar as it fits our times—seeing how often our people have bungled the opportunity <note>original: "die schantze versehen," an idiom meaning to miss a chance or fail in a task</note>, so that they quickly lost the lands, cities, and castles they had conquered with heavy cost, effort, and labor, solely through a lack of foresight.

But so that we may keep such conquered lands and properties, two things will be necessary: namely, military funding <term>Kriegskosten: the financial resources required to maintain an army and its occupation</term> and good laws. The military funding must come first and be used for as long as it takes (even if the people are not rebellious) until all things are properly settled and agreed upon; before then, one should not withdraw the garrison <term>Besetzung: the military force stationed in a town or fortress to maintain control</term>, so that one has no further fear of any revolt. Once this is done, it follows that one should provide that same area with good orders and laws, and abolish all extra costs as well as the garrison, so that the province may recover and thrive again. But before one knows the mind of the province and ensures that the neighbors all around are satisfied, one should not remove the soldiers and the garrison. One should also deal with the officials <note>original: "Amptleuten," referring to local administrators or bailiffs appointed by the crown</note> of the territory so that they behave correctly and do what they are duty-bound to do. As for the establishment of jurisdiction, great diligence will be needed there, for that same thing must endure continually, and all other matters depend upon it and flow from it. And what we have said above concerning the preservation of the kingdom and the usage and order of war, since it belongs here, I must repeat some of it.

It is known, however, that it is far more difficult to protect a newly conquered province than to maintain that which belongs to the ancestral inheritance and the crown. Therefore, necessity requires that one be alert to all dangers that may occur, as well as the ways and means by which a conquered province can be lost again. If it is seen that they conduct themselves faithfully and uprightly, they should be relieved of such burdens at the first opportunity. And the superior or commander over these people can achieve much through his kindness and friendliness. And if he comforts them and promises them that they shall have protection and defense under him, and that he will not allow any violence to be done to them, their wives, children, or their goods, they will be greatly strengthened by this.

If the King himself should also stay for a time in the same <term>Province</term> <note>original: "Prouintz"</note>—if it is situated such that it were possible—and shows himself gracious toward the people, there would be no doubt that they would thereby gain love and favor for him and be well satisfied with him.

It was the custom among the ancients that one imposed upon the peoples who had been conquered in war the requirement to give hostages, according to the size of each city, so that the others might be kept in obedience all the more easily. Our people could also do this, for which one can certainly devise an honorable reason—namely, that the people should become accustomed to us and become knowledgeable in our language, or something similar. And such means must be used if one fears they might become rebels or disobedient, or are not fit for war. But if one has hope that they will keep their faith, one should make them alert and ordain <term>Pay</term> <note>original: "Besoldung"</note> for them and place them among our <term>Soldiers</term> <note>original: "Kriegsvolck"</note>, so that they may learn our customs of war and become used to our manners, and thus gradually begin to love our people. Whatever heads and officials, or whoever else are the most prominent among them, these should be provided with better offices; and one should show benefit not only toward them but also their friends, and provide them with <term>Pay</term>. For through such means they are reconciled, and the others also gain hope of attaining the same. But they become especially joyful and willing when they notice that one places trust in them. In addition, they can also be maintained with less and lower <term>Pay</term> and burden than the foreign, contracted soldiers. Even if they are not equal to our soldiers in the beginning, they will nevertheless become better practiced over time, especially those of the <term>Nobility</term> <note>original: "Adel"</note> and those who come from good families.

The Romans, Greeks, and others who were renowned in matters of war had this custom, which I cannot think of or see how one can long maintain a territory or <term>Province</term> in which one needs a garrison, unless we bring the inhabitants over to our side and use their help. The Turkish Emperor <note>A reference to the Ottoman Sultan.</note>, the grandfather of the currently reigning Emperor, did this when he became master of the Greeks and acquired many other lands. When he saw that he would not be able to defend all those same lands with his own soldiers, he had the best and most capable children chosen from our religion of the Christians, out of those <term>Provinces</term> which he had conquered. He accustomed them to war from their youth and thereafter used them for his own person. These are the Turkish soldiers who—

# Of the Government of the Crown of France

...whom one calls <term>Janissaries</term> <note>original: "Janitscher"; elite infantry units of the Ottoman Sultan's household, historically composed of conscripted Christian youths</note>. However, although it is a cruel and almost <term>Turkish</term> <note>The author uses "Turkish" here as a period-typical synonym for tyrannical or "unchristian" behavior</note> un-Christian undertaking—which will also lead to the Turk's great disadvantage and eventual downfall—for the Janissaries, as brave and practiced soldiers, will finally grow weary of the tyrannical and inhuman government and incite a rebellion. In this, they will divide and partition the Turkish state among themselves; and this is all the more likely because they have neither houses nor hope, but must live solely from their <term>Pay</term> <note>original: "besoldung"</note>. Therefore, the way mentioned above is much more tolerable, Christian, and convenient.

The second point is that the locations of the same land should be so arranged that they can be defended, especially when they are situated on the <term>Frontier</term> <note>original: "Frontir"; the border regions</note>. For this reason, they should be provided with every necessity and fortified so that they can withstand a siege for a year and a day, for which no small amount of resources is required. And if something is neglected through a lack of diligence, the person responsible shall be seriously punished. Therefore, it is most advisable to staff such places with excellent <term>Captains</term> <note>original: "Hauptleuten"</note> and <term>Soldiers</term> <note>original: "Kriegsvolck"</note> in sufficient numbers. These commanders and soldiers should be of such character that they can and will do and suffer everything that is proper, and by no means surrender the fortress while they have hope of being relieved. They should also accept no private <term>Terms</term> <note>original: "Pact oder Condition"; private deals or surrender agreements</note> from the enemies and give up the fortress unless they can no longer hold out for their own sake but are forced to it by the utmost necessity. Therefore, it is safest to use foreign soldiers for this purpose, who have neither houses nor fields in that place, for they will have all the less reason to be swayed. The Captain should be a brave and experienced man, whom the soldiers fear and hold in high regard, and who lacks nothing in military skill. For you will find those who cannot be improved upon when one is to fight the enemy in the field, but who are of no use in a garrison when they are besieged, nor can they provide much counsel when necessity is at hand. But besides experience, it will be necessary for the Captain also to be prudent, to know how to provide counsel for occurring deficiencies, to speak courage into the hearts of the men, and to be diligent in ensuring that no <term>Mutiny</term> <note>original: "Meuterey"</note> arises among them, to distribute the <term>Provisions</term> <note>original: "Prouiant"</note> and other things most equally, and to provide everything for the best.

However, such a Captain must also be held in the highest regard and be well-provided with pay and all necessities, so that he does not have to do something against his duties out of poverty or need. Furthermore, he must not be too greedy or covetous. For such fellows have often shamefully surrendered the fortresses they held for the sake of money—which is the primary concern with such people. Since they are greedy for money, they often neglect necessary things in order to save costs. If the soldiers also become aware of this, they hold them in even less regard, especially when they notice that they wish to have much fellowship with the enemy outside, which cannot happen without danger.

# The Second Book

Therefore, it is best and safest that one commands the soldiers with nothing other than the guarding of the city or castle, and that they have nothing to do with the <term>Civil Government</term> <note>original: "Bürgerlichen Regiment"; the administration of the townspeople as opposed to military rule</note>. Indeed, they should not wander far or have much interaction with the citizenry, but rather attend to their garrison duty and allow no one into the fortress except those they cannot avoid for daily necessities. For such conversations and strolls sometimes give cause for great disadvantage. I have said this much regarding how one should maintain and defend the <term>Provinces</term> <note>original: "Landschafften"</note> that we have conquered through war. Now, I will also briefly remind you of what Law and <term>Justice</term> <note>original: "Gericht"</note> should be used; for this discipline is much more necessary and urgent in such provinces than in ancestral and inherited lands, although we are now experiencing almost the opposite.

Although it can be sufficiently understood from what we have related above how to establish the <term>Civil Administration</term> <note>original: "Policey"</note> and <term>Jurisdiction</term>, how people are to be brought to war, how they should be provided with provisions and other necessities, how <term>Commercial Trade</term> <note>original: "Kauffmañshändel"</note> should be organized, and how disputes should be settled, I cannot refrain from explaining some of these in particular. There is a general commandment which extends quite far: namely, that one should show as much kindness as possible to the common people, provided it can be done without disadvantage to the King and the conquered province. First, when one holds court, one should not look at the person but maintain equality, sharing the law with one as well as the other. For this purpose, upright, honorable, and sensible people must be appointed. Through this, our Lord God is appeased, and the common man is made willing and obedient; also, those who hoped to obtain something from the judge out of favor—when they do not obtain what they desired—must recognize their error, feel ashamed, and hold the judge in much higher esteem.

Secondly, it serves the cause no small amount that in matters which do not greatly affect the King or Prince, one lets the people have their will and live as they please—that is, according to their <term>Customs</term> <note>original: "gebrauch"</note>—and does not force them to discard their old habits and practices. Rather, it is more advisable that the foreigners who are among them adapt themselves to the locals as much as possible, unless it be a case where they willingly submit to our statutes and ordinances.

Just as ***Alexander the Great*** <note>original: "Alexander Magnus"</note> also used this method, and thereby gained great favor and goodwill among those he had overcome in war. Because he conducted himself and conformed to their manner and customs, they believed nothing else than that he thought very highly of them and that they had great favor with him. If, however, time permits later on, one can gradually bring and encourage them to live according to our manner and order, and to let go of their old customs, just as the ***Romans*** also did.

When it is no longer convenient for the King to remain among them, he should, upon his departure, let it be known that the location of the land pleases him well, and that he would most like to dwell there as much as his other business allows; also, for their sake, he should not begrudge any effort or expense. But he who is appointed as <term>Governor</term> <note>original: "Landpfleger"; a regional administrator or prefect representing the crown</note> or commander must be generous and open-handed, not sparing any expense, but rather making friends of the most prominent people who possess the understanding to be advisory and helpful to him in times of both war and peace. And they must in no way allow the <term>Jurisdiction</term> to fail or be hindered, but rather they should also offer their helping hand. For through this, one creates goodwill among the people. But if one deals with it negligently and poorly, and the judges and officials strive more for their own profit than for the <term>Common Good</term> <note>original: "gemeinen nuß"; a central political concept of the era emphasizing public welfare over private gain</note>, then the people will soon not only become unwilling but will also despise them.

The third point is that the King and his officials should deal with the local inhabitants in the most gracious and friendly manner, showing them all honor, especially to those who are somewhat prominent and have more understanding than others. Thus, where it is to be expected that they should be of use, one should distribute the ecclesiastical and secular offices among them, their children, friends, and relatives, according to what each is suited for. But as for the most prominent offices, upon which the land and the common good depend, these should be given to no one but the best and most distinguished people who are fit for them and who are acceptable to the people and held in good standing. Whatever prominent and valiant people there are in the province (as it cannot be otherwise, for no land is so bad that it does not have some good and upright people within it) who have served the common good well, one may grant them the largest and most prominent offices, provided we are certain that they are loyal to us and will cause no harm with their service.

Since, most powerful, gracious, and most favorable Lords, in this my humble, faithful, and well-meaning speech and reminder, I can expect nothing more certain than that I will be placed under the highest suspicion by all parties; since among so many opinions and views that have recently arisen in the Crown of France, it is difficult for one to behave in such a manner as to strike the right balance and satisfy everyone. However, since out of your gracious and favorable will you have permitted others—who presented themselves in the same way and showed some humility—to speak, I did not want to neglect making this humble exhortation to you. I do not do so with the intention of moving or leading you to a different religion than the one each has already adopted, much less out of any vain confidence I might have in myself, but rather I have ventured to speak based on your gracious and favorable permission. For this reason, I am in completely undoubting hope and confidence, and I humbly request that you pay attention to this my speech with such earnestness and diligence of eyes and ears, just as I am eager to deliver it before you. For I hereby offer to refrain from all insolence and wantonness in my speech, and to bring forward only that with moderation which is permitted by your Grace and Favor and by the current time, and which my office requires of me on this occasion.

To begin with, however, gracious and favorable Lords, I cannot agree at all with those who are accustomed to starting by speaking of the excellence of religion. For I consider that the matter is only made worse and more difficult thereby, and the old wounds are thus renewed. For the division and error of the two religions—namely, the Roman or **Papists**, and the **Protestants** <note>original: *Protestirenden*; the speaker explicitly chooses these labels to avoid more inflammatory insults.</note> (for I have resolved to use these two names, rather than others that are even more hateful, in this my speech)—give birth to nothing but such a resentment that it is better to remain silent than to speak much of it, since nothing but insurrection arises from it, which we intend to counter with the greatest earnestness. As far as my own person is concerned, although two kinds of **sects** <note>In the 16th century, the term "sect" was often used for any distinct religious group, not necessarily with the modern negative connotation.</note> have now arisen among us, yet there is but one God, one Law, and one Faith, and of these sects no more than one can be right and true. I am in the hope toward God that I shall know how to conduct myself therein in such a way that I can answer for it before the highest Judge and Discerner of all hearts, and give an account thereof. Yet we are not all alike in such discord; rather, one is minded differently than the other, and we do not all shoot at the same target.

Now, although the **Papists** feel a great loathing for the **Protestants**, as those who have fallen away from them and are said to have become **heretics**; and conversely, the **Protestants** hate and scold the **Papists** most vehemently as **idolatrous** people who persist in the foolish **superstition** of their ancestors; nevertheless, we shall
