# Exhortation to the...

...that we all should be so minded, as many of us as remain among the living, that we recognize, worship, and honor the right, true, and only God, who, for the removal of our sins, took human nature upon Himself, and clothed Himself in our poor flesh, was tortured, and suffered death; which the heathens <note>original: "Heyden"</note> regarded as mockery and foolishness, and which has not been believed by the Jews until this hour—with few exceptions—that nonetheless amidst such discord, Almighty God, who governs and mediates these things, visibly performed and accomplished great and wondrous things for the good and best of both parties. Now, if someone were to attribute such works to one party—whichever it might be—claiming that it happened for their benefit and for their sake alone, they would, in my opinion, act unjustly and audaciously, and would seek to moderate, measure, and judge God's eternal decree according to human reason and emotion. 

That this is so is clearly proven by the Conspiracy of Amboise <note>The Conspiracy of Amboise (1560) was a failed attempt by French Huguenots (Protestants) to seize King Francis II and arrest the Catholic Guise family who controlled him.</note>, which we all witnessed, and which was directed against those who, above all, had to manage and provide for the affairs of the kingdom; in which matter all things were so arranged and provided for that one would have had to say it appeared that God Himself wished to send and promote the work toward the end for which it was intended; and nothing was lacking except that the work should be undertaken and completed on a specified day. 

But nevertheless, those who intended to undertake this were, in a single moment, struck by such a terror that their plans were scattered like a whirlwind, and nothing came of it. Is it not true that the Papists <term>Papists: a contemporary term for Roman Catholics, referring to their allegiance to the Pope</term> were thereby visibly helped? And although one of the Protestants <term>Protestants: specifically referring here to the Huguenots of France</term> might say: "Yes, dear friend, you talk well; if such had not happened through our own neglect, it would have turned out differently; we had traitors among ourselves who hindered the matter." 

Oh, listen, dear friend: do you not know that when God wishes to perform and accomplish a miracle, He sometimes uses means, and we ourselves must help? Even if at that time He mediated things such that they turned out for the luck and benefit of the Papists, He did not thereby entirely turn His goodness and grace away from the Protestants and abandon them—which appears clearly enough from this: that several of their leaders fell into the power [of their enemies], such that they would have had to be subject to them, and perhaps even be executed by them. But our Lord God ordained it so that they departed from this world, so that they would not have to be [humiliated].

We have seen that our King Henry <note>King Henry II of France (reigned 1547–1559), who was known for his intense persecution of the Protestant faith.</note> planned gruesome and terrifying things against those whom he held in suspicion regarding religion, and how he intended to punish them. We have also seen that he had five or [six] of his counselors cast into heavy imprisonment on account of religion. Furthermore, we have seen that he took intelligence from several governors against [his own] associates, and that he even released them from their duty. But at the same time, we had to see on that very same day that the same lord king (would to God that he were still alive and in government!) suffered an injury to his head, whereby he first [lost] an eye, and... <note>In June 1559, King Henry II was mortally wounded during a jousting tournament when a splinter from a lance pierced his eye; his death led to a period of great political instability in France.</note>

This page details the shifting fortunes of the Protestant "party" following the death of King Henry II and the subsequent reign of his successors, emphasizing how sudden deaths at court altered the course of religious persecution.</meta>

-># Government of the Crown of France.<-

...lost his life. And just as he committed a shameful deed at his court on the tenth of June—which it is not fitting for me to report <note>The author refers to King Henry II, who was mortally wounded in a tournament accident on June 10, 1559, while celebrating the Peace of Cateau-Cambrésis.</note>—so he passed away in death on the tenth of July, a day well worth noting. This death was also a cause by which the great and terrible fire of persecution was, to some extent, stilled and settled. Yet his successors in the government, after they had brought their affairs to order and gained power, immediately took up that same undertaking of persecution once more. They showed themselves so cruel in this that all the towers and dungeons were packed full of prisoners for the sake of the Religion <note>original: "Religion halben." This was the common term for the Protestant/Huguenot faith during the French Wars of Religion.</note>, who had nothing more certain before them than that they must and should die a cruel and shameful death.

But in the meantime, the Conspiracy of Amboise <note>The Amboise Conspiracy (1560) was a failed plot by Huguenots to seize the young King Francis II and remove him from the influence of the Catholic Guise family.</note> took place. When it came to fruition, it so terrified and changed the minds of those regents and great lords that—regardless of how bitterly they had previously been incensed against the poor people—through a wondrous act of God’s providence, they were the first to see fit that the prisoners should be set free. I do not say this to disparage or prejudice those same great lords; I well believe that regarding what they undertook against the Protestants, they knew no better than that they could not avoid it due to the requirements of their office. But I must say this for the sake of showing how Almighty God can, in a moment and a twinkling of an eye, overturn and change the minds of men and bring their counsels to nothing.

Subsequently, the fear among those same great lords partially subsided, so that they were determined within themselves to punish those suspected of being involved in or devoted to the Conspiracy of Amboise. Nothing was left undone regarding what human diligence and reason required; among those involved, a distinguished, great, and powerful man <note>Likely Louis, Prince of Condé, a leader of the Huguenots who was arrested and sentenced to death for his alleged role in the conspiracy.</note> came into the highest danger of life and limb. But just as Almighty God in ancient times looked upon and preserved the pious Isaac when his father Abraham wished to sacrifice him, so was this man—along with countless others, just as they were about to be executed—preserved. The unforeseen fatal passing of a single young prince <note>King Francis II died unexpectedly of an ear infection in December 1560, which led to the fall of the Guise family's power and a temporary reprieve for the Protestants.</note> was the cause by which all such bloody designs, terrifying threats, and gruesome un-Christian persecutions throughout all of France ceased, were extinguished, and vanished.

Who can now be so crude and senseless as not to recognize and say that all these aforementioned actions occurred through a special providence of God? Indeed, it is as wondrous as if one had seen a dead man brought back to life in ancient times. Since God has helped us so miraculously, should we now rise up against the other party and take our revenge upon them? By no means. For just as this party was miraculously rescued from the danger of the ordained pains and punishments and escaped them, so too did the other party escape the Amboise Conspiracy and alliance through Divine means (since all things had been so craftily planned), which otherwise would not have been so easily...

->### Admonition to the...<-

...it could have happened, had God chosen to show and manifest Himself with such mighty power.

These are the great and wondrous counsels and works of God. If we were now to presume to measure and fathom them with our foolish and mortal reason <note>original: "närrischen vnd todten vernunfft," literally "foolish and dead reason."</note>, it would be nothing else (if the truth be told) than what was said in ancient times of the Giants: that they piled one mountain upon another, intending to drag our Lord God down from heaven <note>A reference to the Gigantomachy from Greek mythology, where the Giants attempted to storm Olympus by piling Mount Ossa on Mount Pelion.</note>. However, the Almighty is such a good and righteous God that He distributes His goodness and benefits without distinction between the pious and the wicked. He does not look to us—nor will He allow it—to judge what is good or evil, but wishes to reserve that judgment for Himself alone. The Papists <note>The Catholic party.</note> have been wonderfully delivered from danger, while the Protestants <note>original: "Protestirende."</note>, against all human reason, have been defeated three times. What else should we take from this (setting aside for a moment the question of which religion is right or wrong) than that the Lord God has not abandoned us in such discord? Rather, He has sustained us and wishes to remind us that it is His divine will that we do not hate one another for the sake of religion—much less seek one another's lives—but instead carry and maintain a calm and quiet conscience toward one another, thus obeying the divine law of love. This is His meaning; these are His commands with which He has reminded us, which I also now intend to use and take to heart, so that you may govern yourselves accordingly.

I am not of the opinion, most powerful Lords, that I intend to approve of sects or hold them to be right; for may our Lord God graciously preserve me from such temporal opinions and thoughts, so that they do not enter my heart. It seems to me that I know well (praise be to God) which teaching is to be preferred over the others, but the opportunity and the place do not allow for an accounting of that now. But God willing, in time you shall learn that I will declare myself clearly on this matter. In the meantime, and as we have now come together to speak of this and to deliberate on how we might prevent and encounter the burdensome uprisings which weigh upon us from all sides, I will (so far as I can avoid it) not attribute so much to one sect that I would take anything away from the other or wish to offend them. Rather, my mind is set on placing every man’s conscience on an equal path, and to leave the judgment of the rest to Him who alone can know our hearts, consciences, and all thoughts.

Now, in order that we may more comfortably and fitly reach a settling of such impending uprisings (since we have understood from the examples just told that it does not please God, nor does He want us to burden, plunder, or wretchedly slay and murder the other side, or otherwise behave toward them in a tyrannical manner), there is, in my estimation, no more convenient, better, or more tolerable way than that you make an ordinance in your Common Assembly that in one place there be two kinds of churches: one—

# Government of the Crown of France.

...the Catholics <note>original: "Papisten."</note>, the other for the Protestants <note>original: "Protestirenden."</note>, be maintained and permitted. Although I have no doubt that some among your assembly <note>original: "Mittel," referring to the gathered council or representatives.</note> will not be entirely satisfied with this proposal of mine—for it is indeed a proposal that requires reflection and carries significant weight—you might perhaps answer me thus: "What are you saying? When people become divided in opinion, especially in religion—which usually occupies and moves our hearts and minds most intensely—can it truly be managed in France, where a uniform form of religion has been held and practiced for so long, that a new sect and religion can be permitted and tolerated without tumult and riot?"

To this, high and mighty Lords, I give this report: that it may well happen. I ask you also to hear my reasons for it. I say, first, that it has happened in other places. Secondly, I say that given the current state of affairs here in France, it is of the highest necessity. I say further, thirdly, that if you permit this path, it cannot result in any disadvantage to our Lord the King.

As for what concerns the necessity, I will call upon you yourselves as witnesses; I desire no other testimony than your own conscience: whether matters must not, out of necessity, be directed so that the Protestants must either be suppressed and eradicated, or must have free passage among us. Now, they cannot be suppressed unless it be through driving them into exile and misery, or by striking them dead altogether. As for exile, it will be difficult to bring them to the point where they allow themselves to be deterred from their opinion by the threat of misery. Even if you say you would permit them to sell their goods and property and move out of the kingdom, allowing them to settle and establish themselves in other lands, this is also in vain and will not work. This is because such people face so many obstacles: namely, the love of one's fatherland, wife, children, and servants, which prevents one from leaving; and further, the circumstances of their property, for whoever must sell in such a way must give their goods away for almost nothing. In truth, these are no small hindrances when one is expected to leave his fatherland and go to foreign places. And suppose such an edict were issued, and everyone concerned behaved obediently according to it: what else would you have done or accomplished but to have made the noble Crown of France entirely desolate and waste in both money and manpower—and this not among common people, but among the best and most noble estates <note>The "Estates" refers to the social hierarchy: Clergy, Nobility, and Commoners.</note>.

But if you wish to resist the matter with the sword and have the people judicially condemned to death as a deterrent to others—as has happened before, where sword, water, and fire were used—what has it helped? Or what benefit has it brought? Nothing else than that the people, after recognizing the Divine Truth, became all the more eager, and the ignited fire became all the greater. Thus, the more and more harshly they were punished, the less they cared for it, and the more steadfastly they persevered—to such an extent that when one was killed, a hundred others came in his place and confessed to the truth. But if you wish to... <note>The text breaks off mid-sentence; the catchword indicates the next word is "judges."</note>

->Exhortation to the<-

### B

judge, execute, and root them out, then see what kind of fire and what kind of war you will kindle in the noble Crown of France; what burdens you will bring upon the poor subjects, especially since they have not yet entirely recovered from the previous hardships of war, if they are once again to be made a prize for the hungry throats of war <note>original: "Kriegsgurgeln," a vivid term for mercenaries or the ravenous nature of military pillaging</note>. I know what I am talking about. And the defeat at Orléans <note>original: "Aurelianische niderlag," likely referring to the Siege of Orléans in 1563 during the first French War of Religion</note> should rightly be a mirror to us, as we experienced it with such great damage.

And even assuming that you could exercise such foresight that the people in the countryside were secured from the soldiery and remained unburdened, you must still especially consider this: that the Protestants <note>original: "Protestierenden"</note>—who are by no means insignificant people—will not allow themselves to be so oppressed. For one must confess that they are equal in power to the Catholics <note>original: "Papisten"</note>—if not in number—and can hold the balance; indeed, they may be far superior. Therefore, you must not think that you will be able to come away from them without a bloody victory. And even if it should happen that you kept the upper hand and the victory—which you certainly should not take for granted—that the Protestants would be entirely rooted out, it is nonetheless not possible for this to happen without great and gruesome bloodshed, nor without the loss of many great, honorable, and good people of your own. Ultimately, nothing else will result from it, even if you do keep the upper hand, than that you will have to sacrifice and lose many people over it. You will not only rob your King of his subjects but also deliver him naked into the fists of the enemy (who could well intervene in the meantime). This is to say nothing of what you should well consider—since the King is of such a tender and young age—that no small danger stands upon it if one were to make another the Supreme Commander and allow the power of the entire kingdom to come into his hands and trust. And let this be seen above all—to speak briefly of the matter—that one will not be able to root out and destroy the Protestants without our own damage and ruin, nor without great danger to the Lord King.

It is no different in this business than with a human body: when a limb has begun to become rotten and dead, one does not usually wait long, but soon cuts it off so that it may not rot further. But if it is overlooked until it has eaten so far around itself that it has attacked the best and noblest members of the body, and one then wished to cut those away, one would do nothing other than completely kill and destroy the entire body for the sake of the rotten limbs. Thus, even the wisest people in the world have almost always been of the opinion that they advised how new sects <note>original: "Secten"</note> might be dampened with sword and fire in the beginning, before they gained the upper hand. But when they have gained the upper hand and become many—as has now happened among us, and matters have reached the state we see before our eyes—one must hold and advise quite the opposite. This is done in such a way that one has not begun to doubt without special cause: whether even a heretic <note>original: "Ketzer"</note>, who has taught against the Christian faith and persisted in it, can be judged from life to death.

->Government of the Crown of France /<-

And to give an example / There was in former times a heretic / named Priscillian <note>Priscillian of Avila (died c. 385), a Spanish bishop who was the first person in the history of Christianity to be executed for heresy by a civil court</note> / from whom those / who followed his sect / were called Priscillianists / he confused the Persons of the holy and venerable Trinity / held flesh to be impure / and ate none of it / He permitted divorce / upon the request and consent of only one party / And this same bishop held more such errors / with which he led astray and deceived countless people / This man was first declared wrong in a Roman Council / and subsequently in a meeting at Bordeaux <note>original: "Burdegalischen versammlung," referring to the Council of Bordeaux in 384 AD</note> by Saint Martin / and other great / pious and learned men / he was declared a heretic.

Against this Priscillian, Ithacius and Ursacius <note>Ithacius of Ossonoba and Ursacius, bishops who campaigned for Priscillian’s execution</note> / were moved by a particular holiness and devotion (as they imagined) / to accuse him before the Emperor Maximus as a heretic / from which it followed / that he was sentenced from life to death / and up to three thousand of his followers perished. But Sigebert, a monk / of the Benedictine Order / has conversely recorded regarding Saint Martin / that he and his brothers / who had previously condemned Priscillian / similarly banished Ithacius and his followers from the Christian Church. And just as those / who followed Priscillian were called Priscillianists / so also those who followed Ithacius were called Ithacians / because they held with Ithacius / that those / who err in religion / should be punished with death. But what happened? The fear of the ban <note>excommunication</note> nevertheless worked so much / that of those / who had been condemned to death / and lay imprisoned / none were executed.

Although the Pope / because he was inclined toward Ithacius and Ursacius / dealt with Saint Martin multiple times / and finally strictly mandated and commanded him / that he should be in agreement with them / and lift the ban from them / He nevertheless never allowed himself to be moved to do so / unless / the Emperor would set the poor imprisoned people free from their captivity again / and leave them unburdened / as he hoped / and did not doubt / they would return to the right path / and think better of it.

And at that time it was an unheard-of thing among Christians / that a brother / even if he had erred in an article of faith / should be punished with death / Rather, the first master of this business was Dominic <note>Saint Dominic (1170–1221)</note> / who founded one of the four mendicant orders / which are called the Preaching Monks <note>The Dominicans</note> / From which it followed / that the Inquisition thereafter remained and continued with these same monks. # Admonition to the
<meta>catchword: can</meta>

...must and confess, that necessity requires that the Protestants be allowed to live and remain among us alongside the Papists <note>The author uses the term "Papists" (Papiſten) to refer to Roman Catholics, reflecting the polemical language of the 16th century.</note>, since they are fundamentally united in the basis of faith and are baptized Christians; and they should not be allowed to suffer harm to body or property. And this is not only because it is seen as good by human wisdom—which otherwise is foolishness before God—but also because those who are regarded as having advised and recognized this for the sake of their holy life believe it was not contrary to the Divine will.

Now, if you concede to me (as it can hardly be otherwise) that the Protestants may live and dwell among and beside us, then you will also in like manner permit and confess that they must either be brought to the Roman faith through Christian reminders and good examples and admonitions, or be allowed to remain in their way of believing. But that they should be brought back from their religion to Papistry—that will hardly succeed, unless one wished to strip from the clergy the goods <note>Referring to the ecclesiastical lands, wealth, and tithes that were a central point of conflict during the Reformation.</note> over which they contend with them concerning religion. And even if it were to be undertaken through a General or *National Council* <note>original: "National Concilium"</note>, I fear that it would not achieve a successful outcome. Firstly, because the Bishops, Archbishops, and Prelates—who would not remain un-accused—would want to be both parties and judges therein, which is not fitting. Secondly, because the upright Protestants would not allow themselves to be turned away from the Divine Truth, which they have once recognized and accepted, even by a *Council*. In the same way, the Papists would not want to deviate from their old and long-established religion either. For *Councils* only have their proper effect when one side as much as the other is satisfied with what is negotiated and decided, and when one undertakes dealings either regarding abuses or the changing of ceremonies.

The sect of the Arians <note>Arians followed the teachings of Arius (c. 256–336 AD), who argued that Jesus Christ was not co-eternal with God the Father. This was the most significant theological conflict in the early Church.</note> was in former times so large (not to say larger) than that of the Protestants, and was also unanimously condemned in the *Council of Nicaea* <note>original: "Nicenischen Concilio," the first ecumenical council of the Church held in 325 AD.</note> with great deliberation by many learned people. But tell me, did they cease immediately thereafter, or did the Arians become fewer in number? No, indeed. What, then, eventually weakened them? Nothing but time, and not the *Councils*. This was also the direction of the counsel of that precious man *Gamaliel* <note>Gamaliel was a leading authority in the Jewish Sanhedrin; his famous advice to the council regarding the early apostles is recorded in the Bible.</note> when he said, in the fifth [chapter] of *Acts* <note>original: "Actorum am fünfften," referencing Acts 5:38–39.</note>: Leave these men alone, let them go; if this work be of men, it will perish; but if it be of God, you cannot suppress it. Therefore, I also say: if the Protestants' opinion is of God, then it will surely remain, and all human counsel will be able to do nothing against it. But if it is of the Devil, then it must by necessity become rotten and come to nothing, and no medicine or force will be able to help it. Yet I cannot say otherwise than that your *Council* is rightly to be praised, provided only that you ensure one side may be heard and considered as much as the other, and that no partiality creeps in. In the meantime, however, and before the *Council* begins, it will be necessary—since it is not fitting that the Protestants should be put to death, nor hereafter...

Now, whether this same opinion is right and true or not, I will not *dispute* <note>original: "disputiren"</note>; for I initially stipulated that I do not wish to be a judge of which religion is right or wrong. <meta>This page continues the author's critique of the Roman Catholic Church's history and institutional structure. # Exhortation to the...

...specific opinion according to his own passion and discretion; ultimately so many heresies (if indeed they were all heresies) have arisen.

It has also followed from this that the four Mendicant Orders <note>The "four Mendicant Orders" (BettelOrden) refers to the Franciscans, Dominicans, Carmelites, and Augustinians—monastic groups who originally survived by begging rather than through property ownership.</note>—vain, godless, and useless people, who are liked by no one—have never been recognized as good or righteous for the common good, nor were they permitted or accepted by our ancestors with their will. This is clearly seen in the books of William of Saint-Amour <note>original: "Guilhelmi Sanctamorij." A 13th-century academic at the University of Paris who famously opposed the influence of the mendicant friars in the church.</note> and Almain <note>original: "Alkamani." Likely referring to Jacques Almain, a theologian known for his critiques of church power.</note>, which are still available today. These four Mendicant Orders (I say) saw that the parishes were so negligently established and so poorly provided for that, during the time of King Charles VI of France, they obtained a privilege <note>original: "Privilegium"</note> in which they were granted and permitted by the Pope to demand and collect tithes, because they were to fulfill that which was neglected by the rightful parish priests and pastors—despite the fact that the Pope himself was and still is a cause and the beginning of this untimely business.

If one also pays proper attention to the time when the Pope began to grow and exalt himself, to the point that he dared to claim for himself the title of **Supreme Bishop** <note>original: "Obersten Bischoffs"</note> (which happened under the Emperor Phocas <note>Emperor Phocas (reigned 602–610 AD) allegedly issued a decree recognizing the See of Rome as the head of all churches.</note>), one will find that at that very same time, under the Emperor Heraclius (who came to the Empire soon after Phocas), the great and harmful heretic and deceiver Muhammad <note>original: "Mahomet"</note> arose. He scattered his poisonous seed throughout the entire **East** <note>original: "Orient"</note> and increased to such an extent that it will hardly be checked (so far as human help is concerned). Thus, the Pope in the **West** <note>original: "Occident"</note> also expanded his splendor and majesty, just as Muhammad did.

Now, if someone asks why I might speak so much of this matter in passing, they should know it was not done with the intention that I would presume to judge these great and difficult matters. Similarly, Alexander Severus <note>Roman Emperor from 222 to 235 AD, noted for his relative tolerance toward Christians.</note> (who is highly praised in history for his great virtues) permitted—even though he was a heathen—the Christians to build a church in Rome, the capital of his entire Empire. Should he now have weakened his authority and majesty by doing so? 

On the other hand, let someone tell me: what primarily earned Emperor Constantine the title of "Constantine the Great" and confirmed it, other than that he was the first to ordain and grant a church to the Christians, contrary to the intentions and edicts of his ancestors (almost all of whom were enemies of the Christians and had persecuted and killed them)? He did this in such a way that they were not burdened on account of their religion, just like the heathens, and had their own churches. It is impossible to say what great and terrible unrest, harm, strife, quarreling, and ill-will were thereby abolished and prevented; and by contrast, how peace and quiet were planted in the entire Empire. Because of this, he was also gifted by God with a magnificent victory and great fortune.

And so that we do not search for foreign or distant examples, history teaches us that when the Franks <note>The Germanic tribes that conquered Gaul and eventually gave France its name.</note> first came into Gaul <note>The Roman province that became France.</note> and took possession of it, they were still attached to their idols—such as Jupiter, Apollo, Mars, and others. Even though the Gauls already held the baptism and the Christian faith and had torn themselves away from the Devil's yoke, the Franks nevertheless let them remain in their faith, despite the fact that they held the upper hand and were powerful. Indeed, it is found that the Franks persisted in their idolatry until the time of their fourth king, being the conquerors and having subdued the Gauls; yet the Gauls remained and were preserved in their religion and Christian faith.

The great and mighty Turkish Emperor <note>The Sultan of the Ottoman Empire.</note> who now reigns in Constantinople—who leads some fifteen or sixteen kingdoms and lands, and is as large and powerful as France—has he or his ancestors acted so unwisely, or diminished his empire and power, by permitting such means and tolerance? Not at all, Great Princes and Lords; rather, he became stronger and more powerful because of it. For if the Turks had attempted to force their subjects into the Mohammedan faith by violence, they would have accomplished nothing except to stir up one riot after another, and the people would have abandoned their lands and homes, and there would have been no booty for them. 

Therefore, those are far mistaken who believe and think that tolerating two different sects within the Crown of France would be detrimental and harmful to the land and the Kingdom, or that the slightest bit of our King’s authority and power would be lost. For everyone remains with their own religion and is left in peace, [just as] the order of the Church at Geneva is also maintained.

From this, it is clearly [evident] that it is a much different and greater seriousness when it concerns a man's consci[ence], for which he must give an account and answer before the Last Judgment of G[od]. In that judgment, he will have the Word of God on his side, which cannot and will not fail him. For if someone has only a base delusion and mere opinion for themselves, and wants to defend it solely for the reason that it has been handed down from olden times and many years—it is as if one were to defend the mad Carnival customs <note>original: "Faßnachtiſchen gebräuch"; the author compares holding onto religious traditions purely for the sake of "tradition" to defending the rowdy, often pagan-rooted festivities of Shrove Tuesday</note> simply because they [originated] long ago, and to hold fast to them for that reason alone.

And if someone were to [oppose] this, and instead complain about that which is honorable, Christian, and in accordance with the Div[ine Word], claiming that people want to [destroy] the Old Religion and set up and defend new sects—well, these two things are as far apart from each other as Heaven and Earth. One has a [different] origin than the other. Therefore, you should also not allow yourselves to [be misled] when you think or imagine that you want to help one side and sustain them; for such a thing cannot [happen] without the injury of the other side—indeed, to the marked disadvantage and distress of the whole [community]—because people will not allow themselves to be forced in such a manner.

And because I cannot avoid (Great and Mighty Lords) also considering your [own] welfare, I wish to [put forward] what is to be said in general. For I would a thousand times rather be dead than to learn that even the slightest suffering or evil should befall you. And although I hope it will [not] come to that, it is nevertheless to be feared that [such a thing] might happen. Or do you not worry—since such a burdensome [dispute] has lasted so long and so many brave people have perished in it—that perhaps a Scaevola <note>Gaius Mucius Scaevola, a legendary Roman hero famous for his attempt to assassinate a king and his indifference to physical pain; here used as a metaphor for a desperate political assassin</note> or some such foolhardy [individuals] might be found? People who might have the thought that, even if they were to [die] for it, they would not care much, as long as they could [avenge] their side? ...but rather has a great compassion for him (not knowing how he came to such misfortune). Instead, this has happened—and still sometimes happens—to great kings, emperors, princes, and lords.

So that I may prove and demonstrate this, do you also believe that the apostate Emperor *Julian* <note>Julian the Apostate (r. 361–363), the last non-Christian Roman emperor, who attempted to revive paganism</note>, who was a terrible persecutor of the poor Christians, died in any other way than by being shot through with an arrow by a Christian in battle? They were persuaded to do this by a powerful woman named *Fredegunda* <note>Queen consort of Chilperic I, notorious for her role in the bloody Merovingian civil wars</note>, so that she might finally rid herself of the long and difficult siege with which *Sigebertus* was distressing the city of *Samarabrigam* <note>Amiens</note>. 

Should you not also then take heed and fear that the same might happen to you from those who have been burdened and oppressed for so long? Those assassins undertook such bold deeds solely to save themselves and their kin, for which they could expect nothing but a gruesome and terrible death and severe punishment. What do you think those of the present day—who consider not only their earthly life but also the salvation of their souls, and for whose sake they risk everything they have in the world <term>in die Schantze setzen: to venture or risk everything at stake</term>—will or might do?

This can be seen in Saint *Peter*, who was moved by anger to defend the Lord Christ against the high authorities with a sword. Undoubtedly, he would have attempted even more violent acts if he had not been forbidden by the Lord Christ and told to put away his sword.

Religion is a high and great matter which weighs heavily upon people and moves them to great deeds—and not without reason, as so much depends upon it. It especially strengthens people in their conscience and spirit. Had Philip the Conqueror <note>original: "Philippus Acquisitor"; refers to King Philip II Augustus of France (r. 1180–1223)</note> not been warned so that he had to flee from them, it would have happened to him in the same manner. Even our dear King, Saint Louis <note>Louis IX of France</note>, had to evade those desperate people. So little did they fear anyone, and they had set their minds to killing the Princes and the powerful even in the midst of their own people, solely for the sake of defending and preserving their perceived false religion. Because of this, even to this day, the word **Assassin** has the meaning among us in France that it is used when one wants to say of someone that they have murdered someone willfully, outrageously, or treacherously, or have otherwise committed or carried out a treacherous, evil deed.

In the same way, we also read that in our times there was a professor or schoolmaster in Milan named *Carolus Mantuanus* <note>Likely referring to Cola Montano, a humanist teacher who incited his students to assassinate the Duke of Milan</note>, who in all his lectures impressed nothing so strongly upon his students as the idea that one should let no tyrant live, and should endure no tyrannical government. He taught that those who murdered a tyrant would be holy and worthy of praise, both here and in the next world. Whether he was moved to this by his own desire for revenge, or by the love he bore for the common good and its liberty, one cannot truly know. However, it followed from this that among his listeners, this opinion was so strongly impressed upon three of the prominent nobility that they could not forget it. Instead, when they were grown, they went into St. Stephen's Church <note>The Basilica di Santo Stefano Maggiore in Milan</note> to kill the Lord of Milan, *Johannem Galeatium* <note>Galeazzo Maria Sforza, Duke of Milan, assassinated in 1476</note> (regardless of the fact that they could well consider that they would hardly escape with their lives because of the guards and servants waiting upon him). What do you think can be stirred up among the common man in daily public sermons if one speaks of the unjust power with which the subjects are burdened, suggesting that one should think of ways to cast it off?

Therefore, Most Mighty Lords, I wish to have prayed that you would well consider these examples and let them weigh upon you. If you will not do these things for the sake of the common good and the best interests of the people—which should be the primary concern for you, the rulers—then do so for the sake of the common good...

# Government of the Crown of France.

...you should take the greatest care; therefore, consider your own person, your wife and children, your welfare, body, and life, and how you might be secured in them.

Consider also and take to heart—if you intend to persist in your resolve to exterminate the Protestants and not allow them freedom of conscience regarding religion—what danger you will place yourselves in.

A cat has the nature and quality that it cannot be caged. If it is caged and pursued, it retreats and leaps from one place to another as long as it can. But if one tries to corner it too harshly, it leaps directly at the face of the one tormenting it; and what it cannot achieve by retreating, it intends to accomplish in its fury with its claws, caring no longer whether it must lose its life in the process.

I am indeed no patron of the Protestants, but a simple <note>original: "schlechter"; in this context meaning "common" or "ordinary" rather than "bad"</note> citizen of modest means. However, I have been taught that I should fear the **L O R D** God and keep Him before my eyes. And since I have seen such a great storm and discord arising because of religion, I have reflected that nothing could be more fitting or better for me than to stay at home and apply myself with all earnestness to ensuring that the common good may be maintained in peace and quiet. Above all, I wish that our Lord King may remain in his dignity and glory, and that you also, my Lords, may be preserved in your status, honor, and calling.

Therefore, I pray to God that you will not undertake this matter with the sword or do violence to our consciences. For indeed, we all—both Papists <note>A contemporary, often derogatory term for Roman Catholics; used here in a plea for mutual recognition</note> and Protestants—bear the Christian name and are united with one another through the sacrament of holy baptism. Thus, we have one God whom we serve, whom we honor and call upon. Even if it is not done in the same manner, we should nonetheless strive to do so in a way that we do not follow our own whims, but rather as God demands and desires from us.

Furthermore, the next thing is that we love one another, wish each other the best, and mean well toward one another with true loyalty, just as our **L O R D** Christ specially, earnestly, and diligently imposed and commanded us. Therefore, you should also grant as much to one side as to the other. I could not find within myself any reason why you should hate and persecute one side more. But what cannot be reconciled between parties might be postponed and left to rest until a <term>Council</term> <note>original: "Concilium"; a formal meeting of church leaders to settle points of doctrine</note>, if it should please you.

Consider what discord arose in the very beginning of the Christian Church regarding doctrine and the practice of the Lord's Supper (for this discord is not being brought to the fore for the first time now). For we find in the <term>Church History</term> <note>original: "Historia Ecclesiastica"; likely referring to the work by Eusebius</note> that in ancient times between Anicetus, the Roman Bishop, and Polycarp—who were both later [declared] holy...

# A beautiful Preface to the Reader
## in which is reported the Kind and Nature of the Human Race, and how the same is governed and maintained by Divine and Secular Laws.

<image-desc>A large decorative woodcut initial 'D' featuring ornate foliage and vine patterns within a rectangular frame.</image-desc>
Since human beings from the beginning—through the fall of our first parents Adam and Eve—have been so corrupted and weakened <note>original: *entwicht*; meaning to be made unstable or lacking in spiritual weight</note> that no one, according to the Law of Nature, does or provides for another what he would have done for himself, much less lives according to God’s Law and will. Instead, wherever one can deceive, disadvantage, overreach, revile, and finally deprive another of body, honor, and goods, <margin>Cain and Abel.</margin> one does not refrain from it, as was immediately seen in the case of Cain and Abel. For this reason, there is so much to manage and defend in all places, and authorities must be appointed throughout the world. Thus, there is almost no village so small that it must not have an overseer, such as a bailiff <term>Bailiff (German: *Vogt*): a high-ranking official representing a territorial lord, responsible for administration and justice</term>, a judge, a mayor <term>Mayor (German: *Schultheiß*): a local magistrate and tax collector</term>, or the like. Even among us, who wish to be Christians, to whom Saint Paul says: *You shall owe no one anything except to love one another.* So Christ himself speaks in John: *This is my commandment, that you love one another as I have loved you,* etc. In addition, it is fitting for Christians that they follow their Master and Lord Christ in this, and submit themselves under the Cross, as Christ says in Matthew 10: *Whoever does not take up his cross and follow me is not worthy of me; whoever finds his life will lose it, and whoever loses his life for my sake will find it,* etc. Now, if such teaching were in full effect <note>original: *im schwang gienge*; an idiom meaning "in common practice"</note>, one would need neither court, law, nor authority. Instead, each would do to the other what was pleasing to him, and what was right and fair for himself. Because one

Law: *He who is about to pass sentence*. Code on Punishments; that is, a judge who takes notice of a crime ought to investigate everything, and not condemn precipitately, unless the accused is convicted through confessions or proofs, so that he cannot deny the crime he committed.

The judge who intends to pass a sentence should maintain this measure: that he by no means lets a final judgment be passed on someone in <term>capital cases (peinliche Sachen)</term> <note>Literally "painful matters," referring to criminal cases involving physical punishment, torture, or the death penalty.</note>, or otherwise, unless the person has been convicted of adultery, manslaughter, or some other vice, through his own confession or through the unanimous testimony of those who were examined and searched out regarding it with <term>judicial torture (peinliche Frage)</term> <note>The standard early modern legal procedure of "painful questioning" to extract a confession when evidence was strong but not yet conclusive.</note>, and have confessed against him. # Preface to the Reader.

...is killed, [it] pertains to necessity and shall not be curtailed, etc.

The Greeks also punished homicides severely, yet they also maintained a distinction between those that were intentional and willful, those done out of necessity and self-defense, or those that occurred through pardonable accident. In cases of willful homicide, which in Athens were heard before the high judges—those who sat on the <term>Areopagus</term> <note>The Areopagus was the supreme court of ancient Athens, held on a hill of the same name dedicated to Ares.</note>—this procedure was followed: after taking the oath of good faith <note>German: "Aids für geferde" (Eid für Gefährde). This was a legal oath where parties swore they were acting honestly and without malicious intent to deceive the court.</note>, the case was related before the judges plainly, without any emotional display or any introduction, exactly as it had occurred. 

Thereafter, witnesses and testimonies were heard; however, the judges were not permitted to deliberate among themselves. Instead, each gave his verdict using a black or white stone, according to whether he wished to find and hold someone guilty. As the poet says:

> It was an ancient custom to use white or black pebbles; with the latter to condemn men, and with the former to absolve them of guilt. <note>original: "Mos erat antiquus niueis atrisue lapillis / His damnare viros illis absoluere culpa." This is a quote from Ovid's *Metamorphoses*, describing the ancient Greek method of voting in criminal trials.</note>

Now, if there were more of the black stones than the white ones, such a murderer was sentenced with the sword, from life to death.

If, however, it was a case where one had to defend oneself, and <term>self-defense</term> <note>German: "nottwehr."</note> was proven by him, then the defendant was acquitted of the charge and declared free; nor was there any injury to his honor or his civil status.

But if one brought another to his death by an unforeseen accident, he was banished from the land into exile. Thus <term>Telamon</term> <note>In Greek mythology, Telamon was exiled from the island of Aegina by his father, King Aeacus, after he accidentally killed his brother Phocus during a game of discus or athletics.</note> had to remain in exile because he had accidentally killed his brother during a game.

Regarding this, it is particularly to be noted that one who killed another out of self-defense was shown more leniency and less

# There follows a fine and useful

## Treatise by Guido de Suzara, regarding how and when one should proceed against evildoers with criminal interrogation—so that one does not do too much or too little to them.

<image-desc>A large, ornate woodcut decorative initial 'A' filled with intricate vine and leaf motifs.</image-desc>

As we proceed in the present matter concerning the severity of sharp interrogation <term>judicial torture</term> <note>original: "peinligkeit in scharpffer frag." In early modern law, "sharp interrogation" was a standard euphemism for the use of torture to extract a confession.</note>—about which various concerns arise daily—so that one may know how to proceed in an orderly fashion and deal with it rightly and with moderation, it is first necessary to know that every authority / whether he be a Bailiff <term>Vogt</term> <note>A regional administrative or judicial official representing a lord.</note>, a Judge, or a Mayor, should diligently pay attention to five articles. This is so that not everyone acts according to his own whim (when a poor person has been brought to prison and accused of a misdeed) against the regulations of the Law, which is by no means proper, as the Law strictly forbids such things in the Code of Justinian, Book 9, Title 4, Law 2 <note>original Latin: "L. 2. C. de custodia reoru." Referring to the *Codex Justinianus* regarding the custody of defendants.</note>.

->I.<-

First, that every judge or authority should reflect diligently and not allow himself to be easily moved to attack someone with criminal interrogation <note>original: "peinlicher frage"</note> without preceding sufficient causes and *indicia* <term>legal signs of guilt</term> <note>In this legal context, "indicia" refers to circumstantial evidence or indicators that suggested a person's involvement in a crime.</note>. Much less should he repeat the interrogation, even if these causes and signs appear likely to be the truth or "verisimilar" <note>original Latin: "verisimilia," meaning appearing to be true or probable.</note>. This is especially true where one might learn the truth of such matters through another and easier way—namely, the misdeed for which the prisoner is blamed and through which he has come to prison. This is according to the Law of the Divine Pius in the Digest, Book 48, Title 18, Law 1 <note>original Latin: "L. diuus Pius. ff. de quæstionib. & L. i. ff. eo." Referring to the *Pandects* or *Digest* of Roman Law.</note>. There it is said that one should not begin with torture <note>original: "Tortur"</note>. See also the Edict in the Code, same title, and the Law "whenever" in the Digest, Book 6, Title 1 <note>original Latin: "L. edictum. C. eodem. & L. quoties. ff. de rei vend."</note>.

->II.<-

Second, it is well to note and to be careful that a Bailiff or Judge does not proceed to criminal interrogation for any minor cause, nor without distinction of the person, so that he does not commit a legal error. Which persons may be criminally interrogated will be found distinguished hereafter.

->III.<-

Third, one should also know that not all *indicia* <note>signs or evidence</note> lead to criminal interrogation...

<header>How to deal with evildoers</header>

interrogation / to attack someone with it / must be sufficient / because one should not proceed to torture / unless one has clear *indicia* <term>legal signs of guilt</term> and suspicion / which are so strong / that it can be understood and concluded / that the prisoner cannot deny it. <note>original Latin: "d. l. 1. ff. de quæstio." Referring to the Digest of Justinian, Book 48, Title 18, Law 1.</note>

## IIII.

Fourthly / it should be noted / that no one shall be attacked with criminal interrogation <term>judicial torture</term> / unless two things come together / Namely / that *indicia* are present / and that the prisoner is so capable in body and mind / that he can withstand and endure such sharp interrogation. <note>original Latin: "l. 1. in princip. ff. de quæstio." Digest 48.18.1, at the beginning.</note>

---

## V.

Fifthly / it is to be known / that the Judge or authority is duty-bound to maintain such moderation in criminal interrogation / that he does not do too much to the body / and does not let the poor prisoner be stretched and hoisted up as often as the accuser seeks and desires / but only as much as can be endured / in such a way / that the prisoner is not tortured to death / but may remain alive / So that he may enjoy [the benefits of] his innocence / or receive his proper reward <note>meaning his legal punishment if found guilty</note>. <note>original Latin: "l. Parag. quæstioni. ff. de quæstio." Digest 48.18, paragraph 'quaestioni'.</note>

---

## What criminal interrogation is.

And it follows to know what criminal interrogation is / And criminal interrogation is nothing other / than an inquiry into the truth / upon the human body / through painful compulsion / such as the thumbscrew / ladder <note>A form of the rack where the victim was stretched over a wooden frame.</note> / branding <note>original: "Brannt"</note> / and other pains / through which a person is attacked with agony and pain / so that it hurts him. Likewise / one can also torment someone with hunger and thirst / so that he must tell the truth / therefore the judges do wrong / when they do not feed the prisoners / who are to be questioned criminally / <note>original Latin: "teste Bartho. in l. 1. Par. diuus. ff. eodem." Citing the famous medieval jurist Bartolus de Saxoferrato on the Digest.</note>

## Which persons may be questioned criminally / and which not.

As was said above / all persons may be questioned criminally / except those who are forbidden by law to be questioned / yet the Imperial Law <term>Keyserrecht</term> <note>Referring to the *Corpus Iuris Civilis*, the Roman law used as the basis for legal practice in the Holy Roman Empire.</note> says / that in certain cases / all persons without distinction may be addressed criminally / <note>original Latin: "vt C. de quæstionibus. l. milites"</note> where the Emperor / without distinction / speaks of such vices and cases / for which all kinds of people can be questioned / except those / who are in authority / <note>original Latin: "vt C. de infamibus. l. nullum."</note>

# How to deal with offenders
...must [consider] how strong, how old, or how weak they are, and also whether the crimes are minor; so that, depending on the circumstances, he must sometimes question more sharply and harshly, and at other times more mildly, and diligently consider such circumstances. <note>original Latin: "ff. de re militari. Par. finali. & l. si quis in graui. Par. Ignoſcitur. ff. ad S num. l. quæstionis modus. ff. de quæstionibus." — These are citations from the Digest of Justinian regarding military law and the specific protocols for judicial torture (quæstio).</note> This is a matter that a pious Judge should especially concern himself with.

## When many are captured / with whom to
## begin the criminal questioning.

If many prisoners are present at once and are to be questioned, no fixed rule can be prescribed for such a case. Instead, a steady Judge who is cunning and knows the various natures of people [must decide] with whom to begin so that he may discover the truth. It is known that prisoners are seldom of the same nature; one is bolder, another more fearful than the other. In that case, one should begin with the more fearful. <note>original Latin: "l. & l. vnius. Par. 1. ff. de quæstionem." — Referring to Roman law on the order of interrogation.</note> Similarly, [one should begin with] whoever has the most suspicion <term>Verdacht</term> against them, or is otherwise of a weak constitution <term>Complexion</term> <note>In the 16th century, "complexion" referred to a person's physical and mental temperament based on their bodily humors.</note>. Likewise, if a father and son are to be questioned, the Judge may begin with the son and have the father watch, so that he might confess all the sooner. <note>original Latin: "l. isti quidem in fine. ff. quod metus causa."</note> A woman also tends to confess sooner and cannot hold out as firmly as a man. <note>original Latin: "l. filia in orbitate. C. de in officio. testa. c. ſerus de verb. ſignifica."</note> Likewise, a youth confesses sooner than an old person.

It is also to be known here, and especially well noted, that when a Judge wishes to question the prisoner criminally <note>that is, under torture or the threat of it</note>, he must be careful in his questioning and not ask in such a way as: "Did you strike Gaius <note>original: "Gaium" — Gaius is a traditional placeholder name used in legal texts, similar to "John Doe."</note> with the sword or spear in the arm on that day and at that place?" For such a thing is more instructed than asked, showing the prisoner what he should say, pointing the way, and what he should confess. <note>original Latin: "l. 1. Par. qui quæſtionem. ff. de quæſtio."</note> Therefore, he should ask in general terms how he came to be at odds with Gaius and how the matter occurred. See Angelo <note>Angelo de Gambiglioni, an influential 15th-century Italian jurist</note> in the section "following public rumor," third point. Otherwise, the prisoner might say things he had never even thought of.

## It follows for what reasons someone should
## or may be questioned criminally.

To this it is answered that criminal questioning <note>torture</note> takes place and is permitted not only in criminal cases but also in civil cases and matters where the truth cannot otherwise be found. <note>original Latin: "l. diuus. d libero. ff. de quæstio."</note> That is, when someone is accused and brought forward in civil court regarding criminal matters. However, it is handled differently in civil cases than when a criminal offense is present. According to Baldus <note>Baldus de Ubaldis (1327–1400), a renowned professor of law</note> in his commentary on the chapter *diligenti* in the Decretals <note>original: "extra de appella." — referring to the Liber Extra, a collection of Papal decrees.</note>.

[header: how one shall proceed in criminal interrogation.]

## When people should be subjected to criminal interrogation.

It is not intended that everyone, without distinction of person, in all matters, or at any time, should be subjected to criminal interrogation <note>original German: "peinliche frag." This refers to judicial torture used to extract a confession in capital cases.</note>. Rather, one should not undertake such questioning until the truth cannot be reached by any other means, and there is sufficient cause and indices <term>Indicia</term> <note>From the Latin "indicia," meaning signs, marks, or circumstantial evidence that suggest a person's guilt.</note>. Otherwise, one should never begin with criminal interrogation, as was mentioned above. This is required by reason and all fairness, as Abbas <note>Likely referring to Panormitanus (Nicolaus de Tudeschis), a famous 15th-century canon lawyer known as "Abbas."</note> in chapter *cum in contemplatione, extra de reg. iur.* and also the Law 1, in the principle *ff. de quæstio.* <note>original Latin: "ff. de quæstio." refers to the Digest of Justinian, Book 48, Title 18, regarding interrogations.</note> have established. Namely, that the indices and suspicions upon which criminal interrogation is to be undertaken must be lawful and sufficient. Otherwise, the poor person—to whom too much would have happened in such questioning—could be helped neither by appeal nor restitution, since many must lose their lives when they are attacked in such a manner. *L. aut damnum. Par. 1. ff. de pœnis. L. milites. & l. cum cognitio naturaliter. C. de quæst. licet alij legant, cum cognitio naturalis.* <note>These are citations from the Digest and the Codex of Justinian regarding punishments and the "natural knowledge" or "natural investigation" of a case.</note>

## Now follows what indices are sufficient and necessary when one wishes to interrogate someone criminally.

Regarding this point—what indices and signs are necessary and sufficient, and should precede the decision to interrogate someone criminally—the following ruling is given: no thorough report or stable doctrine can be found or given in the law. Rather, it rests primarily in the discretion of the Bailiff <term>Vogt</term> <note>A local administrative official or magistrate.</note> or Judge. *L. 3. in principio. ff. de testibus.* Just as punishments that are not explicitly stated in the law are left to the discretion of the Judge, *L. hodie. & l. sanctio. ff. de pœnis.* Thus, one cannot give a certain measure or rule regarding the timing. Nevertheless, this general rule can be given and used: that a modest and prudent Judge should apply all possible diligence in investigating and inquiring into the truth when someone is brought before him who is said to have committed a misdeed. This is so that he may have certain indices, because indices are closest to proof, and point to the truth as if with fingers; they are a help or strengthening of the conviction. In this, he should not rest but apply his best diligence. *l. instrumenta. & l. finali. C. de proba.* <note>Refers to the Codex of Justinian, Book 4, Title 19, "On Proofs."</note>

A Bailiff or Judge should conduct diligent research and inquiry into which people and in which places the prisoner—who is to be tortured <term>Torquirt</term>—associated with, because bad company is an indicator of bad actions. *L. plures. ff. de administra. tuto. Parag. affidue.* It is often the case that even pious people are led astray and made evil by bad company. *L. ædilem. Par. pedius. ff. de edilitio edicto.* As Aristotle <note>The text uses the abbreviation "Aristo." for the Greek philosopher.</note> also says: a person usually keeps the kind of company that matches their own nature.

# How one should proceed with criminals

Likewise, certain situations provide great presumption of guilt. For instance, if stolen goods are found in someone's possession; or if a young man is seen leaving the house of a beautiful woman <note>In the legal context of the time, this was often considered evidence of adultery or illicit behavior.</note>; or when someone is found near a dead person with a drawn weapon; or if someone is seen leaving a house where a person has been stabbed or strangled, carrying a bloody weapon and appearing pale of face. However, it should be noted here that even if stolen goods are found with someone, if they otherwise have a clean record regarding theft, it is not sufficient presumption on its own. Rather, it must be demonstrated that he is accustomed to dealing with such stolen property; otherwise, it does not create such a great suspicion against him. <note>original Latin: "Alex. in conf. 5. 2. col. primi volum." refers to the legal opinions of the 15th-century jurist Alexander Tartagnus.</note>

Likewise, one should consider what kind of reputation <term>geschrey</term> <note>Literally "outcry" or "shouting," referring to the public reputation or "fama" of a person in their community.</note> the suspect has in the city or in the place where he has stayed. For people generally hold an opinion and speak of everyone according to how they are accustomed to behaving. <note>original Latin: "l. de minore. Parag. Tormenta. ff. de quæstionibus." refers to the Digest of Justinian, specifically the section on torture and interrogations.</note> <note>original Latin: "l. fi ab eo fidei de rei vend. Auten. de testam. Par. Sancimus. colla. 7." refers to further sections of civil law regarding property and wills.</note>

It is also important to consider whether the perpetrator was previously an enemy to the victim or bore them hatred. From this, one may presume—because he previously hated the victim—that he might have plotted further to see how he might cause them additional harm. <note>original Latin citations refer to the Digest titles "On those to whom as unworthy" and "On the taking away of legacies."</note>

Furthermore, a judge may take evidence <term>Indicia</term> and signs from the suspect's demeanor: whether he is steadfast or terrified when he is meant to answer; whether he speaks with a trembling voice; whether he turns pale; or if his hands shake. All these signs are quite useful so that one may arrive at the foundation of the truth all the sooner. <note>original Latin: "d. Par. Tormenta. ff. de quæstio." refers again to the section on judicial torture in the Digest.</note>

In the same manner, it shall also be investigated whether the perpetrator had previously threatened the victim. If this occurred, it is presumed that he followed through on the threat with the deed. This is because a man’s deeds and works are usually measured by his speech. <note>original Latin citations from the Codex "If anyone should speak ill of the Emperor" and the Digest "On the legacy of household goods."</note> This must be applied with discretion, however, according to the circumstances and the character of the person who made the threat; for one often finds people who swear death upon someone many times and yet let them live.

Furthermore, it is to be investigated whether he has previously engaged in such dealings, and whether he even has the power to act in such a way. <note>original Latin: "L. famosi. ff. ad L. Iulian. maies. l. ibi, an potuerit facere & an quid simile fecerit" translates to: "The law on famous criminals... whether he could have done it and whether he has done anything similar."</note> For if it were a person who lacked the capacity to bring about or carry out such a case, one could not proceed against them in this manner without especially great evidence <term>Indicia</term>.

Likewise, if he fled immediately, a presumption would be drawn against him from that act. <note>original Latin citations: "ff. de fœneratoribus" (On usurers) and "ff. de testib" (On witnesses).</note> From these and other...

It emphasizes that while these signs are vital for reaching the truth, they must be weighed against a person's character and actual capabilities.</summary>

...more circumstances, a diligent and careful judge or magistrate should exert as much effort as possible so that he may arrive at a thorough discovery of the truth.

## What the effects of judicial interrogation are.

Finally, it is also necessary to know what the effect of judicial interrogation <note>The term "peinliche Frage" (painful questioning) refers to judicial interrogation, which in this era frequently included the use of torture to extract a confession.</note> is. In this regard, it should be noted that if someone confesses to a crime voluntarily and outside of the interrogation chamber, both ancient and modern writers say that he should not be immediately condemned based on such a confession. Instead, the judge should wait one, two, or three days—depending on the person and the gravity of the case—and afterward, he should have the prisoner brought before him again. He should ask whether he still confesses to the act and whether he intends to persist in such a confession. The reason for this is that a confession in criminal matters does not immediately constitute complete proof, as stated in *Book 2 of the Code on the custody and production of defendants* <note>original Latin: "L. 2. C. de custo. & exhibi. reorum"</note>. This text is understood to mean that it makes no difference whether the confession happened out of fear of judicial interrogation or voluntarily. The text in *Law 1, Paragraph "divus," in the Digest regarding interrogations* <note>original Latin: "l. 1. Parag. diuus. ff. de quæstionibus"</note> is understood in the same way, where it says: *Nor should crimes be immediately considered proven.* <note>original Latin: "Nec statim habere pro exploratis facinoribus"</note>. Likewise in the paragraph *If anyone voluntarily...* <note>original Latin: "si quis vltro"</note>.

It is also to be known that a distinction is made between confessions in civil and criminal matters: in civil confessions, persistence [in the confession] is not necessary as it is in criminal ones. And it is no wonder that one investigates things more diligently and precisely in criminal matters than in civil ones, since the law says: *Where greater danger is involved, a weightier investigation must be held.* <note>original Latin: "vbi maius periculum vertitur, ibi grauior habenda inuestigatio." Citing "L. qui sententiam. C. de pœnis" and "c. vbi periculum de electio. lib. 6."</note>

Although <term>Ludovicus Relegamus</term> <note>Likely a reference to a legal commentator or a specific interpretation of the law regarding exiled persons ("relegati").</note> rejects this distinction and says that in both instances the ratification or confirmation of the confession is necessary, according to *Law 2 on the custody of defendants* <note>original Latin: "l. 2. de custodia reorum"</note>. For if the confession were not repeated and stood by, the judge would proceed too quickly against the criminals, which would be against the law. For although the text says in the *final law under the same title* <note>original Latin: "l. fina. eo. title"</note> that the judge should proceed swiftly with punishment against criminals, the <term>Gloss</term> <note>The "Glossa Ordinaria," the standard medieval commentary on Roman law which judges used as an authoritative guide.</note> says alongside it that he should nonetheless not exceed the mark but maintain the right measure and order as is fitting.

And it does not matter that this is required when the confession occurs during judicial interrogation, for it is not forbidden by other means, namely, when the confession occurs voluntarily.

Therefore, a magistrate or judge should use this caution: he should have the prisoner repeat his confession, whether it was made during judicial interrogation or <term>amicably</term> <note>original: "in der güte," meaning a voluntary confession made without the threat of force.</note>. This is primarily because one should also allow the one who confesses his defense <note>original: "Defension"</note> and not cut it off. However, when one [confirms] his statement with...

->How to Deal with Evildoers<-

Repetition confirms it, and when a person confesses a thing for a second time, then a defense alone can have little power. So too does a person often confess to what he has done, even if the situation is found to be otherwise, as we find in a fine text in *Law: "If anyone voluntarily," in the Digest regarding interrogations* <note>original Latin: "li quis vltro.ff.de quæſtionibus"</note>. There, a servant confesses that he committed a murder so that he would not have to return to his master, from whom he had fled. The text says: "You have acted quite wisely, reasonably, and prudently, dear Saxa, in that you took the servant Primitius—who had falsely taken a murder upon himself and confessed it so that he would not have to return to his master—and sentenced him based on such a false report. But nonetheless, you also wished to learn from his companions (whom he had also falsely named) so that you might arrive at a more certain discovery of the truth. Just as your foresight was not in vain, for you found through judicial interrogation <term>judicial interrogation: "peinliche frag," the formal process of questioning a suspect, which at this time typically involved the use of torture to ensure the truth of a confession</term> that his companions knew nothing of it, and he himself had fabricated the murder. Therefore, you may set aside and revoke the judgment and have the servant sold, so that he does not come back into the power of his master. Even if the master receives the money for the servant, we are certain that he would be glad to be rid of such a servant."

## When someone is judicially interrogated and confesses against another, whether such a confession should be given credit?

In this question, you must use this distinction: you must know whether the prisoner was questioned about his companions or about himself. If he is questioned about his companions, one should proceed accordingly: *Law: "None," in the Code regarding assessors, at the end* <note>original Latin: "L. nullus. C. de aſſeſſoribus in fine"</note>; *Law 1, Paragraph: "Interrogation," in the Digest regarding interrogations* <note>original Latin: "L. 1. Parag. quæſtionem. ff. de quæſtionibus"</note>. Thus says Marcus Tullius [Cicero] in his *Topics* <note>original: "Tropici," referring to Cicero's "Topica," a work on legal and rhetorical arguments</note>: when someone confesses through judicial torture, blows, fire, or burning, it is as if it were the truth itself speaking. Excluded from this is when one speaks of his enemy or confesses against him, for in that case, one should not believe it so easily. However, one should not consider it entirely untrue, but rather conduct further inquiry to see if it is so or not: *Law: "Faith of witnesses," in the beginning, in the Digest regarding witnesses* <note>original Latin: "l. teſtium fides in principio. ff. de Teſtibus"</note>.

When, however, the prisoner is questioned about his own person and about others at the same time, and confesses nothing of himself or against himself, then the aforementioned words may stand. But if he confesses against himself and his companions or others, then according to the opinion of Azo <note>original: "Afonis," likely referring to the influential medieval jurist Azo of Bologna</note>, which is preferred over others, the rule is held: when the prisoner confesses against himself under judicial interrogation, he should not be questioned about others, especially about his companions: *The final law in the Digest regarding interrogations* <note>original Latin: "L. finali. ff. de quæſtionib."</note>; *Law: "Just as," in the beginning, in the Code on the same* <note>original Latin: "L. ſicuti in princip. C. eo."</note>; *The final law in the Code regarding accusations* <note>original Latin: "L. fina. C. de acculationibus"</note>. If it now happens that one is questioned about others, or confesses against others without being asked, such a confession is not to be relied upon, except in those cases where the law investigates. If someone confesses therein, he may be judicially interrogated about his companions, provided that prior evidence <term>evidence: "Indicia," signs or circumstances that suggest guilt but do not yet constitute full proof</term> against them is at hand, of which approximately six are enumerated.

<meta>This page continues the legal analysis of when a confession given under judicial interrogation can be used to implicate others. It specifically lists six legal exceptions where the standards for evidence are slightly lowered to allow for the questioning of accomplices.</meta>

->how one should proceed in judicial interrogation.<-

<margin>I.</margin>
The first case concerns highway robbers and those who provide money or instructions to harm others. These individuals may indeed be questioned about their companions, the nature of their associations, who gave them orders, who hired them, and who provided them housing. <note>original Latin: "L. diuus Hadrianus. ff. de custo. reo. & l. penulti. C. de ferijs" — referring to the laws of Emperor Hadrian regarding the custody of the accused and court holidays.</note>

<margin>II.</margin>
The second case concerns the counterfeiting of coins. <note>original Latin: "L. finali. C. de falsa moneta" — the final law in the Code concerning counterfeit money.</note>

<margin>III.</margin>
The third: when a servant <note>the term "Knecht" refers to a laborer or domestic worker under a master's authority</note> is judicially interrogated <term>judicially interrogated: "peinlich fraget," the formal process of questioning a suspect, which at this time typically involved the use of torture to ensure the truth</term>, one may also question him sharply regarding his companions. <note>original Latin: "L. fina. ff. ad exhibendum" — the final law in the Digest regarding the legal obligation to produce property or persons.</note>

<margin>IIII.</margin>
The fourth concerns sorcerers and soothsayers, who are not only executed with the sword, but also those who seek their counsel. And if they go into other houses and practice their devilish arts, they shall be burned, as shall the person who employed them and consulted them. <note>See Albertus de Gandavo’s chapter on sorcerers and "mathematicians" (a term often used legally to mean astrologers or fortune-tellers).</note>

<margin>V.</margin>
The fifth: if someone confesses to the death of his master, one may inquire after his companions and who ordered the deed. <note>original Latin: "L. qui prius. & L. si percussor. ff. ad Silla." — laws relating to the Silanian Decree, which held a household accountable if a master was murdered.</note>

<margin>VI.</margin>
The sixth is found in the law of Neratius regarding the Aquilian Law <note>The Aquilian Law was a Roman law providing compensation for damage to property</note>. It is important to note that even in these cases, evidence <term>evidence: "Indicia," specific signs or circumstances that point toward guilt</term> must first be present; otherwise, a person could not be questioned about others. <note>original Latin: "L. 1. C. de quæstio." — the first law in the Code regarding interrogations.</note> And although the jurist Angelus argues that certain cases should be exempted—such as the crime of high treason <term>high treason: "crimine læsæ maiestatis," an offense against the dignity or safety of the sovereign or state</term> and cases that cannot be committed without a group—it is stated in his treatise and in criminal matters <term>criminal matters: "Malefiz," serious crimes involving capital punishment</term> that in cases where one may be questioned about companions or accomplices, a person may indeed be seized for judicial interrogation based on such a confession. Yet, he spoke too mildly on this point; it remains true that one must have a presumption <note>a "presumption" (Vermutung) is a legal suspicion based on probability</note> if one is to seize someone for judicial interrogation based on another's confession. <note>original Latin: "L. fin. C. de accusatio." — the final law in the Code regarding accusations.</note>

Now it is asked: when a presumption exists, should one then proceed with judicial interrogation against those who have been named by another during their own interrogation? To this it is answered: in other cases, such evidence and presumption must be "ready at hand"—meaning legally sufficient to justify interrogation—whereas in the six cases mentioned above, the evidence is not sought as strictly or precisely, as shall be further mentioned shortly hereafter.

But what if the person named during judicial interrogation already has a bad reputation and is notorious for ill deeds? Can that same person be judicially interrogated based on such a confession, even outside of the six cases mentioned above? To this I say no, if sufficient evidence is not already present, and it can...
