Meanwhile, they—the judges—though they also occasionally "reach in" <note>take bribes or steal</note>, remain pious and innocent. And it is true that the judges should not rest, according to the aforementioned decree, when something is lost, but should be diligent. Yet it cannot be proven from this that they should have the right and power to attack a thief with torture more than once without preceding indications. Rather, they may indeed address someone with judicial interrogation in that case more than in other cases without preceding indications, but still not more often than once, so that the judges do not overstep the path of the law. And for that reason, the Emperor tells them to be diligent in investigating such lordly property, or when it is lost or alienated, to seek it again; for otherwise they themselves are obligated to restore it, or they otherwise fall under suspicion as if they had alienated it themselves and had thereby become thieves. Accordingly, it is not at all the Emperor's meaning that torture or judicial interrogation should be used in any way other than what is proper in law—much less without cause or more than once—since even the Emperor does not have the power to put someone to death without cause. But one nonetheless finds those who do not care for such rules, but rather wish to be praised for their severity. If he then confesses, the matter takes its course. But if he will not confess, the judge should keep him secured in prison until he may obtain new indications. Only then may he approach him again with judicial interrogation. If, however, the judge cannot obtain new indications, he may appoint and set a legal deadline for the accuser to proceed legally with his complaint against the prisoner. # How to deal with evildoers

And since new <term>indications: "indicia," or circumstantial evidence required by law to justify the use of torture</term> and suspicions are being discussed, it is important to know what is considered new evidence. If the first grounds upon which a prisoner was questioned are distinct—for example, if it is first said that the prisoner has a bad reputation or is an enemy of the victim, and then a second witness comes forward saying they saw the accused strike a blow, or another says they saw him with an unsheathed weapon—these are distinct. However, if a later witness simply repeats the same rumors of a bad reputation that the previous witnesses already stated, this cannot be counted as a new indication. Rather, it is merely a confirmation of the previous suspicion. In such a case, the prisoner may not be further burdened or attacked with <term>judicial interrogation: "peinlichkeit," referring to interrogation under torture</term>. Otherwise, many an innocent person would be torn apart by painful martyrdom before they confessed; and even if they did confess, they would be executed despite being innocent of the deed. This is something for which one could never answer before God. Now, further.

But how, one might ask, if someone is held captive based on existing indications and suspicions and is about to be attacked with the painful question? Suppose the prisoner addresses the <term>Magistrate: "Vogt," a local administrative and judicial official</term> or Judge and says: "Lord Judge, I beg you not to rush me, a poor prisoner, but rather grant me leave to present my <term>exceptions: "exceptiones," formal legal objections to the trial proceedings or the evidence</term> and my <term>defense: "defension," the legal arguments for the accused</term> before I am burdened with torture. For I am of the hope that, according to the law, I might provide enough information and report such things to you that you would have no cause to question me painfully. And even if there are indications present upon which I am to be questioned, I am ready and willing to refute them immediately and take action against them." Should a judge grant such a plea from a poor prisoner or not? Should he allow the prisoner the space and time for such a <term>defense: "schutzwehr," literally "protective-weapon" or legal shield</term> before he is questioned?

To this, one must answer: Although some are of the opinion that such a request from a prisoner should not be granted by the judge—and some even cite legal grounds for this, which shall be omitted here for the sake of brevity—the opposite is actually true. Therefore, you should say that in such a case, the judge is duty-bound to allow the prisoner his legal shield and defense before the painful attack begins. This is especially true when the defenses are of such a nature that, if they hold up to testing and can be proven, they would exempt him from the torture. This is based on this rational cause: if the poor prisoner were to be subjected to torture before his defense was permitted, even if he were to prove his innocence immediately afterward, the damage done to his body and limbs through the torture could never be restored to him—to say nothing of the shame and <term>injuries: "Iniurien," legal term for wrongs or insults to one's honor and person</term> that would follow. It also happens that a person may perish during the painful questioning and give up their life, so that they can no longer protect themselves afterward. <note>original: "L. aut damnatos Parag. 1. ff. de pœ." Refers to a section in the Digest of Roman Law regarding the rights of those condemned or accused.</note> And since the law even allows one who has already confessed to offer a defense of their innocence, <note>original: "l. 2. C. de custo. reorum." Refers to the Code of Justinian regarding the custody and rights of the accused.</note> how much more should the judge in this case not spare nor hinder the prisoner's defense? As...

how one should proceed in the painful questioning.

The rule of law says: To whom the greater is granted and allowed, the lesser cannot be refused. <note>original Latin: "Cui enim licet quod plus esset, vtique licet quod est minus." This is a fundamental legal maxim: if a person is entitled to a major right, they must also be entitled to the minor rights included within it.</note> In summary, the laws state clearly and expressly: as often as a defendant or prisoner desires to be allowed to protect and defend himself during a trial, the judge is bound to hear him and permit it. <note>original Latin: "l. vnius Paragra. cogniturum ff. de quæstionibus," a reference to the Digest of Justinian regarding interrogations, where it is said: "Quamuis defensionem quocunq; tempore postulante reo negari non oportet," meaning "A defense requested by the defendant at any time should not be denied."</note>

However, the judge should pay close attention to what was said above and not forget it: namely, if the prisoner indicates that he wants to prove his innocence immediately or refute the <term>indications: "indicia," the circumstantial evidence or signs of guilt required by law to justify torture</term>, the <term>defense: "defension"</term> must be structured such that, if it is upheld, it exempts the prisoner from the <term>painful questioning: "peinligkeit," referring to interrogation under torture</term>. If the judge is petitioned and requested to grant the prisoner his defense before the torture, he should not refuse it—unless the higher authority <note>original: "Oberkeit"</note> that has command over him does not wish it. In that case, the judge is excused, and the authority that refuses it must answer for the consequences, as <note>Baldus de Ubaldis (1327–1400), a renowned Italian jurist.</note> says in his commentary <note>original: "in Rubrica C. de poena iud."</note>. It is safest for a <term>Bailiff: "Vogt," a local administrative and judicial official</term> or judge, or even the Mayors in the cities, to consult those who have authority over the <term>Capital Court: "peinlichen Halßgericht," a court dealing with crimes punishable by death or physical punishment</term>, who should either be Doctors of Law themselves or have Doctors of Law assisting them.

# Another question.

But what if it happens, as occurs daily and often, that witnesses must be questioned under torture, and someone so questioned confesses something during the torture and martyrdom which he later contradicts before the verdict, saying he was in error—should he be allowed to retract such an error? To this it must be answered: there are two types of error, those of law and those of fact. If it is an error of fact, he may well retract it before the verdict and sentence for this reason: it is not held that one who errs has truly confessed. <note>original Latin: "l. 2. in princip. ff. de confess."</note> Furthermore, such an error cannot harm a person until the verdict is given. <note>original Latin: "l. error. C. de iuris & facti igno."</note> For if someone confesses something during the <term>painful questioning: "peinlicher frag"</term> and persists in it until a verdict is reached, they are still permitted to prove their innocence; if they do so, they are absolved and set free. <note>original Latin: "l. 1. Par. si quis vltro ff. de quæstionib."</note> How much more then should someone be heard who wishes to prove his error and does not persist in his confession, but retracts it before the verdict? Likewise, if someone confesses that they only did so because they feared the painful questioning and appeals for that reason, they shall be heard. <note>original Latin: "l. 2. C. quorum appella. non recipiuntur."</note>

But suppose that someone confesses something during the <term>painful questioning: "peinlichkeit," a common euphemism for judicial torture</term>, but does not persist in such a confession; does such a confession have any effect? To this, it is answered that it does have some effect: namely, it constitutes "half proof." <note>original Latin: "L. r. custodia reorum. L. 1. But what if a prisoner confesses something during the painful questioning, and such painful questioning was initiated against him without any prior sufficient administration and <term>indications: "Indicia," the legal signs or circumstantial evidence required to justify the use of torture</term>? Instrumen."</note> For it is important to know that the <term>indications: "Indicia"</term> are a <term>substantial: "Substantial," an essential legal requirement</term> and a main part of the painful questioning. Without these indications, which must come first, no one should or may be questioned painfully, for one should not begin with the painful questioning. <note>original Latin: "L. 1. ff. de quæstio."</note> If no indications are present upon which one can question, whatever is undertaken without them is entirely void. <note>original Latin: "L. non dubium. C. de legib."</note> However, what someone confesses outside of painful questioning and in other matters, and testifies voluntarily, is indeed something to rely upon; so much so, that a person can be condemned based on such a voluntary confession, and a judgment can be recognized and proceeded with against him. <note>original Latin: "Confessus enim pro iudicato habetur," meaning "He who confesses is held as one already judged."</note> <note>original Latin: "L. vnica. C. de confessis."</note> Furthermore, the confessions of the accused made during interrogations are not held as proven crimes unless they persist in them; indeed, even if they do persist, and yet their innocence appears later, they are to be freed by the Prince. <note>original Latin: "d. l. 1. He says this text is unique on this point, and likewise, a confession made during torture or out of fear of torture are equal; so also held <note>Albericus de Rosate (c. 1290–1360), a celebrated Italian lawyer and commentator.</note>.

Another question follows: There is a statute in a city that no one should be questioned with torture except in certain specifically expressed cases. The bailiff or mayor wants to see it through and learn the basis of the truth; he addresses the prisoner, though not with torture, outside of such special cases so that he might not fall under the penalty of the statute. Instead, he lets him lie in the <term>dungeon: "Kärcker or Thurn"</term>, forbids giving him anything to eat, and makes him stand naked and bare in the wintertime until he confesses. However, if the judge questions someone outside of the dungeon, in his house, or where he is accustomed to sit in judgment, and threatens him to confess or else he will have him led to the tower and questioned with torture until he must confess: it is asked whether the confession given by the wrongdoer upon such a threat may be regarded as having happened out of fear of pain? To this it is to be answered: that this should happen and be undertaken in the <term>bailiff's room: "Büttelstuben," the administrative office of the local constable</term> or otherwise in a common place where the ladders and other <term>tools: "Gezeug," referring to torture devices like the rack</term>, as well as the <term>executioner: "Scharffrichter"</term>, cannot be seen. Then the prudent officials and judges—when they [ask] the prisoners in such a manner whether they wish to persist in their confession after hearing it read back—should take several <term>lay judges: "Schöffen," local citizens appointed to assist the judge</term> or other credible people and have an open <term>instrument: a formal legal document</term> drawn up. In this document it shall be recorded that the person has today, on this date, as it was read to him, again confessed that which he confessed in the painful statement, and confirmed it with such a confession in the presence and witness of such-and-such lay judges and <term>honest men: "Biderleute," upright citizens of good standing</term>, etc. In doing this, they act rightly and well. <note>original Latin: "L. 2. C. de custod. reorum, ibi sub publico testimonio," referring to the Code of Justinian, Book 9, Title 5, Law 2, regarding the custody of defendants and "under public testimony."</note>

<margin><unclear>another point regarding confirmation</unclear></margin>
But here another question arises: When someone has confessed something in painful questioning, how much time should be allowed for them to confirm it, so that they might persist in it? To this it is answered: that in the law no specific time is named. For although it stands in <note>original Latin: "l. ff. de custo. reo. post modicum tempus," referring to the Digest of Justinian, Book 48, Title 3, meaning "after a short time."</note>—that is, after a little time or after a short time—one cannot determine from this how short or how long such a time should extend. Therefore, this stands at the discretion of the judge, who must know how to guide himself according to the circumstances of the person and the weight or insignificance of the crime. For as often and wherever the time or other matters are not expressed in the law, the same is placed at the judge's discretion. <note>original Latin citations: "l. 1. ff. de iur. deliberandi. l. hodie. ff. de poen. l. 1. ff. de effracto." These refer to the Digest regarding the right of deliberation, sentencing, and housebreaking.</note>

Furthermore, it is asked: Who should be present at the painful questioning? To this it is answered as in <note>original Latin: "l. si postulauerit. Par. quæstioni. ff. ad L. Iuliam de adulterijs & stupro," referring to the Digest, Book 48, Title 5, "On the Julian Law regarding adultery and debauchery," in the section on questioning.</note> where the text says that the accused or evildoers, and their patrons or <term>advocates: lawyers or legal representatives</term>, as well as the accuser, may be present. However, whatever the tortured person testifies, the judge should take down in secret. For it is the same thing with such painful questioning as it is with a witness who is to be heard: where one allows the opposing party and the advocates to be present for the presentation and the swearing-in, but when it comes to the <term>examination: "Examen," the actual questioning</term>, they must step away, and the judge and the witness, together with the <term>notary: "Notario"</term>, remain alone together. As was the case in the situation of <note>Bartolus de Saxoferrato (1313–1357), one of the most influential continental jurists of the Middle Ages.</note> in the said law.

# ...how one shall proceed in criminal questioning.

if he should request it <note>original: "si postulaverit"</note>. From the paragraph on questioning <note>original: "Par. quæstioni"</note>, it is clearly concluded that the advocate should not be present during the interrogation of the witness, but should only be allowed to be present at the swearing-in and the recording of the testimony; see Bartolus <note>Bartolus de Saxoferrato (1313–1357) was a towering figure in medieval Roman law whose commentaries were often treated as law itself.</note> on this point.

It is also asked: whether a **free man** may be <term>questioned painfully: "peinlich gefragt," the contemporary legal term for judicial torture</term>, since the entire title in the Digests and the Codex <note>The *Digest* and the *Codex* are the primary components of the *Corpus Juris Civilis*, the foundation of Roman Law used in 16th-century Germany.</note> concerning "painful questioning" appears to suggest that it does not speak of or deal with free people, but only with one’s own <term>serfs: "Knechten," individuals in legal bondage</term>, and is understood as such. Some say that a free man may only be <term>tortured: "torquirt"</term> and painfully questioned in certain cases—for instance, when someone is to give testimony regarding a transaction where he was personally present, yet he wavers and will not stick to one story: see the law *Concerning a free man* in the Digests under *Questioning* <note>original: "L. ex libero. ff. de quæstionibus"</note> and the law *If any decurion* in the Codex under *Forgery* <note>original: "L. si quis decurio. C. de falsis"</note>. 

Briefly, however, you should say that it is not only the serfs—of whom the laws speak (although such are now rarely found, and are abolished almost everywhere here in **Germany**)—but also **free-born people** who may be subjected to the rack and questioned. For if the meaning were such that these free people could not be attacked with the "sharp questioning," then, in the opinion of Bolognini <note>Ludovico Bolognini (1447–1508) was a prominent Italian jurist.</note>, not one crime in a thousand would be punished, contrary to the law *So wounded* in the Digests regarding the *Aquilian Law* <note>original: "L. ita vulneratus. ff. ad L. Aquiliam," a law concerning liability for damages</note>. This is because witnesses are not always present during crimes and misconduct to convict the perpetrators, and those who act evilly usually shun the light and base their affairs upon denial. Accordingly, it is rightly concluded that a free man may be questioned not only against himself but also against others, as the occasion demands.

But what if a <term>bailiff: "Vogt," a local administrative official</term> or judge were so clumsy and reckless that he allowed a poor prisoner to be attacked so harshly with painful questioning and thus tortured that he died on the rack, or had his limbs torn out? Is he also to be punished for this? Say by all means: **yes**. And this is by virtue of the Law, which also does not wish for a serf to be attacked with excessive pain, where the text says in the law *According to Labeo* <note>Marcus Antistius Labeo was a famous Roman jurist from the 1st century.</note>: "But even if someone carries out this questioning by order of the Master, yet has exceeded the limit, Labeo says he is held liable" <note>original: "Sed etsi iussu Domini quis quæstionem hanc habeat, modum tamen excesserit, teneri eum Labeo ait"</note>. 

That is: even if a judge had detained a serf by order of the master and attacked him with painful questioning, but nonetheless did too much to him in such questioning and exceeded the right measure, he shall nonetheless be recognized as deserving of punishment, according to the opinion of Labeo. And it is to be known that this is no small or trivial question when a poor sinner has been tortured to death through painful questioning. Therefore, the officials, judges, bailiffs, and <term>mayors: "Schulthieſſen"</term>, and those who are accustomed to dealing with such matters—such as <term>lay judges: "Schöpffen"</term> and <term>town clerks: "Stattſchreiber"</term> (among whom enough incompetence is sometimes found)—should keep their eyes and ears open and listen with diligence. For some maintain that a judge or bailiff is only punishable in this case if he acted with deceit against the poor prisoner, and not if he otherwise did too much with the painful questioning out of negligence. ## How one [deals] with criminals

On the contrary, it is said: If a judge goes too far with the <term>judicial torture: "peinlichkeit"</term> of a sinner and has him [interrogated] too severely, against the order of the law, so that he must give up the ghost <note>meaning: the prisoner died during the interrogation</note>, then he is not to be regarded as a magistrate or judge, but as a private person. It is concluded from this that it is the same as if he had strangled the poor prisoner with his own fist. And he is just as much to be punished as a guardian who has represented his ward [wrongfully] and unjustly in his administration. For one should not place such a person on a pedestal or at the head of the table because of such improper management; rather, if he cannot account for his actions and it is found that he has wronged those under his care, he must suffer punishment just as any other. <note>original: "L. interdum. Parag. qui tutelam. ff. de furtis. L. qui f. Parag. Si tutor. ff. pro empto." These are references to the Digest, a massive collection of Roman legal writings.</note> And in many more places it is said that the judge cannot be accused if someone dies during the <term>judicial interrogation: "peinlichen frag," usually implying torture</term>, especially if the judge had several <term>indicators: "Indicia"</term> in his favor and these were found in the case records; in that case, he would be excused. But this only holds true if he did not exceed the measure of judicial interrogation. From this, one finds and concludes that if the judge has exceeded the measure in the judicial interrogation such that [the person died], he is to be punished for the excess, transgression, and disorder. If it is in doubt whether the judge did too much or not, the judge shall not be judged. But whoever brings a claim against him must prove the opposite. This is because judicial interrogation is undertaken so that the truth may come to light, and yet the innocence of the [accused] or perpetrator should not be suppressed. But if the judge or magistrate does not keep the proper measure therein, he has fallen into punishment. Just as in the case where one friend sometimes punishes another—he need not be punished by the <term>executioner: "Hencker"</term>—but if he exceeds the measure in such punishment, he is nonetheless punishable. <note>original: "L. 1. C. de emenda. Propinquoru." A reference to the Justinian Code regarding the "correction of relatives."</note> His office cannot excuse the judge; for a judge or authority is excused as little as a private person when they commit a crime. <note>original: "nec Magistratus. ff. de iniurijs." Latin: "nor a magistrate," from the Digest section on injuries or wrongs.</note>

Here, many legal grounds and reasons are attached by **Guido** <note>likely Guido de Marsiliis, a 15th-century Italian jurist famous for his work on torture</note>, along with [legal] arguments, to excuse the magistrates and judges even if they have done too much. These I will not [reproduce] for the sake of brevity, but will leave them as they are. Since this is the [main rule]: if the judge has done too much in the judicial interrogation, he is to be punished. <meta>This page continues the discussion regarding the legal requirements and evidentiary standards for "peinliche frag" (judicial interrogation involving torture). While the previous page focused on the judge's liability for excessive force, this page examines whether a single witness or public rumor provides sufficient grounds to begin such a procedure.</meta>

# [how one] should proceed in judicial interrogation.

**In the law "moritur," in the Digest concerning interrogations** <note>original: "L. moritur. ff. de quæstionibus." The Digest (or Pandects) was a massive compilation of Roman legal opinions used as the foundation for law in the Holy Roman Empire.</note>, where the text clearly states: **"The testimony of one is not to be believed,"** <note>original: "vnius testimonio non esse credendum"</note> it is also the case that all **Laws** and rights that speak of suspicions and **indicators** <term>Indicia: legal clues or circumstances that point toward guilt</term>—upon which one should judicially interrogate—speak in the **plural**. That is to say, there must be more than one indicator, and nowhere is it written that a single **indicator** is sufficient. **In Law 1, Response 2 of the Digest concerning interrogations** <note>original: "L. 1. Respons. 2. ff. de quæst."</note>, it says "and by other arguments"; therefore, one alone cannot be enough where many are required. But be that as it may, despite such arguments and the fact that otherwise a single witness is regarded as no witness at all and nothing can be proven thereby, it is concluded by **Guido** <note>likely referring to the influential 14th-century jurist Guido de Baysio</note> that if a misdeed can be brought to light against a wrongdoer by one witness, then that person may be attacked with "the sharpness" <note>a common euphemism for torture</note>. However, two points are to be noted here: First, that the witness must be an honorable, blameless man and not a loose or flighty person; for such a flighty witness who has a bad reputation cannot provide a sufficient **indicator** for judicial interrogation. **In Law 1, Paragraph "item Cornelio" in the Digest concerning interrogations.** <note>original: "L. 1. Parag. item Cornelio. ff. de quæstio."</note> Secondly, the witness’s statement must be directed straight at the misdeed itself, and not based on a suspicion or an **indicator** of the misdeed. Thirdly: unless there are other circumstances present which contradict this single witness, in which case this single witness’s statement could have no standing, nor create any **indicator** to judicially interrogate someone. This is well worth noting for this reason: if some suspicions can be brought forward for the prisoner which excuse him, then the suspicions brought against him must be strong and powerful and outweigh the others; otherwise, they cannot hold.

### Whether a matter may be proven by public outcry—called *Fama* in Latin—such that one may be judicially interrogated.

There are indeed some who hold that if a public outcry or rumor is proven against a prisoner, he may be attacked with judicial interrogation, and they hold it to be as significant as if something had been proven by a witness. But the opposite is true: namely, that public rumor alone is not sufficient to interrogate someone with "the sharpness." For rumor is a very weak, minor, uncertain, and flighty thing; it can be easily manufactured and blown up like a fire, and painted with such a color that one would swear it were so. But when one looks at it in the light and explores the truth, it is nothing other than a fabricated and lied thing, by which judges and other authorities are often badly led astray and deceived, and must afterwards be ashamed. However, if someone were accused of a misdeed and he took flight because of it, then one might well be attacked with judicial interrogation.

Furthermore, a question arises here: if, alongside common talk or <unclear>rumor</unclear>, another **indicator** <term>Indicium: a legal clue or piece of circumstantial evidence that suggests guilt</term> were also present, and the rumor were strengthened by <unclear>one</unclear> witness, would that be enough for judicial <unclear>interrogation</unclear>? <note>The text refers to "peinliche frag," the formal process of questioning a suspect under torture to extract a confession.</note>

To this, the answer is: "Yes." Likewise, if someone were beaten or even <unclear>killed</unclear>, and the rumor was that Sempronius <note>A traditional placeholder name in Roman legal texts, similar to "John Doe."</note> had done it, <unclear>and</unclear> it was said alongside this that the accused had <unclear>been</unclear> hostile toward the deceased and had held enmity with him; for such a thing brings great suspicion. **From the section "Furthermore" in the Digest concerning interrogations.** <note>original: "Par. præterea. ff. de quæstio." The Digest was the primary source of Roman law used in early modern German courts.</note> Or, if the accused let it be heard <unclear>that he</unclear> intended to cause harm to this or that person, or to beat or kill them; for a great **indicator** and suspicion is taken from this, <unclear>that he</unclear> committed the <unclear>deed</unclear> against him. **In the Code, under the law regarding insults to the Emperor, and in the same place: "let us weigh the deeds of men."** <note>original: "L. vnica. C. si quis Imperatori maledixerit... hominum facta pensemus." This legal principle suggests that a person's prior threats or character should be weighed when evaluating their actions.</note> That is: We are accustomed to weigh the deeds and works of <unclear>men</unclear> by their character. Further, if the accused had <unclear>been seen</unclear> fleeing from the place where the misdeed occurred; for <unclear>that</unclear> accuses and blames the one who flees, and creates a suspicion <unclear>against</unclear> them. **In the Novels, concerning the presentation of the accused, in the section "but if."** <note>original: "Auten. de exhibitione reo. Parag. si verò." The "Authenticum" or "Novels" were later additions to the Roman Body of Civil Law.</note>

Likewise, if one who has a bad reputation, or of whom the <unclear>rumor</unclear> persists that he is said to have committed the misdeed, is also a frivolous <unclear>person</unclear> and such a human being who is accustomed to dealing in such matters, <unclear>and</unclear> has committed similar deeds more times before—**according to the law concerning minors, in the section on Torments, under the title on interrogations, and the law "he to whom," in the same section, in the Digest concerning accusations**—then such a person could <unclear>also</unclear> be proceeded against.

In this way, one should act and conduct oneself when, alongside the <unclear>rumor</unclear>, another **indicator** also occurred; for a diligent and careful <unclear>judge</unclear> or magistrate will know to pay close attention to this with diligence, and to direct and conduct himself according to the <unclear>status</unclear> and circumstances of the person and the weight of the crime. <unclear>And</unclear> when another **indicator** occurs, and the <unclear>rumor</unclear> or report can be proven, then a sufficient sign and <unclear>indicator</unclear> is made of it, through which one can have a certain grounds to subject the <unclear>prisoner</unclear> to judicial interrogation—notwithstanding that the rumor or talk <unclear>in itself</unclear> is not considered a sufficient **indicator**.

whether they might, in good faith and according to their conscience, employ judicial interrogation when an **indicator** <term>Indicium: a piece of circumstantial evidence or a legal clue that suggests guilt but does not provide full proof</term> was not sufficient, or could not be proven; whether he, by virtue of such discretion or freedom, may fulfill that same deficiency? To this, you say: No. This is for the reason that it is not held that such freedom or discretion is given to a judge by which a prisoner’s rights are cut off when he is to be attacked with judicial interrogation <note>The German "peinliche frage" literally means "painful question," referring to the formal process of extracting a confession through torture.</note>, namely, that sufficient and lawful indicators must not precede it; **for the question of fact is in the power of the judges, not the authority of the law.** <note>original: "facti enim quæstio est in potestate iudicantium non iuris auctoritas"</note> This is to say (as I understand it in my simplicity): that a judge, in matters consisting of **fact** <note>original: "in facto"</note> and thus in the deed itself, may well be permitted some room to act; however, should he venture to act against the order of the Law, that is not permitted to him, nor can it be within his power. **Law regarding the order, Paragraph 1, in the Digest "On Municipalities."** <note>original: "L. ordine. ->How to [proceed] with evildoers<-

...who was recently strangled/lying there; such would truly be such a strong **presumption** <term>Vermutung: a legal presumption or suspicion based on circumstances rather than direct proof</term> that one might not only be questioned under **torture** <note>The German "peinlich gefragt" refers to the "painful question," the formal process of extracting a confession through torture.</note>, but even be condemned and sentenced, **through the law "Let all know" in the Code [of Justinian] regarding proofs, by indicators and indubitable proofs** <note>original: "per l. Sciant cuncti. C. de probatio. indicijs ad probationem indubitatis"</note>. And it is well to note that **pallor** <note>original: "Bledheit" (Blässe); turning pale was considered a physical sign of a guilty conscience.</note> is a particular indicator, when someone has turned pale, according to the **law regarding the questioning of minors** <note>original: "l. de minore quæstio."</note>. Furthermore, if he carried a bare sword, because no good is presumed of those who carry weapons with them, according to the **Authentica regarding things given by Princes, final paragraph** <note>original: "Autent. d-datis Principum. Parag. final."</note>. This is especially true if the weapon or the sword was bloody, as usually happens when someone is stabbed or slain, that the weapon of the one who committed the deed or the murder must be bloody. From such qualities and circumstances, one is accustomed to draw or take a presumption—which must not be slight or minor—even though such great and indubitable indicators rarely occur.

Another indicator may also happen or occur which brings with it indubitable proof, which is sufficient for **torture** <term>Tortur: the physical application of pain to extract a confession</term> and the **judicial interrogation** <note>original: "peithen frag" (peinliche Frage)</note>, and which can often occur. Namely, that a man named **Titius** <note>Titius and Seius are standard placeholder names used in Roman and medieval legal texts, similar to "John Doe" and "Richard Roe."</note> was slain in a vineyard, and **Seius** has been frequently blamed for it, yet no witness could be found or brought forward who saw such a homicide with their own eyes. However, these following indicators have nevertheless been proven against him, Seius: First, that at the very time Titius was deprived of life, he fled. Second, it has been shown that there is a public rumor and outcry that Seius committed such a homicide. And third, that Seius was a mortal enemy to Titius. Fourth, that Seius alone held a bare weapon in his hand. Such four indicators (although each specifically for itself would be too weak) nevertheless constitute sufficient proof and presumption, when they are proven simultaneously, not only for judicial interrogation but also to sentence someone to a criminal penalty.

Likewise, another example of indubitable presumptions: namely, Seius is accused of having Titius strangled, though no witnesses can be produced who saw it. However, the following indicators are proven against him: Initially, that he was a mortal enemy to Titius. Item, that the said Seius, after the homicide was committed, took the murderer into his house. Third, that the murderer was related to Seius by service and was his household companion. Fourth, that there was a common outcry that Seius had Titius strangled. Fifth, that Seius had let it be heard and known that he had caused Titius to be killed. Sixth, that Seius was also the kind of fellow who dealt in such murderous deeds. Seventh, it was also known that they had been at odds and in conflict with each other. All of which indicators are sufficient not only for judicial interrogation, but also for sentencing, if they are all proven.

->how to proceed in painful interrogation.<-

And one should not be surprised that so many **indicators** <term>indicia: legal clues or signs that point toward a person's guilt</term>, which on their own might not be sufficient to subject someone to **painful interrogation** <note>The "painful question" or "painful interrogation" (German: peinliche Frag) refers to the legal process of extracting a confession through torture.</note>, may nevertheless constitute an indubitable **indicator** against someone when they are proven together. Par. si vero nullus horum, colla. 6."</note> since two or more things that are incomplete can make one thing that is complete, <note>original: "l. cum scimus. in princ. C. de Agrico, & censitis lib. 11."</note>. As the Poet says:
> And things that do not help individually, help when there are many. <note>original: "Et quæ non prosunt singula, multa iuuant." This is a quote from Ovid's *Remedia Amoris*.</note>

However, one should be very cautious in such cases and not interpret things in such a way that, when many suspicions coincide, one immediately proceeds to a judgment and wishes to deprive someone of their life. Instead, one may sentence the prisoner to a fine, but not condemn them to death.

Although it is also provided in the law that even when one cannot have the clear ground of a misdeed, one may nevertheless sometimes judge and rule upon it through other arguments and suspicions, <note>original: "l. Non omnes, Parag. à barbaris. ff. de re militari"</note>, where it is said:
> Even if this cannot be clearly proven, it must nevertheless be understood through arguments <note>original: "Etsi hoc liquido probari non possit argumentis tamen cognoscendum est"</note>

That is, although the matter cannot be proven so clearly, one must look at the arguments through which it must be recognized, regardless of the fact that it is a criminal matter.

And a diligent reader can find many more such examples of indubitable suspicions that are sufficient for proof. We shall leave it with those just recounted and ask further about certain persons—such as soldiers, judges, bailiffs, and councilors in cities—whether they may be subjected to **painful interrogation**.

### I.

Now, concerning the soldiers of these times: if someone asks whether they may also be subjected to **painful interrogation**, the answer is yes. For since they no longer observe the old military customs, and show themselves neither in their lives nor in their military conduct as the ancients did, they therefore also have no right to enjoy the **privileges** <term>Priuilegien: special legal exemptions or protections</term> that soldiers held in former times, <note>original: "ut in Autentica de mandatis Principum. Par. fina. colla. 3."</note>. This is briefly the opinion of **Guido** <note>Guido de Suzaria, a 13th-century jurist.</note>, and **Ludouicus Bologninus** <note>Lodovico Bolognini, a prominent 15th-century Italian lawyer.</note> ultimately concludes the same with him.

### III.

Thirdly, if a soldier—out of error or ignorance of the Law—has forgotten or left out his **exceptions** <term>exceptions: legal defenses raised by a defendant to delay or stop a lawsuit</term> and other necessities in a legal justification, it is provided for by Law that even after a judgment has been issued, but before the execution of the sentence has begun, he shall be permitted to submit them. <note>original Latin: "l. 1. Soldiers also retain such a **privilege** regardless of whether they are being sued by others or if they are suing one another; for since ignorance is present on both sides, the Law remains the same one way as the other in this case. <note>original Latin: "Ita decidit Barth. in l. 1. ff. de iuris & facti igno." citing Bartolus again on the equality of ignorance.</note>

Alongside this, however, it is important to know that just as the **privilege** is permitted for soldiers to use against others, they must also endure and suffer the same Law from others against themselves. For this is naturally right and fair in itself: that it should go for the plaintiff as it does for the defendant, according to the rule: "the plaintiff is not permitted what is not permitted to the defendant." <note>original Latin: "non licet actori quod reo licitum non est l. petenti. C. de tempo. in integ. resti."</note>

[...if he] knew [the law], but did not wish to allege it, but rather relied upon his **privilege**, then he could not be assisted by it, nor should it be granted to him; for it is only ignorance of the Law that excuses soldiers. <note>original: "l. professio. C. de muneribus patrimoniorum, lib. 10." refers to the Justinian Code regarding public duties.</note> From this it follows that if the soldier’s opponent can prove that the soldier employed legal scholars or had studied Law himself (as often happens), then his **privilege** can neither support nor help him in that instance.

### III.

Though it is true that soldiers may bring forward **allegations** after a judgment has been delivered, this can no longer occur once the **execution** of the sentence has been carried out.

### IIII.

While soldiers may make use of the aforementioned **privilege** in permitted cases, this does not extend to knights, whom some are also accustomed to calling "soldiers" <note>original Latin: "milites"</note> out of error. This is not because they are unworthy of such a privilege and freedom, but because such men are usually intelligent and courageous people of great knowledge and experience; they are not merely poor foot-soldiers <term>Landtknecht: a type of mercenary infantryman often viewed as socially inferior to knights</term> who are accustomed to walking only with weapons, and thus "relying only on iron and spirit," as Livy says. <note>original: "l. 1. ff. de milita. testamento." refers to the Digest section on military wills.</note>

### V.

From this it also follows that legal scholars—such as Doctors and Advocates, who are also called "soldiers" <note>original Latin: "milites" - in the sense of 'milites legum' or soldiers of the laws</note>—are not eligible for the aforementioned **privilege** of soldiers. Indeed, it would be a disgrace if they did not know the very Law which they handle daily and upon which they advise others. Likewise, the clergy are excluded; <note>original Latin: "l. 2. § Seruius Sulpitius. ff. de origine Iuris."</note> for the "unrefined and unlearned are not to be admitted to holy orders." <note>original Latin: "Rudes autem atque indocti ad ordines non sunt admittendi." from the section on most holy Bishops, paragraph on clerics.</note>

## Whether a soldier may also be subjected to painful questioning <term>painful questioning: a common legal euphemism for judicial torture used to extract confessions</term>.

Although we heard above what Guido de Susaria <note>A 13th-century Italian jurist known for his work on criminal law.</note> said on this matter, and concluded that soldiers today may be subjected to **painful questioning**, Oldendorpius <note>Johann Oldendorp (c. 1487–1567), a highly influential German jurist and reformer.</note> holds the opposite view and says: No. This is based on the Law "Soldiers" <note>original Latin: "l. Milites. C. de quaestionibus"</note> in the section on interrogations, where it is stated: "For soldiers cannot be questioned [under torture] nor subjected to the punishments of commoners in criminal cases." This was also established for veterans in the Law "All Judges." <note>original Latin: "l. omnes iudices. C. de decurionibus."</note>

C. de Aduocatis diuersorum iudicum"</note>. ### Finally, and in conclusion, it is asked whether
### clerical persons, as well as judges and councilors in a
### city, may be subjected to criminal interrogation.

Concerning these persons—such as clerics, priests, as well as judges and advocates—much has been said above. Although the author states that by law they should not or cannot be subjected to criminal interrogation, he nevertheless admits that a different custom has arisen through practice. Furthermore, cases are distinguished in such a way that in certain instances no one is spared, though one person might be treated less harshly than another, depending on age, status, the gravity of the deed, and similar factors, as has been heard and detailed at length above. Whoever desires to know more of this matter may read Gandinus <note>Alberto Gandino (c. 1245–1310), an Italian jurist known for his work on criminal law</note> in his treatise on criminal matters <note>original: "Malefiz sachen"</note>, under the title *Concerning Presumptions and Evidence* <note>original Latin: "De præsumptionibus & indicijs"</note>. I intend to translate this treatise into the German language in time for the benefit of the common good. For now, in haste, I have attached several necessary questions regarding this subject from Paulus Grillandus <note>Paolo Grillandi (fl. 1500s), a judge and author of famous works on criminal law and witchcraft</note>, which are very useful and necessary to know, for the benefit of all court officials, which the reader may take in good part.

## I.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'A' featuring ornate scrollwork, foliage, and a small figure nestled within the curves of the letter.</image-desc>Initially, it is asked what "criminal interrogation" <term>peinliche frage: a legal term for a judicial examination where physical pain is used to extract a confession</term> is. To this it is answered: that criminal interrogation is nothing other than the seeking out of the truth through physical assault, which is painful to the body and causes hurt <term>The Law "According to Labeo," Paragraph "interrogation," in the Digest "on injuries," joined with Law 1, Paragraph "interrogation," in the Digest "regarding the Syllanian Decree of the Senate."</term> <note>These citations refer to the *Corpus Iuris Civilis*, the foundational Roman law code used throughout early modern Europe.</note> From this it is to be understood that if a prisoner or wrongdoer is simply spoken to, questioned, or threatened, it cannot be considered a criminal interrogation <term>The same law "According to Labeo," Paragraph "interrogation," the version regarding "naked" [questioning]</term> <note>original: "nuda," meaning simple questioning without the use of instruments or force</note> according to the opinion of **Azo** <note>Azo of Bologna (c. 1150–1230), a highly influential medieval jurist</note>, who insists that one should not assault poor prisoners with criminal interrogation as harshly as the accusers desire, but rather with reasonable moderation <term>Law "on the minor," Paragraph "Torments," in the Digest "on interrogations."</term>

Next, it is asked what **torture** <term>Tortur</term> or **torment** <term>Marter</term> is, for some are accustomed to making a distinction between torture and criminal interrogation. They say that "criminal interrogation" refers to the Judge who carries it out against the prisoner; **torture**, however, refers to the pain or torment itself which the prisoner must suffer. And torment is such a means and way to provide proof that it should not be used until one can find no other way to reach the truth, as **Baldus** <note>Baldus de Ubaldis (1327–1400), a renowned expert in civil and canon law</note> says <term>Law "if anyone to anyone," in the Code "regarding the Julian Law of Majesty."</term> This is because ordinary means and ways are preferred, such as when one proves and makes something known through witnesses or written documents <term>Law "Let all know," in the Code "on proofs."</term>

This makes more or less fear, pain, and smarting in the human body depending on whether it is applied harshly or mildly, and according to the person, the deed, and its nature, and also whether the <term>Indicia: legal signs or clues of guilt</term> and suspicion are heavy or slight.

However, for the sake of greater accuracy in this criminal matter, I have gathered the facts together into five <term>Gradus: degrees</term> or <term>Species: types</term> concerning the cords: how they should be pulled tighter or looser, and how they should be set up and used according to the situation of the person, their age, and the crime. But before I come to that matter, I will first show which <term>Indicia</term> are sufficient for criminal interrogation.

->III.<-

### The third question is: what are lawful and sufficient <term>Indicia</term> for criminal interrogation? 

Before I answer such a question, we want to first see what an <term>Indicium</term> is, what a "common rumor" is, and similar things that must precede before one may proceed to the <term>Inquisition: a formal judicial inquiry</term> and criminal interrogation. I say that the <term>Indicia</term> are of two kinds: one is a half or incomplete <term>Indicium</term> or suspicion; the other is a completely full and sufficient <term>Indicium</term>, as Baldus says in the Law "Indeed that" in the Code on Accusations <note>original: "L. ea quidem. C. de accusa."</note>.

A half or incomplete or doubtful <term>Indicium</term> is that which gives one a strong suspicion to believe or not believe something, according to the Law "Since proof" <note>original: "L. cum probatio"</note> in the Digest on Proofs, and Gandinus in the title "on presumptions."

A total or complete <term>Indicium</term> or suspicion, however, is an indication through signs that are indubitable and sufficient to create a belief in someone.

However, since in criminal matters—especially when proceeding by way of "inquisition" <note>Inquisitorial procedure was a legal method where the judge acted as the investigator and prosecutor, rather than just an arbiter between two parties.</note>—it commonly occurs that one speaks and acts based on the rumor or outcry regarding the evildoer, as the <term>Doctors: legal scholars</term> say in the chapter "how and when," regarding accusations. Therefore, necessity requires that we set down something here regarding good and bad reputation. A good reputation <note>original: "gerücht"</note> is nothing other than the unimpaired or uninjured standing of a person, which is sufficient according to the law and the custom of honest and good morals. *Law "kinds of knowledge," Digest "on various and extraordinary knowledge".*

From this, it can easily be inferred what <term>infamia: infamy or ill-repute</term> or a bad reputation is: namely, a deprivation of a good name <note>original: "leumat"</note> due to an event that occurs against nature. Or, to put it more clearly, "infamy" or a bad reputation is nothing other than an injury to the majesty or dignity of a person's good name, regarding their honor and good reputation; by this description, the opposite of a good reputation is recognized.

But a common rumor <note>original: "gerücht"</note> is that which is spoken among the people and has spread about a person or a thing; this may be called a "speaking rumor," since it speaks of someone continually, called <term>fama: public reputation</term>.

<term>Rumor: hearsay</term>, however, is a completely uncertain outcry and gossip that has spread among the common people and many others, upon which one can neither speak nor build <note>meaning: one cannot base a legal argument on it</note>.

And although there are many other degrees of investigation before one arrives at the true truth, during which the judge's mind remains constantly in doubt—such as <term>presumption: an assumption</term>, suspicion, <term>legal fiction: a legal assumption</term>, argument, <term>support: corroborating evidence</term>, conjecture, ignorance, error, probability, notoriety, the manifest, etc., of which <term>Bartolus: a famous 14th-century jurist</term> makes mention in the law "of admonishing" in the Digest "concerning oaths," and which are recounted at length by <term>Grillando: the author Paolo Grillando</term>—I have nonetheless left them untouched, as they belong more to the school <note>i.e., academic study</note> than to the Town Hall <note>i.e., the practical courtroom</note>. Whoever desires to know the differences between these things may look for them there.

## Now follows how many degrees there are of torture.

## IV.

In the fourth part, we shall now see how many degrees <note>original: "Gradus"</note> of criminal interrogation <note>interrogation under torture</note> there are. It was mentioned above that there are five degrees of torture, which we wish to examine one after the other, beginning with the least and proceeding to the greatest and most severe, just as one climbs up a ladder.

# Necessary questions/ as they occur in and during the

jerking, thrusting, or the strappado <note>original: "Strapecordi" — a form of torture where the prisoner’s hands are tied behind their back and they are hoisted up by a rope.</note>. This involves a mild interrogation which one may proceed to when there are *indicia* <note>original: "indicia" — legal signs or evidence of guilt</note> that appear to provide some provable suspicion, but are not entirely sufficient and are somewhat questionable. For example, if someone were present, as mentioned above, who had seen the defendant commit the crime, but that witness was not of such a standing that one could or should accept their testimony without objection <note>original: "excipiren" — a legal term for entering an exception or challenge against a witness</note>; or if two witnesses were present who had heard about the crime but had not seen the accused prisoner commit it. Such and similar presumptions and *indicia*, though they are not perfect, might cast enough suspicion on the accused that one may use this second degree. According to the opinion of Baldus <note>Baldus de Ubaldis (1327–1400), a highly influential Italian jurist.</note>, this is considered a minor torture or "painful question," in the same way that someone might have a slight or minor fever but can still go about their business. However, I personally do not agree with Baldus in comparing this second degree of torture to a minor fever, because the degree of a "painful question" <note>original: "peinliche frag" — the legal term for interrogation under torture</note> is a completely different matter than a fever, regardless of the illness. For if someone has a small or minor fever and can still walk about the city and other places, he can also go to the Town Hall and thus has no excuse, nor reason to complain against anyone. But even if one is not attacked more harshly with pain than this second degree entails, it is still not possible for it to pass without suffering. Even if he is only hoisted up a little, and even if the pain is minor, it is still pain, and furthermore, such a thing is injurious to the body of the tortured person. Therefore, it must be regarded as a "painful question." I have never made it a practice to use this degree of torture unless I had very explicit and provable *indicia* beforehand, especially if the person is of the nobility <note>original: "vom Adel"</note> or otherwise of a good family. However, if it is a common, unknown person who is inconsistent in their speech, terrified, and accused or suspected of some misdeed, and the *indicia* of the deed are as follows, then one might well subject them to this second degree of the "painful question" as mentioned. Likewise, the statement and confession resulting from such a "painful question" must be ratified <note>confirmed as true after the torture has ceased</note> just as in other cases where someone is properly subjected to torture; *according to Law 2 of the Code on the custody of defendants.* <note>original: "d. l. 2. C. de custo. reorum"</note>

The third degree of the "painful question" is when the prisoner is hoisted up and remains hanging in the weight for as long as it takes to recite a *Miserere* <note>original: "Miserere" — Psalm 51, "Have mercy on me, O God"</note> or a *Pater noster* <note>original: "Pater noster" — the "Our Father" or Lord's Prayer</note>, or a little longer, but without the "stretching" or jerking of the cords or ropes by which a person is tortured. The authorities or the judge may proceed to this degree as often as the prisoner is suspected of a misdeed and the *indicia* brought against him are proven and demonstrated—even if the transgression or misdeed were not so gruesome or urgent, such as if he had committed a minor theft or wounded someone, provided the wound is not fatal; *Law 2 and there Bartolus, Digest on public trials.* <note>original: "l. 2. & ibi Barth. ff. de publicis iuditij." — reference to Bartolus de Saxoferrato, a famous medieval jurist, commenting on the Digest of Roman law.</note> But if the crime is somewhat coarse, and the *indicia* are clear and manifest, but the person is of the nobility, or otherwise of an honorable and stately family—

->IIII.<-

The **fourth degree** of the painful question <note>original: "peinliche frag" — the formal legal term for interrogation under torture</note> is when the prisoner is hoisted up <note>This refers to the "strappado," where a person's hands are tied behind their back and they are lifted by a rope</note> and must remain hanging in the weight for a good while, such as a third part <note>likely twenty minutes</note> or a half hour, or even a full hour, depending on the circumstances and the gravity of the matter or the person. The executioner gives them one, two, or three "jerks" with the cord, or beats them on the shins so that the martyr’s pain becomes even greater. This is done especially when the crime is significant, the person has strong limbs, the *indicia* <note>legal signs or evidence</note> are great and well-founded, and the prisoner is under heavy suspicion. When all these elements coincide, or at least the majority of them, it is sufficient to proceed with this degree of the painful question. Likewise, this applies when the crime is of such a nature that a great scandal would result if it were to go unpunished—such as when someone has committed a major theft, broken into a church, committed a wanton homicide, forged Imperial or Papal letters, or carried out similar misdeeds for which clear, sufficient, and provable *indicia* are present. For instance, if a witness exists against whom no objection could be made, who saw the crime the prisoner is alleged to have committed; or if two or more witnesses exist who can prove the other signs and circumstances according to the nature of the crime, as **Albertus Gandinus** <note>A 13th-century Italian jurist who wrote extensively on criminal law</note> writes further in his treatise on doubtful and certain presumptions, and as the Canonists <note>experts in Church law</note> write in the section *on accusations*.

->V.<-

The **fifth and final degree** of the painful question is when the prisoner has been hoisted up and, as mentioned above, is left hanging in the torture, and the lines or cords are pulled several times and the shins are beaten, but the prisoner disregards all of this and persists in his denial. To increase the severity of such martyrdom and pain, several weights are hung on his feet, such as stones or iron shackles, and he is hoisted up with the weight and left to hang there while his shins are beaten. This is the **greatest and highest degree** of the "sharp question" <note>original: "scharffen frag" — another term for severe torture</note> used on prisoners and evildoers. The Doctors of Law who have written on this subject say that by this means the human body is torn and the limbs are pulled apart, so that often a person is made a cripple and deprived of their health. Therefore, it is also said that it is a heavier pain than if someone had both fists chopped off, according to the law *that no judge...* <note>original: "Auten. vt nulli iudicum."</note> in the paragraph *but because*. Thus **Cassiodorus** <note>A Roman statesman and writer (c. 485 – c. 585 AD)</note> says in his letters that one would rather be dead than be tortured and stretched in such a manner, for these are his words:

> It is easier to seek death from you than to endure the cruelty of torments, in-

...during the final gasps of extreme distress, it is better to die than to live <note>original Latin: "Inter supremas anhelitus angustias melius est perire quàm viuere"</note>, etc. As it often happens that one confesses, out of fear of the pain, to things they never thought of in their entire life; for this reason, such severity is seldom undertaken. They have such strength in their limbs; some are so flexible in their arms that their limbs part from one another very easily and without pain, so that they can clap their arms together backwards over their heads and yet feel little or no pain, as I have often seen and experienced.

In this regard, I cannot leave the reader unnotified that some thirty or forty years ago, while I was still in Leipzig, I was credibly informed that at one time a man was taken into custody (I know not for what gross misdemeanor). However, when the prisoner, who still lay upon the ladder, heard this, he called the executioner to him with the candles still burning and addressed him with these words: **"Dear Master, I still have some hair back here, etc.; please singe it off for me."** The executioner had not expected this at all, as he had otherwise attacked him so harshly with the fire; he therefore asked him if he was in earnest, to which he answered, "Yes." Although such a thing is nearly unbelievable, one nonetheless sees from the preceding examples, and experiences daily otherwise, what such people and wicked, daring knaves dare to venture. # Torture is Wont to Occur
Ppp ij
<meta>catchword: confess-</meta>

...the use of **fire** <note>original: "deß Brandes"</note> was mentioned during the judicial torture <note>original: "peinlichen frag"</note>, and even Grillandus <note>Paulus Grillandus was a famous 16th-century Italian jurist known for his writings on criminal law and witchcraft</note>, in the most severe degree of pain, did not mention fire; thus, I wonder how judges and bailiffs come to the conclusion that they may so easily attack poor prisoners with fire if they do not wish to confess quickly. Truly, one should not deal so swiftly with these poor people (unless the utmost necessity requires it). Although I must also say and admit that in ancient times fire was also used in judicial torture, as can be seen from **Cicero in his *Topics*** <note>original: "Cicerone in Topicis"</note>, where he says: what those who are painfully tortured by fire and blows confess is held for the truth. Excepted, however, is what one says of his friend; that is not so easily to be believed, but also not to be entirely despised; rather, it will be necessary to take diligent inquiry as to whether the matter holds true or not.

Regarding this, I must relate a story here which truly happened. A wicked knave came to a **shoemaker** in a city and desired a pair of shoes from him; but when the shoemaker would not give him the desired shoes without money, the knave went away in anger and said with threats: he would remember this. However, when that same knave was afterwards seized on account of a **murder** <note>original: "Mordthat"</note> which he had committed on the road, and among other things was asked under torture who had helped him in such a murder, he immediately confessed against the shoemaker. The shoemaker was then arrested upon such a confession and immediately questioned, and also **stretched** <note>Referring to the strappado or the rack</note> for so long that he had to confess out of the agony of torture that he had helped to accomplish the reported murder. 

Thereupon, they were both led out, and the authorities intended to execute them with the **wheel** <note>The "breaking wheel" was a gruesome form of execution used for capital crimes like murder</note>, as indeed happened. But the knave—so that he might see his conceived envy brought to fruition before his death—earnestly begged the judge to let the shoemaker be executed first. The judge granted this. Now, as the arms and legs of the poor, innocent man were being smashed to pieces with the wheel, the villain cried out to the **executioner** <note>original: "Hencker"</note> that he should stop and lay no further hand on the shoemaker, for he was innocent of the deed. When he was asked by the judge why he had accused the poor man, doing him such evil and accusing him in an innocent manner and letting him be tortured, he answered: He had once asked him for a pair of shoes, which he had refused him; he had to repay him for that. 

If I were now a judge and had let myself be deceived by such a villain, believing his words and not looking further, nor having conducted a proper **investigation** <note>original: "inquisition"</note> and research, I would not be able to forget it for the days of my life. Therefore, I pray and exhort all judges, and those in authority, for the sake of the **Last Judgment**, that they will indeed not hurry with prisoners, but inquire well into all circumstances before they let someone be executed, so that they do not shed innocent blood. Now follows further.

# Necessary Questions Regarding Judicial Torture
<note>original header: "Notwendige fragen/so in vnd bey der"</note>

...among the final gasps of distress, it is better to perish than to live <note>original Latin: "inter supremas anhelitus angustias melius est perire quàm viuere"</note>, etc. It happens all too often that one, out of fear of pain, confesses to that which they never thought of in their entire life. For this reason, such severity is seldom recommended. Furthermore, judges and bailiffs should not easily allow themselves to be moved, nor should they attempt to use this severity, except in certain specific and great cases. These include the **crime of high treason** <term>lèse-majesté|Latin: "crimine læsæ Maiestatis"; the crime of violating majesty, or treason against the sovereign</term> or **heresy** <note>original: "hæreseos"</note>, such as when one has acted against the Emperor or the Empire, or is a heretic, or has committed a crime against the Fatherland and betrayed it, whereby the same was placed entirely or for the most part in great need and danger. Also, if one has committed a great **assassination** <note>original: "Assassinamentum"</note>, that is, if he has been commissioned to murder and do away with a high-ranking person, such as a Prince or a Cardinal; such persons have no privilege to help them <note>The author cites several Roman and Canon laws here (Code of Justinian and others) regarding the prosecution of treason, sorcery, and heresy to justify why these prisoners lose their usual legal protections</note>.

However, many are found among the prisoners who are of such a body, and also so fearless, that they do not dread any torture, nor do they feel any woe or pain, even if they are hoisted, stretched, and tortured a hundred times. Such strength do they have in their limbs; some are so flexible in their arms that they pull apart very easily and without pain, so that they can strike their arms together behind their heads, and yet feel little or no pain, as I have often seen and experienced.

Here I cannot leave the reader without mentioning that a good forty-three years ago, when I was still in **Leipzig**, I was credibly informed that once a man was imprisoned (I know not for what gross misdemeanor) and when they attacked him with the **judicial torture** <term>peinliche frag|The formal legal process of questioning a suspect using physical pain to extract a confession</term>, and he would not confess—regardless of how long they held the **evidence** <note>original: "indicia"</note> against him—the judge had him attacked most severely with fire. When the **executioner** <note>original: "Scharpffrichter"</note> said he knew of nothing more to do against this man at this time, he took his hand full of the lights <note>candles or torches used for burning</note> with which he had burned him and intended to extinguish them and put them away. But when the prisoner, who was still lying on the rack, heard this, he called the executioner to him, while he was still holding the burning lights, and addressed him with these words: "Dear Master, there are still some hairs back there, etc., which you should singe off for me." The executioner could not understand this at all, because he had otherwise attacked him so harshly with the fire; he therefore asked him if he were in earnest. To which he answered: "Yes." And when he held the light to the place and burned it so that it smelled, the prisoner said: "Right there, dear Master, right there, that tickles me; my thanks to you, dear Master." And thus he let the judge, with his records, and the **hangman** <note>original: "Hencker"</note> withdraw again. Although such a thing is almost unbelievable, one sees it from the preceding examples, and otherwise experiences what such people and wicked, daring rogues will not attempt. Nevertheless, I wish to remind the reader of this and also of something else alongside it—

# Torture Often Occurs.
<note>original header: "Tortur pflegen fürzufallen."</note>

I have mentioned the use of **burning** <note>original: "deß Brandes"; referring to the application of heat or hot irons as a method of torture</note> during judicial torture. Even though *Grillandus* <note>Paulus Grillandus, a 16th-century Italian jurist and influential writer on criminal law and witchcraft</note> does not mention burning even in the most severe degrees of torture, I wonder how judges and bailiffs come to use it so easily on poor prisoners when they do not confess immediately. Truly, one should not deal with poor people so hastily (unless extreme necessity requires it). 

However, I must also admit and acknowledge that in ancient times, burning was used in judicial torture. As understood from *Cicero in his Topics* <note>original: "Cicerone in Topicis"; a work by Marcus Tullius Cicero on legal argumentation</note>, he says that what those who are painfully tortured by fire and blows confess is held to be the truth. Excepted is what one says regarding his friend; that is not so easily believed, yet it is not to be entirely disregarded either. Instead, it is necessary to conduct a diligent inquiry to see if the matter holds true or not. 

I must tell a true story here regarding this. A wicked knave came to a shoemaker in a town and asked for a pair of shoes. When the shoemaker would not give him the shoes without payment, the knave left in anger, threatening: "I will make you regret this." Later, this same knave was seized for a murder he committed on the road. When asked under torture who had helped him in the murder, he immediately accused the shoemaker. Based on this accusation, the shoemaker was arrested and immediately questioned and stretched <note>likely on the rack</note> until, out of agony, he had to confess that he had helped commit the murder. 

Both were then led out to be executed on the **wheel** <term>the wheel|a horrific method of execution where the prisoner's limbs were shattered with a heavy wagon wheel</term>. To see his spiteful plan fulfilled before his death, the knave begged the judge to have the shoemaker executed first. The judge granted this. As the poor, innocent man’s arms and legs were being smashed with the wheel, the villain cried out to the **executioner** <note>original: "Hencker"</note> to stop and lay no further hand on the shoemaker, for he was innocent of the deed. When the judge asked why he had accused the poor man and caused him such suffering, he answered that he had once asked for shoes and been refused, and he felt he had to repay him. 

If I were a judge and had allowed myself to be deceived by such a villain—believing his words without looking further or conducting a proper investigation—I would not be able to forget it for the rest of my life. Therefore, I pray and exhort all judges and those in authority, for the sake of the **Last Judgment**, not to hurry with prisoners. Instead, they should investigate all circumstances thoroughly before allowing someone to be executed, so they do not shed innocent blood. What follows next:

***

# Necessary questions / which in and during the

...certain verses which, if they are used against those who have bewitched themselves so as not to confess (or are unable to), are believed to dissolve their sorcery so that the prisoners then suffer great pain and torment. The reader must reflect upon this; I, for my part, cannot promise anything regarding such remedies <note>original Latin: "remedia"</note>, as I have neither seen nor experienced anything of the sort.

Fifthly, when the question is asked for which crimes and deeds one may undertake the painful question <term>peinliche frag: a formal legal term for judicial torture used to extract a confession</term>, you may answer that commonly it may be used for all misconduct, provided that sufficient indicators <term>indicia: legal signs or circumstantial evidence that suggest guilt</term> are present and the truth cannot be discovered otherwise. This follows the rule found in *Law 1, in the preface of the Digest, concerning interrogations* <note>original Latin: "l. 1. in p ff. de quæſtionibus," a reference to the Corpus Juris Civilis, the foundation of Roman law used in the Holy Roman Empire</note>. However, one should not begin the criminal process and examination with torture. But when necessity requires it, and the laws command the judge to proceed, and the truth cannot be discovered except by means of torture, then the judge may make use of it. Now, when the criminal process is thus established by the judge, it is his duty not to proceed so poorly against everyone without distinction, but to look around and consider whether it is the type of person whom he may subject to the painful question. For some persons are of such a status that they may not be tortured, as shall be said further in the next chapter. And it is to be noted here that this refers to the condition and quality, or the distinction of the person, and not the crime or transgression; for in the transgression there is no distinction, because where the law makes no distinction in that case, we should also make none. For a crime remains and is a crime, regardless of who committed it, according to the *Digest, concerning arbitrators* <note>original Latin: "ff. de Arbitris"</note>.

Now, although it might be argued against this—according to the *law on the edict of interrogations* <note>original Latin: "l. edictum de quæſtionibus"</note>—that the painful question should not always be undertaken for every crime nor used by judges, but only in high cases where one has forfeited their life, and such great and terrible crimes cannot be solved except through the painful question of one's own servant <note>This refers to a specific Roman law tradition regarding the testimony of enslaved persons or servants</note>; from which it would be concluded that in minor crimes, the painful question should not be used, but should be forbidden in the aforementioned places. However, this is to be understood thus: it is true that in minor criminal cases and transgressions, one should not use extreme severity with the painful question, as was mentioned in the distinctions above. Nevertheless, if one cannot otherwise get to the bottom of the truth, one may well use the first or second degree of the painful question <note>Torture was often applied in "degrees" of increasing severity, starting with the showing of the instruments and moving to binding or stretching</note> in such minor cases, according to the *law on which defects [in the edict of the building inspectors]* <note>original Latin: "l. ob quæ vitia. Par. fin. ff. ædilitio edicto"</note>. This applies primarily when the prisoner is a person of low status and the suspicion is great that he committed this or that deed. But if the prisoner is an honorable, high-ranking person, such as a member of the nobility, etc., then in minor criminal cases, one cannot proceed to any torture, no matter how great the suspicion may be, so that the dignity or nobility of the prisoner is not thereby...

Torture is usually applied based on the circumstances. Therefore, the text does not say in vain, *in the Law concerning soldiers, the section beginning "It is necessary," in the Code concerning interrogations: "If the status of the persons requires it,"* <note>original Latin: "in l. milites. This is also how the "Gloss" <note>A standard medieval legal commentary on Roman law</note> views it *in the aforementioned Law regarding slight offenses,* <note>original Latin: "in d. l. Levia"</note> namely, that such measures should be understood as applying to suspicious, lowly, and dishonorable people. And although it is otherwise a common rule of law that the slightest physical pain and punishment is to be considered greater than the largest monetary fine (regarding this, see *the Law concerning servants, in the Digest concerning punishments* <note>original Latin: "in l. Seruorum. ff. de poenis"</note>), it still happens that if someone cannot pay a monetary fine due to poverty, they may be punished physically instead (*Law 1, the final paragraph, in the Digest concerning punishments* <note>original Latin: "l. 1, Paragr. fina. ff. de poenis"</note>).
