->VI.<-

### Which persons may be subjected to the painful question.

Sixthly, a further question arises here: which persons—or whether all persons without distinction—may be tortured and subjected to the painful question <term>peinliche frag: judicial torture</term> in criminal matters. To this it is answered: Yes, provided that the measure and order are maintained as the laws have reasonably provided for them, and if sufficient and lawful indicators <term>indicia: legal signs or evidence of guilt</term> precede and are present. For the judge must continually look to the rule and must not forget that one should not begin with the painful question and torture, as has been mentioned several times above. Thus, no one is exempt or excluded from such painful interrogation except those whom the laws have specifically and expressly indicated (*the aforementioned Law 1, in the beginning, in the Digest concerning interrogations, and the aforementioned Law concerning soldiers, the section beginning "It is necessary," in the Code under the same title* <note>original Latin: "d. l. 1. in principio. ff. de quæstionib. & d. l. milites. Par. oportet. C. eo. tit."</note>).

From this rule, however, many persons are exempt who cannot and should not be tortured. Firstly, military men, who according to military law and custom have the freedom to be spared from such painful measures (*the aforementioned Law concerning soldiers, in the beginning* <note>original Latin: "d. l. milites. in prin."</note>).

Secondly, the councilmen <note>German: "Rahtsherrn"</note>, and their children and daughters, as long as they are in office, because of the dignity of the office (*the Law concerning decurions and the Law concerning the Divine Marcus, in the Code concerning interrogations* <note>original Latin: "l. decuriones. & l. diuo Marco. C. de quæstionib."</note>). And the Emperor says *in the Law beginning "Whoever," in the Code concerning the Julian Law on Majesty* <note>original Latin: "in l. quisquis. C. ad l. Iul. Maie."</note> that the councilors are a part of his own body.

In addition, it is also rightly asked: whether the soldiers of our time, as well as the princely councilors or councilors in the cities, are eligible for this privilege <note>original Latin: "Priuilegij"</note> of being spared from the painful question. Bartolus <note>A famous 14th-century Italian law professor</note> says *on the aforementioned Law concerning soldiers* that yes, they are eligible for such a privilege so that they should not be physically assaulted with torture. Likewise, Cynus says *on the Law concerning the Divine Marcus.* Also, Salicetus *on Law 1, in the second-to-last column, in the Code concerning ignorance of law and fact,* <note>original Latin: "C. de iuris & facti ignorantia"</note> though they say it is nonetheless poorly observed in practice. Thus, I have often experienced the opposite in Rome, even though Barbatius <note>A 15th-century legal scholar</note> in his notes on Sali-

<header>Necessary questions / as they occur in and during the</header>

...as the law regarding the Divine Marcus <note>original Latin: "in d. l. Diuo Marco in fine"</note> states at the end, supporting the authority of Bartolus and the opinion that if there were a common usage or custom in a place or land to subject soldiers, councilmen, or knights to the painful question <term>peinlich fragen: to subject to judicial torture</term>, such a custom should not be valid but rather be null and void. For a case is cited by the aforementioned Bartolus in the law titled "All Judges" in the Code concerning Decurions, book 10 <note>original Latin: "omnes Iudices. C. de Decurionibus, lib. 10."</note>, where the Emperor decrees that judges, officials, governors, and others shall not make use of such improper and insolent customs. Namely, they are not to burden princely councilors or city councilmen with torture <term>peinlichkeit: the "painful question" or torture</term> when they have committed an error or some other offense. Any judge who acts against this shall be punished with twenty pounds of pure gold and shall be and remain infamous. Furthermore, if someone is able to prevent such a person from being tortured <term>Torquirt: tortured</term> and fails to do so, they shall forfeit forty pounds of gold to the Imperial Treasury.

In the same manner, it is held that Doctors of Law and advocates also possess such a privilege that they should not be tortured, as Jason expressly states in the law "concerning which" in the Digest regarding laws <note>original Latin: "in l. de quibus. ff. de legib."</note>. Likewise, Baldus says in Law 1 of the Code concerning advocates of various judges <note>original Latin: "l. 1. C. de aduoca. diuersorum iudicum"</note>: *A Doctor and Advocate cannot be tortured, since he has been established in dignity, and not only during his service as an advocate, but also after leaving the office; and therefore he says that whenever an oath is to be taken from him, a Notary should be sent to his house as to an eminent person.* <note>original Latin: "Doctor, & Aduocatus torqueri non potest, ex quo est constitutus in dignitate, & non solùm durante officio aduocationis, sed etiam eo deposito, & ideo dicit, quòd quoties per ipsum capiendum sit iuramentum, debet mitti Notarius ad domum suam tanquam ad egregiam personam"</note> This means that neither a Doctor nor an advocate may be tortured or seized, not only while they are in office, but even after they have retired. Therefore, whenever one must take an oath from them or they are to give testimony, a Notary should be sent to their home as befits a highly respectable person.

Thirdly, minors <term>Minores: those under the age of majority</term> or those who are under 14 years of age are exempted. Because they are too weak and tender due to their age to be subjected to such gruesome torture—at which every person would be horrified—they are rightly spared from it. If they have committed an offense or if one wishes to investigate and learn something from them, rods may be used instead <note>Meaning corporal punishment/caning rather than rack-torture</note>, according to Law 1, the paragraph regarding minors, in the Digest concerning the Silanian Senate-decree, and the Law concerning interrogations, the paragraph regarding minors <note>original Latin: "l. 1. Parag. impubes. ff. ad Syllania. & l. de quaest. Par. Impubes. ff. de quæstio."</note>.

In the same way, fourthly, women who are pregnant are exempted; they are rightly spared the painful question so that the fruit of their womb is not aborted. Furthermore, they should not be subjected to torture after they have delivered the child until they have returned to their health, which is after 40 days, according to the law regarding pregnant women in the Digest concerning punishments, and the law of the Emperor, and the commentary by Baldus there in the Digest concerning the status of men, and Hyppolitus de Marsiliis in Law 1, at the beginning, in the 5th column of the Digest concerning interrogations <note>original Latin: "l. prægnantis. ff. de pœnis. & l. Imperator. & ibi Bald. ff. de Status homi. Hyppolitus de Mars. in l. 1. in princip. in 5. col. ff. de quæstionibus."</note>.

Fifthly, servants <note>Knecht: in the context of Roman law citations, this often refers to slaves (servi)</note> are exempted, not in the sense that they may never be tortured, but only against certain persons in certain cases, as in the law regarding servants in the Digest concerning interrogations <note>original Latin: "l. Seruos. ff. de quæstionibus."</note>.

<header>Torture as it is accustomed to occur /</header>

Sixthly/ some also hold that old people/ who are so weakened by great age that they can no longer endure the **painful question** <term>peinliche frag: judicial interrogation under torture</term>/ should also be exempted/ Especially Gandinus/ <note>Albertus Gandinus (c. 1245–1310), an Italian jurist who wrote one of the first systematic works on criminal law.</note> who cites the law "It is forgiven" in the Digest regarding the Silanian Decree/ <note>original Latin: "l. 3. Paragra. Ignoscitur ff. ad Syllanianum"</note> and in this he is joined by Bartholomaeus, Angelus, and Hyppolitus de Marsiliis/ <note>Hippolytus de Marsiliis (1451–1529) was a Bolognese jurist known for documenting various methods of torture.</note> as well as all the other Doctors of Law.

But I hold the contrary view/ regardless of what the aforementioned Doctors and others may say in this case/ for their opinion cannot be sustained nor proven/ Thus, it cannot be forced from the aforementioned paragraph "It is forgiven" that this was the intended meaning/ namely, that an old man may not be **painfully questioned**/ Therefore it remains according to the rule/ as found in the first law of the Digest regarding interrogations/ <note>original Latin: "d. l. 1. ff. de quæstio."</note> and the law "Soldiers" and the law "Decurions" in the Code under the same title/ <note>original Latin: "l. milites l. Decuriones C. eo. tit."</note> where certain persons are singled out who may not be **tortured** <term>Torquiren: to subject to judicial torture</term>/ among whom the elderly are not found/ Therefore it is concluded/ that the others/ who are not exempted in the law or in the aforementioned places/ are and remain subject to the **painful question**/ And thus conclude Baldus, Salicetus/ and others/ in the laws concerning soldiers and decurions. As for the paragraph "It is forgiven"/ although it does indeed wish for the elderly not to be **tortured**/ it must be known/ that this third law in the Digest regarding the Silanian Decree was established/ for the sake of lazy, unfaithful servants/ who did not wish to come to the aid of their master when he was attacked/ before he was killed/ for which they then fell under suspicion/ that they had acted deceitfully and maliciously toward their master/ and consented to such a murder/ and all those who were in the house/ when the master was killed/ and did not help him/ so much so that they might have at least raised an outcry/ and avenged his death/ are to be **painfully questioned**/ so that one might discover/ whether they were guilty of or participants in his death. However, certain persons are nonetheless exempted there/ whom one may not **torture**/ in that specific case, such as the elderly/ not because of their person/ but for the reason/ that due to their inability they could not have helped their master/ and therefore such suspicions could not be held against them/ as they were against the other servants/ who were young and strong/ and had no hindrance/ neither in weakness nor age/ I could therefore not see nor know/ how the elderly/ outside of this specific case/ could be freed from the **painful question**/ Provided that one otherwise has a **painful access** <term>peinlichen zutritt: legal grounds to proceed to torture</term> to them through sufficient indications, information, and proof/ especially if one deals with them mildly/ and only employs the first or second degree/ as mentioned above.

But if I were a judge/ and such a case were to occur/ I would apply all possible diligence/ so that I might discover the truth through other means/ than through the **painful question**/ and if I truly had to undertake and use it out of necessity/ I would use it moderately/ and would not step beyond the second or third **degree** <term>Grad: levels of torture intensity, starting with the showing of instruments</term>/ unless a very crude and inhuman case was at hand/ and the prisoner or perpetrator was a base, lowly person/ and under great suspicion.

**Ob**

He advises judges to use "mild" degrees of torture for the elderly only as a last resort in serious cases.</summary>

<header>Necessary questions / such as in and during the</header>

Whether there are more persons who should be spared and excluded from the **torture** <term>Tortur: judicial interrogation involving physical pain</term>, regarding this, see Hyppolitus de Marsiliis in the law "Edict" under the title on interrogations. <note>original Latin: "Hyppolitum de Marsi. in l. edictum de quæstio." Hippolytus de Marsiliis (1451–1529) was a prominent Italian jurist and expert on criminal procedure.</note> There, several more types of persons are recounted by him, among whom are mentioned those who are primarily useful to the **common good** and can serve the same. He cites the law "Regarding Wild Beasts" in the Digest, <note>original Latin: "L. ad Bestias. ff." The Digest (Pandects) is a major part of the Body of Civil Law (Corpus Juris Civilis) compiled under Justinian.</note> where the laws say: that he who has been judged and condemned by law to be thrown to the wild beasts—if that same person were useful to the Roman people—he must be spared from such punishment at the request of the people. This, however, I interpret to mean that he should not be so severely tortured that his limbs might be ruined in such a way that he is no longer fit for work, or might even die from the torture (which, however, seldom happens). Otherwise, he can well be of service to the common good, even if he has been accused once, which is not the case when one is thrown before wild beasts, where one is torn apart by them and brought from life to death.

Such exemptions and exclusions from the **painful torture** <term>peinliche marter: judicial torture used to extract confessions</term>, however, have no place in the exceedingly grave cases, such as in the **crime of lèse-majesté** <term>crimine læsæ Maiestatis: treason against the sovereign or the state</term>, where someone has committed an offense against the Emperor or the Empire. In such a case, no one is spared, be he as noble and worthy as he may; no privilege helps him whereby he might escape the painful torture. <note>original Latin: "l. quisquis. C. ad l. Iuliam Maiestatis." Refers to the Julian Law on Treason in the Justinian Code.</note> To this, the Canonists and others also add the heretics, <note>original Latin: "c. vergentis de hæreticis." A reference to a famous decretal by Pope Innocent III equating heresy with treason.</note> and finally also the sorcerers, as seen in the Code regarding magicians and astrologers, <note>original Latin: "C. de Maleficis & mathematicis"</note> and the law "Even if exempted." In these cases, all must be subject to the painful torture without distinction, as the aforementioned Hyppolitus de Marsiliis indicates at length in the said law "Edict."

->VII.<-

Seventh and lastly, this question arises: Whether one may subject a person to the **painful question** <term>peinliche frag: torture used specifically for interrogation</term> in **civil matters** <term>Bürgerliche sachen: non-criminal legal disputes, such as those regarding property or debt</term>. To this, I give the answer: that it may occasionally happen, but not in all cases, nor against all persons, but only against **slaves** <term>Knecht: in this legal context, referring to the Roman 'servus' or bondservant</term>, when one cannot get to the truth otherwise. The law "Divine Pius" in the Digest regarding interrogations <note>original Latin: "l. diuus Pius, ff. de quæstionib." Referring to Emperor Antoninus Pius.</note> says the text thus: *The Divine Pius wrote back that it is possible to hold an interrogation of slaves in a monetary case, if the truth cannot otherwise be found, but this is done so that an interrogation is not lightly held in a monetary matter.* And Marcianus writes there very modestly that in such a case one should not undertake the painful question unless one cannot come to the truth in any other way against the same person for a second time. And it is to be known that this is the distinction between criminal and civil matters: that in civil matters, only the slaves of others shall be painfully questioned, and even then (as mentioned) only if one cannot otherwise come to the truth; which is not the case in criminal matters, where one may also **torture** <term>Torquiren: from the Latin 'torquere', to twist or torture</term> free people. From this, such a rule can be concluded: that no free person may be painfully questioned in civil matters, according to the said law "Divine [Pius]" in the Digest on interrogations.

# Torture usually occurs.

This rule, however—that in civil or monetary matters, no free person should be subjected to **painful interrogation** <term>peinliche frage: judicial torture used to extract a confession</term>—is to be understood as follows: when the free person is a *principal party* <note>The "principal" is the main person involved in the lawsuit, rather than a witness.</note>. However, if he is a witness and wavers in his speech or refuses to speak out, one may well apply pressure to him <note>original: *anzepffen*, literally "to tap," a metaphor for beginning the process of legal pressure or torture</note>, as the text says; likewise Bartolus also states in the law "Regarding a free person" in the Digest, title on interrogations. <note>original Latin: *l. ex libero. ff. de quaestio.* The Digest (or *Pandects*) was a massive collection of legal opinions from Roman jurists.</note> This occurs not from the nature of the main case itself, but from a circumstance—namely, the wavering of testimony. Reference is made to the law "A free man," at the beginning, and the law "of one," paragraph "witnesses," in the Digest, under the same title; and there also Bartolus and Hippolitus de Marsiliis. <note>Hippolytus de Marsiliis (1451–1529) was a renowned Italian lawyer.</note> The Canon lawyers <note>Experts in church law.</note> say in the chapter "gravis" concerning deposits, that one may come to the **painful interrogation** even in monetary matters if they involve a criminal forfeiture <note>original: *peinliche verwirckung*</note>, as Panormitanus clearly says in that place.

Likewise, Paris de Puteo <note>A 15th-century Neapolitan jurist.</note> says that, by virtue of this text, he has decided and ruled that merchants who have gone **bankrupt** <term>Banckerot: from the Italian "banca rotta" or "broken bench," referring to the destroyed stalls of failed money-changers</term> and are on the run <note>original: *auff flüchtigem Fuß stehen*</note> may indeed be attacked with **painful interrogation** if they refuse to disclose where they have put the goods they borrowed from people and obtained through lies, and afterwards claim they do not know where they put them. This opinion is also followed by Hippolitus de Marsiliis in the law "The Divine." And although he mentions that it is quite difficult and unjust that one should be tortured for money—since the **debtor** <term>Debitor: the person who owes money</term> must suffer more in such torture while the truth is being sought than the matter itself is worth—it is also true that the slightest physical punishment is to be esteemed greater than the largest monetary fine, according to the law "In the case of slaves" at the end of the Digest, title on punishments. <note>original Latin: *l. In seruorum. ff. de poenis, in fine.*</note> Nevertheless, he provides this explanation: that in this place and in this case, the **torture** <term>Tortur: the use of physical pain to extract information</term> is not a "punishment," but rather a physical pain in the body or limbs used to discover the truth, according to the law "Likewise according to Labeo," paragraph "interrogations," in the Digest, on injuries. <note>original Latin: *L. Item apud Labeonem. Par. quaesti. ff. de Iniurijs.*</note> For this reason, there are two distinct titles in the law: "on punishments" and "on interrogations," as Grillandus further explains here. But some give another reason: namely, that this rule and order—that one may not use painful interrogation in monetary matters—does not apply to common and lowly people, but rather to distinguished and great people, such as the **nobility** and the like, who in such cases involving money should in no way be interrogated with pain, however powerful they may be. And so that one may move on from this business and be guided by it, you should note this rule: that in civil or monetary matters, one should not proceed to **painful interrogation** unless it concerns certain persons and cases that are excepted, as mentioned above. However, regarding the cited chapter "gravis" concerning deposits, and likewise the law "As in forgery" in the Code, title on forgery, <note>original Latin: *L. sicut falsi. C. de falsis.* The Code (Codex) was another part of the Roman law collection.</note> stating that one may undertake torture therein—the reason is that the crimes of **theft** and **forgery** are attached to them; therefore, they cannot be considered or called purely monetary or civil matters in all things. It appears, therefore, that in such a case it must be more of a criminal matter than a monetary one. And the judge shall in every way consider with diligence, when someone is accused before him, what the sort and nature of the complaint is: whether it is *from a contract* or *as if from a contract*, or *from a crime* or *as if from a crime* <note>original Latin: *ex contractu, vel quasi, vel ex delicto, vel quasi*</note>; that is, whether the complaint arises from a contract or from a forfeiture

# Necessary questions that [arise] in and during the...

...will [arising] therefrom; as in the Institutes <note>original: *vt Instit. quibus modis re contrahitur obligatio, & gatio. quæ ex delicto nascuntur*—The Institutes was a foundational textbook of Roman Law. The titles cited here refer to "how an obligation is contracted through things" and "obligations arising from crime."</note>. One must know that in the first case—namely, in contracts—**painful interrogation** <term>peinlichkeit: judicial torture</term> has no place. It only applies in the other case, where one is accused of **criminal matters** <term>Malefiz sachen: serious crimes or "malefice" often carrying the death penalty</term> and transgressions. This remains true even if, in the first case, the truth cannot be found through any other means; for the law has ordained other means and ways that one may use in such civil and pure monetary matters. For instance, if the defendant is overcome and the plaintiff has fully proven the case, the defendant is recognized as guilty and judged accordingly; as in the law "if to a debtor" in the Digest <note>original: *L. si debitori. ff. de iudicijs*</note>.

However, if the plaintiff has only a "half-proof" <note>original: *halbe beweisung* or *semiplenè*. In medieval law, "full proof" usually required two eyewitnesses; "half-proof" might be one witness or strong circumstantial evidence.</note> and has proven only partially, as often happens, then to complete such half-proof, an **oath** <term>Iurament: a formal legal oath</term> is imposed and permitted, provided the plaintiff is an honest person and the claim is not excessively large. This is debated at length by Bartolus and several of the modern commentators in the law "of warning" in the Digest, under the title "on oaths"; also Baldus <note>original: *B*</note> on "good faith" in the Code under the same title; and Panormitanus <note>Niccolò de' Tudeschi (1386–1445), a famous canon lawyer.</note> and others in the final chapter of the same title.

If the plaintiff in a civil matter has proven neither fully nor half-way, but even less—for example, if he perhaps had witnesses who did not agree, or "singular" witnesses <note>Witnesses who testify to different facts rather than confirming the same event.</note>, or those of such a character that they could be objected to—then in such cases, a completed oath is not permitted. Instead, as the mentioned doctors say in the final chapter, the **oath of purgation** <term>iuramentum purgationis: an oath by which an accused person clears themselves of a suspicion</term> is imposed upon the defendant. After performing this oath, the defendant is acquitted of the claim.

If, however, the plaintiff has proven nothing at all against the defendant regarding the articles he brought before the judge in his complaint, then the defendant is acquitted and declared free without any oath. Conversely, the plaintiff is ordered to pay the expenses and court costs; as in the law "who to accuse" in the Code, under "on publishing" and "on probation." Thus says the common legal rule: **When the plaintiff does not prove the case, the defendant is acquitted.** <note>original Latin: *Actore non probante reus absoluitur.*</note>

These are the means by which civil cases must and should be decided, and not through **painful interrogation**, provided they are purely civil and have no criminal attachment. Such cases cannot be called criminal, and therefore it is no wonder if judges must occasionally allow or use **painful interrogation** therein to discover the truth—not for the sake of the civil matter, but for the sake of the criminal attachment. For torture must have been devised for criminal matters where it is not a question of money, but where a criminal case could not be fully proven. It is used against cunning rogues and wicked, malicious knaves, as Baldus <note>original: *dus*</note> says in the second law of the Code, "those whose appeals are not received," and Panormitanus in the chapter "since temptation" regarding the rules of law. 

And although **painful interrogation** should not be a punishment in itself, even in criminal cases, it does happen sometimes in cases where someone should give money in a criminal matter and has none, and yet must be punished, that they are subjected to the **torture** <note>original: *Tortur*</note> according to the common rule: **He who has not the means in money, let him pay with his body.** <note>original Latin: *Qui non habet in ære, luat in corpore.*</note>

<summary>This page outlines the legal distinction between civil contract disputes and criminal cases, explaining that torture is forbidden in pure monetary lawsuits where oaths and proof-levels (full vs. half-proof) determine the outcome. It notes that torture is reserved for criminal cases or civil cases with "criminal attachments," often as a last resort against "rogues" or those who cannot pay fines.</summary>

<keywords>judicial torture, civil law, criminal law, half-proof, oath of purgation, legal procedure, Bartolus, Panormitanus, Baldus, court costs, debt punishment</keywords>

->[How] Torture is Wont to Occur.<-

That is: He who cannot pay with money must pay with his skin; especially because the defendant is a loose, worthless person <note>original: *l. 1. Par. fin. ff. de poenis*—A reference to the Digest of Roman Law, specifically the section on penalties, which suggests that those without means may face corporal punishment instead of fines.</note>. It also happens that if someone has committed a minor theft, he may be punished and tortured with **torture** <term>Tortur: the use of physical pain to extract a confession or as a corporal punishment</term> because of it, particularly if they are worthless knaves who have nothing <note>original: *Auten. vt iudices sine quoquo suffra. Parag. ex diuers.*—Referring to a Novel (Authenticum) of Justinian regarding the conduct of judges.</note>.

Here, a question might be attached—of which mention is made in the Law <note>original: *in l. Repeti. ff. de quaestio.*—"On the repeating of questions" in the Digest section on interrogations.</note>—regarding whether and when one who has been **painfully questioned** <term>peinlich gefragt: interrogated under judicial torture</term> once may be seized further or a second time for painful interrogation, and when one has been "properly and competently" questioned. Likewise, if the prisoner were to die during the **torment** <term>marter: physical torture</term>, whether the judge could be accused and punished for it, and what the punishment should be. Likewise, if the defendant were seized with painful questioning and the judge allowed no **indications** <term>indicia: legal evidence or clues required to justify the use of torture</term> to precede it, or if such evidence was present but not sufficient for painful questioning, or was not recorded in the court acts. Furthermore, if the prisoner desires a transcript and copy of the court records and these are not shared with him by the judge but are refused, yet he is nonetheless proceeded against with **painful methods** <term>peinlichkeit: judicial torture</term>, and thereafter in the torment he confesses to another misdeed for which no evidence was present, or for which the evidence was insufficient. Likewise, whether the confession of the prisoner, which has been **ratified** <term>ratificirt: formally confirmed as true after the torture has ceased</term> before the judicial bench, may bring harm to him for his sentencing or in other ways, and in what manner. Likewise, if it should happen that a person who was otherwise privileged and exempted in the Law—such that they should not be addressed with pain, such as due to old age, or a woman with a pregnant body, or a similar person—but they were nonetheless tortured with pain because of it, and the poor human had confessed some misdeed in such painful torment, and also persisted in court when he was questioned again by the judge, and thereby ratified his statement: whether he may be sentenced in such a case. Likewise, if one wished to explain all these questions at length and in full detail as is proper and as necessity requires, such would be more an' excess than a necessity, since all the **Doctors** <note>In this context, "Doctors" refers to Doctors of Law or high-ranking legal scholars.</note> have otherwise concerned themselves with it and written about it, both old and new; these one may consult: Such as **Bartolus** <note>Bartolus de Saxoferrato (1313–1357), a highly influential medieval jurist.</note> in the first law and the final law in the Digest on questioning <note>original: *l. 1. & l. fina. ff. de quaestio.*</note>, and regarding the law of soldiers <note>original: *l. milites. Para. oportet. C. eod. tit.*—Referring to the Code of Justinian.</note>. **Baldus** <note>Baldus de Ubaldis (1327–1400), a student of Bartolus.</note> in the second law in the Code on those whose appeals are not received <note>original: *l. 2. C. quorum appella. non reci.*</note> and the first law in the Code concerning confessions <note>original: *l. 1. C. de confess.*</note>. **Angelus Aretinus** <note>Angelo Gambiglioni (d. 1461), an Italian jurist.</note>. Likewise **Gandinus** <note>Alberto Gandino (c. 1245–1310), pioneer of criminal law theory.</note> in his *Treatises on Misdeeds* <note>original: *Tractatibus maleficiorum*</note>. **Hippolytus de Marsiliis** <note>An Italian jurist (1451–1529) known for his work on torture.</note> in the first law, paragraph on the question, in the Digest on questioning <note>original: *in l. 1. Parag. ad quæstionem. ff. de quæstio.*</note>. **Panormitanus** <note>Niccolò de' Tudeschi (1386–1445), a famous canonist.</note> in the chapter "When in Contemplation" concerning the rules of Law in antiquity <note>original: *in c. cum in contemplatione de regu. Iuris, in antiq.*</note>. Finally also **Guido de Suzaria** <note>A 13th-century Italian jurist.</note>, who is to be found herewith.

But regardless of this—with what measure, gentleness, or severity, when necessity requires, the **painfulness** <term>peinlichkeit: judicial torture</term> against the poor prisoner may be undertaken, and which **evidence** <term>indicia</term> are sufficient for torture or not, and when someone is properly and painfully examined and questioned, or when one has **purged** <term>purgiert: cleared oneself of the weight of evidence</term> his evidence or not—all of this the laws leave to the discretion of an honest, pious judge, since therein is no fixed measure

### Necessary questions [to be] asked in and during torture, etc.

...or [no fixed] rule can be prescribed, because of the constant changes [in cases]—one is always different from the other, with different qualities and circumstances than the next. Therefore, one must act and behave according to the quality of the deed, the nature of the land, and the local use or custom, taking into account other circumstances and qualities, as Baldus says <note>original: *in d. l. i. rum appella. non recip.*—Referring to Baldus de Ubaldis (1327–1400), a renowned Italian jurist, commenting on a law stating that appeals are not accepted in certain criminal matters.</note>. Likewise, in the law "milites," paragraph "oportet," and Bartholus <note>original: *Barthol. ff. de quæstionibus*—Bartolus de Saxoferrato (1313–1357), perhaps the most influential medieval jurist, writing on the Digest section regarding interrogations under torture.</note>, and Panormitanus <note>original: *Panorm. in d. c. cum contempla. de reg. iuris*—Niccolò de' Tudeschi (1386–1445), an expert in canon law, writing on the rules of law.</note>.

However, finally: when the prisoner has been **painfully questioned** <term>peinlich gefragt: interrogated under judicial torture</term> once or even several times, and has confessed to some misdeeds under such painful questioning, but afterwards—when he is in the constable's room or before the **court bench** <term>Gerichtsbanck: the formal seat of the judge where legal rulings are delivered</term>—is asked to acknowledge and confirm his confession, yet he denies it again and recants, saying he did not commit the deed but only confessed because of the **torment** <term>marter: physical torture</term>, what should the judge do and undertake against such a prisoner in this case? Regarding this, the judge should take him and hoist him up again for painful questioning, letting him hang on the torture device for as long as he thinks is sufficient in such a case. And if he then moves away from such a recantation and confesses as he did at first, the judge should hold him to that and have the prisoner ratify and strengthen his confession again before the court bench.

But if he—as one often finds—refuses to persist in it and recants again, then the judge should release him, according to the opinion of Bartholus <note>original: *in l. si quis vltro. & l. Repeti. de quæstio.*—Referring to laws in the Digest regarding voluntary confessions and repeated interrogations.</note> and Hyppolitus de Marsiliis <note>Hyppolitus de Marsiliis (1451–1529) was an Italian lawyer famous for writing a manual on torture; he famously claimed to have invented the "water cure" and documented many practical cases.</note>. The latter writes that such a case happened to him when he was an official in Milan: a consummate rogue was brought before him who allowed himself to be painfully tortured often and always confessed while on the rack, but whenever he was brought before the court, he always recanted. He kept this up for so long that the judge had to set him free and cancel and annul the proceedings. When he was asked after his release why he confessed and then recanted in that way, he answered that it had been his highest necessity, as he had to choose the better of two evils. Therefore, he thought it was better to let himself be tortured by the arms several times with the **hoist** <term>marter: here referring to the strappado, where a victim is jerked up by rope</term> than to let someone tie his throat shut once <note>The prisoner is making a dark joke: the damage from torture can be healed, but hanging is permanent.</note>. For many people are found who can help one's arms, even if they are broken, so that they become straight again; but no one is found who could help him if his throat had been stretched on the gallows for even a little while. I have also heard and seen those who say: "I give my mouth food and drink so that it must speak and say what I want, and not what another wants."

# To the Well-born and Noble
## Lord, Lord Hans Heinrich the Elder, Count and Lord of Schwarzburg, etc., to his Gracious Lord, Georgius Lauterbeck wishes his most willing and diligent service above all.

Well-born and Noble Count, Gracious Lord, since the Imperial **Feudal Laws** <term>Lehenrecht: The body of law governing the relationship between a lord and a vassal, specifically regarding the holding of land (fiefs).</term> have until now been so disorderly arranged and thrown together that almost no one could find their way through them, and for that reason several people have necessarily had to try their hand at bringing them into a better and more correct order—in my opinion, no one has proven better at this than **Doctor Ulrich Zasius**. And although he, as a highly learned and experienced man, has otherwise written many excellent books, yet this book especially is praised above others, and his diligence and understanding are felt within it: for he has very skillfully composed and contained the entire summary of Feudal Law within twelve chapters. And it is no small wonder that he was able to bring such a great light out of such darkness.

Therefore, I have also been motivated to translate this book into the vernacular <note>original: "zuuerteutschen" (to translate into German). While the original author translated the Latin into German, this present edition provides the text in English for modern readers.</note> as briefly as possible, not word for word, however, but rather that which I considered necessary to know. But what belongs in the schools <note>Referring to academic or scholastic disputes that were of interest to university lawyers but less practical for the nobility and landowners.</note> (though there is very little of that), I have left out. Since I know that **Your Grace** is accustomed to reading such books with special diligence, and I also wish to show myself grateful for the many graces and benefits shown to me—especially those I experienced from Your Grace during the **past war** <note>Likely referring to the Schmalkaldic War (1546–1547), which caused significant upheaval in the German territories.</note>—I wished to dedicate this humble work to Your Grace according to ancient custom. By this, I intended primarily to serve those who grant and receive, or accept, fiefs; for many fine rules are contained therein

# Preface of Doctor Ulrich Zasius
### concerning the concise summary of the Imperial Feudal Laws.

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'N' featuring floral motifs and foliage patterns within a rectangular frame.</image-desc>

**N**ow that I have undertaken to explain and interpret as briefly as possible the customs of **Feudal Law** <term>Feudal Law: Referred to as 'Lehenrecht', these were the laws governing the relationship between a lord and a vassal, specifically regarding land held in exchange for service.</term>, which are unfamiliar to other general written laws but are nonetheless accepted elsewhere, I find that they have been tossed together quite disorderly. Furthermore, they are composed so poorly in **Latin** <note>Zasius, a legal humanist, often complained about the "kitchen Latin" or unpolished legal language used by medieval scholars, preferring a return to classical clarity.</note> that it is difficult to be guided by them or to derive much benefit from them. However, because these laws are not only useful but also necessary to know—especially for those who govern the common good and who must grant and receive **fiefs** <term>Fiefs: 'Lehen' in German; land or rights granted by a superior to a subordinate in the feudal system.</term>—I wish to remind and urge those who are accustomed to the proper Latin language not to let such disorder and awkwardness lead them astray. Instead, they should pay diligent attention only to that which is found to be useful within these laws. For my part, I will apply the greatest possible diligence so that all matters are brought into a correct order, and whatever might be confusing or tedious to the reader shall be changed and removed. And I shall not be deterred by the fact that many excellent men have already written on feudal laws and explained and interpreted them. They had different purposes and reasons for writing; after they had most diligently considered and weighed all matters belonging to feudal law, they wrote large volumes about them according to their great understanding. I, however, have only wanted to provide a short guide, perhaps in a different order, manner, and intention than has been done by others until now; yet it shall not be inconvenient, but

### A brief excerpt of the
# Origin, Name, and
## Description of Fiefs.
### The First Chapter.

In my opinion, legal scholars have not sufficiently handled or considered this first part regarding the origin of <term>fiefs</term> <note>original: 'Lehen'; a landed estate held on condition of feudal service.</note>. For that reason, I will also omit that same scholarly order here. However, so that one may know how the matter stands, I consider it to be that fiefs took their origin from the customs and habits of the ancient Romans. For several authors write, such as **Dionysius of Halicarnassus** <note>A Greek historian and teacher of rhetoric who lived in Rome during the reign of Augustus.</note> and also **Gellius** <note>Aulus Gellius (c. 125 – after 180 AD), a Roman author known for his *Attic Nights*.</note>, that the first king, **Romulus**, permitted and allowed the citizens—and especially the rural inhabitants—that each might choose for themselves, according to their circumstances, a <term>patron</term> <note>original: 'Patron'; a protector or advocate in Roman society.</note> and protector to represent and shield them if they were to be burdened or oppressed by the rich and powerful. These people were then called <term>clients</term> <note>original: 'Clientes'; individuals who were under the protection of a patron, often in exchange for services.</note> by the patrons, and subsequently, both parties were obligated and bound to one another to a certain degree; the clients submitted themselves and their property to the protection and defense of the patrons.

And at that time, it was a great honor if a patron had many clients. Thus **Valerius Maximus** <note>A Roman writer and author of a collection of historical anecdotes.</note> writes of **Appius Claudius** that he moved from the Sabines to Rome with five thousand clients. From this ancient custom, I believe that fiefs later originated. For after the Romans had triumphed in wars here and there, not only in France but also in Germany, and thereby brought many kingdoms, principalities, lands, and people under their power, the Roman military for the most part settled there and inhabited those lands. And those lands which they themselves could not inhabit, they handed over to their neighboring residents, who in turn had to obligate themselves to the Romans and earn the granted estates. From this, over time (as all things change), the feudal customs arose. This is also the view held by **Gregor Haloander** <note>Gregor Haloander (1501–1531), an influential German legal scholar who edited the *Corpus Iuris Civilis*.</note>, an excellent and learned man, along with several others. The **Saxon Municipal Law** <note>original: 'Sächsische weichbild'; a 13th-century collection of laws for Saxon cities.</note> agrees with this opinion in Article 7 of the commentary, although **Alvarotus** <note>Jacobus Alvarotus, an Italian legal expert mentioned in the preface.</note>—to whom ancient history was unknown—held a different opinion.

...the second is the vassal. However, a <term>fief</term> <note>original: 'Lehen'; a landed estate held on condition of feudal service.</note> (to write of it briefly, according to the opinion of **Joannes Reinaldus** <note>A legal scholar, likely Giovanni Reinaldo.</note> as cited by **Petrus Rebuffus** <note>Pierre Rebuffi (1487–1557), a prominent French jurist and expert on feudal law.</note>) is nothing other than a free, gracious, and voluntary granting of an immovable good—or something equivalent to it—assigned and delivered to the <term>knighthood</term> <note>original: 'Ritterschafft'; the class of individuals eligible to hold military fiefs.</note> by the Emperor or other princes and lords. For this reason, the word "honorably" is included, meaning that knightly service must be honorable and not shameful, as shall be further addressed in the final chapter.

# On the Distinction of Fiefs.
## The Second Chapter.

<image-desc>Large historiated woodcut initial 'D' depicting a seated figure at a desk, likely a scholar or jurist, surrounded by decorative foliage.</image-desc>
Many <term>feudalists</term> <note>original: 'Feudisten'; scholars specializing in feudal law.</note> have exerted themselves to distinguish between various types of fiefs and have created many different classifications. For instance, **Alvarotto** <note>Gerardo Alvarotto, a 15th-century Italian jurist.</note> identified eleven types, while **Baldus** <note>Baldus de Ubaldis (1327–1400), a highly influential student of Bartolus and a master of civil and feudal law.</note> identified twenty-two. Others have done the same, each according to his own mind, proposing more or fewer categories. We shall, as far as necessity requires, make the following distinctions.

Firstly, some are Royal Fiefs, such as those one receives from the Empire, the Emperor, or the King. These include Margraviates, Principalities, Counties, Lands, and Lordships, which are now commonly called <term>Banner Fiefs</term> <note>original: 'Fahnenlehen'; high-ranking fiefs granted by the Emperor specifically through the ceremonial presentation of a banner, symbolizing military command.</note>. The reason for this name is that the Emperor customarily grants them under a banner. Others, however, are simple or "plain" fiefs and are not Banner Fiefs; these are granted by other, lower lords and not by the Empire, Emperor, or King, etc.

Regarding this distinction, one might ask: if the Emperor, King, or Prince wished to give away certain cities or castles within his kingdom or principality, would he have the power to do so? To this it must be answered: A King or Prince certainly has the power to grant a city, castle, or village, but with this proviso: that he reserves for himself a right concerning his <term>sovereignty</term> <note>original: 'Hoheit'; supreme power or authority over the territory.</note>. As the Doctors of Law say in the chapter *Intellecto* regarding the taking of oaths <note>original: 'c. intellecto. de Iureiurando'</note>; **Jason** in his *Preludes on Fiefs*, column 28 <note>original: 'Iason in præludijs feudorum'</note>; and **Bartholomaeus** in the Law *Prohibere*, section *Planè*, in the Digest concerning force or stealth <note>original: 'Barth. in L. prohibere. Par. planè. ff. quod vi aut clam'</note>. Thus one sees that in such cases, princes reserve for themselves taxes, military service, tolls, or similar rights. If, however, a King, Prince, or Lord wished to give away now this city, now another castle, whereby the land would be noticeably weakened, then he could not do so, as **Egidius Bellamera** <note>Gilles Bellemère (1342–1407), a French canonist and bishop.</note> says in his twelfth Counsel, in the third section regarding doubts <note>original: 'Consil. 12. versicul. Tertio dubitatur'</note>. And even if he did so, such a gift or <term>donation</term> <note>original: 'Donation'; a formal gift.</note> would be invalid and could be revoked by his heirs or successors.

Secondly, some fiefs are noble, and some are non-noble. Noble fiefs

# A Short Extract of the

...are those which ennoble their possessor, such as <term>Principalities</term>, <term>Margraviates</term> and <term>Landgraviates</term>, <term>Duchies</term>, <term>Counties</term>, and <term>Lordships</term>, which <term>Electors</term> <note>The high-ranking princes of the Holy Roman Empire who had the right to elect the Emperor.</note>, Princes, Counts, and Lords receive from the Emperor. Similarly, there are <term>Noble Fiefs</term> which those of the nobility receive as fiefs from Princes—although some make a distinction and call these "lesser noble" here, as noted by <note>original: "vt Iacob. de Beluis."</note> **Jacobus de Belvis**, whom <note>Jason de Mayno (1435–1519), a celebrated Italian jurist.</note> **Jason** mentions in the *Introduction to Fiefs*, and <note>original: "Petrus Rebus in arb. feud."</note> **Petrus Rebuffi** in the *Tree of Fiefs*. Yet, this distinction is not to be regarded as so great, nor is it of such importance whether a nobleman is not as highly ennobled as a Prince or a Count; rather, he should be satisfied that he nonetheless becomes Noble, as one sees the nobility doing in such cases. Therefore, we shall also let the matter rest with the aforementioned distinction, of which further mention shall be made hereafter.

But <term>non-noble fiefs</term> are those held by <term>vavasors</term> <note>original: "Valuasorn"; vassals who held land under a lord but who themselves had vassals under them; here used for those below the high nobility.</note>—that is, those held by other citizens, farmers, merchants, rich and poor, ahead of the nobility—which are then called "Burg-fiefs" or <term>sub-fiefs</term> <note>original: "Afterlehen"; a fief granted by a vassal to a third party (a "rear-fief").</note>. These do not grant nobility, nor do they carry <term>knightly rights</term>, as the noble fiefs do; regarding this, more shall also follow hereafter.

Thirdly, some fiefs are proper, right, and natural, while others are improper or unnatural. All fiefs are held to be right and natural unless they have been altered by a special <term>pact</term> <note>A formal legal agreement or contract.</note> and deprived of their natural character, as shall be set forth in the final chapter. A "right" fief, however, is by its nature and character one that extends only to male heirs, and the closest <term>sword-kin</term> <note>original: "Schwertmagen"; male relatives related through the paternal line who were eligible to inherit "sword-fiefs."</note> may be enfeoffed with it at the same time. Also, a vassal cannot easily be stripped of such a fief without a specific, lawful cause, as stated in <note>original: "c. 1. de natura feudi."</note> **chapter 1, *On the Nature of Fiefs***. What improper or unnatural fiefs are will be shown at length at the end of this book.

Fourthly, some fiefs are "real" <note>original: "dinglichen"; pertaining to the thing or estate itself (in rem).</note>, which extend to the heirs and do not end with the person, as almost all fiefs do. For this reason, it is held that every man desires to provide not for himself alone, but also for his heirs; thus, such fiefs are of the right kind and nature. Temporal fiefs, however, are "personal." They are called personal for two reasons. Firstly, because they end with the person and do not extend to the heirs, but instead revert to the Lord when the person who was enfeoffed with them has died. Secondly, they are called personal if neither the Lord nor the heirs of the enfeoffed person receive anything after the death of the person who held the fief. For instance, if a "provision" <note>A grant of resources for maintenance.</note>—whether in money, wine, or grain—was made by the <term>liege lord</term> to a <term>person of rank</term> (that is, one of the nobility who has fallen into poverty) and he was enfeoffed with it for the duration of his life. This would be a personal fief. But such personal fiefs do not possess the right, natural qualities of a fief, as can be understood in the final chapter.

Fifthly, some are <term>Ecclesiastical</term> or <term>Spiritual Fiefs</term>, and they are called "church fiefs" for three reasons. Firstly, if they are leased by the Church. Secondly, if they are received from the Church. Thirdly, if they are granted by or taken by a spiritual person, of which mention will be made in the sixth chapter. Some, however...

**Secular Fiefs** / are so called because they are granted and taken or received by secular lords and <term>vassals</term> <note>A person who held land from a lord in exchange for loyalty and service.</note>. And because these are the most prominent types of fiefs, this book deals with them most frequently.

Sixthly / there are certain **Male Fiefs**; these are the ones in which only male heirs may succeed, and which are granted to male heirs alone. Indeed, these are considered the "proper" or natural fiefs, which are solely for men, because women cannot succeed in a fief unless it is granted to them out of special grace and favor, or if it is expressly provided for through a specific <term>Pact</term> <note>A formal legal agreement or contract.</note>. In such a case, they are then called and named **Female Fiefs**. Parag. hac quoque."</note>

Seventhly / some are called **Old** or **Paternal Fiefs**, while others are called **New**, being those which one has newly obtained and thus begin with the person of the <term>vassal</term> <note>The person currently being granted the land.</note> and do not come from ancestors, but instead descend to one's own heirs. This is discussed in the next chapter, and by *Baldus on the paragraph "this also," concerning the succession of a fief, chapter 1, on the degrees of succession.* <note>original: "Bal. in Par. hac quoq;. de success. feudi. c. 1. de gradib. success."</note> However, this distinction is maintained: those fiefs that come to us from our forefathers and <term>agnates</term> <note>Relatives related through the male line.</note> beyond the fourth degree are called **Old Fiefs**. But those which come to us from our father, grandfather, great-grandfather, or his father, up to the fourth degree, are called **Paternal Fiefs**.

Finally, it is to be known / that some fiefs are **binding** and some are **non-binding**. These are called binding fiefs when the vassal must bind himself to serve his lord against everyone else and allow himself to be called to service. **Non-binding Fiefs**, however, are so named when the vassal exempts one or more persons against whom he does not wish to be bound to serve his lord. Let this be enough regarding the distinctions of fiefs. For although many other distinctions could be made, they are of little consequence; those I have recounted are the most necessary to know.

Likewise, if the father or vassal / surrendered his fief to the Lord / with this attached request / that the Lord would grant it to his (the vassal's) sons / the fief does not cease to be an Old or **Ancestral Fief** <note>German: "Stamlehen"; a fief that has been in the family for generations.</note> through such a new investiture / such that it would become a New Fief / namely if nothing else therein was changed or renewed / it remains an Old or Paternal Fief. ### A Brief Excerpt of the...

...according to the law, they may grant no other than old <term>fiefs</term> <note>Land held on condition of loyalty and service to a lord.</note>. Therefore, even if a Bishop or Abbot expressly stated and indicated in the <term>enfeoffment</term> <note>The formal process of granting a fief.</note> or the feudal charter that he had given or granted an old fief, such words would nevertheless have no special force or effect. They would not be granted legal validity but would instead be regarded as a fraud, since they are forbidden from granting other types of fiefs. For this reason, such words would be in vain, even if the <term>Chapter</term> <note>The administrative body of a cathedral or monastery.</note> had given its consent alongside the Bishop. However, if such words were already present in the old feudal charters, then this suspicion would not apply, and they could be granted by the Bishop or Abbot in that same manner.

But with secular Kings, Princes, and Lords, the meaning is different, for they may well include such words in their feudal charters or otherwise employ them—namely, that it is an "old fief"—and in that case, it becomes an old fief and is regarded as such. For it acquires the nature and character of an old fief, even if it had previously been a new fief, if it is granted as an old one; this is an important point to note.

If it should happen, however, that two parties are disputing over a fief and neither has possession of it, then it shall be held to be an old fief rather than a new one. This is unless other and greater presumptions are present suggesting it must be a new fief, the determination of which is left to the judge’s discretion. <note>original: "c. 1. de gradib. success." — Chapter 1, on the degrees of succession.</note> It is, however, a strong presumption that a fief is paternal if a person has held and maintained it in long-term possession, as *Alexander* says <note>original: "conf. 15." — Consultation 15 of Alexander Tartagnus, a famous medieval jurist.</note> and *Baldus* in <note>original: "l. si de feudo controuerf. fuerit inter do. & agna." — On the law regarding controversies over fiefs between lords and agnatic (male-line) relatives.</note> and *Præpositus* in his <note>original: "præludijs feudorum sexta diuif." — The sixth division of his introductions to feudal law.</note>

Finally, a question arises here: If a nobleman possessed several ancestral estates and surrendered them to a Prince or Prelate—as may sometimes happen—on the condition that the Lord would grant and lease them back to him as a proper <term>man-fief</term> <note>A standard fief held by a male vassal.</note>, should such a fief be considered new or old? To this, it is answered: it shall be held to be a new fief, especially if it is not otherwise understood in the enfeoffment and the feudal charters that it was given and granted to the man in the place of an old fief. Therefore, one must take great care in the feudal charters; for without this, and if a property were made into a new fief in such a manner, a brother could not succeed the other if he died; instead, the land would <term>revert to the Lord</term> <note>original: "wider heim fiele" — Escheat; the return of land to the lord when there is no legal heir.</note>.

And much more could be set down here concerning old and new fiefs. However, since it will often happen that these must be dealt with in the following chapters of this book, I have chosen to let the matter rest in this chapter with what has already been set down here.

# Which Assets May be Granted
->and Received as Fiefs.<-

### The Fourth Chapter.

<image-desc>Decorative initial 'I' featuring intertwined floral and foliate motifs.</image-desc>

IN this fourth chapter, I wish to point out first that it is not my intention to set down or dispute anything regarding those assets which cannot be <term>alienated</term> <note>Alienation refers to the legal transfer of property ownership to another person.</note> and are not in human use: such as ecclesiastical Church properties and those dedicated to the common good. Similarly, I wish to exclude from this chapter the assets of those who are not masters of their own affairs and may not alienate them without the knowledge of other people, and especially the authorities, their curators, and guardians. These include the assets of <term>minors</term> <note>Under the law, those who have not yet reached the age of legal majority.</note>, the insane, spendthrifts, the mute, and similar persons who cannot administer or manage their own property, much less sell or alienate it. Likewise, if a statute were made in a city or elsewhere stating that one should not sell any landed property to a foreigner, etc. For whatever assets may not be alienated also cannot be granted as a <term>fief</term> <note>Land or rights held by a vassal from a lord on condition of loyalty and service.</note> to anyone. Therefore, we shall dispute and write only regarding those assets which are within our power to do with as we please, as these alone can be granted and received as fiefs; and they are of four types.

First are immovable grounds, such as cities, towns, castles, villages, forests, landscapes, estates, meadows, fields, and the like, all of which can be made into fiefs. And it is to be noted that along with such immovable grounds, the fruits, usage, and other rights that belong to them or grow upon them are also granted as part of the fief—for instance, the fish in ponds, lakes, and waters. This would exclude fish that have been placed in a holding tank or fish-well to be kept and preserved there; these do not belong to the estate, as anyone can easily understand for themselves. Otherwise, if I were <term>enfeoffed</term> <note>The formal process of being given legal possession of a fief.</note> with a lake or pond, it must be understood that the fish therein are also granted to me and must therefore follow the estate: <note>original: "Par. Sciendum. de feudi cognitione." — Referring to the legal section "It should be known" regarding the recognition of fiefs.</note>

Secondly, there are certain assets attached to the immovable grounds which are also granted as fiefs, such as houses and other buildings. Such assets are sometimes granted with the ground, and sometimes without the ground and soil; and it may well happen that the building is granted to one person, while the ground or the site upon which such a building is placed is granted to another. <note>original: "Instit. de rerum diuis. Par. cum in suo." — Justinian’s Institutes on the division of things, section regarding building on one’s own land. "Feudista, tit. hic finit lex. Par. si vasal." — Commentary on feudal law, section on the end of the law regarding vassals.</note>

Thirdly, those things are also given as fiefs which are reckoned among immovable assets, such as annual pensions, interest, and dues—not only in money, but also in grain, wine, livestock, and other things. For these in all—

## A short excerpt, which

considers certain rights as immovable property: In the *Clementines*, "He went forth from Paradise" <note>Latin: *Exivi de Paradiso*. This refers to a specific papal decree from 1312 regarding the rule of St. Francis.</note> and "annual revenues" <note>Latin: *annui redditus*</note> in the section "concerning the meaning of words" <note>Latin: *de verborum significatione*</note>. This applies primarily when such rents or income come from immovable property <note>Property that cannot be moved, like land or buildings.</note>, according to the opinion of some legal experts. But others believe it is all the same whether they come from movable or immovable property. For instance, if someone deposits money for exchange at a certain place, he may certainly grant that right to another. For although such yields and income do not come from immovable property, they are nevertheless based on a trade or business, which is then counted in place of an immovable asset.

However, if the income or pension comes from a person <note>A personal obligation rather than an asset tied to land or a business.</note>, it could not be made into a <term>fief</term> <note>A grant of land or rights held by a vassal from a lord.</note>, just as one cannot make a fief out of a debt.

And it is also to be diligently noted that rents and income which are openly usurious <note>Charging excessive or illegal interest.</note> and unseemly can by no means be made into fiefs. For example, if one took interest from an exchange bank where public usury was practiced, or if one took payments from dice and other shameful games at fairs and church festivals—which should not be tolerated at all.

However, if someone had a yearly income of certain bread, these might be granted just like grain, excluding the "usury-bread" <note>Likely referring to bread distributed as interest or as part of a questionable ecclesiastical endowment.</note> which is usually given to the <term>canons</term> <note>Priests who serve in a cathedral.</note> in the foundations; in my opinion, these cannot be made into fiefs.

From this, some wish to conclude that even the income generated annually by a Bishop's seal may be made into a fief and granted. Since the Bishops in German lands have no less duty to govern land and people than princes, and therefore must use the seal in many matters, provided that it is not made into a matter of public extortion, I consider it possible for this to occur.

But tolls, <term>taxes</term> <note>Original: *Schoß*, a medieval land or property tax.</note>, and <term>safe-conducts</term> <note>Original: *Geleit*, a fee paid for armed escort or protection while traveling.</note>, or the like, can certainly be granted; there is no doubt about this, regardless of whether they come from immovable property as mentioned above. In short, whatever one can derive use from—be it annually, twice a year, monthly, weekly, or however it may be—such rights, whether they involve hunting, fishing, quarrying, and the like, may all be made into fiefs. It also does not matter if such income is not always uniform; rather, it is just the same if one receives grain one year and wine or money the next.

From this it follows that jurisdictions and other subordinate rights (where no other obstacles stand in the way) may be granted, provided one acquires the <term>possession</term> <note>Original: *Gewehre*, a legal term for the outward sign of ownership or right.</note> through patience or neglect [of the lord]. And where one grants a castle or a lordship, it is held that the jurisdictions have been granted along with it, unless the feudal lord has expressly reserved them for himself.

### Imperial Feudal Law

...and thus the <term>fiefs</term> <note>A fief was a grant of land or rights held by a vassal from a lord in exchange for service.</note> would have to perish along with the goods. For if one were to keep them but not be allowed to use them, they would provide no benefit. Furthermore, fiefs are of such a nature and character that the ownership must remain with the <term>lord</term> <note>The superior who grants the property.</note> while the usage remains with the <term>vassal</term> <note>The subordinate who holds the property; here called the "Lehenmann" or fief-man.</note>: which, however, cannot be the case in this instance involving movable goods <note>Because movable goods like food or money are often consumed when used, meaning ownership and usage cannot be easily separated.</note>. And although some believe that if one provided security or a deposit—as is customary in some cases—one could then grant and receive such movable goods as fiefs, this opinion cannot stand, nor does it override or refute the reasons already cited.

However, if someone had sworn an <term>oath</term> <note>original: "jurament"</note> or performed a duty to a lord and thus received such movable goods as a fief, this would be valid—not as a proper fief, but as a different kind of contract. This is because such an oath can be kept without endangering the salvation of one's soul. Nevertheless, Andreas de Isernia <note>A prominent 14th-century Neapolitan legal scholar known for his expertise in feudal law.</note> cites many grand reasons to prove that such an oath is void and powerless; I would rather agree with him, as his opinion is better founded.

As far as <term>tithes</term> <note>A "Zehend" or tithe was a tenth of agricultural produce or income paid to support the church.</note> are concerned, it is asked whether these may also be granted as fiefs, since they are spiritual goods of which mention is made in Holy Scripture—and it was heard above that such goods cannot be granted as fiefs? To this, it should be known: Although the law provides that spiritual goods cannot be granted as fiefs, one can nevertheless grant tithes, especially those which laypeople received from the Church before the <term>Lateran Council</term> <note>The Third (1179) and Fourth (1215) Lateran Councils strictly prohibited laypeople from "owning" church tithes.</note>. Likewise, those which have been in use since time immemorial are permitted, for such tithes are considered to have been granted before the aforementioned Council.

However, if such a tithe had ever reverted back to the Church since the said Council, the Church could not grant it further to a layperson (regardless of the fact that some hold the opposite view and would like to make a distinction between these and other tithes). This is because no consistent distinction can be made between those and other tithes, and the law clearly provides that tithes cannot be granted to laypeople.

Much less can one layperson grant a tithe to another, even if he held it as a fief and possession and it had been granted to him before the Lateran Council. However, this is not observed among the Germans, as one sees daily that lords grant such tithes to the nobility just like other properties. Because they have now

A Brief Excerpt of the

# Who May Grant and Take
## or Receive Fiefs.

### The Fifth Chapter.

<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial 'I' decorated with floral vine patterns.</image-desc>
**I**n this chapter, it is first established who may grant and bestow <term>fiefs</term> <note>A fief was a grant of land or rights held by a vassal from a lord in exchange for service.</note>, and subsequently, who may receive them. As far as the first point is concerned, there would be much to debate and discuss. However, we wish to summarize it as briefly as possible so that the volume does not become too large. Accordingly, it is to be known here what kind of <term>regalia</term> <note>From the Latin *iura regalia*, these are "royal rights" or privileges—such as coining money or collecting tolls—that belong exclusively to the sovereign.</note> there are: Principalities, Lordships, Marches, and Counties. These the <term>Emperor</term> <note>Specifically the Holy Roman Emperor.</note> alone grants; and those who receive such fiefs are Princes, Margraves, Counts, and Lords, etc., and according to feudal law, they shall be called Imperial <term>Captains</term> or heads. The <term>Feudists</term> <note>Scholars and lawyers who specialized in feudal law.</note> say, moreover, that the Pope would also like to claim such regalia and magnificence for himself, if the opportunity should arise and if such were permitted to him.

And although the Emperor in the Holy Roman Empire of the German Nation has the power to enfeoff Archdukes, Princes, Dukes, Margraves, and Landgraves, along with other Counts and Lords, other Kings in their own kingdoms may also grant and bestow such fiefs and dignities (except for the <term>Electors</term> <note>The high-ranking princes who held the specific right to elect the Holy Roman Emperor.</note>). For the Feudists say that a King has more authority and power in his own kingdom than the Emperor has in the Roman Empire; they wish to prove this by the fact that Kings are usually born to their kingdoms, whereas the Emperor is elected to his. Other kingdoms fall to their heirs, but the Emperorship does not. Furthermore, the very name of such fiefs carries their significance with it, in that they are called <term>regalia</term>, which means Kingly and Imperial fiefs.

Now we wish to provide an indication here, as briefly as may be done, of where the Dukes, Margraves, and Counts, etc., have their origin. And it is held that, as far as the name <term>Duke</term> <note>In German, *Hertzog*.</note> is concerned, the name itself has its origin from the Romans, whom they called leaders, in Latin **Duces** <note>original: "Duces," meaning leaders or military commanders.</note>, and were thereafter endowed by the Emperor with certain duchies or lands, provided that they must receive and earn them from him as fiefs; and yet they have retained the name, being called Dukes.

Regarding what concerns the <term>Counts</term> <note>In German, *Graffen*.</note>, although one finds many different accounts in the histories, it is nonetheless certain that the status of Count must be very old. For **Cornelius Tacitus** <note>A famous Roman historian (c. 56–120 AD) who wrote *Germania*, an account of the Germanic tribes.</note> writes in his book on the Germans that among the ancients it was the custom that to every war-captain or Prince, twelve Counts were assigned, by whose counsel he acted; these men were also required to be present with him and to wait upon him.

It also explores the Roman and ancient Germanic origins of noble titles like Duke and Count.</summary>

-># Imperial Feudal Law.<-

As to where the **Margraves** <note>A Margrave (from the German *Markgraf*) was a Count specifically appointed to govern and defend a "Mark" or border province.</note> originated, there are various opinions and views. However, the most prominent authors hold—and also prove from history—that the Margraves were originally appointed by the Empire to guard the borders, so that enemies or those who do not belong to the Empire might not make an incursion. These same men had the power, if they perceived a threat, to summon the nearest neighboring inhabitants so that they might offer more substantial resistance and defense against the enemies.

And thus, the Margraves were nothing other than **overseers of the borders** <note>original: *Limitanei præpoliti*</note>, that is, administrators or protectors of the frontier. This is evident in the Margraves of Baden, who were commanded to guard the Rhine. Whatever territories these same Margraves took from or forced away from the enemies, as **Lampridius** <note>Aelius Lampridius, a Roman historian often cited in the Middle Ages for precedents on border administration.</note> indicates, they kept for themselves and were enfeoffed with them, so that they would be all the more diligent in guarding the border.

Furthermore, it is to be known that every King or Emperor has the power to create Dukes, Princes, Margraves, Counts, and Lords, and to enfeoff them with such dignities and **regalia** <note>Royal rights or privileges, such as minting coins, collecting tolls, or mining minerals, which normally belong only to the sovereign.</note>.

Likewise, not only the Emperor but every King or **Monarch** may grant the regalia, which belong solely to the Imperial or Royal majesty. What these **regalia** are, you will find in **chapter 1, "What the Regalia are"** <note>original: *c. 1. Quæ ſint Regalia*, referring to a specific section of the *Libri Feudorum*, the standard collection of feudal law.</note>. However, in a general grant—such as when high and low courts are granted to someone—the other regalia are not meant to be included nor incorporated unless they were explicitly stated as having been granted by the Emperor or King out of **certain knowledge and his own motion** <note>The legal phrase *ex certa scientia et mero motu* indicated that a ruler was acting deliberately and by his own will, not just through a standard bureaucratic process.</note>.

However, if certain regalia were expressed and named in the enfeoffment, and a general grant followed it, it would have a different meaning: namely, that the other regalia must also be understood as included. For instance, if the King said: "We enfeoff this person with tolls, escorts, and all other regalia, **privileges**, etc.," in such a case, the other regalia would rightly be included as well.

Secondly, if the King had nothing else to grant at that specific location except regalia, and he used such general words in the enfeoffment, then by necessity the other regalia must also follow and be understood as granted.

Thirdly, if because of the office being assigned it is presumed that such regalia must be granted to a Prince or Count, etc., so that he may otherwise perform and fulfill that same office—or if the office could not be carried out without those same regalia—as for example, if a Count were granted the regalia so that he might have people escorted and brought through his territory with **safe-conduct** <note>The right of *Geleidt* (escort) allowed a lord to charge travelers for protection through his lands.</note>, in that case, it would be presumed that the Count of that place must also collect tolls and escort fees, and that he was enfeoffed with them.

Fourthly, if a grace or favor were granted to a Prince or Count by the King or Emperor—for example, if the King gave a County to one of his friends as a gift—the regalia would go with it. Likewise, if it happened that Princes...
