# A Short Extract

Yet these four pieces are not to be understood as anything other than common **regalia** <term>Regalia: Sovereign rights and privileges belonging to the crown, such as taxing, mining, or judicial authority.</term>. However, if they were particularly great and distinguished regalia, they could not be granted without specific expression. Namely, such things as: striking one's own coins, legitimizing children born out of wedlock, appointing notaries, establishing universities, and the like; for these, one requires a special grant of grace.

Although in current times this is not so strictly observed, especially regarding the coinage. Since almost all cities have their own coinage, particularly in the land of Saxony, regardless of the fact that they have no mines; thus, some of them also mint coins, which some people believe should not rightly be allowed.

Although the Emperor had the power to grant all regalia, whether high or low, it is nonetheless important to know that he cannot grant them—neither through **fiefs** <term>Lehen (fief): Land or rights granted by a lord to a vassal in exchange for service.</term> nor in other ways—to the detriment or diminution of his successors or the Empire.

In this regard, it is also asked: If the Emperor were to enfeoff two people with the same property, and such enfeoffment occurred at different times—so that one was enfeoffed first and the other afterward—and the last person was given formal possession, which one should keep the fief? Although some here wish to distinguish and make a difference, saying that if it happened by way of contract, the first should keep the fief; but if it happened by way of a gift of grace, then the last should keep it. However, I hold that the fief should rightly remain with the first, regardless of the possession granted to the second.

For the Emperor, just like anyone else, has made himself bound through such a promise given. Thus, he is obligated to hand over and vacate the fief to the first person, unless it would result in significant detriment to the Empire (or, where it is a Prince, to the **Principality** <note>original: *Fürstenthumb*</note>). For it is also held thus in **ecclesiastical fiefs** <note>original: *Geistlichen Lehen*; these are church-held lands or offices.</note>: when a fief or **prebend** <note>A stipend or land grant given to a member of the clergy.</note> is granted to two people, even if the last one obtains the **investiture** <term>Investiture: The formal ceremony where a person is officially given possession of a fief or office.</term>, the first is preferred.

Since this is the case in spiritual matters, it should rightly proceed the same way in secular fiefs; for the Emperor is no less bound to keep his word than the Church is. And just as it behooves the Church to guard itself against deceit, there is nothing more praiseworthy in the Emperor (as the laws say) than **good faith** <note>original: *guter Glaube*, referring to the legal principle of *bona fides* or honest dealing.</note>. A Prince—as **Isocrates** <note>A famous Greek orator (436–338 BCE) who wrote extensively on the ethics and duties of a ruler.</note> says—should strive for this in all his life and being: that more trust be given to his simple words than if another had sworn an oath to the matter. And this is enough regarding the regalia for now.

Furthermore, there are other large fiefs, such as if a Prince were to grant his land, or part of it, further to another. But such fiefs have no **regalia** or dignity like those mentioned above. Nevertheless, those who are enfeoffed with them may be called **Captains** <term>Capitanier: A term often used for high-ranking military or administrative officials who held land from a prince rather than directly from the Emperor.</term> and be regarded as such.

After the Imperial fiefs, there are also other fiefs which [originate] from...

# Imperial Feudal Law

grants are given to princes, dukes, margraves, and counts; and those who receive such **fiefs** <term>Fief (Lehen): Land or rights granted by a superior to a subordinate in exchange for loyalty and service.</term> are called **Vavasours** <term>Vavasour (Valsasor): A feudal tenant who ranks immediately below a baron or a high captain.</term>. However, because there are many kinds of Captains and Vavasours, the matter is briefly structured as follows:

Firstly, there are the **Captains of the Empire** or feudal tenants, such as **Prince-Electors**, **Princes**, **Margraves**, **Landgraves**, and other **Counts**. Secondly, there are the **Great Vavasours**, who are enfeoffed by Princes and Counts. Thirdly, those are also called **Captains** who hold fiefs from the Emperor or a Prince without any **regalia** <term>Regalia: Sovereign rights, such as the power to mint coins or collect certain taxes.</term>. For some fiefs are called **Royal**, meaning those that possess regalia and lordships, which only the Captains of the Empire—such as Princes, Counts, etc.—receive and are capable of holding. Others, however, are not Royal fiefs, as they possess no lordship or regalia, even if they are granted directly by the Emperor or a Prince.

Thus, there are also four kinds of feudal tenants, or four grades of the same. In the **First Grade** are **Prince-Electors**, **Princes**, **Margraves**, **Counts**, etc. This grade bestows nobility and brings its dignity with it, in such a way that even if a principality were granted to a peasant, he would be considered a Prince by virtue of such a fief, just as he is effectively made a Prince by it. As **Aeneas Sylvius** <note>original: "Aeneas Syluius" - refers to Enea Silvio Piccolomini, who became Pope Pius II and wrote extensively on European history.</note> writes concerning the first prince in **Bohemia**, that he was a peasant <note>This refers to the legend of Przemysl the Plowman, the mythical founder of the Bohemian Přemyslid dynasty.</note>. It is also known from history how **Decius** and **Phocas** <note>Gaius Messius Quintus Decius and Phocas were Roman/Byzantine Emperors who rose from lower military ranks.</note> rose from humble origins to the Imperial throne.

In the **Second Grade** are the most prominent of the nobility, such as the house of **Werther** in **Thuringia** and **Meissen**, and the house of **Bünau**, who have other nobles beneath them as feudal tenants. However, the fiefs with which they are endowed must be of such a nature that they bestow nobility; otherwise, if they were merely citizen or peasant fiefs, the dignity would not follow the fief, so that the tenant could not become noble through it. This would only be possible if the Emperor or Prince had specifically provided for it out of special grace. Those in this grade are called the **Great Vavasours** or feudal tenants.

In the **Third Grade**, although it mostly concerns and commonly includes the nobility, it nonetheless sometimes extends to those who are not noble. These are called **Lower** or **Minor Vavasours**; because they commonly receive their fiefs from the Great Vavasours, they do not become any more noble through such enfeoffment than they were before. Yet they may further grant land to those in the **Fourth Grade**, such as citizens and peasants; and those in the fourth grade are usually called **Vavasinos** <note>original: "Valsasnos"</note>, which is to say, **sub-vassals** or **rear-vassals** <term>Afterlehenleut: Tenants who hold their land from a middle-man (a vassal) rather than directly from the sovereign.</term>.

However, by custom, it is sometimes handled differently, so that the Emperor and the Captains and Princes of the Empire give fiefs not only to those of the nobility but also to others, such as **merchants**, **clerks**, **lawyers**, etc., who are not noble.

In summary, all those who have the administration of their own property and are **laypeople** <term>Laypeople (Leyen): Individuals who are not members of the clergy.</term>, whether man or woman, may either renew old fiefs or have their properties turned into fiefs, even if they were peasants or were in mortal peril. For one may even conclude a marriage on one’s deathbed, provided that both spouses are of sound mind.

# A Short Extract / of the

That a woman may also grant a **fief** <term>Fief (Lehen): Land or rights granted by a superior to a subordinate in exchange for loyalty and service.</term> is an open and clear text in the Title [of the Law], "Who Can Grant Fiefs." From this, the feudal legal scholars <note>original: "Feudisten"</note> conclude that a woman may also hold jurisdiction over her **vassal** <term>Vassal (Lehenmann): A person who holds land under the feudal system and owes allegiance to a lord.</term>: however, if the woman conducts herself improperly and seeks to waste the fief, this shall not be permitted to her.

## Concerning Wards and Minors.

Furthermore, it is asked whether a **ward** <note>original: "Mündlein" – an archaic term for a minor under legal guardianship.</note> or a minor—who are treated the same in this case—may grant fiefs? To this, the answer is: if they are old or paternal fiefs <note>Fiefs inherited through the male line of the family.</note>, he may renew them. And although a minor cannot transfer the **possession** <term>Possession (Posseß): The legal right to occupy or hold a property.</term> to another or assign it to them without the presence and consent of guardians, he can nevertheless grant an old fief—provided he has sufficient understanding—even without the presence of the guardians. In such a case, he releases himself from the obligation by which he would otherwise be bound to the heirs and **agnates** <term>Agnates (Agnaten): Relatives whose kinship is traced exclusively through the male line.</term> of the vassal. For if minors or wards grant old fiefs without the presence of their caretakers or guardians, they cannot bind themselves to any further obligation through this act. However, the vassal who receives the fief in such a manner and obtains it from the minor is also excused, and the grant remains valid without change or disadvantage.

## Concerning Guardians and Proxies, etc.

Likewise, if it is asked whether guardians, caretakers, and **proxies** <term>Proxies (Procuratores): Legal representatives authorized to act on behalf of another.</term> may perform the granting of a fief? The answer is: if they were old fiefs, the caretakers or guardians may grant and bestow them even without the presence of their wards. This is because they have the command and power to manage the property and to sell or exchange it for compelling reasons, excluding transactions with their own blood relatives or friends; and especially if the proxy has a proper and complete administration and management of the property. But neither wards nor minors can grant new fiefs, even with the authority and full power of their caretakers and guardians. Much less may the caretakers and guardians do so on their own behalf, unless it occurs through legal proceedings and thus **by decree of the judge** <note>original: "cum Decreto Iudicis".</note>.

## Concerning Clerical Persons: How and When They May Grant Fiefs.

Now follows the section on clerical persons, and in what manner they may give and grant fiefs, regarding which point the following rules are to be noted.

## The First Rule.

Firstly, that all ecclesiastical **prelates** <term>Prelate (Prelat): A high-ranking member of the clergy who has jurisdiction, such as an archbishop, bishop, or abbot.</term>, such as archbishops, bishops, abbots, and abbesses, as well as **provosts** <term>Provost (Pröbst): A high administrative official in the church hierarchy.</term>, may grant **fiefs** <term>Fief (Lehen): Land or rights granted to a person in exchange for loyalty and service.</term>, specifically "old fiefs" which have customarily been granted in the past. This rule also extends to lower prelates, such as **deans** <term>Dean (Dechant): A cleric with supervisory authority over a group of parishes.</term> and parish priests. This is to be understood such that every superior prelate may grant the property which he holds in his administration or management <note>original: "Administration oder verwaltung"</note>, or which belongs to his church and does not belong to the subordinate churches. An exception is made for the Pope, who desires to have the power to grant the fiefs of every church, since he holds authority over every prelature collectively. Furthermore, what is said here concerning prelates may also be understood regarding those who are suspected of squandering <note>original: "verschwendung halben verdächtig" — individuals suspected of mismanaging assets or wasting wealth.</note>: for these may nonetheless grant fiefs, unless they are formally accused and it is forbidden to them.

## The Second Rule.

Secondly, that a prelate can also grant a fief to someone without the consent of the **Chapter** <term>Chapter (Capittel): A governing body of clergy that assists a prelate in managing the affairs of a cathedral or collegiate church.</term>; this is also commonly held in practice.

## The Third Rule.

Thirdly, that a **college** or chapter may also grant a fief when the prelature is vacant and the prelate has died, unless it were a **Cathedral Chapter** <note>original: "Thumcapittel" — the specific body of clergy attached to a cathedral.</note>. Furthermore, abbesses and lower prelates can grant fiefs without the consent of their superiors, and an abbess is compared to an abbot in the administration of assets.

## The Fourth Rule.

Fourthly, that fiefs which **escheat** <note>original: "heimfallen" — when a fief reverts to the lord or the church because the holder died without heirs or committed a crime.</note> to the church may be granted by an ecclesiastical prelate not only to strangers but also to blood relatives, provided they are otherwise fit and not burdensome to the church, following the example of Christ, who made his friends Apostles.

## The Fifth Rule.

Fifthly, when it is asked which assets may be granted as fiefs by ecclesiastical prelates, the answer—according to the opinion of the legal scholars—is that they must be assets which have been fiefs for 40 years and have been granted at least twice, and that to a receiver who is in good faith. Otherwise, the granting would need to be confirmed by the Pope. For such a confirmation is the same as if the fief had been a church fief for 40 years. In the same manner, a fief could be granted because it was so old that one could not actually know when it was first granted.

Thereupon another rule follows: namely, that no **prelate** <term>Prelate (Prelat): A high-ranking member of the clergy, such as a bishop or abbot, who has authority over a specific territory or religious house.</term> except for the Pope can grant church properties that are not customarily granted. No distinction is to be made here; it applies equally to new or old **fiefs** <term>Fief (Lehen): Land or rights granted to a person (a vassal) in exchange for loyalty and service.</term>. If a grant were made for such goods, it could be hindered or revoked not only by the liege lord but also by those who have a legal interest in the matter. However, the Pope can grant such goods, as stated above. But if it were another prelate and the grant was revoked, if the recipient did not act in good faith, he would be required to restore the **fruits** <note>original: "Früchte" — in a legal sense, this refers to the income, rents, or produce generated by the land.</note> he had received.

Regarding this, there is no doubt that a prelate may grant his own private property as a fief. Whether church goods can be considered the prelate's own is not necessary to detail here, as it belongs to another discussion. One point to note: if someone receives a forbidden property as a fief and does not act in good faith, he must restore the fruit. Rule: "He who acts against [the law]" <note>original: "Qui contra, de reg. iuris" — referring to the legal maxim 'Qui contra legem facit' from the 'Rules of Law' in the Digest.</note> and the law "In what manner" <note>original: "l. quemadmodū C. de agrico. & co." — a reference to the Code of Justinian regarding the status of agricultural workers and colonists.</note>.

It is also to be noted here, should it happen that church lands are taken by force by a lord, and he refuses to return them or will not recognize the church as the liege lord, then the church may grant such lands to another lord of equal power. This new lord may then use force to reclaim the land from the one who holds it and restore it to its proper legal standing. The legal scholars say such a grant is legally valid. However, one should take care that no fraud occurs in such a case, and that one does not willfully stir up war or trouble over such fiefs. Instead, one should first employ all possible human diligence to regain the goods through law or other suitable means or negotiations. But if it were a tyrant who publicly refused all such means, one might proceed with the grant more boldly.

In the same manner, church goods might also be granted if the church were pressured by poverty or other necessity, even if they had not been granted as fiefs previously. For necessity, as the saying goes, has no law. Although some maintain that such a grant should be made with the consent of the **Chapter** <term>Chapter (Capittel): The governing body of a cathedral or collegiate church, consisting of canons.</term>, it is nonetheless held that if the situation were so urgent that time would not permit a delay, the grant would be valid and upheld, even if the Chapter had not yet consented; however, it must afterwards be brought before the Chapter to be **ratified** <note>original: "ratificirt"</note> and confirmed.

If the church were impoverished so that it suffered lack, and some fiefs were to fall back [escheat] to it, the church might keep them for its own use.

A prelate should also—which is well worth noting—when he grants fiefs, not change the old feudal customs or the feudal charters, especially if this would result in disadvantage or harm to the church. For example, if the prelate attempted to grant a proper **male fief** <note>original: "recht Man̄-Lehen" — a fief restricted to male heirs.</note> to a woman.

### Who Can Receive Fiefs and Who May Be Eligible for Them.

As far as the other part of this fifth chapter is concerned/ namely/ who may receive fiefs and who may be eligible for them/ it can be briefly said/ That all those may receive fiefs/ to whom it is not explicitly forbidden in the law: so/ that even **servants** <note>original: "Knechte" — in this context, the author refers to the classical legal concept of a bondman or slave.</note> may be eligible for fiefs/ provided the lord knowingly enfeoffs them: and in that case, the lords of those servants acquire such fiefs/ and they must also earn them.

But if a lord enfeoffs his own servants/ they would thereby be made free/ so/ that they were no longer servants and owned. And although such servants <note>referring to absolute chattel slaves</note> are not found in our **German lands**/ there are nevertheless in many places **serfs** <note>original: "eigene Leute" — literally "own people," referring to individuals bound to the land or a lord, common in the feudal system of the Holy Roman Empire.</note>. Now if one of them/ were enfeoffed in such a manner/ he would thereby also be made free/ and no longer held to be a serf. The same applies to **monks**/ so far as they can have fiefs/ if one were enfeoffed/ then such a fief would have to benefit the monastery. Although monks/ as they have other things to concern themselves with/ should rightly renounce fiefs: it also pairs poorly/ monks and fief-estates/ which belong only to **knightly people** to receive and earn. Yet there are some cases/ in which a monastery may also receive fiefs/ though it is not necessary to dispute that here.

The **son** who is still under his father's authority/ may also receive fiefs: and it does not hinder/ even if the liege lord had been mistaken in the condition. For the son in that case is not incapable/ but eligible for fiefs: and in that case, the **usufruct** <term>Usufruct (Vsufrucht): The legal right to use and enjoy the profits or produce of property belonging to another.</term> would not belong to the father/ as with other goods/ but would remain the son’s. However, all this is to be understood regarding new fiefs/ for in this point one does not speak of old fiefs/ unless they are especially and specifically expressed.

**Women** may receive maternal, paternal, and new fiefs/ namely/ in those cases in which the fiefs extend to women: regarding which more will be set down later in the eighth chapter.

In the same way, **minors**, **underage persons**, and the **senseless** <note>original: "Sinnlose" — referring to the mentally incapacitated or "insane" in a legal sense.</note>/ may receive fiefs/ though differently/ and as follows.

If the **minor** <term>Minor (Mündlein): A child or ward under the protection of a guardian.</term> or ward cannot speak/ he cannot receive the fiefs without the presence of the **guardian** <term>Guardian (Vormünder): A person legally responsible for the interests of a minor or incapacitated person.</term>/ but he must be there and present. However, the guardian may well receive them on behalf of his ward/ even if the minor is not at hand: just as the **letter of enfeoffment** <term>Letter of Enfeoffment (Lehenbrieff): The formal legal document recording the grant of a fief and its conditions.</term> shall be issued in his name.

Here now arises a question. A man of noble birth has fathered several sons with his wife/ who was also noble. # How Fiefs are Given, and What Legal Rights the Vassal Acquires Thereby.

## The Sixth Chapter.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial letter 'I' featuring floral and vine motifs within a square frame.</image-desc>
IN this sixth chapter, two main subjects are treated. First, how fiefs should be granted. Secondly, what legal rights the **vassal** <term>Vassal (Lehenmann): One who holds land from a lord in exchange for allegiance and service.</term> gains and acquires in the fief. As far as the first part is concerned, fiefs are granted in two ways. First, through **investiture**, that is, when one is actually brought into **possession**. Secondly, when the **lord** <term>Lord (Lehenherr): The person who grants a fief to a vassal.</term> gives something into the hand of the man, such as a ring, a sword, or a spear, etc., and says alongside this: "We enfeoff you with the castle," or "city," etc., "along with its appurtenances," or however the custom of the land otherwise dictates. And such **enfeoffment** <term>Enfeoffment (belehnung): The formal act of investing someone with a fief.</term> should happen in the presence of at least two fellow vassals, who are called **peers of the court** <note>original: "Pares curis" — likely a corruption of the Latin "Pares curiae," meaning equals in the lord's court who witness legal acts.</note>. Otherwise, such enfeoffment would be invalid, unless a public instrument <note>A formal legal document.</note> were drawn up and executed before witnesses. And what is said here regarding **oral enfeoffment** pertains to "old" fiefs: for if they were "new" fiefs, then such oral enfeoffment would not be enough; rather, the lord would have to actually induct the vassal into the property—unless the oral enfeoffment took place on the site of the fief itself, or the site was so close that one could see it and point it out to the vassal; in such a case, actual physical induction would not be necessary.

# A short extract of the

yet the **vassal** <term>Vassal (Lehenmann): A person who holds land or rights from a lord in exchange for loyalty and service.</term> may take possession of the same for himself after the **investiture** <term>Investiture (Belehnung): The formal ceremony and legal act of granting a fief.</term> has occurred, primarily if these following words were used in the grant: namely, "We enfeoff, grant, give, and deliver." And if someone held a **fief** <term>Fief (Lehen): Land or rights held under feudal law.</term> in such a way for some time, and it was acknowledged therein, even if he could not prove the investiture in any other way than through this oral grant, it would nevertheless be sufficient.

Furthermore, it should not be overlooked that a proper fief cannot be obtained other than through **formal installation** <term>Formal Installation (Einweisung): The physical act of placing a vassal in possession of the property, often done on the land itself.</term>, if it is to have the characteristics of a true fief and extend to the **heirs**. And it is not enough if the Lord had told him to take the fief if no fellow-vassals were present. However, if the Lord had commanded the vassal to do so in the presence of several other **vassals** <note>original: "belehnten Mañ" — literally "enfeoffed men." In feudal courts, one's peers (other vassals of the same lord) acted as witnesses to ensure the legality of the transaction.</note>, then such a command or order should be counted as the formal installation. If the Feudal Lord could perhaps not obtain the vassals for some reason, and other honest people were available, such as the Lord’s **councilors** <note>original: "Herrerähte."</note> or others—as I have often seen—it would be the same; provided they are included as witnesses in the **feudal charter** <term>Feudal Charter (Lehenbrieff): The written document recording the grant and the conditions of the fief.</term>.

Now, if a vassal had been in possession of the fief for a **year and a day** <note>A standard legal period in the Middle Ages and early modern era; if a situation went unchallenged for a year and a day, it often became legally binding.</note> upon such a command and will of the Lord, and had performed his services, and the Lord had allowed it and been satisfied with it, then the vassal would have obtained the fief thereby; and it would be just as if he had been **invested** <note>original: "inuestirt" — formally given the legal title.</note> in the ordinary manner.

However, if the Lord had enfeoffed the man with a **sword**, **spear**, or as mentioned above, even if he did not yet have **possession** <note>original: "Possession" — actual physical control of the land.</note> through it, the Lord is nonetheless obligated to install the vassal in such a fief immediately. He cannot release himself from this obligation by paying the **monetary value** <term>Value (Interesse): The legal "interest" or financial worth of the fief if the physical land cannot be delivered.</term> of the fief; and if any damage should occur to the vassal due to the delay, the Lord is bound and obligated to compensate for it.

Unless the Lord had afterwards given the actual **installation** to another person; in that case, the second person keeps the fief, and the Lord can release himself from the first person by paying the **value** it is worth; for the first person must also be satisfied with that. This remains true even if the Lord had said that the actual installation of the second should not harm the **legal rights** <note>original: "Gerechtigkeit."</note> of the first. For these words would have no effect here.

If a fief were granted to two people and they both had obtained **possession**, and yet it could not be known which of them obtained possession first, the fief remains with the one who can prove the first **legal grant** or title to it.

If the Lord enfeoffs someone with the **spear**, **ring**, or similar symbol, such an investiture must always happen before the vassal takes his **oath** <note>original: "die pflicht thut" — performing the duty or oath of fealty.</note>. But the installation (which is then the true investiture) should always happen after the oath has been performed.

But if the Lord had given someone a **fief belonging to another** <note>original: "frembd Lehen" — land the Lord did not actually have the right to grant.</note>, which the vassal could not maintain but was won away from him by the rightful Lord of that fief, would not the Lord be obligated to compensate the man for this? ...whether it is a foreign fief or if he is unaware of its status, especially if he is legally challenged by the **fief-measurer** <note>original: "Lehenmaß" — an official responsible for verifying the boundaries and legal status of feudal holdings.</note> regarding it. However, if the person receiving the fief had known that it was a foreign fief, the Feudal Lord would not be held liable or indebted to him for it.

Furthermore, if a Lord has granted a person a feudal estate which is still in the possession and occupation of another, but which would revert to the Lord upon the current possessor's death: such a grant is legally valid under feudal law. However, the recipient has no actual right to it until the fief is vacated and opened by the death of the current possessor. At that time, the Feudal Lord or his heirs—following the previous promise and assurance, and by virtue of such a grant—must confirm the possession and formally hand over and deliver the fief. In our custom, such arrangements are commonly called **Grace-fiefs** <term>Grace-fief (Gnadenlehen): A legal promise of a fief that is currently held by someone else; the new recipient must wait for the current holder to die before taking possession.</term>.

However, it is also important to know that if this were a spiritual or church fief, it must be vacated and then granted again to the one to whom it was promised while the **promisor** <note>original: "Promissor" — the Feudal Lord who made the promise.</note>, that is, the Feudal Lord who promised the fief out of grace, is still alive. But if that same Feudal Lord dies before the fief becomes vacant and open, the grant is void and expires with the Lord; this is a point well worth noting. In this case, it does not help if the grant was made **formally** <note>original: "solenniter" — in a solemn, official legal ceremony.</note> and in a grand manner immediately after the promise was made during the lifetime of the current possessor, as if the possessor had already passed away: for such a grant would still be invalid. This is because the grant should not and may not happen until the proper time has arrived. Therefore, it is necessary to act carefully and wisely in how feudal charters are executed.

Particularly and above all things, one should ensure that in the old fiefs, the manner and the **tenor** <note>original: "Tenor" — the exact wording, phrasing, and legal intent of a document.</note> of the old feudal charters are not changed: for these cannot be changed to the detriment of a third party. For example, if the feudal charter was originally issued to both a husband and wife, and the grant was made upon that basis, it could not later be changed or revoked to apply to the husband alone without the prior knowledge and consent of the other co-beneficiary. For the first grant is the root and foundation according to which all others must proceed. From this, it follows that in feudal law, matters are usually judged and maintained according to the feudal charters, and the **lay courts** <term>Lay Courts (Schöpffenstülen): High judicial benches, such as those in Magdeburg or Leipzig, where expert judges ruled on matters of common and feudal law.</term> deliver their verdicts accordingly.

However, the fact that this **clause** <note>original: "Clausel"</note> is commonly placed in all feudal charters—"(As much as we have the legal right to grant therein)"—matters very little and is quite useless. For if someone else has a right to such a fief, the Lord cannot take it away from them through this grant. But if others have no right to it, the clause is inserted in vain and can have no legal effect.

But this **clause** which the Lords are accustomed to putting in their letters of favor, namely, "(Without prejudice to our fiefs)," is not to be despised or omitted. For even if a Lord gives permission for the **vassal** <term>Vassal (Vasall): A person who holds land from a lord and owes him loyalty.</term> to mortgage his fief—as sometimes happens—the Lord is not obligated to pay anything toward it if the fief falls back to him, about which more shall be set down hereafter.

<header>A Brief Extract of...</header>

...yet the **vassal** <term>vassal (Lehenmann): A person who holds land from a lord in exchange for loyalty and service.</term> may take possession of the same after the **investiture** <term>investiture (Belehnung): The formal act of granting a fief, often involving a symbolic gesture or specific legal phrasing.</term> has occurred, primarily if the following words were used in the grant: "We invest, grant, give, and deliver to him." If a person has held a fief for some time in such a manner, and it is later challenged, even if he cannot prove the investiture in any other way than through the verbal granting, it shall be sufficient.

Furthermore, it should not be overlooked that a proper fief cannot be obtained except through **induction** <term>induction (Einweisung): The physical act of placing the vassal on the land to take control, as opposed to the symbolic ceremony.</term>, if it is to have the characteristics of a true fief and extend to one's heirs. It would not be enough if the Lord had simply told him to take the fief if no formal act accompanied it. However, if the Lord had commanded the vassal to take it in the presence of other **peers of the fief** <note>original: "belehnten Mann" — other vassals who hold land from the same lord and serve as witnesses to legal acts.</note>, then such a command or order shall count as induction. If the Feudal Lord perhaps cannot have the presence of the other vassals for some reason, and other honorable people are available—such as the Lord's **Privy Councilors** <note>original: "Secret-rähte"</note> or others, as I have often seen—it would be just as valid. However, these people must be recorded as witnesses in the **feudal charter** <term>feudal charter (Lehenbrieff): The written document proving the grant of a fief.</term>.

If a vassal has been in possession of the fief for **a year and a day** <note>In medieval law, "a year and a day" was a standard timeframe after which a legal status (like possession of land) became permanent or harder to challenge.</note> upon such a command and order from the Lord, and has performed his services, and the Lord has allowed it to happen and been satisfied with it, then the vassal has thereby obtained the fief. This would be the same as if he had been formally **invested** <note>original: "investirt" — from the Latin *investire*, to clothe or formally install.</note> in the regular way.

However, if the Lord has invested the man with a **Sword, Spear, or Ring** <note>These were symbolic objects used to represent different types of fiefs; for example, a sword often represented a "fief of the sword" involving military service.</note>, as mentioned above, even if he does not yet obtain **physical possession** <note>original: "Possession"</note> through that act, the Lord is nonetheless obligated to grant the vassal immediate entry into such a fief. The Lord cannot release himself from this duty simply by paying **damages** <note>original: "Interesse" — a legal term referring to financial compensation for a loss or delay.</note> equal to the fief's value. If any damage should occur to the vassal due to the delay, the Lord is obligated and bound to compensate him for it in that case.

This is unless the Lord later performed a physical induction for a second person. In that case, the second person keeps the fief, and the Lord can settle with the first person by paying **compensation** <note>original: "Interesse"</note> for what the fief is worth; the first person must be satisfied with that. This holds even if the Lord had stated that the second physical induction should not prejudice the first person's legal rights, for such words have no effect here.

If a fief were granted to two people and both had obtained possession, yet it could not be determined which of them was the first to receive possession, the fief remains with the one who can prove the earlier **claim or title** <note>original: "ankunfft oder Titel"</note> to it.

When the Lord invests someone with a Spear, Ring, or the like, such an investiture must always occur before the vassal takes his **oath of fealty** <note>original: "pflicht" — the formal promise of loyalty made by a vassal to his lord.</note>. But the induction (which is the true granting of the fief) should only happen after the oath has been performed.

If, however, the Lord has granted someone a "foreign" fief <note>A fief that actually belongs to someone else or falls under a different jurisdiction.</note> which he cannot guarantee to the vassal, and it is won away from him by the rightful Lord of that same fief, is the Lord not obligated to compensate the man for it? Answer: Yes, he is obligated. And it is the same whether he knew...

# Imperial Feudal Law.

...whether it is a foreign **fief** <term>fief (Lehen): Land or rights granted by a lord to a vassal in exchange for allegiance and service.</term>, or if he does not know it—provided he is otherwise legally sued by the **vassal** <term>vassal (Lehenmann): The person holding the fief and owing service to the lord.</term> because of it. However, if the grantee had known that it was a foreign fief, the Lord could not be held liable or indebted to him for it.

Beyond this, if a Lord has invested someone with a fief which another person currently holds in **possession and title** <note>original: "possession vnd gewehr"</note>, but which would nevertheless revert to the Lord after the death of the current possessor: such an **investiture** <term>investiture (belehnung): The formal legal act of granting the fief.</term> is valid under feudal law. Yet, the grantee has no right to it until the fief is vacated and opened by the death of the current possessor. At that time, the Feudal Lord or his heirs—according to the previous assurance and promise, and by virtue of such investiture—must grant him the title and have the fief truly assigned and delivered to him. Such grants are commonly called **fiefs of grace** <note>original: "Gnadenlehen" — a grant of a future interest in a property currently occupied by someone else.</note> among us.

However, it must also be known that if such a grant concerns a spiritual or church fief, it must be vacant at the time it is granted again to the one to whom it was promised, provided that the **grantor** <note>original: "Promissor" — the person making the legal promise or grant.</note> (that is, the same Feudal Lord who promised the fief out of grace) is still alive. If, however, that same Feudal Lord dies before the fief becomes open and vacant, the investiture is void and expires with the Lord; this is a point well worth noting. In such a case, it does not help if the investiture was performed solemnly and in a grand manner by the Lord immediately after the promise was made while the current possessor was still alive, as if the possessor had already passed away. Such an investiture would still be invalid, because it should not and may not occur until the proper time has arrived. Therefore, it is necessary to look ahead carefully and wisely regarding how such **feudal charters** <term>feudal charter (Lehenbrieff): The formal written document recording the terms of the fief.</term> are to be executed.

In particular, and above all things, one should ensure that in old fiefs, the manner and the **substance** <note>original: "Tenor" — the exact wording and legal intent of the document.</note> of the old feudal charters are not changed. These cannot be changed to the detriment of another party (such as a third party). For example, if the feudal charter was originally issued to both husband and wife, and the investiture had occurred on those terms, it could not later be changed or revoked to apply to the husband alone without the prior knowledge and consent of the other co-grantee. For the first investiture is the root and foundation, according to which all others must proceed. From this, it follows that in feudal law, one usually follows and adheres mostly to the feudal charters, and the **Benches of Lay Judges** <term>Benches of Lay Judges (Schöpffenstülen): High courts of legal experts and lay assessors that provided authoritative rulings on feudal and municipal law.</term> deliver their judgments accordingly.

Furthermore, the fact that this **clause** <note>original: "Clausel"</note> is commonly placed in all feudal charters—"(As much as we have the right to grant by law)"—does little for the matter and is quite useless. For if another person has a right to such a fief, the Lord cannot take it away through this investiture. But if others have no right to it, the clause is inserted in vain and can have no effect.

However, this clause which Lords are accustomed to putting in their letters of favor, namely: "(Without prejudice to our fief)," is not to be despised or omitted. For even if a Lord gives permission for the **vassal** <term>vassal (Vasall): The holder of the land.</term> to mortgage his fief—as sometimes happens—the Lord is not obligated to pay anything toward that debt if the fief reverts to him, about which more shall be set down hereafter.

# A short excerpt of...

Although a proper and natural **investiture** <term>investiture (Belehnung): The formal legal ceremony where a lord granted a fief to a vassal.</term> is of such a nature that it is attained through a perpetual feudal right, it is handled differently when a man is invested with a **fief** in which a woman's **morning gift** <term>morning gift (Morgengabe): Property or wealth settled on a wife by her husband the morning after the wedding, intended for her financial security.</term> is included. For if the man dies, that same fief reverts to the wife, just as the morning gift and other goods <unclear>owed</unclear> to the woman must be paid. In such a case, after the death of the husband, the investiture has no further effect and is thereby extinguished.

Furthermore, we stated above that if a **vassal** <term>vassal (Lehenman): A person who held land under the feudal system in exchange for service and loyalty.</term> were orally invested, he might take possession and occupy the **feudal estate** <note>original: "Lehengut"</note> by virtue of such investiture. But what if the fief were large, extensive, and divided into many pieces? Is it necessary for the vassal to be personally inducted into every single piece, or is it enough if he is inducted into one piece as the principal part of the fief? To this, we answer: Although there are various opinions on this matter, it is generally held that if a fief has many belonging parts but there is one main part among them from which it takes its name and to which all others are connected, then inducting the vassal into that one part is sufficient. However, if there are many pieces and they are located far apart from one another and are not connected, then by receiving and being physically inducted into only one of them, he would not have acquired the others.

Fiefs may also be granted and received in any place, provided that the location is safe and not dishonorable. Since the feudal bond is an honorable, knightly matter which belongs only to noble persons to grant and receive, it would be entirely unsuitable and improper for them to be granted or received in dishonorable places.

Furthermore, fiefs may also be acquired and obtained through **prescription** <term>prescription (Verjährung): The legal process by which a right or title is gained through long-continued possession or use over a fixed period of time.</term>. For if someone has held and possessed a fief for thirty years and a day, and has also performed the **knightly service** <note>original: "Ritterdienst" — the military or administrative duties owed by a vassal to his lord.</note> required of it, he has fully acquired and obtained the fief even if he were never officially invested, and even if he performed that service only once during those thirty years. For it is not necessary to serve every year and at all times, but only when the Lord requires it and the vassal is called upon. Thus, it may well happen that knightly services are often not performed for several years.

Excluded from this rule, however, are **ecclesiastical fiefs** <note>original: "Kirchlehen" — land grants belonging to the church.</note> and those which serve the common good. These cannot be acquired in thirty years; rather, forty years are required for the proper prescription of such fiefs.

And if a dispute should arise regarding the same fief after thirty years, the vassal would not be required to provide proof, unless the Lord had held the fief only **as a pledge** <note>original: "Pfandweise" — held as collateral for a debt rather than as a permanent grant.</note> during that time. In such a case, the vassal would not have acquired it through prescription, even if he had held it for thirty years or more.

In the same manner, a Lord may also make a feudal estate into his own **freehold property** <term>freehold property (frey Gut): Land held in absolute ownership, free of feudal obligations or services to a superior lord.</term> within the same timeframe. Namely, if no vassal has requested or held that same fief for thirty years, it becomes the Lord’s free property.

Imperial Feudal Law.

## Regarding the Second Main Point of the Sixth Chapter.

Concerning the second main point of this sixth chapter—namely, what legal rights the **vassal** <term>vassal (Lehenman): A person who holds land from a lord in exchange for loyalty and service.</term> acquires over the feudal estate through the **investiture** <term>investiture (Inuestitur): The formal legal ceremony of granting a fief.</term> or enfeoffment—it is important to know that through investiture, the vassal gains **subordinate ownership** <note>original: "Unterherrligkeit," referred to in Latin as *utile dominium*</note>. By virtue of this, he may legally claim the fief from any possessor. He can not only claim it but also represent it in court, meaning he can sue and be sued. If a judgment is rendered in these matters that is detrimental to the lord—whether the lord knows of it or not—it still affects the lord, such that he must accept whoever won the case as his new vassal. This is because the representation and protection of the fief belongs to both the vassal and the lord himself.

Similarly, the vassal may bring legal action against the lord regarding the properties if he is challenged concerning the fief, or if he had received a foreign fief from him, provided the lord had promised to guarantee or secure it for him.

Furthermore, the **feudal lord** <term>feudal lord (Lehenherr): The superior who grants the land.</term> is obliged, upon the request and petition of the vassal, to point out and mark the boundaries of the fief. However, it is better if these are expressed piece by piece in the **letters of enfeoffment** <note>official documents recording the grant</note> and specifically detailed, so that nothing is hidden from the vassal or otherwise forgotten during such a demonstration of boundaries.

If a vassal dies and leaves a son, that son is to some extent considered the possessor of the fief even before it is formally handed over and granted to him; however, this is only by legal fiction <note>original: "gedichter weise"</note> and not in truth or reality. Consequently, if a stranger were holding such a fief and the son wished to sue him for it, he would not be permitted to do so, since in such a case he could not have been **dispossessed** <note>original: "spoliert"</note>. For this reason, he could not claim it using an **injunction for recovery** <note>original Latin: *interdicto recuperandæ*, a legal tool to bring a stolen or lost fief back into one's possession</note> unless he has been formally invested. Once he has received the fief, his **possession** <note>legal control of the land</note> is thereby confirmed; it is as if the fief were actually handed over and delivered to him, and he may use all legal necessities to maintain it.

Just as a vassal may both sue and, if sued, answer in court regarding his fief, he can also enter into amicable settlements, giving and taking terms <note>The original cites "Præpo. c.1. quid sit inuest. col. 2.", referencing standard legal commentaries of the time.</note>. However, this must not be done deceitfully, and the lord should be notified of such agreements whenever possible.

Some, however, doubt whether a vassal may **enter into arbitration** <term>arbitration (Compromittiren): Resolving a dispute through a neutral third party rather than a formal court.</term> and bind himself to settle matters concerning the fief before **arbitrators** <term>arbitrators (Scheidsrichtern): Private judges chosen by the parties to resolve a conflict.</term>. But despite such objections, it is ultimately concluded that this may indeed happen, and such arbitration agreements are legally valid and permissible, provided that if the vassal, through a judgment by the arbitra-

Furthermore, if a **fief** <term>fief (Lehen): Land held on condition of feudal service.</term> should grow <note>referring to land accretion or "accession," where the physical size of the property increases through natural means</note>, the question arises: Does such growth belong to the **feudal lord**, or to the **vassal**? To this, it is generally answered: If a dispute should arise between the lord and his vassal because of this, and the vassal says he had received and obtained the land from the lord with all its future growth, and the lord conversely claims that he had reserved such growth for himself, then the vassal would be obliged to prove his right either through the **Peers of the Court** <note>original Latin: "Pares Curiae," meaning other vassals of the same rank who serve as judges</note>, or through the other vassals, or through the **feudal letters** <note>the formal deeds of the grant</note>, which must then be allowed and permitted to him. This is unless the vassal already had the growth in his use and possession. If, however, the lord had not expressly reserved anything for himself regarding the growth of the fief, then it would belong to the vassal and not to the lord.

Should it also happen that the vassal grants the fief to another **sub-vassal** with all its growth, as might well occur, then the growth belongs to the sub-vassal so long as the first vassal is alive; but after his death, the growth falls back to the lord.

And it is to be noted here that there are two kinds of growth: one comes from **flowing waters** <note>original: "Wildwasser," referring here to "alluvion," the gradual deposit of soil by a river</note> when the water brings something to the feudal estate; the other is manifest when an island arises in the water. And although mention is otherwise made here of many kinds of growth, because not much is found regarding them in the text of the law, we deem it unnecessary to set down anything further about them.

### Imperial Feudal Law

...to use the same / so they are obligated to follow the **fief** <term>fief (Lehen): land held on condition of feudal service</term> within a **Year and a Day** <note>original: "Jar vnd Tag," a standard legal deadline in Germanic law</note>, as is legally provided for and also maintained in custom.

Likewise / if there be two / who are to seek and receive the **fief**, and one sells his share to the other before the **enfeoffment** <term>enfeoffment (Belehnung): the formal granting of a fief</term> / as sometimes happens / then the one who has sold his share is nonetheless obligated, along with the other, to follow the fief within the proper time and to perform the **feudal duty** <note>the formal oath of loyalty and service</note>.

However, regarding the timing, it is understood thus: that the period does not begin until the son or kinsman has learned that the fief has become vacant / and that the father or relative has died / from that time they are obligated within a period of a year and a month / or a **Year and a Day** / as cited differently above / to seek the fief / upon pain of losing the same.

Furthermore, there are other significant causes by which a **vassal** <term>vassal (Lehenmann): a person who holds land from a lord in exchange for loyalty</term> may be hindered so that he cannot follow the fief within the proper time / namely if he be captured or imprisoned / likewise if death, war, enmity, or **feuds** <note>formalized private warfare between noble families</note> were at hand. And if one of these causes occurs / then the vassal would be excused / even if he could not follow the fief in the proper time / or had sought it / provided that no fraud was intended therein. As soon as such hindrances cease / the time begins to run again / in which the vassal is obligated to seek the fief.

The vassal shall seek the fief in appropriate places: the **lord** <term>lord (Lehenherr): the grantor of the fief</term> shall also grant the same to him in proper places: accordingly, it is justly considered a reproach to the vassal / if he should wish to seek the fief in inconvenient places / such as during a meal / in the church / in the bath / or at night / unless he could not otherwise encounter the lord / in which case he would be excused.

Also, if the lord should summon the vassal to a suspicious or unsafe place for the receiving of the fief / and the vassal complains / offering / that he would receive it in other convenient and safe places / and yet could not obtain this from the lord / then the vassal would be excused / if he could not follow the fief within the proper period / and at the right time / and seek it.

Furthermore, the specified time does not bind the vassal / but he is excused / if he does not possess the old **ancestral fief** / and could not obtain the same without extensive litigation / provided that no deceit may be attributed to him here.

The vassal is also excused / if he did not know that the property was a fief / but instead held it to be **ancestral property** <term>ancestral property (Erbgut): land owned outright (allodial) rather than held from a lord</term>.

If two feudal lords should also quarrel over a fief / and each one wants / the vassal to receive the fief from him / then the vassal is excused / if he does not receive the fief / until the two lords have reached an agreement: provided that he protests / that the lack or failure is not his / but that once the two lords agree / as to who shall keep it / he will then receive it from that one without refusal.

## On Feudal Duties.

As to what / and how the vassal shall swear to the Lord / it is widely disputed here and there. But in summary / the **Oath** <term>Oath (Jurament or Eyd): a sacred legal promise of loyalty</term> <note>original: "Jurament oder Eyd"</note> shall comprise these following parts. Furthermore / if the Lord has lost something / to apply all possible diligence to recover the same for him / and to reveal his secrets to no one.

Yet it is also to be noted / that although the vassal shall act against the Lord neither with counsel nor deed / by virtue of the cited articles included in the Oath: he nevertheless would not have acted against such duties / if he advised or acted in a way / that serves the best interests of the general **commonwealth** <term>commonwealth (Landschafft): the organized political community or territory</term> / or the Lord and his children / even if it were against the person of the Lord: such as if the Lord were witless / a spendthrift / or otherwise a tyrant. ## ...then the fief reverts to the Lord, and not to the father or grandfather.

### The Second Conclusion.

Since those in the descending line are at hand, such as **sons** and **grandsons**, they shall succeed to the **fief** <term>fief (Lehen): an estate of land held on condition of feudal service</term> and entirely exclude the **agnates** <term>agnates (Agnaten): relatives related exclusively through the male line</term> who stand in the collateral line. In this matter, it is of no consequence whether the sons are under the father's legal authority or outside of it. However, attention must be paid here: if the ancestor or grandfather should die and leave behind one son along with several grandsons from another deceased son, the grandsons would be admitted in the place of their father just as well as the surviving sons. This rule is maintained continuously with grandsons; regardless of the fact that they are one degree further removed than the sons, they nevertheless step into the place of their deceased father and, for his sake, succeed simultaneously to the fiefs.

### The Third Conclusion.

When an "old" or **paternal fief** <note>A fief that has been in the family for generations, rather than one newly granted.</note> falls to the descendants and none of them remain alive, then those who are most closely related to the descendant from the side in the male line follow—namely the nearest agnates or **sword-kin** <term>sword-kin (Schwertmagen): male relatives capable of bearing arms, who were the only ones eligible for most feudal inheritances</term>, as is the custom. This is most easily understood through an example: namely, Titz <note>A standard legal placeholder name, similar to "John Doe," derived from the Latin "Titius."</note>, a member of the nobility, has acquired a fief. Upon his death, it falls to two of his sons. These sons are in the second degree of kinship and are brothers to one another. According to common **Imperial Law** <term>Imperial Law (Kayserrechten): the legal system based on Roman law used in the Holy Roman Empire</term>, the children of these brothers are in the third degree, and the grandsons in the fourth degree. Thus, all agnates from the side follow one after another, according to who is closer in degree than the other—yet with the distinction mentioned in the next conclusion. Some say that in the fiefs of Counts or other great Lords, should the last Lord of that lineage die, the agnates may follow him even after five hundred years, no matter how distant they may be. And if the entire lineage has passed away, but one of the same name and tribe remains—even if he were in the thousandth degree, were that possible—he should be admitted to succeed as an heir.

However, if those two sons of the aforementioned Titz had divided the estate, and one had received the **allod** <term>allod (Erbe): land owned outright, without feudal obligations</term> and the other the fief, it would be a different matter. In that case, only the agnates descending from the son who received the fief in the division would be admitted to succeed to the fief, and the descendants of Titz’s other son would be entirely excluded.

But when no more male heirs are present from that son who received the fief, only then do the sons, grandsons, or agnates of the other brother follow. And in this case, the fief may fall to those in the ascending—

## The Fourth Conclusion.

Since it sometimes happens that a man grows in debt, and because he may not encumber the **fief** <term>fief (Lehen): land or rights granted by a Lord to a vassal in exchange for service, which usually could not be used as collateral for personal loans</term>, he becomes more indebted than he can pay with his **allodial estate** <term>allodial estate (Erbe/Erbgut): private property owned outright, distinct from the fief, which could be seized to pay debts</term>, even though the estate is of great value: from which it follows that sometimes a person accepts the fief and succeeds to it, but must renounce the private inheritance. Now, if the fief is so established that the **vassal** <term>vassal (Lehenmañ): a person granted the use of land in return for homage and fealty</term> received it for himself and his heirs, and the Lord had granted it to him in such a manner—namely, to him and his heirs—then the descendants, such as sons and grandsons, cannot renounce the inheritance and keep the fief; rather, they must either keep both or let both go and renounce them. And this rule applies not only to new but also to old fiefs, without any distinction.

Likewise, if the vassal were **enfeoffed** <note>original: "belehnt"; the formal legal act of granting a fief.</note> with simple words, and it were not expressly stated that he was enfeoffed for himself and the male heirs of his body by the Lord, it would also be understood that he was enfeoffed solely for himself and his heirs.

However, by "heirs," no one other than male heirs—such as sons or **agnates** <term>agnates (Agnaten): relatives related through the male line</term>—and not outside heirs, must be understood.

And this conclusion cannot apply if the enfeoffment was made with these words: "To give and lend to him and his children or sons," etc. For in such a case, the sons could renounce the inheritance, if it were not advantageous to them, and still keep the fief, because they are there as sons and not as heirs.

Now if someone were to say, since by "heirs" only sons and male heirs are to be understood, there might be no difference between the cases mentioned, but it is the same whether the name "heirs" is expressed in the enfeoffment or not. To this it must be answered that fundamentally there is a great difference between these words "Heirs" and "Sons." For where "heirs" are mentioned, or the word "heirs" is set and expressed in the enfeoffment, it follows that the sons may succeed not only as sons but also as heirs: and those who make and receive the enfeoffment in such a way are considered to not want—nor is it their intention—that the sons should be capable of holding the fief unless they were also heirs. But in the other case, if mention is made only of the sons, they may succeed to the fief even if they are not heirs or do not wish to be: and thus the sons are served, so that they may not be forced to accept the inheritance along with the fief, if such would prove burdensome or impossible for them; as it often happens that an allodial estate is so burdened with debts (as mentioned above) that it is more convenient and better for the heirs to renounce it than to accept it.

# A brief extract / of the

Although it is now common in all **letters of investiture** <term>letter of investiture (Lehenbrief): the formal document by which a Lord grants a fief to a vassal</term> to see these words: "We grant and bestow," and "grant to him and his male fief-heirs," etc.

And this distinction also has its place in **sub-fiefs** <term>sub-fief (Afterlehen): a fief granted by a vassal to their own subordinates, rather than directly from the Prince or high Lord</term> which lords are accustomed to grant to their subjects. For it is a very different thing if a father holds the fief for himself and his heirs, rather than for himself and his children. In the first case, the sons may not renounce the inheritance and still keep the fief-property, as they might in the second case.

However, regarding this point—where it is said that one cannot divest oneself of one and not the other—it should be noted that this rule does not hold in several cases, but rather fails.

Firstly, if the sons had already accepted the inheritance, they could certainly divest themselves of the fief, since the Law has been satisfied and provision has been made for the creditors.

Secondly, it also fails if the sons were not appointed to the entire inheritance, but only to a named or appropriate portion of the father’s estate, while other heirs were appointed to the whole inheritance. In that case, the son might keep the fief and renounce the inheritance, for he would not be obligated to carry the burden of the inheritance in this instance.

Thirdly, if a son were passed over in silence in the father’s will <note>This refers to the Roman law concept of 'praeteritio,' where an heir is neither disinherited nor instituted, which could potentially invalidate a will.</note> and did not wish to contest his father’s last will, he could not be forced to do so, and yet he could still keep the fief.

Here a question arises: If a father specifically disinherits his son, can he still keep the fief? To this, it is answered: No. Unless the father’s will were declared invalid; for if he were disinherited for lawful reasons which would make him **infamous** <note>In a legal sense, "infamous" (anrichtig) meant losing one's legal standing or honor, which was a requirement for holding a fief.</note>, he would be rightfully excluded not only from the paternal inheritance but also from the fief. For a son can be excluded from the fief for the same reasons a father may disinherit him—specifically, if the reasons are of such a nature that they make the son (as mentioned) infamous, so that he would not be good enough for the Lord as a vassal, but rather would be unfit. Yet the son may keep the old paternal fief, even if he is disinherited by the father, if, for example, the father dies but the grandfather is still living <note>The fief would bypass the "unworthy" father and pass from the grandfather directly to the grandson.</note>.

Fourthly, the son may also divest himself of the inheritance and accept the fief if, during the father’s lifetime, he had renounced the inheritance by means of a **physical oath** <note>original: "leiblichen [Eid]"; a solemn oath made with a hand on a sacred object or the body.</note>, as such a renunciation can in no way extend to the fief. And this could also apply to a daughter, if **female fiefs** <term>female fief (Weibliche Lehen): a rare type of fief that could be inherited by women, common in certain regions like Saxony</term> were at hand and the inheritance was too heavily burdened with debt.

Fifthly, if the son had made an **inventory** <term>inventory (Inuentarium): a legal list of assets and debts that protects the heir from being personally liable for more than the estate's value</term> when he accepted the inheritance. For even if nothing remained of the inheritance because the multitude of creditors took it away, he would still keep the fief by virtue of the inventory.

Sixthly, it also fails in the case of ancestral fiefs, which the grandson...

Seventh, if no paternal inheritance <note>This refers to personal property, debts, and assets outside of the feudal grant.</note> were available, the son might keep the **fief** <term>fief (Lehen): land or rights granted by a Lord to a vassal in exchange for service and loyalty</term> so that he would not have to suffer want and necessity. Similarly, one could also say that the son could divest himself of the inheritance and keep the fief if he were reinvested with the paternal fief anew with the consent of the agnates. However, if it should happen outside of these cases now recounted at length that the son wished to divest himself of the paternal inheritance and keep the fief, such would not be permitted to him; instead, the fief would fall to the **sword-kin** <term>sword-kin (Schwertmagen): male relatives entitled to inherit a fief</term> or agnates, who may then claim it.

### The Fifth Conclusion.

On the other hand, the agnates or sword-kin, such as cousins, etc., may leave the inheritance—if they are burdened with it—and divest themselves of it, while nevertheless keeping the fief. This is not permitted or allowed to the sons, as just heard. The reason cited for this distinction is that the agnate does not receive the fief by virtue of his own person or the merit of the deceased **vassal** <term>vassal (Lehenmann): the holder of a fief who owes allegiance to a Lord</term>, but rather through the gracious and mild grant of the Liege Lord.

### The Sixth Conclusion.

When the vassal dies and leaves behind old or paternal fiefs, and also has brothers on one side and nephews <note>original: "Brüderkinder" (brothers' children)</note> on the other, those same nephews inherit together with the brothers **by the root or branch** <term>by the root (in die Wurzel): also known as "per stirpes," where descendants share the portion their deceased parent would have received</term> and not **by the head** <term>by the head (in die Häupter): also known as "per capita," where each individual receives an equal share</term>. That is, the nephews—no matter how many of them there are—take or inherit no more than their father might have inherited had he lived to see the occasion.

However, if the vassal were to die leaving no brother but only nephews, how they should follow was once a matter of great quarrel and discord among the legal scholars. **Azo** <note>Portius Azo (died c. 1230), an influential medieval Italian jurist.</note> in his *Summa* held that nephews should follow their deceased cousin "by the head." **Accursius** <note>A celebrated Roman law glossator (died c. 1263).</note> was of this opinion as well, along with several others. But **Bartolus** <note>Bartolus de Saxoferrato (1313–1357), one of the most famous medieval jurists.</note> and many others—indeed, nearly the majority and the most prominent, namely Baldus, Cynus, Paulus de Castro, Angelus, and Raphael—held the opposite view. Such discord lasted until our time, when the opinion of Bartolus and his followers was rejected. Firstly, by a clear text in the **Authentica regarding heirs coming from an intestate person** <note>original: "Auten. de hæredib. ab intestato venientibus." This refers to the *Novels* of Justinian regarding those who die without a will.</note> in the paragraphs "but also to them" <note>original: "sed & ipsis"</note> and "if however with brothers" <note>original: "si autem cum fratribus"</note> in the same title. Subsequently, the opinion of Bartolus was also rejected by a special constitution by **Emperor Charles V**.

However, this conclusion does not hold: First, if the brothers, with the Lord's knowledge and consent, had made a special agreement <note>original: "pact"</note> regarding the [succession] <unclear>...</unclear>; namely, that one should succeed the other in such a case; then the Lord would be excluded and would have to reinvest the brother with such a fief, regardless of it being "new."

Nonetheless, the surviving brother must be repaid and delivered his due amount of money. The same holds true if one brother had bought a fief [on behalf of] himself and his brother.

Thirdly, if the brothers had acquired and obtained a fief in war, whether they had been in the war with the Emperor as the Lord of the Fief, or with another Lord, they could succeed one another.

Fourthly, if a **fief** <term>fief (Lehen): land or rights granted by a Lord to a vassal in exchange for service</term> had been granted to two brothers as a proper and noble fief, to each specifically in full, then in such a case one would succeed the other, thereby excluding the Lord.

Fifthly, where the fief, which is newly granted to two brothers, is of such a nature that it cannot be divided—such as **hunts, fisheries, jurisdictions, and services**—if a brother dies without male heirs of his body, his portion of such feudal rights falls to the [surviving] brother, provided that he compensates the Lord for the value of such rights. The brother then holds such a portion, for which he has compensated the Lord, not as a fief, but as his own and purchased property, unless it is otherwise agreed upon and negotiated.

However, there are two cases in which the Lord is not obliged to accept the value, but has a closer right to it than the brother. The first is if the Lord had given the fief to the two brothers solely for the sake of the deceased, because he was a skilled and valiant man and had served him well; whereas the one still living were a **fantasist** <note>original: "Fantast"; implying someone unreliable, eccentric, or a dreamer</note> or otherwise a worthless person, then the fief would fall back to the Lord, though he would have to pay the [surviving brother] half the value. The other case is when the portion of the fief that has become vacant is better [more valuable]; in that case, it is also at the Lord’s discretion whether he wishes to redeem the lesser portion for himself as well. For the greater part takes the lesser with it. <note>original Latin: "l. sancimus. Par. ne autem, C. de dona."; referring to the Code of Justinian, Book 8, Title 54, Law 34, which discusses the rules of donations and indivisible property.</note>

Sixthly, the eighth conclusion does not apply to **sub-fiefs** <term>sub-fief (affterlehen): a fief granted by a vassal to a third party</term>. For in such fiefs, when a brother dies, his portion falls to the other.

## The Ninth Conclusion.

In new fiefs in which one brother succeeds another, whether through a pact or in other ways as previously stated, such following or **succession** <term>succession (Succession): the legal act of inheriting a title or property</term> lasts among the descendants forever and without end. But in those successions that occur collaterally and come from the other brother, the succession does not extend further than the **seventh degree** <note>The "seventh degree" is a traditional legal limit for calculating kinship; beyond this, relatives were often considered too distant to inherit under certain feudal customs.</note>, including that same degree. Although this conclusion is not considered entirely settled and is difficult to maintain among us **Germans**, it is nevertheless not established entirely in vain or without cause. For if a fief that someone has newly acquired becomes a paternal fief among the descendants, then one rightly succeeds therein forever. However, if it comes to a lineage or a brother through a pact or agreement, then the succession may well be moderated and cut off after the seventh degree.

Finally, it is also to be known that if the **vassal** <term>vassal (Lehenmann): the person holding the fief</term> had sons and received a fief from the Lord for himself and his brother’s sons, then the brother’s sons immediately acquire a half-share of the fief. Unless he had requested that the Lord should enfeoff him first, and after his death, his brother’s sons. In this case, his own sons would be closer [in line] than the brother’s sons.

### A brief excerpt of the
## The Second Part of the Eighth Chapter / How
## women succeed and follow in fiefs.

AS far as it concerns how and in what manner women may succeed and follow in **fiefs** <term>fief (Lehen): a landed estate held on condition of feudal service</term>, the following conclusions are to be understood.

### The first conclusion.

FIRSTLY, that according to the nature of **Feudal Law** <term>Feudal Law (Lehenrecht): the legal system governing the relationship between lords and vassals</term>, women may not follow in feudal estates, even if the **vassal** <term>vassal (Lehenmann): a person granted the use of land in return for homage and service</term> had received the estates for himself and his heirs in fief: for even in that case, only male heirs are intended and understood. According to the opinion of legal scholars, the reason is this: That women are neither fit nor capable for **knightly services** <term>knightly services (Ritterdiensten): the military and courtly obligations a vassal owes to a lord</term> and wars, for the sake of which such estates are most often granted. And it serves little here what some point out—how the **Amazons** <note>The author refers to the legendary tribe of female warriors from Greek mythology to dismiss historical precedents for women in combat.</note> and other women, according to history, once waged war and performed many knightly deeds. For they would otherwise have to be capable of more things: such as keeping the Lord’s secrets and being advisory to him in his obligations, as well as doing other things required by feudal duty, of which more was said at length above in the seventh chapter. However, how well women keep silence, and what advice they can give even in important matters, is for everyone to consider for themselves; the old proverbs and daily experience also give enough evidence of this. <note>The author reflects the common sexist prejudices of the era, suggesting that women are naturally unsuited for the confidentiality and political strategy required of a vassal.</note>

This conclusion—that women cannot follow in fiefs—also holds true in the case of **purchased fiefs**. For even if someone buys a fief, it does not thereby change its nature, but remains a fief one way or the other, and excludes women.

Some may wish to say that if the fief were purchased, then women might follow by virtue of the contract or purchase, and not by virtue of the fief. But their opinion is false and incorrect. It would only be so if someone were to buy a **county** or another knightly estate with an attached **pact** <term>pact (Pact): a formal legal agreement or treaty</term> and condition that he should give a **rent** <term>rent (Zinß): a regular payment in money or goods, rather than military service</term> for it annually, and did not have to perform knightly service for it. In such a case, a woman might well follow: although such estates are to be counted more among the **rent-paying estates** <term>rent-paying estates (Zinßgüter): land held in exchange for money rather than feudal service</term> than among the feudal estates.

However, the aforementioned conclusion—that women may not follow in feudal estates—may not hold in certain cases. Firstly, if an express provision had been made for the women through a pact of the enfeoffment, stating that they should not be excluded but might follow.

Secondly, if the estate were a **Maternal Fief** <term>Maternal Fief (Mütterlich Lehen): a fief specifically granted to a woman and her heirs</term>. That is, that it was granted to the mother for herself and her heirs. In that case, if she had nothing but daughters, they might succeed and follow the mother in such a fief without an intermediary or any specific pact.

Thirdly, if the vassal should leave a daughter behind, and the
