[The Lord] enfeoffed the same—perhaps because they bought the **fief** <term>fief (Lehen): a landed estate held on condition of feudal service</term>, or he granted them such enfeoffment for the sake of their father's loyal service—then the **agnates** <term>agnates (Agnaten): male relatives who share a common male ancestor</term> would have no right to contest such a fief. The daughter would also not be obliged to return it or step away from it. However, the fief must be situated such that it has either reverted to the Lord, or the Lord otherwise has the power and authority, by law or custom, to bestow it as a grace upon someone.

Fourthly, if there were a local custom that women may also follow in fiefs alongside male heirs—as in the Kingdom of Sicily, and among us Germans in Swabia, where women follow in many fiefs, especially those which are **church fiefs** <term>church fiefs (Kirchenlehen): estates held from the church rather than a secular lord</term> and those that do not involve nobility—then women could not be excluded, since **feudal law** <term>feudal law (Lehenrecht): the legal system governing the relationship between lords and vassals</term> must and shall be regulated according to custom, and arises from custom.

Here a question arises: Whether a woman may also follow in **Frankish fiefs** <term>Frankish fiefs (Franckenlehen): "free" fiefs where the holder owes loyalty but no military service</term>. And they are called Frankish fiefs, or free fiefs, for which the **vassal** <term>vassal (Vasall): a person granted the use of land in return for homage and service</term> need not serve, except that he is obliged to be loyal and faithful to the Lord. From this, I believe the proverb originates: "The free Franks" <note>original: "Die freyen Francken"</note>. To this, the answer is briefly: No. For although such fiefs are not "earned" through service—and thus women could well receive and hold them despite the lack of **knightly service** <term>knightly service (Ritterdienst): military obligations owed to a lord</term>—they are nonetheless hindered by the other reasons mentioned above.

### The Second Conclusion.

Even if it should happen that a fief is granted by the Lord to a vassal for himself and his descending male and female heirs, the female heirs shall nonetheless not be admitted alongside the males as long as male heirs are present. Only when the males are no longer living do they follow at last: and it does not help even if it stands in the **feudal deed** <note>original: "Lehenbrieff"</note>, "To him and his male and female heirs." For even if such fiefs fall vacant, the women do not follow sooner, unless no male heir is left.

It would be different if the son died shortly after the father; in that case, the daughter would also be admitted to the fief: and it would be the same as if no son had existed at all, or if it were a **conditioned fief** <term>conditioned fief (conditioniert Lehen): a fief granted for a specific purpose or under specific terms</term> which was dedicated or obligated to a certain service. For if such a fief is granted to someone and his male and female heirs, then the female heirs follow alongside the males, regardless of the fact that it is against the nature and character of fiefs: for it has been regulated and tempered by the **contract** <note>original: "pact"</note> that was attached to it. However, if the female heirs were not mentioned in the enfeoffment, they could not follow, even if it were a conditioned fief.

Thirdly, female heirs also follow if a fief were granted to the vassal in such a manner: namely, "We enfeoff him along with his heirs, the females together with the males," or "the females as the males." For since such words are bright and clear, there is no doubt to be had; the women will be admitted from it as justly as the male heirs.

# A Brief Excerpt

Fourthly, if two brothers were simultaneously **enfeoffed** <term>enfeoffed (belehnet): formally granted possession of a landed estate (fief) in exchange for service and loyalty</term> with the following words: "We enfeoff you and your male and female heirs," and one brother should die leaving no son but rather a daughter, that same daughter excludes her father’s brother and his sons by virtue of such an enfeoffment. This is because, in such a grant, it is held that each brother has made provision for his own descendants.

And it does not contradict what is set down below—namely, that my daughter’s child excludes the **aunts** <note>original: "Muhmen"; here used specifically for the father's sisters</note>, that is, the father’s sisters. For in this case, the two were not enfeoffed together; rather, the enfeoffment passes from one person to the other.

->### The Third Conclusion.<-

If a man is enfeoffed by the Lord with a **fief** <term>fief (Lehengut): an estate held under feudal tenure</term> in the following manner—namely, that the Lord says: "We enfeoff him and his male heirs," with the addition that "should male heirs no longer be present, then the female heirs shall follow and succeed"—then the female heirs cannot succeed as long as a male heir (whether from the male or female line) is present who belongs to the first-enfeoffed man. For in this case, primary and sole regard must be given to the origin and source of the enfeoffment, as **Alvarotto** <note>Jacobus Alvarotto (1385–1453), a renowned Italian legal scholar who wrote extensively on feudal law</note> indicates. Therefore, they cannot succeed simultaneously, but only one after the other. Thus, if a **vassal** <term>vassal (Lehenmann): a person who holds land from a lord and owes him loyalty</term> who is enfeoffed in this way dies, the son takes precedence and excludes the daughter.

In the same manner, if the vassal should die leaving two daughters, one of whom had a son and the other a daughter, the aunt would be excluded by the son. This also holds true if the vassal left two sons, one of whom left a son after his death and the other a daughter; in such a case, the son is also preferred and excludes the daughter.

Furthermore, this rule applies if the vassal dies in the case recounted above and leaves only a daughter, and that same daughter then has two sons, named **Titius and Seius** <note>traditional placeholder names used in legal examples, similar to "John Doe" and "Richard Roe"</note>. Titius dies and leaves behind two daughters; Seius then dies as well and leaves a son. In this case, the son is again preferred and the daughters are excluded. And although this may seem strange, and might even be considered disputable and doubtful, it nonetheless remains the rule that Seius's son shall be preferred. This is based on the principle that no fief may or should come to female heirs as long as a single male heir exists from the vassal who first acquired the fief as the "stem" of the lineage—regardless of whether he was related to the vassal only through a side branch.

The same principle also holds if the aforementioned daughter had a son and a daughter, and that daughter later had a son (and thus a grandson was born), and the first son died; the grandson's aunt—that is, the father's sister—would be excluded, just as she would have been excluded by her brother had he been present.

# Imperial Feudal Law.

If a man were to acquire a **fief** <term>fief (Lehen): an estate of land held on condition of feudal service</term> with the provision that both male and female heirs should and might succeed to it, and he then died leaving no male heirs but only two daughters, namely Julia and Portia, they would follow him and succeed by virtue of that **enfeoffment** <term>enfeoffment (Belehnung): the formal process of granting someone legal possession of a fief</term>. However, if one sister, Julia, were to die leaving a son, the question arises: may this same son oust his mother's sister, Portia, from the fief in which she has already been established and enfeoffed? To this it must be answered: although some have held that the son can exclude his mother's sister, that opinion is incorrect, regardless of their claim that Portia only succeeded on the condition that no male heir was present. For whatever someone—be it man or woman—has once obtained in a legal and proper manner, they should rightly be allowed to keep. And the rule of feudal law which prefers male heirs over female heirs cannot prevent this. For that rule is understood to apply only to those cases where the inheritance is *yet* to be obtained, and not to those where it has already been obtained and settled.

This rule (which states that women or female heirs are excluded by male heirs) also applies to the receiving of fiefs, in the sense that one should not receive a fief from women as long as male heirs are present. Women should also neither grant nor lease them, as can be clearly understood through the following example. Sempronius receives a fief from his lord and further enfeoffs another with it, named Titius <note>original: "Titzen"; Titius is a standard placeholder name used in legal texts, similar to "John Doe"</note> (for some fiefs have the characteristic that they may be further granted). Afterwards, Sempronius dies and leaves behind two sons, who also die: one leaves a daughter, the other a son. The question is: From whom shall Titius receive his fief? From the surviving daughter or from the son? To this it is conclusively answered that he must receive it from the deceased brother’s son and not from the daughter, as he must receive it from the male and not from the female heir. From this it follows: although a woman can grant both old and new fiefs, she cannot do so in this case where one **vassal** <term>vassal (Vasall/Lehenmann): a person who holds land from a superior lord</term> enfeoffs another and leaves behind grandchildren of both male and female gender. For the vassal cannot receive the fief from the surviving granddaughter.

However, if a man had converted his **ancestral estates** <note>original: "Erbgüter"; these are properties owned outright (allodial land) as opposed to held as a fief</note> into a fief and granted them to another, and then died leaving behind sons and daughters, the vassal would be obliged to receive such a fief not only from the sons but also from the daughters within the proper time. Otherwise, he forfeits his right to the fief; in this case, it would not be sufficient for him to receive the said fief only from the son.

Once a woman is excluded from the fief, she must then remain excluded from it forevermore. Accordingly, if a vassal

# A short summary:
When a man dies and leaves both a son and a daughter, the **fief** <term>fief (Lehen): an estate of land held on condition of feudal service</term> falls to the son and not to the daughter. Even if the son should later die without male heirs, the fief does not pass to the sister; instead, it returns to the Lord as a vacant possession. Just as the daughter is excluded, her entire lineage—both male and female—born of her is likewise excluded. Such a conclusion may also hold weight in **statutes** <term>statute (Statut): local or municipal laws that often governed inheritance alongside broader imperial law</term> in which daughters are sometimes excluded from their parents' inheritance. When this occurs, even if no brother is present, the daughters may not succeed to the estate because the statute has deprived them of it; instead, the abandoned inheritance falls to the nearest **agnates** <term>agnates (Agnaten): male relatives related through the male line</term>. She might, however, succeed her brothers and inherit from them directly. But if a statute provided that female heirs could not succeed as long as male heirs were present, and the male heirs died out, then the inheritance would fall to the women by virtue of that statute.

## The third part of the eighth chapter: Whether one may grant or ordain anything in or from fiefs by way of a Last Will and Testament.

As far as succession by **testament** <term>testament: a person's will</term> regarding fiefs is concerned, this rule is briefly to be noted: a **vassal** <term>vassal (Lehenmann): a person granted the use of land in return for homage and fealty</term> has no power to make any decree concerning fiefs. Specifically, if a father wished to ordain how one son should succeed before another, or that one son should have three parts, another two, and the third only one part of the fief, and such things. For the text of the Feudal Law clearly forbids this when it says: *Everything that is ordained through a testament regarding fiefs shall remain null and void.* This is also the conclusion of **Alvarotto** <note>original: "Aluarot"; refers to Jacobus Alvarotto (1385–1453), a leading legal commentator on feudal law from Padua</note>, who states that the vassal has no power to dispose of anything in fiefs through a testament.

Accordingly, if the vassal had decreed something in such a case contrary to Feudal Law, the descendants—such as the sons and agnates—may contest and overturn it. If he had neither sons nor agnates, but had appointed strangers as heirs to the fiefs, the testament would be void in itself, and the fief would return to the Lord.

Regarding the fact that a father may not grant more to one son than to another in fiefs, this reason is cited: that the vassal has no right to alter or overturn that which has been established by legal decree and by long-standing custom, and which he received through the lord's **enfeoffment** <term>enfeoffment (belehnung): the formal act of investing a person with a fief</term>. Likewise, because the Lord has as much interest in such a fief as the vassal does. Thus, the vassal cannot change anything in it for himself unless it happens with the Lord’s consent.

However, one must maintain this distinction: namely, whether these are the kind of fiefs given to the vassal and his heirs, and are thus **hereditary fiefs** <term>hereditary fiefs (Erblehen): fiefs intended to pass down a specific line of descent</term>.

# Imperial Feudal Law

For example, if the Lord says, "We **enfeoff** <term>enfeoff (beleihen): to grant land or a title in exchange for service</term> Titzen <note>a placeholder name, similar to "John Doe"</note> and his heirs," in such a place, the term "heirs" is understood to mean only the sons. If the grant were made in this manner, the sons would not be able to challenge the father’s decree or his **Last Will** <term>Last Will (letzten willen): a legal declaration of a person's wishes regarding their property after death</term>. 

However, if the grant is made to Titzen and his sons or children—rather than just "heirs"—and these children have taken possession of the father’s goods without making an **inventory** <term>inventory (Inuentarium): a detailed list of inherited property used to protect heirs from the deceased's debts</term>, they also cannot contest the father's testament. But if they had prepared an inventory, the father’s testament could not bind them, unless it was a **new fief** <term>new fief (new Lehen): land recently granted to a family for the first time, rather than ancient family land</term>. In such a case, some argue that the sons cannot challenge or refute the father's testament and decree.

Even if the grant were made to Titzen and all his heirs of every kind, such a grant could not extend further than the persons who are otherwise permitted by feudal law. Therefore, no vassal can, by virtue of such wording, include other "foreign" heirs <note>meaning relatives or outsiders not usually eligible to inherit the land</note> in a testament.

The only exception would be if the **Overlord** <term>Overlord (Lehenherr): the high-ranking noble who granted the land</term> consented to it. I have seen such a **deed of enfeoffment** <term>deed of enfeoffment (Lehenbrieff): the legal document proving ownership of a fief</term> which Duke George of Saxony gave to the von Minckwitz family regarding Sonnewald; in it, he permitted that they might bequeath up to two thousand **guilders** <note>a gold coin used for high-value transactions</note> from the estate by way of testament. Or, it could be allowed if a different custom has been established. For there is no law so strictly ordained that it cannot be changed through a pact, mutual consent, or long-standing custom.

## The Fourth Part of the Eighth Chapter.

Fourth and finally, we must deal here with **succession** <term>succession (Succeſſion): the process of inheriting a title or property</term> in general. First, it is important to know that while in all fiefs it is not strictly necessary for the vassal to be physically **invested** <term>invested (inveſtirt): the formal ceremony of putting someone in possession of land</term> or inducted, it is enough if he is enfeoffed by word of mouth, the deeds are renewed, and the **oath of fealty** <term>duty (Pflicht): the solemn promise of loyalty made to a lord</term> is sworn. 

However, for heirs to fiefs that carry a specific **rank or dignity** <term>rank or dignity (Stand oder Wirdigkeit): high-status positions like being a Prince or Count</term> and are held directly from the Emperor, they cannot succeed according to feudal law unless they have first been formally enfeoffed. This applies to **Principalities** <term>Principality (Fürſtenthumb): the territory of a Prince</term>, **Margraviates** <term>Margraviate (Marggraffſchafft): the territory of a Margrave, a high-ranking nobleman</term>, and Earldoms or Lordships. This is because these positions depend more on selection than on simple succession. Although, in our current times, it is held differently; namely, that in such fiefs, one follows succession almost entirely as one does with other feudal estates.

Yet, one point is necessary to note here: according to the nature and character of fiefs, "choice" may still play a role in such great estates. Although it is generally held and practiced that the eldest son is appointed to the **government** <term>government (Regiment): the rule or administration of a territory</term>, a Lord or father nevertheless has the power to appoint that son to rule who, by reason of his skill, understanding, and wisdom, is better suited to serve the common good and the subjects.

# A Short Excerpt

...could be preferred over the eldest. For although custom holds that the **eldest** should take precedence in governance, it must and should rightly [pass to the younger]—as also mentioned previously—provided that the younger is more fit for it. However, in my opinion, the consent of the **Overlord** <term>Overlord (Oberlehenherren): the high-ranking noble who originally granted the land and holds ultimate authority over it</term> is necessary for this.

Some are of the opinion that it would be unfair to set the eldest aside and appoint a younger man to governance in his place. They say that if the eldest were unfit, he should not be cast out for that reason, but rather be given a **Guardian** <term>Guardian (Curatorem): a legally appointed administrator for someone unable to manage their own affairs</term>, **Caretaker** <term>Caretaker (Pfleger): a person appointed to look after the person or property of another</term>, or **Steward** <term>Steward (Hoffmeister): a high-ranking official or manager of a noble household or estate</term>. Such an opinion shall not be upheld unless the other brother were fit and capable, or if the eldest had already held and received the governance for a long time.

Several jurists, such as **Baldus** <note>original: "Baldus" — referring to Baldus de Ubaldis (1327–1400), an Italian expert in civil and feudal law whose writings were foundational in Europe</note>, make this distinction: if the eldest son were permanently unfit, then the one next in line should be promoted and chosen for governance. However, if he had an incidental or temporary incapacity which might soon pass, then a **Guardian** should be assigned to him. But the [previously mentioned] arrangement is more practical.

However, it sometimes happens that a **vassal** <term>vassal (Lehenmann): a person who holds land from a lord in exchange for loyalty and service</term> has a son who is either mute, deaf, blind, or lame, and is therefore unfit to represent or earn the **knightly estates** <term>knightly estates (Rittergütern): lands held specifically on the condition of noble or military service</term>. Therefore, it is necessary to discuss here whether and how such individuals may succeed to the **fief** <term>fief (Lehen): the land or rights granted by a lord to a vassal</term> and perform service. And because this is a complex question upon which various arguments and answers have been offered and held, one can best navigate it with this distinction: namely, one must pay attention to whether they are **Ancestral Fiefs** <term>Ancestral Fiefs (Väterlich Lehen): land that has been in the family for generations</term> or **New Fiefs** in which the mute, blind, deaf, or lame person is to succeed.

For in **Ancestral Fiefs**, where the disability is not natural <note>meaning from birth</note> but accidental <note>resulting from injury or illness later in life</note>, the one who is mute or deaf may indeed succeed. The reason for this is that if the disability is not natural nor innate, but accidental, then there is hope that with time it might pass away and the sick man might become healthy again to earn the fief—which is not to be hoped for if he were born deaf, mute, blind, or lame.

But in **New Fiefs**, the mute, deaf, blind, or lame person is not fit to be admitted. An **Overlord** would have to be quite reckless to grant a **knightly estate** to one who could not earn it and was by nature unfit to do so.

Indeed, even if such persons who are endowed with **New Fiefs** later become frail and unfit due to an accidental illness, they cannot keep the new fief because the reason for which they were enfeoffed has ceased—namely, that they can no longer earn it through service. Although such persons, who cannot succeed in a fief due to frailty but are excluded from it, should be provided with **maintenance** <note>meaning financial support or alimony</note> so that they do not suffer want, especially if the fiefs are substantial and those excluded are in need. Enough has been said of this for now; another question follows.

Furthermore, it is asked: when a woman is enfeoffed with a **Feminine Fief** <term>Feminine Fief (Fräwlichen Lehen): a rare type of land grant that specifically allowed for female inheritance and succession</term> and her status changes <note>meaning she gets married</note>, whether she should give such a fief to her husband as a **contribution**...

...could be transferred as a gift? This question was once quite debatable, but it has now become customary and upheld that a woman has the power to do so. However, the husband may not succeed his wife in such a fief after her death, regardless of the fact that a husband otherwise inherits from his wife under common law <term>Common Law (gemeinen Rechten): the general legal principles derived from Roman law used across the Holy Roman Empire</term> when no other heir is present.

Whether a father may give a fief to his daughter as part of her **morning gift** <term>Morning Gift (Morgengabe): a gift given by a husband to his bride on the morning after the wedding, intended for her financial security</term> shall be discussed later.

It is important to know here that it sometimes happens that sons are excluded from the **succession** <term>Succession (Succession): the legal right to inherit a title, office, or property</term> and inheritance of the fief through a **pact** <term>Pact (Pact): a formal legal agreement or contract between parties</term> made by the parents. For example, if a man first had a wife of the nobility and fathered several sons with her, and then later took a wife who was not of the nobility, with the pact and condition that if they were to father sons together, those sons should not succeed to the fief.

In the same way, a woman may make provision so that the children born of one marriage may succeed, while those from another marriage are excluded.

However, it should be known that such pacts are unfair and unequal; therefore, they should not be extended or upheld further than in those places where they have been accepted and established by tradition. Indeed, in those places where they are still upheld, they should rightfully be abolished.

Item, it might be asked here whether and in what manner **natural children**—those fathered outside of marriage with a **concubine** or mistress—can succeed to a fief. To this, the short answer is that they should not be admitted at all, neither to old paternal nor maternal fiefs. This remains true even if natural children otherwise inherit **allodial property** <note>original: "Erbgüttern" — property held in absolute ownership, unlike a fief which is held from a lord</note> from the mother. The only exception is if they have been **legitimized** <note>original: "geehelicht" — literally "made legitimate" or "brought into marriage" by legal decree</note> by the Emperor, which may well happen. However, the charter granted to them for this purpose must mention the fiefs specifically and in express words—namely, that they are legitimized in such a way that they may also succeed to fiefs. Without this specific mention, a person could not attain the succession of the fief through a simple and common legitimation, even if performed by the Emperor, because a general act of legitimacy does not extend that far.

If, however, there were otherwise right, natural, and legitimate sons or **agnates** <term>Agnates (Agnaten): male-line relatives who share a common male ancestor</term> present who belonged to such fiefs, it would be unfair for the Emperor or Prince to legitimize someone to their disadvantage and prejudice. For no one should be deprived of their rightful due—unless a special cause arose where the common good was significantly at stake.

And just as the Emperor cannot legitimize someone so that they become capable of holding **clerical fiefs**, neither can the **Pope** legitimize anyone to make them fit to receive **secular fiefs**, so that the **scepters** <note>A reference to the "Two Swords" doctrine: the separation of worldly (Imperial) and spiritual (Papal) authority</note> are not mixed together.

But this is beyond all doubt: if a man fathers natural sons with a mistress and later takes that same mistress as his wife, those sons are thereby legitimized in such a way that they also [succeed] in fiefs...

And do not be mistaken / even if another marriage occurred in between / as when I father a natural son with Julia / my companion <note>original: "Beyschläfferin"; at this time, a woman living with a man without a formal marriage, often translated as concubine or mistress</note> / thereafter take Portia as my wife / and father a legitimate son with her: Portia dies / and only then do I finally take Julia, my companion, as my wife / the son I previously fathered with her would thereby become legitimate / and could likewise succeed to and follow in the fief along with the son born to Portia / without any distinction or hindrance. It might also be asked / if a vassal <term>Vassal (Lehenmann): a person who holds land from a lord in exchange for loyalty and service</term> became a cleric / and entered a monastery / whether the monastery might succeed to the fief on his behalf? This question may have once been necessary: but now (God be praised) since it is known what monastic life truly is / I do not believe that anyone of the nobility would wish to leave their knightly estate / in which they are ordained by God / to enter a monastery.

If it were also asked / if someone had obtained a fief through prescription <note>original: "verjarung"; the legal acquisition of property or rights through long-term, uninterrupted possession</note> / even if he had not been formally granted it / whether the descendants might succeed to it? To this it must be answered / that they may do so.

Finally, it is asked / when two brothers are to succeed together in a fief / one being from both sides / that is / from father and mother / the other from the father alone (the Saxon <note>referring to the *Sachsenspiegel*, the most influential legal code of the German Middle Ages</note> calls them brothers of full and half birth) / whether the one from the father alone may be excluded by the other? And to this it must be answered / No / rather they succeed at the same time / regardless that the one has a twofold relationship / which is not considered in fiefs / but rather it is enough that he has the relationship of the father. Thus Franciscus Curtius maintains in the 6th question regarding the succession of collaterals <note>original Latin: "in transuersalium successione"</note>. He cites Baldus and Alvarotto <note>famous legal commentators of the Middle Ages</note> in the 1st chapter on the degrees of succession <note>original Latin: "de gradib. success."</note>, and Alexander’s 9th counsel in the fifth volume, which is worthy of note.

Imperial Feudal Law. 398

# On the alteration and sale 
# of fiefs.

## The Ninth Chapter.

In the alteration of <term>fiefs</term><note>A fief (Lehen) was land or rights granted by a lord to a vassal in exchange for loyalty and service, particularly military service.</note> / there used to be various uses / customs / and opinions at the courts: for one might have altered a fief in whole / in half / or in part as one pleased / and even pawned it up to half. In some places / it was permitted in times of <term>dearth</term><note>original: "Thewrung"; a period of high prices, often caused by famine or crop failure, where a vassal might need to sell land to survive.</note> / to sell a part of the fief / to create <term>sub-fiefs</term><note>original: "affterlehen"; a secondary fief where a vassal grants part of his land to a lower-tier vassal.</note> from it / and such things.

But afterward / such alteration was completely abolished and forbidden / so that fiefs may now be neither halfway nor entirely pledged / pawned / sold / exchanged / or otherwise altered by the <term>vassal</term><note>original: "Lehenmañ"; the person holding the fief from a lord.</note> / in any way: and those who act against this / forfeit their fiefs thereby: and the notaries or scribes who prepare legal instruments regarding this / shall be deemed <term>infamous</term><note>original: "anrichtig"; losing one's legal standing or honor.</note> / and lose their hands: as this was first enacted in part by Emperor Lothar <note>Lothair II, Holy Roman Emperor (reigned 1133–1137), who issued early decrees against the alienation of fiefs.</note> / and subsequently fully ordained and decreed by Emperor Frederick <note>Frederick I "Barbarossa," who codified much of the feudal law in the 12th century to strengthen central imperial authority.</note>.

And such a strict prohibition was caused by the fact that in such alteration and handling / which people practiced with the fiefs / much and various fraud occurred. For many sold / pawned / or otherwise altered their fiefs solely so they would not have to perform <term>knightly service</term><note>original: "Ritterdienst"; the fundamental military obligation of a vassal to provide armed knights for the Emperor's campaigns.</note> / which resulted in significant detriment and reduction to the Empire and the common good. For when the Princes / Counts / and Lords / at the Emperor's summons / or otherwise in the face of imminent necessity / were to arm themselves / they could hardly bring together even half of the vassals: and thus they could not fully perform and provide their service to the Emperor and the Empire.

And this prohibition by Emperor Frederick / regarding the alteration of fiefs / extends not only to future cases / but also to past cases / which occurred before Emperor Frederick's time / these shall also be canceled and void.

Neither can such alteration / sale / and pawning of fiefs / be validated by any <term>prescription</term><note>original: "verjarung"; a statute of limitations where a long-standing illegal act becomes legal over time.</note>.

Furthermore / the vassal cannot worsen the fief / though he may well improve it: accordingly / he cannot impose any <term>servitude</term><note>original: "dienstbarkeit"; a legal burden or easement placed on a property that restricts its use or value.</note> upon the fief.

In addition to this / the vassal cannot give any fief to his daughter as a <term>dowry</term><note>original: "Ehesteuer"; the property a woman brings into her marriage.</note>: for in such a case / the fief would also be altered / because the dowry does not remain with the father / but follows the daughter.

A woman / however / may well give her own fief to her daughter / since the <term>morning gift</term><note>original: "Morgengabe"; a gift given by a husband to his wife on the morning after the wedding night, which often returned to her own control or her family.</note> falls back to her / as mentioned above.

However, a father may pledge the use and <term>usufruct</term><note>original: "Usufruct"; the legal right to use and derive profit from property belonging to another, provided it is not damaged.</note> of a <term>fief</term><note>A "Lehen" or fief was land held from a lord in exchange for service.</note> to his daughter as a marriage portion and dowry, and bind himself to that. The contracts or writings of many of the nobility in our times, who are accustomed to providing their daughters with <term>fief-estates</term> as a marriage portion, must be understood in this way: such a dowry does not extend further than the use of the property.

This is the case unless the feudal lord has consented to such a dowry, for then it would be valid. But if the lord granted consent with the provision that the dowry of the fief should not be damaging to his own legal rights—and if the <term>vassal</term><note>original: "Lehenmañ"; one who holds land from a lord.</note> and his wife should pass away without heirs to the fief, or if the fief were otherwise lost, that it should revert and return to him—then it must remain and be settled in that manner.

Likewise, if the lord grants consent—especially in the case of ancient fiefs—and the <term>expectant heirs</term><note>original: "A[n-]"; likely "Anwärter" or "Anverwandten," referring to kinsmen who have a legal expectation to inherit the land.</note> have not given their consent to it, they have the right to challenge such a dowry, because they also have an interest in the fief, which the lord cannot give away through his consent alone, as will be further demonstrated below.

Next, know that the lord himself cannot alter his fief in such a way that the vassal would be forced, against his will, to submit to and be directed by another feudal lord. However, whether the lord, by doing so, forfeits the rights he has over the fief will be further indicated below in the next chapter.

From this it follows: if a fief, which was situated in many places, were granted to me, and the lord wished to sell a part of it or otherwise alter it, then I, as the vassal, would not be obliged to recognize or accept anyone other than the old or original feudal lord: except if the lord turns over or sells the fief to a **Church**, which must then be <unclear>permitted</unclear>. In that case, the vassal must allow himself to be directed to the Church and accept them as feudal lords, even if it happens to his disadvantage. Otherwise, the Church could remove him from the fief or keep him as a vassal, as they please. Although, in this matter, too much has been granted to the Church and the clergy. For if the Church is allowed to take a fief in such a manner from a well-deserving or even an innocent vassal, how can she then protect and uphold justice, as she is rightly supposed to do and as the clergy boast of doing? But just as in former times great advantage was given to the Church and almost everything was turned over to it: so now one sees the opposite, that almost everything is being taken from the Church. And it is to be feared that the clergy, through their own injustice, as well as their disorderly lives and un-Christian behavior, have given cause for more to be taken from them all at once now than was given to them over many years.

A lord can, however, alter a fief if he sells his entire land with all its appurtenances, provided that the fief is specifically named and expressed in the contract of sale, as mentioned above. Likewise, if a vassal alters his fief without the knowledge of the lord—whereby he would have forfeited the fief—even if he were to regain that same fief afterward, the lord may nevertheless take it for himself and keep it as a forfeited property.

# Imperial Feudal Law

...and if the <term>vassal</term><note>original: "Lehenmañ"; a person who holds land from a lord in exchange for service and loyalty.</note> could not settle or compensate for such a violation.

Furthermore, a vassal cannot rent out his <term>fief</term><note>original: "Lehen"; an estate of land held on condition of feudal service.</note> for a long number of years, regardless of the fact that the lease might appear to be a minor matter, because it is considered that the fief might be altered through such an arrangement. However, it is generally held that if the lease were set for approximately nine years or less, it might be permitted.

Finally, although it is said that "necessity has no law"—to the extent that a father, in times of famine and hunger, may even sell his son—a vassal in times of need still cannot sell or alter his fief without the consent of the lord. This may certainly be seen as burdensome, but it has its reason: namely, that the vassal is not the absolute master of the fief. Instead, the lord holds the <term>ownership</term><note>original: "eigenthumb"; referring here to 'dominium directum' or legal title, while the vassal has the 'dominium utile' or right to use the land.</note> of it, which the vassal cannot and should not take away from him.

However, this rule stating that the vassal may not sell or otherwise alter his fief has several exceptions, which we shall set forth one after another.

First, the vassal alters the fief if he <term>assigns</term><note>original: "auffschreibet"; to formally surrender or sign over the rights of the fief back to the lord.</note> it back to the lord, which he may do if it is an "old fief" (one inherited from ancestors). However, such an assignment cannot harm the <term>agnates</term><note>original: "Agnaten"; male relatives related through the father's side who have a claim to inherit the fief.</note>; rather, it lasts no longer than the lifetime of the one who assigned it and his male descendants. When they are no longer living, the agnates may then claim their rights to it.

From this it follows that if a vassal assigns his fief to the lord in such a way that he wishes the lord to <term>enfeoff</term><note>To grant someone a fief.</note> his daughter with it, such an assignment is valid and lasts as long as the vassal lives. If he dies without male heirs, the brother or other agnates take the fief back to themselves. But neither the father nor his descendants, while they are alive, can demand such a fief back.

Secondly, the <term>vassal</term><note>original: "Vaſall"</note> may grant his fief further to another, as was the custom among the ancients and also in our own times: provided, however, that it is not harmful to the lord or the agnates, and that no fraud is intended—meaning that he does not sell the fief-estate or otherwise take money for it under the pretense of <term>sub-infeudation</term><note>original: "affterbelehnung"; the practice where a vassal grants part of his fief to a third party, becoming a lord to that person.</note>. Likewise, provided that the person who receives the sub-fief is of equal or lower status than the vassal, and not of higher status, and is capable of performing the required service. However, in such cases, one must look to local usage and the custom of the land.

But the vassal could not grant his fief further or turn it into a sub-fief if he had received it from the lord with the <term>agreement and condition</term><note>original: "pact vn̄ geding"</note> that he should not grant it further or alter it in any other way.

Thirdly, the vassal might pledge the fief, provided he nonetheless kept it in his <term>possession and control</term><note>original: "beſitz vn̄ gewehr"</note>. For in such a case, where he retains the <term>possession</term><note>original: "Poſſeſſion"</note>, it cannot be cited as an "alteration."

From which it further follows that if there were three brothers who held a <term>fief</term><note>original: "Lehen"; land or rights held from a lord in exchange for service.</note>, and one surrendered or <term>resigned</term><note>original: "Resignirte"; formally gave up his share of the property.</note> his portion to the others; if that same person who gave up his portion should die or become a <term>cleric</term><note>original: "Geistlich Mann"; entering the church often legally "ended" one's secular life regarding inheritance.</note>, the two living brothers would succeed to the resigned portion together. The reason for this is that since all three were previously provided for with the fief, one should not have taken advantage of the others or given anything away to their detriment.

Furthermore, it is important to know that if one of the <term>agnates</term><note>original: "Agnaten"; male-line relatives with a potential claim to the inheritance.</note> had consented to a sale or change of a fief simply for himself, and died after such consent, leaving a son, that son would not be bound by such consent; instead, he could revoke it after his father's death.

That is, unless the father had not only consented to the change but had also committed himself not to contest it: in that case, the son would be obliged to uphold what the father had committed to.

From this it follows that if the agnates—who were not called to give consent when the <term>vassal</term><note>original: "Vasallen"; the person holding the fief.</note> changed the fief—later become his heirs, they could not then revoke the changed fief, unless they had made an <term>inventory</term>. For an inventory is so legally powerful that it preserves all and every right of inheritance for the heirs. <note>original Latin: "l. fina. Par. In computatione. C. de iure delibe."; a reference to the Code of Justinian, specifically the final law in the section regarding the "right to deliberate" on whether to accept an inheritance.</note>

However, the agnates must pay diligent attention to this point and not forget: if a fief is changed or sold without their consent, they must be mindful to revoke and contest that sale within the <term>period of one year</term>. Otherwise, they could not pursue it afterward, but would be considered to have remained silent: for it would be viewed as if they had given <term>tacit consent</term>.

These prescribed instructions regarding the change and sale of fiefs only apply to <term>old and ancestral fiefs</term><note>original: "alten vnd Väterlichen Lehen"; property that has been in the family for generations.</note>. For if the vassal changed a <term>new fief</term><note>original: "new Lehen"; a recently granted property.</note> without the consent of the lord, it could be revoked neither by the sons nor by the agnates; instead, it would <term>revert to the lord</term><note>original: "fiele dem Herren heim"; the legal term "escheat," where property returns to the grantor if conditions are broken.</note>.

Seventhly, if the vassal changes the fief in a proper manner—that is, with the knowledge and consent of the lord—and it is a new fief, then the change is valid. For the lord alone has an interest in such a fief, and the sons have no grounds to object to it.

However, if it should happen that the lord granted a new fief to two brothers with the <term>agreement</term><note>original: "pact"; a formal legal contract or clause.</note> that one should follow the other in it, and one brother changes the fief, then the other brother could revoke it, because he would have been disadvantaged by the action, regardless of whether it was a new fief.

But if someone sold an old fief or otherwise <term>alienated</term><note>original: "Alienirte"; to transfer ownership to another person.</note> it, and both the sons and the agnates consented to such a change, there is no doubt that the change is valid. But if only the sons had all consented together, but the...

### A Brief Extract of the...

...<term>agnates</term><note>original: "Agnaten"; male-line relatives who share a common male ancestor and have claims to the inheritance.</note> do not [consent], then that same approval lasts no longer than the <term>vassal</term><note>The person currently holding the land from a lord.</note> and his sons remain alive. If the sons did not all agree, the one who did not consent may revoke the sale during the father's life and return the money to the buyer. The same applies to the agnates who are the next in line after the sons. If some or all of them did not consent, they may, after the death of the vassal, revoke the <term>fief</term><note>original: "Lehen"; the property or rights held under feudal law.</note>, because they did not consent or agree to such a sale: regardless of whether it happened with the lord's approval. 

The agnates also have an advantage over the sons: if they revoke the fief, they do not have to return the purchase price to the buyer. However, if the agnates wish to reclaim the altered fief immediately and during the lifetime of the vassal, and pay for it as a stranger or outsider would, or redeem it for as much as it was sold for, they are free to do so and it must be permitted.

As far as the lord's approval is concerned, the question is asked here: in cases where the lord must consent, is an express approval necessary, or is it enough if he remains silent and does not contest the change? To this it must be answered: If the lord were present, such that he saw and heard the vassal sell and <term>alienate</term><note>original: "alienirte"; the legal transfer of property to another.</note> the fief and did not contest it, he would have consented through such silence, according to the common rule of law which says: "He who is silent, consents."<note>original: "Wer schweigt/ der williget"; a reference to the Latin legal maxim *Qui tacet consentire videtur*.</note> Since he was free to prevent such a sale or alienation and not permit it. 

But if the lord were not present, even if he had knowledge of the change, it could not be drawn as an approval. And although the <term>feudalists</term><note>original: "Feudisten"; legal scholars specializing in feudal law.</note> are somewhat divided on this point—some holding that such knowledge is detrimental to the lord—the first opinion is fundamentally more stable. For legal scholars hold that if one knows of a thing and is not present, he is more likely to be contesting it than approving and accepting it, where it causes him harm. Unless the lord had been written to regarding the matter and he had remained silent and given no answer, or if other presumptions were at hand.

In this, however, there is no doubt: even if the lord did not consent to a sale or change of the fief at the beginning, he can still do so afterward; and it is the same as if he had given his approval at the very start.

Here a question now arises: if it should happen that a vassal receives an estate from the lord as a fief and then grants that same property to another as a <term>sub-fief</term><note>original: "afterlehen"; a secondary fief where a vassal acts as a lord to another person.</note>, as often happens: if the sub-vassal wants to change that sub-fief, is he obliged to seek the approval of both lords, or just one of them—either the lower or the upper lord? 

To this it is answered: regardless of what might be argued—that because the lower lord received the power and authority from the upper lord to grant the fief further, he also has the power to give approval when it is to be changed, and other similar [arguments]...

# Imperial Feudal Law

...to act: that it was therefore sufficient if he applied for approval to the sub-lord. However, it is held that it is proper to seek out the over-lord. For he who granted the <term>sub-fief</term><note>original: "affterlehen"; a secondary fief created when a vassal grants part of his held land to another person.</note> to the sub-vassal no longer possesses the full right he once had in the fief; instead, he has transferred and assigned that right to the sub-fief holder. Thus, he is not a true lord, but possesses only the shadow and name of a lord; and when he dies, the sub-fief or under-fief is ended and has lapsed.

Furthermore, it might be asked here whether a lord, when he consents to the alteration of a fief, might damage his own ownership by such consent? The answer is: No; rather, he retains his ownership continually. It is held that he has consented to nothing further than the extent of the vassal's existing rights. Therefore, regardless of such consent, if the vassal dies, the fief reverts back to the lord. However, to prevent strife and error, it is not improper for the lord to grant consent in such a way that it is "without prejudice to his ownership."

However, if the lord were to grant such a generous consent that it also extended to the ownership itself, the situation would be different. If I were to alter a fief with such consent and then later bring it back into my possession, it would be my own property and not a <term>fief-holding</term><note>original: "Lehengut"; land held under feudal obligation rather than owned outright.</note>, because the lord has surrendered his ownership through such consent.

Furthermore, if I, with the lord's consent, sold a fief to someone—let us say to Titius <note>A traditional name used in legal examples, similar to "John Doe."</note>—as a sub-fief, in such a way that Titius must pay me five Guilders or more in annual interest, then I retain those same five Guilders as a fief. And if I bring such a sub-fief back into my possession, I hold that same fief from the lord in no other way than as a sub-fief; and I give the lord the interest, namely the five Guilders, though it remains a fief nonetheless. For if I were to forfeit it or otherwise lose it, it would revert back to the lord.

Also, if the lord allowed the vassal to sell the fief to a specific and named person, the vassal could not sell it to any other person; for such permission or consent could not extend to another and no further. Yet it should be noted here: if the <term>vassal</term><note>A person who holds land from a lord in exchange for loyalty and service.</note> sold the fief to another who was of equal standing to the one the lord had approved, and the lord had no disadvantage to expect—but rather it was likely that if this person had been proposed to the lord, he would have consented—then such a sale is also valid.

Finally, if a vassal sold his fief to someone who did not know it was a fief, and the <term>agnates</term><note>original: "Agnaten"; male-line relatives with a potential claim to the inheritance.</note> or even the lord himself wanted to contest the sale and revoke the fief, then the buyer's purchase money must be refunded to him, even if nothing was handled regarding the <term>warranty of title</term><note>original: "getwehr"; the legal guarantee that the seller has the right to sell the property and will defend the buyer against other claims.</note> in the sale. But if the buyer knew that it was a fief, and was thus a <term>buyer in bad faith</term><note>original: "emptor malæ fidei"</note>, then the money would not have to be returned to him; instead, the buyer must lose it. Yet such money would not go to the seller or the vassal, but to the <term>Treasury</term><note>original: "Fisco"; the public or royal purse.</note>.

Furthermore, even if the <term>vassal</term><note>A person granted the use of land by a lord in return for homage and service.</note> had provided a guarantee of security to a buyer who was acting in <term>bad faith</term><note>original: "bösen glauben"; in a legal sense, knowing that the transaction is illegal or that the seller does not have the right to sell.</note>, he does not recover his money but must lose it. Additionally, the scribe who prepares a deed or contract for such a sale shall also be subject to punishment.

## Concerning the Division of Fiefs.

Until now, we have spoken through several concluding points about the alteration of fiefs. Now we wish to briefly report how fiefs may be divided; for the division of some also has the character and appearance of an alteration. In this regard, it should be noted that it is not forbidden by law, but rather permitted, to divide fiefs. To be sure, it is more practical for it to remain undivided than for it to be partitioned. Therefore, brothers—when they divide the estate after the death of their father—sometimes grant the fief to one brother so that it remains whole, and grant the <term>allodial inheritance</term><note>original: "das Erbe"; property owned outright, distinguished here from the "Lehen" or fief held from a lord.</note> to the other, making a settlement between them.

Furthermore, if a man leaves many fiefs behind after his death, one may be assigned to one heir and another to another. Through such a division, the type and nature of the fief is not changed.

If a fief is divided in such a manner, and the person who has received a portion of the fief dies without <term>male heirs of the body</term><note>original: "Männliche Leibserben"; biological male children, who were traditionally the only ones eligible to inherit feudal property.</note>, in that case, the fief does not revert to the Lord, but rather to those who were part of that division and are still living. This is the case unless it was otherwise provided for or expressed through a special <term>pact</term><note>original: "pact"; a formal legal agreement or contract.</note>.

Here, one might ask: Can jurisdiction and other incorporeal things and legal rights also be divided, since these are also customarily granted as fiefs? To this, it must be answered: although such things cannot be physically divided because they have no "body," they can nonetheless be assigned to one person, or used alternately by one after the other, with the assurance that one does not hinder the other in such use.

However, great and Princely fiefs should not be divided according to the letter of feudal law—such as <term>Principalities</term><note>original: "Fürstenthumb"</note>, <term>Margraviates</term><note>original: "Marggraffschafften"</note>, and <term>Countships</term><note>original: "Graffschafften"</note>. Instead, they should be kept together and undivided so that they may remain all the more stately and powerful. Nevertheless, despite these legal provisions, such fiefs and principalities are divided almost as much as other, lesser fiefs, because the Roman Emperors permit and look on it with favor. # On the Loss of Fiefs.

## The Tenth Chapter.

This chapter deals with two matters. First, concerning the loss and confiscation of <term>fiefs</term><note>Land or rights granted by a lord to a vassal in exchange for service and loyalty.</note>. Second, concerning the escheat and reversion of fiefs when they become vacant or "extinguished."

As far as the first point is concerned, fiefs are forfeited and lost for many reasons; regarding this, we shall set out several concluding arguments in order.

### The First Concluding Argument.

If the <term>vassal</term><note>The holder of the fief.</note> alters or sells his fief in an unseemly or improper manner, he has lost it. Likewise, if someone allows his fief to pass to another through an amicable agreement, yet did not have sufficient reason to suspect a certain and long-lasting dispute (as has been mentioned previously), he has thereby lost the fief. And it is to be noted here: if the vassal altered the fief entirely in such a manner, he would have lost it entirely; but if he had altered only a part of it, he would only have been able to forfeit that same part. And it is not as some say—that if the vassal had altered only a single piece of sod from the fief, he should thereby have forfeited the entire fief—for their opinion is false and wrong, and it is not upheld. For the punishment should not be greater than the <term>forfeiture</term><note>original: "verwirckung"; the loss of a right or property due to a legal violation.</note> itself.

Now, if the vassal has once lost and forfeited his fief in such a way, even if he brings it back into his possession, it may not help him; rather, as soon as it is improperly altered, it is forfeited and falls to the Lord, in such a way that this alteration immediately carries with it the enforcement of the law, so that the Lord may take possession.

This is true unless the vassal were to bring the fief back immediately and "on the spot," as they say: then and in that case, he would be fairly spared such punishment. For such an alteration is regarded no differently than if it had never happened; just as a thing that is born and dies in the same hour is not considered a birth. And this point is to be understood thus: when it is said that the vassal shall bring the fief back to himself "immediately," it means that it happens within a few days, and before he is sued for it by the Lord.

Secondly, if the man sells his fief and yet has not handed it over, but kept it in his power and possession, in that case, he could not be judged to have lost the fief, for the reason that while he still has the fief in his power and <term>possession</term><note>original: "Posses"; a legal term derived from the Latin *possessio*, referring to the actual physical control of the land.</note>, it is not yet completely altered. For the alteration <insert>is</insert> through the actual handing over and granting occur—

### A brief summary/ which

must be made. If, however, someone sells a <term>fief</term><note>An estate held from a lord on condition of feudal service.</note> and nevertheless keeps it in his possession, but only <term>at the pleasure of</term><note>original: "bittweiß"; a legal term meaning holding property only as long as the owner allows.</note> the buyer, even though he physically holds or keeps it, this is still to be considered a true transfer of ownership. Consequently, the seller loses the fief because the buyer may demand it at any time, even against the seller's will, and may physically remove and drive him from the estate.

Thirdly, if both parties—the <term>vassal</term><note>original: "Lehenmann"; the person holding the fief.</note> who sells the estate and the one who bought it—did not know that it was a fief, the vassal would not have forfeited the fief. Instead, the buyer would have to return the fief to him and take back his expended purchase money, which the vassal is then obliged to return to him in that case. For <term>feudal law</term><note>original: "Lehenrecht"</note> spares the vassal from punishment in such a case where something is done out of ignorance and without fraud.

However, his simple words are not believed in this matter; rather, he must confirm it with an oath that he did not know it was a fief.

But the vassal shall not be permitted to take such an oath unless he has some presumption in his favor: namely, if he obtained the fief from someone who had not served the Lord for a long time. But if the vassal had some presumption against him—such as if he had been personally <term>invested</term><note>The formal ceremony of being granted the fief.</note> or had been summoned to service by the Lord—then he would rightly not be believed, nor should he be permitted to take the oath. This is so that no occasion is given for <term>perjury</term><note>original: "meineyde"</note>, but rather to help prevent it in every way possible.

If, however, the vassal wished to claim that he indeed knew it was a fief, but did not think or know that it was forbidden under feudal law to transfer the fief without the consent of those who have an interest in it—and thus <term>alleged ignorance of the law</term><note>original Latin: "ignorantiam iuris Allegierte"</note>—he would not be heard. This remains true even if the vassal were a soldier or a woman, who are otherwise exempted and excused in <term>common law</term><note>The general legal system as opposed to specific feudal statutes.</note> if they do not know the law.

Now, if the vassal has sold a fief in such a manner—namely, unknowingly—and the buyer were sued in court either by the Lord or by the vassal to return the fief and step away from it, it would be at the buyer’s discretion whether he wished to return it to the Lord or the vassal. And it is no error here that the feudal laws say in another place that the buyer should return the fief to no one other than the vassal. For that is understood provided he wishes to recover his expended money or interest, which the vassal is then obliged to reimburse. For if he were to return it directly to the Lord, he would gain nothing by it in such a case; nor is the Lord obligated or indebted to pay him anything. Therefore, it would be a folly for the buyer not to prefer returning the fief to the vassal, from whom he could demand and obtain the purchase price, rather than to the Lord. But if it should happen that the buyer returned the fief (which was sold to him unknowingly) to the Lord, then the vassal could demand and obtain the same back from the Lord, since it has not been forfeited. Yet he may thereafter seek his claimed justice again in an [orderly] way through the law/ in which case he shall then be heard and permitted.

But a question arises here: Namely, if a **Prelate** <note>A high-ranking member of the clergy, such as a bishop.</note>, such as a Bishop or perhaps a wealthy Abbot, had a **mistress** <note>original: "Beyschläfferin"; a woman living with a man without being married to him.</note>, and the vassal went to her secretly and slept with her, would he also have forfeited the fief thereby? To this it is to be answered: Although the legal scholars hold that a vassal may lose his fief if he dishonors the Lord's mistress, it is a different matter and situation with **Clerical Lords**. Because between Prelates and their mistresses no civil partnership may exist, but rather an unseemly and damned existence. Accordingly, it would be unjust for the vassal to be punished by the Lord in a matter for which the Lord himself is punishable in the highest degree; indeed, it would be worthy that for the sake of such a mistress, both should be removed: the Prelate from his office and the vassal from his fief. <note>The text cites Canon Law here: *c.erubescant. 32.dist.* refers to the "Decretum Gratiani," and *c.sicut.in fine, de cohab.clerico* refers to the "Decretals" regarding the cohabitation of clerics.</note>

But to return to our previous point: namely, where we said that the vassal shall make no friendship with the Lord's enemies under penalty of losing the fief. This is to be understood if the friendship resulted in a disadvantage to the Lord, or was made for that purpose, and not otherwise. Yet, to avoid suspicion, it is more convenient and better for the vassal to distance himself from the Lord's enemies as much as is ever possible, so that he is not forced to purge himself <note>A legal term for clearing one's name or proving innocence through an oath.</note>, or give cause as to why he entered into friendship and involvement with the Lord's enemies.

Following this, the vassal loses his fief if he reveals the Lord’s **secrets**, primarily if such a revelation comes from evil intent and would result in insult and disadvantage to the Lord. But where it happens that the vassal spoke something unexpectedly out of simplicity or otherwise, which the Lord wanted to have kept secret, the fief could not be taken from him by that, since he used no deceit (which must happen intentionally) in the matter. Unless he had overlooked it so grossly that one must consider and hold it to be a fraud. In that case, he could not excuse himself, but would have fallen into the penalty of the fief. Just as the vassal also cannot be excused if he intentionally brings the Lord’s secret to light...

# Imperial Feudal Law.

If the Man <note>vassal</note> should claim he did not do it with the intention of harming the Lord, he must prove it, since the legal presumptions in this matter stand against him. And although according to common law, a **Negative** <note>original: "Negatiua"; the legal defense of denying that an event occurred.</note> is difficult to prove—as when someone says they have not done a thing—he must nevertheless point to enough circumstances from which it can be presumed that he did not intend to cause the Lord any harm with these words. For example, if he proves he was sitting among good friends, did not speak ill of the Lord, showed no angry or unfriendly gestures, but rather spoke too freely in a guileless and simple manner, and said more than was appropriate according to his duties.

If the evidence on both sides were doubtful, such that one could not discern which side was right or wrong, the vassal may clear himself with an oath and be set free.

If it is another person who is a vassal, such as a **Councilman** or a **Mayor**, and he blabs maliciously and deceitfully from the Council, he shall be stripped of his dignity and status.

But the man loses his fief to the Lord if he acts physically against him: violently attacking him in his house where the Lord resides with his wife and child. This remains true whether the violent act occurs on horseback or on foot, with firearms or in other ways, especially if it was an unprovoked attack on his honor. According to **Saxon Law** <note>original: "Sachsen Recht"; referring to the *Sachsenspiegel*, a foundational legal code in German territories.</note>, he must prove his defense with at least two fellow vassals, who are called **Peers of the Court** <note>original: "Pares Curiæ"; vassals of the same rank who served as judges in a Lord's feudal court.</note>. It is enough that the vassal knew the house or castle belonged to the Lord, whether the Lord was present at the time or not, and whether the man knew the Lord was inside or not.

In the same way, the vassal is also found punishable if he strikes the Lord or surprises him with an unsheathed weapon. Although some excuse the vassal and say that if he merely reaches for the weapon but does not draw it, nor strikes the Lord, it should not be held against him. However, if it reaches the point where he does not stop of his own accord, but people have to intervene to pull the man away from the Lord so he does not harm him, then he cannot be excused; he has fallen into the penalty of losing the fief, no less than if he had actually injured the Lord.

Likewise, if the man lays violent hands on the Lord, binds him, or otherwise brings great disgrace upon him, he loses the fief.

Furthermore, if a vassal had sworn to kill the Lord, yet did nothing and had done nothing to him, the fief could not be taken from him for that reason—unless he had done and sworn such a thing through a **Conspiracy** <note>original: "Conspiration"</note> alongside others against the Lord.

...testimony given in **criminal matters** <note>original: "Peinlichen sachen"; specifically referring to capital crimes or cases involving corporal punishment.</note>, however minor they may be. And the law establishes in that place that the vassal has lost the Lord's grace or favor through such proceedings, or has fallen into the Lord’s displeasure; yet this is not to be understood as anything other than the loss of the **fief** <note>original: "Lehen"; the land or rights granted to a vassal by a Lord.</note>. He would also lose his fief if he voluntarily allowed himself to be used as an **advocate** <note>a lawyer or legal representative</note> against the Lord. However, if he were forced to do so by virtue of his office or other necessity, he would rightly be held excused in that matter.

Secondly, if the Lord has a legal claim against the vassal—as can sometimes happen that a Lord must sue someone before the vassal—and the vassal refuses to grant the Lord his right and justice, as the **overseers or bailiffs** <note>original: "Vorsteher oder Vögte"</note> of monasteries sometimes tend to do. Thirdly, the vassal is declared to have lost his fief if someone has brought a criminal complaint against his Lord and the vassal allows himself to be used as a **guarantor** <note>original: "Bürgen"; one who takes legal responsibility for another's debt or appearance.</note> for the one acting against the Lord.

Fourthly, if the **vassal** <note>original: "Vasall"</note>, in a matter of great importance, has passed a **sentence** <note>original: "Sentenz"</note> or verdict against the Lord, which verdict is found to be unjust and is overturned upon **appeal** <note>original: "Appellation"</note> based on the court records: from which it can be presumed that such a thing occurred out of malice or gross ignorance (since he could well have consulted wise people to learn the law), but which he did not do, but rather simply and carelessly judged to the Lord’s detriment; in such a case, there is no doubt the Man has lost the fief. This is especially true if the negligence, deceit, or ignorance is of such a nature that he (had he been an ordinary judge) could be punished for it. If, however, it occurred out of simple innocence—namely, that he could not otherwise be blamed—one should rightly have patience with him, and he would not be subject to the penalty of losing the fief. Therefore, vassals must take good care in such and similar cases, so that they do not lose their fiefs through lack of foresight; for mistakes can easily be made in these matters.

But regarding what was said above—that the Man may not bring a criminal complaint against the Lord without the loss of his fiefs—this is to be understood as: if he cannot prove the criminal complaint he has brought. For if he proves it, then it remains without penalty.

Secondly, if the vassal complained against the Lord regarding actions that the Lord had committed against the **Emperor**, the **Princes**, the **Empire**, or the **Common Good**, then in that case he would be excused.

Thirdly, if the vassal complained against the Lord regarding **injuries** <note>original: "Iniurien"; from the Latin *injuria*, referring to legal wrongs or insults to one's person or honor.</note> and damages which the Lord had committed against him or his family, this would be harmless to his fief.

As far as testimony is concerned, as mentioned before, it is not harmful to the **vassal** <note>original: "Mañ" (Mann); the tenant who holds land from a superior Lord.</note> if he gives testimony against the Lord in matters regarding **investiture** <note>original: "Belehnung"; the formal legal act of granting a fief.</note> or other concerns specifically regarding the fief. ## The Seventh Conclusion.

It is also to be known that the vassal forfeits the fief if he knowingly denies it to the Lord when the Lord claims it, or if he says it is an "old" or "rightful" fief when it is actually "new" or "wrongful" <note>These terms refer to the legal history of the land grant, which determined how it could be inherited or taxed.</note>. If he is convicted of this, he loses that same fief. However, if he denies it unknowingly and without fraud; likewise, if the fief did not belong to him but to another who is quarreling with the Lord over it, and he denies the fief unlawfully even if he knew the truth and kept silent—this would still be harmless to him, perhaps for the reason that no one should force themselves into giving testimony or volunteer information of their own accord.

If the **vassal** <note>original: "Vasall"</note> mismanages the **fief** <note>original: "Lehengut"</note> and ruins it so that it is diminished in value by something significant and noteworthy, he may be deprived of the fief.

For they are not appointed and ordained to treat poor people in such a way, but rather to protect and maintain them. And more could certainly be written here on that subject; however, since things are going so strangely with the monasteries in these times <note>A likely reference to the social and religious upheavals of the 16th-century Reformation.</note> that almost no one knows who is the Abbot or who is the Bailiff, we shall let it rest here. ### The Ninth Conclusion.

Ninth, if it should happen that the **vassal’s** <note>original: "Lehenmañs"</note> [son] grossly injured the **Lord** <note>original: "Lehenherren"</note>, and the Lord demanded the son in order to punish him for such injury, the vassal is obligated to deliver his son to the Lord or to **disown him** <note>original: "sich deß zu enteussern"; literally to alienate or distance himself from the son</note>. If he does neither of these, he would forfeit his fief thereby.
   In the same way, he is also obligated to hand over his other household members—with the exception of his wife—to the Lord in such a case, or to disown them, for he has the choice in this matter. And he can thus clear himself of the accusation by showing that he wishes to have nothing to do with the Lord's enemies, and that such injury did not happen by his command, nor with his will and knowledge.
   However, the person who injured or damaged the Lord shall not be punished more harshly by the Lord than the crime itself warrants.
   But if that same person refused to be brought before the Lord (which, among us **Germans** <note>original: "Teutschen"</note>, and especially among the nobility, would be difficult to carry out), then—if it were the son—he might be excluded from the fief by the Lord after the death of the father, unless he reached a settlement with the Lord regarding the matter.

### The Tenth Conclusion.

When the **sub-vassal** <note>original: "Vnterlehenmann"</note> has injured the **Overlord** <note>original: "Oberlehenherrn"</note>, whereby he would have forfeited the fief, that same fief does not revert to the Overlord (despite the fact that he was the one injured), but rather to the person to whom the Overlord originally granted the fief <note>i.e., the immediate Lord who sits between the Overlord and the sub-vassal</note>.
   If, however, that same [immediate Lord] were requested by the Overlord to punish the **sub-vassal** <note>original: "affterlehenmann"</note> for such a violation, and he refused to do so, then they would both have lost the fief, and it would then revert back to the Overlord as his rightful Lord. And it does not matter if it is argued that the Overlord is not the direct Lord of the sub-vassal. For if the rightful vassal forfeits his fief against the Lord, then the sub-vassal has also lost it. For according to the general rule: **where the right of the giver ends, there also ends the right of the receiver.** <note>original Latin: "cap. 1. de alien. feud."; referencing Chapter 1 of *On the Alienation of Fiefs* in the *Libri Feudorum*</note>. This is unless the Overlord had consented to the sub-granting of the fief: in that case, if the rightful vassal died or the fief was otherwise "opened up" <note>reverted to the Lord</note>, the sub-vassal might step into his place.

# Imperial Feudal Law.

### The Eleventh Conclusion.

Eleventh, a man forfeits his **fief** <note>original: "Lehen"</note> if he is cited and summoned by the **Lord** <note>original: "Herren"</note> to three **court sessions** <note>original: "gedingen"; specific judicial meetings held at set intervals</note> within the proper period and time, regarding matters concerning the **fiefdom** <note>original: "Lehenschafft"</note>, and remains disobediently absent; in such a case, the Lord may then, after the three sessions, be legally installed into the **possession** <note>original: "Posseß"; from the Latin *possessio*</note> of the fief. If the **vassal** <note>original: "Lehenmann"</note> then remains in such disobedience for **a year and a day** <note>original: "Jar vnd Tag"; a standard legal deadline in Germanic law</note>, he has lost the fief. However, if the vassal immediately indicates that he does not intend to appear, there is no need to summon him further; instead, the court may proceed directly with the penalty of the fief.

### The Twelfth Conclusion.

Twelfth and lastly, a man forfeits the fief in any and all dealings which he may commit against his **feudal duty** <note>original: "Lehenspflicht"</note> toward his Lord, some of which have been mentioned above.

Likewise, if it is proven that he has betrayed the Lord.

If he refuses, without sufficient cause, to perform his **knightly service** <note>original: "Ritterdienst"</note> for the Lord.

If he does not release the Lord should he be captured, provided it is in his power and he is able to do so.

If a great damage was imminent for the Lord, and the man knew how to prevent it but neglected to do so.

If he lays violent hands upon the Lord or **ensnares** <note>original: "bestrickt"</note> him.

If he deserts and abandons the Lord in war without a great and weightily honest reason.

If he deceitfully plots against the Lord to his detriment, or is present and nearby when such is done by others.

If he seeks the Lord's life and endeavors to take it, whether with poison, weapons, or by other means.

Finally, if he should offend the Lord in cases which are not specifically expressed in the **feudal laws** <note>original: "Lehenrechten"</note> (as one cannot express every case that may occasionally happen), but which are of such a nature that they carry with them a great **ingratitude** <note>original: "vndanckbarkeit"</note>, he thereby loses his fief. However, such cases not expressed in the law are left to the **discretion** <note>original: "willköhr"</note> of a sensible judge, who shall diligently weigh all circumstances and compare the offense for which the vassal is accused against the expressed cases, and guide himself accordingly with the **judgment** <note>original: "Vrtheil"</note>.

But if he should be in doubt as to whether he should condemn a vassal or declare him free: in such doubt, he should be more inclined to release than to condemn.

In addition to this, it is to be known: if the vassal captures his own brother, even if he does not kill him but holds him in harsh imprisonment, from which he...

## A Brief Excerpt / Which
