This occurs when a **vassal** <note>original: "Lehenmañ"; a person granted the use of land in return for homage and service</note> is burdened or notorious for the heavy vice of **parricide** <note>original: "Parricidij"; here used broadly to mean the murder of any close relative</note> (that is, when he has strangled his father, mother, brother, sister, his children, or any other of his closest blood relatives). Even if he has not directly harmed the **Lord** <note>original: "Herren"</note>, the Lord may still strip him of the **fief** <note>original: "Lehen"</note>; such a man shall not be considered good enough to remain a vassal because of such maltreatment.

From all of this, it is easy to see what a burdensome and troublesome thing it is to be a vassal: something for which a man should not rightly long. For this reason, it is not without cause that some call it a form of **servitude** <note>original: "Dienstbarkeit"; implies a state of being subject to a master, similar to bondage</note>. However, the vassals of today do not care much about this, and it goes with them as it does in all stations of life: nothing remains in its proper order, but instead, everyone does as they please without any fear of the Law. And sometimes the Lords are as powerful over the vassal as **Roland was with his sword** <note>A proverbial expression referring to the legendary knight Roland, suggesting a lord acting with absolute, perhaps arbitrary, power or overwhelming force</note>, as the saying goes. But enough of that; let us continue.

Now, if the **Church** <note>original: "Kirche"</note> held a fief from a Lord, and the **Prelate** <note>original: "Prelat"; a high-ranking member of the clergy, such as an abbot or bishop</note> of that church harmed the Lord, would the Church also lose the fief because of it? To this, it must be answered that the Church has indeed forfeited the fief through such maltreatment and injury, and must do without it as long as the Prelate of that church is alive. After his death, the Church regains the fief. Therefore, in this case, the Prelate does not harm his Church for longer than he lives. Conversely, if the **Feudal Lord** <note>original: "Lehenherr"</note> should harm the Prelate as a vassal, what the law is in that matter and how it is upheld shall be spoken of shortly hereafter.

But if a **City** <note>original: "Statt"</note> holds a fief from a Lord, and a portion of the citizens commit an offense against the Lord, should the entire City lose the fief and have it forfeited? The answer is: No. For the part that has broken the law cannot harm the other innocent part with its forfeiture.

Now another question arises: When the vassal has committed an offense against the Lord by which he forfeits the fief (as has been heard in several cases so far), is it necessary to hold a trial and pass a **judgment** <note>original: "Urtheil"</note> upon it? Or does the Lord have the power to depose the man for such a crime without a prior **legal process** <note>original: "Proceß"</note> and **judicial ruling** <note>original: "Rechtlich erkantniß"</note>?

In this, it is to be known that in all cases where the vassal forfeits the fief to his Lord, a judicial process according to the order of **Feudal Law** <note>original: "Lehenrecht"</note> is necessary, so that the vassal is recognized as having forfeited it by judgment and law and is then stripped of the fief.

Excluded are certain cases in which the vassal, by his own act, strips himself of the fief and loses it, so that no special judgment needs to be pronounced. Namely, if the vassal had altered his fief in some way (as mentioned above) and in other such cases. Furthermore, if the vassal had reached an agreement and settlement with the Lord that should he act against him, he would thereby wish to lose the fief. Nevertheless, such a situation must still be declared through a judgment.

# Imperial Feudal Law

...and it is held thus: That the **vassal** <note>original: "Lehenmann"; a person granted the use of land in return for homage and service</note>, as soon as the judgment is passed, is obligated to deliver to the Lord or the **agnates** <note>original: "Agnaten"; relatives whose kinship is traced through the male line</note>, whichever party it was awarded to, all fruits and income he received from the time he forfeited the fief and acted in bad faith. From that point on, the fief no longer belonged to him but fell back to the Lord. Further mention of this shall be made later.

But what if the vassal committed a **felony** <note>original: "felony"; in feudal law, this specifically refers to a grave breach of the bond of trust and service between a vassal and their lord</note> against the Lord—that is, if he became unfaithful to the Lord or otherwise seriously harmed him, such that he would lose his fief—and yet the Lord did not challenge or sue the man during his lifetime? The question arises: can the Lord, after the vassal's death, sue the son for this or refuse to grant him the fief? Answer: No. For the father's crime may not harm the sons in this case. Unless the Lord did not know that the vassal had acted against him in such a manner; in that case, he could bring the son before the **feudal court** <note>original: "Lehengericht"; a specialized court dealing with disputes over land held in fief</note> even after the father's death. For no one is considered to have given up their right through ignorance. Secondly, if the Lord had prepared to sue the vassal but the man died before the suit began, the son would have to answer for it. Thirdly, if the act was of such a nature that the man deprived himself of the fief by the deed itself—as mentioned above—since such an act brings immediate execution of the penalty, the son could also be sued for it.

Conversely, if the Lord knew the vassal had harmed him but did not sue, even though he was able to do so, then the Lord's son would not be heard if he tried to sue the vassal after his father's death. Because the father did not sue, it is assumed he forgave and pardoned the **felony** or injury; for just as such things happen, the Lord may also forgive the man.

However, if the Lord were a **prelate** <note>A high-ranking church official, such as a bishop or abbot</note>, such as an abbot or bishop, he could not pardon the **felony** of the vassal without the consent of the **college, chapter** <note>original: "Collegij/ Capitels"; the governing body or assembly of the religious institution</note>, or assembly, unless the injury affected only the person of the prelate himself.

Finally, consider such a case. The Lord had promised and agreed to give me a fief and invest me with it. But before the investiture takes place, I commit an offense against the Lord and harm him. I nevertheless petition the court to order the Lord to deliver the promised fief and invest me. The Lord **files an exception** <note>original: "excipiert"; from the Latin *exceptio*, a legal defense used to block a claim</note> and says he is not obligated to do so because I acted against him and harmed him. If the Lord proves this **exception** against me, he is not obligated (despite his previous promise) to deliver the fief. However, if the Lord cannot prove such an **exception** immediately, and the matter would cause a long delay for further investigation, then the Lord should deliver the fief to the man and invest him with it—though **without prejudice** <note>original: "unbégebeñ"; meaning the Lord retains the right to pursue the matter later</note> to what he might have to say regarding the **felony** and injury. # How the Lord Forfeits His Fief.

Hitherto it has been shown at length how and in what cases the **vassal** <note>original: "Lehenmañ"; a person granted the use of land in return for homage and service</note> loses his fief to his Lord. Now it will also be necessary to see whether and in which cases the **Feudal Lord** <note>original: "Leher"; likely an OCR shortening of Lehenherr</note> loses or forfeits his fief or the **ownership** <note>original: "eigenthumb"; here meaning suzerainty or the ultimate proprietary right to the land</note> of the fief to his man. And so that we may come quickly to the matter and avoid long-windedness, it is necessary to note well this **feudal law rule** <note>original: "Lehenrechts Regel"</note>: namely, that the Lord can lose the ownership he has over the fief to the vassal in all cases in which the man would forfeit his fief to the Lord. And it applies equally whether the vassal has **sworn** <note>original: "geschworen"; taken a formal oath of loyalty</note> to the Lord or not. In such a case, the Feudal Lord and the man shall be treated equally. However, if the vassal refused or had refused to perform his feudal duty, and yet was obliged to perform it, the Lord might have injured him without being so greatly at fault that he would have forfeited his ownership over him.

Regarding the cited rule, it follows that if the Lord violates the **spouse** <note>original: "gesponß"</note> or the wife of the man, or dishonors or misleads his daughter or sister, or gives evil incitement or makes indecent advances, etc.—as was previously detailed regarding the vassal—then he has lost his ownership to the vassal.

Likewise, if the Lord murders his own brother or his brother’s son, and is burdened with the crime of **parricide** <note>original: "Parricidij"; in this legal context, the murder of a close relative or a person to whom one owes a special duty</note>, as mentioned above: and if he is not only convicted of this but a criminal sentence has also been passed, such that he is not good enough for the man to serve as a Feudal Lord, then he has lost ownership of the fief in the same manner as the vassal forfeits his fief to the Lord in such cases, as has been indicated.

Further, just as the **vassal** <note>original: "Vasall"</note> loses his fief if he does not seek it from the Lord within the proper time when it becomes vacant, so too if the Lord does not grant the fief to the vassal upon his request within the proper time, he loses his ownership of it.

If the Lord’s son should also injure the vassal, the Feudal Lord is obliged to deliver the son to him so that he may punish him for the mistreatment he committed against the vassal, in the same manner as was stated above regarding the **son of the vassal**. Otherwise, if the Feudal Lord does not do so, the son shall lose the ownership [succession rights] if he intends to follow the father; thus, the vassal would not be obliged to recognize him as a Feudal Lord, as the **feudal laws** <note>original: "Lehenrecht"</note> clearly show. How this is maintained, however, one will have to learn well from experience.

Likewise, as the vassal loses the fief if he alters it in an unlawful manner, as cited above, so must the Feudal Lord...

In the same manner, if the Lord refused to grant the vassal his right and justice—that is, if he denied the vassal legal process, primarily in that the Lord, upon the vassal's request, did not convene the **Peers of the Court** <note>original: "Pares Curiæ"; these were fellow vassals of equal rank who served as a jury to ensure a fair trial according to feudal custom</note>, or if a dispute arose concerning the fief and the Lord would not hold the other vassals to their duty to testify about it, etc.—then he would be deprived of his **ownership** <note>original: "Eigenthumb"; in this context, the Lord's superior right to the land, which would then pass fully to the vassal</note>. He would forfeit it no less than the vassal would forfeit the land to the Lord if the vassal had denied the Lord his legal rights, as heard above.

However, if the **Feudal Lord** is a **Prelate** <note>original: "Prelat"; a high-ranking church official such as a bishop or abbot</note> and commits an offense against the vassal such that he forfeits ownership through his misconduct, the vassal retains that ownership of the fief only as long as the Prelate is alive. After the death of the Prelate, the land reverts back to the Church. This is because, as indicated earlier in this chapter, if the **vassal** <note>original: "Vasall"</note> were a Prelate and injured the Lord in such a way that he lost the fief, the Lord would keep it as long as the Prelate lived, but no longer.

From these examples and cases, one may also understand others that might arise, according to the rule: in whatever cases the vassal loses his fief to the Lord, in those same cases the Lord can also lose the ownership he holds over the fief to the vassal. Yet, the vassal should be very careful if he wishes to sue the Lord, ensuring he has a certain case and that the injury is sufficient under feudal law, so that a judgment is not rendered against him instead.

## To whom vacated fiefs revert.

Now follows the second part of this chapter, namely, to whom **vacated fiefs** <term>original: "eröffneten Lehen"; a fief that has become "open" or available because the previous holder's rights have ended</term> revert. Regarding this, one must clearly understand that fiefs are vacated or made available in four ways.

First, when someone **renounces** <note>original: "auffsaget"</note> or surrenders his fief to the Lord.
Second, when the fief becomes vacant through death <note>meaning the holder died without legal heirs</note>.
Third, if someone forfeits the fief.
Fourth, when someone is unable to hold the fief due to a physical or legal disability.

As far as the renunciation of fiefs is concerned, it is handled in this way: Although the Feudal Lord and the vassal are considered equal in many matters and cases—so that what is right for one should also be right for the other, as has been heard—one might conclude from this that it would not be proper for a vassal to renounce the fief against the Lord's will, otherwise the Lord should also be allowed to do the same, which would not be inconsistent with **Common Law** <note>original: "Gemeinen rechten"; likely referring to Roman Law influences prevalent in the Empire</note>. But despite such arguments, it is clearly provided for and permitted in feudal law that the vassal may surrender his fief to the Lord even against the Lord's will. For

# A Brief Excerpt of the...

It is a clear point of law that anyone may waive and renounce a benefit that has been granted to them by right. Since a **vassal** <note>original: "Lehen" (here referring to the person holding the fief); usually "Lehenmann"</note> cannot terminate his **fief** <term>fief: a landed estate held by a vassal from a Lord in exchange for military service and loyalty</term> to the detriment of the Lord—as the Lord is to expect no harm from it, but only benefit—it is not unfairly ordained in **feudal law** <note>original: "Lehenrecht"</note> that, in this case, the Lord’s intent shall not be considered the same as the vassal’s. This means that the Lord may not renounce or revoke the vassal's fief against his will in the same way that the vassal has the power to do here. And this principle also holds even if the **vassal** <note>the text is clipped: "Lehenmann"</note> had previously granted that same fief to another person; for he may certainly surrender it to the Lord and divest himself of the rights he held.

Although it was stated earlier in this chapter that the right of the **recipient** <note>original: "Nemers"; the one receiving the fief</note> cannot last longer than that of the **grantor** <note>original: "Gebers"; the one giving the fief</note>, but that one must end with the other—from which it would follow that through such a surrender, the **sub-vassal** <term>sub-vassal: a person who holds a portion of a fief from a primary vassal rather than directly from the high Lord</term> must also lose his **sub-fief** <note>original: "Vnterlehen"</note> and be turned out—nonetheless, this specific rule does not apply here. Instead, the **sub-vassal** <note>the text is clipped: "Affterlehenmann"</note> nonetheless remains in possession of his fief, even if his Lord (the primary vassal) has terminated it. This is provided that he offers to serve the high Lord and acknowledges him as his **Feudal Lord**. However, he may not sue his immediate Lord for **warranty** <term>warranty: a legal guarantee (Gewehr) that the grantor has the right to give the land and will defend the recipient's title</term>, because he knew that his Lord also held the land as a fief from another and that it was not his own property. Thus, his right as the recipient cannot last longer than that of the grantor, as just mentioned. Had he not known this, it would be different, and he would have cause to sue for the warranty. The same applies if the sub-vassal had a specific promise and agreement regarding the warranty.

Furthermore, regarding this point of the renunciation of fiefs, it should be noted: if a man surrenders his fief to the Lord and it is a **new fief** <term>new fief: a "feudum novum," or a fief granted for the first time to a specific individual rather than one inherited through generations</term>, it reverts to the Lord, regardless of the fact that this harms the sons. This is unless the aforementioned fief was initially granted by the Lord not only for the sake of the father but also in consideration of the sons.

If, however, it is an **ancestral fief** <term>ancestral fief: an "alt Lehen" or "feudum antiquum," which has been passed down through a family</term> and is renounced by the vassal, it falls to the **male bodily heirs** <note>original: "Männlichen Leibslehens Erben"</note>. In this case, it is all the same whether the vassal renounced it specifically for the benefit of the sons or simply in general.

How a fief becomes vacated and "open," and to whom it reverts in the event of death, is sufficiently explained at greater length above in the eighth chapter, where it is stated how one person should succeed another in a fief.

A fief is also vacated through **infirmity** <note>original: "gebrechlichkeit"</note> and falls to the Lord if the person who would otherwise be entitled to the fief (provided he were not incapacitated) is either mute, deaf, or a cripple. When such a case occurs, if it is an ancestral fief, it falls to the sons or brothers—except in those cases where they cannot keep the fief, as mentioned before. But if it is a new fief and the vassal cannot succeed to it due to infirmity, it falls back to the Lord, who then excludes both sons and kinsmen.

If a vassal were to become a priest or a monk—as sometimes happens—and therefore could not keep his **fief** <term>fief: a landed estate held by a vassal from a Lord in exchange for military service and loyalty</term>, the following occurs: if it is a **new fief** <term>new fief: a property recently granted to a specific person for the first time</term>, the fief passes to the sons, if any are present. If no son is present, it reverts to the Lord. However, if it is an **old fief** <term>old fief: an ancestral estate that has been passed down through a family line</term>, it passes to the sons; or in their absence, to the closest **agnates** <term>agnates: male relatives related through a common male ancestor</term>, and not to the Lord, according to the ordinances of feudal law.

We have previously discussed at length how fiefs are "opened" <note>The "opening" of a fief refers to it becoming vacant and available for a new grant, often due to the death of a vassal without heirs or due to a legal forfeiture</note> through misconduct, and the various ways vassals may forfeit them. Regarding the point when such forfeited fiefs revert to the Lord, there is extensive debate, as fiefs are forfeited not only through **unauthorized transfer** <term>unauthorized transfer: also known as "alienation," this is the act of selling, gifting, or mortgaging a fief without the Lord's permission</term> but also through other forms of misconduct. Therefore, regarding such transfers, you must take careful note of the following conclusions.

## The First Conclusion.

Whenever a new fief is transferred in an improper manner, it immediately reverts to the Lord, as stated above. In such a case, both the sons and the agnates must be excluded and shall be deprived of it. However, if an old fief is transferred in such a manner, it passes to the agnates and not to the Lord, and the sons are excluded. But where the fief has been transferred in a reasonable or permissible manner, the son may revoke the transfer, and the agnates must allow him to do so. If the son had received nothing from his father’s **inheritance** <note>original: "Erbschafft"</note>, even if the fief were transferred in an improper manner, he must still be permitted access to it and cannot be forced out or excluded from it.

## The Second Conclusion.

Should it happen that two brothers make a **pact** <note>original: "pact" (agreement)</note> with one another that one shall succeed the other upon his death and inherit from him, and in the meantime, one of them improperly transfers the fief, then upon the death of that brother, the fief reverts to the Lord, and the surviving brother is excluded.

## The Third Conclusion.

A **vassal** <note>original: "Lehenmann"</note> may certainly transfer and sell the **fruits** <term>fruits: the crops, rents, or profits generated by the land, as opposed to the ownership of the land itself</term> of the fief for a specific, named period of time; he does not lose his rights to the fief in favor of the Lord through such a transfer.

### A brief excerpt of the

...judgment were awarded; likewise, if such a thing happens through an amicable agreement, without malice and deceit, or if the **vassal** <term>vassal: (Lehenmann) a person who holds land from a Lord in exchange for loyalty and service</term> did not know that it was a **fief** <term>fief: (Lehen) an estate of land held on condition of feudal service</term>, etc., then no such modified fief is "opened" <note>An "opened" fief (geöffnet) is one that has become vacant and available for the Lord to reclaim or reassign.</note> to anyone, as has been set forth more extensively above.

But concerning the misconduct or injury committed by the man against the Lord, through which he loses his fief, the following conclusions are to be noted.

## The First Conclusion.

In those cases where the **vassal** is deprived of his property, his sons and other descendants are likewise deprived of it, whether the forfeiture occurred against the Lord or against others. For just as the father, through such forfeiture, becomes unfit to represent the fief with honor, so too the son becomes unfit and cannot be considered a **vassal**. This would only be otherwise if the fief had been given to the father in such a way that his sons and all descendants should be enfeoffed with it, or had already been enfeoffed, as is commonly the custom. For if the enfeoffment had occurred in such a manner, the father's misconduct could not cause harm, since they would follow the fief not through the person of the father, but for themselves and by reason of their own acquired rights.

Secondly, if the fief, at the time the father forfeited it, were still in the hands of the grandfather. For if the father should die during the grandfather’s lifetime, or were deprived of the succession of the fief by a judgment because of such misconduct, and then the grandfather died, the injury caused by the father could not harm the grandson. However, if the grandson's father—that is, the grandfather's son—had followed his father into the fief and received it, then the grandson would inherit through the person of the father and not the grandfather. Therefore, the misconduct of his father could indeed harm him in that case.

## The Second Conclusion.

If the **vassal** <term>vassal: (Vasall) a subordinate holder of a fief</term> should injure the Lord or commit an offense against him upon a specific proposal or intention—namely, so that he might forfeit the fief and thereby perhaps deprive the **agnates** <term>agnates: (Agnaten) male-line relatives who share a common male ancestor</term> of it—in this case, it is held that the Lord may not take it. Instead, it remains with the **agnates**, which is also the common practice among the Germans.

## The Third Conclusion.

If a **new fief** is forfeited by the **vassal** through an injury against the Lord of the fief, the same immediately reverts to the Lord, and neither the **agnates** nor the descendants may have any part in it.

## The Fourth Conclusion.

If the **vassal** <term>vassal: (Lehenmann) a person holding land from a Lord</term> injures the Lord and holds an old or ancestral fief, and he forfeits the same through the injury, then the fief reverts to the Lord and excludes both the descendants and the **agnates** <term>agnates: (Agnaten) relatives related through the male line</term>. <note>original: "gloss. in Para final. c. 1. de pace iuramento firman Francif. Cur. in quinta principali parte, sic tenet, & pulchrè declarat." — This refers to a legal commentary on the "Peace Confirmed by Oath" section of feudal law, cited by the jurist Franciscus Curtius, who "holds this view and declares it beautifully."</note>

However, if the injury occurred with the Lord's knowledge, perhaps specifically so that the fief might be taken away from the agnates; likewise, if the Lord gave the vassal cause for the forfeiture, or otherwise turned a blind eye, etc.—in such a case, the fief would not fall to the Lord, but rather to the agnates.

But if the Lord injures the vassal, or insults him, whereby the vassal is provoked to self-defense and in such defense injures the Lord in return, the vassal cannot be punished with the loss of the fief for that reason.

Furthermore, if the vassal were enfeoffed in such a way, and the feudal deed so stated, that the fief should pass from one to another, or that many had earned such a fief together, and one of them committed an offense against the Lord such that he was judged to have forfeited his fief, the fief would not fall to the Lord for that reason, but rather to the others who were enfeoffed with it at the same time, according to the wording of the enfeoffment. As was also indicated above, in certain cases the sons are not excluded.

In the same manner, if a fief were granted to a man because he had saved the Lord from death, robbers, or otherwise from the hands of enemies: in such a case, he could not be deprived of the fief for any kind of guilt or ingratitude.

## The Fifth Conclusion.

If the vassal does not commit a crime against the Lord himself, but otherwise forfeits and behaves in such a way that he must lose the fief—such as if he were to slay his own brother, or otherwise commit a murder against a blood relative—if the fief were new, it could not fall to the descendants nor to the agnates, but directly to the Lord. But if it were an ancestral or old fief, the Lord is excluded, as are the descendants, and the forfeited fief falls to the

If, however, the witnesses were of such a character that they had a bad reputation among honorable people, the Lord shall leave the vassal unburdened by this and shall not be heard in the matter. <note>original Latin: "c. 1. quot testes sint necessa. ad probandam ingra." — referring to Chapter 1: How many witnesses are necessary to prove ingratitude.</note>

If the vassal dies before the 14th day of February, the fruits of the fief from that same year belong to the Lord. If, however, the vassal dies after the 14th day of February and before the month of August, the fruits belong to the heirs. If he dies after the month of August, the Lord takes the fruits. This is to be understood, according to the opinion of the most prominent **feudalists** <term>feudalists: (Feudisten) legal scholars specializing in feudal law</term>, as follows: that one begins to count the year from September until the **Calends of March** <note>original: "Calendas Martias"</note>, which is, as mentioned, around the 14th of February. Now, if the vassal dies during that time, the heirs take nothing of the fruits of that year until September. But if he dies after the 14th of February until the month of August, including that month, up until September, then the fruits belong to the heirs: as one may see further in **Alvarotto** <note>Jacobus Alvarotto (1385–1453), a highly influential Italian legal scholar who wrote extensively on feudal law.</note>.

## The Eleventh Chapter.

<image-desc>A large ornamental drop cap 'A' decorated with flowing vines and grape clusters, initiating the first paragraph of the chapter.</image-desc>

In order that one may better navigate these matters, it is first necessary to know regarding this eleventh chapter: Although the vassals whom one calls **Peers of the Court** <term>Peers of the Court: (Pares Curiæ) vassals of equal rank who sat in judgment over one another</term> are usually appointed to judge in matters concerning fiefs, not all vassals are called **Peers of the Court**. Rather, they are distinguished in such a way that those are considered **Peers of the Court** whom a Prince, Count, or Lord has sitting under him in his Principality, County, or Lordship, and who belong together in one **legal assembly** <term>legal assembly: (geding) a specific jurisdictional district or court meeting</term>.

However, those who live outside the Principality and do not belong to the same assembly, and yet nevertheless hold fiefs from the same Prince or Count, may not be called **Peers of the Court** along with the others. For example, the vassals in **Austria** are Peers of the Court among one another; likewise, the vassals in the **Breisgau** <note>A historical region in southwestern Germany.</note> are also Peers of the Court among one another. Austria and those in the Breisgau are not called **Peers of the Court** <note>original Latin: "Pares Curiæ" — vassals of the same rank who serve in the lord's court</note> together, but each part for itself: even if they are all vassals of the same Prince, they are considered separately. Secondly, it is to be known that some **fiefs** <term>fief: (Lehen) an estate of land held on condition of feudal service</term> are called **chamber fiefs** <term>chamber fief: (Kammerlehen) a fief where the lord retains the majority of the income or "rents" while granting a portion to the vassal</term>; that is, when the Lord has certain rents and income from a village or farm and enfeoffs someone with it, yet keeps the major portion for himself. Others are called fiefs outside the chamber, namely when the Lord grants someone an estate or farm in a village, along with certain appurtenances, as well as the jurisdiction and **ban** <note>the legal power to command, prohibit, and punish</note> in the village.

But so that this point may be understood somewhat more clearly, this is the general meaning: The Lords who have outlying estates, villages, or their own territory usually have a **manorial court** <term>manorial court: (Dinghoff or Curia) a central administrative and legal hub for a specific district</term> in that same district, to which the other surrounding villages and subjects must be drawn and hold themselves, and from which they truly take their origin. Now, if the Lord grants one of these properties as a fief or **sub-fief** <term>sub-fief: (Afterlehen) a fief granted by a vassal to another person</term> to someone, it is called a **court fief** <term>court fief: (Curtlehen)</term> because it originally belonged to the Lord’s castle or estate.

But when the Lord, who has jurisdiction and authority in a village or castle, grants certain fiefs that are incorporated into the manorial court—as often happens with **soldier's fiefs** or **steward's fiefs** <term>steward's fief: (Vogtlehen) land granted in exchange for acting as a protector or administrator</term>, as mentioned above—or when a fief is granted for a time to an advocate, notary, or procurator <note>a legal representative</note>: these are fiefs that are *not* incorporated into the manorial court or the lordly court. This agrees closely with what was stated above.

As far as the vassals called **Peers of the Court** <note>original Latin: "Pares Curiæ"</note> are concerned, it is clearly to be understood from what was said at the beginning of this chapter: if it happens that the Lord must hold a **vassal court** <term>vassal court: (Manngericht) a court where a lord’s vassals sit as judges over their fellow vassals</term> and appoint the men who can and should be summoned for it, these should specifically be those who belong to the manorial court or *Curia* and are seated within that same Principality, County, or Lordship. For one often sees that the Lords, for such a vassal court, also summon and appoint those who do not belong to that jurisdiction and are seated in another district; conversely, they leave out those who belong to it by inheritance and are incorporated into that manorial court. This is an error and rightly should not happen.

Furthermore, it is to be known here that among the martial <note>war-ready or knightly</note> feudal people, there are some who, besides the fief that is in dispute, also hold several other fiefs from the Lord which are not contested. Others, however, have no other fief from the Lord except the one in dispute. We shall call the first group "proper and certain **vassals**" <term>vassal: (Vaſall) a person who owes loyalty and service to a lord in exchange for land</term>, but the others we call "uncertain"—perhaps because if they lose the disputed fief by law, they can then no longer be the Lord's men, since they otherwise hold nothing as a fief from the Lord.

Now, in the following part of this chapter, we wish to handle two things. First: who may properly judge in feudal law. Second: what kind of process should be followed in feudal law.

...second, between the Lord and the **vassal**. Third, between the vassal and a stranger who is not a vassal. Fourth, between the Lord and a stranger who does not belong before a feudal court. Of these four, we wish to set down the following propositions.

### The first proposition.

Those who are **Captains** <term>Captains: (Capitanier) high-ranking vassals who hold their land directly from the sovereign</term>—that is, those who are enfeoffed by the Emperor or King (as mentioned above in the second chapter), such as Princes, Marquises, Counts, etc.—if two of them have business with one another and each claims he is enfeoffed by the Emperor or King, then the Emperor or King alone has the authority to judge the matter. Likewise, this holds for vassals of a lower status who are nevertheless enfeoffed by the Emperor or King; they also have the Emperor or King as their ordinary judge.

### The second proposition.

But if disputes regarding fiefs should arise among other **vavassors** <term>vavassors: (Vassasorn) vassals who hold their land from a lord other than the King, such as a baron or count</term> or vassals who are not enfeoffed by the Emperor, but have another feudal lord—even if they be **Bannerets** <term>Banneret: (Panerherr) a knight or lord entitled to lead a company of men into battle under his own banner</term>—whether the dispute concerns the whole fief, or part of the boundaries, or other appurtenances of the same: then the Lord of that fief has the right to judge the matter, without the presence of the other vassals.

And this proposition also holds if the judge is an ecclesiastic and the vassals are secular, or if the judge is secular and the vassals are ecclesiastics. For in this case, the clergy are not only bound to appear before the secular judge, but that same judge may also carry out the execution of the sentence passed in such a matter; regardless of how the clergy are otherwise privileged and exempt from secular jurisdiction. <note>original Latin: "c. verum, & c. ex transmissa. de foro compe." These are citations to the Decretals of Gregory IX, a collection of canon law, specifically the title regarding "the competent court."</note>

### The third proposition.

If a dispute arises between two people, whether over the whole fief or over a part of the same, and one is a true and rightful vassal, but the other is not a true and rightful vassal: then that same dispute shall and must be settled before the **Peers of the Court** <note>original Latin: "Paribus Curiæ" — vassals of equal rank to the parties involved who serve as judges in the lord's court</note>, and thus be decided by the vassals.

And it is to be noted that those are called "rightful vassals" who hold from the Lord not only military fiefs, but also other fiefs that are not in dispute. The others, however, who hold nothing more than a military fief from the Lord, are called "uncertain" or "not rightful" vassals; perhaps for the reason that it is still uncertain whether he will keep the military fief and remain the Lord’s man or not, as mentioned above. ## The fourth proposition.

**IF** a dispute now arises over a fief between rightful or uncertain vassals <note>The text refers to "uncertain" vassals as those whose claim to hold the fief from the Lord is the very subject of the conflict.</note> (that is, those who do not hold their fief from the Lord, which is why the conflict arose, as shown above), and one party says it is an "old fief" <note>An "old fief" (alt Lehen) is one inherited through ancestry, whereas a "new fief" (new Lehen) is typically one recently granted or purchased.</note> while the other says it is a "new fief." If the one who claims it is a new fief demonstrates that he bought his portion of the fief from the Lord for money: then neither the Lord may be the judge—since he must stand as guarantor for the buyer of the fief—nor may the fellow vassals be judges, as they may reasonably be suspected of bias toward the buyer on the Lord's behalf. Therefore, in this case, the matter shall be brought before the [Lord's] sovereign and ordinary judge.

However, had he not bought it for money, the matter should be decided by the fellow vassals, provided that the Feudal Lord stays out of it; otherwise, it might appear that the Lord is representing his own interests and wishes to be the judge in his own cause.

If, however, both parties say it is an old fief, then the Lord shall decide the matter alongside the vassals. <note>original: "c. 1. de invest. in marit. fact." refers to a chapter in the *Libri Feudorum* (Books of Fiefs) regarding investments made by a husband.</note> And although it is not explicitly stated, reason dictates this, because the Lord cannot be suspected of bias in this instance, as he is not obligated to guarantee the title for either party.

Regarding this proposition, I must recount a case that occurred during the time of Emperor Maximilian <note>Maximilian I (reigned 1493–1519), known as the "Last Knight," who significantly reformed Imperial administration.</note>, as it belongs here and was finally settled only after great expense.

A certain nobleman named Tiz had an only son and held a magnificent fief. It happened that the son perished in the war. For this reason, the father petitioned His Imperial Majesty—to comfort him in his distress—that his daughters might be enfeoffed with the male-fiefs <term>male-fiefs: (Mannlehen) lands traditionally inheritable only by male descendants and usually closed to female heirs.</term> in the son's stead. His Imperial Majesty—not only as the Feudal Lord and Archduke of Austria but also as the Emperor acting out of his full power and authority—granted this, and provided the daughters with all the necessary legal documents to share in and hold the fief.

But when the agnates <term>agnates: (Agnaten) male relatives related through the father's side who would typically inherit if there were no direct male heirs.</term> learned of this, they opposed it. Subsequently, the matter was brought before the Court of Male-Fiefs <term>Court of Male-Fiefs: (Mannlehengericht) a specialized feudal court dealing with inheritance disputes over male-only estates.</term> at the Imperial Court. After long dispute and much quarreling, the matter was finally dismissed and the claim rejected, regardless of the Imperial enfeoffment and grant of grace. The nobility insisted so strongly on their customary feudal laws that even in such cases they do not ask much of the Lord; which is not unjust, for in all matters and dealings that come before the Feudal Lord...

In this regard, one should also note that if a case arises in which the Feudal Lord alone—or alongside those named with him—is or may be the judge, and yet the Lord refuses to act, thereby preventing the vassals from their rights, he then forfeits his jurisdiction. The matter may then be brought before the Sovereign or an ordinary judge to be complained of and resolved. The Feudal Lord may also be compelled by proper legal means to allow justice to be done for the vassals.

## The fifth proposition.

**WHEN** a dispute arises between the Lord and an external vassal—that is, one who holds his fief outside the Lord’s principality and lands—the matter must be carried out before the ordinary judge and not before the Court of Vassals <term>Mannlehengericht: A feudal court composed of a lord's vassals who acted as peers to judge disputes involving other vassals.</term>

In the same manner, when the Lord has a legal dispute with someone—or someone with the Lord—regarding a fief, but that person is not a vassal (for example, if a dispute arises over the boundaries or a pledge <term>Pfandschafft: A mortgage or security interest placed upon the land.</term> of the fief, or something similar), such a dispute does not belong before the vassals, but before the ordinary judge.

## The sixth proposition.

**HOWEVER,** if disputes arise between the Lord and his vassal, whether concerning investiture <term>belehnung: The formal ceremony and legal act of granting a fief.</term>, forfeiture, or the calling up of the fief, then the matter shall be judged by the fellow vassals. <term>Chapter 1, penultimate paragraph, concerning the prohibition of feudal alienation by Frederick <note>original Latin: "c. 1. Par. penul. de prohi. feud. alie. per fede." referring to a constitution of Emperor Frederick II in the *Libri Feudorum*.</note></term> In such a case, the vassals [to act as judges] shall be chosen by both parties. If they can reach an agreement, the matter proceeds; if not, the Lord may first choose one or more, and then the vassal shall choose just as many. In this way, one party chooses as many for the Court of Vassals as the other, and equality shall be maintained in this matter.

It is also held that this procedure may apply when a dispute arises between the Emperor himself—or another potentate <term>Potentaten: Powerful rulers or sovereign princes who recognize no higher earthly authority.</term> who has no superior lord—and a vassal. In such a case, the selection of the vassals to occupy the Court of Vassals shall be undertaken in no other way than as mentioned above.

Should a dispute arise, however, between a Lord who has a superior lord and an uncertain vassal—where the Lord does not wish to recognize or hold the person as a vassal and claims the estates are not fiefs but allodial lands <term>Erbgüter: Private property held in absolute ownership, inherited outside of the feudal system and free from its obligations.</term>—then the matter shall be brought before the ordinary judge, regardless of whether the Lord or the vassal brings the complaint. If the ordinary judge finds that it is indeed a matter belonging before the Court of Vassals, he shall remit <term>remittiren: To formally refer or send a case back to a different court or jurisdiction.</term> and direct the matter there.

<meta>This page continues the legal discussion regarding the composition and fairness of feudal courts, specifically addressing the rights of vassals to have an impartial hearing and the limitations of a Lord’s power to appoint judges unilaterally.</meta>

<header>A Short Extract of the</header>

Yet some Lords maintain the practice, when they have dealings with their vassals <term>Lehener: A tenant or vassal who holds land from a lord under the feudal system.</term>, of appointing the Feudal Court <term>Lehengericht: A specialized court that handled disputes regarding feudal tenure and land rights.</term> according to their own pleasure with associate judges, choosing the men for it alone, and completely excluding the other party—the vassal. This is not only contrary to Imperial Laws, but also to reason and equity. In a court (as mentioned above), a fair balance must be maintained, and no single side should have an advantage. Therefore, those who claim they are not obliged to stand before any men except those they themselves have chosen and appointed should not be heard, as such a situation carries a great suspicion of bias. Accordingly, Feudal Law well and rightly provides that in such cases, the vassals of the court shall not judge unless they have been appointed by the consent of both parties, or chosen alternately by each. For neither the Feudal Lord alone—nor alongside his men, if he were to expect a particular profit or benefit from the other—can be the judge; much less can they be judges in matters that concern themselves. If this were permitted, it would be nothing else than a man becoming his own judge in the person of another. For there is no distinction between the one who judges and the one who appoints another to be his judge. Since equality must be maintained in courts, as has been said, this custom can in no way be permitted or followed: namely, that the vassal must stand trial before the Feudal Court for the Lord, where the Lord alone has chosen and appointed the judges.

And even if a Lord wished to say that such a thing is the customary heritage <term>herkomen: Traditional or established custom that often held the weight of law in feudal territories.</term> in that place—that when the Feudal Lord has dealings with the vassal, or the vassal with the Feudal Lord, in matters belonging before the Feudal Court, the Lord has the power to choose the men at his pleasure and to seat the court—it is nevertheless held (subject to better judgment) that he should not be heard in this. This is despite the fact that custom is highly regarded and given great weight in Feudal Law. For such a custom, being clearly against the Law, may not stand. The natural Law also dictates otherwise, which says: What you do not wish to be done to you, do not impose upon another.

And since the Lords, without doubt, would not be so foolish as to wish to accept as judges those whom the vassal has proposed and chosen, they should fairly not exercise such an advantage themselves. And since this holds true for secular Feudal Lords, it should hold even more so for ecclesiastical Feudal Lords, as the Feudal Law says that the Church is a mirror of justice and lets no one be burdened against equity.

One should also know this: although the Court of Vassals <term>Mannlehengericht: A court made up of one's peers (other vassals) within the feudal hierarchy.</term> is an established right, it is not a "common law" <term>gemein Recht: Here referring to a general court accessible to all citizens for everyday disputes.</term> that anyone having business with a Lord or vassal might use. Rather, it is established only for the Feudal Lords and their vassals, and in matters concerning the fief. Therefore, if someone is summoned before such a court who does not belong there, it is not unnecessary for him to appear and show cause as to why he does not belong under that court’s jurisdiction. <note>original: "gloss. nota. c. 1. de invest. in maritum. ibi Doct."</note> See the noted gloss in Chapter 1 of "On the investiture of a husband," and the legal scholars cited there.

<header>Imperial Feudal Law. 415</header>

Here one might ask whether a vassal <term>Lehenmann: A person who holds land from a superior Lord in exchange for loyalty and service.</term> could also be compelled to sit down as a vassal-judge or associate, and to judge and pass sentence between the Lord and another vassal—just as judges are otherwise compelled to pass judgment in common Imperial laws? To this, it must be answered that, according to Feudal Law, the men <note>In this context, "men" refers specifically to the peers or fellow vassals of the court.</note> may not be forced to take a seat: unless it were the case that he had already helped to begin the court proceedings, or that the vassal had sworn to do so alongside others during his investiture <note>The formal ceremony where a vassal receives his land/title from the Lord.</note> (as is usually brought about by the common wording of the feudal oath, where the vassal swears to sit at the Lord’s request and to judge between the Lord and a vassal, and to grant justice to every party). However, where the men cannot be found, or where they refuse to take their seats, they must, in the event of their dispute or disagreement, go before the ordinary judge and let the matter be decided there.

Secondly, it might be asked: if a dispute regarding possession <term>Possessorij: Legal matters concerning the right to current possession of property rather than ultimate ownership.</term> should arise in the vassal-court, whether the vassals have the power to judge therein. Although many different opinions have been held on this by the feudalists <term>Feudisten: Legal scholars who specialized in the study and interpretation of feudal law.</term>, it is nevertheless considered that this case also belongs before the vassal-court like others. This is done in such a way that if a dispute should occur between two vassals—so that they are in conflict over possession—the Feudal Lord may judge and pass sentence upon it. But if the dispute is between the Feudal Lord and a vassal, it is proper that the matter be carried out before the fellow vassals.

But what if the Lord "spoils" the man, and thus removes him from his fief by force, or drives him out, or has done him violence in other ways? May the vassal then sue him for a criminal act, or otherwise with sharp words, such as an **interdict regarding force** <note>original: "interdicto vnde vi." This is a Roman legal action used to recover property that was taken by force.</note>—that is, claiming that he has done him violence? To this, it is to be answered that the vassal should not sue the Lord either for a criminal offense or with other sharp, insulting words. Rather, if he has cause to complain against the Lord, he should bring it forward with simple and mild words, in such a way that he does not attack or injure the Lord’s honor.

Furthermore, can the vassals be recused <note>To challenge or disqualify a judge on the grounds of bias or conflict of interest.</note> as suspicious judges and rejected like other judges? To this I say briefly: No. For since the vassal-court or Feudal Court is an ordinary jurisdiction (as was mentioned above) and is clearly provided for in common Imperial laws—which state that an ordinary judge may not be rejected as "suspicious"—then the vassals likewise cannot be recused and rejected. However, it is permitted by law that if the vassals consider themselves too biased, one may be appointed to join them in holding the vassal-court, so that such suspicion may be removed and completely cut off.

# A short extract / of the
eight. Now follows the second part, in which the process of the Vassal Court <term>Manngericht: A specialized court where a Lord’s peers or other vassals acted as judges in matters of feudal law.</term> shall be handled. However, we do not wish to set down everything at length here—namely, how one should issue citations and other legal documents—but rather the Feudal Laws shall be examined for that purpose. <note>original: "Gloss. mag. c. 1. de milite vasal." — This refers to a standard legal gloss or commentary on the laws regarding knights and vassals.</note> Furthermore, the Imperial Laws provide sufficiently and at length on these matters. Therefore, we wish to set down several conclusions regarding the proof and the tender of the oath, and when the Lord is obliged to perform the investiture <term>Belehnung: The formal ceremony where a Lord grants land or a title to a vassal.</term>, and similar matters in succession.

## The first Conclusion.

**F**irstly, when the Lord dies, and the vassal comes before the Lord's son or the new Liege Lord and requests to be invested anew, presenting the letters of fief <note>Formal documents proving the vassal's right to the land.</note> which the previous Liege Lord had given him, and the new Liege Lord refuses to acknowledge them, then the vassal can legally bring him before the Peers of the Court <term>Paribus Curiæ: The fellow vassals of the same rank who served as the judges of the feudal court.</term>. The peers shall then legally direct and require the Lord to grant the vassal oral investiture until the matter reaches a judicial resolution. At that time, and not before, shall the vassal perform his proper feudal duty <note>The "Lehenpflicht" included the oath of fealty and the promise of service.</note> to the Lord.

If, however, the vassal also held other fiefs from the Lord which the Lord acknowledged and which were not in dispute, the vassal-judges shall recognize the investiture for those, and the man shall immediately perform the feudal duty to the Lord, regardless of the fact that the disputed fief has not yet been decided. From this, two things follow:

The first is that a true vassal—namely, one who holds more than one undisputed fief from the Lord (as explained above)—is obliged to do homage <term>Huldung: A formal declaration of loyalty and submission to a lord.</term> to the Lord, even if he is only orally invested and the disagreement over the disputed fief remains undecided between the Lord and him, because it can bring him no disadvantage or danger.

The second is that an uncertain vassal, even if he has received oral investiture, may not be forced to perform the feudal duty until the main legal case has reached its proper conclusion.

## The second Conclusion.

**W**hen it is found that a property is indeed a valid fief, but only the status of it is in dispute—such as when one person claims it is an ancient fief <note>An "alt Lehen" was one inherited through generations, often carrying more prestige or different rights than a "new" one.</note> and the other claims it is a new fief, or one claims it is a true and proper fief and the other that it is not a proper fief, etc.—it shall be held to be an ancient rather than a new fief, or a true and proper fief rather than an uncertain fief, unless there is some strong evidence to the contrary. <term>original Latin: "c. 1. Par. final. de gradib. succes. & c. 1. si de feudo controuerf. fuerit inter dom. & vasal." — These refer to chapters in the "Books of Fiefs" regarding the degrees of succession and disputes between lords and vassals.</term>

### The third Conclusion.

From this follows the third conclusion: namely, if someone wishes to qualify a thing—whether he be the plaintiff or the defendant—such as if he wanted to say this was a Bailiff's Fief <term>Schultheiß Lehen: A fief granted specifically to support the office of a village magistrate or bailiff.</term> or a Pledge Fief <term>Pfandlehen: A fief held as security for a debt or mortgage.</term>, then he must prove that specific quality. However, if the other party wishes to present and prove the contrary—that the Bailiff’s or Pledge Fief had been turned into a proper, hereditary fief—he shall also be heard and permitted to do so.

### The fourth Conclusion.

When a vassal quarrels with the Lord, or two vassals quarrel with each other over a property, although the one who possesses the disputed <note>original: "kriegische" — literally "war-like," but used here in the legal sense of "litigated" or "contested."</note> fief does not have to provide proof (and is spared from doing so), the oath shall nevertheless be imposed upon him in the event that the opposing party cannot provide proof. However, how this conclusion is to be understood, and when it takes effect, you may see further in the next chapter under the first conclusion.

### The fifth Conclusion.

When two people quarrel over a fief, whichever party then presents sufficient proof has won the case; there is no doubt about this, as it is a fact in itself. But if the one who is supposed to provide proof proves nothing, then the oath <note>Specifically a "supplementary oath" used to settle a case when evidence is insufficient.</note> shall be imposed upon the other party who possesses the property. If, however, neither party is in possession of the property, and one party manages to bring forward half-proof <note>A legal concept where evidence is suggestive but not conclusive on its own.</note>, then the oath shall be granted to him to complete such proof. If both parties are equal in their proof, it is left to the discretion of the judge to decide upon which party he wishes to impose the oath. <note>original: "cap. 1. Par. sacramentum, de consuet. recti feud." — Chapter 1, Paragraph "The Oath," concerning the customs of proper feudal law.</note>

### The sixth Conclusion.

Lastly, if a disagreement and dispute arises regarding the additions or growth of a fief <note>Referring to "accession," such as new land formed by a river or additional rights attached to the original grant.</note>, and the vassal proves through the documents of investiture that such additions belong to him, he shall rightfully be left in possession of them. If he cannot prove it, but wishes to maintain his claim with an oath, he shall be permitted to do so. One may also impose the oath upon him, unless the Lord could prove that he had reserved such rights for himself in the investiture, or that he held the same in possession and title <term>Gewehr: A technical legal term for "seisin" or the outward manifestation of legal possession.</term>. <note>original: "cap. 1. Parag. si quis de manso. de controuerse. inuesti." — Chapter 1, Paragraph "If anyone [disputes] a farmstead," concerning the controversy of investiture.</note>

And it is also to be known here that in a Feudal Court <term>Lehengericht: A court specifically for feudal matters, presided over by the Lord and his vassals.</term>, other witnesses are not used nor permitted except for those who are the Lord’s invested men <note>Vassals of the same Lord who are peers of the litigants.</note>; although in certain cases, other witnesses might have been permitted at times. For instance, when an oath has been imposed upon someone, and twelve others were sworn with him—

### The twelfth and last Chapter.

<image-desc>A large ornamental drop cap 'A' featuring intricate floral scrollwork and leaf patterns within a square frame.</image-desc>
At the beginning of this book it was mentioned / that some are proper and natural / while others are improper or unnatural fiefs. Since it is now established / which are proper and natural fiefs / one can then easily judge / what unnatural / improper / or atypical fiefs are.

Briefly, however, proper and natural fiefs have this nature about them.
First, that they are inherited and pass from one to the next through the male feudal heirs <term>Agnaten: Male relatives descended from a common male ancestor; in feudal law, these were the primary heirs to a fief.</term> / forever and ever.
Second, that they proceed freely from the gracious benevolence of the Lord / so that they are given to each person by the Lord.

Third / that the vassal <term>Vasall: A person who held land under the feudal system in exchange for loyalty and service to a lord.</term> binds himself in return to the Lord with the duty of an oath / to earn such fiefs in a proper manner / and likewise to be true and loyal to the same.

Fourth / that they are immovable goods <note>In legal terms, "immovable goods" refers primarily to land and the buildings permanently attached to it.</note> / or the equivalent thereof.

Fifth / that such fiefs cannot be changed / without the prior knowledge of the Lord / and the nearest male kin.

Sixth and last / that righteous fiefs cannot be taken from the feudal tenant without a specific forfeit <note>original: "verwirc-kung" — a legal term for the loss of a right or property due to a crime or breach of contract.</note>: unless / he were to renounce them by his own will.

These points are typical of proper fiefs / and define what such fiefs are. Those, however, which do not have this character and nature / but rather acquire another quality through a contract or otherwise / are not proper and natural / but rather improper and unnatural fiefs.

And if someone wished to say / that this or that was not a proper or natural fief / he must prove it. For every fief is held to be proper and natural / unless the opposite is demonstrated. *Salicetus in the law "neque," the Code, on proofs.* <note>original: "Salice. in l. neq; C. de proba." — A reference to the legal scholar Bartholomaeus Salicetus (1348–1411) commenting on the *Codex Justinianus* (the Code of Justinian) regarding the burden of proof.</note> Just as otherwise, according to common Imperial Law / every person is considered upright and honorable / until something else is proven against him.

<meta>This page continues the final chapter regarding the classification of fiefs, moving from the definition of "natural" (standard, hereditary) fiefs to "unnatural" or "improper" fiefs, specifically focusing on those granted for a fixed term or specific administrative office.</meta>

# Imperial Feudal Law.

Which, however, are improper or unnatural fiefs will be understood through the following conclusions. First, one should know this for a clear understanding of the matter: namely, that although a feudal estate is sometimes granted in such a way that it has several unnatural parts, it nevertheless remains proper and natural in other points. For example, if the Lord has permitted the vassal to secure a sum of money against the fief, or allowed that daughters may also succeed in such a fief. These points are indeed contrary to the proper and natural type of fief, but they do not thereby make the entire fief unnatural or improper. Now we will set down the conclusions one after another.

### The first conclusion.

First, the Office Fiefs <term>Vogtlehen: Fiefs granted in connection with a specific office or "Vogtei" (bailiwick), often involving administrative or protective duties over a territory or castle.</term> are contrary to the species and nature of proper fiefs: for the Lords may take these back to themselves after the end of the year, which cannot happen in proper fiefs. And the Lord is not obligated to return the entry fee <term>Lehengelt: A fee paid by the vassal to the lord upon being granted the fief.</term> to the man in that case. They are called Office Fiefs when a Lord grants someone an office, castle, or lordship to rule, protect, and preserve, and enfeoffs him with it for one year or longer. Now, when that same time has expired, the fief is at an end, and the Lord may take it back to himself to give to another and enfeoff him with it, if he does not wish to let the first man have it any longer. <note>original: "c. 1. de feu. Guar. & ibi Iacobi de Bel." referring to the Libri Feudorum, "Concerning the Garrison," and the legal commentary by Jacobus de Belvisio.</note>

From this it follows that if a Lord appoints and accepts someone as a Procurator <term>Procurator: A legal representative or fiscal agent.</term>, Advocate, or Chancellor, and then enfeoffs him with such service-money, he may revoke such a fief after the expiration of the year—or the term of the enfeoffment—and take it back to enfeoff another with it. Some wish to include here the fiefs called Magistrate's Fiefs <term>Schultheißlehen: Fiefs associated with the office of a local judge or administrative official.</term> or Shield Fiefs <term>Schildlehen / feuda scutifera: Fiefs traditionally held by those of knightly rank, sometimes associated with specific military service or symbols.</term>. They are, however, not common in German lands, and the situation is much like our Leasehold Estates <term>Lasgüter: Lands granted to tenants for a specific term or under specific conditions, rather than as a permanent hereditary fief.</term>, which are also granted to people for a term of years. If, however, a Lord wanted to revoke or take back such an Office Fief before the appointed time, this would not be permitted—especially if he did not have sufficient cause—but it must remain a fief for the designated time, and he may not remove the enfeoffed person before that time.

It is also to be known that, even if such fiefs as just mentioned are given and granted in place of a salary, one may nevertheless give and take feudal fees for them. And the Feudal Lord is not obligated, if he takes the fief back, to return the money to the vassal. Rather, the one who paid such feudal fees must bear the loss himself, since he knew—or certainly should have known—how such fiefs are structured and situated. <note>original: "Arg. l. 1. ff. de condict. indeb." An argument based on the Digest of Roman Law regarding the recovery of payments made in error.</note>

Now, with this first conclusion, this question arises: A person possesses a feudal estate and considers it his proper and natural fief; the Lord, however, insists it is an Office Fief, or otherwise an improper or unnatural fief. The question is...

# A Brief Extract [of...]

<note>This heading continues the title from the previous page regarding the "Imperial Feudal Law."</note>

...which person should rightly be believed, and which side must therefore provide proof? To this, it must be answered that some hold that the burden of proof should be placed on the Feudal Lord <term>Lehenherr: The superior who grants the land.</term>, for through possession <note>original: "Poſſeſſion"</note> the vassal is relieved of the need to provide proof. Conversely, some believe that the vassal <term>Vaſall: The person receiving the land in exchange for service.</term> must prove his claim. From this, it appears that the laws on this point may seem contradictory. Therefore, I say briefly: If the vassal—who considers his fief to be a proper and "natural" one—acknowledges that the Lord has commanded him to hold the bailiwick <term>Vogtey: An office of administration or protection, often temporary.</term>, then he must prove that his fief is not an Office Fief, but a proper and natural hereditary fief. However, if he says that the bailiwick was not commanded of him by the Lord, then the Lord must prove such a thing. And when the Lord has proven it, the vassal is then bound by that judgment, such that he must henceforth allow the fief to be a Guard Fief <term>Quardien: From the Latin 'feudum guardiae', a fief granted specifically for the purpose of guarding a castle or territory.</term> or an Office Fief and treat it as such. This remains the case unless he can show and prove that the disputed fief was a proper and natural fief before, during, or after he was commanded with the bailiwick.

If the enfeoffed bailiff or vassal, while holding such an office, should receive one or more additional fiefs from the Lord, these should be regarded more as Bailiff or Guard Fiefs rather than proper fiefs. For one easily suspects deceit from bailiffs, supervisors, and administrators, whom the Lords sometimes tend to favor. Indeed, a similar case occurred not long ago between a Bishop and a nobleman. The nobleman had received an estate from the Bishop as a proper, natural fief; alongside that same fief, he had also acquired many fine, wealthy fiefs by way of mortgage <note>original: "pfandweiß," referring to lands held as security for a loan</note>, all of which were situated under the Bishop's jurisdiction but did not belong to the aforementioned hereditary fief. When the Bishop wanted to redeem the mortgaged estates, the nobleman claimed the estates belonged to his hereditary fief. However, the matter was eventually settled peacefully through mediation.

## The Second Conclusion.

Secondly, those are called "improper" <note>original: "vnartige," meaning atypical or not following the 'natural' hereditary rules</note> fiefs which are dedicated to certain and specific services. For example, if the vassal must wait upon the Lord's wife, or walk before or behind her. For the nature and character of a proper fief is founded not on specific and certain services, but on uncertain <note>i.e., general military service or loyalty rather than a specific chore</note> services. Thus, the people of Masmünster <note>modern Masevaux in Alsace</note> must, in the event of a dispute, keep the keys to the city of Ensisheim <note>the administrative capital of the further Austrian territories</note> as the chamber of the Archduchy of Austria, even if they are outside the country, to lock and unlock its gates. Likewise, some vassals must, upon the arrival of their Lord or Prince, provide him with food, escort him, or otherwise follow him, and do other similar things. These are called Residence Fiefs <term>Seßlehen: Fiefs that required the holder to reside at a specific place or perform localized services.</term> by some.

In what manner, however, and whether these same fiefs may be officially recorded <note>original: "auffgeſchrieben," referring to being entered into the official feudal register</note> is touched upon above in the tenth chapter, where it is said that they may not be recorded without the consent of the Lord, as legal scholars commonly hold. However, it should be noted here that although this is the common opinion, and the legal scholars put forward this reason...

--- Page 958 ---
<meta>This page continues the legal analysis of "improper" fiefs, specifically examining whether a vassal’s ability to renounce a fief is affected by the type of service (fixed or uncertain) required by the lord.</meta>

->**Imperial Feudal Law.**<-

...that the obligation to specific services is more powerful and should bind the **Vassal** <term>Lehenmann: A person who holds land from a lord in exchange for service.</term> more strictly than those obligations for uncertain services. However, such reasoning is inconsistent with and contrary to the text of the Feudal Law <note>original: "c. 1. ad finem, de vasall. qui contra consti. Lotha"—referring to the *Libri Feudorum*, specifically the chapter "Concerning the vassal who acts against the constitution of Lothair."</note>, which states without any distinction that it is permitted for the **Vassal** to <insert>record as a resignation</insert> <note>original: "auffzuschreiben." In this legal context, "writing up" or recording the fief back to the lord refers to the formal act of renouncing or resigning the tenure.</note> his fief to the **Lord**. Since the law makes no distinction in this case between **Vassals** who are obligated to uncertain services and those obligated to specific ones, we should also rightly refrain from making such a distinction, unless a grave and significant reason were present to cause us to distinguish them—which cannot be shown here. For the obligation to uncertain services binds the **Vassal** just as strictly as the obligation to specific services. And if the **Vassal** who is bound to uncertain services may renounce the fief to the **Lord** regardless of his feudal duty, it follows that he may also renounce his fief to the **Lord** when he is bound to specific services. It is the same thing whether one commits to uncertain services or if they were explicitly named and expressed from the beginning. Therefore, it must finally be concluded that either no **Vassal** may renounce or resign his fief, or that all **Vassals** may renounce their fiefs. Since no one can or will say the first—namely, that a **Vassal** does not have the power to renounce his fief to the **Lord**, as the Feudal Laws state otherwise—then the other must be and remain true: that a man may renounce his fief to the **Lord** by permission of the Feudal Laws. This is also commonly held to be the practice in **Germany**. Nevertheless, everyone is entitled to a better opinion, provided they can demonstrate it with reasonable arguments.

Regarding these fiefs—which are called **Fixed Fiefs** <term>Sestlehen: Fiefs tied to a specific residence or a fixed, permanent service.</term> by some and are dedicated to a specific service—it is well to note that if the service is of such a nature that it cannot be divided and must be performed by one person alone, and the **Vassal** dies leaving behind three, four, or more heirs, they are not all required to serve. Instead, they may appoint one among them as the **Fief-bearer** <term>Lehenträger: The specific individual designated to hold the fief and perform the required duties on behalf of multiple heirs.</term> who is fit for the task. Thus, only one **Prince of Saxony** or one **Marshal of Pappenheim** carries the sword before the **Emperor**. However, if the service *can* be divided, then they shall all serve, each as much as he is obligated to by virtue of his share.

### The Third Conclusion.

Just as a **Lord** can buy a fief for money and take possession of it, he may also grant such a fief to another in exchange for money. And although this is permitted under Feudal Law, it is nevertheless contrary to the true character and nature of fiefs, because fiefs should be granted for free and solely out of grace and favor, as the definition or description of what a fief is clearly implies.

# A Brief Extract [of...]

This concluding argument has been somewhat disputed by several people, but it is nonetheless fundamentally correct and permitted, just as common practice itself demonstrates: **Fiefs** <term>Lehen: A property or right granted by a lord to a vassal in exchange for service and loyalty.</term> are bought and granted in exchange for money. In doing so, they lose their right and natural character <note>The author suggests that a "natural" fief is granted for service/merit, whereas a "purchased" fief is a legal hybrid of a sale and a feudal grant.</note>; however, in other chapters, they remain proper and natural **Fiefs**. Just as the **Vassal** <term>Lehenmann: The holder of a fief who owes service to a lord.</term> is obligated to perform the **Feudal Duty** <term>Lehenspflicht: The specific obligations, such as military aid or attendance at court, required of a vassal.</term> as is fitting, to earn the grant, and to be faithful and loyal to the **Lord**, as is the case with other **Fiefs**. They are also lost and forfeited for the same reasons as other **Fiefs**.

Here it might be asked: Can **Women** also succeed in such **Fiefs** <note>i.e., can they inherit a fief that was originally purchased?</note>? To this, it is to be answered: although some wish to argue that **Women** should succeed by virtue of the **Contract** rather than by the virtue of Feudal Law and the nature of the **Fief**, the following rule must still be held—which was also mentioned previously—that **Women** are excluded from all **Fiefs**, unless they are explicitly named and required for that purpose.

Secondly, it is to be noted here: although one may buy a **Fief**, a **Pledge** <term>Pfand: Property given as security for a debt (a mortgage).</term> cannot be made into a **Fief**, especially if these words were used in the pledging: "I pledge this ground or this estate to you, with the condition that if I do not redeem it within the specified time, it shall herewith be made a **Fief** to you." For such a **Contract** is rejected in the law <note>original: "c. 1. de feudo. da. in vicem. l. commis." — referring to the section of the *Libri Feudorum* on fiefs given in exchange and the Roman law prohibition of the *lex commissoria*, a clause that allows a creditor to keep a pledge if a debt is not paid.</note>, where it is said that **Fiefs** should be granted out of favor and not for the sake of money. This, however, must be understood as applying to such improper and rejected **Contracts**, and not in a general sense.

But if I sell an estate to someone and make it a **Fief** with this provision or **Pact** <term>Pact: A specific agreement or clause within a larger contract.</term>: if someone else offers me more for it within a certain time, I may cancel the sale to the first person and sell and grant it to the other; or with the condition that if I regret the sale, I may revoke it; or if I grant you a **Fief** only until I sell it. Such **Conditions** and **Pacts**, since they are not rejected in common Law but are accepted and permitted <note>original: "l. 1. & 2. ff. de in diem ad." — referring to the Digest of Justinian, title *De in diem addictio*, which permits a seller to cancel a sale if a better offer is received within a certain period.</note>, are also allowed to remain in Feudal Law and are held to be powerful and binding. And according to how the **Contracts** which are made with such **Conditions** as just mentioned reach their conclusion once the **Condition** is fulfilled, one is also obligated in such a case to return the **Buyer's** money. The **Buyer** also keeps the **Fruit** <note>In a legal sense, "fruit" refers to the profits, crops, or rents produced by the land during the time the buyer held it.</note> and is not bound or obligated to pay for them.

An estate can also be sold with this **Pact**: if the **Buyer** does not make the payment on the appointed date, he shall then hold and possess the said estate not as an **Inherited Estate** <term>Erbgut: Allodial land held in absolute ownership, which could be passed to heirs without a lord's interference.</term> but as a **Feudal Estate**, and shall serve for it, while nonetheless fulfilling the payment. The same applies if it were agreed in the **Contract** that if the money were not paid in full, or in part, by the named date, the **Buyer** shall hold the estate, in whole or in part, as a **Fief**. Such purchases with these attached...
