Therefore, this case is permitted, while the other is not.

### The Fourth Concluding Argument.

When the **Lord** grants an estate to someone and acknowledges in the grant or **Feudal Charter** <term>Lehenbrieff: The legal document that serves as the deed for a fief.</term> that he has received a certain amount of **Marks** or **Guilders** <note>Historical currencies; the Mark was a unit of weight for silver, while the Guilder (Gülden) was a common gold coin.</note> from the **Vassal** for it, with the provision that when the Lord is able, he may repay that same sum of Guilders to take the estate back—and that the money used to redeem the pledged estate should be further reinvested as a fief, as often happens among the **Princes and Lords of the German Nation**—such are also not "true" fiefs. Firstly, because they are not granted freely and for nothing. Secondly, because they can be redeemed with money. Yet, in other sections of the law, they remain proper and natural fiefs: specifically, that the **Vassal** must perform his **Feudal Duty**, earn the fief, and be faithful and loyal to the Lord; also, he cannot lose it without fault, nor can the Lord take it from him. If he were to forfeit it through misconduct, however, he could lose it just as easily as any other fief. No injustice is done to him in this, which a **Vassal** should rightly know is part of the character and nature of a fief.

In such **Pledge-fiefs** <term>Pfandlehen: A hybrid arrangement where a fief acts as security for a loan, blending mortgage law with feudal law.</term>, as long as they remain in effect, it is customary for only **Male Heirs** and not **Female Heirs** to succeed. For it is a certain rule, as also mentioned before, that women are not admitted to fiefs unless they are specifically and expressly summoned for that purpose.

Furthermore, if the Lord repays the money and takes the fief back, because the clause was attached stating that such money should be made into a fief again, the **daughters** <note>original: "Meidlein," literally "little girls" or maidens, used here to refer to female descendants.</note> cannot inherit it. If, however, the clause had not been attached, it is considered that the daughters should rightly be admitted. Nevertheless, it has otherwise come into use in the present day that women succeed in **Pledge-fiefs**; and the good **Princes** are sometimes persuaded by the **Vassals** to acknowledge in the charter that it is a **Pledge-fief** and that they have received a significant sum of Guilders for it—even though at times not a single penny was paid—solely so that women may also succeed in such fiefs. This, however, is fundamentally contrary to feudal law.

# A Short Excerpt of the...
## The Fifth Concluding Argument.

It may happen that a **Fief** <term>Lehen: A grant of land or rights held by a vassal from a lord in exchange for service and loyalty.</term> is granted in such a manner that not only the recipient shall hold it, but also anyone to whom he might give it; such a case is considered an **Improper or Unnatural Fief** <note>In standard feudal law, a vassal could not transfer land to someone else without the lord's explicit permission. An "improper" (unnatural) fief breaks these traditional rules.</note>. For in this way, the **Vassal** <term>Lehenmann: The person who holds the fief and owes service to the lord.</term> can sell or grant such a fief even without the lord's prior knowledge or consent to any person, whether man or woman. There are five points to consider regarding this concluding argument:

First, such a fief retains the nature and character of a proper fief as long as it remains unchanged by the vassal: for he must still perform the **Feudal Duty** <term>Lehenspflicht: The specific services or obligations the vassal owes the lord.</term> to the lord and earn the fief as is fitting. Likewise, it can be forfeited through misconduct just like other fiefs, and only **Male Feudal Heirs** <term>Männlichen Lehenserben: Traditional feudal law usually restricted inheritance to the male line to ensure military service could be fulfilled.</term> may succeed to it.

Secondly, when someone buys such a fief that the lord has granted in this manner, the buyer may indeed possess and keep it as his own inheritance and property. In this case, he is neither required to perform duties to the lord nor to "earn" the fief; nor can he forfeit it as one might with other **Feudal Estates** <term>Lehengüter: Lands or properties held under feudal tenure.</term>. This is only different if the **Feudal Charter** <term>Lehenbrieff: The formal document recording the grant of the fief.</term> specifically states: "We grant and lease this to *Sempronio* <note>original: "Sempronio" – a placeholder name used in legal texts, similar to "John Doe."</note>, and to anyone to whom he shall grant or sell it as a fief." In that case, the property would retain the nature and character of a fief, except that it could be changed without the lord's consent; otherwise, those who had purchased and acquired such a fief would have to possess and hold it as nothing other than a feudal estate.

Thirdly, it should be noted: Although the buyer of such a fief is not obligated to perform an **Homage** <term>Huldung: A formal ceremony where a vassal swears fealty to a lord.</term> or feudal duty to the lord for it, as mentioned before, he is nevertheless required to give the lord an "acknowledgment." In this document, he declares that such property originally came from the lord and was originally his fief. This is done for the reason that, if the property should ever become vacant in the future, the lord or his heirs may know to claim it and take it back unto themselves.

Fourthly, when a man sells such a fief, he is not required to reinvest the purchase money into another immovable feudal estate; instead, he may do with it as he pleases, as with his own money. The feudal laws can no longer bind him in this, since he has stepped outside of them and waived them through a special **Agreement** <term>pact: A specific legal contract or treaty (from the Latin 'pactum') that overrides general law.</term>.

Fifthly, even if the lord grants someone a fief in such a way that he may change it and sell it to whomever he wishes, the vassal may not, by virtue of such an **Enfeoffment** <term>belehnung: The act of formally investing someone with a fief.</term>, grant the property to himself. For in common legal speech, the person who is speaking is always excluded from the general terms of the grant <note>Essentially, a person cannot "sell" or "grant" something to themselves to bypass the lord's rights or change the legal status of the land for their own benefit.</note>.

## The Sixth Concluding Argument.

Furthermore, these are also improper and unnatural fiefs which are arranged so that **Women** <term>Weibspersonen: Female heirs.</term> may succeed to them; whereas otherwise, feudal law clearly provides that women shall not succeed to fiefs—

...unless they are specifically and expressly named, as has been mentioned many times before. However, if it should become the custom that female persons are also permitted to succeed to **Fiefs** <term>Lehen: A grant of land or rights held by a vassal from a lord.</term>, the fief would not lose its "rightful nature" simply because it fell to a woman. According to the opinion of legal scholars, such a custom could indeed be introduced.

## The Seventh Concluding Argument.

It is also an **Improper Fief** <note>In this context, "improper" (unrecht) does not mean illegal, but rather "non-standard" or "atypical" because it does not follow the usual rules of hereditary land tenure.</note> when someone is granted a dwelling in a house or a castle. This is a personal fief and does not extend to the heirs, unless it was otherwise provided for and expressed in the **Feudal Letters** <term>Lehenbrieffen: The formal written contracts documenting a feudal grant.</term>. This is because, according to common law, if a dwelling is assigned to someone in a will, that right cannot be extended to their heirs.

## The Eighth Concluding Argument.

Eighthly, **Chamber Fiefs** <term>Kammerlehen: A fief consisting of a regular cash payment from the lord’s treasury (chamber) rather than a grant of land.</term> are considered improper fiefs. This occurs when the lord grants the **Vassal** <term>Lehenmann: The recipient of the fief who owes loyalty to the lord.</term> certain annual rents, payments, or income from his treasury, out of his customs duties or other revenues, which are paid to him yearly. They are called "improper" or "unnatural" because the heirs of the vassal may not be entitled to them. Furthermore, they are not paid to the vassal if the treasury's income is so diminished that the lord would suffer want or hardship, or if the treasury is burdened with significant debt. 

Some, such as **Alvarotto** <note>Jacobus Alvarotto (1385–1453) was a famous Italian jurist known for his influential commentaries on feudal law.</note> and others, have held that such a fief should end with the death of the giver—that is, the **Liege Lord**. However, they have erred and are mistaken in this, because this is not a **Soldier’s Fief** (which is personal in every respect, as shall be said in the next concluding argument). This Chamber Fief is only personal as far as the receiver (the vassal) is concerned, and not the giver (the lord). Nevertheless, such a Chamber Fief remains "proper and true" in several aspects, much like other fiefs: it involves **Knightly Service** <term>Ritterdienst: The military obligation a vassal owes his lord.</term>, the formal "seeking" of the fief, and the swearing of **Feudal Duty** <term>Lehenpflicht: The oath of loyalty and service.</term>. Also, the vassal may not change or transfer it without the lord's consent, and he holds it in legal possession and protection. The vassal is considered to have gained **Possession** <note>original: "Posseß"</note> of such a fief once the grant has been paid to him two or three times.

## The Ninth Concluding Argument.

Likewise, if a member of the nobility has fallen into poverty and the lord provides him with maintenance under the title of a fief—not out of his treasury or cavalry funds, but in another way—this is called a **Soldier’s Fief** <term>Soldaten Lehen: A personal maintenance grant given to support a soldier or noble.</term>. This is entirely personal, for it is extinguished with the person of both the giver and the receiver: that is, by the death of either the lord or the vassal.

## The Tenth Concluding Argument.

If the Lord grants a **Vassal** <term>Lehenman: A person who holds land or rights from a superior lord in exchange for service and loyalty.</term> a **Fief** <term>Lehen: A grant of land or income held under feudal conditions.</term> in such a way that, instead of the required **Knight Service** <term>Ritterdienst: Military service traditionally owed by a vassal to their lord.</term>, the vassal is to provide a certain amount of wine, grain, or money annually, this is contrary to the nature of **Feudal Law** <term>Lehenrecht: The body of law governing the relationship between lords and vassals.</term>. Feudal law traditionally requires that knightly service be "uncertain"—meaning it should be provided whenever the lord calls for it, rather than being a fixed payment. Nevertheless, in all other respects, it remains a valid and "natural" fief. Even if something else is provided to the lord in place of knight service, it does not change the core substance of the fief; it remains a fief regardless.

## The Eleventh Concluding Argument.

Even if the **Feudal Lord** grants a fief along with full **Ownership** <term>Eigenthumb: Total legal possession, which is unusual in a feudal system where the lord typically retains the ultimate title while the vassal only has use of the land.</term> and all legal rights (as is said to be the case when the Kingdom of **Sicily** is granted), although such a grant is against the standard nature of fiefs, it remains a fief nonetheless. This is true despite the fact that some legal experts, such as **Oldradus** <note>original: "Oldrat"; referring to Oldradus de Ponte, a renowned 14th-century jurist.</note> and others, have argued against this view. While such **Contracts** <note>original: "Pact"</note> may go against the typical nature of a fief, they do not abolish its legal substance; they allow it to remain a fief. Even if the vassal receives ownership of the fief, he remains bound to the lord—not only regarding knight service but also in his obligation to be faithful and loyal, as has been sufficiently discussed previously.

Conversely, if a fief were granted for use only, and the lord retained not only the ownership but also the **Underlying Lordship** <term>vnderherrligkeit: The lord's retained sovereign rights and jurisdiction over the fief.</term>, such a fief is valid, yet it lacks the "true nature" of a standard fief, as has been stated.

## The Twelfth Concluding Argument.

It may happen that a lord releases a vassal from his **Feudal Duty** <term>Lehenspflicht: The formal obligations, including service and attendance at court, that a vassal owes to their lord.</term>, so that he does not have to swear an **Oath** <term>Eydt: A formal religious and legal vow of loyalty (homage) to a lord.</term>. When this occurs, the fief has lost its "rightful nature," even though feudal law allows for a vassal to be released from the oath. However, the vassal is no less bound to fulfill everything that the oath entails, just as if he had sworn it. This is by virtue of the **Fidelity** <term>Trew: The fundamental bond of trust and loyalty between vassal and lord.</term> that a vassal owes his lord because of the fief, whether he has sworn an oath or not. This fidelity is a duty that cannot be waived.

If **Frankish Fiefs** <term>Fränckischen: Also known as "Freylehen" or Free Fiefs; these were noble holdings that were often exempt from traditional military service.</term> are granted to someone so that they do not have to perform any knight service, these are also "improper" fiefs and do not possess the nature of true fiefs. # Imperial Feudal Law.

...just as with others we have described in other articles regarding **fiefs** <term>Lehen: A grant of land or rights held by a vassal from a lord in exchange for service.</term>, and the core substance is not taken away by this: for one who holds such a **Franconian Fief** <term>Fränckisch Lehen: A specific type of noble tenure, often associated with greater freedom or specific regional customs of the Franks.</term> must nevertheless swear to the Lord—unless the Lord waives it—to be true and faithful. He must not only refrain from harming the Lord or seeking his life, but is also bound to warn him of potential damage with his greatest diligence. It might be asked, however, whether such a Franconian or **Free Fief** <term>Freilehen: A fief held with fewer restrictions than a standard feudal grant.</term> may be sold or altered without the permission and prior knowledge of the Lord? To this I say: No. The reason being, if the **vassal** <term>Lehenman: One who holds a fief and owes loyalty to a superior lord.</term> had offended the Lord or harmed him, he could not be properly punished by the Lord if he had the power to change the fief as he pleased; he might thereby withdraw himself from punishment.

## The Fourteenth Concluding Argument.

When someone receives a fief without actual **investiture** <term>Einweisung: The formal legal ceremony of putting a person in possession of their land or office.</term>, it loses its right and natural character; this occurs when the vassal takes **physical possession** <term>Cörperliche Possession: Actual, tangible occupancy of the land.</term> of said fief even with the knowledge and will of the Feudal Lord. If the vassal were to die before the end of the year, his feudal heirs could not succeed him in such a fief. However, if he had been in possession for a **year and a day** <note>In medieval law, "a year and a day" was a standard timeframe required to establish a permanent legal right or status.</note> and had performed his proper **knight service** <term>Ritterdienst: Military service traditionally owed by a knight to his lord.</term> to the Lord, it would thereby have become a proper fief.

## The Fifteenth Concluding Argument.

It is to be noted here that the nature and essence of feudal law rests upon two points. First, on written customs. Second, on the custom of each individual land, as has been often stated in this book: that feudal laws for the most part rest on custom. Accordingly, if one looks at the written customs, the **succession** <term>Succession: The process of inheriting a title or property.</term> in feudal estates that carry a dignity with them—such as **Principalities** <term>Fürstenthumb: The territory or jurisdiction of a Prince.</term>, **Margraviates** <term>Marggraffschafft: The territory ruled by a Margrave, traditionally a border province.</term>, and **Counties** <term>Graffschafft: The domain of a Count.</term>—has changed its proper nature. But if one looks at current custom, succession does not change its proper nature, but retains the essence of the fief in this manner: if a Principality, Margraviate, or County were found today which was not hereditary, it would not be unfair to call it an "improper" fief; such as the Principality of **Spoleto** <note>original: "Spolet"; a city and former duchy in central Italy.</note> and the County of **Campania** <note>original: "Campanie"; a region in southern Italy.</note> are said to be, yet they do not lose the name of a "fief" because of it.

Since in all matters that may arise regarding fiefs, it is customary to be guided by the **feudal charters** <term>Lehenbrieffen: Legal documents recording the grant of a fief and its specific conditions.</term> and to pay diligent attention to them, as this serves primarily to ensure that

## A short summary,

from which one can recognize whether a **fief** <term>Lehen: A grant of land or rights held by a vassal from a lord in exchange for service.</term> is proper and natural, or improper and unnatural: for this reason, the **pacts** <term>Pact: The specific legal agreements or contracts governing the conditions of a feudal grant.</term> regarding the manner in which the grant was made must be considered with the greatest diligence, as those who have experience in feudal law well know.

If, however, the pacts of the grant were improperly altered through either error or fraud, one should not look to the new and altered grant or **fief-charter** <term>Lehenbrieff: The formal written document certifying and detailing the terms of a feudal grant.</term> in this case, but rather to how the grant was made in ancient times; for in all dealings, one should consider the beginning and the foundation of the matter. This is unless such a change occurred with the knowledge and consent of both parties, in which case it would be right to let it remain so.

## The seventeenth and final concluding argument.

Whether a fief be old or new, if no other pact or change is added to it, it remains a proper and natural fief. In this, there is no error in the fact that there is otherwise a great difference between old and new fiefs: namely, that an old fief extends with **succession** <term>Succession: The legal right of an heir to inherit property or titles.</term> to the **agnates** <term>Agnaten: Relatives through the male line of descent.</term>, which cannot happen in new fiefs, as was discussed at length above in the third chapter. For there is no fief so old that it was not once new. Therefore, they cannot lose their right nature simply because they are an old or new fief, since a new fief can also be granted in place of or for an old fief, and the new fief may take upon itself the type and nature of an old one. But an old fief cannot be made into a new fief unless it occurs with the consent of the **co-vassals** <term>Mitbelehnten: Persons who hold a fief jointly with another.</term> and the agnates.

As far as **church-fiefs** <term>Kirchlehen: A fief held from the Church or pertaining to ecclesiastical property.</term> are concerned, the grant or the fief-charter may not be altered to the detriment of the Church. For example, if one wanted to make an old fief out of a new one, or a **female fief** <term>Weiblich Lehen: A fief that can be inherited by women.</term> (or one that extends to women) out of a proper **male fief** <term>Mannlehen: A fief intended to be inherited only by male heirs.</term>. Since, however, sufficient mention of this was made above in the third chapter, we will let the matter rest here and have thus concluded.

->End of the Summary of the entire Imperial Feudal Law, described by<-
->Doctor Ulrich Zasius, and translated by Georg Lauterbeck.<-

# To the Stern and Honorable Chris-

->toph Wolff Schrencken, Captain at Walhausen,<-
->Georgius Lauterbeck wishes his willing service.<-

Stern, steadfast, and gracious Honorable Captain, some time ago—while I was held in a state of restriction <note>original: "bestrickung"; this term suggests a period of personal difficulty, legal entanglement, or perhaps house arrest which afforded the author the leisure to write.</note>—I wrote a small book on courtly life and allowed it to be published. I did this partly so that I might prepare a path for young and inexperienced people who have not been at court before, showing them how they should conduct themselves there. I also did it partly so that I might create a reminder for myself and a kind of guide <term>Richtscheid: A straight-edge or ruler used by craftsmen; here used metaphorically to mean a moral or professional standard.</term> by which to model my own actions and behavior at court. For life there is so fashioned that no one is so wise, skilled, or sensible that he does not occasionally need a reminder. 

You have no doubt experienced this yourself. You will also have frequently heard and understood this from your dear, late father, who was indeed a true courtier. I may well say that, having previously been in schools and at the university where I attended to the quiet of my studies, it seemed to me that I had entered another world when I came to court. Your father’s guidance <note>original: "Kundschafft"; here meaning the practical knowledge, acquaintance, or mentorship provided by the elder Schrencken.</note> served me in no small way, as I had much to do with him and was often sent away with him on important matters.

And as I remember your father, I cannot omit to write this of him: that among the other virtues with which he was significantly gifted by God, he maintained the habit of always faithfully advising toward peace and unity. Frequently, through his skill and tact <term>gelimpff: An archaic term for moderation, propriety, and a conciliatory manner.</term>, he prevented no small amount of discord. It would be highly desirable if we had many more such people.

# Preface

In governments <note>original: "Regimenten"; referring to the administration of a state, territory, or a ruler’s household.</note>, things would proceed better than they actually do. For just as it is a very noble and precious thing to have such a man who is peaceful in government—especially in places where there are many lords, and one is minded differently than the other, and for that reason they cannot agree on all things—so too is a person at court who is restless and wants to fight <note>original: "feuchten," likely a variant of "fechten" (to fence/fight); meaning to aggressively contend or push issues to a contentious extreme.</note> for everything to the utmost a most harmful guest. 

As history bears witness, there is no lack of such companions. Whatever good they may have accomplished, the opposite is written of them. If there is now one who has a desire to enter the Chronicles in such a manner, like Ahithophel <note>A biblical counselor to King David who betrayed him to join Absalom's rebellion; his name became a historical shorthand for a treacherous or overly-clever schemer.</note> and his like, he may try it—understand me, the gamble <note>original: "schanz"; a term from gambling or military positioning, meaning a risky opportunity or a "shot" at something.</note> may easily succeed. But **LORD God**, one must surely consider what misery and lamentation such a restless person causes, and how heavily he will have to answer for such things in his conscience. Yet such fellows are usually treated according to what they are worthy of and have well deserved. 

Indeed, if I wished to run through history, I could show enough examples that testify to this; but since I have neither time nor opportunity, I must leave it out here, as I have striven for brevity throughout this entire little book. And for those who wish to betake themselves to court, I have simply prescribed some short rules, so that they may conduct themselves accordingly (provided they do not know any better). 

In particular consideration, although it is a strange thing and troublesome enough regarding courtly life, it is nonetheless a fact that not only are courts different, but also many pious, honorable people—from the nobility, and others both learned and unlearned—daily go to court, to whom the circumstances and the customs of courtly life are not entirely known. Nonetheless, I have wanted to give them a reminder, instruction, and warning, so that they might not immediately stumble at the entrance or lose their way. For just as it pleases a person very well when he is in a strange, unknown place and finds someone who shows him the path and all g- <note>The text breaks here; the catchword "gent" suggests the next page continues with "gelegenheit" (circumstances/opportunities) or "gentlich" (properly/entirely).</note>

# Preface. 424

...circumstances of that same place, according to which he can conduct himself. Thus I also believe it will not be unwelcome to those—especially young and inexperienced people—who come to court and would like to have guidance on how they should properly and well adapt themselves to courtly life, when they read this little book. Although it might not unfairly be held against me that I should rightly abstain from this business and consider my own situation—in such a way that I cannot prove through my own actions that which I have presented here for others to learn—nevertheless, they must admit that it is the same with other things. And to give an example: is a whetstone <note>original: "Wetstein"; a stone used for sharpening blades. The author is using a classical rhetorical trope: he claims to be "dull" himself, but capable of sharpening the minds of others.</note> not a coarse and entirely dull thing, such that one cannot even properly cut a roll of butter in two with it? Yet it nevertheless makes fine and sharp cutting knives, which one may use for all sorts of things.

And although these are brief and bare rules, which might well require a broader explanation, I am nonetheless hopeful that they will not have been written by me entirely in vain, but will occasionally be of use to someone who knows how to use them. And because I often debated, spoke, and dealt with these matters with your dear late father, I wanted to dedicate this little book—which I have improved slightly—to you in his memory. With a very friendly request: that you would take it in no other way than I intended, and thus understand it for the best. With this, I commend you to God. Given at Mansfeld,

# Preface to the Reader.

<image-desc>Large decorative drop cap 'D' containing floral and leaf motifs within a square border.</image-desc>
This short and simple report on court 
life (Dear Reader) I have put on pa-
per for no other reason, and now let go 
forth again, than so that those to whom 
court life is still unknown, and who do not 
know better, might have a modest and simple guide 
when they come to court; for there, everything happens 
quite differently than in the cities and among common 
people. It explains how they should then behave and 
adapt themselves to court life. However, I have not 
wished to take in hand or tackle the true description of 
court life and its shining poverty <note>original: "hochscheinenden armut"; a common 16th-century rhetorical trope describing the "splendid misery" of the court—where a servant might look wealthy in livery but possesses no personal freedom or stability.</note>, for that would 
stray too far and could not be accomplished or grasped in a short 
space. Furthermore, court life is all too well known in itself, 
and has already been sufficiently depicted by Hutten <note>original: "Hutteno"; referring to Ulrich von Hutten (1488–1523), a famous German knight and satirist who wrote scathingly about court life.</note>, Cornelius 
Agrippa <note>original: "Cornelio/ Agrippa"; referring to Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa (1486–1535), known for his critiques of human institutions.</note>, and others, so that it is unnecessary to describe 
it further. I have only wished to show here how someone—
perhaps a young man in his youth, while he is still 
inexperienced—who has entered into service for a 
Prince or Lord and would like to know how he should 
behave, might act rightly toward him and thereby 
attain honor and fame. This is indeed necessary for a young 
fellow, whether he be of the nobility or otherwise, 
especially since envy is so great at court that no one 
instructs another on what is becoming or un-
becoming of him. Instead, when someone comes to court 
and does not know how to behave properly, they 
mock him and laugh at him; indeed, some of them do not 
even consider other people to be human, but rather like 
animals, and they consider themselves alone to be wise 
and understanding, though they themselves also 
occasionally fail.

The poets of old wrote much about a Labyrinth <term>Labyrinth: in Greek mythology, an intricate maze designed by Daedalus to hold the Minotaur.</term>, 
which was such a building that once one entered, 
he did not know how to find his way out again. When 
he had thus lost his way and came to the Minotaur <note>original: "Minotauro"; a mythical creature with the head of a bull and the body of a man.</note> (who 
was half man and half ox, and thus a terrible 
monster), he had to be eaten by him, and no one 
came out again except Theseus, to whom Ariadne, 
the King’s daughter from Crete, provided a guiding thread <note>original: "Richtfaden"</note> 
to which he had to tie himself and be guided, so 
that he came out of the Labyrinth again without danger. 
Now, whoever comes to court has entered into a true 
Labyrinth and is well in need of a guiding line <note>original: "Richtschnur"; literally a builder’s plumb line or a string used to ensure a straight path.</note>, 
so that he does not lose his way, but rather, if he has 
gone somewhat astray, he might find his way back. 
To this end, this short instruction—though not in 
all things, yet in part—can be useful to a servant. 
And it might well happen, if time and occasion 
allow, that I shall write more extensively of these 
things. For now, may you accept this short 
report, which I have in truth written with 
the best intentions, and be com-
mended to God.

# A Memorial and Record / How a Prince’s or Lord’s Councilor / or Servant / should behave in his actions and being in all respects / so that he may derive Honor and Renown therefrom.

<image-desc>A large ornamental woodcut initial letter 'A' entwined with vine and leaf motifs inside a square border.</image-desc>Initially, it will be necessary for one who intends to enter a Lord’s court or service to look well before and around himself as to what kind of Lord he chooses for himself; it is no less necessary than when one wishes to marry <note>original: "freyen"; while today this means "to be free," in this 16th-century context it refers to wooing or seeking a spouse.</note>, that he look well ahead. For Lords are not all alike; rather, one is poor, the other rich; one young, the other old; one pious, the other wicked. Likewise, one is generous and rewards his servants faithfully and well, while on the contrary, another is stingy and gives no one anything. One also finds those who are Papist <note>original: "Papistisch"; a common Reformation-era term for Roman Catholics, used here with a cautionary tone typical of a Protestant author.</note> and godless, or who otherwise deal in absurd matters, in which it is not good for a servant to let himself be used.

And it causes great heartache when one gets such a Lord, whom he has served long and faithfully, and yet his service is not recognized; instead, he must see with his own eyes that one person here and another there is cast out—though they served faithfully—just so that the Lord does not have to reward them, and in their place worthless soup-eaters <note>original: "Suppenfresser"; a derogatory term for parasites or idle hangers-on who serve only for a meal and provide no real value to the court.</note> are taken in, who cut the bread from the others' mouths.

In contrast, one must (as mentioned) think and look ahead well at the beginning, so that he knows what kind of Lord he is getting and what he may hope for from him.

It is also not a bad thing, if one has such an intention, to call upon God for grace regarding it, as we rightfully should in all our actions and being.

But it is to be noted that one should by no means easily enter the service of a Lord who is wicked, quarrelsome, tyrannical, and godless; for since such Lords are also frequently punished here in this temporal life for their godless nature and their tyranny, his servants must fear that they might fall into danger along with the Lord—not only in their property, but also in their bodies, honor, and good reputation. And it is much better to abstain from such a Lord at the beginning than to have to part from him later with ill will.

In particular, no servant should flatter <note>original: "hofieren"; literally "to court," meaning to fawn over or provide "lip service" to the lord's preferences regardless of truth.</note> his Lord in matters of religion, nor abandon the truth of the Divine Word for his sake.

Likewise, if a Lord has a righteous cause and falls into danger because of it, a servant should stand faithfully by him and see him through.

Now, if a servant has found a Lord who pleases him, and has bound himself to that same Lord with oath and duty, he should apply himself with diligence so that his [commission...]

<header>Of Court Life.</header>

...that an appointment <note>original: "bestallung"; a formal written contract or commission specifying duties and pay</note> be established, so that he may know what he should do, and in return, what his salary shall be, so that he need not serve "on grace" <note>To serve "on grace" meant working without a fixed salary, relying entirely on the Lord's occasional whims or gifts.</note>, as some do, whom they are then accustomed to reward with "mercy" <note>The author is being cynical here: instead of being paid what they are owed, these servants are treated like beggars receiving charity.</note>. And once he has the appointment and knows what his office is, he should pay attention with particular diligence, so that he may know how he can best please the Lord. And if he finds that a task is in accordance with honor and fairness, he should carry it out with all diligence.

But if he finds a Lord who will not allow himself to be understood <note>original: "auslernen lassen"; literally "to be fully learned," referring to a lord who is unpredictable or keeps his intentions hidden</note>, but is of one opinion today and another tomorrow—which are usually suspicious people who trust or believe no one, nor wish for anyone to align themselves with them, etc.—a servant may bear such a Lord with patience and carry out that which has been commanded of him. But how difficult it is to serve such Lords who trust no one, those who have experienced it will know. Therefore, it is no better than to let them remain in their own minds, while each person looks to his own opportunity and considers his own best interests. For that is why they are Lords: so that they may do what they wish. Indeed, I have heard tell of a Lord who had three kinds of people at his court: The first could do no wrong, whether they did things well or poorly. The second could have made things better, but also worse. The third could earn no thanks, whether they did things well or poorly.

Next, let him see to it that in such service he fears God above all things, and diligently guards himself against falling into shame or vice through good fortune or complacency <note>original: "sicherheit"; in this context, it refers to a dangerous sense of false security or moral overconfidence</note>. Rather, he should lead a fine, reserved, discreet, earnest, and God-fearing life, so that he may have all the more luck, blessing, and prosperity before God and the world in his deeds and undertakings. For what kind of luck can public murderers, adulterers, robbers, and thieves have? And even if things go well for them for a time, and they wish to use the proverb, "The worse the rogue, the better the luck," <note>original: "Je erger Schalck je beſſer Glück"; a common 16th-century saying suggesting that villains often prosper materially while the virtuous suffer.</note> it cannot last in the long run. Through such public vices, they have already received the greatest damage and misfortune to their good name, honor, and reputation.

Especially let one who is new to court and has not yet learned the courtly ways, nor knows the people, take diligent care that he does not trust everyone. For the world is full of unfaithfulness, and just when he thinks he has found a good and faithful friend, he is betrayed and sold out. Also, if he should obtain a profitable office <term>genieſſlich Ampt: a lucrative position that provides a good income or specific perks</term>, there are easily ten who will envy him and strive to remove him from it, because they would gladly be in his place. Therefore, they investigate and listen day and night with all diligence, seeking to hear something he has said against the Lord, so that they may go to court with it and slander him.

And so that one may see what belongs to a right and true friendship, and how few righteous friends are found now even among us who wish to be Christians—for which reason it is most highly necessary to look out for oneself in this matter—I will here relate how true friend-

<meta>Continuity: This page continues the author’s advice on navigating the dangers of the royal court. Having previously discussed the difficulty of serving unpredictable or untrusting Lords, the author now transitions into the nature of true friendship—contrasting the ideal, selfless friendship of the ancients with the deceptive and secretive atmosphere of contemporary court life.</meta>

<header>Of Court Life. 426</header>

Friendship among the ancient Romans—as wise, sensible, and upright people—was depicted and described with its loyalty, characteristics, and all its proper circumstances. Specifically, they had a youth depicted with an **uncovered head** and in a **coarse garment**. At the bottom of the hem was written **Death and Life**; at the top on the forehead, **Winter and Summer**. The left side was entirely open, so that one could see the **heart**. And the youth has his arm lowered and points with his finger to the heart, and standing written there is: **Far and Near**. This image, along with its description, has been signified and interpreted in the following manner:

The form of the youth signifies that friendship shall remain forever and always new, and never grow cold, nor be extinguished, nor cease. The uncovered <note>The original German text here says "bedeckte" (covered), but this is likely a printer's error, as the previous paragraph and the subsequent explanation ("open to everyone") confirm the head is "unbedecktem" (uncovered).</note> head signifies that the head should stand open to everyone, and that every person should acknowledge his friend at all times and in no way be ashamed of him. The coarse garment shows that a true friend should have no fear—even of something great—and should be willing to endure and stand by his friend even in the most extreme poverty. The writing at the bottom of the garment, **Death and Life**, indicates those who love their friends uprightly and from the heart; for these will even place themselves in the peril of death for their friend’s sake. As one reads concerning the two friends, **Pylades and Orestes**: when the King <note>King Thoas of Taurica.</note> did not know which one was Orestes—who was to be sacrificed to the goddess **Diana** according to the custom of the land in **Taurica** <note>The Crimean Peninsula, where in Greek mythology Orestes was nearly sacrificed by his sister Iphigenia.</note>—Pylades cried out and said *he* was Orestes. But Orestes also stood firm and confessed that *he* was Orestes, and that Pylades wished to make him look poor by his confession and keep him alive. Ultimately, Orestes was set free by his sister **Iphigenia** when she recognized him. The two words **Summer and Winter** remind us that one should not abandon a friend in either prosperity or in adversity and misfortune. The open side down to the heart signifies that one should hide nothing from a loyal friend that is worth mentioning. The arm that bows down, however, and the finger that points to the heart, show that word and heart are one thing; the heart should answer to the words, and the words to the heart, and they should be equal. Finally, the words **Far and Near** remind us that true and upright friendship never ceases, nor should one friend forget the other, no matter how far they are from one another.

From this, one may clearly perceive what belongs to a constant and right, truthful friendship, and how few such people—who are of this kind and nature—are to be found who show such loyalty and friendship, and who dare to do and venture everything for a friend's sake. Therefore, one must take great care not to accept everyone as a friend and trust them with everything—**especially at Court**, where usually everything happens in a hidden manner, and one rarely looks the other in the eye honestly. One must do this if he does not wish to fall into distress and danger. But he who will not believe it and guard himself may experience it at his own adventure <note>In this context, "adventure" implies a risky or perilous experience.</note>.

Therefore, nothing is better for him than to keep a close watch on his mouth and see what he says. As the **Wise Man** says:

> He who guards his mouth, guards his life. <note>original: "Wer seinen Mund / verwaret / der hat sein Leben verwaret." A reference to Proverbs 13:3.</note>

And because it sometimes cannot

But otherwise, be friendly toward everyone; he shall speak ill of no one, nor dismiss them, or snap at them with wicked, proud words. <note>original: "vber das Maul fahren"—literally "to drive over the mouth," meaning to speak harshly or rudely to someone.</note> Only toward his enemy should he show himself earnest, so that the enemy does not think he must be afraid of him.

No one should he disparage to the Lord, much less falsely accuse; instead, when he hears such things from others, he should speak the best of the matter and excuse the absent person until they can give their own answer. For many a person is falsely accused who afterward cannot come to their own defense; and as someone is first presented to the Lord at court, so they remain in suspicion, and it is difficult to talk the Lord out of that opinion.

In summary, <note>original: "In summa."</note> he should use court life in no other way than he uses fire; he must take great care to manage it so that he can warm himself by it and not freeze, yet conversely, not press so close that he burns himself, both of which are harmful. It also happens sometimes, when people wish to be negligent and sleepy, that they suddenly fall into the fire at court and perish—of which I could tell examples, if it were necessary.

And let this be enough of general matters; <note>original: "Generalibus."</note> now we wish to see how he should behave in specific matters. <note>original: "Specialibus."</note>

## Firstly, when one has become an
## Official. <term>Amptmann: A high-ranking administrative officer or bailiff who governed a district and administered justice on behalf of a territorial lord.</term>

<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial 'I' with floral motifs.</image-desc>If the servant has come to an office, he should know the circumstances of that same office, and investigate with all diligence, and take reports from them: how things stand there. He should keep peace with the neighbors and settle matters amicably, yet allow nothing to be withdrawn from his Lord’s rights and jurisdictions; <term>Gerechtigkeit: In this context, it refers to the legal entitlements, revenues, and sovereign rights of the nobleman being served.</term> rather, he should uphold them most strictly. For there is a common proverb: *One buys little justice for a penny.*

He should listen gladly to those associated with his office and give them good counsel. For the sake of favor or gifts, he must not hinder or block anyone’s righteous cause, nor promote anyone’s evil cause. Instead, he should protect and defend every person in that which they have a right to; to the people who have business before him, he should speak kindly. But the wicked scoundrels, when they come, he should punish earnestly; that maintains fear and good governance <term>Regiment: The system of order, rule, and disciplined administration within a territory.</term> among the subjects.

To the Lord, he should always be an advisor toward peace rather than toward strife and discord—whenever it might be to the Lord's disadvantage—with the reminder that the most unjust peace is better than the most just war, etc. <note>A common Renaissance sentiment, often echoing Erasmus or Cicero: "Iniquissimam pacem iustissimo bello antefero."</note>

And by all means, he should not become arrogant in his office, nor despise or belittle others because of it.

### Follows Concerning the Chancellery.

Since much depends on the Chancellery for a Lord, he should see to it that he staffs it with learned, faithful, and pious people, and that he also maintains them appropriately, so that they have no reason to look away from him and move to other Lords. This causes much disorder for a Lord when he has many new servants in the Chancellery, just as it brings little advantage in other matters if a Lord often changes his servants without special cause—as I have seen and experienced much myself.

Now, as for what concerns the office of a Chancellor <term>Chancellor: The chief administrative officer and head of the legal and record-keeping department for a nobleman or prince.</term>, it is to be known that it is a great and excellent, as well as a magnificent office, upon which a Prince's or Lord's heart rests, as the saying goes: *That the Chancellor is the Heart of the Prince.* <note>original: "Quòd Cancellarius sit Cor Principis."</note> This is to say that the Chancellor is the Prince's heart, for it cannot be otherwise: the Lord must at times open and entrust his heart and secrets to him more than to any other. Therefore, it will be necessary that such people as Chancellors and Secretaries <term>Secretaries: High-level administrative officials who handled private correspondence and the prince's "secrets" or private business.</term> conduct themselves faithfully, diligently, discreetly, and modestly in return.

And since a certain Philippus Beroaldus <note>Philippus Beroaldus (1453–1505) was a famous Italian humanist scholar and poet whose works on courtly conduct were widely read in the Renaissance.</note>, an Italian, wrote several of his verses about this office, I could not omit placing them here, so that primarily young fellows who belong to the Chancellery might see themselves reflected therein and have something to remember; and the verses read as follows:

I would have very much liked to translate these verses into German rhymes, according to my usual custom. Indeed, a person is not worthy to be counted among the number of scribes if he cannot write and understand a Latin letter as well as a German one.

Although one finds those who pass themselves off as such, they should nonetheless not be recognized as scribes. Yes, and what is more, I have seen some who have had themselves created as Notaries <term>Notary: A legal official authorized to draw up and certify contracts, wills, and other "instruments."</term>. Furthermore, I would like to know what would happen if a situation arose where a legal instrument had to be sent to a foreign nation, such that it had to be drafted and prepared in the Latin language—how such a Notary would manage? In the Chancery, everything should be still and quiet, and no one should enter except those summoned there, so that things a Lord wishes to keep secret do not become known. Every member of the Chancery should be primarily concerned that foreign, unknown people are not drawn into the Chancery without cause or command.

### Of the Treasury.

Whoever wishes to be a <term>Treasurer</term> <note>original: *Rentmeister*; the official responsible for managing the revenues, taxes, and expenditures of an estate or territory</note> at court is advised, firstly, that he should guard his money-chest well and not give money easily to anyone unless he has sufficient command from his Lord. He should also keep that command safe so that he may present it later, for Lords easily forget and afterward may not wish to know anything of such a command.

Secondly, he should not spend even the smallest amount unless he has first recorded and written it down; otherwise, it cannot fail that he will occasionally forget an entry and not know what became of the money. Through this, he must fall not only into worry but also into financial loss, as I have often seen and experienced.

Thirdly, he should diligently strive to settle his <term>accounts</term> <note>original: *Rechnung*</note> every year and not allow himself to be delayed or hindered by his Lord or other people. This is for the sake of the danger that could arise not only for him but also for his wife and children should he pass away before the accounts are settled; for no one easily steps into another man's accounts—

## If, however, he were a Court Councilor or servant, and were called into council.

If one is called into council by the Lord, he should pay diligent attention to the **proposition** <note>original: *Proposition*; the formal presentation of the matter or question at hand for discussion</note> and toward what end the Lord would like to see that advice directed.

Also, what other people sitting in the council say about it; likewise whether they are matters of necessity or otherwise important matters upon which the land and people depend.

Whether they can suffer delay or not, or whether they are simple and minor matters.

Now, if the matter is itself important and great, and the Lord's opinion is correct, where the council is to begin, he has to say: He can perceive nothing else than that his [the Lord's] opinion stands on good ground. Nor does he know how to improve upon it, much less challenge it; yet he must also hear the opinion and good judgment of the other councilors.

But if the matter were great and important, and the Lord's opinion were wrong, then he should say: the matter is great and important and beyond his understanding, and therefore, in his **simplicity** <note>A common rhetorical trope of the era where a courtier uses "simplicity" or "humility" as a shield when disagreeing with a social superior.</note>, he knows little to say about it. Except that he fears the matter will not allow itself to be handled or undertaken in this way; and besides indicating the reasons, he should, if he can, propose a more convenient and better or safer way. Namely, he might suggest that this way would be easier and safer, yet he would leave it to **His Grace** <note>original: *S. G.*, abbreviation for *Seine Gnaden*</note> and other Lords for further and better consideration.

In addition, it can do no harm for him to remind the Lord—because so much depends on these matters—that if he can find the time, he should take them into further consideration; also, where necessity requires it, to seek the advice and consideration of his other lords and friends therein.

## When someone is dispatched with credentials and a commission, how he should behave therein.

**I**f someone is commanded to travel to a place—be it to a Prince, Count, or City—dispatched with **credentials** <note>original: *Credentz*; formal documents establishing the envoy's authority and identity</note> and a **commission** <note>original: *werbung*; the specific diplomatic message, request, or negotiation task being delivered</note>, it will be necessary for him to primarily grasp the matter well and rightly understand the cause for which he is traveling. He must also know how to present the commission according to his **instruction** <note>original: *Instruction*; the written orders and guidelines provided by his employer</note> as necessity requires; and it is better that he asks questions than that he does not know what he should do and accomplish.

And when he wishes to travel, let him not boast much about it nor make a great stir, so that he may expect less danger on the road <note>Discretion was a security measure for early modern travelers carrying sensitive political documents</note>.

Much less should he let anything be known of his business and dealings in places where it is not appropriate.

But when he has arrived at the places where he is to perform his commission, he must first present himself at the proper quarters, reporting that he has been dispatched by his Lord with credentials and a commission, and therefore request that a hour be appointed for him so that he may be heard regarding his commission.

He may also deliver the credentials immediately, or wait until the time when he is appointed to perform his commission; he can then make a beginning of his affairs with them, for the credentials must precede all other things.

Once the credentials have been delivered, he should then indicate that he was dispatched by his Lord to announce to the Prince, Lord, or Council his humble and friendly service, or favorable greeting, grace, and all things good—all according to the status of the rank. And just as one should not do too much and make oneself obligated and subordinate in a place where it is not owed, it is likewise not fitting to infringe upon anyone’s glory, title, and freedom. When such an announcement of willingness to serve has been made, he should further report and then present his commission as he was commanded, in the most proper way possible, to the Lord or to whomever is commanded to hear it. For it is not always convenient for a Lord to hear the envoys and messages himself; therefore, he must occasionally command others [to do so]. Should the envoy, however, have a strict command to reveal his commission to no one but the Lord himself, he will know how to behave according to such a command in this and other matters, since the legal rule says: *The limits of the mandate are to be diligently observed.* <note>original Latin: *Quod fines mandati diligenter sunt custodiendi.*</note>

# Of Court Life.

Once he has now delivered his **commission** <note>original: *Werbung*; the specific diplomatic message or request</note> and wishes to make his conclusion, or if the **instruction** <note>original: *Instruction*; the envoy’s written orders</note> itself dictates the closing, he may most graciously add that he had received orders from his Lord to report such matters. He should therefore ask that they might receive and understand his words more favorably and better than he, in his **simplicity** <note>a standard rhetorical gesture of humility</note>, was able to speak and present them.

If a good answer is then given, and the envoy has obtained and achieved that for which he was sent out, he shall most highly give thanks for the granted **audience** <note>original: *Audienz*; a formal hearing with a person of high rank</note> and the subsequent friendly or gracious reply. He should offer to report this to his Lord or superior upon his arrival and to praise it with diligence, stating that he has no doubt that his Lord will be mindful to earn such favor in equal and even greater measure.

But if a negative answer is given, the envoy should say that he has heard, on behalf of his Lord, what was given as an answer to his commission and proposal, but that according to the state of affairs, he could by no means have expected such an answer. However, because he cannot change it or press further, he must let the matter take its course and rest there.

Yet if the matter is absolutely unbearable, he may address the **Councilors** <note>the advisors to the prince or city leadership</note> and ask them to take the matter into better consideration or to deliberate further, in view of what is at stake.

Once he has applied his possible diligence and forgotten nothing, and thereupon received his leave to depart, he should diligently record everything that was said and handled there so that he forgets nothing of the answer given to him. This is so that he may provide a complete **relation** <note>original: *Relation*; a formal, detailed written or oral report delivered to his employer</note>, for as much depends upon the report being delivered properly and truthfully as depends upon the commission itself.

It is also to be noted here that when an envoy finds that he can direct the negotiation onto a better path and obtain something more for his Lord than he was commanded, he may well do so. For I consider that it would have to be a strange head indeed who, upon being informed that his envoy had made the matter better, would not be satisfied but would take it poorly; as I have heard a great Prince say, and something of this was mentioned above. Let this be enough regarding envoys and their commissions.

...official request <note>original: *siges ansuchen*; likely a transcription of *solches ansuchen* (such a request) or *hiesiges ansuchen* (this request)</note> to appear here with your opposing party; a gracious command has been issued to summon and require you today for a proper hearing. ### When they have now been heard from both sides
### as necessary, how he should speak:

It is considered by my Gracious Lord that you have been heard from both sides with complaint and answer quite sufficiently and as necessary; therefore, let both parties withdraw. When my Gracious Lord has deliberated upon it, if he wishes to consult further with one party or take a report from them, they will be summoned back.

### When someone has a good case.

If someone should have a good case, then the objection of the opposing party should be repeated and reiterated, with a reminder and a reservation: should it come to a **legal judgment** <note>original: *zum Rechten*; referring to a formal court ruling</note>, it is to be feared that he would not only obtain nothing, but would also be sentenced by law to pay the **expenses** <term>Expens: the legal costs and out-of-pocket expenses incurred during a trial</term> and costs to the plaintiff. Thus, it would not be fitting among Christians to so stubbornly and so insolently withhold from one’s neighbor that which is his, contrary to equity, and thereby cause him wanton damage and delay.

### But if the plaintiff should have a bad case.

But where the plaintiff has a bad case, from which it can be perceived that he will obtain nothing, it may be presented to him that his complaint, and the answer and counter-report of the defendant, have been heard in full. It has been found that he, the plaintiff, has a bad and unfounded case in which nothing can be obtained; therefore, it is a matter of no small wonder that he dared to come forward with such a **holey case** <note>original: *löcherigen Sache*; an idiom for a weak or flimsy argument</note> and trouble the Prince or Count with it. Their Graces also take no pleasure in this and earnestly desire that he desist from it.

Should the complaining party then persist further, he may be given as an ans-

<header>Of Court Life.</header>

...word will be given. One would gladly exert diligence to see whether something might be obtained from the defendant through amicable means.

If, however, the [plaintiff] party had such a poor case that one could not, with a good conscience, press the defendant, nor extract anything from him in kindness, then it is best to dissuade the plaintiff from such wantonness and impose eternal silence upon him. And even if such a wanton plaintiff demands "the law," it should not be granted to him to willfully lead someone into court costs without any cause.

Otherwise, if the parties cannot be reconciled through amicable diligence, and the matter is doubtful—so that one cannot readily determine which side is right or wrong—then one may refer them to the law and let it decide the matter.

If the matter were of such a nature that it must be decided by a judgment, the Lord or judge may, with the knowledge and consent of both parties, formulate a question and have the case set down as it actually occurred in itself, and let whatever is spoken therein remain as the decision.

But if the matter is important, one may submit it to arbitration <term>Compromittiern|To submit a dispute to the decision of chosen arbitrators rather than a formal judge</term> for three or two sessions; also, if it is requested, one may allow a "purification" <note>original: *leutterung*; a legal remedy in Saxon law for clarifying or appealing a judgment</note> as is the custom in Saxon Law <note>The *Sachsenspiegel* or subsequent Saxon legal codes which were highly influential in German territories</note>.

However, no one should be persuaded or forced against their will to leave the ordinary law for arbitration or "narrow law" <note>original: *enge Recht*; likely referring to summary proceedings or restricted jurisdictions</note> which they could rightfully refuse.

Likewise, I cannot highly praise the practice of summoning parties on short notice <note>original: *auff stracken Tag*; literally "on a straight day," meaning a fixed, immediate deadline</note> to dictate their legal needs directly to the pen <note>meaning to have their oral testimony transcribed immediately for the record</note> and to conclude immediately for judgment, as great inequality is perceived and found therein.

Namely, that the plaintiff has more advantage in this case than the defendant, in that he can prepare himself with the complaint, especially if the complaint was not inserted into the citation <term>Citation|A formal summons to appear in court</term>.

But the defendant must make his objection <term>Exception|A formal legal defense or plea used to delay or defeat a plaintiff's claim</term> immediately <note>original: *incontinenti*</note> and without any delay, which is directly against the order of laws, which intend that the defendant should have better standing than the plaintiff <note>original: *non licet &c.*; likely referring to the principle that it is not permitted to disadvantage the defense</note>.

Also: "Defendants are to be held in greater favor than plaintiffs" <note>original: *fauorabiliores rei potius quàm actores habentur*; a Roman law principle emphasizing the presumption of innocence or the favor shown to the party being sued</note>.

And to ensure things do not go correctly anywhere, it is customary to direct the parties, when it comes to recording the case, to the court chambers <term>Hofstuben|The common rooms or administrative offices of the court</term>, where there is often such a clamor—since everyone runs in and through there—that one cannot hear their own words, let alone consider what is fair for their party's needs.

With this, I wish to leave every Lord's court custom uncensored—

<header>Of Court Life.</header>

...left unspoken; for there are enough people who understand the Law and can see to it that no one is deprived of their rights. Thus, I also intend to establish no judicial process here, since more than enough of them are otherwise at hand and found in print, from which the Court Council <term>Hofraht|The advisory council to a prince or lord, which handled administrative, legal, and political affairs</term> may see what is further required in that case.

### How a Lord is accustomed to accepting a new servant, and how to address him.

After the Illustrious or Well-born <note>original: *Durchleuchtige oder Wolgeborne*; standard honorifics for high-ranking nobility and lower nobility, respectively</note>, etc., My Gracious Lord, has considered taking you as a servant, and you have also willingly offered yourself to serve His Grace, His Grace accepts your willing offer with gracious favor.

And thereupon we command that the following intention be presented to you: namely, that you wish to promise and vow to His Grace to be faithful and upright, to warn of His Grace’s harm, and to promote his prosperity and best interests to your highest ability. Whatever is entrusted to you by way of counsel, or otherwise in secret, you shall keep hidden within yourself until the grave, and reveal it to no one to the disadvantage of His Grace or the Lordship. You shall also not allow yourself to be moved thereto by bribes <note>original: *Gifft*; while it means poison today, in this context it refers to "gifts" or "corrupting influences"</note>, gifts, friendship, or enmity, but rather behave in every way as befits and is well-suited to a faithful servant. This you shall vow and promise to His Grace with a handshake in good faith.

When he has now promised and vowed such things with hand and mouth, it is customary to present him with the oath, which he must swear to God with raised fingers <note>The "Schwurfinger": a traditional gesture where the thumb, index, and middle finger are raised to represent the Holy Trinity</note>, as follows:

> What I have spoken and vowed, that I will hold steady and firm, so help me God and His holy Word.

Lords are usually accustomed to having one of their Counselors speak such things; therefore, I have also wished to set it down here with such words. Whichever Lord has another custom will know how to command it according to the same.

### How a Lord’s servant should show and conduct himself toward foreign people when they come to the Lord’s court.

When it happens (as indeed occurs quite often) that foreign nobles, ambassadors, or other honorable people come to the Lord’s court, if the servant or Counselor is a person for whom it would not be fitting (such as a Chancellor, Doctor <term>Doctor|In this period, usually a Doctor of Law serving as a high-ranking official or advisor</term>, or the like) to wait upon them or drink with them, he should nevertheless speak to them in a friendly manner. And if he finds that they lack something, he should—as much as possible—remedy that, also faithfully and with diligence...

<header>Of Court Life.</header>

...promote diligence so that they are heard first, not long delayed, and finally receive a favorable decision <note>original: *bescheid*; a formal legal or administrative answer from the lord</note>.

If, however, the guest were young and had nothing to lose, the servant should provide good company and use all diligence to ensure such people are honored and well-maintained. He should also ensure that nothing is said at the table by which the strangers might be embarrassed or take offense. In summary, he should behave toward them in all ways as he would wish others to behave toward him in a foreign place. It is a great honor for those servants of a Lord who gladly tend to strangers, and they are praised often and much by others, which is a virtue <term>Tugend|A central concept in courtly manuals, referring to the moral excellence and social grace expected of a nobleman or official</term> that is rightly found both in a courtier and in others.

It is also fitting when strangers or ambassadors are staying in inns and waiting for a decision, that one visits them occasionally, speaks kindly to them, and, as much as possible, provides them with company.

### How one should receive strangers on behalf of a Lord.

When he is commanded to accept or receive strangers or ambassadors, he should do so with all reverence and respect, mentioning that his Gracious Lord is highly delighted by his or their arrival, and requests that they present themselves to His Grace, go to their chamber, or to the inn, and wait with good will. As soon as it can be expedited, he shall be assisted, his mission <note>original: *werbung*; refers to the specific message or request an ambassador brings to court</note> heard, and he shall be provided with a gracious and favorable answer.

### How a servant should behave toward his Lord’s enemies.

If a Lord has adversaries who do not wish him well, a counselor or servant should have no association with them whatsoever. Instead, he should keep them at a distance, so that he does not fall under suspicion with the Lord, as if he favored the enemies more than him. Yet, he should not show open enmity until it is commanded of him, or unless the Lord’s honor and necessity demand otherwise.

Some wish to defend their Lords against enemies even when they have no orders to do so; for that reason, they sometimes receive a blow for it, and they are not only mocked by the Lord for their interference, but also by others. Whatever else such a new servant needs to know, time and daily experience will surely teach him.

->Let this be enough for now.<-

<header>Of Court Life. 433</header>

One thing I must still mention here, which a court counselor <note>original: *Hofraht*; a high-ranking official who advises a prince or lord</note> should diligently remember and follow: namely, that he should carefully guard himself so that he does not allow himself to be moved by the "dative case"—that is, by gifts and presents—to depart from the truth and give his approval to injustice. Nor should he, for the sake of gifts, suppress or hinder one person's good cause, while conversely helping to dress up and defend another person's bad cause. For even the Scripture forbids the taking of gifts.

Although it has, alas, now come to the point that almost all matters are settled and promoted through trickery <term>finantzen|In this era, this term referred specifically to shady financial dealings, usury, or bribery rather than general accounting</term> and gifts, I have indeed seen those who dare to demand gifts. Yes, some even boast that they are entitled to take such "finance" and presents, which one must now allow to happen. However, he who has an upright mind and wishes to strive for honor and integrity, and to flee from evil rumors, may well take heed that he does not allow himself to be overcome and bribed by gifts. This is truly not the least of the rumors one might face, and therefore everyone will need to know how to guard themselves well against it.

For it will surely happen that if one takes a gift, he will occasionally speak a word or several more in favor of that person than he otherwise would have. Thus, the Scripture will not lie when it says: *You shall take no gift, for a gift blinds the eyes of the wise and subverts the cause of the righteous.* <note>original Latin: "Munera non accipies, quia excæcant homines, & subuertunt verba iustorum." This is from Exodus 23:8.</note> Write that on your chamber door so that you have it to remind you, and do not quickly grab for it when a gift is offered to you.

Alongside this, he should take care with all diligence when he speaks before the Lord or otherwise, that he refrains from hateful words from which bitterness might arise. Rather, he should use all moderation <note>original: *gelimpff*; a crucial early modern concept of propriety, fairness, and social grace</note>, according to the rule which says: *Moderation is more profitable than the whole rule of law.* <note>original Latin: "Glimppffius est plutiis, quàm tota Regula Iuris."</note> Often a hateful word can cause great bitterness, while conversely a kind and moderate word can create great friendship. Such people are praised above others for the sake of this virtue. Such a man was Doctor Fuchs in Leipzig. <note>Probably referring to a noted jurist or professor at the University of Leipzig known for his diplomacy.</note> One should especially refrain from such hateful words in writing, for writings remain and can be spread far and wide.

### Of Court Life / Hans Wilhelm Kirchhoff /
### in the Little Book of the Secular Estate.

There is no Lord ever so evil, bold, and roguish that he does not have some pious servants who are disciplined, honorable, and modest. Conversely, one finds no Lord so God-fearing, just, kind, and honorable that some of his servants are not godless, unmerciful, blasphemers, and inclined toward injustice. Although Cicero says: *The state is such as are the characters of its princes,* <note>original Latin: "Talis est ciuitas, quales sunt Principum mores." From Cicero's *De Legibus*.</note> this is said not only of Princes, who hold the highest power and sometimes do not remain in all things within their required calling, but much more of those whom the Princes have appointed as subordinate governors. For this reason, the plural form—"the characters of the princes"—is used...

# Seneca on Court Life.

At court one finds great power,
Everything appears magnificent in many ways.
He who seeks to venture there
Gains much power and honor.
And is held in high esteem at court,
Just as the world now desires.
Yet he must also watch for danger,
And take care that he does not stumble.
I have had my fill of it; I would rather be
In my own house, though it be small.
It matters not, so long as I may
Spend my days there in peace.
And need not fear such peril,
Letting my time and years slip by.
In peace and stillness, remaining unknown
To the great lords of the land.
When the end finally comes,
I die, and care not whether I am...
Despised or among the common masses,
And I far prefer it this way. <note>original: *gan viel mehr*; likely an archaic form of *gern* (willingly) or *gahn* (go), expressing a preference for the humble path.</note>
For another, such power and honor
Will make death truly heavy.
He who is known to everyone,
Yet cannot know himself. <note>This is a famous paraphrase of lines 391–403 from Seneca’s play *Thyestes*, a classic Stoic warning against the burdens of fame.</note>
He goes along blindly and madly,
Which the world considers a success.
One must let them be,
For the world treats them no differently.
Yet the world shall surely learn,
When its turn comes at last.

->Georgius Lauterbeck.<- <note>Lauterbeck (c. 1510–1578) was a prominent German administrative official and author known for his "Regentenbuch," a guide for Christian rulers.</note>

<term>Frankfurt am Main</term> — The center of the German book trade and home to the famous Book Fair.

<term>Sigmund Feyerabend</term> — A dominant figure in Renaissance publishing who helped popularize woodcut illustrations.
<term>Colophon</term> — The final note in a book providing details about its production; in modern books, this information is usually found on the copyright page at the beginning.

### Binding Transcription

<margin>Left decorative vertical roll (top to bottom)</margin>

<image-desc>A panel depicting the Resurrected Christ holding a victory banner (vexillum).</image-desc>
The Lion has conquered <unclear>Lion</unclear>
<note>original: *VICIT LEO*. A reference to the "Lion of Judah" from the Book of Revelation, symbolizing Christ’s victory.</note>

---

<image-desc>A panel depicting the Crucifixion of Christ.</image-desc>
O Death, I will be your death
<note>original: *MORS ERO MORS TVAQ*. A traditional Latin phrase derived from the Book of Hosea, frequently used in Reformation-era art to show Christ triumphing over personified Death.</note>

---

<image-desc>A panel depicting the Resurrection of Christ emerging from the tomb.</image-desc>
I have arisen
<note>original: *RESVRREXI*. The standard Latin liturgical opening for Easter Sunday, spoken in the voice of the risen Christ.</note>

---

<image-desc>A panel depicting Moses and the Brazen Serpent on a pole.</image-desc>
Just as Moses
<note>original: *SICVT MOSES*. This refers to the biblical passage "Just as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness," which Christians interpreted as a prophecy or "type" of Christ being lifted up on the cross.</note>

<term>bookbinding</term> — The process of physically assembling a book and securing it within protective covers.
<term>leather</term> — Typically calfskin or pigskin was used for these sturdy Renaissance bindings.
<term>blind-tooling</term> — A decorative technique where heated brass tools or rollers are pressed into dampened leather without using gold leaf, creating a darkened, recessed design.
<term>Renaissance iconography</term> — The specific set of symbols and visual motifs used during the 14th–16th centuries to convey religious or philosophical meanings.

<summary>This page describes the ornate, blind-stamped leather binding of a 16th-century volume, featuring symbolic panels that connect Old Testament prophecy with the Resurrection of Christ. The artwork serves as a visual sermon, reinforcing the religious themes of the text contained within.</summary>
<keywords>bookbinding, blind-tooling, Renaissance art, Christology, Moses, Resurrection, Reformation, religious symbolism</keywords>
